title: Barau Counters Osinbajo, Defends Tinubu’s Economic Reforms
body: …Blames poor communication for public discontent, cites NELFUND, highway projects Sunday Aborisade in Abuja The Deputy President of the Senate, Senator Jibrin Barau, has challenged former Vice-President Yemi Osinbajo’s gloomy assessment of Nigeria’s economy and democratic governance, insisting that President Bola Tinubu’s administration is addressing longstanding structural challenges but needs to communicate its policies and achievements more effectively to Nigerians. Barau acknowledged the validity of concerns raised by Osinbajo, particularly those relating to economic hardship, declining public confidence in democratic institutions and inadequate youth participation in electoral politics. He, however, argued that the perception of poor government performance was partly attributable to the failure of political leaders to adequately explain their policies, interventions and ongoing development projects. The Deputy Senate President spoke on Tuesday in Yola, Adamawa State, during a public lecture titled, ‘ Democracy and Development: Rethinking the Leadership Question,’ organised to mark the 59th birthday of Governor Ahmadu Umaru Fintiri. Osinbajo, who served as vice-president between 2015 and 2023, had expressed concern about the growing dissatisfaction with democratic governance across Africa, despite nearly three decades of uninterrupted democratic rule in several countries. Drawing on findings from Afrobarometer surveys, the former vice-president highlighted widespread economic anxiety, declining public confidence in government, rising living costs, unemployment, inadequate healthcare and diminishing youth participation in electoral processes. He noted that although 64 per cent of Africans preferred democracy to other forms of government, only 38 per cent were satisfied with how democracy was functioning in their respective countries. Osinbajo also cited survey findings indicating that 59 per cent of Africans considered their national economies to be in bad shape, while 51 per cent believed their economies had deteriorated. He warned that persistent economic hardship and the failure of democratic institutions to meet citizens’ expectations could undermine public confidence in democracy, particularly among young people. Responding to the presentation, Barau praised Osinbajo’s intellectual depth but questioned whether the gloomy picture reflected the full extent of government interventions and ongoing efforts to address the country’s challenges. “I know he is a very good orator, a good public speaker and an intellectual to the core,” Barau said. Explaining why he had decided to respond despite initially intending to avoid making a speech at the birthday celebration, the senator described Osinbajo’s presentation as thought-provoking. “Having said that, I am compelled to make some comments on the paper. It is a very beautiful and thought-provoking paper,” he said. Barau identified inadequate communication between political leaders and citizens as a major factor contributing to public dissatisfaction, arguing that governments needed to do more to explain the policies and programmes designed to improve living conditions. He said: “What I want to say is this: one important reason for the gloomy picture portrayed by the surveys, particularly those conducted by Afrobarometer, is what the professor talked about and specifically observed: the issue of communication between the leaders and the led. “There is no proper communication,” he said. The senator maintained that although Nigerians were entitled to demand better living conditions and hold public officials accountable, citizens also needed adequate information about the challenges confronting the country and the measures being taken to address them. He cited interventions in education and infrastructure as examples of the Federal Government’s efforts to tackle structural deficiencies that have constrained economic growth and limited opportunities for millions of Nigerians. On education, Barau highlighted the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND), introduced under Tinubu’s administration, describing it as an intervention designed to expand access to tertiary education, particularly for students from financially disadvantaged backgrounds. He argued that access to education remained critical to addressing the long-term consequences of poverty, unemployment and social exclusion, especially in a country with a large and growing youth population. “Before now, it was very difficult for a child who did not have the means to go to school. Now, everyone, except a child who does not want to go to school, can go to school in Nigeria with the NELFUND introduced by this administration,” he said. The Deputy Senate President also underscored the importance of infrastructure development in stimulating economic activity, attracting investment and improving the standard of living. He cited the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, the Badagry-Sokoto Highway and road projects across the North-east and North-west as evidence of ongoing efforts to address the country’s infrastructure deficit. According to him, investments in roads, water supply and other essential infrastructure are necessary to connect communities, facilitate trade, reduce transportation bottlenecks and create conditions for sustainable economic prosperity. He said: “When we talk about economic prosperity, you cannot achieve it without a certain level of infrastructure, including road networks, water supply and other essential infrastructure. “This is what is happening currently in this country under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration. Roads are being constructed everywhere to propel the process of bringing economic prosperity. That is being done. “It is a long journey, but it is being done. Yet, there is no proper communication.” He urged political leaders and public officials at the federal and state levels to prioritise sustained public engagement, insisting that government policies could not achieve their intended impact if citizens remained inadequately informed about their objectives and implementation. The senator also attributed part of the pressure on household incomes and the rising cost of goods and services to international economic developments, arguing that Nigeria’s current difficulties could not be considered in isolation from global events. He pointed to the Russia-Ukraine war and conflicts in the Middle East as factors that had disrupted international supply chains, increased energy costs and raised production expenses across several economies. Barau also cited tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic international oil transit route, as one of the factors contributing to volatility in global energy markets. According to him, “The fact is that these challenges are not peculiar to Nigeria; they have an international dimension. The rising cost of living is partly attributable to conflicts in different parts of the world, including the Middle East, as well as the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. “These conflicts have disrupted global supply chains, driven up energy prices and increased the cost of goods and services worldwide.” The senator, who is also the First Deputy Speaker of the ECOWAS Parliament, argued that developments in international energy and commodity markets could have significant implications for Nigeria, given the country’s exposure to global trade and the cost of imported goods and production inputs. “Nigeria is not an island,” he said. Barau’s intervention came against the backdrop of continuing public debate over the effects of Tinubu’s economic reforms, particularly the pressure on household incomes, transportation costs and prices of essential commodities. While the Federal Government has defended its policy direction as necessary to address longstanding economic distortions, the scale of the immediate hardship has continued to generate public concern over the pace at which the benefits of the reforms would translate into improved living conditions. Osinbajo’s lecture similarly drew attention to the wider democratic implications of persistent economic difficulties, particularly the possibility that citizens could lose faith in democratic institutions if governments failed to respond adequately to their expectations. Barau, however, argued that bridging the gap between public expectations and government performance required political leaders to communicate more clearly, explain policy choices and provide credible information on the progress of ongoing interventions. He called on public officials and other stakeholders to take collective responsibility for improving public understanding of government policies, stressing that effective communication should complement, rather than replace, tangible results. For the Deputy Senate President, the challenge confronting Nigeria is therefore not only the implementation of policies to address economic and infrastructural deficits but also ensuring that citizens understand what the government is doing, why the interventions are necessary and how they are expected to improve their lives. He maintained that sustained engagement between leaders and the electorate would be essential to rebuilding public confidence, strengthening democratic institutions and securing broader support for the country’s development agenda.

title: ADC PCC Alleges Plot To Shift Presidential Election, Insists on January 16
body: Chuks Okocha in Abuja The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council warned that reports of pressure on the Independent National Electoral Commission to shift the 16 January presidential election, just 80 days away, cannot be dismissed. The ADC PCC said that plot to shift the presidential election was to be hinged on Ebola. A statement by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, said, “If President Tinubu believes Nigerians want another four years of his government, he should face them at the ballot box, not seek more time through the back door.” According to the ADC Presidential Campaign Council Director of of Strategic communications, “The Council has received information that the INEC Chairman is to be summoned to the Presidential Villa and instructed to shift the election. “We are raising the alarm before that meeting takes place. President Tinubu must abandon any such attempt. Professor Joash Amupitan must refuse any instruction to change the timetable and immediately make any such approach public. “The election date belongs to Nigerians. It must not be rewritten behind closed doors at the Villa”, the statement stated. The ADC presidential campaign Council said that “Nigerians have endured three and a half years of soaring prices, shrinking incomes and relentless hardship. “They have the right to judge this government at the ballot box on 16 January. A government that has made life this difficult for Nigerians must not be allowed to postpone its day of judgment.” The ADC presidential campaign Council said that “Ebola is a serious public health concern. Health professionals must be free to contain it, and INEC must take every necessary step to protect voters and election workers. “The NCDC Director General has said there is currently no reason to postpone the election. That position must not be twisted into a political excuse for delay. “The Council puts INEC, domestic observers and international election monitors on notice: any proposal to change the timetable must be made openly, supported by published health evidence and subjected to public scrutiny. The Presidency must not use a health emergency to escape an electoral verdict.” Shuaib stated

title: No Shady Deal in Kwara Social Investment Programme, Says DG, Tejidini
body: Hammed Shittu in Ilorin Director General of the Kwara State Social Investment Programme (KWASSIP) Dr. Abdulwasiu Tejidini, has said that, there was no any shady deal in the financial operations of the agency. He therefore said all the financial operations and approved funds disburshed to the beneficiaries were applied with the objectives of the mandate of the agency. Dr. Tejidini in a statement issued in Ilorin, signed by the agency’s Press Secretary, Mrs. Yusuf Bola Shade, stated that the agency maintains records of beneficiaries across the 193 wards of Kwara State under programmes that includes Owo Isowo, Owo Arugbo, and the skilled and unskilled workers scheme. Dr. Tejidini positions came on the sidelines of the recent called for a probe of the agency by the 52- youth coalition in the state that backed the call of the governorship candidate of the National Democratic Congress (NDC) for 2027 election, Professor Abdulmumin Yinka Ajia to look into the financial operations of the agency since its inception. The statement read, “The Kwara State Social Investment Programme (KWASSIP) has taken note of recent allegations concerning the management and implementation of its programmes. “KWASSIP assures the public that funds approved and released to the agency have been applied in accordance with the objectives of its mandate. “The agency maintains records of beneficiaries across the 193 wards of Kwara State under programmes including Owo Isowo, Owo Arugbo, and the skilled and unskilled workers scheme. “The Kwapreneur programme has also supported beneficiaries in establishing and expanding businesses, creating employment opportunities, and contributing to economic activity in their communities. “These outcomes reflect the agency’s efforts to promote sustainable economic empowerment and support livelihoods across the state”. The statement added, “In response to economic challenges, KWASSIP has, at various times, provided assistance to businesses, individuals, and households affected by difficult circumstances. “This includes support provided to businesses affected by the #EndSARS protests at Palms Mall, which enabled affected operators to resume activities and rebuild their livelihoods. “The agency also recently disbursed ₦90 million to 12 young entrepreneurs to support business expansion, strengthen enterprise development, and promote job creation across Kwara State. “KWASSIP remains committed to transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement in the delivery of its programmes. Its activities and records are available for appropriate review, in accordance with applicable procedures and requirements. “The agency welcomes constructive criticism and public scrutiny. It is important that public discourse remains guided by facts, evidence, and a genuine concern for the welfare of the people, rather than political considerations or unsubstantiated claims. “KWASSIP therefore urges all stakeholders to assess its performance on the basis of verifiable information, documented programme outcomes, and credible evidence. “KWASSIP will continue to work with relevant stakeholders to ensure that its interventions reach intended beneficiaries and contribute meaningfully to the social and economic development of Kwara State”.

title: Israel Election Count: Netanyahu’s Bloc Leads With 54 Seats, Eisenkot-led Bloc 49, Arab Parties 17
body: Israel’s election count has revealed a political deadlock, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led bloc leading with 54 seats, while the bloc led by Yashar party chief Gadi Eisenkot has secured 49 seats and Arab parties hold 17 seats. According to Times of Israel reports, with more than 84 per cent of ballots counted, neither side has secured the 61 seats required for a parliamentary majority, leaving the formation of the next government uncertain. The latest figures give the anti-Netanyahu bloc a combined 66 seats when the Arab parties are included. However, forming a coalition remains complicated by campaign promises from several party leaders not to partner with Arab-led parties. The Joint List chief signalled readiness to support efforts to remove Netanyahu’s government, declaring: “We’re ready to pave the way to oust Netanyahu government.” Despite the uncertainty, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot expressed confidence in their ability to form the next government following exit poll results released on Tuesday night. The exit polls suggested that the election had produced a stalemate, with neither political camp able to form a coalition without making difficult political compromises. The pro-Netanyahu bloc was initially projected to win between 51 and 52 seats, below the number it currently holds in the Knesset. Subsequent partial results increased its projected strength, although the latest count placed the bloc at 54 seats. Meanwhile, reports indicate that Eisenkot’s bloc is exploring ways to use its votes, alongside those of the Arab parties, to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a member of Likud. No candidate has reportedly been agreed upon, but Yisrael Beytenu lawmaker Oded Forer and Yashar’s Elazar Stern have been mentioned as possible options. Netanyahu’s Likud also performed strongly in Kiryat Shmona, Sderot and other communities severely affected by the war, according to reports by The Times of Israel. Political parties across the spectrum celebrated their performances despite the inconclusive results, while several leaders urged patience until the final count is completed. Although more than 84 per cent of ballots have been counted, the final outcome may take several days to emerge. Remaining votes include “double envelope” ballots cast by Israel Defense Forces soldiers, diplomats and other voters who did not vote at their assigned polling stations. The final results will determine whether either camp can assemble a governing coalition or whether further negotiations will be required to break the political deadlock

title: Customs Hands Over N5.8m Seized Unregistered Drugs To NAFDAC In Sokoto
body: Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto The Sokoto/Zamfara Area Command of the Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has handed over seized unregistered pharmaceutical products valued at N5,804,062.06 to the National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) for further investigation and necessary action. The handing over ceremony was held on Wednesday , October 28, 2026, at the Command Headquarters in Sokoto, in line with existing inter-agency collaboration and the directive of the Comptroller-General of Customs, Bashir Adewale Adeniyi. Speaking during the ceremony, the Acting Customs Area Controller, Sokoto/Zamfara Area Command, DC Haliru Isah Abdullahi, said the items were intercepted by gallant patrol teams along the Illela-Sokoto road, following credible intelligence and the commitment of officers of the Command. He listed the seized items to include 360 packages of anti-cold containing 50 cards each with 4 tablets per card, 500 packages of Amodiaquine containing 25 cards each with 3 tablets per card, 140 packages of Paracetamol containing 100 cards each with 10 tablets per card, and 100 packages of Quinine containing 10 cards each with 10 tablets per card. Abdullahi said the importation of the unregistered drugs contravened Section 55 of the Nigeria Customs Service Act 2023 and NAFDAC regulations, noting that the drugs posed great danger to the health of Nigerians as they were not certified for consumption. He warned smugglers and dealers in unwholesome products that the Sokoto/Zamfara Command under his watch would not tolerate any form of smuggling, stressing that the Command remained vigilant and committed to safeguarding the health of citizens and the nation’s economy. He commended the officers who made the seizure possible for their diligence and bravery, and appreciated NAFDAC for its continuous partnership with the Service. “I hereby formally hand over these seized items to the NAFDAC team for further necessary action,” Abdullahi declared. Responding, the Coordinator of NAFDAC, Sokoto State, Abdulsalam Lawan, commended the Nigeria Customs Service for the inter-agency collaboration that had helped in curbing the entry of fake drugs into the country. Lawan noted that the agency and Customs had enjoyed wonderful collaboration which had led to the ridding of unwholesome products from the country, and urged the Customs Service to sustain the tempo. He assured that NAFDAC would carry out further investigation on the seized products and take necessary action in line with its mandate to protect public health and ensure only certified drugs circulate in the country.

title: YAWC Network calls for revocation of licences of teachers convicted of sexual abuse
body: The Executive Director of the Young African Women Congress (YAWC) Network, Daniel Osei Tuffour, has called for the revocation of the teaching licences of teachers found guilty of sexually abusing students, arguing that transferring offenders to other schools is not enough to protect children. He has urged the Ghana Education Service (GES) and other relevant authorities to impose stricter sanctions on teachers who commit sexual offences against students, including prosecution and the withdrawal of their professional licences. Mr Tuffour made the call at the YAWC Network’s 10th anniversary celebration in Accra on Monday, October 26. His comments follow a JoyNews documentary by investigative journalist Manasseh Azure Awuni that exposed allegations of sexual abuse involving the headmaster of Obuasi Senior High Technical School. Mr Tuffour questioned the practice of transferring teachers accused of sexual misconduct to other schools, warning that it could expose more students to abuse if appropriate disciplinary and legal action was not taken. “GES and other authorities should bring stricter sanctions. I don’t see why a teacher will molest a girl and the sanction is just to transfer them to a different school, and they will go and continue such atrocities,” he said. “Apart from being made to face the full rigours of the law, their licences must be revoked,” he added. Calls for stronger protection for victims Mr Tuffour said sexual abuse could leave victims with long-term psychological trauma and urged authorities to ensure that cases were investigated and prosecuted regardless of the perpetrators’ backgrounds or affiliations. He also expressed concern about the handling of the Obuasi Senior High Technical School case, insisting that sexual offences involving children must be treated with the seriousness they deserve. The YAWC Network executive director further attributed the reluctance of some victims to report abuse to victim-blaming attitudes and financial difficulties. He said inadequate support systems could prevent victims from speaking out, reporting offences and pursuing justice. “There are a lot of victims, but because there’s no support system, there is no support anywhere, we find them not being bold to report some of these cases,” he said. Mr Tuffour encouraged victims of sexual abuse to seek help and report their experiences, assuring them that the YAWC Network was prepared to offer support.

title: Reps propose road concession, toll gates to tackle Nigeria’s infrastructure deficit
body:
The House of Representatives has called for the concession of eligible federal roads to private investors and the reintroduction of toll gates on selected highways as part of measures to address the country’s deteriorating road infrastructure.
The call was made in a motion jointly sponsored by Esosa Iyawe (APC, Edo), Olusola Fatoba (APC, Ekiti), Abdulmaleek Danga (PDP, Kogi) and Uche Okonkwo (NDC, Anambra) during Wednesday’s plenary.
Presenting the motion, Mr Iyawe said the poor condition of several federal roads was largely caused by prolonged neglect, inadequate maintenance, insufficient funding and the pressure from heavy-duty vehicles.
He said the situation has led to avoidable accidents, loss of life, vehicle damage, higher transportation costs, and delays in the movement of people and goods.
Mr Iyawe, in particular, highlighted the condition of federal roads in Edo State, describing the state as a major transportation corridor linking the South-South and South-east with other parts of the country.
He identified the Benin-Lagos, Benin-Asaba, Benin-Warri, and Benin-Okene corridors as roads requiring urgent rehabilitation.
According to him, the poor condition of the roads has affected commercial activities, increased the cost of transporting agricultural produce and other essential commodities, discouraged investment and imposed economic hardship on residents, commuters and businesses.
The lawmaker said relying on annual budgetary allocations to rehabilitate and maintain the extensive federal road network has not consistently delivered the required level of infrastructure renewal.
He therefore proposed using transparent Public-Private Partnership arrangements to attract private capital, technical expertise, and efficient project management for the rehabilitation, operation, and long-term maintenance of eligible federal roads.
He also called for the reintroduction of toll gates on selected rehabilitated highways, arguing that tolling could help private investors recover their investments while providing funds for routine maintenance and road safety operations.
“The reintroduction of properly regulated toll gates on selected rehabilitated federal highways could provide a sustainable mechanism for recovering private investment, financing routine maintenance, supporting road safety operations and generating revenue for the Federal Government,” the motion stated.
Mr Iyawe said toll gates could also create direct and indirect employment for host communities through toll administration, security services, traffic management, road maintenance and other businesses.
He further argued that strategically located toll plazas could serve as additional points for lawful security presence, intelligence gathering, emergency response and monitoring of vehicular movements when properly coordinated with security agencies.
However, he stressed that any tolling arrangement must be transparent, affordable and technologically efficient, with enforceable service standards to ensure motorists receive measurable improvements in road quality and safety in return for their payments.
He asked the House to urge the Federal Ministry of Works to develop a national framework for concessioning eligible federal roads to private investors under transparent PPP arrangements, prioritising roads requiring urgent rehabilitation and major economic corridors.
He also urged the Ministry, in collaboration with the Infrastructure Concession Regulatory Commission, the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency, and other relevant agencies, to assess the federal road network and identify roads suitable for concessioning, rehabilitation, operation, and long-term maintenance.
Mr Iyawe further called for the reintroduction of toll gates on selected federal highways after substantial rehabilitation and the establishment of clear concession agreements.
The lawmaker said toll charges should be determined through transparent economic assessments, public consultation and affordability considerations.
Lawmakers seconded the motion, and Ajang Iliya (APC, Plateau) adopted it without debate.
Speaker Abbas Tajudeen, who presided over the plenary, referred the motion to the Committees on Public Assets, Works and Finance for further legislative action.
The committees are expected to engage relevant agencies on the proposed framework and report to the House within four weeks for further legislative action.

title: Oman calls for economic and security pact between Iran and Gulf countries
body: Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Al Busaidi has called for a peace agreement between the Arab Gulf states and Iran, which would see the countries collaborating on security and the regional economy. The agreement would take the form of a security pact that includes Iran, as well as Iraq and Yemen , where Tehran has active armed proxies, he said during a visit to the UK on Wednesday. The US should continue to play an economic role in the Gulf and Iran, rather than a military one, he added. "The idea of a Gulf security architecture that doesn't include Iran is inherently unstable, structurally unsound," Mr Al Busaidi told the BBC's Radio 4. "Iran is an objective fact and closing our eyes doesn't make it go away. I want to fully engage it and bring it to the fold, I want to see peace in the Gulf," he said. Mr Al Busaidi first made the proposal on Monday, during a lecture at the University of Cambridge, where he said that the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz had become "impossible to resolve" because "external powers continue to define the terms of engagement". “What holds us back is that issues, which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed," he said. “They are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.” But on Wednesday, he sought to give assurances that a security pact would not mean that the Gulf was seeking less US involvement in the region. "The US and other friends can still be involved and can invest substantially more in the economic promise of the region. They can be real partners," he told the BBC . "It is time for a change of emphasis, a transition from the military only to the more lucrative economic sphere for all of us," he said. Mr Al Busaidi blamed the US air strikes on Iran in February for sparkling the war and greater instability in the region. Iran has repeatedly attacked energy sites across the Gulf, and its Yemeni armed proxy the Houthis have attacked infrastructure and civilian airports in Saudi Arabia. "All these recent events [are] as a result of the war that was waged against Iran by the United States," he said. Oman has good relations with Tehran and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, and has typically served as a mediator for the US and western allies. But it is not involved in the current ceasefire negotiations between the US and Iran, which are being led by Pakistan and Qatar. Earlier this year, US President Trump reportedly threatened to bomb Oman, claiming the country was getting "in the way" by seeking an alternative agreement with Iran on reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. There was a historical precedent for a regional agreement such as the one he proposed, Mr Al Busaidi said. "We have been there before in 1976 when all the eight countries gathered to try and forge that," he said, referring to meeting in Muscat, in November that year, of foreign ministers from the eight Gulf countries. "Except, then, major events took place subsequently, including the Iranian revolution, the Iran-Iraq war, the invasion of Afghanistan." But the circumstances that had postponed the possibility of a pact were "no longer there," Mr Al Busaidi said. "Today we want to reconvene a proper inclusive process between all the countries in the region."

title: No Western sanctions will divert Russia from path of cooperation with Africa, BRICS — MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Western sanctions will not force Moscow to abandon cooperation with African countries, and its partners among BRICS members and within the Eurasian region, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said.
"No sanctions <…> will knock us off this path. We will continue to cooperate across all areas: with our African partners, with BRICS members, and with our neighbors within the greater Eurasian space," he told reporters on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
Speaking about Europe’s negative reaction to the Russian-Africa summit, Ryabkov noted that European countries have "cut themselves off from cooperation with Russia." "We certainly welcome the immense interest in the Moscow event on the African continent and beyond. The Russia-Africa Forum is an event of global significance, without exaggeration," he stressed.

title: UK Chancellor Healey delivers budget to deal with 'global economic storms'
body: British Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey on Wednesday set out the government's latest tax and spending measures in his first ​budget , ​seeking to boost economic growth while ​maintaining control of public finances. He described it as a “budget for the working people of Britain, ⁠for British businesses, big and small, delivered at a time ​when global uncertainties and pressures are swirling worldwide and hitting people here at home”. Mr Healey said the UK was facing “global economic storms with trade tensions acting as a drag on global growth”. He said Russian President Vladimir Putin's invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago and the war in the Middle East were significant drivers ​of economic ⁠forecasts. The Chancellor said the government would continue to work with ‌allies to end the regional conflict and restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. He said he had chosen to use some of the fiscal headroom to “absorb the impact of the Iran war to protect the economy, and to protect family budgets”. Mr Healey announced plans for a new cost-control framework to drive down energy bills. He announced a £100 payment for 20 million households “to take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring”.

title: Putin outlines goals of ongoing Russia-Africa summit
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. The ongoing Russia-Africa summit in Moscow serves as a platform not only for communication among national leaders but also for exchanging experience and planning joint projects, Russian President Vladimir Putin said.
"We wanted to give this year’s Russia-Africa Forum greater momentum, and we still want to do so. We want to make it more engaging and accessible. Of course, it is important for senior officials and heads of state and government to sit down together and exchange views, but that alone is not enough in today’s world. We wanted to make the forum more inclusive, accessible, substantive and focused. Our goal is to direct participants’ attention, both during this process and at our meetings, toward what we consider the key development priorities for the world, Russia, and African countries," the president said at the Russia-Africa summit.
"We also wanted to showcase the areas in which Russia, in our view, has achieved tangible results and made significant progress, as I mentioned in my address. We want to show that we are ready to share our experience with our friends, partners, and allies in African countries. We also want to draw the attention of the business community, media representatives, and my friends and colleagues who lead African countries and governments to the most important and promising areas for cooperation," he added.
Putin then invited forum participants to visit a thematic exhibition showcasing ongoing Russian-African projects and Russia’s advanced technologies, which Moscow is ready to share with its partners across the continent.
"We would like to invite you to visit the exhibition now and see what we have to offer in terms of cooperation, where we see the greatest potential, and where we expect our joint efforts to achieve the best results. I hope you will find it both interesting and useful," the Russian president concluded.
The Russia-Africa summit is being held for the third time and, for the first time, in Moscow. The previous summit took place in St. Petersburg in the summer of 2023, while the inaugural summit was held in Sochi in the fall of 2019.
Russia’s relations with African countries have been marked by a longstanding atmosphere of friendship. Moscow maintains that, unlike Western countries seeking to preserve their remaining influence on the continent, Russia was never a colonial power in Africa. As a result, engages with its African counterparts without prejudice, treating them as equals and pursuing mutually beneficial partnerships.

title: NPP drags Mahama to Supreme Court over interpretation of 2-term limit
body: The New Patriotic Party (NPP) has filed a suit at the Supreme Court seeking an interpretation of the constitutional provisions governing presidential term limits, in a case that could determine whether President John Dramani Mahama is eligible to seek another term in office in 2028. The writ of summons and statement of case, dated July 28, 2026, were filed by the party’s solicitor, Godfred Yeboah Dame of Dame & Partners, with the Attorney-General named as the defendant. The party is asking the court to clarify whether the constitutional limit of two presidential terms applies regardless of whether the terms are served consecutively or are separated by a period out of office. In its statement of case, the NPP is seeking declarations on the interpretation of Articles 58(2) and 66(1), (2) and (3)(a) of the 1992 Constitution. Among other reliefs, the party wants the court to declare that the presidential term limit means a maximum of two terms, whether consecutive or non-consecutive. It is also asking the court to affirm that a person cannot be elected President more than twice and cannot hold the office for more than two four-year terms, amounting to eight years in total. The NPP is further seeking clarification on the eligibility of a Vice-President who assumes the presidency for more than half of a predecessor’s unexpired term. It wants the court to declare that such a person would be eligible to contest for election as President for only one term. The party is also asking the court to clarify whether a person who has previously served one presidential term may serve only one additional term, regardless of whether the two terms are consecutive. The suit follows public debate over whether the constitutional phrase “two terms” could be interpreted to mean two consecutive terms rather than two terms in total. The NPP argues that such an interpretation could allow a person who has served one term, lost an attempt at immediate re-election and later returned to office to serve two additional terms. The party describes that interpretation as a threat to the constitutional framework governing presidential tenure. “Plaintiff considers this proposition not only absurd but dangerous for the democracy, peace and stability of the nation,” the statement of case reads. It argues that adopting such an interpretation would effectively introduce words into the Constitution that are not contained in the text. “Acceding to this interpretation will condone and sanction manipulation of clear provisions in the Constitution as it involves inserting words into the constitutional text—it will involve amending the Constitution through judicial fiat,” the party states. The NPP’s arguments also draw on international examples, including the United States’ 22nd Amendment, which limits the number of times a person may be elected President. The party further refers to constitutional developments in other African countries and argues that attempts to alter presidential term limits have contributed to political instability in some jurisdictions. It also cites the Constitution Review Commission’s 2011 report, which recommended an amendment to clarify that a person who has served two presidential terms would not qualify to stand for re-election. title: John Darko calls for stronger women’s representation in Parliament
body: The Member of Parliament for Suame, John Darko, has called for greater representation of women in Parliament and other leadership positions, warning that their underrepresentation limits the range of perspectives shaping national decisions. Speaking at an event organised by the Young African Women Congress Network (YAWC Network) in Accra on Monday, October 26, he said Ghana was missing out on the skills, experience and ideas women could contribute to national development. “A democracy that excludes women from meaningful participation in political and economic decision-making deprives itself of the competence, experiences and perspectives of substantial portions of its citizens,” he said. Mr Darko described women’s participation in political leadership as essential to an effective and representative democracy. He noted that although women make up approximately half of Ghana’s population, their representation in Parliament remains disproportionately low. “Ghana’s Parliament presently comprises 276 members, of whom only 41 are women. Women constitute approximately half of our population, yet their presence in the principal institution responsible for making laws, approving national expenditure and scrutinising our executive authority remains disproportionately low,” he said. Representing the Minority Leader at the event, Mr Darko urged stakeholders to intensify efforts to remove barriers preventing women from participating fully in political and economic decision-making. YAWC marks 10 years of advocacy The event formed part of activities marking the tenth anniversary of the Young African Women Congress Network, which advocates greater opportunities and representation for women and girls. The network’s Global President, Dr Stephanie Wirba, said that despite progress over the past decade, many girls and women continued to face barriers to education, healthcare, employment and leadership. “We have won battles, but we have not won the war. Our girls are still out of school, our mothers are still dying in childbirth, our girls are still married before they can vote, and a woman is still asked for sex to get a job,” she said. Dr Wirba’s remarks highlighted what she described as persistent challenges facing women and girls, despite efforts to advance gender equality. Calls for stronger implementation of affirmative action The Executive Director of the Young African Women Congress, Daniel Osei Tuffuor, called on public institutions to move beyond commitments and take concrete steps to expand opportunities for women and girls. He questioned the progress made in implementing Ghana’s affirmative action legislation and urged authorities to demonstrate greater commitment to putting agreed measures into practice. “It’s been how many years now since we passed the affirmative action bill, have we been able to achieve even 20% of that? Our authorities have to be intentional about implementation these bills. Until they are intentional, we will go and come, go and come and still be at where we are,” he said. He added that public authorities had a responsibility to implement measures designed to improve women’s representation and participation. Network shifts focus towards opportunities and mentorship As it marks its tenth anniversary, the YAWC Network says it intends to place greater emphasis on securing practical opportunities for women, alongside its advocacy work. Mentorship will also be a priority over the next decade, with established members expected to support younger women seeking to enter leadership positions. The initiative is intended to help more women develop the experience, confidence and networks needed to participate in decision-making across public and private institutions.

title: Spanish Navy's second F110 frigate hits the water
body:
Navantia has launched Roger de Lauria (F112), the second of five F110-class frigates being built for the Spanish Navy, at its shipyard in Ferrol, Spain, four months ahead of the scheduled delivery.
The frigate entered the water for the first time during a ceremony on October 27, 2026. Construction will continue alongside the shipyard quay, with delivery scheduled for 2029.
The F110 program is intended to provide the Spanish Navy with five multipurpose escort vessels designed to counter air, surface and submarine threats. The frigates will also operate alongside other naval units and support civilian authorities in maritime security missions.
The first ship in the class, Bonifaz (F111), is undergoing systems installation and start-up, with sea trials scheduled to begin in 2027. Construction of the third frigate, F113, is also underway, with five hull blocks already on the slipway. Initial work on the fourth vessel, F114, has begun at Navantia's Digital Block Factory.
The F110 frigates will feature Navantia's SCOMBA combat management system, which processes information from sensors, radars and weapons, and the integrated platform control system (SICP).
The ships will also incorporate an integrated mast designed to consolidate antennas and sensors, optimize electromagnetic spectrum use and reduce radar signature, according to the shipbuilder.
Another key feature is a digital twin, a virtual replica of the vessel developed by Navantia in cooperation with the Spanish Navy and Spain's Directorate-General for Armament and Materiel. Using sensor data and technologies including the Internet of Things, cloud computing and machine learning, the system is intended to support vessel management and maintenance.
The frigates will also have the integrated services system (SSI), a sensor network connected to the vessel's lighting infrastructure. The F110 design is intended to accommodate future capability upgrades without requiring a fundamental redesign of the platform.

title: Russia-Ukraine ceasefire holds in southern Ukraine city, officials say
body:
A planned six-day ceasefire in and around a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night, officials said Wednesday, but Moscow and Kyiv continued to batter each other elsewhere.
The localized truce in the devastated southern city of Oleshky began Tuesday and is due to last through Sunday as a humanitarian operation races to get urgently needed food and medicine to about 2,000 remaining residents, as well as evacuate those who want to leave.
If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time since Russia’s invasion of its neighbor more than 4 1/2 years ago that the two sides have observed a significant truce. Previous attempts to stop the fighting have either failed to take hold or quickly unraveled amid deep mistrust.
Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be sent to Oleshky before any evacuation corridors are opened.
Russia’s occupying forces impose strict limits on who can enter Oleshky, and there was no news on how the humanitarian operation was unfolding.
Russia’s ombudsperson Yana Lantratova and Ukraine’s human rights ombudsperson Dmytro Lubinets both said Wednesday there had been no ceasefire violations in Oleshky for 30 hours.
The plight of the city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region caught the attention of U.S. first lady Melania Trump, and the White House said she brokered the humanitarian mission.
Pope Leo XIV also spoke this month with presidents Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine and Vladimir Putin of Russia, urging them to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky and the safe evacuation of civilians, the Vatican said.
Both Ukrainian and Russian officials, eager to win U.S. President Donald Trump’s approval as he pushes for an elusive peace settlement, thanked Melania Trump for her role.
The ceasefire coincided with U.S.-led plans to bring Moscow and Kyiv officials back to the table next month for technical talks on how to move forward on ending the war, even though neither side shows signs of backing down from their key demands.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, speaking in Helsinki on Wednesday, said Kyiv “will never accept any formula at the cost of our sovereignty or territorial integrity.”
Talks between delegations from Ukraine, Russia and the United States that are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in November have not yet been scheduled because Washington is awaiting developments in the Middle East, Zelenskyy told reporters in remarks Tuesday that were embargoed until Wednesday.
Zelenskyy said the leaders of Finland and Norway, who spoke to Putin by phone Tuesday, told him that Russia is “serious” about discussing steps to de-escalate the war.
The Ukrainian president said these could include a pause in attacks targeting energy infrastructure and commercial sea traffic, further prisoner exchanges, and a discussion of formats for possible meetings at leaders’ level.
The call to the Kremlin by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb was surprising. European countries have sought to diplomatically isolate the Russian leader since the invasion.
But since Putin’s summit with Trump in Alaska last year, Zelenskyy noted, European governments have quietly resumed contacts with Moscow at the level of national security advisers and between intelligence agencies.
The Iran war has depleted stocks of U.S.-made Patriot air defence systems that Ukraine desperately needs to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Ukraine is now getting an average of 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month this year — a sharp drop from delivery rates in previous years, Zelenskyy told reporters.
“Imagine this: you can count on getting 150 missiles a year from America, while you have to shoot down 150 ballistic missiles a month,” he said.
Patriot delivery delays appeared to be part of a trend of U.S. disengagement with Kyiv, Zelenskyy said, following disruptions in vital internet satellite links and intelligence sharing as well as a recent Trump administration agreement to purchase Russian diesel and waive sanctions.
A Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight wounded five people, including a four-year-old child, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said.
The jet-powered drone attack started a major fire that set alight an apartment building, private house and an industrial building, the emergency services said.
In Russia, meanwhile, the Defense Ministry said that air defences downed 531 Ukrainian drones from late Tuesday through early Wednesday.
Officials said apartment buildings and industrial infrastructure in three regions were targeted, wounding eight people.

title: Instagram to allow creators upload videos up to 90 minutes
body: Instagram is testing a new feature that will allow selected creators to upload videos lasting up to 90 minutes, marking a major shift from the platform’s traditional focus on short-form content. The feature, called “Features”, will allow users to watch longer videos, including podcasts, interviews and comedy shows, directly on the Meta-owned platform without switching to other services. Instagram announced the test on Monday, with the company expanding its efforts to compete in the growing market for long-form digital video content. Instagram head Adam Mosseri, who previously opposed introducing longer videos on the platform, said the company had decided to embrace the format for several reasons. “For a long time, I have been against doing long-form video on Instagram,” Mosseri said in a video shared alongside Tessa Lyons, the company’s vice president of product. “But we are actually going to lean in for a bunch of different reasons,” he added. Lyons described the move as a new phase in Instagram’s video development, noting that the platform was beginning to explore ways of accommodating longer storytelling formats. “It feels like a full circle moment that we’re here now talking about the beginning of our journey on the long-form video,” she said. Under the new feature, users who come across short vertical clips on their feeds will be able to tap a prompt to watch the full video in a horizontal format within the app. The development is expected to make it easier for podcasters and other creators to use Instagram not only to promote their content but also to distribute complete episodes. Mosseri explained that creators currently use Instagram to attract audiences before directing them to other platforms to watch full-length videos. “You slice it up, you use platforms like Instagram as the top of the funnel to raise awareness, and then you kind of go to, you know, a podcast player or YouTube or wherever to watch the full-length thing,” he said. The new feature is designed to eliminate that extra step by allowing audiences to access complete videos without leaving Instagram. According to reports, creators will also be able to connect up to eight short clips to a single long video, giving users different entry points through which to discover full episodes. The feature, previously tested in Brazil, is now being expanded to selected creators in the United States, according to reports by The Hollywood Reporter and other media outlets. Instagram is also expanding its presence on television screens through Instagram for TV, which supports viewing videos on devices including Apple TV, Samsung, Amazon Fire TV and Google TV. The company is further testing a feature called “Series” to organise episodes of recurring shows and exploring additional ways for users to discover livestreams. The expansion comes as YouTube continues to attract audiences for video podcasts, interviews and other long-form entertainment. Lyons said Instagram wanted to strengthen its position as a destination for social entertainment by giving creators more ways to tell stories and helping audiences discover content. “Our goal is really to be the best place for social entertainment,” she said. “To do that well, we need to broaden the way that we enable people to tell stories through video and enable audiences to discover them,” she added. However, Instagram has yet to announce a comprehensive payment system for creators producing long-form videos comparable to YouTube’s advertising revenue-sharing programme. Mosseri has also acknowledged challenges with previous attempts to introduce broader creator payment programmes, according to Business Insider. For now, the 90-minute video feature remains in testing, with Instagram yet to announce when it will become available to all creators. The post Instagram to allow creators upload videos up to 90 minutes appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Senate Confirms Tinubu’s Rights Commission, FRC Appointees
body: The Senate has confirmed President Bola Tinubu’s appointees to the boards of the National Human Rights Commission and the Fiscal Responsibility Commission. Those confirmed for the National Human Rights Commission are Dr. Salamatu Hussaini Suleiman as Chairman, alongside ten others as members. Also confirmed are appointees for the Fiscal Responsibility Commission, with Dr. Abdullahi Maikano Saidu as Executive Chairman, and six other members representing the geo-political zones. title: Full list: Winners of the GJA Ashanti Media Excellence Awards
body: The Ashanti regional chapter of the Ghana Journalists Association, on Saturday, October 24, recognized and celebrated the impactful work of journalists in the region. The Ashanti Media Excellence Awards were aimed at promoting excellence in journalism and qualitative media practice by recognising and competitively rewarding outstanding journalistic work produced in 2025. The journalists were celebrated for their outstanding storytelling and investigative reporting across 10 competitive categories. Here is the full list of the winners and runners-up for the various categories. Special Awards Breast Cancer Awareness : Prince Kwadwo Boadu (Hello Fm) – From Survivor to Advocate: A woman’s Journey against Breast Cancer. Inclusion Reporting : Ivan Korshie Heathcote – Fumador (ULTIMATE FM / GHONE TV) – Visually Impaired in Ghana Appeal for Accessible Apps for Digital Financial Transactions. Honorary Award: Veteran journalist, Mr. Kofi Badu , Chief of Staff of the Manhyia Palace Overall • Ashanti Region Journalist of the Year 2025 : Emmanuel Bright Quaicoe (LUV FM / JOYNEWS) – Exceptional reporting of the August 2025 Helicopter Crash at Adansi Akrofuom, in addition to winning the Best Feature Production and Best in Agriculture Reporting. This year’s Awards event is under the theme: “ Celebrating Excellence, Championing Credibility: Journalism in the Age of AI ”.

title: FESF Foundation calls for stronger rice production to boost food security
body: The FESF Foundation has called for increased investment in Ghana’s rice sector, saying stronger domestic production is critical to food security and economic growth. The Foundation says Ghana must move beyond simply producing more rice and focus on improving productivity, quality, irrigation, mechanisation, storage, processing and access to finance. The call was made at the 5th FESF Foundation Food Security Lecture, held under the theme “Rice: A Global Crop for Food Security and Economic Growth.” Rice is one of the world’s major staple foods and supports millions of people across the agricultural value chain, including farmers, processors, traders and transporters. For Ghana, however, growing demand for rice has meant a heavy reliance on imports. According to data cited by the Foundation, Ghana’s rice import bill increased nearly 30-fold in 21 years, rising from GH¢104 million in 2004 to GH¢3.23 billion in 2024. The Foundation attributed the increase partly to global shocks, including the COVID-19 pandemic, the 2022 commodity price shock and Vietnam’s export restrictions in 2023. It said these developments directly affected Ghana’s import bill and household spending on rice. The Foundation believes this situation presents both a challenge and an opportunity for Ghana. It said reducing the country’s dependence on imported rice could help conserve foreign exchange, create jobs, strengthen rural economies and support broader economic growth. The Foundation stressed that food security cannot be achieved simply by producing enough food. It said food must also be available, affordable, accessible, nutritious and safe. This, it said, requires investment across the entire food system, from production and storage to processing, transportation, distribution and consumption. The Foundation also described food security as a national security issue, arguing that a country that cannot reliably feed its population remains vulnerable, particularly during periods of crisis. “A nation that can feed itself in normal conditions and in times of crisis is in a better position to defend itself, develop itself and determine its own future,” the Foundation said. According to the Foundation, Ghana’s rice sector has the potential to become a major driver of economic transformation. It said a stronger rice industry could attract investment, create jobs for young people and women, support smallholder farmers and promote the growth of agro-processing. However, it stressed that this will require closer collaboration between government, farmers, financial institutions, researchers, development partners and the private sector. The Foundation further called for policies that encourage investment, financing systems that reduce risks for farmers and research that responds directly to the needs of producers. The Foundation also warned that climate change could pose a major threat to rice production. It cited changing rainfall patterns, floods, droughts, rising temperatures, pests and diseases as challenges that farmers will increasingly have to deal with. It therefore called for greater investment in irrigation, climate-smart technologies, improved rice varieties and sustainable management of land and water resources. The Foundation expressed hope that discussions at the lecture would produce practical recommendations for developing Ghana’s rice sector and strengthening food security across Africa. It urged stakeholders to look beyond the challenges and explore ways of turning rice production into a driver of economic growth, job creation, industrialisation and rural development.

title: What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
body:
As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP and shared first with NPR, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.
The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.
What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.
The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."
And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.
Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.
Meghan Maher and her mom Connie Cadwell. In order to help her mother through cancer treatment and care for her young children, Maher had to leave her career. Maher family hide caption
At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.
She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.
Stay up to date with our Politics newsletter, sent weekly.
She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.
Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.
Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.
About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.
Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.
Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.
When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.
With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.
What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In May, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said to the Senate committee. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood , an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.
Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.
If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.
The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."
In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.
Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.
In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.
A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.
"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."
Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series " What It Takes " for NPR.
A previous version of this story incorrectly said that the Senate special committee on aging hearing where Meghan Maher spoke was held in April. It took place in May.
