title: Cybersecurity: EFCC strengthens digital systems to combat financial crimes – Official
body:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission ( EFCC ) says it is strengthening its digital systems and cybersecurity capabilities to combat increasingly sophisticated financial crimes.
‎EFCC chairman Olanipekun Olukoyede, represented by Nwanyinma Okeanu, deputy director, public affairs department of the commission, said this at the second edition of the International Cybersecurity Conference (ICSC) 2026 in Abuja on Tuesday.
‎The two-day conference has its theme as ‘Cyber Resilience in the Age of AI: Defending Minds, Networks and Nations’.
‎Mr Olukoyede said criminals were increasingly exploiting digital technologies to target thousands of people, move funds across borders and conceal their activities.
‎“For us in law enforcement, the message is clear: as crime evolves, our response must evolve with it,” he said.
‎He said the commission had embarked on a digital transformation programme to reduce manual processes, improve access to information, automate workflows and enhance operational efficiency.
According to him, the initiative has produced several digital platforms supporting the commission’s operations, including the e-Petition Platform, Enterprise Case Management System (ECMS), Fraud Risk Assessment and Management System, and Asset Management System.
‎“Every new system and digital service creates opportunities, but it also introduces risks,” he said.
‎The EFCC chairman said the anti-graft agency was strengthening network and information security, improving security monitoring and access controls, and enhancing incident response mechanisms.
‎Momo Cyprus, the chairman of the Defence, Intelligence and Security Committee of the Liberian Senate, called for responsible use of AI to protect citizens, institutions and national security.
Mr ‎Cyprus, who represents Lofa County in his country’s senate, said AI offered significant opportunities to improve public services, expand education, accelerate research and empower African innovators.
‎However, he warned that the technology could also be exploited to spread disinformation, facilitate fraud and undermine public confidence in political institutions.
‎“Our task is not to fear technological progress, but to ensure that it serves humanity responsibly,” he said.
‎ The Liberian senator cited the 2026 African Cyber Threat Assessment Report by the International Criminal Police Organisation (INTERPOL), which highlighted the growing sophistication of cybercrime and the increasing use of AI by criminals.
‎He called for digital literacy, critical thinking, public awareness and responsible communication to help citizens identify and avoid online deception.
‎“We must encourage every citizen to pause, verify and act carefully before sharing information or responding to suspicious requests,” Cyprus said.
‎On defending networks, Mr Cyprus said governments, banks, hospitals, communication systems and energy infrastructure increasingly depended on secure digital networks to function effectively.
‎He said Liberia had taken steps to strengthen its cybersecurity framework through the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the National Cybersecurity Strategy for 2025 to 2029 with ways of creating adequate implementation in mind.
‎The two-day conference brought together policymakers, cybersecurity professionals, law enforcement agencies and other stakeholders to discuss strategies for strengthening digital resilience in the age of AI.

title: Egyptian court orders closure of news website and fines editor-in-chief
body: An Egyptian court ordered the closure of Mada Masr , one of the country's best-known independent news websites, after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of running it without a licence. The New Cairo Misdemeanour Court gave her the maximum fine of three million Egyptian pounds (about $54,000) and ordered the confiscation of the outlet's equipment and property. Attalah was taken into custody after the ruling and released several hours later after the outlet paid the fine, according to a statement it published, in which it also said the lawyers plan to appeal the ruling. The verdict came at the end of the trial's first hearing. Hossam Bahgat, executive director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and a former Mada Masr editor, was in court. He told the outlet after the trial that the judge rejected all of the defence's procedural requests and appointed a lawyer for Attalah that her eight-member defence team did not know. He added that the court read out the conviction “amid shouts and protests from the defence counsel”. In its statement, Mada Masr said Attalah has also learnt of a separate one-year prison sentence issued against her in absentia in 2024 on charges of spreading false news and running an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged that ruling, and a retrial hearing is set for November 11. The case was brought under Article 105 of Egypt's 2018 media law, which carries fines of one million Egyptian pounds to three million Egyptian pounds and allows a court to close an unlicensed website. The Supreme State Security Prosecution questioned Attalah for more than six hours on October 21 about a recent report her outlet published. She was released on bail of 100,000 Egyptian pounds. The next day, prosecutors sent her to trial on the licensing charge. Mada Masr was founded in 2013 and has been blocked in Egypt since 2017. This is the sixth case against the outlet or its journalists in six years. The outlet says it applied for a license three times, in 2018, 2020 and 2023, and its latest application is still pending. Before the verdict, dozens of rights groups and media organisations issued a joint statement calling for Mada Masr to be granted a licence. Amnesty International called the ruling “a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt”.

title: Ethiopia receives 12 Su-35 fighter jets from Russia — premier
body:
NAIROBI, October 28. /TASS/. Ethiopia has received the first 12 4++-generation Su-35 fighter jets from Russia, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reported.
"In accordance with our prior agreement with the Russian government, we have today taken delivery of the first twelve Su-35 4++ Generation fighter jets," he wrote on the X social media platform. He did not specify the total number of fighter jets to be delivered under the agreement.
The prime minister expressed his gratitude to Russian President Vladimir Putin for facilitating the delivery of the aircraft a year ahead of the agreed-upon schedule. According to him, by acquiring these fighter jets Ethiopia has taken the lead among sub-Saharan African nations in terms of modern combat aircraft capabilities.
Abiy Ahmed emphasized that receiving the new weapons marked an important step in strengthening the country’s defense capabilities and ensuring national security. He noted that enhancing the combat readiness of the Ethiopian armed forces would help deter potential aggression and contribute to regional stability.
The prime minister’s statement came against the backdrop of the third Russia-Africa Summit, taking place in Moscow on October 28-29, in which he is participating. Russia and Ethiopia have been developing military-technical cooperation for many years. In July 2021, the two sides signed a series of agreements aimed at modernizing the Ethiopian armed forces, transferring technology, and training military specialists.
Arms deliveries are taking place against the backdrop of an escalating situation in the region. Since late September, armed clashes between government forces and rebel groups have continued in northern Ethiopia. At the same time, Addis Ababa’s relations with neighboring Eritrea have deteriorated sharply, and diplomatic ties with that country were severed in early October.

title: Why Jaguar's new electric car is designed to divide opinion, according to the people who built it
body: Rawdon Glover is unequivocal. “Jaguar is back,” proclaims the managing director of the British car maker, speaking about its new all-electric Type 01 . “It feels surreal to finally be in here [at this point] and we’re very keen to get the car out and see what the reaction is. I’m often reminded of the magnitude of feeling for the brand.” It’s a magnitude that generates some strong opinions. When Jaguar unveiled its Type 00 concept car two years ago, the reaction was divided, to say the least. Critics said it showed Jaguar had abandoned its heritage and classic styling cues in favour of something more akin to a minimalist spaceship. And the critics were dismissed as out-of-touch traditionalists. There was even more confusion around Jaguar’s rebranding: the car was pink; the promotional material populated by a very cosmopolitan bunch with bold haircuts and a sci-fi style of dress. It was, in short, not very “middle-aged, middle-class white guy in a country pub”, Jaguar’s long-time homeland. That was the point: Jag Man is dying out. “Our new customer is more likely to be younger, more urban, wealthier, interested in design, but have a unifying mindset of wanting the kind of brands that not everyone else has,” says Glover. “They are after individuality.” And, to drive that point home, what people cannot fail to notice is that Jaguar has pushed on with its new look regardless of the heat it received. If production cars tend to differ, often quite dramatically – and disappointingly – from the concept cars that inspire them, the similarity between the Type 01 and the Type 00 is clear, even if the 01 was all but finished before the 00 was unveiled as an extreme take on it. Indeed, according to Carlee Hardacre, Jaguar’s global head of marketing, the Type 01 shows the company is effectively preparing to shed part of its historic customer base with the aim of winning a new one – by, counter-intuitively perhaps, doubling down on divisiveness with a GT car design it knows many people will hate, but that enough will love. That pushes Jaguar into more of a low-volume, high-price strategy – the Type 01 will start at about £130,000 ($174,250) – a turnaround on its prior high-volume positioning that, arguably, aimed to please too many people with vehicles that also felt too much like the competition’s. But perhaps more importantly, the Type 01, which has been six years in the making, also returns Jaguar to the design ethos of its more golden years, Hardacre says. “When the E-Type was launched [65 years ago this year], some said it was the worst car they had ever seen. And Enzo Ferrari said it was the most beautiful,” she says. “It’s important to us that some people don’t like the Type 01. We decided that the worst thing would be to make a car that everyone thinks is all right but nobody really wants to buy.” Focus group testing only underscored the divide. Before production began, Jaguar asked about 5,000 potential customers around the world – its most extensive run of clinics, as the car industry calls them – to give their reaction to the Type 01, scoring it from one (cannot stand it) to 10 (must have it). Hardacre sounds pleased with the fact that the car scored the greatest number of ones in Jaguar’s history of such surveys, but also the greatest number of 10s. “Once you move beyond commodity pricing then anything you buy becomes about want, and not about need. That realisation came to the design team [behind the Type 01] very early,” says Glover. “Deciding to make it an electric vehicle was secondary. First of all, it had to be a Jaguar [of the old school].” There is, he adds, a lot of “homogeneous design” in the automotive industry right now, with electric cars especially following a “very cookie-cutter shape. I think we’re starting to see an approach with luxury brands that cuts through that”. Shape is an example of the many engineering feats that have gone into the Type 01, leading to about 360 new patent applications. They are feats that, sadly, are all too easy to overlook, even when you know the Type 01, with more than 1,000 hp, is Jaguar’s fastest and most aerodynamic car to date. Indeed, the company says that, early in the development of the Type 01, it had a profile in mind and was determined that engineering would have to find workarounds to make that profile possible. So, for example, many electric vehicles tend to follow a boxy form — because the battery cells are centred under the cabin, in part to keep them away from crash zones — but the Type 01 puts a sixth of them at the front of the car. This helps to give it much better balance – 50/50 front/rear, the company claims – and extends its range. But it also allows for a sleek, low roofline and more legroom in the back. Yet achieving this required the development of an industry-first structural design Jaguar calls the Tri-Apex Node, capable of absorbing and stopping 26 tonnes of force in a head-on collision. “From an engineering point of view, putting battery cells towards the front of a car is a bit crazy,” says Thomas Muller, Jaguar’s chief technology officer. “Of course, it’s never the case that your first attempt [at a solution] works. There’s a lot of time spent standing in front of a whiteboard.” There is also the pressure of getting a new model to market as planned. “Delivering a car to the schedule is important, but if you’re spending a week longer on some aspect when you’re deciding on the future of the brand, it’s worth it,” he adds. It’s Muller’s team that has also developed a suspension system that allows the Type 01’s giant 23-inch wheels sufficient travel up and down, while still fitting snugly within the wheel arches. The team is also behind what the company is calling the “impossible panel”, a one-piece rear quarter panel that brings together four planes and which Jaguar’s design simulation software told them couldn’t be done. After 1,500 hours of tooling, the resulting seamless piece helps create the Type 01’s sense of the monolithic, as though the car was carved out of a single block of aluminium with brutalist intent. This, of course, is where the rubber really hits the road when it comes to divided opinion: in the look of the Type 01. From the super-slim wraparound headlights setting off a short overhang at the front, to the windowless rear where instead there’s a bold, grille-like “strike through” graphic arrangement into which a wraparound, Tron-like taillight is embedded, there’s little doubt that the car is unmistakable from either end. There are shades of the Rolls-Royce Phantom, of Tesla’s equally divisive Cybertruck, of the industrial form-follows-function of a Rimowa suitcase, but with much bigger wheels. Inside there’s a complete lack of leather and mahogany – it’s all organic forms covered seamlessly in a super-light, super-tough laminate textile called Ultra Fabric, and the seats are individually sculpted like pieces of space-age furniture. There is, at least, some carpet – covering not just the floor but continuing up into the lower quarter of each door. The Type 01 is, in a sense, a design object before it’s a car. Perhaps this is even a car for people who aren’t even that into cars – but are into their chairs, lamps, phones and trainers. “Reimagining Jaguar from a blank sheet of paper was part of the process with the Type 01. We wanted the result to feel very fresh and modern,” says Alexey Andreev, lead exterior designer for Jaguar. “It follows quite a reductive design philosophy, with every line following a certain visual logic that sets it in a certain place that will still make sense 30 years from now. The thing is that a lot of this kind of thing is easy to do on a concept car, and not so easy on a production car.” Andreev reckons that even if the initial reaction is uncertainty – and so soon after the Type 01’s launch, the jury is still out – more people will warm to the model when they see it on the road. But he adds that, from his perspective, it is no bad thing for people to feel “a little bit uncomfortable” when they see something for the first time. “It suggests that’s because it’s something they haven’t seen before,” he says. “And, ask yourself, have you ever seen a car like this before?” The answer is no – and, by breaking the monotony of so much car design, it will either push Jaguar back into the sunlit uplands or, as some industry commentators have feared, mark its final farewell. Glover says that he can’t do anything “about tariffs or the Chinese [car makers]. I can only focus on the stuff I can control and do what I can to help Jaguar”. Then he adds that tagline again: “Jaguar is back.”

title: Britain told it can lead world in metamaterials
body: Britain can become a global leader in metamaterials if it acts now to turn its research into commercial products, and the Ministry of Defence’s chief scientific adviser has welcomed a new government roadmap setting out how, according to the Institute of Physics. Metamaterials are engineered materials whose properties come from their internal structure instead of their chemical composition, which lets them respond to energy in ways conventional materials cannot. British-developed examples are already being applied to knee implants, impact protection, fifth generation connectivity, noise reduction and electric vehicle batteries, and the field holds potential for earthquake shielding, wireless charging, targeted ultrasound and cloaking against radar and the human eye. Professor Tim Dafforn, chief scientific adviser at the Ministry of Defence, said: “MOD is encouraged by this government signal designed to translate metamaterials opportunities created by the world-leading UK academic base, to drive commercialisation in this important dual-use emerging technology domain. “In line with the Strategic Defence Review and UK Industrial Strategy, this strongly supports UK freedom of action, resilience, and advantage economically and for defence and national security, at a time of heightened global uncertainty.” The Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap, published by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, warns that the global race to commercialise the technology is already running and that Britain’s window is closing, with countries across Asia, Europe and North America competing for the economic and national security benefits. Earlier research by the Institute of Physics found Britain ranked third in the world for academic papers on metamaterials, behind only China and the United States, but fourteenth for patents. Tom Grinyer, chief executive of the Institute of Physics, said: “The UK has the outstanding research foundations, underpinned by physics, to be a world leader in metamaterials. What we need now is the ambition and coordination to turn that unique advantage into innovations that deliver the UK’s strategic priorities and economic growth, beginning with a properly developed funding plan from research to commercialisation. “If we get this right, uniting public and private sectors behind long-term priorities to unlock the scale of investment needed, the UK can lead the way for the next global technology revolution through metamaterials. If we don’t, we risk the UK falling behind and becoming just one part in the pipeline of an extraordinary future.” Chris McDonald, the Minister for Science, Innovation and Investment, said: “Metamaterials represent a significant opportunity to strengthen the UK’s technology and industrial base, supporting economic growth, and solving societal challenges. Realising this opportunity will depend on our ability to translate cutting-edge research into commercially viable products and new industrial solutions. “I welcome the publication of the Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap and its vision for accelerating innovation, attracting investment and building the partnerships needed to position the UK at the forefront of the transformative potential of metamaterials.” The roadmap identifies fragmented funding and investment, limited manufacturing scale-up, skills gaps and a lack of standards as the barriers, and sets a ten year plan to build the world’s first integrated manufacturing value chain for the technology, with scaled manufacturing and commercialisation capabilities in place by 2035. It builds on more than £80 million of government investment through the National Materials Innovation Programme. The Metamaterials Strategy Action Group behind the work includes the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory alongside the business department, the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council, Innovate UK, the Institute of Physics, the UK Metamaterials Network, the High Value Manufacturing Catapult and the National Physical Laboratory. Professor Alastair Hibbins of the University of Exeter and Dr Claire Dancer of the University of Birmingham, who co-lead the UK Metamaterials Network, said: “Building on the UK’s world-leading academic excellence, research, training, and metamaterials community the launch of the UK Metamaterials Commercialisation Roadmap represents a defining moment, positioning the UK at the forefront of an enabling and transformative technology. “We see the Roadmap charting a course towards the UK becoming a global leader in commercialising metamaterials research and innovation, contributing to our nation’s security and prosperity. Realising this ambition depends on coordinated community action, driven by the community activities of the UK Metamaterials Network’s c.1300 academic, industry, and government members, to fully harness the UK’s competitive advantage in metamaterials.” The post Britain told it can lead world in metamaterials first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Five Things To Know Today
body: Today’s ‘Five Things’ leads with President Tinubu’s new foreign borrowing request, a six-month transport allowance for federal workers, an updated death toll from the Taraba killings, INEC’s investigation into suspicious photographs in the voters’ register, and the findings of the inquiry into deaths in NSCDC custody. 1. Tinubu seeks approval for $20.5 billion and €1.05 billion in fresh foreign loans President Bola Tinubu has asked the National Assembly to approve approximately $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion in external borrowing under the Federal Government’s 2026-2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan. The request was presented to the Senate on Tuesday, 27 October. The President says the financing will support infrastructure, power, transport, healthcare, agriculture, education and employment-related projects across the country. Senate President Godswill Akpabio referred the request to the relevant committees, directing them to report within one week. Former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar has urged lawmakers to withhold approval pending greater disclosure of project details. The borrowing has not yet been approved. Why it matters: The proposed borrowing is substantial and could have long-term implications for Nigeria’s debt obligations, public finances and infrastructure investment. Watch: The Senate committee’s findings, project-by-project disclosures, loan terms and the Debt Management Office’s assessment of repayment obligations. 2. Federal Government approves ₦70,000 monthly transport support for workers A conciliation meeting between the FG and the leadership of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC). X/@LabourMinNG The Federal Government and the Nigeria Labour Congress reached several agreements during Tuesday’s negotiations in Abuja, easing immediate tensions over threatened industrial action. The government approved a ₦70,000 monthly transport intervention for federal public service workers across all grade levels, beginning in November 2026 and lasting six months. It also agreed to pay outstanding peculiar-allowance arrears in three monthly instalments and settle 19 months of outstanding health workers’ allowances over three months, beginning in December. However, the parties did not reach agreement on the effective date for a revised national minimum wage. They agreed to establish a negotiation committee and review implementation after one month. Why it matters: The intervention could provide temporary relief to federal workers facing high transport and living costs. It is not a permanent wage increase. Watch: Publication of payment guidelines, evidence that November disbursements begin as promised, the new wage committee and organised labour’s formal response to unresolved demands. 3. Taraba killings: Emergency agency puts death toll at 62 Nigeria’s National Emergency Management Agency has reported that at least 62 people were killed and 52 injured in last Friday’s attack on Binnari community in Karim-Lamido Local Government Area of Taraba State. The updated figures were reported by the Associated Press, following information from NEMA officials on Tuesday. Authorities said 52 bodies had been recovered, including 15 from the Benue River, while searches continued. Thousands of residents have reportedly been displaced. Security agencies have deployed additional personnel, and the state government has begun providing relief materials. Why it matters: The attack is one of the deadliest recent assaults on a rural Nigerian community, with serious consequences for civilian safety, displacement and livelihoods. Watch: Reconciliation of the casualty figures, arrests, protection for neighbouring communities and humanitarian assistance. 4. INEC investigates suspected AI-generated photographs in voters’ register FILE: Residents check their names in the voters register during the Ondo governorship election on Saturday, November 16, 2024. Photo: Taiwo Adeshina/Channels TV The Independent National Electoral Commission says it is investigating suspicious photographs, including images suspected of having been generated by artificial intelligence, in the preliminary voters’ register published online on Monday, 26 October. INEC acknowledged on Tuesday that questionable entries had been identified during the earlier physical display of the register. The commission says the online version is preliminary and does not reflect all ongoing corrections. It has promised to investigate possible technical and procedural lapses before certifying the final register on 15 December 2026. The presence of suspicious images has been reported; their origin and the extent of any irregularities have not yet been established. Why it matters: The accuracy of the register is central to the credibility of the January 2027 general elections. The commission’s review offers an opportunity to identify and correct questionable records. Watch: INEC’s investigation findings, removal of verified invalid entries, public access to corrected records and independent scrutiny before certification. 5. Niger detention deaths: Federal panel blames suffocation and recommends ₦1.4 billion compensation A Federal Government investigative panel has concluded that detainees who died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps in Minna, Niger State, in September suffered acute respiratory failure caused by overcrowding, poor ventilation and extreme heat. Presenting its report on Tuesday, panel chairman Jonathan Kure said officers failed to respond to detainees’ distress calls. The committee recommended ₦1.4 billion in compensation, the dismissal of responsible officers and institutional reforms. Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo pledged to implement the recommendations and ordered the suspension of officers implicated in allegedly destroying evidence. There is a discrepancy in reported casualty numbers: Channels Television’s account of the committee’s presentation identifies 33 verified deaths. Why it matters: The findings raise serious questions about detention conditions, custodial accountability and the protection of people held by security agencies. Watch: Publication of the full report, reconciliation of the death toll, disciplinary or criminal proceedings and implementation of compensation. The post Five Things To Know Today appeared first on Channels Television .

title: TikTok is going after Yelp and Google Maps with an in-app restaurant guide
body:

For years, the app helped local restaurants go viral. Now, TikTok wants to offer crowdsourced reviews, reservation booking, and curated discovery.﻿

TikTok is launching an in-app restaurant guide in a challenge to other platforms like Yelp and even Google Maps.
The company on Wednesday announced the launch of Must Eat, a new section of the TikTok app built on 40 million posts, reviews, and comments about dining on the platform. The new feature uses videos and discussions of buzzy local businesses to create restaurant recommendation guides. Users can leave reviews of restaurants, call and make reservations, and search for nearby businesses on a map.
At a launch event this week, TikTok US CEO Adam Presser called Must Eat “the compilation of all of the conversation that’s happening on the TikTok platform across creators, restaurateurs, [and] individuals” who make videos or leave comments about local restaurants. Among the featured restaurants in New York are Golden Diner ( home of very viral pancakes ) and hard-to-reserve spots like Semma and Via Carota.
Must Eat falls somewhere between Yelp and more curated recommendations from publications like The Infatuation. Must Eat is divided into two category tabs: “everyday eats” and “elevated dining.” Users can sort and filter by rating, distance, cuisine type, and what’s currently open, and each page for a restaurant links to videos about the business posted to TikTok. Diners can also bookmark businesses to save them for later. The feature is initially available in a few select regions — New York City, Los Angeles, and the Bay Area. The company says restaurants can’t pay to be featured in the recommendation lists.
It’s not the first time TikTok has tried to bridge the gap for users between seeing a video about a place and actually visiting in person. Earlier this year, the company added the ability to book hotels and attractions through the app. That feature, TikTok Go, allowed content creators to tag and link to locations; Must Eat is an expansion of that earlier capability.
TikTok’s deeper move into the dining space is fitting, given the app’s profound impact on restaurants. Content creators have angled to become the food critics of the short-form video era, each with their own schtick or eccentricities. The popularity of food videos has even changed what restaurants put on the menu to begin with , like extra-long cheese pulls or dramatic presentations. In its press release announcing the launch of Must Eat, TikTok says 27 million US diners went to a restaurant, cafe, or shop for the first time thanks to the platform last year.

title: Iran’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity: AEOI spox
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – A spokesman for the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI) has stated that the country’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and has now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants.
Behrouz Kamalvandi, who is also the deputy for the International, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, made the remarks in an interview with the Islamic Republic of Iran News Network (IRNN) on Wednesday, expounding on the significance of the development of the nuclear energy in the world.
Clarifying the objectives and significance of the presence of the participation of the Iranian delegation in the International Conference of Nuclear Power in South Korea, Kamalvandi emphasized that global nuclear industry is divided into two sectors: energy and non-energy. Nuclear medicine, agriculture, and industry are among the fields where nuclear technology is applied within the non-energy sector, while nuclear power generation constitutes a significant part of the nuclear industry.
The sixth ministerial conference on nuclear energy is currently underway in South Korea, he said, adding, “Perhaps one of the reasons for the increased attention given to this subject in recent years lies in global environmental challenges, issues that have become a serious concern for the international community and further underscore the necessity of shifting toward nuclear energy.”
Given the development of modern technologies, including artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and the electrification of vehicles, the demand for electricity is steadily increasing. Hence, the expansion of nuclear power generation has become an undeniable necessity, the spokesman stressed.
In technical terms, nuclear-generated electricity is referred to as "baseload" power. It differs in this respect from certain other clean energy sources, such as wind and solar, where power generation depends on atmospheric conditions, the intensity of sunlight, or wind speeds.
In contrast, nuclear power plants provide stable and continuous electricity generation; this characteristic has further underscored the importance of developing such facilities, he continued.
Regarding Iran’s standing in the utilization of modern technologies, Kamalvandi stated, "Given my approximately 14 years of continuous service at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, I can say with confidence that the nation’s nuclear industry has reached full maturity, and we have now achieved self-sufficiency in the construction of nuclear power plants."

title: ANALYSIS: The criminalisation trap in Africa’s responses to artisanal mining
body:
Thirty-seven boys and young men died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State, last month. Accused of being ‘illegal miners’, they were arrested during raids by the Mining Marshals – a special NSCDC unit targeting illegal mining.
Yesterday, an investigative panel found they died of asphyxiation in ‘inhumane conditions’, calling the deaths preventable. Recommendations to compensate families, dismiss and prosecute the officers involved, and implement institutional reforms (among others) are significant, as they address the gravity of abuses and the need for holistic responses.
Such incidents are not unique to Nigeria, and offer a critical lens for examining recent human rights abuses at artisanal mining sites across Africa.
These sites are guarded by multiple actors, including state security, paramilitary outfits like NSCDC, private security, mercenaries and armed groups. Crimes they mete out against miners include trafficking, enslavement, extortion, sexual violence, child labour, forced recruitment and labour, arbitrary detention, torture and murder.
Artisanal miners and traders face not only abuses by government security forces, but also state failure to protect them from violations by non-state actors, including other miners.
In Central Africa, Institute for Security Studies research reveals that security forces in Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the Central African Republic (CAR) have perpetrated violence, including summary executions, against artisanal miners and mining communities. In the DRC, miners suffer abuse both from the Rwanda-backed M23 and private security guards .
South Africa’s zama zamas illustrate how illegal mining networks intersect with organised crime. Groups reportedly seize abandoned mines, extort other miners for protection, and steal gold from legal operations. Entangled in turf wars that inflame community conflict, these activities are compounded by alleged police corruption, limited enforcement capacity, and weak oversight of abandoned mines.
The Krugersdorp gang-rape case highlights the severe security risks zama zamas pose . Similar patterns exist in the CAR, where the Séléka and Anti-Balaka profit from the country’s diamond trade, sometimes taking over mining sites.
Artisanal and small-scale miners (ASM) in Africa number roughly 13.2 million. There are 2.6 million in Central Africa alone, an increase of over 2,500 per cent from approximately 100,000 in 2013 – driven by a rising demand for mineral resources amid a surge in global commodity prices. Gold hit a record high of $4,000/ounce in 2025, with similar spikes in critical mineral prices.
Across Africa, ASM supplies substantial shares of mineral production, with an annual foreign exchange value of around $3 billion-$5 billion. ASM accounted for 32-41 per cent of Africa’s total gold production in 2022 and 52-74 per cent of global tantalum production between 2017 and 2023, underlining its significant role in the extractive economy.
The scale of ASM in Africa must also be understood in the context of low educational attainment and high unemployment. ASM appeals to young people with few livelihood options. For many, including out-of-school children, it’s a means of survival.
Regulatory gaps further expose miners to human rights abuses. Mining laws across Central Africa generally permit ASM, often within designated areas, and criminalise unlicensed activity. But artisanal miners struggle to obtain permission, facing bureaucratic delays, high administrative costs and complex permit procedures that leave many operating outside legal protections.
The state’s coercive implementation of regulations enables abuses at mining sites. And the criminalisation of ASM exposes miners to exploitation and violence by criminal elements, who commonly demand ‘taxes’, intelligence or ‘protection’ money in exchange for miners’ freedom to pursue their livelihoods. This coerced cooperation increases artisanal miners’ vulnerability, as criminals violate these agreements with lethal violence.
Without differentiating between survival miners and criminal networks, such transactional relationships can be misread as collusion, thereby legitimising security force targeting of miners.
The situation is exacerbated in countries like Chad and South Africa, where political elites and military personnel reportedly sponsor or engage in mining, employ artisanal miners, provide logistical support and receive gold in exchange for private protection. This creates conflicts of interest – and influences selective enforcement of regulations.
Many miners are driven by poverty. Criminalising ASM perpetuates their vulnerability, exposing them to unhealthy working conditions and exploitation, while governments penalise small-scale miners and not concession owners. It can also lead to unrest. In Ghana, some communities have resisted enforcement efforts, saying they threaten their livelihoods.
Criminalisation does not solve the problems posed by ASM; it merely drives miners underground, further exposing them to danger and exploitation, and fuelling crime. Crackdowns and lethal attacks against artisanal miners reveal a limited state understanding of ASM’s complexities, reluctance to confront entrenched mining interests, and inconsistent enforcement due to uncertainty over how to regulate it.
There are valid concerns about ASM’s economic, environmental, infrastructural and human security impacts in Africa and globally. However, purely coercive responses to this complex social phenomenon are counterproductive.
Recent events point to the securitisation of mineral wealth, state desperation to assert sovereignty over ungoverned spaces, minimal accountability and human rights protections, and environmental and governance failures. These dynamics suggest a tacit admission that mining regulations in resource-rich African countries have failed, while states continue to conflate ASM with illegal mining.
The October meeting in Accra on strengthening ASM across the continent was timely. It was attended by political and traditional leaders, the United Nations, the African Union, the private sector, media and international partners, and followed on from last year’s summit on the issue.
But authorities also need to recognise artisanal miners as partners in extractive economies. That requires legislative reforms that define ASM’s scope and protect artisanal miners from human rights abuses by rogue security and law enforcement agents and others. Where infractions occur, investigations and prosecutions should follow.
Countries should expand income-generating opportunities for youth to reduce recruitment into armed conflict and dependence on exploitative mining. That could include investing in industry-aligned vocational training, entrepreneurship, digital skills and creative industries that support their aspirations and economic independence.
Titilope F Ajayi is a Senior Research Consultant, and Oluwole Ojewale is a Senior Researcher in the Central Africa Observatory at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS).
(This article was first published by ISS Today, a Premium Times syndication partner. We have their permission to republish).

title: Tech stocks rebounding ahead of U.S. interest rate announcement
body:
The bond market swung, while U.S. stocks held relatively steady after the Federal Reserve decided not to raise its main interest rate to bring down high inflation.
The S&P 500 rose 0.3 per cent Wednesday. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 0.3 per cent. In the bond market, the two-year Treasury yield initially jumped after the Fed held its main interest rate steady. It then reversed course after traders pared expectations for coming hikes to rates.
Higher rates can help get high inflation under control, but they can also hurt the economy.
The action was much stronger in the bond market, where the yield on the two-year Treasury initially climbed after the Fed announced its decision to hold rates steady. It got above 4.79 per cent from 4.70 per cent late Tuesday after the Fed said two officials actually wanted to raise the federal funds rate at their meeting, only to get outvoted by their peers.
The central bank last month raised its main interest rate for the first time in three years in hopes of bringing down inflation, which has remained above the Fed’s two per cent target for years and has been discouraging Americans broadly.
But the two-year Treasury yield, which closely tracks expectations for Fed action, quickly reversed course. It dropped as low as 4.69 per cent after Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the central bank wants to see how conditions play out before making its next move on rates.
He pointed to how rates for loans going to businesses and others across the economy have already climbed recently and how lenders and investors have become “more discerning.” He said the overwhelming judgment among Fed officials at their meeting was that “monetary medicine” is “starting to work some.”
Along with signals that the U.S. economy continues to grow, Warsh said that “broadly, these developments go in the direction” of helping the Fed achieve its two goals of a healthy economy and relatively low inflation.
Traders on Wall Street still see further increases to rates by the Fed as likely, but they pared back bets for how many may come by next summer, according to data from CME Group.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury, which moves on expectations for inflation and economic growth in upcoming years, had its own yo-yo moves following the Fed’s meeting but was largely steadier. It rose to 5.04 per cent from 4.99 per cent late Tuesday.
Higher rates push downward on stock prices, which has raised the pressure on companies to deliver growth in profits to counteract that. Several companies rallied Wednesday after joining the list of those beating analysts’ expectations for the summer.
GE HealthCare Technologies jumped 6.4 per cent after delivering both profit and revenue for the summer that surpassed analysts’ expectations. It also raised its forecasts for revenue growth and other financial measures for the full year.
Etsy climbed six per cent after its profit for the latest quarter blew past analysts’ forecasts. CEO Kruti Patel Goyal said the online marketplace saw growth in active buyers from prior-year levels for the first time in two years, while its active seller base grew at its fastest rate in two years.
Stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry were also relatively solid. They’ve stabilized this week following big swings on worries that high borrowing costs will undercut the boom in AI data centers largely built with borrowed money.
AI stocks got an additional boost after a major player in the industry, South Korea’s SK Hynix, soared 10.9 per cent in Seoul following its latest profit report. The seller of memory chips said it’s in the midst of a virtuous cycle of rising AI usage, and it expects demand to continue to outpace supply through 2030.
On Wall Street, Micron Technology rose 5.4 per cent and was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500. It also sells memory for computers.
Outside of tech, Wendy’s jumped 14.6 per cent to $7.04 after Trian Fund Management, run by investor Nelson Peltz, offered to buy the chain for $7.35 per share in cash.
That helped offset a drop for Boston Scientific, which fell 4.1 per cent even though the seller of medical devices reported a milder drop in profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for profit in the current quarter that fell short of analysts’ expectations.
Robinhood Markets sank 3.9 per cent after reporting weaker profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped 6.6 per cent following SK Hynix’s leap. Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1 per cent, while France’s CAC 40 edged down by less than 0.1 per cent.

title: Road crash injuries fall 15% in September as police intensify TraffiTech-GH sensitisation
body: The number of people injured in road crashes across Ghana fell by 15.02% in September 2026 compared with the same period last year, the Director of Education, Research and Training at the Police Motor Traffic and Transport Department (MTTD), Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Alexander Kwaku Obeng, has disclosed. He attributed the decline to increased sensitisation and caution notices sent to motorists under the TraffiTech-GH pilot project. ACP Obeng said the police recorded 1,194 people injured in road crashes in September this year, down from 1,405 in September 2025. “Within twenty days of September this year, when we enhanced sensitisation, gathering evidence and confronting vehicle owners with it with an embedded message, with GPS, MTTD sender ID sending messages saying ‘speed kills, reduce it now’ with your vehicle number, time and place of the offence,” he said on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show on Wednesday, October 28. He said a comparison of crash data for the two periods showed a significant change in driver behaviour. “If you compare the data of crashes from September last year (2025) with the same period this year, we have seen a significant change in behaviour of drivers,” he added. ACP Obeng also disclosed that road crashes declined from 1,108 in September 2025 to 1,003 in September 2026, representing a 9.4% reduction. The number of vehicles involved in crashes also fell from 1,928 to 1,693, a decline of 12.19%. TraffiTech-GH is currently under a pilot project and has not yet been rolled out nationwide. TraffiTech-GH is an automated system developed by the Ghana Police Service to enforce road traffic laws and regulations and improve road safety in the country. The system uses cameras and sensors to automatically take a picture and or video of vehicles that flout road traffic laws and regulations, such as speeding and running a red light

title: Violence Mars Gov Radda’s Funtua Campaign Flag-off As Supporters Report Injuries, Property Losses
body: Violence erupted along the route to the Tinubu–Dikko campaign flag-off in Funtua Zone on Wednesday, leaving several supporters of the All Progressives Congress (APC) injured and their property destroyed. The victims, who said they were travelling in the convoy of Katsina State Governor, Malam Dikko Radda, alleged that they were attacked by groups of angry youths and hoodlums while heading to the campaign venue, where the Governor was scheduled to present his administration’s Building Your Future scorecard. Some of the affected supporters told reporters that mobile phones, clothing and other personal belongings were destroyed during the incident, while several people sustained varying degrees of injuries. According to the victims, the attackers, whom they described as armed with machetes, knives, stones and bottles, assaulted them without provocation. “We were simply on our way to attend the campaign flag-off when we encountered some angry youths who attacked us with stones and bottles. Many people were injured, and our property was destroyed. We cannot afford to replace what we lost,” one of the victims said. The victims appealed to security agencies and relevant authorities to investigate the incident and bring those responsible to justice. Earlier, at the Malumfashi town roundabout linking Bakori Local Government Area, stones were seen scattered across the road, while several vehicles reportedly had their windscreens damaged, suggesting earlier disturbances in the area. Despite the disruption, Governor Radda proceeded with the presentation of his administration’s Building Your Future scorecard, highlighting achievements recorded since assuming office and outlining ongoing projects across key sectors ahead of the 2027 governorship election. The statewide campaign is designed to deepen grassroots engagement by taking the administration’s performance and development agenda directly to communities across the three senatorial zones of Funtua, Daura and Katsina, covering all 34 Local Government Areas and 361 wards. Authorities had not issued an official statement on the reported attack at the time of filing this report. The post Violence Mars Gov Radda’s Funtua Campaign Flag-off As Supporters Report Injuries, Property Losses appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Finland and Japan sign new defence agreement
body:
"The agreement will open up significant growth opportunities for our defence industry and technology companies," Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) said.
Finland and Japan have signed an agreement on transferring defence equipment and technology, according to the Finnish defence ministry.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) signed on Finland's behalf during his visit to Japan this week, the ministry said in a press release. Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi signed on behalf of Japan.
"I would like to thank the Japanese Minister of Defence for the good negotiation process. The agreement will open up significant growth opportunities for our defence industry and technology companies," Häkkänen said in the release.
"The international security environment requires democratic countries to cooperate more closely in the development of the defence industry and technology. Japan is an important partner for Finland," he continued.
According to the ministry, the agreement outlines the terms and conditions for transferring defence equipment and technology. Cooperation may include research, development or production projects, coordinated by a joint committee from both countries.
Häkkänen has been in Japan for the past few days, accompanied by a business delegation of 20 Finnish defence and dual-use tech companies.
According to a separate release issued by the Finnish embassy in Tokyo, Häkkänen was scheduled to meet with Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.
Finnish companies joining the trip will present their latest technologies at business seminars and meetings in search of commercial opportunities.

title: UK extends permission to conduct business with Lukoil's Bulgarian subsidiaries until Feb 26, 2027
body:
The UK Treasury's Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation (OFSI) has extended a license due to expire on October 29, 2026, for transactions with Lukoil's Bulgarian entities under the imposed sanctions restrictions until February 26, 2027.
According to the agency, this concerns interaction with the companies Lukoil Bulgaria EOOD, Lukoil Neftochim Burgas AD, Lukoil Aviation Bulgaria EOOD and Lukoil Bunker Bulgaria EOOD.
The UK added Lukoil to its sanctions list on October 15, ordering all business transactions with the company to be wound up by November 29. Then, on November 14, OFSI issued a license to continue those transactions until February 14, 2026, later extending this deadline to August 13 and then to October 29.
The United States Department of the Treasury included Lukoil in its sanctions list on October 22, 2025, issuing a license to wind up operations, the validity of which it also repeatedly extended. The oil company soon announced its intention to sell its foreign assets. Negotiations with potential buyers are currently underway.
Lukoil began operating in Bulgaria in October 1999, purchasing a controlling stake in the Burgas oil refinery with a capacity of 8.8 million tonnes. It also manages a network of over 500 filling stations in the country. Due to the EU's ban on imports of Russian oil, Lukoil has had difficulty running its operations in Bulgaria in the last three years. It said that the group had begun reviewing the strategy for its assets in Bulgaria, including the sale of the business.
As reported, on November 14, 2025, the Bulgarian National Assembly passed a law introducing external management at Lukoil Neftochim Burgas AD, Lukoil Bulgaria EOOD and other enterprises of Lukoil Group in the country. In this connection, management of the affected companies was transferred to a special commercial manager from November 17, 2025. In order to protect its rights and legitimate interests, on February 19, 2026, Geneva-based Litasco SA, which is part of Lukoil Group and is the direct shareholder of Lukoil Neftohim Burgas AD and Lukoil Bulgaria EOOD, sent Bulgaria a notification that it considers the introduction of external management of the company's assets to be expropriation without compensation and may go to court.

title: Iran among 5 countries in eye stem cell transplantation
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) –The head of the Iranian Ophthalmology Society announced that the success rate of eye stem cell transplantation in Iran exceeds 85%, placing the country among the world’s top five in this field.
According to published reports by local Iranian media, the treatment is used for certain severe eye injuries caused by chemical and thermal burns. The cost of the treatment is also covered by government funding, according to the head of the Iranian Ophthalmology Society.
Eye stem cell transplantation is a treatment method used to restore the ocular surface in patients whose limbal stem cells, located in the cornea, have been destroyed or impaired by severe injuries, including chemical and thermal burns. These cells play a role in maintaining and regenerating the corneal surface, and damage to them can lead to vision loss.
Eye stem cell transplantation is a treatment method used to restore the ocular surface in patients whose limbal stem cells, located in the cornea, have been destroyed or impaired by severe injuries, including chemical and thermal burns. These cells play a role in maintaining and regenerating the corneal surface, and damage to them can lead to vision loss.
The scientific secretary of the Iranian Ophthalmology Congress also identified diabetes and its effects on the retina as major threats to eye health. He also warned about the consequences of prolonged computer use and the development of dry eye.
Diabetes can damage the blood vessels in the retina, potentially leading to visual impairment. Dry eye is also a common problem associated with prolonged screen use and may cause symptoms such as burning, a foreign-body sensation, and intermittent blurred vision.
In recent years, Iran has made progress in developing treatments for eye diseases, including corneal transplantation and the use of advanced technologies to restore vision.

title: Russia could implement projects worth billions of dollars in Sahel countries — Novak
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Moscow could implement projects worth several billion dollars in Sahel countries (Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger) at the initial stage of its partnership with them, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told reporters.
"Russia is interested in it. We have a wide range of projects that could be implemented in Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, the Sahel countries. We will discuss all those investment projects, and financing mechanisms on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Forum. <…> At the initial stage this amounts to several billion dollars. Overall, Africa holds great potential for investment across various countries," he stated on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
That said, only those investment projects that are economically beneficial to both investor and country will be implemented, Novak added.
"The range is quite broad, including geological exploration and our advanced technologies. We are currently actively promoting various projects related to digital platforms in African states. Yandex is already present in many countries. Therefore, there is a broad range of proposals across various sectors that we are ready to discuss with our African partners, and we have already shared certain proposals with them," he explained.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Russia sincerely interested in cooperation with all African countries — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia is sincerely interested in strengthening cooperation with all African countries, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
"Russia is sincerely interested in further comprehensively developing and deepening trade, economic and humanitarian cooperation with all African countries," the Russian leader said.
Putin expressed confidence that the forum and the thematic meetings, roundtables and negotiations held as part of it would help address the challenges facing Russia and Africa. He also emphasized that participants would be able to learn about a sovereign development platform for African states developed in Russia. Its main areas are presented at a dedicated exhibition.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Russia has full tech stack to create large generative models — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia has a full technology stack to create large generative models, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
"I must emphasize that our country possesses the full tech stack to build large generative models. In particular, we have two proprietary large language models," he said.
As the President noted, innovative Russian companies have developed technologies that radically transform the quality of services and created platform-based solutions that allow citizens to seamlessly perform banking transactions and order goods and services.
"Digital solutions in healthcare, which are being rolled out nationwide, make it possible to significantly boost doctors' productivity, improve access to medical care, and diagnose diseases at their earliest stages. Naturally, the list of such achievements is much broader," the Russian leader concluded.
TASS is an official media partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Wontumi is safe in Nsawam prison; he’s not getting preferential treatment – Prisons Service
body: The Ghana Prisons Service has stated that the convicted former Ashanti Regional Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Bernard Antwi-Boasiako, also known as Chairman Wontumi, is well and safe in its custody at the Nsawam Prisons. The assurance follows Wontumi’s claim that some inmates at the Nsawam Prison had attempted to poison him; a claim the Prison authorities say they are investigating. “It’s something that the spokesperson of Wontumi drew the attention of the Prison authorities to. But let me repeat that, it’s not a complaint coming from Wontumi himself directly to the Prison authorities. It’s something that the PRO has said. So, by that, we have also set up investigations to launch investigations into the matter, to find out first and foremost the truth in that matter. And if it has any truth, then we will know the steps to take to avoid that,” Chief Public Relations Officer of the Ghana Prisons Service, CPS Abdul Latif, told Myjoyonline . Read Also: We’re investigating Wontumi’s claim of an attempt to poison him – Prisons Service CPS Latif said there was no cause for alarm as far as Wontumi’s safety was concerned. “We can say that Wontumi is safe and there’s nothing to worry about when it comes to his security in the prison.” The Chief Public Relations Officer also disputed claims that Wontumi was receiving special treatment in prison. “I think the Prisons are governed by rules and regulations, and those rules and regulations don’t segregate or discriminate between prisoner A and prisoner B. You understand? So, I can tell you that Wontumi is being subjected to the same rules and regulations that other prisoners are being subjected to. So, the claim that Wontumi is being given preferential treatment in prison is not true and cannot be true. Also, the prison is already overcrowded. We all know the situation in Nsawam.” “A facility that’s supposed to hold about 851 inmates is now holding 3,000-plus inmates. So, I can tell you there’s no truth in that claim, and it’s something that perhaps is being put out there for attention.” The Chief Public Relations Officer, however, denied claims by Wontumi’s spokesperson that some five prison inmates have been relocated from their cells following the alleged attempted poisoning incident. “No, I cannot confirm that”, CSP Latif said when Myjoyonline specifically asked him about that claim.

title: Ex-President Kufuor backs 5-year presidential term despite NPP opposition
body: Former President John Agyekum Kufuor has backed a proposal to extend the country’s presidential term from four to five years, arguing that the additional year would give governments more time to implement their policies and development projects. In an exclusive interview with JoyNews ’ Evans Mensah, Mr Kufuor said the current four-year term was insufficient for governments to deliver on their programmes while also preparing for another election. He said a five-year term would provide a more practical timeframe for governments to execute their plans, with the fifth year accommodating campaign activities ahead of the next election. “Four years is too short for a young nation that is trying to develop,” he said. According to him, the proposed arrangement would allow a government to devote four years to its development agenda before the final year is dominated by electioneering. “… fourth year is an election year, election year anywhere in the world is a mud year, everybody is going around promising and talking, and then the election comes, and you have to pay something to the voter to put you back, what is the benefit?. Fourth year, if the government is good, the people will know, and then the fifth year is election year, allowing the politicians,” he noted. “I believe in the two terms (a system that allows an individual to become president for two separate terms), but four years for a developing young country like ours, and I have gone through the experience, so I spoke from practical experience, and it was my last state of the nation address that I brought it up, I didn’t say it to lengthen my stay,” he added. Mr Kufuor’s endorsement comes despite opposition to the proposal from the New Patriotic Party (NPP), of which he is a member. “Now I say five years, if for whatever reason my party (NPP) says no, that is their point of view,” he emphasised. The proposal forms part of the ongoing constitutional review process and is yet to receive parliamentary approval and presidential assent before it can become law. The debate over the presidential term has centred on whether extending the period in office would give successive governments sufficient time to implement policies and complete development projects before seeking a renewed mandate from voters. Watch excerpts of the interview aired on JoyFM’s Midday News.

title: Russian forces strike Kharkiv, killing one and injuring three
body:

title: Inside Amazon’s Echo hardware event
body:
Amazon swapped its usual big fall hardware showcase this year for a series of smaller launches throughout October. So far this month, it has announced new Fire TV devices, colorful new Kindles, the Alexa Tablet Pro 12, Ring’s first smart lock, new hardware from AI-wearable startup Bee, and new Blink 4K cameras.
Then this week, it hosted journalists at a small event in New York City’s financial district to showcase its new Echo hardware.
[Image: Panos Panay speaking to journalists at an event in New York City this week https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0026.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Panay next to an “exploded” version of the new Echo Show 16 smart display. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0193.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: He demoed the new Alexa Photo Frame with pictures of his own family https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0118.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Panos Panay, senior vice president of devices, Alexa, and Leo at Amazon, kicked off proceedings by explaining the company’s approach this year. “We have so many products we’re launching that are meaningful,” he said. “However, we get to this point when we do everything at once; not all your children get enough attention.” This longer rollout allows for more focus on each launch. He also teased two more launches still to come — from Ring and some “Echo on the Go” news — before explaining that today’s focus is “the most important focus we have, which is the home.”
He then spent about 45 minutes introducing five new Echo smart speakers and displays — the Echo Show 16, Echo Time, Alexa Photo Frame, Echo Studio with Home Camera, and a new Echo Dot — with each product sitting on plinths in the warehouse-like space.
He demoed several new software features for the Echo Show smart displays that will start on the Show 16 and trickle down to existing Show products, including dedicated home screens, an interactive 3D map view for smart home control, and a meal planning feature.
[Image: The new Echo Studio with Home Camera can act as a video calling device for a Fire TV. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0087.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Panay demoed this feature by calling his parents. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0099.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Panay also revealed that they have “opened up Alexa Plus’ brain a little bit more,” unlocking a new layer of understanding in the generative-AI-powered smart assistant. He pointed out that AI in the home is still relatively new, and while it’s everywhere else, from your computer to your phone, the home has been harder to unlock.
Amazon is looking to change that with Alexa’s “new brain” — an updated version of Alexa Plus with new capabilities including the ability to do “deeper research” alongside its usual use cases, such as controlling lights, setting timers, and playing music.
To manage these deeper conversations, a new “Card” interface on Show devices collects each chat. Cards also appear in the Alexa app and on Alexa.com, so you can continue chats with the assistant wherever you are.
[Image: The Echo Time is a new smart alarm clock that Panay says could replace the need to have your phone by your bed. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Time_JTuohy_0012.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Time_JTuohy_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Alexa Cards are a new feature that allows you to go back to previous conversations with the smart assistant. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Show_16_JTuohy_0024.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Panay demos the new Alexa interface on the Show (relayed to a Fire TV) https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Show_16_JTuohy_0025.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
[Image: Panos Panay and Ring founder Jamie Siminoff show the new map view feature on Echo Show and Fire TVs, which cleverly integrates Ring cameras. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Show_16_JTuohy_0026.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The event continued in a selection of small rooms designed to feel like home spaces, where product engineers and designers demoed the new devices and explained their features.
