( Guardian ) + Software flaws in US voting machines threaten election security. ( Axios ) + A blueprint for using AI to strengthen democracy. ( MIT Technology Review ) 2 Starlink restrictions have driven US allies to rethink their dependence Restrictions in Ukraine have spooked officials across Europe. ( Bloomberg $) + And given European firms a new pitch for their rival services. ( Axios ) + An Israeli spy firm allegedly targeted Starlink users . ( Reuters $) + Stratospheric internet could take off this year. ( MIT Technology Review ) 3 Greenhouse gas levels keep reaching new records worldwide Carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide are all on the up. ( New Scientist $) + Trump is making it easier for fossil fuel companies to leak methane. ( Verge ) + The IPCC is fighting for survival. ( Nature ) + How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster. ( MIT Technology Review ) 4 Monkeys’ brains have revealed new clues about consciousness Their neural activity encodes images that escape their awareness. ( Nature ) + Bees’ feelings are also changing views of consciousness. ( New Scientist $) + Debates over AI consciousness are a trap. ( MIT Technology Review ) 5 Chinese scientists have developed a catalyst to make Mars rocket fuel It converts Martian atmospheric carbon dioxide into liquid methanol. ( SCMP ) 6 Tech billionaires have teamed up against California’s wealth tax Sergey Brin, Eric Schmidt, and others have funded a major campaign. ( NYT $) 7 Delaware plans to let AI agents run entire businesses The proposal could let owners evade responsibility for harm. ( Ars Technica ) + A better web for AI agents could hurt humans. ( MIT Technology Review ) 8 Palmer Luckey has unveiled plans for American-made military laptops Anduril will build rugged PCs in Ohio using Qualcomm chips. ( WSJ $) 9 Gen Z is turning away from the social media it grew up with Young people are fueling a boom in digital detox tools. ( Guardian ) 10 Trump now wants to ban the term “artificial intelligence” He’s demanding we all start using “Super Intelligence.” ( Gizmodo ) Quote of the day “For the next two years, we’re going to be living in a state where, on average, every week there is a critical, internet-wide vulnerability.” —Matthew Prince, Cloudflare’s chief executive, tells the New York Times that AI is currently finding software vulnerabilities quicker than they can be patched. One more thing Inside the controversial tree farms powering Apple’s carbon-neutral goal In 2020, Apple set a goal to become net zero by the end of the decade. To hit that target, the company is offsetting its emissions by planting millions of eucalyptus trees in Brazil. Apple is betting that the strategy will lead to a greener future. But critics warn that the industrial tree farms will do more harm than good. Here’s why the plans have sparked a backlash . —Gregory Barber We can still have nice things A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .) + Ugly shoes have become beautifully mainstream . + Scientists have built a stunning new simulation of the early universe. + Guitarist Kent Nishimura has stripped Thriller back to a mesmerising acoustic performance . + A photographer who snapped punks and mods in 1980 has tracked them down for an emotional reunion 46 years later.

title: UAE oil spill: Sharjah closes all beaches as clean-up effort continues
body: Sharjah on Wednesday announced the temporary closure of all beaches as a precaution against marine pollution from an oil spill off the coast of Umm Al Quwain . The measure comes as authorities across the Northern Emirates take action after a supertanker oil spill in the Arabian Gulf. Specialised teams in Sharjah are acting to protect the emirate’s coastline and keep pollution from reaching its beaches, the media office said. The public and those heading out to sea have been urged to follow official instructions, rely on information from authorities and avoid spreading rumours. A Ministry of Climate Change and Environment team detected marine pollution from the spill and confirmed it on October 22. Umm Al Quwain Municipality intensified efforts to limit pollution and protect marine habitats. The civic body said teams immediately started clean-up, containment, cordoning and remediation work to limit the environmental impact. All beaches and coastal areas in Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed while technical teams assessed the situation and determined the measures needed to protect the public and the marine environment. Sharjah previously closed Al Hamriyah Beach as a precaution to prevent pollution from reaching the coast. Ras Al Khaimah authorities announced on Saturday that all public beaches in the emirate would remain closed until further notice. Authorities have not identified the tanker involved or confirmed the spill's cause. But in recent days, UAE residents have reported a strong, acrid fuel smell in the air . The Environment Ministry said the odour posed no health risk, but advised the public to stay away from any oil that washes ashore. Satellite images from the EU’s Copernicus Earth observation programme showed the oil slick widening between October 19 and last Saturday, with oil spreading towards the Umm Al Quwain coastline, Reuters reported on Monday. While authorities worked to contain the spill and monitor the situation to determine the extent of the pollution, experts told The National that swift containment was vital to limit damage to the environment and the UAE's marine ecosystems. When dealing with oil slicks, preventing pollution from reaching the coast is typically a top priority. If that happens, clean-up becomes harder, and habitats can suffer lasting harm. “Once it hits the shoreline, you have to do a lot of clean-up and remediation,” said Rob Mortimer, chief executive of Dubai-based Fuelre4m, which supplies substances used to disperse oil slicks. He said the initial priority should be “to keep it all together” using floating barriers known as booms, allowing as much as possible to be recovered from the sea surface. Prof Richard Thompson, director of the Marine Institute at the University of Plymouth, said cleaning a wide, sandy beach would typically be a less complex task than dealing with a rocky shoreline. “If you have intertidal habitats with a large range of organisms, it’s going to make it more difficult to clean than if you can capture it [the oil] at the sea surface,” he said. “If it’s among rocks or mangroves or seagrass, it’s going to be very difficult to clean … Ideally what you’re trying to do is catch it before you get the encounters between the creatures and the oil.”

title: Beskrestnov suggests introducing road blackouts due to Russian optical navigation
body:
Blackout measures might be introduced on roads if Russian occupiers massively deploy optical navigation modules on their drones and missiles during nighttime strikes against Ukrainian territory, suggested Serhiy Flash Beskrestnov, Advisor to the President of Ukraine on Defense Technologies.

"If our enemy begins to massively use Susanin optical navigation module on Geran-5 and other UAVs (missiles) at night, we may have to reconsider the issue of blackouts. This particularly concerns the lighting of roads and highway sections," he wrote on Facebook on Wednesday.

As Beskrestnov noted, blackouts were introduced in Ukraine in 2022 "out of fear and misunderstanding." "And now, we will probably have to act consciously," the presidential advisor added.

title: Amazon’s new Echo line is here: the 6 biggest updates
body:
Amazon has just taken the wraps off a bunch of new devices as part of a string of fall announcements. Today’s news focuses largely on new Echo speakers, with a few new smart home gadgets sprinkled in.
Here’s a roundup of all of the updates Amazon revealed on Wednesday.
Echo Show 16 adds a larger display and other upgrades
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Show_16_JTuohy_0046.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Amazon’s new Echo Show 16 has a 16-inch display in an anodized aluminum frame that the company says is nearly 40 percent thinner than its predecessor. There’s a new Nanomatte display option to reduce glare, along with an audio architecture with micro woofers and two tweeters for clearer audio.
The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel camera, which Amazon says offers the “widest field of view” on an Echo Show device so far. It has 20 percent more computing power and an upgraded Omnisense fusion platform, allowing Alexa to turn up the heat when the room is too cold or turn on a light when you enter the room.
The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder today and costs $499.99, with the Nanomatte option priced at $569.99.
The Alexa Photo Frame picks pictures to put on display
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Alexa_Frame_JTuohy_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Amazon is launching a new digital photo frame with a semi-matte, 10-inch touchscreen. The device syncs with Amazon Photos, allowing Alexa Plus to automatically pull up pictures based on who’s in it, when it was taken, and sentiment. You can also choose people you want to feature in your frame, as well as ask the device to show you specific pictures.
The Alexa Photo Frame costs $199.99 with a black frame or $229 for the birch and walnut frames.
[Media: https://www.youtube.com/shorts/ffs_wdJAZD4]
Echo Dot gets a bigger role in the smart home
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Dot_Fall_2026_JTuohy_0001-2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Amazon is rolling out an upgraded Echo Dot with a built-in smart home hub that can control devices around your home without a separate hub. Like the Echo Show 16, the Echo Dot also has the company’s Omnisense fusion platform to detect room temperature and presence. It has Amazon’s custom AZ3 chip as well, along with four microphones, a new full-range driver for 50 percent more bass than the previous generation, and a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender. You can buy the Echo Dot today in black, white, green, and pink for $99.99.
An Echo Studio with a built-in camera
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Fall_2026_OGrove_0087.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Amazon built a camera into the Echo Studio. With this update, you can tap into a livestream of the room while you’re away from home, or ask Alexa questions about something in front of the camera. As an example, Amazon says you can hold up a board game to ask about the rules, or show it a box of cereal to order a different flavor. The Echo Studio with Home Camera will soon connect with compatible Fire TVs, too, giving you the ability to hold video calls on a larger screen.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available in black for $249.99, while its optional stand costs $39.99.
Amazon’s Echo Time smart alarm clock can wake you up in a lighter sleep
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Time_JTuohy_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
Amazon has revealed the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock with a circular, 3.2-inch touchscreen that you can customize with different clockfaces and layouts.
The Echo Time offers an optional smart alarm feature that can wake you up when you’re in a lighter sleep — 10 to 60 minutes before your alarm — rather than at the exact time you want to wake up. It uses Amazon’s Omnisense technology to determine when to wake you up based on temperature and presence. The display also adjusts throughout the day, gradually brightening in the morning before dimming at night.
The Echo Time is available today for $199.99 in black, white, and pink, while a Kids Echo Time starts at $209.99. There’s also an adjustable stand available for $39.99.
Amazon can soon build an interactive map of your smart home
[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Echo_Show_16_JTuohy_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
A new Alexa Home Map feature creates an interactive 3D map of the inside and outside of your home. It displays your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other smart home devices, which you can control directly through the map.
Amazon says you can create a map by entering your home address, scanning each room with a compatible iPhone, and then placing each smart home device. You can access your map in the Ring app, too, where you can view live animations of people and cars outside your home.
Alexa Home Map is rolling out in preview later this year on iOS in the Alexa Home Map, Alexa, and Ring apps. It’s also coming to larger Echo Show devices, the Ember Artline Fire TV, and new Alexa Tablets.

title: Ukraine’s parliament approves 2027 state budget in first reading
body:
Ukraine’s parliament has backed a 2027 budget that puts defense at the center of government spending, as Russia’s full-scale war continues to drive the country’s financial needs.
With security and defense allocations accounting for around two-thirds of planned expenditure and a projected deficit of nearly Hr 1.7 trillion ($37 billion), the budget highlights the challenge of funding the war while maintaining economic stability and meeting social commitments.
A total of 239 MPs voted in favour of the draft, above the 226 votes required. Twenty-five voted against and 26 abstained.
The government’s proposal forecasts revenues of Hr 5.65 trillion ($123 billion) and expenditure of Hr 7.27 trillion ($159 billion). Around Hr 4.89 trillion ($107 billion) is allocated to security and defense, equivalent to 43.8% of projected gross domestic product.
Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi said the budget reflects the realities of Russia’s full-scale war and the country’s key needs for the coming year.
"First and foremost, this means the necessary funding for security and defense, maintaining financial stability and meeting important social commitments to the people," he said.
The draft also assumes economic growth of 1.3% in 2027, annual inflation of 8% and an exchange rate of Hr 47.1 to the U.S. dollar. The proposed minimum monthly wage is Hr 9,546 ($203), while the subsistence minimum is set at Hr 3,559 ($78).
Approving the budget in the first reading allows the government to revise the draft in line with parliament’s recommendations and submit an updated version within two weeks. MPs and parliamentary committees submitted more than 5,000 proposals and amendments.
The government is expected to submit the final draft for a second reading in November.

title: Zelenskyy arrives in the Netherlands
body:
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in the Netherlands, where he will meet with Prime Minister Rob Jetten.

"Arrived with the team in the Netherlands for a meeting with Prime Minister Rob Jetten. We are strengthening our partnership and working for greater protection of Ukraine. We will talk about defense and economic cooperation, strengthening Ukrainian air defense, and new steps to support Ukraine," Zelenskyy wrote on his Telegram channel on Wednesday.

In addition, the President will meet with representatives of Ukrainian and Dutch businesses and will have an audience with King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands.

"I am grateful that the Netherlands supports Ukraine and advocates for the protection of life. We are working together to strengthen our shared security," he added.

title: CBD COP17: Indigenous groups urge UN to halt wildlife carbon, biodiversity credits
body:
Indigenous Peoples and civil society groups have called on the United Nations to halt the monetisation of sacred animals and nature as “natural capital” for carbon and biodiversity markets, warning that the practice could contribute to wildlife extinction.
The groups made the call on Tuesday on the sidelines of the ongoing 17th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
They expressed concern that animals such as buffalo, jaguars, orangutans and whales were being incorporated into offset schemes that, they argued, could allow oil and mining companies to portray themselves as environmentally responsible without addressing the damage caused by their operations.
“Alarmed that buffalo, jaguars, orangutans and even whales are being converted into offsets to greenwash oil and mining companies, Indigenous Peoples and civil society demand that the United Nations immediately stop monetising their sacred animals and nature as ‘natural capital’ for carbon and biodiversity markets because it will contribute to their extinction,” the groups said.
The concerns come amid contentious negotiations over Article 8(j) of the Convention, which calls on parties to respect, preserve and maintain the traditional knowledge, innovations and practices of Indigenous Peoples and local communities relevant to biodiversity conservation.
The provision also recognises the importance of the knowledge and practices of Indigenous Peoples and local communities to the conservation and sustainable use of biodiversity.
The dispute over nature-based financial mechanisms comes as delegates at COP17 continue negotiations on how to implement the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which sets global targets for halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030.
Since negotiations began last week, major questions have remained over which countries and stakeholders should contribute to international biodiversity financing, how much funding should be mobilised and the mechanisms through which the resources should be channelled.
Parties also remain divided over language on reducing or phasing out incentives harmful to biodiversity, including certain agricultural subsidies.
Other unresolved issues include which commercial users of digital sequence information should contribute to the Cali Fund, arrangements for a new permanent body on Indigenous Peoples and local communities under Article 8(j), and how biodiversity action should align with climate commitments and other international obligations.
Against this backdrop, Indigenous representatives and environmental organisations have warned that carbon and biodiversity credit schemes could undermine conservation efforts if they allow companies to offset environmental damage rather than prevent it.
Aimee Robeson, executive director of Cultural Survival, said biodiversity conservation should not depend on assigning monetary values to animals and ecosystem services.
“If we truly care about biodiversity, we should not be tempted to monetise our relatives nor ecosystem services like carbon sequestration, because they have inherent value that cannot be reduced to a dollar amount,” Ms Robeson said.
She described market-based schemes as false solutions that could worsen existing environmental crises, arguing that they could lead to biodiversity loss and the degradation of ecosystems.
“There can be no sacrifice zones, no trade-offs and no offsets if we want life on Mother Earth to survive for generations to come,” she said.
Tom Goldtooth, executive director of the Indigenous Environmental Network, said Indigenous Peoples regard nature as a relative rather than a financial asset.
“For Indigenous Peoples, nature is not an asset class, she is our Mother,” Mr Goldtooth said.
He specifically rejected the use of buffalo in carbon credit schemes, describing the animals as central to Indigenous identity and heritage.
Mr Goldtooth recalled that commercial slaughter reduced the buffalo population from an estimated 60 million to 70 million in 1853 to only a few thousand by the 1880s.
He criticised proposals to use buffalo-related soil carbon storage to generate credits that could allow polluters to continue emitting greenhouse gases.
“Our buffalo, Tanka Oyate, are part of our genesis, not ‘bison bonds’. Carbon trading is an offensive scam that threatens the future of humanity. Bring back the buffalo, not colonialism!” he said.
Wilmer Lucitante of UDAPT, Friends of the Earth-Ecuador and the Indigenous A’i Kofán Nation of the Ecuadorian Amazon also criticised the use of jaguar habitats to generate carbon credits.
He said monetising the animals could provide cover for extractive industries while failing to address the threats posed by oil drilling and mining.
“Turning our sacred jaguars into carbon credits is a false solution to climate change that accelerates their extinction, while greenwashing extractive industries. Instead of monetising wildlife, we need to stop oil drilling and mining in the Amazon,” Mr Lucitante said.
In Indonesia, Andine Fahira Lubis of the North Sumatra regional office of WALHI, also known as Friends of the Earth-Indonesia, raised concerns over biodiversity offsets involving the critically endangered Tapanuli orangutan.
With fewer than 800 individuals remaining, the species is considered one of the world’s rarest great apes.
Ms Lubis alleged that the orangutans were being used in biodiversity offset schemes associated with the Martabe Gold Mine in Sumatra, operated by PT Agincourt Resources, a subsidiary of Jardine Matheson.
The mine is located in the Batang Toru ecosystem, within Indigenous Peoples’ territories.
“Not only is the sheer hypocrisy of orangutan offsets staggering, but as our report clearly shows, offsets cannot redeem the irreplaceable,” she said.
The debate also extends to mining projects in Armenia, the host country of COP17.
Nazeli Vardanyan, director of Armenian Forests, said the controversial Amulsar gold mine planned to use biodiversity offsets in areas associated with the Caucasian leopard and brown bear, species whose habitats could be threatened by the project.
She said civil society groups had campaigned against the mine for 20 years and that its approval shortly before the opening of the biodiversity summit had heightened concerns about the use of offsets to address environmental damage.
The groups warned that placing financial values on wildlife and their habitats could allow companies to claim conservation benefits while continuing activities that threaten biodiversity.
Cassandra Smithies, an offsets expert with the Global Justice Ecology Project, said the United Nations should not support schemes that allow extractive industries to use Indigenous territories and ecosystems as sources of carbon credits.
“Putting a price on nature will not save nature, it will destroy her,” Ms Smithies said.
She argued that Indigenous Peoples’ lands, animals and oceans should not be treated as carbon sinks for industries responsible for greenhouse gas emissions.
“The United Nations must not be complicit with green colonialism,” she said.
While Indigenous representatives criticised the monetisation of nature, other conservation organisations at COP17 called for stronger commitments and more effective implementation of existing biodiversity targets.
Sue Lieberman, vice president of international policy at the Wildlife Conservation Society, said negotiations had made some progress but had yet to produce the level of ambition and concrete action required to meet the 2030 biodiversity targets.
She said delegates needed to strengthen commitments in the global review process and ensure that governments, communities and donors followed through on their pledges.
“The key is ambition. The key is to work with countries, communities, and donors to make sure everything they commit to happens,” Ms Lieberman said.
She added that conservation efforts must translate into practical action on the ground and in aquatic ecosystems, particularly at national and regional levels.
Alfred DeGemmis, the society’s director of international policy, said Armenia and a growing number of governments were supporting civil society calls to identify subsidies that harm nature and redirect the resources towards conservation.
However, he said proposed language that could establish measurable milestones towards the 2030 targets remained unresolved in the negotiating text.
“Ministers are now expected to try to resolve this behind closed doors in the summit’s final days,” Mr DeGemmis said.
The competing positions highlight a broader question confronting delegates at COP17: how to mobilise the financing needed to protect biodiversity while ensuring that financial mechanisms do not undermine conservation, Indigenous rights and the integrity of ecosystems.

title: Senate confirms Eze Anaba, 15 others to NHRC board
body: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Senate has confirmed the appointment of the President of the Nigeria Guild of Editors (NGE) and Editor of Vanguard Newspapers, Eze Anaba, and 15 other nominees to the governing board of the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC). The confirmation followed the consideration of a report presented on Wednesday by the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters, Senator Adeniyi Adegbonmire (SAN, APC, Ondo Central). The Senate also confirmed Dr Salamatu Hussaina Suleiman as chairman of the board and Dr Anthony Ojukwu (SAN) as Executive Secretary. Other confirmed nominees are Mrs Roseline Tasha, Ambassador Adam Yubak Baku, ACG Felix Lawrence, Edmund Chinonye, Chinonye Obiaku (SAN), Oluwakemi Asiwaju Okere-Odo, Professor Adedeji Ogunji, Kingsley Chidozie, Mohammed Adelodu, Maupe Ogun Yusuf, Otunba Francis Meshioye, Patience Patrick Udoh and Hawwa Ibrahim. President Bola Tinubu had in April written to the Senate, seeking the screening and confirmation of the nominees as part of efforts to strengthen the country’s human rights protection framework. The letter was read on the floor of the Senate by the President of the Senate, Senator Godswill Akpabio. In the letter, Tinubu sought the reconstitution of the commission’s governing board in line with statutory provisions. The President said the nominations were made pursuant to Section 2(3) of the National Human Rights Commission (Establishment) Act, 2010, which empowers him to constitute the board, subject to Senate confirmation. The nominees were drawn from diverse professional backgrounds, including the media and legal sectors. The NHRC is mandated to promote and protect human rights, investigate alleged violations and encourage compliance with national and international human rights standards. The reconstitution of the board is expected to strengthen the commission’s institutional capacity to discharge its statutory responsibilities. title: Getting good at AI takes time and practice
body:
Many people think 1 that getting “good at AI” is trivial. Sure, with some early models there were tricks you had to learn, 2 but current models don’t need them. Even if there are different tricks 3 that work on current models, the next generation will render them obsolete, so why bother? Just tell the model what you want it to do.
This take is particularly popular with the anti-AI crowd, who scoff 4 at the idea that AI-reluctant people are being left behind, or that it might be irresponsible to advise other engineers to avoid AI use entirely. According to them, if AI does ever become capable enough to be worth using, they’ll be able to start using it with no learning curve. Is that right?
No. Like most things, getting good at using AI isn’t just about clever tricks. It requires developing long-term skills 5 , which takes time and practice.
One failure mode I’ve seen with people who are new to AI is expecting it to read their mind: for instance, asking it to “solve my issue” without ever saying what the issue is, or asking it about some Slack-related problem without actually connecting your agent to Slack. Agents are flexible and will try their absolute hardest to guess what problem you’re facing and how to solve it, but the guesses will be largely wrong. Skilled AI users will pick up on the fact that the agent is missing key context and backtrack.
Skilled AI users will also reflexively include why they want to achieve their current goal, so that the agent has enough context to make decisions. This is often non-trivial: most of us know what we want to do but have to take a second to think about the broader reasons behind it.
AI capabilities are weird : they are very good at some tasks and very bad at others, and it’s hard to predict which task falls into which category. For instance, I know that I can ask an agent to come up with new architectural ideas for how to structure a service, but that I shouldn’t ask it to come up with new features that the service can offer. Worse still, there is a third category 6 of tasks that AI models are bad at but can be prompted into being good: for instance, writing PR descriptions.
Of course, this changes with new models, but less than you’d think. In general, new models get much better at the tasks the old models were already good at, and a little better at the tasks the old models sucked at. So developing a sense of what AI can and can’t do is a surprisingly durable skill.
Really internalizing what the model can do is trickier than it sounds. For instance, I initially struggled to set up MCP servers for GitHub Copilot before realizing 7 I could just ask Copilot to install its own MCP servers. I now reflexively ask AI agents to do local testing of changes — standing up servers, hammering them with curls, running through variations and edge cases — but it took me a while to realize I could ask for that. I have only just started scheduling a job for 6am my time for an agent to go through messages that have come in from different timezones and do some preliminary investigation. What other capabilities 8 am I leaving on the table?
Reviewing AI-generated code is a substantially different skillset from reviewing human-written code. There are whole categories of bugs — off-by-one errors, for instance — that human-written code is prone to but AI-generated code is not. Similarly, there are mistakes that are rare in human-written code but are very common in AI-generated code. I’ve written about how these tend to be mistakes of misalignment : over-engineering some areas that humans would know aren’t important, or trading off important requirements in order to satisfy made-up ones, and so on.
Reviewers used to human-written code are often dazzled by the superficial fluency of AI-generated code. It’s always exhaustively commented and tested and uses sophisticated language features. If a human programmer produced code like this, you’d be inclined to trust their judgment that a mutex is required in this case — but with an AI programmer, you ought to be very suspicious about new mutexes, which are often introduced to satisfy completely insignificant edge cases.
This skill is kind of silly, but it’s so practically important I have to include it. AI models produce a lot of useful output, but it’s often lost in a thick forest of verbiage. Once you’ve read enough of it, you can sort of just let your eyes flow over the phrasing until you get to the specific claims and evidence. If you’re not used to this, you will waste a lot of time and emotional energy trying to cut through the foliage.
It’s possible that these skills are also temporary. Maybe in the future the agent will just do what we want perfectly, freeing us from the need to actually read its output. Maybe model tooling will get good enough to automatically supply the right context, and the models will get good enough to be able to do everything and make no mistakes. Maybe! But that would require the models to get so good that humans aren’t needed at all.
Don’t be a doomer. Like chess, software’s centaur age — the period where a human-machine pairing can beat individual humans or machines — may last decades . Developing skills for the centaur age is still worthwhile, just like it was worthwhile to learn Angular or React even though it seemed likely that those frameworks would be obsolete 9 in a decade.
I’ve left a lot of skills out: knowing when to abandon or steer an agent session, how to break work up between agents, when to trust AI claims and when to verify, how to minimize costs by using smaller models, and so on. On top of all that, even though it’s not durably useful to stay up to date with the current set of tricks (plus knowing which model is the best for which tasks), it’s still very useful in the short-term. Keeping up without getting lost is a skill in its own right.
It shouldn’t be surprising that working with AI involves actual skills. It’s like working with a really weird person: a savant with mad skills in some areas and huge gaps in others, a prolific but inexpert communicator, a workaholic with no long-term memory, and so on. If you were a manager and had someone like that as your employee, you could likely get a lot of value out of them, but it would take time 10 to figure out how.
If you’re deliberately avoiding using AI, you are likely being left behind by the people who aren’t. If you’re advising other people to avoid AI completely, you are doing them no favors. I do think it’s a mistake to go fully into AI, because LLMs reward expertise , which is best gained by hand. However, if you never practice using AI, you are never going to get good at it.
I see it all the time, most recently here and here (in fairness: that post does think there’s skill involved, just not durable skill).
Like asking it to think step-by-step or saying “you are a skilled software engineer” at the start of the prompt.
In fact, they often believe that AI users are literally damaging their brains. As I’ve said a few times , I think this idea is mistaken.
Incidentally, the reuse of the word “skills” to refer to “job-specific dynamically-loaded prompts” has made this post a nightmare to write.
There’s not even consensus on which tasks are in which category. Many people think LLMs are great at writing prompts for other LLMs, but I think they’re terrible (overly prescriptive, etc). This is obscured by the fact that LLMs can manage swarms much more efficiently than humans, but I think most people agree that having a single subagent is worse than just doing it on the main thread.
Shout out to my brother, who told me to stop being stupid and just ask the robot to do it.
I could list like six other things here (e.g. asking agent sessions to get second opinions from the latest Gemini/OpenAI models). If you want me to write a post on that, email me.
As it turned out, those people were wrong: React was pretty good, and the end of ZIRP meant that the framework treadmill stopped, so React skills continue to be useful today.
In no small part because you can’t trust their own claims about their abilities.
If you liked this post, consider subscribing to email updates about my new posts, or sharing it on Hacker News .
Here's a preview of a related post that shares tags with this one.
Early AI agents were basically enthusiastic idiots. Working with them required you to tell them precisely what you wanted them to do (for instance, “method A exists on class B, please add an equivalent method to classes C through F”). Otherwise they’d go off and do entirely the wrong thing. But as AI agents have improved, this has changed.
When frontier models go off and do the wrong thing today, they don’t do it because they’re confused, they do it because they make an incorrect assumption about your goals or priorities. For instance, when GPT-6-Astra thinks it’s writing code for itself, it will produce minified code . It’s perfectly capable of writing human-readable code — at least in Golang, where I’ve produced several thousand lines of acceptable code with the model — but you have to tell it that humans will be reading the code. Continue reading...

title: Ontario pauses some skills training funding for unemployed people: career colleges
body:
In addition to freezing Ontario Student Assistance Program payments to all private post-secondary institutions, the province has paused at least some funding through Better Jobs Ontario, which helps unemployed people get skills training.
But the government won’t explicitly say so.
There has been no public communication from the government about the status of the program that aims to get people off social assistance and into the workforce, but people who were depending on the program and the institutions that were set to train them are taking note.
Reece Daniel was hoping to begin an HVAC program in London, Ont., on Oct. 19. The government had initially scheduled a meeting for Oct. 13 to give him information about the funding agreement, but a few days before that they cancelled and said applications were under review.
The next intake for the HVAC program is in May 2027.
“This course was something that was going to get me jumped back on my feet,” Daniel said.
“I’m still probably going to be presented with the opportunity to go to school next year, but the significant delays … waiting for so long, putting off work for so long, it’s a little bit disappointing and frustrating.”
Pathways Employment Help Centre had been assisting Daniel in his application, and is seeing other clients experiencing the same delays and uncertainty with their Better Jobs Ontario funding decisions, the CEO said.
“Despite our agency’s repeated efforts to obtain clarification, the absence of a definitive decision prevented Reece and other clients from proceeding with their planned training as scheduled,” Ben Cecil said.
Career Colleges Ontario said the association has heard from member schools that Better Jobs Ontario funding for students at career colleges has been paused, but it has not received any formal communication from the government.
“We are concerned about any disruption to funding for students attending compliant institutions,” it wrote in a statement.
“As with OSAP, we are urging the government to restore access to funding for students attending institutions where there are no identified compliance concerns. We continue to advocate for a targeted approach that allows students to access the support they need while maintaining strong accountability across the sector.”
Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced earlier this month that OSAP payments are paused for students at all private post-secondary institutions, after preliminary audit findings raised serious concerns about financial aid usage at some career colleges.
Trillium College has suspended classes due to the OSAP pause, and wrote in a letter to students that it is a temporary measure due to the uncertainty caused by that freeze and “the separate funding interruption affecting Better Jobs Ontario-funded students at Trillium College.”
When asked recently if Better Jobs Ontario funding was also paused, Quinn’s spokesperson said little.
“Preliminary audit findings point to serious, systemic concerns about OSAP usage at private post-secondary institutions,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote.
“OSAP payments to students at these institutions are paused, and other streams of provincial funding to private institutions past and present are under review.”
Giacoboni refused to list those other streams of funding.
Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said if the government is taking action against another source of funding they should come out and say it.
“It’s happening,” he said. “They know it’s happening and I don’t know why they’re afraid to say it.”
NDP Leader Marit Stiles said the government is ducking accountability.
“This government is terrified of facing the music,” she wrote in a statement.
“They won’t even do the bare minimum of explaining themselves. They’re leaving thousands of people who rely on this program to build a better future and find good jobs without any certainty or support. This is not how you protect Ontario in the face of growing job losses.”

title: Defense Forces of Ukraine strike Tor-2M SAM, radar, and EW station inside Russia over past day – General Staff
body:
Units of the Defense Forces of Ukraine on Tuesday and overnight into Wednesday struck three air defense elements of the Russian occupiers inside Russia, as well as a logistics depot in the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk region, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.

According to its information, in Kursk region of Russia, a "Tor-2M" anti-aircraft missile system was struck in the area of Rzhava, along with a radar station near the settlement of Male Horodkove. In Bryansk region, an electronic warfare station was hit in the area of Semyachki.

title: Rosoboronexport delivers first batch of Su-35 fighter jets to Ethiopian Air Force
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the state tech corporation Rostec) has delivered the first batch of Su-35 multirole fighter jets to the Ethiopian Air Force, the company CEO Alexander Mikheyev said in an interview with the Vesti TV channel.

title: Zelensky tasks PM with assembling Kyiv winter preparations team, says Klitschko 'can't do it alone'
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 27 that he had asked Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi to create a task force to help the Kyiv City Administration complete its resilience plans, adding that the city remains unprepared for winter.
"As president, I can't just sit back and watch the mayor (Vitali Klitschko) try to handle this on his own. Why?" Because it's impossible," Zelensky told journalists.
Koretskyi has been tasked with assembling a managerial team to help Kyiv with winter preparations, which are trailing behind schedule as Russia has resumed its attacks on energy infrastructure.
"It would be wonderful if Kyiv could protect itself or at least prepare for the dangers. But that didn't happen in any of these areas. Now, the only way to get through these challenges is for all the institutions to work together," said the president.
According to the president, Klitschko has been unwilling to accept help from other institutions, as he "gets the impression that someone wants to replace him."
Earlier this month, Zelensky pointed out that Kyiv is less prepared than some front-line regions, hinting at apparent shortcomings by city authorities.
"Look at how well Kharkiv is prepared. It's a different level. They have serious challenges of their own, and glide bombs are still hitting the city," Zelensky praised the hard-hit city some 30 kilometers (about 20 miles) from the Russian border.
"It's really good when every city has a team of managers who can solve problems and keep the situation under control," added the president.
Klitschko has faced criticism for insufficiently preparing the city for another winter. Hundreds of people gathered in front of the city council on Oct. 17 to demand his resignation, improvements to the shelter system, protection of green spaces, and transparency in winter preparations.
Zelensky named people he would like to join Koretskyi's task force, including Vasyl Maliuk , a former head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU); Oleksandr Kubrakov , a former infrastructure minister; and Volodymyr Groysman, Ukraine's former prime minister.
Serhii Sukhomlyn , the head of the State Agency of Restoration and Development of Infrastructure, "declined as soon as he heard it was about Kyiv," the president added.
"No one wants to get involved, because no one will thank them afterward, and others will keep talking about politics."
Zelensky and Klitschko's long-running relationship has been marked by tensions and open conflict, with both officials often trading accusations. While Zelensky has criticized Klitschko for his alleged inaction as Kyiv's mayor, the latter has hit back at the president over centralization of power and withholding of funds.
"He (Klitschko) should be the one calling all these people and meeting with them, not me. In a war like this, it doesn't matter whose bridge it is on paper," said Zelensky.

title: LibreOffice Development/AI Policy
body:
Anubis could not load its JavaScript. The server may be overloaded. Please reload the page to try again.
You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.
Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.
Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.
Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

title: Russia exports 13 mln tons of agricultural products to Africa in nine months — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia’s exports of agricultural products to African countries totaled 13 million metric tons in the first nine months of this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.
"In the nine months of 2026, our country exported 13 million metric tons of agricultural products to Africa. Deliveries to some countries increased many times over. They increased by many times, not by percentage points," Putin stressed.
Meanwhile, Africa possesses its own agricultural potential and can provide itself with food on its own, the Russian leader said.
"I believe that this is one of the key tasks for the continent," Putin said.
"We offer advanced agrarian solutions, seeds, fertilizer, agricultural equipment and transport, store and process food products. We have very good plans with some states of the continent for building hubs both for agricultural products and equipment," the Russian leader said.

title: Kraken Cryptocurrency Exchange Receives Preliminary Approval in Kazakhstan
body: Kraken, a cryptocurrency exchange based in the United States, has received preliminary approval to operate in the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC). The company plans to launch a trading platform in Kazakhstan and hold digital assets on customers’ behalf. However, trading through Kraken’s local subsidiary is not yet available because the company has not obtained its final license. The local subsidiary, Payward Kazakhstan, would give customers access to Kraken’s global trading network, allowing them to buy and sell cryptocurrencies with traders in other countries. The preliminary approval was issued by the Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA). Kraken has not yet announced a launch date or the terms of service for customers in Kazakhstan. The expansion was also discussed at AI & Digital Bridge 2026, an artificial intelligence and technology forum in Astana, where Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov met with the company’s co-chief executive, Dave Ripley. The Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development signed a memorandum of cooperation with the company covering digital finance and blockchain technology. The memorandum itself does not authorize cryptocurrency transactions. Kraken, founded in 2011, allows individual investors and financial institutions to trade cryptocurrencies. The exchange is operated by the international Payward group. The approval comes as Kazakhstan tightens oversight of cryptocurrency trading platforms. On October 20, AFSA announced that the AIFC Court had issued restrictions against six cryptocurrency platforms , including Coinbase and HTX, formerly Huobi Global. The court orders, issued in September, prohibit the companies from offering or advertising digital asset services within the AIFC without the required licenses. They also provide for restrictions on access to the platforms through mobile app stores. AFSA warns that an international exchange’s reputation does not, by itself, mean it is authorized to operate in Kazakhstan . The regulator recommends checking a platform’s license in its official register , as customers using unlicensed platforms may not receive the legal protections available to customers of regulated exchanges. Kraken would join other international exchanges, including Binance and Bybit, which already hold licenses to operate within the AIFC. In September, the government approved a plan to develop the digital asset industry. It also said that the country’s national cryptocurrency reserve had reached $700 million, although the National Bank of Kazakhstan said that only about $200 million of the portfolio had been invested at that stage.

title: Ghana, Canada agree on youth skills development and support for Women’s Development Bank
body: Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has announced a series of agreements between Ghana and Canada aimed at creating job opportunities for young people, supporting the establishment of Ghana’s Women’s Development Bank and promoting sustainable mining practices. The agreements followed what Mr Ablakwa described as positive and meaningful discussions with Canada’s Secretary of State for International Development, Randeep Sarai. In a Facebook post on Wednesday, October 28, the minister said the discussions had produced commitments in areas including skills development, peacekeeping, environmental protection and economic cooperation. “I have held very positive and meaningful discussions with the distinguished Canadian Secretary of State for International Development, Honourable Randeep Sarai,” he wrote. One key outcome is a proposed partnership to improve employment opportunities for young people in Ghana and equip them with skills to compete in the global job market. According to Mr Ablakwa, the two countries will collaborate on labour mobility and skills development, focusing on digital literacy, internationally recognised certification, the energy transition, and technical and vocational education and training (TVET). The partnership is expected to help young people acquire relevant skills and improve their access to employment opportunities both locally and internationally. However, the minister did not provide details on the implementation timeline or the number of young people expected to benefit. Canada has also committed to providing technical support for the establishment of Ghana’s Women’s Development Bank, which is intended to improve women’s access to financial services and support their participation in economic activities. Mr Ablakwa listed the commitment among the outcomes of the discussions, stating that “Canada will offer technical support for the establishment of Ghana’s Women’s Development Bank”. Ghana and Canada have further agreed to strengthen their collaboration with the Kofi Annan International Peacekeeping Training Centre (KAIPTC). Mr Ablakwa said the partnership would help the Ghanaian institution expand its contribution to regional stability and counterterrorism efforts. Environmental protection, land reclamation and sustainable mining were also discussed, with the two countries agreeing to cooperate on modern approaches to environmental protection and the rehabilitation of degraded land while promoting legal and sustainable mining practices. Another outcome is an agreement to coordinate a broader Africa-Canada dialogue next year, focusing on the continent’s economic transformation. The proposed discussions will cover trade, industrialisation, railway development and value addition. Mr Ablakwa said Africa’s development ambitions should be driven by stronger economic activity and productive investment rather than continued dependence on aid. He described the approach as one that prioritises “trade, industrialisation, railway development, value addition and not aid”. The minister also praised Mr Sarai for his relationship with Ghana, citing the Canadian official’s decision to make the country his first destination after his appointment last year. “The Honourable Randeep Sarai is a great friend of Ghana, as demonstrated by his conscious decision to make Ghana the first country he visited last year immediately after his appointment,” Mr Ablakwa said. “We reaffirm our buoyant Ghana Canada relations,” he added.

title: Geospatial intelligence contract goes to CGI
body: CGI has won a contract from the Ministry of Defence’s National Armaments Director Group to provide technical and project support for PICASSO, the programme that develops and sustains Britain’s national geospatial intelligence capabilities, according to the company. The PICASSO Client-Side Support contract was awarded competitively through the department’s Digital and IT Professional Services framework, and covers client-side technical leadership and specialist project support across several sites. The work takes in geospatial intelligence, imagery, meteorological and live operational services. Neil Timms, senior vice president for space, defence and intelligence in the United Kingdom and Australia at CGI, said: “PICASSO is a strategically important programme for UK Defence, and we are pleased to continue supporting the Ministry of Defence as it evolves these critical geospatial intelligence capabilities. Drawing on well over a decade of experience supporting the programme, together with the expertise of our partner organisations, we will provide the client-side technical leadership and specialist support needed to help deliver its next phase of evolution.” The company said the contract introduces a flexible delivery model letting the department draw on specialist expertise as requirements change, and listed outcomes including maintaining operational continuity across critical services and supporting the adoption of modern approaches to data, cyber security, artificial intelligence, architecture, agile delivery and service management. CGI will deliver the work alongside QinetiQ, AtkinsRéalis, i3Works, Warleggan Consulting and 5Eyes Consulting. It has supported PICASSO since 2011 and also works on the Borealis and Nostromo programmes for the department. Geospatial intelligence covers the collection and analysis of imagery and mapping data to describe and assess physical features and activity on the ground, and underpins targeting, planning and operational awareness across the services. The post Geospatial intelligence contract goes to CGI first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Military childcare staffing shortages leave families struggling to find care
body: Low wages, lengthy hiring processes and limited availability are leaving some military parents unable to work and making it difficult for childcare centers to recruit and retain staff. For Jessica Maloney, the inability to find childcare has meant giving up the chance to work while raising three children under 6. The Army spouse at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, said her family depends on her income, but without reliable childcare, she cannot earn one. Her family has turned to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, to help put food on the table. Even with that assistance, she said, it is not enough. “Our family is a two-income household and with childcare not being regularly available, I am not able to work,” Maloney said. “We’ve been feeding our kids on SNAP, and I still struggle to have enough of what they need.” Without dependable childcare, Maloney said, finding a way back into the workforce remains out of reach. “It shouldn’t be this hard to go to work,” she said. The Department of Defense operates the nation’s largest employer-sponsored childcare program. Yet staffing shortages and difficulties recruiting and retaining workers have contributed to long waitlists and delays in finding care. In June, the Government Accountability Office reported that the military services employed about 19,000 childcare workers paid with nonappropriated funds who cared for nearly 172,000 children of service members and Defense Department civilian employees in fiscal 2024. The department’s list of unmet childcare needs included nearly 9,000 children in 2025, according to the GAO. More than one-third of those needs were concentrated in five areas: Hawaii; the National Capital Region; Norfolk, Virginia; San Antonio, Texas; and San Diego, California. Low pay and lengthy hiring processes make staffing harder At Camp Pendleton, California, Karen Cunningham, a youth services coordinator, said staffing and demand became overwhelming at the program where she worked last year. “We aren’t supposed to have more than 20 children, but we had nearly twice that many,” Cunningham told Military Times. “We were over capacity, but understaffed and that caused all of us who worked there to pay a very heavy price, mentally, physically and emotionally.” Cunningham said eventually it became too much for her, and she had to take a step back. In a 2024 report based on visits to eight installations, the GAO identified lengthy onboarding processes and stressful work environments among the challenges facing military childcare programs. Officials at the installations reported that onboarding could take one to six months. Background checks and other screening requirements can add time before applicants are cleared to work, making it harder for programs to fill vacancies. Pay presents another obstacle. During a meeting of the President’s Military Spouse Commission, Andrea Ruiz, spouse of the Sergeant Major of the Marine Corps Carlos A. Ruiz, compared entry-level childcare wages at installations in Southern California. Ruiz said workers at Miramar and Camp Pendleton earned about $18 to $19 an hour, while workers at Navy facilities at Point Loma earned $21 an hour. Kimberly Weimer, spouse of the Sergeant Major of the Army Michael R. Weimer, described locality pay differentials of roughly $3 to $5 an hour at some high-cost installations. The commission discussion focused on how military childcare programs compete with employers outside the gates for employees. Weimer also noted that childcare providers can gain certifications and training through their jobs, making them eligible for other positions that may offer higher pay. Tameeka Pethel, who worked as a childcare provider at Joint Base San Antonio, said she enjoyed working with the children and her colleagues, but said the wages were not enough to make the job financially sustainable. “If I could afford to have kept that job, I would have never left,” Pethel said. “It’s pretty sad that I earn more money at Taco Bell than I could’ve as a childcare provider.” In April, the Army launched a new pay model intended to bring staffing at its child development centers above 90%, Stars and Stripes reported. The initiative included higher pay for direct-care workers and childcare discounts for employees’ own children. At the time, the Army said only 22 of its 68 installations had staffing levels at or above 90%, while nearly 3,000 children were waiting for space in Army centers. The GAO has also documented the use of recruitment bonuses, retention incentives, childcare discounts and professional development to attract and retain workers. When military childcare doesn’t fit the mission For military families, finding a provider is only part of the challenge. Care must also fit their schedules and remain available through moves and changes in duty requirements. Tiffany Orner, an Air Force veteran and military spouse who serves on the board of Operation Childcare Project, told Military Times that she regularly sees requests for childcare help in spouse groups connected to installations along the coast. “The posts never change,” Orner said. “I need a sitter for a shift that starts at 0500. We PCS in three weeks, who has an opening. The CDC hours changed and I have no Plan B.” For dual-military couples, Orner said, the problem can be especially difficult when both parents have to report for duty and their planned childcare falls through. “Childcare is mission-critical. End of story,” she said. When military-run care is unavailable, the Defense Department’s Military Child Care in Your Neighborhood program provides fee assistance for eligible families using approved civilian providers. But the GAO has found that providers can face accreditation or state quality-rating requirements, administrative burdens and unclear communication about eligibility. From fiscal 2019 through fiscal 2024, all four military services increased the number of community-based providers and children participating in fee assistance, according to the GAO. That growth does not establish whether a family can find an available provider nearby, afford the remaining cost or secure care that accommodates nontraditional work hours. The most recent meeting of the President’s Military Spouse Commission described a five-location pilot, operating to allow eligible military families to use fee assistance for certain faith-based childcare providers that are legally exempt from state licensing requirements. The locations being piloted are Arlington, Norfolk and Virginia Beach, Virginia; Naval Base Kitsap, Washington; and Naval Base Point Loma, California. The commission said it was looking into whether Coast Guard families could also participate. However, Stars and Stripes reported Oct. 21 that neither the Pentagon nor the White House had independently confirmed that the pilot was operational. The pilot provides a pathway for certain legally license-exempt providers to participate under applicable requirements. Commission members also discussed extending fee assistance to other license-exempt providers, including certain family, friend and neighbor care arrangements, public and private school programs, part-day and short-duration programs, and government or institutional sites. Members also discussed ways to improve recruitment and retention, including more consistent pay across installations, faster hiring and screening and benefits that help workers afford childcare for their own children. Orner said the initiatives need to reach families who are struggling to find care, rather than remain limited to pilots or best practices at selected installations. “The spouse in survival mode deserves to hear that plainly,” she said. She urged the commission to “measure who gets hired and who stays, not who pledged, and get the help to the spouse before the pilot ends.” The cost of care that never comes For Maloney, the question is not whether she wants to work, but whether she can find the care that would make it possible. Until that changes, her family will continue relying on food assistance to help make ends meet. Her experience underscores what staffing targets and program expansions cannot measure on their own: whether a parent can secure dependable care, take a job and count on that arrangement to last. For families facing the same barriers, the consequences reach beyond a childcare waitlist. They shape household finances, employment decisions and the ability to plan for what comes next. The military depends on service members being ready to meet the demands of their jobs. For parents, that readiness can also depend on knowing their children are cared for when duty calls. When reliable childcare remains out of reach, families are left to absorb the consequences. “Military kids have to go through enough hard things,” Maloney said. “Going to bed hungry should not be one of them.”
