The most recent meeting of the President’s Military Spouse Commission described a five-location pilot, operating to allow eligible military families to use fee assistance for certain faith-based childcare providers that are legally exempt from state licensing requirements. The locations being piloted are Arlington, Norfolk and Virginia Beach, Virginia; Naval Base Kitsap, Washington; and Naval Base Point Loma, California. The commission said it was looking into whether Coast Guard families could also participate. However, Stars and Stripes reported Oct. 21 that neither the Pentagon nor the White House had independently confirmed that the pilot was operational. The pilot provides a pathway for certain legally license-exempt providers to participate under applicable requirements. Commission members also discussed extending fee assistance to other license-exempt providers, including certain family, friend and neighbor care arrangements, public and private school programs, part-day and short-duration programs, and government or institutional sites. Members also discussed ways to improve recruitment and retention, including more consistent pay across installations, faster hiring and screening and benefits that help workers afford childcare for their own children. Orner said the initiatives need to reach families who are struggling to find care, rather than remain limited to pilots or best practices at selected installations. “The spouse in survival mode deserves to hear that plainly,” she said. She urged the commission to “measure who gets hired and who stays, not who pledged, and get the help to the spouse before the pilot ends.” The cost of care that never comes For Maloney, the question is not whether she wants to work, but whether she can find the care that would make it possible. Until that changes, her family will continue relying on food assistance to help make ends meet. Her experience underscores what staffing targets and program expansions cannot measure on their own: whether a parent can secure dependable care, take a job and count on that arrangement to last. For families facing the same barriers, the consequences reach beyond a childcare waitlist. They shape household finances, employment decisions and the ability to plan for what comes next. The military depends on service members being ready to meet the demands of their jobs. For parents, that readiness can also depend on knowing their children are cared for when duty calls. When reliable childcare remains out of reach, families are left to absorb the consequences. “Military kids have to go through enough hard things,” Maloney said. “Going to bed hungry should not be one of them.”

title: I don't trust Lean code from AI
body:
So, I wrote a post about why I am not nearly impressed with OpenAI's preprint regarding the Partition Principle. But that is not nearly the whole story. Let me tell you one more thing.
I saw a few people who commented on my previous posts through various social posts and reposts. Many of them were understanding of the plight of mathematicians. Some were trying to make the following point: I claimed that I did not (nor I intend to) read the Lean proof generated by ChatGPT. Some people felt like this is a deal breaker, like this is a reason to disregard everything else I had to offer, because I will not accept this bit of code.
So, let me explain why this is the case. Because I think that if you are not a pure mathematician, you might miss some subtle point in the discource here.
Firstly, Lean is not as sound as you'd think it is, and long code is just codename for trouble. It is known that Lean has soundness issues in its kernel. There are bugs that allow you to peove, in Lean, that \(0=1\). Clearly, this is a false statement. But from a false statement (under the theory that runs Lean) we can prove anything else. When humans write code, we have both accountability and ovresight. Humans produce code at a certain speed, and not any faster than that, so it is not too hard to follow and verify that the code does what it needs to do. I do not have the ability to write a whole new kernel, nor I'd want to do that. I do not think that soundness issues are necessarily problematic when human-generated content is at play, because humans are slow. We produce proofs at a slow rate, which allows us to self-verify.
On the other hand, when ChatGPT produces, in the span of two weeks, several thousands, hundreds of thousands, or even millions, of lines of code... Well, who's going to go through it all to verify that this is all legit? Now we have two problems. The first, which is more famously common, is that the formalisation of a statement is not what the statement actually mean. This is an issue, because if I try to prove that every polynomial over the complex numbers has a root, and the notion of polynomial is not formalised correclty, then the Lean code that I ended up with might not prove what I actually want it to prove. So, if I was writing the code by myself, presumably someone would follow me around and check,as I go along, that I have formalised all the objects correctly, etc. But with ChatGPT, producing a million lines of code, this is not feasible.
The other problem goes much much deeper. AI agents, to the best of my understanding, are very much goal oriented beings. I am sure that you've heard of that agent in Australia that was told to book a gym class, and decided to hack the gym to delete existing bookings of other people and circumvent the five classes a week limitation, just so it can book more classes for its user. The point is that AI is very very good in figuring out exploits and using them. When anyone generates, out of the blue, millions of line of code, we need to be suspicious of this endeavour. Even more so when the entity generating the code is coming from a family of entities that is renowned of finding exploits, bugs, and hacks.
In short, if ChatGPT produced three million lines of code in Lean, I am all but ready to believe that these contain an exploit to obtain the correct result. Even if in the case of the Partition Principle I am willing to accept that the formalisation of the statement itself is easy enough to do right. This trust does not extend to anything beyond that.
Which is what most people outside of mathematics are missing: Lean is not infallible (neither is mathematics, of course). Indeed, Lean is full of fallible problems. And an AI that is bound to find bugs and exploit them (rather than disclose them), is extremely problematic as a certificate. So, that is why I did not intend on reading the Lean code, nor I planned (or plan) to run and test it.
To add to that, it might be worth pointing out that there is another reason (which I hinted at before) for not engaging with OpenAI at this point: mathematical research is done in a very specific way (at least in pure maths), and it is not a particularly fast pace kind of way. OpenAI (and other AI companies) are disruptors. They disrupt the way people do things, and they are trying to insert themselves as "the new way of doing it". Sometimes it works, like how we all ask AI bots for recommendations instead of going on a search engine and trying to figure out how to consolidate a bunch of websites into a small and coherent bit of knowledge.
And this is where the problem lies. It may or may not be the case that mathematical research needs to be disrupted (I don't think so, but I can understand why some people might think otherwise). But the way OpenAI is trying to disrupt mathematical research is entirely based on "everyone outside of maths already think that ChatGPT is an all knowing God, now let us make the maths people bend the knee!". It is evident in the way they release hundreds of "preprints" whose quality is subpar even to some cranks' manuscripts. But, the public perception is that ChatGPT is a god, so many people expect that the mathematical community is going to engage with these "proofs" because they come from ChatGPT. But, as I said before, if OpenAI really wanted to contribute to the progress of mathematics, they would contact experts on each problem, and try to get some feedback and collaboration before going public.
And so, since it is in the interest of OpenAI to write bad proofs, to not vet the Lean code properly, and to lie to us, I am not trusting their produced code. And there are plenty of examples recently to support my doubts. It is just not quite there yet. Maybe in the future, maybe even soon, this won't be a problem anymore. I am excited to see that kind of future, and I am excited to see what kind of use we can make of these AI tools. But I want us to get there together, as a community, not as adversaries. Not while we hate OpenAI, or we are split in how we view and use AI in our research.
So, to all the tech companies. Work with us, not against us. Progress is done through collaboration, not competition.
P.S. I also saw people complain that mathematicians insist that OpenAI produce output that we can read. Well, what is mathematics, as a whole? Is it the production of more and more logically valid statements, or is it the study of understanding and human comprehension of mathematics? I have seen many attempts to define "mathematics", but ultimately the only one that actually fits is "mathematics is a social activity that mathematicians do together". In that sense, if OpenAI claims to prove things, but the claims are unreadable and subpar, then these are not mathematical claims, as they do not participate in our common discourse. There are a dozen cranks who post "preprints that refute Cantor" every single day, let alone the Reimann Hypothesis. There is a reason we do not pay much attention to those. And no, it is not because of arrogance. I am sure that OpenAI does not want to be classified with these people, and for that, we—the mathematical community—need them to play with us, not against us, not disrupt our work. With us. C'mon Sam Altman, if you do this well, you might get a bottle of whisky.

title: Vice President Erlan Karin: Strategic Decisions Will Shape Country’s Future
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s annual presidential address outlines strategic priorities that balance national interests with public well-being, Vice President Erlan Karin said, commenting on President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s address to the people of Kazakhstan. Vice President Erlan Karin. Photo credit: Akorda “History is shaped not by time itself, but by strategic decisions made at the right moment. Today’s presidential address is proof of this. It takes into account both the interests of the state and concern for the well-being of the people,” Karin wrote on his Instagram. He emphasized the strategic importance of Tokayev’s priorities, which aim to advance the country’s development. In his address, Tokayev identified key areas for the country’s further development , with particular attention to strengthening sovereignty and domestic stability, developing the economy , and advancing science and modern technologies. He also called for large-scale modernization of Kazakhstan’s infrastructure, allocating 6.5 trillion tenge (US$14.3 billion) to the initiative by the end of 2029. Economic development was another major focus of the address. Tokayev called for a unified investment management system and instructed the government to develop a dedicated plan to support medium-sized businesses. President Tokayev also outlined Kazakhstan’s strategic objectives for its next stage of development, emphasizing the responsibility to pass on a fundamentally renewed country to future generations. The post Vice President Erlan Karin: Strategic Decisions Will Shape Country’s Future appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Ocean’s ability to absorb carbon is weakening as climate change intensifies, UN warns
body:
The ocean absorbs around 30 per cent of human-caused carbon dioxide ( CO₂) emissions and 90 per cent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. But climate change has already reduced its capacity to absorb carbon by approximately six per cent, a new UN report warns ahead of the COP31 climate conference in November .
The report was a collaboration between the UN’s environment agency, UNEP, and the UN climate secretariat, UNFCCC, which co-organises COP31.
“ For a long time the ocean has been doing us an enormous climate service, but that service is under increasing pressure ,” Sara Traerup, lead author of the report, told UN News .
Rising temperatures and changes in ocean chemistry, circulation and ecosystems are weakening its ability to absorb and store carbon, leaving more CO₂ in the atmosphere.
And this process “ can definitely accelerate ” in the foreseeable future, Ms. Traerup warned.
A major challenge is the lack of reliable ocean monitoring data, particularly in the Southern and Indian Oceans, the Arctic and many coastal regions.
The report therefore calls for stronger “ocean carbon intelligence” – using science, technology, data and local knowledge to better understand and manage ocean carbon systems.
“As of now, we don’t have full information about the ocean, and what we don’t know, we cannot manage and protect,” Ms. Traerup explained.
UNEP looked at three main types of ocean climate technologies, each offering different opportunities and risks.
The first is ocean monitoring : observation systems, sensors, data systems and modelling. Ms. Traerup called these the most mature technologies and the most immediately needed.
The second is blue carbon ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrasses and salt marshes. They already sequester around 407 million tonnes of CO₂ a year, and restoring them could add significantly more. They also protect coastlines, support biodiversity and sustain livelihoods.
The third is marine carbon dioxide removal , which aims to extract CO₂ from the atmosphere and store it over the long term. While potentially promising, these approaches remain highly uncertain and require further research, monitoring and regulation.
“We shouldn’t treat ocean-based technologies as a shortcut,” Ms. Traerup cautioned, as they must complement, not replace, emissions reductions and ecosystem protection .
Small Island Developing States (SIDS) contribute less than one per cent of global emissions, yet are “on the front line of ocean and climate impacts ,” Ms. Traerup noted.
The report called for greater access to finance, technology transfer and capacity-building to enable these countries to develop ocean solutions tailored to their needs. Some islands are already showing how this can work.
In 2015, Seychelles , for instance, benefited from a debt-for-nature swap, which involved restructuring part of its foreign debt in exchange for marine conservation commitments. This enabled the country to set up a trust fund to finance marine conservation, climate resilience and the sustainable blue economy.
In the Pacific, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Solomon Islands and Vanuatu received support to map seagrass meadows and mangrove forests, and measure how much carbon they store. As a result, more than 100 people were trained in blue carbon assessment, giving governments data to feed into their national climate plans.
The report also stressed the importance of integrating local and Indigenous knowledge.
“Communities have been coping with climate change for many, many years,” Ms. Traerup said, pointing to their experience in protecting coastlines through natural habitats and in managing fisheries and coastal resources sustainably.
Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Tuesday.

title: Record heat-related deaths in 2023, WHO-partnered report finds
body:
Climate inaction continues to harm and kill people in all countries with a record 710,000 estimated deaths globally from heat in 2023, a UN-partnered report warned on Wednesday. For the first time, more than seven in 10 fatalities were attributable to human-caused climate change.
The latest Lancet Countdown report in association with the World Health Organization ( WHO ), finds that health harms from climate change are accelerating, with expanded fossil fuel extraction holding back progress and threatening “catastrophic” health risks .
“Heat-related deaths, drought and other climate-related risks (are) increasing faster than a decade ago, even as clean energy investments and climate action begin to deliver health benefits,” the report’s authors state.
Other findings indicate that the global area affected by extreme drought “has grown more than 700 per cent faster than it did in 2006–2015”, with droughts affecting 51.8 per cent of land on earth for at least one month in 2025.
The report also examines the link between rising temperatures and rainfall patterns to dengue transmission, finding that conditions suitable for dengue transmission by Aedes albopictus mosquitoes increased by 24 per cent between 1981-90 and 2016-25, while suitability for transmission by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes rose by seven per cent.
And in a warning that too little is being done to mitigate climate change, the report also notes that the world’s 100 largest oil and gas companies plan to produce “150 per cent more fossil fuels by 2040 than is compatible with keeping warming to 1.5°C [above pre-Industrial Revolution temperature averages], up from 138 per cent a year earlier”.
These and other worrying findings highlight the urgent need to formally recognize climate change as a global health emergency, the authors maintain, in support of stronger, health-centred climate action ahead of the UN COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye.
Priorities include accelerating reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, increasing support for adaptation and expanding investments that strengthen health system resilience.
WHO responds to climate-related health risks through surveillance, early warning systems, health adaptation planning, technical guidance and emergency response teams .
The agency is also closely following the expected health impacts of the ongoing El Niño event through a global incident management team, mobilizing expertise, health intelligence and support to countries most at risk.
WHO also oversees the work of ATACH (the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health), the only network of health ministries and partners working together to develop climate-resilient, low-carbon and sustainable health systems at the country level.
The report – produced by researchers and institutions from all over the world and led by University College London – analyses global trends across 54 indicators linking climate change and health.
It shows that heat-related deaths increased by nearly 36 per cent in the years following the 2015 Paris Agreement on climate change compared with the previous decade. The report also highlights worsening drought conditions, increasing exposure to water-related extremes and substantial economic losses linked to heat exposure.
In more positive developments, important progress has been made in resisting the health impacts of climate change, the report notes, pointing to a record $2.1 trillion global investment in clean energy last year .
“ Many countries that have lowered fossil fuel-related air pollution are estimated to be protecting thousands of people from premature deaths each year,” it adds.
The report also notes advances in climate-resilient health systems, including increased adoption of national health adaptation plans and climate-based early warning systems.
Around one in four countries now have a national plan for adapting health services to climate change , up from just 14 WHO Member States in 2015; 47 have separately completed a vulnerability assessment to underpin plans.
The development follows a warning by the UN World Meteorological Organization (WMO) that levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases accumulating in the atmosphere reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term temperature increase for the planet.
The ocean absorbs around 30 per cent of human-caused carbon dioxide ( CO₂) emissions and 90 per cent of excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases. But climate change has already reduced its capacity to absorb carbon by approximately six per cent, a new UN report warns ahead of the COP31 climate conference in November .
Levels of carbon dioxide (CO2) and other major greenhouse gases in the atmosphere caused by burning fossil fuels reached record highs in 2025, locking in more long-term global warming, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said on Tuesday.

Amazon is giving its premium smart speaker a camera. The new Echo Studio with Home Camera, announced today as part of Amazon’s big blast of announcements, has a built-in camera for monitoring a room while you’re away, showing things to Alexa, and, soon, to use with video calls on Fire TV devices. It’s an iteration on the revised Echo Studio announced last year, which had a brand-new design.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera also offers some audio updates. Amazon says a new feature called “Advanced Room Adaptation” will continuously tune sound to the space that the speaker is in. There’s also an “Adaptive Volume” feature that raises or lowers volume depending on where you are in a room so that “your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”
The new Echo Studio with Home Camera will cost $249.99 and come in graphite. Amazon will still sell the standard Echo Studio at its $219.99 price .
Amazon is also updating the Echo Dot, and the new version is powered by Amazon’s custom-designed AZ3 chip and has a fourth microphone to improve your conversations with Alexa. The Dot also now has a built-in smart home hub, supporting Zigbee, Matter, and Thread, and has a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender that Amazon says can add up to 1,000 square feet of coverage.
The updated Echo Dot is available starting today for $99.99 in graphite , glacier white , agave green , and coral pink .

Kroger’s $1.65 billion proposed acquisition of Giant Eagle might not only consolidate the grocery market, but also a vast surveillance network that includes Flock cameras, a new report warns.
Beyond standard concerns that a merger could decrease competition and increase prices, the American Economic Liberties Project (AELP), which advocates for competition policy reforms, says that the consolidation could also expand customer surveillance by a single company. It comes at a time where Americans are particularly on-edge about surveillance technologies like Flock cameras and surveillance pricing , heading into a midterm election largely defined by affordability issues.
A combined Kroger-Giant Eagle — which would add Giant Eagle’s 200-plus stores to Kroger’s 2,700 — could pose risks in two ways, according to AELP. The first is by enabling Kroger to acquire data on customers across a broader geographic area, which it can use to serve customers personalized pricing based on inferences about their backgrounds and shopping behaviors. It could also use that data to fuel its retail media arm , which repackages consumer insights for other brands. The second is by expanding or combining an existing physical surveillance network consisting of technologies like Flock cameras and Cooler Screens , a company that previously touted its ability to scan shoppers’ faces but backed off that messaging after public backlash. Kroger has shared data from its Flock cameras with police in Columbus, Ohio, The Columbus Dispatch reported in August. Kroger has denied using in-store facial recognition to serve customers’ prices, but has acknowledged in its privacy policy that it uses facial recognition at some stores for security purposes. Kroger and Giant Eagle did not immediately respond to The Verge ’s requests for comment.
“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled”
Similar privacy concerns were raised during Kroger’s earlier attempted merger with Albertsons, a much larger deal that courts blocked in late 2024 after the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general challenged it. AELP argues that the proposed merger with Giant Eagle is also deserving of scrutiny, because of the way it could significantly reduce options in places like Columbus, Ohio , and also because of Kroger’s buying patterns and incentives. They urge the FTC and Ohio attorney general to seek to block the merger, though experts have predicted they might not , both because of the relatively small size of the deal compared to Albertsons, and the Trump administration’s more open approach to settlement deals than the prior administration.“Buying bleach or yogurt now comes with the prospect of being scanned, tracked, and profiled,” the report says. “With every store Kroger buys, the data and surveillance apparatus grows.”

title: Amazon’s first digital picture frame lets you add voice notes to photos
body:
Amazon’s screen-equipped smart speakers have long been able to display your family’s photos, but its new Alexa Photo Frame is purpose-built for that task. It’s designed to compete with other digital picture frames from companies like Aura, and Amazon’s incorporates a smart speaker with access to Alexa Plus’ capabilities through voice commands. However, unlike the Echo Show and Amazon’s other smart home hubs, the Alexa Photo Frame only ever displays your photos, and you’ll never be served an ad.
The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today; it’s $199.99 for a black frame or $229 if you want to upgrade to a frame made from birch or walnut wood. It pulls images from Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members, but otherwise the frame doesn’t require a subscription. The Amazon Photos app can back up photos from your Android or Apple devices and pull images from iCloud Photo, but importing from Google Photos isn’t supported yet.
[Image: A black frame is included with the $200 option, but for $229 you can opt for a birch or walnut wood frame. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/268832_Amazon_Alexa_Frame_JTuohy_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
The frame has a 10-inch touchscreen display with a “semi-matte, anti-glare finish” to simulate the look of physical prints. A light sensor adjusts the display’s brightness throughout the day, and it sits on a detachable stand.
[Image: The frame includes volume controls tucked behind one edge and a microphone mute button. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/alexa3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
You can select specific people or albums through Amazon Photos, or let Alexa Plus curate what’s displayed. Alexa selects the best images based on lighting, when people are smiling, and the current season, so you may get more Halloween costumes this time of year, while intelligently skipping images like receipts or screenshots. Alexa can also display similar photos with unique connections as side-by-side pairs, such as pics of a child 10 years apart with a similar pose. If there’s something specific you want to see, like last summer’s beach trip, you can just ask Alexa to dig those up.
[Image: You can use the Amazon Photos app to record voice notes connected to specific photos, and eventually record them using the frame itself. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/alexaframe2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
You can use the Amazon Photos app to add voice notes to images that will play through the frame. An option to record them on the frame itself is coming later. If you plan to buy the Alexa Photo Frame as a gift and purchase it through Amazon, you can preload photos or albums with voice notes that play once the recipient sets it up.

title: Which Local LMs are Best For Which Tasks
body:
A local language model is one whose actual weights, the enormous file of learned numbers that constitutes the trained model, you download and run entirely on your own hardware.
Someone spends an evening reading "best local LLM" roundups, settles on whichever name keeps showing up at the top, downloads it, and points it at the thing they actually needed help with that week, say, cleaning up a Python script. But it's mediocre at that. Not broken, just unimpressive, in the specific way a generalist is unimpressive at a specialist's job. The model wasn't bad. It was never a coding model to begin with, and nothing in the roundup that recommended it ever said so.
That mismatch is the entire reason this guide exists. "Best" was never a single ranking, and treating it like one is how a genuinely capable model ends up feeling disappointing for no fault of its own. This article works the other way around: what a local language model actually is, why running one on your own hardware is worth doing at all, and then, model by model, with real cited proof rather than vibes, exactly what each one is good at. It closes with one table built specifically to answer the only question that actually matters: for the task in front of you right now, which model should you reach for?
A language model is, at its core, a system trained to predict text: given everything that came before it in a conversation or a document, what's the most plausible next piece of text? That simple mechanism, applied at enormous scale, is what lets a model answer questions, write code, summarize a document, or hold a conversation. Every well-known AI chat product, whether it's ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini, is built on top of a language model doing exactly this.
" Local " describes something about how you access that model, not what it is. A local language model is one whose actual weights, the enormous file of learned numbers that constitutes the trained model, you download and run entirely on your own hardware. No API call leaves your machine. No account is required to use it. No company's server ever sees your prompt. That's a genuinely different relationship to the technology than using a hosted model through a website or an API key, where every request travels to someone else's infrastructure and the model itself is something you can query but never actually possess.
Ollama , the tool that's become the de facto standard for running these models locally, hosts a public library of ready-to-pull GGUF builds for every model covered in this article, and the real download numbers behind some of these models, covered in detail later in this piece, run into the tens of millions.
This is the idea the rest of the article is built around, so it's worth making explicit. A single aggregate benchmark score, or a raw parameter count, tells you surprisingly little about whether a specific model will actually serve you well on a specific task. A model can score well on general knowledge and still write mediocre code. A small, efficient model can lead its entire weight class on tool calling while trailing badly on creative writing. Treating any one number as "the" ranking is how people end up disappointed by genuinely good models used for the wrong job.
It helps to know, briefly, what the benchmarks that show up throughout this article are actually measuring, since they're not interchangeable. Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) tests broad general knowledge across dozens of academic subjects, a reasonable proxy for how much a model "knows."
HumanEval specifically tests whether a model can write correct, functioning code for a given problem, a direct measure of coding capability rather than general intelligence. MT-Bench measures how well a model follows instructions and holds a coherent multi-turn conversation, closer to what " feels good to actually talk to " captures. Keep those distinctions in mind as the numbers show up model by model below, since a model leading on one says nothing certain about where it lands on the others.
Seven models make up this article: six general-purpose chat models plus one embedding model that plays a different but essential role in any local retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) setup. Every claim below is checked against the model's own official card or a cited independent benchmark, not repeated secondhand.
Phi-4-mini is Microsoft's answer to a specific question: how much real capability can you fit into a genuinely small model? Per Microsoft's own Phi-4-Mini Technical Report , it scores 67.3 on MMLU (5-shot) and 70.4 on BigBench-Hard, competitive numbers for a model roughly a fifth the size of many 20B-class competitors.
A separate, independent 2026 evaluation of reasoning consistency across foundation models found Phi-4-mini leading its comparison group on step-by-step reasoning accuracy specifically, per a cross-platform reasoning capabilities study . That's a meaningfully different claim than just "knows a lot of facts"; it suggests the model's actual reasoning process holds together reliably even at this size.
Gemma 4 is Google DeepMind's current generation of open-weight models, released April 2, 2026, and verified directly from Google's own model card . The E2B and E4B variants are the two smallest in a five-size family. They are natively multimodal, accepting text, images, and, on these smaller variants specifically, audio too. Both carry native function-calling support trained directly into the model weights rather than bolted on through prompting, and a 128K context window even at this small size.
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct posts 74.2 on MMLU and 84.8 on HumanEval according to Qwen's own technical release notes , genuinely strong numbers on both general knowledge and coding for a 7B model. The dedicated coding variant, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct , pushes further still, reaching 88.4 on HumanEval in independently logged evaluation results, a real jump over the general-purpose version specifically on code generation.
Qwen3.5-9B is a genuinely current release, verified directly on its own Hugging Face model page : natively multimodal from the ground up rather than adapted after the fact, a 262K native context window, and a Mixture-of-Experts architecture built around Gated Delta Networks for efficient inference relative to its total parameter count. It's Apache 2.0 licensed, meaning it can be fine-tuned and deployed commercially without restriction.
Mistral 7B remains one of the most widely fine-tuned open-weight base models in the entire ecosystem, verified via Mistral AI's own Hugging Face organization page . Its defining trait was never raw benchmark-topping capability; it's the clarity and reliability of its instruction-following, producing clean, well-structured output with comparatively little prompt engineering required to get there.
Llama 3.1 8B 's real, verified size and release come directly from Meta's own model card and Meta's official launch announcement . One factual note worth being precise about, since it trips up a lot of guides: Meta's later Llama 3.3 release exists only as a 70B model. There is no official Llama 3.3 8B, so Llama 3.1 8B remains the correct, current reference point at this specific size within the Llama family.
This is the one model on this list that isn't a chat model at all, and arguably the most quietly essential one for anyone building a local RAG pipeline. Per a June 2026 benchmarked comparison of every major Ollama embedding model , nomic-embed-text runs at 137 million parameters with a footprint under 300MB and supports an 8,192-token native context window. Note that Ollama's default listing sometimes shows a smaller 2,048 figure, so explicitly set the context length rather than assuming the larger number applies automatically. As of that comparison, it had accumulated 85.6 million pulls on Ollama, the single clearest piece of real, measurable adoption evidence anywhere in this article.
Here's the payoff this entire article has been building toward, the one table worth bookmarking.
All seven models are available as ready-to-pull GGUF builds through Ollama, a single ollama pull <model-name> away, with no separate conversion or setup step required for any of them.
The useful question was never "what's the best local model?" It's "what am I actually trying to do right now?" The honest answer to that question changes depending on whether the task is writing a cover letter, debugging a Flask app, or building the retrieval layer of a RAG pipeline.
Seven models, seven real, cited reasons each one earns its place on this list. Match the model to the task in front of you, not the other way around, and the disappointment that opened this article stops happening at all.
Shittu Olumide is a software engineer and technical writer passionate about leveraging cutting-edge technologies to craft compelling narratives, with a keen eye for detail and a knack for simplifying complex concepts. You can also find Shittu on Twitter .

title: Can This Open-Source Model Beat AI Detectors? Let’s Test It Locally
body:
Can a free, open-source AI humanizer beat paid tools? We tested a 12B model locally and compared the results against AI detectors to see if the hype is real.
You do not need to pay for an expensive subscription to rewrite AI-generated content anymore. Open-source models like Humanizer let you do it locally, without monthly fees, API costs, or sending your writing to a third-party service. The model is gaining attention in the open-source community, with more than 143,000 downloads and 2,100 likes reported on Hugging Face in early October 2026. Its developer also claims that 95% of 210 rewritten English drafts were classified as human-written by Originality.ai , although that result has not been independently verified.
In this tutorial, we will download the 12-billion-parameter Humanizer model, run it locally on a Linux machine using llama.cpp with NVIDIA CUDA support, and use it to rewrite AI-generated text. We will then test the results against popular AI detectors, including Originality.ai, GPTZero , and Copyleaks , to see whether this free, open-source alternative can actually deliver on its claims.
Humanizer is an open-source, 12-billion-parameter model built on Google's Gemma 4 12B . Unlike general-purpose language models, it is specifically fine-tuned to rewrite AI-generated content into more natural, human-like writing while preserving the original meaning, facts, and important details.
The model was trained on 28,598 pairs of AI-generated drafts and real human-written text , collected from sources such as academic papers, government reports, emails, Reddit, and Hacker News. It first learned to transform AI-written drafts into human-like text through supervised fine-tuning. The developers then used Direct Preference Optimization with 3,918 preference pairs, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization , where a large language model (LLM) judge evaluated rewrites for factual accuracy, unnecessary copying, and changes in meaning.
When you provide a draft, Humanizer rewrites the wording, adjusts sentence structure, removes repetitive AI-style phrasing, and varies sentence length while trying to keep the original information intact. Interestingly, the developers did not use AI detectors during training . Instead, they focused on improving writing quality and factual consistency.
According to the developer's evaluation, 95% of 210 English rewrites were classified as human-written by Originality.ai , while the quantized Q8_0 version achieved approximately 93%. These results are developer-reported, and the model can still introduce factual errors or perform differently across detectors.
You can also download the desktop application for Windows and macOS and run it offline without writing any code. For advanced users, Humanizer supports llama.cpp, Ollama , Transformers , MLX , and vLLM .
In this tutorial, we will run the Q8_0 model locally on Linux using llama.cpp with NVIDIA CUDA support.
First, we need to set up llama.cpp, an open-source inference engine that lets us run LLMs locally without relying on cloud APIs. We will use its llama-server component to serve Humanizer through a local HTTP API. Since our Linux machine already has NVIDIA CUDA installed, we can build llama.cpp with GPU acceleration to make text generation faster.
Clone the llama.cpp repository and build the server with CUDA support:
Once the build is complete, verify the installation:
Next, we will download the 8-bit quantized version of Humanizer from Hugging Face. Quantization reduces the model's memory requirements, making it easier to run on consumer GPUs without loading the full-precision weights. We will use the Q8_0 version, which offers a good balance between model quality and memory usage, and then launch it using llama-server .
Download the model weights and prompt configuration:
The Q8_0 model requires substantial GPU memory. If your GPU has less VRAM available, you can try the smaller humanizer-12b-Q6_K.gguf version instead.
Here, -ngl 99 offloads all model layers to the GPU, -c 8192 sets the context window, and -fa on enables Flash Attention. The server runs on port 8910 and is accessible only from the local machine.
Open another terminal and check whether the model is available:
If the server returns the loaded model information, Humanizer is ready to accept requests.
Now that Humanizer is running locally, we can test it on AI-generated content. We will create a short article, send it to the model through the local API, and save the rewritten version to a text file. The model uses a specific prompt format to guide the rewriting process, so we will load the official configuration rather than writing our own instructions.
First, create a file called draft.txt and add an AI-generated article of around 200 words. For this experiment, we used an article about running AI models locally, which GPTZero flagged as 100% AI-generated, as shown in the screenshot below.
Next, create a Python file called humanize.py :
The script loads the original draft, combines it with the model's recommended instructions, and sends it to the local llama-server . We use a temperature of 1.0 and a top_p of 0.95 , following the developer's recommended generation settings. The rewritten text is then saved automatically.
The rewritten article will appear in your terminal and will also be saved as humanized.txt .
We then tested the rewritten article using GPTZero, and the results were quite promising. The AI detection score dropped from 100% to 49%, while the human-written score increased to 51%. GPTZero was uncertain about the text but indicated that it would likely be considered human-written. This shows a noticeable improvement after running the article through Humanizer, although results may vary with different content and detectors.
After testing Humanizer on multiple AI-generated articles, I found the results to be quite hit or miss. Sometimes, the rewritten content was classified as human-written, while other times, detectors still flagged it as AI-generated. Based on my testing, it felt like a 50-50 chance of getting a good result.
I am not entirely sure why the results were so inconsistent. I followed the instructions from the official repository, used the recommended settings, and ran the model locally. Even then, I could not consistently reproduce the developer's reported results.
But there is another issue here: AI detectors are not always reliable. They can produce false positives, sometimes flagging text as AI-generated even when a human wrote every word. This makes it difficult to judge how effective a humanizer really is based on detector scores alone.
Overall, I can see why Humanizer is getting so much attention. You can download it, run it locally, and rewrite content without paying for expensive subscriptions or API calls. It is an interesting open-source alternative, even if the results are not always consistent. I would recommend trying it yourself, reviewing the rewritten text for accuracy, and not relying too heavily on AI detection scores.
Abid Ali Awan ( @1abidaliawan ) is a certified data scientist professional who loves building machine learning models. Currently, he is focusing on content creation and writing technical blogs on machine learning and data science technologies. Abid holds a Master's degree in technology management and a bachelor's degree in telecommunication engineering. His vision is to build an AI product using a graph neural network for students struggling with mental illness.

title: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
body:
Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals.
There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers.
Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas. With the midterm elections looming, the data center fight “is the issue in Texas,” says Bledsoe. The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction. Their grievances are just as diverse as their membership: concerns about how much water the industry consumes in a state as dry as Texas, qualms about tax subsidies, and objections to new gas plants and wind farms built to meet rising electricity demand. Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state.
If there’s one thing a broad range of voters can agree on this election season, it’s that they hate data centers and are unhappy with the status quo. A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found. That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents.
After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state. The state’s high-profile Senate race is no less of a nail-biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico. In each race, candidates have to win over voters who think data centers are coming for their water, land, and livelihoods. Republican and Democratic hopefuls alike are trying to distance themselves from an industry that’s taken deep root in the state — and so far, voters aren’t buying it.
“You’re talking about Democrats, libertarians, independents, Republicans, all in one fight … we have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall … fighting one big enemy,” says Jet Parker, who cofounded a group called Save Rural Texas that is now part of the We the People Texas coalition.
Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma. Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project. That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups.
She’s got a warning for Republicans: If they keep backing data centers, they’ll lose Texas. “You just pissed off a lot of people in rural Texas who are supposed to carry you across the [finish] line,” Parker says.
Abbott is in particularly hot water. “You brung it, so you dance with it. That’s Texas talk, you know,” Parker says. “That’s what Abbott’s done, but we’re the ones having to dance with it … we didn’t want to be in the dance at all.”
For years, however, Texas has taken among the most welcoming stances toward data centers in the country. The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry. In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs. As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years. That essentially rolled out the red carpet for companies that need abundant electricity to power energy-hungry data centers.
Since then data centers have had a massive growth spurt in order to support new generative AI models — and that’s costing the state. The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015. But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years.
The state’s energy woes go further than that. Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand. Bledsoe is concerned about air pollution for communities around new gas plants. Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found. Parker, meanwhile, can’t stand solar and wind farms built near farmland. Neither wants to see new transmission lines snaking through their communities.
Data centers can also put pressure on already stressed water supplies, especially in a drought-prone state like Texas. While they can reuse water used on-site to cool servers, the larger part of data centers’ water footprint comes from electricity use. Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems.
Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates. Meanwhile, data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, around 0.4 percent of total water use, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). By 2030, that figure could grow to up to 2.7 percent of the state’s total annual water use, HARC estimates. And water consumption can be much higher when zooming into certain communities. Another study by the University of Texas at Austin estimated that data center water use statewide could rise to as high as 9 percent by 2040.
Virginia has historically been the state with the most data centers, but it’s running out of space. Virginia still beats Texas 287 to 170 when it comes to the number of planned data center projects as of April, according to Pew Research. But as data centers get bigger, they’re moving out of cities and into rural areas — particularly in Texas. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power it draws, and in this measure, Texas already takes the crown with 26GW of existing and under-construction capacity compared to 13GW in Virginia.
Facing backlash to data centers, Abbott has changed his tune. In June, he directed the state Public Utility Commission to require that data center operators cover the costs of new infrastructure built to serve them. Since then, he has also announced statewide moratoriums on permits for data center projects pending audits on their electricity and water use. He’s also said that he would support a repeal of the sales tax exemption for data centers and greater oversight of data centers’ water and electricity use.
Even so, he’s reportedly taken millions in campaign contributions from data center interests, and We the People Texas coalition members are not convinced he’s turned the page. “Is he doing enough? Absolutely not,” Parker says.
The NAACP sent a letter to Abbott’s office last month criticizing his moratoriums for not going far enough because the state is only auditing projects that connect to the power grid. However, more so than any other state, Texas has data centers building their own power supply on-site, without needing to connect to the grid. Bledsoe’s concerned that these private energy projects will be subject to less regulatory scrutiny, while also harming air quality in nearby neighborhoods. Projects that already have permits are still being built. And an October investigation by advocacy group Public Citizen and FracTracker found public records indicating that state agencies are still processing permits for data centers, although Abbott’s office denies that they have issued any approvals since he directed them to pause permitting. To Bledsoe and other coalition members, he says, the temporary moratorium looks like “an attempt to run out the clock before the election.”
Data center hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others have formed their own trade group called the Data Center Coalition (DCC). For what it’s worth, DCC isn’t endorsing any candidates. But in an interview with The Verge, Jess Heck, the group’s director of Texas government affairs, says, “It’s very clear that our members share the same goals as Gov. Abbott and the legislature. We want to be true partners, good neighbors in every Texas community where we operate.” Heck didn’t confirm whether any of its members are providing any campaign support for Abbott.
Eduardo Leal, press secretary for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email to The Verge that “Under [Abbott’s] standards, data centers must pay for their own electric infrastructure, add power instead of only adding demand, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, not disrupt residential neighborhoods, and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives.”
Abbott signed a state Senate bill into law last year that directs the Public Utility Commission of Texas to reassess how it allocates transmission costs in order to keep rates from rising disproportionately for residential customers. And this June, he proposed more measures to force companies to cover the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve their data centers.
Abbott’s biggest competitor, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has eked out a narrow lead recently in some polls after strengthening her language against data centers — calling for a moratorium on development until the state legislature passes more protections.
“Greg Abbott invited data centers into Texas with the richest tax breaks in the country, took millions of dollars in donations from the data center interests, and has spent months lying to Texans about his record to save his political career,” Hinojosa said in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Working Texans are supporting my campaign because I’m not corrupt.”
“I think her campaign has made a ton of inroads into moderate Republican communities because of her stance on data centers,” says Anthony Elmo, public education funding defender for Good Jobs First, which recently cofounded another coalition pushing for data center reforms in Texas alongside other advocacy groups.
Hinojosa has skyrocketed from a relatively obscure local official to a serious contender for the governor’s seat, largely on a populist message that caters to residents’ frustration with Big Tech companies grabbing land for data centers. Even so, she might not be convincing enough for conservative rural voters.
Candidates from both sides of the aisle were pretty soft on data centers up until the party conventions earlier this year, says Miriam Cobb, who cofounded the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers earlier this year (which is also part of We the People Texas). Texans can see the political posturing from Hinojosa, too, she says. One of Hinojosa’s major donors has been the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, which recently formed an “American Infrastructure Alliance” with OpenAI and data center developers.
“[Voters] know she wasn’t against it from a place of understanding or sincerity, it’s something she knows she has to say now,” Cobb tells The Verge, adding that she’ll be writing in an independent candidate come Election Day. Even with many conservatives — some of them now claiming to be single-issue voters on data centers — skeptical of both parties’ candidates, Cobb still expects Republicans to lose seats.
Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, is attempting to atone for his previous support of data centers. He voted for the sales tax exemptions as a state senator in 2013, although he now says he’d support a repeal. In September, he announced an investigation into hundreds of data centers’ water use. Paxton also launched an investigation into the case in Taylor over whether it’s legal for land deeded for parkland to be developed into a data center. And he’s aligned himself with Abbott’s proposals to impose stronger light and noise restrictions on data centers, limit construction in rural areas, and push developers to cover the costs of new energy infrastructure. But he also reportedly received hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign funding this year from data center interests.
Talarico, meanwhile, has a similar plan to stop data centers “from jacking up our utility bills.” But he also claims to want to “empower local communities to decide whether they want a data center in their town,” a jab at Republicans including Paxton who have either stayed mum on whether counties should be allowed to make permitting decisions on data centers rather than the state or have actively curtailed their ability to do so. Abbott signed the so-called “Death Star” bill into law in 2023 barring counties and municipalities from crafting regulations that contradict state law. Some Republicans have cited the Death Star law in legal challenges to local moratoriums on data centers.
While the Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is in the national spotlight over the prospect of a Democrat flipping the seat, it’s probably less important for Texans concerned most about data centers, advocates tell The Verge. The race is too politically polarized to flip voters on the single issue, Cobb says, and neither candidate has given a very convincing position on how to rein in data centers anyway. Neither campaign responded to press inquiries from The Verge.
Working at the federal level, the best thing the senator-elect could do would be to push back against President Donald Trump’s data center agenda and ensure Texas can moderate data center development without interference, she says.
“We want assurances that you’re gonna let us deal with it instead of what’s been happening, where Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in,’” Cobb tells The Verge.
Cobb still sees construction traffic clogging two-lane rural roads leading to data center projects that have avoided Abbott’s partial moratorium. Residents are worried about the traffic jams blocking emergency vehicles, especially when fire weather kicks up. In some areas, Texans have seen property values drop, she adds. Farmers are giving up land that their families have tended to for generations. In other neighborhoods, an influx of new workers arriving for the data center “gold rush” is exacerbating housing shortages and making rent more unaffordable for locals. In either case, data center opposition coalition members say they’re worried about a loss of culture.
“It’s not for nothing,” Cobb says. “They have real community … and now they’re losing it.”
Update Oct. 28: This post has been updated with a statement from Gina Hinojosa.

title: Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
body:
Living digital twins are helping industrial plants run more like living systems, and setting the stage for industries that work in sync.
Most people associate industrial environments with cold steel and clockwork machinery. Functionally, though, a plant or factory is more like a living thing: It has a pulse, even a metabolism. It goes through wear and tear as it ages, and signs of deteriorating health often show up as barely perceptible irregularities.
Digital twin technology has long aimed to mirror that dynamism and model anomalies that may be symptomatic of larger problems. But earlier implementations were a few beats behind physical reality; they were incapable of real-time analysis and unable to proactively address any issues detected. They focused more on simulation, observation and what-if scenario planning, rather than closed-loop execution. Rather than serving as a digital mirror of reality that can spot anomalies or suggest optimizations, a living digital twin combines a dynamic, high-fidelity digital representation of complex operations with the capacity to intervene in the physical world through operations and control systems.
AI is at the center of this change. Rob McGreevy, chief product officer at AVEVA, likens newer, AI-infused digital twins to organisms that grow and evolve. These “living” versions are adaptive, evergreen models of a plant’s assets and processes. Because they keep pace with live conditions and connect systems that once ran in isolation, they provide a previously missing layer of visibility and orchestration that better reflects the organic rhythms of the facility itself.
Now, agentic AI is also enabling industrial systems to move beyond diagnostics or suggestions and act of their own accord. As the technology progresses toward greater autonomy, it’s starting to develop the reflexes for a kind of industrial homeostasis, in which small, constant adjustments keep a plant or factory healthy and humming.
All that said, human judgment and operator oversight still play an instrumental role by defining what healthy looks like to begin with—and flagging when AI systems are falling out of alignment. Living digital twins provide the means for human engineers to monitor what AI is doing and ensure execution is on track.
Living digital twins link engineering and design information with real-time operational data through a digital thread, or a connected record of an asset that follows it through its lifecycle. A couple of notable technological shifts have helped string this thread together: Sensors (which have gotten more affordable in recent years) now stream telemetry from IoT devices and industrial control equipment, and software platforms bring that information into user-friendly interfaces. Predictive and physics-based models can also provide AI-enriched insights into how a machine or process might behave.
The lenses through which operators view digital twins have evolved in turn. “You can look at the digital twin through the lens of sustainability: What are my emissions?” says McGreevy. “Or, through the lens of maintenance: Is this asset performing in a healthy way? Or, through a performance metric: Is it producing the number of widgets I need?”
The next phase is letting AI act on select insights those lenses illuminate. For their part, manufacturers are eager for this chapter: In a 2026 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey of manufacturers (opens in new tab) , 66% said they are using or plan to use agentic AI in their operations, and 40% expect some degree of factory autonomy by 2030. At the same time, they’re wary of the potential risks: In Deloitte’s 2025 smart manufacturing survey (opens in new tab) , 65% of executives ranked operational risk, including the potential for business disruption, among their top concerns.
Source: MIT Technology Review Insights with data from Manufacturing Leadership Council (opens in new tab) , 2026
“There is a lot more refinement to be done, a lot more proof points, testing, and validation needed,” McGreevy says about the ongoing process of making AI autonomous. In the near term, McGreevy expects agentic AI to follow the path seen in other industrial technologies like SCADA systems. “The ‘S’ in SCADA means supervisory, and supervisory means there’s a human in the middle,” he says. He sees AI working mostly in that advisory mode for the foreseeable future, with full autonomy limited to narrow, highly repetitive tasks.
As for the role human operators play, the day-to-day is evolving. Workers who once specialized in a single process line or maintenance task can now take on multiple disciplines. They can spend less time and effort approving routine actions one by one, and more on defining acceptable operating limits. Because AI can reinforce patterns in the data it receives, catching missteps early is a core part of the job. Human knowledge and experience in interpreting what AI is seeing and doing is instrumental.
Governance on a company- and industry-wide scale, too, needs to adapt to the times. Organizations must establish clear guardrails for which decisions AI can make on its own and how its actions are monitored and audited. Still, many have yet to set up comprehensive safeguards: In a recent study from AVEVA and IMD (opens in new tab) , 43% of organizations said AI has changed decision-making and accountability across ecosystem partners only slightly or not at all, while just 23% reported a significant or fundamental change. (Only 27% reported sharing data substantially or extensively with partners.)
In the meantime, regulators are starting to define some of the rules. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI safety components used in critical infrastructure as high-risk and imposes requirements for human oversight. Companies are setting up their own structures as well; AVEVA, for one, has a responsible AI governance board and a published set of principles for how AI is developed and deployed.
Inside the semi-autonomous systems already running, that oversight looks different from one deployment to another. In some cases, an operator approves every action; in others, AI acts on its own while people oversee and define the boundaries it can operate within. McGreevy cites several examples of what machine autonomy and human-plus-machine collaboration looks like among AVEVA customers:
The same synchronization that was once missing from individual plants’ technology systems has also been lacking on a larger scale. “Manufacturing and critical infrastructure have operated as siloed systems for the last 50 years,” says McGreevy. But certain emerging technologies, he suggests, are creating opportunities for more holistic coordination.
On an enterprise level, this might involve the integration of physical AI: systems that pair robotics and sensing technologies with AI-powered decision-making. Drones that fly over pipelines and power lines, for instance, can feed visual inspection data to algorithms that spot gas leaks and other hazards. Not only does this create a more accurate and interconnected flow of information, but it spares humans from needing to physically enter potentially dangerous environments. “The robotics-meets-software convergence will mean fewer incidents, fewer outages, and a more sustainable way of operating,” McGreevy predicts.
A bigger-picture version extends beyond any one plant or process to entire industrial networks, something McGreevy dubs the “integrated value chain.” “Living digital twins make digital manifestations of the entire value chain possible,” he says. “This allows companies to react quickly to supply chain changes, demand changes, tariffs, and material availability.”
Amid today’s realities of turbulent geopolitics and shifting regulatory demands, such resilience will be “an absolute necessity,” adds McGreevy. “Without it, it will be very hard to run an effective business.”
This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: Ukraine’s indigenous ballistic missiles could put Russia’s best-defended targets at risk, Turkish expert says
body:
Sitki Egeli, a military and security analyst and associate professor at Izmir University of Economics who has worked with leading Turkish defense companies, said this in an interview with Ukrinform .
“ Ukraine’s production of ballistic missiles will complicate things for Russia, because some of the best-defended targets will become vulnerable. Ballistic missiles are very difficult to intercept. You need a big investment in development and deployment. The Israelis and Americans have found out in the Iran war that the number of incoming missiles is always larger than the number of interceptors available,” Egeli said.
According to him, he Israelis and Americans have found out in the Iran war that the number of incoming missiles is always larger than the number of interceptors available.
The expert also expressed doubts about the claimed capabilities of Russia’s missile defense systems.
“I think Russian ballistic missile defence capabilities have been exaggerated from the outset. They claim the S-300 or S-400 can engage ballistic missiles, but I have never seen actual testing, as we have seen with and the Chinese or Europeans. Russia’s capacity has always been more theoretical than actual,” Egeli said.
“All indications are that S-400 is a big hoax when it comes to ballistic missile defence capability. You have to mesh radars, interceptors and all those things, and test and verify it. On top of that, modern ballistic missiles manoeuvre and use countermeasures, including decoys, to deceive missile defenсes,” he added.
As Ukrinform previously reported, military expert and founder of the Reactive Post charitable foundation Pavlo Narozhnyi said that Ukraine had successfully used its homegrown FP-7 ballistic missile against a target in Russia for the first time. He assessed the strike as successful because Russian S-400 systems had failed to intercept the missile.

title: How Dubai Fitness Challenge changed lives, from finding love to losing 50kg
body: What began in 2017 as an initiative encouraging Dubai residents to exercise for 30 minutes a day over 30 days has grown into one of the emirate's largest annual community events. Dubai Fitness Challenge returns for its 10th iteration from October 31 to November 29, bringing thousands of free activities and fitness experiences across the emirate. Under this year's theme, What's Your 30?, residents and visitors are once again being encouraged to embrace a more active lifestyle, with flagship events including Dubai Run , Dubai Ride, Dubai Yoga and Dubai Stand-Up Paddle . Launched by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed , Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, the initiative has recorded more than 16 million participants since its inception, bringing together people of different ages, nationalities and fitness levels. Beyond the numbers and large-scale events, the initiative has transformed lives. Here, three Dubai residents share, in their own words, how the city's fitness culture has touched their lives. Tania Lolla Kaddoura: 'I met my future husband at the finish line' When I arrived in Dubai from Serbia in September 2017, I was a stranger to the city, carrying a bag, a lot of dreams and the hope that this new chapter would bring new opportunities. I was already a physiotherapist, personal trainer and athlete, so when I heard about the first Dubai Fitness Challenge, I knew I wanted to be involved. Everyone was talking about it, and there was a real sense of excitement across the city. One of the events was a Spartan Race in Hatta, which I had planned to take part in. But just days before the race, I suffered an injury and realised I wouldn't be able to compete. I didn't want to miss the experience altogether, so I contacted the organisers and asked whether I could volunteer instead. I ended up helping to hand out medals at the finish line. I'd previously seen a fellow athlete on Instagram who was also injured but had decided to take on the race anyway. It involved 30km and 30 obstacles, and I had sent him a few messages of support. Then, while I was handing out medals, I placed one around a finisher's neck and congratulated him. He suddenly recognised me and said, "Lolla, that's you!" It was Mohammed, the same man I'd been messaging. He'd completed the race, and I remember feeling genuinely happy and emotional for him. That moment led to him inviting me for coffee. He would eventually become my husband. If I hadn't been injured, I would have been competing instead of volunteering. If I had arrived a little later or been assigned somewhere else, we might never have met. I truly believe that race in Hatta brought us together. What started as an unexpected love story eventually became a family tradition. Every year, we look forward to the challenge and the opportunity to take part in activities together. Our son Noah was only seven weeks old when we took him to the first Dubai Run in 2019. He later joined us for other events, including Dubai Ride , when we cycled along Sheikh Zayed Road with thousands of other participants. Watching him grow up with these experiences has been incredibly special. I've always wanted to raise a family that enjoys being active together, and the challenge has given us a reason to make that a priority every year. I've also had opportunities I never imagined, including becoming a Dubai Fitness Challenge ambassador alongside my husband, a Spartan ambassador for the Middle East and an Asics FrontRunner. When I think about everything that has happened since 2017, I'm grateful I decided to volunteer at that finish line instead of staying home. If there's one thing I'd tell someone thinking about taking part for the first time, it's not to underestimate what can come from trying something new. You never know where it might take you. Husam Mohamed: 'I lost 50kg, but gained much more' I first heard about Dubai Fitness Challenge in 2017, but I wasn't particularly interested. Fitness and an active lifestyle weren't things I thought about. It wasn't until the second edition in 2018 that I began to take the challenge seriously. I've always admired how Sheikh Hamdan leads by example when it comes to fitness, and seeing him participate personally inspired me to give it a chance. At the time, I was overweight; my fitness level was almost zero, and I was very shy about participating in public activities. I'd never been involved in sports, gone to the gym or paid much attention to living healthily. I wasn't fully committed during those first 30 days, but something changed. For the first time, I made a commitment to my health and started noticing results, physically and mentally. I began thinking beyond the challenge, and eventually exercise became part of my lifestyle. Since then, I've lost 50kg. But the biggest transformation hasn't been the number on the scale. I've become mentally stronger, more confident, more open and more focused on achieving my goals. Movement is now an essential part of my daily routine. I often say that movement is medicine, but it's also a language of love. It's something I enjoy sharing with others because it brings people together, helps us connect and allows us to support one another. For a long time, I was a very shy and private person. Being overweight affected my confidence, and I didn't think I had anything worth sharing. But as my transformation progressed, people began asking how I'd done it. That's when I realised my story might encourage someone else to begin. I hadn't done anything extraordinary. I'd simply started, remained patient and kept going. What I love most is how it brings together people from different backgrounds and fitness levels. For that month, it feels as though the entire city becomes one enormous gym. If I could offer one piece of advice to someone starting where I did, it would be to enjoy the journey. Don't rush or focus only on the final result. Celebrate the small achievements and document your progress. One day, you'll look back and realise just how far you've come, not only physically but mentally and emotionally. Danny Cousins: 'Running became about more than personal bests' My first memories of Dubai Fitness Challenge are of seeing how much the city changes when it comes around. I've taken part a couple of times over the years, but even when you're not actively participating, it's hard not to notice the sense of community it creates. Places such as Kite Beach really come alive. I've always been naturally competitive as a runner, but DFC reminded me that running and fitness don't always have to be about racing or chasing a particular time. While Dubai Fitness Challenge wasn't the direct inspiration behind the launch of SubClub DXB in 2025, it helped foster the city's growing fitness culture, which played a part in our decision to start the running club. With SubClub, we wanted to create something between a social running club and a serious training environment. The idea came from those "sub" targets. Whether you're chasing a sub-20-minute 5km, sub-25, sub-30 or simply trying to run a distance faster than before, everyone has their own version of a personal best. Some of the most rewarding moments have been watching people achieve something they didn't think was possible. A personal best might belong to one person on paper, but when you've trained and struggled together, it starts to feel like a shared achievement. Building SubClub has changed how I think about running. Technically, it's an individual sport, but I've discovered how much of the experience can be shared. That's what I appreciate about DFC. Dubai brings together people from different backgrounds and fitness levels, and for one month everyone is encouraged to work towards the same goal.

title: Call of the Wilde: Jacob Fowler with a sparkling 46-save shutout as the Montreal Canadiens win a third straight defeating the St. Louis Blues
body:
Without Nick Suzuki and Ivan Demidov, two forwards from the top-six, the Montreal Canadiens have done well so far. They’d prefer to have their stars, but learning how to win without them has its value as well.
The Canadiens looked to continue success in St. Louis against the Blues, and they did thanks to Jacob Fowler. He stopped 46 shots in a 2-0 shutout.
It was a third straight start for Jacob Fowler, and you could hardly blame Head Coach Martin St. Louis for making the same choice again. Fowler started the night fourth in the league in Goals Saved Above Expected while Jakub Dobes is 68th of 70 goals in the league.
Dobes will get a chance to figure out what ails him eventually, but, at the moment, the Canadiens need wins, and they know with key injuries on offence, they need to be at their very best on defence.
Fowler is the choice to give them the best chance. He stopped 34 of 35 shots in a masterful performance in Winnipeg. He was awarded the third star for the week in the league on Monday, then on Tuesday, he was even better.
Fowler was showing off his technical skills again. They are the cornerstone of his success. On one occasion, a rebound came so quickly, and from such a vastly different angle than the first shot that it seemed like a sure goal, but Fowler was perfectly in position and standing tall to make the difficult rebound look easy.
In the third period, there was a scramble situation that produced four shots. The puck went left. It went right. It kept landing on Blues’ sticks, and despite all of that pressure Fowler was in perfect position to stop the next shot every shot.
Fowler with another outstanding GSAE to show he is among the elite in the NHL right now. Fowler with a 3.8 GSAE in St. Louis. He now has a 9.9 for the season. He passes Jake Oettinger at 9.4 to lead the entire league.
