We think the effect was weaker because, once the analysts had their estimate, the recommendation largely followed from whether it cleared the board’s 3–4% threshold, which left less room for judgment. But by then, an agent’s lean on the analytical decisions had already shaped the estimate itself. Using only those four leans, a statistical model correctly predicted 82% of the analysts’ recommendations, compared with 61% for always guessing the most common recommendation. (This excludes analysts who proposed an extension.) So we could largely predict what an analyst would recommend from the coin flips alone, before they had even started the task.
Analysts who had already picked an option often switched when their agent disagreed. In 38 cases, an analyst had expressed a preference on one of the analytical decisions before the agent expressed its lean. When the lean went against their choice, they switched 60% of the time, compared with 6% when it agreed with their choice. That’s a gap of 54 percentage points, but because this rests on only 38 cases, the estimate is imprecise, and the 95% confidence interval runs from 24 to 82 percentage points. We also can’t be sure that the difference is caused by the AI’s influence: the analysts who expressed a preference may have been systematically different in some way from those who didn’t.
Experience and expertise did not predict who deferred. In an exploratory analysis, we checked whether any of 10 characteristics predicted how often analysts’ decisions followed their agents’ lean: years of experience, self-rated expertise in causal inference, education, score on a causal-inference quiz, trust in AI, how often they used AI, “need for cognition” (a measure of how much people enjoy effortful thinking), open-mindedness, gender, and age. Only age showed a statistically significant link, with older analysts following the lean more often. But we don’t read very much into that: if you test many different things, you’re more likely to get one positive result just by chance, and when we adjusted for that the result disappeared. Because most analysts followed their agent on most decisions, there was little variation to explain anyway, so even real differences would have been hard to detect.
Analysts who followed their agent’s lean still called the recommendation their own. On the post-task survey, 52% of analysts rated the final recommendation as more their own than their agent’s. The rest said it was more the agent’s recommendation. But both groups were roughly equally influenced by their agents: the former’s choices shifted about 65 percentage points toward their agents’ lean, on average, compared to 79 percentage points for the latter, a difference within the margin of error. Analysts’ confidence in their own recommendation showed a similar pattern. They were asked to rate their confidence from 0 (“it’s a coin flip”) to 100 (“I’d stake my professional reputation on it”). Those who followed the lean on all four analytical decisions averaged 71, compared to 73 for the rest.
Analysts explained their choices in their agent’s words. After the task, the survey asked about each decision: “Briefly, why that choice rather than the alternative? If it wasn’t an active choice, just say so.” Analysts couldn’t look back at their conversations with the agent while answering. Even so, 77% repeated their agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and only 15% credited the agent anywhere.
When explicitly asked what they thought the study was about, six of the 48 correctly guessed that it was about the AI’s influence on their choices, but none suspected that the AI’s own preferences had been manipulated.
Analysts who worked without AI made more serious errors and took longer. Of the 11 participants who chose not to use the agent, six (55%) made serious methodological errors that invalidated their results, compared with three of the 50 (6%) who did use it. Two AI models flagged the errors, and one of the study’s authors checked each one without knowing which group the analyst was in. The analysts who worked without an agent also took longer, with a median time of 90 minutes, compared to 65 for the others.
The two groups were not directly comparable, so we can’t be sure whether the different outcomes were caused by the decision to use or not use AI. Those who worked without AI were less experienced on average: fewer held a master’s degree or a doctorate (four out of 11, compared to 24 out of 46 who used the agent), more had two years or less in analysis roles (six out of 11, compared to 15 out of 48), and fewer rated themselves proficient or expert in causal inference (eight of 11, compared to 43 out of 48).
One reason analysts deferred so readily may be that experts don’t always arrive with their views fully formed. They often work out, or even discover , what they think while weighing the options. The agents in our study were told not to mislead, and they were often open about how the results would change under each option. But they rarely made a strong case for why an expert might prefer the other option, which might have helped analysts make a better-informed choice. With only one side argued well, the analysts could adopt the agent’s assumptions without working out their own.
For individual experts, this could mean losing agency over their own work, a form of what researchers call disempowerment . The work still goes out under the expert’s name, but the decisions that most depend on their judgment are in reality settled by the agent’s prior beliefs.
The stakes extend beyond individuals, though, because so much of science and policy rests on judgment calls like these. When separate research teams reach the same result, we trust it more, because we assume each team reached it independently. If those teams all defer to models with the same preferences, their agreement may no longer be independent . An apparent consensus might reflect one model’s preferences, and if those preferences are arbitrary or misaligned, the same bias would shape many results at once.
The same problem applies to AI safety research. Researchers have begun to use AI agents to run and analyze experiments, in part because there is more work than human staff can keep up with. Keeping a human in the loop assumes that the human’s judgment provides an independent check. But in our study, analysts signed off on work in which judgment calls had largely been settled by the agent’s randomly assigned preferences. Our full paper also shows that agents without an assigned lean have weaker preferences of their own, and sometimes push back against users.
Deferral of this kind is hard to detect. Checking AI-assisted work for errors, or against a reference answer, assumes there is a correct answer. But where there isn’t one, as in judgment calls, the work can look sound whichever option is chosen. Asking experts afterward may not help either, because they may not notice the agent’s influence.
This isn’t an argument for using AI less. Used well, AI could expand people’s agency rather than eroding it. We suggest three areas for future study:
Measuring deferral. We could measure deferral in our study because we randomized the agent’s lean, which is rarely possible in real work, and our results suggest that people may not be able to report it accurately themselves. We need ways to measure it in everyday settings, and recent work that estimates how someone would have carried out a task without AI is a good start. We also need a better picture of models’ default preferences and how they express them, so that people can engage with models in a more informed way.
Designing agents differently. Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one. But this could quickly become overwhelming for users. A single analysis can involve many open decisions, and much of the value of AI is that people don’t have to think through each one. Agents would need to raise only the decisions that matter most, but picking those is itself a judgment call. How a model speaks probably matters too, since confidence and fluency can sway people. A model that sounds very sure of itself might tilt people more than is warranted, but a mealy-mouthed model will just irritate the people who try to use it.
Changing institutions. Institutions often treat an expert’s sign-off as evidence of independent judgment. As AI does more of the work, that assumption becomes shakier. Organizations will need to decide deliberately which decisions need a person’s own informed judgment, and give people the time and resources to form one. Judgment also depends on skill, and people who stop making these decisions may lose the ability to make them. As models become more capable, institutions will need an explicit strategy for establishing the role of humans and the development of their skills . Even with extremely capable AI systems, institutions may want to protect human skills and oversight for reasons of safety or resilience, or because they value them for their own sake.
There may be no single right division of labor between people and AI. Some decisions may be fine to hand over, and others worth keeping. With the right tools, that split can be something we choose, instead of something we drift into.
This project was led by Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren, and Alex Tamkin. Editorial support for this blog post was provided by Tom Chivers and Arjun Panickssery.
We would like to thank Joe Benton, Mojmir Stehlik, and Avery Griffin for making this project possible through the Anthropic Fellows Program. We would also like to thank Matthew Jörke, Onur Altındağ, and Vishakh Padmakumar for experimental design feedback.

title: 2027 State Budget draft approved in first reading
body:
Ukrainian MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak reported the development in a Telegram post, according to Ukrinform.
“The budget has been approved in the first reading — 239 votes,” the post said.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi thanked lawmakers for their cooperation, emphasizing that the document reflects the realities of the full-scale war and the country’s key priorities for the coming year. These include, above all, adequate funding for security and defense, maintaining financial stability, and fulfilling important social commitments.
“The government will review the parliament’s budget conclusions and prepare the draft for the second reading,” Koretskyi stressed.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada’s Budget Committee backed an amendment to next year’s state budget draft providing for increased salaries for military personnel.

title: First Greek Olympic Youth Team Departs For Youth Olympics
body: The first group of Greece’s Youth Olympic Team departed for Senegal on Wednesday, October 28, to represent the country at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games, which will run from October 31 to November 13 for athletes aged 18 and under. The first group includes seven athletes competing in coastal rowing, judo, beach volleyball, badminton and swimming. The athletes are Iason Mouselimis (coastal rowing), Io Eirini Papadotheodorou (judo), Angeliki Charissaki and Grigoria Anna Margaritopoulou (beach volleyball), Ioannis Saourgiannidis (badminton), and Nikolaos Papadotheodorou and Eirini Zervou (swimming). Dakar 2026 marks a milestone for the Youth Olympic Games, as an African country will host an Olympic sporting event for the first time. Organisers expect approximately 2,700 athletes from around the world to compete across 25 sports, with 153 medal events scheduled. title: Kazakhstan GDP Forecast Rises to Nearly $398 Billion
body: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects Kazakhstan’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) at nearly $398 billion in 2026. The figure places the country 47th in a global ranking published by Visual Capitalist , based on the IMF’s October forecasts. The fund expects Kazakhstan’s economy to grow by 4.4% this year after adjusting for inflation, compared with global growth of 3.1%. An earlier ranking , published in January, placed Kazakhstan 50th, with projected GDP of about $320 billion for 2026. The tenge, Kazakhstan’s currency, gained approximately 18% against the dollar over the year to October 28. A stronger tenge increases the dollar value of Kazakhstan’s economy, even without an equivalent increase in actual production. Kazakhstan remains Central Asia’s largest economy by nominal GDP. Uzbekistan, the region’s second-largest economy, is projected to have a GDP of $178.17 billion in 2026. Turkmenistan’s projected GDP is about $83 billion, Kyrgyzstan’s is $26.69 billion, and Tajikistan’s is $21.11 billion. Kazakhstan’s nominal GDP per person is projected to exceed $19,000 in 2026. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of National Economy estimates that the economy grew by 4.2% in January–September 2026, with the non-resource sector expanding by 5.4%. Construction output increased by 11.5%, while manufacturing, transportation, and trade also grew. Oil production, meanwhile, fell by 8.3%. According to the ministry’s October 13 report , manufacturing accounted for 14.1% of GDP in the first half of the year. Machinery production grew by 22.8% in January–September, while chemicals and pharmaceuticals also recorded strong growth. The IMF expects Kazakhstan’s real economic growth to accelerate to 4.9% in 2027.

title: Ice patrol ship will miss a second Antarctic season
body: HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season, leaving Britain without an ice patrol ship in the South Atlantic for a second consecutive year while the government looks at how to cover the gap, according to an answer given in Parliament. Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what steps are being taken to ensure an ice patrol vessel is available for the coming season. Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Due to unforeseen circumstances, HMS Protector will not deploy to Antarctica for the 2026/27 season. The Ministry of Defence is working apace with partners across Government to develop options to support the UK’s Antarctic requirements in the absence of an ice patrol ship in 2026/27 and restore an ice patrol capability as soon as possible. “The Defence Investment Plan announced plans to replace HMS Protector with a more modern variant to maintain this essential presence and support Government activities in the Arctic and around the British Antarctic Territory. Decisions on the method of procurement and the exact replacement timeline will be taken in due course.” Answering a separate question, Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, confirmed that the ship last went south during the 2024-25 season. Pollard told Parliament last week that Protector could not sail from Teesside to Devonport under her own power this month because of propulsion defects and had to be towed, and that she missed the 2025-26 season because of prolonged essential and mandatory maintenance. The ship is the Royal Navy’s only ice patrol vessel and carries out Britain’s survey and inspection commitments under the Antarctic Treaty, alongside supporting the British Antarctic Survey and maintaining a presence around the British Antarctic Territory. She was bought in 2011, originally built as the Norwegian vessel Polarbjørn, and was taken on initially as a short-term replacement for HMS Endurance, which was crippled by flooding in 2008 and never returned to service. The post Ice patrol ship will miss a second Antarctic season first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Oil prices up due to Houthi strikes and US threat to renew Iran war
body: Oil prices rose on Wednesday, recovering losses this week, as more Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the prospect of a renewed US military offensive against Iran kept supply fears elevated. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was up 0.87 per cent at $114.87 a barrel at 2pm UAE time. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, added 1.59 per cent to $101.49 a barrel. Crude prices were up by more than 2 per cent earlier in the session, and are virtually flat for the week after retreating about 1.6 per cent on Tuesday. Oil remains at multi-month highs as tensions linger in the Middle East. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels towards Taif on Wednesday morning. Before that, the Houthis claimed a drone strike on Abha International Airport, although there was no immediate confirmation of the attack from the Saudi side. Meanwhile, there are hopes that talks between the US and Iran to end their conflict are progressing. Qatari mediators presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the US-Israeli war on the country, which Tehran is considering and is expected to respond to by the end of the week, an official told Reuters on Wednesday. Markets are also concerned about the possibility of the US resuming large-scale attacks on Iran. On Sunday, President Donald Trump said he had a “decision to make” on Iran, as talks have yet to yield a deal. The Wall Street Journal reported that Washington has warned several Gulf Arab countries to prepare for a possible renewed US military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned that any Israeli-instigated military escalation in the Gulf could have a devastating impact on international markets. With Middle Eastern crude supply remaining volatile and geopolitical uncertainty persisting, Swiss lender UBS revised its oil price projections upwards, expecting Brent to remain near the $110 level until the end of the year. “Middle Eastern flows, while improving, have not yet fully normalised,” Giovanni Staunovo, a strategist at the Zurich-based bank, wrote in a note. Global inventories have fallen sharply as pledged strategic oil reserve releases have largely been completed, he added. “An undersupplied market could push commercial stocks lower and should sustain oil prices. Record freight costs, constrained tanker capacity and recovering Chinese imports are other factors likely to keep oil prices high,” he said. “Uncertainty around our forecasts remains elevated, reflecting both the unpredictable nature of the Middle East conflict and the pace of recovery in Gulf production and global oil demand.” Traders are also watching Israel's election, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is in the lead, according to early returns.

title: Israel After the Election: Who Will Form a Government?
body:
The formation of a new government looks set to be a complicated process after the Israeli election on Tuesday. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc is slightly ahead of the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, former chief of staff of the Israel Defence Forces, but with around two-thirds of the votes counted neither camp appears to have secured the required majority of 61 seats. The provisional final result is expected on Thursday.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
NRC (Netherlands) sees Israel facing an uncertain political future:
“Netanyahu has suffered a setback but is not yet out of the running. ... Given the deadlock over cooperation with the Arab parties, Israel may be heading for a general election in 2027 – a scenario in which Netanyahu would remain in office as interim prime minister. For Israel’s longest-serving leader and his supporters, this is of course not a bad outcome. But for Israelis who yearn for domestic political change, the memory of the marathon of five elections between 2019 and 2022 is still fresh.”
Polityka (Poland) sees the Arab parties in the role of kingmaker:
“History shows that the politician tasked with forming a government will succeed in doing so. ... Everything indicates that without the support of the Arab parties, none of the candidates will be able to form a government. Eisenkot potentially has the better chances, even though hypothetical coalition partners announced ahead of the elections that they would not enter into an alliance with the Arabs. The Arab parties could play their part in forming a minority or even a majority government if the main opponent of this solution, Avigdor Lieberman, were to withdraw into the opposition.”
A coalition led by Eisenkot would be possible, says La Stampa (Italy) :
“President Isaac Herzog must decide who has the best chances of forming a government, while taking into account two major currents of public opinion: those who are horrified by the massacre of 7 October, and those – mostly from the Arab minority – who are equally shocked by the destruction of the Gaza Strip. Reconciling these two sides will be Eisenkot’s task, should he be given the mandate to form a minority government. The alternative would be to hold another election in three months’ time.”
Change depends on certain ministers losing their posts
On news website Spotmedia (Romania), journalist Irina Olteanu sees a fundamental change of direction within reach:
“A government that is not dependent on politicians like [Minister for National Security Itamar] Ben Gvir and [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich could take more decisive action against settler violence. It would refrain from encouraging the emigration of Palestinians and the disintegration of the Palestinian Authority. Such a government would be more open to initiatives from the US and regional actors on Gaza and other issues. However, it would also inherit the same unresolved questions how to disarm Hamas, who will rebuild Gaza, and who will restore order and respect for the law in the West Bank.”
Die Zeit (Germany) sees a chance for reason and level-headedness to prevail once more:
“For an end to the never-ending drama and hysteria that Netanyahu embodies. In the final phase of his campaign, the prime minister circulated AI-generated images of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv. His message: it’s either me or the apocalypse. This excessive behaviour, this tendency to throw all caution to the wind can only harm Israel, as it would any country. Benjamin Netanyahu has still been able to mobilise plenty of support for his doomsday rhetoric. But not a majority.”

title: Calgary city council approves stiff hikes to water rates over the next 4 years
body:
Calgarians and local businesses are set to pay more for water over the next four years after city council approved a slew of fee increases proposed by city administration Tuesday.
Those increases are set to amount to nearly 20 per cent for drinking water, 15.2 per cent for wastewater and 5.8 per cent for stormwater annually between 2027 and 2030.
Water rates for the average household are set to increase from $119 monthly this year, to $134 per month in 2027, eventually increasing by $90 to $206 monthly by 2030.
Mayor Jeromy Farkas called the hikes an “accountability moment” after what he said was more than 10 years of underinvestment in the city’s water system.
“Us as a council, we’re taking charge, we’re committing to Calgarians that we are addressing this and we are not going to tolerate failure of the fundamental responsibility of a municipality, which is safe and clean drinking water,” Farkas told reporters.
The increases are set to help pay for a $6.5 billion capital invesment over the next four years to renew critical infrastructure, expand drinking water, wastewater and stormwater capacity, reduce water loss and improve emergency readiness.
Challenges with the city’s water system have been highlighted by two catastrophic breaks along the Bearspaw feeder main, one of the city’s most critical water lines that carries more than 60 per cent of Calgary’s drinking water.
“This is not a one-off, this is a sign the entire system needs investment and needs work,” said Michael Thompson, chief operating officer of the city’s water utility.
According to Thompson, the city tried to keep water rates “low and affordable” over the last 10 years.
“I think what happened over that last decade was we focused on rates and not on the infrastructure as well,” he told council.
A report from administration warned of “major risks” within the city’s water system and delaying investment could leak to an increase service disruptions, emergency repairs and long-term costs.
“This isn’t all of what is needed, but it does scratch the surface,” Farkas said. “This is the bare minimum that we need to avoid the literal ‘crap-pocolypse’ of our stormwater, wastewater and water system failing again.”
City council voted 9-6 in favour of the new water rates, which will be included in the upcoming four-year budget deliberations in November. Councillors Landon Johnston, Rob Ward, Kim Tyers, Mike Jamieson, Jennifer Wyness and Dan McLean opposed.
McLean told reporters he hoped city administration would look at alternate funding mechanisms for water infrastructure, like municipal bonds, to help offset the impact on Calgarians’ water bills.
“I understand the need for this but I don’t think we’ve looked at every other option,” McLean told reporters. “This is too much on top of what we’re looking at for a proposed municipal property tax, so I just could not support it at this time.”
City administration said any funding the city receives from other orders of government could reduce rates in the future.
Although Ward 10 Coun. Andre Chabot included an amendment to review the rates next year instead of halfway through the budget in 2028, there were no attempts from city council to reduce the hikes from administration.
“I was hoping that my fellow colleagues would see the cries from Calgarians, from small businesses, from large businesses… saying please slow this down,” Tyers told reporters. “During the budget, there’s definitely room for us to revisit this.”
Businesses are also facing an “egregious” rate hike, according to the Calgary Chamber of Commerce.
A medium sized business using 400 cubic metres of water monthly could see its bills increase from $1,661.33 per month this year to $3,093.19 monthly in 2030.
“It really renders our businesses very uncompetitive, it will squeeze their bottom lines significantly,” said Chamber of Commerce president Deborah Yedlin. “When you think about the fact that 95 per cent of Calgary’s businesses are small and medium sized enterprises, this is a huge concern.”
When pressed on the increases facing businesses, Farkas suggested using less water to reduce the costs.
“For us to give, say, a big break to our largest industrial users and redistribute that burden to the local residential class, that doesn’t make sense to me,” he said.

title: Zelensky lands in Netherlands to discuss air defense, economic partnership
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the Netherlands on Oct. 28 for talks with Dutch officials, as Kyiv seeks to drum up European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten will welcome Zelensky at his official residence, Catshuis, in The Hague, after which the two will hold bilateral talks, according to the Dutch government.
"We will discuss defense and economic cooperation, strengthening Ukrainian air defense, and new steps to support Ukraine," Zelensky said on X upon his arrival.
The visit comes just as the Netherlands confirmed a 1.2-billion-euro ($1.3 billion) package of non-military assistance over the next three years, aimed at supporting Ukraine 's recovery and reconstruction.
In addition to economic support, the Netherlands has provided Kyiv with about $10 billion in military aid as of mid-2026, providing F-16 fighter jets, Patriot air-defense launchers, and funding for packages under NATO's PURL program.
Ukrainian delegates will also hold talks with Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen and Dutch Defense Minister Dilan Yesilgoz-Zegerius, followed by a meeting between Ukrainian and Dutch business leaders.
Separately, Zelensky is scheduled to meet Dutch King Willem-Alexander at Huis ten Bosch, the royal palace in The Hague.
The president's trip coincided with Dutch Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma's visit to Kyiv for talks with Ukrainian officials.
Sjoerdsma outlined details of the three-year support package for Ukraine, including 40 million euros ($45 million) for the Ukraine Energy Support Fund and 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies for their Ukrainian partners.
Ukraine braces for another harsh winter as Russia has already begun striking the country's energy infrastructure, still heavily battered after the previous winter.

title: China’s disarmament union calls on IAEA to boost supervision of Japan's plutonium stocks
body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) needs to strengthen surveillance measures over Japan in a situation where the country is building up its plutonium reserves, Chairman of China Arms Control and Disarmament Association Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He said that Japan's plutonium reserves now stand at 44.4 tons. "The IAEA should proactively strengthen the scale and frequency of comprehensive control measures for Japan. And all countries should approach nuclear cooperation with Japan with caution to ensure that such cooperation is used exclusively for peaceful purposes," he said.
Dai Huaicheng added that Japan had long justified the plutonium reserves growth by developing a nuclear cycle and intending to produce MOX fuel (Mixed-Oxide fuel - mixed uranium-plutonium oxide fuel). However, in light of the facts, this justification does not stand up to criticism. Firstly, there is a serious imbalance between supply and demand," said the head of the association.
"After the 2011 accident at the Fukushima nuclear power plant, many of Japan’s nuclear reactors were shut down for a long time, and the number of reactors in which plutonium is actually loaded and consumed is very limited, which is why significant amounts of plutonium only enter [reserves], but are not consumed."
Secondly, the expert pointed out, this runs counter to Japan's obligations to the international community.
"In 1997, Japan gave the IAEA a written commitment to ensure the ‘absence of excess plutonium.’ That is, that all the separated plutonium will be used in reactors [as fuel], but today it has accumulated dozens of tons of excess plutonium, which means we see a difference in what they say and what they do. Thirdly, plutonium stored abroad can also be used for military purposes. As soon as Japan makes a political decision, more than 30 tons of plutonium stored outside the country can theoretically be quickly delivered [to Japanese territory]," Dai Huaicheng said.
The MOX technology uses secondary nuclear production materials for the production of fresh fuel - depleted uranium and plutonium extracted from irradiated nuclear fuel.

title: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
body:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.
Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion , according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., speaks during a campaign event on October 17, 2026 in Marietta, Georgia. Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images hide caption
The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.
The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.
The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May , according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history . It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.
The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.
With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition 's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.

title: Stonebwoy featured on soundtrack for Hollywood action comedy ‘Wrong Toes’
body: Ghanaian musician Stonebwoy has joined an international collaboration featured on the official soundtrack of upcoming action comedy Boyz Trip , scheduled for worldwide theatrical release in 2027. The award-winning recording artist features on Wrong Toes , a song bringing together Stonebwoy from Ghana, American recording artist Mashanda Faust and Atlanta-based musical group Hero The Band, blending African and American musical influences. The Boyz Trip entertainment project, comprising the feature film, its original soundtrack and the Wrong Toes music video, is executive produced by Alan Key and Kyle Scott, co-founders of KeyScott Entertainment, headquartered in Brisbane, Australia. The concept for Wrong Toes originated with Alan Key, whose creative vision laid the foundation for the song and its accompanying music video. Kyle Scott spearheaded the creative development and execution of that vision, bringing the project together musically and visually while working alongside recording artist Mashanda Faust to shape the song’s musical direction and overall presentation. Written by Alan Key and Faten El Sayed, Wrong Toes has evolved into an international collaboration featuring artists from Ghana and the United States. The official music video was recently filmed at Cape Town Film Studios in Cape Town, South Africa, with two-time award-winning creative director Warren Gray leading its creative direction. Stonebwoy brings Ghanaian music to the global stage Stonebwoy’s participation presents another opportunity to showcase Ghanaian music through international cinema. Known for his blend of Afrobeats, reggae and dancehall, Stonebwoy contributes his signature sound to a soundtrack designed to connect audiences across Africa, North America, Europe and Australia. His collaboration with American artists Mashanda Faust and Hero The Band also underscores the growing creative relationship between the African and American entertainment industries. Wrong Toes is part of a collection of original music being developed for the Boyz Trip soundtrack through KeyScott Entertainment’s newly launched music division, which focuses on original film music, publishing, artist development and international collaborations. About the film: Boyz Trip Boyz Trip is an upcoming international action comedy starring Desi Banks, Rome Flynn, Algee Smith and South African actor Siv Ngesi. Set against the backdrop of Cape Town, South Africa, the film follows four longtime college friends who reunite for what is supposed to be an unforgettable international vacation. However, their dream getaway quickly spirals into chaos when they become entangled in the dangerous world of a notorious criminal figure known as Le Serpent. What begins as a celebration of friendship turns into an action-packed comedy filled with unexpected twists, dangerous encounters and unforgettable moments. The film blends Hollywood-style action comedy with African culture, international locations and a globally influenced soundtrack. An international production with African roots Boyz Trip is executive produced by Alan Key and Kyle Scott under the banner of KeyScott Entertainment, an international film and television production company headquartered in Brisbane, Australia. The film is directed by Kyle Scott, an American filmmaker and executive producer whose international production experience spans more than 41 countries across six continents. The production team includes: Executive producers: Alan Key and Kyle Scott Director: Kyle Scott Lead producer: Autumn Bailey-Ford Co-producers: Sarsha Venord and Jamez T. Associate producers: Ama K. Abebrese, Lya Castillo and Shayla Hill Global theatrical release and international premieres Boyz Trip is being prepared for an international theatrical rollout in 2027, with official release date announcements expected in early 2027. The production is planning premiere events in five international markets: Cape Town, South Africa Atlanta, Georgia, USA London, England Los Angeles, California, USA Brisbane, Australia Further announcements regarding the film’s theatrical distribution, official soundtrack, music releases and promotional activities are expected as the production approaches its 2027 launch. About KeyScott Entertainment KeyScott Entertainment is an international film, television and music production company based in Brisbane, Australia, focused on developing commercially driven entertainment for global audiences. Through its expanding music division, the company is developing original soundtracks, music publishing opportunities, artist collaborations and new platforms for bringing international musical talent into film and television. The upcoming release of Boyz Trip and its associated soundtrack forms part of the company’s broader vision to connect storytelling, music and culture across international markets.

title: A warehouse by day, homes by night: Russian jet drones keep hitting Kharkiv
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); A Russian jet-powered drone set homes on fire in Kharkiv’s Osnovianskyi district during the night, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) reported . A small child was among the people hurt. Around 13:00 on 28 October, another Russian drone hit the same district, starting a fire, killing one person and injuring two, Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said . Of the 88 Shahed-type drones Russia launched from 18:00 on 27 October, 38 were jet-powered, the Air Force reported . By its preliminary count at 08:00, defenses had downed or jammed 31 of those 38. Several drones were still in the air. Russia also fired an Iskander-M or S-400 ballistic missile from Taganrog. Even so, Russian weapons hit eight locations, and debris fell on two more. One strike, a casualty count that shifted Kharkiv Oblast head Oleh Syniehubov reported a drone strike on the district at 22:42 on 27 October. At 23:12, he clarified that a child hurt in the strike had acute stress reaction. At 23:39, he listed four people hurt: women aged 32 and 65, a 56-year-old man, and a 4-year-old boy. Three went to hospital. Eight minutes later, he added that a 65-year-old woman had acute stress reaction. His morning summary of the day’s strikes lists two 65-year-old women in Kharkiv, one wounded and one with acute stress. Aftermath of the strike on Kharkiv. Photo: State Emergency Service of Ukraine in Kharkiv Oblast The SES put the number of people hurt at five, including the child. Rescuers said a jet-powered drone struck the area, starting a 2,500 m² fire. Kharkiv’s last two days The Osnovianskyi fire was part of a run of Russian strikes on Kharkiv and the area around it. On the evening of 26 October, Russian multiple rocket launchers hit the city’s Novobavarskyi district, killing two people and hurting four. That night, jet drones struck three places in Kharkiv district, which surrounds the city. One hit, in the settlement of Vilshany, left people hurt. The SES counted three injured that night. Explore further Russia strikes publishing house warehouse in Kharkiv on Ukrainian Language Day, adding to a campaign against Ukrainian literature and culture During the day on 27 October, another Russian jet drone hit a warehouse in the city’s Slobidskyi district. Preliminary reports showed no casualties. Drones also hit the Shevchenkivskyi district that afternoon, wounding one person, Terekhov said . Another hit damaged an administrative building in the Kholodnohirskyi district, he added . Hours later came the strike on Osnovianskyi. Across Kharkiv Oblast, 14 people were hurt over the past day, including a child, Syniehubov’s morning summary shows. In Osnovianskyi, rescuers were again working under the threat of repeat strikes. Hours later, Ukraine shows photos to US senators

Meta has launched a “tamagotchi-style” pet game called Waddle World, with virtual creatures that chat with users and create doodles to illustrate conversations.
According to its Apple and Play Store listings, the “16-bit pet care game” is not really a game, but “a daily journal disguised as a pet.” Users should talk, not type, with their pets, the description says, as well as play “cozy games” like stacking groceries or word games. The Play store description says:
A little friend that listens. A cozy world that’s yours. Waddle World is a cozy 16-bit world where your pixel pet lives. Hatch a virtual pet, visit whenever you like, and let it get to know you. No pressure, no streaks to protect, no scores to chase — just a warm little escape in the cracks of our day.
The app, noticed by social media consultant Matt Navarra, is listed as free and only available to adults in the Philippines. The cutesy, 16-bit pets come as Meta pushes a sickeningly sweet mascot and small Charm gadgets for its Muse AI agent .
Meta also quietly launched an AI fashion app called Style Sketch , which Navarra says is only available in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. We were not able to verify the location restrictions ourselves.
It’s not clear whether Meta plans to release Waddle World or Style Sketch in the US or elsewhere. We’ve reached out to Meta for more information about these apps and their availability.

title: Athens Students March to Commemorate October 28 Anniversary
body: Athens marked Greece’s October 28 national anniversary on Wednesday with a student parade through the city centre, attended by representatives of the country’s political, state, military and religious leadership. Students from schools across the Municipality of Athens marched along the capital’s central streets in favourable weather, accompanied by the Municipality of Athens Philharmonic Orchestra. Each participating school was represented by a selected group led by a flag-bearer and five flag escorts. The parade honoured the anniversary of the historic “Ohi” (“No”), commemorating Greece’s refusal to accept Italy’s ultimatum in 1940 and remembering those who fought for the country’s freedom. Athens’ October 28 anniversary events The commemorations began at 06:47 with a ceremonial gun salute from Lycabettus Hill, while musical units from the Armed Forces and security services performed the traditional morning reveille. At 08:00, officials raised the Greek flag on the Acropolis. An hour later, at 10:00, Archbishop Ieronymos of Athens and All Greece led the official doxology at the Metropolitan Cathedral of Athens. Representatives of the political leadership and public authorities then laid wreaths at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Syntagma Square. Those who laid wreaths included Parliament Speaker Nikitas Kaklamanis, Education Minister Sofia Zacharaki, New Democracy MP Angelos Syrigos, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas and PASOK representative Dimitris Mantzos. Zoe Konstantopoulou, leader of the Course of Freedom party, had also visited Syntagma Square earlier. title: Four Killed, 16 Injured In Lagos Road Accident
body: Four people have been reported killed, while 16 others were injured in an accident on Alaro City Bridge after a truck carrying a container overturned on a passenger bus at Berger Bridge, inward Eleko, along the Ibeju-Lekki Expressway in Lagos. The accident occurred in the early hours of Wednesday, according to the Lagos State Emergency Management Agency (LASEMA). While providing further details, the Agency noted that the articulated truck conveying a 20-foot container with an unknown registration number and a Toyota Hiace with registration number GME-589 ZU collided due to overspeeding, with the truck ascending the bridge at high speed, losing control, and overturning onto the bus. According to the Permanent Secretary of LASEMA, Dr. Olufemi Damilola Oke-Osanyintolu, they received a distress call regarding the fatal accident, and the ‘Beta Whales Team’ from Epe Base was deployed to the scene immediately. LASEMA also noted that the impact of the collision was severe. “The impact was severe and tragically resulted in the loss of four (4)adult males who were confirmed dead at the scene, while sixteen (16)other adult males sustained varying degrees of injuries. The Agency said the recovery operation is ongoing, and traffic management measures have been deployed to ensure safety. LASEMA towing truck involved in the accident Reacting to the development, the Lagos State Government commiserated with the families of the deceased and wished the injured victims a speedy recovery. Another truck accident was also reported around Vetland School, inward Agege Pen Cinema along Old Abeokuta Road at around 4:09 am, with the Tiger Team from C3 Base responding to the accident. The agency said the team observed a truck with registration number KTU-940XT which had rammed into a solar-powered streetlight pole before mounting the road median and obstructing vehicular movement as a result of reckless driving. According to the agency, they immediately implemented traffic diversion to prevent secondary incidents and to ease movement. “With the arrival of the Agency’s heavy-duty recovery equipment, Elephant, the affected truck was successfully recovered and conveyed to Abattoir Police Station for further investigation and safekeeping. The roadway has since been cleared and reopened for normal vehicular movement”. LASEMA also reported another accident at Igando along LASU-Igando road at Lanre Bus stop involving a DAF Truck with registration number SMK 795 XY which collided with a Toyota Corolla with registration number AKD 169 EA. They said, “Information gathered at the scene indicated that while a broken-down truck on the other side of the road had caused traffic build-up, the DAF Truck driving against traffic collided with the Corolla, blocking half of the road inward to Igando”. However, the agency recorded no loss of life, but the driver of the Corolla sustained a minor head injury, was taken to Igando General Hospital by his associate. The agency noted that the Corolla has been towed to Igando Police Station, “While the Agency’s heavy-duty equipment, Super Metro, has been deployed to recover the DAF Truck to a lay-by to fully restore traffic flow. The operation is ongoing”. The post Four Killed, 16 Injured In Lagos Road Accident appeared first on Channels Television .

title: SBU detains 2 collaborators wanted for aiding enemy in occupied Kherson
body:
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) has detained two enemy accomplices who cooperated with the occupiers during the capture of Kherson and, following de-occupation, attempted to evade criminal responsibility, the SBU reported.
On its Telegram channel on Wednesday, the SBU noted that based on evidence collected by the Ukrainian special service, both perpetrators were sentenced in absentia to prison terms in 2025 and 2026 and placed on the wanted list. Following their detention, both convicts were delivered to places of sentence execution.
"One of the convicts is a local resident who, during the temporary occupation of the regional center, voluntarily joined the regional 'branch of Russian Railways' created by the Rashists," the agency specified.
According to the report, this perpetrator was appointed head of the "signal and communications distance" department, and in this "post," he participated in organizing rail service for the needs of Russian armed formations on the southern front.
For this purpose, according to the SBU, the individual recruited personnel and supervised repairs of damaged sections of fiber-optic lines and communications equipment.
"After the liberation of Kherson, the Rashist accomplice fled to the temporarily occupied left bank of the region, where he subsequently joined the Communist Party of Russia and ran for local occupation authorities. After an unsuccessful attempt to obtain a 'deputy mandate,' the collaborator left for an EU country," the report states.
During an attempt to return to Ukraine, SBU employees detained the convict directly at the state border of Ukraine.
Another collaborator, according to the SBU, was detained by Security Service officers in Kherson: a local taxi driver who, during the occupation of Kherson, took a job at the "Russian Federal Penal Correction Service."
"In this pseudo-institution, he was appointed 'junior inspector of the security department' and granted the 'rank of private of internal service.' Carrying out the occupiers' instructions, the perpetrator guarded cells in the prison seized by invaders, where Rashists held members of the resistance movement," the statement reads.
It was further established that, attempting to evade justice, the collaborator changed his place of residence and hid from law enforcement officers.
However, SBU employees established his location and detained him at his temporary residence.
Based on the SBU's evidence base, one of the perpetrators was sentenced to 13 years of imprisonment with property confiscation, while the other was sentenced to 12 years of imprisonment with property confiscation.
Their crimes are qualified under two articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine: Part 7 of Article 111-1 (collaborative activity) and Part 1 of Article 111-2 (aiding the aggressor state).
"Currently, both convicts have been delivered to places of sentence execution," the SBU emphasized.
The investigation was conducted by SBU employees in Kherson and Zakarpattia regions under the procedural guidance of the Zakarpattia and Kherson regional prosecutor's offices.

title: Greece Showcases New Weapons Systems at Thessaloniki Parade (VID)
body: Greece showcased new weapons systems, advanced air-defence platforms and domestically developed military technologies at the major military parade in Thessaloniki on Tuesday, October 28, marking Greece’s national anniversary. The parade began at 11:00 on Megalou Alexandrou Avenue, attended by President of the Republic Konstantinos Tasoulas, Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis and the country’s political and military leadership. The new systems made their first appearance at the parade, attracting particular attention to Greece’s multilayered Achilles’ Shield air-defence initiative and technologies developed by the Hellenic Navy and the Hellenic Aerospace Industry (HAI). The displays highlighted the transformation of the Greek Armed Forces through modern technology, unmanned platforms, electronic warfare capabilities and advanced systems designed to detect and counter aerial and maritime threats. Defence Minister Nikos Dendias has linked the modernisation drive to the government’s Agenda 2030, which aims to strengthen Greece’s deterrence capabilities, introduce new technologies and develop the country’s domestic defence industry. Dendias has also pointed to the new force structure, long-term defence procurement planning, cyber defence, autonomous systems, reserve-force strengthening and domestic innovation as key elements in building what he has described as the strongest Armed Forces in the history of the modern Greek state. New air-defence and missile systems Among the most prominent displays were the DRONE DOME command-and-control vehicle, the SPYDER and BARAK MX air-defence systems, and the STUNNER interceptor associated with the DAVID’S SLING system. The DRONE DOME platform supports signals intelligence, image intelligence and counter-drone operations. Depending on its configuration, it can interfere with GPS signals and communications, image transmission and navigation systems used by hostile drones and other targets. Its cameras and radar displays also help operators build an electronic picture of the battlefield. The SPYDER mobile, all-weather air-defence system features 360-degree radar coverage and an AESA radar designed to detect and track aerial threats. It uses DERBY and PYTHON missiles and can engage targets at short and medium ranges, according to the system specifications presented. The BARAK MX system can deploy different interceptor missiles against a range of threats, including aircraft, helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles, cruise missiles and tactical ballistic missiles. Its missiles use active guidance, with radar activation during the final stage of flight. The parade also featured a missile resupply vehicle carrying STUNNER interceptors associated with DAVID’S SLING. The STUNNER uses a hit-to-kill mechanism, destroying its target through direct impact rather than a conventional explosive warhead. Its guidance system combines electro-optical and infrared sensors with radar. Domestic drones and unmanned ground vehicles Greece also presented several domestically developed unmanned systems designed for surveillance, reconnaissance, logistics and combat support. The ANEMOGIANNIS unmanned surface vessel (USV), designed and built in Greece, can carry out maritime surveillance and attack missions against hostile naval targets. It uses electro-optical and infrared sensors, autonomous navigation and satellite and radio communications. The vessel can reach speeds of up to 75 km/h and carry a 50-kilogram warhead. The ANTΕOS unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) supports logistics, casualty evacuation, surveillance and reconnaissance. Its six-wheel design can carry a payload of up to 600 kilograms and operate for up to eight hours. It can also serve as a communications platform or weapons carrier. The AGEMA is a fully amphibious unmanned ground vehicle designed for difficult terrain, including rivers, lakes, swamps and flooded areas. Its potential roles include search and rescue, cargo transport and route surveillance using thermal cameras, supported by artificial intelligence and advanced autonomous functions. The domestically developed ARPYIA is a mini-cruise, one-way attack unmanned aerial system designed for precision missions. It can follow a programmed route autonomously and fly at low altitude, while its low radar signature makes detection more difficult. The parade also featured a mobile drone-production unit capable of manufacturing first-person-view (FPV) drones in the field. The systems, developed by military technical units, can operate during both day and night. Surveillance aircraft and battlefield intelligence Several unmanned aircraft demonstrated Greece’s growing emphasis on real-time intelligence and surveillance. The V-BAT is a vertical take-off and landing aircraft designed to provide operational forces with real-time intelligence. It can remain airborne for up to 12 hours and operate at distances exceeding 200 kilometres, supporting extended surveillance and reconnaissance missions. The French-made PATROLLER unmanned aerial vehicle provides long-range surveillance, target recognition and intelligence-gathering capabilities. Its electro-optical and infrared sensors allow it to transmit information in real time and support operations across land and maritime areas. The ARCHYTAS, developed through cooperation between the Hellenic Naval Academy, the National Technical University of Athens’ School of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Greek private-sector companies, can take off and land vertically. It is designed for surveillance and reconnaissance missions from land bases and Navy vessels. The Navy also presented the A-900 vertical take-off and landing unmanned aircraft, which can operate from fleet units or land bases and transmit a detailed surface picture in real time. The Camcopter S-100, manufactured by Austria’s Schiebel, is expected to operate initially from the Navy’s new FDI-class frigates. Its capabilities include detecting threats and transmitting an over-the-horizon picture to command centres, supporting engagement decisions at extended ranges. Electronic warfare and counter-drone systems The M1117 electronic warfare vehicle has been adapted for electronic surveillance. It carries a high-performance infrared camera, a high-gain data antenna and a drone that extends its intelligence-gathering and reconnaissance range. Real-time battlefield information helps commanders make faster operational decisions. Greece also displayed the KENTAVROS counter-drone system, developed through cooperation between the Hellenic Centre for Defence Innovation and HAI. The system can detect and neutralise hostile unmanned aircraft and has undergone operational testing aboard Greek Navy frigates in the Red Sea as part of the European Union’s ASPIDES operation. The HYPERION counter-drone system, which HAI is developing, has entered advanced testing. Designed for installation on ships or land bases, it aims to provide integrated detection and neutralisation of hostile drones. The Navy’s wider unmanned operations also include surface and underwater platforms. These systems can work together with crewed assets and, in certain configurations, operate in coordinated groups to support maritime surveillance and offensive missions. Artillery and armoured vehicles The parade included the PULS multiple-launch rocket system, a modern rocket-artillery platform with a stated range of up to 300 kilometres. Its long-range strike capability and rapid deployment are intended to strengthen the Greek Armed Forces’ ability to engage targets at a distance. The Stryker M1126 eight-wheeled armoured vehicle also appeared in the parade. Designed primarily to transport infantry, it can carry up to nine personnel and accommodate a remotely operated weapon station armed with a .50-calibre machine gun or a 40 mm Mk 19 grenade launcher. The related M1296 Dragoon variant carries a 30 mm cannon. HMMWV Humvee vehicles equipped with drone operators demonstrated how the Armed Forces are integrating small unmanned aircraft into surveillance, reconnaissance and attack operations. Naval unmanned vessels and underwater systems The Hellenic Navy showcased several systems supporting its transition towards a fleet that combines crewed vessels with unmanned platforms. The domestically designed PYRPOLITIS unmanned surface vessel, developed by the Navy, measures five metres and can reach speeds of up to 40 knots. It is designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, anti-surface warfare and one-way attack missions. Its equipment includes electro-optical systems, surface radar, communications and navigation sensors. The Navy also presented the CORSAIR, an autonomous surface vessel developed by US company Saronic. It can operate autonomously or under human control and supports maritime surveillance, intelligence gathering and broader naval operations. The VICTA special-operations craft combines the characteristics of a high-speed surface vessel and a submersible. It is designed to transport special forces covertly into hostile areas while limiting detection by radar and thermal cameras. It can carry a crew of two and six additional personnel, reach 40 knots on the surface and operate underwater at speeds of up to eight knots, with a stated diving depth of 30 metres. For mine-countermeasure missions, the Navy displayed the Italian-made PLUTINO and PLUTO GIGAS underwater vehicles. PLUTINO is designed to locate and neutralise naval mines, particularly in shallow water. PLUTO GIGAS supports operations at greater depths and can use specialised explosive charges or cutting and trapping tools to disable submerged mines. The display also included Seahake Mod 4 heavy torpedoes, manufactured in Germany by Atlas Elektronik. Designed for submarine launch, they use fibre-optic guidance to allow operators to update targeting information during their approach to a target. The Navy’s ROTINOR dive scooters provide underwater demolition teams with a quiet, fast means of reaching operational areas. Their electric propulsion and underwater navigation systems support covert movement. Communications and emergency-response equipment The Armed Forces also presented mobile communications and command systems designed to support military operations and disaster response. The AMPHIKTYON mobile base communications station, installed in a Mercedes-Benz Sprinter van, can restore or extend communications in areas affected by natural or technological disasters. It provides connectivity for deployed personnel and affected residents when local infrastructure fails. The DEFKALION mobile command centre supports the coordination of disaster-response operations. Built on a MAN 6×6 vehicle, it includes work and meeting rooms, modern radio communications, satellite connectivity and access to military data networks. It can communicate with land, sea and air assets and coordinate with civilian emergency services. Two drones and a thermal and optical observation camera provide live imagery to military command centres. A mobile first-aid station was also displayed. The self-contained unit carries modern medical equipment and can deploy rapidly to provide emergency treatment and operational support to military units. The METOIKOS communications system, designed and assembled by the Hellenic Air Force’s telecommunications and electronics facilities, provides a flexible communications hub. It supports satellite, microwave, 4G/5G LTE and wired IP links, and can operate independently for up to 13 hours using its onboard generator. Together, the systems displayed in Thessaloniki underscored Greece’s drive to modernise its Armed Forces through advanced air defence, unmanned technologies, domestic defence production and more resilient battlefield communications.
