title: Iran ranks among world’s top 5 countries in eye stem cell
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iran has been ranked among the world’s top five countries in eye stem cell transplantation with a success rate exceeding 85%.
Head of the Iranian Ophthalmology Association Hamed Ghassemi revealed the news on Wednesday, emphasizing, “The treatment is used for patients with severe eye injuries caused by chemical and thermal burns.”
Regarding the costs and success degree of eye stem cell transplants in the country, he stated that costs are fully covered by the government, and the procedure has a success rate of over 85 percent.

title: KNU community shares vision for university's future – rector-elect Kopiika
body:
Valeriy Kopiika, the elected rector of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv, stated that winning in the first round represents a major responsibility for him.
"Already in the first round, our university community elected me rector of Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv by a majority of votes. For me, this is a great honor and an even greater responsibility. Thank you for your trust and for the fact that our vision for the university's future has become shared," Kopiika wrote on Facebook.
He also addressed those who voted for other candidates, noting that their thoughts and ideas are extremely valuable to him. "We heard a great deal from you: interesting ideas, sound proposals, candid words, painful questions, and accurate remarks. Each of these thoughts will become part of our shared plans. And there are many plans, so come forward, propose, let us create together!" the elected rector added.
In turn, former KNU Vice-Rector for Research Hanna Tolstanova, who received 18.62% of the vote, thanked everyone who supported her candidacy. "Your trust, support, and every warm word give incredible strength! Enormous gratitude to my team and like-minded people—everyone who was by my side all this time, helped, believed, and brought our common result closer. You are my main pride and inspiration!" she wrote on social media.
Additionally, former KNU Vice-Rector for International Cooperation Kseniia Smyrnova, who received 4.16% of the vote, noted that the academic community's choice places responsibility for the future development trajectory of higher education. "I want to thank the team of like-minded people, to thank those who were ready to move according to a vision consistent with shared values!" she wrote.
As reported, in the elections for rector of KNU, which took place on October 27, Chairman of the Academic Council Valeriy Kopiika won in the first round, receiving 51.74% of the vote.
Under the law On Higher Education, the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine must sign a five-year contract with the elected university rector no later than one month from the day of election.

title: Gunmen kill three women, abduct child in Twic East
body: Three women were killed, an 11-month-old baby was injured and a two-year-old child was abducted in an attack by armed men in Twic East County, Jonglei State, on Tuesday, the county commissioner said. James Magok Mabiei, the caretaker county commissioner, told Radio Tamazuj that the women were transporting dried fish to Panyagoor, the county headquarters, when they were attacked in Apiir, Lith Payam, at about 4 p.m. Mabiei said he suspected the attackers had come from the neighbouring Greater Pibor Administrative Area (GPAA). “Yesterday at 4 p.m., some women were attacked in the area of Apiir in Lith Payam while attempting to transport their dried fish to Panyagoor,” he said. “Three women were killed, an 11-month-old baby was injured, and a two-year-old child was abducted.” He condemned the attack and called on authorities in the GPAA to arrest those responsible. “We condemn these barbaric acts and appeal to our counterparts in the GPAA to have these culprits arrested. Targeting innocent road users threatens peaceful coexistence,” Mabiei said. Several attempts to reach Jacob Werchum Jouk, the caretaker GPAA information minister, for comment were unsuccessful. Kenya Mach, an activist with the Jonglei State Women Association, also condemned the attack and called on the government to take action to improve security. “Women are breadwinners. Attacks on businesswomen destroy livelihoods and affect their ability to pay for their children’s needs, including school fees. The government should address these security crises so that our roads become safer again,” she said. The post Gunmen kill three women, abduct child in Twic East appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: Flavio Bolsonaro On Way To Ecuador From Argentina After Fleeing Brazil
body: Defeated right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro was on his way to Ecuador after fleeing Brazil, Argentina’s government said on Wednesday. Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s runoff election to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on Sunday, entered Argentina on Tuesday night before boarding a flight to Ecuador, the country’s National Directorate of Migration said on X. The 45-year-old entered Argentina “with valid travel documents and no legal impediment,” it added, despite a court order banning his exit. Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters boarded “a private flight operated by the company Baires Fly S.A. bound for the city of Guayaquil, Ecuador,” the government agency said. According to data from the Flightradar24 website, the flight took off just after midnight (0300 GMT) on Wednesday from the Argentine town of Puerto Iguazu in the country’s northeast. Baires Fly did not immediately respond to AFP’s request for comment. US media citing anonymous sources had earlier reported that Bolsonaro had arrived in the United States on Tuesday. The US State Department said it would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family but did not confirm their travel plans. Brazil’s Supreme Court banned Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to hand over his passports. He is under investigation for alleged corruption and money laundering, and his election loss is also set to lose parliamentary immunity. A police source told AFP that Bolsonaro’s Brazilian and diplomatic passports had been cancelled, but the senator has held Italian nationality since 2023, according to an Italian parliamentary document seen by AFP. ‘Shameful’ Reports of Bolsonaro’s exit from Brazil came as a shock to his political camp. “We still don’t have any news about his whereabouts,” Bolsonaro’s campaign manager Rogerio Marinho told reporters in Brasilia on Tuesday. “I received a text message from him this morning, where he said he would let some time pass today and then would talk with us, and that was it,” he said. “That was the only communication we had.” Bolsonaro said in a video posted on Instagram a day earlier that he “never had any intention of leaving the country” and the ban on his exit was a scare tactic. Lula, who won the election with 51.8 percent of the vote, called fleeing the country a “shameful” act. “A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide,” he said in Brasilia during his 81st birthday celebration. Following his loss, Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the result, citing the decision to extend polling hours over transportation difficulties that prevented some citizens from voting. Lula had requested the extension, as had Bolsonaro, over bad weather in parts of the country. US President Donald Trump, a close ally of Flavio’s father and Brazil’s former leader Jair Bolsonaro, said that the elections were “rigged.” All bets were on a Bolsonaro win after he came out on top in the first round of elections earlier this month. He campaigned on a pledge to liberate his father, who is under house arrest for coup-plotting after his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never conceded defeat and left the country on the eve of his rival’s inauguration, only returning to Brazil three months later. The post Flavio Bolsonaro On Way To Ecuador From Argentina After Fleeing Brazil appeared first on Channels Television .

title: No confirmation yet regarding Putin-Trump-Xi summit on APEC sidelines — Russian MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. There is no final confirmation yet as to whether a summit meeting of the leaders of Russia, the United States, and China - Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump, and Xi Jinping - will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said.
"At the moment, our Chinese friends - who are the hosts of this summit - are working on it. I say 'if' such a summit takes place, because there is no final decision or confirmation yet. But should it happen, the agenda would naturally include various topics agreed upon by the three states. If any of these topics were deemed unsuitable by one of the parties, it would not be included on the agenda," he said in response to a question on the matter.
When asked whether the topic of arms control would be addressed during the summit, Rudenko clarified that the agenda itself is still under discussion.
"There is no definitive confirmation yet that the summit will take place. Yes, there is a possibility, but for now, we are speaking of it strictly as a possibility," he added.
Previously, Trump suggested that a trilateral meeting involving himself, Putin, and Xi could be held in China. Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that during a meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Putin discussed the potential for a trilateral meeting with Trump and Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which is scheduled to take place in Shenzhen on November 18-19.

title: Ukraine has found a way to respond to Russian attacks on data centers, Zelensky says
body:
Zelensky made the remarks in an interview with The Sun, as reported on his official Telegram channel, according to Ukrinform.
“Many people have not seen that Russia has been attacking our data infrastructure and cyberspace for a long time. Then we found a way to undermine Russia’s strategy and respond to its attacks on our data centers,” he said.
He then said, “This is where we are different. Ukraine is more technologically advanced. The Russians have attacked our data centers so many times, but we have continued to have mobile communications and internet access because we have decentralized and advanced digital infrastructure”.
The president emphasized that “our retaliatory strikes are more painful for Russia because its systems are much more centralized. They have a different strategy. They have a lot of air defense systems and simply protect what they have. We do not have as many air defense systems — we are facing a shortage. That is precisely why we have decentralized everything, not just data. But we always try to respond, and we do so only after Russian attacks against us.”
As reported, Zelensky has said that Ukrainian forces will not target ships carrying Russian diesel fuel bound for the United States.

title: Ukraine lacks unified vision for postwar reconstruction – IMF Alternate Executive Director Rashkovan
body:
Funding for Ukraine's recovery following Russian aggression, which the World Bank currently estimates at $588 billion, should be viewed as part of a broader model and institutional architecture for reconstruction, with a vision for the postwar country being a key element, Vladyslav Rashkovan, Ukraine's Alternate Executive Director at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), believes.
"This vision must be shared and supported by the majority of Ukrainians. Frankly speaking, we do not yet have such a vision," he said in an interview with Interfax-Ukraine on the sidelines of the Annual Meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank Group, held in Bangkok on October 12–18.
Rashkovan said that the IMF does not develop such a vision because the Fund's task is to ensure current macrofinancial stability: preventing high inflation, sharp currency depreciation, and crises in the banking sector, the budget and the balance of payments.
"Structural reforms are being implemented for this purpose, but overall, this is merely a foundation for further development. Some criticize Ukraine's IMF program for lacking ambition. But its purpose is to sustain our resilience," Ukraine's representative at the Fund explained.
According to him, the Future Economy initiative, launched by the Ukrainian government and the Ministry of Economy, is intended to help shape a broader vision. The IMF participates in the initiative as an analyst rather than a strategist. "The World Bank provides more active assistance, but the key role belongs to the Ukrainian authorities and society," said Rashkovan, who has been working on issues related to Ukraine's reconstruction for many years.
He added that an interesting discussion is also underway around the Prosperity Plan: what Ukraine should become after the war and how much funding and investment will be needed for it to become a new European tiger.
"However, neither this plan nor the Future Economy initiative is a Marshall Plan at this stage. They are more like ideas that need to be developed. Money does not solve everything: an institutional architecture is needed that can sustain reconstruction over several political cycles in Ukraine and partner countries," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
He added that Ukrainian ownership of the process is one of the key principles on which reconstruction should be built. "No one will take better care of us than we do ourselves, and no one will shape a vision for Ukraine's future on our behalf," Rashkovan explained.
The expert said that this vision must be translated into strategies. "We already have many regional and sectoral strategies, perhaps even too many. They need to be aligned. And again, it is important not merely to have strategies but to live by them. All of them must contribute to realizing a shared vision," the IMF's alternate executive director said.
In his view, reconstruction is not a task that can be completed in a day or a few months; it will take decades, if not generations. Therefore, it must be planned, and the necessary institutions must be established in advance.
In addition to the IMF program focused on macrofinancial stability, without which long-term investment planning is impossible, he also cited security guarantees as a prerequisite for reconstruction.
At the same time, Ukraine's representative at the IMF believes that the end of the war is not a mandatory condition for beginning reconstruction.
"We are already rebuilding a great deal despite the war. Not on the scale we would like, but billions of dollars have already been spent on recovery," he said.
Among the other elements of the reconstruction model, he also cited European integration, noting that if Ukraine is moving toward the European Union, reconstruction should be planned in accordance with EU standards.
As for financing, Rashkovan noted that a considerable number of instruments are already available. These include the Pillar 2 investment component under the Ukraine Facility; the EUR 1 billion European Flagship Fund for the Reconstruction of Ukraine, managed by Dragon Capital and Amber Infrastructure; projects supported by the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC), resources from the European Investment Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD); and the Co-Investment Platform, which brings together 19 development finance institutions from different countries.
"All of these are working for Ukraine's benefit, but we are still far from the scale required. We need to understand that the probability of all $588 billion coming from public funds provided by international partners is zero. Historical experience shows that 75–85% will come from private sources," Ukraine's representative at the IMF said.
He clarified that private investment typically arrives significantly later than donor funding, which is why Ukraine is currently relying more heavily on donor resources.
Finally, Rashkovan said the importance of structural reforms to attract private capital, including protection of property rights and the continuation of land and anti-corruption reforms. He recalled that the Czech Republic and Poland attracted most of their private investment before joining NATO and the European Union, driven by strong investor expectations.
"If the world expects Ukraine to join the EU and we maintain the pace of reforms, the same could happen here, especially amid friendshoring – the relocation of production and procurement to geopolitically friendly countries," the expert believes.

title: Six-fingered ‘trolls’ working for Georgia’s authorities: Myth Detector identifies 445 fake accounts
body: Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia The organisation Myth Detector has identified a new network of so-called “trolls” comprising 445 fake accounts. The findings follow monitoring of the Facebook pages of TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2, whose editorial policies align with the government’s agenda. The accounts operate in a co-ordinated manner, liking posts by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili. The posts cover topics including bans on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and threats to the country’s sovereignty. Myth Detector believes the aim is to create the impression of widespread public support for the government’s rhetoric. In an earlier investigation, the same organisation identified 434 similar profiles. Myth Detector concludes that the emergence of new accounts indicates that the practice is continuing. Pro-government media in Georgia use fake accounts in campaign against ex-PM On 13 January, Irakli Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in prison on charges of “legalising illicit proceeds”. Monitoring revealed several common characteristics across the network of fake accounts: identical profile pictures; anatomical and geographical inconsistencies typical of AI-generated images; recurring first and last names; and similar patterns of behaviour on social media. According to Myth Detector , most of these accounts were created within a two-day period. A total of 329 profiles were registered on 25 August 2026 and another 109 on 26 August. Of the 445 accounts identified, 316 use AI-generated profile pictures. The remaining 129 feature images of public figures, landscapes, posters or photographs belonging to other social media users. The organisation says some of the newly discovered accounts overlap with profiles identified in October by the non-governmental organisation ISFED. What do the fake accounts like? According to Myth Detector’s analysis, the suspicious Facebook accounts were mobilised around posts published by TV channels Imedi and Rustavi 2. Their activity focused primarily on political statements by Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili and Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze. Co-ordinated likes were particularly noticeable under posts about a possible ban on opposition parties, Western interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and alleged threats to the country’s sovereignty from Western institutions. The fake accounts actively liked posts by Irakli Kobakhidze and Kakha Kaladze concerning a lawsuit against opposition parties filed with the Constitutional Court. Co-ordinated activity was particularly evident under a Rustavi 2 post in which Georgia’s Foreign Ministry described critical comments by EU representatives about a possible ban on opposition parties as interference in Georgia’s domestic affairs and an attempt to put pressure on the Constitutional Court. Accounts mobilised around statements by Shalva Papuashvili supported the argument that foreign interference threatens freedom and democracy in Georgia. Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under posts criticising the methods used to disperse protests in France and other European cities, drawing parallels with the situation in Georgia. The accounts’ activity is not limited to engaging with posts by senior officials. According to Myth Detector , co-ordinated likes also appeared under posts by pro-government philosopher Zaza Shatirishvili. He is one of the leading ideologues of the ruling team and the anti-Western platforms associated with it. His rhetoric closely echoes the narratives of the ruling party and its affiliated People’s Power movement. Co-ordinated likes were also recorded under a post showing Bidzina Ivanishvili attending a party event, as well as under material covering a statement by Georgia’s Foreign Ministry. Fake accounts involved in campaign against Duchenne muscular dystrophy drugs in Georgia — Myth Detector The investigation identified 75 fake accounts AI-generated images and identity theft According to the investigation, a significant proportion of the fake accounts attempt to imitate real people’s profiles. They use photographs and biographical details of people with different ages, professions and interests, creating the impression of a diverse group of government supporters. The profiles list a wide range of employers, including municipal and government institutions, banks, insurance companies, microfinance organisations and major media outlets such as Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and even the Pirveli TV channel. In some cases, the stated place of employment does not match other information in the profile. For example, an account registered under the name Levan Kavtaradze features a photograph of a man standing beside a car during the grape harvest, yet lists the perfume and cosmetics retailer Voulez-Vous as his employer. Keti Giorgadze’s profile lists Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty as her employer, while the accounts of Temo Khitarishvili and Nutsa Simonia name the news service of Pirveli TV. According to Hive Moderation , there is more than a 90% probability that the photographs found in the 445 accounts were generated using artificial intelligence. In some cases, the probability reaches 100%. The images contain anatomical defects, inconsistencies in the surrounding environment and distorted text — all characteristic signs of AI-generated content. In some pictures, the number or shape of fingers looks unnatural, while others show altered architectural details, logos and national symbols. A photograph posted by an account under the name Simoniko Janashia shows a person holding a cup with their left hand, which has six fingers instead of five. A mark associated with images generated by the Gemini AI model is also visible in the bottom-right corner of the picture. In other examples, a hand holding a wine glass is missing its little finger, while hands appear unnaturally fused together or blended into clothing. A photograph shared by Tako Dvalishvili shows a person holding a book. However, the text on its cover is distorted: instead of the words “History of Georgia”, it displays something illegible. The organisation also identified geographical inconsistencies. Comparisons with genuine images of well-known locations in Georgia show that AI alters architectural details and surrounding landscapes, sometimes even adding structures that do not actually exist. Reproducing the visual appearance of old profiles The investigation found that some of the newly identified accounts use profile pictures that had previously appeared on accounts uncovered by Myth Detector and later removed by Facebook. In some cases, these visual similarities include identical anatomical flaws characteristic of AI-generated images. For example, photographs used in personal profiles under the names Tako Chagelia and Nia Gamkrelidze show the same finger defect previously observed in the profile picture of an account attributed to Maiko Vibliani. The investigation also identified other common patterns in the behaviour of some accounts. A total of 196 profiles had liked the Tbilisinews.ge page, 14 had liked Ai Politika and three had liked Rustavi 2. Fake accounts identified by the organisation in previous investigations had also liked the Ai Politika page. Most of the suspicious profiles have no friends at all, while some have only one or two. The investigation also uncovered accounts created in 2024 with friend lists ranging from 169 to 4,800. Fake pro-government accounts in Georgia

title: IDF kills numerous terrorists in Gaza strikes, including Oct. 7 kidnapper of Alexander Dancyg
body: The IDF struck targets in the Gaza Strip in the past week, killing multiple terrorists from the military wing of the Hamas terrorist organization, according to the military.Anas Akram Muhammad Humaida, a Nukhba commander who raided the Sufa military post during the October 7 massacre, was killed in a strike in the Khan Yunis area.In addition, terrorist Ashraf Mahmud Youssef Dahlan, a platoon commander in the East Jabalia Battalion who infiltrated Israeli territory during the October 7 massacre, was killed in the Gaza City area.Two days ago, terrorist Mahmud Othman Abdullah Alwan, a Nukhba commander in the West Jabalia Battalion, was also killed in the Gaza City area.Terrorists killed last week took part in October 7The IDF killed three terrorists on Thursday, including a Hamas Nukhba who infiltrated Kibbutz Nir Oz and took part in the abduction of Israeli civilians during the October 7th massacre, the military said on Wednesday.Ahmed Muhammad Ahmed Baraka, a Nukhba terrorist in Hamas' military wing, was killed in southern Gaza during Thursday strikes, the military announced.The terrorist was responsible for abducting Israeli civilians during the October 7 massacre, including Alexander Dancyg from Kibbutz Nir Oz, the IDF said.According to the military, he also held several hostages during the war, including Nimrod Cohen in the southern Gaza Strip.Additional terrorists killed in northern GazaThe military also announced that the other two terrorists killed were targeted in Friday strikes on northern Gaza.The IDF said that Omar Awadallah, a Nukhba platoon commander, and Moataz Mahmoud Mohammed Al-Nimr, a Nukhba terrorist, were confirmed killed during the strikes.According to the military, both terrorists were operating to "restore the Hamas terrorist organization's capabilities," while also carrying out advanced terrorist attacks against IDF soldiers and Israeli civilians.The military also said that, prior to the strike, steps were taken to mitigate harm to civilians, including the use of precision munitions and aerial surveillance.

title: Romania Orders Mobile Military Landing Radar Systems from Thales
body:
Romania’s Ministry of National Defense, through its General Directorate for Armaments, signed a contract on October 27, with a consortium comprising THALES ROMANIA SRL and THALES LAS FRANCE SAS to acquire four mobile precision approach and landing radar systems.
The contract is valued at approximately 326.5 million Romanian lei (RON) or nearly $70 million , with phased deliveries scheduled to begin in 2028.
The systems will identify and track aircraft and guide them during approach and landing in difficult weather conditions and hostile electromagnetic environments. They will support military and civil aircraft operations, day and night, and transmit information to Romanian national and NATO air command-and-control systems.
Their mobility will enable deployment at alternative locations, reducing reliance on fixed airbase infrastructure and improving operational flexibility and resilience.

title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
body:
NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.
The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.
Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”
One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.
Later in 2024, Macmillan employees were encouraged to use NOA to generate their goals for performance reviews. “We built a specialized prompt to have NOA write goals for you!” one email read.
Several Macmillan employees say NOA was unhelpful and unreliable. “It was terrible, and no one used it,” one says. WIRED spoke with multiple publishing employees for this article, including some who have since left their employers. WIRED is not naming these employees, nor the authors we interviewed, because they are concerned about professional repercussions.
In October 2025, Macmillan staff learned via a company-wide email that Chaptr would be sunsetting NOA. Since then, workers say, leadership has been attempting to integrate Google Gemini into the publishing process. Some staffers subsequently experimented with using Gemini to evaluate submission letters from literary agents, but the Gemini-generated evaluations were “useless,” according to one editor.
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, Kelly Collins, vice president of communications and community at Macmillan, says the publishing house uses Gemini for its “business” but “there has not been any directive from Macmillan leadership to use Gemini for any part of the publishing process, including to evaluate submission letters from agents.” She also says “the points shared do not accurately reflect how NOA was rolled out and communicated” but did not provide further elaboration when WIRED asked which aspects were inaccurate.
Collins notes that the company “takes a thoughtful approach to AI, focused on employee awareness and education while always keeping people front and center.”
Macmillan is usually cited as the smallest of the Big Five US book publishers based on the number of books sold each year. Its imprint Farrar, Straus and Giroux publishes literary fiction heavyweights like Sally Rooney, Yiyun Li, and Ben Lerner while Tor Books is a home for science fiction and fantasy authors John Scalzi, Martha Wells, and Nnedi Okorafor.
Since I first reported on the creep of AI in the publishing world, I’ve heard from staff at all of the Big Five who claim that executives are pushing them to use AI tools, even as Hachette, Macmillan, and Penguin Random House Verlagsgruppe (its German-language division) are suing some of the leading AI companies for copyright infringement.
At the same time, multiple bestselling Big Five authors say they’ve gone to “war” with their publishers over AI and are considering abandoning traditional publishing altogether.
At Penguin Random House (PRH), the largest of the Big Five after the 2013 merger between Penguin Books and Random House, several workers say they’ve been encouraged to use ChatGPT Enterprise in AI learning sessions, even though PRH’s German division is suing OpenAI for copyright infringement.
In February, representatives from Hay House—a new-age self-help publisher acquired by Penguin Random House in 2023—presented a slide deck to some PRH employees about how ChatGPT Enterprise had become a “core productivity, creativity, and collaboration tool” since they adopted it a year prior. One of the four return-on-investment pillars in the deck was “Creativity,” including “idea generation, content development, and storytelling innovations.”
Despite encouragement from the C-suite, all of the PRH workers WIRED spoke with say they’re avoiding ChatGPT whenever possible. “It makes it harder for us to do our jobs,” one employee says. Other staff say their managers have explicitly asked them not to use AI for creative tasks like publicity copy and cover design, which has caused some confusion.
“Penguin Random House approaches AI as we would any significant new technology,” says Claire von Schilling, executive vice president and director of corporate communications and social responsibility for the publisher, via email. “We are exploring ways it may appropriately support our work, guided by clear principles and safeguards, including protecting the intellectual property of our authors and the company and preserving the essential role of human creativity and judgment in publishing.”
Von Schilling also says that PRH’s “publishing groups and imprints have discretion to determine whether and how AI tools may be appropriate for particular workflows, including areas such as marketing, publicity, and design.”
Meanwhile, several bestselling Big Five authors say their relationships with publishers have suffered over the past year due to AI use. Combined, the Big Five authors WIRED spoke with have sold more than 30 million copies. One bestselling author says they received marketing copy that included AI-hallucinated quotes from their book, but the publisher insisted they were not AI-generated. “I was gaslit on all of it,” the author says. During a recent round of contract negotiations, another bestselling author says they could not get a single Big Five publisher to promise no AI would be used in any way on their books.
“It’s undermining the necessary sense of trust that has to exist between writers and publishers,” one author says.
“It’s also frustrating to watch publishers get these massive settlements [from] AI companies and then embrace AI to do their work,” another author says. “It feels like they’re feeding at both sides of the trough.”
Authors say cost-cutting layoffs at the Big Five have contributed to deteriorating conditions for their editors and forced some to embrace AI for survival. “We’re seeing editors not reading the material at all and using Claude to create marketing language that barely has any relation to the book,” one author says. Other authors and agents say they’ve been asked by editors to write their own plans for revisions “because the editors don’t have time to do it themselves.”
All of the authors I spoke with say they want publishers to communicate when and how they’re using AI. “The bare minimum we're asking for is disclosure,” one author says. Another wishes the Big Five “would get together and come up with a set of principles around AI that they intend to adhere to.” But some bestselling authors say their publishers’ use of AI is forcing them to consider publishing future books on their own.
“What are authors even doing with traditional publishers anymore if they’re going to outsource everything to a machine?” one bestselling author says. “Why can't an author do that themselves?”
Following WIRED's previous reporting, several high-profile authors condemned the adoption of AI tools in publishing. “I have never looked down on other publishing models (zine girly from way back) & every day, self pub looking ever more possible for future work,” Mo Ryan wrote on Bluesky. Her most recent book, Burn It Down: Power, Complicity, and a Call for Change in Hollywood, was published by HarperCollins.
John Scalzi, the sci-fi novelist who signed a 10-book deal with Macmillan’s Tor Publishing Group in 2024, wrote, “I would be EXTREMELY annoyed to discover my PR is ‘AI’-generated, and as someone bombarded with dozens of ‘AI’-generated emails daily, I assure you the stink of ‘AI’ is immediately noticable [sic] and immediately dismissible. Publishers are not doing their new books any favors in using it.”
Bestselling authors who have already accumulated huge readerships say they don’t need the institutional support of a Big Five publisher to sell copies. Brandon Sanderson, for instance, publishes some of his fantasy novels through Tor Books, an imprint of Macmillan, but raised more than $15 million in 24 hours from his readers on Kickstarter to publish four books on his own in 2022.
“Publishers have always seen authors as a bit of a nuisance, and now there’s a desire to make us obsolete,” says one bestselling Big Five author. “What’s fascinating to me is that in the process of trying to make authors obsolete by using AI, the publishers are rendering themselves obsolete.”

title: BAE Systems tests adaptable deck launcher for US Navy
body:
BAE Systems has completed the first live-fire test of its adaptable deck launcher (ADL), a deck-mounted missile launch system designed to expand missile deployment and reloading options for the US Navy.
Developed under a US Department of War (DoW) contract for the NATO Seasparrow Project Office (NSPO), the system provides the reliability of a vertical launching system (VLS) and low-cost operation by using an existing Mk 41 VLS logistics and electronics suite.
The ADL’s capability for expedited reloading at sea provides a key operational advantage by helping to ensure ships maintain high rates of fire without returning to port, according to BAE.
The ADL will enable anti-air defense and flexible maritime operations across aircraft carriers, amphibious ships and other surface combatants. The system is also optimized for unmanned warfare, offering compact configurations ideal for medium unmanned surface vessels.
Furthermore, as the mechanical design agent for the Mk 41 VLS family, BAE Systems developed the ADL for full compatibility with Evolved SeaSparrow Missile Mk 25 Quad-Pack canisters, which provide surface-to-air defence for ships against supersonic anti-ship missiles, aircraft and other aerial threats.
“The successful demonstration of the Adaptable Deck Launcher is a major milestone in our commitment to enhancing the Navy’s combat effectiveness and readiness,” said Jason Casciotti , vice president of Weapons Systems at BAE Systems.
“The ADL complements the Mk 41 VLS — the foundation of naval missile integration — by providing a capability for rapid replenishment, using standard shipboard equipment and offering the fleet additional flexibility in how it sustains combat loads at sea.”
Last year, BAE Systems was awarded a $22 million contract by the US Navy to produce missile canisters for the Mk 41 vertical launching system.

title: Court dismisses Emeka Ike’s N10bn damages suit against Wike’s aide, INEC
body: The Federal High Court in Abuja on Wednesday dismissed N10 billion rights suit filed by the Nollywood actor Emeka Ike against Lere Olayinka, Senior Special Assistant to FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). Justice Salim Ibrahim, in a judgment, upheld the preliminary objections of the respondents on the grounds that the suit was incompetent and improperly constituted. Justice Ibrahim also dismissed the main suit on the ground of lack of proof. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that Ike, who aspired to vie for the House of Representatives’ seat for AMAC/Bwari Federal Constituency, Abuja, for the 2027 general elections on the platform of the Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC), lost the bid in a primary poll. The FCT minister’s aide, through a post on X in May, was alleged to have mocked Ike by leaking his confidential voter registration details on social media. The post was said to have shown details of Ike’s voter registration transfer from Imo to the nation’s capital. Meanwhile, Ike, in the suit filed by L. T. Adeh, sued Olayinka and INEC as 1st and 2nd respondents in the suit marked FHC/ABJ/CS/1272/2026. He asked the court to declare that Olayinka’s decision to publish his database on X without his approval “amounts to gross breach and violation of the applicant’s fundamental right to privacy and the protection of personal data”. Ike argued that Section 37 of the 1999 Constitution, Article 12 of the universal declaration of human rights, and Sections 24 & 39 of the Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023 guaranteed his right to privacy and protection of personal data. The actor asked the court to declare that INEC owes him and other voters a “statutory duty of care” to protect their private data against unauthorised access. The applicant, therefore, prayed the court to award him N10 billion against Olayinka and INEC as aggravated and general damages, to be paid jointly and severally for violating his fundamental right to privacy. He sought a declaration that the press release by INEC dated June 2, in reaction to the viral publication and circulation of his personal voter information and private data on social media by Olayinka, amounts to a tacit admission of guilt and liability to him. Ike, equally, sought an order directing Olayinka to immediately retract and pull down the offensive post and publication on his social media X handle, @OlayinkaLere, containing screenshots of his personal voter information and private data. He sought an order directing him to immediately tender an unravelling apology in writing for breach and violation of his fundamental right. But responding in a separate counter-affidavit, INEC and Olayinka prayed the court to dismiss the suit in its entirety. INEC, in its response, said the issue complained about in the suit filed by Ike was neither classified, sensitive nor confidential information. The commission, in the counter affidavit deposed to by Anthonia Makwe, an Assistant Director/Data Protection Officer in the Legal Drafting and Clearance Department, said that such information is displayed and published in accordance with the Electoral Act, 2026. It stressed that the electoral body has the “statutory and constitutional power to make available information of its voters to the general public without the consent of any registered voter.” It said its “statutory responsibility includes the compilation, maintenance, display, publication, certification and management of the register of voters in accordance with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 (as amended), the Electoral Act 2026, and the National Data Protection Act 2023. It said what was alleged to be posted by Olayinka on his X handle did not emanate from the commission. “The 2nd respondent, as a data controller, has never breached its statutory duty of care, custody and protection of personal voter information and data; it owes the applicant and other voters under its secured portal and restricted database.” On his part, Olayinka, in the counter-affidavit he deposed to, said the reliefs Ike sought were in bad faith. He said the only information contained in the document he published was Ike’s name and passport photograph and that the information was already in the public domain. He said, contrary to Ike’s averment, the information he published was not only in the public domain but was not accessed through any unlawful means. Olayinka stated that he did not owe the actor any duty of care and confidentiality and did not require his consent to publish his name and passport photograph that was already in the public domain. He said Ike, who brought himself to contest election into the lower house, cannot be traumatised by the circulation of his name and passport photograph. which he personally presented to the public when seeking to contest election and as a Nollywood star. He argued that information supplied in voters’ cards is not private data because, by the provision of Section 19(1) of the Electoral Act, 2026, INEC is mandated to publish this, no later than 90 days to a general election. He said contrary to Ike’s deposition, the only information contained in the document published by him was his name and passport photograph. He said the publication was done when Ike led a team of hoodlums to the INEC office to disrupt INEC’s activities immediately after he declared his intention to contest the election. According to him, the publication was to remind him that he just transferred his voter registration area. He said it was also to draw the public attention to the statutory provision to avoid any breach of the law. He said contrary to Ike’s submission, the applicant who submitted his personal data and information to INEC and to general public when he decided to contest cannot feel unsafe and traumatised by the publication of his name and passport photograph. Olayinka said contrary to Ike’s averment, INEC admitted in its press release that “there was no external breach of its CVR database, no hacking incident and no unauthorised external access to the commissions ICT infrastructure.” He argued that the purported injury suffered by Ike was not caused by him, who is not a data controller under the Nigerian Data Protection Act, 2023, and who does not owe him any obligation to safeguard his documents. Olayinka stated that the reliefs sought, including the N10 billion, were in bad faith and “an indication that the applicant is a gold digger who wants to reap where he did not sow.” He insisted that he cannot pay damages for information that was already publicly accessible at the time of the publication. He, therefore, urged the court to dismiss the suit in the interest of justice. (NAN) The post Court dismisses Emeka Ike’s N10bn damages suit against Wike’s aide, INEC appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Thierry Henry explains Yamal joke after fans accuse him of disrespect
body: Former Arsenal and France striker Thierry Henry has explained his controversial remarks about Barcelona forward Lamine Yamal during the 2026 Ballon d’Or ceremony, insisting that he had no intention of disrespecting the young footballer. Henry, who co-hosted the awards ceremony alongside Kate Scott on Monday, faced criticism after jokingly questioning whether Yamal really wanted the Kopa Trophy, an award presented to the best young player in world football. Yamal won the trophy for the third consecutive time, but Henry’s comments sparked reactions from fans who interpreted them as a suggestion that the teenager was overly concerned about winning individual honours. Responding to the backlash in a video shared on Instagram, Henry said his remarks had been misunderstood, stressing that he was a huge admirer of the Barcelona star. “For Lamine Yamal, I wasn’t checking his ego at all. I just thought that, as the third time that he’s winning that trophy, I just asked him if that’s the one that he really wanted,” he said. The former Barcelona forward explained that he had expected Yamal to compete for the main Ballon d’Or award, which was eventually won by England captain Harry Kane. “I am a big fan of Lamine Yamal. I wasn’t checking his ego whatsoever. That you didn’t like the joke, I can understand, but please don’t do that. He’s one of the players that I will pay to watch. I love him,” Henry added. He described Yamal as an exceptional talent whose performances he enjoys watching, expressing regret that the youngster did not claim the night’s biggest prize. “Unfortunately, he didn’t win it, because he’s a hell of a player that I enjoy to watch,” he said. Henry also addressed a separate controversy involving his co-host, Scott, after viewers criticised him for making a joke about her pronunciation of the name Socrates, the late Brazilian football legend. The former France international denied disrespecting Scott, maintaining that the exchange was planned and that she was aware of the joke before it was delivered. “Kate was with me on that joke,” Henry said. “And you can ask Kate, by the way. She did it on purpose, to say Socrates. And I had to say Socrates [with a different pronunciation].” He urged critics to stop portraying the exchange as an attempt to embarrass his colleague. “Again, that you didn’t like the joke, I understand. But please stop saying that I disrespect Kate. I will never do that,” he added. The 49-year-old further clarified his comments about Kane, explaining that although he supported fellow Frenchman Kylian Mbappe, he had congratulated the England striker on winning the Ballon d’Or. Henry said he praised Kane for his dedication and work ethic, describing the striker as a deserving winner. “I just said to him [Kane], ‘You are a worthy winner. You deserve it. You are the example of what I always call: work ethic is a talent, working hard is a talent,” he said. Henry also revealed that he had called Kane “Sir Harry Kane” since the World Cup, reiterating his respect for the striker’s achievements. Concluding his response, the former Arsenal captain urged fans to stop reading disrespect into his jokes, reaffirming his admiration for Yamal and Kane and his respect for Scott. “So please, people out there. Relax. I love Harry Kane, I love Lamine Yamal. And I didn’t disrespect Kate. She was in on the joke with me. Have a good night, see you soon,” he said. The post Thierry Henry explains Yamal joke after fans accuse him of disrespect appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Russia’s largest bookstore chain says it has spent millions of rubles pulling banned books from sale. They’re shredded on camera.
body: Russia’s largest bookstore chain, Chitai-Gorod–Bukvoed, has spent about 100 million rubles in recent years pulling books that violate Russian law from sale and destroying them, the chain’s head, Alexander Brychkin, said in an interview with the Russian business news outlet RBC. “Mostly it’s the inability to return the goods to the supplier, so we have to write them off as a loss. We can’t just throw these books in the trash. They’re toxic waste. So they have to be disposed of, and that’s also at our expense. On top of that, no one compensates us for the costs of pulling them from the shelf, sending them back to the warehouse, having it all transported somehow, and then processed at the warehouse. All of this adds up to an enormous amount of work and fairly large expenses,” Brychkin said. Brychkin described how the disposal process works: “The disposal process looks like this: a service provider destroys the books on camera using an industrial shredder.” Brychkin said a book is pulled from sale after the chain receives notice from the Russian Book Union that “there are suspicions regarding a particular book.” The chain then stops selling it “until clarity is reached.” “Of course, there can be no complete clarity in this situation. Because even if the Russian Book Union doesn’t find anything in the book, there’s no guarantee that some parallel expert assessment isn’t happening at the same time somewhere within another organization,” Brychkin added. Brychkin said Russian readers have shown no noticeable interest in books by Lyudmila Ulitskaya and Boris Akunin pulled from sale. “Some of Boris Akunin’s books are still sitting in the warehouse, and we haven’t disposed of them yet. It’s not possible to return them to the supplier. In a sense, you could think of it as a special restricted storage,” Brychkin said. In recent years, Russia has regularly pulled books from sale at the demand of authorities or pro-government organizations. For example, in October 2026, Russia’s media regulator, Roskomnadzor, banned the novels Dvesti tretiy den zimy “The 203rd Day of Winter” and Vesna vody “The Spring of Water” by writer Olga Ptitseva. title: Rostec’s new Obereg GR body armor incorporates bleeding control system
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. The modernized Obereg GR body armor, manufactured by the Oktava plant (managed by RT-Capital, a subsidiary of the Rostec State Corporation), has been equipped with a bleeding control system, the corporation’s press service reported.
"The Oktava plant has modernized the Obereg GR body armor for humanitarian demining specialists. The gear includes an integrated automatic tourniquet system that allows users to quickly stop blood loss in critical situations, thereby increasing the chances of saving a life. A prototype of the equipment is currently undergoing testing," the press service said.
It noted that one of the key advantages of the Obereg GR is its low weight and comfort, combined with a large area of body protection. The body armor weighs about 5 kg and does not restrict movement, allowing it to be worn for extended periods of work.
Rostec specified that the mechanism built into the Obereg GR operates on the same principle as a household blood pressure monitor. Along with the body armor, the deminer wears cuffs with airbags on the arms and legs, and a battery-powered pump is located on the back of the gear. A system of tubes runs through the inside of the gear. These tubes inflate the cuffs with air to constrict an injured arm or leg, functioning like a tourniquet. The system’s control panel is located in a protective pocket on the chest. To use it, the wearer must pull a special cord. Then, using the four buttons, the operator can select which limb needs to be constricted. Both arms and both legs can be constricted, if necessary. When help arrives, the cuffs can be unfastened, or the valve can be opened to release the air. In an emergency, the user can cut the pneumatic tourniquet.
"The modernization of the Obereg GR is a direct response to the real needs of specialists working in high-risk environments. The combination of reliable ballistic protection and new features makes the gear as effective as possible in the field. Stopping bleeding is a key step in first aid for limb injuries, and with the new version of the body armor, this can be done independently using a remote control in a matter of seconds. This saves precious time before evacuation to a hospital and increases the chances of a favorable outcome. A prototype of the new equipment has been created, and testing is currently underway," Rostec reported.
According to the state corporation, the Obereg GR is being supplied to humanitarian demining teams in new regions. The gear features ballistic inserts with special protection classes C2 and Br1+. They can withstand pistol bullets and shrapnel, as well as protect against the main types of modern anti-personnel mines. The body armor is equipped with a large collar, eliminating gaps when worn with a helmet with a visor, and it provides extensive protection for the groin and inner thighs. At the same time, the gear is highly ergonomic - a deminer wearing this equipment can work kneeling on one knee.

title: Hunger beats tenure: Advice for junior engineers
body:
This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them. It had a good run: Being able to quickly define problems and find elegant solutions was a weak but useful predictor for how successful you’d be on my teams. Small coding challenges in real code did tell us something meaningful about candidates.
That’s no longer true. There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests.
The coding interview was, despite its ubiquity, never popular. I suspect that established engineers will still have strong reactions to its disappearance — if only for what it says about the evolution of our roles. Plenty of ink has been spilled to describe how AI is a challenge for junior developers, especially those trying to land a job. Now that I’ve seen junior people work with AI for a bit, I have a more hopeful take: Impact is less bounded by how many years of accumulated knowledge in frameworks and libraries you’ve gathered.
I’m seeing engineers who are comparatively new fly past people who are probably better coders and have been around much longer. Hunger beats tenure.
This post is my best advice for junior engineers, though “junior” is the wrong word. It’s really for engineers without social capital, status, or power.
First, know both your advantage and handicap.
Fresh eyes, even naive ones, have long been considered powerful. When I joined Stripe, founder Patrick Collison implored us newcomers to pay close attention to things that seem odd to us. His bet was that newcomers would spot friction and opportunities that old-timers had long stopped noticing.
In 1991, James March wrote that organizations depend on “maintaining an influx of the naive and ignorant”. When Orson Welles was asked how he got the confidence to try shots nobody had tried, he said : “Ignorance, sheer ignorance — you know there’s no confidence to equal it. It’s only when you know something about a profession, I think, that you’re timid or careful.”
When I joined Notion, one of my interviews involved designing an offline-mode architecture. I was baffled to hear that they considered it a “trick” interview, since an offline mode was deemed impossible. The data model was too complex for easily syncing an entire Notion workspace, and downloading individual pages was a user experience CEO Ivan Zhao would never allow. The data model complexity turned out to be true; the founder resistance didn’t. People considered it such common knowledge that nobody had checked. I, an ignorant newcomer, didn’t know better than to just ask.
It’s easy to read anecdotes like this one and see people making bad decisions. I cannot overstate how hard it is to spot these mistakes when you’re the one making them. Shortly after joining Notion, I wanted to outfit teams with large TVs to display live dashboards. I ran into organizational walls, failed, and didn’t care enough to start a whole fight.
A year later, Ji Pei joined as a new hire with the same idea. I scoffed and told him not to bother; I’d already tried. He’d already asked. The TVs showed up the next day. Somewhere in that year, I had become the old-timer.
The only problem with all that ignorant power: Nobody cares what you think. Most tech companies have layers of middle management to translate larger business goals into execution. Structurally, companies are often built around the idea of a few people green-lighting or blocking individual ideas. In a world where execution is expensive, you normally have to grind your way to some social status before the entire organization would “take a bet” on your idea. Org charts tend to change at a glacial pace, so even companies that believe in AI often expect junior people to simply execute their tasks faster rather than ambitiously go after business goals.
Well, good news: Execution isn’t expensive anymore.
(1) Pick business impact over backlog: In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Attach yourself, he advised, to the parts of a company that make money. Start there: Understand what your company is actually trying to accomplish (or, at a larger one, what your group or department is). Then find the right altitude — understanding what kind of goals your manager’s manager has is often a useful proxy.
(2) Pick a radical idea: Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious!
(3) Build it over a weekend: I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype.
(4) Focus on one good idea: In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype, hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. If your prototype involves the creation of a new programming language, a backend, and also somehow mobile apps, you’re not going to be successful. The point of creating a working prototype is to communicate an idea so well that leadership quickly understands both the opportunity and that you’re the one who can run with it.
(5) Lean into your fresh perspective: If you’re working on something user-facing, you have a unique amount of empathy for users and thus a much better sense for how the product works or doesn’t work for them. My colleagues at Slack and Notion had a hard time internalizing what using Slack or Notion is like as an external user.
If you’re working on infrastructure or tooling, you have the benefit of never having learned all the reasons things are considered “impossible”.
I don’t think the coding interview is going to come back. It’s easy to get sentimental given how many copies of “Algorithms and Data Structures” were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future — or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction.
At the same time, as a longtime hater of promotions by tenure, I can’t help but be optimistic. I’ve already seen my fair share of popular apps and products made this way.
At Anthropic, people got so used to using Claude Code as a command-line interface (CLI) that it took two relatively new engineers ( Anthony Morris and Alice Zhao ) to whip up a working prototype over one weekend. The first public version shipped roughly eight days later. You won’t be surprised to hear that a good graphical interface for Claude Code is a very popular product.
I'm probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI. I haven't quite gotten there yet — but I'm scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I'd love to hear how.
The image for this post is by J. M. W. Turner, “ The Fighting Temeraire ” (1839)
Felix Rieseberg I'm an EM at Anthropic, where I've so far led engineering for Claude.ai, Cowork, and Claude Code Desktop. I'm co-maintainer of Electron and various other open source projects. I've previously worked on and for Notion, Stripe, Slack, and Microsoft.

title: Rosgeo launches gold exploration in Central African Republic
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Rosgeo has launched gold exploration operations in the Central African Republic (CAR), announced Alexey Desyatkin, General Director of Zarubezhgeologia and head of international operations at Rosgeo.
"To give a few examples, in the Central African Republic, we carried out predictive metallogenic mapping between 2021 and 2023, identifying promising zones based on the findings. We are now conducting gold exploration work there," he said.
Discussing Rosgeo’s track record and ongoing projects in Africa, Desyatkin noted that the company had completed satellite imagery analysis in Chad, recommending promising areas for further study. Since this summer, Rosgeo specialists have been conducting airborne geophysical surveys there. In the Libyan Desert, the company’s experts continue to search for groundwater.
Furthermore, Desyatkin mentioned that the company resumed geological exploration in Benin "just yesterday" and is currently carrying out airborne geophysical surveys.
He added that Rosgeo is also fully prepared to sign agreements to assess hydrocarbon potential and explore gold and precious metal deposits in Niger. According to Desyatkin, Rosgeo has hands-on experience operating in more than 15 African nations.
Rosgeo is a Russian diversified geological holding company providing a full range of services related to geological exploration. One hundred percent of Rosgeo’s shares are state-owned. Zarubezhgeologia is an operator of Rosgeo projects abroad.
TASS is an official media partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Aweil farmers look to China to boost rice production
body: Rice farmers in Northern Bahr el Ghazal state are seeking better equipment and farming technology to increase production, as the World Food Programme (WFP) explores potential cooperation with China to expand cultivation on flood-prone land. Santino Akech, a 45-year-old farmer in Aweil, said his community had turned to rice after repeated floods damaged sorghum crops grown in low-lying areas. “When flood came, it affected some farm in the lowland area. It affected sorghum, but the rice succeeded,” Akech said. Farmers harvested 42 bags of rice, each weighing 90 kilogrammes, from four feddans last year, he said. He still had 13 bags in storage at the time of the interview. Income from rice had helped farmers pay school fees and medical expenses, while working in groups enabled them to expand cultivation and save through village savings and loan associations, he said. But farmers need equipment, including ox-ploughs, to prepare land on time and increase production. “We are not demanding tractor,” Akech said, explaining that government tractors were not always available when needed. Some farmers already owned bulls and could contribute towards the cost of ox-ploughs, he added. Expanding Cultivation Haileselassie Berhanu, head of the WFP Aweil Field Office programme, said the agency was working with communities to cultivate flood-prone land with rice rather than lose crops to excess water. Repeated flooding had damaged sorghum, a major crop in the area, prompting WFP and farmers to begin experimenting with rice before gradually expanding cultivation, he said. More than 2,100 farmers or households were involved in rice cultivation this year, with about 1,000 hectares planted under the wider initiative, Berhanu said. The programme needs machinery, improved seeds, training and equipment for harvesting, drying, threshing and polishing rice. Technical expertise on rice varieties is also important, he said, pointing to possible cooperation with China. Chinese Ambassador to South Sudan Ma Qiang, who visited agricultural activities in Aweil, said the area had favourable conditions for rice production and that the initiative could help improve local food supplies. China had previously donated agricultural machinery to local communities, and further cooperation on farming technology was possible, he said. “There are great potentials,” Ma said, adding that cooperation with national and local authorities and international partners could increase food production. He also warned that natural resources, including water, required proper management, highlighting the need to address flooding. Food Security WFP Country Representative Muntina Chimuka said rice cultivation could improve food security by enabling communities to grow their own crops and diversify food sources. The crop at the site visited appeared promising despite dry conditions affecting other agricultural areas, she said. But expansion would depend on funding and stronger cooperation with the government. WFP relies on voluntary contributions to finance its operations, Chimuka said, adding that climate change and unpredictable weather were making farming increasingly difficult. She urged state and national authorities to work with communities to identify suitable growing areas and rice varieties. Deng Deng Bol, caretaker minister of agriculture, environment and forestry in Northern Bahr el Ghazal state, said farmers needed equipment, training and storage facilities to increase production and preserve their harvests. The state had fertile land suitable for agriculture, but changing weather patterns remained a challenge, he said. Flooding damaged crops last year, while drought had affected rice, sorghum and other crops this year. For farmers such as Akech, access to equipment is essential to expand cultivation and harvest crops on time. Rice has shown promise in low-lying areas repeatedly affected by floods, but scaling up production will require improved technology, training, funding and better water management. The post Aweil farmers look to China to boost rice production appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

title: SiFive positions RISC-V as the control layer for AI accelerators
body:
SiFive is positioning its Intelligence-series RISC-V processors as programmable controllers for custom AI accelerators. The approach illustrates how RISC-V’s commercial value is moving beyond the ISA towards specialized system integration, data movement, and accelerator orchestration.
As AI workloads grow more complex, attention is increasingly turning to the processors that manage specialized accelerators, rather than the accelerators’ performance alone.
Clifton Robin, director of technical product marketing, argues that programmable RISC-V processors can provide an effective control layer for custom AI accelerators , handling data movement, scheduling, and coordination, while allowing dedicated compute engines to concentrate on their primary tasks.
According to Robin, there are several limitations in conventional accelerator control architectures. Hardwired state machines can be difficult to modify as algorithms change, shared buses create potential bottlenecks, and relying on the host CPU for low-level orchestration consumes processing resources and adds latency.
SiFive proposes using its Intelligence-series processors as Accelerator Control Units (ACUs), providing a programmable interface between the host processor and custom accelerator hardware rather than a generic state machine/DMA approach.
The approach combines RISC-V scalar and vector processing with three interfaces designed to reduce the overhead of accelerator control and data movement.
The interfaces allow the RISC-V processor to prepare and transfer data, dispatch accelerator operations, and perform ancillary calculations, such as activation functions or data formatting. Changes to the control logic can be implemented in software or firmware rather than requiring modifications to fixed-function hardware.
There are several Intelligence family processors. The X100 series targets control-intensive applications where low latency and modest area are priorities, while the X200 and X300 series offer greater vector bandwidth and computational capacity for more demanding workloads.
Google data centers already use the Intelligence X200 as an AI compute host, and there is an X100 license to an unnamed Tier 1 US semiconductor company for industrial edge AI applications.
This is a useful illustration of a theme running through our latest RISC-V Quarterly Report : The value is moving beyond the ISA. SiFive is selling a way to solve a practical systems engineering problem: how to control specialized compute engines, move data efficiently, and retain flexibility as AI workloads evolve. The differentiation lies in SiFive’s implementation. What the processor does, and how effectively it fits into the broader architecture, matters much more than the instruction set.
RISC-V is entering a more mature phase. Customers are not simply looking for an alternative CPU architecture; they are looking for proven IP that reduces effort, risk, and time to market. SiFive recognizes that the opportunity is increasingly to provide a useful part of a larger computing platform.
Anyway, this seems to be a signal that RISC-V does not have to displace Arm or x86 as the main processor to gain a meaningful position in AI infrastructure. It can find its way into the control plane of increasingly heterogeneous systems.

title: Dozens are dead in a high-speed train crash in Spain
body:
Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday. Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press via AP hide caption
URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year.
The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies.
The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January.
"Today all of Spain is grieving," Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning.
This framegrab taken from a video provided by Spain's Guardia Civil shows an aerial view of carriages and first responders on the site of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, Wednesday. Guardia Civil via AP hide caption
Sánchez called for increased safety measures to restore confidence in a high-speed rail system that was once a source of national pride .
"It is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year," said Sánchez, who faces a national election on Nov. 29.
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the central province of Toledo, involving two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading south in the same direction from Madrid to Seville.
A train operated by the state-owned RENFE company struck the rear of another train operated by private company IRYO that was stopped. The collision derailed two carriages on the tail of the IRYO train and the front of the RENFE train.
Samy Paul, a British tourist, described the shock of the impact to The Associated Press after being rescued from the RENFE train.
"Suddenly, everything started falling apart. Bang! We fell down," he said. "We realized carriage two, carriage one, all gone, all smashed. There was blood all over."
David Gómez, a construction worker, was working nearby when he heard the crash and ran to help, he told the newspaper El País.
"People were trying to get out through the windows ... We cut through some fences to access the area and treated people with the first-aid kits we had brought until emergency services arrived," he said. "As I was trying to pull a young woman out, there was a piece of a leg."
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.
Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente said that the crash was caused by what he called the "inexplicable" order from a central command center for Spain's trains after a security system had failed. He said the train engineers were not to blame.
Puente said that at 8:30 a.m. the security system on a stretch of 63 kilometers (39 miles) stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop. But the central command told the RENFE train to start running again without any speed restrictions, and it ended up colliding with the stopped IRYO train at 8:53 a.m.
Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since there was still a "stop signal" active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.
Authorities were still studying information to see how fast the train was going, but it could have been at 200 kph (124 mph) for that stretch of the track, Puente said.
"I am not attributing responsibility to anyone, I am just stating the facts," Puente said.
The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left carriages shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.
Passenger Ignacio Relaño was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.
"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."
Authorities said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.
Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses. A military emergency brigade was deployed to help.
Spain's King Felipe VI also visited the crash site.
"We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected," Spain's royals said in a statement.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."
Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.
The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 46 people died in southern Spain when an IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-meter (13-foot) slope.
That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.
Before this year, there had been no fatal crash on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992.
Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 kph (155 mph) and over — turning it into a world leader.
Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometers (2,400 miles) of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometers (28,000 miles) for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.
Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. The Italian-owned IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.
A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union, Joan Rodríguez, said increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.
"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodríguez told TVE on Wednesday. "I am not saying it was a determining factor (in the crashes), but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

title: Quoting Terk Terkowitz
body:
If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing. Document why, share it with your community of peers, bring it to your manager, and work to find solutions.
