title: How OPay is taking financial inclusion closer to more Nigerians
body:
From drivers receiving payments on their phones to small businesses serving customers without relying only on cash, digital finance is changing how Nigerians manage money. OPay is part of this shift, as new data show progress in financial inclusion and the need to make access more useful.
For a commercial driver, receiving payment quickly can mean having enough money to buy fuel and continue working. For a market trader, a digital transfer can help pay a supplier without leaving the shop. For a family, sending money to a loved one can take seconds instead of a long journey. These everyday moments show what financial inclusion should mean: giving people practical ways to receive, send and manage money, regardless of their income or where they live.
Nigeria is making progress. The 2026 Access to Financial Services in Nigeria survey by Enhancing Financial Innovation and Access (EFInA) found that 79% of adults, about 94.2 million people, used a financial product or service. Formal financial inclusion reached 73%, up from 64% in 2023, while financial exclusion fell from 26% to 21%. Digital financial services reached 64.4% of adults, compared with 45% in 2023.
Yet access alone does not guarantee financial security. EFInA found that three in four Nigerian adults are not financially healthy. Formal credit reaches only 10% of adults, while insurance reaches 5%. These gaps show why the next stage of inclusion must help people do more than open accounts or make payments. It must help them manage risks, build savings and support their livelihoods.
OPay, which began operations in Nigeria in 2018, is helping bring everyday financial services closer to consumers and businesses through mobile payments, transfers, bill payments, savings, debit cards and merchant services. Its model allows customers to carry out many transactions without travelling to a bank branch.
The value is especially clear for people who earn and spend money daily. OPay’s technology is designed to work on a range of phones, including entry-level devices, and under unstable network conditions. According to company disclosures, more than 99% of transactions started on its app were completed successfully on the first attempt in the first half of 2026. Reliable service matters when a failed payment could delay a purchase or interrupt a day’s earnings.
Small businesses are another important part of this story. OPay reported more than one million merchants and businesses on its network as of June 2026. Digital payments give shops, food sellers, and other businesses another way to collect payments, while eligible merchants that provide financial services can earn commissions. Easier payment collection can save time, support daily trade and help business owners serve more customers.
OPay also contributes to local employment. The company has publicly stated that 99% of its workforce in Nigeria is Nigerian. Its operations require people in customer support, technology, compliance, sales and other roles, while its merchant and agent network creates additional income opportunities. These are meaningful contributions.
Customer service is central to making these benefits last. A customer with a delayed transfer needs clear information. A trader facing a payment problem needs practical help. A first-time user may need guidance on how to protect an account. Listening, giving timely updates and resolving complaints can turn a difficult experience into an opportunity to earn trust.
Policy also has a role to play. The Central Bank of Nigeria’s new ATM guidelines require card issuers to deploy at least one ATM for every 7,500 payment cards issued, with full compliance due by 2028. Improving access to cash is important, especially for people and communities that still depend on it. However, card numbers alone may not show how people now access financial services.
As more Nigerians use mobile payments and nearby merchants, it is worth considering how ATM access targets can work alongside digital channels rather than diverting attention and resources from them. Cash and digital payments will continue to serve different needs; financial inclusion policy should make both work safely and efficiently.
Other gaps deserve attention. CBN policy already recognises the need to simplify customer identity checks, strengthen agent networks and promote digital financial services. The challenge is to keep these measures practical for low-income customers, rural communities and small businesses while maintaining strong safeguards against fraud.
At the launch of Payments System Vision 2028, the CBN set out a goal of a secure, inclusive, and innovative payment system, with collaboration and interoperability as guiding principles. EFInA’s CEO, Foyinsolami Akinjayeju, has also called for providers and policymakers to judge progress by what financial access enables people to achieve, not simply by the number of accounts opened.
For OPay, the opportunity has been to keep turning technology into practical value: reliable payments, stronger merchant relationships, local jobs and easier access to financial services. The ultimate measure of inclusion is not how many people can open an account, but how many can use financial services to earn, save, trade and withstand unexpected costs.
When a driver can receive payment, a shop can keep trading, and a family can send money when it matters, financial inclusion becomes real. That is the impact digital finance must continue to deliver: one customer, one business and one transaction at a time.

title: Russia will continue supplying agricultural products to Africa — MFA
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russia will continue to supply agricultural products to markets in Africa and other regions of the world, Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko told reporters.
"Russia will surely continue to supply agricultural products to markets in Africa and other regions of the world. We understand that many countries are in need of Russian grain or other agricultural goods, and we are always ready to meet our partners halfway and provide assistance to them," he said.
Russian Ambassador to Turkey Sergey Vershinin said earlier that Moscow continued discussing measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea, including with Ankara, adding that the previous Black Sea initiative failed to progress due to Kiev’s stance.
Meanwhile Kenya's Ambassador to Russia Peter Mathuki noted in an interview with TASS that the logistics of grain shipments to Africa were facing serious challenges amid the situation in the Black Sea region.

title: Spain Train Collision Kills At Least 10, Many Injured
body: A collision between two high-speed trains south of Madrid killed at least 10 people on Wednesday, a regional government spokeswoman said, warning the toll could rise. “The information we are receiving is not good at all. There are at least 10 dead and it is possible that the number will increase,” Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the government of Castilla-La Mancha, told local media CMM. Local authorities said the crash resulted in injuries to numerous people. “Two trains have collided — there are people injured,” Manuel Galan, mayor of the town of Urda, told public broadcaster TVE. A spokesperson for the Spanish emergency services told AFP the trains collided just before 9:00 am (0800 GMT) but added it was too early to speak of injuries. “All resources are currently being deployed,” the spokesperson said, including “several fire crews, three helicopters, and two mobile intensive care units”. Rail infrastructure company ADIF also confirmed a collision had taken place, warning in a social media post that the high-speed rail line from Madrid to the south had been suspended. The accident comes less than a year after a rail crash in Adamuz in southern Spain left 46 dead. The post Spain Train Collision Kills At Least 10, Many Injured appeared first on Channels Television .

title: LOTN showcases aviation maintenance and modernisation capabilities
body:
Backed by 80 years’ experience in the aerospace industry, Slovakia-based Letecké Opravovne Trenčín (LOTN) is offering its expertise to local and international partners. The company is this week exhibiting at Afridex 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria.
Earlier this year, its specialist aviation workshops showcased their advanced its capabilities for the first time at Europe’s largest general aviation exhibition Aero 2026 in Friedrichshafen, Germany, in April.
“LOTN has evolved into a high-tech MRO (maintenance, repair, and overhaul) hub that seamlessly bridges legacy Soviet-era platforms with state-of-the-art NATO technology,” the company said. “Our workshops are specialised ecosystems equipped with purpose-built tooling and in-house design capabilities, able to execute complex modernisation programmes.”
Besides modernisation services, the company executes maintenance and repairs of aviation equipment down to the component level of platforms such as Mi-8 and Mi-17/171, UH-60 Black Hawk multi-purpose transport helicopters, as well as F-16 Fighting Falcon fighter jets, L-39 jet trainers and L-410 transport aircraft.
“Thanks to our company-owned and operated airfield, our customers can fly-in and fly-out, a service model that minimises downtime for both military and civil operators,” the company explained. “While our primary mission remains the readiness of the Slovak Air Force, our reputation has attracted a diverse portfolio of international armed forces and private collectors.”
A 100% government-owned joint-stock company under the Slovak Ministry of Defence, LOTN is the only facility of its kind in Slovakia.
Its flagship commercial facility is the state-of-the-art painting and refinishing workshop, designed to accommodate a wide range of aircraft sizes. It undertakes a comprehensive process to protect the aircraft against corrosion and aerodynamic drag. Precision chemical and mechanical stripping precedes detail structural inspections, repairs and hermetic sealing, before the application of specialised high-durability coatings in a climate-controlled environment.
The company further boasts an upholstery workshop, chemistry and metrological laboratory, surface treatment and a plexiglass workshop. This latter workshop specialises in the dismantling, repair and assembly of plexiglass, windows and laminate covers, such as for radars and other protective components.
LOTN is now rapidly expanding into the digital battlefield and towards autonomous flight.
“We are proud to serve as the main industrial partner in the Slovak 3D Radar project,” the company stated. “This involves the sophisticated manufacturing of microwave modules, which require extreme precision and clean-room conditions.”
The LOTN UAV Production and Assembly division is currently developing capabilities for the next generation of unmanned aerial systems. “By integrating our traditional MRO expertise with modern composite materials and drone electronics, we are preparing for a future where manned and unmanned platforms operate in tandem.”
Late last year, LOTN together with it partner Airvolute, delivered two of its Ellipsis VTOL (vertical take-off and landing) unmanned aerial vehicles to the MR Štefánik Armed Forces Academy Simulation Centre in Liptovský Mikuláš.
It is a modern tactical drone designed for advanced ISR (intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) missions. Equipped with a powerful autopilot, it offers top computing power, modular architecture, high reliability and rapid readiness for military, security and civilian deployments. According to the company, its software is customisable for the required mission application, from border protection, perimeter security to rescue missions.

title: Ukraine receives 12 Patriot missiles per month from US, Zelensky says
body:
Ukraine has received an average of 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month from the U.S. throughout 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalist on Oct. 27 at a closed-door press briefing.
Ukraine needs to intercept around 150 Russian ballistic missiles per month but receives about 150 Patriot missiles from the U.S. annually, according to Zelensky.
The president said some European countries have agreed to provide additional missiles from their stockpiles, but the transfers require approval from Washington. Zelensky pointed to documents awaiting action by U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth .
"We want the Americans to start signing off on the supply of antiballistic missiles – interceptor missiles – to Ukraine from the countries we've reached agreements with. Because without Hegseth's signature, it's simply impossible," Zelensky said.
Zelsnky said on Oct. 26 that Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems. Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as an example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, including NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), a mechanism through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the United States .
The shortage also affects missiles for NASAMS air defense systems, which Ukraine receives through the PURL initiative .
Zelensky also said he had asked U.S. President Donald Trump for a special package of interceptor missiles ahead of winter during a meeting in New York on Sept. 22. Trump promised to make efforts to secure the missiles, Zelensky said, but noted that the U.S. also needed them for their own defense.
"These are the circumstances I live in today: every week, we have to put together new packages, find new missiles, and secure new air defenses. We need them every day to save the lives of our people from Russian ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky, Russia has launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since Oct. 14.
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to "bad weather conditions."
Zelensky added that the war in the Middle East has reduced military and financial support for Ukraine, making it more difficult for Kyiv to secure the air defense supplies needed to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.
"The war in the Middle East is having a negative impact on the whole world. The energy challenges around the world are caused exclusively by the Strait of Hormuz. All the other challenges are also affecting Ukraine. The military and financial support Ukraine receives has definitely declined because of the war in the Middle East," he said.

title: Kenyan Army receives MD500s from South Korea
body:
The Kenya Army Corps of Aviation (KACA) has inducted into service refurbished MD500 helicopters from South Korea, which will be used to equip a new unit to support United Nations peacekeeping missions.
The Kenyan Ministry of Defence said the helicopters were received on 23 October at Embakasi. In 2021, South Korea pledged to provide ex Republic of Korea Army MD500MD Defender helicopters to Kenya.
In December 2023, the first six of the 16 donated MD500s were shipped from the Korean Army Logistics Command’s general maintenance depot in Jinhae to the US for repairs and maintenance before delivery to Kenya under US State Department auspices.
The Kenyan Ministry of Defence (MoD) did not state how many helicopters were delivered on 23 October, but imagery of the handover event showed at least five – in a statement, UN Under-Secretary-General for Peace Operations Jean-Pierre Lacroix announced the donation and thanked South Korea for supporting the UN’s air mobility capabilities, saying eight aircraft were delivered.
“The US Government facilitated the installation of advanced digital systems on the helicopters and supported the training of Kenya Army pilots and technicians to enhance their skills in operating and maintaining the modernised aircraft,” the Kenyan Ministry of Defence said, adding, “this milestone marks an important step in the continued development of Kenya Army’s military aviation capabilities and underscores the value of modern aircraft in supporting operational effectiveness.”
Speaking during the occasion, the Cabinet Secretary for Defence, Soipan Tuya, noted that the modernised MD500 helicopters would enhance the Kenya Defence Force’s (KDF’s) capabilities in reconnaissance, aerial support, mobility and critical security operations.
The Chief of the Defence Forces (CDF), General Charles Kahariri, commended the trilateral partnership between Kenya, the Republic of Korea and the United States, noting that it provides a strong foundation for enhanced security cooperation. He highlighted that the new capabilities would enhance security, counter-terrorism efforts, peace support operations and humanitarian assistance.
The Kenya Army Commander, Lieutenant General David Keter, expressed appreciation for the partnership between Kenya, the Republic of Korea and the United States, noting that the collaboration strengthens Kenya Army’s aviation capabilities. He thanked the Government and people of the Republic of Korea for their support and commended the United States Government for providing the technical expertise required to install advanced digital systems on the aircraft.
Ambassador Kang Hyung-shik of the Republic of Korea underscored the deepening diplomatic, economic and security ties between the Republic of Korea and Kenya. He highlighted that the transfer of military equipment reflects mutual trust and a shared commitment to regional peace and stability.
Susan Burns, Chargé d’ Affaires of the United States, underscored the importance of the trilateral security partnership between Kenya, the United States and the Republic of Korea in promoting regional stability and addressing shared security challenges. She noted that modernised military equipment and international cooperation strengthen Kenya’s role as a trusted security partner, from counter-terrorism efforts in East Africa to peacekeeping missions abroad. She added that sustained investment in security creates the stability and confidence necessary for economic growth and long-term prosperity.
Brigadier General Jayson Becker, the Deputy Commanding Officer for the Combined Joint Task Force – Horn of Africa highlighted the trilateral partnership between Kenya, the United States and the Republic of Korea as a demonstration of their shared commitment to regional peace, stability and security. He described Kenya as a trusted partner and a key pillar in efforts to stabilise the Horn of Africa.
He noted that the helicopters, their technical support, training and Kenya’s investment in human capital would strengthen capabilities to address complex security challenges in East Africa and beyond.
Kenya’s military already operates the MD500, with 40 delivered by the United States between 1980 and 1985, along with 2 100 TOW anti-tank missiles. These were recently augmented by six new MD530Fs delivered from the US in December 2019. They were acquired to assist with operations in support of the AMISOM mission in Somalia (now AUSSOM).
The Kenya Army also operates nine AS550C3 Fennecs donated by the United Arab Emirates in 2018 and five Harbin Z-9W helicopters. The Air Force has a larger rotary wing fleet, comprising three Bell AH-1 Cobra attack helicopters, over a dozen MD500s, three Pumas, half a dozen Bell 205s, eight UH-1 Hueys, three AW139s and several Mi-171 helicopters.
Korean Air’s aerospace division built some 280 MD500s under license between 1976 and 1984, but these are being replaced by newer aircraft, including the Korea Aerospace Industries (KAI) Light Armed Helicopter (based on the Airbus EC155 Dauphin).
The Kenya Defence Forces are considered to be the most powerful in East and Central Africa. They have built a reputation for comparative combat effectiveness and have taken part in a number of operations across Africa.
The KDF has established a reputation for competence, stemming from their experience in operations in various parts of Africa and beyond, having fought in neighbouring Somalia and taken part in numerous peacekeeping operations. Kenya is consistently among the top ten defence spenders in Africa, with the result that all three branches of the KDF are regarded as being well equipped, outclassing most of their fellow East African states.
While defence spending has declined slightly in real terms over the past decade, both the Kenyan Army and Air Force have seen a modest level of capital expenditure, allowing for the procurement of a limited number of more modern vehicles, aircraft, and other advanced weapon systems. This modernisation continues as the country fights terrorism mainly emanating from Somalia and participates in various AU and UN peace initiatives.

title: Tata Advanced Systems Limited gaining a foothold in Africa
body:
One year ago, it was reported that Indian conglomerate Tata Advanced Systems Limited (TASL) was opening an armoured vehicle production plant in Morocco. Hyderabad-based TASL, part of the Tata Group, this week showcased some of its innovative technologies, including the African-built vehicle, at the inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) 2026 in Lagos.
The Moroccan facility was established to produce TASL’s 8×8 wheeled armoured platform (WhAP) following a 2024 agreement for the supply of 150 vehicles. The first WhAP was handed over to the Royal Moroccan Army in December last year. By establishing the 20 000 square metre manufacturing plant in Morocco – the first overseas defence factory by a private Indian company – TASL neatly aligns with the North African country’s aim to grow its own defence industry. These vehicles could also be exported across Africa. Apart from the WhAP, plans are afoot to also produce TASL’s Light Armoured Multi-Role Vehicle (LAMV) there.
The formidable portfolio of 20-year-old TASL covers aerostructures, aero-engines, airborne platforms and systems, defence and security, as well as land mobility products and services.
Its flagship product, the WhAP 8×8 wheeled armoured platform, is India’s first amphibious infantry combat vehicle in wheeled configuration. According to the company, it has developed the system by “benchmarking its features with some of the best-in-class products across the globe” and evaluated its performance through rigorous trials in extreme conditions and terrain.
TASL stated that it was designed jointly with India’s DRDO (Defence Research & Design Organisation) for optimal survivability, all-terrain performance and increased lethality. “Modularity and scalability help this platform to be easily customised to cater to various missions and operation conditions.”
The 24 tonne WhAP accommodates a crew of three plus nine to 11 infantry soldiers. It is powered by a 600 hp Cummins ISX/ISXe engine paired with an Allison 4500SP automatic transmission, giving a top road speed of 100 km/h and a range of 500 km. Rear-mounted water jets give an amphibious swimming speed of up to 10 km/h.
The WhAP features modular composite/steel armour meeting STANAG 4569 (Levels 1 to 4) and mine blast resistance rated at Level 3. It can be configured with a 30 mm cannon, 7.62 mm remote controlled weapon stations, automatic grenade launcher, or anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) systems.
Adhering to the philosophy of ‘Make in India’, the company offers a vast range of military vehicles, ranging from 4×4 MRAP (mine-resistant armour-protected) vehicles, ambulances and troop carriers to a family of large trucks. The Tata LPTA family is available in configurations from 4×4 through 6×6 to 12×12. Some of these have also been supplied to Morocco.
Besides land mobility platforms, TASL has long been involved with the likes of Lockheed Martin, Sikorsky and Airbus to manufacture aerostructures and components of C-130 Hercules/C-130J Super Hercules, Sikorsky S-92 and C-295 platforms for the Indian Air Force. The company also produced wings for the F-16 Fighting Falcon and fuselages for Boeing’s AH-64 Apache helicopters.
TASL’s defence and security division manufactures artillery systems, rocket and missile launchers, air defence systems, C4I, radars, optronics, and cybersecurity systems.

title: Netherlands confirms $1.3 billion in non-military aid for Ukraine through 2029
body:
The Dutch government on Oct. 28 outlined a package of non-military aid worth 1.2 billion euros (about $1.3 billion) for Ukraine, to be disbursed over the next three years and directed toward the country's economic recovery.
"Support for recovery and reconstruction can't wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now: military support, but also social and economic assistance," Dutch Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma said during his visit to Kyiv.
"However successful you are on the battlefield, it's also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over."
The package includes 878 million euros (close to $977 million) previously outlined in the Dutch government coalition agreement, plus an additional 327 million euros ($364 million) announced on Sept. 15.
The funds will be disbursed between 2027 and 2029 and are separate from Dutch military aid to the war-torn country.
The Netherlands unveiled further details about the package on the occasion of Sjoerdsma's visit to Ukraine's capital, which comes as the country braces for another brutal winter of Russian attacks against energy infrastructure.
The bulk of the package will be directed to support Ukraine's energy and water sectors.
Under this assistance, the Netherlands will provide 40 million euros ($45 million) to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund by the end of the year, as well as 55 million euros ($62 million) to fund energy equipment from Dutch companies via the Netherlands Enterprise Agency.
The package also includes support for Ukraine's private sector, and Sjoerdsma will sign a memorandum with Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko on 10 million euros ($11 million) for Ukraine's Ramstein initiative — a project aimed at restoring and modernizing the country's industrial base.
A significant part of the aid will be channeled to Ukraine via the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the World Bank, and the European Investment Bank (EIB).
"We will be with Ukraine however long and whatever it takes," Sjoerdsma told the Kyiv Independent in an interview, noting he will hold talks with Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi and other Ukrainian officials during his visit, and possibly hold a call with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The Dutch minister added that "if demands change, if the situation changes, whether it's in Kyiv or in Ukraine, we will adapt our support accordingly... because it's not about what we want to offer you, it's about what Ukraine needs."

title: U S Air Force Tests General Atomics XQ-67A Autonomous Aircraft for Future Combat
body:
The U.S. Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and Air Combat Command’s Experimental Operations Unit have flown the XQ-67A Autonomous Collaborative Platform (ACP) at the Nevada Test and Training Range.
The flight was conducted under the Demonstration of Autonomous Collaborative Platform Performance and Effectiveness (Demon APE) program. Through this program, the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) is testing how multiple aircraft can communicate, share information and coordinate missions to help military personnel make faster decisions.
The XQ-67A demonstrated integration of latest sensors, mission computers, and power and thermal management hardware designed for demanding combat environments. Additionally, the integration of Beyond Line-of-Sight datalinks and live, virtual and constructive simulations during the flight demonstrated management of uncrewed platforms across distributed theaters, bolstering deterrence through resilient, layered command and control.
The XQ-67A development effort aims to extend the operational reach of crewed fighter formations, improve commanders’ situational awareness and add affordable operational capacity while reducing risks to human aircrews.

title: The missing middle in Nigeria’s youth employment push
body:
On the fifth floor of the ITF Building in Iponri, Surulere, guests at ALX’s Lagos office sat around tables, each group working through the same question. “Nigeria channels real money into preparing its young people for work, why does so little of it lead to sustainable jobs or new businesses?”
The gathering, a roundtable titled From Funding to Outcomes, brought together foundations, non-governmental organisations and development partners from across Nigeria. Its host, Ruby Igwe, Regional Manager for West and Central Africa at ALX , believes the answer sits in a stage of the process that rarely draws attention.
In her words, “There is real money going into youth skills and employability in this country, but too many programmes do not deliver the jobs and the change they promised. They rarely fail at the funding stage, because they lose their way in the middle, in how they are delivered, and that is the gap we want to close.”
That middle where that loss happens is where the work gets difficult. A programme can be funded, launched and publicised, and still fail to reach the young people it was designed for, or fail to carry them through to employment. Igwe argues that funders need partners who can manage that stretch between the cheque and the job.
The session was designed to be an interactive one, allowing attendees to trade pain points and possible solutions at their tables, and use the networking time to continue those exchanges.
Participants shared what is working in youth development and where programmes fall short, but the discussion also turned to young Nigerians themselves, their readiness to enroll on structured learning platforms, their motivation to study, and, in many cases, the absence of both.
During the session, ALX asked partners how to make its learning platform accessible to more young people. It is positioning itself as a technical, delivery and implementation partner for any organisation seeking to run youth programmes at scale, and it points to its record in Nigeria, where more than 150,000 young people have gone through its programmes.
Commenting further on the event, Igwe said, “We did not bring people from different sectors into one room by accident. No single organisation can solve this alone. When foundations, NGOs, development partners and implementers work together, we can reach far more young people than any of us could on our own, and we can build the capacity to serve them well.”
The proposition was direct for the funders in the room. Collaboration, in ALX’s view, would extend the reach of its work and increase its capacity alongside partners, so that the benefit reaches more young people.
ALX is part of the African Leadership Group, which has spent more than two decades widening access to opportunity for young Africans. ALX reports that 347,100 learners have graduated from its programmes across the continent and that 257,900 young people have moved into work. It counts 154,300 graduates in wage employment and 43,400 running businesses or freelancing, and says alumni entrepreneurs have created more than 60,000 jobs for others.
The platform’s support does not end when training does. Graduates have access to mentorship, and ALX runs regular grant readiness sessions to help them position themselves for funding opportunities.
The same emphasis on measurable results runs through ALX Enterprise, ALX’s business-to-business offering, which works with organisations across Africa to develop leaders, strengthen teams and build digital skills. Each engagement starts with a consultation on the client’s specific challenges, and results are measured against the change agreed at the outset.
Whether that collaboration takes shape will depend on what the partners around those tables do next, and this was framed as a question in Igwe’s next step.
She asked, “Our question to partners is simple. What is working, what is not, and how can we help? If you are funding young people, we want to make sure that funding ends in a job, a business or a career.”

title: Building the future of Africa’s defence industry
body:
Africa’s defence and security landscape is facing growing security challenges, rapid technological advances and increasing interest from international manufacturers, creating new opportunities for the continent’s defence sector.
At the same time, African companies are gaining recognition for developing practical, reliable solutions tailored to some of the world’s most demanding operating environments.
Matthew Harman, Afridex Content Advisory Board member and founder of Greypoint Advisory Services, said these developments point to a future in which African defence businesses play a far more prominent role in regional and international markets.
With more than three decades of experience across global defence industries, Harman believes Africa’s future success will depend on combining innovation, industrial partnerships and operational expertise with a deep understanding of local requirements.
“Africa represents an enormous opportunity for the international defence industry, but it is important to recognise the diversity of the continent and the different requirements of individual countries,” he said.
Harman noted that one of the biggest mistakes defence companies can make is assuming Africa can be approached as a single market. “This is particularly relevant in Africa, where political, commercial, geographical and operational considerations can vary significantly between markets,” he explained.
The continent faces a range of security challenges, from piracy and terrorism to trafficking, insurgency and the protection of critical national infrastructure. Yet these challenges exist alongside growing economies, increasing technology adoption and considerable industrial potential.
For companies seeking to enter African markets, Harman argues that success requires careful preparation and long-term commitment.
“Companies need to approach these markets with a clear understanding of local requirements, appropriate commercial preparation and a willingness to establish long-term relationships. Those that take the time to understand the operating environment will be much better positioned to identify meaningful opportunities,” he said.
Understanding operational requirements must always be the starting point. Africa’s diverse environments, from deserts and rainforests to extensive coastlines and remote regions with limited communications infrastructure, place unique demands on defence equipment and systems. As a result, reliability and sustainability are often more important than cutting-edge specifications.
“Defence manufacturers must consider how their products will perform over extended distances, how they will be maintained and whether they can remain operational when access to technical support or replacement components is limited,” he said.
The growing importance of Africa within the global defence market is also being driven by wider technological and economic developments. Improvements in communications networks, mobile connectivity and satellite-based services are changing the equation. These advances are increasingly influencing defence and security operations, where access to information, communications and situational awareness are central to mission success.
For international manufacturers, this creates opportunities to establish industrial partnerships, introduce new technologies and support capability development. However, Harman stressed that meaningful success requires patience.
“Businesses must recognise that individual countries have different political structures, commercial practices and procurement requirements. The opportunity is significant, but it must be approached with a proper understanding of the markets involved,” he said.
Harman also sees substantial opportunities for African defence manufacturers to expand beyond their domestic and regional markets.
One of Africa’s greatest strengths, he argues, is the practical experience companies have gained operating in difficult conditions.
“If a manufacturer can demonstrate that its equipment is robust, reliable, relatively straightforward to operate and capable of being maintained over an extended service life, those qualities can be highly attractive to international customers,” he said.
Many countries outside Africa face similar challenges, particularly in parts of South America and the Middle East.
“The opportunity is to take equipment and solutions that have demonstrated their effectiveness in African operating environments and introduce them to other markets where similar requirements exist,” he said.
Strong partnerships, he argues, remain fundamental to building sustainable businesses across Africa. “Businesses should avoid becoming dependent on individual political relationships. The objective should be to establish commercially credible partnerships capable of operating successfully over the long term,” he said.
“The strongest relationships are those in which both sides benefit and where the partnership contributes to the long-term development of local industrial capabilities.”
Industrial cooperation will be increasingly important as African manufacturers seek to strengthen their international competitiveness. Partnerships can combine advanced international technologies with African operational knowledge, engineering expertise and proven solutions.
“That combination can create products that are technologically capable, commercially competitive and particularly well suited to demanding operational environments,” said Harman.
One of the biggest challenges confronting manufacturers is scaling production after developing a successful technical solution. “Partnerships can help accelerate that development by bringing together complementary expertise and industrial capabilities,” he explained.
Technology transfer is another area where Harman sees significant opportunities. “Successful technology partnerships need to deliver benefits in both directions,” he said. Rather than importing finished products, he advocates collaboration spanning manufacturing, software development, component production and long-term support services.
“By combining international expertise with African manufacturing and engineering capabilities, companies can develop solutions that meet domestic requirements while also creating export opportunities,” he said.
Perhaps the most significant driver of change across the defence sector is the emergence of new technologies. Harman said recent conflicts have demonstrated how rapidly military priorities are evolving, particularly in relation to unmanned systems and autonomous capabilities. “We are witnessing a fundamental change in military operations, particularly within the maritime environment.”
Advances in drones, artificial intelligence and autonomous technologies are altering how armed forces evaluate future investments. Lower-cost systems that can be manufactured efficiently, upgraded rapidly and deployed at scale are becoming attractive alternatives to traditional large platforms.
“One of the most significant changes is the increasing importance of lower-cost systems that can be manufactured at scale, adapted quickly and improved continuously in response to operational experience,” Harman explained.
“This creates interesting opportunities for African industry, particularly in unmanned surface vessels, unmanned underwater vehicles and associated maritime technologies,” he said.
Countries such as Nigeria face growing maritime security requirements linked to the protection of critical infrastructure and economic activity within the Gulf of Guinea. Harman believes international technology partnerships could help develop solutions tailored to these requirements while opening export opportunities.
“One of the most significant developments is that sophisticated military capabilities do not necessarily require the same level of investment associated with traditional large defence platforms,” he explained.
The growing accessibility of technologies such as artificial intelligence, autonomous systems and advanced sensors is lowering barriers to entry and creating opportunities for a broader range of companies to participate in defence programmes.
However, Harman cautioned that innovation alone is not enough. “Manufacturers must also be able to produce equipment at scale, maintain quality and respond quickly to changing operational requirements. Companies that can combine technical innovation with efficient manufacturing and sustained product support will be well positioned,” he said.
Against this backdrop, Harman believes Afridex has the potential to become an important catalyst for industrial growth and international cooperation. “The exhibition creates an opportunity for organisations to meet directly, exchange knowledge and identify areas where their capabilities and requirements may complement one another,” he said.
For African manufacturers, it offers a platform to showcase technologies, engage with international partners and explore opportunities beyond domestic markets. For international companies, it provides valuable insight into African operational requirements and industrial capabilities.
“What makes Afridex particularly interesting is its pan-African ambition and the opportunity to bring together participants from across the continent and the wider international defence community,” said Harman.
For Harman, Afridex arrives at a pivotal moment for both Africa and the wider defence industry. As technologies, operational requirements and international supply chains evolve, the continent has an opportunity to demonstrate the depth of its innovation, expertise and industrial capability.
“Afridex should encourage organisations to think beyond traditional markets and established relationships. There is an opportunity for African defence industries to contribute meaningfully to the future of international defence and security,” he concluded.

title: ASIS Boats strengthens African footprint
body:
With nations increasingly relying on rigid-hulled inflatable boats (RHIBs) in support of maritime security, riverine operations, naval patrol, and law enforcement on water, ASIS Boats showcased its highly sought-after boats at the inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) 2026 in Lagos, Nigeria.
The exhibition follows the company’s participation in the Seapower for Africa Symposium (SPAS) in Lagos in June this year.
“Our rigid-hulled inflatable boats (RHIBs) are built for specific missions, serving military, government and professional operators around the world,” said Mario Hoyek, Business Development Manager. “ASIS Boats has delivered 28 boats across Africa in 2026, including two to the Nigeria Customs Service just last month.”
According to the company, it builds every rigid-hulled inflatable boat for specific mission applications. Offering various selections, seating configurations, and accessories, ASIS Boats can provide complete customisation of every aspect of the RHIB to fit a customer’s specific needs.
The pair of 6.5 m RHIBs delivered to the Nigeria Customs Service is configured to support enforcement operations across Nigeria’s waterways. Each boat, delivered with navigation, communication and safety systems installed, is powered by twin Yamaha 100 hp four-stroke outboard engines, allowing a top speed of 30 knots, and is able to carry up to nine personnel. The vessels feature deep-V fiberglass hulls paired with heavy-duty Hypalon 1670 dtex inflatable tubes. Their construction includes non-slip decks, triple fender strakes and reinforced cone ends.
The 20-year-old Dubai-based company prides itself on having delivered boats to more than 80 countries and over 50 government agencies over the years. Each boat is built to order around its mission, from the hull and Hypalon or PU tubes to propulsion and mission-specific equipment.
Hypalon is technically known as Chlorosulfonated Polyethylene (CSM), which offers superior UV (ultra-violet) resistance, chemical tolerance, structural durability, and a significantly longer service life.
As the company explains: “For military, coast guard, and SAR operators running vessels 200+ days per year in UV-intense or chemically harsh environments, Hypalon is not a luxury; it’s an operational requirement.”
From 2024 to date ASIS Boats has delivered eleven 9.5 m RHIBs to the Indonesian Navy.
“We announced the latest delivery, comprising four vessels, in July 2026, which followed the delivery of five boats in 2025 and an initial order in 2024,” Hoyek stated. “The operational configuration of these boats includes Ullman shock-mitigating jockey seats on rails, weapon mounts and a modular deck layout.”
He explained that the seats can be adjusted or removed, so crews can adapt the boat for patrol, surveillance, boarding and tactical operations.
The 9.5 m boats delivered in 2025 feature reinforced deep-V fiberglass hulls with push knees, self-draining non-skid decks and Neoprene/Hypalon 1670 dtex tubes.
Propulsion is provided by twin Yamaha 300 HP four-stroke outboard engines with hydraulic steering. Garmin navigation and radar systems, alongside secure communications equipment, support coordination during missions.
Following the 2025 delivery, ASIS specialists conducted on-site operator training for the Indonesian Navy crews to help personnel familiarise themselves with the vessels and their onboard systems. ASIS trainers draw on military, civilian maritime and firefighting experience to ensure end-users are equipped with the best possible post-delivery training.
ASIS Boats are trusted by military organisations, oil and gas companies, marine and tour operators, and law enforcement agencies for their reliable, high-quality construction.
Last November ASIS Boats delivered 13 fully customised 9.5 m firefighting boats to NAFFCO, the UAE-based National Fire-Fighting Manufacturing Company. Each vessel has been designed and manufactured from Marine Grade Aluminium 5086, renowned for its exceptional strength, corrosion resistance, and durability in the harshest marine conditions, thus ensuring years of reliable performance and safety at sea.
Another innovative solution is the company’s amphibious boat system, which consists of motorised, retractable, and steerable wheels that ensure off-water capabilities. This enables driving straight onto any beach, thus obviating the need for a trailer to move the boat into and out of the water. Not only does the amphibious system allow for extremely fast deployment, but also allows for accessibility to the shallowest water and previously inaccessible areas.
As the company explained: “The entire system is marinised and stays completely out of the water while underway. Once fitted with the amphibious technology, any ASIS boat will be able to travel directly between land and sea by the use of four retractable wheels with a hydraulic system linked to an inboard motor.”
It is available as an option for all ASIS boats ranging from 5.1 m to 12 m.

title: Forestry Commission plans armed camps to protect Subri Forest Reserve from galamsey
body: The Forestry Commission is proposing to establish armed security camps at illegal mining hotspots in the Subri River Forest Reserve in the Western Region to prevent miners from returning to cleared areas. Western Regional Manager of the Forestry Commission, Nana Poku Bosompim, says the strategy will combine armed rapid-response teams, surveillance technology and stronger collaboration among state security agencies to sustain gains in the fight against illegal mining. The move comes amid concerns over the scale of illegal mining in the reserve, where more than 1,000 armed illegal miners are reportedly operating. Mr Bosompim says previous enforcement operations have resulted in arrests, prosecutions and the destruction of mining equipment, but illegal miners often return when security personnel are redeployed elsewhere. Under the proposed arrangement, teams of about 13 armed rapid-response officers will be stationed at identified hotspots after clearance operations. The camps will be equipped with motorbikes, vehicles, CCTV cameras and Starlink internet connectivity to improve surveillance, communication and rapid response. The officers have also undergone specialised training for operations in forest terrain. “We should not allow the Subri River Forest Reserve to fall into that category of a red zone. It would be a failure of epic proportions on the part of all of us if we allow the situation in Subri River to degenerate,” he said. The Commission says the effective area of degraded forestland has declined from approximately 680 hectares to 282 hectares, representing a reduction of nearly 60 per cent. However, Mr Bosompim says the gains remain fragile as illegal miners continue to return to previously cleared sites. The Subri River Forest Reserve covers more than 58,000 hectares and is one of the Western Region’s major ecological assets. He admits that the scale of the region’s forest estate makes sustained enforcement difficult. The Western Region has 19 forest reserves covering approximately 209,333 hectares, requiring continued security operations to prevent further destruction. “Something has been done, but I can also say we are nowhere near winning the fight. There is still more work to be done. That tells us we need to sustain the fight,” he said. Meanwhile, Western Regional Minister Joseph Nelson has called for stronger collaboration among the Forestry Commission, the military, the Navy, the Air Force, the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) and other relevant agencies to tackle armed illegal mining groups. Mr Nelson says joint planning, intelligence-sharing and coordinated deployments are essential to prevent illegal miners from regaining control of cleared areas. He has expressed concern about gaps in cooperation among institutions working to address the same challenge. “The Forestry Commission is doing something on its own. On the same challenge, we have NAIMOS. How is the collaboration like? And interestingly, the two institutions are under the same ministry,” he said. Mr Nelson has urged the agencies to pool their resources and expertise, warning that isolated operations will not deliver lasting results. “Working in silos won’t help anybody,” he stressed, as the Forestry Commission seeks to sustain enforcement gains and prevent the Subri River Forest Reserve from deteriorating into a red zone.

title: Afridex opens to strong exhibitor and delegate interest
body:
The inaugural Africa International Defence Exhibition (Afridex) was greeted with enthusiasm by delegates and exhibitors on its first day. DefenceWeb was there on 26 October and spoke to a number of them to find out what they expected of the show.
Colonel Becky Heyse, the US Director of Public Affairs for the US military’s Africa Command (Africom), said the US was present because Africom “oversees all US military operations and relations with the continent of Africa. And so we work with many of the countries to promote our shared security interests. And the US, particularly for Nigeria, has been a great partner this last year as we have worked together on counter-terror operations specifically. We want to listen, we want to learn, we want to hear about what security concerns our partners have and where those relationships overlap so we can figure out where best we can work together and partner. Our goal is to help enable them with some of the unique capabilities that only the United States has, like some of our very unique precision strike capabilities, our intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities: we want to improve their effectiveness against shared security threats.”
Mateusz Rzymowski, CEO of Revobeam from Poland is keen to expand his business in Africa considering the experience in Poland, “the experience that we have from our neighbourhood in Ukraine plus our experience with Russia. We are now also trying to put solutions in different markets. Our company is focused on electronic warfare solutions and secure wireless communication. So we can provide solutions starting from the components like antennas, like sensors that could be embedded into unmanned solutions like drones or even ground vehicles.”
He added that, “We are open for the different models of collaboration. We are not trying only to sell the solutions but also to set up some kind of joint venture companies here, depending on the needs of the local governments and companies.”
Lieutenant Colonel Nao Otsuji, the Japanese Defence Attache in Nigeria, is attending to find new areas of defence cooperation and to build stronger relations between Africa and Japan. “I’m in charge of Nigeria and Ghana. I am researching what the government in Japan can do to offer to Nigeria. Africa doesn’t just want weapons, and then you dump them. It wants to build the weapons, maintain the weapons. I think maintenance is the most important thing. I focus on Nigerian companies. For example, Terra Industries. They are completely Nigerian and they are exporting. I want to build at least one thing: the best cooperation I can between Japan and Nigeria.”
Thamer Al-Emadi from Qatar is no stranger to Africa. As Managing Director of DICON-SUR he is already in a partnership with the Defence Industries Corporation of Nigeria (DICON) manufacturing uniforms.
“We are here today at Afridex to show our friendship and cooperation and partnership with the Nigerian Ministry of Defence. We are here to expand our partnership. Moreover, we localise and transfer technology to Nigeria. We are also here looking to expand our potential cooperation with the Nigerian forces and with other countries from the different delegations that are here. We see that Nigeria is a good hub for expanding our businesses across Africa.”
Colonel Karen Such, the Australian Defence Attaché to the African Union, is accredited to Ethiopia, Kenya, South Sudan, Djibouti and South Africa, but covers the entire continent. “The organisers reached out to our High Commission in Abuja and I thought this was a good opportunity to come and engage with a lot of African nations considering our need to cover the majority of the continent,” she said.
“What we focus on from a defence perspective here is we offer defence training courses to a number of different African nations. So, we recently had two Nigerian defence members come to Australia to undertake the UN Military Observer Course in preparation for UN Peacekeeping Missions, so that’s something I think that is of particular interest for Australia in our partnership with African countries.
“I also think it is important for countries to have some autonomy and have some ability to protect themselves and defend themselves. I think it does make sense as well for Africa to look across its nations and work together, but I think there’s a lot of opportunities for partners to come in and share and exchange knowledge and experiences and things like that, and I think that’s where this conference is a really good opportunity to do that,” she concluded.

title: American special forces buy Tekever drones
body: United States Special Operations Command has bought uncrewed aircraft from Tekever after a programme of validation and acceptance testing backed by training and an extensive flight programme at several locations, according to the company. Ricardo Mendes, chief executive of Tekever, said: “This procurement represents an important milestone in a relationship that has been built over time through rigorous testing, open dialogue and a clear focus on delivering effective capability. We greatly value the professionalism and engagement of the USSOCOM personnel with whom we have worked, and look forward to continuing to support their evolving requirements.” The number, model and configuration of the aircraft are not being disclosed. Tekever described the system as highly deployable and designed for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance in demanding environments, with a modular architecture bringing together the air platform, mission payloads, communications and mission software. Tekever has an established presence in Fayetteville, North Carolina, where the announcement was made and which sits next to Fort Bragg, the home of United States Army special operations. The company said the purchase is a further step in its commitment to the United States and its special operations community. The Portuguese company is familiar to British readers through its AR5 maritime surveillance aircraft, which has flown over the English Channel under Home Office contracts since 2020. It has also supplied uncrewed aircraft to Ukraine and employs more than fifteen hundred people across Portugal, the United States, France, the United Kingdom, Germany, Estonia and Ukraine. The post American special forces buy Tekever drones first appeared on UK Defence Journal .

title: Press review: Europe seeks restoration of Russia ties as aid operation starts in Alyoshki
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Europe seeks to restore channels of communication with Russia; a humanitarian operation begins in Alyoshki; and Russia highlights the need to safeguard the global gas market. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia
The leaders of Russia, Norway and Finland agreed to maintain direct contact during a telephone conversation on October 27. However, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who initiated the call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, denied they were speaking on behalf of Europe as a whole, Izvestia reports.
The joint call by Finland’s president and Norway’s premier signals that Europe is getting ready for the next round of peace negotiations, Tigran Meloyan, an analyst at the Higher School of Economics’ Institute for Global Military Economics and Strategy, said. Such steps by leaders of NATO and European Union countries are always preceded by diplomatic consultations with allies, so it is safe to assume that the idea had been coordinated with Kiev and Brussels, the expert added.
Western media reports say the European Union is discussing the appointment of a special envoy for talks with Russia. Ultimately, the bloc could select several representatives, European Parliament member Fernand Kartheiser of Luxembourg said. EU member states hold widely differing positions, as some remain skeptical about the very principle of talks, while others, such as Slovakia, seek to normalize bilateral relations with Russia as much as possible. That said, appointing multiple negotiators could better represent the range of opinions within the EU, Kartheiser added.
Yegor Sergeyev, senior researcher with the Institute for International Studies at the Moscow State Institute of International Relations, pointed out that it was still too early to speak of European countries becoming fully involved in the negotiation process. The analyst pointed to the lack of constructive proposals as one of the reasons.
The initiative by Stubb and Store is not part of EU diplomacy but reflects the national interests of Russia’s European neighbors, Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at the Russian State University for the Humanities, told Vedomosti . According to him, the Norwegian premier and the Finnish president did not call Putin as European envoys but as national leaders. "This does not indicate a change in attitude toward Russia or a decline in support for Kiev. This can also be viewed as an effort to avoid being left out of discussions of future European security," the expert noted.
The humanitarian operation in Alyoshki will continue until 10:59 p.m. on November 1, Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova said. Its main goals are to provide civilians with medicine, food and essential supplies and evacuate those wishing to leave the town. A successful outcome could pave the way for the resumption of trilateral talks between Moscow, Kiev and Washington, Izvestia notes.
The Russian army suspended fire in the Alyoshki area at 4:00 a.m. on October 27 to prepare for the humanitarian mission, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump.
Meanwhile, provocations by the Ukrainian armed forces during the ceasefire in Alyoshki cannot be ruled out, military expert Alexey Leonkov told the newspaper. In this regard, he cited 18 artillery strikes and more than 120 drone attacks carried out by Kiev’s forces against Alyoshki and the main roads leading to the town during the week of October 19.
"Numerous ceasefires have been announced since the start of the special military operation. Humanitarian ceasefires were also declared before that, particularly during the period when the Minsk Accords were in effect. Still, Ukraine failed to honor these agreements each time," Leonkov noted. According to him, Kiev could use the pause in fighting to deploy additional troops to this part of the front and replenish its ammunition stocks.
"Ukrainian forces are not currently staging provocations as they have to honor a promise presumably made to Melania Trump. But once the humanitarian ceasefire ends, they could resume attacks on Alyoshki and once again lay mines along roads leading to the town," military expert Viktor Litovkin pointed out. Nevertheless, the ceasefire should be used to the fullest to address humanitarian needs.
However, although humanitarian and political efforts continue in parallel, with the two processes not directly connected, a successful operation in Alyoshki could create favorable conditions for the resumption of trilateral negotiations between Moscow, Kiev and Washington. A new round of negotiations could take place after November 4.
Discussions at the Eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit in Moscow on October 27 focused on volatility in energy markets, driven by tensions in the Middle East, and sanctions on Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin and speakers from other GECF member states discussed these issues in their remarks, Vedomosti reports.
The main issue today is disruptions to gas supplies, which highlight the need to develop ways to optimize transportation routes, taking into account the geographic locations of GECF member states, the Russian leader said. Most GECF members and observer nations called for peace and security to be maintained to ensure stable gas supplies. The situation in the Strait of Hormuz has demonstrated how geopolitical changes could affect the energy sector, GECF Secretary General Philip Mshelbila pointed out.
Moscow has never refused to engage in dialogue with European countries, but the European Union has made a series of short-sighted political decisions, digging a hole for itself rather than for Russia, Izvestia notes, citing Putin.
The 2026 Middle East crisis has worsened the fragmentation of gas markets, Kept expert Nikita Illeritsky said. In his opinion, US liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports are now seeking to strengthen their positions in Europe and Northeast Asia to recoup billions of dollars invested in their facilities.
Still, many European countries continue to prioritize political decisions over their economic interests. In a bid to cut Moscow’s revenues, the European Union has undermined its own economy. Abandoning stable pipeline gas supplies from Russia and shifting to the spot market, where prices are much higher, has dealt a direct blow to European industry. Nevertheless, neither restrictions nor market disruptions can halt the global trend toward a growing role for natural gas as a pillar of the global energy sector, industry and international trade.
The shares of Europe and the United States in financial and economic influence across African countries have fallen to 29% and 10%, respectively. Meanwhile, BRICS countries have broadened their presence, raising their share to 16%, according to Vedomosti estimates.
When it comes to Africa, it’s more accurate to speak of "a fragmented international security market" rather than "zones of influence," as African governments decide which external actors to work with, while global powers compete for access, influence, mineral resources and trade routes.
"This is not a division but ‘a competitive coexistence’ of numerous external forces in one space," said Mikhail Margelov, acting head of the UNESCO Department at Moscow State University’s Institute of Asian and African Studies and vice president of the Russian International Affairs Council. Formal zones of influence no longer exist in Africa, as the colonial-era division of the continent has been replaced by competition among external powers. These changes are especially evident in the Sahel region, where Russia has consolidated its position following the withdrawal of French and US troops.
African nations are increasingly seeking to balance their ties with foreign partners while reinforcing their sovereignty. The West describes this approach as multi-alignment, with countries maintaining relations with several centers of power at once, Denis Degterev, senior researcher with the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, and professor with the Moscow State Institute of International Relations and the Higher School of Economics, explained.
Economic influence in Africa depends not only on trade and investment but also on defense and political cooperation, as well as debt burdens, Degterev noted. Creditors such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have particularly strong leverage. Even Sahel countries, which have rejected military cooperation with the West, remain reliant on these institutions. As for the European Union, it should not be viewed as a single player, because France, Germany and Italy often vie for influence.
Deeper African integration has become a crucial trend, including efforts to develop a continental free trade area, a regional payment system and financial institutions. "The only way for African nations to implement major industrial and infrastructure projects and reduce their reliance on foreign countries is to pool resources. Africa needs industrialization," Andrey Fyodorov, leading researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute for African Studies, emphasized.
Russian oil refineries are ramping up diesel production after the government partially lifted its export ban. The resumption of diesel exports and higher output could help sustain domestic oil production, Rossiyskaya Gazeta notes.
Valery Andrianov, associate professor at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation, pointed out that the return to operation of refineries following scheduled maintenance was supporting Russian oil production. However, growth remains limited by Russia’s quota under the OPEC+ agreement. Earlier, domestic output fell short of the quota because demand from processing facilities had declined and logistics issues had hampered efforts to increase crude oil exports.
According to energy expert Kirill Rodionov, the current level of oil production in Russia is shaped by three factors: oil exports, domestic refining and various fuel export bans. Crude exports are currently hindered by shipping difficulties in the Black Sea. Meanwhile, domestic oil processing depends on the completion of maintenance work at Russian refineries and the regulator’s export restrictions, which are now being partially lifted.
The expert stressed that the Russia-US diesel deal would have little impact on the oil production situation because the export volumes agreed by the two countries were too small. However, a full lifting of the diesel export ban, at least for oil refineries, could pave the way to higher petroleum product exports and oil production.
In Andrianov’s view, Russia could raise oil output by 1.3 mln barrels per day. However, achieving this target will depend on the pace of refinery maintenance and the intensity of attacks on the facilities.
Rodionov identified shipping issues in the Black Sea as another risk. He does not expect Russia to achieve sustained oil production growth before 2027.

title: More than 60 killed after trains collide in Spain
body: At least 64 people died on Wednesday when two trains collided near Toledo, in central Spain , a representative of the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha said. A train operated by state-owmed Renfe and another by Iryo, Spain's first private high-speed rail operator, crashed shortly after 9am local time, causing at least two of the Iryo carriages to derail. The incident also injured 80 people out of the more than 540 passengers. Videos broadcast on the regional Castilla-La Mancha TV showed ​a derailed train with at least one carriage ‌remaining on an elevated section ⁠of track while twisted metal, ​broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an ​embankment ‌beneath the line. The collision ⁠comes nine months after an accident between high-speed trains belonging to the same operators on the same line that killed 46 people. Both accidents occurred on the line running south from Madrid and involved state-owned train operator Renfe and Iryo, a rival operator controlled by the Italian-state. Wednesday’s crash happened about 132km (62 miles) south of Madrid, near the city of Toledo. Miguel, a passenger ​travelling ⁠with colleagues in the rear carriage ‌of one of the trains, described to Cope Radio the moment of the accident. “We heard a massive ​roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train – I imagine it must have been the other one,” he said. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said he was shocked by the accident and remained in contact with Transport Minister Oscar Puente and the president of Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano Garcia-Page. Messages of support Emergency services were working at the scene to help those affected as part of a co-ordinated response, Mr Sanchez said. “My affection, solidarity and support go to all the victims and their families,” he wrote on X. Manuel Galan, mayor of nearby town of Urda, ⁠told the Cadena SER radio network that the town council had been asked to prepare emergency facilities, including at a sports hall, for injured and affected passengers. Spain's Royal Household said it was “deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident”. “We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of the deceased and send our best wishes to the injured and all those affected,” it said in a statement. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed dismay at the “terrible” train accident. “My deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims. Today, Europe mourns with you,” Ms von der Leyen said.

title: Ozon Posts Over $370M in Estimated Damages From Drone Attacks
body:
Russia’s second-largest online retailer Ozon on Wednesday booked 30.1 billion rubles ($373.1 million) in estimated damages from Ukrainian drone attacks that have so far targeted around a dozen of its warehouses across the country.
In its third-quarter earnings release, the company said the estimated losses, some of which were insured, included “damage to goods for sale, equipment disposal and impairment losses, as well as other losses and expenses.”
Ozon said it was still negotiating with insurers as it seeks compensation to offset the financial impact of the drone attacks.
Despite the losses, Ozon reported that revenues rose to 421.2 billion rubles ($5.2 billion) in the third quarter, a 60% increase year-on-year.
Ozon said its net profit between July and September fell to 3.7 billion rubles ($45.8 million) from 10.1 billion rubles in the second quarter of 2026.
Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) reached 93 billion rubles ($1.1 billion), a figure that excludes estimated losses from the drone strikes.
Ozon said it completed 1.2 billion orders in the third quarter, up 76% from the third quarter of 2025. On average, an Ozon customer places 51 orders per year, the company said.
Ukraine began its air campaign against Ozon and its main competitor, Wildberries, this summer on accusations that they help supply the Russian military.
