Everyone was talking about it, and there was a real sense of excitement across the city. One of the events was a Spartan Race in Hatta, which I had planned to take part in. But just days before the race, I suffered an injury and realised I wouldn't be able to compete. I didn't want to miss the experience altogether, so I contacted the organisers and asked whether I could volunteer instead. I ended up helping to hand out medals at the finish line. I'd previously seen a fellow athlete on Instagram who was also injured but had decided to take on the race anyway. It involved 30km and 30 obstacles, and I had sent him a few messages of support. Then, while I was handing out medals, I placed one around a finisher's neck and congratulated him. He suddenly recognised me and said, "Lolla, that's you!" It was Mohammed, the same man I'd been messaging. He'd completed the race, and I remember feeling genuinely happy and emotional for him. That moment led to him inviting me for coffee. He would eventually become my husband. If I hadn't been injured, I would have been competing instead of volunteering. If I had arrived a little later or been assigned somewhere else, we might never have met. I truly believe that race in Hatta brought us together. What started as an unexpected love story eventually became a family tradition. Every year, we look forward to the challenge and the opportunity to take part in activities together. Our son Noah was only seven weeks old when we took him to the first Dubai Run in 2019. He later joined us for other events, including Dubai Ride , when we cycled along Sheikh Zayed Road with thousands of other participants. Watching him grow up with these experiences has been incredibly special. I've always wanted to raise a family that enjoys being active together, and the challenge has given us a reason to make that a priority every year. I've also had opportunities I never imagined, including becoming a Dubai Fitness Challenge ambassador alongside my husband, a Spartan ambassador for the Middle East and an Asics FrontRunner. When I think about everything that has happened since 2017, I'm grateful I decided to volunteer at that finish line instead of staying home. If there's one thing I'd tell someone thinking about taking part for the first time, it's not to underestimate what can come from trying something new. You never know where it might take you. Husam Mohamed: 'I lost 50kg, but gained much more' I first heard about Dubai Fitness Challenge in 2017, but I wasn't particularly interested. Fitness and an active lifestyle weren't things I thought about. It wasn't until the second edition in 2018 that I began to take the challenge seriously. I've always admired how Sheikh Hamdan leads by example when it comes to fitness, and seeing him participate personally inspired me to give it a chance. At the time, I was overweight; my fitness level was almost zero, and I was very shy about participating in public activities. I'd never been involved in sports, gone to the gym or paid much attention to living healthily. I wasn't fully committed during those first 30 days, but something changed. For the first time, I made a commitment to my health and started noticing results, physically and mentally. I began thinking beyond the challenge, and eventually exercise became part of my lifestyle. Since then, I've lost 50kg. But the biggest transformation hasn't been the number on the scale. I've become mentally stronger, more confident, more open and more focused on achieving my goals. Movement is now an essential part of my daily routine. I often say that movement is medicine, but it's also a language of love. It's something I enjoy sharing with others because it brings people together, helps us connect and allows us to support one another. For a long time, I was a very shy and private person. Being overweight affected my confidence, and I didn't think I had anything worth sharing. But as my transformation progressed, people began asking how I'd done it. That's when I realised my story might encourage someone else to begin. I hadn't done anything extraordinary. I'd simply started, remained patient and kept going. What I love most is how it brings together people from different backgrounds and fitness levels. For that month, it feels as though the entire city becomes one enormous gym. If I could offer one piece of advice to someone starting where I did, it would be to enjoy the journey. Don't rush or focus only on the final result. Celebrate the small achievements and document your progress. One day, you'll look back and realise just how far you've come, not only physically but mentally and emotionally. Danny Cousins: 'Running became about more than personal bests' My first memories of Dubai Fitness Challenge are of seeing how much the city changes when it comes around. I've taken part a couple of times over the years, but even when you're not actively participating, it's hard not to notice the sense of community it creates. Places such as Kite Beach really come alive. I've always been naturally competitive as a runner, but DFC reminded me that running and fitness don't always have to be about racing or chasing a particular time. While Dubai Fitness Challenge wasn't the direct inspiration behind the launch of SubClub DXB in 2025, it helped foster the city's growing fitness culture, which played a part in our decision to start the running club. With SubClub, we wanted to create something between a social running club and a serious training environment. The idea came from those "sub" targets. Whether you're chasing a sub-20-minute 5km, sub-25, sub-30 or simply trying to run a distance faster than before, everyone has their own version of a personal best. Some of the most rewarding moments have been watching people achieve something they didn't think was possible. A personal best might belong to one person on paper, but when you've trained and struggled together, it starts to feel like a shared achievement. Building SubClub has changed how I think about running. Technically, it's an individual sport, but I've discovered how much of the experience can be shared. That's what I appreciate about DFC. Dubai brings together people from different backgrounds and fitness levels, and for one month everyone is encouraged to work towards the same goal.

title: Chinese expert points to Japan’s ability to produce thousands of nuclear warheads
body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan possesses more than 40 metric tons of plutonium, theoretically enough to produce several thousand nuclear warheads, Secretary General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA) Dai Huaicheng told TASS.
He pointed out that according to the Japanese authorities, the country possessed 44.4 tons of separated plutonium at the end of 2024, including 8.6 tons stored domestically and 35.8 tons held overseas. In addition, Japan’s stocks of spent nuclear fuel contain about 191 tons of unseparated plutonium.
"The latest report from the Japan Atomic Energy Commission, published in August 2026, says that the total amount of separated plutonium remained at about 44.4 tons at the end of 2025, with 9.9 tons stored in the country and about 34.5 tons held abroad, as the size of the stocks remained vast," Dai said.
"What does this mean? Making a simple nuclear warhead typically requires only a few kilograms of weapons-grade plutonium. According to open sources, Japan’s 44.4 tons of separated plutonium would be enough to manufacture several thousand nuclear warheads," the expert pointed out.
Dai also said that the Japanese authorities justified the country’s substantial plutonium stockpiles by citing plans to use the material as fuel for nuclear power plants. However, this remains a cause for concern amid statements by some Japanese politicians advocating the acquisition of nuclear weapons, the expert added.
"Although most of Japan’s plutonium is reactor-grade, it’s not entirely impossible to use it in nuclear devices. Notably, Japan has the technology and processing facilities needed to separate weapons-grade plutonium, making the distinction between civilian and military use extremely blurred," the expert concluded.

title: Chinese expert says it would take Japan only a few dozen days to develop nuclear weapons
body:
BEIJING, October 28. /TASS/. Japan could develop a nuclear explosive device in a matter of weeks if its government decided to pursue nuclear weapons, according to Dai Huaicheng, Secretary-General of the China Arms Control and Disarmament Association (CACDA). Speaking to TASS, Dai said Japan’s advanced industrial base and existing plutonium stockpiles could allow it to achieve this far more quickly than other countries. "From a technical and material standpoint, Japan is already on the ‘nuclear threshold’ when it comes to overcoming the hurdles involved in producing even a single nuclear explosive device. As one American expert aptly put it, Japan ‘only needs to turn a screwdriver’ to acquire nuclear weapons," Dai said.
"Based on statements by various Japanese officials and analyses by both domestic and foreign experts, Japan could theoretically produce a nuclear explosive device in a very short time if it chose to take that risk. Some estimates suggest the process could take just over 100 days - or perhaps even as little as a few dozen days," he added.
"On the other hand, from a technical standpoint, creating a full-scale nuclear arsenal requires completing stages such as weaponization, testing, and systems integration. However, the international community must remain on guard: Japan possesses long-standing stockpiles of nuclear materials, technologies, and delivery systems, meaning the time it would take for the country to complete this process would be significantly shorter than for other nations," the expert noted.
"This is precisely why the misguided statements and actions of the Japanese authorities in the nuclear realm pose a particular danger: they are attempting to remove the final political and legal barrier preventing Japan from crossing the 'nuclear threshold’," Dai concluded.

title: Nestoil pays further $40 million to lenders after EFCC intervention
body:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) intervention in the debt settlement dispute between local energy firm Nestoil Limited and a consortium of lenders has yielded further positive results, with the company paying an additional $40 million to the creditors.
The fresh payment on 19 October brought the total paid to the lenders so far to $100 million, people familiar with the matter told PREMIUM TIMES.
It marks major progress in the structured repayment plan Nestoil and the lenders agreed to at a meeting earlier organised by the EFCC, which yielded an initial payment of $60 million from the oil firm to the banks.
The agreement set out a framework for repaying the outstanding debt, based on the parties’ agreed terms and applicable laws.
The EFCC’s mediation in the dispute centres on certain financial transactions involving Nestoil, its affiliate Neconde Energy Limited, and the banks.
The lenders welcomed the latest payment as a key, encouraging development and reaffirmed their commitment to continued cooperation with the EFCC and other relevant stakeholders to ensure full settlement of the debt.
The EFCC’s media department could not be reached for comment.
The feud between Nestoil and the lenders is a complicated legal battle that came to a head at the Supreme Court of Nigeria in June, prompting the court to annul a Court of Appeal order freezing the assets of Nestoil and Neconde Energy.
The lawsuit seeks to recover debts of more than $1 billion and N430 billion allegedly owed by Neconde and Nestoil, as well as Azudialu Obiejesi and Nnenna Azudialu-Obiejesi, their top promoters.
In October 2025, police officers acting on an order issued by Dehinde Dipeolu, a judge of the Federal High Court, Lagos Division, sealed Nestoil’s headquarters in Lagos. The order gave FBN Quest Merchant Bank and First Trustees leave to take over Nestoil’s assets.
Justice Dipeolu granted multiple orders freezing the defendants’ bank accounts and shares held with more than 20 financial and other institutions in Nigeria.
The court also authorised Abubakar Sulu-Gambari (SAN), the receiver/manager appointed by the plaintiffs, to take over Nestoil’s headquarters and other identified assets.
Justice Dipeolu also directed multiple security agencies to help enforce the receivership.
Following Nestoil’s complaints about the proceedings, John Tsoho, the chief judge of the Federal High Court, reassigned the case to another judge.
On 20 November 2025, J. Osiagor, the new Judge, revoked the earlier receivership-enforcement order.
FBN Quest Merchant Bank and First Trustees appealed against the decision on 22 November 2025.
In November 2025, the Court of Appeal issued a restorative injunction in an ex parte application filed by the financial institutions.
The order reversed Justice Osiagor’s decision and also forbade Nestoil, Neconde and their agents from obstructing the receiver/manager pending the hearing of the appeal.
In January, the Supreme Court ordered all the parties in the suit to return to the Court of Appeal to resolve a major procedural issue.
It held that the appeal court had to resolve the issue of legal representation.
Consequently, in January, the Court of Appeal disqualified Wole Olanipekun, Muiz Banire, and other lawyers appearing with them from representing Neconde and Nestoil.
It ruled that the receivership of Mr Sulu-Gambari had suspended Mr Azudialu-Obiejesi’s powers.
But in June, the Supreme Court ruled that the appellate court exceeded its authority by issuing an ex parte application against the oil firms.
It ruled that the Court of Appeal assumed jurisdiction and granted an injunction against Neconde and Nestoil when the dispute was not properly before the court.
It also rebuked the lower court for misusing the judicial process in granting a stay of proceedings at the Federal High Court, Lagos.
The court consequently annulled the freezing order on Nestoil’s and Neconde’s assets.
“Prior to the Court Action, Nestoil obtained several bilateral loan facilities from eight (8) lenders dating back to 2010 and serially defaulted on all the various repayment obligations,” the consortium of lenders said in a statement following the Supreme Court’s ruling.
“Nestoil subsequently proposed restructuring the bilateral loan facilities to bring the Lenders into a Global Club to ease the administration of the indebtedness. Lenders, in good faith, agreed to this restructuring, but Nestoil has again serially defaulted on its repayment obligations since the restructuring became effective in 2023,” the lenders added.
According to a May press release, Nestoil’s alleged $2 billion distressed loan has triggered “a historic balance sheet reset” and “a lack of dividend payments” at some major Nigerian banks.
The statement listed First Bank, United Bank for Africa, and Access Bank among the financial institutions most affected by Nestoil’s bad loans.

title: Poland’s F-35A fleet at home reaches 10, with more deliveries expected by year-end
body: The Polish defense ministry announced the latest arrival on October 27. Aircraft 3518 completed final assembly and testing at Cameri, Italy, and made its first test flight on September 15. Deliveries to Poland began in May, and Lockheed Martin representatives have indicated that another two or three aircraft could arrive before year-end. Two further fighters, numbered 3519 and 3520, made their first test flights at Cameri in October. Kolejny, dziesiąty “Husarz” wylądował w Polsce. Wkrótce wielozadaniowy samolot F-35 będzie wykonywał swoje zadania z 32 Bazy Lotnictwa Taktycznego w Łasku. Ochrona polskiej i sojuszniczej przestrzeni powietrznej to jeden z naszych priorytetów. Budujemy siłę i zdolności polskich sił powietrznych, budujemy bezpieczeństwo naszych obywateli. — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) October 27, 2026 Poland ordered 32 F-35As under an agreement with the United States signed in January 2020. The aircraft will equip two Polish Air Force tactical aviation squadrons. F-35A deliveries are also continuing elsewhere in Europe, with Finland recently receiving two more aircraft to bring its total in the country to four .

title: Ceasefire in Oleshky enters 30th hour as Russian strikes kill 2, injure 17 elsewhere in Ukraine over past day
body:
Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 28 that the first 30 hours of the ceasefire in the town of Oleshky had passed "without a single incident," while Russian attacks killed two people and injured 17 others in other regions of Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson , the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
The ceasefire, which took effect in the early hours of Oct. 27 and is set to last until Nov. 1, initially covered Oleshky and surrounding areas in Kherson Oblast. It is intended to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and the delivery of humanitarian aid over the coming days.
At the same time, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump announced on Oct. 27 that the ceasefire had taken effect across the entire region.
Kherson Oblast Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said no strikes against critical or civilian infrastructure were reported in the region over the past day. The governor added that four people who had suffered injuries in "previous days" had sought medical care.
Pavlo Drohal, a spokesperson for the Ukrainian Navy's Marine Corps, also confirmed that Ukrainian and Russian forces were observing the ceasefire as of 8 a.m. local time.
Meanwhile, Russia continued to attack other regions of Ukraine. Russian forces launched an Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missile and 88 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine, including 38 jet-powered drones, overnight on Oct. 28. Russia also used a low-cost S8000 Banderol/Dan-T cruise missile and decoy drones in the attack, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 71 drones, 31 of which were jet-powered.
Russian weapons struck targets at eight locations, while falling debris was reported at two others. The Air Force did not specify whether the strikes were caused by drones or the ballistic missile.
In southeastern Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , a Russian strike on the Synelnykove district killed one person and injured another, while three people were injured in the city of Dnipro on Oct. 27, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks injured two men and two women in the regional capital of Kharkiv. Two more people were injured in other settlements across the region over the past day, the local military administration said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , two people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia District, according to the local military administration .
In northern Sumy Oblast , drone strikes injured a 51-year-old man in the Sumy community and a 43-year-old man in the Bilopillia community, the local military administration said.

title: NEDO Plans 4,000 Observers, AI Monitoring for 2027 General Election
body: Folalumi Alaran in Abuja With public confidence in Nigeria’s electoral process under pressure and shaky, five civil society organisations have unveiled plans to deploy more than 4,000 observers and use artificial intelligence to scrutinise results and document irregularities during the 2027 general election. The initiative, under the Nigeria Election Data Observatory (NEDO) Consortium, is designed to strengthen independent monitoring of voting, result collation and transmission, while enabling participating organisations to cross-check electoral information and expose discrepancies. The consortium, comprising Dataphyte Foundation, Yiaga Africa, BudgIT Foundation, the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID), and DEAN Initiative, was launched in Abuja yesterday. At the heart of the initiative is a shared data platform that will combine information from election observers, media organisations and technology systems to build an independent evidence base against which official election information can be examined. The platform will use artificial intelligence (AI)-powered optical character recognition (OCR) to convert result-sheet images published on the Independent National Electoral Commission’s (INEC) Result Viewing Portal (IReV) into machine-readable data, enabling the system to flag potential discrepancies for further verification. Under the arrangement, figures recorded on result sheets can be analysed for inconsistencies, including discrepancies between votes recorded and relevant voter figures. The system is also designed to identify errors ranging from typographical mistakes to potentially serious irregularities. The consortium said the technology would support the identification and documentation of questionable figures as result sheets are uploaded, rather than leaving discrepancies to emerge only after the collation process. The initiative came against the backdrop of persistent concerns about electoral credibility. A September 2026 national voting intentions survey by Yiaga Africa found that only 34 per cent of respondents expressed confidence in INEC’s ability to conduct credible elections. Speaking on behalf of the consortium, Dataphyte Foundation Country Director, Oluseyi Olufemi, said NEDO was established to address fragmentation in election observation, civic data management and information sharing among organisations working to protect electoral integrity. The consortium said the difficulties surrounding IReV during the 2023 general elections had demonstrated the importance of coordinated civic resources capable of consolidating observation data and independently checking electoral information. With more than 4,000 observers planned for the 2027 elections, the initiative will draw on participating organisations’ networks, including Yiaga Africa’s Watching The Vote observers, to document voting, electoral incidents, collation, and results. Information gathered from the field will be compared with official results and other available evidence to help identify inconsistencies, verify competing claims and provide a stronger basis for public reporting. CJID will also connect the initiative to participating newsrooms and fact-checking networks, enabling journalists to seek corroboration from observers in relevant locations before publishing claims about electoral incidents. The consortium said the arrangement would help counter misinformation and conflicting reports while giving the media access to a broader body of independently gathered evidence. It also unveiled the NEDO App, through which field observers will document developments throughout the electoral process. Dataphyte Foundation Programme Manager, Abdulahi Adebayo, said the application would feed information into a shared evidence repository for analysis, reporting, visualisation, advocacy and public communication. However, the consortium acknowledged that the technology itself would require protection against deliberate interference. It said it was working on transparency, accountability and auditing mechanisms, including engagement with INEC on technical glitches and system integrity. The initiative will also include pre-election surveys and assessments led by DEAN Initiative to examine electoral preparedness, citizens’ perceptions and emerging risks. Findings will inform a National Election Readiness Report, regional briefs, and periodic situation reports. After the elections, the consortium plans to analyse its evidence alongside official results and publish a post-election report, with relevant data made available for research, advocacy, and electoral reform.

title: Shanghai, 1937: An Urban Warfare Project Case Study
body:
Liam Collins , Jayson Geroux , John Spencer and Amanda Zhao | 10.28.26
One historian wrote that it “presaged urban combat as it was to be waged . . . throughout the remainder of the twentieth century.” A journalist said that it was “as though a Verdun had happened on the Seine” or “a Gettysburg was fought in Harlem.” International media compared the siege of one building where defenders made a desperate last stand to the Alamo.
It isn’t the Battle of Stalingrad. It isn’t Manila, Hue, Mogadishu, or Grozny. It is the 1937 Battle of Shanghai, one of the earliest major engagements of the Second Sino-Japanese War. Between them, the Republic of China and the Empire of Japan committed a million troops to the battle. It was fought over more than three months, for control of what was at the time the second-largest metropolis in Asia. And the city’s large foreign-controlled sectors made it an incredibly complex urban battlefield.
The seventeenth installment in MWI’s Urban Warfare Project Case Study Series examines the Battle of Shanghai, extracting its most important and enduring lessons—from the critical factor of legitimacy in a fight for a globally connected city to challenge of synchronizing combat power in complicated, often chaotic, urban conditions. You can read it here , and be sure to follow the Urban Warfare Project for future case studies and continuing exploration of the challenges faced by military forces operating in cities.
Liam Collins, PhD is the director of Madison Policy Forum and a distinguished military fellow with the Middle East Institute. He is a retired Special Forces colonel with deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan, Bosnia, the Horn of Africa, and South America. He is the coauthor of The War for Karabakh: Strategy, Technology, and Victory, coauthor of Understanding Urban Warfare , and author of Leadership & Innovation During Crisis: Lessons from the Iraq War .
Major Jayson Geroux is an infantry officer with The Royal Canadian Regiment and is currently with the Canadian Army Doctrine and Training Centre. He has been a fervent student of and has been involved in urban operations training for twenty-five years. He is an equally passionate military historian and has participated in, planned, executed, and intensively instructed on urban operations and urban warfare history for the past thirteen years. He has served thirty-one years in the Canadian Armed Forces, which included operational tours to the former Yugoslavia (Bosnia-Herzegovina) and Afghanistan.
John Spencer is chair of urban warfare studies at the Modern War Institute, codirector of MWI’s Urban Warfare Project, and host of the Urban Warfare Project Podcast . He served twenty-five years as an infantry soldier, which included two combat tours in Iraq. He is the coauthor of The War for Karabakh: Strategy, Technology, and Victory, author of Connected Soldiers: Life, Leadership, and Social Connections in Modern War , and coauthor of Understanding Urban Warfare .
Amanda Zhao is an undergraduate student in the Georgetown School of Foreign Service, majoring in international politics (international security concentration) and minoring in government. She served as the lead researcher and author on this case study.
The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

title: Urban Warfare Project Case Study #17: Battle of Shanghai
body:
Liam Collins, Jayson Geroux, John Spencer, and Amanda Zhao | 10.28.26
The Battle of Shanghai occurred from August 13 to November 11, 1937 , and was the first major battle of the Second Sino-Japanese War (1937–1945). Following Japan’s invasion of Manchuria in 1931, the two countries engaged in periodic skirmishes. The deadliest of these was 1932’s “ Shanghai incident ,” in which thousands of soldiers and ten thousand civilians lost their lives. Despite this, the nations avoided full scale war until July 7, 1937. The war started with the “ Marco Polo Bridge incident ” in northern China, but its focus quickly shifted to Shanghai. On August 9, 1937, Chinese police officers shot and killed Japanese First Lieutenant Oyama Isao and his driver when they attempted to enter Shanghai’s Hongqiao Airport in violation of the 1932 ceasefire agreement. Soon thereafter, tensions escalated into a major battle for Shanghai that ultimately ended in a Japanese victory.
Due to colonialism, Shanghai had evolved into a city with control divided between three governing bodies. A joint municipal council governed the 8.35-square-mile international settlement. The settlement stretched across the center of the city from west to east and contained a large American, British, and Japanese presence. To its south the French consulate general administered control over the 3.9-square-mile French concession . The Chinese Municipality of Greater Shanghai governed the remaining fifteen square miles of the metropolis and the most populous parts of the city. From west to east the Zhabei, Hongkou, and Yangshupu districts were situated within the Chinese municipality north of the international settlement. The Zhabei district was an industrial area and a major transportation hub where roads, waterways, and railways converged. The Sihang Warehouse was located at its southern tip. The Old City and Nanshi districts were located within the Chinese municipality south of the French concession. The underdeveloped Pudong district sat on a peninsula opposite the international settlement on a bend formed by the Huangpu River . The river flowed from south to north with a sharp bend at Shanghai, before emptying into the Yangtze River fifteen miles north of the city.
The 150-foot-wide Suzhou Creek with its steep seven-foot banks bisected the city. It ran from northwest to southeast along the border of the Zhabei district and the international settlement and then through the international settlement before emptying into the Huangpu River’s bend. There were few subterranean spaces within Shanghai due to the water-saturated soil . The city’s streets were a mix of asphalt and dirt arranged in a mostly grid-like pattern intersected by narrow, maze-like alleyways. Most buildings were multistory and constructed of wood. The combination of narrow streets, dense building clusters, and limited avenues of movement created canalized engagement areas where defending forces could mass fires against advancing troops.
Trade had transformed Shanghai into a metropolis. In 1937, its population of 3.5 million made it the second-largest city in Asia (Tokyo was the largest) and the fifth largest in the world. The city’s residents included seventy thousand foreigners from forty-seven countries. The largest group (twenty thousand Japanese) was concentrated in the eastern half of the international settlement, Little Tokyo (in the Hongkou district’s south), and parts of the Zhabei district.
The international settlement was divided into four defense sectors run by Italy, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Japan to defend the international residents. The United States defended its sector—the westernmost part of the international settlement—with its 4th Marine Regiment. The United Kingdom defended its sector—the central portion of the international settlement—with British forces commanded by Major General Alexander Telfer-Smollett. Observing that the fight for the city was impending, a multinational Shanghai Volunteer Corps and additional British and American military personnel began building concrete blockhouses and machine gun posts reinforced with barbed wire to defend their respective sectors.
The Japanese defense sector was the largest. It included the eastern portion of the international settlement and the southern part of the Hongkou district. The Japanese forces stationed in Shanghai included 2,500 members of the Special Naval Landing Forces, marine infantry units. They were stationed at their headquarters —a two-block, fortress-like, four-story building with a roof made of two layers of reinforced concrete—as well as other positions throughout the district and within the Japanese defense sector. The headquarters building, located in Little Tokyo, included a dense network of machine gun positions protected by sandbag walls, concrete emplacements, and barbed wire obstacles. The marines had light armored vehicles, tanks, and artillery. On August 11–13, the Japanese Navy’s 3rd Fleet reinforced the garrison with another 2,500 marines who arrived on twenty-one warships that moored near where the Suzhou Creek joined the Huangpu River. Over the course of the battle, Japan would land additional divisions that participated in the battle in and around Shanghai. Japanese naval and army aviation units, including the 1st Combined Air Group, supported the battle. In total, nearly three hundred thousand Japanese forces would participate in the three-month battle.
General Zhang Zhizhong, a veteran of 1932’s Shanghai incident , commanded the Chinese 9th Army Group at the beginning of the conflict, which conducted most of the urban combat. These forces included twenty-two thousand soldiers from the 87th and 88th Divisions, a half-strength brigade (2,500 soldiers) from the 98th Division (at the disposal of the 87th Division), and two regiments (five thousand soldiers) from the 36th Division, all located in the Shanghai North Railway Station. The 55th Division (six thousand soldiers) was positioned in the Pudong district on the eastern bank of the Huangpu River. The 87th and 88th Divisions had undergone modernization plans before the start of the war and were trained by members of the German advisory corps, which consisted of seventy officers. As a result, their soldiers were more competent than typical Chinese soldiers and on par with their Japanese adversaries. Also present was the Peace Preservation Corps, a Chinese paramilitary group and the only Chinese force permitted to operate within Shanghai as stipulated by the 1932 ceasefire agreement. A total of seven hundred thousand Chinese soldiers would ultimately participate in all three phases of the Shanghai campaign as additional forces arrived throughout the battle.
Other elements supported these infantry forces, but they lacked sufficient size, training, combat power, and experience. Artillery units possessed several types of guns, the largest being 150-millimeter, but their crews and forward observers were undertrained. Chinese armor consisted of sixteen light tanks but their crews suffered from the same lack of training. Air defense units were equipped with an insufficient number of German/Swiss Solothurn S-18/100 20-millimeter antitank rifles. The Chinese air force included 250 functional aircraft . Their pilots were being mentored by retired United States Army Air Corps Captain Clair Chennault, but they still lacked sufficient skill.
Both sides entered the battle with weapons and equipment that shaped the character of the urban fight. Japanese forces employed modern infantry weapons, light machine guns, mortars, artillery, and naval gunfire support from ships positioned along the Huangpu River. These systems proved highly effective in suppressing many Chinese assaults before they could get close enough to destroy Japanese defensive positions. Chinese forces possessed some modern German-supplied equipment, but a majority lacked the training and coordination to employ it effectively. In the dense urban terrain, machine guns, artillery, and naval fires dominated streets, intersections, and avenues of approach, making movement in the open extremely costly.
China’s objective for the operation was to eradicate Japanese forces from Shanghai and to prevent Japan from landing additional forces near the city. Chinese forces’ concept of operations was to occupy and fortify key terrain within the city, identify weak points in the Japanese defenses, and then vigorously assault to push the Japanese forces out of the city . The battle unfolded in three phases . During Phase I (August 13–23), both sides prepared for and initiated the battle. Phase II (August 23–October 24) was focused on operations both inside and outside of Shanghai. Phase III (October 24–November 11) included the Chinese withdrawal from the northern parts of Shanghai, a major battle at the Sihang Warehouse, and combat operations in Shanghai’s Nanshi district.
Japanese forces sought to defend their positions within Shanghai while maintaining control of the Huangpu River to support, resupply, and reinforce their marines in the city. As the battle developed, Japanese forces sought to transition to the offensive by landing additional divisions north and south of Shanghai to isolate the Chinese forces and force their withdrawal .
Recognizing the waterway was Japan’s main logistical route, the Chinese sunk two old steamers and dozens of junks at critical spots along the Huangpu River on August 12 to impede river transit . Simultaneously, soldiers from the 87th and 88th Divisions filed into Shanghai from Nanjing, the Kuomintang capital several miles upstream on the Yangtze River, and started digging trenches throughout the Zhabei district.
Seeing that the urban fight was coming and fearing a repeat of 1932’s Shanghai incident, tens of thousands of Chinese residents started fleeing to the countryside and the international settlement, the latter receiving fifty thousand at the onset of the conflict. Likewise, thirty thousand Japanese civilians fled from Shanghai and China’s interior, crowding the city’s wharves as they waited to be ferried back to Japan. Yet hundreds of thousands of civilians remained. The United States ambassador requested that Chinese forces not enter the international settlement, which the Chinese agreed to only if the Japanese agreed not to base in the settlement. This proved effective at keeping the battle—other than errant bombs or stray bullets—out of the American and British sectors. The American commander ordered the 4th Marines to prevent entry into the American defense sector by all means necessary.
The battle started in the morning of August 13 with meeting engagements between small Japanese and Chinese patrols. The patrols had advanced through the narrow alleys to minimize detection and met at the Peace Preservation Corps barricades at the northern edge of the Yangshupu district, near the Commercial Press Building in Little Tokyo, and at the Chih Chih University in the Zhabei district. Japanese forces reacted to Chinese sniper and machine-gun fire by sending out search-and-destroy parties to conduct house-to-house searches and setting any buildings on fire that were thought to contain Chinese positions. That evening a heavy rainstorm moved over the city.
Throughout the night and into the following morning, both sides indiscriminately fired mortars and artillery in the direction of one another. While Japanese forces worked to fortify their positions in western Hongkou, American and German military advisors recommended to their respective Chinese leaders that they conduct an air and ground offensive the following day. Captain Chennault helped the Chinese plan close air strikes—which would start in the morning and continue throughout the day—to destroy the 3rd Fleet’s ships anchored in the Huangpu River to prevent the ships from supporting the battle. The ground offensive was to begin in the late afternoon and would focus on destroying Japanese forces that had taken up positions throughout western Hongkou and then close with and destroy the Japanese marine headquarters at the northern end of that district .
Chinese leader Chiang Kai-shek had selected Shanghai as the location for the first major battle of the war because of the large number of foreigners who lived there. He hoped that a battle in Shanghai would attract global attention and result in foreign support for China. But to maintain that support, he knew he had to prevent Chinese forces from endangering foreign civilians. As such, he forbade Chinese forces from travelling through the American and British defense sectors to advance on Japanese forces. German military advisors, however, recommended to their Chinese counterparts to ignore the agreement to stay out of the international settlement. They argued that Japanese forces were expecting Chinese forces to attack from Zhabei and, thus, had heavily defended positions on the western side of Hongkou. If Chinese forces instead advanced through the American and British sectors, they could hit the Japanese rear where they had no defenses. Chiang, however, refused to rescind the order recognizing that while it might be tactically advantageous, it would be strategically disastrous because it risked the loss of international support.
On the morning of August 14, the Chinese air force began its bombing campaign. It was nothing short of an unmitigated disaster due to the rainstorm turning into a typhoon . Chinese aircraft flew a paltry six missions because most of their pilots could not fly under such difficult conditions. Even their best pilots struggled. The weather forced the pilots to fly at an extremely high altitude, and they failed to adequately adjust their bomb sights to account for the altitude and high winds. Despite dropping many bombs, only one hit a Japanese ship, the cable-laying Okinawa Maru . At 4:27 p.m. , two bombs struck the Cathay and Palace Hotels in the international settlement, resulting in the deaths of 150 civilians . The hotels were located on the bank of the Huangpu River southwest of where Japan’s 3rd Fleet was anchored. At 4:45 p.m. , two bombs hit the Great World Amusement Center in the French concession and killed an additional 675 civilians . As a result of the errant bombings, the date became known as “ Bloody Saturday .” The incident highlighted the difficulty of employing airpower in dense urban environments and demonstrated how quickly civilian casualties could undermine strategic objectives.
The Chinese ground operation fared no better. As Chinese forces worked their way through the multistory buildings and narrow alleyways from Zhabei into Hongkou, they routinely stumbled into well-concealed Japanese defensive strongpoints within buildings that were hard to see through the typhoon’s torrent rain. Chinese forces repeatedly advanced along predictable avenues of approach and conducted frontal assaults against prepared Japanese strongpoints. These attacks exposed advancing units to concentrated machine-gun fire, artillery, and naval gunfire that inflicted heavy casualties before Chinese troops could close with and destroy the defenders .
Since the Chinese air force had failed to destroy the Japanese fleet, the ships’ naval guns could support the Japanese marines within the city. The powerful naval guns helped decimate Chinese assaults, which allowed the Japanese forces to counterattack into the flanks and rear of advancing Chinese forces. In the confusing urban terrain, Chinese commanders at all levels had only a vague understanding of where their personnel were located and what was happening . The Chinese had kept their artillery well to the rear to protect their few guns, so they were too far away to support the attack. Yet even if they were positioned farther forward, their crews were so poorly trained that they likely would have done little more than produce collateral damage and civilian casualties. Chinese casualties quickly grew so high that General Zhang called off the ground attack only hours after having ordered its start.
The battle paused on August 15–16 as both sides waited for the typhoon to pass before recommencing operations. During this time the Japanese brought in reinforcements , rebuilt defensive strongpoints, placed large obstacles on the streets, and positioned tanks and armored cars at critical locations in Hongkou. Understanding the Japanese forces were more than likely strengthening their defenses, the Chinese attackers sought to press the attack before the Japanese defenders could fortify their positions even more. Thus, they brought in their own reinforcements and created an improved plan , Operation Iron Fist. Instead of attacking into the Zhabei district, the plan called for an attack into the eastern and northern portions of Hongkou. General Zhang ordered the 87th Division, reinforced with 2,500 soldiers from the recently arrived 98th Division, to assault into Hongkou from the less fortified Yangshupu district. He ordered the 88th Division to assault into northern Hongkou, move through Hongkou Park, and advance south toward the Japanese marine headquarters.
The Chinese forces also adjusted their tactics given the failure of their frontal attacks during the battle’s first two days. General Zhang directed that once Chinese forces discovered a Japanese position, they would use the minimum combat power necessary to pin down the defenders and set the building on fire. Meanwhile, other forces would attempt to find and exploit gaps between defensive positions by moving inside buildings using mouseholes or on rooftops to advance beyond Japanese positions and then attack them from the rear. The 88th Division’s German advisor recommended that dismounted soldiers advance behind creeping artillery barrages . When performed correctly, Japanese forces would seek cover from the artillery and when it lifted, the Chinese forces would be at extremely close range, thus negating the defenders’ inherent advantage. Chinese commanders believed that if they could squeeze the Japanese defenders into Little Tokyo and cut the defense into three sectors , they could they could then defeat the isolated forces in succession and force the remaining Japanese forces to retreat to the Huangpu River and out of the city on ships. The tactics might have been effective had the Chinese conducted sufficient reconnaissance prior to the attack, but they felt pressured to press the attack as soon as the weather lifted to prevent the Japanese from fortifying their positions any further.
At 5:00 a.m. on August 17, the two Chinese divisions began their assault and immediately ran into challenges. Recently emplaced obstacles, newly arrived Japanese armored vehicles and tanks, and reinforced strongpoints surprised the Chinese attackers. They found the strongpoint positions too challenging to eliminate despite attempting, unsuccessfully, to implement General Zhang’s new tactics. Likewise, communication challenges undermined the 88th Division’s attempts to advance using creeping artillery barrages. The Chinese soldiers trailed too far behind the artillery shells, which allowed the Japanese defenders sufficient time to regroup and effectively engage the advancing Chinese soldiers after the artillery fire had lifted. The 88th Division lost an entire battalion while attacking a single building.
When Chinese units did seize a building, they often lost it a short while later to Japanese counterattack. Buildings often changed hands several times, thus preventing a breakthrough. Chinese commanders found it difficult to track their units advances due to the confusion of the urban terrain, which was compounded by some units exaggerating their successes or being unable to identify their exact locations. One regimental commander from the 87th Division became so frustrated that he issued orders for his subordinate units to remove street signs and send them to their headquarters so that staff officers could monitor units’ progress. When Chinese commanders eventually realized they were not making any forward progress, they paused offensive operations to create another plan of attack.
Civilians tried to avoid the battle, but many could not. Although the fighting had remained outside the international settlement, 2,700 British and American civilians departed Shanghai. In Hongkou, Japanese soldiers and civilian thugs killed an unknown number of Chinese civilians. Likewise, Chinese civilians attacked individuals suspected of being Japanese or accused of collaborating with Japanese forces.
On August 18, 1,400 Japanese marines and 5,000 Chinese soldiers from the 36th Division arrived in Shanghai and entered the battle the following day. With Chinese forces having performed so poorly in Zhabei and Hongkou, General Zhang positioned his newly arrived forces east of the Hongkou salient in Yangshupu and had them conduct an offensive through Yangshupu in the hopes that they could reach the Huangpu River and cut Japanese forces in half. The remainder of the 88th Division was right-forward, the 87th Division left-forward, and the 36th Division’s two regiments of five thousand were in the center when they attacked that morning .
When the Chinese forces restarted their attack, they once again demonstrated limited proficiency in urban combat by advancing along open streets and through open areas. Japanese soldiers in defensive positions on the top floors of buildings easily engaged the Chinese soldiers, who were often forced to use their dead comrades as cover to return fire. Nevertheless, through sheer mass in numbers the Chinese troops slowly advanced to Broadway Road, one block north of the Huangpu River, before they ran into a wall with large iron gates that surrounded Japanese-owned factories on the river’s wharves. The Japanese forces had turned the area between the wall and the river into a series of fortified strongpoints with positions along the top of the wall. After failing to advance beyond the wall, the Chinese brought three howitzer artillery guns forward to breach the wall in direct-fire mode, but all three malfunctioned . Chinese soldiers desperately attempted to scale the walls, but they were cut down by Japanese machine-gun and naval gunfire.
On August 19–21Chinese forces continued to press the attack but failed to make headway due to poor coordination between their infantry, armor, and artillery forces. Chinese forces often conducted narrow advances, which allowed Japanese marines, supported with tanks, to move up adjacent streets and attack their flanks. With their forces lacking antitank weapons, Chinese commanders sent tanks forward to support the dismounted troops. They, however, deployed them in piecemeal fashion and without infantry protection, which resulted in the destruction of two the 87th Division’s tank companies. To protect their artillery, the Chinese forces hid them in the Pudong district’s bamboo groves on the south bank of the Huangpu River.
By this point of the battle the Japanese military had gained air superiority, thereby grounding the Chinese air force. Meanwhile Japanese fighters and bombers destroyed bridges, railways, and airfields and forced the Chinese forces to conduct large movements of personnel and supplies at night . Although the Chinese forces possessed German/Swiss Solothurn S-18/100 20-millimeter antitank rifles , they did not use them against aircraft for fear of revealing their locations and receiving swift retribution from Japanese aircraft. They did, however, employ them against Japanese marines. By the third week of August, the Chinese 88th Division had suffered so many casualties that it became combat ineffective and the 36th Division’s two regiments had suffered two thousand casualties. On August 21 the Japanese received another one thousand marine reinforcements, which boosted their numbers to approximately 6,300 personnel . Realizing their attack had failed, Chinese commanders ordered a withdrawal.
On August 23, Japan landed another 7,500 soldiers from the 11th and 3rd Divisions at Wusong, roughly fourteen miles north of central Shanghai, and at Chuanshakou, about thirty miles northeast of the city, along the southern bank of the Yangtze River. In early September, three more divisions—the 9th, 13th, and 101st—landed. Chinese leaders recognized the threat these forces posed. The new Japanese divisions could easily move south and isolate the Chinese forces within the city. As a result, they left the depleted 88th Division to defend within the Zhabei district and directed the remaining Chinese units north to meet the Japanese divisions. For the next two months the forces clashed north of the city in a slow battle of attrition, but the Japanese forces slowly pushed the Chinese forces back to the city by late October . These amphibious landings fundamentally altered the campaign by extending the battlespace beyond Shanghai itself and placing Chinese forces at growing risk of encirclement.
With his forces now under great threat of being trapped, Chiang directed the 88th Division to defend in Zhabei, while the rest of the Chinese forces were to begin their withdrawal to Nanjing on October 23 . Chiang directed the 88th Division to disperse into small, independent units to conduct guerrilla warfare . His goal was not to defeat the Japanese forces but to prolong the fighting until the Nine-Power Conference in Brussels in early November, to demonstrate to Western nations that China had not been defeated. This conference was being convened to discuss Japanese expansion and policies to halt it. Chiang hoped the West would force Japan to cease all offensive actions, which would allow him to hold Shanghai.
While conceptually sound, the plan was not suited to the conditions on the ground. General Sun Yuanliang, commander of the 88th Division, did not believe the conditions were conducive for practical reasons. Sun did not believe that many of the soldiers were capable of operating independently because only 20–30 percent of his reinforcements had combat experience. He also did not believe that small, independent groups could resupply themselves or evacuate casualties. Moreover, many of the buildings in Zhabei had been damaged or destroyed, which he believed rendered the terrain unsuitable for guerrilla warfare. Sun effectively argued his case with Chiang and convinced him to leave only a single battalion behind to defend from one large, fortified strongpoint. This, he believed, would demonstrate the capability and will of the Chinese to fight for the city without losing too many soldiers .
General Sun selected the twenty-thousand-square-meter Sihang Warehouse complex, which had served as his division headquarters, for the battalion’s strongpoint. The complex rested on the northern bank of the Suzhou Creek and was located at the southern tip of Zhabei. It was a sound tactical position. Its two six-story buildings offered clear visibility in all directions, and if all of the debris on the streets and open areas could be cleared, the Chinese battalion would have ample kill zones in which to engage advancing Japanese forces. The buildings’ walls were made of ten-foot-thick steel-reinforced concrete, which included dozens of large firing ports. The British defense sector was located on the opposite bank of the Suzhou Creek meaning the warehouse would only have to be defended to the north and east. The Lese Bridge joined the warehouse complex with the British sector. British soldiers defended the bridge to their sector behind sandbags and barbed wire . General Sun believed the proximity of the British sector to the warehouse would discourage Japanese forces from using airstrikes or artillery .
Lieutenant Colonel Xie Jinyuan, the commander of the 524th Regiment, commanded the defense, which was comprised of Major Yang Ruifu’s 1st Battalion. The battalion included three rifle companies and a machine-gun company, totaling four hundred soldiers . The battalion, however, had become separated during earlier fighting, so two of the companies were presently withdrawing with the rest of the Chinese forces, leaving Xie with a single rifle company in his possession and Yang with another.
On the evening of October 26 Lieutenant Colonel Xie ordered Major Yang to send messengers to his two withdrawing companies directing them to move to the warehouse to join the battalion’s defense. Withdrawing Chinese units had enacted an urban “ scorched earth ” policy, setting fire to thousands of buildings to impede the Japanese advance. But this also made it difficult to recall Major Yang’s two companies. Nonetheless, the companies reached the warehouse complex by 9:00 a.m. on October 27, apart from one platoon that became entangled in a firefight with a Japanese column near the Shanghai North Railway Station four blocks northeast of the Sihang Warehouse. The platoon finally reached the complex at 10:15 a.m. after a two-hour firefight.
The first Japanese troops arrived at the warehouse complex at 1:00 p.m. They then initiated their assault after seeing Chinese troops defending from the outer wall and from some of the structures around the complex including the Bank of Communications building, which neighbored the warehouse. By this point of the battle, the Chinese troops had learned some of the Japanese tactics. Japanese units rarely attacked Chinese strongpoints directly. Instead, they would often seize an undefended or less defended neighboring building to stage from and then launch their attack from there. Lieutenant Colonel Xie believed the Japanese troops would try this tactic to seize the Bank of Communications building before attacking the Sihang Warehouse. As a result, the Chinese company defending from the bank building rigged a nearby bunker with grenades and mortar rounds. They put up a light defense at the bank building and bunker, withdrew, and then detonated the explosives in the bunker after the Japanese soldiers stormed it . Soon thereafter, a group of Japanese soldiers attempted to crawl through the rubble-filled streets to infiltrate into the complex, but they were easily observed. Once they were close enough, Chinese soldiers threw hand grenades from rooftops which forced the advancing Japanese soldiers to withdraw .
On October 28 the Japanese forces attacked the Sihang Warehouse in greater force, starting with a close air strike at 7:00 a.m. The aircraft, however, failed to drop their ordnance after the Chinese defenders engaged them with Maxim machine-guns from rooftops. Fearing the contested aircraft might errantly drop their bombs on the nearby international settlement, the Japanese commander waved off the airstrike. Japanese ground forces spent most of the day moving into position, emplacing machine-gun teams atop neighboring buildings (including the Bank of Communications), moving five artillery pieces forward to be used in direct-fire mode, and cutting electricity and water to the complex. They initiated the attack at 3:00 p.m. For the next two hours Chinese defenders repulsed repeated Japanese advances using machine-guns and hand grenades and mortar rounds thrown from the upper floors.
Now under siege, Major Yang enacted a ration plan, placed guards around the water reserve, and ordered urine to be stored for firefighting purposes. That evening he directed continued improvements to the buildings’ defenses, organized medical evacuations across the Lese Bridge, and, as part of a deception plan, further directed evacuating troops to inform journalists that there were eight hundred defenders within the complex . International media picked up the story and dubbed the fighting at the warehouse the “ Chinese Alamo .” Throughout the battle Chinese civilians provided intelligence and logistic support to the outnumbered defenders. During the day, Chinese civilians observing the battle from the other side of the Suzhou Creek cheered any Chinese success and created large signs of encouragement. They also telephoned the defenders to send heartfelt messages and inform about Japanese troop movements. They gathered food, clothing, medicine, cigarettes, and other supplies. Some fasted to provide funds and obtain supplies for the defenders while others begged British soldiers to pass food to them. With the support of the municipal council and the Shanghai Volunteer Corps, Chinese civilians transported ten truckloads of supplies over the Lese Bridge, sometimes under fire .
On October 29 the Japanese repositioned forces from within the city to support the attack. The Japanese forces attacked at 2:00 p.m. using armor and artillery (in direct- and indirect-fire modes) to support the infantry advance. After an hour-long artillery barrage, infantry troops stormed the warehouse carrying ladders that they placed against the walls in an attempt enter the large firing ports on the building’s second floor . The Chinese defenders, however, pushed the ladders away while raining intense small-arms and machine-gun fire on the advancing troops. The Japanese forces made multiple attempts with similar results. One individual Chinese soldier was rumored to have conducted a suicide attack by strapping grenades to his body and running into a group of Japanese soldiers who were attempting to explosively breach the warehouse wall.
At 2:45 p.m. British soldiers observed two small Japanese pinnaces sailing up the Suzhou Creek with thirty marines to attack the warehouse from behind . A British officer contacted the Japanese consul general and ordered him to turn the vessels around since they were intruding into the British defense sector and warned that if they did not, the British would assume they were being attacked and would open fire to destroy the pinnaces. The British were pro-Chinese due to a Japanese aircraft strafing the British ambassador’s car earlier in the conflict, the accidental killing of the three British soldiers by Japanese shelling and bombing during this battle, and Japan’s illegal occupation and fortification of British property in the Yangshupu district. Due to Britain’s pressure, the Japanese military turned the pinnaces around. Fighting continued into the evening and throughout the night as Japanese aircraft bombed the complex while tanks and artillery inched closer. The Japanese forces used large spotlights at night to help illuminate their targets.
The Japanese forces continued the attack on October 30 as both sides exchanged small-arms fire throughout the day and into the evening. Despite using aircraft, tanks, and artillery, the Japanese forces lacked the combat power to seize the hardened objective without taking high casualties. The Chinese, however, could not defend indefinitely given their tenuous supply lines. That evening, Chiang Kai-shek, who had received hundreds of telegrams from military and civilian supporters begging him to save the defenders, directed that the battalion had met its objectives and that they were to withdraw into the international settlement , something the British had also recommended multiple times during the previous two days.
Japanese forces continued pummeling the complex with munitions while the Chinese planned, with the help of the British , their withdrawal for the early morning hours of October 31. A platoon with a heavy machine-gun formed the rearguard, covering the four companies as they raced across the Lese Bridge under fire in small groups of two to three. After crossing the bridge, they surrendered to the British forces. Major Yang’s battalion wanted to leave the British sector and rejoin the Chinese army, but the British commander forbade it. To do so would have violated international agreements and given the Japanese a pretext to invade the British sector . Fighting at the Sihang Warehouse resulted in the death of roughly two hundred Japanese and fifty Chinese soldiers, with many more wounded.
On November 5, the Japanese 10th Army landed at the weakly defended Hangzhou Bay, approximately twenty-five miles south of Shanghai on the East China Sea, and easily pushed the surprised Chinese 8th Army Group north to the city. In the Nanshi district south of the French concession, China’s 55th Division continued fighting against Japanese forces well into November . With the battle at the Sihang Warehouse complete, the Japanese forces sought to eradicate all Chinese forces from Shanghai and began attacking multiple areas of the district to overwhelm the Chinese defenders. During this time Japanese tanks adopted a new tactic of opening fire down alleyways at Chinese positions and then immediately backing away to prevent retaliatory antitank strikes. The Japanese forces’ advance in Nanshi was slowed by the district’s numerous canals, which required pontoon bridges to move from one block to the next. Nonetheless, the Japanese made steady progress. As they had done at the Sihang Warehouse, many Chinese soldiers in the Nanshi district made a final stand before withdrawing and surrendering to the French military in the French concession.
On November 11, Japanese forces secured control of Shanghai following the withdrawal of the remaining Chinese forces and the collapse of organized resistance within the city. The Battle of Shanghai, including fighting outside the city, involved one million combatants including seven hundred thousand Chinese soldiers and three hundred thousand Japanese marines and soldiers. Casualty estimates vary, but Chinese forces suffered approximately 187,000 casualties before withdrawing toward Nanjing , while Japanese forces suffered over 9,000 killed and more than 31,000 wounded. By the end of the battle the population within the international settlement had swelled from 250,000 to four million as residents moved there to avoid the violence. The battle produced tens of thousands of civilian casualties for those who were not lucky enough to flee. The battle also resulted in the destruction of 2,900 of Shanghai’s 5,255 factories , and damage to the lone railway into the interior resulted in the decrease of trade from $31 million to $8.3 million after Japanese occupation.
The first strategic lesson from the Battle of Shanghai is that in a globally connected city, the fight for legitimacy can be as decisive as the fight for terrain. Chiang Kai-shek chose to defend Shanghai not only for its economic value, but also because of its international population and foreign-controlled sectors. He sought to draw global attention to gain external support. That objective shaped battlefield decisions. Chinese forces refused to maneuver through the international settlement even when it offered a clear tactical advantage, because doing so risked foreign casualties and the loss of international backing. As a result, Chinese units repeatedly attacked into prepared Japanese positions from less favorable directions. In this case, the strategic objective of influencing international opinion constrained tactical freedom of action and contributed to battlefield failure.
The second strategic lesson is that protected neutral zones within a city fragment the battlespace and restrict maneuver for both sides. In Shanghai, the American, British, and French sectors created areas that neither side risked transiting. These zones forced both Chinese and Japanese forces to fight around them rather than through them, shaping avenues of approach and limiting options to outflank or reposition. Theses neutral zones also imposed constraints on the use of fires. Both forces had to consider the risk of striking foreign sectors when employing artillery and airpower near those areas. Modern cities often contain similar constraints in the form of diplomatic sites, protected populations, or politically sensitive infrastructure that limit how forces can fight.
The first operational lesson is that a force can fail in the urban fight and still win the campaign by controlling access, reinforcement, and maneuver outside the city. Chinese forces focused on defeating Japanese units within Shanghai through repeated attacks in Zhabei, Hongkou, and Yangshupu, but they failed to close the waterway. As a result, the Japanese military was able to bring in reinforcements throughout the battle. These operations threatened Chinese lines of communication and created the risk of encirclement. China’s decision to withdraw was driven by this pressure outside the city, not by a decisive tactical defeat inside it. Control of approaches and sustainment routes proved more important than local gains inside the city.
A second operational lesson is that the value of an urban strongpoint comes from its location and the constraints it imposes on the enemy, not simply its construction. The Sihang Warehouse was a strong defensive position, but its true advantage came from its location along the Suzhou Creek next to the British sector. This limited Japanese forces’ avenues of approach and restricted their use of artillery and airpower due to the risk of escalation. Japanese forces were forced into repeated frontal assaults and could not fully isolate the position. A well-sited position that limits enemy options can be more effective than one that is simply hardened.
The first tactical lesson is that combined arms integration is essential in urban combat, and the failure to synchronize forces often leads to rapid losses. Chinese forces employed infantry, armor, artillery, and airpower, but these elements were not coordinated. Infantry advanced without effective fire support. Tanks that operated in small numbers without infantry protection were destroyed. Air operations conducted independently resulted in little effect on the ground fight. Communication problems made coordination even more difficult. Japanese forces, by contrast, were able to combine fire and maneuver more effectively, including the use of naval gunfire to disrupt Chinese attacks. Urban terrain magnifies the consequences of poor coordination and quickly exposes gaps between units.
A second tactical lesson is that in dense urban combat seizing terrain is not enough. Units must also be able to hold it. Chinese forces were able to capture buildings but often lost them shortly thereafter to immediate Japanese counterattacks. Positions changed hands repeatedly because units could not secure flanks, maintain awareness of adjacent elements, or reinforce gains. Commanders struggled to track unit locations in the dense terrain and lacked a clear understanding of the fight. Without the ability to consolidate and defend, tactical success remained temporary. In urban warfare, the ability to hold ground is what turns local success into lasting progress.
The Battle of Shanghai was one of the first large-scale modern urban battles in which infantry forces, armor, artillery, naval gunfire, and airpower were brought to bear in a dense city. It was not merely a fight for terrain; it was a contest shaped by political objectives, international presence, and constraints imposed by a globally connected city. Chinese forces entered the battle seeking both military success and international support, while Japanese forces adapted by reinforcing from outside the city and expanding the fight beyond the urban core.
The battle demonstrates that success in urban warfare is rarely determined by tactical actions alone. Chinese forces achieved local gains and demonstrated determination but were unable to translate those actions into operational success due to poor coordination, lack of integration, and the inability to counter Japanese maneuver outside the city. Japanese forces, while facing stiff resistance in the urban fight, ultimately achieved success by controlling reinforcement, sustainment, and encirclement. Shanghai reinforces a recurring reality of urban warfare: Cities magnify the consequences of decisions at every level of war. Tactical actions inside the city cannot be separated from operational maneuver, sustainment, political objectives, and international perception. Success in urban warfare depends not only on controlling terrain, but on aligning tactical actions with operational and strategic objectives under conditions of extreme friction and constraint.
Liam Collins, PhD is the director of Madison Policy Forum and a distinguished military fellow with the Middle East Institute. He is a retired Special Forces colonel with deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan, Bosnia, the Horn of Africa, and South America. He is the coauthor of The War for Karabakh: Strategy, Technology, and Victory, coauthor of Understanding Urban Warfare , and author of Leadership & Innovation During Crisis: Lessons from the Iraq War .
Major Jayson Geroux is an infantry officer with The Royal Canadian Regiment and is currently with the Canadian Army Doctrine and Training Centre. He has been a fervent student of and has been involved in urban operations training for twenty-five years. He is an equally passionate military historian and has participated in, planned, executed, and intensively instructed on urban operations and urban warfare history for the past thirteen years. He has served thirty-one years in the Canadian Armed Forces, which included operational tours to the former Yugoslavia (Bosnia-Herzegovina) and Afghanistan.
John Spencer is chair of urban warfare studies at the Modern War Institute, codirector of MWI’s Urban Warfare Project, and host of the Urban Warfare Project Podcast . He served twenty-five years as an infantry soldier, which included two combat tours in Iraq. He is the coauthor of The War for Karabakh: Strategy, Technology, and Victory, author of Connected Soldiers: Life, Leadership, and Social Connections in Modern War , and coauthor of Understanding Urban Warfare .
Amanda Zhao is an undergraduate student in the Georgetown School of Foreign Service, majoring in international politics (international security concentration) and minoring in government. She served as the lead researcher and author on this case study.
The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the official position of the United States Military Academy, Department of the Army, or Department of Defense.

title: Russia-Zimbabwe joint venture discovers gold occurrences during diamond exploration
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. A joint venture between Russia and Zimbabwe conducting diamond exploration in the African nation has identified gold occurrences at three sites, with plans underway to evaluate a transition to pilot-scale extraction, Russian Minister of Natural Resources and Environment Alexander Kozlov said at the Russia-Africa Summit.
"The joint venture is engaged in diamond exploration, with operations currently active across 13 sites. Gold occurrences have been identified at three of them, and the venture has been granted the rights to conduct gold operations. Consequently, gold reserves are being calculated to assess the feasibility of moving to a pilot-scale extraction stage," Kozlov stated.
In late 2019, Russia’s Alrosa and the Zimbabwe Consolidated Diamond Company (ZCDC) finalized a joint venture to prospect for and explore new primary diamond deposits in the country. Alrosa holds a 70% stake in the venture, while ZCDC holds 30%.
TASS is an official media partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: AI driving Formula One with sport now 'best showcase' for the tech
body: The role of artificial intelligence in Formula One is set to grow, with the sport providing the “best showcase” for the technology, according to an executive from Oracle Red Bull Racing. “Data seeps through every element of our business,” Jack Harington, the F1 team's technical partnerships lead told The National at Oracle AI World in Las Vegas. F1 has progressed massively over the past few years and the rate of tech integration has dramatically increased, he said. “I think it is the best showcase for technology . We are heavily reliant on our tech partners to deliver us tools that we can utilise in the running of our cars, the running of our business. It’s a hotbed for testing out technology.” F1 has been among the foremost adopters of AI in recent years. There are 300 to 600 sensors embedded in every F1 car, measuring variables such as engine temperature, tyre pressure, brake wear and aerodynamic loads, according to IMD. Nearly every F1 team has collaborations with leading tech companies , including Microsoft, Oracle, AWS, Google, Dell Technology, AMD and Palantir. Teams use cloud infrastructure and real-time data analytics to run billions of simulations, accelerate car design , optimise race strategy and gain a competitive edge, IMD said in a report last year. Mr Harington declined to be exact on the number of sensors on the cars . Teams remain secretive about the AI plans, he said. “These [the cars] are data-driven monsters. And we need to constantly monitor every element of the car. I think if it were left to the engineers, we would have thousands and thousands of sensors, but every sensor is a weight, and weight in Formula One is very important, so we have to reduce the amount of sensors we have on the car to make sure it is competitive,” he said. “We probably pull around two terabytes of data from the car every session that we're out on track. “There's many millions of data points within that that we have to dig into to really understand whether our car is performing as we want it to, and to maximise its performance over a lap or throughout a race.” One example of using the data is its strategy simulation, he said. “So, we have two kinds of data in F1. You have your known data, which is things like tyre degradation curves – or how long the tyres are lasting for. Then you have unknown data, which is things like a yellow flag, a red flag, an unexpected overtake, safety car, etc.” The team uses Monte Carlo simulations – a computational technique that uses repeated random sampling to predict the probability of different outcomes – ahead of races. Before a race weekend, the team runs eight billion Monte Carlo race simulations to try to plot the fastest way from the start to the finish of the race. During practice sessions, all the data is gathered and collected. “And we introduce that data into our simulations and we run another eight billion Monte Carlo simulations, and then if something happens during the race, we're actually able to update those models live ,” Mr Harington said. As part of the deal with Oracle, the team has transitioned those simulations to the Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. “This is a huge advantage for us as a team because now with the ability to scale the amount of simulations that we're running using Oracle Cloud, we are able to actually kind of play war games. So not only are we simulating what's the fastest route from the start to the finish of the race, we're also simulating, if we make a decision, how are the teams going to react to it?” he added.

title: CAP Plc Champions Lead-Safe Paint
body: Yusuf Ebiti Chemical and Allied Products (CAP) Plc, one of Nigeria’s leading paints and coatings manufacturers, has urged Nigerians to prioritise product safety when choosing paint for their homes, schools and workplaces. CAP Plc also stressed the importance of responsible manufacturing, informed consumer choices and professional training in preventing lead exposure. The call coincides with International Lead Poisoning Prevention Week (ILPPW) 2026, observed from 18 to 24 October under the theme “From Detection to Prevention”. The global campaign highlights the importance of identifying sources of lead exposure and strengthening preventive measures to protect public health, particularly that of children. Through its “Look Beyond the Colour” message, CAP Plc is encouraging consumers to consider more than a paint’s colour, finish and price when making purchasing decisions. The company advised buyers to seek reliable product information, understand the safety considerations associated with their choices and select products suitable for their intended applications.
