title: MultiChoice Unveils New DStv, GOtv Packages Ahead of November 5 Rollout
body: Mmachi Okafor MultiChoice Nigeria, a CANAL+ company, has unveiled a simplified package ‘ Expect More’ lineup for DStv and GOtv subscribers, with the new structure scheduled to take effect on November 5, 2026. The announcement was made at a press briefing held at the company’s headquarters in Victoria Island, Lagos, where executives outlined changes aimed at giving subscribers more choice and better value through packages tailored to their viewing preferences. Under the new structure, DStv subscribers will choose from four packages: Starter, Select, Sports and Premium, while GOtv customers will have Easy, Starter, Select and Sports. The restructuring forms part of CANAL+’s broader strategy to develop a more unified, customer-focused portfolio following MultiChoice’s integration into the group. Chief Executive Officer of MultiChoice Nigeria, Kemi Omotosho, said the changes were driven by customer feedback and shifts in how audiences consume entertainment across television sets, smartphones, tablets and laptops. “Our focus is on giving subscribers better value and access to the entertainment they love,” Omotosho stated during her keynote presentation. “The strength of our platform is the combination of African entertainment, leading international content, and unrivalled live sports in one place. We’ve reimagined our packages to better reflect how customers watch today, with tailored options specifically for general entertainment and sports fans.” During the executive media question-and-answer session, Omotosho explained that the restructuring was intended to reduce package confusion and help subscribers choose options that better match their interests and budgets. She added that, despite the company’s integration into CANAL+, pricing, channel packaging and day-to-day operations remained locally driven, with content tailored to Nigerian consumer demand and economic conditions. During a product presentation led by Senior Vice President of Communications, Tope Oshunkeye, the executive team outlined the prices and content available across the new DStv packages. The entry-level DStv Starter package, priced at N6,000 monthly, will introduce two new channels: SuperSport KICKOFF, which will broadcast the Premier League Match of the Week and selected UEFA Champions League fixtures, and Africa Magic+, a destination for local and international entertainment. DStv Select, priced at N11,000 monthly, is designed for family viewing, combining movies, local and international series, selected football and other sports, children’s programming and Africa Magic Showcase. For sports enthusiasts, DStv Sports will cost N21,000 monthly and offer every Premier League and UEFA Champions League match, alongside WWE, UFC, the Europa League and ESPN content, including the NBA. The package will also include all general entertainment channels available on the Select tier. DStv Premium priced at N44,500 will remain the flagship package, offering all the content available on the Sports tier, alongside motorsport competitions such as Formula 1 and MotoGP, Grand Slam tennis, major golf tournaments and first-run international series on M-Net. Alongside the package changes, MultiChoice announced a refresh of its movie offerings through the introduction of M-Net Movies+, M-Net Stars and M-Net Legends. The company said the changes were intended to provide faster access to new releases and reduce repetitions. For customers who prefer streaming, DStv Stream will be available as a standalone service from N6,000 monthly. The application will allow subscribers to watch content on compatible smart TVs, tablets and mobile devices without requiring a physical decoder or satellite dish. MultiChoice also announced a decoder promotion offering a complete kit, including a dish and one-month entry-level subscription, for N15,000 across both DStv and GOtv platforms. Addressing the transition for existing subscribers, Vice President of Customer Value Management, Onyinye Ezenwa, said active accounts on legacy packages would be automatically mapped to new tiers offering equivalent or greater content selection. She assured customers with advance multi-month subscriptions that they would retain their full prepaid duration without losing service time or experiencing interruptions. Executives also responded to questions about future technological developments, including artificial intelligence and regional content expansion. They said these areas remained under internal consideration as the company continued to assess emerging AI regulations and their implications for content quality and platform integrity.

title: #CourageON: Highlights from #MoveCebu 2026
body: Last week, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brought #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during a public forum to define what a liveable city should be . To solidify our long-term commitment to campus journalism and civic engagement, we proudly signed memoranda of understanding with the University of San Carlos , and the University of the Philippines Cebu . Rappler multimedia reporter John Sitchon , who reports on Cebu and the Visayas region, joined us as we worked directly with participants. You can check out these stories to read more about what happened during the roadshow: Padayon Cebu: A new space to chat how to make the province more livable At #MoveCebu forum, Cebuanos define what a liveable city should be MovePH trains Movers in Cebu on local reporting, civic organizing Taking advantage of the momentum generated by the forum, we dove into focused workshops with 35 newly-trained Movers, and leaders from Cebu’s civil society groups to bridge reporting with civic organizing . Our Movers who chose the civic mobilization track pitched bold, ground-level initiatives tackling community realities across Cebu province. For example, participants designed action plans to address food safety at the Colon Night Market. Some Movers want to address the lack of housing for displaced families in Minglanilla. One Mover hoped to champion the rights of people with dwarfism. Meanwhile, Movers who wanted to specialize in community journalism pitched stories tackling gut issues in Cebu, like substandard flood control projects, child labor, and how neighborhood carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable. Our civil society and academe partners matched this energy during our Partners’ Huddle, where they decided to prioritize four crisis clusters: Ecological, Governance, Services, and Displacement. Together, partners committed to lobbying local councils to prioritize environmental policy over profit, conducting citizen audits, raising awareness of and tackling the energy crisis plaguing Cebu, and fighting for humane relocation sites and protected municipal waters for fishing communities. Movers and partners are already coordinating on next steps in the Padayon Cebu chat room on the Muni app. To be part of the action, you can join the chat room by downloading the Rappler app for free . If you would like to support Rappler’s Cebu coverage , we hope you consider becoming a Rappler+ member. Rappler+ is our premium membership program that allows you to experience the best of our journalism, while supporting our work. You can join Rappler+ here . – Rappler.com

title: Woman killed by Tema-Afienya train as residents demand footbridge
body: An unidentified woman has been killed after being struck by a passenger train on the Tema-Afienya railway line at Mataheko-Sebrepo, prompting residents to renew calls for a footbridge to provide a safer crossing between communities in the area. The incident occurred on Tuesday night, leaving residents at the scene grappling with the aftermath as they waited for the police to arrive. Witnesses said they heard the train sound its horn shortly before the collision, followed by an unusual noise that alerted people to the incident. The impact reportedly left the woman’s body severely mutilated, with her head thrown into a nearby gutter. Some residents and bystanders searched the area to locate it. Residents raise concerns over safety Residents said the incident had revived longstanding concerns about the difficulty of crossing the railway line and the need for a dedicated pedestrian crossing to connect communities in the enclave. They are calling on the relevant authorities to construct a footbridge to reduce the risk of pedestrians being struck by trains. The residents believe such a facility would provide a safer route across the railway and help prevent similar tragedies. According to accounts from people at the scene, several emergency calls were made after the incident, but assistance had not arrived by the time some residents began taking steps to preserve the body. When a news crew arrived at about 9:30 p.m., residents said they had made repeated calls for help. The body was subsequently conveyed by officers of the Afienya-Mataheko Police for the necessary procedures. The identity of the deceased had not been established at the time of reporting, and further details about the circumstances of the incident were not immediately available.

title: French Senate passes bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage
body: The French parliament’s upper house passed a bill Wednesday that would make protesters financially liable for damage caused during street demonstrations, despite warnings from critics that it could curb the right to protest. The bill was drafted in response to riots that followed Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the UEFA Champions League final in May. But it has taken on added significance after weeks of protests over inequality and soaring prices culminated in some of the worst violence France has seen in years on October 17, when thousands of businesses across the country were damaged and looted. The Senate passed an expanded version of the bill by 229 votes to 105, backed by a right-wing and centrist alliance which holds a majority. The legislation has been sent to the National Assembly, which is split between France’s political factions, for debate and voting. Far-right leader Marine Le Pen, whom opinion polls place as the frontrunner to succeed Emmanuel Macron in next spring’s presidential election, supports the legislation. Speaking in parliament, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez stressed the “urgency” of responding to the damage and scenes of chaos seen on October 17. “We can no longer allow the vast majority of our fellow citizens to pay for a minority of vandals,” he said. – ‘Legal travesty’ – Under the legislation, protesters could be ordered to pay up to 10,000 euros for damage caused during street demonstrations. But critics argue that people who took no part in vandalism could nonetheless be held liable if they were deemed to have been associated with those responsible. The bill introduces joint financial liability for anyone found to have “knowingly participated” in a group formed with the intent of carrying out acts of vandalism. It would also apply to individuals who “voluntarily” continued to take part in a gathering likely to disrupt public order after two police dispersal warnings. Welfare benefits and housing assistance could also be seized to help cover the cost of damages under the scheme, a provision that has drawn sharp criticism from left-wing parties and advocacy groups. In the second reading, senators toughened the measure to include other social benefits such as the family supplement, back-to-school allowance and the employment bonus. Left-wing lawmakers accused the government of an “authoritarian drift” at the expense of the freedom to demonstrate. Communist senator Fabien Gay denounced what he called a “legal travesty that deliberately conflates protesters and rioters”. Green senator Melanie Vogel accused the government of responding to social demands with “collective punishment.” Supporters of the bill sought to reassure critics. “We must not give the impression that this bill would criminalise a passer-by or a peaceful protester,” said Olivier Bitz of the centre-right Horizons party. – ‘Disastrous consequences’ – The government has proposed introducing protest bans targeting the most violent individuals. Late Tuesday, the Senate approved a bill allowing authorities to demand the rapid removal of social media content calling for “insurrection or taking up arms against the state”. “As we speak, there are calls circulating for next Saturday that are calls for insurrection. Those are the kinds of content we want to remove,” the interior minister told senators. Platforms would be required to remove such content within 24 hours, or they could face “blocking” or “delisting.” In an op-ed published in French daily Le Monde last week, a coalition of trade unions and student groups warned of a “serious infringement on the freedom to demonstrate.” They argued the measures would disproportionately affect “the poorest families” and encourage “arbitrary police action.” Amnesty International also urged the government to abandon the bill, warning the measures could push “already marginalised families further into poverty”. “If passed, this bill would be a deeply regressive step,” Nathalie Godard of Amnesty International France said on Monday. “Seizing family allowances, housing assistance, or the active solidarity income could have disastrous consequences for some of the most vulnerable people.” AFP The post French Senate passes bill to make protesters pay for unrest damage appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Kano lawmakers back establishment of state police
body:
The Kano State House of Assembly on Tuesday endorsed the Bill to establish a state police service.
The assembly passed the bill during its plenary session presided over by the Speaker, Jibril Ismail-Falgore.
Mr Ismail-Falgore said the house passed the bill after deliberation on clauses 1–26 at the committee of the Whole House.
“In the committee of the whole house, we deliberated on the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 Alteration Bill 2026 from clause 1–26.
“Now, by the powers conferred on us based on Section 9(2) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.
“A bill for an act to alter the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 to provide for the establishment of the state police service and for related matters is hereby considered and passed,” he said.

title: Israel’s Elections: What Happens Next?
body:
Israelis voted on Tuesday in their highest turnout for decades, with exit polls showing the camp of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and that of his rival are neck and neck.
Exit polls from the three mainstream Israeli television networks gave the two blocs around 51 seats each in the 120-member Knesset -- well below the 61 needed to govern -- after initially giving an edge to the opposition led by ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Israeli Arab lists made strong gains, with exit polls showing them winning 17 or 18 seats between them.
The parties will immediately begin negotiations to try to reach a 61-seat majority, but the path forward is far from clear.
President Isaac Herzog will name a candidate who has the best chance to form a government -- not necessarily the party with the most seats.
The Arab Israeli parties, particularly Raam, have voiced openness to working with Eisenkot’s bloc, but the camp has kept them at arm’s length, perceiving their support as a liability during the campaign.
For Netanyahu’s bloc, however, there is no obvious place to pick up more seats after some smaller right-wing parties failed to meet the vote threshold for entering parliament.
Coalition negotiations can be arduous, with parties insisting on parochial interests, and can produce unstable governments.
It took Netanyahu 58 days to form his government after the previous election in November 2022.
If no bloc manages to secure 61 seats, a candidate could attempt to govern without a majority but rather through support on an ad hoc basis from other lawmakers.
In this scenario, lawmakers from the Arab Israeli parties -- whose community makes up 20 percent of the population and generally identifies as Palestinian -- could play a critical role.
Raam, led by Mansour Abbas, has been a kingmaker in the past, having been the first Arab party to join an Israeli government in a short-lived 2021-2022 coalition led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid.
Another Arab movement, the Joint List, has said it would be unlikely to join a coalition government outright, but has offered to provide a “safety net” for anyone that ousts Netanyahu from power.
Political commentator Tal Elovitz said that an especially high Arab turnout “indicates a strong desire for partnership”.
Eisenkot has not even entertained the possibility publicly, and Netanyahu relentlessly told Jewish voters in his campaign that a vote for the opposition could bring Arabs into government.
“Bottom line, at the moment, it appears there is a possibility of forming a minority government headed by Eisenkot, but this could still shift depending on the final results,” Elovitz said.
Considering Israel’s extreme polarisation, the prospect of a national unity government would appear fanciful, but it could theoretically create a less extreme government.
Israeli commentators have often mused on the possibility of a national unity government in which Netanyahu would jettison his provocative far-right allies as well as ultra-Orthodox parties and team up with Eisenkot, who shares Netanyahu’s views on many security issues.
Such a grand coalition would also exclude Arab parties.
A poll published on October 16 found that 55 percent of Israelis would prefer a national unity government over new elections if the vote did not produce a clear majority.
This scenario has a recent precedent. In 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, like Eisenkot a retired general appealing to the centre, reached a power-sharing agreement after three elections in less than a year.
The agreement stipulated a rotation of the prime ministership, but the partnership fell apart after a year, triggering another election.
A unity government in the present situation would face strong opposition from both sides, particularly the opposition bloc, which has built its campaign around ousting Netanyahu, casting him as unfit to lead.
If no candidate manages to form a government, Israel will have to return to the polls.
The country held four elections between April 2019 and March 2021 due to the inability of politicians to forge a lasting coalition.
The candidate designated by the president will, in principle, have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension, although there are other procedural ways to prevent an immediate calling of new elections.

title: US cruise ship ends global voyage due to fuel costs; 200 passengers lose their homes
body:
A U.S. cruise ship on a three-year voyage has suspended its journey in Cambodia due to high fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia -- A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.
Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
“We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses,” Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees” while it tries to restructure.
“The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements,” it said.
Passengers however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.
Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.
Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.
“We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” she said. “We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement.”
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.
Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
“I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it’s a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end,” Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. “You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it's all over.”
Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.
“Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth … I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising,” she said.
The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.
The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.
In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.
After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.
Associated Press writers Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, and Grant Peck in Bangkok contributed to this report.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Trump's cure for Republicans' midterm woes is more Trump. Will it work?
body:
President Donald Trump wants midterm voters to imagine he's on the ballot and has seized the political spotlight in a way that makes such make-believe seem a bit more real
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump likes to play make-believe with his supporters.
“Just close your eyes,” he tells them, “and pretend I'm on the ballot.”
It's a typically self-involved appeal from someone who has been the center of the nation's political gravity for more than a decade. Now, he's finishing the midterms with a cross-country blitz of campaign rallies that allow him to bask in applause when he's otherwise profoundly unpopular.
In a year marked by the war with Iran , fears about artificial intelligence , redistricting fights , high energy prices and increasing concerns about the cost of living , Trump's deeply personal approach might be the election cycle's biggest gamble.
Republicans still love the president, who remains dominant even as he approaches the back half of his second term. But his approval ratings are low enough to potentially sink his party and its bid to maintain control of Congress.
“I don’t think there’s anybody that wants Donald Trump out there at these rallies more than Democratic candidates," said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, which focuses on electing Democratic women who support abortion rights.
Every time there's another Trump event, she said, “we look at that as a win.”
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump is “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”
“The choice has never been more clear,” he said in a statement. “Doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda, or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”
It goes far beyond a whirlwind rally schedule.
The president organized even small details of the first-ever Republican midterm convention last month in Dallas, speaking both nights. He also was depicted there as the Marlboro Man , a cowboy on horseback and with a white Stetson who could ride to the rescue, on everything from baseball caps to beer cozies.
Trump even has a personal spin on his blockbuster attempt to win over voters by pledging big checks if Republicans hold Congress, saying “I’ll give you $5,000” even though the improbable idea would likely need lawmaker approval.
Political groups associated with the president have spent at least around $277 million since Sept. 1 to help Republicans — a staggering sum that nonetheless didn't completely drain the $416 million that Trump’s flagship Super PAC, MAGA Inc. , had in the bank to start last month.
But that wasn't enough for Trump. He used taxpayer funding to run television ads celebrating himself, including one nearly identical to a spot from 2024 — the last time he really was on the ballot.
From expanding executive power , to turning the presidency into a profit center for his family, to molding the White House in his own gilded image , Trump's self regard has escalated since he won back the White House.
“I can do stuff that is unbelievable," he bragged at a rally in Kentucky.
Trump crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes , demolished the East Wing to build a sprawling ballroom and converted the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate. There's also a new helipad that he showed off to Xi Jinping , China's communist leader, during a recent visit.
The president is focused on reshaping Washington as well, dispatching National Guard troops to the streets , closing the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building , planning a towering arch just outside the city and pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course .
Trump has wielded his iron grip on the Republican Party in ways that could hurt its chances in some races. He helped Ken Paxton, who has a history of legal and ethical problems, defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary, making the general election campaign against Democrat James Talarico more competitive.
Trump also clashed with North Carolina Sen. Tom Tillis, prompting him to retire , and pushed Michael Whatley to run. Now Republicans are bracing to lose the seat to former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper.
The Trump-centric approach backfired during his first term in 2018, when a similar presidential rally barrage didn't stop Democrats from retaking House control.
This time, many of the issues that helped Trump win reelection in 2024, such as his handling of the economy, could prove to be liabilities for Republicans.
Just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, as the Iran war keeps fuel prices high and stokes inflation fears, according to an AP-NORC poll conducted in late September.
The White House points to highlights beyond Trump's personal appeal, like efforts to lower prescription drug prices , stimulate domestic manufacturing , crack down on the U.S.-Mexico border and oppose transgender rights.
But longtime Michigan pollster Richard Czuba said the president's decision to focus on himself has prevented Republicans from courting conservative voters disappointed in Trump.
“He’s literally driving people who disagree with him to the Democratic side," Czuba said.
“The dividing line is how voters feel about Donald Trump,” he added. “And there’s a whole lot more voters who disapprove of Donald Trump than approve of Donald Trump.”
A CNN/SSRS poll conducted in mid-October found that about 4 in 10 registered voters suggested they’d think of their vote for Congress as more about sending a message that they oppose Trump. Only about 2 in 10 said they would be sending a message supporting him.
Even while hopscotching the country , the president has generally stuck to reliably red states. When he goes to battlegrounds, he mostly visits conservative areas, thus ensuring especially adoring crowds.
A pre-speech video likens the president to a global savior, booming repeatedly, “God gave us Trump," and he usually spends more of his speeches repeating past grievances than talking about next week's Election Day.
The idea is to energize the Republican base while avoiding backlash in swing states — and also potentially reaching television viewers who see the adulation for Trump and may vote Republican elsewhere around the country.
“I always cater to my base," Trump recently told the Washington Examiner, when asked if he was focusing too much on sympathetic rallygoers, rather than wooing independents.
Trump’s endorsement can be enough for some. Cindy Downes, a 67-year-old retiree from North Liberty, Iowa, cast an early ballot for Rep. Ashley Hinson for U.S. Senate and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' reelection.
“The number one reason: POTUS supports them,” said Downes, who wore a MAGA hat to a recent campaign event. “I trust him. I trust his judgment.”
But LuAnn Bird, 72, of Hales Corners, Wisconsin, said opposing Trump was one of many reasons she’s supporting Democrats.
“It just feels so good, not just to go against Trump, but to go for something,” said Bird, who attended a Milwaukee rally where former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris appeared with the Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley. “I want to see an aggressive, progressive agenda.”
Mackler of EMILY’S List recently spent time in states Trump has visited, including Georgia, Florida and Ohio. She said the president's approach exposes a disconnect with voters who "are so frustrated and fed up with this agenda that’s making their lives worse."
“That’s what’s driving opportunity on the ballot,” she said, "including in states and races and places that we would not have imagined would be in play.”
Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Milwaukee, Hannah Fingerhut in Coralville, Iowa, and Amelia Thomson DeVeaux in Washington contributed to this report.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Russia exposed the weaknesses of international security. What did NATO, the EU, the UN and the OSCE do?
body:
Russia’s aggression against Ukraine has exposed serious limitations in the international security system. Organisations that were established decades ago to prevent conflicts were unable to stop the largest war in Europe since the end of the Second World War. NATO, the European Union, the United Nations and the OSCE responded to the Russian invasion, but each institution has different capabilities and instruments at its disposal.
The greatest problem remains the fact that the Russian Federation continues to participate in organisations responsible for maintaining international peace, while simultaneously using their mechanisms to block decisions directed against its own aggression.
Following 24 February 2022, the European Union began imposing sanctions on Russia, restricting economic cooperation and reducing its dependence on Russian energy resources. At the same time, EU member states became involved in providing military, financial and humanitarian assistance to Ukraine. The reception of millions of refugees and support for Ukrainian agricultural exports were particularly important. The EU demonstrated that it possesses instruments capable of exerting economic pressure on Russia, but it is not an organisation designed to conduct military operations. Its effectiveness therefore depends primarily on the political determination of its member states and their ability to maintain sanctions over an extended period.
NATO’s position is different, as the Alliance is primarily responsible for the security of its members. Russia’s invasion effectively destroyed the previous model of cooperation with Moscow, developed partly on the basis of the 1997 NATO–Russia Founding Act. The Alliance decided to strengthen its eastern flank, increase military readiness and develop its deterrence capabilities.
However, Ukraine is not a NATO member and is therefore not covered by the guarantees provided under Article 5 of the Washington Treaty. Military assistance supplied by Allied countries has been extremely important for Ukraine’s defence, but it has not meant NATO’s direct involvement in the war against Russia.
The greatest controversy concerns the United Nations. Russia remains a permanent member of the UN Security Council and possesses the right of veto, allowing it to block the body’s most important decisions. In practice, a country conducting a war of aggression participates in decisions concerning the international response to its own military activities. This is one of the most serious paradoxes of the collective security system established after the Second World War. Changing this mechanism would require a fundamental reform of the United Nations, for which securing the agreement of all the major powers would be extremely difficult.
However, this does not mean that the UN has remained completely inactive. The organisation launched one of its largest humanitarian operations, supporting refugees, internally displaced persons and civilians in Ukraine. Important achievements included the evacuation of civilians from the Azovstal steelworks in Mariupol and participation in negotiating the agreement that allowed Ukrainian grain exports through the Black Sea.
Access to occupied territories remained a major problem, with Russia restricting the activities of humanitarian organisations. This was particularly evident following the destruction of the Nova Kakhovka dam in June 2023, when Moscow rejected UN requests to provide access to the affected population.
Similar limitations affect the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). For years, the OSCE participated in monitoring the situation in Ukraine and diplomatic efforts concerning the conflict in Donbas. Following the Russian invasion, however, its capabilities were significantly restricted. Russia repeatedly used the consensus mechanism to block decisions, while previously established negotiation formats ceased to fulfil their basic objectives. The organisation itself does not possess military instruments that would allow it to force an aggressor to end hostilities.
Nevertheless, the OSCE’s expert and documentation activities remain important. The organisation prepared reports concerning violations of international humanitarian law, war crimes and human rights abuses in Ukraine. These documents may contribute to future efforts to hold perpetrators accountable. At the same time, the OSCE remains one of the few forums enabling direct communication between Western countries and Russia and Belarus. Excluding Moscow could therefore restrict channels of communication without resolving the fundamental problem: the absence of effective mechanisms for enforcing international obligations.
Russia’s aggression has exposed fundamental differences between the capabilities of international organisations. The European Union can impose sanctions and finance assistance to Ukraine, NATO is responsible for deterrence and the defence of its members, the United Nations conducts humanitarian operations, and the OSCE deals with monitoring violations of international law and diplomatic activities, among other responsibilities. Each institution plays an important role, but none was able to stop the Russian invasion independently.
The greatest challenge remains the effectiveness of the entire system, in which an aggressor can violate international obligations while simultaneously blocking the activities of institutions established to protect them.
The war in Ukraine has demonstrated that the future of European security will depend not only on reforming international organisations, but also on the actual ability of states to deter Russia and respond to further threats.

title: War update: Over 190 clashes on front lines in past day, most Russian attacks on Pokrovsk axis
body:
The General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces said this in a Facebook update on the battlefield situation as of 08:00 on Wednesday, October 28, Ukrinform reports.
Russian forces launched three missile strikes and 68 airstrikes, dropping 258 guided aerial bombs.
In addition, Russian invaders deployed 9,654 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,535 attacks, including 35 using multiple launch rocket systems (MLRS).
Russian strikes targeted Bezsalivka, Koreniok, Tovstodubove, Ulаnove, Rohizne, Neskuchne, Pysarivka, Bachivsk, Vovkivka, Hirky, Kruzhok, Doroshivka, Mohrytsia, Yastrubshchyna, Nova Sich, Khrapivshchyna, Luzhky, Kozache, Obody, Mala Korchakivka, Kindrativka, Korchakivka, Volfyne, Zapsillia, and Ivolzhanske in the Sumy region, and Khrinivka in the Chernihiv region. Fotovyzh was hit by an airstrike.
Ukraine's missile forces and artillery struck a Russian UAV control center.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, Russian forces carried out 37 attacks, three of them using MLRS.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukraine's Defense Forces repelled five attacks. Russian invaders attacked toward Okhrimivka and Mala Vovcha.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces launched three assaults toward Radkivka.
In the Lyman sector, Russian troops carried out six assault operations toward Nove, Stavky, and Lyman.
In the Sloviansk sector, the Russian army launched two attacks near Yampil and toward Orikhuvatka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian troops attacked three times toward Malynivka, Vasiutynske, and Chervone.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 15 attacks were recorded. Russian forces conducted offensive operations near Kostiantynivka and toward Raiske and Pavlivka.
The enemy launched 32 attacks in the Pokrovsk sector, attempting to advance near Sofiivka, Vilne, Vodianske, Vasylivka, Molodetske, and Udachne, and toward Toretske, Kucheriv Yar, Dobropillia, Hannivka, Novohryshyne, Hulive, and Serhiivka.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Oleksandrivka sector.
In the Huliaipole sector, Russian troops launched 17 attacks, attempting to advance toward Ternuvate, Dolynka, Hirke, Charivne, and Yehorivka.
Russian forces conducted no assault operations in the Orikhiv and Dnipro River sectors.
No signs of Russian offensive groupings being formed were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.
Photo: General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces

title: ADGM's Registration Authority issues guidance on crypto mining in emirate's financial hub
body: The Registration Authority of Abu Dhabi’s ADGM has published guidance on cryptocurrency mining in the emirate's international financial centre. The guidance, the first from a financial centre in the region, provides clear directions on commercial licencing to crypto miners and businesses conducting crypto mining within or from the emirate's financial centre, the authority said in a statement on Wednesday. The advice treats crypto mining as a “licencable commercial activity” overseen by the ADGM’s Registration Authority and not as a regulated financial service. The authority has adopted a “technology-neutral approach” across proof of work and proof of stake to ensure responsible mining activities, it said. The move is in line with the ADGM’s broader strategy of promoting innovation, and enabling new business models to develop within a well-governed environment, said Rashed Al Blooshi, chief executive of the Registration Authority at the ADGM. Abu Dhabi’s economy is increasingly being shaped by digital infrastructure, and the emirate regards crypto mining to be at the “intersection of energy, technology and capital”, Mr Al Blooshi said. “With this guidance, ADGM is open for responsible crypto mining,” he said. “We are giving operators a clear commercial licencing pathway, proportionate supervision calibrated to scale and risk, and certainty on where the regulatory perimeter resides.” The guidance builds on the ADGM’s goal to strengthen digital assets and emerging technologies within its jurisdiction, and provide greater regulatory certainty for “responsible crypto mining operators” seeking to increase their activities from Abu Dhabi, the authority said. Businesses that meet governance and transparency standards of the ADGM will find in Abu Dhabi “a jurisdiction where they can plan, invest and grow with confidence”, Mr Al Blooshi added. Abu Dhabi’s financial centre has been maturing its regulatory framework for digital assets as it strives to become a global base for cryptocurrency and digital assets companies and attract global operators. Recent amendments streamline the process through which virtual assets are accepted for use in the financial centre. They also impose appropriate capital requirements and fees for authorised people conducting regulated virtual asset activities. The Registration Authority said its guidance is the first phase of broader plans to develop crypto mining in the ADGM. In a second phase, it aims to develop regulations for mining, with market consultation set to begin in due course. The issuance of the guidance follows an eight-week consultation published earlier in the year , which generated “substantive feedback”, it added.

title: Global South more optimistic about AI jobs, FII survey finds
body: People in the Global South are significantly more optimistic than those in wealthier economies about artificial intelligence creating jobs, even as growing enthusiasm for the technology is accompanied by overwhelming demands for tighter regulation, a new study has found. About 43 per cent of respondents in the Global South disagree that AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys, compared with 70 per cent in the Global North, according to the Future Investment Initiative Institute's Priority Compass report released on Wednesday. In the three Middle East and North Africa countries surveyed – Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco – 66 per cent believe AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys, compared with just 27 per cent in Europe and 33 per cent in North America. The findings highlight a sharp divide between the Global South and wealthier economies over AI's impact on employment, even as 85 per cent of respondents worldwide back a global regulatory framework to ensure greater human oversight. Globally, 54 per cent disagree that AI will create more quality jobs than it destroys. The report surveyed more than 61,000 respondents across 32 countries. The Mena nations in the study were Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. A consistent view in all regions was that they want AI to be subject to more human oversight, with 85 per cent overall saying they want a global framework and rules to regulate the growing technology. The clamour is “underscoring a global demand for human control on emerging technologies”, Maha bint Mishari, chief executive of the FII Institute, wrote in the report. For the acceptance of cryptocurrencies, Africa was the most positive with 81 per cent, followed by the three Mena countries surveyed at 71 per cent. The Global South's overall score was 69 per cent, more than double the Global North's 30 per cent, with Europe's 28 per cent the least positive. Meanwhile, inflation remains the top concern around the cost of living, but energy and fuel costs have risen to become the next biggest worry, the study revealed. The impact of successive crises in the Middle East on fuel prices has been felt most heavily in the Global North, with concern about fuel costs rising to 42 per cent, up from 29 per cent last year. In contrast, low wages still come second in the Global South – at 32 per cent against 17 per cent in the Global North – but energy costs have also become more of a worry in the Global South, rising from 22 per cent last year to 29 per cent in 2026, the FII Institute said. “Half of all respondents continue to cite the cost of living as their number one concern, underlining a global confidence crisis unrepresented in headlines,” Ms bint Mishari said. “People everywhere are feeling the impact of inflation, job insecurity and the pressure of everyday expenses.”

title: Trade deals should open more than markets
body: Trade agreements are powerful tools for economic growth. By enhancing the competitiveness of exports, a nation can drive productivity, catalyse innovation and expand critical or emerging sectors. This is why the UAE moved to connect our ecosystem to the world’s most important economies in 2021 – and why we continue to explore closer ties with high-growth markets around the world. Increasingly, though, we understand that the real value of a trade deal emerges through unlocking the growth potential of foreign direct investment and private-sector partnerships that follow in its wake. Our Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement programme, which has facilitated record flows of resources, merchandise and services to 40 nations on six continents, is now evolving to translate access into sustained, long-term mutual benefit. The Cepa with Canada, which we signed this week , is a key milestone in this process. More than just another addition to our trade network, this deal embodies our wholly integrated approach to economic partnerships, one in which trade policy, investment and business engagement work in parallel. Removing trade barriers isn’t the goal, it’s the first step in building and scaling economic opportunity. Every export requires infrastructure. Before a shipment reaches its customer, it will rely on warehouses, freight corridors, port terminals and local supplier networks. Investment in these assets strengthens the competitiveness of entire business ecosystems, creating opportunities for a broad range of companies. This is where trade policy and strategic investment work together. Importantly, it also means recognising that a manufacturer may now have access to a new market but can’t leverage it without the distribution network required to serve it efficiently. It means understanding that an entrepreneur may identify demand but lacks the financing, local expertise or strategic partners to realise the opportunity. We have seen this in action in India . Following the signing of our Cepa, in 2022, DP World pledged $5 billion to strengthen its integrated supply-chain network, a commitment that built on the $3 billion it had already invested across three decades. The stated objectives include lowering logistics costs, supporting local manufacturing and expanding access to global markets. This investment is designed to improve connectivity, increase efficiency and support industrial growth. Its benefits extend far beyond any single project. The UAE aims to be a platform where businesses can grow, invest, innovate and build partnerships that extend across a number of markets While commercial relationships can – and often do – predate trade agreements, our Cepa programme has delivered the confidence, certainty and regulatory harmony that encourage businesses to pursue larger ambitions and form deeper partnerships. In India, our private sector is now accelerating its investments in integrated food production, logistics networks and energy production because they see how our Cepa has secured bilateral trust and opportunity. This isn’t a by-product, it’s the objective. Our deal with Canada will provide another real-life case study. The forthcoming Cepa will add impetus to the investment framework that has committed $50 billion in capital to sectors such as energy , artificial intelligence, logistics and mining by delivering the complementary foundations for trade, investment and industrial co-operation. The task of the Ministry of Foreign Trade has shifted in parallel. Signing a trade deal is simply the first, albeit important step in the process; the real work is to coalesce other ministries, institutions, sovereign wealth funds and the investment community to ensure these frameworks translate into commercial outcomes. That means identifying opportunities early and approaching implementation with a clear focus on growth from the very beginning. The ministry’s work post-signing must be fully focused on connecting businesses whose capabilities, capital and expertise can support new projects, new investments and new sources of growth. When trade, investment and business engagement reinforce one another, economic relationships gain momentum: commercial success encourages further investment; new investment expands productive capacity; and these opportunities attract new participants and deepen co-operation. The greatest potential of this approach, however, extends beyond any single bilateral relationship. Every new partnership should strengthen not only the relationship between the UAE and a specific country, but also the value of the wider network available to businesses operating within it. A Canadian technology company could work alongside a UAE investor and an industrial partner in another Cepa market. An entrepreneur may use the UAE as a base from which to develop partnerships across several regions. These outcomes are not automatic. They require commercial judgment, investment and compliance with the regulations of each market. Yet they illustrate the scale of the opportunity before us. The UAE has long been recognised as a gateway to regional and global markets. Our ambition today is broader. We aim to be a platform where businesses can grow, invest, innovate and build partnerships that extend across a number of markets. Ultimately, by combining open trade with targeted investment and stronger commercial connections, we can ensure our partnerships deliver sustainable growth and shared prosperity for many years to come. In doing so, we can redefine what globalisation means – and what it can deliver. Our Cepa with Canada is another opportunity to demonstrate it.

title: AMA clears Achimota bus stop to make way for Ayalolo buses
body: The Accra Metropolitan Assembly (AMA) has stepped up efforts to reclaim public spaces in the capital, clearing unauthorised structures around the Achimota New Overhead Ayalolo bus stop to improve access for commercial buses and their passengers. The operation, led by the Accra Mayor, Michael Kpakpo Allotey, on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, targeted structures and trading activities obstructing the bus stop, where Ayalolo and other commercial buses are expected to pick up and drop off passengers. The clearance is intended to provide buses with adequate space to operate, reduce obstructions and improve traffic movement around the busy transport point. The exercise forms part of a broader campaign by the AMA and the Okaikwei North Municipal Assembly to remove unauthorised structures and trading activities from public spaces. Bus stops targeted The assemblies say the operation is aimed at restoring bus stops to their intended purpose and preventing trading activities from interfering with public transport services. The presence of structures and traders around loading and offloading points can restrict access for buses, disrupt passenger movement and contribute to congestion, particularly at busy transport locations. By clearing the area around the Achimota interchange, the authorities hope to enable commercial vehicles, especially Ayalolo buses, to serve commuters without having to navigate obstructions at the designated stop. Broader public-space enforcement The collaboration between the AMA and the Okaikwei North Municipal Assembly is intended to extend the removal of unauthorised structures and trading activities beyond the Achimota bus stop to other areas where public spaces have been occupied. The authorities are seeking to ensure that bus stops remain accessible to public transport operators and commuters, while discouraging trading and other activities that obstruct their use. The clearance forms part of wider efforts to restore order in the city’s transport corridors and improve the movement of people and vehicles. The assemblies are expected to continue addressing the occupation of unauthorised spaces as part of their traffic management and public-space regulation measures.

title: Kazakhstan, UN Discuss Steps to Strengthen Cooperation Among Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. ASTANA – Kazakhstan and the United Nations have discussed practical measures to strengthen cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones and advance the implementation of recommendations from a new UN comprehensive study on the subject. Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations hosted a forum in cooperation with the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) on Oct. 27 to discuss cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones. Photo credit: MFA. The forum was hosted by Kazakhstan’s Permanent Mission to the UN in cooperation with the UN Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) on Oct. 27. The event marked the 20th anniversary of the signing of the Semipalatinsk Treaty and the publication of the new UN study, the first comprehensive assessment of nuclear-weapon-free zones in 50 years. Discussions focused on implementing the study’s recommendations, strengthening cooperation among existing nuclear-weapon-free zones and engaging with nuclear-weapon states. Participants included UN Under-Secretary-General and High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu, Mexico’s Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Porfirio Thierry Muñoz Ledo, Nuclear Threat Initiative Vice President Paul Dean, diplomats from UN Member States, representatives of international organizations and experts in nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. Ryan Musto of William & Mary in the United States moderated the discussion. In his opening remarks, Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov said rising nuclear risks underscored the need to strengthen effective cooperation mechanisms. He called for the study’s recommendations to serve as a basis for concrete joint initiatives and highlighted Central Asia’s contribution to regional security and the nuclear non-proliferation regime. Nakamitsu commended the longstanding partnership between the UN and Kazakhstan, highlighting their joint efforts to promote cooperation among nuclear-weapon-free zones. Earlier, Kazakhstan and UNODA organized international workshops in Astana in 2019 and 2024 to strengthen cooperation between the zones and improve consultation mechanisms. Describing the Semipalatinsk Treaty as an example of successful regional diplomacy, Nakamitsu said the study’s lasting value would depend on the practical implementation of its recommendations. She reaffirmed UNODA’s readiness to support further efforts. Muñoz Ledo emphasized the need to strengthen the institutional capacity of nuclear-weapon-free zones while accounting for their regional differences. He also called for continued dialogue with nuclear-weapon states on legally binding security assurances. Dean highlighted the potential of nuclear-weapon-free zones to reduce nuclear risks, drawing on the experiences of Kazakhstan, South Africa, Brazil and Argentina. He also outlined plans for an interzonal meeting in Vienna and the development of a dedicated online learning resource for diplomats. During the open discussion, the ambassadors of Brazil and the United Kingdom stressed the importance of regular consultations among nuclear-weapon-free zones and constructive dialogue with nuclear-weapon States. Experts and civil society representatives proposed stronger coordination, information-sharing and educational cooperation, including initiatives to engage young people. A representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross highlighted the complementary nature of nuclear-weapon-free zone treaties and the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Concluding the forum, Umarov proposed closer coordination among the five regional nuclear-weapon-free zones and Mongolia to advance shared priorities in dialogue with nuclear-weapon States. As a follow-up, Kazakhstan, with UNODA’s support, will prepare a concise summary of the discussions outlining participants’ key proposals and potential areas for further cooperation. The post Kazakhstan, UN Discuss Steps to Strengthen Cooperation Among Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zones appeared first on The Astana Times .

title: Republicans emphasize transgender ads, putting cultural issues over economy
body:
Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections
NEW YORK -- Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections, betting that struggling GOP candidates can leverage the divisive cultural issue to overcome voters' concerns about President Donald Trump's leadership and the state of the economy.
The massive investment through Oct. 25 produced about 217,000 TV spots nationwide and exceeds the amount Republicans spent on similar ads in 2024, a presidential election year, at the same point before Election Day, according to tallies provided to The Associated Press by data firm AdImpact.
The spending campaign matched messaging from other Republicans on the campaign trail, led by Trump, who has played down surging gasoline prices and other rising costs, but highlighted what he described as an urgent threat to America's children from Democratic policies.
The Republican emphasis on transgender issues offers a consequential test of whether a theme that had worked in past elections — and especially in deep red states — can still be potent when voters consistently say high prices are their chief concern.
Barely five minutes into his speech during Monday night’s rally in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump said that Democrats “promote the transgender mutilization of your children.” During his Sunday rally in Florida, Trump said “men in women's sports” four times and gender “mutilization” — meaning mutilation — another four times.
Having shifted away from abortion, few cultural issues reflect the Republican Party's evolution on social issues in the age of Trump more than transgender rights. Though a tiny number of Americans are directly affected by legislation designed to protect transgender people from discrimination, Republicans have used the issue as a powerful emotional motivator, especially in Republican-leaning states where they need to win to maintain control of Congress.
Texas’ high-stakes Senate contest alone has consumed the largest share of Republican-backed transgender-related spending, drawing an estimated $58 million for more than 50,000 airings, according to AdImpact. But the GOP is also investing heavily in related attacks against Democrats in Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa and Mississippi, according to an AP analysis of the data.
The Republican Party's focus stands in stark contrast to what voters say they care most about this midterm season.
“Republicans clearly believe these issues expose a cultural disconnect between Democratic candidates and a significant portion of the electorate,” said Republican pollster Chris Wilson. “It's not necessarily that transgender policy is a top voting priority, it’s that voters can use a candidate’s position on it as a proxy for their broader values and judgment.”
Only about 1 in 10 registered voters say transgender issues are “one of the most important issues” in the election, according to an AP-NORC poll from October .
That falls well below the roughly 8 in 10 who mentioned the economy or the cost of living , and also falls short of other issues that have surfaced during the campaign, including healthcare and the war with Iran.
Republicans were more likely than independents and Democrats to say transgender issues are highly important to this election, but it still fell below other issues.
The issue resonates with voters like Jerry Casner, a 74-year-old registered Republican and three-time Trump voter, who lives in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. He retired from a nearby Army depot and works 12 hours a week at a grocery store in New Cumberland.
“Well, I don’t like the way the Democrats operate," Casner said, when asked what national issues are important to him. He explained: “If you can’t even determine the difference between a man and a woman, but yet you’re going to make life and death decisions for me, oh, I don’t think so. That’s disgusting.”
Casner said he plans on voting Republican up and down the ballot.
Republicans across federal, state and local races have aired transgender-themed ads during the general election around 217,000 times at a cost estimated at $183 million through Oct. 25, AdImpact found. That's up from $151 million in spending in the 2024 general election as of the same number of days prior to that year’s election.
Democrats have spent roughly $11 million on transgender-related ads, largely to defend themselves from the attacks.
This year's spending was concentrated in a small number of races, according to AdImpact.
Texas PAC, the Republican super PAC largely funded by Elon Musk and supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, has at least three separate TV ads hammering Democrat James Talarico on trans issues.
One of them echoes a Trump ad from the 2024 campaign with the narrator saying that Vice President Kamala Harris is for “they, them. President Trump is for you.” The Texas ad accuses Talarico of supporting taxpayer funding of minors' sex-reassignment surgery, charging that he's “for they them, not you.”
Another Texas PAC ad claims Talarico supports taxpayer funding of gender reassignment surgery for minors, while a third accuses him of backing child abuse charges against parents who do not support transitioning their children.
“If you care about your children, do not vote for James Talarico,” the narrator says in the spot that has aired nearly 17,000 times at a cost exceeding $23 million.
In Ohio, Republican groups led by the Senate Leadership Fund PAC are running multiple trans-themed ads against Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown .
In two of that fund's ads, someone who underwent surgery as a minor and later de-transitioned is featured describing the regret and accusing Brown of supporting such surgeries for minors. Another accuses Brown of supporting “men competing in women’s sports.”
Brown's campaign said the ads were a “total lie” and a distraction from economic issues. The independent organization PolitiFact rated the fund's ad false.
Talarico has publicly stated that he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for minors. And the attack against Brown twists a 2023 interview where Brown stated that a child’s medical decisions belong between families and doctors, not politicians.
Still, the Texas ads have aired an estimated 50,000 times overall at a cost of $58 million, representing roughly 2 in 10 ads run in the Senate race. The Ohio attacks against Brown have cost nearly $26 million.
In deeper-red states like South Carolina, which has emerged as an unlikely Senate battleground, Republicans have spent more than $5 million on transgender-themed ads. And in the Kansas Senate race, Republican transgender ads have aired 7,000 times at a cost of nearly $7 million.
“The interesting question isn’t why Republicans are running these ads, it’s whether they’re still persuading anyone or simply reinforcing attitudes voters already hold,” said Wilson, the Republican pollster. “Those are two very different things, and $100 million in spending doesn’t tell us which is happening."
He added, "We’ll find that out on Election Day.”
Peoples reported from New York. AP writers Linley Sanders in Washington and Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, contributed.
