title: The Signal: The Parties Are Choosing Sides. Will the Voters Follow?
body: Tinubu’s political alliances are expanding, Obi and Kwankwaso are sharpening their challenge, and INEC is under pressure to demonstrate transparency. But as the presidential campaign gathers momentum, Nigeria’s politicians may be discovering that winning endorsements is easier than winning public confidence. There is an interesting contradiction emerging in Nigerian politics. At a time when political parties are supposed to be competing against one another, their leading figures are increasingly finding reasons to work together. In Rivers State, Nyesom Wike is assembling a coalition that crosses party boundaries but supports President Bola Tinubu and other APC candidates. In Osun, Governor Ademola Adeleke supports Tinubu’s re-election while insisting that his political organisation will compete against the APC in legislative elections. Meanwhile, Peter Obi and Rabiu Kwankwaso have established a joint presidential campaign structure, even as other opposition leaders continue discussing the possibility of a broader alliance. And the Independent National Electoral Commission, caught in the middle of growing political suspicion, has taken a step towards addressing concerns about the voters’ register. Welcome to Nigeria’s 2027 election. A contest in which party labels are becoming increasingly flexible, political loyalties are being renegotiated, and the electorate is being asked to distinguish between genuine conviction and political convenience. But beneath the manoeuvring lies a question that could determine the outcome. The politicians are choosing sides. Will the voters follow them? Wike’s coalition: when political boundaries become optional Nyesom Wike has never been a politician easily constrained by conventional party loyalties. His support for Tinubu in the 2023 presidential election, despite his association with the PDP, demonstrated his willingness to pursue political objectives across party lines. Now, with another presidential election approaching, he is taking that approach further. At a political gathering in Eleme, Rivers State, Wike made it clear that his Rainbow Coalition is not simply an arrangement to support Tinubu’s re-election. It also intends to support APC candidates contesting governorship and legislative elections. That is a significant development. It suggests that Wike is attempting to create a political structure capable of influencing elections at several levels, regardless of the formal party affiliations of those participating. There is a certain political logic to the arrangement. For Tinubu, Wike provides an influential ally in a strategically important state. For Wike, cooperation with the President offers a means of preserving political relevance and strengthening his position in Rivers. But what does the arrangement offer ordinary voters? That is the question that deserves more attention. Cross-party cooperation is not inherently objectionable. Indeed, democracies often require politicians to work across partisan divisions. But political cooperation should ideally be based on identifiable policies and shared objectives. When alliances appear to be organised primarily around personalities, voters may reasonably wonder what distinguishes one party from another. There is also the question of whether Wike can deliver the electoral support he promises. Rivers has experienced significant political tensions and competing claims to influence. A political endorsement, however emphatic, does not automatically resolve those divisions. The Rainbow Coalition may prove formidable. But its true strength will be measured at the ballot box, not at political gatherings. Adeleke offers a different interpretation of coalition politics Compare Wike’s approach with that of Governor Ademola Adeleke in Osun State. Adeleke has declared his support for Tinubu’s re-election. But he has also made it clear that this support does not extend to APC legislative candidates. His political organisation intends to support its own candidates in those contests. The distinction is revealing. In Rivers, Wike is promoting a broad electoral alliance with the APC. In Osun, Adeleke is offering presidential cooperation while preserving competition at other levels. Both arrangements reflect the increasingly personalised character of Nigerian politics. But they also demonstrate that support for Tinubu does not necessarily translate into support for his party. That could become important in states where governors and influential politicians maintain strong local organisations outside the APC. It also raises a broader democratic question. If politicians can support one party for President and another for the National Assembly, are voters being offered genuine ideological choices, or merely different combinations of political interests? There is no simple answer. Nigerian political parties have rarely been distinguished by sharply defined ideological programmes. But the growing frequency of cross-party arrangements makes it even more important for candidates to explain what they stand for. Otherwise, the election risks becoming a contest between political networks rather than competing visions of government. Obi and Kwankwaso move from negotiations to confrontation While Tinubu’s allies are consolidating their arrangements, the opposition is beginning to demonstrate a more assertive posture. The Nigeria Democratic Congress has unveiled a presidential campaign council bringing together Peter Obi, Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso and former Bayelsa Governor Seriake Dickson. Dickson chairs the council, Obi serves as co-chairman, and Kwankwaso, the party’s vice-presidential candidate, occupies the position of co-vice-chairman. The structure includes national and state-level coordinators intended to support the campaign across the country. This is an important organisational step. For months, opposition politics has been dominated by discussions about possible alliances, common candidates and negotiations among competing political leaders. The NDC’s decision to establish a formal campaign structure suggests that the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket intends to contest the election seriously. And Obi’s latest criticism of Tinubu indicates that the campaign is becoming more confrontational. Obi has questioned the President’s capacity and energy to govern effectively, sharpening his attack on the administration’s leadership. Such criticism is part of democratic competition. But it presents both an opportunity and a risk. The opportunity is to draw public attention to the government’s performance. The risk is that personal attacks could overshadow the substantive policy differences voters need to understand. The Obi-Kwankwaso partnership has an interesting geographical dimension. Obi’s strongest political appeal has historically been associated with the South-East and reform-oriented voters in other regions. Kwankwaso brings an established political identity in Kano and parts of the North-West. Together, they could potentially appeal to constituencies that have not always supported the same presidential candidate. But that potential should not be confused with guaranteed electoral success. A presidential election requires a broad national coalition. The NDC must demonstrate that it can compete effectively beyond its strongest regional constituencies. It must also explain how it would manage the economy, address insecurity, create jobs and improve public services. The opposition cannot rely indefinitely on dissatisfaction with the incumbent. At some point, it must persuade Nigerians that it offers a better alternative. INEC takes a step towards rebuilding confidence Away from the rallies and political endorsements, another development deserves serious attention. INEC has published the preliminary voters’ register online, following complaints about public access. The development comes after Atiku Abubakar and other stakeholders questioned whether Nigerians had been given adequate opportunity to inspect the register during the previously announced period. The commission’s publication of the register is a welcome step towards greater transparency. But publication alone is not enough. The real test is whether voters can access their records, verify their information and obtain corrections where necessary. INEC has indicated that the final register is scheduled for publication on December 15. That leaves a limited period in which administrative problems must be identified and resolved. The commission should therefore provide clear information about the verification process, the treatment of complaints and the safeguards designed to protect the integrity of the register. There is a wider lesson here. Electoral confidence cannot be manufactured through assurances. It must be earned through procedures that citizens can understand and independently examine. Opposition parties have a legitimate right to scrutinise INEC’s preparations. But they also have a responsibility to distinguish genuine irregularities from unverified allegations. Similarly, the ruling party should resist the temptation to interpret every demand for transparency as an attack on the government. A credible election benefits every participant. The winner gains legitimacy. The losers have stronger grounds to accept the result. And the country avoids the instability that can arise when large numbers of citizens believe their votes have not been properly counted. With the presidential election approaching, INEC’s conduct may prove just as consequential as the campaigns themselves. The economy remains the argument nobody can escape For all the attention devoted to political alliances, the economy remains central to the election. Tinubu’s campaign is defending the reforms introduced during his first term. The government argues that removing petrol subsidies and restructuring the foreign-exchange system were necessary to correct longstanding economic distortions. There have been improvements in some macroeconomic indicators. But the political difficulty is that many Nigerians continue to experience high living costs. Food prices, transportation expenses, housing costs and the burden of running small businesses remain immediate concerns. The Federal Government’s recently announced 90-day economic intervention programme is therefore particularly significant. Its objectives include improving food affordability, supporting households and accelerating the delivery of public projects. The programme is expected to run into the period immediately preceding the presidential election. That creates an unusually direct test of the administration’s economic performance. If Nigerians experience meaningful relief, Tinubu’s argument that his reforms are beginning to deliver results could become more persuasive. If the intervention produces little visible improvement, the opposition will have additional grounds to question the government’s economic record. There is also the unresolved issue of organised labour’s demands for improved wages and relief from rising petrol prices. A breakdown in negotiations could increase political pressure on the administration. But the opposition should not imagine that public dissatisfaction automatically translates into support for its candidates. Voters will want to know what alternative policies are being proposed. Would an opposition government restore petrol subsidies? Would it retain the current foreign-exchange framework? How would it finance wage increases? What would it do to improve electricity supply, agricultural productivity and employment? These are questions that deserve detailed answers. Nigeria cannot afford another election in which economic promises are made without serious consideration of how they would be implemented. Nigeria 2027 Election Watch: the emerging battlegrounds The latest political developments provide a clearer picture of where the contest may become particularly competitive. Rivers State will test whether Wike’s Rainbow Coalition can translate political influence into votes across presidential, governorship and legislative contests. Osun State will provide an interesting example of split political loyalties, with Adeleke supporting Tinubu while retaining his own party’s electoral ambitions. Kano State could become crucial to the Obi-Kwankwaso ticket, particularly if it succeeds in mobilising voters beyond Kwankwaso’s traditional political base. The South-East remains important to Obi’s electoral prospects, although turnout and the strength of competing political organisations will matter. The North-Central states may prove especially competitive because of their diverse political loyalties, security concerns and economic circumstances. And across the country, the influence of younger voters deserves attention. Many younger Nigerians are politically engaged, economically frustrated and increasingly willing to challenge established political assumptions. But their potential influence will depend on voter registration, turnout and the credibility of the choices available to them. Social media enthusiasm can help shape political narratives. It cannot substitute for votes. Political actor current assessment Tinubu and the APC have a strong campaign organisation and extensive political endorsements, but continue to face exposure to economic dissatisfaction Wike’s Rainbow Coalition Clearer electoral ambitions in Rivers; still faces the test of translating influence into votes Adeleke Preserves political flexibility by separating presidential support from legislative competition Obi-Kwankwaso /NDC More defined campaign organisation and a sharper challenge to Tinubu; national mobilisation remains a test Atiku and the wider opposition continued relevance in coalition negotiations and electoral scrutiny, but cooperation remains unresolved. INEC takes a constructive step with publication of the preliminary register; must demonstrate that verification and corrections work effectively. What to watch before Friday Several developments deserve close attention over the next few days. The first is whether the Obi-Kwankwaso campaign can move beyond its organisational announcement and begin demonstrating effective national mobilisation. The second is whether Wike’s Rainbow Coalition attracts additional political support or encounters resistance from competing organisations in Rivers. The third is whether the wider opposition coalition negotiations produce a clearer electoral arrangement. INEC’s handling of the preliminary voters’ register will also remain important, particularly as political parties and civic organisations examine the information made available. And the government’s engagement with organised labour could influence the economic atmosphere in which the campaign unfolds. These are developments that may have more lasting consequences than another round of political endorsements. The final signal: Voters are not political property There is an assumption that runs through much of Nigerian politics. It is the belief that powerful politicians possess votes. A governor controls a state. A former governor controls a political structure. A party leader commands a constituency. And when these individuals enter an alliance, the votes supposedly follow them. But voters are not political property. They may admire a governor without agreeing with his presidential preference. They may support a political party in one election and reject its candidate in another. They may attend a rally without intending to vote for the person addressing them. And they may express enthusiasm for an opposition candidate without ultimately turning out on election day. This is why the political calculations unfolding across Nigeria deserve careful scrutiny. Tinubu’s extensive network of endorsements is a significant advantage. The Obi-Kwankwaso partnership presents an interesting challenge. Atiku’s political experience and networks remain relevant. Wike’s Rainbow Coalition could influence the contest in Rivers. And Adeleke’s carefully limited endorsement illustrates the complexity of political loyalty. But none of these arrangements settles the election. The more important question is whether the candidates can persuade Nigerians that their lives will improve under their leadership. For Tinubu, that means demonstrating that economic reforms are producing tangible benefits. For the opposition, it means offering credible alternatives rather than simply promising change. For INEC, it means ensuring that the electoral process is transparent, accessible and trusted. And for the electorate, it means examining the candidates beyond their alliances, their slogans and the political personalities surrounding them. The parties are choosing sides. The politicians are negotiating their interests. The campaigns are gathering momentum. But when Nigerians enter the polling booths in January, the ballot will belong to the voter, not the governor, the minister or the party leader who claims to speak for them. That is the distinction every campaign should remember. And it may be the most important political signal of all. That is The Signal this Tuesday. EDITORIAL NOTE Political Signals is an independent weekly political analysis produced for Channels Television. It examines political developments, personalities and electoral trends without endorsement of any political party or candidate. Its assessments are based on publicly available evidence and may change as events and evidence develop. The post The Signal: The Parties Are Choosing Sides. Will the Voters Follow? appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Niger governor’s convoy crash kills four students, driver
body:
Five people, including four students of the Federal University of Technology, Minna, have died in a road crash involving a vehicle in the convoy of Niger State Governor Mohammed Bago .
The accident occurred on Monday at Gidan Mangoro in Minna, involving a Toyota Hilux conveying the Director-General of the Government House, Dauda Chikuba, and a vehicle carrying the students, according to a report by PUNCH published on Tuesday.
The four students and the driver of the Government House vehicle died at the scene, while Mr Chikuba was taken to a hospital for treatment, the report said.
The crash reportedly occurred as the governor’s convoy was returning to Minna after a condolence visit to the Etsu Nupe and Chairman of the Niger State Council of Traditional Rulers, Yahaya Abubakar, over the death of Sagi Nupe, Aisha.
The vehicle conveying the students was travelling towards Bida when the collision occurred.
An eyewitness quoted by PUNCH described the incident as a head-on collision and alleged that the governor’s convoy was travelling at high speed.
“It was a head-on collision. We learnt that the convoy was at high speed when the accident occurred. It was a terrible accident,” the eyewitness said.
The report did not independently establish the cause of the crash.
The spokesperson for the Niger State Police Command, Wasiu Abiodun, confirmed the accident and said the police had begun an investigation.
“The accident occurred this morning, and we are investigating it,” Mr Abiodun was quoted as saying.
The police spokesperson did not disclose the identities of the deceased.
Further details about the circumstances of the collision and the condition of the injured government official were not immediately available.

title: Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Largest Steel Plant, Chemical Factory Amid 531 Drone Claims
body:
Ukraine reportedly struck Russia ’s largest steel plant and a major chemical factory overnight on Oct. 27-28, with fires reported at both facilities as Russian authorities reported a massive wave of drone attacks across several regions.
On the night of Oct. 27-28, a missile alert was declared in Russia’s Lipetsk Oblast.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The enemy is attempting to attack the industrial infrastructure of Lipetsk. A massive attack is currently being repelled,” the Russian Telegram channel Radar Lipetsk reported .
Later, the channel reported a fire at the Novolipetsk Steel Plant (NLMK). The Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also confirmed a blaze on the facility’s premises, suggesting that a Russian Pantsir air defense system may have failed to intercept an incoming aerial target.
Igor Artamonov, the governor of the Lipetsk Oblast, later said on Telegram that 45 drones had been shot down over the region overnight.
According to him, drone debris shattered windows in an apartment building in Lipetsk. In one of the region’s gardening cooperatives, a drone fell onto a garden plot next to a house. Another drone fell near a residential building in the Dankovsky District.
“Reports are circulating on social media and messaging apps about a major fire at an industrial facility. This is not true. Drone debris fell in a wooded area, sparking a fire that has now been contained,” Artamonov said.
NLMK is Russia’s largest steel plant and ranks among the 20 largest steel producers in the world. The facility has an annual production capacity of 17 million tons of liquid steel. It was previously targeted in an attack on July.
Early on the morning of Oct. 28, Tula Oblast Governor Dmitry Milyaev also declared a missile alert. He later reported that the region had come under a massive attack by Ukrainian drones.
“As a result of falling drone debris in Novomoskovsk, damage has been recorded to an apartment building, private homes, and infrastructure in the adjacent industrial zone,” Milyaev wrote .
He added that information about possible casualties and the extent of the damage was still being clarified.
Although Milyaev did not identify the specific industrial facility targeted, he said that laboratories from the Tula Oblast state institution Priroda (Nature) and the regional office of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s federal consumer rights protection agency, had been dispatched to Novomoskovsk.
According to Exilenova+ and the Russian outlet Astra, the target of the latest attack in Novomoskovsk was the Azot chemical plant, which belongs to the EuroChem group and is one of Russia’s largest producers of nitrogen fertilizers.
The facility manufactures ammonia, ammonium nitrate, urea, and methanol. These substances are used in various industrial applications, including the production of munitions.
Astra previously reported an attack on the Azot chemical plant on June 26. The facility had also caught fire following a Ukrainian attack on the night of June 14.
The Russian Ministry of Defense reported that air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 531 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) overnight, between 8 p.m. Moscow time on Oct. 27 and 8 a.m. on Oct. 28.
According to the ministry, the drones were intercepted over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, and Tula Oblasts, as well as Moscow Oblast.
The Ukrainian side has not commented on its involvement in the reported strikes as of publication.
On Oct. 24, Ukrainian drones attacked Tolyattikauchuk , a major petrochemical enterprise in Russia’s Samara region.
A fire broke out at the plant, which is owned by Tatneft, and authorities closed nearby streets. The Tolyatti combined heat and power plant (CHP) was also struck, resulting in disruptions to electricity and water supplies for local residents.
Tolyattikauchuk produces monomers, hydrocarbon fractions, and gasoline additives. Its synthetic rubber products are also used in the production of solid rocket fuel for tactical and ballistic missiles.
Julia is a Deputy Head of News and correspondent for Kyiv Post who has previously worked as a parliamentary editor, journalist, and news editor. She has specialized in covering the work of the Ukrainian parliament, government, and law enforcement agencies.

title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up ‘very soon’
body: US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up “very soon.” The announcement came as Trump’s administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year. “There’ll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made,” Trump told reporters. Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks. The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November. Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine. Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of US-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed. In recent days Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war. AFP The post Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up ‘very soon’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: French Parliamentary Report Urges Construction of a Second Aircraft Carrier by 2029
body: A French parliamentary report urges ordering a second next-generation aircraft carrier by 2029 to ensure a permanent Carrier Strike Group presence at sea. French lawmakers are pressing the government to seize a historic opportunity and order a second next-generation aircraft carrier. Doing so would ensure a permanent Carrier Strike Group presence at sea. A newly published parliamentary report argues that a sister ship to the upcoming France Libre must be ordered by 2029 to meet escalating global security threats and cement the French Navy’s status as the leading maritime force in Europe. Authored by lawmaker Yannick Chenevard, the text serves as an official advisory report for the National Defense and Armed Forces Committee. Under the French legislative system, a rapporteur is specifically appointed to investigate and draft formal opinions on complex budgetary or military matters. Although the strong push for a second hull stems directly from Chenevard’s own strategic conclusions following a series of industry hearings, his recommendations are formally submitted on behalf of the broader defense committee to help shape upcoming naval procurement decisions. Currently, the Marine Nationale relies solely on the nuclear-powered Charles de Gaulle . Because of routine and major maintenance cycles, France regularly faces periods without a sovereign carrier strike capability. The Charles de Gaulle will retire around 2038 when the new France Libre enters active service. Between 2035 and 2038, the navy will actually operate both vessels to facilitate crew transfer and training. Dismissing the Life Extension Option Lawmakers looked into keeping the current carrier operational past 2038 to solve the availability gap. However, the report highlights massive technical hurdles. Decades of neutron flux have permanently altered the nuclear reactor vessels. Inspecting the lowest sections of the hull for corrosion presents major engineering challenges as well. Extending the ship’s life would require a fourth major technical refit, including refueling the nuclear cores, at a staggering cost of two billion euros for just a few extra years of service. A formal government assessment on this option is due after the ship’s 2028 refit, but the parliamentary consensus is already leaning heavily against it. The Sister Ship Solution Chenevard makes a firm case for building a direct sister ship to the France Libre . Doing so offers massive industrial and financial benefits. A second hull would cost roughly 30 percent less than the lead ship since research and development expenses are already covered. Building it immediately after the France Libre at the Chantiers de l’Atlantique shipyard in Saint-Nazaire would maximize economies of scale. Inserting civilian cruise ships into the production line would erase these savings. To ensure the two carriers operate on offset maintenance schedules, the report suggests 2029 as the ideal time to place the order. Additionally, infrastructure costs remain low because a second dry dock is unnecessary. A second berth in Toulon can be built cheaply as part of ongoing port upgrades. Rethinking the Double Fleet Myth Critics frequently argue that a second carrier requires duplicating the entire escort fleet, including frigates, submarines, and supply vessels. The report thoroughly debunks this assumption. Maintaining continuous readiness simply means one carrier is deployed or ready while the other is in maintenance or conducting training. It does not mandate two simultaneous strike groups. From a hardware perspective, the French Navy would “only” need to acquire 12 additional Rafale M fighters and two more E-2D Advanced Hawkeyes. Pilots and aircraft can easily rotate between flight decks. Escort duties can be managed without buying new ships by implementing dual crewing on air defense frigates, a strategy already proven successful on the FREMM fleet. Still, lawmakers emphasize that expanding the overall surface fleet to 18 first-rank frigates remains essential for long-term sustainability. About France Libre aircraft carrier Named by President Emmanuel Macron in March 2026 to honor the Free France resistance movement , the France Libre represents a massive leap in capability for the Marine Nationale. The vessel was previously developed under the PANG program. The 80,000-tonne ship measures 310 meters in length and 90 meters at the beam, entirely dwarfing the older 42,000-tonne Charles de Gaulle . Naval Group, Chantiers de l’Atlantique, and TechnicAtome are spearheading the joint industrial effort. Two TechnicAtome K-22 pressurized water reactors provide propulsion. These reactors grant the ship virtually unlimited range and a top speed of 27 knots. The carrier will feature a 17,200 square meter angled flight deck equipped with the US-designed Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System (EMALS) and Advanced Arresting Gear (AAG) supplied by General Atomics. This configuration allows for simultaneous launch and recovery operations, a critical capability missing from the current French carrier. High-intensity combat operations are expected to yield around 60 daily sorties. The air wing will consist of roughly 30 combat aircraft, initially centered on the Dassault Rafale M F5, supported by three E-2D Advanced Hawkeyes and up to six NH90 Caïman helicopters. Looking to the future, the ship is designed to integrate unmanned combat aerial vehicles and a “Next Generation Fighter”. Hull assembly begins in 2032 in Saint-Nazaire, with commissioning scheduled for 2038. The total program cost is estimated at 10 billion euros. The post French Parliamentary Report Urges Construction of a Second Aircraft Carrier by 2029 appeared first on Naval News .

title: Poland UK Sign Three-Year Defense Pact to Counter Russian Threats
body:
Poland and the United Kingdom have signed a three-year Defense Cooperation Plan to strengthen military capabilities, defense-industrial ties and coordination against emerging security threats, including Russian hybrid activities along NATO’s eastern flank.
The agreement was signed on October 27 in Warsaw by Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski also participated in the bilateral talks. The plan follows a bilateral treaty adopted several months earlier and sets strategic priorities for military cooperation through the end of the decade.
Key priorities include artificial intelligence, drones, counter-drone systems, long-range precision capabilities, joint military exercises, personnel training and adaptation to hybrid threats. The agreement also aims to strengthen NATO’s deterrence posture along its eastern flank.
Kosiniak-Kamysz highlighted ongoing defense-industrial cooperation, including Poland’s Miecznik frigate program, the Narew and Pilica air-defense systems, Pilica+ and efforts to establish domestic production of 155 mm ammunition. British participation also extends to Poland’s air-defense investments and its submarine procurement process, which involves a Swedish partner.
Support for Ukraine was central to the discussions. Kosiniak-Kamysz linked Russia’s aggression to its seizure of Crimea in 2014 and the subsequent full-scale invasion, reaffirming Polish-British cooperation in supporting Kyiv.

title: TRAVELOGUE: What happened in Vegas!!!
body:
“What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas.” I had always considered that a remarkably convenient rule. This time, however, I broke with tradition. I returned to Las Vegas for “The Assembly,” the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists ’ conference, and the visit gave me a few stories I could not quite leave behind.
Getting to Vegas was a story of its own. After nearly 20 hours of travel, I boarded the final leg from New York’s JFK Airport to Las Vegas, thinking the hard part was over. It was a domestic flight, so I had imagined a short hop. Five hours later, I was less certain. ‘Na this one dem dey call short flight?’ That one flight was roughly as long as flying from Lagos to Cairo.
Somewhere over the United States, I found myself thinking about the debate over how Africa appears on the world map. It is right to show the continent at its true scale. But a larger Africa on paper will mean more to its people when they can move across it more easily. We need sustainable African airlines, dependable connections and routes that spare travellers the long detours that can turn a journey between African cities into an expedition.
I had been in Vegas for “The Assembly” two years earlier. The city was as dazzling as advertised, bright lights, restless crowds, and buildings seemingly designed to win an argument with the desert. I went home with plenty to say, but obeyed the unwritten Vegas rule. I must admit, it was difficult. This year’s visit felt different. Since my previous visit, I had become more aware of another side of Vegas. Beyond the spectacular hotels and casinos, I saw people sleeping outdoors; some appeared to be struggling with drug use. How could a place that displayed so much wealth also have people living this way? This time, I decided to ask.
They say the best way to learn a city’s secrets is to ask a taxi driver. In my village, we have the ‘mai shayi.’ Order one cup of tea and, before it cools, you may know who quarrelled, who settled and who is pretending they never quarrelled in the first place. Vegas was a long way from my village, but the method travelled well. I asked my driver about the people I had seen sleeping outdoors. “No be gossip o. Na the why I dey find!”
The driver was Ethiopian. His English came in short, sometimes broken phrases, and I had to listen closely. When words failed him, his hands took over. He opened one palm towards the casinos, then drew a small circle in the air as he described a path from gambling to drugs, financial distress and, for some, homelessness. I understood his point. “This is Vegas,” he said. It was one driver’s account, not an explanation for every person I had seen, but his gesture stayed with me, the circle he drew against a backdrop of dazzling buildings.
Vegas also brought back a very different memory. Tupac Shakur was killed in this city, but long before I visited it, his music had already found its way into my secondary school years. In “Changes,” he spoke of a “war on poverty” and questioned why public attention seemed to favour a war on drugs instead. Decades later, I found that question more demanding than I had as a student. It asks whether we measure progress only by the problems we confront, or also by the lives we help improve. It is a question I explored more fully in an earlier PREMIUM TIMES article, “Nigeria’s violence is not holy war; it’s sustained state of deprivation.” There, I argued that we cannot understand violence through its slogans alone; we must also examine deprivation, corruption and the public choices that allow both to persist. Tupac’s line has stayed with me since school.
I never learned to rap, an outcome for which my loved ones should probably be grateful. But that did not stop me from taking the stage at a social night at Federal Government College Kaduna almost three decades ago. I mimed Usher’s “Can U Get Wit It” before an audience. Whether they got with it is a question I have wisely never investigated. Tupac’s words, though, were the ones I learned to listen to. Tupac was killed in Las Vegas in 1996. Thirty years later, and shortly before my return to the city, a jury convicted Duane Davis of his murder. The timing was striking. I had come for conversations about financial crime and accountability, in a city where another long pursuit of accountability had just reached a verdict.
That question of accountability followed me into “The Assembly.” At a session on Artificial Intelligence (AI) and financial crime, Tony Eastin of Google made two points that stayed with me. First, institutions spend heavily on people and processes, yet still miss warning signs that AI can help identify much faster. Second, the contest is unequal: a fraudster needs to get through the defences only once, while those protecting the system cannot afford to miss that one attempt.
AI seemed to find its way into every session I attended. At first, I wondered whether it was taking over the conference. Then my thoughts turned homeward. How prepared was Africa for this change? More particularly, what was Nigeria doing to make it useful to its people? I met a few Nigerian bankers and government officials at the conference.
Their presence brought the conversation closer to home. I found myself wondering how the ideas discussed in Vegas could translate into safer banking and better public services in Nigeria. Being part of the conversation was a useful start; putting the lessons to work would be the real test. For an ordinary Nigerian, the question need not begin with how the technology works. It can begin with something familiar: could it help protect the money in my account? Could it shorten the time I spend chasing a document in a government office? Could it help a teacher with paperwork and leave more time for teaching? These are the kinds of results that would make the excitement worthwhile.
Some of these possibilities were already being tested. In January 2025, the government announced the launch of DeepTechReady, involving 3MTT, Data Science Nigeria and support from Google.org, with a target of training 20,000 young Nigerians in AI and data skills. But training must lead somewhere. Our young people need opportunities to apply what they learn; in banks, schools, hospitals and public offices. Otherwise, we will keep applauding their potential at home and celebrating its fulfilment abroad. Consequently, we must get the basics right through affordable internet, steady power supply and accurate records. If an office cannot find your file today, an expensive AI system will not automatically perform the miracle tomorrow.
For Africa, and Nigeria in particular, the ambition should be to use AI and help build tools that understand our languages and solve our everyday problems. Progress should be measured by what improves for ordinary people, such as safer savings, quicker services and better opportunities for the talent we already have. But enthusiasm must come with judgment.
These reflections reminded me of my late Political Economy lecturer, Mohammed Wader, who introduced me to the seminal works of Samir Amin, Andre Gunder Frank and Immanuel Wallerstein. Years later, in Vegas, Mr Amin’s idea of delinking felt close at hand; our engagement with the world should serve our own development needs. For Nigeria, that means embracing AI while giving our people room to build it. Otherwise, we may enter the revolution with plenty of subscriptions and very little say in its direction.
Furthermore, Eli Wachs, CEO and co-founder of Footprint, emphasised another point that stayed with me. He posits that human oversight remains essential, as trained professionals retain ultimate responsibility for decisions made with the assistance of AI. The machine may draw attention to something unusual; a person must still examine the facts. An innocent customer should not suffer simply because a computer sounded certain. That thought took my mind back to Kaduna. In a recent Daily Trust report, the Vice Chancellor of Ahmadu Bello University, Professor Adamu Ahmed, warned that AI must not replace critical thinking. He urged postgraduate students to verify what these tools produced and remain responsible for their work. That advice belonged in the Vegas conversation too. Whether we are doing some analysis or protecting someone’s savings, “the computer said so” should never be the end of the discussion.
I left “The Assembly” convinced that Nigeria should embrace this revolution with purpose. Start with problems people recognise. Give our young people room to work. Check the results, correct the mistakes and build on what succeeds. Earlier in the journey, I had thought about Africa’s size on the map. In the conference halls, I found myself thinking about its place in the future. We should have a hand in shaping that future, and ordinary people should be able to feel the difference.
Away from the conference, there was another suggestion from my taxi driver to consider. Before we parted, he had encouraged me to try the Big Apple Coaster at (New York Hotel & Casino). One evening, I took his advice and joined the queue. The ride climbed 203 feet, dropped as far as 144 feet and reached 108 kilometres per hour. I had read those figures already. Standing beneath the track gave them a new meaning. Then India came back to me. I had once tried a ride there that was nowhere near this high, yet it frightened me enough to leave a lasting impression. In the Vegas queue, my adventurous self argued that the India experience had prepared me. My other self replied that India was precisely the reason I should go back to my hotel room with its mountain view and make a cup of coffee. Every time the coaster roared overhead, that second voice presented fresh evidence.
Still, I moved forward with the queue. I had come all the way to Vegas. Surely I could manage a roller coaster? Then I remembered that the Vice President of the United States was roughly my agemate, though, between us, “I senior the guy small.” At our age, I thought, one must learn to distinguish courage from unnecessary research into gravity. I stepped out of the queue with what I hoped looked like the composure of an elite observer. A few steps later, I was moving rather faster than an elite observer should. My taxi driver had encouraged adventure; I had listened, considered it carefully and made an honourable retreat. “No be every height person must conquer. Me, dis life no tire me o.” I love my Naija.
One of my more mischievous friends warned me to “be careful with the Vegas nightlife.” “They call it Sin City,” he reminded me, with rather more enthusiasm than concern. My dear friend, Sin City has no case against me. By the time the nightlife began, I was in my room, fast asleep. My body was still eight hours ahead, operating on Nigerian time and refusing all requests to adjust. If anyone claims otherwise, my pillow is my witness. So, there you have it, nothing happened in Vegas. Vegas happened around me while I slept.
Even leaving Vegas came with its own small drama. On the flight back to New York, three hours seemed to disappear. New York was three hours ahead of Vegas, so flying east meant moving the clock forward. The local arrival time made the journey look three hours longer than the time I had actually spent travelling. I had not lost those hours in the air, but it certainly felt as though the day was getting away from me. On the outward journey, travelling west had lent me those hours. Coming back, the clock collected its debt. No be only bank dey recover loan.
Let me leave you here and munch the last of the cheese-flavoured Doritos I imported from Vegas. During the conference, jet lag kept me sleepy, but the Doritos kept me going. Now the packet is almost empty. After everything we went through together, finishing it feels like saying goodbye to a friend. “Ha! Doritos fit stay for Vegas, but these lessons must reach Naija. We no fit travel that far come back with only crumb.”

title: UN holds annual vote on condemning US embargo on Cuba as tensions spill into public
body:
The United Nations is set to vote on a resolution condemning the decades-long U.S. economic embargo on Cuba as President Donald Trump's administration intensifies its campaign to undermine Cuba’s socialist government
UNITED NATIONS -- The United Nations is set to vote Wednesday on a resolution condemning the decades-long U.S. economic embargo on Cuba as President Donald Trump's administration intensifies its campaign to undermine Cuba's socialist government, including by threatening military intervention.
The annual exercise aimed at calling out the U.S. government’s “maximum pressure policy” has been put before the U.N. General Assembly for the past 34 years, and each time the resolution has received overwhelming support from the 193 member states. Last year, the vote was 165-7, with 12 abstentions.
And while it is still expected to pass by a large margin this year, it is unclear if the Trump administration’s overt campaign to influence the vote will result in more opposition or abstentions from key countries — including Western allies — than it has in previous years. While such resolutions are not legally binding, they reflect world opinion.
The vote before the world body comes as Cuba is weathering deepening financial crises while the U.S. increases its already punishing economic campaign. On top of this, Trump, a Republican, last week once again raised the specter of U.S. military intervention, saying U.S. warships could stop over in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war .
The tensions between Washington and Havana have spilled over into public forums at the United Nations.
On Tuesday, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz and Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez found themselves in a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly while debating the embargo resolution.
Shortly after Waltz had begun his criticism of the socialist government, Rodríguez walked down to the podium where the U.S. envoy was addressing the hall and called him a liar while trying to get a point of order from the official presiding over the session.
“This individual needs to back away from this podium. He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America,” Waltz said as U.N. security and personnel tried to intervene. "You understand who you’re dealing with? This is America. Back up.”
In a post on X, Rodríguez reminded Waltz where he was making his remarks, saying he's at the U.N., not at a national security meeting at the White House.
“With his crude lies at the UN General Assembly, the U.S. government has launched another desperate attempt to justify its economic aggression against Cuba and its criminal energy blockade,” he continued.
A week earlier, a similar interaction between Waltz and his Cuban counterpart, Ernesto Soberón Guzmán, took place outside a U.S.-hosted panel with Cuban dissidents and former prisoners that sought to highlight allegations of the oppressive behavior of the island’s government.
It all reflects a clear break from the traditional diplomatic decorum expected at the U.N. and the new phase of contentiousness between the U.S. and Cuba.
The U.S. embargo against Cuba was first imposed in 1960 after Fidel Castro led a revolution that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista and nationalized properties belonging to U.S. citizens and corporations.
As a result, the Caribbean country has spent decades facing the dire impact of longtime economic and financial troubles and is now being pushed to a breaking point after Trump announced in late January that he would impose tariffs on any country that sells or provides oil to Cuba. The warning has effectively cut off fuel to the island , leading to widespread power outages that affect basic activities such as cooking, the water supply and internet and telephone services.
Associated Press writer Dánica Coto in San Juan, Puerto Rico, contributed to this report.

title: Federal judge rules top US prosecutor in Los Angeles isn't legally serving
body:
A federal judge has ruled that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles
LOS ANGELES -- A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles.
The ruling is the latest roadblock to the Trump administration’s effort to extend handpicked acting U.S. attorneys beyond the 120-day limit set by federal law. The strategy was designed to bypass confirmation by the U.S. Senate — something that generally requires a degree of bipartisan support.
Essayli “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote.
The order won’t take effect until the court rules on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said he doesn’t agree with the court’s order. He said the president and Attorney General “have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”
“Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then,” he said in a statement.
The former state lawmaker was appointed by the Trump administration last year to serve as Acting U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, which includes Los Angeles. Just before the 120-day mark, then-U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi appointed him as First Assistant U.S. Attorney.
But in October 2025, Seabright disqualified Essayli from overseeing several criminal cases, concluding he had stayed in the temporary job longer than allowed by law. He was allowed to continue to serve as a First Assistant U.S. attorney.
The administration never appointed another acting U.S. attorney, effectively making Essayli the top prosecutor. He’s been a face of the administration’s sparring with California on everything from alleged health care fraud to recent claims of widespread noncitizen voting. California has pushed back on federal efforts to prevent election officials from counting ballots of up to 20,000 people the Trump administration suspects are not U.S. citizens.
On Tuesday, Seabright wrote that Essayli's status faced new questions following an August appeals court ruling in a similar case. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Sigal Chattah, the Trump administration’s initial pick for U.S. attorney in Nevada, was unlawfully appointed to lead federal prosecutions in the state.
Seabright wrote that Bondi’s appointment of Essayli as a special attorney and designation of him as the FAUSA “is identical” to her appointment of Chattah in the same roles.
Despite a new designation by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche that cut a few of Essayli’s duties, the judge said that “nothing in the revised designation order materially distinguishes it from the Chattah designation order deemed improper in" the appeals court ruling.
Judges have found a number of interim U.S. attorneys installed by the administration are unlawfully serving in their positions.
A judge in New Jersey last year disqualified acting U.S. attorney Alina Habba and in January a judge ruled that John Sarcone was not lawfully serving as acting U.S. attorney for the Northern District of New York.
Essayli is a former federal prosecutor and Republican state lawmaker. In the Legislature, he took up conservative causes and criticized the state’s COVID-19 restrictions. He has been outspoken against California policies to protect immigrants living in the country illegally, and he has aggressively prosecuted people who protest Trump’s ramped up immigration enforcement across Southern California.
