title: Hackers target US FEC system, disrupting campaign finance disclosures days before midterms
body: NEW YORK, USA – The US Federal Election Commission’s website was targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency’s electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections. The hack comes as so-called super PACs and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races. The elections will determine whether President Donald Trump’s Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years. In a statement, the FEC said, “At this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service.” The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10 pm ET on Monday (0200 GMT; 10:00 am Tuesday Philippine time). Around 8 pm ET on Tuesday (0000 GMT; 8:00 am Wednesday Philippine time), a new status message said the issue “has been identified and a fix is being implemented.” The FEC did not immediately return a message seeking comment and a notice on its website said its filing system remained offline. The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters’ ability to cast ballots. The outage does prevent organizations from filing the FEC’s 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races. “I’ve never seen this in 26 years,” said Steven Mele, president and CEO at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. The FEC posted the notice to its website after campaign finance officers could not file mandatory reports late on Monday. “We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services,” an FEC electronic filings officer said in the email to several campaign compliance firms that night. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC. The midterms are now the most expensive US election in history with roughly $11.21 billion spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. They have surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when $11.2 billion was spent on all races, including $3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said. Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions. The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds. Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over $50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added. “It’s a big deal,” he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online. “These are the key reports that tell us what is happening,” Glavin said. “In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money’s being spent” and who’s spending it. – Rappler.com

title: Did Zelenskyy reject peace in 2023? Ukrainian MP’s claims raise serious doubts
body:
Ukrainian MP Oleksiy Honcharenko claims that in 2023, Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejected a proposal to end the war on terms significantly more favourable to Ukraine than those currently available. According to the MP, Russia was allegedly prepared to withdraw from most of the territories it had occupied since February 2022, provide hundreds of billions of dollars for the country’s reconstruction and accept Western security guarantees. The problem is that his account of events contradicts the Kremlin’s position at the time.
Oleksiy Honcharenko, a member of Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada, has presented details of an alleged 2023 peace proposal that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reportedly rejected. According to his account, Moscow was prepared to agree to withdraw its troops from most of the territory of four Ukrainian regions whose annexation it had declared in September 2022.
The new line of demarcation would have run approximately along the positions held by Russian forces before the start of the full-scale invasion. Russia would have retained de facto control over Crimea and the previously occupied part of Donbas, while Ukraine would have committed not to attempt to regain these territories by military means. This would not, however, have amounted to formal recognition of Russian sovereignty over the peninsula.
Honcharenko also claims that the Russians were prepared to return the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant to Ukraine, consider withdrawing from Melitopol and accept the use of approximately USD 300 billion in frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s reconstruction. Moscow would, at the same time, have retained Tokmak and obtained guarantees that a land corridor to Crimea would remain operational. The agreement would have been backed by NATO member states, which would have provided Ukraine with security guarantees.
At first glance, this appears to be an exceptionally favourable proposal for Kyiv, particularly when compared with Russia’s subsequent demands. This is precisely why the account raises serious doubts. Honcharenko has not presented any document confirming that Putin accepted such terms. Nor has he explained why the Russian leadership would have agreed to such far-reaching concessions.
Honcharenko has long been one of Ukraine’s most recognisable and controversial parliamentarians. Originally from Odesa, he began his political career in local political structures before becoming associated with the Party of Regions, the political base of Viktor Yanukovych.
Following the Euromaidan events, he joined Petro Poroshenko’s political camp, with which he remained associated for several years. He served as an MP representing the Petro Poroshenko Bloc and subsequently European Solidarity. His political career demonstrates a significant evolution in his views and an ability to navigate different political alignments.
Over the years, the MP has built his public profile through media appearances, outspoken statements and political provocations. He has repeatedly used international forums to criticise the Russian authorities, with his actions often intended to attract widespread media attention.
In October 2026, however, the MP began attracting attention for a different reason. He has become increasingly active in promoting the idea of ending the war through negotiations, allowing for compromises that have previously been rejected by a significant proportion of Ukraine’s political establishment.
The options he has considered include Ukrainian neutrality, abandoning NATO membership, partially lifting sanctions against Russia and discussing the future status of Donbas. The politician argues that continuing the war is devastating the country and that negotiations should begin before Ukraine’s position deteriorates further.
Honcharenko has also criticised Zelenskyy, accusing him of being unwilling to engage in an open discussion with the public about the costs of the war and possible concessions. He also claims that some MPs privately share his position but are afraid to express it publicly.
Contrary to opinions sometimes expressed, Ukraine made efforts to end the war through diplomatic means from the very first days of Russia’s full-scale invasion. The first meeting between delegations from the two countries was organised on 28 February 2022 in Belarus. Talks continued in March, both through further direct meetings and remotely. Turkey also became involved in the diplomatic process, hosting the two countries’ foreign ministers, Dmytro Kuleba and Sergei Lavrov, in Antalya on 10 March. Despite the absence of a breakthrough, negotiations continued, with their most important stage taking place towards the end of the month.
It was during the meeting in Istanbul on 29 March that the Ukrainian delegation presented a proposal for the country’s neutrality in exchange for international security guarantees. Kyiv declared its willingness to discuss abandoning NATO membership, as well as a multi-year negotiation process concerning Crimea’s status. These were significant concessions, demonstrating that the Ukrainian leadership was genuinely seeking a diplomatic solution to the conflict. However, Russian demands concerning limitations on Ukraine’s military capabilities and the mechanism for future security guarantees remained problematic. Moscow sought to secure influence over the activation of these guarantees, which could have undermined the effectiveness of the entire agreement.
The prospects of reaching a compromise began to diminish as the military situation changed and crimes committed by Russian soldiers in Bucha and other towns in Kyiv Oblast came to light. The withdrawal of Russian troops from northern Ukraine, followed by further successes by the Ukrainian army, also changed both sides’ calculations. The counteroffensive in Kharkiv Oblast was particularly significant, enabling Ukraine to regain substantial areas of territory in September. The Kremlin responded by announcing partial mobilisation, while towards the end of the same month, Putin declared the illegal annexation of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts.
The Russian leader’s decision further reduced the prospects of an agreement. Zelenskyy subsequently approved a position ruling out negotiations with Putin, while Ukrainian diplomacy focused on building international support for its own vision of ending the war. This was based on the ten-point peace formula presented by the Ukrainian president during the G20 summit in November. Among other provisions, it called for the restoration of the country’s territorial integrity, the withdrawal of Russian troops, nuclear and energy security, and the release of prisoners of war.
Diplomatic initiatives continued in the following months, although their nature changed considerably. Instead of direct negotiations between Kyiv and Moscow, consultations involving third countries became predominant, with these states attempting to establish the basis for a future agreement. In February 2023, China presented its own twelve-point document concerning a political settlement of the conflict. Several months later, a delegation of African leaders travelled to Ukraine and Russia, also seeking to initiate peace talks.
At the same time, Kyiv sought international support for its peace formula. One of the most important events was the August meeting in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, attended by representatives of more than 40 countries. Similar consultations were subsequently held in Malta, and the process led to the organisation of a peace summit in Switzerland in June 2024. No Russian delegation participated in any of these three meetings, limiting the possibility of directly negotiating the terms for ending the war.
The talks only gained new momentum following Donald Trump’s return to the White House in 2025. The US president initiated intensive contacts with Moscow and Kyiv, declaring his intention to bring the conflict to an end. One outcome of these efforts was the resumption of direct negotiations between Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Istanbul in May, more than three years after the previous talks held in the city.
The course of these events is important when assessing Oleksiy Honcharenko’s latest claims. Numerous peace initiatives were indeed undertaken in 2023, but these primarily involved diplomatic consultations and attempts to establish a common position among countries engaged in seeking a resolution to the conflict. No draft agreement negotiated with the Kremlin that envisaged the withdrawal of Russian troops almost to their pre-February 2022 positions was publicly presented at the time. This makes the claim that such far-reaching concessions were accepted by Putin and subsequently rejected unilaterally by Zelenskyy all the more questionable.
The most serious problem with Honcharenko’s account is that it contradicts Russia’s official policy. In September 2022, Putin announced the annexation of four Ukrainian regions. From that point onwards, the Russian authorities consistently presented them as integral parts of the Russian Federation. In the following months, Kremlin representatives repeatedly emphasised that any future agreement would have to take account of the so-called new territorial realities. Moscow’s claims were not limited to the territories it actually occupied but extended to the entirety of these regions within their administrative boundaries.
According to Honcharenko, however, Putin was already prepared to relinquish most of these areas in 2023. This version of events contradicts public statements made by the Russian leadership. In 2023, Russia was still counting on exhausting Ukraine’s military capabilities and weakening Western support. Russian forces were expanding fortifications in southern Ukraine, while the Kremlin was preparing its economy for a prolonged conflict. Moreover, in June 2024, Putin presented peace terms that went significantly further than those described by Honcharenko. He demanded the complete withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts, including areas that remained under Kyiv’s control.
The Russian president also demanded that Ukraine abandon its aspirations to join NATO, adopt neutrality and recognise Russia’s territorial claims.
Moscow has sought to restrict Ukraine’s strategic sovereignty for years. Even before the start of the full-scale invasion, in December 2021, the Russian authorities presented the United States and NATO with draft agreements concerning the European security architecture. Russia’s demands included blocking further NATO enlargement and limiting the Alliance’s military presence in Central and Eastern Europe. Ukraine was therefore one element of a much broader Russian strategy.
Following the start of the invasion, the Kremlin demanded Ukrainian neutrality, demilitarisation and restrictions on military cooperation with Western countries. In this way, the Russian leadership sought to establish lasting influence over the security policy of its neighbouring state. For this reason, reducing Russia’s objectives solely to the issues of Crimea and Donbas is a mistake. Even retaining control over these territories would not guarantee Moscow the achievement of all its strategic objectives.
From the Kremlin’s perspective, it would also be advantageous to create a situation in which Ukraine remains formally independent but its ability to cooperate militarily with the West is restricted, while Russia retains instruments of influence over its domestic and foreign policy. This is why the nature of the security guarantees that would supposedly have accompanied the alleged 2023 agreement remains such an important question.
The entire affair therefore appears primarily to be an attempt to use vague information about behind-the-scenes diplomatic contacts for current political purposes. Honcharenko presents events from three years ago in a way that makes it possible to hold Zelenskyy responsible for prolonging the war while simultaneously justifying his own calls for negotiations to begin quickly. In Ukraine’s current political situation, with growing public war fatigue and increasingly difficult prospects for ending the conflict, this is a message that could attract a wide audience.
However, the manner in which this information has been disclosed is itself unconvincing. The MP presents an account of enormous significance for assessing the decisions of the Ukrainian authorities, but does not explain how he knows the details of the alleged arrangements or why he has decided to reveal them now. The names of those involved in the talks, documents and independent confirmation of his account are all missing. Instead of answers to these questions, the public is presented with a ready-made interpretation of events in which responsibility for a missed opportunity for peace is attributed to the Ukrainian president.

title: Injury toll from Russian attack on Kharkiv rises to five
body:
The Main Directorate of the State Emergency Service of Ukraine in the Kharkiv Region announced this on Facebook , according to Ukrinform.
"Kharkiv: five people were injured in a Russian attack, including a four-year-old child. A large-scale fire broke out," the statement said.
According to rescuers, Russian forces again struck the Osnovianskyi district of Kharkiv overnight with a jet-powered drone. The impact set fire to a two-story apartment building, a private house, outbuildings, and three industrial buildings. The fire covered a total area of 2,500 square meters. Multi-story residential buildings, garages, and passenger cars were also damaged.
Units of the State Emergency Service, the National Police, medical personnel, volunteers, and municipal services are working at the scene under the threat of further attacks. Emergency Service psychologists are providing assistance to affected residents.
Earlier reports said that Russian troops struck an apartment building in Kharkiv's Osnovianskyi district. Four people were initially reported injured.

title: Trump expects to meet with Putin, Zelensky soon
body:
WASHINGTON, October 28. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump said that he expects to meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and Vladimir Zelensky soon.
"I think we're making a lot of progress with Russia and Ukraine. There'll be a meeting set up soon, and I think a lot of progress is being made," he told reporters at Joint Base Andrews. When asked to clarify who he plans to meet with, Trump noted: "With President Putin and <…> Zelensky."

title: Poland to Host Patriot PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility First Outside the U S
body:
The United States, in coordination with Lockheed Martin and European allies, has selected Poland to host Europe’s first Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) missile maintenance facility outside the United States.
The announcement was made on the sidelines of NATO’s Conference of National Armaments Directors (CNAD) meeting.
The facility will provide regional maintenance, repair and overhaul capabilities, aiming to reduce turnaround times, secure critical supply lines and improve operational readiness across NATO’s air and missile defense forces. Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden will support supply-chain integration, while the Polish hub is expected to provide additional maintenance capacity during crises and periods of heightened demand.
The project advances defense-industrial commitments made at NATO’s Ankara Summit in July 2026 under the “NATO 3.0” framework, which seeks to strengthen regional resilience and enable European allies to assume greater responsibility for conventional defense.

title: World Acclaimed Pianist Calls Greece His Love and Inspiration
body: Internationally acclaimed French-Canadian pianist Alain Lefèvre will perform works by George Gershwin and Leonard Bernstein with the Athens State Orchestra at the Athens Concert Hall on Sunday, 1 November, in a concert that brings together the energy of jazz and the richness of the symphonic tradition. Under the baton of American symphonic music specialist Carl St. Clair, Lefèvre will perform Gershwin’s Piano Concerto in F and the legendary Rhapsody in Blue, followed by Bernstein’s Symphonic Dances from West Side Story. In an interview with the Athens-Macedonian News Agency (AMNA) and journalist Giorgis-Vyron Davos, Lefèvre discusses his enduring love for Greece, his admiration for Greek composers, changes in the classical music industry and his concerns about artificial intelligence (AI) and the future of artistic creation. Greece, a lifelong love Lefèvre has developed a particularly close relationship with Greece, which has also inspired his own compositions. His connection with the country began when Thessaloniki served as European Capital of Culture. “Greece is a long love story for me,” he says. He recalls how Christos Lambrakis, an influential figure in classical music, heard him perform and immediately invited him to appear at the Athens Concert Hall. The performances attracted full audiences, and he later performed at the ancient theatre of Epidaurus. “After these experiences, I realised that I was a happy person when I was in Greece,” he says. His affection for the country extends beyond its natural beauty to its people, culture and historical heritage. “Greece offers me, first of all, an exceptional culture. Many people will tell you, ‘Oh, I love Greece, it is a beautiful country.’ I will tell you something that may surprise you: I love the country, but I also love the Greek people.” Lefèvre believes Greeks retain a powerful sense of freedom at a time when, in his view, that quality is disappearing around the world. Although he recognises the difficulties many Greeks face, he believes the country’s historical legacy continues to shape its identity across generations. He says his love for Greece has inspired at least 30 of his compositions, including Helios and Philotimo, the latter being his most recent work dedicated to the country. “I have always admired Greek culture. I am always convinced that Greece must remain fundamentally free and that Greeks must never forget who they are and where they come from,” he says. Asked whether he might perform one of his Greece-inspired compositions as an encore on 1 November, Lefèvre acknowledges that many people would welcome a recital devoted entirely to his own music. However, he believes the upcoming concert offers a particularly compelling programme. Gershwin and Bernstein bridge jazz and classical music Lefèvre considers Gershwin’s Piano Concerto in F one of the great works for piano and praises Rhapsody in Blue for its ability to communicate directly with audiences. He also describes Bernstein’s West Side Story as a masterpiece that demonstrates the depth of American music beyond popular culture. “When we look at what is happening musically, particularly in pop music, people often associate the United States with the pop side of music. Yet America has also produced very great composers,” he says. Lefèvre argues that Gershwin incorporated jazz into his compositions with exceptional sophistication, making him a distinctive figure in the relationship between jazz and classical music. He hopes audiences will embrace the programme’s combination of orchestral richness, rhythmic energy and melodic appeal. Lefèvre praises Greek composers but criticises limited opportunities The pianist also expresses admiration for Greek composers, particularly Manolis Kalomiris, whose work reflects a deep engagement with Richard Wagner, and Nestor Taylor. “I am a Wagner lover, and what has always fascinated me is this great Greek composer, Kalomiris, who created almost a tetralogy as a tribute to Wagner,” he says. However, Lefèvre laments the lack of opportunities for contemporary Greek composers working outside pop music. “Unfortunately, very talented Greek composers who want to create music that is not pop music have absolutely no platform at the moment,” he says. He argues that successive governments have failed to provide emerging composers with sufficient opportunities to have their work performed and heard. Many talented young Greek musicians, he adds, dream simply of hearing their compositions played before an audience. Lefèvre also criticises what he sees as an increasingly commercial classical music industry that rewards technical speed and volume over interpretative depth. “The industry promotes various pianists who appear on stage, play fast, play loudly, but have absolutely nothing to say,” he says. He contrasts this approach with performances that establish a profound intellectual and emotional connection between musicians and listeners. He cites recordings of Johannes Brahms’s Ballades performed by Arturo Benedetti Michelangeli, as well as Dinu Lipatti’s performances and German conductor Hans Knappertsbusch’s interpretation of Wagner’s Parsifal at Bayreuth. For Lefèvre, such performances demonstrate how music can communicate a deeper message that transcends technical excellence. AI poses a growing threat to artistic creation Lefèvre’s concerns about the loss of artistic depth also extend to artificial intelligence, which he believes poses a real threat to composers and other creators. AI systems can now generate music that imitates the styles of celebrated composers, raising questions about originality, copyright and the future of creative work. “We are already facing a real danger,” he warns, describing how record companies might use AI to generate music on demand. He gives the example of a request to compose a second movement for a piano concerto in the style of Mozart. The pianist also raises concerns about legal disputes involving the use of musical themes in advertisements and television productions without appropriate compensation for their creators. “I don’t want to sound pessimistic on the phone, but I am not really optimistic about the direction our society is taking,” he says. Culture, spirituality and the future of society Beyond music, Lefèvre expresses concern about social tensions, young people’s frustration and what he sees as society’s growing emphasis on financial wealth at the expense of cultural and spiritual values. He argues that spirituality plays an essential role in human survival and social progress, although he stresses that spirituality does not necessarily involve religion. “Society has made a huge mistake: it has forgotten that humanity has a fundamental need for spirituality in order to survive,” he says. He believes modern society increasingly measures people’s worth by their financial resources rather than their character, knowledge or contribution to the world. Despite his concerns, Lefèvre hopes younger generations will restore education, artistic access and historical knowledge to the centre of public life. “The future lies in the hands of a generation, and I hope it will realise that a person’s true value lies in education and in the ability to access art and history,” he says. His album Consolation, like his own compositions, reflects his desire to reconnect audiences with deeper human values. “There is a dangerous void in our humanity. Through my compositions and my album Consolation, I wanted, very humbly, to express the fact that there are two important values in life for me: love and tolerance,” he concludes. title: Greek Roast Lamb and Potatoes: A One-Pan Classic With an Orange Twist
body: Greek roast lamb and potatoes is the one-pan dish that fills Greek homes with garlic and oregano. Greek roast lamb and potatoes with an orange and mustard marinade. Photo: Allrecipes What makes Greek roast lamb so special? In Greek, the dish is called arni sto fourno me patates, which simply means lamb in the oven with potatoes. Families cook it through the cooler months, and it also turns up on many Easter tables. The Easter tradition is a whole lamb on a spit, as our story on the Easter Sunday spit explains. Still, most home cooks have no spit, so arni sto fourno does the job. This version comes from Diana Moutsopoulos, who shared it on Allrecipes. In Athens, her aunt told her to swap the usual lemon juice for the juice of one orange. As a result, this Greek roast lamb has a gentle sweetness. Because the orange and mustard stay in the background, the meat, garlic and oregano still lead. The recipe holds 4.4 out of 5 from 13 ratings, and 25 home cooks say they have made it. Ingredients for four serves Greek roast lamb and potatoes needs only eight ingredients, shown in US measures with metric equivalents: 1 large orange, juiced 3 US tablespoons (about 45 ml) brown mustard, or more to taste 4 teaspoons dried oregano 3 US tablespoons (about 45 ml) olive oil Salt and pepper, to taste 10 Yukon Gold potatoes, peeled and cut into 5 cm chunks 1 half leg of lamb on the bone, about 1.4 kg (3 pounds) 5 cloves garlic Yukon Gold potatoes are hard to find in Australia, but any creamy, yellow-fleshed potato suits arni sto fourno. Dutch cream or Nicola potatoes work well, while floury, dry ones do not. Moutsopoulos prefers a leg on the bone, since the bone adds flavour. She also likes a dark brown or Dijon mustard, although almost any mustard works. Go easy on the oregano , because too much makes Greek roast lamb bitter. In addition, the cook suggests Greek oregano and fresh orange juice rather than bottled. How to make arni sto fourno Allrecipes lists 30 minutes of preparation and about an hour in the oven. So, Greek roast lamb with potatoes takes roughly 90 minutes from start to finish. First, heat the oven to 190°C (375°F). Whisk the orange juice, mustard, olive oil, oregano, salt and pepper in a large bowl. Toss the potatoes in this marinade, then lift them into a large roasting pan with a slotted spoon. Next, cut small slits in the lamb and push a garlic clove into each one. Rub the rest of the marinade over the meat and sit it on top of the potatoes, then pour over any that is left. Roast the arni sto fourno for about an hour, until the potatoes are soft and the lamb reaches medium, or 60°C (140°F) inside. Check the pan every 30 minutes, and add 60 to 125 ml of hot water if the potatoes look dry. Finally, if the lamb is ready first, move it to a board and cover it with foil while the potatoes finish. For a boneless Greek roast lamb, Moutsopoulos says to take the meat out at 57°C (135°F). Then let it rest until it reaches 63°C (145°F). Tips from home cooks Allrecipes shows seven written reviews for this recipe, and eight of the 13 ratings are five stars. Ana had never cooked lamb before she tried this arni sto fourno. She wrote that “this recipe was easy and I had rave reviews!” Her only change was Greek seasoning in place of plain oregano. Some cooks worry about the orange, but watscooking found it “very subtle” . That reviewer also used a lamb rub of rosemary, cumin and other spices. Marinating time came up often with this Greek roast lamb. Inge Lewis wished she had marinated her roast for longer, while Karue4U left a boneless roast in the marinade for several hours. Karue4U also added carrots and onions to the pan. By comparison, sharshep used a sweet hot mustard, a little white wine and smoked paprika. That cook found the arni sto fourno needed about 1½ hours. Not every reviewer was won over. Sabray gave three stars and found the seasoning too bland, although the texture came out great. LisaMR12 served it at Christmas dinner and may reduce the pan juices into a sauce next time. Serving ideas and leftovers Greek roast lamb and potatoes needs little else on the table. Serve it with a village salad , crusty bread and a bowl of tzatziki . If you love lamb in other forms, try our souvlaki skewers with lemon and oregano on the barbecue. For a slow one-pot meal, our stew with green beans suits a cold night. Arni sto fourno also has a close cousin. Unlike this open pan, kleftiko seals the meat in paper or foil to cook it slowly in its own juices. According to nels5637, the leftovers make excellent sandwiches. Moutsopoulos notes that the same Greek roast lamb method works with beef or chicken. You can find the full recipe on the original Allrecipes page . title: Experts outline conditions for Russian investment in African countries
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russian investment in Africa should be concentrated in countries and projects where established trade flows or anticipated long-term demand already exist, according to the authors of a report titled "Africa’s Investment Landscape: Conditions, Opportunities, and Models for Russian Business Presence," prepared by the Financial University, the Roscongress Foundation, and Vedomosti business newspaper.
The report noted that Russia’s offerings to Africa have a distinct sectoral focus. Investments are most frequently associated with energy, nuclear technologies, mineral fertilizers, geology, mining, metallurgy, mechanical engineering, transportation solutions, and education.
Meanwhile, Chinese companies primarily invest in large-scale infrastructure and production chains, companies from the Gulf states favor logistics, energy, and real estate, while Western companies focus on mining, finance, and services. "It would be more rational for Russia to focus its capital where technological expertise is combined with existing trade flows or guaranteed long-term demand," the report’s authors believe.
Russia holds strong positions in the agricultural sector, where Russian suppliers account for approximately 20% of the African fertilizer market, as well as in energy, particularly when it comes to large integrated projects, and mining, where Russian expertise can be applied not only through asset acquisitions but also through geological exploration, engineering services, equipment supplies, and energy provision.
Russia is also interested in exporting educational services to Africa. "This interest is linked to training specialists for projects, as shortages of qualified personnel often directly limit the extent to which operations can be localized," the report said.

title: Ghana’s universities face hard truth: Degrees alone will not deliver development
body: At the inaugural matriculation ceremony of Rosebank International University College, its Vice President, Professor George Kwabena Asamoah, delivered a message that deserves national attention. He argued that Ghana has reached a stage in its development where universities must produce graduates who establish enterprises, strengthen institutions, and create opportunities for others. Rather than merely seeking employment. His remarks come at a time when the relationship between higher education and economic development is under increasing scrutiny. Ghana has expanded access to university education significantly over the past three decades. Yet graduate unemployment remains a persistent challenge. Data from the Ghana Statistical Service (GSS) show that 22.3% of individuals experiencing long-term unemployment between 2022 and 2023 possessed tertiary qualifications. While 77.4% of all unemployed persons were youth aged 15 to 35. These figures present a troubling contradiction. Ghana is producing more graduates than ever before. Yet too many struggle to find meaningful employment or transform their knowledge into productive enterprises. The question therefore is not whether university education has expanded. The more pressing question is whether it is producing the kind of graduates capable of driving the country’s next phase of economic transformation. Limits of Job-Seekers Model The traditional assumption that a university degree naturally leads to salaried employment is becoming increasingly difficult to sustain. Every year thousands of graduates compete for a limited number of opportunities in government institutions, financial services, telecommunications companies, and multinational firms. The challenge is not uniquely Ghanaian. But it is most significant in developing economies where economic growth often lags behind graduate output. Recent labour market assessments indicate that graduate unemployment remains high, despite continuous expansion in tertiary education. Historically, countries that achieved rapid development did not rely primarily on graduates seeking jobs. They relied on graduates creating them. The economic rise of the United States was powered by university-linked innovation ecosystems that produced companies such as Google, Hewlett-Packard, and Cisco. Stanford University alone has been credited with helping create thousands of companies that collectively generate trillions of dollars in economic value. Similarly, Israel transformed itself into the world’s “Start-Up Nation” through strong collaboration among universities, government, investors, and industry. The lesson is clear. Universities become engines of development when they produce entrepreneurs and innovators rather than merely supplying labour to existing organisations. Missing Entrepreneurship Ecosystem One reason graduate unemployment persists is that entrepreneurship remains peripheral rather than central to many university experiences. Students often spend years mastering academic theories but graduate without practical exposure to innovation, product development, venture creation, or market validation. Entrepreneurship is frequently taught as a course instead of being embedded within the culture of the institution. This contrasts sharply with global best practice. At Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), entrepreneurship is integrated across disciplines, and students are encouraged to transform research into commercial ventures. Research has consistently shown that companies founded by MIT alumni would constitute one of the largest economies in the world if treated as a nation. Likewise, Singapore’s universities deliberately connect research, industry, and government policy. The result has been a highly innovative economy capable of competing globally despite limited natural resources. Ghana cannot expect different outcomes while continuing to operate under educational models designed primarily to produce employees. The challenge therefore extends beyond curriculum reform. Universities must establish innovation hubs, business incubators, startup accelerators, and industry partnerships that expose students to real-world problem solving before graduation. Neglected Dimension of Development Perhaps the most important aspect of Prof. Asamoah’s remarks was his emphasis on institution building. Economic development is often viewed through the lens of infrastructure projects, industrialisation programmes, and investment flows. Yet decades of research by scholars such as Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson demonstrate that nations prosper largely because they develop strong, accountable, and effective institutions. Ghana’s development challenges frequently stem less from policy formulation than from policy implementation. Many public and private organisations struggle with governance weaknesses, leadership deficits, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and accountability challenges. Universities therefore carry responsibilities that extend beyond technical training. They must cultivate graduates who can strengthen public administration, improve corporate governance, enhance transparency, and build sustainable institutions. A country with competent leaders but weak institutions struggles. A country with competent leaders who strengthen institutions creates lasting prosperity. Quality versus Quantity The matriculation address also raises an important question that education stakeholders often avoid. Has expansion been matched by quality? Universities today produce significantly more graduates than they did two decades ago. However, employers regularly report concerns regarding communication skills, problem-solving abilities, adaptability, digital competence, and workplace readiness. The global economy increasingly rewards creativity, innovation, critical thinking, and technological literacy. Yet many educational systems continue to reward memorisation and examination performance. This disconnect helps explain why employers frequently report skills shortages while graduates continue searching for employment. The issue is therefore not simply the number of graduates entering the labour market. It is whether graduates possess capabilities aligned with the needs of a rapidly changing economy. Why This Matters Professor Asamoah’s comments arrive at a particularly significant moment in Ghana’s development journey. The country faces growing demands for employment creation, industrial expansion, technological innovation, and improved public-sector performance. These objectives cannot be achieved through government action alone. The private sector must become more dynamic. Existing enterprises must expand. New businesses must emerge. Public institutions must become more efficient and responsive. Innovation must become more widespread. Universities occupy a strategic position within this ecosystem. They train future business leaders, entrepreneurs, public servants, educators, engineers, healthcare professionals, policymakers and journalists. Their influence therefore extends far beyond their campuses. When universities produce graduates who create enterprises, they contribute directly to employment generation. When they produce graduates who strengthen institutions, they contribute to governance and national stability. When they produce graduates who innovate, they contribute to competitiveness and economic growth. The nation’s development trajectory is therefore closely linked to the effectiveness of its higher education system. What Ghana Can Learn from Rwanda Closer to home, Rwanda offers valuable lessons. During the past two decades, Rwanda has deliberately aligned higher education, innovation policy, and entrepreneurship development with its national transformation agenda. Universities have been encouraged to support technology transfer, startup development, and practical skills acquisition. While Ghana’s economy is larger and more diversified, Rwanda demonstrates how deliberate alignment between education and economic policy can produce measurable development outcomes. The critical lesson is that universities must be viewed not merely as centres of teaching but as strategic instruments of national development. Beyond Rhetoric to Reform The true test of the Vice President’s vision will not lie in the applause generated by the speech but in the actions that follow. Universities must rethink curricula, strengthen industry partnerships, expand experiential learning, and create stronger innovation ecosystems. Students must be exposed to real-world challenges and encouraged to develop solutions. Entrepreneurship must become integral to university culture rather than an optional add-on. Government, industry, and academia must also collaborate more closely. Universities cannot produce entrepreneurial graduates in isolation from the economy they are expected to transform. Likewise, students themselves must embrace a broader understanding of success. The most impactful graduates may not necessarily become employees of prestigious organisations. They may instead be those who build sustainable enterprises, create jobs, and solve pressing social problems. Necessary Challenge Prof. George Asamoah’s message was not merely inspirational. It was diagnostic. Ghana’s development challenge is not simply a shortage of graduates. It is a shortage of graduates who create enterprises, strengthen institutions, drive innovation, and expand opportunity. As the country seeks sustainable economic growth, universities will increasingly be judged not by the number of students they enroll or degrees they award. But by the economic and social value their graduates create. Countries that transformed themselves, from Singapore and Israel to South Korea and Rwanda, did so by building higher education systems that generated innovators, entrepreneurs, and institution builders. That is the standard Ghana’s universities must now aspire to meet. And that is the challenge that the inaugural matriculation ceremony at Rosebank International University College has rightly brought into the national conversation. By Dr. Ebo Afful

title: Greek Navy Leads Six-Nation Mine Hunt Near Athens
body: Divers, fast boats and helicopters hunted sea mines near Athens during Aegean Seal 26-I, a multinational exercise led by the Greek Navy with five allied countries. The Hellenic Navy General Staff released dramatic photos from the drills on Tuesday. Held from 11 to 22 October, the exercise covered the South Euboean Gulf and the Saronic Gulf. Alongside the Hellenic Navy , personnel and equipment came from Estonia, the United States, Spain, Italy and Poland. Aegean Seal targets mines in shallow water Greek forces took part with special warfare craft, AETOS-type fast boats and S-70B Aegean Hawk helicopters. The navy’s Underwater Demolition Command also sent personnel and equipment. In addition, mine clearance teams, divers and autonomous vehicles that find and destroy mines joined the training. Medical and support staff took part as well. During the drills, the teams worked through several training scenarios. Their main task was to locate and neutralise mines in very shallow waters, the navy said. In particular, the training focused on mine warfare amid multiple and asymmetric threats. Teams practised dealing with both standard and improvised explosive devices, at sea and on land. Greek Navy seeks more minehunters The Greek Navy holds Aegean Seal every year. Its goal is to train the units that clear explosive devices and sea mines, and to help them work better together. According to the General Staff, this year’s exercise helped maintain and boost operational readiness. It also improved cooperation between the forces of the six countries, the navy added. The 2025 edition of Aegean Seal was based at Marathon, where US Navy mine-clearance teams trained alongside Greek special forces, US Navy photos show. Greece hosted the ARIADNE25 naval drills in March 2025. Athens is working to strengthen its mine warfare fleet. Earlier in October, Greece discussed taking two used minehunters from Italy . The navy currently has only two operational minehunters, Greek City Times reported. title: Police, emergency services searching for people, vehicles trapped in southern Israel floods
body: Israel Police and volunteer rescue units are searching for people and vehicles reported lost or trapped in flooded areas of the Negev and Arava as heavy rainfall has created dangerous conditions on Election Day.Rescue teams conducted ground and air searches to locate the missing individuals and vehicles.In Beersheba, parking lots and shopping malls flooded, and residents reported that several traffic lights stopped functioning.Israel Police and volunteer rescue units are searching for people and vehicles reported lost in flooded areas of the Negev and Arava on October 27, 2026. (CREDIT: Israel Police Spokesperson's Office)Power outages caused by the weather also disrupted voting in Meitar, causing a polling station to be temporarily closed. Roads closed due to flooding, flash flood riskFlooding and the risk of flash floods closed multiple roads in southern Israel and the Dead Sea area, including all roads leading to and from Eilat, according to Ynet. Police closed Route 90 due to the severe weather. Yoni Stern, a resident of Neot HaKikar, where residents have been stranded in their vehicles due to closures, told Ynet, "Many Arava residents, myself included, are stuck on the road and cannot exercise our right to vote. We're getting no response from the Central Elections Committee or the police. I'm stuck at Arava Junction and need to get to my polling station. They need to extend voting hours or reopen the road."Near Eilat, Ynet reported 17 millimeters of rainfall fell in just three hours on Tuesday. Other parts of the Arava also saw heavy rainfall, with Neot Smadar receiving nearly a quarter of its annual rainfall in one afternoon, the report added.

title: Trump Says Putin-Zelensky Meeting Will Be Arranged ‘Very Soon,’ Claims Progress on Ukraine Peace
body:
US President Donald Trump said Wednesday, Oct. 28, that a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin would be arranged “very soon,” claiming progress in US efforts to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
“There’ll be a meeting set up very soon,” Trump told reporters, referring to a possible meeting between Putin and Zelensky.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We’re making a lot of progress with Russia-Ukraine,” he added.
The remarks come ahead of planned trilateral negotiations involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives in November.
Trump did not specify a date or venue for the proposed meeting, and neither Kyiv nor Moscow has publicly confirmed that the two leaders have agreed to meet.
The announcement came just six days before the Nov. 3 US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Arizona Baby Found Alive in Hospital Morgue After Four Hours
body: An 18-month-old boy in Arizona suffered devastating, life-altering injuries after hospital staff declared him dead and transferred him to the hospital morgue, where an employee discovered him alive nearly four hours later. The incident began on the afternoon of 8 February, when Vincent wandered out of sight during a family gathering and was found unconscious in a backyard swimming pool. His relatives immediately began administering first aid until emergency responders arrived and rushed him to Mercy Gilbert Medical Center, where medical staff continued resuscitation efforts. According to police reports, a nurse detected a pulse and alerted the medical team. However, the attending physician, Arian Tousi, reportedly refused to reassess the child. Citing his medical training and blood gas measurements that he believed were incompatible with life, he allegedly dismissed signs that the boy remained alive, halted further interventions and officially declared him dead. He even requested a minute of silence. Later, a police officer reportedly heard sounds resembling attempts to breathe and alerted hospital staff. Despite the warning, staff transferred Vincent to the hospital morgue between 7:18 pm and 7:23 pm. The toddler remained there for approximately four hours. At around 11:30 pm, an employee from the medical examiner’s office arrived to collect the body and was shocked to discover that Vincent was breathing and still alive. Staff immediately arranged an air transfer to a hospital in Phoenix for specialised treatment. Toddler faces lifelong care Eight months after the incident, Vincent is now two years old, but his condition remains devastating. The four hours he spent without medical treatment in the morgue caused catastrophic consequences. He can no longer walk, speak, sit independently or swallow. He receives all his nutrition through a feeding tube and will require lifelong care. His mother, Alexus Fiordilino, says the child is no longer the same baby she once knew, who loved climbing and waving at everyone. The family has been cleared of any wrongdoing in connection with the swimming pool accident. They are now pursuing legal action against the hospital and its staff, seeking justice for what they describe as a catastrophic medical error that has permanently changed their son’s life. title: How my son escaped wife’s murder attempt – Father
body: The father of a 30-year-old man allegedly stabbed by his 18-year-old wife in Dass Local Government Area of Bauchi State has recounted how his son escaped an alleged attempt to slit his throat before being stabbed in the stomach hours later. Malam Yunusa Yusuf told Daily Trust that the incident had thrown his family into confusion and grief, as they struggle to understand what led to the attack. The Bauchi State Police Command had earlier confirmed the arrest of Fatima Dalha over the alleged stabbing of her husband, Usama, during a domestic dispute in Lirr Bajar, Dass LGA. The police said the incident occurred at about 6 am on Sunday, October 25, 2026, following a disagreement over money, wrappers and a phone allegedly in the husband’s possession. Yusuf, however, said the trouble started on Friday night after the couple returned to their respective homes following prayers. He said his son later told him that he was lying on his bed when he felt something sharp against his neck. “He said the light was already off when he felt a knife on his neck. It was his wife who allegedly sneaked in and tried to cut his throat,” Yusuf said. According to him, his son woke up and challenged his wife, leading to an argument that attracted neighbours. Yusuf said the matter was brought to him because the couple’s house was a short distance from his own. He pleaded with them to allow tempers to cool before discussing the issue the following day. He said he advised his son not to sleep in his matrimonial home that night because the disagreement had escalated to the use of a knife. “I sat him down and told him that since the misunderstanding had reached the point where someone could take a knife to cut his throat, he should not sleep in the house. They were the only occupants of the house. “He listened to me and slept in my house alongside his siblings,” he said. Yusuf said the attack occurred around 5 am on Sunday when his son returned to his house to fetch a kettle and water for ablution ahead of the dawn prayer. “He said his wife sneaked up behind him and stabbed him in the stomach. He screamed for help, and we rushed to the scene. “To my surprise, while he was screaming in pain, she held his clothes close to his neck until people intervened and rescued him,” he said. A female relative of the husband, who requested anonymity, alleged that the dispute was linked to claims of infidelity. She said the wife had previously caught her husband with another woman in their matrimonial bedroom, adding that members of the family were aware of allegations that he pursued other women. Another relative said the disagreement escalated after Usama returned from Port Harcourt three days before the incident. He alleged that the couple argued on Friday after Usama told his wife he was going to visit a girlfriend. The relative claimed he returned home around 11 pm, prompting his wife to demand the return of her money, wrappers and phone. The police said the injured man was taken to hospital, where he was receiving treatment. The suspect was detained, while the knife allegedly used in the attack was recovered. The police added that the case would be transferred to the State Criminal Investigation Department for further investigation.

title: Oil revenue: PANDEF seeks 50% derivation for oil-producing states
body: The Pan-Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF) has called for an increase in the derivation allocation to oil-producing states from the current minimum of 13 per cent to 50 per cent to address environmental damage and years of underdevelopment in the Niger Delta. The forum also urged the Federal Government and the National Assembly to abolish the onshore/offshore dichotomy in revenue allocation, arguing that offshore oil exploration also affects coastal communities and their sources of livelihood. PANDEF made the demands in a communiqué issued after a meeting of its Board of Trustees and National Executive Committee in Abuja on Tuesday. The communiqué was read by its National Chairman, Dr Godknows Igali. The forum said the current derivation rate, provided for under Section 162(2) of the 1999 Constitution, had remained unchanged for more than two decades despite the environmental and developmental challenges facing oil-producing communities. It said increasing the allocation would enable the states and communities to tackle infrastructure deficits, pollution, health hazards and the social and economic effects of oil and gas exploration. PANDEF argued that offshore oil operations affect maritime ecosystems and fishing grounds on which coastal communities depend, adding that oil spills and other incidents could damage livelihoods regardless of whether the resources were located onshore or offshore. It called on the Federal Government, the Revenue Mobilisation, Allocation and Fiscal Commission and the National Assembly to take urgent legislative and constitutional steps to address the issue. On environmental protection, the forum called for adequate, sustained and transparent funding for the Ogoni clean-up programme and urged the government to extend the remediation exercise to other affected parts of the Niger Delta. It specifically identified Nembe Creek in Bayelsa, Odidi in Delta and Kula in Rivers as areas requiring urgent attention. It also asked presidential candidates to present practical and time-bound plans for environmental restoration and sustainable development. The forum welcomed plans to modernise the ports in Warri, Port Harcourt and Calabar, as well as proposals for deep-sea ports in Akwa Ibom, Rivers and Bayelsa states. It urged the Federal Government to establish sustainable funding arrangements for the projects. PANDEF also described the completion of the 750-kilometre Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as non-negotiable, saying it would improve connectivity, boost trade and unlock the economic potential of coastal communities. The forum called for greater investment in the region’s gas resources, including power generation, mini-LNG plants, LPG and CNG hubs, petrochemicals and other gas-based industries. It also urged the Federal Government to prioritise modular refineries through appropriate funding, licensing and technical support, while ensuring environmental compliance. To reduce dependence on oil, PANDEF asked the Federal and six South-South state governments to develop a coordinated agricultural programme focusing on crops such as palm oil, rice and cassava, alongside processing, storage, rural roads and access to affordable financing. As the 2027 general elections approach, PANDEF urged residents of the South-South to vote peacefully for candidates with credible programmes for the region’s development. The forum, which reviewed its first decade of activities, also cited the establishment of the South-South Development Commission and its advocacy for infrastructure, maritime development and greater participation in the oil and gas industry among its achievements.

title: NCCE unveils new curriculum for colleges of education
body: The National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE) has unveiled a new curriculum and a five-year strategic plan aimed at improving teacher education and strengthening the capacity of colleges of education to award degrees alongside the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE). The commission’s Executive Secretary, Dr Angela Ajala, said the reforms were intended to move colleges beyond awarding certificates to producing competent teachers equipped with modern teaching skills, digital knowledge and practical experience. Ajala spoke on Tuesday at a national retreat and workshop on the implementation of the dual mandate and the NCCE Medium-Term Strategic Plan (2026–2031) in Abuja. She said the dual mandate provided an opportunity to reposition colleges of education, expand academic pathways and improve the professional preparation of teachers. Ajala said the new curriculum, developed through consultations involving academics, curriculum specialists, professional bodies and regulatory agencies, incorporated digital competencies, inclusive education, entrepreneurship and innovative teaching methods. She warned that the curriculum could not deliver the desired results without adequately trained lecturers, modern facilities, effective quality assurance and appropriate funding. She urged provosts and other college leaders to assess their institutions’ readiness for the dual mandate, including staffing, infrastructure, curriculum delivery, governance and financial sustainability. The Minister of State for Education, Prof. Suwaiba Sa’id Ahmad, said the success of the policy would not be measured by the number of colleges introducing degree programmes but by their ability to maintain academic standards. She said participating institutions must demonstrate adequate qualified personnel, appropriate facilities, functional quality assurance systems and sound governance arrangements before commencing or expanding degree programmes. Ahmad also urged the NCCE to ensure that the new curriculum was properly disseminated and consistently implemented, with mechanisms to monitor compliance and assess learning outcomes. She said colleges should align their development plans, annual budgets, staffing strategies and infrastructure priorities with the objectives of the strategic plan. The minister called for stronger collaboration among the Federal Ministry of Education, NCCE, National Universities Commission and college managements to ensure effective implementation and avoid duplication of regulatory responsibilities. Ahmad formally unveiled the new dual-mandate curriculum and the NCCE Medium-Term Strategic Plan for 2026–2031, urging stakeholders to work together to improve teacher preparation and learning outcomes nationwide.

title: Kogi gov justifies airport project
body: Kogi State Governor, Usman Ododo, has defended the state’s international airport project at Zariagi, near Lokoja, describing it as a strategic investment to unlock the state’s economic potential, improve connectivity and attract investment. Ododo spoke on Tuesday during an inspection visit to the ongoing project, where he expressed satisfaction with the pace of construction and credited President Bola Tinubu’s support for enabling the state to pursue the infrastructure initiative. The governor said Kogi’s geographical location, with access to several major commercial centres, including the Federal Capital Territory, made an airport a strategic necessity for strengthening economic activities and connectivity. He noted that despite the state’s location and commercial links, Kogi had operated without its own airport until the Tinubu administration approved the project and supported its execution. Ododo said his administration would continue to monitor construction to ensure compliance with required standards and timelines, expressing optimism that the project would reach an advanced stage of development by next year. He also urged critics questioning the feasibility of the airport project to visit the site and assess the level of work, insisting that construction was progressing beyond claims circulating about the initiative. “Please, I want them to come here to see things by themselves. It is not an AI thing. You can see the equipment working, and they are working day and night. We are not going to make noise about it; we invite them to come and see,” he said. Ododo described Tinubu’s support for the project as evidence of the Federal Government’s commitment to extending critical infrastructure development to states, adding that the airport was intended to deliver long-term benefits to Kogi residents.

title: VIDEO: Boy bids farewell with sister after shooting by Israel
body: TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – A Palestinian boy bid a final farewell to his sister, who died from her injuries after being shot by Israeli forces in Al-Mawasi, west of Khan Younis, in the Gaza Strip.

title: Presidency seeks private sector funding for state police
body: The Presidency has urged the Organised Private Sector (OPS) to develop a financing and implementation plan for the proposed state police system. The Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Femi Gbajabiamila, made the call during a session on “Security, Stability and Economic Resilience” at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja. Gbajabiamila challenged the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG), chambers of commerce and business associations to propose practical ways to finance and manage state police, with measures to ensure accountability. He said businesses had a stake in the success of the reform, noting that insecurity had led to abandoned investments, delayed factory expansions and lost economic opportunities. He said President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to establishing state police provided an opportunity for businesses to help build security institutions that could support economic growth. He urged the NESG to take the discussions beyond the summit and engage state governments and lawmakers on financing and implementing the proposed system. “Bring forward a considered private sector contribution on financing and implementing state police, with practical proposals for accountable partnerships,” he said. He, however, warned that private sector involvement must be transparent and should not compromise the independence of the police. The Chief of Staff said states seeking to establish their own police services must demonstrate their ability to meet the financial obligations of running them. He said providing vehicles, uniforms and other equipment at the start would not be enough without sustainable funding for salaries, training and maintenance. He warned that failure to pay officers regularly could expose them to pressure from private interests and unlawful demands. Gbajabiamila assured Nigerians that federal police would continue to operate in states that were not financially or institutionally ready to establish their own services. On concerns that state police could be used against political opponents, he said the proposed legislation would provide safeguards, national professional standards and independent oversight.

title: FG to pay workers N70,000 monthly transport allowance
body: The Federal Government will pay workers a N70,000 monthly transport allowance for six months, beginning in November 2026, to cushion the effects of economic challenges. This is contained in a resolution reached at the end of a conciliation meeting between the Federal Government and the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) on Tuesday in Abuja. The meeting was convened by the Federal Ministry of Labour and Employment to address workers’ welfare concerns, following the NLC’s demands for improved conditions of service and economic relief. The resolution was signed by Dr Muhammad Dingyadi, Minister of Labour and Employment, Mr Tanimu Yakubu, Director-General, Budget and Dr Garba Abdul, Permanent Secretary, Service Welfare Office, Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, on behalf of the federal government. Mr Joe Ajaero, NLC President, and Mr Olowoye Gbenga, National Secretary of the Joint National Public Service Negotiation Council (JNPSNC), signed for the labour unions. The resolution stated that the transport intervention would commence in November 2026 and cover workers across all levels for six months. “That transport intervention of N70,000 commencing from November 2026, would be paid across all levels for a period of six months,” it stated. The meeting also agreed that payment of peculiar allowance arrears would commence in November 2026, with the outstanding amounts to be paid in three equal monthly instalments. The resolution stated that the peculiar allowance had been approved by the Federal Government, effective from May 1, 2026. The meeting further agreed that 19 months of outstanding allowances owed to health workers would be redeemed within three months, beginning in December 2026. On the national minimum wage, the parties agreed that the Minimum Wage Negotiation Committee would be constituted and commence meetings immediately. However, the resolution noted that both parties disagreed on the effective date for implementing the minimum wage. On tax relief for workers, the meeting agreed that the matter would be referred to the National Executive Council, as taxation was a statutory issue. It also said that the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security had submitted the list of beneficiaries and cost implications for agricultural workers’ hazard allowances to the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission (NSIWC) for verification. It added that the verification was expected to be completed within two weeks, after which the commission would issue the implementation template. On the Consolidated Health Salary Structure (CONHESS), the NSIWC was expected to complete an updated cost assessment within three weeks to enable the Presidential Committee on Salaries to decide on the adjustment. The resolution urged state and local governments to participate in the intervention process and called on unions to pursue the implementation of the agreed measures. It added that both parties would reconvene after one month to assess the level of implementation of the resolutions. (NAN)

title: October 28, 1940: Snow and Frostbite Plagues Greek Troops
body: On 28 October 1940, as Italy invaded Greece, Greek soldiers began fighting not only the enemy but also severe weather across the Pindus Mountains, the Greek-Albanian border and the mountain passes of Epirus. Torrential rain, mud, snow and bitter cold made conditions increasingly difficult for troops during the Greco-Italian War. Historical records from operations on 29 and 30 October document snowfall at Kiafa, at an altitude of approximately 2,400 metres, where Greek soldiers already struggled with the cold and found it difficult to hold their weapons with frozen hands. Meanwhile, torrential rain fell at lower positions, including the Muka height. Soldiers became soaked and exhausted as they fought in exceptionally harsh conditions, with the weather varying dramatically between mountain peaks and lower parts of the front. From autumn rain to winter blizzards Meteorologist Stefanos Papanagiannakis preserved valuable evidence of the weather during the war. Mobilised as a reserve second lieutenant, he served at the front and later compiled observations from meteorological stations across the region. In 1951, he gathered records from locations including Ioannina, Kastoria, Florina, Korçë and Moscopole. According to an analysis of the data by the National Observatory of Athens, rainy autumn weather prevailed from the start of military operations through most of November, although snow also fell in mountainous areas. Persistent rain and high humidity hindered troop movements, while snowfall on higher peaks created additional hazards for soldiers operating along the front. December brought extreme cold Conditions deteriorated dramatically in December, the coldest month of the winter of 1940–1941. Temperatures fell to −5°C in Ioannina, −10.5°C in Kastoria and −17°C in Florina. At Moscopole, approximately 1,200 metres above sea level, meteorological records registered −19°C on 30 December and −20°C on 14 January. Papanagiannakis estimated that temperatures on snow-covered mountains above 1,500 metres could fall even lower, particularly on clear nights. Meteorologists took these measurements at approximately 1.5 metres above ground level. Conditions close to the snow-covered surface could be even harsher. Frostbite became a second battle The extreme cold posed a direct threat to the soldiers’ lives and physical well-being. Troops spent hours wearing wet uniforms and boots, crossed snow-covered slopes and struggled with shortages of dry clothing and adequate protective equipment. Figures cited by meteo.gr from Papanagiannakis’s work illustrate the severity of the conditions. Between 8 and 21 December, one Greek division recorded 1,148 deaths and injuries from military operations, compared with 2,711 cases of frostbite. The figures highlight the devastating impact of winter weather on Greek forces during the campaign, when exposure to freezing temperatures added another major challenge to the fighting against Italian troops.
