title: I can take a bullet for Tinubu – Uba Sani
body: Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani, has declared his readiness to defend President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid in 2027, insisting that his support for the president is based on conviction despite public discontent over economic hardship. “I have no apology supporting President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and I will continue to support him till the last minute,” the governor said during an interview on Trust TV’s Daily Politics programme on Tuesday. Asked whether he was prepared to take a political bullet for the president, Sani said he was confident he would eventually be vindicated for his position. “I can tell you today, tomorrow, and next tomorrow, that I will be vindicated,” he said. Rivers Rainbow Coalition retains Chinda, allocates 33 slots to APC, 15 to PDP Bangkok’s debt debate: Can Africa secure fairer development finance? The governor said his support for Tinubu was informed partly by their long-standing relationship, which dates back to 1994 when they were involved in the struggle for the restoration of democratic rule. He recalled that Tinubu, who was associated with the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO), supported pro-democracy activists during the military era, despite the risks that forced some of them into exile. Sani said their shared experience in the struggle for democracy and the devolution of power had shaped his assessment of the president. He also cited projects and appointments he said had benefited Kaduna State under Tinubu, including the approval of four federal university initiatives and the reconstruction of the Kaduna-Birnin Gwari road. The university initiatives he listed were the Federal University of Applied Sciences in Southern Kaduna, Federal University of Education in Zaria, Federal University of Petroleum Resources in Rigachikun and the proposed conversion of Kaduna Polytechnic into a federal university of technology. He said the projects were benefits to the state rather than personal favours to him. “The favour he has done is not to me, because he has not given me. It’s to the state,” he said. The governor also cited the appointment of Kaduna indigenes to senior federal positions as evidence of the state’s representation in Tinubu’s administration. On whether northern voters would support Tinubu for another term despite the economic hardship, Sani argued that opposition parties must present a credible alternative rather than merely asking Nigerians to reject the president. “When you say don’t vote for Asiwaju, you must bring an alternative,” he said. He said poverty in northern Nigeria predated Tinubu’s administration but had worsened over time, comparing the region’s challenges to a dilapidated building that had been neglected until it became difficult to repair. “If we had addressed this problem even before Asiwaju ever thought of becoming president, we wouldn’t be where we are,” he said. The governor added that he had previously urged northern leaders to examine their records and accept that they had let the people down, but said his calls had not received sufficient attention. “The northerners are their own problem. We shouldn’t run away. The only way to help, I think, is for us to sit down and look at ourselves in the mirror, and accept that we are the problem,” the governor said. Sani’s comments come amid growing political positioning ahead of the 2027 general elections, with the performance of the Tinubu administration, economic hardship and insecurity expected to feature prominently in political debates. On insecurity in Kaduna State, the governor acknowledged continuing concerns, particularly attacks in Millennium City. He said he had discussed the situation with military and security officials and that plans were being made to strengthen the security presence in the area.

title: Flavio Bolsonaro and family to receive US visas after leaving Brazil, State Department says
body: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday, Reuters TV images showed.Bolsonaro lost Sunday's presidential election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and did not comply with a Supreme Court order to turn in his passports to federal police on Tuesday.Reuters TV images showed Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters disembarking from the Gulfstream G400 and heading into Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport.Their journey to the United States captured attention across the region. They entered northern Argentina late on Tuesday evening, according to the country's migration department, and then took a private jet to the Ecuadorean city of Guayaquil. From there, they flew to Miami.Neither Argentina's presidency, Ecuadorean ministries nor Baires Fly, the operator of the private jet, responded to requests for comment.Bolsonaro, who has yet to officially concede to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, left Brazil after refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to surrender his passports.The ruling relates to a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing.The location of Flavio, his wife, and two daughters was not immediately clear. One source close to the family said Flavio had landed in Florida, but declined to say where."The State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States," a senior State Department official said.Trump approves of Bolsonaro arrival to USTrump said on Wednesday he approved of Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election."Well, I would approve," Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews on his return from a campaign trip to Texas, adding that he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina."I think they're fine people," Trump said. "The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible. It's gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market."He added, "I think it's so terrible to see it. I didn't take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well."Trump was referring to former President Jair Bolsonaro, whom he has previously alleged to have been a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil."The father was treated really badly. I thought, but I wasn't involved," Trump added. "That's Brazil. It's a different country." Brazil-US rift growsBolsonaro's departure threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. Lula has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.Trump has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil. The elder Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.Trump made no mention of Flavio Bolsonaro's departure in comments to the press on Monday, but said the Brazilian vote "looked like another rigged election."Lula, speaking in Brasilia, said he had just heard that Flavio had left the country, and called it shameful, saying he should have stayed in Brazil and proved his innocence.Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to Lula.Ordered to hand over passportsOn Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports, but they were canceled after the deadline lapsed, two sources said. In a court ruling seen by Reuters, the Supreme Court cited the risk of Bolsonaro fleeing Brazil and his "significant financial resources" in ordering his passports seized.Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee."I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."His departure appeared to have caught his campaign manager off guard."We are surprised by the news because, just yesterday, we discussed the need for Flavio — given the 60 million votes he received — to take on this role as leader of the opposition," Senator Rogerio Marinho told reporters.Bolsonaro's Liberal Party acknowledged Lula's victoryAlthough Bolsonaro has yet to officially concede defeat, saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities. His Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro did not leave the country through any regular border crossing.Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move."If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

title: 'Cognitive erosion' has become a new target of disinformation – expert
body:
Paolo Cesarini, Chair of the Executive Board of the European Digital Media Observatory (EDMO), said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
According to the expert, the ultimate goal of such attacks is not persuasion but to push audiences into a state of apathy in which they stop believing in any facts or sources of information.
"Classic disinformation operations, like classic influence operations, had been known to be designed to persuade people. More and more, especially after AI took a huge role in the production and distribution of information online, you see that the strategy is no longer persuasion or motivation. Now it is cognitive erosion," the expert said.
In his opinion, this leads to disengagement, cynicism, and the defiance of any form of state authority or government institutions.

title: PANDEF@10: Leaders push for 50% derivation
body: By Henry Umoru ABUJA—THE Pan Niger Delta Forum, PANDEF, the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone has called for a total overhaul of the region, demand an increase in the derivation allocation to oil-producing states from the current minimum of 13 percent to 50 percent. It also wants accelerated completion of the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and urgent environmental remediation across the Niger Delta. PANDEF urged the Federal Government, the Revenue Mobilisation, Allocation and Fiscal Commission, RMAFC, and the National Assembly to initiate measures to raise the allocation to at least 50 percent, just as it argued that the minimum 13 percent derivation allocation had remained unchanged for more than two decades, despite the environmental damage and economic difficulties facing oil-producing communities. Addressing newsmen in Abuja, yesterday, after a meeting of the organisation’s Board of Trustees and National Executive Committee, virtually to mark the 10 years of existence of the organisation, PANDEF National Chairman, Amb. Godknows Igali, said: “The minimum 13 percent derivation allocation had remained unchanged for more than two decades, despite the environmental damage and economic difficulties facing oil-producing communities. We are demanding an upward review to 50 percent. “We also demand the abolition of the onshore/offshore dichotomy in revenue allocation. We insist that offshore oil and gas operations could damage marine ecosystems and fishing grounds relied upon by coastal communities.” The meeting was attended by the Board of Trustees Chairman and former Akwa Ibom State Governor, Obong Victor Attah, former Attorney-General and Minister of Justice, Kanu Agabi, SAN, PANDEF National Publicity Secretary, Minimising Obiuwevbi, alongside political leaders, traditional rulers and other stakeholders from the six South-South states. Further Igali said: “We propose exploring a market-based South-South investment fund to mobilise resources from individuals, businesses, institutions and other stakeholders for investment in critical sectors. The proposed fund would support enterprise development, improve regional connectivity and create jobs, with the organisation planning to engage private-sector players and other partners to develop a workable framework.” On the 2027 elections, he said: “We called on the people of the South-South to exercise their civic responsibilities peacefully and vote according to their conscience, choosing candidates at all levels whose programmes, commitments, and demonstrate capacity align with the aspirations of the region and who can contribute meaningfully to the peace, progress, and development of the Niger Delta. “Also as the country prepares for the elections, we are calling for a framework that extend to environmental remediation to other polluted communities. We urged presidential candidates in the 2027 elections to present measurable and time-bound plans for restoring the region. “The development agenda of the candidates must also address the region’s infrastructure deficit. Also, the completion of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway as non-negotiable.” On the environmental damage in the region, he expressed concern that communities across the Niger Delta continued to bear the consequences of more than six decades of oil and gas exploration, identified Nembe Creek in Bayelsa State, Odidi in Delta State and Kula in Rivers State as areas requiring urgent intervention, while demanding sustained and transparent funding for the Ogoni clean-up programme. “We called for adequate, sustained and transparent funding of the Ogoni clean-up programme. The Federal Government must to develop a comprehensive framework for extending environmental remediation to other affected communities across the region. “While we welcome the Federal Government’s decision to retain the original broad alignment of the 750-kilometre project, the highway could improve connectivity among coastal states, stimulate trade and unlock opportunities in the blue and marine economy.” Further, he said: “We advocate support for modular refineries through appropriate financing, licensing and technical assistance, alongside environmental compliance measures. Modular refineries could complement large-scale refining projects, support local businesses and reduce dependence on imported petroleum products.” The post PANDEF@10: Leaders push for 50% derivation appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Stop using money to manipulate elections — Inusah Fuseini warns vote-buying politicians
body: Former Tamale Central Member of Parliament Inusah Fuseini has cautioned against the growing use of money to influence internal party elections, saying financial inducements threaten electoral integrity even when they fail to determine the eventual winner. He said the presence of vote-buying in the recent National Democratic Congress (NDC) constituency executive elections was troubling in itself, warning that political parties risk undermining democratic values when candidates use cash to court delegates. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, October 27, the former member of Parliament’s Constitutional and Legal Affairs Committee said the outcome of the elections showed that spending more money did not necessarily translate into electoral victory. “When we produced our report, we said that we did not believe that the influence of the use of money would influence voters to cast their vote one way or the other. But the fact that it was present was bad in itself,” he said. Mr Fuseini said voters could still exercise independent judgement despite attempts to influence their choices, adding that the experience should serve as a warning to politicians who believe money can secure electoral success. He welcomed comments by a person who had spoken against the practice, saying such a position could discourage candidates from relying on financial inducements to win votes. He said the central concern was not simply whether a candidate who spent heavily won or lost, but whether the use of money had the potential to distort the electoral process. “What we are concerned with is the undue influence that has the potential to corrupt the outcome of elections that affects the integrity of elections,” he said. Mr Fuseini warned that the increasing reliance on money in internal party contests risked shifting attention away from the candidates’ competence, ideas and commitment to public service. He said such a trend could also exclude candidates who lacked the financial resources to compete, regardless of their leadership qualities or support among party members. Voters’ conscience To illustrate his point, Mr Fuseini referred to the election results, arguing that some candidates who reportedly distributed more money than others did not win. He mentioned Babar and Jamal while discussing the results, saying the outcome challenged the assumption that the candidate who spent the most would necessarily emerge victorious. He also cited the case of a candidate who received only one vote and, according to his account, had not given money to voters. “And again I go back to also there was one person who got only one vote, and that person never gave anything,” he said. Mr Fuseini questioned whether the candidate’s failure to distribute money explained the result, while suggesting that voters retained the ability to make their own choices. “Is it because that person never gave anything that he got one vote, and who was this person who voted? That person was a voter of conscience who received but decided that he would act one way or the other and not be influenced by what he had received?” he said. His comments highlight the distinction between the presence of financial inducements and their actual influence on voting decisions. Even where voters reject attempts to influence them, he suggested, the practice remains damaging to the credibility of elections. Safeguarding internal democracy The debate over vote-buying raises broader questions about the conduct of internal party elections and the ability of candidates without substantial financial resources to compete fairly. Although Mr Fuseini said money might not always determine the outcome, he warned that its presence could compromise the integrity of the process and weaken confidence in party democracy. His remarks come at a time when political parties face recurring concerns about the role of cash and other inducements in contests for internal leadership positions. Ensuring transparent elections, enforcing party rules and encouraging delegates to assess candidates on their leadership records and ideas are among the measures that can help strengthen internal democracy.

title: Last moments of Katsina cleric, Masussuka
body: Family and neighbours of the slain Islamic cleric, Sheikh Yahaya Ibrahim Masussuka, have recalled the chain of events preceding his gruesome murder in front of his residence in Dutsin-Ma, Katsina State, on Monday evening. Masussuka was shot dead alongside his associate, Adamu Abubakar, in an attack claimed by the extremist group Ansaru. The killing has plunged his family, followers and associates into mourning. This is as Amnesty International called on the government to conduct a thorough investigation into the killing and ensure that those responsible were brought to justice. Hours before the incident, at a gathering in his father-in-law’s residence where relatives and well-wishers had assembled to mourn a deceased family member, the cleric had reportedly spoken about the inevitability of death and the need for people to live harmoniously. ‘How my 5 children died in tricycle-tanker crash’ Bangkok’s debt debate: Can Africa secure fairer development finance? Masussuka was said to have reminded the mourners that differences in race, tribe, nationality and social standing should not divide humanity because everyone would eventually return to Allah. A resident, Murtala Narega, who was familiar with the cleric’s final hours, said Masussuka used the gathering at his father-in-law’s residence to remind mourners that differences among people should encourage understanding rather than hostility. “He reminded us that Allah created people differently, but those differences should not be a reason for division or hostility,” Narega said. According to him, the cleric also spoke about the certainty of death, regardless of a person’s wealth, position, or circumstances. “He told us that this world is only a temporary place and that everyone will eventually return to Allah. He advised us to use the time we have to do good and serve humanity,” he said. Narega said the message had become particularly painful following the cleric’s death just hours later. “None of us imagined that we would be mourning him so soon after listening to him speak about death. His words have stayed with us because he reminded us that life is temporary, but we did not know that his own end was so close,” he added. After the gathering, Masussuka reportedly returned to the studio at his residence, where he regularly delivered religious lectures to his followers online. The wife of the late cleric, Hajiya Fatima, recalled that Masussuka had reminded her of the oneness of Allah before he stepped out on the fateful day, adding that shortly afterwards, she heard gunshots. “My husband spoke to me about the oneness of Allah before he left home. Shortly after he left, I heard about four gunshots. Then I received the news that he had been killed,” the widow recounted briefly. “I pray that Allah forgives his shortcomings and grants him Aljannah Firdausi.” The circumstances surrounding the attack have left relatives and associates searching for answers, including whether the assailants knew the cleric’s movements or had monitored him before the shooting. His death has also renewed attention to the religious disagreements that surrounded some of his teachings. Cleric’s followers urged to remain calm Muhammadu Sabi’u, deputy to the late cleric, said the entire community was shocked and devastated by the incident. “We are shocked and devastated by his death, but we believe that Allah will grant him Aljannah Firdausi,” Sabi’u said. He noted that thousands of Masussuka’s followers had been admonished to remain peaceful and calm during the difficult period, warning against actions or statements capable of escalating tensions. Another close associate, Bello Danwaire, who said he influenced Masussuka’s relocation to Dutsin-Ma from Bauchi in 1988, described the deceased as a man of honour who respected people irrespective of their religious affiliations. Danwaire said the cleric’s respect for human dignity was among the most important lessons he learnt from their relationship. He said Masussuka demonstrated through his conduct that differences in religious beliefs should not prevent people from treating one another with respect and understanding. Malam Yahaya Bani Adam, who taught Masussuka, also urged the cleric’s followers to maintain harmonious relationships with others. He described the deceased as someone whose life was worthy of emulation and cautioned his followers against making statements capable of inciting violence. Bani Adam said the ultimate judgement belonged to Allah, while the investigation into the killing remained the responsibility of the relevant authorities. He added that the family and followers were awaiting the necessary government approval before concluding arrangements for the burial. Also, a prominent Islamic scholar, Sheikh Ahmad Gumi, urged the public to remain calm and allow the authorities to take appropriate action. Gumi appealed in a statement posted on his verified Facebook page hours after the cleric was killed, describing the incident as a serious mistake that could trigger conflict within the Muslim community. The scholar warned that the incident could be exploited to create confusion and division among Muslims, urging people not to take the law into their own hands. He also cited verses from the Qur’an to support his call for restraint, cautioning against actions that could lead to unrest and urging people to refer security-related matters to the appropriate authorities. Quoting Qur’an 4:83, Gumi emphasised the importance of referring matters concerning security and fear to those in authority rather than spreading information without proper investigation. He further cited Qur’an 24:63, warning against actions that could lead to trials or painful consequences. Gumi prayed for peace and an end to conflict within the Muslim community. “May Allah grant us peace and remove every form of conflict and division from the community of Prophet Muhammad (peace and blessings be upon him). Amen,” he said. ‘Masussuka’s controversial preaching’ The cleric’s approach to Islamic scholarship was not without controversy. Masussuka was known for his Qur’an-centred approach, particularly Tafseerul Qur’ani bil Qur’an, a method of interpreting passages of the Qur’an through other passages of the same scripture. His positions on certain Hadith traditions generated disagreements with some Islamic scholars and religious organisations. A prominent Islamic scholar in Katsina State, Muhammad Yunusa, said although he had no personal animosity towards the late cleric, he strongly disagreed with his religious doctrines and method of preaching. Yunusa said his disagreement with Masussuka centred on what he described as the cleric’s rejection of the Sunnah of Prophet Muhammad, as well as aspects of his preaching that he believed challenged the integrity of other Islamic sects and their followers. He said, “You see, if I really understand Yahaya Masussuka, he preaches the Qur’an but vehemently rejects anything that has to do with the Sunnah of the Prophet of Islam. That is where we parted ways, but I’m not against him personally.” However, Isma’il Zakariyya, one of the slain cleric’s closest associates, offered a different assessment, describing Masussuka as a peaceful man whose preaching during his lifetime was consistent with the teachings of the Qur’an. Zakariyya, who said Masussuka had studied under his father, maintained that the late cleric was committed to religious preaching and peaceful coexistence. He also rejected reports linking Ansaru to the killing, insisting that he did not believe the group was responsible for the attack. Mourners at Masussuka’s residence in Dutsinma, Katsina State yesterday. “As people who believe in destiny, we never and will never believe that Ansaru is responsible for the killing, and we have left everything in the hands of God,” Zakariyya said. Zakariyya further disclosed that Abubakar, who was killed alongside the cleric, would be buried at his residence in Katsina on Wednesday. He explained that Abubakar had travelled from Nasarawa State to attend a gathering scheduled for Saturday, October 31, in Katsina before he was killed alongside Masussuka. “Adam Abubakar came from Nasarawa State for our next Saturday’s gathering here in Katsina, and as God willed, he was killed alongside Masussuka. His relatives came and accepted that he should be laid to rest at my residence in Katsina,” he said. Meanwhile, the gathering organised by the Qur’anic Believers Harmony for Peace Initiative under Masussuka’s leadership is expected to hold on Saturday as scheduled, despite the killing of its leader, Daily Trust gathered. The event is intended to feature prayers for peace, security and violence-free elections. Zakariyya also said that, barring any unforeseen circumstances, Masussuka’s funeral prayer would take place on Friday at the palace of the Emir of Katsina in Kofar Soro. The cleric’s remains had been deposited at the Federal Teaching Hospital, Katsina, for a post-mortem examination. Masussuka’s killing has left his followers mourning while raising questions about the motive for the attack and the identity of those responsible. Despite the religious disagreements surrounding his teachings, his associates have urged calm, leaving the investigation into his death to the relevant authorities. The doctrinal differences between Masussuka and some of his fellow scholars have attracted renewed attention following his killing. In November 2025, the Katsina State Government reportedly summoned Masussuka after complaints about aspects of his preaching. Reports at the time also indicated that the cleric had complained about insults and threats allegedly directed at him. The government reportedly referred the dispute to the Katsina Emirate Council for discussions, although the outcome of the proceedings has not been clearly established. Amnesty demands thorough investigation Amnesty International Nigeria condemned the killing and called on the authorities to investigate the incident effectively and bring those responsible to justice. “The Nigerian authorities must immediately and effectively investigate the incident and ensure that those suspected of being responsible are brought to justice,” the organisation said. The human rights organisation described Masussuka as a preacher who consistently used his teachings to promote cooperation, peaceful coexistence, interfaith dialogue and understanding among Muslim faithful. It also noted that he spoke against violent extremism and radicalisation. Amnesty International further said the cleric had faced threats to his life and intimidation during his lifetime, raising concerns about whether earlier warnings were adequately addressed. The organisation’s intervention has added to calls for the authorities to establish not only who carried out the killing but also whether previous threats or complaints could have provided warning of the danger. The extremist group Jama’atu Ansarul Muslimina Fi Biladis Sudan, popularly known as Ansaru, has reportedly claimed responsibility for the killing. According to a report by PREMIUM TIMES on Tuesday, the group made the claim in a video in which it cited Masussuka’s advocacy for peaceful coexistence among people of different faiths as one of the reasons for the attack. The report said the group also criticised the cleric’s religious positions and issued threats against others whose views it opposed. Tinubu orders probe President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has condemned the murder of Masussuka and his friend. The president also ordered a thorough investigation into the circumstances leading to their killing, noting that perpetrators should be brought to book. Bayo Onanuga, Special Adviser to the president on Information and Strategy, said the President was deeply saddened by the news of the killing. The President described the act “as heinous and an assault on the values of peace and sanctity of human life.” Onanuga said President Tinubu had extended his heartfelt condolences to the families of the deceased, their followers, as well as the government and people of Katsina State, over the tragic loss. “The president has directed the Nigeria Police Force and other relevant security agencies to move swiftly, intensify efforts already underway by the Katsina State Police Command, and ensure the perpetrators are tracked down, apprehended, and brought to justice. “President Tinubu prayed for the repose of the souls of the departed and for comfort for all those who mourn their death,” he stated. Police launch manhunt The Katsina State Police Command said two armed men riding on a motorcycle opened fire on Masussuka and his associate before fleeing. The attack occurred at about 7:30pm in front of the cleric’s residence in Dutsin-Ma, according to the police. Both victims sustained fatal gunshot injuries and were taken to a hospital, where they were pronounced dead. The Commissioner of Police, Ali Umar Fage, ordered the deployment of tactical and operational teams to track down the assailants, while the command said an investigation had commenced. The police also expressed condolences to the families, friends and followers of the deceased and assured residents that efforts would continue to apprehend those responsible. The cleric’s remains were subsequently deposited at the Federal Teaching Hospital (FTH), Katsina, for postmortem examination. His funeral prayer has been rescheduled for Friday at the palace of the Emir of Katsina in Kofar Soro. The funeral committee announced the change in arrangements, citing ongoing investigations. No findings from the postmortem examination had been made public as of the time of filing this report. By Abdullahi Izma Yamadi, Katsina; Baba Martins, Abuja & Mohammed Ibrahim Yaba, Kaduna

title: Digital currencies could become new payment tool for Russia, Africa — report
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Central bank digital currencies could become new instruments for facilitating cross-border settlements between Russia and African countries, according to the authors of a report titled "Russia-Africa: Routes for Capital, Goods, Information, and Specialists," prepared by Vedomosti business newspaper and members of the New Generation International Club of Young Economists with the participation of the Roscongress Foundation.
The report also noted that currency swaps and settlement facilities between the Bank of Russia and African central banks could serve as other effective instruments, with priority given to Egypt, Nigeria, Ethiopia, and South Africa.
The report’s authors point out that the shift away from currencies of unfriendly countries in settlements, along with the risk of secondary sanctions and the lack of direct correspondent banking relationships and ruble-denominated accounts, is keeping trade between Russia and African countries below its potential level.
Other challenges include high costs and delays associated with multiple currency conversions, the near-total absence of accessible direct currency conversion channels for small businesses, and a lack of hedging instruments for currency pairs.
Trade between Russia and African countries totaled approximately $27 bln in 2025. Under the pessimistic scenario outlined by the report’s authors, payments will continue to be routed through third countries at considerable cost through 2030, sanctions could tighten, and bilateral trade could reach $27-30 bln by 2030.

title: Northern Ashanti Mines challenges Minerals Commission over Konongo takeover, disputes $8.3m debt
body: Northern Ashanti Mines Limited (NAML) has challenged the Minerals Commission’s justification for taking over its Konongo premises, accusing the regulator of making false claims about its debt and mining activities. In a statement responding to the Commission’s defence of the takeover, the company described the regulator’s account as containing “falsehoods, untruths and half-truths”. NAML said it had invested more than US$100 million in developing the mine since taking it over in 2019. It accused the Commission of acting in bad faith and seeking to undermine a Ghanaian-owned business. The company disputed the Commission’s assertion that it had met the requirements of Section 68 of the Minerals and Mining Act, 2006 (Act 703). According to NAML, it received no notice identifying a statutory breach before the revocation of its mining lease and prospecting licence. It said the only correspondence received was a letter dated April 30, 2026, communicating the revocation. Although that letter referred to an earlier notice, the company maintained that it had not received such a notice. “The Company finds the claim and actions of the Minerals Commission perplexing and in complete bad faith,” the statement said. NAML also challenged the Commission’s claim that the revocation related to debts of US$8,332,000 and US$49,000 associated with its mining lease and prospecting licence, respectively. The company said an audit communication from the Commission in May 2026 put its debt at approximately US$2.4 million. It argued that this was separate from a legacy debt of about US$8.3 million attributed to the mine’s previous operator. NAML said it had paid more than US$1 million towards reducing its outstanding balance. The company said it had requested time to settle its obligations because it was still developing the mine, including constructing a processing plant, and had not begun producing gold or earning revenue. “The Minerals Commission has at no point expressed any disagreement to this proposal,” it said. NAML rejected the claim that it had undertaken no meaningful mining operations on the concession for more than two years. It argued that mine development and investment in processing infrastructure are essential to responsible mining. The company said the Commission had issued permits for projects, including a new processing plant and mining activities to stockpile ore ahead of full production. It cited two permits issued on February 7 and February 17, 2026, both due to expire on December 31, 2026. NAML maintained that it was carrying out mining activities under those permits. The company said it had turned to the courts to protect its investment and its ambition to build an indigenous mining business. It also alleged an emerging pattern of “horrible, unlawful takeovers” of Ghanaian-owned mining assets, which it accused the Commission of instigating or facilitating. Despite the dispute, NAML said it remained open to dialogue and a resolution that would protect confidence in Ghana’s mining investment environment.

title: Why 5G remains out of reach for most Nigerians
body: •High cost of devices, coverage remains uneven •As smartphone market contracts 11% amid rising device prices •Africa’s budget smartphone shipments plunge 34% amid rising costs By Juliet Umeh Nigeria’s mobile market has shifted significantly towards newer network technologies over the past three years, but 5G remains out of reach for most consumers. High smartphone prices, uneven network coverage and rising infrastructure costs continue to limit adoption, despite growing demand for mobile data. In May 2023, 2G accounted for 58.36 percent of reported mobile connections, while 4G represented 25.06 percent and 5G just 0.12 percent. By August 2026, 4G had become the leading technology at 54.77 percent, while 2G fell to 36.05 percent. 5G increased to 4.92 percent. The data from the Nigerian Communications Commission, NCC, show progress but underline how slowly the newest technology is reaching the wider population. Chief Technology Officer of NATCOM Development and Investment Limited, trading as NTEL, Kingsley Uwazie, said Nigerians had a strong appetite for data consumption, but the cost of accessing 5G remained a significant barrier. “The 5G ecosystem is in its maturity phase. It has been proven that there is an appetite. Nigerians have an appetite to consume data. But there is a barrier to acquiring the devices and using the technology,” he said. High cost of compatible devices Consumers need 5G-enabled smartphones to access the technology, but rising device prices are making upgrades increasingly difficult, particularly for low-income earners. Uwazie said 5G devices remained expensive despite subsidies offered by some operators. “5G, at the moment, is not a cheap technology to deploy or to own. The cost of 5G devices has been high,” he said. He cited MTN Nigeria and Airtel Nigeria as operators subsidising selected devices, adding that a phone available for about N50, 000 with a subsidy could cost more than N200, 000 without it. The affordability challenge has intensified as Nigeria’s smartphone market contracted by 11 percent in the second quarter of 2026, according to technology research firm Omdia. Rising memory-chip costs, partly linked to growing demand from artificial intelligence, AI, data centres, have increased pressure on manufacturers and consumers. Across Africa, shipments of smartphones priced below $100 fell by 34 percent year-on-year during the quarter. In Nigeria, a market assessment published by technology news platform Condia found that prices of selected Tecno, Infinix, Oppo and itel models increased between January and June 2026. The midpoint price of the itel S-Series Ultra rose from about N263, 500 to N316,400, while the Infinix Zero Series increased from approximately N550,000 to N637,500. Omdia warned in June that Nigerian smartphone prices could rise by another 15 to 30 percent through the remainder of 2026 if component costs continued increasing. These developments could discourage consumers from upgrading, slowing the growth of the 5G user base. Coverage remains uneven Even consumers who can afford compatible devices may struggle to access reliable 5G connections because coverage varies by location. MTN’s 2023 pilot announcement identified Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Ibadan, Kano, Owerri and Maiduguri as intended launch cities, subject to coverage. Airtel began its rollout in Lagos, Ogun, Rivers and the Federal Capital Territory, focusing on selected locations. However, a rollout in a city or state does not guarantee availability in every neighbourhood. A December 2025 report based on Ookla analysis put Lagos’s average 5G coverage gap at 55.4 percent, meaning a compatible phone could not connect to 5G for more than half of the measured time. The gap was approximately 50 percent for MTN and 77 percent for Airtel. In Abuja, the average gap stood at 47.4 percent. These figures measure time-based access gaps, not the proportion of land without coverage, but they illustrate the difficulty consumers face in obtaining consistent service. High operating costs slow expansion Expanding 5G requires substantial investment in network infrastructure, electricity and transmission. Operators must determine whether the number of potential subscribers in an area can justify those costs. Uwazie estimated that operating a telecommunications site in Nigeria could cost between $2,000 and $3,000 monthly, compared with about $300 in China and $500 in India. He said the costs included power and transmission. “If you deploy 5G in areas where only two people have 5G-enabled phones, it means those two people can’t cater for the operating expenditure required to deploy 5G. The operating expenditure of running mobile networks in Nigeria is extremely high. It is a combination of both power and transmission, keeping that site up.” The limited number of compatible devices can, therefore, weaken the business case for expanding coverage, particularly in areas where operators expect low subscriber numbers. Digital inclusion at risk The challenge extends beyond 5G adoption to Nigeria’s broader digital inclusion ambitions. The GSMA’s smartphone adoption report found that only 27 percent of Nigeria’s population owned a smartphone in 2024, while the mobile internet usage gap remained close to 60 percent. The NCC said in April 2026 that it was exploring ways to make cheaper smartphones available. Nigeria was also selected for pilot initiatives coordinated by the GSMA’s Handset Affordability Coalition to expand access to affordable 4G smartphones. However, rising global component costs threaten to undermine these efforts. Affordable devices and reliable connectivity are essential for mobile banking, digital education, online commerce and employment opportunities. Expanding network coverage alone will not connect consumers who cannot afford internet-enabled phones. For 5G to reach more Nigerians, compatible devices must become cheaper, coverage must improve and operators must find sustainable ways to reduce deployment costs. Until these barriers are addressed, 5G will remain largely inaccessible to many consumers, with adoption concentrated among those who can afford compatible smartphones and live in well-served locations. title: US national debt hits record high of over $40.5 trillion
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – The US national debt has surpassed a record $40.5 trillion, according to US Treasury Department data.
The US national debt has surpassed a record $40.5 trillion, according to US Treasury Department data analyzed by TASS.
According to figures published by the department, US sovereign debt stood at $40.52 trillion as of October 26, an all-time high. The debt exceeded $38 trillion in October last year and crossed the $40 trillion mark in August this year, having increased by $20 trillion in less than a decade.
According to estimates by the Peterson Institute for International Economics, the country’s debt could reach $50 trillion in six years unless government spending or taxation is reformed.

title: Oman to see El Nino effect in three months of 2027
body:
Muscat: The El Niño is likely to affect several governorates across the Sultanate and it is possible that related conditions will arise particularly during February, March, and April of next year. As temperatures begin to rise and the season transitions from winter to summer, the environment will become highly conducive to the formation of these massive thunderstorm cells. According to Abdullah bin Rashid Al Khadouri, Director General of Meteorology at the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) told @ShababRadioOman, "This does not, however, imply that November and December will be dry; we anticipate the arrival of further weather disturbances, especially from mid-November onward. The current weather system will gradually taper off by Sunday, followed by a relatively calm period lasting about a week to ten days. Thereafter, based on current forecasts there will be a new weather system taking effect November or from mid-November through December." He added from today until Saturday, conditions will be favorable for rainfall of varying intensity across the Al Hajar Mountains, including the central Al Hajar range, Al Dakhiliyah, Al Dhahirah, and North Al Batinah governorates. The Musandam Governorate will also fall within the affected area today, besides North al Sharqiyah, South al Batinah, and Muscat Governorate. For Wednesday, there are chances of rains around the coastal areas of the Muscat Governorate. During the next three to four days, there are chances for rainfall in the coastal parts of the Muscat Governorate, as well as the South Al Batinah and North Al Batinah governorates. "Over the past few months, we have witnessed climate extremes, which is referred to experiencing either exceptionally intense rainfall or extremely dry weather." According to World Meteorological Organization, "For the 2026–27 season, in the Northern Hemisphere, a large increase in probabilities for above-normal temperatures covers Africa, southern Europe, the Arabian Peninsula, the Indian Subcontinent, Eastern Asia, western coastal parts of North America south of 60°N, northeastern regions of North America,Central America, the Caribbean, and the Arctic Circle north of 60°N. Model consistency across these regions is moderate to strong."

title: Marquez’s plan as chief justice bet: No more overburdened courts by 2032
body: MANILA, Philippines – Associate Justice Jose Midas Marquez made a big promise when he faced the Judicial and Bar Council (JBC) for his interview as a chief justice candidate. Marquez, who once served as head of the Supreme Court’s (SC) Office of the Court Administrator, said there will be no more overburdened courts six years from now if he is selected as Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo’s successor. “By 2032, we should no longer have [an] overburdened court,” said the aspiring chief justice during his public interview on Monday, October 26. “While a courtroom or a courthouse is a physical representation of justice, the true measure of a court is not its buildings or facilities, but the quality of justice it provides. Citizens do not come to court because of the structure that houses it; they come because they seek protection of their rights, resolution of disputes, and assurance that the rule of law will prevail,” Marquez added. Marquez is one of the five SC associate justices in the running to become Gesmundo’s successor. The JBC concluded the interviews on Monday and will proceed to deliberations. Afterwards, the council will submit to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. a short list of nominees. Marcos will then appoint the country’s 28th chief justice. Marquez is currently the most junior among the candidates and is holding seat no. 12 at the High Court. If chosen, he will serve as chief justice for 10 years, or until 2036. Plans for the judiciary During the interview, Marquez said the judiciary faces three perennial problems: congestion of court dockets, delay in resolution of cases, and the perception of alleged corruption. “ So to enhance our court processes, court management, pagandahin pa natin ‘yong internet connectivity not only here in NCR (National Capital Region), but especially in far-flung areas para mas papabilis ang takbo ng resolution ng mga desisyon, ” the magistrate said. “ Dapat po meron tayong continuous monitoring of the dockets of all courts nationwide, ‘di lang ang congested courts ,” he added. (So to enhance our court processes, court management, let’s improve our internet connectivity not only here in NCR, but especially in far-flung areas to improve the resolution of cases. We should have a continuous monitoring of dockets of all courts nationwide, not only those which are congested.) Marquez said that if selected, he will launch his Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations 2.0 (SPJI) that will run from 2028 to 2032. SPJI is the brainchild of outgoing Chief Justice Gesmundo which contains the innovations for the judiciary, including digitalization. It has been running since 2022 and will conclude in 2027. The aspiring chief justice said his SPJI 2.0 will focus on the following: Sustain and institutionalize SPJI reforms Invest in people development and people encounter Reinforce the Court as both a place and a service Strengthen the Judiciary’s independence and fiscal autonomy Harness technology and digital transformation to address judicial inefficiencies Continuous monitoring of the Rules of Court Initiatives for the Philippine Judicial Academy, which is the “training school for justices, judges, court personnel, lawyers, and aspirants to judicial posts.” Initiatives for the JBC More power to the Judicial Integrity Office (JIO). This is the SC office that handles administrative disciplinary cases and ensures accountability within the judiciary. More power to Office of the Judiciary Marshals. This office was established under Gesmundo to deal with threats and violence against members of the bench and court personnel that affect not only their lives and safety, but also undermine judicial independence. Play Video When asked to give at least three laws that the Congress may pass to help the judiciary, Marquez said he wants legislation that will will focus on the creation of more courts – both regular and Shari’ah (Islam) courts. He said that he also wants a law that clearly defines the role of the Department of Budget and Management in the preparation of the budget of government branches and agencies. Marquez added he also wants a law that will strengthen the mandate, powers, and authority of the SC’s JIO. As to additional courthouses, Marquez said the construction of halls of justice is not only a concern of the judiciary, but also of local government units (LGU). “ Para sa akin po, ‘yong construction ng hall of justice po, kasi kasama po sa trabaho ng LGU, pasensya na po (For me, the construction of hall of justice is part of the LGU’s job, I’m sorry). Because if you want your LGU to be the best LGU, you have to provide all these services,” he explained. Marquez also said he wants to standardized the allowances of judges. He explained that it’s an independence issue that some of the judges are receiving allowances from LGUs where their courts are located. “ For me, para po talaga mawala na ‘yong usapin ng independence [of our judges] being encroached upon by the LGUs, may siguro dapat pong pag-usapan or pag-isipang mabuti how we can increase the allowances of our judges and give that allowance ,” he said. (For me, to eradicate the issue on our judges’ independence being encroached upon by the LGUs, maybe we can talk or think carefully how we can increase the allowances of our judges and give that allowance.) From intern to chief justice? During the interview, Marquez was also asked about the SC’s power of judicial review – or the mandate to revisit whether another branch of government erred in following rules and in case it violated the Constitution. He explained that his years as associate justice were honed by his past experiences inside the High Court. He explained that when resolving cases involving other branches, he always looks at the mandate of that specific branch. “That’s the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court, the judiciary. Maingat na maingat po ako doon (I am really careful about that). I don’t want to overstep the mandate or overreach the mandates of either the executive or the legislative,” the magistrate said. If he becomes chief justice, Marquez said he will lead, like Gesmundo, with collegiality. “ Kung paano ang naging pamalakad ni Chief Justice Gesmundo, palagay ko po kaya ko rin pong gawin, tularan, o kung kaya pong higitan pa, gagawin po natin (I can emulate the leadership style of Chief Justice Gesmundo, and if I can go beyond it, we will),” he added. Marquez also revealed during the interview that his age and experience in the bench – being the most junior candidate – were part of the things he considered when he accepted the nomination. The justice said he rose from the ranks – he started out as an intern, court lawyer, spokesperson, and court administrator. Marquez said he will lead by example if chosen as the next head of the judiciary. “ Para sa akin, I’ve always led by example. So pinapakita ko lang po na inire-respeto natin silang lahat, nagtatrabaho po tayo nang maayos, at nakikinig po tayo sa lahat ng dapat pong pakinggan (For me, I’ve always led by example. So I just show that I respect everyone, I work professionally, and we listen to those who need to be listened to),” Marquez said. “You just have to do your work…. Do not look for promotion. Just do your work and do it well. There’s no substitute for hard work,” he added. – Rappler.com

title: Kabul’s Qosh Tepa Canal and Water Security Challenges for C5
body: The Astana Times provides news and information from Kazakhstan and around the world. Domestic political, economic and security dynamics in Afghanistan directly impact countries in close proximity to Kabul. This includes Central Asian states, which find themselves impacted by the ongoing Qosh Tepa Canal project . It originates from the Amu Darya River in Afghanistan’s Balkh province and extends to Jawzjan, Faryab while finishing at the Andkhoy district. Conceived in the 1970s under President Daoud Khan , feasibility studies were conducted in 2020, a year before the U.S. withdrawal from Kabul in 2021. Since then, the interim Taliban government prioritized its development as an integral, water driven project to address food security shortages amid dwindling reserves and massive poverty. Photo credit: The Times of Central Asia/Stephen M. Bland Spanning 285 kilometers, a width of 100 meters and depths of 8.5 meters, the Qosh Tepa’s intake is located adjacent to Uzbekistan’s Surkhandayra region near Termez. It is financed entirely through Afghan revenues generated from customs and taxes with Phase II of the project dealing with excavation witnessing significant progress. As per Kabul’s National Development Corporation, excavation reached 98% completion while structural construction of canal embankments and slope readiness stood at a readiness of 90.5%. Institutional shifts have also been underway in Phase 1. However, despite assurances from the Taliban that regional cooperation for Qosh Tepa needs to take place, the project has resulted in lingering mistrust between Afghanistan and downstream riparian states. The Taliban has opted for unilateral measures on water management resulting in large amounts of water being potentially lost to sandy soils in the absence of concrete walls and reinforced banks . The unilateral completion of the Qosh Tepa clearly constitutes an existential water security threat as it alters the balance of influence of countries along the Amu Darya River basin. While Central Asian states have a vested stake in witnessing Afghanistan’s domestic prosperity and water security, the unilateral pursuit of Qosh Tepa intensifies water stress levels for the Central Asian states along the northern border. Alarm bells rang as early as March 2026 when Uzbekistan’s water resources minister cautioned that Afghanistan’s annual withdrawals of approximately four billion cubic meters could translate into significant agricultural risks for Tashkent. Uzbekistan remains particularly vulnerable as large swathes of its agricultural land remain dependent on Amu Darya water in regions of Karakalpakstan and Khozerm. Lack of unfettered access to critical water supplies during peak periods would hence, entail significant losses to Uzbekistan’s crop yields which, in turn, increases operational costs for water management and negatively impacts rural areas acting as agrarian ecosystems. This is significant in the year 2026 as the Amu Darya River remains integral for localized irrigation systems otherwise damaged due to the decades long dryness of the Aral Sea which initially lied between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. The Tuyamuyun Reservoir for example fell by more than 600 mcm with volumetric depletion resulting in larger salination risks. Additionally, unilateral pursuits from Kabul come amid Central Asian states having to contend with rising temperatures , glacial melts, possibilities of Glacial Lake Outburst Flooding (GLOF) and seasonal variations as existential threats. Amid this backdrop, Kabul continues to invest in capacities beyond water historically allocated to it in the absence of being a party to post Soviet regional water sharing mechanisms. Turkmenistan’s case is another pertinent one in this regard. As another increasingly dependent country, on the Amu Darya River for agricultural sustenance, reduced access to water increases competition for Ashgabat between three key nodes of its local economy including production of crops, agricultural settlement needs and environmental requirements. These issues can potentially be addressed through pursuing bilateral technical cooperation with Afghanistan towards more durable and predictable water mechanisms for irrigation efficiency in downstream networks. This however, remains dependent on the Kabul regime being open to pursuing bilateral cooperation with states directly affected which has so far remained elusive amid the unilateral pursuit of the Qosh Tepa Canal. Fluctuations due to seasonal flows, jolts to reservoir operations and hydropower development challenges also remain integral for countries such as Tajikistan that are heavily reliant on agricultural sectors and remittances to support local economies. The Qosh Tepa Canal, however, makes existing frictions with Afghanistan over water allocations more pronounced given that Dushanbe has to balance its energy requirements with declining water levels. With almost half of the project complete and maximum completion slated for 2028, downstream countries are clearly facing multidimensional challenges from Kabul’s unilateral pursuits. The threat remains palpable despite calls for regional cooperation. Central Asian governments can hence propose the establishment of an Amu Darya Dialogue with Afghanistan for permanent contact groups with relevant ministries and technical experts. There is also a need to negotiate a practical water management mechanism for dispute resolution with proper monitoring of the Qosh Tepa to avoid discrepancies. These measures however, remain dependent on Afghanistan being open to pursuing this project through multilateral frameworks (which it has politically), but is concomitant with its unilateral pursuits. For all five Central Asian states however, the water security threat is real and the key is to act now. The author is Hamzah Rifaat, the president of Initiate Futures, a policy think tank. He is also an author for the Trends Group in Abu Dhabi and is cooperating with Nightingale Int. title: Experts identify African countries attractive for agricultural investment
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Zambia, and several West African countries offer different agricultural investment environments for Russian investors, according to the authors of a report titled "Africa’s Investment Landscape: Conditions, Opportunities, and Models for Russian Business Presence," prepared by the Financial University, the Roscongress Foundation, and Vedomosti business newspaper.
The report’s authors point out that what unites these African countries is not the type of agriculture they practice, but the potential to increase productivity and domestic value added. "The most obvious areas of Russian interest are fertilizers, agricultural machinery, and grain supply chains. However, a more sustainable presence emerges when product deliveries are complemented by services, agronomic support, training, storage, irrigation, and processing," the report said.
Ethiopia is highlighted in particular, as its industrial zones accommodate agricultural processing, making the country attractive for investment and creating opportunities to link agricultural resources with industrial facilities, "although the foreign exchange and transportation environment still requires separate analysis," the experts added.

title: Trump claims credit for Netanyahu's election gains as vote count continues
body: U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday claimed credit for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's stronger-than-expected showing in Israel's parliamentary elections, saying his endorsement had helped turn what appeared to be a likely defeat into a close contest or even a potential victory. Trump's remarks came as Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc continued to outperform preelection polling, first in Tuesday night's exit polls and then by an even wider margin in preliminary official vote counts. The results remain fluid, however, with most ballots still being counted and neither of Israel's main political blocs assured of the 61 seats needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.   "I hear he did very well. It's pretty close, very good," Trump told reporters while returning from a campaign rally in Texas. "When the endorsement came out, it helped him a lot." "But actually, I heard he did pretty well. He's probably winning or tied. But I heard he's doing pretty well," he added. Trump acknowledged that the results were far from final but suggested Netanyahu had significantly exceeded expectations. "It's still a little early. But I hear in Israel, I mean, top people are saying, 'Wow, he did much better.' Something like a tie, maybe even a win. We'll see what happens." The comments followed an election campaign in which Trump publicly backed Netanyahu, lending the Israeli leader the support of a U.S. president who remains popular among much of Israel's political right. Before the election, several opinion polls had suggested Netanyahu's governing bloc was headed for defeat against an opposition alliance led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Tuesday night's exit polls indicated a considerably tighter race, with Netanyahu's bloc performing better than many preelection surveys had anticipated. As the official count progressed overnight, the prime minister's position improved further. By 6:02 a.m. Wednesday, with 41.09% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party was projected to win 28 seats, compared with 21 for Eisenkot's Yashar party, according to figures from the Central Elections Committee. The updated projections gave Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc 57 seats, compared with 47 for the rival pro-change bloc. Predominantly Arab parties were projected to hold the remaining 16 seats. Although Netanyahu's bloc had established a lead over its principal rival, it remained four seats short of a parliamentary majority. The figures were preliminary and subject to change as additional ballots were counted and the final distribution of seats became clearer. The results have raised the prospect of difficult coalition negotiations, with neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot enjoying a straightforward path to forming a government. Trump also amplified claims about the impact of his endorsement in a post on Truth Social, sharing a statement attributed to Irving C. Schwartz that credited the U.S. president with reversing Netanyahu's electoral fortunes. "When President Trump endorsed Bibi Netanyahu, the whole tide turned, and now, rather than a decisive defeat for a Great Prime Minister, it looks like a big come-from-behind stalemate, or even a WIN for Netanyahu," the statement read. "It all took place AFTER the Endorsement by President Trump, who only wants what is good for the Middle East, Israel, and the United States of America!"

title: Iran ready to expand electricity connection with reg. states
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iran is ready to expand electricity interconnections with neighboring countries and strengthen regional cooperation in the power sector.
Iran’s Energy Minister Abbas Aliabadi said at the 30th Belarusian Energy and Ecology Forum.
The Iranian energy minister emphasized Iran has established electricity connections with its western neighbors and with Pakistan and Afghanistan to the east, adding that links with Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Turkey and Iraq are also in place.
Iran is seeking to connect its electricity network to Russia through a neighboring country, Aliabadi stressed.
He said that regional cooperation is increasingly important as electricity demand rises, particularly with the growth of artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies.
He also highlighted the need to expand energy storage and electricity interconnections to balance power generation, distribution and consumption.
The minister said Iran's electricity generation capacity has grown from 7,000 megawatts at the time of the 1979 Islamic Revolution to nearly 97,000 megawatts. He added that Iran manufactures power plant equipment domestically and exports such equipment to regional countries.
Aliabadi said Iran remains committed to developing its electricity industry and is prepared to cooperate with other countries and make use of their capabilities despite sanctions and war.

title: State Police: Presidency seeks private sector support for funding, blueprint
body: By Johnbosco Agbakwuru ABUJA—THE Presidency has challenged Nigeria’s organised private sector to develop a comprehensive financing and implementation blueprint for the proposed state police system, saying that businesses must take an active role in building the security institutions required to protect investments, create jobs and strengthen economic resilience. Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Mr. Femi Gbajabiamila, who made the challenge, tasked the Nigerian Economic Summit Group, NESG, chambers of commerce and business associations with producing practical proposals for financing, institutional management and accountable partnerships to support the decentralisation of policing. Speaking during a plenary session on “Security, Stability and Economic Resilience” at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit, in Abuja, on Monday, Gbajabiamila said President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to establishing state police presented an opportunity for businesses to contribute directly to the development of security institutions capable of supporting sustainable economic growth. According to him: “I, therefore, ask the Nigerian Economic Summit Group to carry this engagement beyond our meeting. Bring forward a considered private sector contribution on financing and implementing state police, with practical proposals for accountable partnerships. ”Take that work into the legislative process and into your engagement with state governments. For our part, we remain answerable for turning reform into protection that people can rely on,” he said. Gbajabiamila urged business leaders to engage governors and legislators on the proposed reform, drawing attention to the relationship between effective local policing, employment generation and investment decisions. ”Your participation should also improve the substance of the reform. As the legislative process proceeds, examine the proposals for financing and oversight. Bring your experience of managing institutions and controlling expenditure to that discussion. Help us understand the security failures that prevent viable projects from proceeding,” he stated. He, however cautioned that private sector involvement must be transparent and should never compromise the independence of police institutions. ”Where businesses provide resources, those contributions need published accounts and independent scrutiny.‎ ‎”Public funding must remain dependable, and a donation must never purchase influence over an investigation or preferential treatment. The object is to strengthen a public service on which every citizen can rely,” he warned.‎ ‎He said providing vehicles, uniforms and other equipment at the commencement of operations would be insufficient without sustainable arrangements for personnel salaries, professional training and operational maintenance. ‎”Financial readiness is equally important. A state taking on policing must be able to sustain the service after the initial purchase of vehicles and uniforms.‎ ‎”Regular pay and continued training are essential to professional conduct. An institution that cannot meet its obligations to its officers becomes vulnerable to private patrons and unlawful demands on the public,” he cautioned.‎ He assured that federal policing would continue in states not yet financially or institutionally prepared to establish their own police services.‎ ‎Providing an update on the legislative process, Gbajabiamila confirmed that 24 State Houses of Assembly had approved the constitutional amendment providing for state police as of October 23, meeting the required two-thirds threshold.‎ ‎He disclosed that the Presidential Working Group had submitted the draft National Policing Bill and 29 consequential amendment bills to the Federal Ministry of Justice on October 19 for legislative review. The United States Mission in Nigeria has announced a major breakthrough in the fight against transnational cybercrime, with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, FBI, arresting nine suspects in Nigeria in an operation targeting scam centres stealing billions of dollars from Americans. FBI Director, Kash Patel, disclosed this in a post on X which was reposted by the US Mission in Nigeria, saying the operation, code-named Operation Blackout, is taking the fight directly to international cybercriminal networks. According to Patel, the Nigeria operation delivered nine arrests, seizure of 53 electronic devices and identification of $11 million in potentially freezable funds across multiple countries. “Operation Blackout is taking the fight directly to the international cybercriminal networks stealing billions from Americans,” Patel said. “These scam centers exploit innocent victims, steal life savings, and operate across international borders believing they are beyond the reach of law enforcement. They’re wrong,” he stated. He commended Nigerian law enforcement and partners in London for their cooperation. “Thanks to Nigerian law enforcement and our partners in London for their outstanding cooperation,” Patel said, warning: “To the criminals targeting Americans from overseas: Justice will fibd you.” While the FBI did not name the Nigerian agency involved or the locations of the arrests, the operation is part of a wider international enforcement exercise coordinated from London. According to the US Department of Justice, the broader crackdown resulted in 28 arrests across Nigeria and Ghana and the seizure of hundreds of electronic devices. The operation also involved Meta and 14 other technology companies, leading to the removal of more than 3.7 million fraudulent accounts, pages and groups linked to West African scam networks. Reports indicate that 19 of the arrests were made in Ghana, where 117 victims, said to have been trafficked and forced to work in a residential compound running scam operations, are pending repatriation to Nigeria. The arrests come amid heightened US-Nigeria cooperation on cybercrime. In September, South African authorities handed over six Nigerians to FBI officials over allegations of defrauding more than 100 women in a romance scam scheme. In August, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, extradited two Nigerians to the US over alleged online sexual exploitation and sextortion of two teenage boys who later died by suicide. In August 2025, the FBI arrested 22 Nigerians for alleged involvement in financially motivated sextortion schemes linked to a rise in suicides among American teenagers. The FBI said Nigerian authorities will prosecute the nine suspects arrested in the latest operation for violations of Nigerian law, while investigations continue to freeze the $11 million identified across several countries.
