U.S. policy experts have also floated an alternative type of assistance that could facilitate Kyiv’s efforts to hunt Russian missile launchers, suggesting Ukraine could use extended-range attack munitions (ERAM) fired from its F-16s . The United States has already approved the sale of these munitions, but currently Ukraine can only use the missile in its older Soviet aircraft. Ukraine’s F-16s also lack the software and hardware integration needed to dynamically update targeting locations for the ERAM , a necessity for hunting mobile launchers. Upgrading this technology would be fairly straightforward, and this would give Ukraine both the targeting support and munitions it needs to go after Russian launchers.
Either type of support would enhance Ukraine’s ability to prevent ballistic missile attacks at their source, but neither offers anything close to a guarantee of success. Indeed, the fundamental challenges associated with any effort to find and destroy mobile missile launchers would remain.
Ukraine would also face obstacles that the United States did not have to grapple with in Iran. Whereas the United States had the ability to operate across Iranian territory without restrictions, U.S. senators have only asked that Ukraine be given permission to use Starlink 300 km into Russia. Russia’s large size would allow it to simply move launchers outside this range and then continue attacks. On top of this, Ukraine’s limited F-16 fleet is already under strain , lacking sufficient spare parts, waiting for repairs, and facing a shortage of pilots. Ukraine might succeed in destroying some number of Russian launchers, but it is unlikely to prevent severe damage to the country’s cities and infrastructure in the coming winter.
Even if Ukraine could reliably strike Russian missile launchers with a high rate of success, however, giving Kyiv this capability would be a mistake for the United States. Whether it provides more advanced munitions, upgrades Ukraine’s F-16s, or provides Ukraine access to Starlink over Russian territory, enabling Ukraine’s hunt for ballistic missile launchers inside Russia would substantially expand the U.S. role in the war and drag it ever closer to a direct conflict with Russia.
After all, if the Trump administration gives into Kyiv’s demands, Ukraine would be using U.S. intelligence, U.S. satellite networks operating over Russian territory, and possibly U.S. aircraft and weapons to shoot targets inside of Russia. Ukrainians would still be pulling the trigger (or firing the missile or launching the drone), but in all other ways, the mission and its execution would be an American one.
Russia would surely see this as a serious provocation and use it as justification for an expansion of its alleged hybrid campaign against NATO members . This, in turn, could worsen the pre-existing risk of a wider war that drags the United States in, caused by miscalculation or an uncontrolled escalation spiral. Russia might also increase support to Iran or other U.S. competitors by providing weapons and intelligence, putting U.S. forces elsewhere in danger.
Finally, there is the precedent that the United States would set by allowing the use of Starlink over Russian territory. For now, it is only Washington with access to the type of global satellite capability that Starlink provides, but soon Russian and China will have their own networks. Once the United States has allowed the use of Starlink over Russian territory by a third party, there is nothing to stop Moscow or Beijing from making the same decision with their own versions of the technology, leaving the U.S. homeland more vulnerable in the future.
When Ukraine asked for Tomahawk missiles in 2025, the Trump administration wisely broke Biden’s cycle by denying the request on the grounds that stockpiles were too scarce and the capability too escalatory. Trump should do the same today. A campaign to hunt Russian missile launchers would only marginally reduce attacks on Ukraine’s cities and would do so at an unacceptably high cost to American interests in the near and long-term.

title: Call of Duty 4: Injecting American empire right into the veins
body:
Next in the latest version of the first-person shooter classic: the US military must be everywhere, lest North Korea and Russia take over
The good folks at Activision and Infinity Ward have outdone themselves this time.
For more than two decades, Call of Duty has dominated the world of first-person shooter games, selling more than 500 million copies worldwide. What began in 2003 as a gripping, cinematic rendition of some of World War II's most heroic battles has gradually morphed into an immersive Beltway military fantasy in which millions of players experience the world of geopolitics through Washington's eyes, complete with its familiar enemies, justifications for military intervention, and warnings about the dangers of American withdrawal.
The latest installment of the saga, Modern Warfare 4, takes this formula to extraordinary lengths, plunging players into a world where North Korean brutality and Russian expansionism threaten global stability, while American military power remains the indispensable answer.
Of course, this is nothing new to the series. In 2019's Modern Warfare, players encounter the aftermath of a Russian massacre along fictional Urzikstan's "Highway of Death," a warped inversion of the real-life slaughter of retreating Iraqi forces by the American-led coalition in 1991. Throughout the series, players are constantly hunting down and executing political and military leaders with names that are sometimes a little too on the nose, from Khaled Al-Asad to Iranian Quds Force Major Hassan Zyani. In recent years, the fall release season has become something of an annual opportunity for Activision to show us what's next on the menu of the Beltway's voracious appetite for military confrontation. This year's offering is North Korea.
The campaign opens with players assuming the role of South Korean Private Park Hyun-Jun, enjoying a routine night out with his fellow Marines when the North Koreans launch an unprovoked, full-scale invasion of South Korea. The assault begins with a citywide blackout, followed by a devastating strike on a bustling civilian market that leaves soldiers and civilians dead.
The story then rewinds five days, to a North Korea mourning the death of its longtime ruler who is replaced, after a palace coup, by his blood thirsty war criminal daughter.
The player, now acting as a North Korean soldier, meets the daughter in “Following Orders,” a brutal mission that again leaves little to the imagination. Searching for a defector, you and your comrades ravage a village, torturing North Korean civilians for having illegal MP3 players, novels, and heart medication. Then, once the sister has made you hang the defector, the whole village is executed en masse for harboring him. Watching the gameplay of this mission, I was reminded of My Lai and Blackwater’s Nisour Square massacre. The game’s intended audience won’t be.
Meanwhile, Russian ultranationalists, who are helping North Korea wage its war against the South, are also taking advantage of American military withdrawals from strategic positions around the Black Sea and the fictional state of Urzikstan.
American operatives are furious that Washington is abandoning the work they have accomplished abroad. When one questions why policymakers are undoing all their good work, another offers a simple explanation: "It's a flawed system,” the consequences of which are spelled out moments later: “Russia's taking ground. We withdraw, they move in."
The flawed system, it seems, is the very democratic process that allows the American public and its elected representatives to question Washington's military commitments abroad. As Americans increasingly reckon with the disastrous consequences of decades of interventionism and debate the wisdom of further military entanglements in Ukraine, Taiwan, and Iran , Activision offers a familiar Beltway warning: American restraint only emboldens our enemies.
Roger Stahl, a professor at the University of Georgia who studies the military-entertainment complex, sees a familiar pattern in the franchise. "The enemies are - surprise! - the very same enemies that animate the narratives of official U.S. foreign policy," he told me, arguing that the franchise advances "a powerful narrative” that lets U.S. interventionism “off the hook."
Toward the end of the campaign, players discover that American restraint almost brought all of Europe to the brink of catastrophe. Once North Korea is liberated from the tyrannical Ri Ju-Young, whom you execute, you learn that the whole invasion was a Russian testing ground for an EMP device. The ultimate plan, orchestrated by Russian ultranationalists, was to use the same technology to conquer Europe, beginning with Ukraine and Poland and eventually reaching the United Kingdom.
The game ends in a dramatic fight sequence where you murder a man who appears to be the Russian minister of defense.
Throughout the campaign, players are given freedom to make a bevy of choices: from which brand of ramen to buy at a Korean convenience store, to what ways and for how long they toy with North Korean civilians. Yet these choices have little bearing on the larger narrative of the game already laid out for the player.
Matthew Alford, a scholar of the military-entertainment complex, succinctly described this illusion of choice : "The player has tactical freedom within a political framework they cannot question: how to fight is interactive; why we fight is settled in advance."
Stahl wonders how Americans would react if the Russians or North Koreans developed an equally popular game in which players conduct covert operations to infiltrate Washington and assassinate the American president. Would anyone dismiss that as just another video game?
Activision has also enlisted MrBeast, YouTube’s most popular creator, to promote its latest military fantasy through a million dollar Call of Duty competition that has already attracted nearly 50 million views . The video-game spectacle concludes with contestants scrambling aboard a Chinook helicopter that takes off from the feet of an enormous statue bearing an eerie resemblance to current North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
At a time when young men, this game's target audience, are beginning to question the legacy of America's disastrous foreign policy over the last two decades, this game feels painfully outdated. It offers a packaged fantasy of a world where American restraint invites catastrophe, Washington's enemies display irredeemable and insatiable evil, and U.S. military intervention is the only conceivable solution to curb said evil.
Such a narrative, if left unexamined, could leave a player's energy recharged, his imagination captured, and his consent manufactured for America's next war by the time he puts down the controller.
Activision did not return requests from comment from RS.

title: Europe went from leading Iran diplomacy to slavishly following US
body:
The continent played a crucial role in the JCPOA, but now it finds itself on the sidelines and supporting war
There was a time when Europe was serious about diplomacy — diplomacy as the patient, often frustrating business of engaging adversaries, rather than merely issuing condemnations and imposing sanctions.
Ten years ago, on October 25, 2016, the European Parliament adopted a report on relations with Iran that embodied precisely this understanding of statecraft. Drafted under the leadership of British MEP Richard Howitt, it offered a forward-looking strategy for engaging Tehran following the conclusion of the 2015 nuclear agreement, the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) – a diplomatic achievement in which the European Union and its member states the United Kingdom, France and Germany played a leading role.
As a foreign policy adviser in the European Parliament, I had the privilege of working closely with Howitt throughout the report’s preparation, negotiations, and eventual adoption, including a fact-finding mission to Tehran. The report was adopted by an overwhelming majority of 456 votes to 174, with 67 abstentions.
But its significance extended well beyond parliamentary numbers: it represented a moment when Europe appeared capable of acting with strategic foresight. The engagement with Iran was a pragmatic instrument for advancing European security and economic interests; fostering moderation in Iran; and stabilizing the Middle East .
Ten years later, EU-Iran relations are in tatters. Europe has lost much of its economic leverage, its diplomatic influence has diminished dramatically, and its role in addressing the region’s security crises has become marginal.
To understand the scale of this decline, one needs to look back at how pragmatic and ambitious Europe’s approach once was.
The Howitt report proposed developing relations in key areas, including political dialogue, trade,academic exchanges, human rights, and regional security. It offered European expertise to assist Iran in fulfilling the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) criteria – a key step toward economic reform.
The report departed from the mantra promoted for years by hawkish circles in the U.S., Israel and some Arab capitals , which had depicted Iran as the sole source of regional turmoil. Instead, it recognized Iran as an indispensable actor in addressing conflicts in Syria, Iraq, and Yemen. It called for European diplomacy to encourage rapprochement between Tehran and Riyadh – an appeal acted upon years later, by Beijing , not Brussels.
Crucially, the report did not remain a simple exercise in parliamentary rhetoric. Just a few weeks after its adoption, the EU Foreign Affairs Council endorsed the parliamentary approach for engagement with Tehran. It also supported the establishment of an EU delegation in Tehran. Here was a case where parliamentary diplomacy had contributed to shaping the broader political position of the EU.
Reactions to the report were revealing. The National Iranian American Council (NIAC), a Washington-based pro-diplomacy group, welcomed it enthusiastically. Its founder and then-president, Trita Parsi, now executive vice president of the Quincy Institute, praised the strategy of expanded relations while warning against renewed isolation and military threats.
Perhaps the best evidence of the report’s impact was its hostile reception by forces committed to confrontation. Pro-Israeli groups, such as the AJC Transatlantic Institute (TAI), the Brussels office of the American Jewish Committee, denounced the text for allegedly failing to confront Iran’s threats against Israel; its support for Hezbollah in Lebanon and the Assad regime in Syria; and its human rights abuses.
The false choice between defending human rights and engaging with Tehran was peddled relentlessly by the report’s critics. However, the report contained substantial criticism of Iran’s record in that area, including input from Human Rights Watch.
We proposed to anchor discussions on human rights in a broader framework of dialogue rather than simply issuing condemnations. As Howitt said during the parliamentary debate, addressing his critics, “they knowingly imperil the leverage that we do have with Iran and make the improvements in human rights less, not more, likely”.
Reactions from Tehran were equally instructive. The Foreign Ministry’s spokesman acknowledged that “a number of promising points exist in the document which can help open new horizons in and expand relations between the EU and Iran.”
Yet spoilers existed on the Iranian side, too. Mohammad Javad Larijani, then secretary-general of the Iranian judiciary’s High Council for Human Rights, objected to the establishment of an EU delegation in Tehran, suggesting it could interfere in Iran’s internal affairs.
The allegation was ludicrous: 22 of the EU’s then-28 member states, including the United Kingdom, already maintained embassies in Tehran, while the EU had delegations in numerous countries whose governments had profound disagreements with Brussels.
Larijani’s objection reflected a suspicion within parts of Iran’s political establishment that closer relations with the West would invite political subversion. This strengthened precisely those European voices that portrayed engagement with Tehran as futile or even dangerous.
In 2015 and 2016, however, the spoilers on both sides seemed unlikely to derail the positive trajectory. There was reason to believe that the JCPOA, in the view of the then-EU foreign policy chief, Federica Mogherini , was indeed only the floor, not the ceiling, for EU-Iran relations.
That optimism proved tragically short-lived.
When President Donald Trump unilaterally withdrew the U.S. from the JCPOA in 2018, despite international verification of Iran’s compliance at the time, the EU formally opposed Washington’s decision. But the gap between the EU’s declarations and its capacity to act to preserve the agreement soon became painfully obvious.
European companies withdrew from Iran under the threat of secondary U.S. sanctions. Banks refused transactions. The EU attempted to preserve trade through mechanisms such as INSTEX, but these proved woefully inadequate . The promised economic benefits for Iran of the agreement never materialized.
Meanwhile, in a misguided attempt to appease Trump, the E3 (the U.K., France, Germany) themselves adopted an increasingly hawkish line on Iran, accusing it of destabilizing the region and developing ballistic missiles . The latter charge caused particular indignation in Tehran as these same European countries were increasing the supply of sophisticated arms to Iran’s regional rivals. From Tehran’s perspective, its missiles were vital to national defense.
The lesson for Tehran was unmistakable: Europe might disagree with Washington but it was incapable of protecting the nuclear deal. That inability was arguably a major factor in Tehran’s subsequent pivot to Moscow, which led to it supporting Russia’s illegal invasion of Ukraine, in exchange for military-technical cooperation — and which, in turn, made EU-Iran relations more adversarial.
The consequences of this failure have become stark during the 2025 and 2026 U.S.-Israeli wars against Iran. Rather than acting as an independent diplomatic bridge capable of mediating between Washington and Tehran, Europe has struggled to define a meaningful role.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wholeheartedly supported the Israeli aggression, notoriously hailing it as Israel doing “the dirty work” for Europeans. The only major European leader who unequivocally opposed the aggression was Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who banned the use of Spanish military bases for the war despite Trump’s attempts to bully Madrid into submission.
Where Europe once led diplomacy with Iran, it is now reduced to issuing bland and toothless statements while Pakistan, Turkey and the Persian Gulf states have stepped in as more consequential diplomatic actors.
The contrast with the approach of 2016 is staggering. The question, then, is not merely how Europe traded its leverage over Iran for moral grandstanding and diplomatic irrelevance, but whether it can recover the understanding of statecraft that once made that leverage possible.

title: 'We have the world's best toilets': Norway's toilet humor flushes Trump's 'shithouse country' jab
body: Norwegians have responded with dismissal, amusement and contempt in recent days to the latest insults from U.S. President Donald Trump, who described their country as a "shithouse country" during a campaign rally Sunday night, apparently angered that he had once again failed to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Trump made the remarks at a campaign rally in Michigan ahead of next week's U.S. midterm elections, where he also declared that immigrants from Norway were not welcome in the United States. Bluntly stating that "Norway sucks," he said he would welcome immigrants from certain countries, but not Norway, because he had not received the coveted prize awarded by the independent Nobel Committee based in Oslo.   "I'm not in love with Norway," Trump said. "As a matter of fact, Norway sucks. Norway has actually become a shithouse country." Trump has previously used similar language to describe countries such as Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen. Earlier this month, he said the failure to award him the Nobel Peace Prize was an "indelible stain" on Norway. Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide responded diplomatically to the latest remarks, telling Norwegian public broadcaster NRK that Trump knows perfectly well that the Nobel Committee is independent and does not accept directives, instructions or recommendations from the Norwegian government. Other Norwegians seized the opportunity to poke fun at the U.S. president. Visit Norway, the country's official tourism organization, published a mocking social media post that read: "We've heard some chatter about a 'shithouse country.' Well, what can we say, we do have some of the world's most spectacular toilets. Love, Visit Norway." The post included a link to a feature on its website showcasing what it calls some of the "world's most beautiful toilets," scattered across the Scandinavian country's breathtaking landscapes.   The website features photographs of remarkable public restrooms at Norwegian tourist destinations, explaining that "the toilets along the Norwegian Scenic Routes are architectural masterpieces." It describes Norway's impressive collection of restrooms as examples of how something as ordinary and mundane as a toilet can become a tourist attraction. The Norwegian Public Roads Administration, which is responsible for developing the country's scenic routes and their facilities, still has a few tricks up its sleeve, the website adds. In a response column published in the Norwegian newspaper Dagbladet under the headline "Straight into the toilet," the writer declared: "Yes, Donald, we are a 'shit house country.' Norway is, after all, the home of the outhouse." The columnist explained that Norwegians are among the last people likely to take offense at being associated with outdoor toilets, which many connect to the country's traditions and its cabin culture, where such facilities were once commonplace.     "Trump has complained about the Nobel Peace Prize so many times that it almost seems like an obsession," the columnist wrote. "No matter how many times both the prime minister and the Norwegian Foreign Ministry explain that the government has absolutely nothing to do with awarding the prize, he continues to blame them." The writer added: "An overwhelming majority of American voters agree with the Nobel Committee: Trump certainly does not deserve any peace prize. Quite the opposite. The war in Iran is a major source of criticism of Trump, including among his own supporters, second only to the cost of living and the period of inflation and soaring prices. He promised to end the endless wars, particularly in the Middle East. Instead, he joined Benjamin Netanyahu in a war he cannot find a way out of."     Trump's remarks about Norway also drew criticism in the United States. Democratic Sen. Bernie Sanders, a leading figure on the American progressive left, wrote on X: "Norway is one of the most democratic and prosperous countries on Earth. Free health care. Free college Strong democracy. Free press. Trump says 'Norway sucks' and is a 'shit house country' because it won’t give him the Nobel Prize. Insane. We have a mentally unbalanced president." Sanders' praise for the Nordic country was hardly exaggerated. Norway, with a population of just 5.6 million, is among the wealthiest and most developed countries in the world. Its sovereign wealth fund, known as the Government Pension Fund Global or the Oil Fund, was established in the 1990s using revenues from oil and gas production and is the largest of its kind in the world.   The fund is worth approximately $2.3 trillion and holds an average stake of about 1.5% in all publicly listed companies worldwide. On the United Nations Human Development Index, which measures life expectancy, education and income, Norway ranks second globally alongside Switzerland, behind Iceland. Its gross national income per capita is also among the highest in the world. This year marked the 10th consecutive year that Norway topped Reporters Without Borders' World Press Freedom Index. Trump has argued since his first term in office that he deserves the Nobel Peace Prize, and his demands intensified last year after he claimed to have secured eight peace agreements. In practice, these were not comprehensive peace treaties but primarily ceasefires or conflicts that broke out, some with his backing, and ended relatively quickly when he sought their conclusion.   This year's Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former judge at the International Criminal Court in The Hague from South Africa and an outspoken critic of Israel who also authored a report accusing the country of genocide. The Michigan rally where Trump made his remarks about Norway was the same contentious event at which he compared Muslim Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed to the terrorists responsible for the September 11, 2001, attacks. Trump also made crude remarks about the backsides of other politicians within his MAGA movement and about that of his supporter, rapper Nicki Minaj.

title: Araghchi congratulates Lula on Brazil election win
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi congratulated Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on winning Brazil's 2026 presidential election during a phone call with Brazil's foreign minister, Mauro Vieira.
Iranian Foreign Minister Seyyed Abbas Araghchi congratulated Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva on his victory in the country's 2026 presidential election during a phone call on Tuesday evening with Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira.
The two sides also exchanged views on the most important regional issues and the latest international developments.
