title: Blackstone plans fourfold growth in Gulf assets amid infrastructure spending boom
body: Blackstone has committed more capital to the Gulf region in the past 12 months than at any point in its history, and it plans to invest more despite geopolitical headwinds, its chief executive has said. Despite the months-long war , the investment appeal of the Gulf remains intact, Steve Schwarzman, who is also chairman and co-founder of the world's largest alternative asset manager, told The National . The $1.3-trillion investor aims to substantially grow the percentage of its assets under management in the Gulf, within its broader Europe, Middle East and Africa portfolio, by the turn of this decade. “I would say it would surprise me if it weren't three to four times larger from the current level,” Mr Schwarzman said, without disclosing the dollar number. Last year, he said that the company’s combined asset base in Europe and the Middle East had grown to $400 billion and there was an opportunity to boost it to $500 billion in Europe alone by 2035. Deals flurry Blackstone, which has been in the Gulf for more than 15 years, has already stepped up the pace of investment in the region through a flurry of deals over the past 12 months. In July, the firm invested $16 billion, in partnership with global investors, in the Kuwait Oil Company's crude oil pipeline network. In March Blackstone also announced a $250 million allocation in Abu Dhabi's Advanced Digital Gaming Technology. The group followed that with another partnership in April, teaming up with Dubai Aerospace Enterprise to invest about $1.6 billion annually in aircraft leasing. Maturing Gulf The big-ticket $16 billion investment in Kuwait reflects the company’s growth ambitions in the region. Global investors such as Blackstone have historically focused on capital-raising from the region. However, they are now pivoting towards investing; competing for opportunities in the region's digital infrastructure, technology, real estate, and energy sectors. The Gulf's role as a global capital exporter is reversing, with a rapid rise in its own financing needs, Mr Schwarzman said. “That has to do with the maturity of the region and people look at it and say, ‘there's something going on here’ [and] that is changing the way we're looking at this region,” he said. In October last year, Blackstone created Glide, a $5 billion logistics platform, in collaboration with Abu Dhabi’s Lunate. A month before that, Blackstone had participated in a $525 million financing round for UAE property portal Property Finder. Blackstone, which manages more than $200 billion in data centres and AI-related infrastructure, has also expanded its tech investment footprint in the Gulf. Its portfolio company AirTrunk struck a $3 billion data centre deal with Saudi Arabia's Humain, which is the first of potentially many deals elsewhere in the region, including the UAE, he said. "There are opportunities to collaborate with what's going on in Abu Dhabi, which in AI, is the most progressive, most informed, most advanced," Mr Schwarzman said. "It also has the advantage of nuclear power and it's pretty remarkable all the things that are being done in Abu Dhabi. Global investors who visit the region can see changes that are "really fascinating", he said, and when a place such as the Gulf reaches critical mass, “all of a sudden it becomes really interesting”. Growth ambitions Blackstone, which established its first office in Abu Dhabi in 2010, is rapidly growing its regional presence. The company has expanded the scope of its Abu Dhabi licence. It has also opened an office in Kuwait and is about to officially launch dedicated private wealth operations in Dubai. “We're going to have offices, in pretty much every country,” Mr Schwarzman said. “We expect to be over time putting more capital in the region from a global perspective, because you tend to make more money in our lines of business, where there's rapid economic growth." Undeterred Blackstone, like its global peers, remains undeterred despite the continuing Iran conflict that is now in its eighth month. “It obviously changes the risk profile of the region, but we're longer-term investors, and I think the people who deal with the region, who provide capital, realise that there are very smart people running these countries,” Mr Schwarzman said. Sovereigns in the region, he said, are willing to spend whatever it takes to expand the infrastructure, which will kickstart a new construction boom as soon as the conflict is over. “From talking with the heads of these countries, it's pretty clear they're going to spend whatever it takes to create a much safer environment, for their long-term economic plans,” Mr Schwarzman said. “The commitment to engineering safety and to protect their infrastructure over the next two to three years is going to be a very intense period, and so in that sense, they'll rebuild their economies.” Headwinds The US-Iran war has severely disrupted economic momentum in the Gulf region, with the International Monetary Fund estimating a 4.8 per cent contraction this year. It is set for a 9.1 per cent rebound in 2027 . “But what's interesting, beyond that, is that it is temporary and we expect all of the Gulf to go into rapid growth mode once this conflict is resolved,” Mr Schwarzman said. Construction boom The push to protect and expand the infrastructure will be among the main drivers of the next phase of economic activity, he said. “One of the things that's going to happen in the Gulf, that's probably been underestimated, is the amount of spending to protect the infrastructure,” Mr Schwarzman said. Blackstone anticipates a “very substantial construction boom”, as countries in the region push to move vulnerable infrastructure underground. Gulf nations will need to rebuild their economies if Iran remains “a structural problem” for them for years to come, Mr Schwarzman said. “I'm not enough of an expert to know what the response will be, but there are a lot of different scenarios that you could have, and it strikes me that just being a recipient of that aggression forever is an unlikely scenario.” Infrastructure basket Currently, the broader Middle East and North Africa region requires an estimated $900 billion in financing for infrastructure projects. British lender HSBC estimates that the finance pipeline in the UAE alone is more than $190 billion, about 22 per cent of the broader Menat total. The report, released last week by HSBC, has identified $872 billion worth of individual project packages within a wider $1.4 trillion pipeline of planned and unawarded infrastructure projects. “I can speak for us, but I don't think others like us are particularly different, and we see this as a very good long-term place for growth,” Mr Schwarzman said.

title: 'Eretz Nehederet' tackles Israel's election-night drama with Gal Gadot, political satire
body: As Israelis anxiously awaited the results of one of the most crucial elections in history on Tuesday night, Israeli-born Hollywood superstar Gal Gadot appeared on a special two-part broadcast of Eretz Nehederet (Wonderful Country) on Channel 12.Eretz Nehederet's staff of quick-thinking writers did what they could to make people smile despite the somewhat grim denouement of a divisive campaign (CREDIT: COURTESY).Gadot and the regular cast entertained a politically divided nation as the polls started to close, and Israelis were unified at last in their shared suspense.Her presence was a high point on an unusual broadcast: half of it was shown before the polls closed and the other half was broadcast after the exit polls showed an inconclusive result, far from the definitive victory both sides had craved.In the first half, one sketch featuring Asher (Yuval Semo), the chatty cabbie who always says exactly what is on his mind, focused on a few of the 70,000+ Israelis returning from abroad to vote.Asher is never speechless, but he was definitely shocked when Gadot stepped out of the airport and into his cab. Their upbeat, emotional conversation captured the euphoria and emotion of many Israelis who returned to vote after years abroad.“So, did you come back to vote? Or to be an artichoke on The Masked Singer?” Asher asked Gadot, who posted an Instagram story earlier in the day showing herself voting and saying she had backed one of the opposition parties, although she did not reveal which one.“No, I came to vote,” she said.“Good for you! Good for you,” Asher responded.“Absolutely,” she said.“What a Zionist! What a patriot,” he said enthusiastically.“If not now, when?” she said, echoing the famous quote from the Jewish sage, Hillel the Elder.“Tell me, how long have you been living abroad?” Asher asked Gadot.“Almost 12 years,” the actress, who has starred in two Wonder Woman movies and about a dozen others since she made the move, replied.“So, I can scam you like a tourist!” he said.Asking her who she was voting for, she agreed to whisper her choice to him.As soon as she did, Asher grabbed his megaphone and announced her choice to all the cabbies from his station, but the party's name was bleeped out, and he promised the other cabbies wouldn't tell anyone, as she laughed.She also spoke candidly about the difficulty of being an Israeli and a Jew in Hollywood in a period of rising antisemitism.“It's hard these days to be an Israeli abroad,” she said, and even said that she often wore masks when she went out, as if it were still the pandemic era.She said she often tried to give “context” that would help Americans understand the issues.“There's a lot of hate. I try to explain to them that what you see from there isn't what we see from here. And what we see here, you don't see there.” She said she planned to return to Israel with her husband and four daughters, three of whom were born in the US, and that they were building a house here.Finally, frustrated by the Israeli traffic, she told Asher she would drive, since she had starred in Fast & Furious. After some daredevil moves with his cab, she turned it into a flying car, heading up into the clouds in her quest to make it to a polling place in time to vote.Eretz Nehederet featured sketches about election candidates IN THE first, more optimistic half of the broadcast, the show outdid itself with an opening sketch in which the political opponents were depicted as professional wrestlers in appropriately absurd costumes.They fought each other in over-the-top wrestler-style, with weapons like a sawed-off shotgun wielded by Gadi Eisenkot (Yuval Semo), head of the Yashar party, and a huge gold suitcase of cash thrown around by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (Mariano Eidelman), a reference to how his government allowed suitcases containing millions of dollars from the Qatari government to be given to Hamas in Gaza.In a panel discussion moderated by host Eyal Kitzis, Channel 12 political analyst Amit Segal (Roy Bar Natan) appeared distracted, busy writing a victory speech for Netanyahu, a reference to the fact that Segal is alleged to have given the prime minister advice on his campaign speeches.Another panelist, Dana Weiss (Alma Zack), Channel 12's political and diplomatic correspondent, ignored calls from an increasingly unhinged Tally Gotliv (Liat Harlev) from the Otzma Yehudit party.Netanyahu appeared at a shopping mall and tried to spark fear in voters, saying everyone would die tonight if they did not vote for him.He brandished a toy ceramic mushroom, saying it was a mushroom cloud, a joke about an AI image the prime minister actually released in the final days of the campaign that purported to show Tel Aviv destroyed by an Iranian nuclear bomb.Eretz Nehederet ribbed Naftali Bennett (Eran Zarahovitsch), the head of the B'Yachad Party, for his campaign visits to “parliamentim,” informal political discussion groups of older citizens around the country.On Election Day, he had spent so much time with these groups that he realized he had missed his chance to vote and seemed forlorn. Eisenkot, in turn, looked terribly awkward courting the youth vote with a moronic influencer (Liat Harlev).Expanding on this theme, Eretz Nehederet went back in time and showed AI commercials to former prime ministers, including Golda Meir, Yitzhak Rabin, Menachem Begin, and Ariel Sharon, all of whom completely missed the point. Meir seemed especially mystified when she was handed an e-cigarette.Writers attempt to inject comedy into initial election results In the second part of the show, after the exit polls were revealed, the writers had to try hard to find comedy in the fact that neither side had won enough seats to form a government.One sketch showed the leaders of the three opposition parties, Eisenkot, Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman (Sharon Taicher) of Yisrael Beytenu, playing a game show called “Excuse the Promise,” trying to retract their campaign promises not to collaborate with Arab or haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties.Ofer Winter (Yaron Berlad) and Yoseph Haddad (Eli Finish) showed up upset that their party, People of Israel, had not gotten enough votes to enter the Knesset.Haddad was especially incredulous, saying he couldn't understand how he seemed to be the only Arab not elected to the Knesset, a reference to the fact that the Arab parties did much better than expected.Meanwhile, a grim-faced Netanyahu was shown in the defense headquarters, boasting he was starting up the war with Iran to cement his power as the head of state.Eretz Nehederet's quick-thinking writers did what they could to make people smile despite the somewhat grim denouement of a divisive campaign, and the prospect of more uncertainty to come.One unsettling element was that, instead of Kitzis's usual sign-off line about Israel being a wonderful country, the second broadcast ended with him simply handing the show back to Channel 12 news anchor Yonit Levi.

title: Iran's UN envoy counters US claims with martyrs' photos
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iran's UN envoy responded to US Ambassador Mike Waltz's claims by showing photos of martyrs from the recent war, urging him to speak based on facts, not accusations, and saying the US is the aggressor and Iran the victim.
Iran's ambassador and chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, responded to claims by US Ambassador Mike Waltz at the end of a UN Security Council meeting on Iran on Tuesday, showing photos of martyrs from the recent war and saying, "Speak based on facts, not accusations."
Darzi said the US representative could not provide any valid argument or justification for his country's blatant aggression against Iran and instead resorted to repeating lies and baseless accusations about Iran's peaceful nuclear program. He said Waltz repeated lies and raised baseless accusations to hide the truth, evade responsibility and escape accountability.
"Let us speak based on facts, not fabricated accusations," Darzi said. "The facts are clear: the United States and the Zionist regime have committed acts of aggression, including repeated military attacks on Iran's peaceful nuclear facilities that are under IAEA safeguards."
He said Iran is the victim of this war, not the aggressor. The aggressors are the United States and the Israeli regime, which have committed war crimes against the Iranian people. Residential areas, schools, hospitals, bridges, airports, energy facilities, sports complexes, cultural heritage sites, the railway network and other critical infrastructure were deliberately targeted and attacked.
While showing images of children and martyrs of the aggressive attacks against Iran to the world, Darzi said no amount of propaganda can change the facts, erase the suffering of the Iranian people or absolve those responsible of their international legal obligations. Those who ordered, carried out or facilitated these horrific crimes must be held accountable, not granted impunity.
Darzi stressed that the United States is the aggressor and Iran is the victim of this aggression. The positions of aggressor and victim must never be swapped. The United States cannot commit aggression, cause widespread civilian casualties and then use the UN Security Council to portray itself as the victim.
He said the United States, along with the Zionist regime, has carried out devastating attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure. They have committed war crimes and will sooner or later be held accountable for all these horrific crimes against the Iranian people. They cannot escape or evade their responsibility.

title: Tanzania announces first gas discovery in more than 10 years
body: Tanzania has discovered an estimated 223 billion cubic feet of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the country’s south, its energy minister announced on Tuesday. Energy ​minister Juma Homera said the reserves ⁠were found at the Kasa-1X ST2 ​well, explored jointly by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum ​Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil company Maurel & Prom The find is Tanzania’s first gas discovery in ​more than 10 years Homera said ​that TPDC and Maurel & Prom had drilled three ‌wells — ⁠MB-5, MS-2 and Kasa-1X ST2 — that would help to boost the country’s gas supply Maurel & Prom has said that first ​gas production ​could ⁠start as early as next month Homera said TPDC was already in ​talks with four investors planning ​small-scale ⁠liquefied natural gas projects Before the latest announcement, Tanzania’s discovered reserves stood at about ⁠57.5 ​trillion standard cubic feet, ​according to the energy regulator

title: This is not sustainable
body:
What a week , huh? High fives all around—October is "Cybersecurity Awareness Month", and I think we've all done a stellar job. If both the New York Times and NPR report on one of the at least four or five concurrent fires I'm fighting, then I think we can say that yeah, people are aware of cybersecurity. Mission accomplished, so... could we maybe turn it down a bit?
The current situation is not sustainable: 0-days are dropping left and right, pre-notifications and embargoes are broken for marketing purposes , AI companies compete first on who commits the most crimes and then pretend to sell you protection in the form of a DoS on the Open Source community. " Nice project you got there. Be a shame if somebody dropped an 0-day on it." 1
Companies are not staffed for this, and no matter what the industry wants to tell you, you can't AI your way out of this. Vulnerability discovery has fundamentally changed, disclosure processes are effectively broken , and patch management has been a losing proposition for years now. Severe vulnerabilities are identified and disclosed at a pace that defenders are unable to keep up with.
This is because it still takes significant resources to accurately assess the feasibility of a given vulnerability within your environment; it takes time to discover your attack surface relevant to the given attack vector, and it takes even more time to deploy a fix. As I've said before , development of the fix is not the bottleneck. Let me illustrate with examples from the last couple of days:
Initially disclosed as a "KVM escape", this vulnerability also applies to other virtualization as well as containers, although that angle hasn't really gotten much attention. You now need to assess which possible mitigations might be in place across your fleet of systems, then determine whether you can livepatch your kernels with the custom patches you pull from upstream or if you want to wait for your upstream OS provider to deliver a new kernel 2 and then all you have to do is reboot a few thousand systems.
How does AI help you here? Maybe you spend a few thousand dollars on tokens to use the most advanced cyber cyber models to develop your own exploit, but in the end, that doesn't really tell you anything you didn't already know, and your defensive position and tasks at hand remain the same.
This one's fun, isn't it? Sure, browsers were all set quickly, but guess what, there's a few other things that might use TLS in your environment. Like... everything . So again, having the fix is not the bottleneck. Waiting for upstream packages to release an update only blocks you if you actually know that you need to pull in that update.
Oh, you have a detailed package inventory or, dare I say it, SBOMs? That's really nice. Do show me where that lists the various vendored or hard-coded CA trust bundles . Yeah, I didn't think so. 3
(At least this incident was not AI generated, detected, or triggered. Just one of your wholesome, classical, a-human-going-"huh" kind of discoveries. It's almost reassuring that we still get these, too.)
The PHP vulnerability that supposedly affects "over 70% of websites" (a widely quoted, but never attributed statistic) was disclosed under embargo to several organizations. If you were part of this inner circle, then this should have reduced your panic-mode somewhat, buying you at least some time to deploy protections for your customers and do the tedious work of sifting through your inventory and, again, identify the attack surface, affected systems, possible local mitigations, etc. etc. The usual.
Unless the embargo is broken. Then you get to scramble again. And you need to keep up to date with all the rapidly published (and increasingly verbosely AI polluted) breathless blog posts driven by cyber security vendors' marketing teams eager to beat each other as the first to detect 4 , first to exploit, first to brag, all of which adds to the distraction.
And of course you still need to do the actual work of determining the accuracy of the various exploits floating around the internet, some put together by people with a clue and many, many slopped together by those lacking a full understanding of the bug 5 . (More on that below.)
And then, by the time Thursday rolls around, people start to see a NodeJS security advisory , which includes as the third "high" severity vulnerability an issue with the "Node.js Brotli decoder". Alright, attack surface enumeration, software inventory check, start to deploy updated packages,... the usual.
Except, of course, once you take a closer look, it begins to dawn on you that this goes well beyond just Node.js 6 . And so once again, having the upstream fix available is absolutely not your bottleneck, because you still need to find the plethora of frankenstances of brotli across all of your stacks first.
Of course at that point in time OpenAI starts to go "Us! It was us! We found it!" even though the issue was fixed back in February and Mozilla noted the critical security impact as far back as April. It seems there's no vulnerability, no compromise, no cyber crime AI companies are not willing to claim as their credit.
All of this was going on over the course of one week, and doesn't even account for the previous set of weekly Linux local privilege escalation vulnerabilities 7 . And no doubt there will be more such disclosures—many more.
AI companies are incentivized to continue the onslaught, with the most benevolent interpretation of mass disclosures of findings being a canonical example of " verschlimmbessern ", with less friendly interpretations observing that it's profitable for a company to create the disease for which they're selling you the treatment (and never the cure). They've got a new toy, it's a hammer, and by golly they're gonna swing it.
Millions of dollars have been spent on identifying vulnerabilities using so-called "frontier AI models", and we know that adversaries are feeding, e.g., the Linux kernel commit messages into their models to analyze them for exploitable vulnerabilities on the fly. Today, vulnerabilities are found independently by multiple parties on a regular basis, so you already have to assume that a disclosure embargo only contains the massive exploitation by opportunistic adversaries at best.
At the same time, I'm observing a worrying trend on the defensive side of cyber security, which mirrors the same de-skilling trend across the industry: AI generated vulnerability reports are often much, much too verbose to be digested easily by human readers. They drown you in details, overwhelm your attention with unnecessary information. Because defenders don't fully understand the vulnerabilities described here, they tend to believe the generally exaggerated severity claims, and feed the full report into their AI to reproduce or generate a proof of concept.
Several thousand tokens later, you end up with a binary handed to you by a meat-proxy that's supposed to trigger the vulnerability, but nobody actually understands why it works. Which, more often than not, it actually doesn't , because your environment is different, your AI was missing context the meat-proxy didn't (know to) provide, because the code base differs from upstream, or who knows what else. When you ask for clear instructions on how to run the exploit, what pre-conditions need to be met, and how it works—you know, the kind of one-pager that offensive engineers used to be able to produce—you get back, you guessed it, an AI-vomited 7,000 word README.md . 8
Fighting one fire at a time is taxing enough. Each one of the above examples would have been a once-a-year incident not too long ago. Having multiple such incidents at the same time is burning out all your incident response staff, your engineers, your comms and legal teams.
(And it always is more or less the same set of people driving each incident. I have not seen organizations properly staffed and not relying on the same set of ghostbusters—the heroes and company-elders with the required tribal knowledge to make up for the gaps in your software inventory, attack surface enumeration, and documentation, because who else are you gonna call?)
Context switching between each of these incidents means you can't focus on any one of them, making you more likely to miss important information, to fall for sensationalistic headlines, to succumb to pressure and to rush fixes you don't understand for vulnerabilities that might not apply in your environment. Which, in turn, makes more people more susceptible to the appealing lure of quick and confident answers from the bot, and subject-matter non-experts start to paste their prompt results into incident response channels.
Oh, lol, sorry, I mislead you. When you ramble and rant, you're supposed to end on an upbeat note, provide a solution 9 , proffer suggestions on how we can all roll up our sleeves and work together and solve the problem. Alas, I have no idea.
Ah, but surely all of this is just temporary , right? AI will find all the vulns, we slog through this dark winter of disclosure chaos, and then come out in a world where all software vulnerabilities have been found and fixed.
If you're able to believe that, I envy you. I don't see it happening. If you try to tell me that software developers should just use AI to generate patches, remember that over 50% of the time , AI either doesn't fix the issue, introduces a new vulnerability, or changes the application's behavior in the process. Reducing our own understanding of complex software while simultaneously producing more and more code is a recipe for more vulnerabilities, not fewer. And, at the risk of sounding like a broken record, getting the vulnerability fixed is not the bottleneck .
Even if the current status were temporary—for how long? A year? Two? And what are we supposed to do in the meantime? Hiring more infosec staff isn't likely to happen in this economy . Investing into overhauling your entire infrastructure such that you can at least pull in and deploy updates automatically and reboot your fleet and do all that safely is equally unlikely: companies have gotten away with not doing that for decades, and who wants to be the VP or executive who shifts funding away from "moar code moar faster"? Not to mention that such a project would take several years as well.
The last option left is to simply accept the status quo. There will be more vulnerabilities, including RCEs, and you won't be able to keep up with them. Your only option is to limit the blast radius. Assume compromise, detect exploitation, limit exposure, lateral movement, privilege escalation, etc. If that sounds like an old hat, well, yes, that's what sane infosec practitioners have been asking for funding for for decades. (We used to call it "Zero Trust", before that became an empty marketing term.) But that funding instead goes to the next singing and dancing, AI-based vulnerability management SIEM dashboardmajing, which will only miss 40% of your infrastructure and assets. Hooray!
[1] The same racket works even better with businesses: " Nice supply chain you got there. Be a shame if somebody dropped hundreds of 0-days for most of your dependencies. Better subscribe to our service to get pre-notification. " ↩
[2] As of 2026-10-27, 12 days after initial disclosure, Canonical, to name one example, still doesn't ship a fixed kernel , considering the issue of "medium" severity. ↩
[3] Your best bet in some cases is to just run a simple fetch using the language/framework in question. I also have a script to detect and update bundles for you. But that doesn't scale, either. Good luck, tho! ↩
[4] Detection of exploit attempts is a critical signal to help you assess the urgency of your response and can influence disclosure timelines. Announcing you've observed per-disclosure exploitation without sufficient confidence is harmful to all responders. ↩
[5] And don't get me started on using setjmp(3)/longjmp(3) for error handling in any even remotely complex program. Sure, it's clever , but writing clever is rarely the same as writing safe code. I'm not convinced you can use this mechanism safely in all but the most trivial cases, and wouldn't be surprised if additional vulnerabilities are lurking here. And now that the Eye of Sauron is trained on this codebase... ↩
[6] By the way, does anybody know why Google Docs insists on hyperlinking node.js ? .js is not a TLD. Is it really stupid enough to just go by [a-z0-9.-]+\.[a-z]{2} ? Oh, it totally is. Brilliant. ↩
[7] Disclosures like " Linux kernel LPEs: ZcopyReaper (CVE-2026-43502) and 20 more are pretty much par for the course after we got " DirtyFrag ", " GhostLock ", " FragGap ", " ZapScape ", " Januscape ", and I forgot what else in a constant trickle earlier this year. ↩
[8] Granted, that's only marginally more than some dude's ranting all-over-the-place blog post. But at least that was 100% human generated. ↩
[9] I would like to say that one way forward here is accountability . To hold companies accountable for what they do—including what they enable or allow their software, their models, their bots to do. That certainly is necessary for the various reckless AI companies as they continue to fail to restrict their malware. I'd also like to hold vendors accountable for shipping software with known vulnerabilities, but I don't know how that is supposed to work for Open Source, nor do I think it solves the disclosure-as-ddos problem. ↩

title: 'Not just empty talk': Ra'am's Abbas signals willingness to join next government
body: Ra'am party leader Mansour Abbas said Tuesday that joining a new government could bring meaningful change to the country's Arab minority, after exit polls projected his Islamist party would win seven seats in parliament amid a significant increase in Arab voter turnout. "If we join a government of change, we will be able to see substantial changes, not just empty talk," Abbas told ynet after the first exit polls were released.   Early projections showing a narrow advantage for the opposition's pro-change bloc initially suggested that Ra'am could emerge as a pivotal player in negotiations to form Israel's next government. But overnight revisions shifted the advantage toward Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc, sharply reducing the likelihood of a minority government supported by Ra'am from outside the coalition. Under Israel's parliamentary system, a governing coalition generally needs the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset. Arab parties could play a decisive role if neither major political bloc secures a majority on its own. Despite the shifting projections, Abbas welcomed the substantial increase in voting among Arab citizens of Israel, including unusually high participation by religious figures. "We received seven seats according to the polls. We hope to secure an eighth seat so we can bring down the current government and become part of the camp for change, with the aim of fighting crime and violence, home demolitions and racism," Abbas said. Crime and violence in Arab communities, along with disputes over housing demolitions and allegations of discrimination, have been central issues in Ra'am's political agenda. Abbas acknowledged that his party still faced significant challenges in translating electoral support into political influence. "We still have a long way to go before we have an influential voice and a meaningful position on the ground," he said. "We must bring about change across all institutions and invest every effort and resource available to us to achieve that." He thanked Arab voters for their support, singling out residents of the Negev region in southern Israel, where Ra'am has a significant political base. "We have invested tremendous efforts to reach where we are today. We have faced challenges and paid a price," Abbas said. "We have endured criticism and attacks, including on a personal level, but despite everything, we will continue on our path with determination." Abbas reports calls after exit polls Abbas said he had received numerous telephone calls following the release of the exit polls but declined to identify the callers or disclose the substance of their conversations. "I received many phone calls after the poll results were published, and I will not reveal their contents," he said. "We want to carefully examine the political landscape, and we will adopt a series of positions and decisions that serve the Arab public." Ra'am, officially known as the United Arab List, is an Arab Islamist party affiliated with the southern branch of Israel's Islamic Movement. Under Abbas, it has pursued a pragmatic approach to parliamentary politics, emphasizing cooperation with Jewish parties to secure government resources and address problems affecting Arab communities. The party made history in 2021 when it joined the coalition government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, becoming the first independent Arab party to formally participate in a governing coalition. Its potential involvement in another government has become a central point of contention in the current coalition negotiations, with Netanyahu rejecting any government dependent on what he describes as anti-Zionist Arab parties. Ra'am lawmaker Walid Taha described the projected election result as a major achievement. "We have achieved historic success as an independent party," Taha said. "Now the work begins. If we manage to secure the eighth seat, our strength will be even more significant, and that will have an impact on the government." Fellow Ra'am lawmaker Iman Khatib-Yasin said the party's campaign reflected years of frustration among Arab citizens over violence, crime and what she described as hostile government policies. "For four years, we have suffered from many problems that have harmed Arab society," she said. "How deeply we have suffered over the murders and the cries of mothers. We want to act to confront this harsh reality." Khatib-Yasin also criticized those who had accused Ra'am members of betraying their community. "What hurt us most was hearing people call us traitors and slander us," she said. "But that did not deter us or divert us from our path. We will continue working with determination and investing tremendous effort." The final distribution of Knesset seats will depend on the official vote count, leaving Ra'am's ultimate parliamentary strength and its potential role in forming the next government uncertain.

title: El-Rufai’s Alleged 12 Questions to Tinubu: The Facts, The Reforms And The Answers Nigerians Deserve
body: By Gloria Fraser Twelve questions circulating publicly have been attributed to former Kaduna Governor Nasir El-Rufai, although authorship remains unverified. The National Patriots welcomes scrutiny grounded in facts, figures and the responsibilities of every tier of government. 1. Fuel Subsidy: Where Are The Trillions Saved From Subsidy Removal, And What Tangible Benefits Have Nigerians Received? An August 2026 assessment estimated N15.8 trillion in savings: Federal Government N5.43 trillion, states N6.52 trillion and local governments N3.88 trillion. Fiscal space supports infrastructure, N223.8 billion student financing, N150 billion mortgage support, N50 billion consumer credit, healthcare, education, wages and social protection. These are estimated fiscal resources, not a separate bank account. States and councils must turn increased FAAC into schools, clinics, roads and jobs. Citizens deserve transparent accounting. 2. Insecurity: Why Negotiate With Bandits In The North While Taking A Different Approach To Security Issues In The South-West? Defence Minister General Christopher Musa opposes bandit negotiations and ransom payments. Such negotiations predated Tinubu, including during El-Rufai’s governorship. Northern operations face forests and remote settlements; cross-border arms; compromised intelligence; hostage risks; overlapping terrorism, kidnapping, illegal mining and communal violence; and ambushes. Oriire in Oyo and operations in Kwara demonstrate intelligence-led approaches. The National Patriots advocates stronger military operations, border surveillance and community cooperation. Different tactics do not mean different values for Nigerian lives. 3. Electricity: You Promised Nigerians Should Not Re-Elect You In 2027 If You Failed To Fix Electricity. Where Is The Light? Tinubu’s 2022 declaration was rhetorical emphasis—a figure of speech expressing determination, rather than a literal instruction to voters. The Electricity Act of June 2023 empowered state electricity markets. By May 2026, 15 states had assumed regulatory responsibilities: Abia, Anambra, Bayelsa, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Imo, Kogi, Lagos, Nasarawa, Niger, Ogun, Ondo, Oyo and Plateau. Gombe subsequently transitioned; Akwa Ibom received a transfer order. Other states are advancing investments. Abia’s 188MW Geometric plant serves nine Aba-area councils. Lagos has 26MW Akute, 21MW Island Power and 40MW Victoria Island projects; some target December 2026 operations. Edo’s 100MW CCETC project targets December commissioning, with 46MW reportedly installed. Regulatory reform is not electricity already supplied. President Tinubu has delivered the fundamental legislative reform he promised in order to address Nigeria’s persistent electricity outages. With the legal and policy framework firmly established through the exercise of his presidential powers, implementation now rests with state governments and their private-sector partners. The President has fulfilled his commitment within his constitutional authority, laying the foundation for sustainable and reliable electricity supply nationwide. 4. Poverty: With Millions Struggling To Survive, What Concrete Steps Has Your Government Taken To Reduce Poverty, Especially In Northern Nigeria? More than N600 billion in transfers reportedly reached over 10 million vulnerable households. Five new development commissions—North-West, North-Central, South-East, South-South and South-West—complement the North-East Commission through infrastructure and empowerment. The National Social Protection Plan, proposed 90-Day Cost-of-Living Reduction Plan, $1 billion social protection initiative, NG-CARES, SOLID and HOPE address hardship, health and livelihoods. Seven North-West states received approximately N749.7 billion net FAAC in H1 2026. EFCC oversight should ensure local results; immediate relief must accompany sustainable employment. State-by-state analysis appears in Nigeria’s Great Reset: Rebuilding Today for a Prosperous Tomorrow, by Princess Gloria Adebajo-Fraser, MFR. 5. Agriculture: Where Are The Promised Marketing Boards, Guaranteed Prices And Investments To Make Food Affordable? The N200 billion Bank of Agriculture Guaranteed Minimum Price Programme, announced September 8, 2026, targets 500,000 farmers and 11.5 million households. The $500 million World Bank-supported SPIN programme supports a 500,000-hectare irrigation ambition by 2030. A Cotton, Textile and Garment Development Board is proposed. Guaranteed prices protect farmers; irrigation, mechanisation, credit and processing enable multiple harvests, improve supply and ease food costs. Nigeria cannot rely on seasonal rainfall alone. 6. Digital Jobs: Where Are The One Million Digital Jobs Promised To Nigerian Youths? The 3MTT programme reports 135,000 trainees, 300,000 resource users, 1.8 million registrations and approximately 15,000 facilitated career opportunities nationwide. Software, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and data skills can support internships, entrepreneurship and employment. Facilitated opportunities are not necessarily permanent jobs; training must convert into paid work. 7. Industrialisation: How Many Industries Have You Built Or Revived In The North-West, And What Is The Status Of The Akk Gas Pipeline? Initiatives include Kaduna’s Kakuri textile revitalisation, Kano leather and garment activity, Bank of Industry financing and a proposed textile board. The inherited 614km Ajaokuta–Kaduna–Kano pipeline could power factories and create jobs. A $50 billion gas-sector investment initiative seeks private and other investment, not government subvention. Insecurity, worker fatalities, floods, difficult terrain, River Niger engineering and failed Chinese financing delayed AKK; NNPC funded continuation. Oilserv Chairman Emeka Okwuosa cited shorter workdays and rising costs. NNPC reported approximately 95% completion in August 2026. 8. Abductions: Why Does The Government’s Response To School Abductions Appear Different Across Regions? Does Every Nigerian Life Matter Equally? Absolutely. Rescue decisions reflect intelligence, terrain, hostage safety, coordination, community information, operational flexibility and demographics—including population density, settlement patterns, languages, population movement and school locations. Oriire illustrated intelligence-led operations; Kwara and Niger reportedly saw 308 abductees rescued in August 2026. Headlinenews.News examined Oriire. Government should be judged by its lawful efforts to protect citizens and secure their release, not by whether every operation follows identical procedures. Every Nigerian life matters equally, irrespective of ethnicity, religion, geographical location or demographic circumstances. 9. Sunday Igboho Versus El-Rufai: Why Act On The Pleas Of Yoruba Monarchs Regarding Sunday Igboho But Seemingly Ignore Northern Traditional Rulers On Comparable Security And Justice Concerns Involving El-Rufai? Igboho’s case concerned separatist agitation and security allegations; El-Rufai’s concerns statements about alleged interception of the National Security Adviser’s communications. DSS proceedings followed a February 2026 interview. El-Rufai deserves presumption of innocence and due process. Monarchs can seek reconciliation, but cannot override courts; equality requires lawful procedures, not identical outcomes. 10. Governors’ Accountability: You Asked Nigerians To Hold Governors Accountable. What Practical Mechanisms Will You Provide To Make That Possible? On October 1, 2026, EFCC Chairman Ola Olukoyede announced presidential approval to monitor state and local FAAC. Citizens should demand budgets, project records and measurable outcomes. Education, healthcare, agriculture, roads, drainage, water and community jobs are subnational responsibilities. Increased allocations must improve daily life. 11. Kaduna Promises: You Made Promises About Jobs, Agriculture, Security And The Akk Pipeline In Kaduna In 2022. Which Have You Fulfilled? Tinubu commissioned the 300-bed Bola Ahmed Tinubu Specialist Hospital in June 2025, with cancer and nuclear-medicine ambitions. Barau Dikko Teaching Hospital announced relocation of 14 clinics on October 26, 2026: gastroenterology, cardiology, rheumatology, dermatology, endocrinology, nephrology, pulmonology, neurology, psychiatry, general surgery, orthopaedic surgery, urology, neurosurgery and oncology. One hundred CNG buses reportedly carried 3.2 million passengers, saving N3.5 billion. Projects include Kafanchan and Kauru–Kubau roads, Abuja–Kaduna–Kano highway, N178 billion Mando–Birnin Gwari road, 203km Kaduna–Kano railway and proposed 50km Kaduna Light Rail across two corridors, estimated at N1 trillion, with June 2026 mobilisation. AKK, textile initiatives and Governor Uba Sani’s agricultural and vocational programmes support jobs. Some projects remain ongoing. 12. Trust: If You Were A Nigerian Struggling Under Your Administration, Would You Trust Your Promises A Second Time? My personal answer is YES. I rate Tinubu 85%; the remaining 15% reflects bureaucracy and states and councils failing to translate FAAC into visible improvements. Nine considerations support my assessment: subsidy, currency and revenue reforms; over $15 billion in NNPC remittances to the CBN over three years, as examined in Nigeria’s Great Reset; increased FAAC; social protection; NELFUND and vocational education; youth programmes—3MTT, NATEP, iDICE, NiYA, YEIDEP and NYSP; roads, rail and electricity; the $50 billion gas initiative; and irrigation-led agriculture. Tinubu is a humanitarian who does not want Nigerians to suffer. His reforms are difficult, but his social interventions show compassion and his determination deserves recognition. Good intentions must still produce household benefits. As the Hausa proverb says: “Jumma’a mai kyau tun daga Laraba ake gane ta.” The Friday that will be good can already be recognised from Wednesday. My answer remains an unequivocal YES. I would vote for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu again in 2027, and I encourage Nigerians across the country to do the same. We know his determination and achievements. The twelve questions have been answered with facts, figures, policies and evidence of implementation. There is no compelling reason to deny him a second term. Absolutely none. He deserves the opportunity to consolidate reforms and turn stabilisation into prosperity. THE NATIONAL PATRIOTS POSITION We welcome scrutiny and distinguish completed, ongoing and proposed initiatives. We can document at least 100 reforms, achievements and development initiatives across the economy, infrastructure, electricity, agriculture, healthcare, education, youth, security, social protection and industry. State and local governments must account for FAAC. The ultimate test of Nigeria’s Great Reset is not merely how much government collects, but how much Nigerians benefit. Imagine what Nigeria would become in another 3 years with the electricity decentralisation in full swing nationwide, industries sprouting up, irrigated farms producing food crops all year round, gas ecosystem opened up, education system repositioned with more youths engaged through the various free programmes to learn skills, social protection plan in full steam, National security architecture plan in full operation, what a lovely country Nigeria would become. That is President Tinubu’s vision and mission from our evaluation with objective analysis of credible evidence and facts. Further analysis appears in Nigeria’s Great Reset: Rebuilding Today for a Prosperous Tomorrow, by Princess Gloria Adebajo-Fraser, MFR. •Princess Gloria Adebajo-Fraser, MFR President, The National Patriots

title: Economic Summits and Developmental State
body: Kayode Komolafe With the 2027 general elections in view, perhaps no political party or candidate would deny the urgency of the theme of the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit: “Growth That Works: Delivering Jobs, Productivity and Shared Prosperity.” The differences, if any, would probably arise over the strategies and tactics required to achieve these central economic objectives. At the risk of sounding repetitive on this page, the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG), an eminent think tank and ad-vocacy forum, deserves lavish commendation. It has sustained for over three decades, an important platform for public-private sector dialogue on the Nigerian economy. Indeed, the NESG remains one of the enduring examples of how sections of the Nigerian elite can forge a consensus around the imperative of harvesting ideas for national development. In a sense, the theme of the 32nd Summit of NESG is a derivative of the economic objectives already enshrined in the Chapter II of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Paradoxically, this is hardly acknowledged by our economic experts and pundits. Some of the participants at the summit which ended yesterday might even contest this assertion. Specifically, Section 16 of the constitution provides a foundation for the management of the economy in the interest of the wel-fare, prosperity and socio-economic justice especially for the people. Inexplicably, in more than a quarter of a century of experimentation with liberal democracy, political parties and candidates have hardly drawn sufficient inspiration from this constitutional provision in formulating their manifestos, programmes and development strategies. However, whenever electoral disputes arise, or controversies emerge over intergovernmental relations, politicians and their lawyers are quick to invoke the constitution as the fundamental law of the land. Yet remarkably little attention is paid to the fact that the constitution is not merely a charter of formal political freedoms. It also embodies a vision of socio-economic justice. Indeed, the constitution provides a broad framework for economic management. The Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles of State Policy, contained in Chapter II, are particularly relevant in this regard. The constitution has as an objective an economy managed in such a manner as to secure the maximum welfare, free-dom and happiness of every citizen based on social justice and equality of status and opportunity. It also stipulates the state to direct its policy towards ensuring the planned and balanced economic development of the country. In particular, Chapter II of the Constitution puts the matter in Section 16 like this: “(1) The State shall, within the context of the ideals and objectives for which provisions are made in this Constitution. “(a) harness the resources of the nation and promote national prosperity and an efficient, a dynamic and self-reliant economy. “(b) control the national economy in suck manner as to secure the maximum welfare, freedom and happiness of every citizen based on social justice and equality of status and opportunity. “(c) without prejudice to its right to operate or participate in areas of the economy, other than the major sectors of the economy, manage and operate the major sectors of the economy. “(d) without prejudice to the right of any person to participate in areas of the economy within the major sector of the economy, protect the right of every citizen to engage in any economic activities outside the major sectors of the economy.” In the same Section 16, the Constitution also stipulates as follows: “(2) The State shall direct its policy towards ensuring: “(a) the promotion of a planned and balanced economic development. “(b) that the material resources of the nation are harnessed and distributed as best as possible to serve the common good. “(c) that the economic system is not operated in such a manner as to permit the concentration of wealth or the means of produc-tion and exchange in the hands of few individuals or of a group; an “(d) that suitable and adequate shelter, suitable and adequate food, reasonable national minimum living wage, old age care and pensions, and unemployment, sick benefits and welfare of the disable are provided for all citizens.” These are not empty constitutional declarations. They represent a conception of the responsibility of the state for economic development and social progress. As for the question of justiciability, specific laws have been subsequently made to make as-pects of Chapter II enforceable in areas of access to primary healthcare, basic education and social welfare. So, Chapter II is not dormant. In essence, the constitutional provisions offer a solid basis for the emergence of a developmental state in Nigeria. Think tanks such as the NESG should devote greater intellectual and policy attention to this constitutional question.. Perhaps the relative neglect of this constitutional dimension of economic management can be explained by the dominance of neoliberal ideas in the Nigerian policy arena over the last few decades. Under this ideological influence, the assumption has often been that development would follow almost automatically once the role of the state was sufficiently diminished and market forces were allowed to operate with minimal interference. Planning was consequently treated as an obsolete idea, while the state was increasingly conceived primarily as a provider of “an enabling environment for private enterprise.” The underlying illusion is that the market, left substantially to its own devices, would deliver the structural transformation necessary for national development. Yet, the limitations of this neoliberal orthodoxy have become increasingly evident, not only in neo-colonial states, but also in advanced capitalist economies. Across the world, governments are rediscovering the importance of industrial policy, strategic public investment, economic planning and purposeful state intervention in shaping development outcomes. The debate is no longer simply about whether the state should play a role in economic development. The more pertinent questions concern the nature, quality, capacity and strategic direction of that role. This changing global ideological climate should provide an opportunity for a more fundamental interrogation of the philo-sophical assumptions underlying economic policy in Nigeria. One striking weakness of the Nigerian political economy is the relative absence of clearly articulated schools of economic thought in the formulation of public policy. Elsewhere, competing development strategies are often rooted in identifiable philosophical underpinnings, whether liberal, conservative, Keynesian, social democratic, developmentalist or otherwise. The influence of economists such as Friedrich Hay-ek and Milton Friedman on the neoliberal turn in Western economic policy is a familiar example of the relationship between economic thought and political choices. There is a story that at any time you would likely find a copy of Hayek’s book in Mar-garet Thatcher’s handbag as she studiously demolished the British welfare state. Equally, the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, who wants to repair the cumulative socio-economic damage done to the political economy of the UK since the days of Thatcherism, is also advancing from a clear ideological vantage. Similarly, the postwar experience of several East Asian economies demonstrates the importance of strategic state capacity, in-dustrial policy and long-term developmental planning. In Nigeria, however, economic policies are too often presented as technical prescriptions detached from their philosophical and ideological foundations. Reforms are announced, defended or criticised without sufficient interrogation of the economic theories, assumptions and historical experiences informing them. Consequently, public debate frequently revolves around isolated policy instruments rather than competing conceptions of development. This huge intellectual deficit should concern organisations such as the NESG. To achieve the much-discussed elite consensus necessary for national transformation, Nigeria needs a more rigorous debate about the character of its political economy and the role of the state in development. Such a consensus need not imply unanimity on every economic policy. Nor should it eliminate legitimate political differences. Rather, it should establish what may be described as the irreducible minimum conditions for national development. These would include a shared commitment to economic diversification, productive employment, industrialisation, infrastruc-ture, education, healthcare, technological advancement and the reduction of poverty and inequality. The constitutional basis for such a consensus already exists. But politicians and experts alike have strangely ignored this reali-ty. Section 16 of the Constitution should, in this respect, become something of a battle cry for development. Its provisions should inform the manifestos and programmes of political parties, irrespective of their political differences. Ordinarily, this should not be a Herculean task, especially given the limited ideological differentiation among the political par-ties in Nigeria. What is lacking is not necessarily agreement on the desirability of development. Virtually every political actor professes a commitment to growth, employment generation and poverty reduction. What is missing is a sufficiently serious engagement with the economic ideas, institutional arrangements and strategic choices necessary to translate these aspirations into reality. If the constitutional objectives became the common foundation of party programmes, political competition could then be ele-vated to a more rigorous level. Parties and candidates would be challenged to explain their preferred strategies, policy in-struments, institutional reforms and implementation mechanisms for achieving broadly agreed developmental goals. The debate would move beyond rhetorical promises to the comparative merits of alternative development pathways. For example, what should be the relationship between public investment and private capital in industrialisation? How should the state promote domestic productive capacity? What institutional mechanisms are required to coordinate economic transformation? How should economic growth be linked deliberately to employment creation and social inclusion? These are questions that cannot be answered adequately by the ritual invocation of “an enabling environment for the private sector.” Certainly, in Nigeria’s context a vibrant private sector is indispensable to economic development. Private investment, entre-preneurship, innovation and enterprise are essential components of any successful development strategy. But the historical experience of development does not support the proposition that private enterprise, operating without strategic public coor-dination, will necessarily deliver structural transformation. A developmental state is not synonymous with an overbearing state or an indiscriminate expansion of government bureaucra-cy. Nor does it necessarily entail hostility to markets or private capital. Rather, it is a state equipped with a nationalist vision, institutional capacity, policy coherence, developmental vision and po-litical commitment to mobilise public and private resources towards clearly defined national objectives. Such a state does not merely react to market outcomes. It consciously shapes the conditions under which productive invest-ment, technological learning, industrial upgrading and social development can occur. It is precisely this strategic capacity that Nigeria must build if the economy is to make the developmental leap that has re-mained elusive for decades. However, the next stage of this dialogue should go beyond the familiar repertoire of policy prescriptions. It should be enriched by a conscious effort to locate the provenance of the economic ideas informing policy proposals. The philosophical foundations of competing approaches to development should be made explicit and subjected to rigorous de-bate. This would deepen the intellectual quality of economic policymaking and help to move political discourse beyond the superfi-cial contest of personalities, slogans and promises. More importantly, it would enable Nigerians to evaluate the development strategies of political parties and candidates based on coherent economic visions rather than disconnected policy announcements. The challenge is, therefore, not simply to persuade politicians to endorse the worthy objectives of growth, jobs, productivity and shared prosperity. No politician would openly reject those objectives. Ultimately, Nigeria’s developmental challenge cannot be resolved merely by improving the environment in which market forces operate. It requires a purposeful, capable and accountable state working in productive partnership with the private sector. Such a state could be described as developmental. All told, it is time the idea of a developmental state was squarely placed on the agenda of the nation’s s political economy.

title: Vote-buying: High cost of politics is pricing out people with integrity – Inusah Fuseini
body: Former Tamale Central MP Inusah Fuseini says the growing cost of politics is pushing people with integrity out of public life and fuelling corruption. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he warned that the demand for money was narrowing political participation. Women, young people and people with valuable skills were being priced out. His comments come amid reports of widespread vote buying during the NDC’s latest internal executive elections. “It is a fact that what is happening is excluding a lot of people from the political space,” he said. “Those heavily impacted by what is happening are women and the youth because they might not have the required resources to be able to do that.” Mr Fuseini said the financial burden was also discouraging people whose integrity and reputation could benefit the country. He warned that heavy political spending creates pressure to recover the money after gaining power. “A politician is not an NGO and so when people spend that amount of money, they expect to recoup that, and that fuels corruption on a national scale.” The former NDC legislator said efforts to tackle inducement in internal elections had exposed a gap in the party’s constitution. According to him, the constitution did not clearly give the relevant party bodies authority to handle such cases. That leaves disciplinary action open to challenge. “In fact, the committee had said, our committee had said that having admitted that that thing had happened in the elections, there was a need for sanctions, but also appreciated the fact that there was no legal mechanism in our constitution to deal with that.” Fuseini said the committee was considering which institutions should handle complaints and what should count as inappropriate financial support. “How much money can we say is appropriate in the circumstances? If somebody gives a delegate GH¢200, is it an inducement or what is it?” He also raised the difficulty of dealing with payments described as transport support when the amounts exceed reasonable travel costs. The proposed framework could give constituency councils of elders authority to act or refer cases to the party’s national headquarters. Recommendations would feed into the party’s constitutional amendment process. “So yes, it’s a work in progress.”

title: Brazilian lawmakers call for Bolsonaro to be stripped of Senate seat — TASS source
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 28. /TASS/. Several Brazilian lawmakers have called for Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election, to be stripped of his Senate seat following his flight to the United States, a source in the South American country’s National Congress told TASS.
"His career is over. Several lawmakers have already called for Flavio Bolsonaro to be stripped of his Senate seat following his flight to the United States," the source said. The source added that lawmakers were also demanding an immediate suspension of the politician’s salary payments.
It was reported earlier that Flavio Bolsonaro had secretly left Brazil in defiance of an order by Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes to surrender his passports as part of a criminal investigation into money laundering allegations.
Brazil held the second round of its presidential election on October 25, with incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro competing for the country’s top office. The politician fled the country as the votes were being counted, prompting sharp criticism from both his political opponents and his own allies.

title: US energy secretary says further diesel supplies from Russia possible
body:
NEW YORK, October 28. /TASS/. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright has not ruled out additional shipments of diesel fuel from Russia in the future.
"Quite possibly," he said in an interview with CNBC when asked whether more tankers carrying Russian diesel fuel would follow.
On October 9, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump held a telephone conversation during which they discussed, among other things, supplies of petroleum products. Putin said Moscow had reaffirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.
Earlier on Tuesday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russia had already dispatched three tankers carrying Russian diesel for export, with a fourth scheduled to depart on Thursday.
Russian companies could export 500,000 metric tons of diesel as early as October under agreements covering supplies to the US and global markets, Novak said, adding that Rosneft could account for the bulk of the exports.

title: Sanctions equal economic terrorism, Iran tells UN
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iran's UN envoy said unilateral sanctions amount to economic terrorism and that blockades imposed by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law.
Iran's chargé d'affaires to the United Nations, Gholamhossein Darzi, said unilateral sanctions amount to economic terrorism and that blockades imposed by armed force are acts of aggression under international law.
Speaking at a UN General Assembly meeting on the need to end US economic, commercial and financial sanctions against Cuba, Darzi said it was the 34th time the assembly has declared its firm opposition to unbridled unilateralism, reckless foreign policies and unilateral coercive measures imposed by a government that considers itself above international law while continuing systematic and severe violations.
Darzi said unilateral sanctions, including those states impose independently, are rooted in unilateralism and coercion and therefore endanger multilateralism, destabilize international relations and undermine the UN Charter and international law.
He said the sanctions, as a tool for collective punishment of targeted nations, violate fundamental human rights, obstruct peace, weaken the right to development and block a just, peaceful and equitable international order.
Darzi said more than six decades of unilateral US sanctions and blockade against Cuba are a clear example of coercive pressure against a sovereign state, imposing widespread suffering on its people, undermining their fundamental human rights and hindering their development.
He said the intensification of these measures under the hypocritical pretext of "promoting democracy" reveals the deep contradiction between claimed goals and devastating humanitarian consequences. This approach, he said, instrumentalizes democracy rather than promoting it.
No government has the right to dictate the political future of an independent nation, Darzi said. From any perspective, such policies and actions, including economic warfare, are illegal, immoral and inhumane. The illegal and inhumane blockade that has lasted decades must end immediately, the imposing government must fully compensate the Cuban people for all damages, and all those involved in perpetuating these policies must be held accountable, he said.
Darzi said the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has itself faced aggression and the consequences of US economic pressure and blockades, once again declares its clear and firm opposition to any sanctions against independent and sovereign states, including Cuba.
He said such sanctions harm ordinary people, especially women, children and the elderly, undermine their health, security and welfare and create serious obstacles to development, which is necessary for the full enjoyment of human rights. These measures, by instrumentalizing the "human rights" of a nation, in fact grossly violate the human rights of that same nation. This is not a defense of human rights but blatant hypocrisy, he said.
Darzi recalled the US president's so-called "help" promise to the Iranian people, saying: "Help is on the way," and days later, on his orders, US forces bombed an elementary school in Minab, ruthlessly killing 168 children aged 7 to 12.
He said the UN General Assembly must compel the United States to implement dozens of resolutions adopted with the overwhelming support of the international community that reject the Cuban blockade and call on the US to end its economic, commercial and financial blockade. The serious legal consequences of unilateral coercive measures for the international legal order must not be ignored or underestimated, especially in the current turbulent international environment, he said.
Darzi said the UN Charter, as stated in Articles 1 and 2, is founded on the principles of sovereign equality, international cooperation and the development of friendly relations among nations. Unilateral coercive measures violate all these principles as well as the principle of non-intervention, especially when their aim is to force states to change their domestic policies, while Article 2(7) prohibits intervention in matters essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of states.
He said invoking human rights can in no way justify measures that impose widespread suffering on innocent people, since sanctions imposed in the name of protecting human rights themselves violate rights such as health, food, development and a dignified life.
These measures target ordinary people and in practice act as a form of collective punishment, hitting the most vulnerable hardest, he said. This is not protection of human rights but denial of human rights through economic pressure, a instrumentalization and weaponization of human rights.
Darzi said that while the Charter considers international cooperation necessary to solve global problems and promote friendly relations among nations, unilateral coercive measures instead strengthen confrontation, deepen divides and weaken the foundations of peaceful coexistence.
He said these measures directly conflict with the text, spirit, subject and purpose of the Charter. Sanctions are a form of economic terrorism, while blockades enforced by armed force constitute acts of aggression under international law, he said. Despite differences in form and severity, these measures share a deeply worrying feature: they undermine the sovereignty of states, cause human suffering and substantively violate international law, and are therefore both illegal and illegitimate.
Darzi said a policy that sacrifices the welfare of millions for political ends is incompatible with the principles of humanity, morality and international solidarity.
He reaffirmed Iran's firm solidarity with the government and resilient people of Cuba in their struggle against the blockade and other unjust coercive measures. Iran will continue to support the elimination of unilateral coercive measures and calls on the assembly to intensify efforts to end these measures immediately, including sanctions against Cuba.
The time has come to end these illegal and inhumane measures, Darzi said. Their continuation is not only a failure of international responsibility but a clear manifestation of humanitarian and moral bankruptcy.

title: Iran slams West attempts to whitewash U.S. misconduct
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iranian Foreign Ministry Spokesman Esmaeil criticized certain states for attempting to whitewash the US misconduct in violating its commitments.
"Washington’s contempt for diplomacy is once again laid bare. President Trump’s admission that he never believed in the Islamabad MoU and considered it a waste of time exposes the hollowness of their diplomatic commitments. For Iran, this is nothing new. Washington has a long record of reneging on its commitments and treating international obligations as disposable whenever they become inconvenient," Baghaei posted on X.
"There is absolutely no justification for European states and other apologists for Washington to continue whitewashing U.S. misconduct and shielding it from accountability."
"Broken commitments cannot be excused, international law cannot be applied selectively, and no amount of political spin can absolve Washington of accountability."

title: Putin and Pezeshkian Honor Khamenei, Killed in US-Israeli Strikes, and Challenge US Influence
body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that the Middle East could resolve its conflicts without the US, as Tehran and Moscow pledged to deepen an increasingly consequential partnership spanning military cooperation, energy and regional security.
Speaking on the sidelines of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, Pezeshkian thanked Putin for Russia’s political and economic support and called for closer cooperation among countries facing US sanctions.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“I believe we are capable of resolving our problems in the region without relying on the US,” Pezeshkian said.
He argued that Washington’s actions were encouraging Iran and Russia to work more closely together and strengthen a multipolar international order.
“Our trade is expanding and growing day by day. US actions in the region make it easier for us to move towards greater multilateralism and strengthen our cooperation with you and other countries subject to unilateral US sanctions,” he said.
The statements highlighted the deepening relationship between two governments whose military cooperation has already had direct consequences for Ukraine.
Iran has supplied Russia with drones and ballistic missile technology used to support its invasion of Ukraine, according to US and European authorities. Moscow, meanwhile, has reportedly provided Iran with military equipment, drone technology and intelligence assistance amid its confrontation with Washington and Israel.
The cooperation has raised concerns that technology and battlefield experience gained in Russia’s war against Ukraine could also strengthen Iranian military capabilities in the Middle East.
The Russia-Iran relationship has evolved beyond diplomatic coordination and economic cooperation into an increasingly important military partnership.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Iranian-designed Shahed drones have become a major component of Moscow’s long-range strike campaign.
Russia subsequently established domestic production and modified the drones, improving their capabilities for use against Ukrainian targets.
US and European officials have reported that Russia may be transferring upgraded Shahed drones back to Iran, incorporating improvements developed during the war in Ukraine.
During Tuesday’s talks, Pezeshkian expressed confidence that Moscow and Tehran could deepen cooperation across several sectors, explicitly including security and military affairs.
He thanked Putin for supporting Iran politically and economically, arguing that US pressure had created greater incentives for countries under sanctions to cooperate.
“After the Americans began taking such aggressive steps in the region, it became clear to everyone that we must work toward creating a multipolar world,” Pezeshkian said.
His remarks came amid the continuing confrontation involving Iran, the US and Israel, which escalated with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran last week. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi subsequently said the two countries had never worked so closely.
Both leaders paid tribute to Iran’s late Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
Addressing the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, Pezeshkian praised Khamenei’s foresight, initiative and support for the organization, describing his contribution to its development as substantial.
Putin echoed the tribute, crediting Khamenei with playing an active role in establishing the forum.
“You rightly recalled the role of the former spiritual leader of the Iranian people, Ayatollah Khamenei, who was indeed one of the active participants in establishing our forum,” Putin said.
“We rightly remember him with gratitude.”
Putin used the meeting to emphasize the economic foundations of the partnership.
He said bilateral trade increased by 10.4% during the first eight months of 2026 and reaffirmed Moscow’s commitment to ongoing joint projects.
“We are fulfilling all our obligations under all our projects,” Putin said.
The Russian president highlighted continued construction at Iran’s Bushehr nuclear power plant, where Russia is a major technology and construction partner.
He also noted that nearly 10,000 Iranian students were enrolled at Russian universities.
Pezeshkian announced that Iran had cleared the way for Russia’s state television broadcaster VGTRK to establish a bureau in Tehran, following discussions during Lavrov’s recent visit.
The expansion of Russian state media operations would add another dimension to an increasingly broad relationship involving government institutions, energy companies and security establishments.
At the gas exporters’ summit, both presidents criticized Western sanctions and efforts to restrict their countries’ participation in international energy markets.
Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of undermining global energy security through military attacks on Iranian infrastructure and restrictions affecting the country’s energy exports.
He urged major gas-producing countries to oppose what he described as destabilizing unilateral measures.
Putin echoed those criticisms, arguing that Europe’s efforts to reduce dependence on Russian gas were harming European industries and households.
“Any attempts to exclude Russia from the global gas market or restrain the development of our industry carry serious consequences,” he said.
The Russian president accused European governments of imposing excessive costs on their own economies by rejecting Russian energy supplies.
The EU has pursued restrictions on Russian energy imports as part of broader efforts to reduce the revenue available to Moscow for financing its war against Ukraine.
Despite Pezeshkian’s call to reduce US influence in the Middle East, Putin signaled that Moscow remained open to cooperation with American companies in the energy sector.
Speaking at the forum, Putin said Russia was considering joint projects with US partners in the Arctic.
“Until recently, European partners worked alongside us in our fields, and Chinese partners are still working there. Now, we’re exploring the possibility of joint work with American partners,” Putin said.
He did not identify prospective American companies or specific agreements.
