title: Rains to continue across parts of Oman
body:
Muscat: After two days of moderate to heavy rainfall across several parts of Oman, more thunderstorms, strong winds and possible hailstorms are forecast for Wednesday and Thursday, October 28 and 29, as local cloud formations continue to develop over the country. The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said convective cloud activity is expected to continue over the two days, mainly over the Al Hajar Mountains, with chances of extending to coastal areas of South Al Batinah, North Al Batinah, South Al Sharqiyah and Musandam governorates. According to the National Multi-Hazard Early Warning Centre, the ongoing weather activity is linked to the influence of a low-pressure trough, which is expected to continue affecting Oman until the end of October. The latest forecast maps indicate rainfall activity across several northern governorates, including parts of Muscat, Al Dakhiliyah and North Al Sharqiyah, with varying intensities. The CAA has also issued yellow-level alerts for moderate rainfall and downdraft winds in coastal areas and adjacent parts of Al Batinah. The rainfall alert takes effect at 12 noon on Wednesday, while the wind alert begins at 1 pm. Some areas could experience heavy downpours accompanied by strong winds and hail, increasing the risk of sudden runoff in wadis and low-lying areas. Authorities have urged residents and motorists to exercise caution, avoid crossing flooded wadis and follow official weather updates.

title: No clarity on Israel's next PM; Arab parties get 15 seats
body:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing bloc has widened its lead over the opposition in the country's parliamentary election, but remains short of a majority, Israeli media reported on Wednesday. With around 50% of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc was projected to win 56 of the 120 seats in the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, seven more than the opposition camp led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party was set to emerge as the largest party with 27 seats, followed by Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party with 21 seats. With neither side reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority, it remained unclear who would become Israel's next prime minister. Vote counting is continuing, with the country potentially facing weeks of difficult coalition negotiations. Arab parties were projected to win a combined 15 seats and could play a decisive role in determining who becomes Israel's next prime minister. Eisenkot would need the support of Arab parties to form a government, but several opposition parties have so far rejected such an arrangement. Initial exit polls after voting ended on Tuesday had suggested the opposition would finish ahead of Netanyahu's bloc. But the picture shifted overnight, with the prime minister's camp gaining ground. Netanyahu's coalition, which relied on far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties, won 64 seats in the last election in late 2022.Netanyahu calls for strong right-wing government Netanyahu called for a strong right-wing government early on Wednesday, projecting confidence despite the inconclusive election outcome. Eisenkot, meanwhile, said the Israeli people had "voted for change" and pledged to form a government quickly. "We have made history! The public has voted for change," Eisenkot told supporters. "The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu continuing to serve as prime minister of Israel," he said, adding that he would work to "respect the will of the people." "Israel is on the path to a new era - an era of hope, mutual responsibility and solidarity," Eisenkot said.Highest turnout in decades The election, the first since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent Gaza war, was seen as a watershed moment for the deeply divided country. At stake was whether Netanyahu would remain in power or whether his political opponents could muster enough support to bring about a change of government. In a sign of how much Israelis felt was at stake, turnout was exceptionally high, with the Central Elections Committee reporting the highest participation since 1999. The committee said 77.7% of the country's roughly 7.3 million eligible voters had cast their ballots. According to media reports, more than 70,000 Israelis travelled home from abroad to vote, as most citizens are not permitted to cast their ballots overseas.

title: Inzaghi blames fatigue as depleted Al Hilal suffer shock defeat at Al Shamal
body: Al Shamal produced the biggest result of their AFC Champions League Elite campaign on Tuesday, beating an understrength Al Hilal 3-1 at Al Bayt Stadium to hand the Saudi Pro League leaders their first defeat of the league phase. Algerian winger Riyad Mahrez marked his second start for Shamal with two assists. The Qatari side went ahead early through Wesley Said before Al Hilal captain Salem Al Dawsari levelled. Baghdad Bounedjah restored the hosts’ advantage three minutes into the second half, and Mohamed Ben Romdhane struck six minutes later to secure a memorable victory for David Prats’ side. The result leaves Hilal on six points from three matches, while Shamal move to five after drawing their opening two games. For Simone Inzaghi, it was a third defeat since taking charge of Hilal in the summer of 2025 and one that exposed the cost of a depleted squad. Midfielders Ruben Neves and Sergej Milinkovic-Savic were unavailable, while Gabriel Martinelli was injured and Crysencio Summerville suspended. Split open, finished in style. ✨ Wesley Saïd races through and sweeps a lovely left-footed finish beyond the goalkeeper to put Al Shamal ahead. #ACLElite | #SHAvHIL pic.twitter.com/HgbTWzsO3H — #ACLElite | #ACLTwo (@TheAFCCL) October 27, 2026 “We put in a fine first half, but in the second half, because of fatigue, we did not deliver the expected performance,” Inzaghi told Saudi newspaper Asharq Al Awsat . “We will return to Riyadh and prepare for our upcoming commitments.” Shamal needed only eight minutes to take the lead, with Said finding the bottom corner with a low strike after the hosts had made a bright start. Al Dawsari, making his first start of the season, restored parity in the 32nd minute when he finished a counterattack after Theo Hernandez had powered forward down the left. Al Hilal at their flowing best. ✨ A slick team move is rounded off clinically by Salem Al Dawsari to bring the visitors level. #ACLElite | #SHAvHIL pic.twitter.com/oifLL7EWdo — #ACLElite | #ACLTwo (@TheAFCCL) October 27, 2026 But Hilal were unable to maintain their level after the interval. Bounedjah struck three minutes into the second half off a Mahrez assist to put Shamal back in front before Ben Romdhane pounced from close range after more fine work from Mahrez to give the hosts a two-goal cushion. Al Dawsari admitted Hilal had been below their best. “This result is not satisfactory for us,” he said. “There were many mistakes, but we will review our mistakes and make up for them in the next match.” One touch is all Mateusão needs! 🤩 #ACLElite | #SAHvEST pic.twitter.com/bE6pe3Bjqf — #ACLElite | #ACLTwo (@TheAFCCL) October 27, 2026 Shabab Al Ahli joined fellow UAE club Al Ain on nine points with a 2-0 victory over Esteghlal in Dubai. Mateusao volleyed Sardar Azmoun’s looping cross into the net in the 68th minute before Juan Alvina sealed the win six minutes from time. The defeat ended the Iranian club's unbeaten start to the league phase and moved Shabab Al Ahli up to second place behind Al Ain. The top eight teams in each 16-team western and eastern league progress to the knockout stages, with the quarter-finals, semi-finals and final to be staged in Saudi Arabia in April and May.

title: Russell Brand told police he never had non-consensual sex
body: Russell Brand told police in interviews in response to allegations of rape and sexual assault that he had been “very promiscuous” in the past, but had never engaged in “non-consensual sexual activity”, a court has heard. Officers interviewed Brand four times between 2023 and 2025. The TV and media personality is currently on trial at Southwark Crown Court in London on three counts of rape and other offences. He denies all the charges. Jurors heard on Tuesday that he gave a prepared statement in each police interview. In November 2023, he said: “I have repeatedly stated publicly and written extensively that I led a very promiscuous life, that I have spent years openly denouncing. I have never engaged in non-consensual activity.” Russell Brand’s wife Laura accompanied him to court on Tuesday Brand went on to say the allegations were made in “a defamatory and fictitious documentary”, which he said contained “false and anonymised” interviews. He added that “subsequently both the media and the police publicly invited additional allegations to be made, which has resulted in further encounters to be invented or reimagined”. In court on Tuesday, the jury was also asked formally to find Brand not guilty of a charge of indecent assault. The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, said there was “insufficient evidence to support the charge of indecent assault”. This charge related to a woman who said Brand grabbed her arm and tried to drag her into a toilet in 2001 when she worked at MTV. The jury was then given an amended indictment, which charges Brand with attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to this charge. The prosecution will conclude on Wednesday morning before the defence is expected to start. Brand denies three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of attempted indecent assault.

title: Chaiseri wins Jackal order from Malaysian Army
body:
The Malaysian Army has ordered a fleet of vehicles to support the future arrival of CAESAR 155mm truck-mounted howitzers. This CASEAR support vehicle contract encompasses five vehicle types.
Platforms across four of the categories are believed to be based on Mercedes-Benz 6×6 chassis. These include a total of 18 long-wheelbase 155mm ammunition resupply vehicles, three forward repair vehicles, a medium recovery vehicle and two fire control coordinating vehicles.
The fifth vehicle type in the package is the Jackal forward reconnaissance vehicle developed by Thai firm Chaiseri. The Jackal 4×4 high-mobility vehicle can perform convoy escort, forward observation and reconnaissance for the Malaysian artillery regiment.
The contract for the Jackals, reportedly for 34 vehicles, was signed on 20 October 2026. The signatories were the Thai Defence Industry (TDI)-Chaiseri joint venture and Shafleena Venture from Malaysia.
Advanced Defence System (ADS) will perform final fit-out on the Jackals before eventual handover to the Malaysian Army. TDI-Chaiseri will commence deliveries next year, with production to be split between Malaysia and Thailand.
Unveiled at the Defense & Security exhibition in November 2025, the 5.2-tonne Jackal is known to have been adopted by the Thai military, with examples appearing near the fractious Thai-Cambodian border.
Powered by a 228hp engine and capable of carrying a 1,250kg payload, the Jackal is more capable than the commercial-vehicle-based 4x4s popular with Southeast Asian militaries.
Through its local partner ADS, KNDS will deliver 18 Renault-based, right-hand-drive CAESAR Mk 1 self-propelled howitzers to the Malaysian Army via a contract signed on 16 June 2026.
This made Kuala Lumpur the 15th CAESAR customer, and full delivery is to occur within four years. ADS will perform final fit-out and localisation at its facility in Pagoh, Johor.
Malaysia and Thailand have a history of cooperation. Indeed, Chaiseri previously supplied 20 customised First Win 4×4 protected vehicles to the Malaysian Army, where the platform is known as the Lipan Bara. That contract had been signed in 2015.

title: US urges Gulf allies to prepare for possible Iran strikes after midterms, report says
body: The United States has urged several Arab Gulf countries to prepare for a short but intense military campaign against Iran following next week's U.S. midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday, citing people briefed on discussions between Washington and regional governments. According to the report, the messages, delivered through diplomatic and military channels, are among a growing number of indications that the United States and Israel are preparing for another round of large-scale military operations against Iran.   U.S. President Donald Trump has not made a final decision on whether to launch an attack but is leaning toward a broad military operation after the midterms, the newspaper reported. Potential targets include Iranian critical infrastructure and nuclear facilities. The alternative remains a negotiated agreement with Tehran. Regional mediators continue diplomatic efforts to avert another confrontation, but those talks have yet to produce a breakthrough. The reported preparations include significant changes to the U.S. military posture in the Middle East. Officials familiar with the matter told the Journal that the U.S. military is moving a Patriot air defense system from Texas to the region to strengthen its defenses against potential Iranian missile attacks. American forces have also been relocated from bases considered vulnerable to attack as part of preparations for a possible escalation. According to several officials cited in the report, U.S. troops stationed in the region have replenished their ammunition supplies, while American bombers and fighter jets are being readied for potential strikes. An additional aircraft carrier strike group and a Marine Corps expeditionary force are expected to join the U.S. military buildup next month, the newspaper reported. They would augment an armada of roughly 20 warships already operating in the Middle East, although some of the incoming vessels could replace ships currently deployed in the region rather than increase the overall number. Netanyahu: 'This is not over' The Journal's report emerged around the same time that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed supporters early Wednesday following Israel's parliamentary election. Netanyahu's Likud party remained the largest in the Knesset, according to exit polls, although his right-wing political bloc appeared to have lost significant ground, leaving his ability to form a governing coalition uncertain.   Netanyahu opened his election-night address by focusing on Iran, declaring that Israel's confrontation with the Islamic Republic was far from over. "We have brought the Iranian regime to the brink of collapse," Netanyahu said. "And yet I tell you, this is still not over. Because as long as this fanatical regime exists, a regime that has defined its very purpose as destroying our existence, it will try again to destroy us." "We have the power, together with our wonderful friend President Trump, to remove this threat once and for all," he added. Netanyahu's remarks came shortly after his main rival Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the Yashar party, called on him to resign, describing him as "a caretaker prime minister without a mandate or public trust." Eisenkot made the comments Tuesday night, before dramatic overnight revisions to the election exit polls altered the projected balance between the political blocs. His warning reflected concerns among opposition figures that Netanyahu could seek to escalate security tensions to complicate efforts to replace him or pressure rival parties into joining an emergency government. Addressing senior defense and security officials, Eisenkot urged them to resist any attempt to involve the security establishment in political maneuvering. "Stand firm against any attempt to challenge you," he said. He then directed a warning at Netanyahu: "Do not dare use Israel's security for your political purposes."

title: Kyiv to allocate UAH 1 bn for water crossings over the Dnipro, Klitschko says
body:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced this on Telegram following a meeting of the Kyiv Defense Council, Ukrinform reports.
“We discussed the safety of bridge infrastructure in the capital at the Defense Council meeting amid the enemy’s escalating attacks on critical infrastructure. In particular, specialists from the city’s relevant institutions are developing additional technical solutions to preserve the structural integrity of bridge crossings over the Dnipro River,” Klitschko wrote.
He added that military officials had presented their proposals on the matter.
According to Klitschko, the meeting also addressed the implementation of a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro and access roads leading to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, which will also require approval from the Kyiv City Military Administration, among others. Following the government’s recommendation, the city will secure UAH 1 billion in funding for the project,” the mayor wrote.
The meeting also addressed the maintenance, construction, and equipping of shelters in the capital, including the installation of mobile shelters.
As previously reported, traffic on Kyiv’s Southern Bridge was restricted following a Russian attack on the capital. Experts are assessing the extent of the damage.

title: 2 men arraigned over alleged disrespect for corpse
body: The police on Tuesday dragged two men before an Iyaganku Magistrates’ Court in Ibadan, over alleged disrespect for a corpse. The defendants are Femi Moshood, 42; and Nureni Oyekunle, 57. They are standing trial on a three-count charge of conspiracy, disrespect to a corpse and conduct likely to cause a breach of the peace. The defendants, however, each pleaded not guilty to the charges. The prosecutor, ASP Femi Olanibi, alleged that the defendants committed the offences sometime in October in the Adegbayi area of Ibadan. (NAN) He alleged that the defendants were found in possession of bones and other body parts suspected to be those of a deceased man. Olanibi further alleged that the defendants showed disrespect to the corpse by possessing parts of the deceased’s body. The offences contravene the provisions of sections 38, 249(d) and 516 of the Criminal Law of Oyo State, 2000. The Magistrate, Mrs Gladys Olanrewaju, granted the defendants bail in the sum of one million naira each, with two sureties each in like sum. The court directed that one of the sureties must be a blood relation of the respective defendant, while the other must be a religious leader. She adjourned the case until Dec. 1, for hearing. (NAN)

title: Oman signs RO 904,000 contract for 21 homes in Habroot
body:
SALALAH: Oman has signed a RO 904,123 contract to build 21 homes for eligible families in Habroot, a remote community in Dhofar near the border with Yemen, with handover scheduled for late 2028. The agreement signed on Wednesday, October 28, moves a previously announced housing commitment into the construction stage. It sets out the cost and delivery timetable for homes in the Habroot Triangle area of Al Mazyunah, rather than adding a new allocation of houses. The Ministry of Housing and Urban Planning signed the agreement with Rikan, the Energy Sector Social Responsibility Development Foundation, in partnership with the Oman Charity Organisation (OCO). Eng Khalfan bin Masoud al Naabi, Director-General of Housing and Urban Planning in Dhofar, signed for the ministry, while Eng Mohammed bin Ali al Shanfari, Rikan’s Manager of Project Execution, signed for the foundation. The contract follows a wider funding agreement announced on October 7, under which Rikan pledged more than RO 2 million towards 71 homes. That programme includes the 21 units in Habroot and 50 other homes under the housing assistance programme across Oman. Construction is expected to take 730 calendar days. Each home will have 199 square metres of built-up space, with three bedrooms, a majlis (traditional reception room), living room, kitchen and service facilities, as well as a separate perimeter wall. The overall contract value is equivalent to about RO 43,054 per home, although this is an average of the agreement value, not a disclosed individual construction price. Construction work has been assigned to Omran Construction and Works, with Hima Engineering Consultancy responsible for site supervision and monitoring progress against the agreed timetable. Saeed bin Amer al Harasi, Head of the Housing Programmes Monitoring and Community Partnership Section at the ministry, said the project followed a nationwide study of villages, particularly remote settlements where families face housing needs and limited access to essential services. He said the circumstances of prospective beneficiaries had been examined and eligibility requirements checked before the project was approved. Ahmed bin Said al Maashani, Director of the Housing Department at the ministry’s Dhofar directorate, said field visits and the remote-villages study had helped identify the specific housing needs in Habroot. The development, he said, was intended to provide suitable accommodation and strengthen family stability in the border community. Al Shanfari said Rikan’s contribution formed part of the energy sector’s social responsibility commitments and its cooperation with government and charitable organisations to improve living conditions for eligible families.

title: 3 docked ‌over alleged theft of N4.2m
body: The police on Tuesday charged three people before an Abeokuta Magistrates’ Court in Isabo, over alleged house breaking and theft of N4.2 million, and other valuables. The defendants are: Ibrahim Habeeb, 25; Jamilu Ibrahim, 27; and Yunusa Zangi, 30. They pleaded guilty to a four-count charge of conspiracy, burglary, stealing and receiving stolen property. The prosecutor, Insp. Opeyemi Lawal, told the court that the defendants committed the offences on Sept. 25 at about 2.38am at No 1, Ola-Oti Street, Obasa Sabo, Abeokuta. (NAN) Lawal alleged that the first and second defendants unlawfully entered into the premises of the complainant, Miss Bolanle Johnson, and stole the cash sum of N4.2 million. He added that Habeeb and Ibrahim broke into the house through the ceiling. Lawal said the defendants also stole a Redmi mobile phone valued at N320,000 and a Techno Spark 20 valued at N320,000. Other items include two power banks valued at N76,000 and a gold earring valued at N40,000, property of Miss Bolanle. Meanwhile, the prosecutor alleged that the third defendant, Zangi, received the stolen items from Habeeb and Ibrahim, knowing them to be stolen. According to him, Habeeb and Ibrahim, unaware of the presence of security guards, were apprehended and subsequently handed over to the police. He said the offences contravened the provisions of section 390(4 a/b) 427 and 516 of the Criminal Code Vol.1 Laws of Ogun 2006. The Magistrate, Miss O.T. Odubanjo, granted the defendants bail in the sum of N500,000 each with one surety in like sum. Odubanjo said that the sureties must be registered bondsmen with the Ogun State Judiciary. She ordered that the defendants be remanded at the Ibara Correctional Centre pending the perfection of their bail conditions. The case was adjourned until Nov. 18 for hearing. (NAN)

title: Greece Seeks Freeze on Foreign Accounts in €120 Million Fraud
body: Greek authorities have requested the freezing of two bank accounts in Ireland and Denmark as part of an ongoing investigation into an alleged large-scale tax fraud and money-laundering operation involving the Choriatiko (Χωριάτικο) bakery chain and hundreds of other businesses managed by its 58-year-old owner, whom investigators identify as the alleged leader of a criminal organisation. The Directorate for Combating Organised Crime submitted the request through the Hellenic Police’s International Police Cooperation Directorate. Investigators suspect the organisation systematically evaded taxes and social security contributions while laundering millions of euros through a network of businesses and foreign bank accounts. Authorities identify €6 million in foreign accounts The two accounts stand in the names of foreign women whom authorities have not arrested. One has reportedly fled to Romania and the other to Germany. Investigators found that the accounts were linked to point-of-sale (POS) terminals used by businesses in Greece. The organisation allegedly channelled proceeds through these accounts before transferring the money back to Greece as foreign remittances. It then used the funds to purchase property, tourism businesses and other assets. Authorities have reportedly identified approximately €6 million in the two accounts. However, they expect the total amount to be considerably higher as the parallel investigation by Greece’s Anti-Money Laundering Authority examines additional bank accounts and safe-deposit boxes. Network operated 433 businesses across Greece According to findings from the police investigation, the organisation operated 433 businesses, mainly in Attica, Rhodes and Mykonos. Of these, 340 were food-service and entertainment establishments, including bakeries, cafés, coffee bars, entertainment venues, nightclubs and strip clubs. The remaining businesses included personnel-hire companies and other commercial operations. The organisation coordinated its extensive network from its headquarters in Attica, where an informal accounting office operated within its premises. A separate specialist accounting firm also supported the operation, with branches in Mykonos and Rhodes. Investigators say the organisation relied on more than 100 front men and women, supported by a close-knit group responsible for overseeing business operations, establishing legal entities and paying the nominees who formally owned or managed the companies. The organisation reportedly paid its front men and women around €1,000 a month. Many came from financially disadvantaged backgrounds or had health problems, making them vulnerable to exploitation. Investigators also found that the network listed fictitious individuals or deceased people as managers of certain businesses. Rhodes beach concessions formed part of the scheme The investigation has revealed that the organisation controlled 28 beach concessions on Rhodes alone. Police arrested 14 of the 59 suspects identified so far on the island. Investigators allege that the network manipulated public tenders for beach concessions administered by the Hellenic Public Properties Company and other state property authorities. The organisation allegedly submitted exceptionally high bids through companies registered in the names of front men, effectively discouraging competing bidders. In one example cited by investigators, a company secured a beach concession with a starting price of €100,000 by offering €1 million for a three-year lease. The company would typically pay the first instalment and then stop making payments for the remainder of the lease. Authorities would eventually record the outstanding debts with the relevant tax office, while the municipality could initiate procedures to remove the operator. Before enforcement measures could recover the money, the organisation allegedly suspended the company’s operations, leaving the debts in the name of the front man. It would then enter another tender through a new legal entity registered to a different nominee and repeat the process. The same method allegedly left unpaid social security contributions and other liabilities with individuals who had no assets, preventing the state from recovering the money. In another scheme, the organisation secured premises at selected beach concessions for periods of up to 10 years and subsequently sublet them to companies. Companies concealed the owner’s control Investigators allege that the 58-year-old suspect used his accounting offices to establish private capital companies, known in Greece as IKE, in the names of front men, often without their knowledge of the full arrangements. The network then opened bank accounts and established businesses that other members of the organisation secretly operated for the alleged leader’s benefit. According to police sources, the principal objective was to evade obligations to the state while shifting legal and civil liability onto the nominal owners and managers. The organisation allegedly used foreign bank accounts, including accounts in Iceland and Denmark, linked to the businesses’ POS terminals to conceal its revenue. Members then transferred the funds to companies controlled by senior figures in the organisation and presented the money as income from abroad. The network allegedly used the proceeds to purchase properties, land, vehicles and investment products. Investigation identifies approximately €120 million in unpaid obligations Police estimates indicate that, over the decade covered by the investigation, the organisation systematically failed to meet obligations totalling approximately €120 million. The estimated losses and unpaid liabilities comprise: €38.8 million in unpaid employer social security contributions to Greece’s EFKA social security agency. €38 million in debts relating to state repayable advances and payroll taxes. €43 million in concealed taxable income, including unpaid value-added tax (VAT) and income tax. Investigators say the organisation adapted its methods to the type of business it operated, consistently seeking to avoid payments to the state. The investigation remains ongoing, with authorities examining additional accounts and assets to establish the full scale of the alleged operation. title: Alleged fake lawyer nabbed after 10 years of impersonation
body: The Police Command in Ebonyi has arrested a man, Ugwumba Enyinnaya, for allegedly impersonating and practising as a lawyer for more than 10 years. The Police Public Relations Officer (PPRO), SP Joshua Ukandu, disclosed this in a press statement issued in Abakaliki on Tuesday. Ukandu said the arrest followed a discreet investigation by operatives of the command after receiving a petition bordering on alleged obtaining of money by false pretence. According to him, the petitioner, Mr David Chukwu, alleged that the suspect collected N650,000 from him in March 2026 to facilitate the processing and approval of a street-naming request in Ohaozara Local Government Area of the state. He said the suspect allegedly presented himself as a lawyer with years of legal experience while collecting the money. Ukandu said preliminary investigations following the arrest revealed that the suspect had allegedly been parading himself as a legal practitioner in spite of lacking the requisite professional qualifications. (NAN) He added that the suspect admitted during interrogation that he was not a lawyer. The police spokesman said a search of the suspect’s apartment led to the recovery of several exhibits, including a Nigerian Bar Association (NBA) seal and a portrait of the suspect dressed in barrister’s regalia. Other items recovered, according to him, included purported Bachelor of Laws (LL.B.) and Master of Laws (LL.M.) degree certificates bearing the name of Enugu State University of Science and Technology (ESUT). The police also recovered a barrister’s robe and wig, court judgments allegedly procured from the court, and various legal documents purportedly prepared by the suspect. Ukandu listed some of the documents as powers of attorney and deeds of conveyance. He said the suspect had been charged to court. The PPRO said the Commissioner of Police in Ebonyi, CP Hope Okafor, had commended the operatives for their diligence in uncovering the alleged impersonation. The police reiterated the need for members of the public to exercise caution when engaging individuals who claimed to be qualified legal practitioners. (NAN)

title: Time to switch to refillable water bottles, suggests EA
body:
Muscat: The Environment Authority (EA) issued a campaign urging people to choose stainless steel bottles over single-use plastic bottles for the benefit of both their health and environment. Steel bottles are BPA-free and suitable for repeated use when cleaned regularly besides reducing plastic bottle consumption and waste. They are also durable and long-lasting; insulated models keep water cold for hours. According to Greenspace, single-use plastic bottles are a major contributor to the global pollution as they take hundreds of years to decompose, releasing harmful chemicals into the environment during their slow breakdown. Producing plastic bottles requires vast amounts of fossil fuels and natural resources. From extraction to manufacturing, transportation, and disposal, the life cycle of these bottles generates a significant carbon footprint. By banning single-use plastic bottles, we can conserve energy and resources. The Environment Authority (EA) and the Foreign Ministry of Oman have banned single-use plastic water bottles inside their buildings, urging employees and visitors to switch to reusable containers.

title: GoldBod’s intervention in forex market gives cedi modest reprieve; one dollar going for GH¢12.15 at forex bureaus
body: The intervention by GoldBod in the foreign exchange market in the last three weeks has given the cedi a modest reprieve. The Board injected a US$130 million spot foreign exchange sale at GH¢11.60 per dollar to shore up the value of the local currency By the close of the fortnight, the local currency modestly clawed back some losses in the interbank market. It appreciated 1.20% against the US dollar and pound sterling to close trading at GH¢11.65 per US dollar and GH¢15.57 per pound sterling, respectively. It also gained 0.16% against the euro to sell at GH¢13.04. In the retail market, the cedi held steady against the American greenback to trade at GH¢12.10. It appreciated by 0.32% against the pound to sell at GH¢15.85 and 1.11% against the euro to trade at GH¢13.50 to the euro. As part of its October 2026 programme, GoldBod planned to supply US$1 billion to commercial banks and provide an additional US$500 million to the Bank of Ghana for reserve accumulation. The planned US$1.5 billion supply forms part of its broader foreign exchange intervention programme, which it says is aimed at supporting the recovery and stability of the local currency. Meanwhile, the cedi began this week going for GH¢12.15 against the US dollar in the retail market. Its year-to-date loss is about 9.0%.

title: 5 killed in attack on Adamawa communities
body: At least five people have been killed in a suspected Boko Haram attack on Gaya-Sikalmi and Gaya-Gartsanau communities in Hong Local Government Area of Adamawa State. Sources in the area said the attackers stormed the communities in the early hours of Monday, killing three residents in a gunfire, while two others died when an improvised explosive device (IED) planted along the main access road detonated. Several houses and business premises were also reportedly burnt during the attack, leaving the communities in distress. The chairman of Hong Local Government Area, Dr Aliyu Saad Yerima, who visited the affected communities on Monday to assess the damage and sympathise with the victims, confirmed the incident. Yerima condemned the attack and pledged to strengthen local security by increasing support for vigilantes, hunters and security forces to protect lives and property. He urged residents to remain vigilant and called for collective efforts to tackle terrorism, particularly the activities of informants allegedly aiding the attackers. The chairman also provided financial assistance towards the burial arrangements of the deceased and prayed for the repose of their souls. Security analysts said the communities remained vulnerable to attacks because of their proximity to Sambisa Forest, which they said provided terrorists with access to the area.

title: US warns $3.4 billion Airbus loan threatens aircraft trade truce
body: The US has warned that European financing for Airbus could threaten its aircraft trade truce with the European Union, saying officials still have not received details of the deal despite repeated requests. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer raised the issue in an October 26, 2026, statement challenging the European Investment Bank’s support for Airbus. The bank approved financing of up to €3 billion, approximately $3.4 billion, earlier this year. “This situation injects substantial uncertainty into transatlantic trade in the aerospace sector,” Greer said. He urged the EU to resolve the issue quickly to avoid violating the agreement. Airbus defended the loan, telling Reuters it was a “standard corporate financing facility” comparable to commercial loans it had previously arranged. A spokesman said the company was willing to share more information with governments and was working with the relevant authorities. The dispute concerns whether Airbus received financing on terms that give it an unfair advantage over Boeing. Under the aircraft agreement, Washington and Brussels committed to providing financing for large commercial aircraft development and production on market terms. The EIB announced the Airbus financing package on June 29, 2026. An initial €1 billion loan was signed as part of the broader €3 billion commitment, the largest corporate financing package the bank had approved. The money is intended to support Airbus research and development in France, Germany and Spain across commercial aviation, defense and space. Greer accused European governments of using support for Airbus to disadvantage US aerospace companies and workers. He said Washington had agreed to suspend tariffs in exchange for a commitment to market-based financing, but still lacked the information it needed about the EIB deal. Boeing had asked the Trump administration in July 2026 to seek more information about the loan, Reuters reported. The EIB has denied offering unusual support, while Airbus Chief Financial Officer Thomas Toepfer previously said the financing was obtained at market rates. The US and EU agreed in June 2021 to suspend tariffs arising from their aircraft subsidy dispute for five years. They also established a working group to address disagreements and committed to greater transparency in government-funded aircraft research. That agreement required more than commercial terms for loans. Both sides also pledged to avoid research funding or other manufacturer-specific support that would harm the other side’s aircraft industry. The tariff pause was extended this summer, according to Greer’s statement. Washington is now seeking details of the Airbus financing to determine whether Europe is honoring its commitments under the agreement. title: Deaths in detention cells in Nigeria were entirely preventable, inquiry finds
body: An inquiry into the deaths of 33 detainees in Nigeria’s Minna state has found they died as a result of severe overcrowding, poor ventilation and failure by officers to respond to distress calls. Forensic and medical evidence showed the “entirely preventable” deaths had resulted from acute respiratory failure linked to prolonged confinement, aggravated by heat stress and dehydration. The evidence did not support initial claims of a disease outbreak. The detainees were found dead on 17 September while being held by the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps on suspicion of illegal mining. The investigation found that the mining sites had been licensed. Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said those found responsible for the deaths would face the full force of the law. He added that investigators arrived after the detention hall had been cleaned, raising concerns about possible attempts to compromise evidence. Implicated officers will face suspension, and the report would be forwarded to the Attorney General of the Federation for further legal action, Tunji-Ojo said. The investigating committee found that the raid on the miners had been conducted without an approved operational order, proper planning or consultation with the Mining Marshals Unit. It said that 50 detainees had been held in a cell measuring about 20 sq m, with no running water or functioning toilet, and inadequate food, drinking water and airflow. Adults and minors were detained together, and some detainees were held beyond lawful detention periods. Officers reportedly ignored repeated calls for help, despite a medical worker having raised concerns about the conditions. “Detainees repeatedly banged on cell doors and walls, shouted for assistance and pleaded for water,” said the head of the investigating team, Jonathan Kure. “These distress calls were heard by officers assigned to nearby duties… but were not acted upon.” Kure said the detention conditions amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. “The tragedy demonstrates the consequences of systemic disregard for detention standards, supervisory responsibilities and the welfare of persons in custody,” he added. The investigating committee also recommended compensation of 30m naira (£16,683; $22,285) for each of the bereaved families and 10m naira for each survivor.

title: Lumby to hold mayoral byelection after two back-to-back elections
body:
Kevin Acton is no stranger to election victories, but winning two elections just one week apart is a first for the longtime Lumby mayor.
Acton won re-election as mayor in the municipal election on October 17 before securing a provincial seat as the Conservative MLA for Vernon-Lumby on October 24.
He says he had planned to run provincially but expected the opportunity to come much later.
“All along, the plan was to run provincially if I got the nod from the party,” Acton said. “We just expected it to be two years from now, not a week after the election.”
Acton had previously said he would accept the provincial seat if he won both races and step down as mayor.
He said his decision was driven in part by a desire to improve the relationship between local and provincial governments.
“I absolutely love the job, love the community,” Acton said. “But there’s been some frustrations in dealing with provincial government that I think I can really help direct the province towards mending.”
He also pointed to what he described as ongoing tension between the province and local governments.
Acton’s departure means Lumby residents will soon be heading back to the polls for a third time to choose their mayor in a byelection.
“Sort of, but you’ve got to do what you’ve got to do,” resident Ann Verhage said when asked whether she was experiencing election fatigue.
Another resident, Paul Gilfillan, said he was not particularly concerned about another trip to the polls, while Irene Yaremcio joked that she was getting tired of voting and hoped it would be the last time.
The byelection is not expected to take place until the new year.
“We would be looking at the end of January, early February as a voting day,” said Bobbe Koenig, the village’s chief financial officer and acting administrative officer.
It means Lumby will go several months without an elected mayor.
“Once Kevin moved on to that MLA seat, we would have an acting mayor system similar to when he goes on vacation, ” Koenig said. “So the councillors that were in place would step on up on a rotating schedule that’s already established.”
Koenig estimates the byelection will cost between $5,000 and $10,000.
Acton has pledged to cover the cost personally, saying he does not want the expense to fall on Lumby taxpayers.
“It was the situation I was put in,” Acton said. “So I joke around sometimes and think that maybe David Eby should pay for half of it as well but I don’t think that’s going to happen. But no, I don’t want to put that responsibility on the taxpayer of Lumby.”
Acton is expected to be sworn in as the Conservative MLA for Vernon-Lumby in mid-November, formally beginning his transition from municipal politics to the provincial legislature.
I feel really excited about the final, the way it all worked out in the end,” Acton said. “I’m really excited to get to work.”

title: Controversial Islamic cleric shot dead in northern Nigeria
body: A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina. Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC. The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said. It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death. It is widely believed in Islam that a person’s soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the Day of Judgement; if not, it is tormented. This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the Prophet Muhammad’s spoken words and actions. This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge for interpreting the Quran, the central religious text of Islam. But Musaylima based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam’s holy book, questioned some of the hadiths, and did not believe that the dead were reawakened. He was jailed for nine months because he teased respected scholars about their belief in this hadith and other teachings. Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching in Quranic schools at age 13. He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies. At home, he had a studio where he recorded videos of his teachings to broadcast on social media for his followers. The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria’s population. Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years. For Masussuka’s efforts, Nigeria’s Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year. Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria – several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009. Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, and the secular government, and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.

title: It’s time to set ego aside: Netanyahu, Eisenkot must form unity government - comment
body: Israelis went to the polls in extraordinary numbers on Tuesday, delivering an election result that, according to initial exit polls, left neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to forming a government.The projections put both blocs around the 50-something mark, with Arab parties slowly approaching a historic 20 seats.The figures are preliminary, and the final seat distribution could still change. Nevertheless, they raise a question that neither leader can easily avoid: What happens when two rival political camps emerge from an election without the parliamentary majority needed to govern?One possibility is a national unity government bringing Netanyahu and Eisenkot together.The truth is, politicians lie, and Israel's politicians are no exception.But there are some ideals we cannot stray from in a post-October 7 world, and the next Knesset cannot set itself up to be held hostage by one faction, be they Haredim (ultra-Orthodox) or Arabs.Eisenkot and Netanyahu must form a true unity government The solution is simple: Eisenkot and Netanyahu must set their differences aside to form a true unity government.The mythical broad Zionist government we've heard so much about. The chance is here, within our reach.The only roadblock is the ego of man.The same ego, by the way, that saw thousands of votes trashed because too-small parties refused to face the music and back out.Too good to be trueSuch an arrangement would require significant compromises from both leaders, who have spent the campaign presenting competing visions for Israel's future.For Eisenkot, entering a government alongside Netanyahu would raise difficult questions about his campaign commitments, particularly his criticism of the prime minister's leadership and the government's responsibility for the failures surrounding October 7.For Netanyahu, partnering with Eisenkot would require negotiating with a political rival whose rise has challenged Likud's dominance and whose supporters have demanded major changes to the country's leadership and priorities.These differences cannot simply be dismissed as personal animosity or political ego. They concern fundamental questions about accountability, democratic institutions, national security, and the direction of the state.The high turnout, reported at 77.7%, demonstrated the importance voters attached to the contest. But participation alone cannot resolve the disagreements reflected in the resulting parliamentary math.True unity seems too good to be true. After all our country has been through, can anyone really compromise? Of thinking outside of yourself and doing what's best for the country.The coming negotiations will test not only the two leaders' willingness to compromise, but also whether their respective parties and potential coalition partners are prepared to accept such an arrangement.Israel's voters have participated in the democratic process. The responsibility for interpreting the result and translating it into a functioning government now passes to their elected representatives.Whether a Netanyahu-Eisenkot unity government can meet that responsibility remains an open question. What Tuesday's election has made clear is that neither leader can resolve the country's political deadlock through declarations of victory alone.The precedent for cooperation already exists.Eisenkot served in Netanyahu's emergency wartime government following October 7, before departing alongside Benny Gantz in June 2024.That experience demonstrated that political rivals can participate in the same government during a national crisis. They simply need to realize that, even without missiles, we are in a crisis.Whether the vote was cast for Netanyahu or Eisenkot, we the people voted for stability.We voted for peace and unity.It's up to them to deliver it.

title: Liverpool v Chelsea: Alexander Isak rediscovers scoring touch after dismal start to life on Merseyside
body: As he started at a new club, hot on the heels of a controversial exit from his previous club, Alexander Isak's beginning at Liverpool was nothing short of disastrous. Having effectively gone on strike to force through a move from Newcastle United to Merseyside, the Swedish striker was in the spotlight last summer. A lack of pre-season training meant he entered the campaign lacking sharpness. Things went from bad to worse when he broke his fibula just 14 minutes after coming on as a second-half substitute – having just scored – during Liverpool's win at Tottenham Hotspur in December. It was only his 10th Premier League appearance of the season for Arne Slot's reigning champions. He managed a meagre four goals in 22 appearances across competitions in his first season at Liverpool. The previous season, at Newcastle, Isak had scored 27 goals in 42 games. Serious questions were being asked about whether he could rediscover the scoring touch that encouraged Liverpool to fork out a British-record £125 million . “It is quite an understatement to say he's had a tough year,” Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk said of Isak in April. “But now he is fit, and we all know what he can bring, and he shows it in training and in games as well. “It is about getting games, confidence, but obviously scoring goals as a striker – that's the main trigger for him. I'm not worried at all about him whatsoever.” Slot was sacked over the summer – paying the price for a disappointing campaign, just one year after winning the title – and replaced by Andoni Iraola , who would need Isak to lead his line. Fellow centre-forward Hugo Ekitike was expected to be out of action until December after rupturing his Achilles tendon in April's Uefa Champions League exit to holders Paris Saint-Germain, which also saw Isak make his first start in four months. As it turned out, Isak appears to be relishing the responsibility. On Sunday, he was in the right place to prod home Bradley Barcola's cross to seal a 2-0 victory over an in-form Brighton side for what was the 27-year-old's sixth goal in seven Premier League games. Only Erling Haaland (nine in eight games) has scored more so far. “I feel good, I feel like I’m in a good place,” said Isak last month. “It has been challenging, of course, with a lot of injuries especially. But there have been some beautiful moments as well, good learning moments. I take all of that as stuff to help me get better and get stronger, not looking back too much and just focusing on what’s ahead.” Notably, all of Isak's goals have come inside the penalty area, with most in or around the six-yard box, showing his poaching skills are intact but, more importantly, Iraola is setting up the team to get the best out of his striker. Ahead of their League Cup last-16 tie against Chelsea at Anfield on Wednesday, the Reds manager talked about how Isak now “feels the trust of everyone” at the club following a tough start to his Anfield career. “Everyone trusts [that] if he moves into good positions he will score goals,” the Spanish coach said. “But I always tell him he has to help us so we can give him the chances, and I think he understands that necessity. I hope that can continue at the same level.” The victory over Brighton lifted Liverpool into the top four and above Chelsea, with Iraola ready to rotate his squad as they juggle a packed fixture schedule. “There will definitely be changes, but we want to win the game,” he added. “We want to be competitive.” Chelsea, meanwhile, are still struggling for consistency under new manager and former Liverpool player Xabi Alonso, who is also a close friend of Iraola. Alonso's team sit just one place and two points behind Liverpool in the Premier League, but fell to a frustrating London derby defeat against Tottenham Hotspur on Saturday. The game at Stamford Bridge had been goalless for 77 minutes until 21-year-old Chelsea goalkeeper Mike Penders, making his first start after Emi Martinez suffered a fractured jaw, managed to punch the ball into his own net. That was quickly followed by Cole Palmer being sent off for a second booking, before a frustrating evening was completed by Mathys Tel making it 2-0 with three minutes left. “We were not happy for sure with the result and performance,” admitted Alonso. “It was a big game, and it could have been better. Now we have moved on and the focus is just on Liverpool.” It has been a rollercoaster start for Alonso, whose team have the third-highest goals tally in the top flight (17), but also the joint third-worst defensive record (with 15 conceded). Alonso will be without the suspended Palmer for the trip north, while top scorer Joao Pedro, who missed the Spurs loss with a thigh problem, is set “to be out for a few weeks" according to the Spaniard. “We will miss him [Pedro], but we have to be ready to deal with that and win games and be competitive with the players we have available … We have to be looking for solutions not for excuses.” As for Palmer's red card, Alonso added: “We spoke and for sure he knows the mistake he made. There are things you can avoid. I hope this is not going to be repeated.”

title: La Pleasure Beach management sues SSNIT, two hotels over demolition
body: The dispute over the management of La Pleasure Beach has taken a legal turn, with the beach’s management committee suing two hotel companies and the Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT) over the demolition of its office and other structures. In a writ of summons filed at the High Court in Accra on October 23, Stanley Anyetei Nunoo, who describes himself as Chairman of the Management Committee of La Pleasure Beach, is seeking declarations confirming the committee’s authority to manage the beachfront, regulate activities, issue licences and generate revenue from its operations. The suit accuses Hotel Investments (Ghana) Limited, La Palm Beach Hotel Limited and SSNIT of involvement in an operation that allegedly destroyed the committee’s management office and other licensed facilities, disrupting its work and affecting operators at the beach. The plaintiff describes the demolition as unlawful and is asking the court to determine whether the defendants had any legal basis for the action. Committee contests authority over beach At the centre of the case is a dispute over who has the legal authority to manage La Pleasure Beach. According to the statement of claim, the management committee was established following a Court of Appeal order dated July 21, 2022, which the plaintiff says dissolved an interim management committee set up by the High Court in April 2013. Mr Nunoo contends that the committee has since exercised management responsibilities, including issuing licences to operators, regulating activities and collecting revenue. The suit also challenges the position of the two hotel companies, which operate Labadi Beach Hotel and La Palm Beach Hotel. The plaintiff argues that the companies have no proprietary or possessory interest in La Pleasure Beach or its management, apart from an access licence granted by the committee. Demolition allegedly carried out at dawn The statement of claim alleges that security personnel from the Ghana Police Service and the Ghana Armed Forces entered the beachfront at dawn on or about October 2, 2026, and pulled down the committee’s management office and other structures. The plaintiff further claims that equipment, furniture, files, records and other property were destroyed or removed during the operation. Staff and licensed operators were allegedly driven away, disrupting the committee’s activities and the businesses operating under its authority. The suit maintains that the demolition took place without a court order or warrant and without prior notice or a hearing for the committee. Mr Nunoo is asking the court to establish the legality of the operation and determine the extent to which the defendants were involved in, or facilitated, the demolition. SSNIT’s concerns over beachfront activities The court action also refers to a press release issued by SSNIT on October 2, 2026, in which the trust said it had sought the intervention of the National Security Council Secretariat over what it described as persistent unlawful occupation, encroachment and unauthorised activities on the beachfront adjoining Labadi Beach Hotel and La Palm Royal Beach Hotel. According to the statement cited in the court documents, SSNIT said the hotels were part of its investment portfolio and that it had a responsibility to protect those investments for the benefit of contributors and pensioners. The plaintiff, however, alleges that the defendants jointly participated in or facilitated the demolition of the committee’s structures. The competing positions bring the management of the beachfront, the scope of the parties’ respective rights and the circumstances surrounding the demolition before the court for determination. The court is yet to determine the claims and reliefs sought in the action.

title: Painting that Paul Guiragossian refused to leave behind is on show in Abu Dhabi
body: Manuella Guiragossian recalls the shelling and gunfire, the family rushing out of the house and towards the shelters. She recalls the painting her father Paul would remove from the wall, from its place above the piano, and bring with him as if “it was a member of the family”. She remembers this detail as a speckle of warmth in an otherwise traumatic cycle during the Lebanese Civil War. As a young girl, she couldn’t understand why her father insisted on bringing the painting along every time they sought shelter. She couldn’t have been the only one. The sight of Paul Guiragossian in pyjamas, on crutches (he had lost his leg in a lift accident in 1974), leading his family to safety with a painting tucked under his arm must have struck many as strange. Amid the violence and absurdities of war, many must have seen Guiragossian’s protectiveness of his painting as an artist’s eccentricity. For the young Manuella, what was strange was not so much the fact her father wanted to protect his work. She knew how dedicated he was to his practice. What confounded her was the fact he always wanted to safeguard this particular piece, this one self-portrait. “I was wondering why it was this painting that was coming with us,” she says. “We are running, we are in a rush, we are trying to make it to the shelter. It is chaos, and this portrait is coming with us regardless.” The painting is one of the works featured in Paul Guiragossian: 100 Years of Art, an exhibition at Abu Dhabi’s Bassam Freiha Art Foundation running until January 17, 2027. It is also the cover image for the exhibition catalogue. The painting shows Guiragossian as a young man. His posture seems to be caught between two moods. One hand hangs from the armrest of his chair, the other holds a brush. His gaze is intense and unwavering. His shirt is unbuttoned, relaxed and wrinkled. The Guiragossian in the image is an artist intently observing himself. He is wary of being observed, yet also trying to exist outside his own eye. The tension is heightened by the dark reds and browns in the backdrop around his head, an ill-defined ring of fire that adds to the intensity of his look. The painting is being exhibited outside Lebanon for the first time. It was an emotional leap to let go of the work that has always remained within the family and the artist’s estate, Manuella says. Yet it was important to include the work in an exhibition that celebrates the centenary of the late artist’s birth. “After my father passed away, whenever we did retrospectives in Lebanon, this portrait would travel by hand with me or my siblings, and always come back by hand,” says Manuella, who is the president of the Paul Guiragossian Foundation, as well as an artist herself. “So you can imagine the emotions when the painting was packed and went outside Lebanon for the first time, the responsibility of letting go.” The painting was produced in 1948 – the same year that Guiragossian and his family were displaced from Jerusalem as a result of the Nakba . In the tumult of the displacement, the artist was forced to leave most of his works behind – among them a self-portrait that he regarded as one of his best at that time. The self-portrait he later produced was a memento of that painting, that experience of displacement – and perhaps of the experience of his parents, who had come to Jerusalem as survivors of the Armenian genocide. Guiragossian’s 1948 self-portrait is displayed in the opening section of his retrospective at the Bassam Freiha Art Foundation. The exhibition is segmented into different phases of Guiragossian’s life. Special attention is also dedicated to the women who influenced his life and career. The exhibition presents a portrait of the artist as a son, husband and father. “They are interconnected chapters, each dedicated to a specific time in the life of Paul Guiragossian,” says Michaela Watrelot, head curator at the foundation. “A lot of people know Guiragossian the artist. But we wanted to tell the story of his life through the women in his life. How his humanity translated into his work. No matter how iconic his works have become, they are rooted in the humanity of who Paul was as a person. We wanted to show works that people had rarely seen before, that may not be associated with Paul.” Guiragossian’s mother, Rahel, is the star of the opening section, In Search of Belonging. Ink and charcoal drawings of her are featured alongside an oil painting, also produced in 1948, that shows her in a palette similar to Guiragossian’s self-portrait. She seems to have bequeathed her son her eyes, yet her gaze is less intense – almost elsewhere. “The first chapter highlights the resilience of his mother and the influence she had on him,” says Watrelot, who co-curated the exhibition with Manuella. These works, along with archival images, give visitors a sense of how close Guiragossian was to his mother. The section also includes other self-portraits as Guiragossian sought to emulate the artists he looked up to in his youth. An oil-on-canvas piece, composed with thick brushstrokes and a subdued palette, features the artist looking out with a sideways glance reminiscent of paintings by Paul Gauguin. The charcoal drawing adjacent to it has feverish swirls and lines apparently inspired by Vincent van Gogh. These early works show an artist experimenting with media and techniques to find himself on paper and canvas. Earth tones dominate the oil paintings, and it is not until the following section – presenting works produced between 1950 and 1959 – that we begin seeing the first signs of the motifs that would become characteristic of Guiragossian, the vibrant colours that would become his emotional palette. “In the beginning, he was almost scared of using colours,” Manuella says. “He had a lot of sadness and pain, and couldn’t imagine using colours. All that changed when he got married and had children. His life became injected with colour.” Sure enough, the paintings he produced in the early to mid-1950s, though still dominated by earth tones, begin to show more vibrant hues. Two, in particular, are ablaze with a mesmerising yellow, which expresses tenderness in Maternité (1953) and anguish in Le Cycle de Vie (1955). Motherhood also manifests clearly as a focal interest during this period. Portraits of the artist's wife feeding their infant children allude to Christian iconography – a testament, Manuella says, to how Guiragossian considered “the mother as a sacred figure”. The archival images and posters in this section reference Guiragossian’s time in Florence, after he received a scholarship to the Accademia di Belle Arti. In 1958, he held a solo exhibition at Galleria d’Arte Moderna La Permanente, where he presented some of his first experiments with figurative abstraction. A few of those works are on show in this exhibition. Here, we see some of the earliest elongated figures, such as in La Famille (1957). The figures appear as colourful outlines, their insides left bare. Manuella says the approach earned praise from Italian critics who came to see the exhibition. The minimalism, she says, was enforced: Guiragossian simply did not have the money to buy more paint and so had no choice but to keep his figures unfilled. Interestingly, there are also works that do not seem like Guiragossian’s at first glance, such as Les Amies (1958) or Femmes en Conversation (1951). Yet we begin seeing here elements that Guiragossian would continue to develop, such as the abstracted figures, stripped of their features and instead depicted in their postural essences. A 1978 portrait of his wife, Juliette, is a highlight of the following section, titled Painting Humanity, which brings together works from 1960 to 1979. The two-metre-long painting shows Juliette poised and upright, but seemingly caught off guard. The colours, though restrained, are more vivid here, the brushstrokes more economical. Here, we begin to see works that are classic Guiragossian in style: vivid, elongated figures, silhouetted and huddled in groups, such as in the mournful Silence , painted in 1968, and the mirthful Rythme , painted in 1978. Physical and facial features are totally abstracted, with postures and colours filling the emotional spectrum of each work. La Lettre (1978) is a strong example. The painting shows children gathered around a mother as she reads from a letter. The child in the foreground appears to be on tiptoe. The letter may be a source of joy or sorrow – the painting can be read either way. But the family is nonetheless experiencing it as one, huddled together as a single dynamic mass, an unbroken assemblage of hues and brushstrokes. It is around this point in the exhibition that we see more of how fatherhood inspired Guiragossian 's work. While there were paintings of his wife and children in the preceding section, he seems to step into the frame through an archival image that is presented alongside portraits of Manuella. The photograph shows Guiragossian entertaining his daughter with a puppet. “During the war, my brothers and sisters travelled abroad,” Manuella says. “For a time, I was alone with my parents. During this period, I became extremely close with my father. There was a lot of complicity between us, inside jokes and humour.” The concluding section, Beyond Time and Form, exhibits the final, artistically intense years of Guiragossian’s life. His paintings ramp up in size. His figures loom over the viewer with the aplomb of Mesopotamian reliefs, albeit colourful, drawing from the people around him instead of mythological deities, but exalting them all the same. This is especially seen in Portrait de Famille and L’Echarpe , both of which were painted in 1986. Guiragossian’s last painting is presented here and was seen by him as the effective culmination of his practice. According to the exhibition catalogue, when Guiragossian finished this painting on November 20, 1993, he told Manuella that “he had finally managed to draw together the many strands he had grappled with as an artist his whole life”. With the achingly apt title of L’Adieu , the painting features a huddle of abstracted figures in thickly layered reds, greens and yellows, brushstrokes fervent in each form, each figure holding its independent logic of motion. What is particularly arresting are the feet of the figures, perhaps their only defined feature – alluding to Guiragossian’s paintings from the late 1940s, in which he depicted porters with enlarged feet. But the final painting of the exhibition is a self-portrait produced in the last year of his life, elegantly bracketing the show between two self-examinations. Here, however, Guiragossian’s gaze is a lot less confrontational. He seems at ease with himself, at ease with what he sees. It is the look of a person who, after experiencing displacement, war, grief, family and love, is intimate with the full spectrum of life, knows that hardship is unavoidable and knows how to find peace and fulfilment within. “There are so many stories, so many moments that are connected to the artworks,” Manuella says. “Once you know them, once you go a little bit behind the scenes, you start seeing how all this evolved gradually. So much humanity. So much beauty in the hardships and the hope. It’s all connected. And that’s what makes the beauty of a retrospective like this.”

title: US national debt hits record high of over $40.5 trillion
body:
WASHINGTON, October 28. /TASS/. The US national debt has surpassed a record $40.5 trillion, according to US Treasury Department data analyzed by TASS.
According to figures published by the department, US sovereign debt stood at $40.52 trillion as of October 26, an all-time high. The debt exceeded $38 trillion in October last year and crossed the $40 trillion mark in August this year, having increased by $20 trillion in less than a decade.
According to estimates by the Peterson Institute for International Economics, the country’s debt could reach $50 trillion in six years unless government spending or taxation is reformed.

title: The real test for medical AI is how many people it helps
body: As artificial intelligence advances at a rapid pace, it provokes both excitement and concerns. There are understandable questions on a number of issues ranging from the threat to jobs to the possibility of machines escaping human control . Yet its potential to improve lives is increasingly irrefutable – and nowhere is this more profound than in the fields of medical research and health care. Recent developments in the UAE illustrate what is possible. UK-based pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca, which relies heavily on AI and other technologies in its work, is investing $50 million in about 30 clinical trials with Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi, targeting cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases. It is also collaborating with American tech giant Oracle and M42, the Abu Dhabi-based tech-enabled healthcare company, to explore how AI and real-world medical data can improve hypertension diagnosis, recruitment for clinical trials and safety monitoring. Elsewhere, M42 has introduced Ossi , an AI platform designed to reduce doctors’ administrative burdens and give them more time with patients. By summarising medical histories and supporting clinical documentation, the system could help doctors focus exclusively on the person sitting in front of them. Research offers possibilities that are just as compelling. American biotech company Insilico Medicine , with scientists based in Masdar City, is using AI to identify potential treatments for blood cancer and develop a non-opioid pain killer. Clinical testing is, no doubt, necessary before their safety and effectiveness can be established, but AI’s ability to speed up the discovery of new drugs is promising. Medical progress should not be measured simply by how fast a drug is discovered, but also by how many people benefit from it – regardless of their socioeconomic status or where they live Technology is having an impact on preventive care, too. The Abu Dhabi Department of Health’s Project Cradle will study whether wearable smart rings can identify warning signs of premature birth among high-risk pregnancies. Another partnership, between the department and US-based wearable tech company Whoop , will explore sleep, cardiovascular health and ageing. Such initiatives are important as they anticipate illness, thereby helping people avoid possible later-stage complications and expensive treatments. All of these developments are coinciding with technology’s increasing ability to streamline public services and business operations. Oracle’s latest agentic AI systems , which take on complex tasks ranging from supply chains to shipping to restaurants, are a case in point. But when it comes to health care, the stakes are much higher. Of course, digitisation carries with it privacy and security-related risks with heightened cybersecurity attacks. Digital systems must, therefore, be equipped with stronger safeguards to protect sensitive medical information and maintain clinical oversight. They should also remain accessible to people with limited digital literacy. Accessibility should also mean ensuring that the benefits of the aforementioned advances do not become the preserve of wealthy patients and those with comprehensive health insurance. To achieve this, governments and insurance providers will need to make equitable access a central principle of health tech innovation. Medical progress should not be measured simply by how fast a drug is discovered, but also by how many people benefit from it – regardless of their socioeconomic status or where they live. Advances will really count when we can measure human lives saved or improved by the incredible technological leaps being made.

title: New Abu Dhabi clinical trials using AI to have ‘massive’ impact on health care
body: Oracle expects its new artificial intelligence partnership with AstraZeneca and Abu Dhabi’s M42 to have a “massive impact” on the region’s healthcare systems by cutting the time and cost of running clinical trials , according to a senior executive at the tech firm. Under the collaboration announced last week, AstraZeneca will pair its scientific development with Oracle’s cloud infrastructure and AI tools to speed up clinical research globally. The first programme with M42 focuses on hypertension care and research in Abu Dhabi. It will help clinical teams identify patients with uncontrolled hypertension (high blood pressure), implement care and improve recruitment for trials, the companies said. “It’s going to have a massive impact,” Seema Verma, executive vice president and general manager of Oracle Health and Life Sciences, told The National in an interview on the sidelines of the Oracle AI World event in Las Vegas. Drugmakers face pressure to lower prices, she said, and bringing a drug to market costs “billions and billions of dollars”, with recruiting patients and running trials among the biggest barriers. The aim is to “rethink how clinical trials are done from the time that you match the patient to the trial, to enrolling them into the trial, and then making the trials easier, faster to conduct”, Ms Verma said. “It’s a very exciting partnership … probably one of the first times you've seen a technology company, a provider, and a pharmaceutical company [come together].” Long gaps persist between scientific breakthroughs and drugs reaching the market, partly because data must be moved manually from electronic health records (EHRs) into the separate electronic data capture systems used for clinical trials – a lag AI is expected to help close. “Why do these need to be two different systems? What if we empowered every clinician to be able to participate in a clinical trial?,” she said. “I don't think anyone's attempting that in the world, but we feel pretty confident that this can be solved. “There's a lot of complexity to matching patients in clinical trials, and AI is the backbone,” she added. Ms Verma expects results within about a year, starting with whether the programme can increase trial participation and identify sites, and ultimately whether it can make trials run faster. The collaboration is expected to expand to projects in the US, Middle East and Europe. Abu Dhabi hotbed for clinical trials Abu Dhabi has become a centre for clinical research in recent years across areas such as oncology and Alzheimer’s, cardiovascular, renal and metabolic diseases. Last week, AstraZeneca separately revealed plans to invest $50 million in dozens of clinical trials in the UAE with Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi . In July, M42, Abu Dhabi’s Department of Health and US company Halia Therapeutics said they would carry out trials of a therapy that could prevent Alzheimer’s disease. M42 last week also launched Ossi, an AI platform built with Microsoft that is estimated to let doctors spend up to 60 per cent more time with patients. It will be available at seven M42 centres in the UAE and Bahrain. The Middle East is “incredibly innovative”, Ms Verma said. “A lot of the population has genomic testing, genomic sequencing has been done, so they're really positioned maybe to be the most innovative place in the world … they're very open to leveraging AI.” Oracle is also adding AI tools to its EHR system, including ambient listening that generates notes from doctor-patient conversations and helps with coding and diagnoses. “AI can automate all of those processes … so that means people are going to be able to access their healthcare providers more easily, get more real-time care, and hopefully that leads to better health outcomes for the patients and for the region,” Ms Verma said. The goal is to prevent disease, prevent the progression of disease, and have better outcomes, she added.
