Not a human replacement Healthcare systems globally are stretched as people live longer and doctors see more patients. “The healthcare system is not prepared for this increased demand, so AI brings a tangible solution to the table,” Ms Verma said. As AI adoption rises, organisations are setting up regulations to deal with the risks, and those using the data must be trained, she said. “If you are relying on AI, make sure you understand where that data came from – so transparency and double-checking. “It's not just putting out technology, but also training people to use the AI tools appropriately and effectively.” Humans have to make the final decision, “and I think this is especially important in health care because health is not an exact science; it’s an art and a science”, she said. AI can highlight the latest treatments, but factors such as patient preference must also be considered. “AI is a very powerful tool, but it doesn't replace humans,” Ms Verma said.

title: The name game: Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate bid tests the limits of US politics
body: El-Sayed, El-Sayeed, El-Sayad – for months, Abdul El-Sayed , an Egyptian American running for the US Senate for Michigan, has had his name mispronounced, sometimes deliberately. US President Donald Trump has frequently mocked his name and said he would call him "Mohammed". He has also faced relentless attacks over his Muslim faith and accusations of having ties to Hamas, the Muslim Brotherhood and Hezbollah – allegations he has vehemently denied. “I'm here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a United States senator,” Mr Trump said at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday. “And nine days from now, the people of Michigan are going to defeat Abdul Mohammed, I'll say it, a man who should never be allowed inside the halls of our great, beautiful Capitol building.” Mr El-Sayed, 41, a progressive candidate and physician, will face Mike Rogers , a Republican ally of Mr Trump, on November 3. If victorious, Mr El-Sayed will become the first Muslim to serve in the US Senate. Michigan is one of the most closely watched and hotly contested states in the midterm elections. The result of the race could help determine control of the Senate, where Republicans currently have a thin majority. At stake is Mr Trump's ability to advance his legislative agenda during his remaining two years in office. Michigan, experts say, is the quintessential purple state, a mix of Republican red and Democrat blue. Mr Trump has won it twice, but the last time a Republican won a Senate seat there was in 1994. It is also home to the largest concentration of Arab Americans in the US, a key constituency for Mr El-Sayed. The Israel question Mr El-Sayed, whose full first name is Abdelrahman, is a former public health official and his campaign has focused on universal health care and higher taxes for the wealthiest Americans. “He's an incredibly skilled debater, very effective on the stump, and he has a great command of social media,” said Jim Manley, a Democratic strategist. “I'm still concerned that independent voters aren't going to buy it, but we'll see.” Foreign policy has taken on unusual prominence in the race, becoming a fault line in a bitter debate over Israel and the war with Iran. The issue intersects with domestic concerns over inflation, petrol prices and the use of taxpayer money. Mr El-Sayed has described Israel's conduct in Gaza as genocide and opposes more military aid to America's long-time ally, breaking with the pro-Israel stance long associated with the Democratic establishment. He has said the US should instead prioritise domestic needs, such as education. In recent weeks, he has said Israel should not be considered a US ally, as its government drew Washington into the war with Iran. His opponent, Mr Rogers, 63, is a former US Army officer and FBI agent. He served in the US House of Representatives until 2015. He has campaigned on bringing manufacturing jobs back to Michigan and lowering the cost of food, petrol and everyday items. But his close alignment with Mr Trump has undermined his message. Mr Rogers is a strong supporter of Israel and backs continued US military aid, saying Israel has the right to defend itself against regional threats. The latest polls show the two candidates are neck and neck. They also indicate that Michigan voters, like voters across much of the country, are primarily focused on the economy and the high cost of living. “Trump is a vulnerability, gas prices are a vulnerability,” John Feehery, a Republican strategist, told The National . “It's not an easy state for Republicans to win, but if they do win it, it shows that they have a lasting coalition that can be successful." Aipac setback In a surprising turn , the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, the most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the US, said last week it would no longer endorse candidates or make direct campaign contributions. Instead, the group will continue operating through its affiliated super Political Action Committee, the United Democracy Project. The development comes amid growing criticism of Aipac, particularly within the Democratic Party, and declining support for Israel among Americans after the war in Gaza. Aipac's involvement in the Michigan race has been particularly contentious. Its super Pac spent more than $30 million seeking to defeat Mr El-Sayed in the Democratic primary and backing Representative Haley Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel. It was the organisation's largest single investment in a contest. Mr El-Sayed won the nomination in August, dealing a major setback to the pro-Israel lobby. Mr Rogers was initially wary of Aipac's involvement, amid concerns that the group's unpopularity could hurt his campaign. He later publicly welcomed its support. Last week, Aipac directed about $9 million to a group supporting Mr Rogers in a last-minute effort to boost his campaign, according to The Washington Post . The money was reported as independent political spending rather than a direct contribution to his campaign. 'The moment we've all been waiting for' During a forum in Ann Arbor, Michigan, on Monday, Mr El-Sayed spoke about promoting universal health care, tackling rising prices, slowing the proliferation of AI to protect jobs and raising taxes on billionaires. He also called for an end to unconditional foreign military aid. “It shouldn't be this hard in the richest, most powerful country in the world to afford a tank of gas or a second bag of groceries,” he told a cheering crowd. Mr El-Sayed was joined on stage by Independent Senator Bernie Sanders. “They can't debate Abdul on the issues, so what they are doing is attacking him because he is a Muslim,” Mr Sanders said. Hundreds of people, mostly university students, gathered in the auditorium. Most said they were drawn to Mr El-Sayed's domestic policy proposals. “I skipped class for this,” said Cal Karbowski, 20, a university student. He said he supported Mr El-Sayed's positions on health care and reproductive rights. But it is not just Mr Sanders – establishment Democrats are starting to fall in behind Mr El-Sayed as well. Last month, former vice president Kamala Harris campaigned with Mr El-Sayed in Detroit in a bid to unite Democrats behind his campaign. The move angered some of his supporters, who blame Mr Trump's predecessor, Joe Biden, for the war in Gaza, but the move underscored the party's efforts to bridge divisions over the issue. On Saturday, Mr Obama headlined a rally with Mr El-Sayed, in a major breakthrough for the campaign. “We have seen this movie before. I starred in it,” Mr Obama said, referring to the attacks he faced over claims that he was Muslim, although he is not, and that he was not born in the US and therefore ineligible to be president. “This stuff didn’t work on me – not in Michigan. It’s not going to work on Abdul.” For Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud, the endorsements are a decisive moment. “This is vice president Harris, this is former president Obama, putting their stamp of approval on Dr Abdul El-Sayed and the things he's advocating for and fighting for,” Mr Hammoud told The National . “He's not changing or shifting his policies to accommodate those who want to endorse him. And I think that's really meaningful.” Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, a journalist who was born and raised in Michigan, went a step further. “This is the moment we've all been waiting for, where pro-Israel establishment politicians are now rallying around a progressive Muslim American who is critical of Israel and actually is championing working-class issues through his own progressive policies," he said. Mohammed Qazzaz, a resident of Dearborn, put it more succinctly: “I hope he wins, because I really don't like the other guy.” Apart from the debate over Israel, a defining point of contention during Mr El-Sayed's campaign has been his faith. Sahar Aziz, a Rutgers University law professor and author of The Racial Muslim: When Racism Quashes Religious Freedom , said Republican political messaging during this election cycle had increasingly relied on anti-Muslim stereotypes , portraying Muslim candidates as threats to democracy, potential extremists or inherently disloyal. Democratic leaders, she added, had done little to counter the stance. “The reason Republicans can continue to do this unashamedly is that there hasn't been pushback. There hasn't been political accountability,” Ms Aziz said. Still, she sees hope in a younger generation of American-born Muslims who are refusing to accept the status quo and working towards change. “They're saying, ‘No, I will run for office, and I will use this opportunity to educate constituents about this form of hate, as well as focus on the policies'.” Mr El-Sayed appears to be seizing that chance. “I don't care how he pronounces my name,” he said of Mr Trump. “Because he can just go on and call me Senator after November.”

title: Iran war puts Republican foreign policy hawks under pressure before midterms
body: US President Donald Trump ’s war against Iran has emerged as a liability for Republicans before next week’s midterm elections, including for several prominent hawks on foreign affairs committees. Democrats are linking Republican support for the Iran war to higher fuel prices and what they say is Mr Trump's lack of a clear plan to end the conflict. The approach has found a receptive audience as voters focus on affordability. An AP-Norc poll found that about eight in 10 registered voters want the next Congress to make lowering the cost of living a top priority. Many also want it to end the war in Iran. The conflict, which the US launched alongside Israel on February 28, disrupted the Strait of Hormuz for several weeks and helped push petrol prices past about $1.13 a litre in the US – still cheap compared to most rich countries but more than 40 per cent higher than at the start of Mr Trump's term. The conflict has shone a spotlight on vulnerable Republicans as the Democrats try to take control of Congress. Dan Sullivan Mr Sullivan , a member of the Senate foreign relations committee, is seeking a fourth term in his home state of Alaska. He voted against a September resolution that would have required Mr Trump to end the war or seek congressional authorisation. He finds himself in an unexpectedly competitive re-election race against Democrat Mary Peltola, with recent polls showing the challenger narrowly ahead. Mr Sullivan has been an outspoken and consistent supporter of Mr Trump’s agenda, particularly on Iran, defence and energy. He backed last year's Operation Midnight Hammer strikes on Iranian nuclear sites and has strongly defended the current conflict, saying Tehran has effectively been at war with the US for decades. The veterans' advocacy group VoteVets launched a $225,000 advertising campaign against Mr Sullivan in August, accusing him of backing the war at the expense of working families. “Alaskans already pay more for everything and Dan Sullivan voted 12 separate times to make it worse," said VoteVets senior adviser Max Rose. The Alaska race is complicated by another candidate who is on the ballot, Daniel J Sullivan, whose presence Republicans say could confuse voters and pull support from Mr Sullivan the incumbent. The Department of Justice last week sued Alaska election officials in a bid to block certification of the results if the incumbent Mr Sullivan loses, arguing that voters could confuse the two candidates. A Reuters/Ipsos poll this month found that 78 per cent of Americans blamed Mr Trump’s policies for price increases outpacing their earnings, reinforcing concerns among Republicans that foreign policy is feeding into voters' economic anxieties. Pete Ricketts Meanwhile, Mr Ricketts, who also sits on the powerful Senate foreign relations committee, is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska. Mr Ricketts has been a staunch supporter of the war in Iran and he has consistently opposed congressional efforts to restrict Mr Trump’s war powers, including by voting against the resolution in September along with Mr Sullivan. Polls show a too-close-to-call race with Mr Osborn in Nebraska, which hasn't elected a Democratic senator for 20 years. Despite his broad support of the Iran war, Mr Ricketts has broken with Mr Trump on economic policies affecting his state's agricultural sector. Mike Lawler Republican Representative Mike Lawler, who sits on the House foreign affairs committee, is in a tight race in New York state against Democrat Cait Conley. At a forum in April, voters challenged him over his opposition to a House resolution restricting Mr Trump’s war powers. He defended the strikes as within the President’s authority, arguing that the campaign was necessary to counter US adversaries. A September Emerson College poll found that 52 per cent of district voters opposed US military action in Iran, against 37 per cent who supported it. Ms Conley’s campaign and Democratic groups have since attacked Mr Lawler over the war and its economic costs. The Emerson poll found Ms Conley leading Mr Lawler 48 per cent to 46 per cent, within the survey’s 4.9-point margin of error Support for Israel has also become a significant part of the race, with both candidates courting Jewish voters while arguing over who would best protect Israel and fight anti-Semitism. Other vulnerable Republicans include Senator Roger Marshall, who has strongly supported the war against Iran and who in March voted against a resolution to restrict Mr Trump’s military authority. Mr Marshall is now facing a competitive race against Democrat Adam Hamilton in Kansas, a Republican stronghold that that Mr Trump won by about 16 percentage points in 2024.

title: Vote-buying: Heavy political spending fuels corruption – Inusah Fuseini
body: Former NDC MP for Tamale Central, Inusah Fuseini, has warned that heavy political spending fuels corruption as politicians seek to recover the money they spend to win power. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the financial demands of politics also exclude women, young people, and people with integrity. “Also, when you spend a lot of money, politics is not Father Christmas. A politician is not an NGO, and so when people spend that amount of money, they expect to recoup that, and that fuels corruption on a national scale.” His warning comes amid reports of widespread alleged vote-buying during the NDC’s latest constituency executive elections. Mr Fuseini said the growing influence of money was narrowing access to political office. Those without substantial resources were being pushed out. “Those heavily impacted by what is happening are women and the youth because they might not have the required resources to be able to do that,” he said. He added that people with integrity and reputations for public service were shying away from politics because they could not afford its financial demands. Mr Fuseini said efforts to address inducement had exposed gaps in the NDC’s constitution. His committee recognised the need for sanctions after acknowledging that inducement had occurred during the elections. However, it found “there was no legal mechanism in our constitution to deal with that”. He explained that the party needed clear provisions defining misconduct and identifying the body authorised to handle complaints. Without those rules, disciplinary action could face challenges. “So we need a framework,” he said. The committee is considering whether constituency councils of elders should handle cases locally. Another option would be to refer offenders to the national headquarters for the Functional Executive Committee to act. It is also examining the boundary between legitimate support and inducement. “How much money can we say is appropriate in the circumstances?” he asked. “If somebody gives a delegate GH¢200, is it an inducement or what is it?” He also questioned how the party should handle payments described as transport allowances when the amounts exceed reasonable travel costs. Mr Fuseini said the party would further scrutinise the proposals before presenting them to a special congress for constitutional amendment.

title: No European leaders except Stubb, Store requested calls with Putin —Peskov
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. No European leaders other than Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store have requested phone calls with Russian President Vladimir Putin in recent days, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS.
"No," he replied when asked whether any other European leaders had requested talks.
On October 27, Putin held a telephone conversation with Stubb and Store at the request of the Finnish and Norwegian sides. The leaders exchanged views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis. They welcomed the agreement to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the United States in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.

title: JetBlue defends its finances as creditors hire restructuring advisers
body: JetBlue is trying to reassure investors it can turn its business around after a group of creditors hired restructuring advisers and the airline reported a deeper quarterly loss despite bringing in more money. JetBlue CEO Joanna Geraghty told Reuters on October 27, 2026, that the airline was not discussing a restructuring with creditors or seeking US government financial support. “We are not in talks with our creditors,” she said. Her comments followed an October 23 Bloomberg report that creditors holding some of JetBlue’s bonds and loans were working with investment bank PJT Partners and law firm Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld. The group includes holders of $2 billion in bonds due in 2031 and a $742 million first-lien loan, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. JetBlue’s latest financial results, released on October 26, showed a net loss of $257 million for the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared with a $143 million loss a year earlier. Revenue rose 21.1% to $2.8 billion, but the airline paid far more per gallon for jet fuel. Its adjusted loss widened to 60 cents per share from 40 cents a year earlier, missing analysts’ forecast of a 55-cent loss, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters. JetBlue ended September 2026 with approximately $1.63 billion in cash and investment securities, down from $2.48 billion at the end of 2025. Total debt stood at about $8.4 billion. JetBlue spent $273 million more running its business than it brought in during the first nine months of 2026, compared with $143 million a year earlier. Its loyalty-backed TrueBlue bonds were trading at about 47 cents on the dollar on October 26, with yields above 30%, Reuters reported. JetBlue says it can borrow another $600 million through an existing credit line. It also expects to raise $250 million later this year through loans secured by its aircraft. The airline also said it had approximately $7 billion in assets not pledged as collateral, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines. Those assets provide financing options, but are separate from its available cash. Geraghty said stronger fares and demand were helping JetBlue absorb higher fuel prices. Revenue per available seat mile rose 18.4%, and the airline said it recovered approximately 87% of the increase in fuel costs during the quarter. Fort Lauderdale was a particular source of growth. Revenue per available seat mile there increased nearly 15% despite capacity rising more than 65%. JetBlue plans to operate more than 150 daily departures at its winter peak, up 39% from a year earlier. JetBlue is also waiting on new first-class seats it is counting on to bring in more money. President Marty St. George said supply shortages are limiting how quickly the airline can install its BlueFirst cabins. Most aircraft are expected to be fitted by the end of 2027, but the work will continue into 2028. “But I would gladly take seats faster if we could,” St. George said on the earnings call. JetBlue aims to earn an operating profit in 2027 and have positive free cash flow in 2028. It expects fuel to cost 85% more per gallon in the fourth quarter than a year earlier. The post JetBlue defends its finances as creditors hire restructuring advisers appeared first on AeroTime .

title: Plans for $1 Billion F-47 Campus at Nellis AFB Move Forward
body: The U.S. Department of Defense has issued further solicitation to industry ahead of bids being tendered for the construction of support facilities for the Boeing F-47 at Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada. The F-47 Future Campus at Nellis is projected to cost $1.057 billion and potentially involve as many as four different contractors. The chosen contractors will be expected to deliver the project rapidly, with the project’s final milestones penciled in for 2032. Contract awards are scheduled to be issued on Feb. 5, 2027. Currently, interested industry partners are asked to make their proposals for milestones two, three, and four. This includes the primary support facilities for the F-47 , with completion desired by 2031. As well as a combined operations and maintenance hangar, projected at 116,000 square feet, the department also requires a new 1.153 million square foot apron complete with sunshades, a simulator facility, reprogramming lab, and assorted utilities and infrastructure. A U.S. Air Force F-35 Lightning II aircraft assigned to the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron taxis at Nellis Air Force Base, Nevada, July 16, 2026. Note the sunshades, | Source: U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Heather Amador Paulino Chosen vendors may then be selected for follow-on works that include a low observable corrosion control hangar (for maintenance of radar absorbent material (RAM) coatings), fuel cell hangar, weapons load training hangar, and additional maintenance facilities. Construction of these additional facilities would begin in 2029, ready for delivery in 2032. While initial testing for Boeing’s sixth-generation F-47 fighter will almost certainly take place at Edwards AFB following the scheduled first flight of a production airframe in 2028, Nellis will be vital as the Air Force works to integrate both the F-47 and the Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) that it is designed to fight with into its combat-ready armada. Anduril delivered the first CCA to the @usairforce last month. Now, USAF operators are flying Fury on their own. https://t.co/HdSLg7MbZZ — Anduril Industries (@anduriltech) September 25, 2026 The U.S. Air Force’s experimental CCA unit, operating the FQ-42 and FQ-44, is based at Creech AFB, close to Nellis. Alongside hosting the U.S. Air Force Weapons School and the Red Flag exercise , Nellis is home to the 422nd Test and Evaluation Squadron (TES), which since 1969 has been the primary unit tasked with operational testing and evaluation of the U.S. Air Force’s newest fighter designs. As we noted in a previous article: Nellis is a huge facility and – despite being on the outskirts of Las Vegas – can offer many areas away from prying eyes. While arriving and departing aircraft will be clearly visible, more sensitive activities involved in supporting the new aircraft will be able to be hidden in plain sight camouflaged by the already sprawling and highly active airfield. Close proximity to the massive Nevada Test and Training Range (NTTR) will allow the F-47 to face a plethora of U.S. and foreign airborne and surface threats, including genuine Russian aircraft and anti-air equipment which has been acquired through the years for use on the range. The F-47 may even face off against classified platforms, which can fly – as the F-47’s prototypes almost certainly have been – from Area 51.

title: Trump factor looms as Herzog weighs next move in election deadlock
body: President Isaac Herzog has a particularly important role to play now that the election is over. He must decide who will receive the first mandate to form a government: Benjamin Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot or perhaps another candidate. Sources close to Herzog say he currently prefers to wait for the official election results, which are expected in several days, before addressing the issue and inviting party representatives to the President's Residence for consultations.   Central Elections Committee Chairman Supreme Court Deputy Chief Justice Noam Sohlberg told Herzog on Tuesday that he expects to submit the official results only next Wednesday, although the results themselves are expected to be published several days earlier. The immediate implication is that Israel is entering a period of uncertainty against the backdrop of a sensitive security situation and the approaching U.S. midterm elections. Until then, according to prevailing assessments, no unusual security developments are expected. The central question is whether the political picture will become clearer and whether the White House and U.S. President Donald Trump will seek to intervene. Sources close to Trump are holding talks overnight with Israeli officials to understand the exit poll results, the prospects of forming a unity government and the significance of the largest party in determining who will form the next government. Washington does not want to see another government that includes far-right elements such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and would prefer a unity government or a stable coalition. The anti-Netanyahu bloc is concerned that the premier could attempt to trigger a regional escalation to complicate its efforts, and perhaps even force an emergency government with Yashar! Chairman Gadi Eisenkot. Eisenkot has categorically ruled out such a possibility, declaring that if it happened, he would "resign the next day."   According to most of Tuesday evening's exit polls, neither bloc has secured the 61 Knesset seats needed to form a government, partly due to the strong showing by the Arab parties. Based on the average of exit polls published by Channels 11, 12 and 13, the predominantly Arab Joint List and Ra'am parties are projected to win a combined 18 seats. As a result, Israel appears headed for a politically complicated period alongside an already complex diplomatic and security situation. All three main television networks project a narrow advantage for the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot, with 52 seats compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. In the days leading up to the election, Trump published two messages endorsing Netanyahu, the latest just over 24 hours before polling stations opened across Israel at 7 a.m. Tuesday. The anti-Netanyahu bloc is concerned that, in the absence of a decisive outcome between the two camps, as the exit polls currently suggest, Trump may seek to assist Netanyahu once more. Sources close to Trump's White House have offered several explanations in recent days for the president's support for Netanyahu. One was the claim that "Netanyahu promised Trump a unity government." Opposition figures, however, believe the endorsement post was effectively compensation for Netanyahu over the postponement of a possible strike on Iran until after the U.S. midterm elections, if such an operation ultimately takes place.

title: Russia launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv in past two weeks
body:
Russia launched over 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region since Oct. 14, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his evening address on Oct. 27, as Moscow's relentless assault on the Ukrainian capital continues.
"In two weeks, more than 100 ballistic missiles have been launched against Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast. We are doing everything possible to protect our energy sector, to protect our infrastructure and our logistics. The task is extremely difficult," Zelensky said .
Kyiv, a city of three million people, has been relentlessly assaulted by Russian ballistic missiles in recent months as Moscow exploits Ukraine's air defense shortage. While its battlefield offensive has slowed, Russia has chosen a strategy of mass aerial strikes against vulnerable civilians, as well as energy infrastructure ahead of the coming winter months.
Zelensky's comments come one day Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack on a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities in Kyiv. The attack killed one person and injured 15.
Zelensky has repeatedly called on allies to supply additional air defense missiles amid the intensification of Russian attacks.
"Everyone hears, everyone sees that right now, it is difficult for us to defend against Russian ballistic missiles. And above all, we do not have enough missiles for Patriots," Zelensky said in his evening address, referring to the U.S.-made air defense system.
Ukraine relies on Patriot systems to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to stop, making timely deliveries critical to the country's air defenses .
On Oct. 26, the Ukrainian president said that Kyiv has been waiting nearly a month for U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to approve missiles for its Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems. Ukrainian officials have described the delays and disruptions as another example of political pressure from Washington that could put civilian lives at risk.
"It’s important that the world sees this, that our partners see it in the United States, on which almost everything concerning Patriots depends, so that we get answers and the necessary authorizations from the Pentagon for Patriot supplies," Zelensky concluded.

title: Igbo youth rebuff of Nigerian Army (II), by Ochereome Nnanna
body: How did the Igbo nation, in about 70 years, move from dominating the officer grades of the Nigerian Army to being begged to fill their quotas today? The simple answer is that the Nigerian armed and security forces have been the primary kinetic instrument used by colonial Britain and its willing vassal post-colonial Nigerian state establishment to oppress and deny the Igbo their rightful place of leadership of the nation. The same Army they once bestrode was not only used to wage the Biafra War against them; it has been weaponised, along with the Northern cabals and Deep State elements, to distance them from power. These barefaced machinations came in waves. The first wave was from 1976 to 1983. When the Generals Murtala Mohammed/Olusegun Obasanjo regime triggered its transition to civil rule programme in 1976, the Northern civilian political class was very open to genuine reconciliation with the Igbo. The National Party of Nigeria (NPN) was essentially more of a reformed and nationalised Northern People’s Congress (NPC). It threw its arms wide open to embrace political leaders from across Nigeria. It offered prominent Igbo leaders like Dr Alex Ekwueme, Dr Ozumba Mbadiwe, Dr J. O. J. Okezie and others cosy positions, with Ekwueme emerging as Vice President of Nigeria under President Shehu Shagari in 1979, barely nine years after the War. The NPN also forged an Accord with Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe’s Nigeria People’s Party (NPP), which enabled the Igbo to produce the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Edwin Ume-Ezeoke, as well as influential ministers. Indeed, the NPN created a zoning formula (North and South) and positioned Vice President Ekwueme to inherit the position of President from Shagari in 1987. This arrangement has been widely acknowledged as the ultimate dealbreaker for the Northern military officers who felt scandalised that the same people who fought them in the war would now rule them. Most of them were still young – in their 30s and 40s – and could not fancy being retired when all they needed to do was grab power. So, they grabbed power on 31st December 1983. The second coming of the military was politically the resumption of the war against the Igbo and self-reward for their roles at the war front. The second wave was in 1999. After the annulment of the June 12 election and the truncation of the handover of the military to the civilians, the National Democratic Coalition (NADECO) became the umbrella under which the agitation for the revalidation of Moshood Abiola’s mandate was waged. Prominent among the NADECO constituents were the Yoruba Afenifere, groups from the East such as the Council for Unity and Understanding (CUU) led by retired Commodore Okoh Ebitu Ukiwe, Dr Arthur Nwankwo’s Eastern Mandate Union (EMU), Chief Anthony Enahoro’s Movement for National Reformation (MNR), and Northern progressives led by retired Lt-Gen Theophilus Danjuma. The primary purpose of Igbo involvement in NADECO through the CUU was to end power monopolisation by the North through a “power shift” mechanism, as propounded by Ukiwe, a former second-in-command in General Ibrahim Babangida’s government. The CUU also wanted to use its involvement in NADECO as a springboard for an Igbo bounce-back into the Nigerian political mainstream. On his own part, Ekwueme, along with Dim Chukwuemeka Odumegwu Ojukwu, led the Igbo delegates to the National Constitutional Conference (NCC) in Abuja, also with the purpose of putting Ndi Igbo back into the centre stage of power. At a summit held in Enugu in April 1994, where the Igbo agenda was forged, Ekwueme resurrected the NPN power-sharing and presidency-rotation mechanism, which he fiercely championed at the Conference. Added to the Igbo agenda was the proposal to create eight geopolitical zones or regions, each closely conforming to the principle of ethno-cultural contiguity and consanguinity, or grouping people of roughly the same ethnic, linguistic and cultural heritage in the regions. At the end of the Conference in 1996, Gen. Sani Abacha showed great leadership. The Provisional Ruling Council (PRC) “approved” power rotation (North and South) and the six geopolitical zones, but declined to enshrine them in the Draft Constitution. Ekwueme came out of the Conference looking very much like the consequential President after military rule. But Gen. Abacha had other plans. He used civilian politicians to form five political parties, which nominated him as their joint presidential candidate. All he needed was to pull off his uniform and contest unopposed. But Ekwueme, leading the G.34 group of prominent politicians from all over the country, held a series of summits in Lagos and Kano. Many of these leaders were rounded up and thrown into detention. However, on 8th June 1998, Abacha suddenly died, shortly after seeing off Palestinian Liberation Organisation (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat at the Abuja Airport. Gen. Abdulsalami Abubakar emerged as Head of State and immediately announced an 11-month transition programme. The G.34 transformed into the People’s Democratic Party, while many pro-Abacha politicians (mostly Northerners) formed the All People’s Party (APP). Later, Chief Bola Ige and his Afenifere group pulled out of the PDP to form the Alliance for Democracy (AD). Ige saw that his presidential ambition had no way forward in the PDP, with Ekwueme poised to take the ticket. It had seemed that the NPN had resurrected in the PDP. But, again, the North-controlled military had other ideas. With the rapid-fire deaths of Abacha and Abiola, the Abdulsalami regime, in cahoots with key international players, decided to appease the Yoruba for the annulment of the June 12 election and Abiola’s murder in detention. Abdulsalami, General Babangida and other top Northern Generals prevailed on Northern politicians to bury their presidential ambitions and support Obasanjo for the 1999 presidential race. The same Obasanjo they had thrown into jail for an alleged coup plot against Abacha was pardoned and given the presidential ticket. Ekwueme and the Igbo nation were again thwarted. Culprit? The Nigerian Army! We end this next Wednesday. The post Igbo youth rebuff of Nigerian Army (II), by Ochereome Nnanna appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Nigeria’s external debt may top N200trn by year end
body: From Abdullateef Aliyu, Lagos; Hussein Yahaya & Mumini Abdulkareem, Ilorin President Bola Tinubu has written to the Senate requesting approval for the Federal Government’s 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan, totaling $20.52 billion and €1.05 billion (approximately $21.5 billion combined), a move that could push Nigeria’s external debt burden higher as the Federal Government seeks additional funds for infrastructure and other critical sectors. The proposed borrowing comprises $20.52 billion and €1.05 billion, equivalent to approximately $21.5 billion combined. At prevailing exchange rates, the facility could translate into about N30 trillion, further increasing the naira value of the country’s external debt. If approved and fully borrowed, the new facility could contribute to Nigeria’s external debt exceeding N200 trillion in naira terms by the end of the year, depending on exchange-rate movements, actual disbursements and other changes in the debt stock. Daily Trust reports that Nigeria’s total public debt rose to N166.79 trillion as of June 30, 2026, according to the Debt Management Office (DMO). The figure showed that the country’s public debt stock increased by N7.44 trillion within three months, rising from N159.35 trillion at the end of March 2026 to N166.79 trillion by the end of June. The DMO is yet to release figure for the nine-month period but with increasing debt numbers, it is projected that the debt profile would balloon further and could hit over N200 trillion by the end of the year if the latest borrowing is added. In a letter addressed to Senate President Godswill Akpabio on Tuesday, Tinubu requested the early consideration and approval of the Federal Government’s 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan. The President said the proposed loans were necessary to bridge funding gaps and address the country’s infrastructure deficit, with investments planned across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory. The projects are expected to cover power, transportation, healthcare, education, agriculture, water supply, security, job creation and financial management reforms. “I submit the attached Federal Government 2026–2027 Supplementary External Borrowing Plan for consideration and early approval of the National Assembly to ensure prompt implementation of our projects,” Tinubu stated in the letter. He explained that the projects had undergone technical and economic assessments to ensure that they deliver significant benefits, particularly in poverty reduction, skills acquisition, entrepreneurship and food security. According to him, the scale of Nigeria’s infrastructure needs and the financial resources required to address them have made additional external financing necessary. “In light of the need for significant infrastructure investment in the country and the vast financial resources needed to address this gap, it has become essential to pursue prudent external borrowings to close the financing shortfall,” the President said. The request was presented to the Senate during plenary, where Akpabio observed that aspects of the borrowing framework had featured in previous government borrowing plans. He subsequently referred the proposal to the Senate Committee on Local and Foreign Debts, chaired by Senator Haruna Manu, for detailed scrutiny. The committees on Appropriations and Finance, Akpabio stated, would also contribute to the legislative review. Akpabio said the borrowing framework had previously received attention in the government’s budget and external borrowing plans covering 2025 to 2027. “However, this request will be looked at by the Committee on Local and Foreign Debts,” he said, adding that the committee would clarify the scope of the proposal before further legislative action. Daily Trust reports that the new request forms part of the borrowing plan to fund the 2026 budget deficit. In the N68.32 trillion budget approved for 2026, the deficit stands at N23.85 trillion and it is expected to be funded through loans. However, the proposed borrowing comes amid concerns about Nigeria’s growing debt obligations and the rising cost of servicing public debt. Many experts have also called for caution over the rising borrowing amidst sustainability concerns. Speaking on the latest borrowing plan, an economist at Al-Hikmah University, Ilorin, Dr Muhammad Bashir-Yusuf, said borrowing to finance critical infrastructure was a normal practice, provided the funds were used for their intended purposes. He said governments resorted to domestic or external borrowing when their projected expenditure exceeded available revenue. He added that infrastructure investment was essential to improving productivity, attracting investors and expanding the country’s revenue base. “If they are borrowing to finance critical infrastructure, I think every country does that, and that is normal. It is when you have infrastructure that you will be able to generate more revenue,” he said. Bashir-Yusuf, however, warned that diverting the funds from the projects for which they were obtained would undermine the purpose of the borrowing and leave the country with debts without corresponding development benefits. “The problem will now be if they have gotten the approval and actually gotten the loan but refuse to use it for what it has been borrowed for. “Then that will be a problem, because eventually, we will be borrowing for people to invest in, and that will not be good,” he said. Addressing concerns over Nigeria’s rising public debt despite the removal of the petrol subsidy, the economist said the country’s total debt figures included obligations incurred by the Federal Government, state governments and the Federal Capital Territory. He explained that the funds distributed to state governments were provided for under the Constitution and were not discretionary allocations that the Federal Government could withhold because of political differences. Bashir-Yusuf said concerns about how the funds were spent should be directed at the respective state governments, while the Federal Government should be held accountable for its own expenditure. He added that the priority should be to ensure that the proposed borrowing translated into tangible infrastructure and economic development, rather than allowing the funds to be diverted from their stated purposes. “What concerns us now is to make sure that this money, since we have said they are going to get it, is used for what they have borrowed it for. If they do that, then we will all see the impact in the nearest future,” he submitted. …Don’t approve the loan, Atiku tells NASS Former Vice-President and African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Candidate, Atiku Abubakar, has said President Bola Tinubu’s request for approval to borrow $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion vindicates his October 12 warning about a loan plan of up to $20 billion. Atiku said the President’s failure to identify the specific projects the loans would fund raises serious concerns that borrowed public money could be channelled through the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, now rerouted inland, to political campaigners and favoured contractors. In a statement issued by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said: “On October 12, I warned Nigerians that President Tinubu was reportedly preparing to borrow up to $20 billion in connection with the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway. I asked him to confirm or deny the plan and publish the accounts. He did neither. Today, he has asked the Senate to approve $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion in external loans. My warning has been vindicated. “The President has listed broad sectors but has not provided a project by project account of what this enormous borrowing will fund. Nigerians have not been given clear project details, costs, locations or contractors to scrutinise. “That silence is especially troubling given the highway’s inland rerouting. Nigerians have every right to ask whether it is becoming a pipeline for borrowed money to reach Tinubu’s campaigners and favoured contractors. Barely 12 weeks before an election, how can the President ask lawmakers to saddle Nigerians with more than $20 billion and €1 billion in debt without identifying the projects and their costs? Is this a development plan for Nigerians or a campaign financing scheme dressed up as infrastructure? “You cannot continue taking frivolous loans on the eve of your departure from office. Let it be on record that one of the first responsibilities I will undertake as President is to scrutinise and investigate every kobo borrowed, especially loans taken in the final year of your tenure. Nigerians will ask questions, and we will find the answers by every lawful means. “I put local and international lenders on notice: any loan granted to this winding down administration must meet all constitutional, statutory and due process requirements. Upon assumption of office, I will scrutinise every such loan. Any borrowing found to have been obtained without proper authorisation or process will be challenged and will not be allowed to stand. “The National Assembly must not approve a single dollar until the President publishes every project, contract, cost, contractor, loan term and repayment obligation. No public money should be borrowed in the dark, and no lawmaker should sign a blank cheque against Nigeria’s future.” Atiku said the burden was on Tinubu to prove that the borrowing would serve the country, not his political interests. He urged lawmakers to publish the proposal and supporting documents and subject them to rigorous scrutiny before any decision.

title: Nigeria’s portfolio investment inflows rise 17.6% to $7.09bn in Q2
body: Nigeria’s portfolio investment inflows rose by 17.6 per cent to $7.09 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up from $6.03 billion in the preceding quarter, according to the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN). The increase of $1.06 billion was driven by higher inflows into long-term general government debt securities, the CBN said in its Q2 2026 Economic Report published on Monday. The report showed that portfolio investment remained the largest component of new financial liabilities recorded during the quarter, significantly exceeding direct investment liabilities. Portfolio investment inflows increased by 17.6 per cent between January and March and April and June, while direct investment liabilities rose by 11.7 per cent to $1.15 billion from $1.03 billion. The CBN attributed the increase in direct investment liabilities to higher reinvested earnings. Other investment liabilities also increased, rising to $2.75 billion in the second quarter from $1.36 billion in the first quarter. The growth reflected higher loan drawdowns by the government and other sectors, as well as increased currency and deposit liabilities of deposit-taking corporations. Consequently, the net incurrence of financial liabilities rose to $10.84 billion from $8.36 billion in the preceding quarter. Portfolio investment inflows were about six times direct investment liabilities in the second quarter. They accounted for about 65 per cent of total net financial liabilities incurred during the period, compared with roughly 72 per cent in the first quarter, as other investment liabilities recorded stronger growth. However, the portfolio investment rose amid a decline in Nigeria’s aggregate foreign exchange inflows.

title: Dangote Refinery’s IPO attracts investors from 120 countries
body: Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has successfully concluded its Initial Public Offering (IPO), attracting investor applications from 120 countries across all six inhabited continents, including every one of Africa’s 54 countries, in an unprecedented demonstration of the continent’s capacity to mobilise capital and broaden ownership of strategic industrial assets. The offering, described as the People’s IPO, achieved 100 per cent geographical coverage of Africa, bringing together investors from across the continent and beyond in a transaction that could redefine the scale, accessibility and international reach of African capital markets. More than a conventional fundraising exercise, the IPO has emerged as a landmark in financial inclusion, demonstrating how digital technology, coordinated financial institutions and innovative distribution channels can connect millions of potential investors to opportunities previously dominated by institutional and high-net-worth participants. The transaction was supported by an extensive network of commercial banks, stockbroking firms, fintech platforms, capital market institutions and distribution partners, whose collaboration expanded access to the offer across national boundaries and created new pathways for retail participation. For Dangote Industries Limited, the conclusion of the IPO marks a defining moment in its industrial journey, transforming the refinery’s ownership proposition from an investment driven by a single entrepreneurial vision into an opportunity for broader African participation. President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, described the outcome as a powerful affirmation of African confidence, enterprise and the continent’s ability to mobilise its own resources for development. “When we set out to build this refinery, many doubted that a project of this scale could be delivered by Africans. We proved that Africa could build it. Today, through this historic IPO, we have demonstrated something equally important: Africans are ready to own and participate in the prosperity created by their own industries. “To have investor applications from all 54 African countries is deeply significant to me. It tells us that our people do not simply want to consume what Africa produces; they want to invest in it, own it and share in its future. This is the Africa we have always believed in,” he said. Dangote said the company’s decision to open the refinery to broader ownership was not driven solely by the need to raise capital but also by its ambition to create opportunities for ordinary Africans to participate in an enterprise of global significance. “We did not undertake this IPO simply because we needed to raise capital. We wanted to open the doors of ownership, give ordinary Africans an opportunity to participate in an enterprise of global significance and establish a new culture of shared prosperity. “The refinery was built in Africa, by African determination, and its future must create opportunities for Africans. Today, we have made history together. But the greater achievement will be the generation of African investors, entrepreneurs and industrialists that this transaction inspires. “Our ambition is not merely to build successful businesses. It is to help build a prosperous, self-reliant Africa whose people are participants in its economic destiny. As we advance our expansion programme and Vision 2030 strategy, we remain committed to strengthening our operational performance, deepening our contribution to Africa’s energy security and building an enterprise that rewards the confidence placed in it,” he said. The IPO’s geographical reach is particularly significant for a continent where capital markets have historically been fragmented by national boundaries, differing regulatory environments and limited retail investor participation. By attracting applications from all 54 African countries, the transaction has demonstrated the potential for a more connected investment ecosystem in which Africans can participate in major industrial opportunities beyond their domestic markets. The offering also highlights the growing importance of digital financial infrastructure in widening investment access. Through partnerships involving traditional financial institutions and technology-driven investment platforms, the transaction created multiple channels through which eligible investors could express interest and submit applications. Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, David Bird, said the international response reflected confidence in the refinery’s operating capabilities, industrial scale and long-term growth prospects. “The successful conclusion of this IPO is a remarkable milestone for Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals. Investor applications spanning 120 countries demonstrate the extraordinary international interest in our business and the confidence that investors are placing in the future of this refinery. “We have built one of the world’s most significant refining and petrochemical complexes, and our focus remains on translating that industrial scale into operational excellence, sustainable growth and long-term shareholder value,” he said. Bird said the breadth of participation made the transaction particularly significant, as it provided investors across Africa and other continents with an opportunity to own a stake in a major African industrial enterprise. “That is a powerful endorsement of the refinery’s potential and of Africa’s growing relevance in global investment markets,” he added. The refinery’s IPO opened on September 14, 2026, offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 per share, representing a proposed capital raise of approximately N2.15tn. Initially scheduled to close on October 13, the offer was extended to October 27 following approval by the Securities and Exchange Commission, allowing additional time for investors across Africa and other international markets to participate. The extension reflected the Group’s stated ambition to prioritise the breadth of ownership alongside the financial objectives of the transaction. Beyond the industrial significance of the refinery itself, the IPO has also established a model for collaboration across Africa’s financial services ecosystem. Its distribution network brought together institutions operating across banking, securities trading, financial technology and investor engagement, demonstrating how coordinated infrastructure can expand access to large-scale investment opportunities. Group Chief Financial Officer of Dangote Industries Limited, Murat Erden, said the transaction had established an important precedent for the continent’s capital markets. “The Dangote Refinery People’s IPO represents much more than a landmark capital-raising exercise. It marks a defining moment in the evolution of African capital markets, demonstrating our continent’s ability to mobilise domestic savings, connect investors across borders and broaden ownership of strategic industrial assets. “Reaching investors in 120 countries, including all 54 African nations, is an extraordinary achievement and a powerful testament to the growing investment appetite across our continent. “By bringing together banks, capital market institutions, stockbrokers, fintech platforms and innovative digital distribution channels, we have demonstrated that African capital markets can transcend national boundaries and connect millions of people to investment opportunities previously beyond their reach,” he said. Erden said the transaction was underpinned by the refinery’s industrial scale, financial performance and long-term growth prospects. “Importantly, this transaction is underpinned by exceptional industrial and financial fundamentals. With US$22.5bn in revenue and US$5.52bn in EBITDA in the first nine months of 2026, Dangote Refinery combines world-class industrial scale, strong profitability and significant long-term growth potential. “Our greatest achievement is not simply the capital we mobilise, but the doors we open and the foundation we lay for future generations of African investors, entrepreneurs and businesses. “We believe the People’s IPO will be remembered not only as a landmark transaction in African capital market history, but as a blueprint for a more inclusive, interconnected and globally competitive African financial ecosystem — one in which Africans increasingly finance, own and share in the prosperity created by their continent’s industrial transformation,” he said. The successful conclusion of the offer comes as Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals pursues an ambitious programme to expand its refining and petrochemical operations, strengthen its distribution network and support greater energy security across Africa. Located in Lagos, the refinery represents one of the continent’s largest private industrial investments and a major effort to reduce dependence on imported refined petroleum products while building domestic processing capacity.

title: Panthers power past Winnipeg Jets as losing streak extends to six games
body:
The Winnipeg Jets’ scoring woes continued as did their losing streak Tuesday night against the Florida Panthers.
Florida scored three powerplay goals en route to a 5-1 win over the Jets at Canada Life Centre. Winnipeg has now lost six straight games (0-4-2) and has just 10 goals during the skid.
The Panthers scored three times in the span of just three minutes in the first period and never looked back.
“We really beat ourselves on this one,” said Jets head coach Scott Arniel. “We’ve only given up four PK (penalty kill) goals until tonight. We’ve done a pretty good job on our coverage and knowing who you have on certain scenarios. Tonight, I know we tipped one in our net but the other ones there – those are mistakes that we knew what we were supposed to do. You didn’t have to tell the player cause the player knew exactly who was supposed to be covering what.”
It was the first time since March of 2024 the Jets surrendered three power play goals in a single game, and they’ve now scored just five goals over their last four games as the losses start to pile up.
“A lot of shooting ourselves in the foot right now,” said Jets captain Adam Lowry. “Just mental errors. Reads, assignments, penalty killing. We give up three goals in three minutes.
“We’ve got to find a way to right the ship here and get this thing going in the right direction.”
The Jets have given up the first goal in four straight contests and in eight of their last 10 games overall.
The Jets power play came up empty again and they’re now 0-for-14 on the man advantage over their last five games.
It hasn’t exactly been the fresh start they were looking for following the Connor Hellebuyck trade and the Heritage Classic.
“It’s frustrating,” Lowry said. “We’re frustrated. We expect more out of ourselves. We expect more out of the team and we’re not delivering the results, so, we felt like going into the Heritage Classic that was going to be a great spot to get us right, didn’t get it done and you want to rebound and it seems like we’re picking ourselves off that mat.
“We got to find a way to get some things going in our favour, just some consistency in our game 5-on-5, shorthanded, on the power play and go from there.”
Carter Verhaeghe scored twice for the Panthers, while the Tkachuk brothers combined for seven points as Matthew picked up four assists, while Brady recorded a goal and two assists.
Lowry scored the lone goal for Winnipeg in the loss, his second of the season. It was his 13th career shorthanded goal to tie him with Thomas Steen for the second most in franchise history, behind only Doug Smail who had 25.
Jets goalie Clay Stevenson allowed five goals on 24 shots, the most he’s allowed in his four starts with Winnipeg.
Florida took control of this one early with three goals in the opening 20 minutes.
After a Cole Koepke holding penalty at about the six-minute mark of the game, the Panthers cashed in with the man advantage.
During a scramble behind the net, Brady Tkachuk was able to chip a loose puck to Verhaeghe in front, who snuck it past Stevenson to open the scoring.
Just over a minute later, defenceman Nikko Mikkola skated in from the point and threw a puck at the Jets net, which hit the stick of Jets defenceman Mario Ferraro and flew over the shoulder of Stevenson to give Florida the 2-0 lead.
The Jets then took a too many men penalty just past the halfway point of the period and Florida once again capitalized as Verhaeghe rifled a shot past Stevenson just 16 seconds into the man advantage, giving the Panthers three goals on their first five shots.
Both teams were able to convert on a Florida powerplay past the midway point of the second period. Panthers goalie Akira Schmid was stripped of the puck behind his net by Lowry, whose wraparound attempt just crossed the line to get the Jets on the board.
But on the same man advantage, the Panthers responded as the Tkachuk brothers and Sam Reinhart converted a tic-tac-toe passing play with Reinhart beating Stevenson to put Florida back up by three.
Brady Tkachuk would score the lone goal in the third period, finishing a rush by deflecting in a pass from his brother.
Tyrel Bauer and Brad Lambert both returned to the lineup for the Jets while Nino Niederreiter and Haydn Fleury were scratched.
The Jets now hit the road where they’ll visit the Tampa Bay Lightning on Thursday night, with puck drop just after 6 p.m., before a rematch with Florida on Friday night.

title: Greece Marks 10 Years Since The Opening Of The Holy Sepulchre
body: Greece marked the 10th anniversary of the historic opening of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem with an event in Thessaloniki on Tuesday, where National Technical University of Athens (NTUA) professor Antonia Moropoulou recalled how her interdisciplinary team opened the sacred monument on 26 October 2016 to protect it from potentially irreversible damage. President of the Hellenic Republic Konstantinos Tasoulas attended the commemorative event at the Thessaloniki Concert Hall, held under his auspices. Organisers also presented the advanced digital exhibition The Holy Sepulchre: The Monument and the Project , developed as part of the EVLOGON programme. The event brought together religious leaders, government officials, academics and representatives of the three Christian communities responsible for safeguarding the shrine. Speakers highlighted the monument’s spiritual significance and the role of scientific expertise in preserving its historical fabric. Religious leaders highlight the message of hope Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew said in a recorded message that the Empty Tomb carried renewed significance at a time when violence, wars and uncertainty were testing humanity, particularly in the Middle East. He emphasised its message that life overcomes death, love defeats hatred and hope endures. Archbishop Ieronymos II of Athens and All Greece, who attended the event, also stressed the continuing relevance of the Holy Sepulchre’s message. He highlighted how faith and science could work together through mutual respect and cooperation. Archbishop Aristarchos of Constantina delivered greetings on behalf of Patriarch Theophilos III of Jerusalem and All Palestine. Metropolitan Philotheos of Thessaloniki said the Holy Sepulchre symbolised life and presence rather than death and absence. He argued that the Resurrection did not remove people from the reality of suffering but challenged them not to let pain become the final truth of human life. He also clarified that scientists had not undertaken the restoration to prove the Resurrection, but to protect the monument that bears witness to it. Deputy Interior Minister responsible for Macedonia and Thrace Konstantinos Gioulekas said the anniversary highlighted the meeting of science, engineering and Christian faith. He praised the scientists who worked at what he described as Christianity’s holiest site. Other speakers included Thessaloniki Concert Hall board chairwoman Eugenia Alexandropoulou, artistic director Christos Galileas and NTUA Vice-Rector for Research, Innovation and Outreach Emmanouil Varvarigos. The Ministry of the Interior’s Macedonia and Thrace sector, the Holy Metropolis of Thessaloniki, the Thessaloniki Concert Hall, NTUA, the Technical Chamber of Greece and its Central Macedonia branch jointly organised the event. Moropoulou recalls why the team opened the tomb Moropoulou, who led the NTUA team and served as scientific director of the study and restoration of the Holy Edicule, said the team’s primary concern was to protect the monument after discovering cracks that threatened irreversible damage. “We opened the Holy Sepulchre to protect it,” she said, explaining that the team needed to address the structural risks before beginning grouting work. The team exposed the burial bed on 26 October 2016. Moropoulou described the experience as extraordinary, saying the atmosphere and the release of energy at the moment of opening made the monument feel alive and capable of speaking to humanity. She also highlighted the event’s international reach. According to her account, National Geographic broadcast the opening worldwide, reaching approximately two billion viewers at the time and three billion by the end of the programme. Moropoulou said the global audience demonstrated how widely people sought hope and responded to the message of the Resurrection. Scientific investigation reveals historic details The team faced unexpected difficulties while using non-destructive testing methods to examine the monument. Moropoulou said the scientific instruments stopped working during efforts to record the Holy Sepulchre’s structure, forcing the team to wait around two hours before resuming measurements. The investigation found that the upper slab of the burial bed had been raised by approximately 80 centimetres and consisted of two pieces of the same rock. Moropoulou suggested that this arrangement might reflect Emperor Constantine’s intention to distinguish the level of Christian veneration from that of the earlier Temple of Hadrian when establishing the Christian shrine. The team exposed the burial bed over 72 hours, during which construction work at the site stopped. Researchers continued investigating the surrounding area and gathered evidence about the underlying rock, the monument’s foundations and a cluster of tombs discovered nearby. Another significant discovery was a cross on the cornerstone at the southeastern corner of the Holy Edicule, bearing the date 15 October 1809. Moropoulou attributed it to restoration work carried out at that time by Komninos the Mytilenean. Using a simulation of the cross, the team installed a new cross on the dome. Moropoulou said the dome had not received a cross since the Mamluk incursion of 1244. She described the restored Holy Edicule, safeguarded by Jerusalem’s three Christian communities, as a monument capable of carrying the message of the Resurrection into the future. Christian custodians honoured at anniversary event The ceremony honoured representatives of the three Christian communities that safeguard the Holy Sepulchre and took part in the historic initiative to restore the Holy Edicule in 2016. The honourees included Patriarch Theophilos III of Jerusalem and All Palestine, represented at the event; Franciscan Custos Father Francesco Patton; and Armenian Patriarch of Jerusalem Nourhan Manougian. Ministers, deputy ministers, members of parliament, local government representatives and other officials also attended, alongside a large audience at the Thessaloniki Concert Hall.
