title: BOI, AFD sign $30m facility to boost Nigeria’s creative sector
body: The Bank of Industry (BOI) and the Agence Française de Développement (AFD) have signed a $30 million credit facility to support Nigeria’s creative and cultural industries. The agreement was signed in Abuja by the Managing Director of BOI, Dr. Olasupo Olusi, and the Chief Executive Officer of AFD Group, Christophe Lecourtier, a statement said yesterday. Olusi described the deal as ‘’a major milestone that builds on the longstanding partnership between both institutions and expands collaboration into a critical growth sector of the Nigerian economy.” According to him, the creative sector, which spans music, film, fashion, design and gaming, holds one of the biggest opportunities for job creation, youth inclusion and economic diversification. “This agreement builds on a very longstanding partnership between AFD and BOI. “The creative sector represents one of the biggest growth opportunities for the Nigerian economy, as it has the biggest capacity to absorb young people and create jobs.” Olusi said the facility aligned with President Bola Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda and the Federal Government’s ambition to grow Nigeria’s economy to a $1 trillion economy, noting that access to affordable finance remains a major constraint for creatives. He added that the facility would prioritize women-led and youth-led businesses and segments of the economy that were typically excluded from financing. “We’re very excited because particular attention will be given to women-led businesses and youth-led businesses. ‘’This financing will bridge a very important gap, not only in providing large quantum of financing but also at an affordable cost,” he said. The BOI MD assured AFD of prudent utilization of the fund to support credible and growth-oriented enterprises. In his remarks, AFD CEO Christophe Lecourtier said BOI remained AFD’s leading development banking partner in Nigeria and its largest partner in terms of non-sovereign loans. He recalled the first partnership, a credit line of over 100 million euros focused on climate issues under the Transforming Financial Systems for Climate (TFSC) programme, and said both institutions shared strategic priorities. “Cultural and creative industries are very important for the French, but you are probably the leader in Africa for that. “I know more and more French people that are listening to Nigerian music and watching Nigerian films. For us, it’s great to be able to work together and support such a growing sector.” Lecourtier said the results from the facility would inspire further collaboration in Europe and disclosed that both institutions were already discussing a next credit line based on Nigeria’s development priorities. He also commended the relationship between Nigeria and France, noting that both Presidents share similar values despite changing global priorities.

title: TotalEnergies finalises $800m sale of Nigeria gas assets
body: TotalEnergies has officially finalized the divestment of its 10% non-operated interest in the Renaissance Joint Venture (JV)—formerly known as the Shell Petroleum Development Company (SPDC) JV—to Vaaris for an aggregate cash consideration of US$800 million. Daily Trust reports that the transaction marks a major milestone in the ongoing restructuring of onshore oil assets in the Niger Delta as TotalEnergies strategically retained full economic interest in the joint venture’s vital gas assets. Under the terms of the finalized agreement, TotalEnergies EP Nigeria (TEPNG) transferred its 10% participating interest across 15 primarily oil-producing licenses within the Renaissance JV framework. These divested fields accounted for approximately 16,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d) of attributable production in 2025. However, the French energy major has carved out a crucial exception for gas production. TotalEnergies retains its full economic interest in the three key gas-producing licenses of the Renaissance JV—OML 23, OML 28, and OML 77. These fields remain central to the domestic and export energy landscape, accounting for 50% of the gas supply to Nigeria LNG (NLNG). The successful closure with Vaaris follows a heavily scrutinized period for international oil companies (IOCs) divesting onshore and shallow-water assets in Nigeria. The transaction marks a notable rebound from earlier divestment efforts. In 2024, TotalEnergies had initially attempted to sell its SPDC JV stake to Chappal Energies for roughly $860 million. However, that deal faced regulatory headwinds and was ultimately rejected by Nigerian authorities.

title: We’ve come a long way from the one-party state lament, by Rotimi Fasan
body: It’s been just a matter of weeks since the political temperature of this country was constantly raised by claims that the governing All Progressives Congress (APC) was bent on making Nigeria a one-party state. We were inundated with stories, not proofs, that the opposition parties were not being allowed to thrive, even when what was most obvious was the failure of the leading politicians in these parties to do the work of opposition parties or provide the leadership necessary for them to succeed. The scant regard for democratic ethos, which some of the politicians themselves like to describe as a lack of internal democracy, would not allow the political parties to thrive. The ADC was a small party that existed only on the sidelines before the likes of Atiku Abubakar, Rauf Aregbesola and David Mark embarked on an aggressive takeover of its leadership. They saw the party simply as a means to achieve an immediate need. It was no more than what Nigerians now call a special purpose vehicle. So, a man like Alhaji Atiku, who has contested for the presidency on different political platforms for nearly forty years, saw nothing wrong in moving into the ADC in 2025 and taking over its leadership because nothing mattered more to him in those circumstances than his obsessive drive to be president. The same was the case with the NDC candidate, Peter Obi, who has also proven to be a political journeyman who has moved back and forth from APGA to the PDP, LP and ADC before finally berthing at the NDC, which is at this moment proving to be very hot for his kind of one-man politics. But for the fact that INEC rules no longer permit any careless hopping around, there is no doubt that Peter Obi would not be in the NDC at a time like this, when he is not having it as smooth as he did when he was dominant in the LP. From the constitution of the party’s campaign council to who keeps the party’s purse, Obi and his followers are being subjected to the discipline of a party not organised around the former Anambra State governor. Seriake Dickson has his own mind and his own agenda for setting up his party, and would not be dictated to by anyone, certainly not Peter Obi or any of his followers. Dickson is definitely not a Julius Abure and would not be tossed around to please one man. He is his own man, who holds court and calls the shots from the private confines of his living room, much like a medieval potentate. When these opposition politicians screamed that Nigeria was being turned into a one-party state, they were not being honest about what their real problem was. It is the ghosts from their past and their lack of preparedness for the game they had enlisted for that are holding them to account. While one would admit that politicians are not averse to underhand practices to outwit their opponents, claims that the political space was being constricted to squeeze out opposition parties in order to make the APC the only political party in the country frequently strained credulity. Established parties that are better positioned than their counterparts try to lure members of other parties into their folds with juicy appointments, contracts or raw cash. We all know this. But it is not often the case that they go out of their way, in a brazen display of might, to snuff life out of their opponents just to ensure that only they exist. Or buy out their leadership, as some of the opposition politicians who are the first to complain have done. Making life difficult for their opponents is the game most politicians play, and that is not limited to Nigeria. It can be seen in many parts of the world. It was rife in the early years of party formation in Nigeria, when politicians could not bear the idea of others competing with them for votes among their base and in what they considered to be their catchment areas. This was the case in the first few years after independence, when certain parties dominated the politics of some regions. In the North, it was the Northern Peoples’ Congress, while the Action Group and the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons were respectively dominant in the Western and Eastern regions. Members of the other parties were openly hounded, brutalised and, in some areas, charged for phantom crimes and thrown into prison. That has so far not happened in the last three and a half years, when the president could be called names, even dubbed a criminal, and openly disrespected, whereas in the past such opposition figures would have been dealt crippling blows, if not mortal termination. We know how the likes of Gani Fawehinmi were beaten within an inch of their lives right in court premises during the military era. President Olusegun Obasanjo was not subtle in his treatment of opposition elements in his second term. He crushed the AD in all the Yoruba-speaking states and boasted that the election through which he made Umar Yar’Adua president would be a do-or-die affair. Even Yar’Adua himself was appalled by what happened. Yes, Bola Tinubu has, in executing his political moves, told Nigerians that all is fair in politics, but he has not been openly hostile in the manner of some of his predecessors. When his opponents, who scream about a one-party state, attack him, they do so as if they expect him to fund and help them manage their political affairs. That is what Nigerians can hear sometimes when Peter Obi tells them that if he becomes president, he would do this and that for opposition parties. He often comes short of saying he would run their affairs for them. The one-party lament is, however, subsiding, and since the APC formally flagged off its campaign in Kaduna last weekend, the opposition has been singing a different tune. What we are now hearing is that the crowds at the APC rally were either AI-generated or hired. One wonders why that should be the business of opposition parties that have been moving from one town hall and party venue to another in the name of campaigning. As they always do, as if they need the APC to prompt all seventeen of them, they are beginning to flag off their campaigns for 2027. Uba Sani has shown the way. We should hopefully sleep now without the noise of a one-party state. The post We’ve come a long way from the one-party state lament, by Rotimi Fasan appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Fake drinks may be causing liver, kidney diseases in Ondo — NMA
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure The Ondo State chapter of the Nigerian Medical Association (NMA) has raised the alarm over the circulation of suspected fake and adulterated beverages, warning that they may be contributing to liver and kidney diseases among young people. The association recalled previous incidents involving suspected adulterated drinks in parts of the state in which at least 50 people reportedly died, and called on the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC) and other relevant agencies to intensify efforts to rid the market of counterfeit alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages. The NMA Chairman in Ondo State, Dr Roland Bola Arohunmolase, raised the concern in Akure while speaking with journalists, saying doctors were encountering liver cirrhosis and kidney disease among younger patients in age groups where such conditions were considered uncommon. He said the association could not yet provide a definitive number of cases linked to suspected adulterated drinks because investigations were ongoing, but described the changing age profile of patients as worrisome. “Traditionally, when you profile some diseases, there are certain age groups in which you do not commonly find them. When a disease no longer conforms to its traditional profile, it becomes a cause for concern,” he said. Arohunmolase said cases of liver cirrhosis among teenagers and liver and kidney diseases among people aged between 22 and 30 required closer medical investigation. “For instance, I don’t expect a child of 15 years or someone between 15 and 18 to develop liver cirrhosis. You begin to wonder why that would happen. Similarly, we are finding liver cirrhosis and kidney disease among young people between the ages of 22 and 30. I think it calls for caution,” he said. The NMA chairman identified the consumption of unhealthy or adulterated beverages as a possible risk factor, while stressing that further investigations were necessary to establish the causes of individual cases. He recalled previous incidents in Odigbo and Irele involving suspected adulterated drinks, which reportedly claimed at least 50 lives, as well as an earlier incident in Ilere linked to methanol consumption. He warned that methanol, an industrial chemical, could cause severe poisoning and organ damage when ingested. According to the association, suspected counterfeit beverages are no longer confined to open markets, as such products have allegedly found their way into supermarkets, hotels, bars and other retail outlets. It warned that beverages produced under unhygienic conditions or made with contaminated water and harmful industrial chemicals could expose consumers to acute poisoning and long-term organ damage. The association called on the FCCPC, the Ondo State Government and other relevant regulatory agencies to conduct aggressive, unannounced inspections of markets, supermarkets, hotels, bars and shops suspected of stocking counterfeit beverages. It also urged the authorities to seize and destroy products that fail to meet safety standards and prosecute those found responsible for their production and distribution. The NMA further called on beverage manufacturers to strengthen anti-counterfeiting measures through tamper-proof seals, holograms, unique QR codes and product-tracking systems to enable consumers to verify the authenticity of their purchases. It advised consumers to be wary of drinks sold at prices significantly below prevailing market rates and to inspect seals, labels and packaging before making purchases. Arohunmolase said the association decided to alert the public without delay rather than wait for bureaucratic procedures to run their course. “As medical professionals who are supposed to be the custodians of public health, we needed to bring this to the public’s notice before writing to the relevant authorities,” he said. He urged anyone who suspected they had consumed a fake or contaminated beverage to seek medical attention immediately, rather than wait for symptoms to develop. “Whenever you consume something you suspect is not okay, it may not be advisable to wait until the symptoms start manifesting. You should seek medical advice on time,” he added. The post Fake drinks may be causing liver, kidney diseases in Ondo — NMA appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Alara Stool: Aramoko kingmakers seek Ooni, Oyebanji’s intervention
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure The Alara-in-Council and residents of Aramoko-Ekiti, Ekiti State, have appealed to the Ooni of Ife, Oba Adeyeye Enitan Ogunwusi, and Governor Biodun Oyebanji to intervene in the selection of a new traditional ruler, six months after the process was suspended. The kingmakers said the prolonged delay had left the Alara stool vacant, affecting traditional institutions, cultural activities and the observance of some festivals and rites in the community. In a statement signed by the Head of Kingmakers and Asao of Aramoko-Ekiti, High Chief Julius Oladiran Adebayo, and the Secretary and Sajowa of Aramoko-Ekiti, High Chief Kolade Oyebade, the council said its appeals to the state government had yet to receive a response. They urged the Ooni, whom they described as a custodian of Yoruba culture and tradition, to appeal to Oyebanji to permit them to reconvene and conclude the selection process. According to the kingmakers, the process began in April 2026 in accordance with the Alara of Aramoko Chieftaincy Declaration and the Ekiti State Chieftaincy Law. They said three princes were shortlisted through an Ifa divination exercise conducted by Baba Araba Elebuibon, after which voting by the 12 kingmakers ended in a tie, with six votes each. The council said a second round of voting was expected to resolve the deadlock but was not held following the postponement of the process by the Commissioner for Chieftaincy Affairs. “However, six months later, the process remains suspended after the Hon. Commissioner for Chieftaincy Affairs postponed it. Our letters to government have not received a response,” the statement said. Appealing directly to the Ooni, the kingmakers said the prolonged vacancy had created uncertainty in the community and affected the performance of some traditional rites. “The stool of Alara remains vacant. Our youths are restive. Our traditional festivals and rites cannot hold,” they said. They urged the Ooni to use his influence to persuade the governor to allow the kingmakers to reconvene and complete the selection process. The council expressed confidence that the intervention of the Ooni and the cooperation of the state government would lead to a peaceful resolution of the dispute. The kingmakers also highlighted the historical and cultural ties between Aramoko-Ekiti and Ile-Ife, describing the selection of a new Alara as important to preserving the town’s customs and traditions. They said they hoped the intervention would protect and strengthen the longstanding relationship between the two communities. The statement added that the kingmakers remained confident in the Ooni’s wisdom and the governor’s respect for law and tradition. The post Alara Stool: Aramoko kingmakers seek Ooni, Oyebanji’s intervention appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
body: A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world suspended operations because of extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia. The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and “temporary living arrangements”. It is unclear how many were on board, but the nearly 200 m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a “continuous voyage around the world”. Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship’s operator said monthly fuel costs per cabin in parts of Asia have risen from $1,800 to as much as $8,000 (£6,000). The company said it had taken “significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port”. But those measures proved insufficient to “offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs”. “Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” it said. The company would spend the next 60 days on “restructuring and recapitalisation”, though “no outcome is assured”, it said. The Villa Vie Odyssey’s voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website. Delays arose as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds. The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before it announced the suspension of its journey on Tuesday, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia. According to its website, the Villa Vie Odyssey has several bars and restaurants, a pool deck, and a pickleball court. Permanent residencies in its cabins range from $120,000 to $440,000. These cabins are also available for rent from $3,500 a month. Bloomberg reported that around 200 passengers were on board when they were ordered to disembark in Cambodia, citing the cruise operator’s founder.

title: What Nigeria can learn from the 2026 Nobel-winning research in Economics
body: Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford, the Winners of the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics, speak to policymakers through their work on “the microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation.” This is because their work helps in explaining how household and business decisions shape the wider economy, and how public policy can respond when growth, employment, and prices move in undesired directions. More importantly, the research of Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford transformed how economists understand these policies as well as illustrate that a broad, top-down view of the economy alone is insufficient because household and business decisions together shape the overall economy. Models based on this idea are called New Keynesian models. The influential economist John Maynard Keynes argued that weak demand for goods and services can increase unemployment and weaken economic growth. When people and businesses spend too little, shops and factories sell fewer goods and services and may thus produce less and hire fewer workers for which reason unemployment can rise and the economy can slow down. Excessive demand, on other hand, can overheat the economy and push up inflation. Stabilisation policy therefore aims to boost demand when it is too weak and curb it when it becomes excessive. Earlier economic models assumed that the economy would respond in familiar ways because they expected prices to rise when employment and production were strong, and to fall when the economy weakened. But the oil crises of the 1970s broke this pattern due to the fact that the surge in oil prices raised the cost of many goods even as businesses cut production and jobs. As a result, inflation and unemployment rose together. Robert E. Hall, for instance, showed how expectations influence household spending by illustrating that household spending depends not only on current income but also on expectations about future income: If families feel hopeful about the future, they may spend more. Based on this idea, Hall argued that household spending should remain fairly stable unless people receive new information about the future. His theory implies that changes in household spending cannot be accurately predicted and later research supported his idea. Michael Woodford’s model on the other hand shows how central banks (CBN) can influence economic activity. In 2003, Woodford introduced a macroeconomic model of how the economy works based on decisions by households and businesses which Policymakers can use to explore questions such as: what might happen to production and inflation if interest rates fall? How much should rates rise to control inflation? The model incorporates Hall’s findings on household spending and shows how changes in interest rates can shape the saving and spending decisions of families. In addition, Woodford’s work explains how a central bank can influence economic activity by adjusting its policy interest rate or the amount of money in circulation such as, for example, hiking interest rate by Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to help moderate inflation which has effects on aggregate demand; and how ‘Ways and Means’ have been used by past administrations to prop demand, and output but as well affect other variables. In the light of the above, it can be argued that: since businesses cannot always adjust prices immediately when demand or costs change and updating price or informing customers takes time and money, prices may stay fixed, a phenomenon economists call price stickiness. If customers buy less; a business may initially keep prices unchanged and instead reduce production or staff hours; continued declines can reduce both output and employment; and businesses set prices by considering future costs and competitors’ prices. Their views about the central bank’s future policies can also affect inflation. This is why clear and credible communication from the central bank matters. Woodford used the idea of the output gap to postulate on this: If actual production is above the level the economy can sustain, demand may be too strong, and inflation may rise. If actual production is below that level, the economy may be weak and inflationary pressure may ease. One aim of stabilisation policy is to reduce this gap. Supply shocks force policymakers to make difficult choices. A sudden increase in energy prices or a disruption to international supply chains can limit an economy’s productive capacity as evident in the recent US/Iran war. Production may decline as inflation and unemployment rise at the same time. In these circumstances, focusing solely on boosting demand is not enough. Policymakers must also account for inflationary pressure and the most effective response depends on the cause of the shock and the state of the economy. The aforementioned facts demonstrate that the research and ensuing postulations by Hall and Woodford provides policymakers with better tools to stabilise the economy. New Keynesian models, building on the work of Hall and Woodford, are now used by central banks and finance ministries in many countries. Policymakers can tailor the models to each country’s economic conditions, and further research is needed to improve on them. The Nobel laureates’ research can help explain Nigeria’s current economic challenges and influence how Policymakers can respond to them because the work can enhance how policymakers understand the responses of people to changes in income, prices, and interest rates, and how firms adjust prices, production, and investment. This framework can deepen the analysis of Nigeria’s current difficulties although it is not a ready-made policy formula. Nigeria faces high inflation alongside relative moderate growth and investment. Although inflation declines to 14.86 % in September 2026 from the 15.39 % in August 2026, subdued economic activity, supply and cost pressures, and slow growth in private-sector credit are still key challenges. In August, private-sector credit was 1.35% and this implies that businesses were delaying investment amid high financing costs, energy shortages, infrastructure bottlenecks, uncertainty about demand and the coming general election. These points indicate that policymakers must take appropriate measures to reduce inflation without further weakening production, investment, and employment. The Nobel laureates’ approach shows how the pressures cited above can affect different parts of the economy. As prices rise, households may spend less, use their savings, or cut essential expenses but low-income families with limited access to credit have less room to adapt. Businesses, meanwhile, consider interest rates alongside energy costs, access to imported inputs, infrastructure, demand, and policy uncertainty when deciding whether to invest, produce, or hire. Higher interest rates can curb borrowing and demand, but cannot, on their own, fix energy shortages, port delays, or other supply problems. When inflation is driven mainly by demand overtaking the economy’s capacity to supply, tighter monetary policy can help curb spending. But when a supply shock pushes up costs while production and employment remain weak, raising rates may further reduce investment and jobs without addressing the source of inflation. A lower rate is not automatically the answer, either. If households and businesses expect prices to keep rising, inflation may persist. In this scenario, CBN must weigh both risks and design how it will respond to new evidence. The Nobel laureates’ output also raises the need for consistency across public policy because CBN’s monetary tools and the government’s decisions on taxes, spending, and borrowing serve different purposes but affect the same economy. When government borrowing boosts demand or competes with businesses for bank funds, it can weaken the effects of monetary restraint. Nigerian policymakers can take the following three practical lessons from this: First, track inflation by its sources and the groups it affects, drawing on data about household spending, wages, business costs, import prices, and expectations; Second, set interest rates with inflation risks in mind, alongside growth, employment, and credit conditions; and Third, strengthen supply and productivity with reliable energy, efficient ports, better transport, and fewer administrative barriers. Targeted support may help protect low-income families as these changes take effect. The theory applies to Nigeria because households and businesses everywhere make decisions that shape economic outcomes. Nevertheless, the country’s high informality, limited household savings, reliance on imports, supply constraints, and banking-sector weaknesses call for locally grounded analysis. The key lesson is to use the Nobel laureates’ framework to understand how policies influence real decisions, while aligning credible monetary policy with sound fiscal choices and practical steps to address high costs and weak investment. Muhammed Muttaka Usman is a Professor of Economics at Ahmadu Bello University Zaria, and member of the Board of Economics, Daily Trust. Views expressed in this article are the author’s own.

title: Is Israel barreling toward another election? 5 scenarios after dramatic night
body: Israel faces the prospect of another election after updated exit polls early Wednesday showed neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his main rival Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to a parliamentary majority, leaving the country confronting a prolonged political deadlock. The projections, including overnight revisions, reinforced what had become increasingly apparent during the election campaign: Neither political bloc appears capable of securing the 61 seats needed to control the 120-member Knesset.   Several scenarios remain possible, including another election, a national unity government, a Netanyahu-led coalition supported by defectors from the opposition and a minority government headed by Eisenkot. But the possibility of an Eisenkot minority government, which appeared viable when the first exit polls were released at 10 p.m. Tuesday, has diminished significantly following overnight updates. One revised projection showed Netanyahu's bloc holding a substantial advantage over the opposition. The unexpectedly strong showing by Arab parties has complicated coalition calculations for both sides, leaving neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot with an apparent path to a majority without their involvement or support. Scenario 1: Another election A return to the polls may be the most likely outcome, although it could also be the most damaging for Israel, particularly as the country continues to face security tensions on several fronts. The large number of seats projected for Arab parties has left both major political blocs struggling to assemble a governing majority without cooperating with them — a prospect that several party leaders have publicly rejected. President Isaac Herzog could attempt to broker a compromise to prevent another election, potentially with assistance from political figures and international actors. Under Israel's parliamentary system, the president consults with party representatives after an election and assigns a lawmaker the task of forming a government, generally choosing the candidate considered most capable of securing parliamentary support. If those efforts fail, Israel could face another election, with Netanyahu remaining in office as caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. That would give Netanyahu a significant advantage by allowing him to retain the premiership despite the absence of a new parliamentary majority. Some figures in the opposition's pro-change bloc also fear that Netanyahu could seek to escalate security tensions to complicate efforts to replace him or pressure rival parties into joining an emergency government. Those concerns reflect the opposition's suspicions rather than any established plan by Netanyahu. Scenario 2: A national unity government led by Netanyahu A unity government headed by Netanyahu remains possible, but only if several political leaders abandon explicit campaign promises. In his election-night address, Netanyahu gave no indication that he intended to break with his existing right-wing coalition partners. He did not directly appeal to leaders of the opposition bloc or explicitly propose a unity government. Instead, he declared that "the Zionist majority must come to its senses and unite," without outlining how such an arrangement might work. Eisenkot, who was introduced as "the next prime minister" during his own election-night speech, appeared equally unwilling to compromise. "A worthy leader would resign that very day," Eisenkot said, referring to Netanyahu and the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel. Eisenkot has repeatedly promised that he would not serve in a government with Netanyahu under any circumstances, even declaring that he would resign the following day if he ever agreed to serve under him. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, leader of the Beyachad party, and Avigdor Liberman, chairman of the nationalist Yisrael Beytenu party, have also ruled out joining a Netanyahu-led government. The updated exit polls, which show Likud and Netanyahu's bloc performing more strongly than initially projected, could further complicate negotiations. With Likud emerging as the largest party, Netanyahu would be unlikely to relinquish the first term as prime minister under any proposed power-sharing rotation agreement, assuming he agreed to such an arrangement at all. That leaves a unity government theoretically possible but politically difficult to achieve. Scenario 3: Netanyahu forms a government with opposition defectors Netanyahu could also attempt to form a government by persuading lawmakers from the pro-change bloc to defect and join his coalition. But the updated projections suggest he remains well short of the 61-seat threshold. Rather than needing one or two opposition lawmakers to cross the aisle, Netanyahu would have to attract a substantial group of defectors to secure a majority. That would be a considerably more difficult political undertaking, particularly after a campaign in which opposition leaders made replacing Netanyahu a central objective. The Likud leader could nevertheless seek the presidential mandate to form a government as a tactical move, even if his prospects of assembling a viable coalition remain slim. Receiving the mandate would give Netanyahu an opportunity to negotiate with potential partners, but it would not guarantee that he could form a government. Scenario 4: An Eisenkot minority government An Eisenkot-led minority government initially appeared possible after the first exit polls were released at 10 p.m., when the pro-change bloc seemed poised to emerge as the largest parliamentary grouping. Under that scenario, Eisenkot could have secured more recommendations from lawmakers than Netanyahu, potentially persuading Herzog to give him the first opportunity to form a government. Minutes after the initial projections were released, Eisenkot announced that he intended to begin working immediately to establish a government, arguing that his bloc had emerged as the largest. Such a government would likely have required parliamentary support from Arab parties without necessarily including them as formal coalition partners. But Liberman, who ruled out a minority government during the campaign, offered no indication in his election-night speech that he was reconsidering his position. He also declined to answer whether he would cooperate with Ra'am, the Arab Islamist party led by Mansour Abbas. Liberman instead called for a revolt against Netanyahu, whom he described as "the head of a criminal organization." The overnight exit poll revisions have made an Eisenkot minority government even less likely, with the pro-change bloc no longer appearing to command enough support to establish a government, even if potential defectors were to join it. Scenario 5: Replacing Netanyahu's caretaker government Another possibility would involve replacing Netanyahu's caretaker administration with a temporary government headed by Eisenkot, allowing the opposition to pursue a limited legislative agenda even without a stable long-term coalition. Such an arrangement could enable the new parliamentary majority to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, and establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attack. A state commission of inquiry, an independent investigative body with broad powers to summon witnesses and examine government conduct, has been a major demand of Netanyahu's critics. The arrangement could also allow the opposition to pursue other parliamentary measures while attempting to negotiate a more permanent governing coalition. But this scenario, too, has become increasingly remote following the overnight revisions to the exit polls. With Netanyahu's bloc performing more strongly than initially expected and Arab parties holding a substantial share of parliamentary seats, the opposition appears to lack the numbers needed to carry out such a transition. For now, the projections point to a fragmented Knesset in which neither major bloc can govern alone, leaving Israel's political future dependent on difficult coalition negotiations, possible reversals of campaign pledges or another election. The final distribution of seats will not be known until the official vote count is completed.

title: After elections, Israeli Arabs now have political power - will their leaders use it? - analysis
body: Late on election night, Mansour Abbas was asked about the conditions Gadi Eisenkot had set for working with Arab parties. His reply went to a more immediate problem: was there a government to be formed in the first place?In the Channel 16 interview, the Ra'am leader put the arithmetic before the negotiations. First establish whether a government is viable, then discuss the terms. With the television projections pointing in different directions, there was a practical reason for that sequence. Abbas was assessing the possibilities available to his party and its voters. He might have leverage. He might discover that the final results left him with very little.Israel's Arab citizens are often discussed abroad as evidence in somebody else's case. Their own political arguments receive less attention. They are invoked as evidence of Israeli democracy, or described through the discrimination they face. Meanwhile, their parties are debating how to exercise influence, what to demand, and how much compromise their supporters will accept.Some of those choices have already changed Israeli history. Ra'am participated in the Bennett-Lapid coalition formed in 2021, helping sustain a government led initially by a prime minister from the Israeli right. This election could again put Arab parties near the center of coalition negotiations. Three broadcasters projected Netanyahu's bloc short of a majority; Channel 14's updated projection put it above one. These remain projections, not the official result.In Israel's 120-seat parliament, 61 seats give a coalition a majority. An Arab citizen's ballot contributes to that calculation in the same way as a Jewish citizen's. Governments can depend on those votes, and governments can fall when parliamentary support disappears. Anyone describing Israel to an international audience needs to give that political power its proper weight.The weight of the word 'apartheid'The word “apartheid” requires more care than an election-night slogan allows. Amnesty International's allegation extends to Israel as well as the occupied territories, and its report acknowledges Arab representation in parliament. Arab electoral rights do not resolve the status of Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank, whose legal and political circumstances differ. Participation also does not erase discrimination inside Israel. Those arguments require scrutiny on their own terms. So does the democratic reality of Arab citizens organizing parties, winning seats and negotiating over how their country is governed.The differences among those parties matter. Abbas wants Ra'am to participate in government. The Joint List, comprising Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad, has offered to negotiate support from outside a government that replaces Netanyahu. Its leader, Yousef Jabareen, has demanded a funded and monitored plan to combat crime, while setting red lines over national issues, including war and settlement budgets. Cooperation would have to survive those disagreements. A shared interest in replacing a prime minister does not settle what comes afterward.Ra'am has taken another striking step by recruiting Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former Yesh Atid lawmaker who once headed Israel's national serious-crime unit. His move to a party with Islamist-conservative roots brings questions about policing, partnership and political identity into the same room. Voters can regard it as an opportunity, a mistake, or an arrangement unlikely to last. The decision is theirs. What interests me is that such a choice exists, crossing a boundary that can look immovable from a distance.There are equally consequential differences among the Jewish parties. When Keshet Neev and I interviewed Eisenkot in September, he described conditions for partnership: acceptance of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, the Declaration of Independence's values, an obligation of service, and recognition that Hamas is a terrorist organization that must be dismantled. He said he saw no Arab party meeting those principles. He later ruled out aligning himself with any Arab party in an October podcast reported by Reuters.These are questions about the responsibilities of government. After October 7, a disagreement over Hamas reaches directly into national security, and the confidence citizens place in those making decisions on their behalf. Arab leaders seeking a governing role should expect close scrutiny of their positions and record, as should their prospective partners. Their proposals deserve attention without anyone assuming in advance that they must be accepted.The mistrust also has a history. In an article published on October 8, 2023, Balad chairman and former MK Sami Abu Shehadeh discussed the attack's strategic significance and potential political gains without condemning the killing and abduction of civilians. He later condemned the massacre, said he had written before understanding the full scale of the atrocities, and said the article should not have appeared in that form. On November 5, 2023, Ra'am MK Iman Khatib-Yasin questioned reports of babies being killed and women raped while discussing footage she acknowledged she had not watched. In that interview, she also condemned the attack as inhumane, contrary to Islam, and unjustifiable. She apologized and retracted her remarks that evening; Mansour Abbas rejected minimization of the massacre and demanded her resignation. The damaging remarks and the responses to them both belong in the record.Naftali Bennett, who led the government that included Ra'am in 2021, now opposes repeating that arrangement. He has explained his objection in terms of the party's non-Zionist character rather than its members' ethnicity. Yair Golan, leader of the Democrats, supports bringing Ra'am into a coalition. Each position carries implications for the kind of government that could be formed and the compromises it would require. Neither can be understood through the seat totals alone.Whether either Arab list belongs in a particular government depends on a workable agreement, its policies and the trust its partners can sustain. Refusing a coalition partnership does not, by itself, establish racism. Equally, an Arab citizen's political legitimacy cannot depend on choosing a party the Jewish majority finds agreeable. A democracy has to keep those distinctions clear, especially when elections make them inconvenient.National identity reaches into the most ordinary parts of Israeli life: the safety of a street, public services, the obligations citizens owe one another. Arab parties differ over how those concerns should shape their political strategy. Jewish parties have their own disputes over the country's character and the price of cooperation. No single leader speaks for an entire community, and a voter's identity cannot tell us everything about the decision made behind the curtain.Abbas began with the question of whether a government was possible. The answer may eventually leave him inside a coalition, supporting one from outside, or sitting firmly in opposition. Any of those outcomes could emerge from democratic politics. The important test will be whether Israel can turn the result into responsible government while preserving the standing of citizens whose representatives remain outside it.That is the future worth imagining: a country secure enough for serious disagreements to be argued through institutions, where equal citizenship survives the collapse of a coalition or the defeat of a party. On election night, attention settles on the seats around the cabinet table. The country's democratic life also depends on what remains true for everyone who has no place at it.

title: Olympiacos Beat Montenegro Team in Champions League Thriller
body: Olympiacos defeated Montenegrin champions Jadran Herceg Novi 19-17 on penalties in Piraeus on Wednesday, after a 14-14 draw in regular time, to secure their second consecutive win in the men’s water polo Champions League group stage. Olympiacos equalised with a penalty from Konstantinos Genidounias just over a minute before the final whistle. However, the Greek champions dropped a point and sit second in Group A behind Sabadell, whom they will host at the Petros Kapagerof pool on 10 November. Olympiacos recover after a difficult start Elvis Fatovic’s team made a poor start, conceding twice in the opening 90 seconds. Olympiacos quickly levelled the score but struggled to get past Australian goalkeeper Lawrence Barker, who made five saves in the first quarter to keep Jadran in the game. Olympiacos took control in the second quarter as their defence and goalkeeper Manos Zerdevas shut down the Montenegrin attack. Jadran went 12 and a half minutes without scoring, allowing Olympiacos to build a 5-0 run. The visitors then scored twice in succession to reduce the deficit, but Genidounias helped Olympiacos establish a 6-4 lead at half-time. Jadran regain the lead in a tense finish Jadran began the third quarter strongly, scoring three unanswered goals to move ahead 7-6. Olympiacos responded through Pap anastasiou and a penalty from Fountoulis, but poor decisions during extra-man attacks allowed Jadran to regain control. Goals from Merkulov and Stupar gave the Montenegrin champions a 9-8 advantage heading into the final quarter. The teams exchanged goals throughout the fourth quarter, but Olympiacos could not take the lead. Barker produced another outstanding save against Angyal during an extra-man attack to keep the score level at 11-11. Nineteen-year-old Strahinja Gojkovic, one of Jadran’s standout performers, scored his fifth goal of the match to put his team ahead 14-13 with 1 minute and 18 seconds remaining. Olympiacos won a penalty after Kharkov drew a foul from Merkulov. Genidounias converted with 1:03 remaining to make it 14-14. Zerdevas then saved Stupar’s shot. Olympiacos could not capitalise on their final attack, with officials missing what appeared to be a foul by Radovic on Alafragkis. Zerdevas saved Gojkovic’s attempt in the closing seconds to send the match to a penalty shootout. Tzortzatos delivers the decisive save Olympiacos converted all five penalties through Fatovic, Fountoulis, Pap anastasiou, Dimou and Genidounias. Goalkeeper Panagiotis Tzortzatos, who had not played during regular time, replaced Zerdevas after the first two penalty attempts. He saved Stupar’s shot to secure the victory and give Olympiacos two points. The result leaves Olympiacos second in Group A, with their next match against leaders Sabadell scheduled for 10 November in Piraeus. Quarter-by-quarter scores: 2-2, 4-2, 2-5, 6-5 Penalty shootout: Olympiacos won 5-3 Referees: Burz (France), Savinovic (Croatia) Olympiacos (Elvis Fatovic): Zerdevas, Angyal, Fatovic 3, Genidounias 4, Fountoulis 4, Papanastasiou 2, Gillas, Spahic 1, Alafragkis 1, Loncar, Kharkov, Dimou 3, Tzortzatos, Pouros 1. Jadran Herceg Novi (Vladimir Gojkovic): Andric, Murisic, Stupar 3, Obradovic, Durik 1, Radovic 2, Merkulov 3, Gojkovic 6, Petrovic, Trtovic, Ukropina 2, Matiasevic, Barker, Vranes. title: Jaiz Bank’s financing portfolio hits N800bn
body: Jaiz Bank has more than N100bn in financing supporting trade in cocoa, cashew and other non oil export products, as its overall financing portfolio approaches N800bn, its Managing Director, Dr Haruna Musa, has said. Musa said more financing was needed for exporters, manufacturers and micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) to expand production, create jobs and grow the economy. He spoke at a breakfast session of the 32nd Nigeria Economic Summit (NES32) in Abuja on Tuesday. He said banks needed to structure financing around the operations and cash flows of businesses rather than apply the same arrangement to every customer. “In the non-interest banking model, we have various contracts, and these contracts must align with the business model and cash flows,” he said. Musa called for increased financing for manufacturing and agriculture, saying support should cover different stages of the value chain, from farm inputs to processing and distribution. He also identified solar energy as an area for financing, arguing that support should extend beyond installing solar systems to businesses across the value chain. He said hospitals and other essential facilities could benefit from such arrangements. The Jaiz Bank managing director called for better access to non-interest finance for women, young people and rural communities, where limited banking infrastructure can make it difficult for businesses to access financial services. He said digital platforms and partnerships with financial technology companies could help banks reach more customers and reduce dependence on physical branches. Musa disclosed that he had gone almost a year without visiting a bank branch because he carried out transactions through his mobile phone. Also speaking, a Professor of Islamic Law at the University of Ilorin, Prof. AbdulRazzaq Alaro, said non-interest finance could support job creation and economic growth by directing funds towards productive activities. “When you channel money to productive economic activities, you automatically create jobs. You automatically get economic growth, and that will ultimately result in shared prosperity for all,” Alaro said. He said the model was based on principles including risk sharing, asset-l backing and transactions linked to real economic activities. Alaro identified agriculture, infrastructure and MSMEs as areas where Islamic finance arrangements could support investment. He said the Salam contract could be used to finance agricultural production, while Istisna could support construction, infrastructure and projects involving the production or delivery of specified assets. He also highlighted Nigeria’s National Halal Economy Strategy, which he said seeks to position the country to benefit from a global halal market estimated at $8 trillion. According to him, Nigeria is targeting a contribution of up to $12bn to its gross domestic product through the strategy over the coming years. He said non-interest banks and other Islamic finance institutions could finance businesses serving the halal market, including those involved in production and trade.

title: Ikare Festival: Ondo monarch urges patience with Tinubu’s reforms
body: By Dayo Johnson, Akure The Owa-Ale of Ikare-Akoko in Ondo State, Oba Adegbite Adedoyin, has appealed to Nigerians to exercise patience with the economic reforms of President Bola Tinubu, expressing confidence in the country’s future under the administration. The monarch also prayed for Tinubu’s re-election, expressing the belief that the President would secure another term in office. Oba Adedoyin spoke at the conclusion of the week-long annual Okemeji Takotabo Festival in Ikare-Akoko, where prayers were offered for peace, development and progress in the community, Ondo State and Nigeria. He said the festival remained an important part of the community’s cultural heritage, inherited from its forefathers, and provided an opportunity to seek divine intervention in the affairs of the kingdom and the country. “The Okemeji Takotabo Festival is part of the cultural heritage we inherited from our forefathers. Ikare is traditionally associated with the festival, which remains an important part of our identity and history,” he said. According to the monarch, the community visited the Okemeji hilltop during this year’s celebration to pray for Ikare-Akoko, Ondo State and Nigeria. He said prayers were also offered for Tinubu, the Ondo State governor, local government officials, ministers, political leaders and residents of the community. “We asked God to guide our leaders and grant them the wisdom to govern effectively. We also prayed for the President to secure another term, believing that he is working towards building a new Nigeria,” the monarch said. Adedoyin expressed optimism that the prayers would yield positive results, saying he expected residents to return at the next edition of the festival with testimonies of answered prayers. He further stressed that peace was essential to the development of Ikare-Akoko, adding that he had continued to encourage peaceful coexistence among residents. Also speaking, the Elemure of Emure, Oba Bankole Adeyefa, commended the Ondo State Government for supporting traditional institutions and promoting the state’s cultural heritage. Adeyefa described the festival as an important initiative for strengthening traditional institutions and preserving cultural values. He added that the celebration provided an opportunity to pray for the kingdom, Ondo State and Nigeria. Similarly, the Olona of Okeagbe Quarter, High Chief Rafiu Okunade, described the festival as historic and symbolic, commending the Owa-Ale for his contributions to community development. The Oniku of Iku Quarter, High Chief Bello Mukaila, also praised the monarch and urged residents to remain law-abiding. title: New tax laws won’t trigger automatic bank deductions – NRS
body: The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has assured Nigerians that the new tax reforms do not empower authorities to automatically deduct money from personal bank accounts, urging taxpayers to understand the laws and embrace voluntary compliance. The State Administrator for Jigawa, Kano and Katsina, Abdullahi Samaila, gave the assurance at an NRS sensitisation and enlightenment programme in Kano, with the theme, “Driving Voluntary Tax Compliance Through Tax Reforms Awareness.” Samaila said the reforms had generated concerns among individuals, businesses and state governments over bank transactions, taxation of family transfers and loans, value-added tax (VAT), and the possible impact on small businesses. He said the concerns were understandable, noting that taxpayers wanted assurances that their money would remain safe, their businesses would not be unnecessarily burdened, and governments would continue to receive resources to provide essential services. “Certainly, there are practical reasons for greater confidence in the new tax regime,” he said, adding that tax collection and recovery must follow the applicable laws and procedures. The NRS official also clarified that the standard VAT rate remained 7.5 per cent, while urging taxpayers to distinguish between money received as loans and actual business income. He explained that a trader who received a loan of N500,000 should not automatically have the amount treated as sales or profit, stressing the importance of keeping proper records and evidence to establish the nature of transactions. Samaila said the tax reforms would be better understood if taxpayers received clear and practical explanations of their obligations, applicable reliefs, record-keeping requirements and channels for seeking assistance. He outlined key areas of the sensitisation programme, including tax provisions affecting companies, individuals and businesses, practical steps towards voluntary compliance, and measures to address challenges confronting taxpayers. According to him, taxpayers should register appropriately, maintain accurate records, reconcile transactions, file returns, pay applicable taxes on time and respond to official correspondence. He also called on participants to identify difficulties they encountered, including confusing tax guidance and challenges with digital processes, to enable the service to develop practical solutions. Samaila said the NRS was responsible for providing clear guidance, consistent treatment and accessible support, while taxpayers were expected to provide accurate information and fulfil their obligations within the stipulated time. “Understanding builds confidence. Clear procedures make action clearer and easier. Clear and responsive services help sustain trust,” he said, urging participants to ask questions and share their experiences to strengthen voluntary tax compliance.

title: BUA seeks large-scale indigenous industries to drive growth
body: The Founder and Executive Chairman of BUA Group, Abdul Samad Rabiu, has called for increased investment in local industries to expand Nigeria’s productive capacity, create jobs and improve living standards. He said the country must move beyond economic reforms to increased production, urging the government and private sector to work together to build a stronger industrial base. Rabiu spoke at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja, where he delivered a keynote address on the theme, “Growth That Works: Building a New Economic Accord for Nigeria.” He commended President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms, particularly improved access to foreign exchange, saying they had helped create a more predictable environment for businesses. He said manufacturers previously struggled to obtain dollars for machinery and raw materials, even when they had enough naira to finance their investments. “Legitimate businesses can now access foreign exchange through the market at prevailing exchange rates, rather than depending on direct allocations from the Central Bank,” he said. Rabiu also acknowledged the removal of petrol subsidy, fiscal and tax reforms, banking sector reforms and infrastructure investments. However, he said the gains must translate into higher production, more jobs and shared prosperity. “We must move from reform to results, from stabilisation to expansion, and from economic adjustment to shared prosperity,” he said. Highlighting BUA Group’s expansion plans, Rabiu said the company was investing in flour milling, pasta, noodles, edible oils, rice milling and feed mills. The projects, he said, are expected to be completed in 2027 and double production capacity across the affected operations. He said the investments would strengthen food security, create jobs, support farmers and suppliers, and increase Nigeria’s capacity to serve markets across Africa. Rabiu disclosed that BUA Foods and BUA Cement, both listed on the Nigerian Exchange, had a combined market capitalisation of more than $17bn. He said Nigeria needed to create at least 100 more major indigenous industrial companies capable of investing in manufacturing, agriculture, mining, technology and other productive sectors. “The question we must ask ourselves is not simply how BUA can continue to grow. It is how Nigeria can create another one hundred BUAs,” he said. The businessman identified access to affordable, long-term financing as a major obstacle to industrial expansion, noting that large manufacturing investments could take 10 to 20 years to realise their full potential. He called for greater mobilisation of funds from banks, pension funds, insurance companies, development finance institutions and capital markets to support productive investments. Rabiu cited the cement industry as an example of what sustained local investment could achieve, noting that Nigeria had moved from importing almost 80 per cent of its cement consumption to self-sufficiency and net exports. “Nigeria must not remain simply a supplier of raw materials or a market for finished products. We must become a nation that processes, manufactures and exports,” he said. He urged the government to ensure policy stability, improve infrastructure and invest in human capital while encouraging businesses to take advantage of opportunities under the African Continental Free Trade Area. Rabiu said Nigeria’s resources and entrepreneurial capacity could drive economic prosperity if they were converted into productive investments.

title: US costs of Iran war rise to over $47B – Pentagon data
body: WASHINGTON, USA – The US military has spent over $47 billion so far to prosecute the war in Iran , more than 25% higher than the Defense Department’s estimate in July, according to Pentagon data obtained by Reuters. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to a request for comment on its estimate, which has not been shared publicly. The disclosure about the rising cost of the Iran war comes as Republicans wrestle with the political fallout of the unpopular conflict ahead of the November 3 election that will determine control of Congress for the next two years. The war’s impact on global energy costs has weighed on support for Republican candidates and hurt President Donald Trump’s approval ratings. Trump’s Republican Party holds a narrow majority in both chambers of Congress. The Pentagon’s latest estimate was tied to the operational costs of carrying out the war, with a projected cost of more than $29 billion to replace expended munitions used in the conflict. More than $6 billion would be needed to replace military equipment and so-called “platform losses,” which include the loss of aircraft including many drones lost during the war. Trump launched the Iran war jointly with Israel in February, predicting ​that the conflict would last a short time. Trump’s initial strategy in the Iran war focused on first using expensive, high-end precision missiles to bomb Iran’s defenses so it could later use less expensive munitions, including gravity bombs like the air-launched JDAMs, which are plentiful. But an April ceasefire gave time for Iran to dig out underground storage facilities, bringing back online some Iranian defenses, as well as missiles and drones that had been inaccessible. Trump has since imposed a naval blockade on Iran to starve it of oil export revenue and held out the possibility of restarting combat operations after the midterm elections. US officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, say the Pentagon has been planning to restart heavy fighting if ordered to do so. The latest Pentagon estimate compares to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ‘s July estimate of $37.5 billion for the cost of the war. While the figures include a host of operational costs, from flight operations to cyber support, the US military’s Iran war cost estimates did not clearly account for the massive expense expected to repair damage to US bases sustained by Iranian missile and drone attacks. Rappler.com

title: FMBN launches non-interest mortgage in Kano
body: Nigeria’s apex housing finance institution, the Federal Mortgage Bank of Nigeria FMBN has launched its first Non-interest product in Kano called Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek also known as Lease-to-Own. According to the bank, the conventional interest-based mortgage model does not align with the personal convictions of some Nigerians arising from affordability, limited access, prompting the bank to mobilise contributions into the National Housing Fund (NHF) and facilitate access to affordable housing. This is to help people access financial services that are consistent with their values and convictions. Speaking at the Launch, FMBN Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer Shehu Usman said the objective is to widen the mortgage market and provide an additional pathway to homeownership such that eligible NHF contributors are not excluded from housing finance. “The product Ijarah Muntahia Bittamleek, is based on Islamic finance arrangement commonly described as Lease-to-Own. Under this structure, the customer occupies a property through a lease arrangement and subject to the agreed terms and fulfilment of the contractual obligations, ownership is transferred to the customer at the end of the arrangement,” said the CEO. He said the product is not for one religious community but an additional housing finance option for eligible NHF contributors who wish to access a non-interest based arrangement. According to him, while the global Islamic finance assets have reached US$5.98 Trillion in 2024, Nigeria’s Islamic finance industry was estimated at over N4.4 trillion in 2024 from N2.5 trillion in 2023 and it is projected to rise. The bank said it has dedicated a housing project financed by FMBN in Bichi as the pilot implementation of the Non-interest mortgage product. Launching the product, Minister of Housing and Urban Development Engineer Muntaqa Rabe Darma said the product launch is consistent with the National Mortgage Industry Policy issued by the Ministry in July this year, directing FMBN to disburse at least 40% of each year’s NHF collection as mortgages and raise its loans ceiling from N50m to N80 million. He also asked the bank to decide application within 30 working days, noting that the product will narrow the housing deficit in the country. Darma said more than six million Nigerians contribute to the NHF yet fewer than 500 individual mortgages are booked in a year with many contributors staying away from the interest-bearing loans altogether. With the launch of the product the Minister said the Bank is expected to process 2000 mortgages this year and 5000 by the year 2028. He charged the bank to scale up from Kano to reach Lagos, Port Harcourt, Enugu,Ibadan, Sokoto and Maiduguri, saying President Bola Tinubu places housing at the heart of inclusive growth and his Renewed Hope Agenda. Kano State Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf represented the Commissioner for Housing and Urban Development, Arch. Ibrahim Yakubu Adamu hailed the introduction of the product which he said will help expand access to housing finance. He said a vast expanse of land in Lambu village was allocated and is being developed as a Renewed Hope City project.

title: Zamfara gets new statistician-general
body: Governor Dauda Lawal appointed Kabiru Jelani as the new Statistician-General of Zamfara State. This was contained in a statement signed by the Zamfara State Head of Service, Shehu Baraya. The appointment follows the elevation of the former Statistician-General, Mu’azu Jibril Guraguri, to the position of Permanent Secretary in the state civil service. The statement added that the appointment was to ensure continuity in the leadership of the state’s statistical administration, which plays a critical role in evidence-based policy making, development planning, resource allocation and monitoring of government programmes. The Head of Service urged the appointee to discharge his responsibility with a high sense of professionalism, integrity and dedication to public service. In the same vein, Governor Dauda Lawal has approved the redeployment of 19 Permanent Secretaries across various Ministries, Departments and Agencies in the state civil service. A statement signed by the Zamfara State Head of Service, Alhaji Shehu Baraya, indicates that the redeployment is meant to broaden the administrative experience of the senior public officers, promote cross-sectional knowledge, and strengthen efficiency, accountability and service delivery across the state civil service. The Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Information and Culture, Alhaji Muhammad Salihu Anka has moved to the General Service. title: Polio: UNICEF, Zamfara move against disease
body: The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), in collaboration with the Zamfara State Ministry of Information and Culture, organised an awareness walk in Gusau to commemorate World Polio Day. The walk commenced at the Gusau Emir’s Palace and proceeded to Dr. Karima Primary Health Care Centre, Gusau, as part of efforts to raise public awareness about polio prevention, immunisation, and the importance of protecting children against the disease. The initiative highlighted the importance of collaboration between government institutions, development partners, traditional leaders, and communities in the fight against polio and other vaccine-preventable diseases. The awareness walk also serves as a platform to encourage parents and caregivers to ensure that their children receive all recommended doses of the polio vaccine to protect them from lifelong disability caused by the disease. UNICEF and the Zamfara State Ministry of Information and Culture continue to emphasise the importance of public awareness, community participation, and accurate information in promoting immunisation and improving children’s health outcomes across the state. The commemoration reaffirms the collective commitment of stakeholders to supporting polio eradication efforts and ensuring a healthier future for every child in Zamfara State. title: 2027: 2.3m electorate to vote in Zamfara
body: Governor Dauda Lawal and 19 other governorship candidates would scramble for 2.3 million votes in the February 2027 governorship election in Zamfara state. Governor Lawal, who is seeking reelection under the platform of the All Progressives Congress, will face 19 opposition candidates in the polls. The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) said the state registered voters have risen to 2,265,175 as of August 2026. The figure represents an increase of 313,115 voters, or 16.04 per cent, compared to the 1,952,060 registered voters recorded during the 2023 general elections in the state. The Zamfara INEC Resident Electoral Commissioner, Dr Mahmuda Isah, disclosed this during the election stakeholders’ meeting on the 2027 general elections and PVC collection on Wednesday in Gusau, Zamfara. “I would like to highlight some important electoral statistics that demonstrate both the scale of our responsibilities and the significance of public participation in the electoral process,” Isah said. “The Continuous Voter Registration exercise recorded 313,115 registrations as of August 2026, representing approximately 16.04 per cent of the 2023 registered-voter figure,” he said. He noted that the figures underscore the importance of sustained voter mobilisation, effective public enlightenment and the need to maintain an accurate, credible and inclusive Register of Voters. “Registration records will continue to undergo the necessary verification and validation processes in accordance with the law and approved procedures,” Isah said. According to him, Zamfara comprises 14 Local Government Areas, 147 Registration Areas (Electoral Wards), 3,529 Polling Units, three Senatorial Districts, seven Federal Constituencies and 24 State Assembly Constituencies. “With an average of approximately 553 registered voters per Polling Unit, based on the 2023 figure, these statistics demonstrate the considerable logistical, administrative and security responsibilities involved in conducting elections across the state,” he said. Isah said successful conduct of the 2027 general elections would require meticulous planning, efficient resource deployment, effective security coordination, continuous voter education and active cooperation of all stakeholders. He emphasised that the Permanent Voter Card (PVC) remained an essential requirement for voter accreditation and participation in elections. “The commission, therefore, attaches considerable importance to ensuring that all eligible registered voters have adequate opportunities to collect their PVCs. “Following the conclusion of the ward-level collection exercise, PVC collection will continue at INEC offices in the 14 Local Government Areas of Zamfara, in accordance with the commission’s approved arrangements. “I appeal to all registered voters who are yet to collect their PVCs to visit their respective INEC local government offices and collect their cards personally,” he said. “INEC Zamfara remains resolutely committed to carrying out its constitutional mandate with independence, impartiality, professionalism, transparency and integrity,” he assured. title: Zamfara steps up Ebola surveillance, screening
body: The Zamfara Government had stepped up surveillance against Ebola by conducting mass screening at the Gusau International Airport and across motor parks. This was done to prevent possible spread of the virus in the state. The Commissioner for Health, Dr Nafisa Maradun, disclosed this while flagging-off the response team at the Gusau International Airport on Friday. She said the state government initiated the response measure following the arrival of a passenger, an indigene of Zamfara, from Saudi Arabia via EgyptAir, who presented with high temperature. Maradun said the measures were aimed at preventing an outbreak of the virus in the state. She said the government had also intensified screening of passengers and commuters arriving at Gusau motor parks and other entry points, noting that raising public awareness remained key to curbing possible spread of the virus. The move, according to the commissioner, follows the reported index case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja. The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention had disclosed that the index patient diagnosed with the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus in Nigeria is a Ugandan-born woman who arrived in the FCT with her husband on October 3. Flagging off the response at the airport, Maradun said: “It becomes necessary as the surveillance team identified a passenger arriving from Saudi Arabia via EgyptAir with high temperature.” She said officials had been deployed to the airport to screen passengers arriving in Zamfara by air to ensure no one imports the Ebola virus into the state. title: Norway allocates nearly $54M in energy support for Ukraine
body:
This was announced in a press report by the Norwegian government, according to Ukrinform.
“Ukraine is about to enter another wartime winter. To ensure the most stable energy supply possible and avoid severe humanitarian consequences, it is crucial that Ukraine receives funding to purchase equipment to strengthen and restore critical infrastructure damaged by Russian bombing,” Energy Minister Terje Aasland said.
During a visit to Kyiv on Tuesday, October 27, Aasland announced that Norway would provide 500 million Norwegian kroner (NOK) to support Ukraine’s energy sector.
The funding is being provided under the Nansen Support Programme, which runs through 2026. The assistance will be channeled through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund (UESF).
This mechanism allows funds to be quickly directed toward repairs, the purchase of new equipment, and investments where they are most urgently needed.
In particular, the Ukrainian side emphasized the need for new power cables to ensure a stable energy supply.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Norway has allocated more than 16 billion Norwegian kroner ($1.72 billion) for gas procurement, repairs to energy infrastructure, and investment in new solutions.
As previously reported, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said Norway would maintain its military, humanitarian, and financial assistance to Ukraine at around $9 billion in 2027.

title: Governor Lawal repositions health sector, motivates medical workers, improves service delivery — NMA
body: Governor Dauda Lawal has been repositioning the healthcare sector in Zamfara state through infrastructural revitalisation, improved healthcare service delivery, institutional strengthening, the Medical Association, (NMA) has said. The NMA Chairman, Zamfara State chapter, Dr Muhammad Murtata Salahu, revealed this at the 2026 Annual Physicians’ Week And Ordinary General Meeting of the association. He reaffirmed the NMA’s readiness to work closely with Governor Lawal’s administration in building a healthcare system that is resilient, accessible, equitable and responsive “A stronger medical profession means a stronger healthcare system, and a stronger healthcare system means a healthier and more prosperous Zamfara,” he said. “On behalf of the entire NMA members in Zamfara let me express our profound appreciation to Governor Dauda Lawal for his visionary leadership, remarkable commitment to healthcare transformation and sustained support for the medical profession. “We acknowledge and commend the determination of the present administration in the state to reposition the healthcare sector through infrastructural revitalisation, improved healthcare service delivery, institutional strengthening and greater attention to the welfare and professional development of healthcare personnel,” he explained. He said. “Governor Dauda Lawal’s commitment of giving the healthcare a priority of his administration demonstrates a clear understanding that a healthy population remains the foundation of sustainable development, economic productivity and social stability. “We particularly appreciate his administration’s responsiveness to the needs and concerns of medical professionals and its efforts towards creating a more conducive environment for effective medical practice. “These initiatives are encouraging and represent important steps towards addressing longstanding challenges within our healthcare system. “The commitment of the state government to healthcare development is commendable, and we assure you of the continued professional support and constructive partnership of the Nigerian Medical Association in translating the state healthcare vision into sustainable benefits for the people of Zamfara. “We equally encourage the governor to sustain this positive momentum through continued investment in healthcare infrastructure, workforce development, improved welfare packages, recruitment and retention of medical personnel, and the strengthening of healthcare services across the state,” he explained. The theme for this year’s Physicians’ Week is, “Securing the Future of Medicine in Nigeria.” Part of the activities marking the week was scientific lectures presentations on polio in Zamfara, Applications of Artificial Intelligence in healthcare, and Diphtheria Case Management.
