title: Inside Capella Dubai: What to expect from the ultra-luxury resort
body: Capella Hotels and Resorts is often ranked among the best in the world, and the group is set to make its UAE debut with Capella Dubai in 2030. The ultra-luxury resort will form part of Dubai Peninsula, a new destination on the Jumeirah coastline, which will also house debut Dubai properties from Aman and Rosewood Hotels. Shahab Lutfi, chairman of Dubai developer H&H, the group behind Dubai Peninsula, exclusively tells The National the project is conceived as a destination "with a distinct identity, bringing together some of the world’s most renowned hospitality brands, exceptional residences and a unique waterfront setting". “Capella brings a different dimension to this vision through its intimate, highly personalised approach to hospitality," Lutfi says. "We see a strong alignment between Capella’s emphasis on individual experiences and sense of place and our ambition to create a destination that offers more than exceptional design and location. Capella Dubai will introduce a more intimate, service-led hospitality experience to the city’s resort landscape, adding depth and character to the overall offering.” What to expect at Capella Dubai Rising nine floors and featuring 115 luxurious rooms and suites, Capella Dubai will open directly onto a stretch of private beach. Guests can look forward to a collection of exciting culinary concepts, including a rooftop restaurant and bar, a rooftop pool, and the Capella Lobby Lounge. A signature feature at the heart of all Capella properties is the Capella Living Room, and Dubai will be no exception. The Living Room serves as a meeting place for guests to connect and converge, as well as a backdrop for workshops and activities. It’s also the home of each property’s Capella Culturist, the brand’s self-described “part neighbourhood expert, part intuitive mind-reader” who can recommend and curate experiences that connect guests to each location’s local community, heritage and culture. Beyond dining, the property will put a strong focus on wellness, with a spa complete with treatment rooms, a plunge pool, a hammam, dedicated male and female relaxation lounges, and a fitness centre. Aesthetically, Capella Dubai is designed as a contemporary beachfront palace, drawing inspiration from Dubai’s long-standing connection to the sea; from its maritime heritage to its modern coastline, water, natural materials and light will cleverly frame every space. Guests will arrive to a sweeping 25-metre-high arrival courtyard with grand marble-clad columns appearing to float within a reflecting pond. Once inside, the subtle nods to Dubai’s seafaring history extend to the interiors, the work of architectural firm Denniston, also behind One&Only One Za’abeel, Aman New York and Cheval Blanc Seychelles. This is translated into refined and modern interior design elements, including graphic motifs, crafted details and intentional material choices. A palette of sandstone, coral stone and dried palm fronds pays quiet homage to traditional coastal dwellings with soft, washed neutral tones laced with pops of washed blue, a chic reference to the surrounding waters. Grand spaces of dramatic scale will lead into more intimate, residential-feeling spots, with framed views and plenty of plants across the public spaces intentionally dissolving the boundaries between inside and out, ensuring the connection to the beachfront setting is always felt. The resort will also feature ample alfresco spaces, with courtyards, gardens, and outdoor terraces woven throughout, all layered with planting, elements of water, and textured marble to create immersive, calming sanctuaries. Capella Dubai will mark the Singapore-based brand’s second property in the region, with Capella Hotels and Resorts debuting in the Middle East with Capella Diriyah, slated to open in Riyadh in 2027. Capella Hotels and Resorts currently has a portfolio of 10 properties across Asia Pacific and Australia. “Capella has always been deliberately selective about where it goes, choosing destinations where we believe we can create something meaningful and distinctive,” says Roland Fasel, president of Capella Hotel Group. “At Dubai Peninsula, our partnership with H&H is the foundation for all that we are building. They share our vision for the intimate, highly personalised experience Capella is known for, one that connects guests more deeply with Dubai, its culture and its people,” he adds. “With the opening of Capella Dubai in 2030, we will further establish our presence in one of the region’s most compelling cities, while remaining true to the approach to hospitality that defines Capella.” Dubai Peninsula: What we know so far First announced in December 2025, the Dubai Peninsula will be located on reclaimed land along the coast in Jumeirah 2, stretching from the Four Seasons Resort Jumeirah. Billed as "an ultra-luxury waterfront destination", it is expected to bring together some of the world’s best-known hospitality brands, as well as a marina lined with restaurants and boutiques, several luxury waterfront and beachfront residential towers and more than two million square feet of botanical gardens. Alongside Capella Dubai, Aman will arrive in the UAE for the first time with an exclusive Kerry Hill-designed Aman Hotel, a collection of luxury Aman Residences and the members-only Aman Club. The all-suite waterfront Aman hotel will feature a 350m private beach and a 2,300 square metre Aman Spa, while the residential element comprises 78 ultra-luxury two- to five-bedroom residences, alongside four villas. Rosewood Hotels & Resorts will also mark its Dubai arrival on Dubai Peninsula, with Rosewood Dubai. Spanning 640,104 square feet, the property will feature 195 rooms and suites plus eight private villa gardens, a private beach and beach club, four dining venues, a dedicated wellness centre and Explorers Club for young guests. A separate residential tower on the same plot will feature 63 refined residences and five exclusive beachfront villas, with resident privileges including 24-hour concierge, a spa, private cinema, library and lounge. The project is scheduled to open in 2030. Speaking on the wider destination, Lutfi adds, “We are bringing hospitality, architecture and landscape together from the outset, ensuring that each responds to the setting and contributes to a coherent vision. For us, the strength of Dubai Peninsula lies in the way its different elements come together, from its shoreline and central park to its collection of hospitality and residential offerings.”

title: ‘A politician is not an NGO’ – Inusah Fuseini on the cost of seeking office
body: Former NDC MP for Tamale Central, Inusah Fuseini, warned that politicians who spend heavily to win office expect to recoup their money, fuelling corruption nationwide. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he linked the rising cost of political contests to corruption and the exclusion of capable people from public life. “A politician is not an NGO, and so when people spend that amount of money, they expect to recoup that, and that fuels corruption on a national scale.” His warning comes amid reports of widespread alleged vote-buying during the NDC’s latest internal executive elections. The controversy has raised questions about the cost of competing and the party’s ability to punish inducement. For Mr Fuseini, the consequences reach beyond the outcome of any single contest. Financial demands are determining who can enter politics and who must stay away. “Those heavily impacted by what is happening are women and the youth because they might not have the required resources to be able to do that,” he said. He said people with integrity and reputations for service were also shying away from politics because they could not afford the sums involved. “Politics is not Father Christmas,” he said. Mr Fuseini said efforts to address inducement had exposed a gap in the NDC’s constitution. His committee recognised the need for sanctions after acknowledging that inducement had occurred during the elections. But it also found that “there was no legal mechanism in our constitution to deal with that”. He explained that the party needed rules that define the misconduct and identify the bodies authorised to handle complaints. Without those provisions, disciplinary action could face challenges. “So we need a framework.” The committee is also examining where legitimate assistance ends and inducement begins. “How much money can we say is appropriate in the circumstances?” he asked. “If somebody gives a delegate GH¢200, is it an inducement or what is it?” He questioned how the party should treat payments described as transport support when they exceed reasonable travel costs. Proposals under consideration include empowering constituency councils of elders to handle cases or referring offenders to the national headquarters. Mr Fuseini said the recommendations would undergo further scrutiny before being presented to a special congress for constitutional amendment.

title: Neil Young again sues Trump campaign for playing Rockin’ in the Free World at rally
body: Rock veteran Neil Young has filed a $10m lawsuit against a fundraising committee supporting US President Donald Trump, citing the “unauthorised” use of his 1989 song Rockin’ in the Free World. The Canadian-American star alleges that the Trump 47 Committee infringed on his copyright when it played the song before Trump took the stage at a 12 October rally in Ohio. The lawsuit says playing the song amounts to an “unauthorised public performance”. The singer-songwriter sued the Trump re-election campaign in 2020 over its use of the same song and Devil’s Sidewalk. Young said the parties settled the matter shortly thereafter. The BBC has contacted the Republican National Committee for comment. The White House referred the BBC to the Republican National Committee for comment. Through his company, Silver Fiddle Music, Young alleges the song was played without a license or Young’s permission at a political event in Youngstown, Ohio, on 12 October. In the US, music used at campaign rallies often requires a public performance licence for it to be played for an audience, even if a campaign has already purchased a legal copy of the recording. According to the US Congress, because sound recordings lack a general public-performance right, permission is needed only from the musical-work copyright holders, which can be obtained directly from them or through performing rights organisations. The five-page federal lawsuit says that Trump “was personally aware that a license would be required to play the Song at rallies,” and that Young “has not, and would not, grant the required license”. It also says the song has been played “numerous times at other rallies”. The Grammy Award winner, 80, who has strongly opposed Trump’s politics, characterises the song as “a blistering anthem that contrasts the hollow promises of American political rhetoric with the harsh realities faced by the poor, homeless and forgotten”. Young says that the song is “the opposite of everything that Donald J Trump stands for”. In 2020, Young sued Trump’s re-election campaign for copyright infringement over the same song, as well as Devil’s Sidewalk. The new lawsuit claims the campaign, at the time, “asserted no defence and immediately settled shortly after it was served”, promising never to use the song without permission again. Young posted about the lawsuit on his website on Tuesday, thanking Trump for coming to so many of his shows in the 1980s and 1990s, but stopped short of allowing him to play his music. “I am sorry it came to this, but money and transactions are something you understand,” he wrote. Young, The Rolling Stones, Rihanna, Adele, REM and the estate of Prince have previously criticised the president for using their music at campaign events.

title: Cosmetic surgery sees slump as weight-loss drugs prove cheaper and simpler
body: Weight-loss drugs are having a significant impact on the beauty business and transforming demand for cosmetic procedures. A recently released international survey has revealed a decrease in the number cosmetic procedures for women over the previous two years, signalling a continuing trend. The International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery asked more than 2,900 plastic surgeons to submit clinical data from 51 different countries and found that a total of almost 17.9 million surgical procedures had been carried out in 2025. Cosmetic procedures for men fell by 14 per cent in 2025 from the previous year and by 7.7 per cent for women. Female demand for cosmetic surgery had already dropped 4 per cent in 2024. In 2025, demand for liposuction fell by 11.4 per cent, following on from a 12.6 per cent reduction the previous year. The popularity of breast augmentation and Botox is also on the slide, with demand for both procedures falling by 17 per cent in 2024 and a further 2 per cent and 7 per cent, respectively, last year. Dr Sanjay Parashar, a surgeon and chief executive of Cocoona Centre of Aesthetic Transformation in Dubai , said cosmetic trends were being driven by the popularity of weight-loss drugs, while economic factors could be behind the fall in men opting for cosmetic procedures. “Technology has improved, as has surgical safety,” he said. “Fewer men choosing cosmetic procedures is more about economic pressure than anything else. Dr Parashar said that wider access to existing GLP-1s could lead to increased demand for excess skin removal and skin tightening. “The amount of liposuction procedures we are doing has definitely decreased because of the oral weight-loss medications now available, helping people reduce that stubborn fat. But what has gone up as a consequence are procedures like facelifts and bodylifts. “People now do not want to resort to non-surgical like fillers to fill up their faces and look unnatural. They prefer to have a tightening procedure to look more natural, and a more cost-effective outcome.” Supercharged weight loss Figures for the UAE were not included in the 2025 survey but featured in the 2024 edition, which showed there were 272,000 surgical procedures in the emirates during that period. Dr Parashar said the emerging band of “triple G” weight-loss drugs that target three hormone receptors simultaneously could further reduce demand for liposuction procedures as they promise even greater weight loss than existing GLP-1 drugs. Regulatory approval has yet to be granted for “triple G” drug retatrutide, but trials suggest potential weight loss of up to 28 per cent. Triple-hormone receptor agonists slow digestion, curb appetite, regulate fat metabolism, and increase energy expenditure to break down stored fat. “These medications will continue to improve, along with the side effect profile,” he said. Weight-loss drugs “will become more easily accessible to people, along with the benefits”. “But what remains a challenge is the ageing effect,” Dr Parashar added. “There still has not been any medical treatment to improve skin elasticity, so there'll always be opportunities for cosmetic surgeons.” Eyelid surgery remained the most popular surgery in 2025, with 2.46 million procedures carried out worldwide. Survey participants completed a questionnaire that focused primarily on the number of specific surgical and non-surgical procedures performed. They were also asked questions related to surgeon demographics and the prevalence of medical tourism. Natural look Dubai-based plastic surgeon Dr Dmitry Melnikov said that while there was a trend for patients to opt for breast lifts rather than implants, the survey did not offer a complete picture of the aesthetic industry in the emirate. “Patients do tend to choose cheaper surgeons for simple breast augmentations and they may simply have not been reflected in the ISAPS survey,” he said. “Fashion standards have changed in the past couple of years. Patients want to have smaller, more natural breasts, but not all of [the patients]. It really depends on the country.” The ISAPS survey showed that demand for hyaluronic acid fillers had dropped by around 25 per cent in 12 months. Dr Melnikov said a “clean-girl” trend was emerging, with a more natural physical appearance, but that the presence of GLP-1 therapies was having a considerable impact. “GLP1 has had an impact absolutely everywhere, it is also very typical for a user’s face to sag,” he said. “Also the assumption that fillers are good, safe and completely resolvable is finally gone. “They migrate, they never fully dissolve and with time they create a tired, swollen look. Patients see that, doctors see that and nowadays opt for procedures that focus on the production of a patient’s own collagen and improving skin quality rather than pumping the face with fillers.” The rise of weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro is also beginning to shape the cosmetics industry. The head of French beauty giant L’Oreal, Nicolas Hieronimus, said weight-loss drugs had made a “phenomenal” impact on the beauty industry. At the release of the company’s latest financial results, Mr Hieronimus told investors that the latest products were designed to work alongside and complement GLP-1 medications to counter the effects of skin sagging. L’Oreal reported significant growth in the third quarter of 2026, with sales soaring 7.2 per cent to €11.6 billion ($12.9 billion) in the three months to September 30. A recent Gallup poll found GLP-1 use had almost quadrupled in the US since 2024, while an estimated 1.6 million people turned to weight-loss drugs in England, Wales and Scotland from 2024 to 2025. Competition Dr Vikas Verma, a consultant plastic surgeon at NMC Royal Hospital DIP, Dubai, said an oversaturation of UAE clinics and price competition could be behind a downturn in aesthetic surgeries. “Intense competition and the sheer number of players push price and quality of work down,” he said. “With so many providers, individual clinics can lose volume even when the market grows.” Elsewhere, regulations are tightening on the industry. The Dubai Health Authority recently told private facilities that medical advertising must be truthful and supported by appropriate evidence, with disciplinary action for non-compliance. Stricter licensing has also aimed to redraw boundaries between medical clinics and beauty salons to reduce the number of bookings driven by social media influencers. “Traditional surgery still matters,” Dr Verma said. “But the preference is shifting towards treatments which are non-invasive, can be done quickly, give immediate results and people can go to work the next day. “GLP-1 drugs are reshaping plastic surgery, mostly by creating a new patient group and shifting demand towards facial and body-contouring work. We are getting more enquiries for such procedures and at a much younger age group.”

title: U.S. to issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro as his whereabouts remain unclear
body:
Flávio Bolsonaro arrives at Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026, in Opa-locka, Fla. Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty images hide caption
RIO DE JANEIRO, Brazil — In his first statement since leaving Brazil, Flávio Bolsonaro declared himself the country's "president-elect," accusing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government of political persecution and electoral fraud, hours after arriving in the United States following his election defeat.
In a lengthy statement posted on X , the former Brazilian presidential candidate addressed "the Brazilian people and the international community", thanking Argentine President Javier Milei for his support and President Donald Trump for "welcoming" him.
"I will not abandon you. I shall be the voice and the free leadership of our nation," he wrote, comparing himself to political figures who went into exile, including Charles de Gaulle, José Martí and María Corina Machado.
He claimed it had never been his "intention to leave my homeland", but said he knew "exactly where this is heading", describing the situation as following "the classic playbook of any coup d'état".
He later reposted the statement with clarifications, describing himself simply as the "leader".
The posts cap 72 hours of high drama for Bolsonaro, who arrived at Opa-locka Airport near Miami early on Wednesday with his family. Uniformed officers carrying large umbrellas escorted the family to a waiting vehicle, obstructing views from gathered media.
Earlier Wednesday, Argentina's migration authority said in a statement on X that Bolsonaro and his family had crossed from Brazil into Argentina late Tuesday.
"Citizens Flavio Nantes Bolsonaro, Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro, and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro entered through the Tancredo Neves International Bridge border crossing in the province of Misiones. They did so with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment to entering the country."
The statement added that at 11:30 p.m. Tuesday, the group boarded a private flight bound for Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to the flight plan.
Bolsonaro, a conservative politician and ally of Trump, lost Sunday's presidential election to incumbent Lula by more than four million votes, three weeks after winning the first round of voting.
While Bolsonaro's Liberal Party has since acknowledged Lula's victory, Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat.
On Tuesday a senior U.S. administration official said that the State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the country.
The visa announcement came as Bolsonaro faces multiple investigations in Brazil, including allegations of money laundering and tax evasion, which he denies. On Monday Brazil's Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country.
In a video released that same day, Bolsonaro said federal police officers had stopped him outside the home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and ordered him to surrender his passports. The former far-right leader is under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his own defeat by Lula in the 2022 presidential election.
"I never thought about leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in the video. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this aberration." He described the order as an attempt to intimidate him. By Tuesday however, Brazilian media were reporting that Bolsonaro had left for the United States. His campaign manager, his lawyer and other political allies had earlier said they did not know his location.
Trump has repeatedly cast doubt on Lula's victory, suggesting on Monday that the election was "rigged", without offering any evidence. He returned to the subject at a campaign rally in Texas on Tuesday night, as he accused Democrats of election fraud.
"Brazil is also doing a good job of it, aren't they? Did you see that? I didn't take sides, but it didn't look very good," he said.
Lula criticized Bolsonaro's departure during celebrations for his 81st birthday in Brasília on Tuesday. "Those who have nothing to hide have nothing to fear," Lula told supporters.
"He could have stayed and proven that the accusations [against him] are not true," Lula said, adding that he regretted Bolsonaro's departure. He described the move as "shameful."
He also took aim at the Bolsonaro family's close ties to the Trump administration. "Brazil is their second home; their first home is the United States," he said.

title: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in US after Brazil cancels his passports
body: Defeated presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro has arrived in the US, hours after Brazil cancelled his passports, sources have told the BBC. The right-wing candidate left the country after its Supreme Court ordered that he surrender his passports amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. Bolsonaro has not been charged and has denied the allegations. His passports were cancelled on Tuesday after he missed a deadline to hand them over to authorities, prompting widespread speculation that he may have left Brazil. Sources told BBC Brasil and BBC Mundo that Bolsonaro met with his younger brother, Eduardo, in Florida – though his exact travel route from Brazil to the US is unclear. Neither brother could be directly reached for comment. His reported arrival in the US came hours after a senior US official confirmed the US State Department would issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country. The BBC has contacted the White House, State Department and embassies in both the US and Brazil. On Monday, Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered Bolsonaro to hand his passports to police within 24 hours as part of its alleged money-laundering probe. At the time, Bolsonaro said he had no plans to leave the country, and insisted that he would stay in Brazil to lead the opposition to his left-wing rival, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who on Sunday won the election. After he missed the deadline, Bolsonaro’s lawyers told BBC Brasil that they were “completely in the dark” about his whereabouts. “We knew nothing about this, and we still have no information about what happened,” one lawyer said. Bolsonaro has not made any public statements since Monday afternoon local time, when he posted a video on social media. Federal officers checked border crossings to establish if Bolsonaro may have travelled to neighbouring Argentina, a police source told BBC News Brasil. However, Argentine authorities told the BBC there was no record of the senator entering their country through any border crossing. Bolsonaro was already under investigation for alleged corruption over the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, who was convicted of plotting a coup and is under house arrest. A separate inquiry involves alleged links to a Brazilian lawyer accused of laundering more than $1bn through a fraud scheme. Police said earlier this month they had discovered Mr Bolsonaro had access to the bank accounts of a company owned by the lawyer. Bolsonaro denied doing business with the lawyer, and described the passport confiscation as an attempt to intimidate him. In addition to that investigation, Brazil’s Supreme Court ordered police on Tuesday to examine Flávio Bolsonaro’s electoral campaign over alleged foreign funding. The 45-year-old senator suffered a stinging defeat on Sunday when Lula beat him in a presidential run-off, a result Bolsonaro had been widely expected to win. His younger brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, lives in Texas, but was in Miami on Sunday, where he cast his vote at a polling station and attended an election viewing event streamed to his followers. Sources have told the BBC that Flávio has already met his brother, Eduardo, in Florida, though details of his exact travel route from Brazil are unclear. It’s also unclear who travelled with him or whether Flávio Bolsonaro intends to stay and live in the US. Opinion polls put him narrowly ahead of Lula, and analysts said Bolsonaro’s first-round win on 4 October meant he was likely to win the run-off. But after an early lead in the count, the veteran incumbent overtook him, becoming the first presidential candidate to overturn a first-round loss to win in the second round. Lula won 51.79% of the vote, while Bolsonaro got 48.21%. Despite trailing by 4.4 million votes, Bolsonaro has not conceded and has called for the election to be annulled. He argues he was put at a disadvantage because polling was extended by two hours on election day, even though both his party and his rival’s requested the extension. He called the extension, which was ordered by a Supreme Court justice, a “dirty trick”. However, the party he represented, the Liberal Party, accepted the result, though it said the extension of voting “merits investigation”.

title: EU seeks to avoid Ukraine’s mistakes in relying on Starlink — Bloomberg
body:
NEW YORK, October 28. /TASS/. Discussions on strengthening defense capabilities have gained renewed momentum in the European Union following slowdowns in the operation of the Starlink satellite system in Ukraine, Bloomberg reported, citing sources.
According to the sources, one of the central topics at the latest EU summit on October 15-16 was the slowdown in Starlink services and the resulting new public dispute between Vladimir Zelensky and US President Donald Trump. European officials discussed the need to bolster their own capabilities, reduce dependence on the United States, and diversify suppliers of "critical technologies."
However, a Bloomberg source stressed that such changes would take years. The most realistic solution under the circumstances is to strengthen Europe’s role within existing structures, such as NATO, the agency added.
Last week, Kiev said that US company SpaceX had restricted the operation of Starlink terminals used by the Ukrainian armed forces, disrupting several Ukrainian military operations. SpaceX founder and entrepreneur Elon Musk, for his part, stated that the Starlink satellite system is not used for offensive military operations but only for defense and civilian purposes. He also said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government and that any restrictions are imposed by the US military and ultimately by the US president. Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal claimed that Musk himself had ordered restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starshield.
On October 22, Trump announced that Ukraine’s access to the military-grade Starshield satellite communications system had been restored. However, he declined to answer a question about who had issued the order.

title: Git for the US Code
body:
Now publicly available as part of global law.
A programmer can point at any line of code and see who wrote it, when, and what the file looked like on any past day. A lawyer reading a federal statute usually cannot, at least not without an afternoon in the notes at the foot of the section. But why shouldn't they have the same, convenient system of record? It is especially relevant given that so much first-pass legal research now runs through language models, which are often unable to utilise the proper lineage of a law, handcuffing its ability to offer interpretation.
Outside the titles Congress has enacted as positive law, the code is only prima facie evidence of the law, and the Statutes at Large govern where the two differ. [ 1 ] The Office of the Law Revision Counsel publishes it as a series of release points, each current through a named public law, and keeps reorganising it; a bill to enact title 41 as positive law was introduced in September 2025. [ 2 ] Which public law wrote a sentence is recorded in amendment notes, in prose. When a change took effect is often in a separate effective-date note, and where Congress said nothing the default rule is that a law takes effect on the day it is enacted. [ 3 ]
The definition of a small business debtor in 11 USC § 1182(1) shows how far apart those answers can be. It was created in 2019 with the existing small business debt limit. [ 4 ] The CARES Act raised the limit to $7.5 million in March 2020 as a temporary measure, later extended to March 2022. [ 5 ] , [ 6 ] That increase lapsed on 27 March 2022, and on 21 June 2022 Congress restored it for two more years, for cases commenced on or after 27 March 2020 and still pending, which reached back over the gap. [ 7 ] The higher limit expired again in June 2024, and after the triennial adjustment in April 2025 it stands at $3,424,000. [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] For a case filed in May 2022, the release point printed at the time gives the lower limit, and only a later Act changes the answer. A history that is useful to a lawyer has to carry the text, the date each change took force, and the scope of any law that reaches back.
A study from the Technical University of Munich this year found two failures in models answering questions on German statutes: they apply rules that were superseded after their training cutoff, and they prefer the newer provision even when an older one governs the facts. One model answered 24% of post-cutoff questions correctly on its own and 87% when the relevant statutory text was retrieved for it, and the authors conclude that temporal validity has to be treated as a hard constraint. [ 10 ] Other recent work trains search agents to respect the date a question is about, with large gains in consistency. [ 11 ]
Asking a model to produce the old text does not solve this. When the same Munich group had a model apply German amending laws to earlier versions, the output looked 93–99% similar to the official text, but only half of single amendments and a fifth of chains of amendments matched exactly, and experts found legally significant errors in the near misses. [ 12 ] The history has to be checkable.
For each pair of release points from 2017 onward, we took the public laws enacted in between, carried out their amending instructions on the older text in date order, and compared the result with the newer version. Of 365 changes across the nine titles, 361 reproduced the next release point exactly. The other four are shown with a label saying how far they could be confirmed. Each change then carries the law and the date it took effect: 261 took effect on enactment by default, 72 by an effective-date note and 29 by a date in the amendment itself. One depends on an agency determination that may never come, and we leave it out of the text rather than guess.
With that record, the reader can answer the questions lawyers ask. You pick a date and get the text in force on it, with the words that read differently today marked. Each phrase is coloured by the Act that wrote it. A change to a defined term lists every other provision that uses it, and you can follow a section to see what has changed since your last visit.
It does not yet show a later law’s reach back on the earlier dates it covers, so for a case filed in the 2022 gap it shows the lower limit without warning that the June 2022 Act changed the answer.
Effective-date notes are read by pattern, and unusual wording falls back to the date of enactment.
Each change links to the law’s own words, and for anything that matters the original should be read.
We're also still thinking about the right form factor this should take.

title: SC: Employees cannot be forced to retire before age 65 without consent
body: MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) has ruled that employers cannot force their employees to retire early without an agreement. In a decision penned by Associate Justice Ramon Paul Hernando, and was made public on Tuesday, October 27, the SC 1st Division said employees cannot be made to retire from their position before the mandatory retirement age of 65 without their clear and voluntary consent. Hernando, in the case, partly granted the petition of Rodolfo Ondevilla and found Colegio de San Juan de Letran (CSJL) in Laguna guilty of illegal dismissal. Ondevilla asserted in his SC petition that he never agreed to retire before 65. The SC accepted his position. Hernando explained that under the country’s Labor Code , the retirement age is set by an existing agreement or employment contract. If there’s no agreement or contract, then the mandatory retirement age of 65 will be applied, along with the minimum age for optional retirement of 60. The ruling explained that optional retirement is based on a voluntary agreement between the employer and employee, and the latter must freely agree to it without pressure or coercion. But the SC said in the Ondevilla case that the early retirement happened despite the lack of a mutual agreement between the parties. Based on the decision, the SC said CSJL never made any proposal for a retirement plan to the petitioner that he could accept or reject, adding that there was no indication that the school was willing to discuss Ondevilla’s retirement. The High Court added Ondevilla’s objection to his supposed early retirement, along with his illegal dismissal complaint, showed that he had no intention of availing himself of optional retirement before reaching the age of 65. “Because his retirement was involuntary, the SC treated it as an illegal dismissal. Ondevilla was therefore entitled to full back wages and separation pay instead of reinstatement,” said the ruling. The SC also awarded him retirement benefits covering his employment from June 16, 2004, until August 29, 2024, when he reached the mandatory retirement age of 65. It directed the arbitration branch to compute the total amount due to him. Case’s background Ondevilla started working for CSJL as a comptroller in 2004, and later worked as assistant vice president for finance. He was renewed for work several times. When the school had a management reorganization in 2018, he was reassigned as controller. Although he objected to this and said it was a demotion, he continued working with the same salary and employee benefits. CJSL considered Ondevilla’s appointment expired on August 29, 2019, when he turned 60. The petitioner then filed a complaint for illegal dismissal. He secured victories from the Labor Arbiter, and then from the National Labor Relations Commission. The case reached the Court of Appeals (CA). It found that Ondevilla had been illegally dismissed, but ruled that a letter he sent to the school showed that he had agreed to retire on July 31, 2020. When he filed the petition with the SC, Ondevilla challenged the CA’s findings and argued that he never agreed to retire early. – Rappler.com

title: GPAA opens 23rd Annual Conference in Techiman with strong calls for primary healthcare action
body: The Ghana Physician Assistants Association (GPAA) has officially opened its 23rd Annual General Conference at the Jemima Grace Kodua Hotel in Techiman, with a resounding call for physician assistants to be positioned at the heart of Ghana’s primary healthcare delivery system. The high-level opening ceremony brought together key stakeholders in the health sector, including the Director General of the Ghana Health Service, Dr. Samuel Kaba Akoriya; the National President of the GPAA, Peter Akudugu Ayamba; the Bono East Regional Minister’s representative, Mrs. Beatrice Kwarteng; and Nananom of the Techiman Traditional Council. “Not Background Noise” — GPAA President Delivers Stirring Message In his address, GPAA National President Peter Akudugu Ayamba delivered a powerful message on the indispensable role of physician assistants in Ghana’s healthcare architecture. “Primary healthcare is not a footnote. It is the headline. And the Physician Assistant is not background noise. They are a frontline instrument of policy delivery,” Ayamba declared. He emphasized that if the nation is serious about moving from policy to practice, there must be a deliberate effort to remove the obstacles that stand between policy formulation and community outreach. “We have to be serious about equipping physician assistants to respond fully to the rate of health needs in the community,” he added. Government Reaffirms Commitment In a speech read on behalf of the Bono East Regional Minister, Francis Owusu, the Regional Planning Officer, Mrs. Beatrice Kwarteng, reiterated the government’s commitment to supporting the work of physician assistants. “Government remains committed to supporting the works of physician assistants by providing more health facilities in rural communities to help in the implementation of the free primary healthcare policy,” Mrs. Kwarteng stated on behalf of the Regional Minister. She further noted that the government recognizes the critical role physician assistants play in bridging the healthcare gap, particularly in underserved rural communities, and assured that efforts are underway to strengthen the system. GHS Director General Charges Practitioners The Director General of the Ghana Health Service, Dr. Samuel Kaba Akoriya, also addressed the gathering, urging physician assistants to remain steadfast in their dedication to the free primary healthcare system. “Remain committed to the free primary healthcare system in order to leave positive names for yourselves,” Dr. Akoriya charged the practitioners. Traditional Council Backs Conference The traditional authority was well-represented at the ceremony. Nana Boakye Ameyaw Pentenpre II, Nifahene of the Techiman Traditional Council, who chaired the occasion on behalf of the Omanhene, urged the physician assistants to make the conference a turning point. “Let this conference be a defining moment for transformative leadership, effective policy execution, and a lasting legacy of healthcare excellence,” he said. The 23rd Annual General Conference, themed “From Policy to Practice: Positioning the Physician Assistant to Deliver Comprehensive Free Primary Healthcare at the Community Level,” is not just a talk shop. Alongside the conference activities, the GPAA has been running a free community health screening across four locations in Techiman — the forecourt of the Bonokyempem Hall, the Regional Coordinating Council (RCC), the Techiman Central Market, and the forecourt of the NHIS office. The screening, which includes breast cancer examinations and general health assessments, targets busy workers who find it difficult to visit hospitals due to their schedules. It is a practical demonstration of the conference theme in action.

title: Ukrposhta cuts network to 7,211 branches over three years, Lubinets says
body:
The ombudsman reported this on Telegram , according to Ukrinform.
“Imagine: the post office in your village has closed. Where do you go now to collect your pension? How do you pay your bills? Will the mobile post office come, and when can you expect it?
These questions arise for a reason. I’ve been receiving complaints about the closure of post offices and the operation of the mobile postal service. That’s why I decided to look into what’s happening and whether people are losing access to essential services,” he wrote.
According to Lubinets, over the past three years, Ukrposhta has reduced its network from 10,000 to 7,211 branches. At the same time, the ombudsman noted, mobile branches accounted for about 28% of the network in 2024–2025.
“The number of mail carriers in 2023–2024 nearly halved—from 12,505 to 6,658. But it’s something else that raises the most questions. During the Ombudsman’s Office’s monitoring, we found that Ukrposhta does not keep separate records of settlements where a stationary branch has been replaced by a mobile one, and those where there is no post office at all. “This means we cannot fully assess where mobile postal services are actually solving the problem, and where people risk being left without services,” he noted.
The Ombudsman stated that Russia’s war against Ukraine is affecting the postal service’s operations. According to his data, from the beginning of 2022 through July 1, 2026, 1,070 postal facilities ceased operations or changed their operating hours due to security concerns.
“I have provided Ukrposhta with recommendations to improve tracking and monitor how the mobile branches are operating and whether people have access to services. It’s not enough to simply close a branch and replace it with a mobile one. We need to ensure that people can actually get what they used to come to the post office for,” Lubinets wrote in his post.
As reported by Ukrinform, city branches of JSC “Ukrposhta” will prioritize processing incoming and outgoing parc els.

title: Putin highlights friendly nature of Russia-Equatorial Guinea relations
body:
MOSCOW, October 28. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin highlighted the constructive and friendly nature of relations between Russia and Equatorial Guinea during a meeting with Equatorial Guinean President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo.
"In recent years, we have met regularly, practically every year, and our meeting reflects the friendly and consistently constructive nature of our relations. Your presence in Moscow in 2025 for the 80th anniversary of our country’s Victory in the Great Patriotic War was particularly significant," Putin said.
The Russian leader noted that Russia values its effective coordination with Equatorial Guinea on the international stage. "Our countries maintain good relations on these platforms and hold similar positions on key issues, advocating a polycentric world order and the right of all countries to independently choose their own path of development. Mr. President, I would like to emphasize once again that we are very pleased to welcome you to Moscow," Putin added.

title: Regina dismantles Core Community Park encampment over fire safety concerns
body:
The City of Regina has dismantled an encampment at Core Community Park, also known as Pepsi Park, with fire officials citing an increased safety risk following a number of fires in recent days.
Police and fire crews cleared the encampment as streets surrounding the park were closed. City officials began erecting a fence around the property, while police placed tape reading “Do Not Cross” around tents.
About 150 people had been living at the encampment over the past three and a half months. Residents were not given notice that the site would be decommissioned, leaving some arriving at the park to discover their tents and belongings were gone.
Natalie, a former encampment resident whose last name was not provided, said she did not know the site was being cleared.
“My tent is gone. I didn’t even know this was happening at all,” she said.
The move also caught community organizers and at least one city councillor off guard.
“This problem just keeps getting worse and I know nobody wants to look at it, but it’s not going away,” community organizer Shawn Koch told Global News.
Last November, city council approved changes to its encampment response strategy, including the creation of the CARE Team and an approach focused on care rather than enforced removals.
Coun. Shanon Zachidniak said she did not know the encampment was being dismantled until the operation was already underway.
“I had no idea this was happening until I found out as it had already started,” she said. “And so I got here as quickly as I could to try and see what is going on, what is the plan, how can we ensure that folks are going to have a safe place tonight.”
Community organizers also raised concerns about what would happen to residents and their belongings.
“When you come back to the spot that you’ve called home for over three months, and nothing is going to be here, none of your friends are going to be there, and none of your belongings are going to be here,” community organizer Mandla Mthembu said.
He said those belongings could include keepsakes, as well as essential medication such as insulin.
Regina fire officials said the decision to clear the site followed an increase in fires and a high-risk assessment conducted over the weekend.
Mayor Chad Bachynski said the city had been working with the province to try to open some type of space where people could get out of the encampment and receive support.
“We were working with the province to try and open up some kind of space, whether it’s a triage space, a transitional space, something so they can get out of the encampment, out of the elements, and into somewhere where they can then navigate people on where they need to go,” Bachynski said.
Those displaced by the closure are now facing questions about what comes next as colder weather settles into Regina.

title: Zelensky: Europe Must Be Included in November Peace Talks
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky insisted Tuesday, Oct. 27, that European countries must be involved in upcoming peace negotiations, warning that no European partner should be excluded from decisions on ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
His remarks came as preparations continued for US-mediated talks involving Ukrainian, American and Russian representatives in November, following renewed diplomatic contacts between Moscow and European leaders.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“We expect a trilateral format in November, with Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives,” Zelensky said in his evening address .
“It is important that Europe also take part in all diplomatic moves. Ukraine has always insisted that Europe must be present and must have a say in the decisions,” he said.
“And this, by the way, applies to everyone in Europe. No one should be left out of the process.”
The Ukrainian president’s comments underscored Kyiv’s position that any settlement must address not only Ukraine’s future but also the security interests of European countries affected by Russia’s war.
The anticipated negotiations are expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, according to statements from Moscow. Discussions are being prepared at the level of negotiating teams, rather than as a summit of the three countries’ presidents.
Zelensky’s appeal followed a rare phone call on Tuesday between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre.
The call, conducted from Helsinki, was initiated by Finland and Norway in consultation with Ukraine and followed diplomatic discussions held in Oslo on Oct. 20.
According to a joint statement published by the Norwegian government , the Nordic leaders sought to convey messages directly to Putin about future negotiations and the need to end the war.
“The discussion was frank and substantive,” Stubb said, emphasizing that the outcome of the war would directly affect European security.
“Ending the war requires direct discussions,” he added.
Støre stressed the war’s human and economic consequences and said the leaders had called for de-escalation.
Both leaders reaffirmed their continued support for Ukraine.
Following the conversation with Putin, Stubb and Støre briefed Zelensky on the discussions.
According to the Ukrainian president’s office , the Nordic leaders told Putin that Russia needed to take concrete steps toward de-escalation, particularly by reducing attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Zelensky thanked them for coordinating the initiative with Kyiv and supporting efforts to bring Moscow back to negotiations.
The leaders also discussed preparations for the November trilateral meeting and possible formats for broader European participation.
Finland and Norway, both of which share borders with Russia, have a particular interest in reliable security arrangements, Zelensky noted.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, said the participants had welcomed plans to resume trilateral negotiations in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November.
Moscow reiterated its position that any lasting settlement must take account of what it describes as Russia’s security interests.
In his evening address, Zelensky said Ukraine was intensifying diplomatic coordination with European partners while working to secure additional military assistance ahead of the anticipated negotiations.
“These days, we are doing our best to secure new support packages,” he said.
“Coordination with our partners is also ongoing to ensure diplomacy and meetings as soon as possible.”
Zelensky also confirmed that Kyiv would remain in contact with Washington as preparations continued.
The renewed diplomatic push follows talks in Oslo involving Zelensky, European leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, who subsequently met Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21.
Following those contacts, both Kyiv and Moscow expressed support for resuming trilateral negotiations, which had stalled after earlier rounds produced limited progress beyond prisoner exchanges.

title: Netanyahu vows to confront Iran threat alongside Trump as exit polls show no clear majority
body: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu declared early Wednesday that his Likud party remained Israel's largest political force, according to election exit polls, and vowed to continue confronting Iran alongside U.S. President Donald Trump, even as projections showed his political bloc falling short of a parliamentary majority. Speaking after exit polls projected Likud as the largest party in the 120-member Knesset, Netanyahu said Israel had dramatically reshaped the Middle East through military operations against Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran, crediting the country's soldiers and his government's decisions for what he described as unprecedented strategic achievements.   "We have accomplished wonders that have changed the face of the Middle East," Netanyahu said. "We eliminated Mohammed Deif, Yahya Sinwar, Hassan Nasrallah and Ali Khamenei. We established security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria. We removed enormous threats hanging over us and struck the Iranian regime." "Iran is weaker than ever, and Israel is stronger than ever," he said, attributing those achievements to "our steadfast soldiers and the decisions we made." But Netanyahu stressed that Israel's military campaign was not finished, warning that Iran would continue to pose an existential threat as long as its current leadership remained in power. "This is not over as long as this fanatical regime exists," he said. "As long as it exists, it will try to destroy us. And together with our wonderful friend, President Trump, we will work to remove this threat once and for all." Netanyahu's remarks came as exit polls suggested his bloc had increased its parliamentary representation but remained below the 61 seats required to form a majority government in the 120-seat Knesset, leaving Israel facing another potentially prolonged round of coalition negotiations. Netanyahu said the exit polls were only a preliminary indication of the election results and urged supporters to await the official count. "This is only the beginning. We are still waiting for the actual results, which we will receive over the next day or two," he said. "Two things have become clear. First, unequivocally, Likud is the largest party in Israel." He accused Israeli media outlets of deliberately understating Likud's electoral strength in preelection polling to discourage his supporters from voting. "Remember how the propaganda channels manipulated public opinion? Likud at 18 seats, 19 seats. They knew all along it was a lie. They were simply trying to suppress you, to keep you from going to the polls," Netanyahu said, as exit polls indicated Likud finishing with 25 seats and over. "Well, the first thing that has become absolutely clear is that Likud is the largest party in Israel. There is no disputing that." Netanyahu also claimed that the election demonstrated overwhelming support for the right among Jewish and Zionist voters, despite exit polls indicating that his bloc remained short of an overall parliamentary majority. "The second thing that has become clear, and they tried to manipulate public opinion about this as well, is that the right-wing bloc has a clear, decisive majority among the Zionist public, among the Jewish public and among all those who support the Jewish state," he said. "That is why I said, and I say again, that we must establish a strong national right-wing government. That is what needs to be done." Netanyahu sharply rejected the possibility of an alternative coalition relying on Arab political parties, accusing them of opposing Israel's existence and siding with its enemies. "We must not, absolutely must not, endanger Israel by establishing a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties, parties that oppose our very existence, that regard Hamas as a charitable organization and call our soldiers war criminals," he said. As supporters chanted "Shame! Shame!" Netanyahu continued: "It is indeed a disgrace. And I ask, how have we reached a point where politicians and media outlets talk about this, normalize it and justify it?" He also attacked the opposition's proposed "alliance of those who serve," a reference to political parties seeking to unite around military service and opposition to exemptions from conscription, especially for ultra-Orthodox men. "How can you talk about an alliance of those who serve when you join forces with those who attack the people who serve — our IDF soldiers?" Netanyahu said. "These are people who not only do not serve the state, but serve the state's enemies." Netanyahu singled out the Islamic Movement, whose southern branch is affiliated with the Arab Islamist Ra'am party and has ideological roots in the Muslim Brotherhood, as well as the Joint List alliance of predominantly Arab parties and the Arab nationalist Balad party. He accused them of opposing Israel's existence as a Jewish state and siding with its enemies, warning against any coalition that would depend on their parliamentary support. "You're talking about an alliance of those who serve with them? This must not be allowed to happen," he said. "The Zionist majority in the State of Israel, the Jewish and Zionist majority, must come to its senses and unite. Only then can we secure Israel's future." Netanyahu thanked the millions of Israelis who supported him and his political bloc, saying they had rejected what he characterized as attempts to remove a right-wing government through politically motivated criminal investigations. "I want to thank the millions of Israeli citizens who placed their trust in us, who placed their trust in me," he said, adding that they had "emphatically rejected the attempt to bring down a right-wing government through criminal political investigations." Netanyahu is standing trial on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate corruption cases involving allegations that he accepted lavish gifts from wealthy benefactors and sought favorable media coverage in exchange for regulatory benefits.  He denies wrongdoing and has repeatedly portrayed the proceedings as a politically motivated witch hunt orchestrated by law enforcement officials, prosecutors and political opponents to drive him from office and undermine Israel's right wing. The prime minister also paid tribute to IDF soldiers, those wounded in the fighting and bereaved families. "From the bottom of my heart, I want to thank our heroic soldiers, those wounded in body and mind, and embrace the bereaved families, my brothers and sisters," he said. Returning to Iran, Netanyahu said Israel faced a unique opportunity to eliminate an existential threat, working alongside Trump. "I want to tell you that Israel stands before a historic, once-in-a-lifetime opportunity, together with our partner President Trump, to remove the existential threat from Iran once and for all," he said. "We must not, absolutely must not, allow any extraneous considerations to divert us from this sacred mission." Concluding his address, Netanyahu struck a defiant tone. "Citizens of Israel, we have prevailed over our enemies, and together we will prevail over them in the future," he said. "Fear not, Israel, fear not, for you are a young lion. The lion has roared — who will not fear? The people of Israel live, and the Eternal One of Israel does not lie. Thank you very much."

title: [Vantage Point] One peso, two fortunes: The hidden energy bill
body: When a household opens a higher electricity bill, it is also confronting a currency problem. The peso’s slide creates a stark divide across the country: extra cash for families receiving dollars, but steeper costs for those earning pesos. Yet even that apparent windfall carries an invisible tax. Because the Philippines relies heavily on imported energy, currency depreciation and global commodity swings compound, draining household budgets, raising operational overhead, and eroding the foreign exchange reserves the broader economy requires to keep operating. For Elena, a nurse in California, the peso’s decline looks like a modest salary increase. Sending $1,000 to her mother yielded P60,000 at a P60 exchange rate; at P64, it yields P64,000 before transfer fees. But for Ramon, a delivery driver paid strictly in pesos, that same currency movement brings costlier pump prices and fewer groceries. Neither has changed jobs, worked longer hours, or shifted productivity, yet their purchasing power moves in opposite directions. Their lived experiences capture the uneven consequences of currency depreciation. Overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) and their dependents appreciate the extra cash, while domestic wage earners absorb the pain of rising prices. Even Elena’s mother cannot treat the extra P4,000 as pure windfall. A good portion will simply cover goods and services made pricier by the weaker peso—starting with her power and grocery bills. On October 27, the peso closed at P64.17 per dollar , extending its slide despite an unexpectedly sharp 50-basis-point policy rate hike to 5.50% by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) the previous week. Must Read Philippine peso sinks to record low P64.17 vs $1 | The wRap The currency’s brief bounce quickly faded, exposing the limits of monetary defense when an economy must continually spend massive amounts of foreign exchange on basic necessities. The underlying vulnerability is a structural imbalance between the dollars the country earns and those it spends. The BSP projects a $19.1-billion current-account deficit this year, equivalent to 3.8% of gross domestic product. Capital flight compounds this strain: BSP figures for January through August show net foreign portfolio investments recording $4.254 billion in net outflows, reversing $4.583 billion in net inflows a year earlier. That nearly $8.84-billion adverse swing explains why dependable remittance receipts have failed to halt depreciation. (READ: Martin Romualdez’s properties: Where and how much? ) Energy sits squarely at the center of this dollar drain. Building a gas-fired power station on domestic soil does not transform imported fuel into a local resource. World Bank trade data show Philippine liquefied natural gas (LNG) import spending jumped 52.6%—from $767.73 million in 2024 to $1.171 billion in 2025. Over the same period, imported physical volumes rose 41.7% to roughly 1.68 million tons. Notably, roughly 79% of that $403.62-million increase came from buying more physical fuel, with higher unit values accounting for the rest. This demonstrates how expanding reliance swells the external bill long before an exceptional global price shock hits. In the broader trade account, Philippine Statistics Authority data reveal that imports of mineral fuels, lubricants, and related materials grew by $2.56 billion in the first half of 2026, accounting for 21% of total import growth and equivalent to 37% of the widening merchandise trade deficit. By comparison, August figures show fuel imports reached $1.85 billion, while electronics imports of $4.51 billion were more than offset by $6.20 billion in exports. Electronics generates net foreign exchange; imported fuels represent an unhedged dollar drain. At the generation level, the arithmetic is unforgiving. Consider an illustrative facility requiring seven million British thermal units of fuel to generate one megawatt-hour. At $10 per unit and an exchange rate of P58, fuel costs alone amount to P4.06 per kilowatt-hour. If international fuel jumps to $30 and the exchange rate weakens to P63, that fuel component surges to P13.23 per kilowatt-hour before factoring in other generation costs. While actual tariff recovery depends on power contracts and regulatory treatment, consumers ultimately face a bill that incorporates both the global commodity spike and the currency depreciation that magnifies it. This dynamic ripples across corporate ledgers and family tables alike. Consider Miguel, who runs a business process outsourcing firm billed in dollars while paying salaries and rent in pesos. Depreciation widens his operating margin, provided clients do not demand price cuts and domestic overhead remains manageable. Freelancers with foreign clients share that advantage. (READ: [Vantage Point] Gig Economy: Growth engine or precarious lifeline? ) Across town, bakery owner Liza faces the painful reverse. Her walk-in customers pay in pesos, but imported flour, packaging, and commercial electric utility bills expose her directly to dollar costs. She must decide whether to raise bread prices and risk customer resistance, or absorb the cost hikes and watch her livelihood shrink. Airlines, import-heavy manufacturers, and firms servicing unhedged dollar debt confront identical pressures. Their resilience depends on pricing power, hedging strategies, and whether they generate dollar revenue. Gas power undeniably provides controllable electricity when other plants falter, and system outages carry severe economic costs. Clean alternatives like solar, wind, and battery storage demand substantial upfront capital, grid expansion, and adequate storage duration. Yet dependable supply must remain affordable under adverse economic conditions. Energy planners must disclose what proposed capacity actually costs when fuel prices spike and the peso tumbles, identifying who truly bears the foreign-exchange risk. A lasting recovery demands firmer foundations: stable foreign investment, greater export earning power, and genuine relief from expensive imported energy. Elena may welcome the extra pesos, and Miguel may enjoy healthier margins. But Ramon and Liza have good reason to worry. The decisive policy test is whether the country can break its avoidable dependence on imported energy before the temporary gains enjoyed by some are completely swallowed by the higher bills imposed on everyone else. – Rappler.com Below are some Vantage Point pieces you might have missed: [Vantage Point] When a paycheck runs out before payday [Vantage Point] How our rooftop becomes a hedge against Meralco Click here for other Vantage Point articles.

title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
body:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms, including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital, are expected to return billions .
Yet, according to Anthropic’s S-1 , none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.
While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.
Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock up front, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.
According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.
As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.
Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.
But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity) in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.
Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.
Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times , and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 8%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from Anthropic through 2033.
While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sells it much of the computing power it runs on.
The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.
The estimate of Google’s fully diluted stake has been updated.

title: Zelensky Urges US to End Month-Long Patriot Missile Delay as Russian Strikes Kill Civilians
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky urged the US on Tuesday, Oct. 27, to approve urgently needed Patriot interceptor deliveries that have been delayed for nearly a month, warning that shortages are leaving Ukrainian civilians vulnerable to deadly Russian ballistic missile strikes.
His appeal followed Russian attacks on Kyiv on Monday evening and overnight that killed a 46-year-old woman and injured 15 others. The strikes damaged the State University of Trade and Economics, including student dormitories and academic buildings, as well as nearby Kyoto Park, residential buildings and transport infrastructure. Five of those injured were university students and staff, Ukrainian officials said.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“It’s important that the world sees this, that our partners see it in the US, on which almost everything concerning Patriots depends,” Zelensky said in his evening address , calling for the necessary Pentagon authorizations to deliver the interceptors.
The president warned that delays in Western air defense assistance were making it increasingly difficult for Ukraine to protect its cities.
“Everyone hears and sees that it is now difficult for us to defend against Russian ballistic missiles. Above all, we lack missiles for Patriots,” Zelensky said.
He said Russia had launched more than 100 ballistic missiles against Kyiv and the surrounding region in the two weeks since Oct. 14.
A day earlier, on Oct. 26, Zelensky revealed that Ukraine had been waiting nearly a month for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to authorize deliveries of missiles for Patriot and NASAMS air defense systems.
“In particular, we have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr. Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS,” Zelensky said, adding that he had instructed Ukrainian officials to raise the matter with Washington again.
The delay reportedly affects missiles already paid for by Ukraine’s allies.
Some of Ukraine’s interceptor supplies are purchased through NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), under which European allies and other partners finance American-made weapons for Kyiv.
Because the missiles are manufactured in the US, transfers from partner countries can require American authorization.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio previously acknowledged that a batch of interceptors might not have arrived but said the delay was not politically motivated.
The Pentagon has maintained that US policy on military assistance to Ukraine has not changed, while emphasizing the need to preserve sufficient American interceptor stocks.
For Kyiv, however, the delay comes as Russian ballistic missile attacks continue to cause civilian casualties and damage critical infrastructure.
“Every support package is an opportunity to protect people’s lives,” Zelensky said Monday.
Ukraine seeks Patriot interceptors from other partners
With US authorization still pending, Ukraine is pursuing additional interceptor supplies from European countries and other partners.
Zelensky said Monday that Ukrainian officials were working through several channels to secure PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles, both used by Patriot air defense systems.
“We are working on several tracks – with the US, Europe, and other partners that have stocks of PAC-2 and PAC-3 missiles,” he said.
“Conversations with other countries are also ongoing.”
The president said preparations were underway for the next meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, known as the Ramstein format, expected in November.

title: Alex Pretti's parents seek answers from DOJ months after son's killing
body:
No one has been charged in connection with the killing of the VA nurse.
It's been more than nine months since Veterans Affairs nurse Alex Pretti was shot by federal immigration agents in Minnesota, and his parents said that they have received no updates, no information and no support from the federal government.
On Tuesday, Susan and Michael Pretti made a public emotional plea to the Justice Department, which has not issued any charges in connection with the Jan. 24 shooting, to release all the evidence it has into its investigation and provide more accountability.
"Michael and I are not asking for any special treatment. We do not want to be on TV we are not political activists, nor do we want to become political activists. All we want is justice for Alex," Susan Pretti told reporters.
The couple held back tears as they spoke to the press, surrounded by pictures of the incident that sparked protests and backlash against the Trump administration, Immigration Customs and Enforcement and other federal agencies.
"The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex, they tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime," Susan Pretti said.
Then Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem alleged their son "committed an act of domestic terrorism," during a news conference hours after the shooting.
A Justice Department spokesperson responded to the Prettis' claims in a statement to ABC News on Tuesday.
"The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed. As is standard practice, communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing," the official said. "Those communications do not typically occur during an investigation."
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office in Minnesota declined comment to ABC affiliate KSTB in St. Paul.
Eyewitness videos reviewed by ABC News show that the 37-year-old nurse appeared to be recording on Jan. 24 when a federal officer shoved a woman into him.
Alex Pretti appeared to try to help her, and then both of his hands are visible -- one holding a phone and the other held up, seemingly to protect himself from pepper spray -- when he's wrestled to the ground.
His firearm, which he had a legal permit to carry, was removed by an officer while he was on the ground and before approximately 10 shots were fired, the videos show.
Noem later said that she did not have all of the information about the incident before she alleged Pretti was a terrorist.
However, she repeatedly refused to retract her statement or apologize when asked by the press and congressional leaders on multiple occasions.
"We are working in those situations where there's a tragic loss of life and that there is something that our agents are involved in, that we continue to deliver information," she said during a Senate hearing in March when asked about the shooting.
Noem was removed from her position days after that hearing. Since her ouster as DHS secretary, Noem was named by Trump to be the special envoy to the "Shield of Americas," a coalition between the U.S. and governments in Latin America.
Michael Pretti said no one from the federal government reached out to his family despite repeated requests. The family says Attorney General Todd Blanche and Dan Rosen, the U.S. attorney for the District of Minnesota, have not provided any more details about the investigation.
The Justice Department said the investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"What we have been treated to is cruelty," Michael Pretti said.
"At every turn they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex's killers," he added.
Steve Schleicher, an attorney representing the couple, told reporters the Hennepin County Attorney's Office was reviewing the case and needed access to all available evidence to determine what happened and whether criminal charges were warranted.
In a statement provided to ABC News, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said: "The federal government continues to obstruct our investigation into Alex Pretti's killing. That's why we continue to pursue our lawsuit in federal court to access the evidence that is being wrongly withheld."
The statement added: "We have repeatedly asked for the cooperation to resume. Those requests have fallen on deaf ears. Alex Pretti died at the hands of federal agents and their bosses continue to hide evidence. It's disgusting behavior that reflects how little they care for the American people, who deserve transparency about a fatal shooting by a federal agent."
Michael Pretti directly addressed Blanche and Rosen during the news conference asking them to cooperate with local investigators.
"Look in your heart and do what is right. Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable," Michael Pretti said.
The father added the family would consider any available legal options as they continue seeking justice for their son.
"We're heartbroken to be here today. We wish we didn't have to be here. We wish Alex was alive," Michael Pretti said.
-ABC News' Luke Barr contributed to this report.
