title: King Abdullah II Officially Opens SOFEX 2026 in Aqaba
body:
The 15th Special Operations Forces Exhibition and Conference (SOFEX 2026), attended by more than 400 official delegations from 75 countries and 350 exhibiting companies from 38 countries, focuses on special operations capabilities, autonomous systems and next-generation defence technologies.
King Abdullah II of Jordan, Supreme Commander of the Jordan Armed Forces–Arab Army (JAF), officially inaugurated SOFEX 2026 at a ceremony in Aqaba on Tuesday, October 27. The opening ceremony was also attended by Their Royal Highnesses Crown Prince Al Hussein bin Abdullah II and Prince Hashem bin Abdullah II.
Organised in coordination with the Jordan Armed Forces (JAF), SOFEX 2026 serves as an international platform for manufacturers and suppliers of special operations equipment. It also provides an opportunity to showcase the latest military technologies, defence solutions and cybersecurity systems, exchange expertise, and develop strategic partnerships.
This year's event is the largest edition in SOFEX's history in terms of exhibition space and the number of participating countries. According to figures released by the organisers, more than 400 official delegations from 75 countries and 350 exhibiting companies from 38 countries are participating in the exhibition.
Technology and International Cooperation Shape the Future of Special Operations
Speaking at the opening ceremony, SOFEX Chairman Brigadier General (Ret.) Ayman Al Batran said this year's exhibition was taking place at a critical juncture amid increasingly complex regional security challenges.
Emphasising the need to enhance preparedness and strengthen international cooperation to respond effectively to the evolving security environment, Al Batran highlighted the importance of establishing integrated strategic partnerships among nations, armed forces, security agencies, innovators and technology leaders in the defence industry.
Al Batran also noted that, over nearly three decades, SOFEX had strengthened Jordan's position on the international defence exhibition scene. He added that the event reflected the Royal vision of establishing Jordan as a regional and international hub for defence innovation and technology.
Following the opening ceremony, King Abdullah II toured the exhibition grounds accompanied by his delegation and visited the stands of local and international companies. Company representatives and pavilion managers briefed the King on the products on display, special operations equipment, smart systems and the latest developments in defence technology. A video presentation documenting SOFEX's evolution over the years and highlighting the modern defence solutions showcased at the exhibition was also presented.
Artificial Intelligence and Autonomous Systems Are Transforming Modern Warfare
Colonel Hisham Al-Huneiti, Commander of the King Abdullah II Royal Special Forces Group, highlighted how emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence and autonomous systems, are rapidly transforming the nature of modern warfare.
He stressed that technological superiority alone was insufficient and needed to be complemented by operational experience and the ability to adapt rapidly to changing conditions on the battlefield.
Al-Huneiti also underlined the importance of establishing close international partnerships to address future threats. He noted that the future of special operations forces would be shaped by cooperation and shared strategic choices.
These assessments reflect the growing importance of unmanned and autonomous systems, smart tactical solutions and advanced security technologies in special operations, all of which feature prominently in the agenda of SOFEX 2026.
High-Level Military and Defence Engagements
Alongside his visit to the exhibition, King Abdullah II held bilateral meetings with senior military and defence officials from several countries on the sidelines of SOFEX 2026.
Those meeting with the King included Major General Hassan Odeh, Chief of Staff of the Lebanese Armed Forces; Michel Menassah, Lebanon's Minister of National Defence; Vice Admiral Edward Ahlgren, the United Kingdom's Defence Senior Adviser for the Middle East and North Africa; General Aurelio Colagrande, NATO's Deputy Supreme Allied Commander Europe; Rear Admiral Samuel Majou of the French Armed Forces; Major General Michał Strzelecki of the Polish Armed Forces; Lieutenant General Datuk Azhan Md Othman, Chief of Staff of the Malaysian Armed Forces; and Brigadier Carlos Lovell, Chief of Staff of the Barbados Defence Force.
Members of the Royal Family, senior military commanders and government officials also attended the opening ceremony.
Taking place from October 27 to 29, SOFEX 2026 brings together equipment and systems designed for special operations forces, alongside defence technologies, cybersecurity solutions and innovative security applications.
In addition to the exhibition, the programme includes live demonstrations, workshops, official engagements and military displays. The event provides an important platform for international stakeholders in the defence and security sectors to assess emerging technologies, exchange experience and explore future cooperation opportunities.
Turkish Defence Industry Participation at SOFEX 2026
Eight Turkish companies are participating in SOFEX 2026. Some are exhibiting at their own stands, while others are participating in cooperation with local partners. The companies are ASELSAN, LASERSAN, ATEŞCİ, ASFAT, DASAL, MKE, YILMAZ Savunma Sanayi (YSS) and YILTEX ARMOR.
On the first day of the exhibition, Prof. Dr. Hakan Karataş, Vice President of Türkiye's Presidency of Defence Industries (SSB), responsible for Corporate Development and Talent Management, visited the stands of Turkish companies. Karataş received briefings from company representatives on their products and ongoing activities in Jordan and other countries across the region.
As one of the official media partners of SOFEX 2026, Defence Türkiye will cover the exhibition on-site over two days, bringing readers the latest developments, notable products, technologies and capabilities, alongside assessments of key trends shaping the defence and security industries.
On October 28, scheduled activities include a workshop for non-commissioned officers, live demonstrations by exhibitors, a workshop addressing the role of women in the armed forces, shooting-range activities, a performance by the Jordan Armed Forces Band and an air show by the Royal Jordanian Falcons.
On October 29, the programme will feature another workshop for non-commissioned officers, tactical displays by exhibitors, a live-firing demonstration, performances by the Jordan Armed Forces Band and the Royal Jordanian Falcons, and the SOFEX 2026 closing press conference. The exhibition is scheduled to close at 5:00 p.m.

title: Fleetwood Town dump Arsenal out of Carabao Cup
body: English Premier League champions, Arsenal, have been dumped out of the Carabao Cup following a 5-3 loss on penalties to Fleetwood Town. The Gunners who finished the match with ten men had been held to a 1-1 draw at full time in the fourth round fixture. Arsenal lost to the lowest-ranked team left in the competition, suffering arguably the biggest shock of the Carabao Cup with the poor outing and shock loss. Aaron Loupalo-Bi scored the opener for the hosts but Viktor Gyokores equalizer restored parity before the home side forced penalties. Arsenal made wholesome changes but went behind on 21 minutes despite fielding players of Premier League pedigree. Loupalo-Bi preyed on one of the youngsters fielded by Mikel Arteta, outmuscling the youngster before slotting the ball into the net for 1-0. Gyokores restored parity on 50 minutes with a scrappy goal, but the London club could not take the lead thereafter and were reduced to 10 players when Max Dowman was sent off for retaliation. Fleetwood goalkeeper Jay Lynch made two saves in added time to ensure the match was decided on penalties. Lynch then produced the only save of the penalties, keeping out Bruno Guimaraes’ attempt before Conor Haughey slotted home the winning kick. Defeat is Arsenal’s first against Fleetwood Town, and is the earliest an Arteta-coached Arsenal will exit the Carabao Cup. Fleetwood Town however reach the quarter-finals for the first time in the club’s history.

title: Mayoral candidates pitch more policing as civic election nears in Winnipeg
body:
Additional police and drones for surveillance won’t reduce social issues despite mayoral candidates vowing to add more officers if elected, experts say.
The Winnipeg Police Service receives 27 per cent or $370 million of the City of Winnipeg’s budget, according to the city’s 2026 budget. The city’s operating budget is at $1.49 billion.
“Per capita, we are pretty high. I think usually a lot of cities that are just slightly smaller than us are around $260-290 per citizen. Winnipeg is over $350 to $360 per citizen,” said Kevin Walby, University of Winnipeg criminologist. “When we put this percentage of our money into policing year after year after year, and we don’t see any reduction in any of those issues — in fact, visibly and statistically they are much worse. You have to start to wonder why are we doing that?”
Operating expenditures for policing in Canada totaled $22 billion in 2024-25, which is up 12 per cent from 2022-23, according to Statistics Canada.
“We are 100 police officers short of the very mere minimum of the per capita right now,” mayoral candidate Kevin Klein said on 680 CJOB.
“We need police officers, we do, we’re both committed to adding more police officers,” mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham said, also on 680 CJOB.
Mike Vogiatzakis said he would introduce drones as a tool to watch over the city and see where problems are at CBC Manitoba’s mayoral debate.
“As mayor, I’m going to instruct the police board and the police chief,” Vogiatzakis said. “I’ll sit with them within my first 30 days. I’ll sit with them and decide how we’re gonna change the city.”
The Winnipeg Police Service declined to comment.
Watch the video above for the full story.

title: Enitan on Mission to Build Civil Service That Works for Nigerians
body: Iyobosa Uwugiaren writes that the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Abel Olumuyiwa Enitan, may have embarked on a tough mission to build a federal civil service that works for Nigerians. For the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Mr. Abel Olumuyiwa Enitan, who was appointed in August by President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the true measure of leadership lies not in the office he occupies, but in the institution he leaves behind: a productive, professional and citizen-focused civil service capable of earning public trust. When the easygoing Head of the Civil Service of the Federation assumed office on August 27, 2026, he took charge of an institution crucial to the machinery of government. Indeed, through the federal civil service, policies are translated into programmes, projects and public services that affect more than 250 million Nigerians. For Enitan, the assignment goes beyond occupying the highest administrative position in the federal civil service; it presents an opportunity to strengthen an institution whose usefulness ultimately depends on its ability to deliver results for the people it serves. His message at the start of his tenure was clear: no individual can transform the civil service alone. According to him, meaningful progress requires the commitment of permanent secretaries, directors, heads of agencies and civil servants across all cadres. This emphasis on collective responsibility offers an insight into the legacy he has promised to build. Rather than make transformation synonymous with one officeholder, Enitan wants public servants to share ownership of an institution that must remain effective long after its leaders have moved on. Following his swearing-in by President Tinubu, Enitan succeeded Mrs. Didi Esther Walson-Jack, who retired at the age of 60. He described his appointment as a call to service, expressed gratitude to the President for the confidence reposed in him, and pledged to discharge his responsibilities with “humility, dedication and integrity.” But rather than pursue sweeping changes simply to distinguish his tenure, Enitan promised to consolidate existing initiatives and improve the systems through which they are implemented. “I am not going to reinvent the wheel. I will rather lubricate the wheel so that it can deliver efficiently and more productively so that I can fulfil the aspirations and expectations of Nigerians,” he stated after his swearing-in. According to one of his aides, the statement reflected a preference for continuity with improvement. In a large bureaucracy, reforms require time to take root, administrative processes must be strengthened, and institutional gains must survive changes in leadership. A system person, Enitan acknowledged his predecessor’s contributions to the transformation of the federal civil service, noting that her tenure advanced key initiatives and established a foundation for further progress. His pledge to continue from where Walson-Jack stopped, according to an insider, signalled an intention to treat these initiatives as institutional responsibilities rather than the personal projects of individual leaders. Going by his stated intentions, the challenge is to turn continuity into measurable improvement. Preserving existing frameworks matters only if they become more effective, weaknesses are addressed, and public servants can demonstrate tangible progress in their work. For the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, the opportunity is to strengthen the foundations already laid while ensuring that the civil service becomes better equipped to meet the expectations of President Tinubu and, by extension, Nigerians. As he stated at the beginning of his tenure, at the centre of his agenda is the EPIC Culture, built around Efficiency, Productivity, Incorruptibility and Citizen-Centredness. These principles define the standards he wants embedded across ministries, departments and agencies. They also provide a practical framework for assessing whether the civil service is fulfilling its responsibilities. In Enitan’s thinking, efficiency requires the responsible use of public resources and the reduction of unnecessary delays. Productivity demands results rather than routine activity alone. Incorruptibility places integrity at the heart of official conduct, while citizen-centredness requires public institutions to respond to the needs and experiences of the people they serve. For many public administration experts, the quality of public administration is often reflected in everyday encounters: how quickly an application is processed, how fairly an administrative decision is made, how reliably a public programme operates, or how respectfully an official treats a service user. These experiences shape public confidence in government. The EPIC Culture, in line with its design, is expected to have lasting value only if it moves beyond official declarations to influence workplace behaviour, management decisions and service delivery. That will require leadership by example, clear performance expectations, effective supervision and consistent adherence to ethical standards. It will also demand that public servants recognise that completing a procedure is not necessarily the same as achieving a useful result. If these values become part of the civil service’s institutional identity, they could outlast the tenure of Enitan, who is currently promoting them. Enitan has identified the effective implementation of government policies, programmes and projects as a central priority. “My task is very simple, and it is just to make the Federal Civil Service more innovative, more productive and more professional, as well as to be more responsive to the yearnings of Nigerians, where the civil service as a body translates government policies, programmes and projects into concrete results,” he promised. To be sure, the statement identifies a critical responsibility of public administration: bridging the gap between government intentions and outcomes experienced by citizens. As experts would argue, policies and public announcements do not automatically improve living conditions; their impact depends on planning, coordination, resource management, execution and monitoring. The civil service occupies a pivotal position in this process, providing professional advice, coordinating institutions and supporting implementation. Enitan’s task is to strengthen this capacity while supporting the federal government’s reform objectives and the Renewed Hope Agenda of his principal, President Tinubu. Permanent secretaries, directors and other senior officials have a particularly important role in ensuring that responsibilities are clearly assigned, implementation is monitored, and administrative obstacles are addressed. Yet the responsibility extends throughout the workforce, because the daily decisions of officers at every level influence the speed and quality of government services. In the long run, the success of public policy must be judged not merely by its announcement or approval, but by whether it achieves its intended purpose. A civil service that consistently delivers on this responsibility would provide one of the clearest measures of Enitan’s contribution. Perhaps that is why Enitan urged civil servants across the federal establishment to embrace professionalism, innovation, accountability and results-oriented service delivery. Those familiar with his policies and programmes said his focus on officers on Grade Levels 8 to 14 underscores the importance of engaging employees who carry out many of the operational and administrative tasks of government. His thinking may be that reform cannot be sustained if it remains the concern of senior officials alone; officers who process applications, maintain records, prepare correspondence and attend to citizens must understand how their work contributes to institutional performance. By encouraging ownership across the hierarchy, Enitan may be seeking to make improvement part of everyday working life rather than an initiative connected exclusively to the Head of Service’s office. This will require clear communication, appropriate professional development and a culture that recognises diligence while addressing misconduct and persistent underperformance. It also calls for openness to innovation as technology and changing public expectations reshape administrative work. In line with Enitan’s statement from day one, collective responsibility is not simply a message of solidarity; it is a practical requirement for improving the performance of a complex institution. Some observers of the federal civil service have argued that Enitan’s leadership will be tested by his ability to turn that principle into coordinated action across the federal civil service. Nevertheless, records show that Enitan brings experience from several important institutions of the federal government. Born on December 12, 1966, and hailing from Osun State, he attended Ajibode Grammar School, Ibadan, and the College of Arts and Science, Ile-Ife. He then obtained a Bachelor of Science degree in Finance and Banking from the University of Lagos in 1988 and a Master of Science degree in Public Policy Analysis from Nasarawa State University, Keffi, in 2015. He had wanted to enrol for a doctorate after his retirement, but his current appointment came along. His academic background combines financial training with public policy analysis, disciplines relevant to resource management, institutional administration and policy implementation. Before his appointment as HCSF, he served as permanent secretary in the Ministry of Police Affairs, the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs, the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Aviation and the Office of the Vice President. These postings exposed him to different dimensions of government administration, coordination and policy delivery. As the most senior permanent secretary, he emerged to lead the federal civil service, a role that demands coordination across numerous ministries, departments and agencies, as well as the ability to promote common professional standards. His experience may have provided a foundation for the assignment. But its ultimate value will be determined by how effectively he applies it to strengthening institutional performance and improving the delivery of public services. Enitan has pledged to help restore public confidence in the civil service, but that confidence cannot be secured through declarations alone; it must be earned through fairness, transparency, competence and consistent performance. Observers have argued that administrative delays, unclear procedures, weak coordination and unethical conduct can undermine trust. Conversely, reliable services, transparent processes and timely decisions can help rebuild it. The practical implications of Enitan’s agenda are therefore clear: public institutions must become more dependable, responsibilities must be taken seriously, and performance must be assessed against results. Progress will require cooperation among the Head of Service’s office, ministry leadership, administrative officers and other stakeholders. It will also demand sustained attention to implementation rather than treating policy statements as evidence of achievement. The extent to which Enitan restores public confidence will ultimately be determined by what Nigerians experience when they interact with government—not simply by what the civil service promises to deliver. What legacy will Enitan leave behind? For a public servant entrusted with leading the federal civil service, legacy is not necessarily defined by the number of initiatives launched or the changes announced at the beginning of a tenure. It is measured by what remains when the officeholder departs: stronger institutions, enduring professional standards and a workforce better equipped to serve the public. Enitan may have set out a clear direction. He wants to strengthen existing administrative frameworks, embed the EPIC Culture and ensure that public servants at every level take responsibility for results. The test is whether these commitments become established practices rather than aspirations associated with his tenure. Will official processes become more efficient? Will integrity guide administrative decisions? Will policies produce measurable benefits? Will citizens encounter a civil service that treats their needs as a central responsibility? The answers will determine the significance of his leadership. Yet the most distinctive measure of Enitan’s legacy may be what happens after his watch has ended. If the systems he strengthens continue to function, if the values he promotes remain part of official conduct, and if public servants sustain improvements without depending on the presence of one individual, his contribution will have acquired lasting significance. That is the subterranean meaning of his insistence that no individual can transform the civil service alone. The leader may provide direction, but the institution must carry the work forward. For Enitan, success will, at the end of the day, mean leaving behind more than a record of policies and initiatives. It will mean helping to build a civil service that works because its people understand their responsibilities, its systems support effective performance, and its commitment to Nigerians endures beyond any single tenure.

title: Osaka ‘not far off’ her best but often ponders future
body: Naomi Osaka says she is “not far off” the form that brought her four Grand Slam titles, but admits she has thought about quitting and often ponders her future. The 29-year-old Japanese star won both the US Open and Australian Open twice between 2018 and 2021, during a glittering start to her career that took her to world number one. She took time out of the sport in 2021 to prioritise her mental health and another 15 months away after becoming pregnant, before returning in 2023 following the birth of her daughter. Osaka now says that she would quit tennis if her three-year-old, Shai, asked her to, despite climbing back up the world rankings and once again challenging for major titles. “It’s tough; sometimes I look towards my future, and I often wonder how long I’m going to play,” Osaka said as she prepares to take part in the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo. “Because if my daughter did say she didn’t want me to travel as much, I’m not the type of person to ignore that.” Osaka acknowledged that her mindset has changed a lot with age and the extra responsibilities that come with parenthood, saying “my daughter is my biggest priority”. “I try my best to put as much energy as I can into tennis,” she said. “I wouldn’t say I’m part-timing it, but my entire day doesn’t consist of that. “If I think about it in certain ways, I’m really proud of where I am now because it’s not like I can dedicate my entire time to the sport.” Osaka has battled back to 19th in the world and is the seventh seed at this week’s tournament, where she faces Italy’s Jasmine Paolini in the opening round. Osaka beat top seed Aryna Sabalenka to reach the quarter-finals of Wimbledon earlier this year, after finishing runner-up at the preceding grass tournament in Bad Homburg, and also reached the last 16 of the French Open and US Open. Osaka also reached the semi-finals in Washington and the last eight in Toronto during the North American hardcourt swing, and eventual champion Elena Rybakina ended her run at Flushing Meadows. “I genuinely don’t feel like I’m that far off,” she said, when considering if she can get back to winning titles. “I think there are certain instincts that I don’t want to say I lost, but maybe I forgot and I’m kind of relearning, but yeah, I don’t think – I hope – I’m not far off. “I think I built a pretty solid base and I’m just excited to see if I can continue learning and going further in tournaments.” Osaka is on the opposite side of the draw in Tokyo from Kazakhstan’s world number one, Rybakina, who enters the tournament after winning her fourth title of the year at the Ningbo Open in China. The defending champion powered past Canada’s Leylah Fernandez 6-2 6-2 in Sunday’s final to claim a first tournament victory since last month’s US Open. Elsewhere, Daniil Medvedev defended his title for the first time in his career, beating Nikoloz Basilashvili 6-7 (6-8) 6-1 6-3 in the Almaty Open final for his 25th men’s singles crown and fourth this season. And at the Lyon Open, the British pair of Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash beat France’s Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti 4-6 6-3 10-8 in the men’s doubles final to record their 12th ATP title together.

title: MultiChoice Introduces Simplified DStv, GOtv Packages for Customers in Nigeria
body: • From Nov. 5, brand-new Sports package including every PL and UCL match MultiChoice Group, a Canal+ Company, introduces its most significant product update in years, bringing more of Africa’s greatest sports and entertainment live to subscribers, live from 5 November 2026. Under the new structure, DStv packages will comprise Starter, Select, Sports and Premium , while GOtv customers can choose from Easy, Starter, Select and Sports . The new package line-up is designed around how customers watch today, with clearer choices, more accessible content and greater value across the portfolio. “Our focus is on giving subscribers better value and access to the entertainment they love,” said Kemi Omotosho, CEO of MultiChoice Nigeria announced at the unveiling of the packages. MultiChoice Nigeria Chief Executive, stressed further: “The strength of our platform is the combination of African entertainment, leading international content and unrivalled live sports in one place. We’ve reimagined our packages to better reflect how customers watch today, with tailored options specifically for general entertainment and sports fans.” For the first time, some of DStv’s biggest channels will be available at significantly more accessible price points for its subscribers. “Starter is the entry-level entertainment package featuring two brand-new channels: SuperSport KICKOFF, which brings the Premier League Match of the Week and selected football from the UEFA Champions League; and Africa Magic+, which offers premium local and international series plus more at only 6,000 Naira. “Select offers a wide variety of entertainment for the whole family at 11,000 Naira. Subscribers will enjoy all movie channels, local and international series, a selection of top football and other sports, as well as the complete kids’ channel offering. “Sports is the first package built specifically for football fans, covering every Premier League and UEFA Champions League match, WWE and UFC. Alongside this extensive sports offering, Sports package includes all the general entertainment channels available on Select for only 21,000 Naira. “Premium re mains DStv’s most comprehensive package, combining everything available on Sports with additional premium sporting titles, including Formula 1, MotoGP, Grand Slam tennis and Golf majors, as well as the best international series on M-Net. DStv’s movie line-up has also been refreshed with M-Net Movies+, M-Net Stars and M-Net Legends, bringing more blockbuster movies, faster access to new releases and fewer repeats. MultiChoice also announced that GOtv customers will also benefit from Its refreshed package line-up, with new GOtv packages launching alongside the new DStv offering on 5 November. “Built around the same principles of greater value, simpler choice and access to more of the entertainment customers love, the new GOtv packages will provide an enhanced viewing experience tailored to local audiences,” she concluded.

title: Golf: Nigeria’s Okoko Claims Maiden Sunshine Devt Tour Title in Kenya
body: Nigeria’s prodigy, Godwin Okoko, claimed his maiden professional title after winning the Rift Valley Championship, the eighth leg of the Sunshine Development Tour – East Africa Swing, which concluded at Nakuru Golf Club yesterday. Okoko, who has been in fine form this season, closed with a five-under-par 68 to secure the title, finishing on a tournament total of 209. His final-round scorecard featured six birdies on holes 3, 4, 6, 10, 11 and 17, alongside a spectacular eagle on the 16th. He dropped shots on holes 5, 8 and 12 but maintained his advantage to seal the win. Speaking after his round, an elated Okoko said, “I’m very happy to win my first title on the Sunshine Development Tour. I’ve been working hard throughout the season, and it feels good to see that effort pay off. The course tested us, but I stayed focused, took my opportunities and kept pushing until the end. This win gives me a lot of confidence as I prepare for the next event back home in Nigeria.” The victory earned Okoko Ksh 400,000 (about N4million) from the Ksh 2 million prize purse, alongside 210 Sunshine Development Tour Order of Merit points. Simon Njogu of Golf Park Golf Club finished second on nine-under-par 210 after another strong performance. His final-round card featured birdies on holes 5, 8, 10, 11 and 16, with his only dropped shots coming on holes 4 and 17. Okoko will now return to Nigeria for the next Sunshine Development Tour event, the Alpha Bravo Golf Classic, scheduled for 18 – 21 November 2026 at Lakowe Lakes Golf Estate. Having secured his first title, he will be looking to carry his momentum into the home event and challenge for another victory. Njogu took home Ksh 214,000 and 172 Order of Merit points. Edwin Mudanyi, who began the final round as the overnight leader, finished third on six-under-par 213 after a challenging start. Dismas Indiza finished fourth on four-under-par 214, while Greg Snow of Muthaiga Golf Club took fifth place on four-under-par 215. John Kagiri finished sixth on one-under-par 218. Sponsored by NCBA Bank, the championship formed part of the Sunshine Development Tour – East Africa Swing, bringing together professional golfers and elite amateurs from across the region to compete for prize money, world ranking points and opportunities to advance their careers.

title: Edo Queens in Cairo for Rescheduled WAFU-B Final with Ghana’s Ampem Darkoa
body: Nigeria’s Edo Queens and Ghana’s Ampem Darkoa will tomorrow in Cairo, Egypt compete for the West African Football Union (WAFU B) representative’s slot following the disputed regional final last month. At the WAFU B final in Burkina Faso, Edo Queens defeated the Ghanaian Ladies 4-1 in penalty shootouts. Regulation time had ended 2-2 before the penalty shootouts. However, the Ghanaians filed a protest against the penalty shootouts, insisting that the rule of the competition provided 30 minutes extra time which the match officials ignored and went into the spot kicks. CAF ruled in favour of the Ghanaians and ordered for the extra 30 minutes be played on a neutral ground. Edo’s objection not to replay after winning the final failed. CAF’s Disciplinary and Appeals Board upheld Ampe Darkoa’s protest. Edo Queens left Nigeria since Monday to prepare ahead of Thursday’s clash with the Ghanaian top women’s team. In the schedule for the 2026 CAF Women’s Champions League released yesterday by the continental body, the winner will join seven other qualified teams, including defending champions AS FAR of Morocco, South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns, Uganda’s Kawempe Muslim Ladies, Mali’s USFAS Bamako, Morocco’s FUS Rabat, Cameroon’s Lekie Football Girls and Egypt’s FC Masar. The group-stage matches will take place from November 1 to 8, with the semi-finals scheduled for November 11, the third-place match on November 14 and the final on November 15. The fixture list confirms that all kick-off times are in Cairo local time, with Suez Canal Stadium in Ismailia and Ismailia Stadium hosting matches during the tournament. The tournament will also carry significant global implications, as the African champions will face North Korean side Naegohyang in the second round of the FIFA Women’s Champions Cup in December. For Edo Queens, securing the WAFU B ticket would provide another opportunity to represent Nigeria on the continental stage and pursue Africa’s top women’s club honour.

title: FG Dangles $3,000 Reward for Gold as Team Nigeria Set to Depart for Youth Olympics in Dakar
body: Duro Ikhazuagbe As Team Nigeria athletes and officials brace up to depart for the 2026 Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, the Federal Government has announced cash rewards of $3,000 for every gold medallist. Speaking at the send forth ceremony for the team in Abuja yesterday, the Director General of the National Sports Commission (NSC), Hon. Bukola Olopade, announced the incentives for the Dakar-bound athletes. According to the NSC DG, any Nigerian athlete who also wins a silver medal will receive $2,500, while bronze medallist will earn $2,000. Beyond the financial incentives, Olopade charged the young athletes to represent Nigeria with pride, discipline and patriotism at the historic competition, which will be the first Olympic event hosted on African soil. He described the opportunity to compete in Dakar as an important milestone in the athletes’ careers, urging them to maximise the experience as they begins their journeys toward senior international competitions, including the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles. Olopade said he believes in the athletes going to represent Nigeria at the Youth Olympiad. The Youth Olympics in Dakar is very historic, and you are making history by being part of the first Olympic Games to be held in Africa. This is why I am very confident that this Youth Olympics will mark the beginning of greatness for all of you,” Olopade stressed He also assured the athletes of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s commitment to their development, particularly in balancing their sporting ambitions with education. Olopade noted that the Commission’s renewed emphasis on grassroots sports development was designed to identify and nurture young talents capable of representing Nigeria at major international competitions. The NSC DG specifically highlighted the Invited Junior Athletes (IJA) programme as part of the Commission’s talent development strategy, adding that the Youth Olympics would provide valuable international exposure for some of the programme’s beneficiaries. The ceremony also featured the formal handover of Team Nigeria from the NSC to the Nigeria Olympic Committee (NOC), with the athletes appearing in their national green-and-white kits ahead of their scheduled departure for Senegal tomorrow (Thursday). Receiving the contingent, NOC President, Engr Habu Gumel, assured the Commission that the athletes would receive the necessary care and support throughout the competition. Gumel also emphasised the importance of clean sport, expressing confidence that the Nigerian contingent would compete fairly and return home without compromising the principles of integrity and sportsmanship. The 2026 Youth Olympic Games will take place in Dakar from October 31 to November 13, bringing together more than 2,700 young athletes from 205 countries to compete for medals and national honours.

title: ASIS Spotlights NSIA’s $300m Renewable Energy Fund to Expand Power Access
body: Deborah Ndinorouba The Africa Social Impact Summit (ASIS) has highlighted the $300 million Nigeria Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE) Fund as a major step towards addressing Nigeria’s electricity access gap, with the initiative expected to channel investment into renewable energy solutions for underserved communities and businesses. The fund, launched commercially by the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA), Africa50 and Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL), is designed to scale up distributed renewable energy projects, including mini-grids and standalone solar systems. The initiative was spotlighted at the inaugural ASIS Global Action Forum in New York, held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly, where policymakers, investors, development institutions and private-sector leaders examined ways to mobilise capital for Africa’s development priorities. The forum, convened by Sterling One Foundation in partnership with NSIA, the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), RALLY and other partners, built on discussions at the fifth Africa Social Impact Summit held in Lagos in July. Co-managed by NSIA and Africa50, with SEforALL providing energy-access leadership, the fund is expected to support the deployment of renewable energy solutions across Nigeria, helping to extend electricity supply to communities and businesses underserved by conventional power infrastructure. Speaking on the initiative, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Renewables Investment Platform for Limitless Energy (RIPLE), established by NSIA, Yusuf Umar, said closing Nigeria’s energy access gap required financing structures that could deliver viable solutions to the people and businesses that needed them most. “Closing Nigeria’s energy access gap requires more than recognising the scale of the challenge; it requires financing structures that can bring viable solutions to the communities and businesses that need them most,” he said. Chief Executive Officer of Sterling One Foundation, Olapeju Ibekwe, said the fund demonstrated how partnerships could move development conversations beyond commitments to practical interventions that respond to the needs of communities. “At the Africa Social Impact Summit, we believe that the true value of development conversations lies in what they make possible beyond the room,” she said.

title: Insurer Advocates for Wealth Protection through Integration of Risk Management
body: The Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer of Mutual Benefits Assurance Plc, Mr. Olufemi Asenuga, has said that Nigeria must integrate risk management and insurance more deliberately into its sustainable development agenda in order to protect households, businesses, public institutions and critical infrastructure against shocks. Asenuga, stated this while delivering a plenary paper on behalf of the Group Chairman of Mutual Benefits, Dr. Akin Ogunbiyi, at the 19th Annual Research Conference & Fair of the University of Lagos recently. Speaking on the theme, “Risk Management and Insurance as Catalysts for Sustainable Development: Protecting Lives, Livelihoods and Critical Infrastructure,” Asenuga examined how insurance could help individuals, businesses and governments withstand financial shocks, preserve development gains and recover from unexpected losses. “Development is not what a nation builds. Development is what survives,” he declared, emphasising the importance of protecting investments and livelihoods against preventable and unforeseen risks. Aligning his arguments with the conference’s focus on food security, health, housing and humanity, Asenuga described insurance as an essential component of national development, rather than a peripheral financial service. He said while risk management helped to identify and reduce potential losses, insurance provided financial protection against covered events, enabling households, businesses and public institutions to recover and maintain continuity. He noted that the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals recognised the importance of resilience and financial protection, particularly Target 1.5, which promotes the resilience of vulnerable populations, and Target 8.10, which encourages access to insurance and other financial services.

title: ACAMB Warns Bank Customers against Phishing Scams
body: Deborah Ndinorouba The Association of Corporate Communication and Marketing Professionals in Banks (ACAMB) has cautioned bank customers against phishing scams, warning that fraudsters are increasingly impersonating financial institutions through fake text messages, cloned websites and fraudulent social media accounts to steal sensitive banking information. The warning follows a fraudulent text message impersonating several banks, which FactCheckAfrica debunked after finding that the link contained in the message directed users to a cloned internet banking website designed to harvest login credentials, Bank Verification Numbers (BVNs), card details and transaction PINs. The incident highlights growing concerns over digital banking fraud as more Nigerians rely on online platforms for financial transactions. In June, Wema Bank suspended its engagements on X following reports of more than 70 fake accounts impersonating the bank and its ALAT platform. Similarly, Zenith Bank Plc disclosed in August that it was investigating unauthorised access to customer data linked to a global cyberattack. ACAMB President, Jide Sipe, said fraudsters were becoming increasingly sophisticated in their attempts to exploit customers’ trust in established banking brands, making it more difficult to distinguish fraudulent messages from legitimate communications. “When a scam message carries your name, your phone number or your bank’s logo, it looks real. That is exactly why customers must slow down. No bank in Nigeria will ask you to confirm your PIN, password, OTP or BVN through a link,” Sipe said. He acknowledged efforts by banks to strengthen fraud detection and customer protection, alongside regulatory measures introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria through its mandatory cybersecurity self-assessment guide. However, he stressed that stronger security systems and regulatory oversight must be matched by greater customer awareness, noting that fraudsters continue to exploit unsuspecting users through deceptive messages and requests for confidential information. “Banks can strengthen their security systems, but fraudsters continue to find ways to exploit unsuspecting customers. We must all remain vigilant. Always pause, verify requests through official channels and report anything suspicious before taking action,” he added.

title: Axxela Hosts Customers, Reaffirms Commitment to Quality Service
body: Axxela Limited, a leading gas and power portfolio company in Sub-Saharan Africa, has reaffirmed its commitment to service excellence and strong customer relationships. The company gave the pledge at its 2026 Customer Appreciation Forum, themed, ‘Energy for Progress, Partnerships for Growth’, held in Lagos. Axxela’s annual Customer Appreciation Forum forms part of the company’s broader commitment to fostering open communication, strengthening customer relationships, and creating value across its markets. Speaking at the event, the Group Chief Executive Officer of Axxela, Moshood Olajide, expressed appreciation to the customers for their continued confidence and partnership, emphasising their importance to Axxela’s growth and long-term ambitions. “This forum is more than an opportunity to express our appreciation; it is also an avenue to reaffirm our commitment to building enduring partnerships, delivering value, and providing energy solutions that cater to your evolving needs. Our evolution into an integrated energy solutions provider reflects our understanding that our customers’ needs are dynamic and will continue to evolve,” Olajide said. In his goodwill message, the Managing Director/CEO of Emmalesson Enterprises Limited, Emmanuel Evue, commended Axxela for their unwavering support, encouragement and reassurance during a challenging period in the company’s journey. “The process of obtaining our take-off approval from the Federal Government was long and challenging. Throughout the journey, Axxela’s customer relationship management team provided unwavering support. Their consistency and commitment reassured us, while their encouragement and practical support gave us the confidence to persevere through a difficult period,” Evue said.

title: THE CARNAGE ON OTEDOLA BRIDGE
body: The authorities must do more to curb the deadly crashes While questions are being asked about the frequency of accidents on the Otedola Bridge, the Lagos State government insists that structural assessments conducted with federal authorities show no core engineering defects, attributing the recurring crashes to reckless driving, indiscipline, and overloaded heavy-duty trucks. But in the latest accident on the bridge located at the Lagos end of the expressway to Ibadan, a diesel tanker carrying 33,000 litres plunged off the bridge and burst into flames beneath the structure. The Lagos State Fire and Rescue Service and others were able to contain the blaze which left two men with severe degree-burns. There are arguments that repeated mishaps on Otedola Bridge may be due to severe structural engineering defects. Indeed, some safety and structural experts contend that the bridge has two major engineering defects. One, the road is too slippery hence the need for resurfacing with more coarse asphalt materials in order for vehicles not to lose tyre grip. Two, the approach to the bridge is downward sloppy which means vehicles descend into a valley and start climbing up almost at the same time, on a very slippery surface. Built in 1978 and named after a former governor of Lagos State, Sir Michael Otedola, the bridge has, over the years, become notorious for deadly tanker explosions, fallen containers and trucks as well as multiple vehicle collisions. In the last three years alone, it has recorded about 15 accidents, many of them fatal. On 1 September 2023, a wheat-laden truck fell off the bridge, killing one occupant while on 7 January 2025, four trucks were involved in catastrophic crashes, killing one person and injuring three others. On 29 March 2025, newly wedded Chidozie and Joan Okoye were burnt alive along with others on the bridge when a tanker laden with gas caught fire. Barely a month ago on 16 September, a containerised truck lost control and rammed into multiple vehicles, trapping passengers and causing severe damage on the busiest transport corridor in the country. But perhaps the defining tragedy on the Lagos bridge occurred on 28 June 2018, when a petroleum tanker lost control, spilled its contents and exploded. The body count was 12 dead, while 54 vehicles went up in flames. Expectedly, the crashes were accompanied by traffic chaos and massive gridlock, some lasting the entire day. To be sure, traffic accidents are commonplace in Nigeria due mainly to bad roads, poor vehicle maintenance, disregard for traffic rules in addition to regulatory failure. But drivers of petroleum tankers, heavy trucks and other articulated vehicles constitute a special risk to other road users across Nigeria as they are a law unto themselves. The manner in which they go about terrorising other road users had always left the impression whether the drivers were under some instruction to break the rules of civilised conduct. The disturbing history of crashes on the Otedola Bridge bears these familiar streaks. The serial fatal incidents are attributed largely to the lawlessness of heavy-duty drivers, speeding, and poor state of the vehicles, including brake failures. The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC) has reported 256 road traffic crashes on Otedola Bridge, the nearby Kara Bridge and the OPIC corridor between January 2018 and June 2020. According to the report, 39 crashes occurred on Otedola Bridge, representing 15 per cent, with speed violations as the chief culprit, in addition to brake and mechanical failures, and tyre bursts. Heavy-duty truck drivers in particular lose control while descending the bridge and negotiating the bends at unsafe speed. While the Lagos State Commissioner for Transportation, Oluwaseun Osiyemi insists that integrity tests jointly conducted with federal authorities have proved conclusively that there are no structural defects with the bridge, there is an urgent need to put an end to these catastrophic crashes.

title: A FRIEND OF THE NORTH
body: The Kaduna rally is the north’s referendum on Tinubu, reckons ABDULAZIZ ABDULAZIZ Through Kaduna, its old political capital, the North spoke on Saturday. And the echo will haunt those who have spent months marketing the lie that the North has abandoned President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. The Kaduna Township Stadium was full beyond capacity, and the mammoth crowd overflowed into the well-adorned streets. It was a confetti of colours, flags raised high and proudly: a sea of red caps, white babban riga, green wrappers, placards of _Sai Asiwaju_. It was a cacophony of languages — Hausa, Fulfulde, Tiv, Idoma, Gbagyi, Yoruba, Nupe, Kanuri, and English. Entire APC governors from the North, supported by their southern counterparts, sat shoulder to shoulder with former governors, legislators, imams, pastors, women leaders, and artisans who trekked kilometres to see the man they still call Jagaba, the leader. The gathering was beyond a rented crowd; it was organic, massive, and emotional. A few photos from the event displayed that spectacularly: the excited trio waving so happily at their president who wound down the window to greet them; the many people who kept vigil at the venue so they could get a good spot to witness history; and the excited young men and women who spent the whole day under the sun waving flags and chanting praises. It was Arewa saying, without apology: we still stand with our friend. As I wrote in February 2023, at the heat of the last campaign when the same suspects tried to whip up ethnic sentiments against him, Asiwaju Tinubu and the North have always been friends. This friendship is not transactional. It is historic. Tinubu’s consequential political journey did not begin in Lagos. It began with the North. In 1991, at the beginning of the aborted Third Republic, when General Ibrahim Babangida midwifed two parties, a young Tinubu had a choice. His kinsman, the great Chief Lateef Jakande, was in the field. Yet he chose to pitch his tent with General Shehu Musa Yar’Adua’s Peoples Front (PF) — the most organised, most progressive political machine of that era. On the SDP platform under that PF, Tinubu became Senator for Lagos West in 1992. When MKO Abiola emerged as SDP candidate, Tinubu was instrumental in pushing Ambassador Babagana Kingibe, a son of Borno, as the running mate. He chose North, again. That choice in 1992 has defined his politics ever since. When President Obasanjo wanted to skin Atiku Abubakar alive in 2007, Bola Tinubu was his saviour. In 2011, he propped up Nuhu Ribadu, and Muhammadu Buhari in 2015 and 2019. In 2011, he supported Aminu Tambuwal for Speaker at a time Tambuwal’s own party, the PDP, was against him. No other Southern politician has invested that much political capital in the North. Indeed, the North doesn’t forget. This is why Arewa for Asiwaju, a political movement of the crème de la crème of the Northern political establishment, is a commendable and timely intervention. At a time when the opposition offers only recycled fuel subsidy — illegal under the PIA — and AI-generated falsehoods which Governor Uba Sani rightly warned about in Kaduna, A4A provides what Arewa needs most: honest conversation, the voice of truth, in Hausa, Fulfulde, Tiv, Nupe, Gbagyi, Kanuri, in every market, motor park, mosque and church. A4A is not just a campaign apparatus. It is a reminder that friendship is a two-way street and that the North is faithful to its values of fairness, justice, peaceful coexistence and national unity. As a political movement, its raison d’être is consensus-building and evidence-based campaigning. The purpose is to counter with evidence the lies that as president, Asiwaju Tinubu has abandoned his old friend, the North. How? With the Ministry of Livestock Development the North craved for 60 years? With the North Central Development Commission and North West Development Commission? With the new Federal Universities in Mubi, Kachia and Kabo? Would the person who abandoned the North rush the completion of the Kano-Maradi rail or the Akwanga-Lafia-Makurdi road? Would he have established cancer centres and upgraded dozens of hospitals and schools? Well, Arewa for Asiwaju is throwing those questions with hard facts. Kaduna provided a ground to further deflate the vacuous noise of the opposition. The North came together in one powerful voice. Eighteen out of 19 governors, an array of former governors from the class of 1999 to date, a horde of Young Turks, an armada of party faithful. It was a spectacle. For months, a small but loud echo chamber in Abuja and on social media had been working hard to sell a fiction — that the North regrets 2023, that the President and his campaigners can no longer enter Arewa, that 2027 is already decided. Kaduna buried that fiction with one picture. As the Campaign Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, said from the podium, everyone that mattered in the North was at the stadium yesterday. Most of them were there in person, a lot more in spirit. The few and scattered dissenters are too insignificant to cause any political upheaval. Vice President Kashim Shettima and Yari did not come to Kaduna to speak grammar. They came with history and with receipts. VP Shettima was as sharp and straight as always. He used a clincher to remind voters from the North of the options before them. “We won in 2023 not because we were the wisest or richest, but because you saw the options before you and knew the alternative was a calamity. We have come to ask you to renew a second term for the APC from top to bottom.” Senator Yari, who was evidently pleased by the turnout across all walks of life, assured: “By God’s grace, Northern Nigeria is 101 per cent behind you, Asiwaju Bola Ahmed Tinubu, and we are determined to deliver our promise on 16 January 2027.” Speaking further in Hausa, Senator Yari said the President should as well go to sleep and wait for victory. Yet, President Tinubu did not just go to Kaduna to excite the crowd or display supporters. He went with deliveries. In a first for campaign rallies, President Tinubu used the occasion to inaugurate the 81-kilometre section of the Kaduna-Abuja highway with a symbolic ribbon-cutting. It is just one of many dividends Kaduna got from the Tinubu administration, as Governor Uba Sani reeled out so many benefits Kaduna reaped from the Tinubu administration in his welcome address. They range from roads to rail to universities and health institutions. The North, as Governor Sani testified, has never had it this good. President Tinubu is repaying loyalty in concrete, steel, and care. From Peoples Front in 1991 to Arewa for Asiwaju in 2026, President Tinubu has always operated as a friend. Kaduna proved it yesterday. On 16 January 2027, the ballot will confirm it louder. Abdulaziz is Senior Special Assistant to the President on Print Media and Director of Media and Communication, Arewa for Asiwaju

title: THE BURDEN OF BREAST CANCER
body: Every person affected deserves timely assessment, and appropriate treatment, write CHIMEZIE ANYAKORA and UJUNWA PRINCESS ONYEKABA Every October, breast cancer awareness campaigns bring the disease into public conversation. Communities organize health talks, organizations share educational materials, healthcare professionals encourage people to pay attention to their breast health, and survivors share experiences that help others feel less alone. These efforts matter. But an important question remains: what happens after someone notices a change in their breast? For Bloom Public Health, that question is deeply personal. We have experienced the pain of losing a staff member to breast cancer. Our colleague’s absence is a reminder that this disease is not merely a statistic or an annual campaign topic; it affects real people, families, workplaces and communities. We cannot undo that loss, but we can let it strengthen our commitment to sharing reliable information and encouraging people to seek care without avoidable delay. Awareness can make a difference only when it is connected to timely medical assessment, accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Where these services are difficult to reach, unaffordable or poorly coordinated, awareness alone cannot bridge the gap. The challenge is not simply to tell people that breast cancer exists, but to help ensure that those who need care can obtain it. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately 2.4 million women were diagnosed with breast cancer worldwide in 2024, and about 694,000 people died from the disease that year. Breast cancer occurs in countries at every income level, yet inequalities in early diagnosis and access to treatment contribute to very different outcomes. In many settings, substantial barriers remain between noticing a symptom and receiving appropriate care. The burden of breast cancer is also evident at the country level. In Nigeria, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) estimated 44,196 new breast cancer cases in 2024, making it the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women in the country. In Zambia, an estimated 1,555 new cases occurred in the same year, with breast cancer ranking second among cancers affecting women, after cervical cancer. These figures highlight the importance of country-specific responses that reflect local health needs and the capacity of healthcare systems to provide timely diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Breast cancer does not always cause pain in its early stages. A new lump or thickening in the breast or underarm, a change in breast size or shape, dimpling of the skin, a change in the nipple, or unusual nipple discharge may require medical assessment. Not every breast lump is cancerous, but anyone who notices a new or unusual change should consult a qualified healthcare professional rather than assume it is harmless or wait for pain to develop. Recognizing a symptom is only the beginning. The next steps may depend on the availability and cost of healthcare, distance to a suitable facility, access to diagnostic services and the effectiveness of referral systems. Fear and stigma can also discourage people from seeking care. Some worry about what a diagnosis could mean for their families, livelihoods or finances; others do not know where to go or what to expect. These barriers should not be seen simply as failures of individual awareness. They also reflect the conditions in which people seek care. An effective public health response must do two things: help people recognize when to seek medical attention and ensure that health services can respond when they do. Primary healthcare facilities often provide the first point of contact for people concerned about breast changes. Frontline health workers need the training and support to assess symptoms, explain next steps and refer patients promptly for further investigation. Depending on the findings, diagnostic assessment may involve imaging, tissue sampling and pathological examination. Together, these steps help establish whether cancer is present and inform treatment decisions. When essential services are unavailable, unaffordable or poorly coordinated, patients may face repeated visits, extra expenses and prolonged uncertainty. Delays can also occur when referral arrangements are unclear or patients receive little support in completing the next steps. Stronger links between primary healthcare, diagnostic services and specialist care can make the journey from first concern to diagnosis more reliable. Evidence from Nigeria illustrates the importance of strengthening access to diagnostic services. Early diagnosis matters, but it must lead to appropriate care. Treatment depends on the type and stage of breast cancer and the individual’s circumstances. It may involve surgery, radiotherapy, medicines or a combination of approaches. Many people, particularly those whose cancers are found early and treated appropriately, have better prospects. A breast cancer diagnosis is not automatically a death sentence; patients deserve accurate information, compassionate support and access to suitable care. Early diagnosis and screening are not the same. Early diagnosis focuses on evaluating people who already have symptoms or signs of possible disease. Screening is intended for people who do not have symptoms and should follow appropriate national guidance and individual risk assessment. Anyone who notices a concerning breast change should seek medical evaluation rather than wait for a routine screening appointment. The journey through suspected cancer, diagnosis and treatment can involve several facilities and healthcare professionals. Patient navigation and continuity of care can help people arrange appointments, complete referrals, understand next steps and access practical or emotional support. Care should be organized around the patient’s journey, rather than leaving each person to coordinate every stage alone. Improving breast cancer outcomes requires coordinated action from governments, healthcare institutions, health professionals, development partners and communities. Public health communication can help people recognize symptoms and find reliable information. Healthcare facilities need trained personnel, diagnostic capacity and clear referral pathways. Policymakers must also address affordability, geographic access, treatment availability and systems that show whether patients are reaching the services they need. Families, friends and employers have a role as well. Someone facing a possible cancer diagnosis may be managing fear, uncertainty, financial pressure and concern for loved ones. Support can be practical: accompanying someone to an appointment, helping with daily responsibilities or listening without judgment. No one should be blamed, shamed or isolated because of a cancer diagnosis. For public health organizations, outcomes depend not only on information, but also on whether services are accessible and work together. Strengthening the systems that connect people to qualified healthcare is essential to turning awareness into timely diagnosis and effective care. Breast cancer awareness should not end when October ends or the pink ribbons are put away. Its impact should be seen in everyday conversations, timely medical assessments, effective referrals and sustained efforts to make diagnosis and treatment more accessible. Success should be measured not only by the number of events held or materials distributed, but by whether people know where to seek help and can obtain the care they need. We cannot undo the loss of our colleague, and no campaign can promise that every life will be saved. But we can honor those we have lost by helping others recognize symptoms, share accurate information and seek appropriate medical attention. The pink ribbon can open a conversation; reliable healthcare services must help carry it forward. Breast cancer does not wait for the right moment, for fear to disappear or for life to become less busy. Neither should we wait to take breast health seriously. If you notice an unusual change, seek medical advice. If someone close to you is concerned, encourage them to seek care and offer support. If you can help make credible information or healthcare more accessible, take that opportunity. Every life matters, and every person affected deserves to receive timely assessment and appropriate treatment. Turning awareness into action means making sure that no one is left to navigate the path without reliable information, support or a fair chance of receiving the services they need. Prof. Anyakora is the CEO Bloom Public Health, while Ms Onyekaba is the Special Assistant on Media to the CEO Bloom Public Health

title: WHO SUCKS?
body: President Trump has stated that ‘Norway Sucks’ after he wasn’t awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, for a second time! His grasp of the English language and its ability to express complex ideas seem to be at odds, given the ‘sucks’ lacks the grandeur a Presidential statement should carry. There is also a lack of understanding that insulting someone that you want something from doesn’t increase the likelihood. Fortunately the committee is honest and will recommend the most deserving person. Donald Trump will be awarded his trophy shortly after ‘hell freezes over’, if not slightly later. The FIFA peace prize doesn’t set a precedent. Dennis Fitzgerald, 28 Landale St., Box Hill, Vic, Australia

title: POLICE EXTORTION ON OLD AVIELE–AUCHI ROAD
body: Reports of alleged extortion by some police officers and local vigilantes along the old Aviele–Auchi Road have raised serious concerns. Motorists and motorcyclists reportedly face demands for money, prompting public reactions and confrontations. While such allegations deserve proper investigation, another question deserves attention: Have we become so eager to demand accountability that we have forgotten the importance of maturity and respect? In today’s Nigeria, it appears that a smartphone camera can turn anyone into a judge, prosecutor, and commander. Imagine a civilian ordering a serving officer to sit on the floor in the name of accountability. Is that the proper way to address alleged misconduct? Let us be clear: wearing a uniform does not place anyone above the law. Any officer found guilty of extortion should face appropriate disciplinary action. However, demanding accountability is different from deliberately humiliating an officer in public. What if such a confrontation escalates into violence? What if an officer loses control and opens fire? The consequences could be tragic, leaving innocent people dead and families devastated. Officers must exercise restraint, while civilians must understand that challenging authority does not require provoking a dangerous confrontation. Social media has also turned serious incidents into public entertainment. A video appears on Facebook, and before the full circumstances are established, people become judges and deliver their verdicts. Recording misconduct can serve the public interest, but a video clip may not tell the whole story. Respect, however, must never become an excuse for extortion. Citizens should not be forced to pay unlawful demands, and officers must not abuse their authority. Voluntary appreciation for an officer’s service is entirely different from money obtained through intimidation. Idris Rufai, idrisrufai744@gmail.com

title: TALES BY MOONLIGHT
body: Atiku’s fate will be decided by voters, argues PAUL IBE Akin Osuntokun’s latest intervention, titled “Atiku Abubakar Cannot Heckle His Way to the Presidency,” published in THISDAY on October 16, 2026, is a curious mixture of selective history, political prejudice and recycled allegations masquerading as informed commentary. It is remarkable that at a time when Nigerians are grappling with unprecedented economic hardship, insecurity and growing uncertainty about their future, Osuntokun considers it more important to excavate alleged private conversations from over two decades ago in an attempt to disqualify former Vice President Atiku Abubakar from seeking the presidency. Of particular interest is his resurrection of a story attributed to former Cross River State Governor Donald Duke, who claimed that former military President Ibrahim Babangida once told President Olusegun Obasanjo that Atiku could not rule Nigeria. This is precisely the sort of tale by moonlight that should have no place in serious political analysis. According to the account, Babangida allegedly pretended to have forgotten his keys, returned to Obasanjo’s private study and whispered a warning about Atiku. We are then invited to treat this extraordinary recollection of a supposed private exchange as a definitive assessment of Atiku’s presidential suitability. But where is the independent corroboration? Has Babangida publicly authenticated those precise words? Even assuming, without conceding, that the conversation occurred exactly as narrated, since when did an alleged private judgment made over twenty years ago become a permanent disqualification from democratic leadership? The irony is that Osuntokun chooses to dwell on what Babangida allegedly said in private while conveniently sidestepping what Obasanjo subsequently declared in public. On October 11, 2018, Obasanjo openly endorsed Atiku for the presidency. He acknowledged their past disagreements, reconciled with his former deputy and offered an unambiguous assessment of his leadership credentials. His words deserve to be recalled: “You surely understand the economy better.” Obasanjo went further, praising Atiku’s business experience, national and international reach, accessibility and capacity to provide leadership superior to that of the incumbent administration. These were not anonymous whispers behind closed doors. They were public declarations made before political leaders, religious figures and the Nigerian media. Indeed, Obasanjo acknowledged that there had once been an understanding for Atiku to succeed him. That documented admission is considerably more relevant than Osuntokun’s speculative reconstruction of conversations from another political era. One would have expected a commentator concerned with historical accuracy to reconcile these facts rather than cherry-pick episodes that reinforce his preferred conclusion. As for Babangida, any serious examination of his assessment of Atiku must account for the full history of their political relationship, including subsequent engagements, rather than elevate an uncorroborated remark into an eternal verdict. Neither Obasanjo nor Babangida holds a hereditary franchise to determine who may govern Nigeria. Whatever they may have thought about Atiku at different points in their political lives, the final authority belongs to the Nigerian electorate. Osuntokun also suggests that Atiku’s age and repeated presidential contests should persuade him to surrender his ambition and become a mentor to younger politicians. This argument is as selective as it is unpersuasive. If age, experience and repeated electoral contests are legitimate subjects of political scrutiny, they must apply equally to all candidates, including President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. They cannot suddenly become disqualifying considerations simply because the candidate under examination is Atiku Abubakar. Age does not confer competence, but neither does it automatically extinguish it. The appropriate questions concern judgment, capacity, policy, integrity and the ability to assemble a credible governing team. Atiku has offered Nigerians his experience in public administration, economic management, enterprise development and national leadership. These credentials are open to legitimate scrutiny, just as Tinubu’s performance after more than three years in office must be subjected to rigorous examination. On zoning, Osuntokun advances the argument that another northern presidency would violate an expectation that power should remain in the South for eight years. Regional balance is important to national cohesion. But zoning is a political arrangement, not a constitutional prohibition against qualified Nigerians seeking elective office. More importantly, it cannot become an instrument for shielding an incumbent from accountability. Nigerians are entitled to consider regional equity alongside competence, performance, national security and economic survival. It is for voters, not columnists, to decide how these considerations should influence their ballots. Osuntokun’s attempt to portray Atiku as the principal architect of opposition fragmentation is equally simplistic. The crisis within the opposition cannot credibly be attributed to one individual while ignoring the ambitions, choices and conduct of other political actors. Political parties are collective institutions, and responsibility for their successes and failures must be assessed accordingly. Atiku has participated in efforts to build a broader opposition coalition and now leads the ADC presidential ticket alongside Rotimi Amaechi. Whether that coalition persuades Nigerians is a matter to be settled democratically, not through predetermined assertions about his supposed unelectability. Then there is Osuntokun’s fascination with Atiku addressing the President as “Bola.” When did addressing a public official by his given name become a constitutional offence or a measure of political desperation? Bola is the President’s name, not an insult. Those who regard its use as an affront should explain why the substance of public accountability matters less to them than presidential titles. The real political pollution is not calling a president by his name. It is the growing tendency to treat legitimate criticism of public officeholders as an act of disrespect. What Nigerians require from political commentators is a searching examination of governance. How have the administration’s economic policies affected household incomes? What has happened to the purchasing power of wages? How secure are communities? What measurable relief has reached ordinary Nigerians? These questions deserve more attention than an alleged conversation about misplaced keys in Aso Rock more than twenty years ago. Osuntokun is entitled to his preferences, prejudices and political conclusions. He is even entitled to believe that Atiku should not be President. What he is not entitled to is the pretense that his personal judgment constitutes the verdict of the Nigerian people. In a democracy, presidential ambition is neither granted nor extinguished by the approval of political columnists. On January 16, 2027, Nigerians will have the opportunity to examine the competing candidates, evaluate their records, consider their proposals and exercise their constitutional right to determine who governs them. They will not be required to consult Osuntokun’s preferred political history before casting their ballots. Atiku Abubakar does not require Akin Osuntokun’s permission to seek the presidency, any more than Bola Tinubu requires his endorsement to pursue re-election. Both must submit themselves to the sovereign judgment of Nigerians. Ultimately, Atiku’s presidential fate will be determined by the votes of Nigerians, not by Akin Osuntokun’s biases, recycled anecdotes or tales by moonlight. That is democracy. And that is the verdict that matters. Ibe, Media Adviser to Atiku Abubakar, writes from Abuja

title: Flavio Bolsonaro arrives in US with family — CNN Brasil
body:
RIO DE JANEIRO, October 28. /TASS/. Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the country’s presidential election, arrived in the United States on Tuesday with his wife and daughters after fleeing Brazil, CNN Brasil reported, citing sources.
The senator followed in the footsteps of his father, former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who also traveled to the United States after losing to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election, the broadcaster noted.
The politician left the country in defiance of an explicit court order. The previous day, Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports to the police and barred him from leaving the country as part of a criminal investigation into money laundering allegations
Earlier, Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that the senator may have secretly crossed the border into Argentina before flying to the United States aboard a private jet, although immigration authorities in neither country had recorded his legal passage across the border.
Brazil held the second round of its presidential election on October 25. According to the final results released by the electoral commission, incumbent President Lula da Silva won with 51.79% of the vote, while Flavio Bolsonaro lost with 48.21%. The politician’s secret flight from the country caused deep disappointment among his political allies, who had expected the senator to personally lead the opposition to the new government in the National Congress.

title: Venus Williams loses again – to opponent 28 years younger
body: Former world number one Venus Williams lost her 16th straight singles match, beaten by an opponent 28 years younger at the Guangzhou Open. The 46-year-old American, who has won seven Grand Slam singles titles, lost 6-2, 6-2 to 18-year-old Lilli Tagger on Tuesday. It is the biggest age gap between opponents in a WTA match this decade and among the largest in tour-level history. Williams, ranked 599th in the world, has not won a match since July 2025 and relies on wildcards to play WTA tournaments. This latest defeat continues the debate over whether she deserves them. Some in the sport argue Williams is taking spots from younger players trying to build their careers, but tournament organisers see the commercial value in inviting an all-time great. The Guangzhou fans clearly appreciated the chance to see the American superstar. A sizeable, enthusiastic crowd encouraged Williams and gave her a huge ovation as she walked off court. Williams won six of her Grand Slam singles titles – plus 30 WTA tournaments – before Austria’s Tagger was born in February 2008. Tagger’s coach Francesca Schiavone – the Italian former world number four who won the 2010 French Open – is the same age as Williams, and lost all eight meetings with the American during her playing career. “When I saw the draw I was super excited and a bit nervous – I respect her a lot,” said Tagger, who is 53rd in the world. “It is funny she used to play with my coach.
