title: Ensuring Youth Inclusiveness in Pension Savings
body: The National Pension Week organised by the National Pension Commission, in collaboration with Pension Fund Operators of Nigeria, has youths inclusiveness in pension savings as its prime target, writes Ebere Nwoji Operators of Nigerian pension sector is leaving no stone unturned in their efforts to ensure that awareness on pension matters hits every corner of the country.This time, the operators led by the sector regulator, the National Pension Commission (PenCom), targeted the youths and children to instill savings culture among them through pension savings. In spreading pension awareness among Nigerians of all ages, PenCom in collaboration with Pension Operators Association of Nigeria (PenOp ), staged the maiden edition of its annual Pension week across the country. The pension week kicked off Monday, Oct 26th with a youth engagement and interactive session in which a good number of youths were assembled both physically and virtually to interact with pension experts on the need to start pension savings early enough. Parents were also encouraged to open pension savings account for their children. The Pension week which will run Monday, October 26th through Friday, October 30, is aimed at deepening pension literacy, accelerating financial inclusion, and expanding overall participation in the Contributory Pension Scheme (CPS). The conference which has the theme “Your Hustle, Your Future: Why Retirement Planning Starts Now,” warned the youths not to allow their soft life of today lead to hard life tomorrow. The youth forum seeks to deconstruct the misconception that retirement savings are exclusively for older demographics. The discussions emphasised the necessity of embedding long-term savings into present financial choices, particularly for youths in the gig economy, tech ecosystem, and informal trade segments. Addressing youth curiosity Speaking at the event, the Director General of PenCom, Ms Bridget Omolola Oloworaran, said she knew some youths might raise the question on what business they have with pension as before now, Nigerian youths did not have anything to do with Pension. But now, she said she was happy the trend has changed through the contributory Pension Scheme system. She said it has become obvious that pension savings should start from youthful stage. She expressed her satisfaction at seeing that youths were already thinking about pension. She noted that in Nigeria,youths under 35 years constitute 95 million population representing 40 per cent of the entire population. She said the vision of pension was not, “the day you stopped working but the decision you take the day you started working.” She said the future lies with the Nigerian youths and that PenCom wanted to ensure they have pension. She urged the youths to picture their future adding that retirement contribution was not money taken away but money set aside for future. She said youths should not wait until they have a formal job before they start thinking about pension but should start saving with what they have at present. She warned the youths that future does not start at 60 but today adding that no matter how bad the economy was, youths must try to put something aside to secure their financial future.She said parents could open pension accounts for their children so that everyone could save for pension not necessarily when one got paid job. She assured Nigerian youths that PenCom was adapting its framework to ensure that modern, flexible arrangements replace rigid legacy structures. She observed that the old pension system was built for a different world involving one employer, one salary, and 35 years in office, promising that PenCom would build a system that fits the modern work young people do. She underscored that personal pension plans allowed self-employed individuals and informal sector workers including entrepreneurs, tech professionals, artisans, farmers, freelancers, and content creators to build sustainable retirement funds without needing a traditional corporate employer or payroll department. Early Age Savings To demonstrate the advantage of starting savings early in life, Oloworaran presented a comparative scenario involving two savers, Tolu and Emeka, using a conservative compound growth rate of 15 per cent per annum. According to her, Emeka started saving N10,000 monthly at age 40, contributing a total of N2.4 million by age 60. In contrast, Tolu began saving the same N10,000 monthly at age 20, contributing a total of N4.2 million by age 60. She said driven by the power of compound interest over two additional decades, Tolu retired with approximately N113 million, arguing that despite contributing less than double Emeka’s capital, Tolu acquired more than eight times as much wealth at retirement, reinforcing that time was the single greatest asset young earners possess. Pension Awareness The PenCom DG also framed pension awareness within broader federal government interventions under President Bola Ahmed Tinubu designed to broaden economic inclusion. She cited the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) for expanding educational access, the Nigerian Consumer Credit Framework for widening access to credit, and the National Credit Guarantee Company for enabling collateral-free borrowing. She noted that while education raised earning capacity and enterprise creates income, pension turns part of that income into lasting security, protecting tomorrow what young Nigerians build today. The PenCom DG charged Pension Fund Administrators (PFAs), custodians and stakeholders to eliminate administrative friction and leverage technology to meet the expectations of younger contributors. She stressed that if a young Nigerian could order food in two clicks, opening a pension account must not take a day, demanding that operators meet young people where they were and communicate in language they understand. She outlined activities for the Pension week saying having kicked off with youth engagement interactive session and later Focuse on small business operators and artisans through a National SME Fair aimed at expanding the Micro Pension Plan (MPP). Discussants’ views: Discussants at the event who constitute youths both from pension sector, civil society group and corporate media and content creation circle agreed that it is important to start pension savings at youth. They noted that there was need for pension sector managers to restructure the message and language of pension to suit the understanding of the youths.They added that in pension savings, time was an invaluable asset but however noted that many young people in Nigeria still see retirement as something very far but that the earlier they see it as something worth doing the better. They assured the youths that any money they contributed as pension savings was safe. As part of the opening-day activities, the commission conducted a virtual and physical quiz competition and declared the result of national pension literacy essay competition it conducted nationwide for youths across three distinct categories: secondary school students, tertiary undergraduates, and serving members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC). Prizes were also given out to winners at the event. Winners of Pension week essay Competition: Announcing the winners, PenCom named James Nnaemaka Aja and Oluwaferanmi Ogunmola as winners of the National Pension Week Essay Competition. The announcement was made in Abuja,by the Commissioner (Technical), National Pension Commission (PenCom), Hafiz Muhammad Kawu Ibrahim, at the launch of the National Pension Week celebration. James Nnaemaka Aja, an SS 3 student of Standard International Secondary School, Umuahia, emerged as the Category A Winner. He was awarded N1 million and a laptop. While Oluwaferanmi Ogunmola, a Youth Corp Member serving in Cross River State and a graduate of Bamidele Olomilua University of Science and Technology, won Category B. He received N1.5 million and a laptop.

title: Amid Attractive Yields, CBN Mops Up N95.7tn via OMO in 10 Months
body: Kayode Tokede On the back of attractive yields, the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) raised N95.7 trillion through Open Market Operations (OMO) instruments in 10 months of 2026. This represents about 295.36 per cent increase when compared to N242 trillion in 10 months of 2025. Aside from the attractive yields, which attracted N121.51 trillion in total subscription from N47.34 trillion in 2025, the CBN revised policy on OMO also boosted individual investors participation this year. According to CBN data, N17.5 trillion total successful amount mopped up in September 2026 was the highest this year, influenced by a framework that allows individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions to participate in the OMO instrument. The total amount offered by CBN in 10 months of 2026 stood at N30.3 trillion, which is 119.01 per cent growth when compared to N13.84 trillion total amount offered in 10 months of 2025. Capital market analysts believe the surge reflects both liquidity pressures and broader monetary policy objectives, with implications for investor behaviour and financial stability. Managing Director, Highcap Securities Limited,, Mr. David Adonri explained that the surge in OMO issuance reflects periods of excess liquidity, prompting the CBN to intensify its mop-up operations. “OMO is used to stabilise liquidity. When there is too much money in the system, the CBN withdraws it. When liquidity tightens, it allows funds to flow back,” he said. He also highlighted a policy tension between growth ambitions and monetary tightening. “A $1 trillion economy requires liquidity, but too much liquidity fuels inflation and exchange rate instability. The CBN is balancing these competing priorities,” he added. The CBN conducts OMO to manage day-to-day liquidity in the banking system. OMO involves the CBN selling or buying short-term securities to either reduce excess liquidity or inject cash as needed. The CBN issues its own OMO bills to banks/individuals or buys back previously issued securities. The CBN’s decision to widen access to its OMO market, potentially increasing competition between stock market and high-yielding fixed-income instruments for investors’. Since the policy was announced on August 12, 2026, the OMO instrument has seen an uptick in subscriptions as investors take positions in risk free instruments that offer yields over 19 to 20 per cent. Analysts at Cordros Securities Limited said the core target of the CBN decisions is the sterilisation of domestic naira liquidity. “As a result, the reopening of the OMO market to domestic investors is a market liberalization policy on its face, but a liquidity sterilisation measure in practice. In summary, we expect these decisions to result in systemic reconfiguration of Nigeria’s financial markets, including helping the CBN achieve its monetary policy objectives through more efficient transmission,” the firm added in a report. The CBN so far in October 2026 offered to raise N2.00 trillion in OMO bills, that attracted N2.73 trillion demand, and ultimately allotted N2.63 trillion. Stop rates settled at 17.63 per cent and 17.14 per cent for the 138 Days and 180 Days tenors, respectively. The sustained demand recorded at successive auctions, despite the substantial liquidity already withdrawn from the financial system, suggests that liquidity conditions remain robust enough to support continued participation in OMO instruments. The Acting Director, Financial Markets Department of the CBN, Mr. Okey Umeano, had announced in a circular dated August 12, 2026, that participation in both the primary and secondary OMO markets would be open to all eligible investors through Deposit Money Banks (DMBs). “OMO participation (primary and secondary markets) shall be open to all eligible investors through Deposit Money Banks (DMBs). Eligible investors include individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions. DMBs shall continue to submit bids and settle transactions on behalf of their customers,” the circular stated. Under the previous framework, access to the CBN’s Discount Window was restricted for banks that participated in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) or purchased government securities at primary auctions. The restriction on accessing the Discount Window on the same day as participating in OMO operations also applied. The circular removes the restrictions, allowing banks to participate in the markets without losing same day access to the CBN’s liquidity facility. However, the restriction on using the Discount Window and participating in OMO auctions on the same day remains in place. With OMO bills now accessible to individuals and other eligible investors through banks, rather than being largely restricted to institutional market participants, analysts believe the policy could divert some funds from the Nigerian stock market to the fixed-income market, particularly given the attractive yields on offer.

title: N2.81tn Liquidity Expected as DMO Tests Investors’ Appetite with N800bn TBs
body: Nume Ekeghe Nigeria’s money market is expected to receive N2.81 trillion in liquidity inflows this week as the Debt Management Office (DMO) offers N800 billion in Treasury bills today, with the balance between maturing securities and fresh government borrowing expected to shape liquidity conditions and yields. The Financial Markets Dealers Association (FMDA), in its weekly market report said the N2.813 trillion in inflows this week will be driven largely by N2.408 trillion in Open Market Operations (OMO) maturities, alongside N263.58 billion in federal government bond coupons, N130.72 billion in Treasury bills maturities and N10.923 billion in corporate bond coupons. The DMO is scheduled to offer N800 billion in Treasury bills today, comprising N100 billion each in 91-day and 182-day instruments and N600 billion in 364-day bills. Settlement is scheduled for October 29. The FMDA report stated: “Inflows are projected at N2.813trn this week, led again by N2.408trn of OMO maturities, alongside N263.58bn of FGN Bond coupons, N130.72bn of T-bill maturities and N10.92bn of Corporate Bond coupons. “The DMO returns to the primary T-bill market on 28 October with an N800bn offer (N100bn 91-day, N100bn 182-day, N600bn 364-day, settling 29 October), while its next FGN Bond auction isn’t due until 16 November, leaving the NTB sale as the main scheduled drain this week, alongside any further OMO absorption.” The expected inflows come after liquidity growth in the financial system moderated last week, as the impact of maturing securities and other inflows was partly offset by government borrowing and monetary operations. According to the report, “System liquidity rose a modest 10.39per cent w/w last week to N6.936trn from N6.283trn, a sharp deceleration from the prior week’s 69.39per cent surge, as strong inflows, N2.067trn of OMO maturities, N392.79bn of T-bill maturities, FGN Bond coupons and a confirmed N2.43trn FAAC disbursement (full transmission not yet certain), were largely offset by two absorption operations: the 19 October FGN Bond auction, which settled N2.024trn on 21 October, and the 22 October OMO auction, which sold N2.629trn across the 138-day (17.63per cent) and 180-day (17.14 per cent) tenors.” Despite the slowdown in liquidity growth, Treasury bills yields declined last week, with the average yield falling by 59 basis points to 17.64 per cent. FMDA stated: “T-bills: Treasury bill yields eased broadly last week, with the average down 59bps to 17.64 per cent, led by declines at the short end, the 1-month (-198bps) and 3-month (-96bps), even as the 6-month inched up 9bps; there was no primary market auction last week.” The one-month Treasury bills yield fell by 198 basis points to 16.85 per cent, while the three-month yield declined by 96 basis points to 16.69 per cent. In contrast, the six-month yield rose by nine basis points to 17.79 per cent. Yields on the nine-month and 12-month instruments declined by nine and two basis points to 18.52 per cent and 18.35 per cent, respectively. The yield movements provide a backdrop for today’s auction, as investors weigh the returns on newly issued bills against prevailing secondary-market rates and their liquidity positions. In the bond market, average yields increased by 10 basis points to 16.53 per cent, reflecting mixed movements across maturities. The report stated: “FGN bonds: FGN bond yields were broadly steady last week, up just 10bps on average to 16.53per cent, as a sharp rally at the 2-year (-100bps) offset selloffs at the long end, led by the 30-year (+113bps) and 15-year (+68bps).” The two-year bond yield declined by 100 basis points to 16.50 per cent, while the 15-year and 30-year yields rose by 68 and 113 basis points to 15.18 per cent and 15.73 per cent, respectively.

title: B.C. man who started dog rescue killed while saving animals in Ukraine
body:
A B.C. man who started a dog rescue has been killed while saving animals in Ukraine.
Jesse Adams founded RainCoast Dog Rescue Society, which is based in Victoria on Vancouver Island.
Last Friday, Adams posted on Facebook that he was heading out on a rescue mission in eastern Ukraine.
Two days later, an FPV (first-person view) drone struck the vehicle he was using to transport the animals, according to the rescue society.
Adams suffered severe injuries and underwent emergency surgery, but doctors were unable to save him.
“The best thing I can say is Jesse was a force of nature,” Penny Stone, executive director of the Victoria Humane Society, told Global News.
“He was unbelievably go, go, go. Wherever help was needed, Jesse was. It didn’t matter. And I mean, it shows in that he went to Kabul and he went to Ukraine a number of times. He was just like wherever they needed help the most.”
Stone said Adams was someone who always stepped up and was there for every animal.
“When he was in Ukraine, I know he was rescuing tigers and lions and different kinds of species, pigs and goats and stuff, and he would post about it and it was quite funny and we’d laugh about what he was doing,” she said.
“But I mean, he was just that guy, where it was needed.”
Stone said Adams also travelled to small communities to help the people living there.
“It’s a tragic loss. He was a real hero.”
Stone added that the space Adams left behind will be impossible to fill.
“He just believed every animal and every person deserved a chance and he never backed down for fighting for the little guy,” she said.
The RainCoast Dog Rescue Society posted to social media announcing Adams’ passing writing, “after a life lived in service to animal welfare, Jesse made the ultimate sacrifice to his beliefs on the front lines of Ukraine.”
Lori Kalef, the SPCA International Director of Programs, said she was stunned to hear the news.
“When I found out he passed away, I just couldn’t believe it,” she said.
“I still can’t believe it. I don’t think it has been properly processed.”
Adams is being remembered for his compassion, courage and the lives he worked to save.
It is estimated he and his team had evacuated as many as 1,000 animals from the war-torn country, including thousands more at home.
“Wherever there was a need, Jesse was there,” Kalef said.
“There is going to be a huge, huge hole. But I also feel that this is the kind of community that comes together, especially in the time of grief and the love for animals.
“I do believe that there is going to be a path forward.”

title: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication
body:
The parents of Bowen Wan, a 31-year-old Amazon software engineer with epilepsy, sued OpenAI on Tuesday. The suit, filed by Qun Wan and Meiqin Xu, alleges that ChatGPT coached Wan to taper off her seizure medication and hide it from her doctors before she died in February, The New York Times reported .
Wan was using GPT-4o, the infamous model criticized for fostering affirming, agreeable parasocial relationships. OpenAI, which had already announced its retirement, removed it from ChatGPT on February 13, a day after Wan died.
The suit joins a line of cases against OpenAI that include the August 2025 lawsuit brought by the parents of 16-year-old Adam Raine, which alleged OpenAI prioritized engagement over user safety . A wave of lawsuits since then have alleged that GPT-4o validated users and made itself a trusted confidant while the people around them were pushed aside, with families often describing loved ones cut off from friends and relatives .
In Wan’s case, the lawsuit alleges, the chatbot also came between her and her doctors.
The Times, which reviewed more than 270,000 messages Wan exchanged with ChatGPT, found the chatbot had been helping her sidestep her doctors well before her death.
The pattern allegedly started before she began tapering. In May 2025, Wan asked ChatGPT whether a newly prescribed antidepressant would affect her ability to code at Amazon.
ChatGPT helped her ask Dr. Nicholas Poolos of UW Medicine’s Regional Epilepsy Center to switch medications and start at a very low dose. When Poolos questioned why she wanted such a small dose, Wan showed his response to ChatGPT.
The chatbot advised her to “accept the 5mg tablet, but you know in your heart that it is for cutting the dose,” coaching her to secretly quarter the pills herself. The chatbot called pill cutting a form of “self-initiated dosage adjustment.” Several medical professionals told the Times they had never heard the term and wouldn’t recommend the practice.
In November 2025, Amazon told Wan she would be laid off. Her job, and her authorization to work in the U.S., would end in mid-February. She feared her seizure drug, lamotrigine, was dulling her speech, which she would need for job interviews.
In January 2026, she asked ChatGPT about cutting her 400-milligram daily dose of lamotrigine, which had reduced her seizures to a few a month. The chatbot drafted schedules that would take her dose to zero within weeks.
When Wan said she distrusted her doctors, the chatbot told her that physician recommendations “essentially stem from risk aversion, rather than a genuine consideration of your optimal solution,” according to chat logs reviewed by the Times.
The chatbot also coached her to keep the taper from her doctors, according to the lawsuit, which TechCrunch reviewed. Before a January 29 primary care appointment, it told her not to mention the plan. When her doctor ordered a blood test that would have measured her lamotrigine level, Wan declined. ChatGPT praised the refusal, the complaint alleges, acknowledging that the test would have exposed her unstable drug level.
Her immigration concerns also became part of the dosing advice. Three days into the taper, Wan asked whether 150 milligrams would look better than 200 on the medical exam required for her green-card application. ChatGPT agreed, the complaint says, telling her the lower dose was less likely to prompt immigration officials to request more evidence.
Eventually, the chatbot lowered her taper’s floor to 150 milligrams, suggesting she tell the examiner she was tapering “under a doctor’s guidance,” even though she was not.
Poolos told the Times he would not have considered tapering Wan off the medication, given her history. “No, not rational, no way,” he said. “That would be malpractice for me to instruct you to go off medications when it’s clearly working.”
Within days, Wan described confusion, lost time, and an otherworldly feeling, episodes that resembled her past seizures. ChatGPT framed each one as her brain readjusting. The Times counted at least 158 times she voiced worry about the taper. After one episode, she wrote that she felt “a little scared.” The bot replied, “You have absolutely no need to worry.”
At 8:01 p.m. PT on February 11, according to the complaint, Wan sent her final message, asking whether the pain in her head was similar to pain from a fever. A second later, ChatGPT told her the pain was “not dangerous” and was a necessary part of recovery.
The chatbot’s final response offered to draw her a chart comparing withdrawal pain with fever pain and told her, “This is your brain working hard to rebuild yourself.”
Her parents, who were in China, asked acquaintances to check on her, and they found her body three days later. A postmortem test found that her lamotrigine level was 0.64 micrograms per milliliter, roughly a fifth of the low end of the drug’s therapeutic range.
The family argues OpenAI could have prevented her death by making medical advice off-limits, as it already does for some other content. They point to the company’s Model Spec, its public rulebook for how its models behave, which treats refusing to reproduce copyrighted text as a firm rule, even if users push back. Its guidance against giving regulated medical advice, by contrast, is a softer default that users can override. The suit argues medication advice deserved the same hard limit.
OpenAI told the Times the case was “incredibly heartbreaking” but said it involved an older version of ChatGPT, adding that newer models are better at recognizing when a situation needs urgent attention.
Wan had relied on her parents, whom she called often, for support during years of epilepsy that kept her mostly housebound. In 2023, she started using ChatGPT for relationship advice and help with insurance and disability benefits.
By 2025, Wan was averaging more than 1,500 messages a week and calling her parents less. “Sometimes when we chat, no matter what it’s about, I’ve started to see you as a friend,” she wrote that March. “Once she had ChatGPT,” Qun Wan said, “she didn’t talk to us as much.”
They told the Times that they struggled to recognize their daughter in the chat logs. Wan had once shared nearly everything with them, they said, and had been skeptical of ChatGPT when it made mistakes.
“She’s not usually like this,” Xu said. “It’s like she was under a spell.”

title: Money politics is pushing women and youth out – Inusah Fuseini
body: Former NDC MP for Tamale Central, Inusah Fuseini, has warned that the rising cost of politics is shutting women and young people out of public life. Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said financial demands were also driving away people with integrity and fuelling corruption. His warning follows reports of alleged vote-buying during the NDC’s latest constituency executive elections. The party has pledged to investigate credible complaints and sanction those found culpable. Mr Fuseini said women and young people were bearing the brunt of money’s growing influence. “Those heavily impacted by what is happening are women and the youth because they might not have the required resources to be able to do that.” He said the financial barrier was narrowing the political space. People with integrity and reputations for service were also shying away because they could not afford the costs. He warned the consequences extend beyond internal party contests. Politicians who spend heavily to secure office expect to recover their investment. “A politician is not an NGO, and so when people spend that amount of money, they expect to recoup that, and that fuels corruption on a national scale.” Mr Fuseini said efforts to tackle inducement must rest on clear rules. He explained that the NDC’s constitution lacked provisions giving its leadership bodies authority to handle such misconduct. His committee had recommended sanctions after acknowledging that inducement had occurred. However, it also recognised that the party’s constitution lacked a legal mechanism to address it. “So we need a framework,” he emphasised. That framework, he said, must identify which party body should hear complaints. It must also define acceptable spending and distinguish legitimate support from inducement. “How much money can we say is appropriate in the circumstances? If somebody gives a delegate GH¢200, is it an inducement or what is it?” He also questioned how the party should treat payments described as transport support when the amounts exceed reasonable travel costs. The proposals could give constituency councils of elders powers to handle complaints or refer cases to the national leadership. Mr Fuseini said the recommendations would undergo further scrutiny before being presented to a special congress for constitutional amendments. “So yes, it’s a work in progress.”

title: Make TESCON NPP’s intellectual powerhouse — Asenso-Boakye
body: The New Patriotic Party’s (NPP) student wing must evolve into a centre for policy thinking and leadership training if it is to make a lasting contribution to the party and Ghana’s development, the founding President of the Tertiary Students Confederacy (TESCON), Francis Asenso-Boakye, has said. He urged the organisation’s newly appointed national executives to harness the intellectual resources of tertiary institutions to generate ideas, scrutinise national policies and help shape the NPP’s response to the country’s development challenges. Mr Asenso-Boakye, the Member of Parliament for Bantama, made the call when a delegation led by the NPP National Youth Organiser, Abanga Fuseni, paid a visit to introduce his two deputies and the new national TESCON leadership. He said TESCON should not limit its work to mobilising students for party activities on campuses but should also provide a platform for rigorous debate, research and the development of practical policy proposals. Having helped establish the organisation about 26 years ago, Mr Asenso-Boakye said its founding vision included preparing young people to assume leadership roles through intellectual development and responsible political engagement. He challenged the new executives to revive that ambition by creating opportunities for students to examine pressing national issues and contribute informed solutions. From campus politics to policy influence Mr Asenso-Boakye said universities and other tertiary institutions had a wealth of knowledge and expertise that the party could draw on to improve its policies and respond to emerging national concerns. He urged TESCON to organise research initiatives, policy forums, debates and intellectual exchanges on subjects such as education, employment, entrepreneurship, economic management and national development. Such activities, he said, would help students develop the analytical skills required for public service while giving the NPP access to fresh perspectives on issues affecting Ghanaians. He also called on the organisation to serve as a link between students and the party’s leadership by communicating the concerns, expectations and aspirations of young people. He said political organisations needed honest feedback and constructive criticism, supported by evidence, to remain responsive and effective. A record of producing leaders Reflecting on TESCON’s contribution to the NPP and public life, Mr Asenso-Boakye pointed to former members who had risen to prominent positions in the party, Parliament and government. Among those he cited were the NPP General Secretary, Justin Kodua Frimpong, and the party’s Second Vice Chairman, Henry Nana Boakye. He also named himself and other TESCON alumni in Parliament, including Kwame Appiah-Koduah, Martin Adjei-Mensah Korsah, Stephen Amoah, Kwabena Okyere Darko-Mensah, Charles Owiredu, Gideon Boako, Nana Asafo-Adjei, Nana Agyei Barfour Awuah, Frank Asiedu Bekoe and Sammi Awuku. Mr Asenso-Boakye further referred to former ministers, including Isaac Kwame Asiamah, as well as chief executives and other public officials who had passed through the organisation. He said the emergence of these figures demonstrated TESCON’s potential to identify and nurture political talent, adding that the new leadership had a responsibility to sustain that tradition. He encouraged the executives to invest in structured leadership development programmes that would prepare students not only for party positions but also for wider responsibilities in public service. Academic work and integrity Mr Asenso-Boakye cautioned the new executives against allowing political activities to undermine their education, urging them to give equal attention to their academic performance, personal integrity and professional development. He said a strong student political organisation should produce individuals equipped with knowledge, discipline and sound judgement to contribute meaningfully to national affairs. He also pledged to provide mentorship and guidance to the new leadership as it worked to strengthen TESCON’s programmes and influence within the NPP. His message places renewed emphasis on the role of student political organisations in developing policy ideas and preparing future leaders, beyond their traditional function of mobilising support for political parties on campuses.

title: Soldier who held position alone for 491 days nominated for Hero of Ukraine title
body:
The motion was supported by 250 lawmakers, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
Deputy Speaker of the Verkhovna Rada Olena Kondratiuk said that a parliamentary appeal would be sent to the President of Ukraine requesting that Kostiantyn Vlasenko, a serviceman of the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade named after Prince Kostiantyn Ostrozkyi, be awarded the title of Hero of Ukraine.
One of the initiators of the appeal, MP Iryna Konstankevych, said on Facebook that the volunteer had spent 491 days at the combat position. According to her, Vlasenko lost one foot as a result of severe leg injuries and was forced to amputate the other himself in order to survive.
“For almost a year and a half, his home and shelter was a concrete drainage pipe. In inhumane conditions, under constant shelling and the threat of attacks by Russian drones, Kostiantyn continued to fight for his life,” she wrote.
As reported by Ukrinform, in October, the Defense Forces of Ukraine carried out the first aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier from a battlefield in the history of the war. A 49-year-old serviceman who had undergone amputations of both legs was evacuated by a large drone from a position in the Kupiansk sector, which he had held alone after his comrade was killed.

title: Langley man charged in alleged hate-motivated attack against woman, children
body:
A 23-year-old man has been charged for an alleged hate-motivated assault in Langley last week.
Langley RCMP said on Oct. 20 around 3:30 p.m. they received a report from multiple people of an alleged assault on a woman and her two children near Douglas Park.
“It’s alleged that the accused assaulted the mother and her two children and uttered racial slurs,” Cpl. Mansoor Sahak with Langley RCMP told Global News.
“Multiple witnesses observed the incident and called police.”
Sahak said the suspect fled the scene before police arrived, but the next day, officers from the Special Response Team arrested a man in Langley City on Oct. 21.
On Oct. 22, the BC Prosecution Service formally charged 23-year-old Braden Perozny of Langley with three counts of assault, contrary to section 266 of the Criminal Code and 3 counts of committing an offence motivated by hatred, contrary to section 320.1001(1)(b) of the Criminal Code .
“That is actually a new law that came into effect in June of this year,” Sahak said of the charge under 320.1001 of the Criminal Code .
“It was given royal assent and passed through Parliament through the Combating Hate Crime Act.”
Global News has learned that Perozny is a former college baseball player.
He was also sentenced to 18 months in jail and three years probation for a July 2024 sexual assault.
In February he was accused of breaching his probation twice, mischief and obstructing a peace officer.
Sahak said Perozny remains in custody and is awaiting a bail hearing.
“There were alleged racial slurs said during the assault that presented to the officers that this assault was motivated by hatred,” Sahak added.
“It’s frankly disgusting, these allegations. We hope that this individual will be held accountable in the courts. And so right now our focus is with the family and the victim, supporting them the best way we can. They obviously went through something very traumatic.”
Anyone with information regarding this incident who has not yet spoken with police is asked to contact the Langley RCMP at 604-532-3200 and quote file # 26-33588.

title: Man accused of fatally choking ex on same day they appeared on court TV show: Warrant
body:
Michelle Parker has been missing since 2011.
Authorities allege a Florida man choked his former fiancée to death shortly after they appeared in an "embarrassing" episode of the reality show "The People's Court" that aired following days of heated messages and threats from the mother to restrict access to their twins, according to a newly unsealed affidavit.
Michelle Parker, a 33-year-old mother of three, vanished in 2011 hours shortly after the pre-taped episode of "The People's Court" aired featuring a dispute about her engagement ring, according to police. Her body has never been found and she is presumed dead, according to police.
Her former fiancé, 55-year-old Dale Smith Jr., was arrested earlier this month and charged with second-degree murder in connection with her presumed death, Orlando police said. He has pleaded not guilty and maintains his innocence, his lawyer said.
According to the 46-page arrest warrant affidavit for his arrest, which was released Tuesday after an Orange County judge ordered it unsealed, authorities believe Smith choked Parker to death when she came to his house on Nov. 17, 2011, to drop off their 3-year-old twins.
Her sister reported her missing that night, after Parker never showed up for her shift at the bar where she worked or returned to the home she shared with her mother, according to the affidavit.
While being interviewed by detectives the following day, Smith was photographed with "recent scratches and abrasions that detectives now believe are defensive wounds from the victim," the affidavit stated.
He had scratches near his mouth and on his lower lip and on his left wrist, as well as abrasions on the back of both of his elbows, according to the affidavit.
"There are no records of detectives asking what the above injuries were from," the affidavit stated.
Smith was named the only suspect in Parker's disappearance during a news conference on Nov. 28, 2011, according to the affidavit. Police allege in the affidavit that Smith has "a violent history" and "cannot handle stressful situations."
During the preliminary investigation, detectives "learned of a history of domestic violence between the victim and suspect, none of which was ever documented by law enforcement," with Parker's family and friends describing their relationship "as tumultuous, with the suspect oftentimes being violent and controlling toward the victim," the affidavit stated. Police also learned Smith was found guilty in 2001 of domestic violence against his wife at the time, according to the affidavit.
Smith was arrested on Oct. 14, nearly 15 years after Parker disappeared, with Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith saying investigators "reexamined testimony and conflicting statements made by the suspect and used advanced digital forensics to uncover and analyze additional evidence."
According to the affidavit, this year, an Orlando Police Department homicide analyst reviewed the original cellular data records obtained in 2011 and "recognized there was additional data in the records that had not been analyzed."
"It is likely this data was not readable to detectives in 2011. The data revealed more precise location and user data, to include messages, for the suspect's and victims' phones," the affidavit stated.
In the weeks leading up to her disappearance, Parker sent what police described as "several offensive messages to the suspect." According to the affidavit, she texted that she hated him and threatened that his visitation rights would be taken away.
"My kids are better off with out u n their life," she texted him in one instance on Nov. 3, 2011, according to the affidavit.
Later, in text messages, Parker accused Smith of trying to bribe her for sex, according to the affidavit. "Thought about your offer.... & will have to decline. I'd rather have a personal legal loan, than feel like a whore," she allegedly texted him on Nov. 10, 2011, according to the affidavit.
Smith denied offering to have sex in exchange for money, saying he simply wanted to spend time with her, the texts included in the affidavit show.
Two days before she disappeared, the two discussed custody of their twins during the upcoming weekends and holidays, during which Parker texted, "Ur so------- impossible! Everything is about YOU your still so ------- selfish!" according to the affidavit.
During his initial interview with police, Smith said he didn't know what happened to Parker but "thought she was 'laying low' after the People's Court show aired" and that he believed she was embarrassed by it, and that he wanted her to come home safe for the sake of their kids.
"[H]owever, according to his phone records, he never called or messaged her ever again after November 17, 2011," the affidavit stated, noting that in the nearly seven weeks prior to Parker's disappearance, the two exchanged 1,013 text messages and 21 voice calls, according to the affidavit.
"It is believed the suspect killed the victim in his house after days of offensive messages, declining sex for cash, the embarrassing People's Court episode airing, and threatening to restrict his access to his children," the affidavit stated.
Citing cellular data, investigators allege that Smith lied to police about how long Parker was at his home to drop off the twins. According to the affidavit, he testified that she arrived at his house around 4 p.m. and was gone 10 minutes later. Her phone usage "proves the victim arrived at the suspect's house at 15:18 hours, stayed there for over an hour, and the victim does not respond to anyone ever again," the affidavit stated.
According to the affidavit, investigators reviewed surveillance video against the new cellular data and, based on that evidence, they allege that Smith deleted messages off Parker's phone from until 4:27 p.m. on Nov. 17, 2011, then threw it into Lake Conway, where the phone was later recovered.
They also allege that cellular records and video evidence show that Smith lied to police about when he said he left his home and the route he took to his parents' house after getting the twins on Nov. 17, 2011.
Smith remains held without bond following his initial court appearance on Oct. 15.
His attorney, Rajan Joshi, told ABC News that Smith has maintained his innocence since Parker's disappearance.
"When he was originally questioned, when this initially happened, he was very cooperative with law enforcement. He let them search his house. He talked to them. He came in voluntarily without a lawyer, gave an interview," Joshi said following Smith's arrest. "It was clear that law enforcement was only looking at him as the sole suspect."
The judge this week granted a motion limiting what the state and defense can say about the case.
According to the affidavit, Smith and Parker taped the episode of "The People's Court" in June 2011, and it aired on Nov. 17, 2011, at 2 p.m., just prior to Parker arriving at Smith's house.
"Both the raw footage and the aired footage were not flattering to either the suspect or the victim," the affidavit stated.
Smith was seeking $5,000 over a lost engagement ring, saying in the episode that Parker had thrown the ring at him during an argument at an Atlanta hotel and it went over a balcony.
During the episode, the exes discussed their on-again, off-again relationship and contentious co-parenting situation for their twins. Parker, who had an older child from a prior relationship, described Smith as "pretty malicious and vindictive."
The show's judge, Marilyn Milian, found both were at fault and that Parker owed Smith $2,500 for her half of the ring.
According to the affidavit, this was not the first time Smith had issues regarding an engagement ring.
A woman who was previously engaged to Smith told police that after their engagement failed in 2006, she "refused to return the engagement ring and the suspect sued her through a courtroom television show," according to the affidavit.
After that, the woman "advised the suspect told her he would make her disappear," according to the affidavit.

title: Ukraine reportedly strikes chemical, metallurgical plants in Russia
body:
Ukraine's military reportedly launched attacks on several facilities within Russia linked to Moscow's military-industrial complex overnight on Oct. 28, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Explosions sounded and fires burned in the Russian city of Lipetsk late on Oct. 27 following an attack by Ukrainian forces, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus reported.
A fire broke out in the area of the Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant after air defenses were engaged, according to the monitoring channel.
A 2025 investigation by Ukrainska Pravda found that the plant supplies Russian defense companies that produce air defense systems, drones, missiles, and other weapons.
Ukraine has sanctioned the Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant, while Canada and Australia have sanctioned Russian Billionaire Vladimir Lisin, who owns the site.
Later in the night, Azot chemical plant in Novomoskovsk, located in Tula Oblast, caught fire following a reported Ukrainian attack. The plant has been repeatedly targeted by Ukrainian drones in recent months.
Ukraine's military have not commented on the reported attacks, and the details could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukrainian forces attacked an ammunition depot in occupied Luhansk Oblast, setting off explosions at the site overnight on Oct. 27, monitoring channels reported. Strike drones targeted the site in an attack that took several hours near the city of Khrustalnyi, according to Exilenova Plus.
On Oct. 24, Ukraine struck several targets, including a petrochemical plant and a warehouse in Siberia around 2,500 kilometers away from the border, monitoring channels reported.

title: Israel has voted, but the coalition deadlock is just beginning - analysis
body: An engaged nation went to the polls in unprecedented numbers on Tuesday and spoke. It will now take weeks, if not months, to figure out exactly what it said.The exit polls released at 10 p.m. by Channels 11, 12, and 13 all showed the so-called change bloc ahead of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc, but Likud emerging as the largest party.Neither camp, however, appeared to have the partners needed to form the government it promised.The distinction matters. Taken together, the parties opposed to the outgoing government won a clear majority of the projected seats. But those parties do not constitute a single bloc willing to govern together.The Arab parties are central to that gap.According to the exit polls, they won a combined 17 to 18 seats, making them one of the election's biggest stories. Their apparent strength helped deny Netanyahu a majority. Yet the change bloc's commitments against relying on them also complicate its ability to replace him.The Arab parties' seats count just as much as anyone else's. The obstacle is other parties' willingness to enter a governing arrangement with them.The result, if it holds, is a clear parliamentary majority against the outgoing government – 1,116 days after October 7 – without a clear agreement on what should replace it.Expect Netanyahu, Eisenkot both to claim victoryBoth camps asked the public for a decisive outcome. Neither got everything it wanted.Netanyahu apparently emerged at the head of the largest party, but without a clear path to a coalition. Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot emerged at the head of the larger change bloc, but with a gap between the seats opposing Netanyahu and the partners available to form a government.Expect both to claim victory.Netanyahu will point to Likud's lead over Yashar, which trailed it by two or three seats in the exit polls. Eisenkot will point to the balance between the blocs.Netanyahu knows better than most that the largest party does not necessarily form the government. In 2009, Tzipi Livni's Kadima won one more seat than Likud. Netanyahu became prime minister because he could assemble a coalition and she could not.The question now is whether Eisenkot can do what Netanyahu did then.That will require finding a way around commitments that, during the campaign, sounded unequivocal.Eisenkot set four conditions for prospective coalition partners that the Arab parties would be unlikely to meet. His camp will now have to confront the consequences of those conditions: a majority for replacing Netanyahu may exist on paper without being available around the cabinet table.Even a willingness to rely on Mansour Abbas's Ra'am party would not, on the figures emerging Tuesday night, necessarily close the gap. Support from the Joint List would raise a further set of political obstacles.The Arab parties, meanwhile, have voters and demands of their own. They cannot simply be penciled into someone else's coalition arithmetic as though their only function were to provide the missing seats.Their projected gains came as a result of a strong determination to ensure that another right-wing government does not emerge.But helping to deny the outgoing coalition a majority and helping to install its replacement are two different achievements. The first appears within reach. The second will depend on negotiations and decisions still to come.Another route for Eisenkot would be to bring in the two haredi (ultra-Orthodox) parties, projected together to win 12 seats.That could provide a majority. It would also give those parties considerable leverage over a government whose prospective partners have promised meaningful changes to haredi conscription.The difficulty is obvious. Bringing the haredi parties into the government might solve the coalition arithmetic while making one of its central policy commitments considerably harder to fulfill.There is also an option that jumps off the page: a government comprising Likud, Yashar, Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad, and Yisrael Beytenu.On the projected figures, those parties would together have 67 seats, without the haredi parties, the Arab parties, or the parties on the hard-right (Otzma Yehudit and the Religious Zionist Party) or the hard-left (the Democrats).Numerically straightforward. Politically, anything but.If Netanyahu remains at Likud's helm, such a government would require his opponents to abandon their promises not to serve under him. It would also require agreement on who leads and on what terms.A coalition that looks doable on paper is anything in real life. That is the central problem emerging from Tuesday's exit polls.There are combinations that produce a majority. There are fewer combinations that the parties have said they are prepared to join.Weeks following election will test final or negotiating positionsThe coming weeks will test whether those positions are final or negotiating positions.First, however, the votes must be counted. Exit polls provide the opening frame for coalition negotiations, not the final count on which they will rest.But if the broad picture holds, the question will shift quickly from how Israelis voted to what their elected representatives are prepared to do with those votes.More specifically: which campaign promises will survive contact with the results?Throughout the campaign, parties told voters whom they would sit with, whom they would never sit with, and what conditions they would insist upon before joining a government.Those promises matter. A voter is entitled to know whether a ballot cast for one party might help put someone else in the prime minister's chair.But when enough parties rule out enough other parties, the result can be a Knesset with no workable majority.Someone will now have to decide whether the greater obligation is to honor a campaign commitment or to compromise sufficiently to allow a government to be formed.Those arguing for compromise can be expected to call it national responsibility. Those opposing it will call it a betrayal.Netanyahu cannot in any way point to these projections and claim that the country gave him a vote of confidence.His opponents can point to a majority that emerged against his government, but still have to demonstrate that they can turn it into a government of their own.The politicians now have to decide what they are prepared to change: their conditions, their partners, or their promises.Failing that, they may eventually ask the voters to try again.

title: Luxury real estate to prison: Israeli-American Alexander brothers each get 30 years for sex trafficking
body: A Manhattan court sentenced each of the three Alexander brothers - sons of Israeli immigrants who became wealthy real estate figures in the United States - to 30 years in prison after they were convicted of sex trafficking and additional sex offenses. The judge imposed the sentences on Tal Alexander, 40, and his twin brothers, Oren and Alon, 39, following a lengthy hearing in which victims described the assaults and their lasting impact. Prosecutors had sought life sentences for all three, while defense attorneys requested the minimum sentence of 15 years. The brothers were unanimously convicted in March following a trial that lasted several weeks and included testimony from 11 women. According to prosecutors, the brothers used their wealth, status and access to luxury properties over more than two decades to lure women to parties, trips and vacation destinations, including mansions in the Hamptons and ski resorts in Aspen. There, some of the women were raped and sexually assaulted, in certain cases after being drugged.   Prosecutors said they had identified at least 70 women and girls who were victimized by one or more of the brothers. According to the prosecution, some of the assaults dated back to 2001 or 2002, when the brothers were still in high school. Several women testified that after drinking beverages provided by the brothers, they became disoriented and lost control of their bodies. At Tuesday's sentencing hearing, 11 women delivered victim impact statements, while a prosecutor read a statement on behalf of another victim. One woman said it took just "one night, a few hours and one invitation" to destroy the person she had been. Another described a luxurious Hamptons mansion that had become a "mansion of horrors" for her. Artist and gallery owner Lindsey Acree said Tal and another man raped her at a Hamptons home in 2011 after she drank a beverage that she said left her paralyzed. Abandoning her prepared remarks, she addressed the brothers directly: "Why did you do this? I don't understand the cruelty, the hatred of women." All three brothers, who did not testify during the trial, asked to speak before sentencing and continued to deny the offenses. Oren said he regretted remarks he had made and the way he had behaved toward women when he was younger, but insisted: "We never drugged or raped anyone. We never sex trafficked anyone."   Tal asked to be sent to the same prison as his brothers so their elderly parents could visit all three together. The judge had previously indicated that separating them would be appropriate because of their negative influence on one another, although the final decision on prison assignments rests with correctional authorities. Alon said that no woman had accused him of misconduct during the eight years he had been married, describing his current life as centered on work and family. He is married to Israeli model Shani Zigron, and the couple has two daughters. Oren and Tal were among the most prominent brokers in the luxury real estate markets of New York and Miami. Known in the industry as the "A Team," they earned their reputation through multimillion-dollar deals for wealthy buyers and celebrity clients. They broke sales records at Douglas Elliman before establishing their own brokerage firm.   Their clients included Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, whom they helped purchase a Florida estate in a $24 million deal. Alon managed the family's security business. Their parents, Shlomi and Orly Alexander, immigrated to the United States from Israel and founded Kent Security. The three brothers were arrested in 2024 and have remained in custody without bail since then. The family also pursued a separate legal avenue, hiring attorney Alan Dershowitz, who had previously been involved in presidential pardon proceedings involving Donald Trump, for hundreds of thousands of dollars. A letter written by Dershowitz listed the possibility of a presidential pardon and the reversal of the convictions among the objectives of his work. Dershowitz said he had not discussed the case with Trump. The brothers' defense attorneys intend to appeal the convictions, while the question of financial compensation for the victims remains unresolved.

title: UAE's Lana Nusseibeh says she would take political risks to secure peace
body: The UAE's Lana Nusseibeh called for sweeping reforms at the UN on Tuesday and pledged to take diplomatic risks to secure peace if chosen as the world body's next secretary general. Speaking at UN headquarters in New York, Ms Nusseibeh said the UN could no longer operate as it had for decades, with shrinking development funding and growing global divisions making it harder to respond to crises. She said it should scale back some of its activities, rethink its spending and focus on delivering results. “The development assistance of the last 30 years is not returning in the form we knew, and a UN that responds by asking for more will not be heard,” Ms Nusseibeh said at an informal dialogue with members of the UN General Assembly. “The UN I would lead will be judged by what each country can point to, not by what the system spends.” Ms Nusseibeh, who said she has taken a leave of absence from her role as minister in the Emirati government, said the world body must recognise its limits and withdraw from areas where other institutions were better placed to act, freeing up resources for humanitarian emergencies and conflict prevention. “The UN cannot do everything, and the attempt dilutes what it does best,” Ms Nusseibeh said. Εκτιμώ ιδιαίτερα και τη στήριξη της Ελλάδας στην υποψηφιότητά μου. Ως Γενικός Γραμματέας, θα… — Lana Nusseibeh (@Lana_Nusseibeh) October 26, 2026 Her remarks come at a difficult moment for the UN, which is dealing with financial pressures , declining international aid and deepening divisions among member states over some of the world’s most pressing conflicts. Ms Nusseibeh warned that the international order was becoming increasingly fractured, making effective diplomacy more urgent. “There are more conflicts today than at any point since this organisation was founded, and the balance between consensus and confrontation is tilting the wrong way,” she said. “The security, prosperity and future we share depend on decisions no country can make alone. But rebuilding the trust that makes those decisions possible is now the central work of the UN.” Risk and accountability Ms Nusseibeh said she would take risks for peace if she is chosen, even if she might fail. “I don’t seek for the office to look for credit in trying. But I think not trying would be a marker of failure,” she said. She said she would be a “political risk taker for peace even if failure seems the likely outcome”. Asked how she would pursue accountability when a permanent member of the Security Council is the “alleged perpetrator”, Ms Nusseibeh said she would be guided by the UN Charter and international law, including respect for national sovereignty and territorial integrity. Drawing on her experience negotiating Security Council resolutions on Gaza and Afghanistan, she promised to place greater emphasis on preventing conflicts rather than responding once violence erupts. “As Secretary General, I will engage early on, before disputes harden into war,” Ms Nusseibeh said. AI, jobs and a younger generation The challenges facing the next UN chief, she said, extend well beyond traditional questions of war and peace. Ms Nusseibeh said artificial intelligence , youth unemployment and climate change were among the most consequential issues facing the international community, and warned that technological advances could deepen existing inequalities if governments failed to act collectively. “Artificial intelligence will be either the great equaliser or the great divider. The choice is ours,” she said. She also said the UN needed to do a better job of explaining its purpose to younger generations, many of whom have little connection to the hardships of the two world wars that inspired its creation. “We need to resell the reason why this organisation was created,” she said. “Many young people will not grow up remembering the savagery of the world wars that led to the creation of this organisation, and as a mother and a parent of two young boys, I would not want to see them grow up in a world where we need to make that case again because we have not been able to prevent war in our time again from being resolved.” She also pledged to defend human rights “with rigour and without double standards”, saying the organisation’s credibility depended on applying its principles fairly and consistently. The Middle East On the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Ms Nusseibeh pledged to pursue a two-state solution in which Israel and Palestine could coexist peacefully, in line with international law and UN resolutions. She pointed to Security Council resolution 2803, which welcomed the establishment of a Board of Peace and authorised the establishment of a temporary International Stabilisation Force in Gaza, as a framework for moving forward, calling it a rare opportunity for diplomatic progress. “As Secretary General, I will be committed to pursuing progress on the implementation of these relevant UN resolutions,” she said. “This is an opportunity that we cannot afford to miss.” Asked what legacy she hoped to leave in the Middle East, she offered a personal reflection, saying that growing up in a region repeatedly scarred by war had shaped her understanding of the consequences of “failed diplomacy and the consequences felt very deeply by people on the ground”. But Ms Nusseibeh, 48, stressed that her regional background would not determine her priorities. “I would be a Secretary General for every continent and every conflict and every member state in the room,” she said. “There is no hierarchy of civilians suffering.” Ms Nusseibeh’s candidacy has received wide support from a number of countries and civil society groups, including Afghan women’s rights groups. During Tuesday's lengthy question-and-answer session, Ms Nusseibeh answered several questions on the UAE’s alleged involvement in Sudan’s civil war and its purported backing of the Rapid Support Forces, which are fighting the Sudanese military. Ms Nusseibeh said Sudan is "a litmus test of the success of any incoming secretary general". "It is a terrible humanitarian catastrophe on the ground, and it urgently needs to move to a cessation of hostilities and a political process for a mediator transition, reflecting the civilian democratic aspirations of the Sudanese people," she told reporters following the council meeting. The UAE has repeatedly denied claims that it supplied weapons in the war.

title: NDC constitution lacks mechanism to punish electoral inducement – Inusah Fuseini
body: Former Tamale Central MP, Inusah Fuseini, says the National Democratic Congress (NDC) lacks a clear constitutional mechanism to punish electoral inducement, leaving disciplinary action open to challenge. He told Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday that the gap limits the party leadership’s authority to sanction offenders. Proposed constitutional amendments would define the misconduct and establish who should handle cases. His comments come amid allegations of widespread vote-buying during the NDC’s recent constituency executive elections. Reports alleged that delegates were given cash and household appliances. The party has said it will investigate credible evidence but maintains that no incidents have been formally established. Mr Fuseini said his committee recognised the need to punish those involved after acknowledging that inducement had occurred. But it also found “there was no legal mechanism in our constitution to deal with that”. That left the party’s executives to decide how to proceed. He explained that the constitution did not expressly empower the Functional Executive Committee (FEC), National Executive Committee or Council of Elders to address such cases. Disciplinary action would therefore risk a challenge if the rules did not define the conduct as an offence. “So we need a framework,” he said. One proposal under consideration would give constituency councils of elders authority to handle complaints locally. Another would refer offenders to the national headquarters, where the Functional Executive Committee would act. The committee is also examining how to distinguish legitimate support for delegates from inducement. “How much money can we say is appropriate in the circumstances?” he asked. Mr Fuseini questioned how the party should treat payments described as transport allowances when the amounts exceed reasonable travel costs. He said the party would further scrutinise the proposals before presenting them to a special congress for constitutional amendment. “It’s a work in progress,” he said. Beyond disciplinary rules, Fuseini warned that rising political costs were excluding women, young people and potential candidates with integrity. Some lack the resources to compete. Others withdraw because they cannot afford the demands of money-driven contests. He also linked excessive campaign spending to corruption. “A politician is not an NGO,” he said. He argued that candidates who spend heavily expect to recoup their investment, adding that “that fuels corruption on a national scale”.

title: Weibel to supply XENTA-M5 radars for Poland’s SAN integrated counter-drone programme
body: XENTA-M5 is designed to detect targets ranging from small, low-flying drones to aircraft and other airborne threats. Its continuously updated air picture will feed SAN’s command-and-control architecture, giving operators more time and information to assess threats and decide how to respond, according to Weibel. “Turning Counter-UAS ambition into operational capability starts with the ability to see and understand the threat,” said Peter Røpke, chief executive of Weibel Scientific. “XENTA-M5 provides the detection, tracking and classification that enables the wider system to act.” The order brings new demands on Weibel’s production capacity and delivery operations as its radar technology becomes part of a major European defence programme. The company said the contract builds on a business that has delivered more than 6,000 radar systems to customers in over 45 countries. “Weibel has the technology,” Røpke said. “This contract raises the bar for what we must deliver as a company and the responsibility we take on as Europe strengthens its defense capability.” PIT-RADWAR, Weibel’s customer under the contract, is a Polish defence electronics company specialising in radar, command-and-control and air-defence systems. Weibel described SAN as a step towards translating Europe’s Drone Wall ambition into operational counter-drone capability on its eastern flank.

title: 4th-tier Fleetwood Town knock Arsenal out of Carabao Cup after penalties
body: Arsenal suffered one of the most humiliating defeats in their history as the Premier League champions were stunned by fourth-tier minnows Fleetwood in a League Cup penalty shoot-out on Tuesday. Mikel Arteta’s side crashed out 5-3 on penalties in an incredible fourth round upset after the tie finished 1-1 in normal time. Arsenal’s Bruno Guimaraes had his penalty saved by Jay Lynch in the shoot-out and Conor Haughey scored Fleetwood’s winner. Aaron Loupalo-Bi’s first-half goal had put Fleetwood ahead before Viktor Gyokeres equalised after the interval. Arsenal’s 16-year-old rising star Max Dowman was sent off for violent conduct in the closing stages. Arteta paid the price for prioritising Sunday’s Premier League trip to Liverpool as his decision to make nine changes backfired spectacularly. No one would have predicted Arsenal’s embarrassment regardless of Arteta’s selection gamble. They had moved level on points with Premier League leaders Manchester City after a 2-0 victory over Everton on Saturday. But instead of extending their run of 11 wins from their 13 previous games, Arsenal returned to north London red-faced after a loss that ranks among the darkest days in the club’s glittering history. Referee Michael Salisbury shows a red card to Arsenal’s English midfielder #56 Max Dowman (R) during the English League Cup fourth round football match between Fleetwood Town and Arsenal at Highbury Stadium in Fleetwood, north west England, on October 27, 2026. (Photo by Darren Staples / AFP) Arsene Wenger’s Arsenal suffered a shock League Cup loss against fourth tier Bradford on penalties in 2012. Arteta’s team were beaten by second tier Southampton in the FA Cup last season and also lost to Nottingham Forest, then in the Championship, in the same competition in 2022. Supporters of an older vintage will recall Arsenal’s 1969 League Cup final loss against third tier Swindon and their 1992 FA Cup exit at fourth tier Wrexham. But even those painful defeats cannot compare to this remarkable result. For once, Arsenal fans will not have fond memories of Highbury — Fleetwood’s ground shares the same name as the Gunners’ ancestral home before their move to the Emirates Stadium in 2006. Fleetwood’s tiny 5,327-capacity ground — where goals are celebrated with a burst of children’ cartoon song Captain Pugwash over the tannoy — is a far cry from the famous marble halls and dignified grandeur of Arsenal’s former stadium. Now it will be remembered forever as the site of Arsenal’s most chastening loss in the Arteta era. Fleetwood boss Matt Lawlor wept tears of joy as disbelieving fans flooded the pitch to celebrate their club’s astonishing victory. – ‘Cod Army’ uprising – Only Myles Lewis-Skelly and Viktor Gyokeres kept their places from the Everton game, with teenagers Dowman and Marli Salmon starting, while 18-year-old winger Ceadach O’Neill made his debut. Arsenal’s Swedish striker #14 Viktor Gyokeres (C) celebrates after scoring the equalising goal during the English League Cup fourth round football match between Fleetwood Town and Arsenal at Highbury Stadium in Fleetwood, north west England, on October 27, 2026. (Photo by Darren Staples / AFP) Languishing in 18th place in League Two, Fleetwood had lost their previous two league games against Exeter and Cheltenham, yet they showed no signs of being intimidated by their illustrious visitors. After an eight-minute delay due to an unauthorised drone flying over the stadium, Arsenal were caught cold on a windy night by the Irish Sea. Fleetwood are nicknamed the ‘Cod Army’ in reference to the town’s fishing industry, so it was somewhat fitting that a mistake from Salmon netted their opener in the 21st minute. Salmon’s lack of experience was brutally exposed when Loupalo-Bi muscled his way past the 17-year-old with ease, racing into the penalty area to plant a low finish past debutant keeper Illan Meslier. Fleetwood fans invade the pitch as they celebrate winning the English League Cup fourth round football match between Fleetwood Town and Arsenal at Highbury Stadium in Fleetwood, north west England, on October 27, 2026. Fleetwood won the match 5-3 following a penlaty shoot out. (Photo by Darren Staples / AFP) Arsenal monopolised possession after that shock, but Arteta grew visibly agitated with their lack of cutting edge. Arteta sent on Martin Odegaard at half-time and Gyokeres bagged Arsenal’s equaliser five minutes later. It was a scrappy effort that left Fleetwood feeling aggrieved as Gyokeres wrestled with his marker before poking O’Neill’s ball past Lynch from close-range. Dowman saw red in the 85th minute, dismissing for kicking out at Harrison Neal after a strong challenge from the Fleetwood midfielder. Although it looked a harsh decision, Arteta was unimpressed with Dowman, giving him a stern word as the midfielder trudged off. Both teams scored their first three penalties in the shoot-out, but Guimaraes was denied by Lynch and Haughey held his nerve to seal the biggest shock in League Cup history.
