title: IPOB urges South-east to withdraw support for APC over Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal
body:
The outlawed Indigenous People of Biafra (IPOB) has asked the people of the South-east and others in parts of the South-South to withdraw their support for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) over the Nigerian government’s delay in listing Nnamdi Kanu’s appeal against his conviction.
Mr Kanu is the convicted leader of IPOB, a group seeking an independent state of Biafra, which it wants carved out of the South-east and parts of South-South Nigeria.
He was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment for terrorism in November 2025 at the Federal High Court in Abuja.
The IPOB leader, who is serving his jail term in a prison facility in Sokoto State, filed an appeal against his conviction and sentencing in February this year.
But the hearing on the appeal has not begun, even after about eight months.
In a statement on Tuesday which was forwarded to PREMIUM TIMES, the spokesperson of the IPOB, Emma Powerful, said South-easterners should reject the APC because the federal government allegedly “deliberately” failed to hear Mr Kanu’s appeal.
“Biafrans must withdraw voluntary political support from the APC, boycott its rallies, refuse its insignia, and deny it community legitimacy,” Mr Powerful said.
“Biafra” is a phrase often used by the separatist group to refer to the
South-east and some parts of the South-South of Nigeria.
The group also uses the phrase “Biafrans” to refer to indigenes of the two regions.
The IPOB spokesperson stressed in the statement that the Nigerian government moved “swiftly” to convict Mr Kanu but failed to hear the IPOB leader’s appeal with the same speed.
“Any regime is preferable to the APC. Under any other administration, the judiciary would at least be free to list and hear all pending legal cases according to the rule of law, rather than being subverted into an instrument of executive terror.
“Rather than facing judicial scrutiny before the Court of Appeal, the state has deliberately left the case unlisted,” he claimed.
Mr Powerful maintained that the federal government deliberately left the appeal unlisted by its failure to file its respondent’s brief.
“Our position is unequivocal: we will not lend our participation, support, or political legitimacy to a party whose government fears facing our leader’s appeal,” he said.

title: Assessing Ghana’s government policy on contract mining and local economic benefits
body: Pursuant to the passage of the Minerals and Mining (Local Content and Local Participation) Regulations, 2020 (L.I. 2431), the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources has announced that indigenous Ghanaian companies are to undertake contract mining for surface mining operations, while underground contract mining should be conducted through partnerships in which Ghanaian-owned companies hold not less than 50 percent interest. For the purpose of clarification, contract mining refers to an arrangement in which a holder of a mineral right engages an independent corporate entity to execute mining operations, including drilling, blasting, excavation, haulage, equipment maintenance, dewatering, and rehabilitation. With this explanation, it is clear that the policy is a step in the right direction. However, for the successful implementation of this policy, the government must consider the myriad challenges that could hinder its implementation while identifying the potential benefits of this groundbreaking policy for Ghana’s mining sector. Contract mining would undoubtedly create opportunities for direct and indirect employment for many Ghanaians. Both skilled and unskilled members of the Ghanaian workforce would have roles to play in mining operations. Operators would be required to operate dump trucks, excavators, drill rigs, service trucks, and other equipment. Some of these positions do not require advanced academic qualifications, although the necessary training, licences, and practical competencies may be required. According to the Ghana Chamber of Mines, nearly 42 percent of employees in mining firms are indigenous people. This suggests that transferring mining operations to local contractors could create opportunities to increase employment among Ghanaians, thereby providing sustainable jobs for the country’s large population of unemployed youth. A Ghanaian-owned company conducting mining operations for a mining company can help retain a greater share of mining-related expenditure within the local economy, in both cedis and foreign currency. The contractor pays its workers from the revenue it earns, purchases locally available spare parts, and engages Ghanaian transport companies to transport its workers and materials. These activities promote the circulation of money within the economy while supporting other businesses. Where local contractors replace foreign service providers, some payments that would otherwise leave the country could be retained in Ghana. This could contribute to reducing foreign-exchange outflows and easing pressure on the cedi, particularly where local businesses also replace imported goods and services. However, the extent of these benefits would depend on the contractors’ reliance on imported equipment, spare parts, fuel, and other inputs. Another potential benefit is an increase in government tax revenue. According to the Minerals Commission, there are sixteen large-scale mining companies in the country. If indigenous Ghanaian companies undertake a greater share of the mining operations currently performed by foreign contractors, government revenue could increase through corporate income tax, PAYE income tax from workers, and other applicable taxes, including withholding tax on contract payments. The resulting revenue could support the government’s efforts to finance development projects across the country. Contract mining also presents an opportunity to develop Ghanaian-owned businesses. A Ghanaian entrepreneur could establish a company specialising in haulage, drilling, blasting, equipment maintenance, or other mining-related services. Existing indigenous mining companies could also take advantage of this policy to expand their businesses, strengthen their operational capacity, and improve their competitiveness in securing mining contracts. In assessing this policy holistically, it is important to consider the challenges that indigenous Ghanaian companies may face in undertaking mining operations. One of the major challenges is access to substantial capital. Surface mining operations, in particular, are equipment-intensive and require considerable investment in the acquisition of dump trucks, excavators, bulldozers, drill rigs, and other machinery. When a mining company transfers its load-and-haul operations to a contractor, the contractor is expected to provide a fleet of equipment capable of hauling ore and waste materials every day. Indigenous companies may struggle to obtain the necessary funding. Therefore, there should be appropriate financing arrangements between financial institutions and contractors. These arrangements should be developed after a thorough cost-benefit analysis and an assessment of the project’s financial viability by qualified engineers and financial experts. The introduction of contract mining should also create opportunities for public-private partnerships involving Ghanaian businesses to establish companies that provide mining-related goods and services. Page 47 of the Ghana Chamber of Mines’ 2024 report details expenditure of approximately US$240.7 million on imported consumables, including drill rods, drill bits, drill pipes, blasting consumables, and mobile equipment consumables such as tyres. Establishing local companies to manufacture or supply some of these goods could help retain a greater proportion of this expenditure within the Ghanaian economy and reduce the country’s dependence on imported mining inputs. The transfer of mining operations to indigenous Ghanaian companies could also raise concerns about workers’ wages, job security, allowances, and other employment benefits. Workers who previously worked directly for mining companies may experience changes in their conditions of service following the transfer of operations to contractors. Differences in salaries, allowances, and medical coverage could generate dissatisfaction among workers. Such grievances could lead to labour disputes, reduced morale, and the loss of experienced workers, thereby affecting the productivity of mining operations. The Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, in conjunction with the Minerals Commission, should therefore be commended for recognising the importance of addressing these concerns. However, there must be effective enforcement of fair wage and allowance standards for contract mine workers. Workers should receive fair and transparent remuneration that takes into account their skills, experience and job responsibilities. Particular attention should be given to basic salaries, overtime payments, night-shift allowances, and adequate healthcare benefits for contract workers. In conclusion, Ghana’s contract mining policy presents a significant opportunity to transform the country’s mining sector into a stronger engine of local economic development. By empowering indigenous Ghanaian companies to undertake mining operations, the policy has the potential to create sustainable employment, promote local entrepreneurship, retain more value within the domestic economy, reduce dependence on imported mining inputs, and increase government revenue. However, the realisation of these benefits will depend on the government’s ability to address the financial, technical, operational, and labour-related challenges that may confront indigenous contractors. Ultimately, the success of contract mining should not be measured solely by the number of Ghanaian companies awarded mining contracts but by the extent to which the policy builds competitive Ghanaian businesses, creates decent jobs, strengthens local industries and improves the economic well-being of Ghanaians. ********* Author: Agyarko Ebenezer (Principal Mining Consultant and Head of Technical Communications, West Africa Cooperatives Networks [WACoN] )

title: Hacker trying to breach US Federal Election Commission system, email shows
body: The US Federal Election Commission's website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting the agency's electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections, according to an email seen by Reuters.In a statement, the FEC said that, "at this time, the FEC's electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service." The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said that users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage.The hacking attempts come a week before the midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections, and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.The outage prevents organizations from filing the FEC's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races.FEC system outage threatens election finance transparency, expert warns"I've never seen this in 26 years," said Steven Mele, a partner at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. "The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections" until it's fixed.A status message posted by the FEC noted that its filing system had been down since around 10 p.m. ET on Monday (0200 GMT Tuesday). The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI did not immediately return messages seeking comment.

title: Time to reform the Ghana Reference Rate: From treasury bill yields to banks’ deposit costs
body: For businesses borrowing to buy equipment, restock a shop or meet payroll, the price of credit affects everyday decisions. The Ghana Reference Rate (GRR) provides a common starting point for that price. Its usefulness depends on whether the formula reflects financing conditions and whether borrowers can understand how it becomes the interest rate they pay. The central weakness is specific. The GRR blends a policy signal, interbank borrowing and government investment returns without directly measuring banks’ deposit costs. Its reserve adjustment also gives Treasury bill movements more influence than the stated 40% weight initially suggests. The evidence supports a review of the benchmark’s weights and a test of a simple formula that directly includes banks’ deposit interest costs. The main questions for this article are: Whose Cost Is Ghana’s Reference Rate Measuring? Why Should Bank Deposit Costs Replace Government Borrowing Rates in the GRR Formula? How the formula works Existing component Weight What it represents Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) 40% The central bank’s policy signal Interbank rate (IBR) 20% The rate banks pay to borrow from one another Reserve-adjusted 91-day Treasury bill rate (T₉₁) 40% Government’s short-term borrowing rate, increased for reserves and vault cash Here, T₉₁ is the annualised 91-day Treasury bill rate. CRR is the cash reserve ratio, the share of eligible deposits banks must hold as reserves. CIV is the cash-in-vault ratio used in the adjustment. The denominator represents the share remaining after these amounts are deducted. The three stated weights sum to 100%. [3, 4] At a 20% CRR and an illustrative 2% CIV, the denominator is 0.78. A 5.38% Treasury bill rate therefore enters the formula as 6.90%, before the 40% weight is applied. The adjustment recognises a cost from funds held in cash and reserves, but its design and size deserve scrutiny. [2, 5] The Treasury bill component has more leverage than it appears With CRR at 20% and CIV at 2%, a one percentage-point rise in the raw Treasury bill rate increases the formula-based GRR by 0.513 percentage points. The same rise in the policy rate increases it by 0.400 points, and an interbank increase adds 0.200 points. These comparisons hold the other inputs constant. Figure 1 A Treasury bill movement has the largest direct effect Sources: Bank of Ghana interest-rate series and reserve information [2, 5]; 40/20/40 formula [3]. Sensitivities use CRR 20% and CIV 2%. One basis point is 0.01 percentage points. The bars show separate responses, not shares that must total 100%. For example, a Treasury bill increase from 5% to 10%, with the other inputs unchanged, would add approximately 2.56 percentage points to the GRR under these assumptions. A business with a floating-rate loan linked to the benchmark could face that increase even without a change in the policy rate or its own creditworthiness, depending on its contract. The formula’s 40% Treasury bill weight is applied to an adjusted rate. Relative to the unadjusted rate that most readers see in the news, the sensitivity is about 51.3%, compared with 40% for the policy rate. This is not an arithmetic error. It is a feature that should be disclosed prominently whenever the benchmark’s weights are explained. The reserve setting changes that sensitivity. At a 10% CRR and 2% CIV, the Treasury bill coefficient is approximately 0.455. At 20% CRR and 2% CIV, it becomes 0.513. Thus, raising reserve requirements changes the GRR’s response to future Treasury bill movements as well as increasing its current level. The required improvement is straightforward: every monthly GRR release should show both the stated weights and the effective sensitivities to the three headline rates. Borrowers should not have to infer this distinction from the formula. Treasury bills dominate the historical movement An analysis of 102 monthly observations from April 2018 to September 2026 shows how significant this design becomes over time. The Treasury bill component, including its reserve adjustment, accounts for 78.8% of the variance in monthly changes in the formula-based GRR. The policy component accounts for 12.6%, and the interbank component for 8.6%. [1, 2] Figure 2 Treasury bills and reserves dominate the model’s variation Data sources: Ghana Association of Banks and Bank of Ghana [1, 2]. Decomposition covers 101 monthly changes in the formula-based GRR. Shares allocate covariance with the total change; they include shared movements and do not establish independent causal effects on published rates. The 78.8% figure concerns variation in the formula-based benchmark, not the percentage of every loan rate attributable to Treasury bills. Nevertheless, it shows that a component with a stated 40% weight has dominated the benchmark’s historical movement. A Treasury bill is an investment available to banks. Its yield is therefore relevant when a bank compares lending with holding government paper. However, an investment return is different from the cost of obtaining deposits. Treasury bill yields can change because of government financing needs, auction supply and investor demand. The formula can transmit those conditions into the starting price of private credit. Using Treasury bill yields in the GRR passes the government’s borrowing pressures on to businesses and households through bank lending rates, rather than directly reflecting banks’ own funding costs (Deposit cost). The policy rate and interbank rate also reflect related monetary conditions. Treating their 40% and 20% weights as independent economic information overstates the diversity of the formula’s inputs. Their relationship does not make the blend invalid, but the allocation needs evidence. BoG and the Ghana Association of Banks should specify whether the GRR measures funding costs, the opportunity cost of lending or monetary policy conditions. If it is primarily a funding benchmark, the present 40% Treasury bill allocation needs to be tested against a measure that includes actual deposit funding costs. A common benchmark does not tell the borrower’s whole story Published rates show that the GRR has a substantial relationship with bank lending. Across 92 matched monthly observations, the statistical fit between the GRR and average lending-rate levels is approximately R² = 0.95. The difficulty is therefore not an absence of connection. It is that the benchmark cannot explain the entire price of a loan or establish whether that price is fair. [1, 2] Figure 3 Lending rates follow the broad cycle but the gap changes Sources: Ghana Association of Banks GRR historical data and Bank of Ghana Summary of Economic and Financial Data [1, 2]. April 2018–September 2026. The MPR line shows prior-month inputs; lending data end in August 2026. Missing lending observations are left blank. The average lending-rate gap above the GRR was 7.34 percentage points in 2019, compared with 1.37 points across the available observations in 2024. By August 2026, the GRR was 10.61% and the average lending rate was 15.94%, leaving a gap of 5.33 points. A changing gap matters to borrowers because a lower benchmark does not guarantee an equally large reduction in the final loan rate. [1, 2] These aggregate gaps are not measures of bank profit or default risk alone. They can reflect funding differences, operating costs, capital charges, risk, loan composition and margins. Fees can raise the annual percentage rate further. BoG’s APR framework distinguishes these additional charges from the reference rate itself. [4] The underlying design problem remains; the GRR contains no direct deposit-cost input, although banks can fund loans with current accounts, savings, term deposits and wholesale borrowing. It also combines overnight and 91-day rates while many business loans run for years. A funding benchmark should acknowledge these differences, with product-specific credit and maturity costs disclosed separately. How the MPR and GRR can move apart The MPR signals monetary policy; the GRR blends that signal with market rates. The MPR is neither a required floor nor a ceiling for the GRR. Comparing 102 published GRRs with their prior-month MPR inputs gives 44 months below, 58 above and none exactly equal. Using prior-month inputs aligns the comparison with the formula’s timing. [1, 2] For the formula-based GRR, let A represent the reserve-adjusted Treasury bill rate. Subtracting the MPR from both sides gives: The gap depends on how the interbank and adjusted Treasury bill rates compare with the MPR. Published gaps can additionally reflect observation dates and calculation conventions. Relationship Period MPR GRR GRR − MPR MPR above GRR Sep 2026 14.00% 10.18% −3.82 pp GRR above MPR Feb 2023 28.00% 33.25% +5.25 pp Nearly equal Aug 2021 13.50% 13.51% +0.01 pp Sources: GAB published GRRs and BoG policy-rate data [1, 2]. The MPR column uses the prior-month input; pp means percentage points. Near equality is not exact equality. When the MPR is greater than the GRR In September 2026, MPR was 14.00% and GRR was 10.18%, a 3.82-point gap. Lower interbank and adjusted Treasury bill inputs pulled the formula below the policy signal. This can weaken the MPR’s influence on the benchmark when other rates remain low. It does not guarantee cheap loans: banks still add contractual margins and charges. When the GRR is greater than the MPR In February 2023, GRR was 33.25% against MPR of 28.00%, a 5.25-point gap. The adjusted Treasury bill input was approximately 41.42%, while interbank was 25.24%. The higher Treasury bill component outweighed the lower interbank component. Government financing conditions can therefore lift the lending benchmark above the policy rate, adding pressure to GRR-linked borrowing costs. When the two rates are equal Exact equality would mean the weighted differences cancel, not that the model is accurate. Hypothetical inputs of MPR 14%, IBR 10% and adjusted Treasury bills 16% produce GRR of 14%. August 2021 was close: GRR was 13.51% and MPR 13.50%. Equality should not be forced through a floor, cap or target. The mismatch also affects changes in the rates. Holding interbank and reserves constant, a one-point MPR cut lowers GRR by 0.40 points, but a simultaneous one-point Treasury bill rise adds 0.513 points at CRR 20% and CIV 2%. The net result is a 0.113-point GRR increase despite the policy cut. The critique is the formula’s mixed signals and indirect funding proxy. The deposit-cost proposal below addresses that proxy; it would not guarantee equality with the MPR. The monthly calculation should be reproducible Using August 2026 month-end inputs of a 14.00% policy rate, 10.20% interbank rate and 5.38% Treasury bill rate, together with CRR of 20% and CIV of 2%, the formula produces 10.40% for September. The published September GRR was 10.18%. The difference is approximately 0.22 percentage points. [1, 2, 5] Under this calculation, the reserve adjustment alone adds about 0.61 percentage points, lifting the unadjusted blend from 9.79% to 10.40%. The question is whether increasing the return on government paper is the best way to represent the cost of deposits held in reserves. An alternative is to calculate that allowance directly from the cost of the funding subject to the reserve requirement. Across the 102-month period, formula-based estimates fall within 0.15 percentage points of published GRRs in 68 months. In 11 months, the difference exceeds 0.50 points. Different observation dates, reserve ratios or conventions may explain these gaps. The comparison cannot identify the cause without the precise inputs used for each announcement. Figure 4 September 2026 shows why input dates matter Sources: GAB historical GRRs; BoG month-end interest-rate series and reserve information [1, 2, 5]. The formula-based estimate uses CIV 2%. Values are rounded. The 0.22 percentage-point difference is a replication gap; it does not establish an error in the published GRR. Under this calculation, the reserve adjustment alone adds about 0.61 percentage points, lifting the unadjusted blend from 9.79% to 10.40%. The question is whether increasing the return on government paper is the best way to represent the cost of deposits held in reserves. An alternative is to calculate that allowance directly from the cost of the funding subject to the reserve requirement. Across the 102-month period, formula-based estimates fall within 0.15 percentage points of published GRRs in 68 months. In 11 months, the difference exceeds 0.50 points. Different observation dates, reserve ratios or conventions may explain these gaps. The comparison cannot identify the cause without the precise inputs used for each announcement. Historical reserve treatment also matters. During the earlier tiered regime, banks faced reserve ratios of 15%, 20% or 25%. A common benchmark should state which ratio was applied and why. BoG subsequently moved to a uniform 20% CRR on 4 June 2026. Any industry averaging and the vault-cash allowance should be explicit. [5, 6] Publication of the calculation-date inputs would settle these questions more effectively than asking the public to approximate the announced rate from separate statistical releases. A simple proposed formula GRR* denotes the proposed rate. D is the annualised, amount-weighted interest cost of eligible cedi deposits across participating banks. The proposal replaces the Treasury bill input with D and keeps the existing weights as a transitional design for testing. It is not an approved BoG formula, and these weights have not been established as optimal. Proposed component Weight Why retain or include it Monetary Policy Rate (MPR) 40% Retains the monetary policy signal Interbank rate (IBR) 20% Retains a traded bank funding rate Reserve-adjusted direct deposit cost (D) 40% Introduces banks’ actual deposit interest cost in place of the Treasury bill yield The 40% policy-rate weight preserves the monetary policy signal. The 20% interbank weight preserves a traded bank funding indicator. The remaining 40% introduces the direct deposit interest cost. Keeping the weights initially unchanged makes the effect of replacing the Treasury bill input easier to assess. How to measure the deposit cost BoG should derive D from total interest accrued on eligible cedi deposits during the month, divided by their average balances, and annualise the result. Pooling the amounts across banks gives an industry rate weighted by deposit balances. Include eligible non-interest-bearing deposits at a zero interest rate; using only advertised fixed-deposit rates would overstate the direct cost of the whole deposit base. Consider an illustrative GH¢100 deposit base: GH¢50 pays no interest, GH¢30 pays 10% annually and GH¢20 pays 15%. Annual interest cost is GH¢3 plus GH¢3, or GH¢6. The direct deposit cost D is therefore 6%, rather than either quoted rate of 10% or 15%. If CRR is 20% and the applicable CIV allowance is 2%, GH¢78 remains after the adjustment. Dividing the GH¢6 annual interest cost by GH¢78 gives an adjusted deposit cost of 7.69%. Its 40% contribution to the proposed GRR is 3.08 percentage points. The deposit balances and reserve ratios must cover the same eligible funding. The reserve and vault-cash treatment should be confirmed and published. Direct deposit cost measures interest expense; operating costs, borrower risk and other loan charges remain separate. This is still a hybrid reference rate, not a complete measure of the cost of lending. How the change would affect the GRR The same August 2026 market inputs used above allow a direct comparison of the two formulas. Hold MPR at 14.00%, IBR at 10.20%, CRR at 20% and CIV at 2%. Only the Treasury bill input is replaced with the illustrative deposit costs below. The existing formula estimate remains 10.40%; it is distinct from the published September GRR of 10.18%. With a hypothetical direct deposit cost of 6%, the proposed formula adds 5.60 percentage points from the policy rate, 2.04 points from interbank funding and 3.08 points from adjusted deposits. The result is 10.72%, approximately 0.32 percentage points above the existing formula’s estimate. Figure 5 Deposit costs determine whether the proposed rate rises or falls Market input sources: Bank of Ghana [2]. All deposit costs shown are hypothetical, not observed industry estimates. MPR 14%, IBR 10.20%, CRR 20% and CIV 2% are held constant. The dashed line is the existing formula estimate using a 5.38% Treasury bill rate, not the published September GRR. If the direct deposit cost were 4%, the proposed GRR would be 9.69%, approximately 0.71 percentage points lower than the existing formula estimate. At 8%, it would be 11.74%, approximately 1.34 points higher. At D equal to the Treasury bill rate of 5.38%, the substitution would leave the formula result unchanged. Three effects follow. First, the benchmark would respond directly to deposit interest costs: a one percentage-point change in D would move the proposed GRR by about 0.513 points at these reserve settings. Second, Treasury bill movements would lose their direct mechanical effect on the formula, although they could still affect deposit pricing indirectly. Third, deposit costs would have to fall before this input could support a lower benchmark. The purpose is a more representative starting point for loan pricing. A lower GRR is a possible outcome, not a guaranteed one. Historical improvements in accuracy or stability cannot be established without a verified deposit-cost series, and borrowers benefit only to the extent that their contractual loan rates reflect the benchmark change. Three priorities for reform 1 Test the deposit cost formula BoG and the Ghana Association of Banks should run the proposed formula alongside the existing GRR for at least three monthly releases. Banks should submit deposit interest accruals and average eligible balances under one reporting definition. Check the submissions, include zero-interest deposits correctly, and publish the comparison before deciding whether to replace the Treasury bill input. Retain 40/20/40 initially to isolate the substitution, then review the weights against measured funding conditions. 2 Publish a calculation that everyone can reproduce Each GRR announcement should show the policy rate, interbank rate, Reserve-adjusted 91-day Treasury bill rate (if replaced by deposit cost as proposed), reserve ratio and CIV allowance, with their observation dates and weighted contributions. Publish the precise deposit-cost definition and explain how the reserve adjustment applies. The inputs should add up to the announced rate, and banks should not recover the same reserve cost again through an unexplained loan margin. Transparent inputs and periodic review are consistent with IOSCO benchmark principles. [7] 3 Show borrowers how the benchmark changes their loan Require each floating-rate loan statement to show the GRR, the contractual margin, fees, the annual percentage rate and the next reset date. BoG should check that rate adjustments follow the contract and that any permitted margin change has a documented basis. Fixed-rate contracts should retain their agreed treatment. This connects benchmark reform to the interest and payments borrowers actually face. [4] A deposit-cost input would give Ghana’s lending benchmark a clearer economic meaning. Its value would come from measuring an actual funding cost, explaining the calculation and making contractual loan pricing easier to verify. Sources and measurement notes Historical comparisons cover April 2018–September 2026. Lending comparisons use 92 matched observations without filling missing values. Formula-based estimates use prior month-end rates, a 2% CIV assumption, the lowest 15% tier during the tiered reserve period and approximate dates for some historical reserve changes. The estimates are distinct from official GRR calculations. Variance shares describe the formula-based series; R² describes statistical association. Exact historical replication requires calculation-date inputs and confirmed reserve conventions. The proposed deposit-cost formula retains the 40/20/40 weights as a transitional design for testing. The deposit-cost scenarios are hypothetical. A verified industry deposit-cost series has not been used to backtest the proposal, so the historical variance shares and lending-rate fit describe the earlier GRR analysis, not demonstrated performance of the new formula. References [1] Ghana Association of Banks. (n.d.). Ghana reference rate historical data, 2018–2026. Retrieved October 23, 2026. Read source [2] Bank of Ghana. (2018–2026). Summary of economic and financial data. Releases from July 2018 to September 2026; monetary policy, interbank, 91-day Treasury bill and average lending-rate series. Read source [3] The Ghana reference rate: A new era? (2018, May 3). Modern Ghana. Historical explanation of the 40/20/40 weights and reserve adjustment. Read source [4] Bank of Ghana. (2019). Annual percentage rates of banks as at September 30, 2019. Explains the GRR components, reserve adjustment and distinction from APR. Read source [5] Bank of Ghana. (2026). Bi-monthly publication of questions from the media July 2026. Confirms the transition to a uniform 20% CRR on June 4, 2026. Read source [6] Bank of Ghana. (2024, March). Monetary policy committee press release. Describes the tiered cash reserve requirements. Read source [7] International Organization of Securities Commissions. (2013, July). Principles for financial benchmarks. Provides standards for methodology transparency, data sufficiency, periodic review and accountability. Read source The recommendations above apply the principles of transparent inputs, a defined economic purpose and periodic methodological review to the GRR. [7] Authors : Williams Kwasi PEPRAH, PhD, Professor of Finance, Andrews University, email: peprah@andrews.edu and Fred Bortey Kyeremeh ACCA, PhD(c), Adventist University of the Philippine, Email: Fbkyeremeh@gmail.com

title: SOCO projects to resume across northern Ghana, Oti Region, after funding delays resolved
body: The National Project Coordinator of the Gulf of Guinea Northern Regions Social Cohesion (SOCO) Project, Elizabeth Ohenewa Agyei, has announced that stalled development projects across northern Ghana and the Oti Region are expected to resume following the resolution of funding delays. She said the World Bank-supported initiative had experienced a temporary disruption in the flow of funds, but the situation had since been addressed, with the Ministry of Finance releasing funds to facilitate the completion of ongoing projects. Speaking at a Ghana–Togo Joint Regional Working Session in Nalerigu in the North East Region on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, Ms Agyei said contractors were already mobilising to return to project sites. “Initially, there was a brief stall in the fund flow, but currently, that has been resolved. So, what we should expect is the pick-up of stalled projects that had to wait a while. I think that they have already started mobilising and coming back to site,” she said. She added that the Ministry of Finance was releasing most of the funding required to ensure the projects were completed. “Currently, we do not have that issue. We have the Minister of Finance actually releasing most of the funding that is required, especially to make sure that these projects are completed,” she stated. Ms Agyei also disclosed that discussions were ongoing about a possible third cycle of the project, expressing optimism about its prospects. “We are also in talks to get to know if we will do the third cycle, which we have high assurances of,” she added. The announcement offers renewed hope to communities across the beneficiary regions, where SOCO interventions aim to improve access to essential infrastructure, strengthen livelihoods and address development challenges that could contribute to social tensions. The working session brought together stakeholders from Ghana and Togo to review project implementation and strengthen cross-border collaboration under the SOCO initiative. The Togolese delegation included the Prefect of Tandjoari, Agbante Oukoure. The North East Regional Minister, Ibrahim Tia, called for stronger cooperation between Ghana and Togo to address emerging security threats, including violent extremism, cross-border crime and illicit arms trafficking. In a welcome address at the session, Mr Tia said the two countries shared longstanding historical, cultural, social and economic ties, particularly among communities along their common border. “These enduring ties constitute a valuable foundation upon which we can build stronger partnerships for peace, security, and sustainable development,” he said. He warned that instability in the Sahel region posed growing risks to border communities, stressing that Ghana’s relative peace and stability should not be taken for granted. Mr Tia said the SOCO Project was important not only for delivering infrastructure but also for strengthening social cohesion, improving livelihoods and enhancing communities’ resilience to conflict and other shocks. The World Bank-supported initiative is being implemented in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Côte d’Ivoire to strengthen social cohesion, improve socioeconomic and climate resilience, and reduce fragility, conflict and violence. In Ghana, the project covers 48 metropolitan, municipal and district assemblies across six beneficiary regions, including the North East Region. Its interventions include investments in education, healthcare, markets, water systems and livelihood activities, particularly for women and young people. Mr Tia noted that poverty, unemployment, social exclusion and competition over resources could fuel grievances that extremist and criminal groups might exploit. “Development must go beyond the provision of physical infrastructure. It must also empower communities, strengthen local institutions, promote inclusion, and create opportunities for people to participate meaningfully in their own development,” he said. He urged stakeholders to assess the project’s impact beyond the number of facilities constructed, focusing instead on service quality, improved livelihoods and the trust built among communities. “Our success must not be measured solely by the number of projects completed or facilities constructed. It must also be measured by the quality of services delivered, the livelihoods improved, the trust built among communities, and the contribution our interventions make towards lasting peace and stability,” he added. The working session, held under the project’s Regional Coordination and Dialogue Platform, aims to strengthen coordination, share lessons, review progress and identify challenges affecting implementation. Participants are also expected to engage communities in areas such as Nakpanduri and Bimbago to hear directly from beneficiaries, identify their concerns and assess the impact of project interventions. Mr Tia called for stronger collaboration among governments, implementing agencies and border communities, emphasising that no single country or institution could address the region’s security and development challenges alone.

title: Olympiacos Beat Benfica in Dramatic Challenge Cup Comeback
body: Olympiacos staged a remarkable comeback to defeat Benfica 3-2 in the first leg of their CEV Volleyball Challenge Cup tie at Rentis, keeping their hopes of reaching the round of 32 alive. Led by an outstanding performance from Bannister, who scored 34 points, the Greek side recovered from a two-set deficit to win 16-25, 23-25, 25-15, 25-22, 15-10 after 139 minutes of play. Benfica took the first two sets, but Olympiacos dramatically raised their level in the third, dominating the remainder of the match to complete the turnaround. Branko Kovacevic’s team must now pursue victory in the return leg in Portugal. If Olympiacos lose, the tie will go to a golden set to decide which team advances. Match statistics Final score: Olympiacos 3-2 Benfica Set scores: 16-25, 23-25, 25-15, 25-22, 15-10 Olympiacos scored through six aces, 65 attack points, nine blocks and 24 opponent errors. Benfica recorded six aces, 61 attack points, seven blocks and 23 opponent errors. title: Danielle Smith faces another leadership review call from UCP constituency board
body:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is facing another call for a leadership review from one of her United Conservative Party constituency boards.
Scott Cyr, a backbencher in Smith’s caucus, says the board of his Bonnyville-Cold Lake-St. Paul constituency association passed the motion Monday.
Cyr, in a social media post Tuesday, said it passed narrowly — 10 votes to nine — in a secret ballot.
But Cyr said he doesn’t agree with the outcome and that it’s time to rally behind Smith’s leadership.
“With the 2027 provincial election approaching, I am concerned about the consequences of continued internal division within the United Conservative Party,” he wrote.
Cyr’s riding is one of a few to recently call for a review of Smith’s leadership, while others have announced their support for her. The party’s annual general meeting in Calgary is one month away.
Mitch Sylvestre, president of Cyr’s constituency association, is a prominent face in Alberta’s separatist movement.
Smith is seeking to rein in separatist elements in her party ahead of the next election, set for October 2027.
Sylvestre and others behind the independence push have set their sights on ousting Smith as party leader over her support for keeping Alberta in Canada.
Last week, three-quarters of Alberta voters in a provincewide referendum affirmed they want the province to stay in Canada rather than hold a second, binding referendum on separation.
Smith called the referendum. She said it was necessary to quell a growing debate in Alberta over its role in Confederation. Critics said there was never such a groundswell of separatist sentiment and that Smith called the vote to appease UCP separatists and keep her job.
After the referendum, she promised there wouldn’t be another separation vote while she’s premier. She said the referendum had settled the debate.
She also urged in-house separatists to find a new home, but Sylvestre has said he’s not going anywhere.
Smith was expected to face questions on the topic later Tuesday, as the legislature was to begin its fall sitting.
The UCP has also lost a legislature member. Backbencher Shane Getson announced Monday he was quitting politics completely and immediately, citing unspecified personal reasons.
Smith’s party now has 46 seats in the legislature. The NDP has 39, and there is one Progressive Tory.

title: Trump reportedly considering lifting sanctions against Russia's investment fund
body:
U.S. President Donald Trump is considering lifting sanctions against Russia's government investment fund, the New York Times reported Oct. 27, citing an unnamed U.S. official.
The White House is assessing how sanctions may be lifted against the fund to improve bilateral relations with Moscow and help end Russia's war against Ukraine, the official said .
Russian officials have also pushed for U.S. sanctions against the investment fund to be lifted because of the financial structure's involvement with Trump's diesel deal with Russia, people familiar with the matter told the New York Times.
On Oct. 9, Trump said that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," he wrote on Truth Social.
The first ship carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel then set sail en route to New York, expected to arrive in early November, Reuters reported Oct. 23, citing London Stock Exchange Group data.
The Malta-flagged tanker loaded its cargo in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is set to arrive in the U.S. on Nov. 7, according to the outlet.
Ukrainian officials also fear the White House could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry , two people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent in an article published Oct. 23.
The proposal would fit an approach in which the U.S. offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war, one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 23 that a new round of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
On Oct. 25, Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled media that the Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day.
As the U.S. considers lifting sanctions, Russia continues to launch missiles and drone attacks against civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people have been injured in the Russian attack , Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.

title: JPost’s Election Day LIVE: Watch exit polls, analyses, and election updates across Israel
body: The Jerusalem Post is bringing you live election coverage from 9:30 p.m. on Tuesday, as Israel awaits the first indications of how the country has voted and what the results could mean for the next government.Our team is bringing you live analysis and discussion ahead of the release of the exit polls at 10 p.m., when Israel's major broadcasters publish their initial projections for the distribution of seats in the next Knesset. The projections will offer an early indication of how Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot have performed, and what coalition possibilities could emerge.The performance of smaller parties, particularly those near the electoral threshold, could prove significant in determining whether either political bloc can secure the support needed to form a government.Exit polls are projections rather than official results, and the political picture may change as votes are counted and verified throughout the night. The Post will continue to bring you real-time coverage of the results and their implications for Israel's political future.Watch the live broadcast above for the latest projections, reactions, and what the results could mean for the next government.

title: Air Force launches next phase of hypersonic missile program with $694M contract award for ARRW
body: The Air Force recently took a major step in its pursuit of hypersonic missiles, awarding Lockheed Martin a $694 million production contract for a boost-glide system that can be carried by B-52 bombers. The deal for the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon (ARRW) was awarded Sept. 29, according to a press release, although the service didn’t announce it until Monday. The announcement withheld key details about the contract, such as quantities of missile purchases and delivery dates, citing a need to protect “operational security.” The award is the latest turn in the saga of the ARRW program, which at one time seemed like it might not survive the budgetary axe following a series of setbacks during its development phase — including at least one failed all-up-round flight test that occurred in 2023 — and the prioritization of another initiative known as the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile (HACM). However, the program was revived, and officials requested funding from Congress in fiscal 2026 to start production. The award for the new production contract came in the final days of fiscal 2026. “This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said in a statement released Monday. “By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems.” The Pentagon has invested billions of dollars to develop hypersonic weapons. In addition to the air-launched ARRW and HACM, other hypersonic systems that the military is working to field include the Army’s ground-launched Dark Eagle and the Navy’s sea-launched Conventional Prompt Strike. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach said in a statement Monday that fielding ARRW will enhance the service’s ability to “hold targets at risk anywhere around the world” and provide the joint force with a “flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments.” In a press release issued Tuesday, Lockheed Martin said the system brings “sustained and maneuverable hypersonic capabilities to America’s Arsenal of Freedom and is the culmination of years of developmental and test partnership between Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Air Force.” Mark Gunzinger, director for future concepts and capability assessments at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies and a former deputy assistant secretary of defense, called the production contract award “a real turning point” for the Air Force and the Pentagon. The U.S. military needs an operational air-launched hypersonic weapon to create a future strike force capable of high-intensity warfare against peer adversaries like China, Russia, and others, he told DefenseScoop. “Frankly, hypersonic weapons is one such capability where China has stolen a march on the United States, and I think this announcement is a real milestone in that effort to catch up and maintain our advantage, technological advantage as well as operational advantages over China. That’s exactly what we need to do to deter possible conflict in the Pacific,” Gunzinger added. Hypersonics are intended to be highly survivable, he noted, “which is a combination of their speed and actual designs to reduce their signatures and so forth.” They would most likely be used against “fleeting” or “time-sensitive” targets, Gunzinger said, such as highly mobile and relocatable weapon systems like missile launchers, and command-and-control platforms. Carlton Haelig, a fellow in the Defense Program at the Center for a New American Security, said the movement of ARRW into production is “hugely” significant. “In general, it’s a big step forward because it provides a, you know, more diverse capability set, but particularly just in the Air Force trying to get itself established and having operational hypersonic weapons capability,” Haelig told DefenseScoop. Just a few years ago, the ARRW program appeared to be shelved, he noted. “They were indicating that they were not going to be moving it to operational use. They concluded its [research, development, test and evaluation] spending. There were some failed or unsuccessful tests, and they were kind of cutting their losses and moving on to other programs. Now, sometime between then and last year when the budget documentation came out … obviously things changed,” he said. “Obviously through their testing and evaluation, they’ve identified that they have a viable, safe and effective platform that they’re comfortable with moving into initial procurement.” Haelig noted that sometimes the military services keep programs in the research and development stage longer than they need to be, and that increases the costs associated with those programs and delays their eventual transition into the field and throughout the force. “So, this could also be the type of decision where they say, ‘Look, we have enough ready to go forward with the Block A variant of ARRW. It’s ready, it’s safe, it’s effective. It can be integrated onto the platforms. Let’s move forward with this, and we’ll continue to iterate on what might eventually be a Block B. We don’t need that Block B solution to get in the way of the Block A capability’ that they seem to have available to them right now,” Haelig told DefenseScoop. Gunzinger noted that ARRW systems will come with a relatively high price tag compared to many other types of munitions. His “informed guess” is that they’ll cost “well over $10 million a copy.” They’re not an “affordable mass munition,” in Air Force parlance, he said. “They’re not going to be a level-of-effort munition that you size their inventory for a large-scale air campaign. They are special capabilities to be used against the … highest value, critical targets that we absolutely need to destroy in order to take down an adversary’s A2AD network and disrupt their command and control, battlespace management operations, and so forth,” he said. The B-52 Stratofortress, which has already been used for ARRW testing, is well-suited to carry the missile, according to Gunzinger. “It’s obvious that the B-52 would be the initial aircraft for integrating this weapon into the Air Force’s arsenal. They’ll be the threshold aircraft because they are very large weapons, and they have to be carried externally because of that, and you would not want to obviously carry ARRW externally on … a B-21 [Raider] or, you know, another aircraft that is stealthy, because that would essentially really create a signature that’s no longer stealthy,” he said. The Stratofortress could potentially carry multiple ARRWs, according to Gunzinger, who said the B-1 Lancer could also carry the missile. Based on the size of the contract, he estimated that the Air Force is probably buying “dozens” of ARRW missiles with this new production deal but less than 100, depending on their exact cost. Haelig said the number of ARRWs being purchased with the new contract is “certainly not hundreds” but “definitely double digits.” He noted that some of the funding in the deal could be allocated toward starting up the production line, not just purchasing the actual missiles. “The Air Force has been really tight-lipped about the details at like the unit cost level and the planned buy inventory for this program, starting with last year when it first moved it into the procurement side of the budget. So, it’s really hard to put an estimate on there, and there’s very few, like, comparable systems to compare it to, to try and get a rough cost estimate,” he said. Haelig said the Army’s Dark Eagle hypersonic weapon is “a completely different system with much different procurement patterns and support systems,” and is “probably much more expensive than the ARRW would be.” Gunzinger also suggested that the ARRW would have a lower price tag than the ground-launched Dark Eagle. According to Army budget documents, the unit cost of an all-up round and canister for the Dark Eagle system in fiscal 2026 was nearly $37 million. However, the unit cost is expected to go down in the coming years. One of the advantages of air-launched hypersonic weapons is that developers don’t have to build them with rocket boosters large enough to get them from the ground or surface level to higher altitudes before their glide body separates, Gunzinger said. “You’re already at altitude and at speed when you launch a hypersonic weapon from an aircraft. So, that reduces the size and cost of air-launched hypersonic weapons. I think that dynamic is pretty important,” he added. It’s unclear exactly when the Air Force will field the ARRW. “I think the intent is to field these weapons and other hypersonic weapons as quickly as possible to restore our ability to deter China and other adversaries, as well as to prepare for contingency operations in the Pacific,” Gunzinger said. “So, I would hazard a guess, not knowing when the [initial operational capability] might be for the ARRW, but I would hazard a guess it’ll be this decade. It won’t be pushed into the 2030s. And of course, that’s not just a matter of how quickly the Air Force can complete testing and so forth with live rounds, but also how quickly Lockheed Martin can produce these weapons to reach an IOC threshold. But I suspect it’s going to be in a couple years, not another five to 10.” Haelig predicted that it will take “multiple years” to get them out to units at scale. The Air Force will have to train air crews and maintainers and prepare to integrate the system with the platforms that will be carrying the weapon, he noted. “Much of that can be done ahead of the actual production at scale of the munition, so that once the munitions start coming off of the production line and being delivered to operational units, those platforms are actually ready to use them and to actually field them. So, if those two tracks are going in parallel, you buy back a lot of time. But the big constraint still remains how quickly they’ll be able to produce that,” he said. In a press release issued Tuesday, Lockheed Martin said it has already funded “efforts, materials, and equipment required to start ARRW’s production, underscoring the company’s commitment to delivering this critical capability to the U.S. Air Force at speed and scale.” The company announced that it broke ground on an expansion effort for Building P-20 in Troy, Alabama, that will add 47,000 square feet of production space for the ARRW program. “The expansion will triple the current facility’s production space and generate new American jobs over the next four years,” according to the press release, which noted that the workforce will build ARRW using advanced manufacturing, robotics and digital technologies. title: X-Bow Systems to supply rocket boosters for U.S. Navy’s CHAOS cruise missile program
body: The missile is intended to engage land and maritime targets, giving allies a strike capability that reduces reliance on expensive legacy stockpiles. CoAspire described it as a mid-range maritime strike weapon and said its supplier network includes 56 first-tier companies across almost every state. The selection is X-Bow’s seventh new propulsion program in 2026, with awards spanning the Navy, Army and Missile Defense Agency. The company recently completed its first major production contract, delivering more than 2,100 combat-ready rocket motors. “Rebuilding the nation’s arsenal demands a fundamentally different industrial base,” said Jason Hundley, X-Bow’s founder and CEO. “Our digital-first manufacturing and proprietary Additive Manufacturing of Solid Propellant™ technology are built to deliver advanced, reliable systems at a cost and velocity the legacy industry can’t match.” X-Bow uses proprietary additive manufacturing technology to produce solid rocket motors for missiles, interceptors and space launch vehicles. The company says that approach allows it to expand production while keeping costs down. “CoAspire is thrilled to support the U.S. Navy with this much-needed, affordable, mid-range maritime strike weapon,” said Doug Denneny, CoAspire’s CEO, owner and founder. “We, and our 56 first-tier suppliers across almost every state, are excited to support PMX-201, NAVAIR, and our coalition partners with an affordable cruise missile solution.” X-Bow said its revenue and backlog have more than doubled since 2023. The company is headquartered in Albuquerque, New Mexico, and operates manufacturing and test sites across the United States.

title: Marine Corps fast-tracks AI-powered ultrasounds, blood coolers to battlefield
body: For the Marine Corps, one lesson to come out of Operation Epic Fury is a clear mandate to move faster on technology that might make battlefield injuries less lethal. And the service is doing just that, ramping up acquisition processes for two new devices, a portable smart ultrasound and a blood refrigerator, that promise to keep troops alive for longer at triage points. In a call with reporters this month, Col. Paul Gillikin, the Corps’ program manager for combat support systems, said he has been closely tracking feedback from Navy surgical teams and Marine Corps medical units deployed in support of the Iran fight and forward-based in the Pacific and elsewhere around the world. “I’m talking with maybe lieutenants running surgical centers; that’s the level of detail we’re getting to,” he said. “I’m talking to that lieutenant, lieutenant colonel over SIPR and NIPR [military networks] to find out exactly what they’re experiencing and how I can make their life better and how I can make operations and support better for them … it’s an all-engine stop affair.” And as a result of that direct feedback, Lt. Cmdr. Kyleigh Hupfl, the Marine Corps’ clinical lead for expeditionary medical systems, said the service is accelerating fielding of the Expeditionary Medical Refrigeration Unit, or EMRU, a compact 62-pound cooler that she said will be critical to establishing a field-ready blood bank operation for distributed units that may need to sustain themselves for longer periods of time before there’s a chance at medevac to a better-equipped hospital facility. It replaces a larger 140-pound unit that required far more manpower to transport and could sustain about 24 hours of refrigeration in ideal conditions, officials said. The EMRU, with rechargeable batteries, is designed for long-term sustainment of what officials call the “cold chain” for blood supplies in field environments. The officials who spoke with reporters said the concept of the Golden Hour, the first 60 minutes after a wound or injury, where triage care and limiting blood loss is critical for survival odds, is taking a backseat to a longer-term concept of care that ensures corpsmen can continue to limit hemorrhage and keep vitals strong with tools that might previously have been reserved for more established medical centers in the rear. “What we’re trying to get after with the equipment is identifying those things that are saving that life in that first hour and ensuring that they can be distributed, they can be applied, they can be carried on the back of a corpsman, and they’re supported logistically,” Hupfl said. “We need to be able to bring cold chain distribution forward without relying on heavy generators, and we need to be able to do that in a sustainable way,” she continued. “We need to be able to warm that blood so that we don’t get that patient in a worse-off situation, and we need to be able to see … whether they have continued bleeding, so that the commander can make a risk decision on putting an evacuation asset at risk to get that patient out.” With the EMRU, which can keep blood bags at a stable cold temperature, but also warm them if they freeze in Arctic conditions, units sent to the Middle East have received positive feedback from medical providers there, Hupfl said. “We were told that the gear was instrumental to their ability to maintain a revolving lead bank to ensure that they had what they needed to be ready to care for injured service members,” she said. An early rollout has now turned into a plan to push the refrigerator into full operational capability status across the Marine Corps, reaching full fielding by the second quarter of 2027, she said, with point-of-need units receiving priority treatment. “We want to get it as far out as we possibly can,” she said. Likewise, she said, a portable ultrasound device, the Kosmos, which allows corpsmen to conduct an AI-assisted fast exam in the field, has been greenlit for expanded fielding. While ultrasounds have traditionally been performed only by Role 2 medical units, or advanced mobile trauma units staffed by doctors, these devices are set to be pushed to Role 1 units, the smaller immediate-aid field units and embedded corpsmen who often provide the first care to patients. “We are not waiting, because we’ve heard that … the units want it now,” Hupfl said. Ease of use and the AI support, she said, enable the more basically trained corpsmen to operate the ultrasound with confidence. “Using the ultrasound probe is not the thing that’s the hard part, right?” she said. “What’s hard is you’re looking at an image, and you don’t know what it means. With the AI assistants, somebody who doesn’t have many years of clinical experience doing ultrasound can look at that screen, and it helps them to identify, ‘Hey, this is what I’m looking at, and there might there’s an injury here.'” Brig. Gen. Tamara Campbell, commander of Marine Corps Systems Command, suggested that these fielding initiatives are part of a greater effort that will move the Marine Corps further away from a three-tiered medical care system in which Role 3 — the military hospital — has often been the urgent and accessible destination. “I think that we need to understand that we will be in a contested environment,” she said. “And whatever we need to apply care to sustain that life until we can get them to a different point of care [will need to be] at that point of injury.”

title: ‘I'll act immediately to replace Netanyahu’: Eisenkot responds to Israel exit polls
body: Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar! party, vowed Tuesday night to act immediately to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government after Israel's election exit polls gave the bloc seeking political change a narrow advantage, although neither side secured the parliamentary majority needed to form a government. "The initial results indicate a complete vote of no confidence in Netanyahu and the government of October 7 by the Zionist majority and the majority of Israeli citizens," Eisenkot said, referring to the government in office during the Hamas-led attack on Israel.   "If these are the final results, this is a victory for the mainstream Zionist majority in Israel," he added. "I will act immediately to implement the people's decision, replace Netanyahu's government and establish a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible." The average of the exit polls published by Kan 11, Channels 12 and 13 gives the change bloc 53 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu's bloc. The Arab parties are projected to win a combined 17 seats, leaving neither of the two main political blocs with the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. Despite the narrow lead for Netanyahu's opponents, Likud is projected to remain Israel's largest individual party, setting the stage for potentially difficult coalition negotiations once the official results are known. Eisenkot's Yashar! projected to win 19 to 23 seats Eisenkot's Yashar! party is projected to win 21 seats in Kan 11's exit poll, 22 in Channel 12's and 23 in Channel 13's. The i24NEWS poll gives the party 20 seats, while Channel 14 projects 19. Across all five exit polls, the former military chief's party averages 21 seats, placing it among the country's largest political factions, behind Likud. Eisenkot, Israel's 21st IDF chief of staff, entered politics in 2022, three years after leaving military service. He joined Benny Gantz's National Unity alliance and was placed third on its electoral list.   Following the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's emergency wartime government alongside his party and served as a minister without portfolio. On December 7, 2023, his son Gal was killed in combat in the Gaza Strip. In June 2025, Eisenkot announced his departure from National Unity. Two months later, he established Yashar!, which subsequently emerged as a leading party in opinion polls ahead of Tuesday's election. In recent months, Eisenkot did not rule out forming a minority government with outside parliamentary support from Ra'am and potentially some members of the Joint List. However, Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman rejected that possibility, saying he would not agree to such an arrangement. With the exit polls showing no outright majority for either main bloc, that disagreement remains a significant obstacle to assembling a governing coalition. Yair Golan: ‘The public has fired Netanyahu's government’ Democrats leader Yair Golan, a retired IDF major general who has expressed support for a government including Ra'am, also welcomed the exit poll results, describing them as an opportunity to replace Netanyahu. "The public has spoken. It has fired Netanyahu's government," Golan said. "We have been given a historic opportunity to establish a genuine government of change in Israel, and we have no intention of giving it up." "We represent an enormous public that has fought in the streets for four years, joined the party and gone out into the field to persuade voters," he continued. "We will do everything we can to ensure that such a government is formed." Golan said his party was prepared to cooperate with other political factions to overcome disagreements and establish a new coalition. "We are ready to work with all our partners, bridge the gaps and take responsibility," he said. "The public has spoken. Now it is our turn to do the work." Sa'ar: ‘The left is celebrating too early’ Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar, a senior Likud figure, offered a sharply different interpretation of the exit polls, warning Netanyahu's opponents against treating the projections as a victory. "The celebrations on the left are premature," Sa'ar said. "According to the exit polls, one thing appears fairly clear: Likud is the largest party in Israel." His remarks highlighted the central uncertainty emerging from the projections. Although the change bloc holds a narrow lead over Netanyahu's allies in the average of the three main exit polls, Likud remains the largest single party, and neither bloc has enough seats to govern independently. The final balance could still change as votes are counted, particularly with hundreds of thousands of special double-envelope ballots from soldiers, diplomats and other eligible voters requiring separate verification. Election officials have warned that the count could continue into Friday morning. Even after the final results are published, President Isaac Herzog will need to consult the elected parties before deciding which lawmaker has the best prospect of forming a government. For Eisenkot and his allies, the projections represent an opening to replace Netanyahu. For Likud, its position as the largest party provides grounds to challenge claims of an opposition victory. The immediate question is not simply which bloc finishes ahead, but whether any candidate can assemble the parliamentary support needed to govern.

title: Putin holding talks with Libyan Presidential Council chairman
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding talks with visiting Chairman of the Libyan Presidential Council Mohammad al-Menfi, a TASS correspondent reports.
