title: Wontumi allegedly targeted in attempted poisoning in prison – Palgrave
body: A senior aide to former Ashanti Regional Chairman of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Bernard Antwi-Boasiako, popularly known as Chairman Wontumi, has alleged that some prison inmates attempted to poison the politician. Dr Palgrave Boakye-Danquah explained that Mr Wontumi had informed him of the alleged incident when he appeared in court on Tuesday, adding that prison authorities had initiated investigations to establish the facts. “Chairman is okay. We haven’t received any medical reports from the doctors. But I have received indications that over the past week, some prison inmates attempted to poison him,” Dr Boakye-Danquah told Accra-based Citi FM as Mr Wontumi marked 100 days in prison. He stressed on Tuesday, October 27, that investigations were underway to verify the allegation. “And so I’ve been informed that there are some investigations that are ongoing to make sure that they verify the truth or otherwise of that,” he added. Dr Boakye-Danquah said he had also spoken to the prison commander, who assured him that the matter was being investigated. “He mentioned that to me today when he came to court, and I have spoken to the commander, and the commander said he has asked them to investigate the matter, so he will come back to me on that issue. This attempted poisoning of his life happened a few days ago,” he said. However, Dr Boakye-Danquah said no medical report had been received in connection with the claim, and the circumstances surrounding the alleged attempt remain under investigation.

title: CCT Chairman Proposes Transformation into National Anti-Corruption Court
body: The Chairman of the Code of Conduct Tribunal (CCT), Dr Mainasara Umar Kogo, has expressed concern that many Nigerians occupying positions of authority appear unaware of their constitutional responsibilities, warning that the pursuit of personal interests continues to undermine national development. Kogo made the remarks while discussing corruption, leadership and the challenges facing Nigeria’s public institutions. He called for stronger institutional mechanisms, improved legal frameworks and a renewed commitment to patriotism, discipline and responsible public service. According to him, public office should be regarded as a responsibility to serve citizens rather than an opportunity for personal enrichment. He maintained that no public official was inherently more important than an ordinary Nigerian and stressed that public resources belonged to the people. Kogo said that diverting even a single naira from public funds constituted a serious moral offence, emphasising the need for integrity among individuals entrusted with public responsibilities. The CCT chairman expressed optimism that corruption could be addressed in Nigeria but argued that existing institutional structures and legal frameworks needed to be strengthened. He also stressed the importance of ensuring that those responsible for adjudication and public administration demonstrated patriotism and discipline. On the tribunal’s ability to prosecute politically exposed persons, Kogo explained that its current powers were limited by the existing legal framework. He said the Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB) was responsible for investigating and prosecuting cases brought before the tribunal, while the Attorney-General also possessed constitutional prosecutorial powers. He noted that the tribunal could not independently determine who should be prosecuted, as it was restricted to handling cases presented through established legal procedures. Kogo disclosed that a proposed legislative reform was intended to address these limitations by allowing anti-corruption agencies to bring relevant cases before the tribunal, regardless of the status of the individuals involved. He also proposed transforming the Code of Conduct Tribunal into a National Anti-Corruption Court with a broader mandate to handle corruption-related cases. Under the proposal, anti-graft agencies and civil society organisations would be able to prosecute relevant cases before the proposed court. The proposal also includes establishing about seven judicial divisions and recruiting 37 additional judges to expedite the handling of corruption cases. Kogo said he had appealed to the Attorney-General of the Federation and the President to consider adopting the bill as an executive bill to facilitate its passage by the National Assembly. He further identified issues such as certificate forgery, falsification of records, academic plagiarism, dual citizenship and foreign bank accounts as matters that could require legal scrutiny beyond asset declaration, subject to the applicable legal framework. Reflecting on Nigeria’s governance challenges, Kogo expressed concern about the declining purchasing power of citizens and the difficulties many households face in meeting their basic needs. He said the country’s economic circumstances had weakened the ability of many Nigerians to afford essential goods and services. He also lamented what he described as an erosion of nationalism, national cohesion and patriotism, arguing that individual interests were increasingly taking precedence over the collective welfare of the country. According to him, Nigeria needs more statesmen who prioritise national development and the welfare of future generations rather than focusing primarily on acquiring political power and wealth. Kogo called on the National Orientation Agency (NOA) to strengthen its role in promoting national unity, patriotism, responsible citizenship and public service. He also discussed the challenges he encountered upon returning to the tribunal as chairman, describing an institution that had deteriorated considerably. He said the building lacked reliable electricity and water supplies, its lifts were not functioning, security was inadequate, and essential working materials were unavailable. Kogo said he had taken steps to restore electricity, provide water through boreholes, improve security and commence renovations. He also highlighted staff development initiatives, the resolution of outstanding promotions and efforts to pay retirement entitlements to former employees. According to him, approximately 70 to 80 per cent of affected retirees had received their entitlements, with some having waited as long as two decades for payment. He added that new allowances and welfare measures had been introduced for staff, alongside a 13th-month salary bonus intended to boost morale and improve productivity. However, Kogo said inadequate funding continued to constrain the tribunal’s operations. He disclosed that the institution received an average of between ₦26 million and ₦28 million in overhead funding, with releases sometimes delayed by two or three months. He also said he had not received any capital allocation since assuming office. To address some of the resource challenges, he said he had approached international donor agencies and other institutions, which provided computers, laptops, printers, photocopiers and other equipment. Kogo also disclosed efforts to recover properties allegedly disposed of by previous tribunal leaderships. He said a property in Wuse II, Abuja, had been recovered following the intervention of the FCT Minister, Nyesom Wike, while another property in Bauchi, which had allegedly been converted into a commercial plaza, had also been recovered. He said the tribunal was seeking funds to renovate the properties and restore them to official use. Kogo maintained that his priority was to establish a functional institution capable of operating effectively beyond his tenure, adding that public officials should focus on fulfilling their responsibilities rather than pursuing personal recognition.

title: What’s next for the BC NDP? Veteran MLA says party must ‘listen and learn’
body:
Following the snap provincial election on Saturday in which the BC Conservatives won a strong majority, many are questioning what is next for the BC NDP.
David Eby resigned from his position as BC NDP leader on Saturday.
BC NDP MLA for Vancouver-Renfrew, Adrian Dix, said Eby took responsibility for calling the election.
“The snap election had a number of effects,” Dix said.
“First of all, it blotted out every other issue. So we want to talk about health care. We have a significant advantage on health care, people support our public health care position, but we couldn’t get the issue beyond the snap election, whether it was that or car insurance or any of the issues we wanted to talk about.”
Dix said the election also demobilized their supporters who didn’t vote because they were responding to an election that they did not see was necessary.
“I’m not going to get into who said what to who here,” he said.
“I think very clearly, if you’re going to call an election in B.C., where every election is close, everyone is close… you’re putting the government and the project at risk. You have to have a very strong and compelling reason to do that. And the voters told us very explicitly we didn’t.”
Dix said they still have people in the BC NDP who want to work and hold the newly-elected BC Conservative majority government to account.
“But we also have to listen and learn,” Dix added.
“We can’t draw all the conclusions now, we gotta go talk to our members and people, especially people in areas that didn’t vote NDP.”
Dix said that includes Surrey and south of the Fraser River, to the Tri-Cities and the B.C. Interior.
He said they have to pick a new leader for their party but they also need time to reflect on what happened and why.
“We’ve had nine years in government,” Dix added.
“There were really significant successes, but there were things that we didn’t achieve as well. And I think this is the opportunity to do that. We’ve got to get to work. I think people voted for a Conservative government last Saturday, but 38 per cent of them voted NDP, and they want a strong opposition, and we’re going to deliver that.”
Dix said in 2001, the BC NDP suffered the biggest loss in the party’s history.
“We came back from that,” he said. “But we can only do that if we listen, we engage, and we do our job as an opposition.”

title: President Zelensky accepts letters of credence from ambassadors of five countries
body:
Zelensky announced this on Facebook , Ukrinform reports.
According to the President, these are different countries with different relationships with Ukraine, but each is important to the country.
“We value the diplomatic presence in Kyiv, alongside our people. Last night, the ambassadors experienced Russian ballistic missile strikes, saw the destruction, and indubitably understand how much Ukraine needs help in protecting lives. Supplies and the strengthening of our air defense – from Patriots to HAWKs – all of this matters every single day,” Zelensky stressed.
The President and the ambassadors discussed efforts to achieve peace and Ukraine’s European integration.
“We also talked about Russia’s blockade of the Black Sea and the food crisis it is already causing in countries that rely on Ukrainian grain. And of course, we discussed current bilateral issues with all the ambassadors,” Zelensky said.
As reported by Ukrinform, Zelensky appointed Vasyl Hamianin as Ukraine’s ambassador to the Gabonese Republic.

title: Early progress on accelerating drug development with Claude
body:
Anthropic’s life sciences team is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: BigHat Biosciences , Bristol Myers Squibb , Divergence Labs , Enveda , Generate Biomedicines , and The Column Group . We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here .
There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like proposing initial designs for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.
Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.
So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.
This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.
In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.
Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering. Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more , and see Generate’s technical report .
Divergence Labs: hit generation. Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more , and see Divergence’s technical report .
BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization. BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more , and see BigHat’s technical report .
Enveda: manufacturing and filings. To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more , and see Enveda’s technical report .
The Column Group (TCG): company creation. Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more .
More recently, we’ve also begun working with Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.
Michael Pourdehnad, MD , Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy.
In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see our technical report .
All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly preclinical— that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.
This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out Claude Science , our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing Claude credits for life scientists . We’ve also created the Life Sciences Verification Program to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an open call for guest investigators in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.
We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.
If you work at an organization focused on drug development and would like to get in touch, complete the following form.

title: Researchers are getting tired of OpenAI gatekeeping its breakthroughs
body:
On Monday, OpenAI announced impressive breakthroughs in mathematics, computer science, and physics, along with what the company says is an evolving approach to communicating its findings. But despite its apparent course correction, researchers who spoke to The Verge are growing increasingly tired of the company’s antics.
It has been a turbulent few months between OpenAI and mathematicians, who are still grappling with the hundreds of preprints unceremoniously dumped on them at the start of October. This time, OpenAI says it is working with expert “shepherds” to decide how best to share its latest breakthroughs.
All three results concern some of the most consequential unsolved problems in mathematics, computer science, and physics. Some extend OpenAI’s previous work and others break new ground. Following advice from OpenAI’s “shepherds,” each has a different release strategy. For the mathematics result, OpenAI released the AI-generated output, “leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.” For its computer science finding, OpenAI will also assemble an external group of researchers “to explain the result.” Physics, meanwhile, has not been released at all, and OpenAI said it will “defer” to an external group of experts about how to release the materials.
* The mathematics result appears striking. It purports to resolve the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions. Roughly speaking, the problem asks how little space is needed to rotate a needle or pencil in every direction. A proof of the three-dimensional version was among the achievements for which NYU mathematician Hong Wang was awarded a prestigious Fields Medal earlier this year. Brown University mathematics professor Brendan Hassett told The Verge OpenAI’s claim “looks well supported,” though he stressed he had not yet checked the Lean formalization, a means of computationally verifying results.
* The physics result explores the Standard Model, the most successful and complete theoretical framework in physics. It concerns quantum chromodynamics, which describes the strong nuclear force, one of nature’s four fundamental forces (alongside gravitational force, electromagnetic force, and weak nuclear force) and its relationship to Yang-Mills theory, a cornerstone of modern particle physics. Yang-Mills theory is also at the heart of one of the seven Millennium Prize problems in mathematics, though OpenAI’s work does not address the unresolved “mass gap.”
* The final result claims to disprove the exponential time hypothesis, a widely held assumption in theoretical computer science that certain problems cannot be solved substantially faster than brute-force approaches. It is closely related to P versus NP, another Millennium Prize problem and one of the field’s biggest unsolved problems, which asks whether problems whose solutions can be easily checked are also easy to solve.
Given the varying levels of disclosure and the complexity of evaluating such work, it is difficult for researchers to fully judge the company’s findings. Even with all of the information, doing so would take time. But experts who spoke to The Verge said there are good reasons to take the results seriously, variously describing them as “huge,” “major breakthroughs,” and “significant.”
But researchers’ excitement about the science was tempered by exasperation with OpenAI’s conduct, a familiar feeling after months of what they describe as an exhausting barrage of AI-generated findings. Many were eager for the wider community to get on with the arduous task of scrutinizing the AI lab’s findings and questioned why OpenAI was putting up additional barriers by handpicking experts to oversee the process.
Most experts The Verge spoke to welcomed OpenAI’s decision to consult outside researchers, but argued that publicly announcing results should also mean making that work available for anyone to scrutinize. “I am fine with them releasing the problems as they did today,” said Constantin Kogler, a researcher at the Institute for Advanced Study, welcoming the more manageable batch of three results compared with the hundreds released previously. But he questioned the decision to restrict access to experts of OpenAI’s choosing. “It doesn’t make any sense that first only a few distinguished scientists can look at them,” he said.
“The fact that they handpick the group is a disaster,” Andreas Karch, a physics professor at the University of Texas at Austin, told The Verge. “The large labs have enough power as it is. They should not be picking winners and losers.” Karch initially suggested selecting researchers through a “competitive process,” though he acknowledged it would likely produce a similar group, which he described as “first rate.” Later, he questioned why OpenAI “can’t release the proof now,” in addition to appointing its team of experts. “This would democratize access while still showing that they care about making the results meaningful and understandable,” he said.
It is exactly the kind of gatekeeping the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence (AGMAI), a group of experts OpenAI had previously pledged to consult on how to share its findings, warned against just a day before the announcement. “We recommend that AI companies do not adopt this practice,” they said, arguing that selecting certain people to receive the output first is “unnecessary,” borrows the reputation of selected researchers, and risks unequal access, biased selection, and delays, among other issues. Instead, they recommended that AI labs release output on scholarly repositories, with formalized proofs and information on how the problems were chosen, and provide funding and other support for people working on understanding the results.
Following the publication of the latest results, AGMAI urged OpenAI to “make public without delay the natural-language and Lean outputs behind its announced” results in physics:
> ”While these are central questions in physics, they are also important questions in mathematics. The existence of quantum Yang–Mills theory is part of a Millennium Prize problem and the construction of interacting quantum field theories in four dimensions has been a goal of mathematical physics for decades.
> We have great respect for the scientists asked by OpenAI to lead this work. But as we explained in our recent statement, understanding should develop in the open, with everyone given the same access. OpenAI have said they delayed release until the Lean formalization was complete. By their own account this is now complete, so there is no scientific reason for delaying the release any further.”
Making the findings openly available could also lead to better science and encourage wider adoption of new tools like AI, Hassett said. “Having many groups around the world wrestle with these results supports rapid adoption of new tools by those that would like to use them,” he said.
Finding a way to communicate with researchers in the fields OpenAI is increasingly encroaching on that satisfies everyone may be impossible. The company says it is experimenting with different approaches and acknowledges that each has tradeoffs. “My sense is that for any approach, there is going to be someone who is upset,” said Stanford mathematician Jared Duker Lichtman. “So it’s just a question of finding the least offensive option.”
Xiaoyu He, a mathematics professor at the Georgia Institute of Technology, thinks the problem is deeper than how OpenAI chooses to announce its findings. ”The results are very impressive,” he said, “but I think they are making a show of trying to be responsible and thoughtful about how they release results while not being able to change the main issues: that fundamental results are being solved so quickly without human contribution, and that the papers are difficult to read and verify.”

title: Raspberry Pi Zero 3W and Pi 4 Model A spotted in device trees
body:
Two new Raspberry Pi boards have quietly turned up in Raspberry Pi’s Linux kernel tree, and neither of them is quite what I’d have guessed. Device tree files for a Raspberry Pi Zero 3 W and a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A have landed ( Phoronix also spotted it ), and whilst there’s no official announcement just yet, device tree files tend to give away a surprising amount if you can decipher them and I gave it my best shot.
The Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W launched almost exactly five years ago (tomorrow, in fact), so a successor has been a loooooong time coming. If you want a refresher on where things stood back then, my Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W benchmarks piece covers the jump from the original pretty well.
The headline from the Zero 3 W device tree is the SoC. It’s the Broadcom BCM2711 , the same quad-core Cortex-A72 chip that powers the Raspberry Pi 4 , replacing the Zero 2 W’s quad-core 1GHz Cortex-A53 RP3A0. If you want an idea of the sort of gap we’re talking about, it’s worth having a look at how those two compare on sbc.compare . That’s a big step up in per-core performance, and if they can get anything close to Pi 4 clocks in that tiny footprint, it’ll be a hell of a lot of compute for a Zero. I do wonder how toasty it’s going to get though, as the BCM2711 isn’t exactly known for running cool, and there’s not a lot of board for the heat to spread into. The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about clock speeds, so we’ll have to wait and see whether it’s been dialled back.
Beyond the SoC, here’s what else stood out to me:
There are a couple of more speculative bits too. The PCIe controller is enabled and there are lines named PCIE_PWR_EN and PCIE_DET_WAKE, and the camera side pulls in a 4-lane CSI configuration rather than the 2-lane one the Pi 4 Model B uses. It’s worth noting that both device trees share a lot of copy-and-paste DNA (the Zero 3 W even has a duplicated “PWR_GPIO” line name), so I wouldn’t read too much into either of those until we see an actual board. I’d love to see PCIe exposed on a Zero, but I’m not holding my breath.
The second surprise is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A . We haven’t had a Model A since the Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+ back in 2018, and the formula has always been the same: take the Model B, strip out the bits most people can live without (RJ45, some USB ports etc), and knock a chunk off the price. The Pi 4 Model A looks to follow that recipe pretty closely, though the price comment may not quite hold. Let’s see!
The device tree doesn’t tell us anything about USB. On the Model B, the USB 3 ports made use of the PCIe bus, and the PCIe controller is enabled here too, so USB 3 is possible, but the 3 Model A+ only had a single USB-A port and I’d probably expect the same here.
Here’s a quick side-by-side of what the device trees tell us, with the Pi 4 Model B thrown in for good measure. Anything marked with an asterisk is my interpretation of the device tree rather than something it states outright.
Quite a lot, I’m afraid. Device trees don’t describe RAM, so there’s no word on memory configurations, and there’s nothing on pricing, clock speeds, connector types or a release date either.
Pricing is the big one for me. Memory costs haven’t exactly been kind lately (I covered the last round of increases alongside the 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 launch ), and a lower-cost Pi 4 variant makes a lot of sense in that context. The BCM2711 is a mature chip at this point, it’s well supported in software, and a cut-down board gives people who don’t need a Pi 5 something cheaper to reach for. The Zero 3 W is a tougher one to call though, as the Zero range has always lived and died by its price, and I can’t imagine the BCM2711 being as cheap to build around as the RP3A0.
On the whole, I like what I’m seeing here. The Zero 3 W looks like the upgrade a lot of people have been asking for since the Zero 2 W landed, and the 4 Model A feels like a sensible way of squeezing more life out of the Pi 4 platform at a time when components aren’t getting any cheaper. The external antenna support on the 4 Model A is a really nice touch if it makes it to the final board.
Saying that, everything above comes from device tree files rather than an official spec sheet, so mileage may vary when the real thing turns up. Kernel support landing ahead of launch is usually a good sign that it’s not far off, and you can bet I’ll be throwing both the Zero 3 W and the 4 Model A onto sbc.compare as soon as I can get one in my hands.
Which of the two are you more excited about? Do let me know in the comments!
Sources bcm2711-rpi-zero-3-w.dts bcm2711-rpi-4-a.dts
Related posts: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W vs Zero W Benchmarks – Pi Zero Showdown – 1GB Raspberry Pi 5 Launched Alongside Price Increases
Bret has worked with Raspberry Pi computers for almost 10 years now and in that time he's benchmarked and tested over 30 Single Board computers. In his day job, he's a systems administrator for a large cloud computing provider.
I have to think that one of the main numbers, figuring into Zero-based projects, is power consumption. I sure hope they aren’t doing with the Zero 3W what they did with the RPi5.

title: I built 18 free agent skills (and the tools behind them run in your browser)
body: Most "AI agent skills" I've tried either do too little or want network access for everything. So I built a set of small, zero-dependency Node tools that each do one audit-type job — and packaged them as SKILL.md skills so any compatible agent can use them. All free: https://github.com/NenadZivotic/lite-agent-skills (17 skills) + https://github.com/NenadZivotic/secret-leak-scan-lite The security set Skill What it does secret-leak-scan-lite Scans files for leaked credentials — AWS keys, GitHub/Slack tokens, private key blocks git-history-leak-check-lite Same, but for diffs — only added lines are scanned docker-security-lint-lite Top-5 Dockerfile mistakes: root user, baked secrets, :latest , `curl {% raw %} ci-cd-security-audit-lite GitHub Actions risks: unpinned actions, pull_request_target + checkout of PR head, secrets in run: http-header-audit-lite Missing security headers in a pasted response cors-misconfig-check-lite Dangerous CORS combos — wildcard+credentials, null origin, reflected ACAO jwt-inspector-lite Decode a JWT locally, claims masked, expiry status env-config-audit-lite .env vs .env.example parity — values are never printed Plus non-security ones: har-to-api-map-lite , broken-link-crawl-lite , seo-quick-audit-lite , geo-audit-lite (AI-search readiness), npm-package-health-lite , github-repo-due-diligence-lite , video-repurpose-engine-lite , contract-triage-lite , cold-email-sequence-lite , meta-prompt-architect-lite . Why lite? Every skill is a cut-down but fully working version — not a demo. The lite tools run offline, take files/stdin, and print JSON. If you want the full version (more rules, more file types, report formats), each README links to it — but nothing nags you. Try them without installing anything I also ported the paste-in tools to run entirely in the browser — same logic, no upload, you can verify in DevTools that nothing leaves the page: JWT decoder Secret leak scanner Dockerfile security lint Security headers checker CORS config checker GitHub Actions security audit .env parity checker AI-search readiness audit Install npx skills add NenadZivotic/lite-agent-skills --skill secret-leak-scan-lite Each skill folder has SKILL.md + scripts/ + tests. No dependencies beyond Node 18+. If any of these save you an audit — a star on the repo helps more than you'd think. What would you lint/audit that isn't covered yet?

title: Code as Norm: Algorithmic Governance and AI Ethics
body:
Posted on Oct 27 • Originally published at dobrepanstwo.org
The article analyzes the transition from traditional legal and social norms to technical architecture, where code becomes a form of ex ante behavioral control. The author argues that algorithms are not neutral but rather implement specific conceptions of the good encoded in their objective functions. Drawing on the thought of Michael Sandel and Chinese concepts such as Jilin (mechanical heart-mind), the text points to the risk of human instrumentalization and the loss of the internal goods of professional practices. The main thesis is that technocracy does not replace value conflicts with calculations, but rather hides political philosophy within system specifications. Consequently, a teleological analysis of AI is essential to prevent moral depersonalization and excessive optimization at the expense of dignity and interpersonal relationships.
