title: How Hubtel is rethinking AI in Ghana: Own your data, rent the intelligence
body: From the trader at Makola checking prices on her phone to the graduate in Kumasi searching for work, one question is getting louder across Ghana. Will artificial intelligence make life better, or will it take away what people already have? Ghana has placed its bet. In 2025 it launched a ten-year national AI strategy, and government has committed $270 million to get the country ready. But for ordinary Ghanaians, the most useful answers may come from a local company that has already tried, stumbled and found a smarter way forward. That company is Hubtel . Head of Engineering, Augustine Adjei, told the national audience during the premiere of the AI & Ghana’s documentary on Joy News, exactly what Ghana’s AI journey looks like from the inside, and why the country does not need to start big to win. About the Digital Economy Forum The Digital Economy Forum is a national thought-leadership platform conceived by Hubtel to create evidence-based conversations about the technologies, policies and ideas shaping Ghana’s economic future. It combines original documentary storytelling with a televised debate on JoyNews and Joy FM, bringing together government, regulators, businesses, academics and everyday Ghanaians. The maiden edition tackled digital fraud and why trust matters in Ghana’s growing digital economy. The latest edition asked a bigger question: AI and the Ghana economy, opportunity or disruption? For Hubtel, which helps Ghanaians pay bills, send money and order goods, the stakes are personal. A digital economy only grows when people trust it, understand it and can benefit from it. The forum is Hubtel’s way of making sure that conversation happens in public, with the facts on the table and ordinary people in the room. Opportunity or disruption? Both, says Hubtel Asked whether AI is good or bad news for Ghana, Augustine Adjei refused to pick one side. “It is both,” he said. “Growth is hard and painful, but the disruption is a setback while the opportunity is exponential.” He compared it to a catapult. You get pulled back first, and that painful pull is what launches you forward. Change will hurt in places, but those who prepare will move faster than ever. When Hubtel tried to build its own AI Hubtel opened an AI lab in 2023, before chat apps like ChatGPT became part of everyday life. It hired skilled Ghanaian engineers to build AI from scratch. The lab’s biggest project helped the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) catch power theft. The system flagged meters that seemed not to be paying, traced back through the records and connected the dots. Hubtel also built its own fraud detection and call-centre tools. Then the world moved faster and cheaper. By 2025, global AI companies were selling far more powerful tools for about $20 to $25 a month. Hubtel did what any smart trader does when a better product appears at a lower price. It stopped trying to outbuild the giants and started buying access. Talent Isn’t the Problem Augustine Adjei explained the decision with a picture every Ghanaian understands. “Would you want an Italian chef to cook your fufu and light soup, or an equally competent Ghanaian chef who has lived here all their life?” he asked. The answer is obvious: the Ghanaian chef. But training that chef takes time and money. Until then, you hire the chef who can feed you today while you plan for tomorrow. He was clear that Ghana’s problem has never been brains. “Talent is equally distributed; resources are not,” he said. Hubtel had the people. What it did not have was the hundreds of millions of dollars global firms spend on AI. Own your data, rent the engine Hubtel did not just sign up for a free chatbot. It negotiated directly with leading global AI companies, which were surprised a Ghanaian firm could pay at that level. Under the deal, Hubtel runs the AI inside its own systems, keeps full ownership of its data, and the providers have promised not to use Hubtel’s information to train their models. Augustine Adjei summed up the rule simply: “Own what you can before you scale.” He also shared a funny but serious warning. When Hubtel tested a free AI model and asked it about the company, the model said Hubtel was headquartered in Kigali. AI only knows what you teach it, so Ghanaians must feed it Ghanaian facts. The best example of this thinking is Hubtel’s virtual call centre. Because so many Ghanaians transact on Hubtel every day, the phones ring constantly. An AI agent now answers first and can check a customer’s order status on the spot. It works because all the information it needs already belongs to Hubtel. It is built in Ghana, trained on Ghanaian data and speaks to customers in a Ghanaian accent. For Augustine Adjei, that is the point. “AI is not a thing, it is us. There is no AI without humans,” he said. “If we are biased, AI will be biased.” Honorable Sam George backs the Hubtel approach Communications Minister of Ghana, Honorable Sam George said Hubtel’s story shows why Ghana must fix its data first. “AI models are only as good as their data sets,” he said. Hubtel had found no simple way for companies in Ghana to share data. The Minister said government is building a national data exchange hub to connect about 48 public registries, from the Ghana Health Service to the National Identification Authority, so developers make one request instead of 48. Companies are welcome to join, as long as they contribute data too. On jobs, he echoed Hubtel’s message that people must grow with the technology. “Those who evolve and adapt will survive,” he said. “Those who fail to evolve and adapt will fall off.” Bright Simmons of Imani Africa, the night’s toughest critic of government spending, held up Hubtel as an example of doing AI in the right order: use a proven global tool first, then build local. “If you don’t define your problem extremely well, AI can’t give you answers,” he warned, adding: “We should not stay on the surface.” Five lessons for every Ghanaian You do not need to be a tech company to learn from Hubtel. Whether you run a chop bar, a boutique or a small office, the same rules apply: Start with what you already have. Your customer list, your records and the way you work are your biggest AI asset. Use what works today. Global AI tools are cheap and powerful, so use them while local options grow. Guard your information. Keep control of your data and know where it goes. Teach the AI about Ghana. If a tool thinks Hubtel is in Kigali, it can get your business wrong too. Think before you upload. Augustine Adjei said his phone holds his 74-year-old mother’s medical record, and he would not run it through a public chatbot without protection. Ghana’s AI future will not be decided by one big announcement. It will be shaped by businesses and individuals who test, learn, adjust and keep going. Hubtel has shown a practical path for the whole country: own your data, rent the engine, solve real problems for real customers and keep your people learning. Through the Digital Economy Forum, it is making sure every Ghanaian gets to hear that conversation.

title: Netanyahu’s party is first in Israel’s elections, but opposition bloc winning more seats
body:
TEL AVIV, October 27. /TASS/. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party is set to win 25 seats in Israel’s 120-seat parliament, according to an exit poll results released by the state-run television channel Kan-11 after the polls closed.
Netanyahu’s key rival from the opposition, Gadi Eisenkot and his Yashar party, are second, winning 21 seats.
Meanwhile, the poll results suggest that the opposition bloc is outstripping the current ruling coalition with 53 seats vs 50 seats of Netanyahu’s bloc. Arab parties are winning 17 seats, but neither the Likud bloc nor the opposition are ready to form a coalition with them, according to forecasts.
Neither of the political forces is getting 61 seats required to forma a ruling majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

title: “It’s always been more of a friendship than music” – King Promise on his relationship with Mr Eazi
body: Ghanaian Afrobeats and Highlife singer-songwriter King Promise says his relationship with Nigerian singer and entrepreneur Mr Eazi has always been built on genuine friendship rather than music, revealing that the two have known each other for more than a decade. Speaking in an interview with Lexis Bill on Joy FM’s Drive Time on Tuesday, October 27, King Promise said their friendship dates back to around 2012, before either of them had a hit song. He recalled that he was still in school when they met, while Mr Eazi was working on his first mixtape, About to Blow , which preceded his breakthrough in music. “For us, it’s always been more of a friendship even than music,” King Promise said. He explained that the two rarely collaborated musically in the early stages of their relationship, but when they eventually made songs together, the results travelled far. “We barely made songs till we made songs. And then whenever we made them, they went far,” he said. King Promise said he values friendships that are not built around what the people involved can gain from each other professionally. He cited his relationships with music group R2Bees and rapper Sarkodie as similar examples, noting that he had known them for years before they worked together on songs. “I try to keep genuine friendships where it’s not because you need me and I need you,” he said. Beyond their friendship, King Promise credited Mr Eazi with influencing his outlook through his honesty, confidence and approach to business. “The influence he’s had on me is that he keeps it a thousand percent. He’s very real and straightforward, direct to the point. If he says yes, it’s yes and if he says no, he says no,” he said. He added that Mr Eazi’s confidence in his work and success in music had also inspired him, particularly when he was still establishing himself as an artiste. King Promise recalled watching Mr Eazi thrive in the industry while they exchanged ideas in the studio. “I was still coming when he was already flying. And that alone was a lot for me, like my guy is smashing it,” he said. The Terminator hitmaker also praised Mr Eazi’s business instincts, saying their conversations sometimes extend to investment opportunities, including stocks. He described Mr Eazi as a businessman whose entrepreneurial interests predated his music career. Mr Eazi, he explained, initially worked as a promoter and booked artistes before venturing into music and later establishing a record label. “It was business that even got him into music,” King Promise said, adding that his friend was a “forward thinker”.

title: AI as a Detector, Not a Decision-Maker
body: Designing Scribe AI’s live path: offline speech recognition, rule-based scripture detection, and a human approval step that keeps a wrong guess off a church screen. Scribe AI listens to a church service and tries to catch scripture references as they are spoken — “turn with me to John chapter three, verse sixteen” — so the verse can be put on screen without a volunteer scrambling to type it. It is a small system, but it operates in an unforgiving environment: whatever it gets wrong is projected in front of the whole room. Two constraints shaped nearly every design decision: the system must keep working without the internet, and nothing it detects should reach the screen without human approval. Offline Is a Requirement, Not a Feature In the settings Scribe is designed for, a dropped connection in the middle of a service is ordinary, not an edge case. So everything in the live path runs locally against local data: microphone capture, speech recognition, detection, Bible lookup, and display. There is no network call anywhere in this path. Speech recognition uses Faster-Whisper’s small model on the CPU, quantised to int8, with greedy decoding (beam_size=1) and voice-activity filtering to skip silence. Audio is captured at 16 kHz and transcribed in five-second chunks. These are deliberate trade-offs for the kind of laptop a church production desk actually has: a smaller, faster model designed to keep up with speech, rather than a potentially more accurate one that falls behind it. Offline operation is not simply a convenience. If the internet connection fails during a service, the system should still be able to do its job. Rules, Where Rules Are Enough It would have been easy to reach for a learned model to find scripture references in the transcript. I did not, because the detection problem does not require one. Spoken references tend to follow a limited number of patterns. The detector covers four common forms: John 3:16 John chapter 3 verse 16 John 3 16 John 316 The last example matters because speech recognition can compress a spoken reference into a run of digits. The patterns match against all 66 Bible book names and common abbreviations. Each match is then checked against the actual number of chapters in that book. For example, Genesis 60 is rejected because Genesis has only 50 chapters. That validation is particularly important for compressed references, where the detector must decide where the chapter number ends and the verse number begins. The benefit is not accuracy for its own sake. It is inspectability. When the detector fires—or fails to fire—the logic behind the decision can be examined. There is no confidence score, and I have not pretended there is one. The detector checks whether a reference is valid according to its rules. This is a useful reminder that not every component in an AI system needs to be another learned model. Sometimes a small, explicit rule set is easier to understand, test, and maintain. References Don't Respect Chunk Boundaries A preacher does not pause neatly every five seconds. “John chapter three” might land at the end of one audio chunk, while “verse sixteen” arrives at the beginning of the next. If each chunk were processed independently, the detector could miss the complete reference. To address this, when a chunk produces no detection, the system carries the last 60 characters of its transcript forward and prepends them to the next chunk. When a chunk does produce a detection, the carried text is cleared to reduce the chance of detecting the same reference twice. It is a small implementation detail, but it reflects a broader engineering problem: real-time systems have to account for the difference between how data is processed and how events actually occur. The audio arrives in chunks. Human speech does not follow those boundaries. The Approval Step A detected reference never goes straight to the screen. Instead, it appears in an operator console: a separate, always-on-top window where a person can approve the detection, dismiss it, or type a reference manually. Only an operator's action—approving a detection or entering a reference themselves—puts a verse on the display. This is the system's answer to a simple question: What happens when the AI is wrong? A misheard reference costs the operator a click. Without the approval gate, it could mean displaying the wrong verse in front of an entire congregation. Manual entry is equally important. The operator is never dependent on the detector. If the system misses a reference, the service can continue without waiting for the AI to recover. The implementation also separates audio processing from the user interface. Audio capture and transcription run on a background thread, while the console and display belong to the Tkinter UI thread. The audio thread never manipulates the interface directly. Instead, it schedules work on the UI thread with root.after, helping prevent the two threads from interfering with the same widgets. The design principle is broader than this particular application: automating detection does not require automating the final decision. Being Clear About What Is Not Connected Scribe also contains a service-state machine—keyword rules that track whether the service is in worship, sermon, prayer, or announcements—and a lyric detector that fuzzy-matches transcript text against a song library. Both are implemented and tested. Neither is connected to the live microphone path yet. They run together in a separate pipeline driven by simulated text. That distinction matters. It would be easy to describe the modules the system contains and leave readers with the impression that everything operates live. But having a working module is not the same as integrating it into the complete application. There are other limitations, too. The lyric matcher's threshold has only been tested on clean text, and the song library contains placeholder data. These limitations belong in the description of the system, not in a footnote. A clear account of what works, what has been tested, and what remains disconnected is more useful than a broader claim that the implementation cannot yet support. What Comes Next There are three main priorities for the next stage of Scribe AI: Build a real-world evaluation set. Use recordings from actual services, including accents, crosstalk, and music, to measure detection performance under the conditions the system will encounter. Integrate the separate pipelines. Create one live entry point that includes service-state tracking and lyric detection, replacing the split between the live path and the simulated pipeline. Make speech recognition interchangeable. Introduce an interface that allows other models—including models better suited to African languages—to be swapped in and compared fairly. These steps move the project beyond demonstrating that its components work in isolation and towards evaluating how well the complete system performs in practice. The Model Is Not the Whole System The general lesson I keep returning to is this: the most important design decision in an applied AI system is often not the model. It is where the model's output is allowed to go, what happens when that output is wrong, and who gets to say no. In Scribe AI, speech recognition proposes what it heard. Rules check whether a scripture reference is valid. A human operator decides whether the verse reaches the screen. That separation is intentional. In a live environment where an incorrect output is immediately visible to everyone in the room, a useful AI system is not simply one that produces answers quickly. It is one designed to handle uncertainty without taking control away from the person responsible for the outcome. Project: Scribe AI — an offline-first system for detecting scripture references during church services, with human approval before display.

title: I Built a Tarot Website, Is My UX Good on Desktop and Mobile?
body: Building a website is one thing. Making it intuitive for people who have never visited it befo re is something completely different. I've been working on Arcanio.xyz, an online tarot and Arcana platform where people can explore tarot readings, card meanings, spreads, and their personal Arcana. One question I've been thinking about lately is whether my website offers the right user experience across different devices. For example, is it okay for the desktop version of a website to look almost the same as its mobile version? Should a desktop layout use the available screen space differently, or is keeping the design consistent across devices a better approach? I'd love to hear honest feedback from developers, UX designers, and anyone interested in web design. What Is Arcanio? Arcanio.xyz is an online tarot platform designed to make tarot exploration accessible to beginners and experienced enthusiasts. A traditional tarot deck contains 78 cards, each with its own symbolism and interpretations. Learning about the cards, understanding different spreads, and exploring their meanings can be fascinating, but it can also feel overwhelming to someone who is just getting started. Arcanio brings several aspects of this experience into one digital platform: Online tarot readings: Explore tarot through a digital reading experience. Tarot card meanings: Learn about the symbolism and traditional interpretations of the cards. Personal Arcana: Discover a personal tarot profile and explore its associated symbolism. Personalized results: Receive results in PDF format where available. Educational content: Read guides about tarot cards, spreads, and different ways to approach readings. You can explore the project here: https://arcanio.xyz/ I've also been publishing educational articles on the Arcanio blog to help visitors understand tarot and explore its different traditions. However, building useful features is only part of creating a good product. People also need to understand how to use them. The UX Challenge: Designing for People Who Are New to Tarot One of the challenges of creating a tarot website is that visitors have different levels of experience. Some people already know the difference between the Major and Minor Arcana. They might arrive looking for a particular card meaning or a specific reading spread. Others might simply search for a free tarot reading without knowing anything about tarot. These visitors have different needs. Experienced users may want quick access to features, while beginners may need clear explanations and guidance. If the interface assumes too much knowledge, new visitors may become confused. If it explains everything before allowing people to interact, the experience might feel unnecessarily complicated. My goal with Arcanio is to make the first visit straightforward. Ideally, someone should quickly understand what the website offers, where to start, and what they can expect from the experience. But there's another UX question that interests me just as much: how should this experience change depending on the device? Should a Desktop Website Look Like Its Mobile Version? This is one of the design decisions I'd particularly like feedback on. A mobile-first approach makes sense for many websites. Starting with a small screen encourages you to prioritize important information, simplify navigation, and avoid unnecessary interface elements. That doesn't mean a desktop website must look completely different, though. Consistency can be valuable. Keeping the same visual identity, familiar controls, and recognizable navigation patterns helps people understand a product regardless of the device they use. For a website like Arcanio, maintaining the same dark visual atmosphere, typography, colors, and overall design language across mobile and desktop makes sense to me. However, visual consistency and identical layouts are not the same thing. A phone has limited horizontal space, so stacking content vertically is often the most practical solution. A desktop monitor offers much more room, which creates opportunities to organize information differently. For example, three tarot cards might appear vertically or in a compact arrangement on a phone, but sit side by side on a desktop. Navigation could use a full menu on larger screens while remaining compact on mobile. The same principle applies to content. A blog article should remain comfortable to read on a desktop rather than stretching across the entire monitor, even if the overall page uses more horizontal space. This raises an interesting question: when does keeping a mobile-style layout on desktop become a usability problem? If a layout stays narrow in the center of a large monitor, it might feel unnecessarily constrained. If it fills the screen but stacks every element vertically, visitors might have to scroll more than necessary. On the other hand, simply making everything wider isn't automatically better. Excessive text width, scattered interface elements, and poorly balanced spacing can create new problems. For Arcanio, I want the design to remain recognizable across devices while taking advantage of the space each screen provides. I'm still interested in where other developers and designers would draw that line. Visual Design Is Not the Same as Usability Tarot has a strong visual identity, which makes design an important part of the experience. Colors, typography, illustrations, spacing, and imagery can help a website feel connected to its subject. A dark, atmospheric interface with carefully presented tarot artwork can create a more coherent experience than a generic interface with cards added as decoration. But an attractive website isn't necessarily easy to use. A visitor might enjoy the design but struggle to find the main feature. A button might look beautiful without clearly communicating its purpose. An interface might work perfectly for its creator but confuse someone who encounters it for the first time. That's why I'd like to evaluate Arcanio beyond its appearance. Can a first-time visitor understand the purpose of the website within a few seconds? Is the primary action easy to find? Does the navigation make sense? Does the mobile experience feel natural, and does the desktop version use its available space effectively? These questions are difficult to answer objectively when you already know how everything works. What I'd Like People to Test If you visit Arcanio.xyz, I'd appreciate feedback on several aspects of the experience. First impressions Open the homepage as if you've never heard of Arcanio. Can you immediately explain what the website does? Is the value clear, or do you need to explore several pages before understanding the product? I'd particularly like to know whether the visual design communicates both the tarot theme and the practical purpose of the platform. Desktop layout Visit the website on a laptop or desktop monitor. Does the layout use the available space well? Does anything feel too narrow, too stretched, or unnecessarily stacked vertically? Would you keep the layout mostly consistent with mobile, or introduce different arrangements for larger screens? I'm especially interested in practical suggestions rather than simply making the desktop version look different for the sake of it. Mobile usability Try the website on a phone if possible. Are the buttons easy to tap? Is the text readable? Does navigation work naturally? Do any sections feel too crowded or require too much scrolling? A responsive design should adapt to different screen sizes without making the experience feel like a completely different product. Navigation and discoverability Try to find a feature you'd naturally want to use. Are the navigation labels understandable? Can you find the reading experience without guessing? Is important information easy to discover? You can also explore the Arcanio blog to see how the educational content fits into the wider website. The beginner experience Imagine you've never used tarot before. Would you know where to start? Are the explanations clear enough? Does anything feel intimidating or unnecessarily complicated? I'd like the platform to feel approachable even to visitors who don't know the traditional meanings of the cards. Accessibility and performance If you have experience with accessibility or frontend performance, I'd welcome those observations too. Are contrast levels comfortable? Is the interface usable with a keyboard? Are there any responsive-layout issues worth investigating? Does the experience feel smooth on different devices? I haven't independently verified every one of these areas, so I don't want to assume that the website already gets them right. What I'm Trying to Improve My goal isn't simply to make Arcanio look more modern. I want to reduce friction between someone arriving on the website and understanding how to use it. That means thinking about information architecture, responsive design, content hierarchy, accessibility, performance, and the language used throughout the interface. It also means recognizing that different visitors have different goals. Someone looking for an immediate reading may need a different path from someone researching The High Priestess or learning about the Major Arcana. Both should be able to find what they need without unnecessary steps. I also want to avoid adding interface elements just because desktop websites traditionally have them. A sidebar, larger menu, or wider layout should solve a real problem rather than simply fill empty space. At the same time, I don't want to limit the experience by treating every screen as if it were a phone. The challenge is finding the right balance between consistency, simplicity, and making effective use of the available space. How Would You Improve Arcanio? I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from developers, designers, and UX enthusiasts. You don't need to be interested in tarot to evaluate the website. Someone unfamiliar with the subject might actually notice assumptions that experienced tarot users would overlook. Here are a few questions I'd love to discuss: What's the first thing you'd improve on the homepage? Is the primary action obvious enough? Should the desktop version use a substantially different layout from mobile? Does the website balance visual atmosphere with usability? What would make the beginner experience clearer? Are there any accessibility or responsive-design issues you'd investigate? What would you simplify, remove, or reorganize? Specific criticism is more useful than simply hearing that the website looks good. If something is confusing or feels unnecessary, I'd rather know so I can improve it. You can visit Arcanio.xyz and share your observations in the comments. Final Thoughts Building Arcanio has reminded me that creating a product isn't just about implementing features or writing code. It's also about understanding how people experience what you've built. Developers become familiar with their own interfaces. We know where every button leads, what every label means, and how each feature is supposed to work. New visitors don't have that context. The same applies to responsive design. A layout that feels natural on a phone might not be the best arrangement for a desktop, even if both versions use the same visual style. I believe the best approach is to preserve a consistent identity while adapting the layout to the needs of each screen. But I'd like to hear how other people approach this in practice. I'm continuing to develop Arcanio and want to make the experience better with each iteration. Try Arcanio and Share Your UX Feedback I'd love to hear from developers and designers who can look at the project with fresh eyes. Explore Arcanio — an online tarot and personal Arcana platform. Try the experience and tell me what you'd improve about its U... Questions for the community What would you change about the desktop layout? Would you keep the mobile layout mostly consistent on desktop, or use a wider layout with different card arrangements, navigation, and content sections? What matters most in a first-time user experience? Would you prioritize a clearer main call to action, simpler navigation, more onboarding, or a different homepage layout? Is the visual design helping usability? Does the dark, mystical tarot aesthetic make the experience more engaging, or would you simplify parts of the interface to make the main features easier to discover? Project: https://arcanio.xyz/ Blog: https://arcanio.xyz/blog Honest, constructive feedback is welcome. Thanks for taking a look!

title: Find Your Next Apartment with Search API: A London and San Francisco Guide
body: TL;DR To build an apartment finder with the Valyu Python SDK, turn a renter's requirements into neighbourhood-specific searches with valyu.search() , retrieve rental pages with their source links, merge duplicate URLs, and review individual listings before shortlisting them. This tutorial builds a Python and Streamlit tool for London and San Francisco , including weekly-to-monthly rent conversion and a downloadable shortlist. The finished tool lets you: Search selected rental websites from one brief. Read the returned evidence and open the original listing. Enter the advertised rent and confirm the details that matter. Download your research, notes and reviewed shortlist. You'll need Python 3.11 or later, as required by the pinned Streamlit 1.66.1 release , and a Valyu API key . We use the official Valyu SDK for search; you don't need a separate language-model API key. The apartment looks great. Then you read the listing. You find a flat that seems to fit your budget. The photographs look good. The location looks promising. Then you notice the price is per week , not per month. Or you're looking in San Francisco, and the advertised price is an effective average after a move-in concession. The monthly base rent is higher. Another promising result is a room in a shared apartment, even though you need the whole place. You now have tabs open across several websites and a notes app full of half-remembered addresses. Let's build something that helps with that specific job: find rental pages worth investigating, keep the evidence together, and produce a shortlist you can use to arrange viewings. We'll work through two searches. The budgets and neighbourhoods below are example inputs, not claims about market averages or guaranteed availability. Requirement London example San Francisco example Home Entire one-bedroom flat Entire one-bedroom apartment Monthly base-rent ceiling £2,200 GBP $3,200 USD Areas to investigate Stratford, Lewisham, Finsbury Park Inner Sunset, Inner Richmond, Bernal Heights Example move-in date 1 December 2026 1 December 2026 Commute to check King's Cross Embarcadero Another question Does the landlord accept a cat? What is the pet policy, including any extra charges? The app lets you change these inputs. It defaults the move-in date to 30 days from the day you run it. How does an apartment discovery tool work? An apartment discovery tool converts a rental brief into searches across relevant websites, then collects the returned pages for review. Valyu Search API supplies ranked results with source URLs and extracted text. Your application manages the renter's requirements, duplicate URLs, price calculations, review state and shortlist. A search result starts the investigation. The reviewed listing determines whether you should contact the advertiser. Our first version has a simple path: Rental brief → One web search per neighbourhood → Source-linked candidate pages → Listing review and rent normalization → Downloadable shortlist For London, the source configuration includes OpenRent, Rightmove and Zoopla. For San Francisco, it includes Zillow, Apartments.com and the San Francisco Bay Area Craigslist domain. These are example web-search filters, not direct inventory integrations or a promise that every website will return accessible results. Keep the vocabulary local. A London query should include “flat to rent” . A San Francisco query should include “apartment for rent” and the city name. Country targeting adds context, but the query still needs the city and neighbourhood. Step 1: Set up the Python apartment finder Create a project and install the Valyu SDK and Streamlit: mkdir apartment-finder cd apartment-finder python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate python -m pip install valyu == 2.13.2 streamlit == 1.66.1 Add a .gitignore before storing credentials: .env* .venv/ __pycache__/ *.pem *.key credentials.* secrets.* shortlist-*.json Set VALYU_API_KEY in the environment of the terminal that will run the app. In Bash or zsh on macOS or Linux, this reads the key without displaying it or putting its value in your shell history: read -s VALYU_API_KEY export VALYU_API_KEY Paste the key at the prompt and press Enter. Keep it in the Python server process, not in browser JavaScript. Step 2: Search rental websites with the Valyu SDK The Valyu Python SDK reads VALYU_API_KEY automatically. Call valyu.search() with search_type="web" and the rental domains you want to investigate. The SDK handles the HTTP request and returns typed results. Save this as first_search.py and run it with python first_search.py : from valyu import Valyu with Valyu () as valyu : response = valyu . search ( " 1 bedroom entire flat to rent in Stratford, London under GBP 2200 per month. " " Move in 2026-12-01. Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms. " , search_type = " web " , country_code = " GB " , included_sources = [ " openrent.co.uk " , " rightmove.co.uk " , " zoopla.co.uk " ], max_num_results = 10 , ) if not response or not response . success : raise RuntimeError ( response . error if response else " Search did not complete. " ) for listing in response . results : print ( listing . title , listing . url ) print ( listing . content ) For San Francisco, use a query such as: 1 bedroom entire apartment for rent in Inner Sunset, San Francisco under USD 3200 per month. Move in 2026-12-01. Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms. Change country_code to US and use the San Francisco domain list from the code below. Putting a budget in a query is not the same as enforcing a numeric price filter. Search can return an area page, a building with multiple units, or a listing that doesn't meet every requirement. We apply the budget after reviewing a specific listing's price. We also avoid a blanket start_date filter. It filters publication dates, which aren't the same as move-in dates or confirmed availability. A page's publication date can be missing, and an older listing may have been updated. Step 3: Search rental websites and preserve the evidence Save this as rental_search.py . The two market profiles supply the local vocabulary, currency, example areas and source domains. discover() reuses one Valyu client for up to three neighbourhood searches, keeps source text and dates, and merges repeated URLs. It records failures separately so a failed search doesn't silently look like an empty neighbourhood. import math from datetime import datetime , timezone from urllib.parse import parse_qsl , urlencode , urlsplit , urlunsplit from valyu import Valyu MARKETS = { " London " : { " country " : " GB " , " currency " : " GBP " , " budget " : 2200 , " areas " : " Stratford, Lewisham, Finsbury Park " , " domains " : [ " openrent.co.uk " , " rightmove.co.uk " , " zoopla.co.uk " ], " home " : " flat to rent " , " destination " : " King ' s Cross " , }, " San Francisco " : { " country " : " US " , " currency " : " USD " , " budget " : 3200 , " areas " : " Inner Sunset, Inner Richmond, Bernal Heights " , " domains " : [ " zillow.com " , " apartments.com " , " sfbay.craigslist.org " ], " home " : " apartment for rent " , " destination " : " Embarcadero " , }, } def monthly_rent ( amount , period ): if not isinstance ( amount , ( int , float )) or isinstance ( amount , bool ): return None if not math . isfinite ( amount ) or amount <= 0 or period not in ( " month " , " week " ): return None return amount * 52 / 12 if period == " week " else amount def clean_url ( url , domains ): try : p = urlsplit ( url ) host = ( p . hostname or "" ). lower () if p . scheme not in ( " http " , " https " ) or p . username or p . password : return None if not any ( host == d or host . endswith ( " . " + d ) for d in domains ): return None params = [( k , v ) for k , v in parse_qsl ( p . query , keep_blank_values = True ) if not k . lower (). startswith ( " utm_ " ) and k . lower () not in ( " gclid " , " fbclid " )] return urlunsplit (( p . scheme , p . netloc . lower (), p . path , urlencode ( params ), p . fragment )) except ( ValueError , TypeError ): return None def discover ( brief ): market = MARKETS [ brief [ " city " ]] rows , receipts = {}, [] with Valyu () as valyu : for area in brief [ " areas " ]: query = ( f " { brief [ ' bedrooms ' ] } bedroom entire { market [ ' home ' ] } in { area } , " f " { brief [ ' city ' ] } under { market [ ' currency ' ] } { brief [ ' budget ' ] } per month. " f " Move in { brief [ ' move_in ' ] } . Individual long-term rental listings, not rooms. " ) observed_at = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ). isoformat () try : response = valyu . search ( query , search_type = " web " , max_num_results = 5 , country_code = market [ " country " ], included_sources = market [ " domains " ], response_length = " short " , include_image_links = False , ) except Exception as exc : receipts . append ({ " query " : query , " error " : type ( exc ). __name__ }) continue if not response or not response . success : receipts . append ({ " query " : query , " error " : response . error if response else " Search did not complete. " , " tx_id " : response . tx_id if response else None }) continue receipts . append ({ " query " : query , " tx_id " : response . tx_id , " warning " : response . error , " warnings " : [ w . model_dump ( mode = " json " ) for w in response . warnings or []], " returned " : len ( response . results )}) for hit in response . results : url = clean_url ( hit . url , market [ " domains " ]) if not url : continue if url in rows : if area not in rows [ url ][ " found_for " ]: rows [ url ][ " found_for " ]. append ( area ) continue rows [ url ] = { " title " : hit . title , " url " : url , " original_url " : hit . url , " source " : hit . source , " content " : hit . content , " found_for " : [ area ], " publication_date " : hit . publication_date or None , " retrieved_at " : observed_at , " rent " : 0.0 , " period " : " unknown " , " whole_unit " : False , " available " : False , " fits_brief " : False , " notes " : "" , } return { " brief " : brief , " rows " : list ( rows . values ()), " receipts " : receipts } def reviewed_shortlist ( rows , budget ): selected = [] for row in rows : rent = monthly_rent ( row [ " rent " ], row [ " period " ]) if ( rent is not None and rent <= budget and row [ " whole_unit " ] and row [ " available " ] and row [ " fits_brief " ]): selected . append ({ ** row , " monthly_base_rent " : round ( rent , 2 )}) return sorted ( selected , key = lambda row : row [ " monthly_base_rent " ]) There are two useful details here. First, source can simply be "web" . Keep the original URL as well, because that's how the renter gets back to the advertiser. The code also keeps tx_id values from successful responses for debugging. Second, URL deduplication is deliberately modest. Removing utm_ tracking parameters can merge repeated links to the same page. It doesn't establish that two different URLs describe the same apartment. The code preserves other query parameters and URL fragments, such as #unit-2 , because they may identify different units. New candidates start with an unknown rent period and unchecked confirmations. We don't extract the first price from a multi-property page and attach it to an arbitrary apartment. Step 4: Add the search and shortlist interface Save this as app.py in the same folder. The interface collects a rental brief, shows the returned source text, and provides a review table. Once you've checked a specific listing, enter its base rent and payment period, then confirm that it is the whole unit, available for your dates, and fits your other requirements. import json from datetime import date , timedelta import streamlit as st from rental_search import MARKETS , discover , reviewed_shortlist st . set_page_config ( page_title = " Apartment discovery " , layout = " wide " ) st . title ( " Find your next apartment " ) st . caption ( " Search London or San Francisco. Review the source, then build your shortlist.
