title: The weakest part of every survey job is the delivery. So we built our own
body:
A South African fixed-wing LiDAR operator on why gigabytes of finished survey data still reach clients as a download link, and what changed when they stopped sending it that way.
We fly fixed-wing drone LiDAR for a living, mostly in South Africa. The flying has become remarkably good, and processing gets faster every year. Yet for a long time our jobs still ended the same way: a download link, a 4 GB LAZ file, an orthomosaic too big for any photo viewer, and a client phoning to ask which program opens it.
Most of our clients are not GIS people. They are farmers, engineers, mine managers, developers and municipal officials. They want to see their site, measure something and pass it on to the next person. A folder of GeoTIFFs lets them do none of that. The last step of the job, the one the client actually sees, was the one that looked least professional.
We have done all four. None of them is a delivery a client remembers for the right reasons.
SurveyDeliver started as our own delivery page. We upload the files we already export from our processing software: GeoTIFF orthomosaics and elevation models, LAS/LAZ point clouds, shapefiles, DXF, GeoPackage and KML. The client gets one link with our logo on it: a map they can measure on, a 3D view of the point cloud, and every file to download. Nothing is installed on either side. In October we opened it to other operators.
What the client opens: the viewers, the downloads and the survey details, under the operator’s own logo. Picture: SurveyDeliver.
The part I would point other operators to first came out of our own mistakes. A site exported in the wrong UTM hemisphere lands thousands of kilometres from where it should be, and you find out when the client phones. Now each file is read on the surveyor’s own computer before anything is uploaded: the coordinate system is found, the footprint is drawn on a map and anything wrong is said in plain words. A file with no coordinate system gets a list to choose from on the spot.
Local grids matter here. South Africa’s south-oriented Lo systems, UTM zones and US State Plane all land where they should, and the client reads coordinates in the project’s own grid.
On the map: distances, areas, spot heights, ground profiles and stockpile volumes; a swipe to compare any two layers; a printable sheet with a title block; exports to KML, CSV and DXF in the project’s grid. In 3D: the aerial image draped over the shape of the ground, the point cloud coloured by height, class or intensity, and cross-sections. And every original file, for whoever needs it next.
The client’s map: the aerial image with contours and the drainage lines, each layer switched on and off in the Layers menu. Picture: SurveyDeliver.
A cross-section drawn across a vineyard in 3D, the point cloud coloured by class, with the chart below. Picture: SurveyDeliver.
From the terrain model the service works out slope, where rain water runs, where it ponds and the wettest ground, each with a key in plain words. These have turned out to be what clients ask about most: a farmer looking at where water sits after rain, an engineer checking drainage before a design. The operator chooses which ones each client sees.
Where rain water runs and where it ponds, worked out from the terrain model, with the key. Picture: SurveyDeliver.
A 2.4 GB orthomosaic was ready for the web in 11 minutes, a 242 million point cloud in 3 minutes 20 seconds and a 2.6 GB surface model in 15 minutes. Uploads of several gigabytes carry on where they stopped if the line drops, and can be sent straight from the processing computer overnight. It works from DJI Terra, Pix4D, Agisoft Metashape and WebODM, and from any GIS or CAD package that writes those formats.
It does not process imagery or LiDAR. You bring finished deliverables from the software you already trust, and the data stays yours. It is simply the last step of the job, done properly.
A real delivery, a LiDAR survey with a 5 cm orthomosaic, is open to anyone at surveydeliver.io/sample . There is a 14-day trial with no card needed at surveydeliver.io . Plans start at US$29 a month, and accounts started by 30 November 2026 get 30% off their first three months on monthly billing.
Charlie Wijnberg is a LiDAR operator and GIS data specialist at 3DroneMapping, a fixed-wing drone LiDAR survey company in South Africa that built SurveyDeliver for its own deliveries first.

title: State Police: Presidency Tasks Private Sector To Develop Comprehensive Funding, Implementation Blueprint
body: Deji Elumoye in Abuja The Presidency has tasked organised private sector in the country to develop a comprehensive financing and implementation blueprint for the proposed state police system. It stated that businesses must take an active role in building the security institutions required to protect investments, create jobs and strengthen economic resilience. Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, who gave the challenge, particularly charged the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG), chambers of commerce and business associations with producing practical proposals for financing, institutional management and accountable partnerships to support the decentralisation of policing. According to him, the private sector has a direct stake in the success of the reform because insecurity was already imposing enormous costs on businesses through disrupted supply chains, abandoned investments, postponed factory expansions and lost economic opportunities. Speaking during a plenary session on “Security, Stability and Economic Resilience” at the 32nd Nigerian Economic Summit in Abuja, Gbajabiamila said President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to establishing state police presented an opportunity for businesses to contribute directly to the development of security institutions capable of supporting sustainable economic growth. “I therefore ask the Nigerian Economic Summit Group to carry this engagement beyond our meeting. Bring forward a considered private sector contribution on financing and implementing state police, with practical proposals for accountable partnerships. “Take that work into the legislative process and into your engagement with state governments. For our part, we remain answerable for turning reform into protection that people can rely on,” he said. Gbajabiamila urged business leaders to engage governors and legislators on the proposed reform, drawing attention to the relationship between effective local policing, employment generation and investment decisions. He explained that the experience of businesses in managing institutions, controlling expenditure and assessing risks could strengthen the design and implementation of the new policing framework. According to him, the organised private sector should also provide evidence of security failures preventing otherwise viable investments from proceeding, enabling policymakers to determine where additional security capacity was most urgently required. “His words: “Your participation should also improve the substance of the reform. As the legislative process proceeds, examine the proposals for financing and oversight. “Bring your experience of managing institutions and controlling expenditure to that discussion. Help us understand the security failures that prevent viable projects from proceeding.” The Chief of Staff, however, cautioned that private sector involvement must be transparent and should never compromise the independence of police institutions. He said businesses could contribute expertise in communications infrastructure, equipment maintenance and financial planning, but insisted that such partnerships must operate within clearly defined legal and accountability frameworks. “Where businesses provide resources, those contributions need published accounts and independent scrutiny. “Public funding must remain dependable, and a donation must never purchase influence over an investigation or preferential treatment. The object is to strengthen a public service on which every citizen can rely,” he warned. Gbajabiamila explained that the administration was determined to establish financially sustainable state police institutions, insisting that states seeking to operate their own services must demonstrate the capacity to meet recurrent expenditure obligations. According to him, providing vehicles, uniforms and other equipment at the commencement of operations would be insufficient without sustainable arrangements for personnel salaries, professional training and operational maintenance. “Financial readiness is equally important. A state taking on policing must be able to sustain the service after the initial purchase of vehicles and uniforms. “Regular pay and continued training are essential to professional conduct. An institution that cannot meet its obligations to its officers becomes vulnerable to private patrons and unlawful demands on the public,” he cautioned. The Chief of Staff assured that federal policing would continue in states not yet financially or institutionally prepared to establish their own police services. Providing an update on the legislative process, Gbajabiamila confirmed that 24 State Houses of Assembly had approved the constitutional amendment providing for state police as at October 23, 2026 meeting the required two-thirds threshold. He disclosed that the Presidential Working Group had submitted the draft National Policing Bill and 29 consequential amendment bills to the Federal Ministry of Justice on October 19 for legislative review. According to him, after the review and the Working Group’s final consideration, the proposals would be presented to President Tinubu for approval before transmission to the National Assembly. He explained that the proposed framework would enable willing and capable states to assume greater responsibility for protecting their residents, while retaining a strong federal police institution to address interstate criminal activities and other specialised national security requirements. Gbajabiamila said the reform was intended to correct the structural imbalance under which state governments were responsible for responding to the consequences of insecurity without possessing corresponding authority to organise policing. “Bringing policing closer to the communities it serves can improve local intelligence and shorten the time between a call for help and an effective response,” he explained. Addressing concerns about the possible deployment of state police against political opponents, he assured Nigerians that the proposed legislation would contain enforceable safeguards, national professional standards and independent oversight mechanisms. “The concern that police powers could be used against political opponents or vulnerable communities is serious. Our answer is to place enforceable limits on those powers and provide remedies when they are abused. “A citizen’s entitlement to protection cannot depend on whom he supports or where she comes from,” the Chief of Staff declared. He said the framework had benefited from consultations with state governments, security institutions, members of the public and a Policy Advisory Committee drawn from the public and private sectors. Explaining why businesses should champion the reform, Gbajabiamila said insecurity affected investment decisions far beyond the immediate financial burden of hiring private security personnel. Said he: “The cost of the present arrangement is already in your accounts. You pay for additional security and disrupted deliveries. “You also bear losses that never appear as a separate charge: a factory expansion postponed, or a productive location excluded from your investment plans.” He argued that companies could not guarantee sustainable operations merely by securing their premises while surrounding communities remained unsafe. According to him: ‘A company can reinforce its perimeter. Its workers still have to travel home, and its suppliers still have to move through the surrounding communities. “Your long-term security depends on the strength of public institutions beyond your gates.” Turning to the administration’s wider security interventions, Gbajabiamila said President Tinubu had supported the modernisation of the Armed Forces through the induction of helicopters into Army Aviation and the restoration of more than 100 refurbished armoured fighting vehicles to active service. He recalled that the President commissioned three additional naval vessels in June to strengthen maritime security, noting that sustained operations against crude oil theft had contributed to improved oil production, foreign exchange earnings and government revenues. On food security, the Chief of Staff disclosed that the deployment of 10,000 Agro-Rangers across 19 states and the Federal Capital Territory was helping to integrate agricultural production with security protection. He explained that the administration recognised that investments in improved seedlings, agricultural credit and other support programmes would achieve little without guaranteeing farmers’ access to their land. “Improved seedlings and access to credit will achieve little on farmland that its owners are afraid to cultivate. Protection makes those agricultural interventions usable,” he said. Gbajabiamila also highlighted the Presidential Forest Guards Initiative, under which more than 7,000 personnel drawn from seven frontline states had completed training by December 2025 to support security operations in areas exploited by criminal groups. He disclosed that President Tinubu had directed the preparation of a National Threat Assessment and a rolling five-year Strategic Defence Operations Plan in August to improve coordination, align security spending with operational priorities and strengthen institutional accountability. Acknowledging that Nigerians continued to face threats of kidnapping and violent attacks despite government investments in security, he said the administration recognised that its achievements must ultimately be measured by the safety of citizens. “Nigerians living with the threat of abduction or attack are entitled to judge us by their own safety. We recognise the distance between an improvement in national capacity and dependable protection in every community.” The Chief of Staff further linked the administration’s security interventions with its economic reform programme, including fuel subsidy removal, foreign exchange restructuring and tax reforms. He acknowledged that the reforms had imposed considerable pressure on households and businesses but maintained that economic productivity and security were mutually dependent. “A government with inadequate revenues cannot sustain the institutions required to protect its citizens. An economy in which people cannot work safely cannot generate the revenues government needs. “We have therefore had to address both problems together, even as the costs of transition have placed considerable pressure on Nigerian households and businesses,” the Chief of Staff explained. Gbajabiamila urged investors to respond to improving security conditions by returning to communities where commercial activities had been disrupted, arguing that renewed investments would create employment, restore local supply chains and expand public revenues. He assured business leaders that the administration welcomed constructive criticism and practical recommendations, stressing that President Tinubu’s willingness to confront longstanding structural challenges required sustained cooperation from all stakeholders. “A farmer returning to his land and an employer reopening a business will be making decisions about their families’ futures. Our work together must give them sound reasons to proceed.”

title: Four Months of Zig
body:
It has been about four months since I returned to Zig after being absent for a few years. In this time, I have written some software in Zig and reengaged with the community, online and in person. I decided to share some of that experience, including what I have liked about Zig so far and what I haven't. I'll include some comparisons to Rust along the way since that was my previous go-to language.
The first project I started in Zig was snurl . It is a library for interacting with the smallnet (Gemini, Finger, Gopher, Spartan, and such). My goal has been to provide an alternative to curl for the smallnet, with similar testing and fuzzing requirements but on a smaller scale. I wanted to roughly follow TigerStyle insofar as it made sense for the project.
Something I ran into early on was that the fuzzer didn't actually work. When getting excited about fuzzing in my last post, I didn't realize that the feature had not yet been completed. This isn't surprising, considering Zig's status, but it was disappointing, especially since the fuzzer is demonstrated in the generated main.zig file provided by zig init . It seems this was based on a misunderstanding of how to use the fuzzer. An issue with documentation, not with the fuzzer implementation.
After this, I wrote a two programs which I have not published yet. The first is a small TUI typer racer. It was simpler than I expected to get a minimum version working so far. The second is an n-body simulator with stellar evolution using raylib.
The most exciting opportunity in the last few months was the chance to go to a local Zig Day. I learned of Zig Day Seattle occurring on Lobsters on August 20th. I was ecstatic to learn that there was a Zig Day in my area. Then I saw Andrew Kelley would be there and became more excited.
Zig Days are local meetups where people interested in Zig hang out, work on their projects together, and talk about Zig. For this Zig Day, I decided to work on snurl. A friend, Evin Yulo also decided to attend.
The event itself occurred in the Bothell library, moved there from the Bellevue library after so many people signed up that capacity was overwhelmed. Having the creator of Zig at the event will do that.
I love the format of these Zig Days and I'm glad they are a part of the community. Since they are run by local groups, it gives the whole Zig community a more interconnected feeling. It's a way to interact with other people who are interested in Zig in person. And, in this case, the creator of Zig itself.
I got the chance to talk with other programmers about their projects. Hopefully some ideological cross-pollination occurred that will make all our projects stronger. I ended up working on snurl with evin, who started work on integrating Zig's standard library TLS implementation as alternative backend.
I also briefly talked with Andrew Kelley. I hope Zig's built-in fuzzing gets fixed sometime soon!
Ryan Hendrickson wrote an excellent article outlining more of the events of that day from his perspective if you want more details.
I will definitely be attending Zig Day Seattle again in the future. I may even head down to Portland to catch one before the next local one comes around. I enjoy the opportunity to connect with other people interested in Zig and its values.
I love anyzig . I've had to use zig master and 0.16.0 for different projects, and anyzig has made that doable.
Unfortunately, it breaks outside of directories without a build.zig.zon , meaning if you have tooling that requires a zig command to work, it can only occur in project directories. This breaks autoformatting for my one-off Zig scripts. Maybe a default zig version could be provided in that case.
I know it frustrates some people, but I love the fact that you have to pass IO and allocator parameters to functions in Zig.
I'll start with allocators, since they've been around longer. For each Zig function you have to accept an explicit allocator parameter. This is different from most programming languages which either use a default allocator that may be changed globally or one changed by a local context (see Odin).
I like being able to change allocators for different parts of code. You might want an arena allocator for some things but need a general purpose allocator for others. Sometimes a FixedBufferAllocator is all you need to perform an operation. Zig's style makes this all obvious to handle.
I prefer Zig's system to Odin's implicit context system since Zig keeps things explicit. It's clear whether a function allocates memory or not, and hard to accidentally pass in the wrong allocator.
This is also superior to Rust's hidden, infallible allocations that panic when memory is exhausted. They're working on adding explicit allocations, but this will be yet another feature tacked onto the language rather than something built from the ground up.
It's much easier to reason about programs that allocate memory in Zig.
The IO parameter is even more powerful, even if it is newer. It is well worth the breaking changes required to bring it about (even if I skipped the 0.15.0 -> 0.16.0 transition). In Zig, every function that interacts with the underlying operating system (with caveats) requires an "IO" parameter. This provides the context for input, output, and everything else. Porting Zig to new operating systems is mostly just porting IO.
Practically, this is really nice for testing. When testing behavior, you just need to put in a testing IO instance that works as you need it to. You can change the input stream however you want, cause writes to fail, and anything else.
Just like with allocation, passing an IO argument makes it clear which programs are pure and which ones are not. You can tell at a glace whether or not a program is going to modify something external.
Zig has a really good track record of keeping things simple while also adding powerful features. Instead of adding 100 small features that do slightly different similar things, it tends to provide one major feature that supports all the various other use-cases. Low floor, high ceiling.
I love comptime. It's a seamless way to do metaprogramming and precomputation all in one. Other people have written more detailed accounts so I shall move on.
Zig's build system is stellar. So much so that companies like Uber have adopted it for their software written in other languages.
One thing I like about it is that I can integrate other tools with it seamlessly in ways that Cargo complains about. This is especially important for one of my projects that involves code generation.
Zig has an excellent dependency culture. The main ethos is simple: avoid. When you don't need a dependency, don't add one. However, when you do, it's often a battle-tested library that Zig can effortlessly integrate with translate-c. You can easily also vendor in external dependencies and audit their code.
Most of my Zig programs have about one or two direct Zig dependencies, with zero indirect dependencies. This makes the codebase much easier to audit and control.
This stands in stark contrast to Rust, where the smallest of my projects regularly have a few direct and dozens of indirect dependencies.
This is thanks both to Zig's dependency culture and the fact that essential features like reflection, random number generation, clean error handling, and JSON parsing are built into the language or standard library rather than maintained as separate individual libraries. No need to depend on serde or syn in every program.
Zig encourages careful consideration before adding dependencies, and I appreciate that.
Zig pushes programmers to handle errors correctly by default. The laziest way to handle errors in Zig is to use the try keyword and add ! to the function's return type.
This contrasts to Rust, which leads programmers to insert panics into their code. The issue is that it's often easier to panic when prototyping, and then leave that in the code longer than it should be. I've used production code written in Rust that panic instead of returning a proper error.
In Rust you can use ? , which is quicker than unwrap , but you also have to do something like Result<Type, Box<dyn std::error::Error> . That's a mouthful! Alternatively, you can use the anyhow crate and return anyhow::Result , which also provides some nice helper methods. But then you have to add a dependency for reasonable error handling. There's also Zig-style composable errors with yet another library.
The core team members at Zig have been doing amazing work at incremental compilation. If you run zig build --watch -fincremental , the compiler will watch for changes, check exactly what you changed, and then modify only what you've changed down to linking. No effort beyond what's required, so it's faster that human perception even for large codebases. Zig was designed from the ground up to support this behavior.
This makes for a really nice workflow. I can just run the compiler in incremental mode right next to my text editor, and get updates on my code as I save. No time to get distracted with something else. With Rust projects 10+ seconds incremental compilation loops were common even in smaller projects. That's enough time to get distracted but not enough time to be productive doing something else, leaving annoying gaps that Zig eliminates.
Rust is disadvantaged here. It's a stable language that needs to maintain backwards compatibility. This means it can't afford to break things in order to improve compilation speed, at least not to any large degree. Meanwhile, if it makes Zig better, the maintainers are willing to break just about anything to ensure the end result will be perfect.
Currently, Zig only supports incremental compilation on x86_64 on Linux and macOS. If you use another operating system or architecture you won't have access to this feature yet, but in that case it's another thing to look out for!
This makes Zig just a bit more wonderful to work with. I'll take it.
Like every other user of Zig, I would like to see the standard library become more stable. I know that's one of the last tasks to do before 1.0, and there are many others before then, but it is frustrating to deal with the constant breakage in the ecosystem. My understanding is that that's why 0.17.0 took so long to be released.
Andrew Kelley said at Zig Day that he would like to see 1.0 more than anyone. I believe him, so I will have patience and trust that the final version will be excellent.
This is the one reason I still use Rust for some projects. Some cases require a stable programming language and the ecosystem that provides. But considering the impressive software that's being built in Zig these days, stability isn't everything. And there are projects for which the niceties of Zig outweigh its instability. I can't wait for 1.0.
I would like to see more assistance with lifetimes in the Zig compiler. Specifically, I would like to see returning local variables to fail in debug mode, either as a kind of built-in lint (as Andrew Kelley has mentioned wanting to implement) or as literally invalidating that memory after the function returns. That way new users quickly learn to avoid that pattern. Currently, it's easy to unintentionally break your code this way, even if you think you understand lifetimes.
Relatedly, the compiler currently accepts code that will be broken in the future. The compiler lets variables live the entire scope instead of the scope of a block. This means that if you stack-allocate a buffer and return it from a block, that buffer should be invalidated but isn't. My understanding is that this could silently break in a future Zig version.
Zig is poorly documented. It has enough to get you started, but to continue onward you have to parse intention from sparse doc comments that are sometimes attached to functions. Examples are rare. I still haven't got Zig's standard library TLS working in snurl because neither I nor a friend can figure out how to set up the buffers correctly.
Because of this lack of documentation, a lot of the knowledge for building solid Zig programs is distributed across the Web. If you're well integrated into Zig communities, having read the existing documentation, watched the presentations, and read the code, you can succeed. If you aren't that well integrated, however, it can be a challenge to work effectively.
The benefit of this is that it encourages people to engage in Zig communities (I'm an admin for the Matrix room, for example). While LLMs seek to demolish human collaboration, we need human-to-human collaboration now more than ever. However, we can still have that and nice documentation too. As we all know, people will still ask questions if you have things well-documented. And a good community knows how to point people towards good resources rather than just saying "RTFM".
I would also be curious to see what the intersection of Zig and literate programming could be. My literate programming tool is written in Rust right now, but that might change.
I would love to parse JSON at compile time. For one of my projects, there is a JSON file that is stored inside the binary. It's static and could be parsed at compile time into a collection of structs.
However, the standard library JSON parser requires an allocator. Because there are no allocators that work at compile time, this means that any JSON parsing must be done at runtime. So that's what I did with my project.
I believe there is an intention of adding a JSON parser that does not require an allocator (the data already exists in the JSON string, after all). That will solve the immediate problem, but there are more general cases that may require an allocator. I believe FixedBufferAllocator worked at compile time before and served this purpose. It could do so again.
Zig's bootstrapping story is impressive. They erased the C++ version of their compiler and replaced it with a small WASM blob and WASM interpreter . The WASM file is a stripped-down version of the compiler that compiles the full Zig compiler to C, which is then compiled by the system C compiler. It's an interesting approach and you should read the linked article if you want more details.
The one caveat to this is that it requires the compiled binary blob checked into the source code. This is better than requiring the full previous compiler (like Rust), but it's not as good as having the full source available for every step of the process at all points. A malicious actor could still sneak something into the blob. More importantly, many distributions (like Debian) cannot properly package Zig at the moment because it's impossible to do so in a way that's compliant with their guidelines.
Their original plan was to use the compiler's C backend to generate a C version of the compiler which would then be maintained separately. They would then have two different source versions. They decided this approach would be too difficult, unfortunately.
Because of this, someone will have to make another Zig compiler in another language (probably C) that will improve the bootstrap process. This is explicitly not something the Zig Software Foundation wants to develop right now. This means that at the moment there is no way to bootstrap Zig fully from source.
This issue isn't just a theoretical problem. Because Zig can't be packaged on Debian, I had to choose another language for one of my projects to ensure wider possible usage.
Fortunately, this issue is temporary. Once Zig is stable, building an alternative compiler should be straightforward. Zig is designed to be a simple language where alternative implementations are humanly achievable, unlike other languages . Currently, the instability means any alternative compiler will be playing a constant game of catch-up, which is probably why the core team doesn't want to manage it while they're rapidly iterating.
Alas, this may also require waiting for 1.0. May it come soon!
I will continue to use Zig. I'm excited about the direction it's going and I look forward to continuing to be a part of its community. So far, I've found no other programming language that I prefer more than Zig, even with its shortcomings. It's just stable enough that I don't have to make massive changes between releases. It will continue to be my go-to programming language for most projects.
One of these projects is ReTangled . It was previously written in Rust but I grew tired of the massive dependency trees and want to take full advantage of Zig's build system.
I've also been looking to contribute more to Zig directly. Between my limited time as a student, Zig's overflow of contributors already, and the poor documentation, this will be a challenge. But I want to contribute back, make an impact on the project, and become a better software engineer. Thankfully, improving contributor onboarding seems to be a priority for Andrew Kelley moving forward.
I'll also be at future Zig Days in Seattle, if you want to meet and work on Zig projects together!

title: Dangote Refinery’s historic IPO nets investors from 120 countries worldwide, 54 in Africa
body:
Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals has successfully concluded its landmark Initial Public Offering (IPO), attracting investor applications from 120 countries across all six inhabited continents, including all 54 African countries.
In a statement on Tuesday, the company described the development as an unprecedented demonstration of the continent’s capacity to mobilise capital and broaden ownership of strategic industrial assets.
The historic offering, widely described as The People’s IPO, achieved 100 per cent geographical coverage of Africa, bringing together investors from across the continent and beyond in a transaction that could redefine the scale, accessibility and international reach of African capital markets.
More than a conventional fundraising exercise, the IPO has become a landmark in financial inclusion, showing how digital technology, coordinated financial institutions, and innovative distribution channels can connect millions of potential investors to opportunities previously dominated by institutional and high-net-worth participants.
The transaction was supported by an extensive network of commercial banks, stockbroking firms, fintech platforms, capital market institutions and distribution partners, whose collaboration expanded access to the offer across national boundaries and created new pathways for retail participation.
For Dangote Industries Limited, the IPO’s conclusion marks a defining moment in its industrial journey, shifting the refinery’s ownership proposition from an investment driven by a single entrepreneurial vision to an opportunity for broader African participation.
President and Chief Executive of Dangote Industries Limited, Aliko Dangote, described the outcome as a powerful affirmation of African confidence, enterprise, and the continent’s ability to mobilise its own resources for development.
“When we set out to build this refinery, many doubted that a project of this scale could be delivered by Africans. We proved that Africa could build it. Today, through this historic IPO, we have demonstrated something equally important: Africans are ready to own and participate in the prosperity created by their own industries.
“To have investor applications from all 54 African countries is deeply significant to me. It shows our people don’t just want to consume what Africa produces; they want to invest in it, own it, and share in its future. This is the Africa we have always believed in,” he said.
“We did not undertake this IPO simply because we needed to raise capital. We wanted to open the doors of ownership, give ordinary Africans an opportunity to participate in an enterprise of global significance and establish a new culture of shared prosperity. We built the refinery in Africa, through African determination, and its future must create opportunities for Africans.
“Today, we have made history together. But the greater achievement will be the generation of African investors, entrepreneurs, and industrialists that this transaction inspires. Our ambition is not merely to build successful businesses. It is to help build a prosperous, self-reliant Africa whose people are participants in its economic destiny. As we advance our expansion programme and Vision 2030 strategy, we remain committed to strengthening our operational performance, deepening our contribution to Africa’s energy security and building an enterprise that rewards the confidence placed in it.”
The statement said the IPO’s geographical reach is particularly significant for a continent where capital markets have historically been fragmented by national boundaries, differing regulatory environments and limited retail investor participation. By attracting applications from all 54 African countries, the transaction has shown the potential for a more connected investment ecosystem, allowing Africans to participate in major industrial opportunities beyond their domestic markets.
The offering also highlights the growing importance of digital financial infrastructure in widening investment access. Through partnerships involving traditional financial institutions and technology-driven investment platforms, the transaction created multiple channels for eligible investors to express interest and submit applications.
Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals, David Bird, said the international response reflected confidence in the refinery’s operating capabilities, industrial scale and long-term growth prospects.
“The successful conclusion of this IPO is a remarkable milestone for Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals. Investor applications from 120 countries demonstrate extraordinary international interest in our business and the confidence investors place in this refinery’s future. We have built one of the world’s most significant refining and petrochemical complexes, and our focus remains on translating that industrial scale into operational excellence, sustainable growth and long-term shareholder value,” he said. “What makes this transaction particularly meaningful is the breadth of participation. The opportunity to own a stake in a major African industrial enterprise has reached investors across every African country and all six inhabited continents. That is a powerful endorsement of the refinery’s potential and of Africa’s growing relevance in global investment markets.”
The refinery’s IPO opened on 14 September, offering 4.1 billion ordinary shares at N525 per share, representing a proposed capital raise of approximately N2.15 trillion.
Initially scheduled to close on 13 October, the offer was extended to 27 October after the Securities and Exchange Commission approved it, giving investors across Africa and other international markets more time to participate.
The extension reflected the Group’s stated ambition to prioritise broad ownership alongside the transaction’s financial objectives. Beyond the refinery’s industrial significance, the IPO also established a model for collaboration across Africa’s financial services ecosystem. Its distribution network brought together institutions across banking, securities trading, financial technology, and investor engagement, showing how coordinated infrastructure can expand access to large-scale investment opportunities.
Dangote Industries Limited Group Chief Financial Officer Murat Erden said the transaction set an important precedent for the continent’s capital markets, speaking to the offering’s execution and broader significance.
“The Dangote Refinery People’s IPO represents much more than a landmark capital-raising exercise. It marks a defining moment in the evolution of African capital markets, demonstrating our continent’s ability to mobilise domestic savings, connect investors across borders and broaden ownership of strategic industrial assets. Reaching investors in 120 countries, including all 54 African nations, is an extraordinary achievement and a powerful testament to the continent’s growing appetite for investment. By bringing together banks, capital market institutions, stockbrokers, fintech platforms and innovative digital distribution channels, we have demonstrated that African capital markets can transcend national boundaries and connect millions of people to investment opportunities previously beyond their reach,” he said. “Importantly, this transaction is underpinned by exceptional industrial and financial fundamentals. With US$22.5 billion in revenue and US$5.52 billion in EBITDA in the first nine months of 2026, Dangote Refinery combines world-class industrial scale, strong profitability and significant long-term growth potential. Our greatest achievement is not simply the capital we mobilise, but the doors we open and the foundation we lay for future generations of African investors, entrepreneurs and businesses. We believe the People’s IPO will be remembered not only as a landmark transaction in African capital market history, but also as a blueprint for a more inclusive, interconnected and globally competitive African financial ecosystem — one in which Africans increasingly finance, own and share in the prosperity created by their continent’s industrial transformation.”
The successful conclusion of the offer comes as Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals pursues an ambitious programme to expand its refining and petrochemical operations, strengthen its distribution network and support greater energy security across Africa.
Located in Lagos, the refinery represents one of the continent’s largest private industrial investments and a major effort to reduce dependence on imported refined petroleum products while building domestic processing capacity.

title: Telecel Ghana rewards subscriber with Hyundai Creta in 15th Dream Car promotion
body: Telecel Ghana has rewarded a lucky subscriber, Eric Ayamgash, with a Hyundai Creta at the end of the 15th cycle of its Dream Car promotion. The initiative forms part of the telecommunications company’s efforts to reward customer loyalty and support the aspirations of its subscribers. Senior Manager in charge of Mobile Data at Telecel Ghana, Carlos Asare Oppong, says the promotion reflects the company’s commitment to creating rewarding experiences and helping customers achieve their dreams. He disclosed that the latest presentation marks the eighth car awarded under the promotion, in addition to six houses given to winners over the programme’s 15 cycles. “We believe that Ghanaians are very aspirational, and as an aspirational brand, we want to be able to support our customers to achieve their dreams and their goals in life. That is why we launched the Dream Car promotion about 15 cycles ago,” he said. Mr Asare Oppong also announced improvements to the 16th cycle of the promotion, including an additional GH¢100,000 cash prize expected to be awarded towards the end of November or December. He further revealed that the next cycle will feature a bigger car, urging subscribers to remain active on the network and participate in the promotion for a chance to win. Meanwhile, winner Eric Ayamgash expressed excitement and gratitude to Telecel Ghana, describing his win as a testament to the authenticity of the promotion. He said after failing to win in the previous year’s edition, he was determined to put in more effort in the subsequent cycle. “Last year, I tried but I couldn’t win. When I saw the video of the winner, I said to myself that the next one I’m going to try and put in more effort. God being so good, I was called that I am the winner for this cycle. I just want to say thank you very much, Telecel. I’m so grateful,” he said. Mr Ayamgash encouraged other subscribers to participate, insisting that the promotion is genuine. The Dream Car promotion, which is approved by the National Lottery Authority, gives Telecel subscribers the opportunity to win prizes by participating through the designated USSD platform. Subscribers can dial *2018# on their Telecel SIM cards to take part in the promotion.

title: Ghanaian music can go global without copying foreign sounds – King Promise
body: Ghanaian Afrobeats and Highlife singer-songwriter King Promise says his ambition is to take Ghanaian music to the global stage without losing the sound and identity that distinguish local artistes from their international counterparts. The Terminator hitmaker said he had previously experimented with music heavily influenced by foreign sounds but eventually realised that Ghanaian artistes should build on their unique strengths rather than imitate what already exists elsewhere. Speaking on Joy FM’s Drive Time with Lexis Bill on Tuesday, October 27, he said his focus had always been on achieving global success while maintaining a strong connection with Ghanaian audiences. “I’d rather them not influencing me so much, rather me influencing the world so much,” he said, referring to the influence of international music on his creative direction. King Promise admitted that there was a period when he was making music driven largely by foreign influences, but he chose not to release those experimental songs. “I was making music that was mainly driven by a lot of foreign influence down home, but that was when I was experimenting. I didn’t drop them,” he explained. He said he subsequently recognised that Ghanaian musicians possessed distinctive musical qualities that could appeal to international audiences. “What they lack in the rest of the world is what we have here. So why would you trade what you have here for what they have?” he asked. According to him, international success should not require Ghanaian artistes to abandon their musical identity in an attempt to appeal to foreign markets. He cited the global popularity of Spanish-language hit Despacito as an example of how music can cross borders without abandoning its original identity. “If Despacito could be a big record in Ghana, why can’t “Mene medofa ahye dam mu” be big in Spain? Or why can’t “Terminator” be played in Singapore?” he said. The singer added that his belief in his music and its potential audience had remained central to his career. “It’s going to work. It has to work. If it doesn’t go this way, we keep going until it goes,” he said. King Promise also discussed the challenge of balancing the tastes of audiences in Ghana with those of listeners abroad. He said he had spent years trying to find a sound that could connect with both markets. He cited songs including Perfect Combi , Paris and Terminator as examples of his efforts to create music with appeal at home and internationally. He also referenced earlier releases such as Tokyo . The singer said he had drawn inspiration from R2Bees, whom he admired while he was in school because of their ability to achieve success both in Ghana and among audiences in the diaspora. He also acknowledged the influence of Nigerian artistes Mr Eazi, Wizkid and Davido, saying their achievements had reinforced his belief that Ghanaian musicians could compete globally. King Promise, who won the Artiste of the Year award, said his international ambitions extended beyond music releases to collaborations and partnerships, including his work with Chelsea Football Club. He maintained that the goal was to help Ghanaian music reach wider audiences while retaining the qualities that make it distinctive.

title: I compete with myself, not other artistes – King Promise
body: Ghanaian Afrobeats and Highlife singer-songwriter Gregory Bortey Newman, known popularly as King Promise, says he is more focused on improving his own achievements than competing with fellow artistes, describing his approach to the music industry as a continuous pursuit of personal growth. The singer said although competition was a normal part of the music business, comparisons between musicians were often driven by fans rather than the artistes themselves. Speaking on Joy FM’s Drive Time with Lexis Bill on Tuesday, October 27, he said his priority was to build on every milestone in his career rather than become preoccupied with the achievements of others. “I’ve never been but with myself. I’m in my own lane,” he said when asked whether he competed with other musicians. King Promise acknowledged that fans often compared artistes and sought to position their favourites against one another, particularly when awards and career achievements were involved. “It’s normal, you know, I believe like when you’re in contention to be at the apex of your career, and people are doing similar stuff, it might not even be the artists, it might be the fans that will put you against each other,” he said. He added that he preferred to use the achievements of other musicians as motivation rather than allow comparisons to create resentment. “Rather than have it feel like negative competition, if there’s anything that I feel the need to compete is to see someone do something like, ‘Oh, this is nice,’ and I like this. It should inspire me rather than put spite in me,” he explained. The musician cited his relationship with Mr Eazi as an example of how another artiste’s success could motivate him. He said watching his friend achieve international recognition had strengthened his belief in what was possible for Ghanaian musicians. King Promise also referred to Wizkid’s achievement of selling out London’s O2 Arena, saying it inspired him to pursue similar milestones. “You see Wizkid do something like, ‘Ah bro, he sold out the O2, I want to do it too one day.’ Why was it him and it’s not me? That’s my mentality,” he said. He explained that his ambition was to keep identifying new levels to reach, regardless of what he had already accomplished. “I’m like, okay, what can we do next? Well, okay, this went this way, I’ve seen that, okay, it has to go this way next, and that’s really what it is,” he said. The singer also spoke about his friendship with Mr Eazi, whom he has known since around 2012, before either of them had a hit song. According to King Promise, their relationship developed from genuine friendship rather than a deliberate effort to collaborate musically. He said Mr Eazi had influenced him through his directness, confidence and business-minded approach, adding that the two often exchanged ideas beyond music. King Promise said he valued relationships built on genuine connections, citing his longstanding associations with Mr Eazi, R2Bees and Sarkodie. Looking ahead, he told Lexis Bill that he had major plans for his career in Ghana and internationally. He also mentioned new music, future music videos, an upcoming album and his Promise Land event as part of his plans. He further hinted that he might release another song before the end of the year, although he did not confirm a date.

title: Herder killed in Plateau community
body: A herder identified as Umar Adamu Jagar was on Tuesday reportedly attacked and killed around Lamor community of Mangu local government area of Plateau state. Herding community said the incident occurred when the deceased was on his way from Lamor to Gotkum communities in Mangu LGA. Ibrahim Yusuf Babayo, State chairman of Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria (MACBAN), who confirmed the attack, condemned the incident, describing it as unacceptable. MACBAN said, “The Miyetti Allah Cattle Breeders Association of Nigeria (MACBAN), Plateau State Chapter, strongly condemns the gruesome killing of Umar Adamu Jagar, who was reportedly ambushed and shot dead on the morning of 27th October 2027 at about 9:30 a.m. while travelling from Lamor to Gotkum in Mangu Local Government Area of Plateau State. Kidnappers break into Kaduna estate, abduct residents 5 suspects arrested over woman’s abduction in Rivers “The deceased was attacked without any provocation and lost his life in the unfortunate incident. We extend our heartfelt condolences to his family, relatives, and the entire Fulani community over this painful loss. We pray that Almighty Allah (SWT) grants him Aljannatul Firdaus and gives his family the strength to bear this irreparable loss. “This latest killing is deeply disturbing and further raises serious concerns about the recurring attacks on innocent Fulani herders and travelers in parts of Plateau State. Such acts of violence threaten peaceful coexistence and undermine ongoing efforts to restore peace and stability in the state.” Babayo further called on security agencies, including the Nigeria Police Force, the military, and other relevant authorities to conduct a thorough investigation into the incident, identify those responsible, and ensure they are brought to justice. “We also urge all Fulani communities to remain calm, law-abiding, and to avoid any form of retaliation while allowing the security agencies to carry out their constitutional responsibilities,” he said. Spokesperson of Operation Enduring Peace, Captain Polycarp Auta, did not respond to inquiries regarding the incident from our correspondent as of press time.

title: How EFCC’s Sting Operation Led to Arrest of 19 Fraudster in Lagos Estate
body: Alex Enumah in Abuja A sting operation by operatives of the Lagos Directorate 1 of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, on Monday, has led to the arrest of 19 persons suspected of fraudulently activities. The sting operation according to the anti-graft agency was carried out at the Applewood Estate, Orchid Road, Lekki, Lagos State. The operatives had embarked on the operation to apprehend suspected cybercrime fraudsters said to be obtaining money from unsuspecting victims through gift cards, crypto currencies and international money transfers by impersonating several individuals. “The operation, carried out by 5am, yielded the arrest of twenty-one(21) suspected cybercrime fraudsters and five exotic cars. The fraudsters were apprehended professionally owing to diligent pre-arrest surveillance and reconnaissance of the activities of the fraudsters. “A young lady that stood in the way of the operation by making telephone calls to alert the fraudsters was held and her phone confiscated until the conclusion of the operation. The phone was later released to her”, the statement signed by the commission’s spokesperson, Mr Dele Oyewale read in part. It noted that preliminary investigations of the arrested suspects indicted 19 persons, while two others not indicted were subsequently released. While assuring that, “All the indicted suspects will be arraigned in court immediately, the EFCC said it would continue its crusade and operational dynamics against economic and financial crimes and other acts of corruption. The anti-graft agency accordingly enjoined the public to keep faith with it and loudly condemn the activities of fraudsters bringing the nation to disrepute. “The Sting Operation at Applewood Estate was professionally carried out, with no record of harassment, intimidation or unlawful arrest of anyone. The Commission is open to constructive engagement by well-meaning Nigerians but blackmailers and alarmists will not be allowed to sabotage its mandate”, the statement added.

title: The next circle of security hell
body:
A few years back I wrote “The modern packager’s security nightmare” . Have things improved since? On the contrary, I feel like we’re slipping down a well-oiled slope with no end in sight. Vulnerabilities are reported at unprecedented rates. A lot of people are doing everything they can to patch them up, which doesn’t necessarily mean they’re not making things even worse. Complex software involves complex trees of dependencies, and every branch on that tree needs tending to. When they stop being reliable, people further down the tree start taking more weight. And there’s a limit of how much a single person can do, so what started as an effort to resolve an issue upstream may quickly become a weakness. Is software less secure these days? It’s tempting to say yes. I’d love to blame the corporate sector for egotistically dumping low quality software on us. I’d love to blame marketing-oriented people developing stuff with the sole goal of making a profit. I’d love to blame Rust for getting people obsessed about memory safety, and ignoring the kinds of vulnerabilities that aren’t caught by the compiler. Finally, I’d really love to blame slop. But the truth is, I don’t know. That’s really beside the point.
The point is that nowadays everyone and their chatbot became security researchers. Projects are being flooded with vulnerability reports. Even though pretty much every bug bounty was discontinued because of slop, people aren’t stopping. And even if we disregard truly invalid junk reports, there’s a lot left, and you have to deal with them somehow. You have to figure out how important they are, and how to fix them (or more likely, whether the fixes submitted are truly valid and don’t introduce regressions), or if you should reject them and why.
In the end, security is tricky. We’re seeing lots of bugs like REDoS, or other kinds of “performance bugs”. Are they really vulnerabilities? Well, it depends on the attack vector. And that in turn depends on how the software is used. Some scenarios are really contrived, and feel like “shell can execute dangerous commands if you type them in”. But then, you also have really serious issues such as “timing attack can be used to guess user’s secret”. You need to know a lot to make that kind of judgment, and sometimes your judgment doesn’t really match users’ expectations.
In the end, what can project maintainers do? Even if they have the expertise and the energy to judge, if they can “know better”, there’s likely a CVE assigned already. It may have absurdly high score. All security scanners will complain unless you fix it, and users will come asking or complaining, or attacking, or forking. I mean, technology can’t handle nuances. More than once I’ve been doing unnecessary security stabilizations over vulnerabilities that didn’t affect Gentoo (for example, because we already unbundled the vulnerable dependencies), to avoid false positives from security scanners. I’ve been also doing meaningless version bumps (with no real changes or no changes that applied to Gentoo) so that our packages don’t get reported as being “outdated”. It’s a hassle and it sucks, but it saves people from worrying.
I’ve said this before and I’ll say it again: most projects aren’t really prepared to handle security issues. And it’s not just about triage. It’s about having LTS or security branches, it’s about making proper security releases with minimal changes. Unfortunately, it’s quite common for security fixes to be combined with new features, deprecations, API changes. In extreme cases, people are caught with their metaphorical pants down, and suddenly need to make a security release in the middle of a major rewrite, or along with barely tested new code. And then, people downstream discover that they need to quickly deal with major API changes to upgrade past a vulnerable version. These things keep piling up.
What happens next? The community reaches a breaking point. People can’t keep up. You discover you can’t rely on others, so you work around them. You start bundling more stuff. Soon enough your workload goes beyond your ability. Software development becomes “every chatbot for itself”. The nightmare becomes worse, and the wheel keeps turning.

title: Ukraine Recaptures Territory, Forces on the Offensive, Zelensky Says
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, Oct. 27, that Ukrainian forces had recaptured significant territory in three major offensive operations this year, strengthening their frontline positions and disrupting Russia’s battlefield plans.
In his evening address, Zelensky highlighted an Air Assault Forces campaign that liberated more than 800 square kilometers (309 square miles), Operation Vivaldi in Donetsk region, where Ukrainian troops reported recapturing 277 square kilometers (107 square miles), and Operation Veles near Kupiansk, where Ukrainian forces turned Russian underground infiltration tactics against Moscow’s troops.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“It is important to note that this year, Ukraine’s positions on the front line remain the strongest they have been in a long time during this war,” Zelensky said, noting that Ukraine would be in a much better diplomatic position if partner support was equally strong, particularly in the field of air-defense systems.
According to Zelensky, the offensive led by Air Assault Forces (DShV) has liberated more than 800 square kilometers (309 square miles). The campaign ran through Jan. 29 through Aug. 12, liberating 26 settlements spanning across three regions – Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, and Zaporizhzhia.
The second, Operation Vivaldi , was carried out by the 3rd Army Corps near Lyman in Donetsk region from July until mid-October. According to Zelensky, Ukraine’s Defense Forces liberated more than 200 kilometers (124 miles) there, in an area where Russia had concentrated its assaults.
When the operation ended on Oct. 14, 3rd Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky said his forces had retaken 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) and more than 16 towns and villages, while inflicting at least 8,000 casualties on Russian troops.
The offensive, he said, pushed Russian forces back from the Slovyansk-Kramatorsk highway, a key supply route for both cities.
In an interview with ArmyInform on Oct. 19 , Biletsky, who is also commander of Ukraine’s Center Grouping of Forces, said Operation Vivaldi had disrupted Russia’s broader plan to encircle the strategically important cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
According to the general, Russian forces intended to advance from a bridgehead along the Chornyi Zherebets River, bypass Lyman and approach Sloviansk and Kramatorsk from the north, while another Russian grouping advanced from the Dobropillya direction.
The commander said Ukrainian forces eliminated the Russian bridgehead, forcing Moscow to abandon its planned northern advance.
Biletsky also reported more than 8,000 Russian personnel losses and approximately 270 soldiers captured, including more than 20 officers.
He emphasized that the operation’s most significant achievement was not the territory liberated but the disruption of Russia’s strategic plans to capture the remaining Ukrainian-held strongholds in Donetsk region.
In a separate statement earlier on Tuesday, Zelensky said he had been briefed on the operation’s results by Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapaty, Deputy Head of the Presidential Office Pavlo Palisa and Brig. Gen. Ihor Oboliensky, the Khartiia Corps commander.
According to the report, Russian forces had previously tried to use underground gas pipelines to slip past Ukrainian positions and launch assaults. Ukraine’s Defense Forces then adopted the method and refined it, making it “far more thought-out and technologically advanced,” Zelensky said.
Repeating figures Khartiia’s Corps first released on Oct. 22, Zelensky confirmed that more than 30 Russian soldiers have been captured, while Russian losses exceeded 100.
At the time, it was reported that more than 30 Russian prisoners were captured, with the maneuver described as the world’s first full-scale underground counteroffensive.
Without any GPS or daylight, Ukrainian troops pushed through more than 15 kilometers (9 miles) of underground infrastructure before emerging behind Russian positions overhead.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Fields Medal-winning UC Berkeley professor ends graded homework due to AI cheating
body: A University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) professor has stopped giving his students graded homework, saying that rampant AI use has made it pointless. According to the New York Post , renowned mathematician Richard Borcherds said that it’s now nearly impossible to tell the difference between a student-written submission and one that’s been created using artificial intelligence. Because of this, he now primarily uses in-person exams with no electronic devices to grade his students and see how well they are doing in his class. “Online exams are now a waste of time as several students just use AI to answer the questions. I cannot tell which students are using AI, but I notice the average score increases a lot in online exams,” Borcherds told the publication. He also added, “Grading for correctness just adds a huge incentive for them to use AI for homework instead of doing it themselves and penalizes students for honesty. And paying to grade AI generated answers is a waste of time and money.” This problem appeared when OpenAI released the first popular LLM, GPT-3.5, in November 2022. But while LLMs were prone to mistakes back then, making their inordinate use easy to spot, the technology has improved to the point that it’s now very hard to tell if it's been used for written work. Various researchers have proven that students routinely get better scores when taking exams online. While they haven’t definitively proven that the students used AI to answer the questions, the difference between the scores was significant enough that the researchers concluded unmonitored online exams are no longer reflective of what the students have learned in the course. A Brown University professor determined this earlier this year when his students scored an average of 96% for his take-home midterms — a huge jump from the historical average of 65% to 80%. Because of this, he made his students take their final exams in person, which resulted in only two students getting a score that’s within 10% of their midterm grades , with only one performing better. However, not all AI tools are as keen to help students cheat, with Cursor AI telling one user to learn coding instead of asking it to generate code. Still, this is just one tool in a sea of many, making it next to impossible to stop students from using AI. As for UC Berkeley, it has already looked at AI-detection software to try and deal with the situation, but determined that it wasn't reliable. Because of this, the University decided to give professors free rein on their own AI policies, as long as they spell out their AI rules in the course syllabi. As for Borcherds, he says that if the worst thing that AI can do is to make it harder for teachers to grade student homework, then he will be “very relieved."

title: How Halifax’s famous donair fueled one man’s goal to run a marathon
body:
A Nova Scotia man says he recently trained for his first marathon in the most Halifax way possible: by eating dozens of donairs.
As part of his training, David Wadden trekked to 59 different locations to devour the pitas filled with spiced meat, fresh onions and tomatoes covered in a sweet sauce. Keeping with local tradition, lettuce was not on the menu.
“At the end of the day, I think it’s the donair itself that just brings everybody together,” he mused.
Wadden moved to Halifax from Cape Breton in 2018. After realizing he had little to offer in terms of donair recommendations whenever friends visited from outside the city, he embarked on a mission to strengthen his bond with Halifax’s official food.
“I decided … what if I ran or did an exercise to get to the donairs? And then the name ‘Donairathon’ came to be,” he said.
Wadden says he jogged and biked more than 800 kilometres across the city in hopes of locating the best donair, while also getting some exercise.
“Thirty-two kilometres was my longest run: 16 kilometres, eat the donair, and then 16 kilometres back,” he said.
In the process, Wadden says he became a donair connoisseur of sorts and documented his journey online.
He shares his donair reviews afterward, based on his own ranking system, which includes noting the donairs’ weight, price and size.
“ I don’t have a background in food. I don’t know if I have the best palate, but I do know that I can tell you what I’m seeing on my plate,” he said.
“So I just broke it down into a quantity category and a quality category of each ingredient in a donair and then kind of gave an overview of what I felt the donair gave me.”
The highest rating? Joann’s Pizza Land in Clayton Park.
“This donair is, it’s a milder spice, but I really like the spice blend that they have and everything that accompanies the donair meat is exactly what I like,” he said.
“It’s a perfect complement to each part.”
The restaurant’s manager, Nidhin George, says the first-place distinction has given them a boost in business.
“It was really good. It really helped us, it really helped the business,” said George. “We started getting new customers. People seemed to love the donair.”
Beyond satisfying his own curiosity and cravings, Wadden used the opportunity to help tackle food insecurity. He partnered with Feed Nova Scotia, and encourages his fans to donate to the charity through its website.
Feed Nova Scotia is even getting a bit creative with the partnership. They’re measuring donations by, what else, donairs.
“So if you donate $10, it’s like you donated a donair, $20, you donated two donairs,” said spokesperson Mandi MacDonald.
With food bank usage rising across the province, MacDonald says community-led initiatives like Wadden’s can go a long way.
“Sometimes just the smallest idea can turn into something that is so, so much bigger,” she said.
As for that marathon, Wadden successfully completed it two weeks ago in the Annapolis Valley.
“It was nice not having a backpack full of camera gear and donair rating supplies on my back. So that definitely helped my time,” he said.
“I did end up training enough, so I did finish the marathon, which was really nice.”
After the nine-month journey, Wadden says he has a newfound appreciation for donairs and the vast community of shop owners and customers that keep the city’s culture thriving.

title: Lockheed Martin expands Alabama plant to produce hypersonic missiles for B-52 bombers
body: The Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon is designed to strike targets at significant standoff ranges while traveling faster than Mach 5. Lockheed Martin said the B-52-integrated missile combines hypersonic speed and maneuverability, with advanced materials and technology intended to maintain accuracy under extreme flight conditions. The company broke ground on an expansion of Building P-20 in Troy, Alabama, that will add 47,000 square feet and triple the facility’s production space. The project will create jobs over the next four years, although Lockheed Martin did not specify how many. The factory will use advanced manufacturing, robotics and digital technologies to build ARRW. Lockheed Martin said it had already paid for preparatory work, materials and equipment needed to start production. “The ARRW production contract award showcases Lockheed Martin’s ability to develop and begin production on cutting-edge systems at unprecedented speed and scale,” said Tim Cahill, president of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control. “ARRW expands our weapon systems portfolio and launches a critical, high-precision, and sustained hypersonic capability that will enhance the U.S. Air Force’s strategic advantage across multiple domains.” The production award follows years of cooperation between Lockheed Martin and the Air Force on development and testing. The company said ARRW’s readiness for production would support rapid deployment of the capability. According to Lockheed Martin, the missile’s advanced materials are designed to withstand the extreme heat of hypersonic flight. Its onboard technology is intended to preserve accuracy and lethality in those conditions and overcome a range of defenses. The ARRW expansion forms part of Lockheed Martin’s planned $8 billion to $9 billion investment through 2030 to meet munitions demand. The company said continued research and development would support the program over the longer term and help accelerate delivery to the Air Force.

title: UralChem intends to supply at least 1 mln tons of fertilizers to Africa annually
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. UralChem Group plans to supply at least 1 mln tons of fertilizers annually to African countries in the coming years, with the intention of eventually increasing shipments to 2 mln tons per year, the company told TASS.
"UralChem plans to supply at least 1 mln tons of fertilizers to Africa annually in the coming years. We plan to boost sales volume to 2 mln tons in the foreseeable future," the company said ahead of the Russia-Africa forum, adding that this can be achieved as effective distribution systems and logistics infrastructure are developed within the continent.
Uralchem ranks among the top five fertilizer suppliers to the African continent, having increased its sales from 100,000 tons in 2018 to around 1 million tons by 2025. Moreover, the company supplied about 135,000 tons of fertilizers to African nations free of charge between 2022 and 2024, while also covering the transportation costs associated with these humanitarian shipments.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Mauritania Students Protest Rising Transport Costs, Poor Study Conditions
body: University students in the Mauritanian capital Nouakchott staged a boycott Tuesday to protest against transport price rises and demand better living and study conditions. The campus was almost deserted as students boycotted lectures at Al Aasriya University, the country’s largest, AFP journalists reported. Some told AFP they were protesting against increases in the price of state subsidised transport from 5 ouguiyas (around $0.13) to 30 ouguiyas ($0.75). They demanded an increase in bus services and for improvements to living and study conditions. Since last Friday, a “Student Front” comprising students and several unions has held several on-campus demonstrations while calling for strikes, sit-ins and marches to obtain “concrete responses” from authorities. On Monday, police used batons and tear gas to disperse a gathering of students on and around the campus. The ministry of higher education recently announced measures aimed at improving the situation, citing rising student numbers as a factor but adding the government had laid on more bus services in response.
