title: Israel awaits election results after turnout soars
body: Read the latest on Israel's election here Israelis are awaiting their general election results after voting in their highest numbers in decades on Tuesday at a pivotal moment for the Middle East. Votes were being counted overnight after a closely-fought contest between Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former army general Gadi Eisenkot. An exit poll by Channel 12 showed Mr Netanyahu's Likud party winning 24 seats in the 120-member Knesset, with Mr Eisenkot's Yashar party on 22. Their potential coalitions were also closely matched. The forecast would mean a loss of eight seats for Likud. The results will set the stage for what could be weeks or months of coalition talks as parties try to assemble the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset. Turnout was high as voters delivered their verdict on Israel's wartime government. Long queues were reported at polling stations. Mr Netanyahu voted in the west Jerusalem neighbourhood of Katamon amid tight security. Mr Eisenkot went to a polling station in Herzliya. Opposition politician Yair Golan escaped unhurt after he was approached by a man carrying a large knife, his party said. In a separate incident, three people were arrested for alleged bribery. Voters from Israel's Arab minority were among those flocking to the polls, some for the first time. People casting ballots at the Nazareth Baptist School, which was being used as a polling station, told The National they were desperate for change after more than three years of “catastrophe” for Arabs living in Israel following the October 7 attacks. Hasar Zoabi, who voted for a Joint List of three Arab parties, argued that “as a minority in Israel we should use our democratic right to vote to try to influence the politics for the good”. The high Arab participation has raised the prospect of parties representing the minority having a kingmaker role in the new parliament, potentially either joining a coalition or tolerating a minority government. Mr Netanyahu remains in office while talks on forming a government take place, with no formal limits on his powers. The prospect of a long interlude has raised fears that he will try to use the situation to his advantage, possibly by initiating a new round of fighting with Iran. Israel has a history of political deadlock. Between 2019 and 2022, the country held five elections as parties repeatedly struggled to form stable governments. Under Israeli law, the process of forming a government follows a strict sequence of legal windows. The President first tasks a lawmaker with forming a coalition, granting them up to 42 days, followed by a second candidate who gets 28 days if the first fails. If both fail, a final 21-day period allows any member of the Knesset to try and gather 61 signatures; if this deadline also expires without a majority, the Knesset automatically dissolves itself and mandates that a snap election be held roughly 90 days later. The election was Israeli voters' first chance to weigh in on Mr Netanyahu's leadership after a four-year term defined by the October 7, 2023 attacks, Israel's destructive war on Gaza and the country's subsequent campaigns in Lebanon , Iran ' and across the region. Opposition supporters used the campaign's final days to call for a formal inquiry into the October 7 attacks, something Mr Netanyahu has resisted. Critics say Mr Netanyahu has deepened Israel's international isolation, with its actions in Gaza and the West Bank causing widespread outrage. Mr Netanyahu defended his record, casting himself as the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes. He ended the campaign with several moves to emphasise his hardline security stance, from warning of a "second Holocaust" if Iran is allowed to rearm, to ordering an operation of questionable military value in the occupied West Bank. Mr Eisenkot kept his policies vague, running on a brand of down-to-earth honesty. But most of the main candidates hold belligerent views towards Iran and few are enthusiastic about the idea of a Palestinian state .

title: Europe must be involved in decisions on ending war – Zelensky
body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said this in his evening address , Ukrinform reports.
“We expect a trilateral format in November, with Ukrainian, American, and Russian representatives. It is important that Europe also take part in all diplomatic moves,” Zelensky said.
According to him, Ukraine insists that European countries be involved in the negotiating process and that none of them be excluded from decision-making.
Zelensky also said that Ukraine plans to hold new contacts with key European countries in the coming weeks.
He added that Ukraine would continue coordinating with the United States and other partners to arrange diplomatic meetings.
“We must protect lives. We must bring peace closer. We must shape policy toward Russia in a way that sparks their interest in de-escalation steps. Without pressure, there is no peace. Peace does not come to the powerless,” the head of state stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said during a joint press conference with Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide in Helsinki that a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin was needed to discuss the most sensitive issues of a peace settlement.

title: Germany’s Helsing promises jet-drone-hunting missiles at under $100,000 a shot—its CEO doesn’t expect them on the market before 2027
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); German defense AI firm Helsing has unveiled Contra, an AI-run air defense system and two interceptor missiles designed to chase Russia’s jet-powered Geran drones, the company announced on 26 October. Officials pitch it as cheap, but it won’t reach the market this winter. That leaves Ukraine on its own defenses as Russia shifts to jet drones. By early October, jet models made up about 40% of Russian drone launches, and Ukraine’s own interceptors for them won’t arrive in needed numbers before late November, Air Force Deputy Commander Yurii Cherevashenko said . Two missiles, one AI brain Contra is the command layer of air defense: it links radars and other sensors, tracks incoming drones and missiles, and assigns a weapon to each target, while people keep control over decisions, Helsing said. Besides the company’s own missiles, it can also use other firms’ interceptors, lasers, guns, or nets. AD-1 Inferno is jet-powered and designed to loiter, swarm, and re-engage targets, while AD-2 Ambush, a solid-fuel rocket, is designed to reach Mach 2.5, over twice the speed of sound, and a range of more than 20 km, the company said. Inferno, with a 700 km/h speed and a 20-km range, would be the everyday shooter. Ambush would handle “leakers,” drones about to hit the ground, said Maxwell Adams, Helsing’s senior product director. Each shot should cost under $100,000, company officials said. Built for the faster Gerans Ukraine once downed 90% of Russia’s slower, propeller-driven Gerans, copies of Iran’s Shahed, Defense News reported. Russia has since fielded thousands of jet Geran-4s and Geran-5s flying at 400–700 km/h, and almost half now get through, Helsing co-founder and co-CEO Gundbert Scherf said. Ukraine’s own nightly rates swing widely. On 28 September, President Zelenskyy put the shoot-down rate for jet drones at 57% . Overnight on 7 October, it exceeded 82%, National Security and Defense Council Secretary Ihor Klymenko said . Russian output of the two models has reached 4,000 a month, Helsing said, citing unspecified intelligence reports. Ukraine already uses Helsing’s HX-2 strike drones. Scherf said they should be integrated into a system like Contra. title: Fixed-wing UAS MOU signed between SPARC AI, European supplier
body:
VANCOUVER, B.C. Defense technology company SPARC AI announced that it entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with a major European uncrewed aerial system (UAS) OEM.
Under the terms of the MOU. the as-yet-unnamed manufacturer will integrate and evaluate Overwatch, SPARC AI's positioning network for GPS-denied environments, on two new fixed-wing UASs, with a defined path to commercial deployment once testing has been validated.
The fixed-wing manufacturer is slated to conduct independent testing and validation, with SPARC AI providing engineering, training, and standby support during the testing program. The MOU, according to the announcement, is set up so that integration and evaluation lead directly to commercial deployment.
SPARC AI officials say that this MOU is one of several engagements it has under way with drone manufacturers and end-user operators in the region; these arrangements range from evaluation of Overwatch on other companies' platforms up to and including commercial discussions.

title: MIKTA envoys, FG seek stronger climate finance partnerships ahead of COP31
body: By Favour Ulebor, Abuja Diplomats from MIKTA member countries and the Federal government have called for improved access to climate finance, stronger international partnerships and increased investment in practical solutions to help developing countries address climate change. The call was made at a MIKTA roundtable on Climate Finance and Implementation Partnerships in Africa, held on Tuesday in Abuja, ahead of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, COP31, scheduled to hold in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20. The discussions brought together representatives of Australia, Türkiye, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Mexico, Ethiopia and relevant stakeholders from the climate change sector to examine ways of translating climate commitments into projects that support economic growth, energy access, agriculture and community resilience. Speaking at the meeting, the Australian High Commissioner to Nigeria, Ms Leilani Bin-Juda PSM, said climate action must deliver practical outcomes, particularly for developing countries and communities most vulnerable to its effects. Bin-Juda said many developing countries continued to face difficulties accessing climate finance because of complex applications, fragmented funding systems, reporting requirements and delays. She said Australia was working with Türkiye towards COP31 and with Pacific partners to ensure their priorities were reflected in the global climate discussions. The High Commissioner also highlighted a Pacific-led Action Plan on access to climate finance for Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries, launched at Pre-COP in Fiji on October 8. She said the initiative sought to simplify funding applications, approvals and disbursement, mobilise private investment and strengthen countries’ capacity to develop investment-ready projects. Bin-Juda urged Nigeria to support the initiative, noting that broader international backing would strengthen efforts to make climate finance more accessible and responsive to the needs of vulnerable countries. “For Australia, COP31 is about turning climate ambition into practical outcomes,” she said. The Turkish Ambassador to Nigeria, Mehmet Poroy, said COP31 should focus on implementing existing commitments and ensuring that climate ambitions translated into measurable results. Poroy said African countries needed adequate financial resources, technology, institutional capacity and support for project preparation to implement their national climate plans. He said climate finance should also support development priorities, including energy systems, sustainable agriculture, food security, green industries and climate-resilient cities. The ambassador highlighted Türkiye’s Climate Implementation Bridge initiative, being developed with the United Nations Development Programme, to help developing countries bridge the gap between climate commitments and investment-ready projects. He explained that the initiative was not designed to establish a new fund or replace existing climate finance mechanisms, but to help countries connect their climate priorities with appropriate financing and private capital. Poroy said cooperation between MIKTA countries and African partners could help strengthen implementation as the international community prepares for COP31 and COP32, expected to be hosted by Ethiopia in 2027. Meanwhile, the Indonesian Ambassador to Nigeria, Bambang Suharto, said the scale of investment required to achieve climate targets in developing countries highlighted the need to combine public resources, private investment and international support. He said Indonesia estimated that it would require about $472.6bn to achieve its climate targets, with annual financing needs of approximately $14.5bn through 2030, compared with an annual state budget allocation of about $4.42bn. Suharto said Indonesia was exploring different financing instruments, including green sukuk, blended finance, thematic bonds and concessional funding, to support climate action. He called for existing international climate finance commitments to be delivered and for greater support for project preparation to help countries develop proposals capable of attracting investment. The envoy also highlighted the importance of ocean conservation and coastal resilience, including mangrove restoration, early-warning systems and sustainable fisheries. He expressed Indonesia’s readiness to consult with Nigeria and interested partners on a possible Indonesia-Nigeria Climate Finance and Resilience Partnership, with potential areas of cooperation including climate-resilient agriculture, land restoration, coastal protection, clean energy and green industrialisation. Similarly, South Korea’s Ambassador to Nigeria, Jeong Yoan, outlined opportunities to deepen climate cooperation with Nigeria through renewable energy, agricultural technology, infrastructure and green investment. Jeong said South Korea was committed to achieving carbon neutrality by 2050 and had set a 2035 target to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 53 to 61 per cent compared with 2018 levels. He said Korea’s cooperation with Nigeria included a planned 2026 to 2030 project involving the Korea International Cooperation Agency, KOICA, and the Food and Agriculture Organisation, FAO, aimed at creating green jobs for young people in agriculture and food systems. According to him, the project is expected to support practical training in climate-smart agriculture and digital technology, with the broader objective of improving food security and strengthening resilience. Jeong also identified private investment and a stable investment environment as important factors in mobilising climate finance, noting that clear regulations, transparent procedures and reliable infrastructure could encourage long-term investment. He noted, Nigeria estimated that it would require about $337bn between 2026 and 2035 to meet its climate commitments, underscoring the need for domestic resources, international financing and private-sector participation. The Mexican Charge d’Affaires in Nigeria, Jose Manuel Briseno Flores, also stressed the need to ensure that climate resources translated into practical outcomes, including renewable energy products. He said climate finance should support solutions that could be deployed to address the needs of communities while advancing the transition towards cleaner energy. In her remarks, the Director-General of the National Council on Climate Change, NCCC, Mrs Omotenioye Majekodunmi, said the country was committed to moving from climate pledges to implementation. Majekodunmi who was represented by the council’s Department of Energy, Transportation and Infrastructure, NCCC, Mrs Jummai Vandu said Nigeria supported efforts to turn its Nationally Determined Contributions into bankable, investment-ready projects that could attract financing and deliver measurable results. She identified adaptation finance, decentralised climate action, gender inclusion and a just transition as key priorities for the country. According to her, climate finance must be predictable and accessible to communities facing environmental challenges, while international partnerships should create pathways for states, cities and local governments to implement projects at the subnational level. She also said women and young people should be empowered as decision-makers and direct beneficiaries of climate investments, adding that the transition to clean energy must protect energy security, job creation and economic equity. Majekodunmi said Nigeria was ready to work with MIKTA, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change and other international partners to ensure that COP31 produced practical outcomes. Also speaking, the Ambassador of Ethiopia to Nigeria, Legesse Geremew Haile, said Africa faced disproportionate climate vulnerabilities despite contributing marginally to global emissions. He called for direct access to predictable, grant-based financing and technology transfers, noting that African countries needed support to implement their climate priorities. The Ethiopian envoy highlighted his country’s Climate Resilient Green Economy Strategy and Green Legacy Initiative as examples of efforts to combine environmental protection, employment and sustainable development. He said Ethiopia was looking forward to hosting COP32 in 2027, adding that the conference would provide an opportunity to place African development priorities, just energy transitions and loss-and-damage delivery at the centre of the global climate agenda. MIKTA is a cross-regional partnership comprising Mexico, Indonesia, the Republic of Korea, Türkiye and Australia. The post MIKTA envoys, FG seek stronger climate finance partnerships ahead of COP31 appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Putin holding talks with Equatorial Guinea president
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin is holding talks with visiting President of Equatorial Guinea Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, a TASS correspondent reported.
The meeting is being held on the sidelines of the 8th summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum. Earlier in the day, the Russian leader supported Nguema Mbasogo’s proposals related to cooperation in the gas sector.
Diplomatic relations between the former Soviet Union and Equatorial Guinea were established on December 7, 1968. From the 1990s through the 2010s, bilateral dialogue was maintained at the level of the foreign ministries. In June 2011, President Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, who has been leading the country since 1979, visited Russia for the first time. In July 2013, he participated in the Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit in Moscow, and in October 2019, he attended the Russia-Africa Summit in Sochi. On both occasions, he met with Putin. In November 2023, he paid an official visit to Russia.
According to Russia’s Federal Customs Service, trade between Russia and Equatorial Guinea was $1.7 million in 2021 (further updates are unavailable). Meat and meat products accounted for 86% of Russia’s exports, which also included cardboard, paper, and timber. Timber and charcoal accounted for 100% of imports.
Currently, Russia and Equatorial Guinea are discussing Russian companies’ potential participating in the Central African gas transmission system project. This refers to an agreement reached in September 2022 by seven oil-and gas-producing countries, namely Angola, Gabon, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Congo, Chad, and Equatorial Guinea, to build a network of major oil and gas pipelines, oil refineries, and power plants to reduce dependence on the refining capacities of developed countries.

title: Tinubu’s Difficult Reforms Beginning To Bear Fruit, Says Adesina
body: Former African Development Bank (AfDB) President Akinwunmi Adesina has said President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms are beginning to yield results, citing increased foreign exchange availability, renewed portfolio investments and a downward trend in inflation. Adesina, who visited Tinubu on Tuesday, described the removal of the petrol subsidy and the harmonisation of exchange rate windows as “very important, difficult reforms”, adding that the government must now focus on translating economic stabilisation into growth and prosperity. Speaking to State House correspondents after the meeting, the former AfDB chief said Nigeria’s international perception had also improved, pointing to the outlooks assigned to the country by rating agencies. “If you look at it, you have a lot more FX available today. You have a lot of portfolio investors that are coming into the country. You have inflation trending downwards. Prices are still a bit high, but inflation is trending downwards,” he said. ﻿ Adesina added that some rating agencies had given Nigeria stable or positive outlooks, describing the development as an indication of changing perceptions of the country. He, however, said the gains from the reforms should be followed by a stronger focus on structural transformation and economic expansion. “Now that’s just the beginning of the work. I think the most critical thing is the president realised this, and everybody knows that being a dentist is not a very difficult job. But you have to also now move from the issue of the reforms and stabilisation, straight into structural transformation and also growth and prosperity, which is what the president is focusing on,” he said. Adesina also expressed his willingness to contribute to Nigeria’s development in any capacity the President considers appropriate, insisting that he was not seeking a political appointment. “I told the President, I’m back at home, here to help and ready to help. It’s my country. I love my country, and I’m ready to help,” he said. Asked in what capacity he could support Nigeria, given his experience on the international stage, Adesina said he was prepared to serve wherever his contribution would be useful. “I’m fully able to help Nigeria in any capacity. I’ve always had that. You know, my heart is always at home. And in any capacity that His Excellency feels I can help, I can help in anything. I’m not looking for a job. I’m not looking for anything. I’m just here to help,” he said. “It’s my country. I have a duty, an obligation, and a responsibility to do so, and I will.” Adesina also briefed Tinubu on his 10-year tenure as AfDB president, which ended after two terms, and the bank’s support for Nigeria during that period. He said the AfDB provided about $7 billion in financing to Nigeria between 2015 and 2025, compared with $11.1 billion in total financing since the bank began operations in the country in 1971. “So, within 10 years, we were able to do 63 percent, literally, of that,” he said, adding that Tinubu was pleased with the bank’s support to Nigeria during his tenure. Adesina said the visit provided an opportunity to report on the achievements of his tenure and discuss the bank’s support for the country. The post Tinubu’s Difficult Reforms Beginning To Bear Fruit, Says Adesina appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Burna Boy-Led ‘For Everybody’ Campaign Wins 15 Awards
body: Sporty Group’s ‘For Everybody’ campaign, featuring Grammy Award-winning Nigerian singer Burna Boy and directed by Dave Meyers, has won 15 awards at the 2026 w3 Awards, including Gold in the Creator/Brand Collaboration category. The campaign features Nigerian football stars Asisat Oshoala, a six-time African Women’s Footballer of the Year, and Kenneth Omeruo, an Africa Cup of Nations winner. Other sporting personalities in the production include Spanish international and FIFA World Cup 2026 winner Nico Williams; French international and Real Madrid midfielder Eduardo Camavinga; Ghanaian football legend Michael Essien; former Tottenham Hotspur midfielder and Kenyan national team captain Victor Wanyama; and South African rugby star Cheslin Kolbe, a two-time Rugby World Cup winner. Released in January, the campaign brings together music, sport and African culture to celebrate the continent’s talent and ambition. Sporty Studios, the production arm of Sporty Group, produced it in collaboration with RadicalMedia, with an international production team working across multiple locations. The production also received 14 Silver Awards across categories including Music Video, Best Use of Cinematography, Brand Storytelling, Branded Content, and Sports and Entertainment. The w3 Awards recognise excellence in digital creativity, content and online experiences. An international panel of industry professionals from organisations including Netflix, the Smithsonian and Apple judged the entries. Commenting on the recognition, Elias Gallego, Sporty Group’s Vice President of Media, Marketing and Business Development, said the campaign was designed to reflect the company’s identity and values. “When we released For Everybody, we wanted to create something that reflected who we are as a Group and what we believe in. The most powerful brand partnerships go beyond advertising to become part of a cultural moment, so seeing the campaign recognised across disciplines, from storytelling and cinematography to music and sport, makes us incredibly proud of what we’ve built together,” he said. The Gold award recognises creator-brand collaborations for their integration of creators and audience impact. According to Sporty Group, the campaign sought to create a production that reflected Burna Boy’s identity and resonated with its intended audience.

title: Israel election 2026: What happens after polls close and when will we know who won?
body: At 10 p.m. Tuesday, most polling stations across Israel will close and the country's three main television networks will release their exit polls, offering the first indication of the outcome of the election for the 26th Knesset. But the end of voting will mark only the beginning of a process that could take days to produce definitive results and weeks or even months to determine who will form the next government. With voter turnout reaching historic levels, hundreds of thousands of special ballots still awaiting separate counting and several smaller parties potentially hovering around the electoral threshold, the results projected on election night may look considerably different from the final distribution of parliamentary seats.   Beyond the count, Israel faces another series of deadlines: the publication of official results, the swearing-in of the new Knesset and the president's decision on which lawmaker will be given the opportunity to assemble a governing coalition. What happens when polling stations close at 10 p.m.? At 10 p.m., Israeli television networks Kan 11, Channel 12 and Channel 13 are expected to publish their exit polls, providing the first estimates of how the Knesset's 120 seats will be distributed among the competing parties. The exit polls are based on surveys of voters and are not official results. While they may indicate which political bloc is ahead, they cannot determine with certainty which parties will enter parliament or who will ultimately become prime minister. One of the most significant uncertainties concerns parties close to the 3.25% electoral threshold. Parties that fail to reach that percentage of valid votes receive no seats, meaning even a small change in the final count could significantly alter the balance between rival political blocs. The official counting process will begin as polling stations close, with results gradually transmitted to the Central Elections Committee. The first counted votes are expected to become available during the night, providing a clearer picture as the hours pass. Although the scheduled closing time is 10 p.m., voters who arrive at a polling station before the deadline will still be allowed to cast their ballots, even if they remain in line afterward. When will the final election results be known? The counting process could continue well beyond election night, primarily because of the large number of special double-envelope ballots. More than 650,000 such ballots are expected from soldiers, diplomats, displaced residents, hospital patients, voters with disabilities and others who cast their votes outside their registered polling stations. Unlike ordinary ballots, double-envelope votes require an additional verification process to ensure that each voter has cast only one ballot. The identifying outer envelope is checked before the anonymous vote is added to the count. Central Elections Committee officials had initially hoped to complete the count by Thursday, October 29, but acting Director-General Dean Livne warned that the number of special ballots could be higher than anticipated, potentially delaying the process until Friday morning. The committee is expected to publish a clearer picture of the election results by Thursday, although the final tally may take longer. Under Israeli law, the official results must be published by November 4. The distinction is important: even if television exit polls show one political bloc holding a parliamentary majority, the actual allocation of seats could change as the special ballots are counted and parties near the electoral threshold learn whether they have secured representation. Historic turnout: 74.3% by 8 p.m. The election has already been marked by unusually high voter participation, with turnout reaching 74.3% by 8 p.m., the highest rate recorded at that hour since 1988. According to the Central Elections Committee, 5,449,277 Israelis had voted out of 7,331,981 eligible voters, compared with 66.3% at the same hour in the November 2022 election. The increase amounts to eight percentage points, or approximately 12% in relative terms. The latest figure also surpassed the previous election's final turnout rate of approximately 70.6%, with two hours still remaining before most polling stations were scheduled to close. Earlier in the day, turnout stood at 66.7% by 6 p.m., compared with 57.7% in 2022. By 4 p.m., it had reached 55.7%, compared with 47.5% four years earlier. Participation was also particularly high among military personnel. According to the IDF, 68% of eligible service members had voted by 5 p.m., compared with 65% at the same hour during the previous election. The surge brought long lines to polling stations in several cities, while severe weather and flash floods in southern Israel complicated voting in some communities, particularly in the Arava region, where road closures prevented some residents from reaching their designated polling stations. Election committee rejects request to extend voting hours The combination of exceptionally high turnout, lengthy waits and severe weather prompted a political dispute over whether voting should continue beyond 10 p.m. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party submitted a request to extend voting hours. The proposal received support from Shas, led by Aryeh Deri, Otzma Yehudit, led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael party. Opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar!, Naftali Bennett's Beyahad and Yair Golan's Democrats, opposed extending voting hours. Following a discussion, Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg, deputy president of the Supreme Court, decided not to approve the request, leaving the scheduled closing time unchanged. The committee nevertheless emphasized that voters arriving before 10 p.m. would be allowed to vote even if they remained in line after the deadline. Violence and confrontations throughout Election Day Tuesday's voting was also accompanied by several reported incidents of violence, intimidation and confrontations between political activists. Israeli singer Ofer Levi was questioned by police on suspicion of incitement to violence after a video circulated online allegedly featuring calls to execute left-wing voters. Levi denied making the statements, claimed the video had been manipulated using artificial intelligence and warned that anyone distributing it could face legal action. He was released under restrictive conditions following questioning. In Rahat, a Bedouin city in southern Israel, a brawl broke out near a polling station following arguments between voters. In the ultra-Orthodox city of Modi'in Illit, youths burned pictures of Moti Leitner, chairman of the Haredi Public party. Campaign booths belonging to the party were also vandalized in Beitar Illit and Bnei Brak, while activists were reportedly called "traitors." In Haifa's Bat Galim neighborhood, a confrontation erupted between city council member Yaniv Ben Shoshan, who heads the Likud faction on the council, and activists at a Democrats party campaign booth. The activists alleged that pushing had occurred. In Bat Yam, Deputy Mayor Kati Piasecki of the Democrats and five other party activists were reportedly assaulted near a school. Earlier in Tel Aviv, police arrested a man carrying a knife who approached Democrats leader Yair Golan during a tour of the city. Golan's party alleged that the incident was an attempted attack, while police confirmed the arrest but did not characterize it as an attempted stabbing. The incidents underscored tensions surrounding the election, even as millions of Israelis continued to cast their ballots. November 10: The new Knesset will be sworn in Once the official results are published, attention will shift to the composition of the new parliament and the process of forming a government. The 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, exactly two weeks after Election Day. Its 120 elected members will formally take office, even if negotiations over the next government have not been completed. Unlike in presidential elections, Israelis do not vote directly for a prime minister. They vote for party lists, with parliamentary seats distributed according to each party's share of the valid vote, provided it crosses the electoral threshold. A party's position as the largest faction in parliament does not automatically entitle its leader to become prime minister. Instead, the president must determine which member of the Knesset has the best prospect of assembling a governing coalition. To do so, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the parties elected to parliament, with each faction recommending a candidate to form the next government. The candidate selected by Herzog will then be tasked with securing sufficient parliamentary support. How long does a candidate have to form a government? The first candidate chosen by the president will have 28 days to form a government. Herzog may extend that period by up to an additional 14 days, allowing a maximum of 42 days for the initial attempt. If the candidate fails, the president may assign the task to another member of the Knesset. That second candidate would receive 28 days, without the possibility of an extension. If the president concludes there is no viable candidate, or a second attempt fails, a further 21-day period allows at least 61 members of the Knesset to submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a particular lawmaker. Should such a request receive the necessary support, the designated candidate would have 14 days to form a government. The president's role is therefore central to the post-election process, particularly if the parliamentary balance is divided and no political bloc can immediately secure the support needed to govern. And if nobody succeeds? If every attempt to form a government fails, the Knesset would be dissolved and Israel would return to the polls for another election, to be held within 90 days. Until a new government is sworn in, the outgoing government remains in office in a caretaker capacity. That means the first exit polls at 10 p.m. may offer only the opening chapter of a political process whose conclusion could remain uncertain for weeks. Even after the official votes are counted and the new Knesset convenes, the question of who will lead Israel may still depend on negotiations between political parties and their ability to assemble a governing majority.

title: Export hurdles and visa waits for Ukrainian companies force Pentagon to slow its drone contest
body:
A soldier holds a remote controller near a GARA unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) at an unnamed location in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
One morning in June, the head of export at Ukrainian drone company Stellarion found himself unexpectedly in need of a U-Haul outside the Detroit Metro Airport in Michigan.
Stellarion was set to test its drones in front of American soldiers at a competition organized by the Pentagon at Camp Grayling, a military base three hours away. But while many of its 48 invited competitors were American companies that had had weeks to modify, prepare, and fit warheads onto their drones, Stellarion was facing a last-minute scramble.
The company's drones had landed that very morning, slowed by Ukrainian export controls and lengthy shipping times, Stellarion's head of exports, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told the Kyiv Independent.
Stellarion performed strongly enough to advance in the competition, but the Ukrainian company's ordeal reflects a broader problem.
Interviews with Ukrainian manufacturers competing in the Pentagon's Drone Dominance Program (DDP), a contest to procure drones for U.S. defense, revealed the companies’ struggles with export controls, shipping times, and visa approvals, sometimes resulting in late product arrivals and rapid turnarounds before competition.
The obstacles to Ukrainian companies are serious enough that, in early October, the Pentagon announced it was pushing back the next phase of the competition, Phase 2.5, which focuses on bomber drones, to November. About half of the 17 companies invited to participate are Ukrainian, a sign of how much the U.S. procurement strategy now depends on drones made in Ukraine.
It is the first time the program has been so visibly forced to accommodate its rules and timeline to meet the needs of Ukrainian companies.
In a statement to the Kyiv Independent, the Pentagon said that "Ukrainian companies have the most battlefield-tested Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems products in the world, and have scaled. We have a responsibility to give American soldiers and Marines the benefit of the best materiel."
The DDP, initiated by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a July 2025 memorandum, is the U.S.’ flagship effort to procure drones at a time when Russia and Ukraine each plan to produce 7 million in 2026 for their respective war efforts. The program is funded to the tune of $1.1 billion and initially aimed to procure 340,000 drones, according to the Request for Solutions released in December 2025.
The Pentagon has prized speed, stating in February in a press release: "We are buying what works — fast, at scale, and without bureaucratic delay."
In the spring, Phase I tested classic one-way attack first-person view (FPV) drones. Over the summer, Phase II tested long-range strike drones and those that operate in close quarters. Other than the U.S. itself, no country sent more competitors to those initial phases than Ukraine. Other competing countries included Israel. Croatia, the U.K., among others.
In July, the Pentagon announced the names of the 17 companies that would be invited to compete in Phase 2.5, spending $30 million to acquire up to 1,200 bombers, according to the Request for Solutions released in July.
Unmanned bombers, which can carry heavier payloads, have played a crucial role in Russia's war against Ukraine. These drones have increasingly been used for logistical, resupply, and rescue missions, with one drone airlifting a 42-kg E-bike to a wounded soldier in July of 2025.
Eight or nine of the companies invited to Phase 2.5, according to the Inside Unmanned Systems blog , have Ukrainian origins: UFORCE, Gurzuf Defence, Skycutter-Skyfall, Meta Bureau, Grim Tech, and F-Drones are publicly Ukraine-based. Two other companies, listed as Achiever UA and UA Defense Tech, have no public presence, nor does the Areya corporation. Ukrainian companies need a registered legal entity in the U.S. to enter the competition.
Ukrainian companies have long struggled with the DDP’s tight turnarounds. In late July, the DDP put out a "Request for Solutions," or an invitation for companies to pitch the Pentagon on participating in Phase 2.5. Responses were due by Aug. 10. Invitees were announced publicly on Sept. 21, and given until mid-October to ship six ready-to-test bomber drones — which can cost up to $20,000 per unit to produce — to Camp Grayling.
But the export obstacles that Stellarion faced in June are still present.
Ukraine has worked to streamline its export approvals, aiming in July to shorten the approval process to 30 days, but it can still take weeks to approve drone exports. Phase II of the DDP required a special deal to get Ukrainian drones out fast.
But shipping the drones to the U.S. can add another two or three weeks, leaving Ukrainian companies with practically no time to make needed modifications or prepare in an on-base testing environment.
A number of Ukrainian companies therefore considered or decided to withdraw from the competition. One is Skycutter-Skyfall, a partnership between a British defense tech startup that works closely with SkyFall, which produces drone hardware in Ukraine.
Skycutter-Skyfall placed first in Phase I of the DDP in March, earning an order of 2,560 of its one-way-attack FPV drones, according to the DDP’s online leaderboard . Yet, Skycutter was the last of 11 companies to deliver its drone contract, the leaderboard shows.
Gurzuf Defence told the Kyiv Independent that it had notified the Pentagon of its withdrawal from Phase 2.5, while another Ukrainian company told the Kyiv Independent, on condition of anonymity, that it considered pulling out of the competition before ultimately deciding to attend.
As of Oct. 13, at least four companies — a quarter of all those invited — declined to audition their drones at Camp Grayling, according to the DDP website . Two of the four were Ukrainian companies.
Now, the Pentagon is postponing Phase 2.5 to November "to best position all participants for success," according to the Drone Dominance website. The Pentagon reached out to companies that had withdrawn to ask them back to the competition. Gurzuf, for its part, still declined, telling the Kyiv Independent it would take them until December to be fully ready.
The Pentagon told the Kyiv Independent that Ukrainian export controls and shipping times were not "in themselves a factor" in the decision to postpone Phase 2.5. Instead, they emphasized that the decision "included a recognition of the time-consuming U.S. visa processes."
The U.S. Embassy in Kyiv does not process traditional business visa applications, meaning Ukrainian applicants need to travel elsewhere to complete the process, which can take weeks or months, depending on the location.
The Pentagon maintains that it holds Ukrainian companies to the same standards as all competitors. In the first two phases of the program, run between February and August, multiple Ukrainian companies, on condition of anonymity, said the Defense Department’s attitude to supply chain challenges could be boiled down to: "These are the rules. You knew them in advance."
The Pentagon’s decision to postpone signals a shift in approach, suggesting the DDP cares more about encouraging Ukrainian participation than preserving its initial, rapid timelines.
The DDP is the largest drone procurement initiative in the world outside Russia and Ukraine. It is a central part of the U.S. defense modernization effort.
A Grim Tech representative, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told the Kyiv Independent: "If you want to access the American market, you need to be there." In its request for Fiscal Year 2027, the Pentagon has asked for $54 billion for drone warfare and procurement. Companies that succeed now stand to benefit from large future American contracts.
Ukrainian companies also know domestic wartime demand will not last forever. Some have begun to modify their products and form new partnerships to make themselves attractive to foreign governments, the Pentagon most of all.
In March, Ukrainian drone producer General Cherry announced a partnership with American military producer Wilcox Industries to produce hardware in New Hampshire. F-Drones, another Ukrainian company, announced in June a major production project in Ohio. Both General Cherry and F-Drones advanced in earlier phases of the DDP.
But these partnerships don't come cheap. As Grim Tech’s representative put it, "We are finding reliable partners in the U.S., but we're still thinking about what we can do. Because it's a high cost. It's a big investment to set up."
Stellarion’s head of exports put it similarly: "Companies that already have some strong representation in the U.S., some U.S. partners, are in a much better position."
"We had to navigate challenges on our own."
Leo Greenberg is a Kyiv-based analyst and writer focused on Eastern European politics, defense strategy, and military technology. He has worked for Warsaw's Stefan Batory Foundation and the U.S. House of Representatives, and holds a BA in History and Philosophy from Yale University.

title: UBA Foundation opens 2026 essay competition to promote literacy among SHS students
body: The UBA Foundation has opened applications for its 2026 National Essay Competition, seeking to strengthen the writing skills, creativity and critical thinking of senior high school students across Ghana amid concerns about declining literacy skills among young people. The competition offers students an opportunity to develop their writing abilities, express their ideas and compete for financial support towards their tertiary education. Regional Head of Brand, Marketing and Corporate Communications at UBA West Africa, Henry Nii Dottey, said the initiative formed part of the foundation’s efforts to support education and nurture the creative potential of young people. He said the foundation had observed a decline in the literary skills of young people and was using the competition to encourage more students to develop their writing abilities. “This is one of our support initiatives to society. We’ve observed that the literary skills of our young people keep declining. So, one of the things we aim to do is to help improve their creative skills by getting them to write,” he said. Mr Dottey said the competition was open to eligible senior high school students nationwide, with applications for the 2026 edition scheduled to close on November 13. He encouraged students to apply through the UBA Ghana website, stressing that the competition offered an opportunity to strengthen their skills while securing financial assistance for further education. “The competition is open from now until November 13. We want to encourage everybody watching that once you’re in a secondary school in Ghana, you’re eligible. There’s good money to support your tertiary education. You have to apply through the UBA Ghana website,” he said. Previous winner urges students to participate For Stephanie Ewuraabena Aidoo, a winner in the 2024 edition, the competition provided benefits beyond financial support for her university education. She said the experience helped her recognise the value of her voice and build confidence in expressing her ideas. “Aside from the major grants from the UBA Foundation to support my university education, I have learnt to value the power of my voice. I have become more confident in expressing my ideas,” she said. She encouraged students to participate rather than dismiss their chances of winning before applying. “So, to every high school student out there, I’ll encourage you to try. A winning essay begins with trying. Don’t disqualify yourself by thinking you won’t be chosen,” she added. The competition has also attracted interest from students who attended a programme promoting the initiative. Emmanuella, Girls’ Prefect of Achimota Senior High School, said listening to speakers at the event had inspired her and encouraged other students to take advantage of similar opportunities. “The programme has been amazing to the very end. Having to sit through and listen to the encouraging words from every speaker has inspired me. So, I encourage every other student out there that it is necessary,” she said. The UBA Foundation says the competition is part of its broader commitment to education and youth development, with the aim of encouraging more young people to embrace reading and writing and build the communication skills needed to contribute to Africa’s development.

title: UralChem prepared to establish joint ventures in Africa
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. UralChem is prepared to share with African countries its expertise in the construction of fertilizer and agricultural product transshipment terminals, as well as to establish joint ventures for distribution, UralChem Group told TASS.
"We are prepared to contribute to the development of the continent’s agricultural sector, including through the establishment of joint ventures to develop distribution in local markets and the transfer of modern agricultural technologies," the company said ahead of the Russia-Africa forum.
TASS is an information partner of the third Russia-Africa Summit and Economic and Humanitarian Forum.

title: Energy cooperation between Russia, Egypt actively developing — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russia and Egypt are actively developing cooperation, including in the energy sector, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) summit.
"Our cooperation with Egypt is developing very actively across many areas, including the energy sector. One of the largest joint projects is the construction of a nuclear power plant, which is being financed primarily through multi-billion-dollar state loans provided by Russia," he said.
Putin described this project as successful. "The project is progressing very successfully with the support of President [of Egypt Abdel Fattah] el-Sisi. And we very much hope to see him in Moscow soon for the Russia-Africa forum," he added.

title: 5 Data Center Power Stocks to Watch Before Earnings
body: Wall Street has spent the last three weeks punishing the companies that build and equip AI data centers, which would make more sense if anyone could point to the orders drying up. As of Friday, that group was down a median 23% since the S&P 500's record close on Oct. 6, while the Big Tech companies actually writing the checks were down only 5%. A dozen of the biggest builders and power suppliers lost more than $300 billion in market value over the stretch, including $54 billion at GE Vernova, $30 billion at Eaton and $25 billion at Quanta Services.  Last Thursday's leg down came after Meta's latest earnings report reignited worries about AI infrastructure spending, but the physical shortage hasn't changed. Jefferies' Aniket Shah told Yahoo Finance that "the biggest constraint right now for the AI build-out is power," U.S. transformer supply is running about 15% short this year according to Wood Mackenzie, and Apollo's Torsten Slk puts lead times at transformer makers at as long as 26 months.  That is the thinking behind this list. Whether the power comes from gas, solar or nuclear, somebody has to build the turbines, transformers, switchgear and batteries it runs through, and those factories are booked years out. Three of the five companies below report within a week, so we are about to find out whether the order books still look the way they did in the summer.  GE Vernova Reports Tomorrow  GE Vernova NYSE GEV would probably like to talk about something other than its stock. Since GE spun it off in 2024 it has been the poster child for the power crunch, and it ended the second quarter with a $176 billion backlog, nearly four times the revenue it expects this year. The shares slid to about $823 last week anyway, their lowest since March 31.  The gas turbine order book gets most of the attention. Customers have signed up for 116 gigawatts of equipment and production slots, although 63 GW of that is reservations rather than firm orders, and CEO Scott Strazik says the company is "implementing actions to produce 30 GW in 2030." GE Vernova is only now reaching a 20 GW annual pace, so the current list is nearly six years of production, and anyone who isn't already in line has a long wait ahead.  The weak spot is Wind, which lost $657 million at the EBITDA level in the first half and helped push GE Vernova to miss Wall Street estimates for adjusted EBITDA in the second quarter. Management expects Wind to come in roughly break-even this quarter, and Bank of America is looking for orders of about $21 billion, up 44% from a year ago, so what matters tomorrow is whether the order book keeps growing while the stock keeps falling.  The Venture Global deal gets less simple the closer you read it. GE Vernova and Baker Hughes signed frame agreements with the LNG exporter this month covering up to 16 gas-fired power islands, and with transformer equipment included the package could be worth $17.2 billion if every purchase order goes through. Venture Global says it expects to place the first one by the end of the year, which is the sort of detail that tends to get dropped from the headline.  Quanta Services Starts Building What It Used to Install  Quanta Services NYSE PWR has spent decades putting up other people's equipment, so its new joint venture with Hyosung HICO to make high-voltage circuit breakers in Pennsylvania says a lot about where the bottleneck is. Quanta pitched it as a supply chain fix for customers, but it reads like a contractor that got tired of waiting on suppliers.  CEO Duke Austin said second-quarter results "meaningfully exceeded expectations," which is fair when revenue rose 41% to $9.56 billion and backlog hit a record $53.4 billion. Which earnings number you use matters more than usual, though Quanta guides to $16.45 to $16.95 a share adjusted but only $11.41 to $11.92 under GAAP, a gap of roughly $5 that comes mostly from amortization of acquired intangibles and stock compensation. The data center money is also a year or so away, since CFO Jayshree Desai says Quanta is being conservative about counting those projects in backlog and meaningful field work doesn't start until the second half of 2027. Quanta reports before the open Thursday.  Eaton Bought Its Way In  Eaton NYSE ETN did not get into the data center business by waiting. Since April 2025 it has paid $1.43 billion for Fibrebond, which builds modular power enclosures, and $9.55 billion for Boyd Thermal, a thermal management business, and CEO Paulo Ruiz says data centers "remain a key growth driver" even as he points out that demand is strong across its other markets. The orders support that, with rolling 12-month orders at Electrical Americas, the unit that sells power distribution gear into data centers, up 41% and backlog across the electrical business up 43% from a year ago.  Sales hit a record $8.53 billion in the second quarter, but earnings fell to $2.11 a share from $2.51 as interest expense nearly tripled and long-term debt more than doubled to $18.5 billion, which is what closing $11 billion of acquisitions in a single quarter will do. Eaton's own guidance has GAAP earnings flat for the year and adjusted earnings up 12%, and the roughly $3 a share separating the two is acquisition costs, restructuring and amortization. Anyone quoting only the adjusted number is leaving that out.  Eaton agreed in June to hand its Mobility business to Dana in a Reverse Morris Trust, due to close in the first quarter of 2027, and the roughly $1.1 billion in cash it expects from the deal can go toward debt. The company reports Nov. 3.  Powell Industries, the One You Probably Haven't Heard Of  Powell Industries NASDAQ POWL has been building electrical distribution gear in Houston for 79 years, mostly for oil and gas, petrochemical and utility customers, and in the quarter ended June 30 its backlog passed $2 billion for the first time, reaching $2.4 billion. Helping get it there was a single order worth more than $400 million for a data center built around its own on-site power generation, the same behind-the-meter idea Venture Global is chasing with GE Vernova's turbines.  CEO Brett Cope says "commercial momentum across our key end markets continues to accelerate," and he has the numbers to say it, with a record $934 million in new orders against revenue of $312 million. At that pace the backlog is nearly two years of sales, so the question is how fast Powell can build, which is why it is expanding its Jacintoport fabrication yard and weighing new plants. Oil and gas customers are still buying too, including a roughly $60 million order tied to LNG export on the Gulf Coast.  Petrochemical revenue fell 49% in the quarter, though, and earnings of $1.42 a share missed the $1.49 analysts expected. Powell is expected to report fiscal fourth-quarter results in November.  Fluence Energy Has a Houston Problem  Fluence Energy NASDAQ FLNC, the battery storage maker AES and Siemens started in 2018, booked $1.44 billion in orders in the June quarter, nearly triple a year earlier, and ended it with a record $6.4 billion backlog. It says it has also secured about $850 million of data center business through July, roughly $550 million of it from a hyperscaler. Building what it has sold is another matter.  Fluence's new contract manufacturing plant in Houston was supposed to average 11 battery units a day in August and September. It averaged less than one in August and about three in early September, according to Latitude Media, because a customized automated welding process ran far below target and crews had to switch to slower manual welding, and as of the Sept. 16 call the plant still wasn't connected to the grid and was running on generators. CEO Julian Nebreda told investors the company had "underestimated the complexity of the ramp-up of the Houston facility," which is one way to put it.  That is how a company that began the fiscal year guiding to $3.2 billion to $3.6 billion in revenue ended up at about $2.4 billion after two cuts in six weeks, with an adjusted EBITDA forecast that swung from a $50 million profit to a loss of about $200 million. The stock fell about 15% the day after the second cut, and law firms have since filed a securities class action covering shares bought between Nov. 24, 2025 and Sept. 16. Those are allegations, not findings.  It is also the second year in a row that a new U.S. factory has dragged Fluence down revenue fell 16% last year on what S&P Global Market Intelligence described as weaker-than-expected production ramps at new U.S. plants, along with project delays and tariff uncertainty.  The timing is awkward because the data center customers Fluence wants most move fast. Nebreda has acknowledged the delay creates problems for them, since they go from lead to contract in under three months, compared with about 18 months for everyone else. Meanwhile the company burned about $299 million of free cash flow in the first nine months of its fiscal year and had $863 million of liquidity at June 30, and CFO Ahmed Pasha says the goal for fiscal 2027 is neutral to positive operating cash flow without outside capital. That plan arrives with full-year results later this fall.  Wall Street can debate whether the AI build-out is a bubble for as long as it likes, but a plant that can't weld fast enough is a much simpler problem to understand.  By Michael Kern for Oilprice.com

title: Favourite Family Recipe: Mahtab’s Golden Saffron Tahchin
body:
Persian Saffron Rice with Chicken and Crispy Golden Crust
Serves: 6–8 Prep time: About 30 minutes Cooking time: About 1 hour 15 minutes
1. Bloom the saffron: Mix the ground saffron with 3 tablespoons of hot water and let it sit for 10–15 minutes.
2. Cook the chicken: Place the chicken, onion, turmeric, salt, pepper and water in a saucepan. Cover and simmer for about 25–30 minutes, until the chicken is cooked and tender. Remove the chicken and shred or cut it into bite-sized pieces.
3. Prepare the rice: Rinse the basmati rice several times. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil and add the rice. Cook for about 6–7 minutes, until the outside of the rice is tender but the centre is still slightly firm. Drain well.
4. Prepare the saffron mixture: In a large bowl, combine the yogurt, egg yolks, melted butter, oil, salt and bloomed saffron. Add the drained rice and gently mix until the rice is evenly coated.
5. Assemble the Tahchin: Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Generously grease a deep oven-safe baking dish. Press half of the saffron rice into the bottom. Add the chicken in an even layer, then cover with the remaining rice and gently press it down. Cover tightly with aluminum foil.
6. Bake: Bake for about 60 minutes. Remove the foil and bake for another 15–20 minutes, until a deep golden crust has formed. Let it rest for about 10 minutes, then carefully flip it onto a serving platter.
7. Garnish: Quickly sauté the barberries in butter for about 30–60 seconds, adding a little sugar if desired. Spoon them over the Tahchin and garnish with slivered pistachios and almonds.

title: Perpetua Resources gets $40M US Army funding to advance tungsten production
body: Perpetua Resources (Nasdaq: PPTA) (TSX: PPTA) has received a new 36-month, $40 million award through the U.S. Army’s Defense Ordnance Technology Consortium (DOTC) from the Portfolio Acquisition Executive Agile Sustainment & Ammunition (PAE AS&A) in Picatinny Arsenal, New Jersey. The award, the company said, will fund a program to evaluate the technical and economic feasibility of producing tungsten concentrate at its project in the historical Stibnite mining district in Idaho. Structured as a cost-share program between Perpetua and the U.S. Government, funding will support drilling to define a potential tungsten mineral resource, collection of material for laboratory and bench-scale metallurgical testing and permitting and engineering of an exploration decline to access areas of known tungsten mineralization. There has been no commercial tungsten mining in the United States since 2015. The US is wholly reliant on imports, with recent Chinese export controls and new federal sourcing restrictions adding to the defense and manufacturing supply risk. The Stibnite mining district has a history of antimony and tungsten production, supplying roughly half of the tungsten and 90% of the antimony used by the United States during World War II. When the war ended, mining for tungsten and antimony concluded, leaving identified mineralized materials behind. In August, Perpetua reported a new gold-tungsten discovery along the southeastern edge of the proposed Yellow Pine pit at its Gold-Stibnite project. Drilling also outlined gold mineralization at the adjacent Huckleberry fault zone and returned antimony-tungsten intercepts at Hangar Flats. The company has said those areas could eventually add to 3.1 million oz. of indicated and inferred gold resources and 99.8 million lb. of antimony resources lying outside the current reserves. Stibnite is expected to produce an average 463,000 oz. of gold annually during its first four years, according to Perpetua’s December technical report. The project is part of U.S. efforts to establish a domestic antimony supply chain for defence and industrial uses. The company said the drilling program at the Hangar Flats deposit returned significant tungsten-antimony mineralization, as previously reported, including 9.8 meters grading 4.6% tungsten, 8.3% antimony; 22.9 meters grading 1.2% tungsten, 3.2% antimony and 3.4 meters grading 1.5% tungsten, 10.6% antimony. The results underpin the new DOTC award which will focus largely on the tungsten mineralization beneath the Hangar Flats pit, Perpetua said. “The U.S. Army’s additional investment in a historically proven American tungsten source at Stibnite underscores the growing strategic value of Stibnite’s mineral endowment and continues to strengthen the partnerships supporting Perpetua’s future,” Perpetua Resources CEO Jon Cherry said in a news release. “Historical production and recent exploration results suggest Stibnite has the potential to be one of the world’s highest-grade tungsten sources,” Cherry said. Perpetua’s proposed program with the U.S. Army includes an initial surface exploration drilling program and metallurgical test work on an existing 550-kilogram sample compiled from prior exploration activities grading 9.2% antimony and 4.2% tungsten. Other work will include the design, permitting, and possible construction of an exploration decline to access the high-grade antimony, tungsten and gold mineralization beneath the Hangar Flats pit. In addition to drilling for tungsten under the DOTC award, the company said it intends to continue to advance its own ongoing exploration activities underneath the currently permitted Hangar Flats pit which contains approximately 1.37 million ounces of gold resources and over 95 million pounds of antimony resources not included in the current mine plan or in the reported mineral reserves. Any activity outside the scope of the currently permitted mine plan will require additional regulatory review and permitting. Perpetua said will design and implement the tungsten exploration project and will match the U.S. Army’s $40 million contribution in the joint investment. The initial 18-month phase is expected to cost approximately $18 million and be shared equally between Perpetua and the U.S. Army. The timing, scope and cost of subsequent phases are subject to ongoing development based on results of prior exploration, testing, engineering and permitting activities, as well as approval of each incremental phase of additional funding. This new award brings total U.S. Government awards to Perpetua for critical minerals to $126 million since 2022. In addition to the announced DOTC grant, Perpetua has submitted proposals for additional grants to further expand its critical minerals program. Perpetua Resources stock was up over 9% Tuesday afternoon in Toronto. The company has a C$3.2 billion ($2.3 billion) market capitalization.

title: 4 students, one lady killed in Niger governor’s convoy road crash
body: By Clare Nnabuike, Minna Five person, four male students and a young lady have died in a fatal accident involving the Niger state governor Mohammed Umaru Bago’s convoy in Minna, the state capital. The incident happened on Monday at Gidan Mangoro community along the Minna–Bida Road. It followed a head-on collision between a high speeding Hilux van in the convoy of Bago, and a private Peugeot 206 car. The lady identified as Mrs Nafisa was driving the car and died at the spot of the accident. She was said to be a staff of an NGO, and Programme Manager at Labspace, and the Founder of Wosh Mart Service Ltd. A resident of Gidan Mangoro, Abdullahi Musa, told Vanguard that the accident occurred at about 11:35am when the governor was returning from Bida. He and his team paid a condolence visit on the Etsu Nupe and chairman of the Niger state council of traditional rulers Alhaji Yahaya Abubakar over the passage of the Sagi Nupe Hajia Aisha. He said the occupants of the private car driven by Nafisa were suspected to be postgraduate students of the Federal University of Technology, Minna. His words, “The people in the private car died instantly, while those in the government Hilux sustained serious injuries with the driver dying on the spot. Nafisa “The accident was caused by wrongful overtaking by the Hilux in the governor’s convoy. The other car was in its lane when the Hilux rammed into it.” A member of staff of Minna General Hospital, where the victims were rushed to told Vanguard that three people died on the spot while two other people died due to high level of injuries sustain from the crash. “Some of the injured victims were subsequently referred to IBB Specialist Hospital for advanced medical care,” he said. Vanguard gathered that one of the occupants of the Hilux van was a former Niger state local government council chairman who sustained fractures to his legs but was still alive at the time of this report. The Niger State Sector Commander of the Federal Road Safety Corps, FRSC Aishat Sa’adu, confirmed the road crash but said that by the time her officers arrived at the scene, the victims had already been evacuated to the hospital. The Police Public Relations Officer of the Niger state command Superintendent of Police Wasiu Abiodun confirmed the incident and said the accident was under investigation. He did not however give the names or numbers of the deceased. “The accident occured this morning and we are investigating it,” Abiodun said. The post 4 students, one lady killed in Niger governor’s convoy road crash appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: GRASAG president calls for sustainable funding for agricultural research in Africa
body: The President of the Graduate Students Association of Ghana (GRASAG), Richard Class-Peters, has called for sustainable financing for agricultural research to improve food security, boost local production and support economic growth across Africa. He made the call at the recently concluded World Bank’s Africa Growth and Opportunity – Research in Action (AGORA) 2026 conference in Palermo, Italy. Mr Class-Peters said African countries must increase investment in research and innovation while strengthening farmer cooperatives to improve agricultural productivity and build more resilient food systems. “Sustainable financing for agricultural research is critical to empowering innovation, strengthening farmer cooperatives and transforming local agriculture for food security and economic prosperity in Africa,” he said. He noted that increased funding for agricultural research could help farmers access improved technologies, raise production levels and develop practical solutions to challenges affecting the sector. Mr Class-Peters also stressed the importance of supporting farmer cooperatives, saying they enable farmers to share knowledge, access resources and improve their productivity. “We must empower our local farmers and cooperatives with the knowledge, technology and support they need to produce more and contribute meaningfully to Africa’s economic development,” he said. He added that stronger domestic agricultural production could reduce African countries’ reliance on imported food, create jobs and improve livelihoods, particularly in farming communities. The AGORA 2026 conference focused on how African countries can develop the skills, businesses and systems needed to translate investment into employment and economic growth.

title: The Food Discourse kicks off its Bodawuro Project in Vane
body: The Food Discourse, a youth-led initiative and community platform, has kicked off its Bodawuro Project with an engagement with farmers in Vane, in the Ho West District of the Volta Region. The project is in line with its objective of promoting sustainable food systems, agroecology and climate resilience in Ghana and across Africa. It aims to highlight grassroots food and climate stories from farmers, identify their challenges and propose possible solutions across five selected regions of Ghana. Vane, the gateway to Avatime, lies at the base of Mount Gayi in the Ho West District of the Volta Region. The majority of residents rely on farming, cultivating crops, among other activities, to support their livelihoods. However, climate change, the high cost of agro-inputs and urbanisation, among other factors, are affecting the farming activities of these rural residents. They also highlighted the difficulties of accessing their farms and transporting farm produce, among other challenges. In effect, The Food Discourse is implementing its Bodawuro Project in the area, hoping to promote climate-resilient practices among farmers and the younger generation to sustain the food system. The farmers were introduced to an eco-friendly solar food storage system and digital extension services in a bid to sustain the system, ensuring access to extension services and adopting measures to prevent post-harvest losses so they earn enough from their yield. They were also introduced to fish farming as an alternative livelihood to sustain them during periods when the climate is not favourable for crop farming. They were trained in setting up a simpler model of a canopy fish pond using easily accessible materials. The Founder of the Food Discourse, Gloria Agyare, said that they aim to protect the food systems at the local level to sustain livelihoods. “They talked about so many challenges, and I closely paid attention. Then I asked them, Why are they still doing this farming thing? Because in their challenges, you have to leave it.” “But all of them said, How will we eat if we stop this work? This highlights the importance of our food system to sustain every life on it. So there’s a need to shape the way the food system is to ensure that we create a balance for people to find jobs and create jobs in it,” she said. She added that the Bodawuro Project was also designed to ensure a transfer of knowledge of the food systems and agriculture knowledge from the older generation to the younger generation. “We are trying to amplify the stories at the grassroots. the indigenous knowledge and bring it to the forefront”, she said. The Paramount Chief of the Avatime Traditional Area, Osie Adza Tekpor VII, lauded the initiative, emphasising its focus on saving the climate. “We have a forest; we have trees, so there’s no need for us to even go into free planting. They forget that as you cut the tree, you are destroying the forest, and as the saying goes, when the last tree dies, the last man dies.” “So, we need this constant awareness. On behalf of the committee, we welcome the project. We will do everything within our capacity and capability to make sure that at least 20 people will start this project this season,” he stressed.
