title: 2027: No rainbow coalition in Imo – Uzodimma
body:
Governor Hope Uzodimma of Imo State has declared that there is no Rainbow Coalition Movement in the state.
Mr Uzodimma insisted that the All Progressives Congress (APC) would win the 2027 elections across all elective positions in the state.
The governor made the remarks on Tuesday during the flag-off of the PBAT Door-to-Door Movement in Imo State and the distribution of campaign vehicles to the group in Owerri, the state capital.
The PBAT Door-to-Door Movement is a support group mobilising for the re-election of President Bola Tinubu in 2027.
The event was broadcast live on Channels TV which was monitored by PREMIUM TIMES.
Mr Uzodimma, who handed the campaign vehicles to the group, told them that they should remain members of the APC and work solely for the victory of Mr Tinubu and all candidates of the party in the next year’s general election.
“The PBAT Door-to-Door Movement, listen to me,” he began.
“You’re members of the APC. If I see you work outside the APC, I’ll collect the vehicles from you,” the governor warned.
“You’re empowered to work for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the APC. There’s no rainbow coalition in Imo State.”
Mr Uzodimma boasted that he does not need the Rainbow Coalition Movement to win the election for Mr Tinubu in Imo, arguing that the president would win the state with “organic votes” in the 2027 election.
The governor maintained that the APC was the “only recognised” political party in the state and urged supporters to vote for the party’s candidates across all levels in the 2027 general elections.
Mr Uzodimma and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, have been in a face-off over the Rainbow Coalition Movement.
Mr Wike, a former governor of Rivers State, runs the Rainbow Coalition, a multi-party political arrangement, to support President Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid.
The All Progressives Congress governors, under the aegis of the Progressives Governors Forum (PGF), have vehemently opposed the coalition, describing it as a political arrangement that could undermine the party and its candidates ahead of the 2027 elections.
The PGF is chaired by Mr Uzodimma, who has picked the APC’s ticket for Imo West District despite the fact that his tenure as governor will elapse in January 2028, six months after the next Senate would have been inaugurated in June 2027.
Mr Wike is officially a member of the opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), but he works under the APC-led government.
The FCT minister’s position on the Rainbow Coalition Movement has been that the movement would work solely for the re-election of Mr Tinubu while his party, the PDP, would push to win other elective offices.
But Mr Uzodimma and other APC governors insist that such an arrangement would work against the election of other APC candidates.
On his part, Mr Wike claimed Mr Uzodimma, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq of Kwara State and their Ogun State counterpart, Dapo Abiodun, were fighting the Rainbow Coalition Movement for “selfish reasons.”
Mr Wike stressed that the governors believe that the coalition would deprive them of the power to secure victory for their chosen APC senatorial and House of Representatives candidates.
The minister said some politicians, including incumbent federal lawmakers, secured PDP senatorial and House of Representatives tickets after the governors allegedly denied them APC tickets.
He specifically said the governors were jittery that the politicians who secured PDP tickets after losing APC tickets could work against their political interests if they win in the general election.
Mr Wike then accused Mr Uzodimma of opposing the coalition mainly because of his belief that it could jeopardise his ambition to become Senate President.
The FCT minister also declared that he would not support Mr Uzodimma’s ambition to become the country’s Senate president.

title: Police arrest 34 foreigners in Benue
body: The Police in Benue State have arrested 34 foreign nationals suspected of engaging in illicit activities in two Local Government Areas of the state. State Commissioner of Police, CP Cletus Nwadiogbu, who disclosed this on Tuesday while parading the suspects and others arrested for various offences at the Command Headquarters in Makurdi, expressed concern over the growing attraction of Otukpo to foreign nationals whose movements have raised security concerns. Nwadiogbu said the arrest consists of 16 Cameroonians picked up in Otukpo town of Otukpo LGA and 18 Nigeriens intercepted at Orokam in Ogbadigbo LGA on October 22. He said the 16 Cameroonians arrested in Otukpo on October 9, claimed they came to settle in the town, but could not provide clear explanations for their purpose. Kano: Man’s body recovered from open water Sheikh Gumi urges calm over Masussuka’s killing Nwadiogbu said, “Otukpo has become a place where they like to go and hibernate. There must be something taking them to that axis.” The commissioner added that the 18 Nigeriens intercepted at Orokam claimed they were travelling to Ikom in Cross River State but could not produce the required travel documents. He said the suspects were being investigated to establish their immigration status and the circumstances surrounding their entry into the country. The police commissioner added that the suspects would be handed over to the Nigeria Immigration Service after the investigation. He recalled that some Pakistani nationals were also recently arrested in Otukpo, raising further questions about the town’s emergence as a destination for foreign nationals whose movements have attracted security attention.

title: CNO Outlines Vision for Fleet Adaptation
body: WASHINGTON — Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle highlighted the critical need for a dynamic and resilient naval force during his address at the Fantail Breakfast hosted by the Navy Memorial in Washington, D.C., Oct. 26, focusing on adaptation, operational endurance, and sustained fleet readiness. Speaking to military leaders and industry partners, Caudle outlined a strategic vision for the future Fleet centered on continuous modernization. He emphasized that to maintain a decisive advantage in the fight, the Navy must be capable of changing itself as problems change, utilizing software, modularity, and uncrewed systems. “When I think about the Navy, we will need in the decades ahead, I keep coming back to two words: Adaptation and Endurance,” said Caudle. “Our advantage cannot depend on getting every prediction right. Our advantage must be our ability to adapt faster than the threat and endure longer than the fight.” To build this self-adapting force, the discussions highlighted the necessity of a highly responsive industrial base and a robust foundry of manufacturing capacity. Caudle called for stronger collaboration with industry partners to accelerate the transition of commercial technologies, open architectures, and software-defined capabilities directly into the fleet. “Innovation that cannot transition to the Fleet, scale in production, or be sustained in combat is not yet the warfighting advantage we need,” said Caudle. “Speed is a weapon. And in the next fight, the side that can translate learning into fielded combat power faster will create advantages its adversary struggles to overcome.” Addressing warfighting endurance, the CNO stressed that long-term operational success depends heavily on the Sailors who generate combat power. He highlighted key “Total Sailor: Fit to Fight” and quality-of-service initiatives, noting that the Navy has expanded Wi-Fi in unaccompanied housing—which currently sits at 90 percent coverage and is rapidly expanding to 100 percent—improved galley food service satisfaction from 56 percent to 80 percent following pilot improvements, and reduced the number of junior Sailors living aboard ships in homeport by more than 80 percent. “Ships do not generate combat power by themselves. People generate combat power,” said Caudle. “Quality of service is not separate from readiness. It’s foundational to our ability to recruit, retain, develop, and sustain the people we send into harm’s way.” Following his formal address, Caudle participated in the Navy Memorial’s SITREP Speaker Series. Marking a milestone for the program, the engagement featured questions from both a live, in-person audience and online viewers for the first time. During the Q&A session, Caudle expanded on his vision for an adaptable force, challenging the traditional reliance on rigid carrier strike group deployments to solve diverse global challenges. “For decades, our normal force generation model has been centered around strike groups. So, you lived in a have and have-not, a poor man rich man problem. A one or a zero,” said Caudle. “Could the Navy do more than a one or a zero? And of course it can. So this idea of packaging our Navy in a way to solve combatant commander key operational problems in a unique way by listening to what they really need, that may not be tied to the strike group.” Using U.S. Southern Command as an example, Caudle noted that an effective, tailored force package for maritime domain awareness might combine uncrewed systems, Littoral Combat Ships, afloat forward staging bases, and U.S. Coast Guard integration rather than a traditional carrier strike group. The engagement reinforced the Navy’s commitment to building a force that learns from real-time global operations, reconfigures quickly, and regenerates combat power to maintain a decisive advantage in any future conflict. From the Navy Chief of Information, Oct. 26. 2026 The post CNO Outlines Vision for Fleet Adaptation appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: American, Israeli Jews report stronger bonds despite challenges of recent years, survey finds
body: A new survey commissioned by the Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA) has revealed that a large majority of American and Israeli Jews feel a deep and growing sense of shared connection, defying prevailing narratives of a widening chasm between the two communities.Mimi Kravetz, chief impact and growth officer at JFNA, told The Jerusalem Post, “Over the last three years, a surge in Jewish engagement here at home has come alongside a rising sense of connection to Jews in Israel too.”“Now there's an opportunity to strengthen those connections using the kind of relationship-building strategies our data show work, including travel, shlichut [emissary work], and community partnerships that our communities have invested in for decades,” Kravetz told the Post.Writing in a JTA op-ed on Monday, Kravetz and Rebecca Caspi, senior vice president for Israel and overseas and director general of JFNA's Israel Office, shared the survey's findings, noting that the survey forms the first part of a two-part analysis exploring where the two communities are aligned and where they differ. “Part two will address where American and Israeli Jews see things differently, and why.”Caspi and Kravetz pointed out that the last three years have been historic for both communities, marked by the trauma of October 7 and ensuing wars in Israel alongside a dramatic rise in security threats, antisemitism, and attacks on Zionism faced by American Jews at home. While it would be understandable if these separate challenges drove the two populations apart, the data reveals that they actually feel closer to one another than they have in years.JFNA surveys over 4,000 American, Israeli Jews on shared identity and connectionThe findings are detailed in the 2026 JFNA Bilateral Relationship Between American and Israeli Jews research initiative published on the Berman Jewish DataBank, which examined attitudes on peoplehood through two separate national surveys conducted earlier this year. The research comprised a national survey of 2,836 adult Jewish Americans conducted by Burson via text-message recruitment between May 4 and May 27, and a parallel survey of 1,323 Israeli Jewish adults conducted by Shmuel Rosner utilizing the Madad Israeli panel and a haredi (ultra-Orthodox) panel between May and June.The study explored how both populations view their bilateral relationship, tracking a noticeable rise in what the report termed the “rise in peoplehood” since previous major assessments. According to the survey data, 75 percent of Israeli Jews reported feeling “a lot” or “some” commonality with Jews in the United States. On the American side, 72 percent of respondents reported feeling a similar connection with Israeli Jews, rising significantly from 59 percent in a 2020 Pew Research Center survey, with those reporting they have “a lot” in common jumping from 19 percent to 29 percent.This strengthening bond is also reflected in how members of both communities characterize their relationship through family metaphors. Among American Jews, the share describing Israelis as extended family or part of their community climbed from 46 percent in 2021 to 62 percent, while those feeling no real connection dropped by more than half from 28 percent to 13 percent. Similarly, the proportion of Israeli Jews categorizing American Jews as extended family or part of their community rose from 45 percent to 53 percent, while those reporting nothing in common dropped from 14 percent to 10 percent.When asked whether Jews around the world, regardless of where they live, share a common fate and must act accordingly, 78 percent of Israeli Jews and 56 percent of Jewish Americans agreed. Furthermore, strong majorities in both countries rejected the notion that diaspora life is a problem to be solved, with 72 percent of American Jews and 72 percent of Israeli Jews affirming that the Jewish Diaspora is a legitimate form of Jewish life.The research highlighted that this connection translates directly into action, particularly through philanthropic support following the events of October 7, 2025. The Jewish federation system raised $908 million through its Israel Emergency Campaign to fund recovery efforts on the ground. 79 percent of Israeli respondents and 67 percent of American respondents agreed that American Jewish philanthropy remains important to Israeli society, while 68 percent of Israelis stated that post-October 7 giving made them feel Diaspora Jews genuinely care about Israel.Travel to Israel strengthens American Jews' sense of shared identityBeyond broad sentiment, the data demonstrates that physical presence and direct engagement dramatically multiply feelings of commonality between the two populations. Among American Jews, travel frequency correlates directly with a stronger sense of shared identity; those who have traveled to Israel once are 1.7 times as likely to feel real commonality with Israeli Jews, those who have traveled more than once are 3.8 times more likely, and those who have lived in Israel are 11.2 times more likely.A similar dynamic exists on the Israeli side, where casual tourism does not significantly shift connection levels, but deeper immersion does. Israelis who participate in Jewish communal life while visiting the US are 2.8 times as likely to feel a sense of peoplehood, and those who serve as emissaries, work at summer camps, or live inside an active American Jewish community are 2.6 times as likely. Overall, 87 percent of Israeli Jews with real, engaged contact with American Jews feel commonality, compared to just 52 percent among those with no contact.When American Jews were asked in open-ended discussions why they feel connected to Israel, the responses revealed a consistent set of core motivations. Respondents frequently pointed to seeing Israel as a safe place for Jews, viewing it as the historical homeland where Jewish identity began, and maintaining a belief that Jews are responsible for one another alongside religious or biblical ties. Others highlighted feeling more whole in Israel, recognizing the necessity created by the Holocaust, viewing Israel as part of their own culture, and taking personal pride in Israelis themselves.Caspi and Kravetz noted that this reawakening of shared peoplehood directly corroborates findings from a separate, comprehensive study conducted by JFNA that tracked trends in Jewish life in the United States. That separate survey revealed that heightened community engagement, known as the “Surge,” had evolved into a sustained behavioral shift rather than a temporary reaction.Specifically, the research showed that 38 percent of the American Jewish community is part of the Surge and has maintained an active increase in participation across three distinct areas: communal involvement like attending synagogues or joining advocacy groups, educational exploration, and social connection such as hosting private Shabbat dinners or participating in workplace affinity groups.“We are in another challenging season for the Jewish people,” Caspi and Kravetz said. “It would be easy to conclude that we have more differences than we have commonalities, and to approach discussions from a place of distance and division. But there is an opportunity in this tense moment to recognize our deep sense that we are one community.”JFNA urges greater investment in travel and community programs to strengthen Jewish tiesRegarding their recommendations for moving forward, Caspi and Kravetz stated, “Our data confirm that today we feel closer than ever, and we recognize that our lives are shaping each other's. Perhaps even more importantly, our data show what we can do to strengthen and perpetuate this trend. We need to keep investing in things we know build a connection: more travel, more Israeli emissaries in North American communities, and more programs that put people in real contact.”“And we need to scale innovation that will enable shared volunteer projects, philanthropic partnerships across both communities, stronger business and professional ties, and digital opportunities to learn from one another. These opportunities can ensure impact when travel is impractical, reach those who are less engaged, and ensure that this sense of connection to and understanding of Jews across the world is accessible to everyone in our greater Jewish family and community,” Caspi and Kravetz said.

title: Villa Vie Odyssey’s ‘Endless’ World Cruise Comes to a Halt in Cambodia as Fuel Costs Soar
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
The residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey anchored off St. Lucia in the Caribbean. The vessel has suspended operations in Cambodia amid soaring fuel costs and financial restructuring efforts. Photo: Villa Vie Residences
Villa Vie Residences has suspended operations of its residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey in Cambodia, forcing residents to disembark as soaring fuel costs push the company toward financial restructuring.
The Fort Lauderdale-based company announced Tuesday that it is evaluating restructuring and recapitalization options over the next 60 days after a sharp increase in fuel expenses made its current operating model financially unsustainable.
According to the company, monthly fuel expenses on an equivalent per-cabin basis have surged from a historical average of approximately $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 in parts of Asia, an increase of as much as 344%.
The company attributed the increases to the conflict with Iran, which began in late February and has disrupted energy markets and shipping operations worldwide.
“Since the conflict began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company said. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs.”
The financial pressures have brought an abrupt halt to a voyage that was marketed as a continuous, around-the-world residential cruise.
In a notice to residents on Monday, October 26, Villa Vie CEO Kathy Villalba said the company had been unable to secure the fuel needed to continue operating. The vessel would enter temporary layup, with crew remaining aboard to maintain essential systems.
Residents were instructed to leave the vessel by 2 p.m. that day, according to a copy of the notice published by resident Randy Cassingham .
The company said it is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements, acknowledging the disruption for residents, crew members and employees.
The shutdown follows earlier efforts to raise additional funding. Cruise Industry News reported that Villa Vie had sought financial contributions from residents, including a recent request for $360,000 to cover fuel expenses. In April, the company reportedly offered residents an emergency loan investment opportunity seeking $3 million, with interest rates ranging from 12% to 24%. It was unclear how much funding, if any, was raised.
Cassingham, writing about the shutdown, said the company’s problems extended beyond fuel prices, citing a combination of weaknesses in the business model, management decisions and rising operating expenses.
The 195-meter Villa Vie Odyssey , formerly Fred. Olsen Cruise Lines’ Braemar , was acquired by Villa Vie in March 2024 and underwent refurbishment in Belfast before beginning its continuous world voyage in October of that year.
The company’s concept offered residents the opportunity to purchase cabins aboard the ship and travel indefinitely, with itineraries taking the vessel to hundreds of destinations around the world. Its Endless Horizons program also offered lifetime cruising through a one-time payment.
The financial crisis comes just three months after Villa Vie announced plans for a second residential cruise ship , Legacy , which was expected to enter service in early 2029.
At the time, the company said more than 85% of available residences aboard Odyssey had been sold. It also announced plans to extend lifetime residency rights to Legacy and introduced a program allowing new buyers to live aboard Odyssey before transferring to the second vessel.
Tuesday’s announcement did not address the future of Legacy or how the suspension might affect residents who purchased cabins or lifetime cruising rights.
Villa Vie said it continues to evaluate financing and restructuring alternatives, but no transaction has been finalized and there is no confirmed timetable for resuming operations.
The company acknowledged that the outcome of its restructuring efforts remains uncertain.

title: Elon Musk says Ukraine’s military violated Starlink’s terms of service
body:

Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink’s terms of service before the recent slowdown, as reported earlier by Ars Technica . According to Musk, “Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” however Ukrainian officials have denied that happened, or that it is actually possible for them to do.
The statement comes nearly two weeks after Ukrainian officials accused SpaceX of putting limits on the military’s satellite internet service that disrupted its drone missions and operations. As reported by Axios , Ukraine uses Starlink for communications, logistics, and to defend against incoming drones. For offensive missions, officials say that Ukraine uses Starshield, the US military-controlled variant of Starlink.
Musk points to a post from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which said Ukraine uses “Starlink from mid-range strikes against enemy military targets,” in violation of Starlink’s policies. However, Serhii Beskrestnov, a defense technology advisor for Zelenskyy, pushed back on this in a post on Telegram, saying Starlink’s systems can only connect to devices traveling between 70 and 90 kilometers per hour (around 43 and 55 miles per hour) and don’t work in Russia. “Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes or medium-range strikes,” Beskrestnov wrote.
Ars Technica also points out a tweet from another former Ukrainian advisor, Serhii Sternenko, that went into more detail, saying that while stationary terminals could be registered (with Starlink) by military personnel or civilians, “for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system… In other words, using civilian Starlink for drone missions was technically impossible. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield.”
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Starlink and Starshield services had been fully restored. With the restriction lifted, Ukraine’s military can now connect to devices traveling at speeds of more than 400km/h (248mph), the Kyiv Independent reports .
Though Musk initially offloaded the blame for the slowdown in Ukraine onto the US government, President Donald Trump responded by saying he “wasn’t involved” and didn’t know who throttled SpaceX’s services. A report from The Wall Street Journal later said Trump asked Musk to lift restrictions on Ukraine.

title: Pentagon creates advisory council on human performance, health
body: After creating a new directorate on warfighter optimization within the Department of Defense, the Pentagon announced it will form a federal advisory committee to weigh in on issues affecting troop performance and health. According to a Federal Register notice Tuesday , the $1.4 million committee will focus “exclusively on human performance,” providing guidance and insight on improving function, combating the physical, mental and emotional tolls of military service known collectively as “operator syndrome,” and preventing physical injuries and operational stress. “The Council will serve as a high-impact, low-cost mechanism for the [DoD] to secure the expertise of the nation’s foremost leaders at the nexus of warrior health and performance,” the announcement stated. The Pentagon established a Warfighter Performance Optimization division earlier this year within Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata’s office. It is intended to oversee and coordinate the individual services’ efforts to improve troops’ readiness and performance. In May, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed Tata to report on existing optimization initiatives across the services to create a department-wide performance optimization plan. Hegseth said he wanted to accelerate fielding technologies that will improve performance — such as wearable devices and other analytics tools — and focus on elevating “cognitive performance as a key to readiness.” “By building on and modernizing the principles of Total Force Fitness (TFF), WPO will deliver a unified operational approach to accelerate readiness, dominance, and peak performance across the Force. We will treat the Warfighter as a readiness capability, held to the same disciplined evaluation, maintenance, and optimization we demand of every asset that preserves combat power,” Hegseth wrote. The services have created their own approaches to health, fitness and human performance within the last several years. Army introduced its Holistic Health and Fitness initiative in 2020 to improve the health of the force and reduce the number of soldiers considered non-deployable because of chronic medical conditions. The Navy introduced its Human Performance Optimization program as a pilot in San Diego in February, providing training and education on nutrition, sleep, injury prevention and stress management. The Marine Corps has had a total fitness strategy since 2023 that combines wellness, fitness, mental health and data to improve the health of members, while the Air Force is building a new human performance optimization facility at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, which is designed to support Air Force Special Warfare airmen. The new advisory committee will have up to 20 members with expertise in an array of scientific and medical fields, including urology, endocrinology, nutrition, neurology, combat stress, orthopedics, preventive medicine, wearable technology or spiritual, psychiatric or psychological health, sleep medicine and human factors engineering. As with all federal advisory committees, volunteers are unpaid and only receive travel pay and per diem reimbursement when conducting council-related business. The announcement described the council as “an exceptionally cost-effective resource.” The newly formed group, the announcement stated, will provide information that helps the services create “lethal, operationally ready warriors prepared physically, psychologically, for successful large-scale, high kinetic, combat operations against peer adversaries who are imbued with the essential Warrior Ethos to win decisively,” the announcement stated. Shortly after Hegseth took office last year, he dismissed the members of roughly 40 Defense Department advisory boards and launched reviews to determine whether they supported his goal to “revive the warrior ethos” in the U.S. armed forces. The Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services and the Defense Advisory Committee for the Prevention of Sexual Misconduct were among those terminated. Hegseth has also created several new advisory boards since being sworn in, most recently, the Homeland Defense Board, announced Sept. 11, which he plans to chair. The board will provide guidance on military support for homeland security missions.

title: A shipwreck, two Nazi spies and the Boy Scout who noticed
body: Editor’s Note: The opening passage is excerpted from Sara Vladic’s The Dangerous Shore: How a Motley Crew of Scientists, Mobsters, Double Agents, Retirees, Volunteer Pilots (and a Boy Scout) Stopped the Invasion of America (HarperCollins, 2026). That night, snow falls in heavy, wet flakes, coating Hancock Point in a thin, white blanket — the first snow of the season. Harvard Merrill Hodgkins, a high school senior and a Boy Scout, drives home from the Wednesday night dance at the Townsend Club. It’s just after eleven, and he’s navigating the winding, unlit road back to Crabtree Neck, as snow drifts down in near-blinding sheets. As he rounds a bend, his headlights catch two figures trudging through the snow. They’re moving slowly, heads down against the wind, dressed in long, city-style overcoats and slacks, clothes that look foreign here in the Maine woods. He slows the car, and the men turn their faces away from the light. It’s bitter cold, but they wear no hats, no boots. Hodgkins finds it suspicious. “You just don’t see folks walking without boots out here when it’s snowy . . . no one around here wears a topcoat in the winter.” He considers offering them a ride; something about them nags at his curiosity. “Shucks, if they were crazy enough to be out on a night like this, maybe I’d let them walk,” he thinks, edging the car to the side as they pass. Their faces are unfamiliar—strangers, he realizes, and in a place where six families live year-round, everyone’s face is familiar. Hodgkins watches them disappear around the bend, their steps trailing off toward the woods and the black sea. It’s a risky time to be out here alone, with recent whispers of spies landing on the Maine coast. He stops the car. He gets out and follows their footprints down the road, then down a little trail that veers off toward Sunset Rocks — a spot he knows well from rabbit hunting with his father, Dana Hodgkins, a deputy sheriff and local guide. Their tracks vanish into the trees near Kent Crabtree’s house. They’d come from the shore, Hodgkins realizes. “There was no reason for them to be coming from down there,” he ponders, unease prickling as he scans the empty coastline. The cottages along Sunset Rocks are empty in the winter — no reason at all for strangers to emerge from that path. Down the road, another local, Mary Forni, mother of three and the tax collector’s wife, is driving home from her weekly card game. It’s nearly midnight when her headlights pick up two men walking along the edge of the macadam highway, close enough that she can make out their thin, city-style coats, their shoulders hunched against the snow. She, too, feels that flash of unease. Forni tells her husband, who brushes it off with a laugh. The encounter with those two strange men lingers in Mary Forni’s mind, keeping her awake long into the night. By morning, she can’t shake her misgivings, so she shares them with her neighbor, Harvard’s mother. “They just weren’t like anyone you’d see here in November,” she said, the unease still fresh in her voice. “Honestly, it’s a wonder I didn’t stop and offer them a ride.” They quickly connect the dots to the two sightings. — ✦ — The strangers were German intelligence agents Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh. On Nov. 29, 1944, U-1230 had delivered them to the Maine coast to gather intelligence in the United States. Four days later, the same submarine torpedoed the Canadian freighter SS Cornwallis off the Maine coast. The ship sank in less than 10 minutes, killing 43 of the 48 people aboard. Only five survived. Now, more than 80 years later, the Nomad Exploration Team has located the wreck nearly 400 feet beneath the Gulf of Maine. The discovery, made on July 11, 2026, followed seven years of research and expeditions to find the long-lost ship. It brings renewed attention to the lives lost and to the remarkable events ashore that wartime headlines would only partly explain. The Nomad Exploration Team recently located the wreck of the Canadian freighter SS Cornwallis. (Nomad Exploration Team) When Harvard’s father, Deputy Sheriff Dana Hodgkins, returned from a hunting trip, Harvard told him about the strangers. Dana initially suspected burglars, but his investigation of the area’s homes revealed nothing amiss. On Dec. 4, while in Bangor, he encountered an FBI agent he knew and mentioned Harvard’s experience. Within an hour, three agents arrived in Hancock to question the teenager. Federal personnel had already been sent to the area following the sinking of Cornwallis. The attack established that a U-boat was operating offshore. Harvard’s account supplied the first evidence of a potential enemy landing. Investigators checked transportation connections and telephone records. But the strangers had moved on. The decisive break eventually came from inside the operation. Colepaugh approached a friend who contacted the FBI on his behalf. Colepaugh surrendered, and the information he supplied enabled agents to arrest Gimpel. In its Jan. 15, 1945, issue, TIME described federal agents following the spies “almost as soon as they landed.” The article reported their arrests but did not explain Colepaugh’s surrender or the roles of Hodgkins and Forni. The effect was reassuring: enemy agents had arrived, and American authorities had been close behind. The fuller story gives civilian vigilance and a spy’s decision to surrender far greater importance. The FBI made the arrests, but that fact alone did not explain how the landing came to light or how the case broke. Along another stretch of Maine’s coast, USS Eagle 56 offers a different example of why wartime accounts deserve careful examination. In April 1945, the patrol vessel sank after a violent explosion. Survivors reported evidence of a submarine, but the official inquiry attributed the loss to a boiler explosion. Decades later, persistent research prompted a reassessment. In 2001, the Navy recognized the sinking as a combat loss caused by a German U-boat. The Nomad Exploration Team also located Eagle 56, finding the wreck in 2018 before its discovery was publicly announced the following year. These were separate events, with different circumstances. Together, they reveal how much the history of America’s wartime shores still rewards investigation. They are among the stories explored in The Dangerous Shore : a war of merchant crews, intelligence officers, sailors, and ordinary Americans confronted with extraordinary responsibilities close to home. For families of those lost aboard Cornwallis, the discovery establishes the ship’s final resting place. For the rest of us, it brings the war off America’s coast into sharper focus. These waters carried merchant crews toward home, enemy submarines within reach of shore, and secrets that would outlast the fighting. Finding Cornwallis was no small undertaking. After years of searching, the Nomad team nearly missed the wreck entirely, finally detecting it in the last 100 yards of a sonar survey. Confirming the discovery required dives into cold, dark water nearly 400 feet deep, with strong currents and conditions that challenged even these experienced divers. With Cornwallis and Eagle 56, the Nomad team has brought renewed attention to two ships whose histories reach well beyond the circumstances of their sinking. In Hancock, that history also survives on an ordinary stretch of road. Before anyone knew the strangers’ names or their mission, a teenager noticed their clothes, and a mother refused to dismiss her unease. Neither knew the whole story. Both recognized something worth telling. More than 80 years later, a team of divers has given us another reason to listen. Sara Vladic is the New York Times bestselling co-author of INDIANAPOLIS and author of The Dangerous Shore , which explores the Americans who defended the home front during World War II.

She, too, feels that flash of unease. Forni tells her husband, who brushes it off with a laugh. The encounter with those two strange men lingers in Mary Forni’s mind, keeping her awake long into the night. By morning, she can’t shake her misgivings, so she shares them with her neighbor, Harvard’s mother. “They just weren’t like anyone you’d see here in November,” she said, the unease still fresh in her voice. “Honestly, it’s a wonder I didn’t stop and offer them a ride.” They quickly connect the dots to the two sightings. — ✦ — The strangers were German intelligence agents Erich Gimpel and William Colepaugh. Four days later, the same submarine torpedoed the Canadian freighter SS Cornwallis off the Maine coast. The ship sank in less than 10 minutes, killing 43 of the 48 people aboard. Only five survived. Now, more than 80 years later, the Nomad Exploration Team has located the wreck nearly 400 feet beneath the Gulf of Maine. The discovery, made on July 11, 2026, followed seven years of research and expeditions to find the long-lost ship. It brings renewed attention to the lives lost and to the remarkable events ashore that wartime headlines would only partly explain. The Nomad Exploration Team recently located the wreck of the Canadian freighter SS Cornwallis. (Nomad Exploration Team) When Harvard’s father, Deputy Sheriff Dana Hodgkins, returned from a hunting trip, Harvard told him about the strangers. Dana initially suspected burglars, but his investigation of the area’s homes revealed nothing amiss. On Dec. 4, while in Bangor, he encountered an FBI agent he knew and mentioned Harvard’s experience. Within an hour, three agents arrived in Hancock to question the teenager. Both recognized something worth telling. More than 80 years later, a team of divers has given us another reason to listen. title: US Army queries industry’s ability to build 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles
body: The U.S. Army is asking whether the defense industrial base can deliver and support nearly 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles . An Army market survey published Monday focuses on two ISV versions: the ISV-9, which carries nine passengers, and the ISV-Utility, which carries five passengers plus a utility bed to haul cargo. “The estimated total requirement is for 20,787 vehicles (9,003 ISV-9 and 11,784 ISV-U), subject to fund availability and requirements from the U.S. Army, other sister services and potential Foreign Military Sales (FMS) customers,” the survey said. “To ensure the most streamlined, competitive, and cost-effective approach, the government is utilizing the results of this market survey to determine the feasibility of several procurement pathways.” The ISV, from GM Defense, is based on General Motors’s commercial Colorado and Silverado pickups. GM Defense was awarded a $697.7 million contract modification last month for engineering changes to the ISV-U and the ISV-U Utility Winch Kit, bringing the cumulative value to $915.6 million. GM Defense announced Oct. 12 that the Army expanded orders for the ISV from an initial 649 to nearly 12,000. In the market survey, contractors are asked to provide the Army with manufacturing cost estimates based on “varying annual production volumes (e.g., 100, 500, 1,000, and 1,500+ units per year) to evaluate economy-of-scale thresholds.” The survey also includes a timeline that begins in fiscal 2028 with an acquisition of 106 vehicles. The acquisition continues to fiscal 2036, with the Army receiving around 2,000 to 2,100 vehicles per year. The survey also listed numerous technical specifications. The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have a maximum vehicle curb weight of 5,200 pounds, plus an operational payload of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-9 and a payload capacity of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-U. Both versions will have a gross vehicle weight rating of up to 10,200 pounds, the survey said. Both vehicles require baseline military modifications, including blackout lights, 24V electrical systems, main power disconnect, run-flat tires, the ability to ford both salt and fresh water, MIL-STD-814/MIL-STD-209K life and tie-down provisions, 24V NATO slave receptacles on the front and rear bumper, an integrated winch and Military Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants (POL) compatibility.” The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have full rollover protection for their passengers. The ISV-U will also have a winch, a 4,000-watt inverter with multiple electrical outlets, towing capacity of up to 6,500 pounds and the capability to carry “non-ambulatory patients as a kit.” The vehicles should be capable of traveling up to 55 miles per hour on good paved roads and 17 miles per hour cross country. “Both the ISV-9 and ISV-U shall be capable of traversing longitudinal grades up to 60% and must reliably meet stringent mobility profile requirements across improved, secondary, and un-improved surfaces (trails and cross-country) without fatiguing the occupants when the platform is operating at GVW [gross vehicle weight],” the Army said.

The ISV-U will also have a winch, a 4,000-watt inverter with multiple electrical outlets, towing capacity of up to 6,500 pounds and the capability to carry “non-ambulatory patients as a kit.” The vehicles should be capable of traveling up to 55 miles per hour on good paved roads and 17 miles per hour cross country. “Both the ISV-9 and ISV-U shall be capable of traversing longitudinal grades up to 60% and must reliably meet stringent mobility profile requirements across improved, secondary, and un-improved surfaces (trails and cross-country) without fatiguing the occupants when the platform is operating at GVW [gross vehicle weight],” the Army said.

title: US Army queries industry’s ability to build 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles
body: The U.S. Army is asking whether the defense industrial base can deliver and support nearly 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles . An Army market survey published Monday focuses on two ISV versions: the ISV-9, which carries nine passengers, and the ISV-Utility, which carries five passengers plus a utility bed to haul cargo. “The estimated total requirement is for 20,787 vehicles (9,003 ISV-9 and 11,784 ISV-U), subject to fund availability and requirements from the U.S. Army, other sister services and potential Foreign Military Sales (FMS) customers,” the survey said. “To ensure the most streamlined, competitive, and cost-effective approach, the government is utilizing the results of this market survey to determine the feasibility of several procurement pathways.” The ISV, from GM Defense, is based on General Motors’s commercial Colorado and Silverado pickups. GM Defense was awarded a $697.7 million contract modification last month for engineering changes to the ISV-U and the ISV-U Utility Winch Kit, bringing the cumulative value to $915.6 million. GM Defense announced Oct. 12 that the Army expanded orders for the ISV from an initial 649 to nearly 12,000. In the market survey, contractors are asked to provide the Army with manufacturing cost estimates based on “varying annual production volumes (e.g., 100, 500, 1,000, and 1,500+ units per year) to evaluate economy-of-scale thresholds.” The survey also includes a timeline that begins in fiscal 2028 with an acquisition of 106 vehicles. The acquisition continues to fiscal 2036, with the Army receiving around 2,000 to 2,100 vehicles per year. The survey also listed numerous technical specifications. The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have a maximum vehicle curb weight of 5,200 pounds, plus an operational payload of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-9 and a payload capacity of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-U. Both versions will have a gross vehicle weight rating of up to 10,200 pounds, the survey said. Both vehicles require baseline military modifications, including blackout lights, 24V electrical systems, main power disconnect, run-flat tires, the ability to ford both salt and fresh water, MIL-STD-814/MIL-STD-209K life and tie-down provisions, 24V NATO slave receptacles on the front and rear bumper, an integrated winch and Military Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants (POL) compatibility.” The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have full rollover protection for their passengers. The ISV-U will also have a winch, a 4,000-watt inverter with multiple electrical outlets, towing capacity of up to 6,500 pounds and the capability to carry “non-ambulatory patients as a kit.” The vehicles should be capable of traveling up to 55 miles per hour on good paved roads and 17 miles per hour cross country. “Both the ISV-9 and ISV-U shall be capable of traversing longitudinal grades up to 60% and must reliably meet stringent mobility profile requirements across improved, secondary, and un-improved surfaces (trails and cross-country) without fatiguing the occupants when the platform is operating at GVW [gross vehicle weight],” the Army said.

title: US and Cuban envoys in shouting match during UN embargo debate
body: Washington’s UN envoy Mike Waltz and Cuba’s Foreign Minister, Bruno Rodriguez Parrilla, clashed on Tuesday during a General Assembly debate on the US's decades-old embargo against Cuba. The 193-member body was debating a resolution calling for an end to the US trade embargo on the island. The confrontation began when Mr Waltz accused Cuba ’s government of enriching its political elite while ordinary Cubans endured food shortages, power cuts and economic hardship. Mr Parrilla repeatedly interrupted the speech, demanding that the American be called to order for what he described as offensive remarks against the Cuban government and its people. As tension rose, Mr Waltz demanded that members of the Cuban delegation move away from the podium. “I’m the representative of the United States of America. Back up,” Mr Waltz shouted. “This isn’t Havana . You’re not going to intimidate me.” The President of the UN General Assembly , Khalilur Rahman, temporarily suspended proceedings and then allowed Mr Parrilla to raise a point of order. Mr Parrilla accused Mr Waltz of lying and violating the dignity of the assembly. “I request you to call to order the Permanent Representative of the United States, who is not only lying grossly, but is beneath the dignity of this forum and member states,” he said. “He is offending the dignity of the people and government of Cuba.” The "point of order", under Rule 71 of the UN, permits a representative of a member state to speak at any time, and the president of the General Assembly has to rule on it immediately. Mr Parrilla interrupted again as Mr Waltz displayed photographs that, he said, showed the lavish lifestyles of Cuba’s ruling elite. Cuba’s Communist leaders love to blame capitalism for their country’s misery, yet they apparently have no problem benefiting from the global luxury goods marketplace. pic.twitter.com/y4ZAI38OOO — Ambassador Mike Waltz (@USAmbUN) October 27, 2026 The UN General Assembly has voted overwhelmingly almost every year since 1992 to call for an end to the US embargo on Cuba , which has been in place for more than 60 years. The resolution is non-binding, and only the US Congress can lift the embargo. Since the start of this year, the administration of President Donald Trump has increased pressure on Havana by restricting oil shipments and threatening to impose tariffs on countries that supply Cuba with fuel. The measures have worsened shortages of basic goods and led to power cuts across the island. Washington has repeatedly blamed Cuba’s economic troubles on the country’s communist government rather than the US embargo, while pushing for a change in leadership in Havana.

title: CFTC sues Utah to block action against prediction markets
body:
The US state filed a lawsuit against Kalshi last week, seeking to recover up to $60 million in profits related to event contracts on prediction markets.
The US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) announced legal action against Utah officials after the state’s attorney general said he would sue to compel Kalshi and its affiliates to return up to $60 million in profits allegedly obtained illegally.
In a Monday filing in the US District Court for the District of Utah, lawyers for the commodities regulator sued the State of Utah and its Attorney General Derek Brown a week after officials announced legal action against prediction market platform Kalshi and its affiliates over allegedly illegal betting.
According to the CFTC, Utah was attempting to bypass congressional intent to “federally preempt state law” by “restrict[ing] the functioning of CFTC-registered exchanges.” CFTC Chair Michael Selig has been claiming for months that the regulator has “exclusive jurisdiction” over prediction markets, leading to several lawsuits between state and federal authorities.
“The event contracts targeted by Utah are ‘swaps’ under the federal [Commodity Exchange Act], and the exchanges that offer these event contracts for trading are CFTC-regulated Designated Contract Markets [DCMs],” said the lawsuit. “Utah’s efforts to prevent a CFTC-regulated DCM from offering CFTC-approved financial products intrude on the exclusive federal scheme Congress designed to oversee United States commodity derivatives markets.”
Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick told Cointelegraph in response to the Utah lawsuit:
The case is another dispute between federal and state authorities over prediction markets that may be resolved only by a Supreme Court decision. In September, New Jersey officials petitioned the high court to weigh in on their case against Kalshi, similar to other lawsuits pending in Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Nevada, Massachusetts, Wisconsin and New York. As of Tuesday, the Supreme Court has not announced whether it will hear arguments in the case.

title: U.S. Navy submarine arrives in Western Australia for Scheduled Maintenance
body: HMAS STIRLING, Australia — The Virginia-class fast-attack submarine USS Colorado (SSN 788) arrived at HMAS Stirling today to begin a scheduled, monthlong maintenance period. The visit marks the fourth submarine maintenance period in Western Australia since the establishment of the AUKUS security partnership and highlights ongoing progress under AUKUS Pillar I. USS Colorado (SSN 788) is the sixth nuclear-powered attack submarine to visit HMAS Stirling following the announcement of the Optimal Pathway and the third to undergo maintenance in Australia in the last 12 months under AUKUS Pillar I. The port visits and maintenance periods are part of the AUKUS Pillar I plan to help Australia acquire, operate, and maintain its own conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarine fleet. On October 26, 2026, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and his Australian and U.K. counterparts issued a joint statement naming USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class fast-attack submarine assigned to Submarine Squadron 3. The boat will help formally establish Submarine Rotational Force – West (SRF-West) upon its planned return in late 2027. Over the coming weeks, more than 30 trained and certified Australian civilian maintenance technicians from ASC Pty Ltd. will perform routine maintenance on a Virginia-class submarine in Western Australia for the first time, working alongside specialists from Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility (PHNSY&IMF). Under SRF-West, up to four U.S. and one U.K. submarines will rotationally operate out of HMAS Stirling. For Australia, SRF-West accelerates its readiness to maintain, operate and sustain conventionally armed, nuclear-powered, submarines while affording greater access to the Indo-Pacific region, the Indian Ocean and adjacent areas which enhances regional deterrence and operational flexibility for allied submarines. “This maintenance period brings us closer to establishing SRF-West,” said U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Doug Adams, director of AUKUS, International & Systems. “Our Lead Maintenance Activity, Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Intermediate Maintenance Facility, is doing a great job ensuring the Australian personnel trained in Hawaii are ready and able to support our submarines.” The maintenance period will demonstrate several new pieces of Australian-built infrastructure. Technicians will use a custom-made metal safety walkway, known as a sail “racetrack.” The team will also leverage recent nuclear-powered submarine-specific upgrades made to HMAS Stirling’s Diamantina Pier and other local solutions, such as a pure water plant, high-pressure air compressor and dehumidifier. “With each visit, Australia demonstrates new organic capabilities,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Jason Pittman, commander of Submarine Squadron 3. “During last year’s maintenance period, we successfully delivered pure water from an Australian-designed and built plant and validated the sail racetrack was fit for purpose. During the U.K.’s maintenance period in February, we validated the high-pressure air compressor and dehumidifier systems. Now, with the racetrack, we’re using it to conduct maintenance, utilizing the pier upgrades, and leveraging a workforce of about three dozen fully qualified and certified Australian civilian nuclear-powered submarine maintenance workers.” “Through these historic port visits Australia has continued to progress our ability to not just host SSNs for longer periods but also deliver maintenance to schedule and get the boats back to sea,” said Royal Australian Navy Rear Adm. David Mann CSC, the Australian Submarine Agency’s head of Virginia Division. The United Kingdom’s Royal Navy will be an active participant in the SMP. “We don’t get many opportunities like this,” said Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the U.K. Prime Minister’s Special Representative for AUKUS. “The more the three nations work together to maintain submarines – whether American or British – the faster we’ll be able to uplift our Australian partner’s knowledge and skills and increase commonality across our submarine forces.” “This maintenance activity represents the ultimate integration of a U.K., U.S., and Australian workforce,” said Mann. “Operating as a single team, we are testing our infrastructure, validating our nuclear stewardship processes, and substantially upskilling our naval and civilian workforces. These maintenance periods have been critical to Australia being on track to start SRF-West in 2027.” “As we approach the establishment of SRF-West, we must remember that our trilateral efforts are being driven by the challenging strategic environment in the Pacific and our collective desire to deter aggression and ensure peace through strength,” said U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Chris Cavanaugh, commander, Submarine Force, U.S. Pacific Fleet. “For decades, the United States, Australian, and British submarine forces have operated together. Through AUKUS, we’re building enhanced integration and increasing interoperability to ensure we collectively preserve the advantage in the undersea battlespace.” For the crew of Colorado, the success of this port visit relies heavily on the close partnership between the boat, the ASC team and personnel from PHNSY & IMF. This joint workforce ensures the submarine remains fully mission-ready for its forward-deployed operations. “The success of any maintenance period comes down to the people on the deckplates, and the Australian personnel stepping aboard our ship are true professionals,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Justin Reeves, commanding officer of USS Colorado. “Their technical skill and dedication are exactly what we need to keep this ship in the fight, and it gives us absolute confidence in Australia’s ability to support the fleet.” About AUKUS Integration & Acquisition (I&A) AUKUS Integration & Acquisition is the central U.S. Navy program office coordinating the delivery of the U.S. contribution to AUKUS Pillar I. The office integrates critical technical, industrial, and programmatic efforts across the Department of the Navy and with international partners. The office serves as the central hub for synchronizing submarine operations, workforce development, hands-on training pipelines, nuclear stewardship protocols, and trilateral industrial base expansion. By supporting Australia in acquiring a conventionally armed, nuclear-powered submarine capability at the earliest possible date, AUKUS I&A actively strengthens our collective undersea advantage, expands the industrial base to meet future defense demands, and upholds the highest global standards of nuclear safety, security, and nonproliferation. From Rory O’ Connor, Oct. 27, 2026 The post U.S. Navy submarine arrives in Western Australia for Scheduled Maintenance appeared first on Seapower Magazine .

title: Show HN: Tar-minefield shows where tar implementations disagree
body:
GitHub haampie/tar-minefield DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23617964
This project provides an extensive test suite and documentation for tar file extraction, with the goal of ensuring that implementations extract tar archives the same way.
There are many implementations of tar, from command line tools to libraries for programming languages. Because the tar file format leaves room for interpretation, different implementations can extract certain crafted tar files in different ways.
This is a security concern for file exchange: for example, when a security scanner and the extractor use different tar implementations, the scanner could inspect other files than the ones that end up on disk.
By assigning identifiers to these ambiguities, and providing test cases and usage data, this project aims for tar implementations to converge on strict parsing and identical behavior.
This project proposes a default policy that rejects the vast majority of ambiguities in tar files that could make implementations extract different files, while ensuring that nearly every source tarball already published can still be extracted. Of the 82,586 source tarballs of Spack, nixpkgs, Guix and live-bootstrap, and samples of PyPI, crates.io and RubyGems, it accepts 99.79% .
This table shows how different tar implementations behave on each test case. A green â is the strict behavior that the default policy asks for; click a row for details about the case.
Each case has a permanent identifier, such as F15, whose letter is its category:
A case's page shows its archive block by block, what every implementation makes of it, and how common it is in release tarballs. An implementation's page, linked from its name above the matrix, lists the cases where it does not do as the policy says.
This section defines a working draft of the default policy 1 , which accepts, tolerates or rejects each case below, based on data from the 82,586 distinct release tarballs of Spack, nixpkgs, Guix and live-bootstrap, and samples of PyPI, crates.io and RubyGems.
The prevalence column is the share of these tarballs that have a case: a first-order approximation of how common it is in general.
1 A policy can be stricter and also reject the tolerated cases, at the cost of rejecting more published tarballs: some tolerated cases are common, such as numbers padded with spaces (F01), and others rare. That suits special-purpose tools, such as an extractor for a single ecosystem, where it can be checked against every tarball ever published there.
The default policy accepts 99.79% of the 82,586 distinct release tarballs of Spack, nixpkgs, Guix and live-bootstrap, and samples of PyPI, crates.io and RubyGems. See the list of the 170 it rejects , and why.
The tarballs by the median mtime of their members, a rough check that the data spans enough years, leaving out the 14,361 whose mtimes are fixed for reproducibility or missing:
This project is looking for contributions from people who work on package managers, registries and tar implementations, in the form of discussions in issues or pull requests on GitHub or by email to harmen at stoppels dot ch, so that the working draft of the default policy can become a reference.
You can also contribute by testing other implementations, or by crafting a tarball that is particularly hard to parse. A case that shows a vulnerability that is not yet disclosed is reported privately first: see SECURITY.md .
