title: IBSF rules to keep Russia’s int’l ban in doubles and four-seat bobsleigh events
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. The Congress of the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation (IBSF) has kept in force its decision regarding the participation of Russian athletes in international events under the organization's purview and extended indefinitely the suspension of bobsleigh athletes in doubles and fours, also upholding the previous decision to allow Russians to compete in skeleton and monobob events under a neutral status, President of the Russian Bobsleigh Federation (RBF) Anatoly Pegov told TASS on Tuesday.
"By a majority vote, the IBSF Congress decided to allow only skeletonists and monobob athletes to participate in international competitions," Pegov told TASS.
"Athletes will compete under a neutral status, but they will be granted it, unlike in the previous season, i.e. without any testing, although we were prepared to do so," the RBF chief continued.
"As for allowing bobsleigh athletes in doubles and fours, Europe is not yet ready to let them in. We intend to fight for their rights together with the Russian Olympic Committee," Pegov added.
Late last July, the International Bobsleigh and Skeleton Federation ruled to allow Russian skeletonists and female bobsleighers to race in monobob competitions at IBSF tournaments under a neutral status during the Olympic qualifying season.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced a decision on July 7 to provisionally lift an earlier-imposed suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) and also recommended lifting restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes in all international tournaments.
On February 28, 2022, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued recommendations to international sports federations to prohibit athletes from Russia and Belarus from participating in international tournaments, citing Moscow’s special military operation in Ukraine as the reason.
Following the IOC’s recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations decided to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.
In late March, 2023, the IOC recommended allowing individual athletes from Russia and Belarus to participate in international sports tournaments, but only under specific conditions. Specifically, athletes from the two countries should not be "actively supporting" Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine and must compete under a neutral status. Russia and Belarus were also banned from participating in international team events.
On October 12, 2023, the IOC suspended the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) until further notice after the Russian organization included the Olympic councils of the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics (DPR and LPR), the Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions as its members.

title: Veteran leader Joseph Lagu dies, Kiir declares national mourning
body: Retired General Joseph Lagu Yanga, a former rebel commander who led the Anyanya movement during Sudan’s first civil war and later served as Sudan’s vice-president and ambassador to the United Nations, died in Juba on Tuesday at the age of 94. President Salva Kiir, who is in Russia to attend the third Russia-Africa summit, declared national mourning for Lagu, describing him as a nationalist and liberation hero who dedicated his life to South Sudan’s struggle for freedom. In a statement seen by Radio Tamazuj, the president praised Lagu’s contributions as a military officer, diplomat and politician, saying he was among the most significant figures in South Sudan’s history. Kiir ordered national flags across South Sudan and at the country’s diplomatic missions abroad to fly at half-mast until Lagu’s burial. He said he would personally bid farewell to Lagu at a state funeral and urged South Sudanese to mourn his death while celebrating his life and legacy. Kiir also called on the public to pray for Lagu’s family, saying the veteran leader had lived to see the birth of the country for which he fought. Who was Joseph Lagu? Gen. Lagu was a central figure in southern Sudan’s struggle for autonomy and helped negotiate the 1972 Addis Ababa Agreement, which ended the first north-south civil war and granted the region self-government. Born on November 21, 1931, in Momokwe, in the Madi area of what is now South Sudan’s Eastern Equatoria state, Lagu trained as a military officer before defecting from the Sudanese army in 1963 to join the southern rebellion. In 1968, he became leader of the Southern Sudan Liberation Movement and commander-in-chief of its armed wing, Anyanya. Under his leadership, the movement negotiated the Addis Ababa Agreement with the government of President Gaafar Nimeiry in 1972, ending a conflict that had begun in 1955. Lagu returned to the Sudanese army after the agreement and rose to the rank of lieutenant-general. He served as president of the High Executive Council of the autonomous Southern Region from 1978 to 1979 and as Sudan’s second vice-president from 1982 to 1985. The agreement granted southern Sudan a decade of regional self-government. Nimeiry abrogated it in 1983, a move that contributed to renewed conflict in the south. Lagu’s forces included young officers who later became prominent figures in South Sudan’s history, including Salva Kiir and the late John Garang, who served under his command during the Anyanya rebellion. After Nimeiry was overthrown in 1985, Lagu settled in Britain before returning to public service as Sudan’s roving ambassador from 1988 to 1990 and again from 1992 to 1998. He also served as Sudan’s permanent representative to the United Nations from 1990 to 1992. After South Sudan gained independence in 2011, Lagu served as a special adviser to Kiir. He had also held an advisory role during the autonomous southern Sudan administration before independence. He later retired from active public service. In November 2022, his family launched the Joseph Lagu Foundation, which focuses on education, leadership development, community empowerment and humanitarian assistance in South Sudan. Lagu completed his memoir, Sudan Odyssey: Through a State from Ruin to Hope , in 2006. His career spanned the southern rebellion, peace negotiations, senior government positions and diplomatic service, as well as the early years of South Sudan’s independence. Lagu is survived by several children, including Josephine Lagu, who previously served as a vice-president in the Transitional Government of National Unity. title: Former Ontario cabinet minister who resigned over expenses scandal defends promotion
body:
Months after resigning from Premier Doug Ford’s cabinet over a hotel expenses scandal, Progressive Conservative MPP Stan Cho returned to Queen’s Park with a new title, a higher salary and scorn from opposition parties.
Cho stepped down as the tourism minister in July after Global News revealed he charged taxpayers $16,000 to stay in downtown Toronto hotel rooms, despite living just six kilometers away from Queen’s Park.
The revelation ignited a summer spending scandal after public records revealed a number of other Progressive Conservative MPPs also billed taxpayers more than $120,000 for hotel rooms despite living within driving distance of the Ontario Legislature.
While MPPs were forced to repay the expenses, Cho was the only member who lost his position within the Ford government and profusely apologized for the “error in judgment.”
“I make a mistake,” Cho told reporters at Queen’s Park. “I made a decision that was convenient for my family, I wasn’t thinking about the people in my riding, working two jobs trying to make ends meet.”
“I took responsibility for that mistake, I paid the money back, I resigned from cabinet.”
That consequence, however, was thrown into doubt after Premier Doug Ford announced Cho would receive a new position just fourteen weeks after he stepped down from the position.
Cho has been appointed as the new parliamentary assistant to Education Minister Paul Calandra – a position that comes with a $22,000 salary increase, on top of his base MPP salary of $157,350.
The appointment was immediately met with pushback from members of the opposition who questioned why Cho was deserving of a promotion “after he ripped off the people of this province.”
“I do not understand how the premier decided it was a good idea to promote a minister, an MPP who has abused the taxpayer dollars, but that’s what we keep seeing from this government,” said NDP Leader Marit Stiles.
Ford, who in part contradicted Cho’s story on his resignation, also rebuffed suggestions that he was given a promotion.
“I don’t call it a promotion,” Ford told reporters.
“I fired him from being a minister, he admitted he made a mistake, he’s paid it back and now he’s going to be a parliamentary assistant.”
Green Party Leader Mike Schreiner said Ford is “failing to hold Cho accountable” by giving him another position within the government.
“What does it say to the people of Ontario that we have the most bloated cabinet in Ontario history, the most bloated Premier’s Office in Ontario history, meanwhile everyday people are struggling to be able to pay the rent,” Schreiner said.
Cho also offered new light on the circumstances that led to the expenses.
According to internal government emails obtained by Global News, Progressive Conservative MPPs were given the green light by the Ford government to charge taxpayers for the hotel perk because the shortened legislative sessions meant more late night sittings at Queen’s Park.
“Those night sittings, they’re tough on schedules especially when you have family circumstances at home,” Cho said.
Many of those night sittings, however, were eventually cancelled and Cho suggested it was too late to reverse the hotel room charges.
“You try and cancel the hotel room with less than 24 hours notice, cause those night sittings were cancelled the morning of … so unfortunately you can’t cancel those,” Cho added.

title: The tenth Hussar has arrived in Poland. Another F-35 for the Łask base
body:
The tenth F-35A Husarz multi-role aircraft has arrived in Poland, as announced by Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The machine is soon to begin its duties at the 32nd Tactical Air Base in Łask. This is the latest delivery under the order for 32 fifth-generation fighters, which includes training and logistics support.
The F-35A deliveries are gradually enhancing the capabilities of the Polish Air Force. Upon reaching operational readiness, they will primarily serve to defend Polish and Allied airspace. The stealth technology utilised in these machines makes them difficult to detect, while advanced sensors enable the identification and tracking of threats. Data from on-board equipment is processed into a coherent tactical picture, facilitating the pilot’s situational assessment and decision-making regarding the use of weaponry. The ability to transmit this information to other aircraft and ground-based air defence systems also allows for the support of other forces involved in airspace defence.
The first three Husarz aircraft landed in Łask on 22 May 2026. A further five reached the country on 28 August, while the head of the Ministry of National Defence announced the arrival of the ninth machine on 1 October. This was the first Polish F-35A assembled at the Italian facility in Cameri.
Kolejny, dziesiąty "Husarz" wylądował w Polsce. Wkrótce wielozadaniowy samolot F-35 będzie wykonywał swoje zadania z 32 Bazy Lotnictwa Taktycznego w Łasku. Ochrona polskiej i sojuszniczej przestrzeni powietrznej to jeden z naszych priorytetów. Budujemy siłę i zdolności polskich sił powietrznych, budujemy bezpieczeństwo naszych obywateli.
Parallel to these deliveries, trials of subsequent units destined for Poland are ongoing. On 15 October in Cameri, the aircraft with tactical number 3520—the twentieth Polish F-35A—conducted its first flight. A test flight is a stage in preparing the machine for handover to the recipient, and some Polish Husarz aircraft remain in the United States for personnel training purposes. Consequently, the number of aircraft that have completed test flights is higher than the number of aircraft already delivered to Poland.
Poland ordered 32 F-35A aircraft under an agreement signed on 31 January 2020. The contract, valued at $4.6 billion (approx. €4.2 billion), also includes training and logistics packages. The machines are to equip two squadrons based in Łask and Świdwin. In addition to air defence tasks, they will be used for reconnaissance, electronic warfare, and striking ground targets.

title: The Diesel Crisis Is Here To Stay
body: The diesel crunch is set to persist well into 2027 as supply remains limited by the Middle East conflict and the damaged Russian refineries, analysts say.  Attempts at transient small supply-side solutions like the Trump-Putin diesel deal are not expected to move the needle in the very tight global market.  Until refineries in the Middle East, damaged by Iranian strikes, return to full operations, oil product flows through the Strait of Hormuz recover, and Russia's diesel exports rebound, the world's supply of diesel will remain below 2025 levels.  Supply Crunch   The rest of the world, including the United States, is producing at full capacity, but it is unable to fully offset the lost supply. Refineries outside the Middle East and Russia have deferred maintenance to produce as much diesel as they can over the past few months. But they cannot delay scheduled maintenance indefinitely because they risk malfunctions and unplanned shutdowns, which would make the supply situation even worse.  Flows of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz may have recovered to nearly pre-war levels, according to many ship-tracking services, but fuel exports remain limited and are more dangerous to ship out of the Persian Gulf because cargoes are more flammable in case of a strike on a vessel. Fuels are also typically being shipped on smaller tankers.  Shipping is not the only  although it's the biggest  issue for the Middle East's oil supply. Refineries including Bapco in Bahrain and Jizan in Saudi Arabia were hit by Iranian strikes in the early weeks of the war. Bapco is now back to three-quarters of full capacity, but Saudi Aramco's 400,000-barrel-per-day Jizan refinery, a major refining hub on the Red Sea, is still shut following multiple hits over the past few months.  Related Saudi Aramco Offers Discounted Oil to Europe as Exports Recover  Adding to the limited fuel exports out of the Middle East is the crash in Russian diesel exports as half of Russia's refineries have been offline for months, due to Ukrainian drone hits, prompting a domestic fuel crisis and a ban on diesel exports.  This ban was partially lifted earlier this month when U.S. President Donald Trump announced a deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel to the U.S. The first tanker shipping about 40,000 metric tons, or about 300,000 barrels, of ultra-low sulfur diesel ULSD out of Russia to the U.S. departed from the Russian Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last week.  "On November 7, the first vessel, carrying a measly 300,000 barrels, less than a tenth of what the US consumes every day, should arrive in New York," Robin Mills, chief executive of energy advisory firm Qamar Energy, wrote in The National.  No Quick Fix  Analysts acknowledge that the 'Russian diesel deal' would have negligible effects on global diesel supply and prices, and certainly not ahead of the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.  There aren't immediate supply-side solutions significant enough to ease the upward pressure on diesel prices as winter approaches and heating oil demand in the Northern Hemisphere will jump, especially in the United States.  According to Qamar Energy's Mills, "the strategic choice is to save on consumption, whenever and wherever possible."  These could include heavy-duty vehicles running on natural gas, public transportation buses on gas or battery-electric power, and a shift toward passenger electric vehicles.  The record-high gasoline and diesel prices have accelerated Europe's shift toward EVs in a significant push away from conventional cars that lawmakers were trying to speed up for years with regulation.  But all of the above demand-side savings on diesel consumption are no immediate solutions to the global diesel crunch.  Until fuel flows from the Middle East and Russia recover to some adequate levels, the risk to prices is tilted to the upside in the near term.  Global fuel markets are set to remain tight until at least the middle of next year as the second quarter of 2027 will see unusually high planned maintenance that refiners have deferred from this year, Morgan Stanley said last week.  The expected drop in refinery utilization in the second quarter of next year would be two and a half times the usual capacity taken offline by spring maintenance globally, and is more than the capacity in the Middle East and Russia that's currently offline, according to Morgan Stanley's analysts.  The IEA also warned in its monthly Oil Market Report for October that the current crunch in the diesel and gasoil markets is set to extend into the middle of next year.  Amid the supply crunch, prices in the U.S. are not easing even after the Administration used every available tool to provide relief.  Last week "Diesel edged modestly higher nationally, and with the national average for gasoline likely to remain above $4 per gallon and diesel above $6 heading into the U.S. election, the relief motorists and policymakers have been hoping for remains elusiveeven as states have moved to cut fuel taxes and the Trump administration has pulled virtually every lever available," Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said on Monday.  With a week to go to the election, U.S. gasoline prices are 42.3c/gal above 2022's election day average, which was the priciest Election Day at the pump ever, De Haan noted. Diesel is nearly $1/gal above 2022's $5.33/gal. Both are on track for the highest Election Day prices on record not all-time highs, the analyst said.  By Tsvetana Paraskova for Oilprice.com

title: Persian leopards hang on in the Caucasus despite landmines
body: There have been few sightings of the endangered Persian leopard in the Caucasus region over the past 20 years: just three in Georgia and 10 in Armenia. But scientists and conservationists are alert to one Persian leopard in particular, whom they’ve named Aren and who is presumed to have journeyed 240 kilometers (150 miles) through cold, mountainous terrain with only three legs. This region of the world — made up of southern Russia, Georgia, Armenia, and Azerbaijan — still contains decades-old minefields from prior conflicts, and it’s believed this is how Aren was injured. Joining the Newscast this week to discuss her story for Mongabay is journalist Kayleigh Long, who explains how this leopard subspecies, Panthera pardus tulliana, persists in the region. She also describes how NGOs like NACRES, operating on extremely thin budgets, continue to monitor the big cats and provide what protection they can. “WWF is also monitoring the leopards. They put some cameras out in the same area as NACRES. So it’s really difficult,” she says. “I mean, these guys … are doing things on an absolute skeleton crew. And that’s partly because of a lack of funding more generally. There’s been a kind of tightening of purse strings around the world.” NACRES, founded in Georgia in 1991 as the Noah’s Ark Centre for the Recovery of Endangered Species and later renamed the Centre for Biodiversity Conservation & Research, has a staff of just three people, led by a zoologist named Bejan Lortkipanidze, who accompanied Long in…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Former MP Svyatas, sentenced to 12 years in Ukraine, detained in Sweden – media
body:
Swedish police have detained former Ukrainian MP Dmytro Svyatash, who was found guilty of justifying Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine and of fraud, according to Expressen.
"He arrived in Sweden last week and landed at Arlanda Airport on Thursday. According to his lawyer, Mark Safaryan, he came to Sweden to attend a Stevie Wonder concert at the 3 Arena in Stockholm. During passport control, Dmytro Svyatash was detained by border police and denied entry. Dmytro Svyatash holds both Russian and Ukrainian citizenship, but reportedly presented his Ukrainian passport during border control," the report reads.
According to his attorney, the official reason for denying entry was Poland's decision to ban re-entry, which was entered into the Schengen Area's shared database. However, Safaryan sees a political subtext in this ban, calling Svyatsh "one of the most wanted individuals in Ukraine."
The lawyer also noted in the appeal that Svyatas opposes his extradition to Ukraine.
"They know they cannot extradite him to Ukraine because it is impossible. It contradicts European practice," he said.
Svyatash is currently wanted both in Ukraine and internationally. The warrant is linked to another court case in Ukraine involving treason. The trial has been ongoing since April of this year.
Svyatash was previously wanted by Interpol, but after his lawyers challenged the warrant, Interpol revoked it in November 2024. In its decision, Interpol noted that the Ukrainian warrant did not comply with established rules.
Through his attorney, Svyatash requested an oral hearing before the Migration Court. On Tuesday, the court rejected this request. According to the ruling, Svyatash must submit written comments and conclude the presentation of his position by 10:00 on Wednesday, after which the court will issue its decision.
Svyatash served as a member of the Ukrainian Parliament from 2002 to 2019. In 2019, he left Ukraine and moved to Russia, where he has lived in recent years. After the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, he publicly supported Russia's actions.
In addition, Svyatash was linked to the Russian occupiers' plans to form an administration under their control in Kharkiv region. He was named as one of the possible candidates to lead the occupied part of the region.
In the summer of 2024, Svyatash was sentenced to 12 years in prison: he was found guilty of justifying Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine and of fraud amounting to UAH 2.2 billion. Since 2023, he has also been suspected of treason.

title: US looking at lifting sanctions against RDIF — media
body:
NEW YORK, October 27. /TASS/. The US administration is looking at lifting sanctions against the Russian Direct Investment Fund (RDIF), The New York Times reported, citing sources.
An unnamed US administration official told the newspaper that Washington is considering an RDIF inquiry for a sanction waiver as part of efforts toward improving Russian-US relations. Apart from that, the official noted the work of the Fund’s CEO and Russian president’s special envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries Kirill Dmitriev, in collaboration with the United States, toward settling the Ukrainian crisis.

title: Amazon's anti-tokenmaxxing memo says engineers should be pickier about using AI
body:
Amazon laid out its AI usage guidelines for software engineers in a memo to staffers, and discouraged employees from turning to "tokenmaxxing" in their push to embrace artificial intelligence tools.
The memo , which was circulated internally in September and posted to the company's website on Tuesday, revises how the company defines the role of software development engineers and managers in the age of AI.
"We're just seeing the beginning of AI's effect on software engineering," the company wrote. "While we have a vision for what the future looks like, there's a lot that's still emerging. We are certain that whatever future best practices are, AI will be at the center of software engineering practice."
Under CEO Andy Jassy , Amazon has rapidly integrated AI across the company's sprawling business operations. Jassy has previously predicted that AI will "change the scope and speed" of day-to-day work, and potentially shrink its corporate workforce in the next few years through automation, though he's noted it will also create "other jobs."
As employees rush to adopt AI tools, companies have grappled with the technology's surging costs and how to reliably measure whether the technology leads to a productivity boost or other valuable returns on investment.
Companies have recently cracked down on tokenmaxxing , in which developers use AI as much as possible with little regard for output. Some companies have set limits on employees' usage of tokens, or the units of data that are processed and generated by AI models, in a bid to slow rising AI bills. Others have switched to cheaper, open-source models for certain tasks.
An Amazon spokesperson said the company hasn't instituted caps on employees' token usage. Amazon in May shut down an internal leaderboard after discovering employees were tokenmaxxing to climb the ranks.
In the memo posted Tuesday, Amazon said metrics like token usage, the rate of adoption of AI tools, and code changes or reviews remain "deeply flawed" ways of measuring teams or organizations' AI usage, adding that they can lead to higher costs and too much complexity.
It stopped short of telling staffers to ignore those metrics altogether, however. Token usage and code generation should be considered "with care and judgment" alongside other data, Amazon said.
"We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," the company wrote.
Marc Brooker, a vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, told CNBC in an interview that the company has looked to metrics such as "feature velocity" to measure how AI is improving engineer productivity.
The metric looks at things like, "how many launches are we doing, how many successful changes are we making in production," he said.
"Broadly, we think about this as a return on investment," Brooker said. "If there is an important problem to solve for our customers, important problem to solve for our business, we're going to invest tools, time, tokens, human effort, etc. into those."
He added, "What we don't want to see is wasted effort where we are going and spending those tokens solving problems that don't matter and sometimes it's hard to know, so we do need to have some appetite for experimentation."
Amazon also discouraged staffers from using AI when it doesn't make sense for a given task.
"If your work does not benefit from current AI tooling, that is a finding, not a failing," Amazon said in the memo.
The company added, "An engineer who can explain where AI does not yet help their work is demonstrating the judgement we are asking for."

title: Russia says it foiled close-range drone attack on Moscow missile defenses
body: Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) said on October 26, 2026, that it had arrested two men accused of preparing a close-range drone attack on part of Moscow’s missile-defense system and an electricity facility, with the aircraft to be launched inside Russia and controlled remotely from Ukraine. The FSB alleged that the men were working for Ukraine’s SBU security service and had retrieved first-person-view (FPV) drones and explosive components from hidden caches in the Smolensk and Kaluga regions. They were instructed to prepare the aircraft, transport them to the Moscow region and activate them before operators in Ukraine took control, according to the agency’s statement carried by Russian state news agency TASS. Russian authorities described the suspects as men from the South Caucasus, born in 1991 and 1998, but did not disclose their citizenship or names. Both men were jailed pending trial on terrorism-related charges, The Moscow Times reported. The FSB did not name the targets or say how the drones would be controlled from Ukraine. TASS separately reported that the FSB released footage showing a suspect giving a confession and scenes purportedly depicting drone assembly and preparation. The announcement follows repeated drone attacks that have disrupted air traffic around the Russian capital. On October 23, 2026, all four airports serving Moscow suspended arrivals and departures as Russian air defenses engaged approaching drones, marking their second simultaneous closure in two days. Restrictions affected Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky airports. Sheremetyevo directed passengers into shelters, including people aboard aircraft parked on the airfield. Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil infrastructure have also become a point of contention with Washington. The US has pressed Kyiv to stop striking refineries , arguing that the attacks contribute to higher energy prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has resisted an unconditional halt. In an interview aired on October 25, 2026, he said Ukraine could stop the attacks if Russia ceased striking Ukrainian electricity infrastructure. He also outlined alternatives involving satellite connectivity over Russian missile-launch sites or additional Patriot interceptor missiles. Russia, meanwhile, has expanded its use of jet-powered Shahed attack drones. Their greater speed and operating altitude have been putting Ukrainian mobile air-defense teams at a disadvantage, with crews describing much shorter engagement windows than against propeller-driven aircraft. Ukraine’s Air Force said an overnight Russian attack on October 9-10 involved 160 drones, including 110 jet-powered Shaheds. By the morning, it reported shooting down or jamming 117 aircraft, including 82 of the jet-powered drones, while strikes were recorded at 14 locations, according to Ukrainska Pravda. The post Russia says it foiled close-range drone attack on Moscow missile defenses appeared first on AeroTime .

title: After election victory, Chow to face budget pressure and new deal with Ontario
body:
Negotiations with the province to help relieve Toronto’s budget pressures loomed over Olivia Chow’s election victory, as she vowed to be the “mayor for everyone.”
Chow fended off challenger Brad Bradford and convinced voters to back her progressive agenda for a second term headlined by free school lunches and a weekly transit fare cap.
She reiterated today her promise to keep property taxes at or around the rate of inflation while fielding questions about negotiations for new budget help from the province.
Chow, who negotiated a 2023 deal set to expire this year for $1.2 billion in operating cash from the province, is facing down a 2027 budget shortfall the city has put at roughly $1.1 billion.
Fresh off Monday’s win, she also deflected questions about whether this would be her last term, saying she intends to spend “every moment” of the next four years “working hard for the people of Toronto”.
Premier Doug Ford congratulated Chow on the victory and says he will “work with anyone to drive the economy to make sure we protect communities and companies and people” from U.S. tariffs.

title: Navy identifies NAS Pensacola sailors killed in car crash
body: The U.S. Navy announced the names of the service members who died in a fiery car crash early Saturday morning in Pensacola, Florida. Aviation Ordnanceman Airman Apprentice Drekwon Bagley, Aviation Ordnanceman Airman Recruit Francois Longdayeyambete and Airman Apprentice David Deanda died in a single-vehicle traffic accident, the service confirmed. Bagley and Longdayeyambete were assigned to Naval Air Technical Training Center, while Deanda was assigned to Naval Aviation Schools Command, both of which operate out of Naval Air Station Pensacola. “The Pensacola Police Department is leading the investigation into the accident,” the Navy said. The Naval Criminal Investigative Service is also conducting an investigation, which the service said was common protocol when there is a non-combat death without medical oversight. The NCIS is working alongside the Pensacola Police Department to uncover the circumstances that led to the crash. Police, who were notified of a vehicle collision around 1:35 a.m. Saturday morning, told local reporters that the car flipped over and caught fire after the driver lost control and smashed into a barrier. Originally from Michigan, Bagley enlisted in the Navy on May 14, 2026. Longdayeyambete, from Massachusetts, enlisted in the Navy on July 9, 2026. And Deanda, who hailed from California, enlisted in the Navy on June 4, 2026.

title: Both sides observing ceasefire in Oleshky, Lubinets says
body:
Lubinets made the statement during a televised broadcast, Ukrinform reports.
“Both sides are observing the ceasefire. I made a verification call to the person on our side who monitors Russian compliance with the ceasefire. I was told that there had been no incidents or violations since 3:00 a.m. Russian forces have not advanced, attempted to seize any islands, or sought to improve their positions. None of that has happened,” Lubinets said.
Roads leading to the town were being cleared of mines, he said.
Once demining is complete, the next step will be to deliver humanitarian supplies, including water, food, medicine, and equipment for the hospital in Oleshky.
Lubinets stressed that another objective of the humanitarian mission was to give Oleshky residents the opportunity to leave the town.
“Once the road has been cleared of mines and humanitarian supplies have been delivered, representatives of three countries—Ukraine, the United States, and Russia—will be present on the ground. Everyone who needs assistance will receive it from the three countries. Everyone who wants to leave for Ukraine will have that opportunity. Those who want to leave for Russia will receive assistance as well. Moreover, there are people who have said, ‘We want to stay,’” Lubinets said.
He added that Ukraine was separately working out ways to assist those who wished to remain in the town.
“As of today, we are making every effort to disseminate information, coordinating this with our Russian counterpart. We are issuing the same messages simultaneously. We have published mobile phone numbers for collecting information. We are gathering information on our side, and the Russians are doing the same on theirs. We are also compiling verified lists specifying what assistance each person needs,” Lubinets said.
The parties were also assessing transport needs, including ambulances for people requiring urgent medical care, according to the human rights commissioner.
“There is a separate category of elderly people and people with limited mobility, and we are working out how to assist them. Those who want to leave for Ukraine will receive dedicated assistance: they will be accompanied, met upon arrival, provided with accommodation, and helped in Ukraine. All government agencies are working on this under our coordination,” Lubinets said.
The human rights commissioner said that US representatives were not yet in Oleshky and would be able to arrive once the roads had been cleared of mines.
He noted that US representatives would monitor how each side fulfilled its commitments under the relevant document signed by Lubinets and his Russian counterpart, Elena Lantratova.
“They are closely monitoring what each side must do and what commitments it must honor. From the 23rd to the 27th, several days have passed. During this period, we have already gone through several stages, and each side has fulfilled its commitments in full,” Lubinets said.
As previously reported, US First Lady Melania Trump said she had secured a local ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine covering only Oleshky, a town in the temporarily Russian-occupied part of the Kherson region.
According to the White House press office, the parties agreed to temporarily cease all military operations in Oleshky to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and prepare for the evacuation of civilians through an agreed safe corridor.

title: Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies
body:
The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday .
It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments.
The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.
This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles . Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups.
According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.

title: Senior Russian, Malian defense ministry officials discuss defense cooperation prospects
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov met with Minister-Delegate (Deputy Minister) of the Malian Ministry of Defense Omar Diarra to discuss prospects for military cooperation between the two countries, the Russian Defense Ministry said.
"As part of preparations for main events of the third Russia-Africa summit, Russian Deputy Defense Minister Vasily Osmakov held a working meeting with Minister-Delegate at the Malian Ministry of Defense General Omar Diarra. During the talks, the sides discussed the current state of bilateral cooperation in the defense sector and prospects for further interaction," it said.
The meeting was held in an atmosphere of mutual understanding and demonstrated the friendly character of Russian-Malian relations, it added.

title: Poland to Host €227M Patriot Missile Service Center
body:
Poland has announced that it will be hosting a European service center for US-made PAC-3 interceptor missiles, aiming to cut repair times for weapons that are already in short supply worldwide and critical to Ukraine’s defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who led Warsaw’s negotiations, called the decision “historic” in a statement on Tuesday, Oct. 27. Three other countries had competed to host the facility, she said, naming Germany, the Netherlands and Norway.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“This success was not a given. It is the result of many months of negotiations and the hard work of the entire team,” Sobkowiak-Czarnecka wrote, noting that the Polish bid had been the highest rated since the application stage.
According to TVP World citing Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, the hub would be the only one of its kind outside the United States. Its cost would be roughly 1 billion Polish zlotys (about $253 million) and would take about a year to become fully operational.
In her statement, the defense minister thanked Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Deputy Prime Minister and Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, who appointed her chief negotiator.
The outcome showed what was possible when the government and the country’s President Karol Nawrocki pulled in the same direction, she added.
PAC-3 missiles, used in US-made Patriot air-defense systems, are currently shipped to the US for servicing, which led Washington to seek a European site to cut turnaround times, TVP World reported.
The US, Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden signed an agreement with manufacturer Lockheed Martin in July, in an aim to explore setting up such a hub.
According to the broadcaster, Warsaw has long pursued the project with hopes that it would eventually lead to Patriot missile production in Poland.
Although the government did not officially name a location at the time of the report, TVP World reported that the WZE electronics plant in Zielonka, located about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) northeast of Warsaw, is widely seen as the leading candidate.
In September, Sobkowiak-Czarnecka toured the plant with US Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno. At the time, the US Embassy in Warsaw noted that the visit highlighted bilateral cooperation on critical Patriot components.
Under a 2019 agreement with Lockheed Martin, the plant already produces and services key PAC-3 MSE components, TVP World reported.
As of Oct. 15, Ukraine has reportedly depleted its stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles.
For the country, the PAC-3 is currently among the very few weapons capable of intercepting Russia’s Iskander-M, a ballistic missile carrying a half-ton warhead strong enough to tear down a quarter to half of a typical apartment block.
The shortfall was particularly felt during Russia’s large-scale attack overnight into Wednesday, Oct. 14, when most incoming ballistic missiles reached their targets. The strike hit three power plants in Kyiv and energy facilities in Kharkiv, killing four people and injuring at least 25 in the capital.
According to CNN’s exclusive , Ukraine fired its last remaining Patriots as the Air Force shot down four Russian ballistic missiles during that same attack.
Around the same time, the US aerospace giant Starlink tweaked parameters and limited terminals above 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour), crippling Kyiv’s drone operations, including interceptor drones used against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones.
As of Oct. 1, Lockheed Martin is in advanced talks over PAC-3 production outside the US over tripled demand, as countries seek to rebuild their stocks amid the war in Iran and Russia’s escalating rhetoric towards Europe.
For much of the year, Ukraine has repeatedly appealed to its Western partners for faster deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
On Sept. 8, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said Germany would deliver PAC-2 missiles to Ukraine from it’s own Bundeswehr stocks, while Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said contracts are being signed with partners for about 1,000 Patriot missiles.
During the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said he made a “final decision” to grant Ukraine the licenses to produce Patriot missiles domestically, after backtracking on the previous July commitment.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Salesforce expands Agent Fabric with AI evaluations to trigger shutdowns when agents fail
body:
Credit: VentureBeat made with ChatGPT-Images-2.5
Salesforce is detailing the next phase of its Agent Fabric platform , with evaluations designed to identify malfunctioning AI agents and initiate corrective action, alongside expanded discovery capabilities and previously announced spending and governance controls.
The October 27 announcement sets a November beta and January 2027 general-availability target for Agent Evals, which MuleSoft first announced at its annual Dreamforce conference in September. It also outlines API Evals, a forthcoming tool for testing the software connections agents depend on, starts a beta for custom agent scanners and schedules an evaluation-triggered agent kill switch for January.
For enterprise buyers, the announcement combines forthcoming capabilities with extensions and existing tools. The basic kill switch became generally available in September, while MuleSoft outlined budget controls, spending dashboards and token-saving features over the summer . The September announcement also described connecting failed evaluations to corrective actions.
The broader proposition is to shorten the distance between discovering a problem and addressing it. A company might know that an agent produces incorrect answers or consumes too many resources, but still need to identify its owner, navigate another platform and obtain permission to suspend it.
In an interview with VentureBeat, Andrew Comstock, senior vice president and general manager of MuleSoft at Salesforce, described familiar problems behind the company’s approach.
“I have too many of them. The technologies are totally different. Nothing talks to each other. Everything runs in a silo,” Comstock said, describing customer challenges that informed Agent Fabric.
Salesforce wants to manage those agents even when customers build them on competing platforms.
“I’ll emphasize, it’s not Salesforce specific. It’s across everything,” he said.
Salesforce had already described Agent Evals at Dreamforce in September , including generating tests, measuring outcomes against success criteria and connecting failures to remediation.
The October announcement adds rollout dates and describes how evaluations can extend beyond testing before deployment to checking agents, language models and Model Context Protocol servers in production. The goal is to identify behavior that falls outside an organization’s thresholds and initiate an appropriate response, including approval steps where policy requires them.
In Salesforce’s illustrative retail scenario, moving an agent to a cheaper model produces worse answers to order-status questions. Evaluations detect the decline and initiate a process to quarantine the agent, obtain approval where required, and revise and retest it. That is a hypothetical workflow, rather than a reported customer result.
Comstock said evaluations can also help companies enforce expectations about how agents communicate. A customer-facing agent that should sound upbeat, for example, should not unexpectedly become sarcastic.
The forthcoming API Evals tool addresses another part of the system: generating functional and performance tests from API specifications. Both evaluation products are scheduled to enter beta in November and become generally available in January 2027.
The kill switch itself is not new to this announcement.
MuleSoft introduced the concept in June and made the basic capability generally available in September . It uses gateway controls to block governed traffic, with options to scope an intervention to a request, session, agent or tenant and restore access afterward.
That distinction matters: blocking an agent’s access through a gateway does not necessarily terminate every process running in the external platform that hosts it.
What Salesforce now puts on the January roadmap is a Triggered-Agent Kill Switch , connecting detected problems to policy-driven intervention. The September evaluation preview had already discussed linking failures to remediation; the October announcement supplies a more specific release target for the triggered capability.
For buyers, the practical distinction is between an available control for stopping governed activity and a forthcoming mechanism that connects evaluation results to that response.
Agent discovery also predates today’s announcement. MuleSoft described its agent scanners in April as a way to identify agents across supported environments.
The addition entering beta today is a Custom Agent Scanner , intended to extend discovery to internal systems, environments behind firewalls and additional platforms. General availability is planned for January.
Comstock said the registry does not require customers to relocate their agents to Salesforce.
“I’ll emphasize, we’re not moving the agent; the agent’s still running there,” he said. “We’re just pulling the pointer so that you can get a universal registry across all of your agents.”
An administrator connects the relevant environments and brings their metadata into a shared registry. Customers do not have to use Agentforce, Salesforce’s own agent platform, to use Agent Fabric, Comstock said.
He also argued that the need depends more on the diversity of a company’s agent deployments than its size. A business using several agent frameworks and providers may encounter coordination problems even without being a large enterprise.
The announcement also highlights a FinOps Dashboard, Model Wallet budgets and policies intended to reduce model consumption.
These are not all newly introduced features. MuleSoft’s August release overview outlined model access, cost optimization, wallets and dashboard improvements. A September explanation of Model Wallet described setting dollar or token budgets by provider or model, with daily, weekly or monthly limits.
The controls address a familiar tension: an individual developer may choose an expensive model to get a task done faster, while the organization needs to understand the combined bill.
Comstock said visibility should extend beyond reducing total spending to identifying the teams and projects responsible for it.
“So it’s not just about keeping the cost down. That’s obviously part of it, but it’s also making sure that you can correlate that with the right teams and projects who are actually driving changes in your organization,” he said.
Salesforce’s October release describes semantic caching, payload compression and response trimming among its optimization techniques. It claims token reductions of up to 75% in test scenarios. That is a vendor test result, not a guaranteed reduction in a customer’s overall AI bill.
Salesforce is also emphasizing Open Policies for applying governance across federated gateways, including Azure, Apigee and Kong.
The underlying capability is not making its first appearance today. MuleSoft described Open Policies in September , while its October release notes document the renaming of Universal Policies to Open Policies and related enhancements.
For enterprises, the attraction is applying common controls across infrastructure they already operate. Actual coverage still depends on the supported integrations and where traffic passes through enforceable controls.
Comstock framed that governance as a prerequisite for broader deployment.
“Nowadays, governance is your actual accelerant because you’re governed. You can answer better questions. You can feel more confident and comfortable, and that makes you go faster,” he said.
Salesforce’s public MuleSoft pricing page lists a starting price of $2,000 per month for the broader portfolio, with Mule Credits used across capabilities.
The page’s agent-management offering includes Agent Fabric functions such as discovery, orchestration, governance and budgets, but directs buyers to contact sales. The $2,000 figure should therefore not be presented as a confirmed standalone price for the specific Agent Fabric configuration described in this announcement.
The pricing material outlines prepaid credit packages, a precommit option with a $50,000 annual minimum and a custom-priced unlimited option. It does not establish a separate public price for Agent Evals or API Evals, or enough detail to calculate what a particular evaluation workload would cost.
The $2,000 project budget Comstock used as an example during the interview was hypothetical, not a product-price disclosure.
Agent Fabric sits in a growing market for managing agents across an organization, although competing products combine oversight and execution in different ways.
Microsoft Agent 365 is a close comparison on enterprise administration. Microsoft describes an agent registry, access and lifecycle controls, analytics and security integrations with products such as Entra, Defender and Purview.
ServiceNow’s AI Control Tower similarly targets discovery, observation, governance, security and measurement across vendors. Its announced capabilities include controls for risky activity and visibility into AI costs and business outcomes.
OpenAI Frontier is another relevant competitor, with a broader proposition that includes building and operating agents, connecting business systems and context, evaluating performance, and managing permissions. The overlap is in enterprise agent management, even though the scope is not identical to Agent Fabric’s emphasis on governing agents across existing environments.
Anthropic’s Claude Managed Agents overlaps at the infrastructure layer but is a less direct comparison. It provides managed facilities for running agents, including execution environments and orchestration. Agent Fabric’s central pitch is discovering and governing agents that may continue running elsewhere.
Anthropic publishes a Managed Agents runtime price of $0.08 per active session-hour , in addition to applicable model and tool charges. That is not directly comparable with MuleSoft’s portfolio starting price or a negotiated Agent Fabric contract.
These distinctions are an interpretation of the vendors’ published capabilities, rather than a claim that the products are interchangeable. An enterprise could need both an agent runtime and a separate governance layer, depending on integration support and its existing infrastructure.
The most immediate addition in this announcement is the Custom Agent Scanner beta. The basic kill switch and highlighted spending controls are already generally available.
Agent Evals and API Evals are scheduled for beta in November, with general availability in January 2027. The custom scanner is also scheduled for general availability in January, alongside the Triggered-Agent Kill Switch.
For buyers evaluating the announcement, the central question is whether Salesforce can connect discovery, testing, spending visibility and enforceable intervention across the agents they actually use. The forthcoming releases will determine how much of that workflow can operate as a connected system.

title: Video: ‘Please, don’t forget your children and I’ – Toluwanisings’ wife breaks down at Tribute Night
body: Akanbi Elizabeth, the widow of late gospel singer Olayemi Bayonile Bolaji, popularly known as Toluwanisings, broke down in tears while paying tribute to her husband at a memorial event in Ibadan, Oyo State. In a video from the tribute night held at Jogor Centre on Tuesday, Elizabeth struggled to complete her speech as she became overwhelmed with emotion while remembering her late husband. “Toluwanisings, my dear husband. I will forever miss you. Please do not forget your children and I,” she said. Several gospel artistes attended the event to honour the late singer, including Adeyinka Alaseyori, Esther Igbekele, Laolu Gbenjo, Akintayo Akinwande, SB Live, Bidemi Olaoba, Mr Gbera, Peterson Okopi and Sarah Apekeola. Nollywood actress Bimbo Oshin was also among the celebrities present at the memorial. Toluwanisings died in Ibadan on October 14, 2026, after reportedly slumping. His death has since generated controversy over allegations that efforts to obtain emergency medical care for him were unsuccessful, disagreements over his burial arrangements and calls for an investigation into the circumstances surrounding his death. Following his death, the singer’s personal assistant, Babadunni Gbolabo, alleged that efforts to secure emergency medical treatment took him to between seven and eight hospitals in Ibadan. The allegations sparked public concern about access to emergency medical services and the circumstances surrounding the singer’s death. The controversy surrounding his death has also extended to his burial arrangements, with disagreements emerging between his widow and members of his paternal family over where he should be laid to rest. Meanwhile, the singer’s grandmother, Sabitiyu Olayemi, alleged that he neglected her for years, adding to the family-related controversies that emerged after his death. title: FBI agents charged with lying about Hunter Biden probes accuse DOJ of 'serious abuse'
body:
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides have been charged with lying to Congress.
A magistrate judge blasted Justice Department attorneys during a hearing Tuesday after the department, in an overnight court filing, added a charge of obstruction to two charges of lying to Congress that were brought Friday against two former FBI agents who investigated Hunter Biden .
The Justice Department on Friday charged Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director for FBI's Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another former senior counterintelligence official, with allegedly making false statements to Congress stemming from a probe into whether investigators in the lead-up to the 2020 election sought to suppress or discredit the veracity of material on the laptop of former President Joe Biden's son that included embarrassing photos and videos.
The DOJ early Tuesday added an obstruction of a congressional proceeding charge -- but in a contentious hearing, magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui slammed the Justice Department for the overnight filing, which prosecutors posted to the case docket without receiving signoff from the judge.
The FBI agent who swore out the complaint also did not include his signature.
"I think they should have filed nothing," Judge Faruqui said. "They never had complaints filed on their record that are unsigned, waiting for a judge to make a probable cause finding. I think that it is inappropriate and harms the defendant. I'm frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night, but I'm much more concerned that it's filed on the public record."
The assistant U.S. attorney in the hearing, John Borchert, struggled repeatedly as Faruqui asked him to explain the government's conduct, which the judge said was unlike any case he had ever seen in the history of D.C.'s district court.
Faruqui ultimately granted the request from Flores' and Benavides' attorneys to strike the amended complaint from the docket and said he would continue Tuesday's hearing to determine whether prosecutors established probable cause in their initial complaint filed last week.
"Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?" Faruqui asked of Borchert. "What is it? It appears that -- it makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause."
"Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said.
The Justice Department alleges that Floris and Benavides knowingly lied to Congress on two separate occasions -- on July 19, 2023, for Floris, and on Sept. 28, 2023, for Benavides.
"The evidence further establishes that probable cause exists to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of minimizing or concealing [the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation," according to the documents filed overnight.
The affidavit alleges that both congressional and FBI witnesses, along with FBI documents, prove that the pair were aware of the Hunter Biden investigation.
"The government's last-ditch filing before the pre-scheduled preliminary hearing in this case is not merely procedurally improper and substantively deficient," Floris' attorneys said. "It represents a serious abuse of the criminal charging process, a troubling disregard for the judicial safeguards governing the initiation of criminal proceedings, and a calculated effort to evade judicial scrutiny and shield the government's allegations from adversarial testing at the scheduled preliminary hearing."
"In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself," the attorneys said. "We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing."
Judge Faruqui appeared on Friday to be skeptical of the charges -- saying the "facts appear to be old" and there are "questions that need to be answered" -- before setting a hearing for Tuesday to consider whether the government established probable cause in its complaint.
Faruqui said the judge who signed off on the complaint needed extra time to determine if there was probable cause or not. "Rare charges" that are "this old" are never charged by complaint, according to the judge.
It was not immediately clear why prosecutors chose to charge the pair through a criminal complaint and not an indictment, which would have required approval by a grand jury instead of a magistrate judge.

title: Margin debt growth slows sharply as stock market warning signs build
body:
The pace at which investors are borrowing money to invest in stocks has cooled substantially, raising concern that the stock market may be due for a fall.
Recent FINRA data shows the annual growth in margin debt fell to 31.4% in September from 53.7% in May, Bank of America technical strategist Paul Ciana pointed out in a Friday note. Ciana warned that slowing borrowing momentum from extreme levels has been associated with previous market peaks.
May's growth rate in 2026 was the fourth highest since 1998, according to a BofA analysis. The three higher extremes took place in 2000, 2007 and 2021 — all of which preceded stock market declines.
Earlier this year, borrowing was increasing much faster than stocks were rising. Analysts view high borrowing levels as a contrarian signal, similar to bull-bear sentiment indicators.
At $1.48 trillion, margin debt in September is 1.5% below June's record of $1.5 trillion.
High leverage can have snowball effects in a market downturn. Lower prices trigger demands for additional collateral or forced sales, which accelerate a downturn.
Individual investors can be hit hard. Tesla investor Hy Luu, for example, refinanced his home to raise $30,000 to pay down margin debt during the stock's 2022 decline.
BofA sees other market warning signs, including widening high-yield credit spreads and a rotation toward defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples.
Paradoxically, the rotation into those sectors has pushed them to "bubble-risk levels," BofA's equity derivatives team said in a note on Tuesday. Similar shifts occurred in the late 1990s dot-com era and Covid rally, they added. "These dynamics provide further evidence that markets continue to move towards a more bubble-like state."
The bull case is that the midterms could alleviate some of the market's uncertainty and trigger a relief rally, Ciana noted. "Typically, risk assets such as the S&P 500 rebound after midterms unless more severe downside risks materialize."

title: Rada withdraws bill that threatened journalists' work – MP
body:
Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration by the Verkhovna Rada, according to MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak (the Holos faction).
"Yes, I would like to report that following constructive negotiations with Andriy Motovylovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction, and the parliament's leadership… Bill No. 10242 has been withdrawn from consideration – both for tomorrow and for the rest of this week," Zhelezniak said on his Telegram channel.
The bill in question provides for amendments to Articles 361 and 361-2 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, increasing penalties for acts involving unauthorized access to electronic systems and the dissemination of restricted information.
According to media reports, the bill was proposed for the agenda by Andriy Motovilovets, first deputy head of the Servant of the People faction.
The bill had already been considered in 2024 – on December 4, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not support the bill in its second reading and sent it back for a repeat second reading. Prior to that, on December 2, media and human rights organizations called on the Rada not to support the bill due to threats to freedom of speech, the work of journalists, and the protection of journalistic sources and whistle blowers in Ukraine.
Chair of the Committee on Freedom of Speech Yaroslav Yurchyshyn called on his colleagues in the Verkhovna Rada to remove Bill No. 10242 from the agenda and draft a new one that takes into account the rights of whistle blowers. However, two weeks later, the bill reappeared on the agenda. On December 17, Media Rukh, along with media and human rights NGOs, appealed to lawmakers for a second time, urging them to withdraw their support for the bill and noting that the revised version had not eliminated the risks. Proposals to introduce effective protection mechanisms for individuals who disclose confidential information in the public interest-particularly journalists and whistleblowers – were not taken into account.
On December 18, 2024, the Verkhovna Rada did not consider the bill, but it was not withdrawn from consideration.
In January 2025, the bill was once again added to the agenda of the Verkhovna Rada sessions without consultation, even though the Committee on Freedom of Speech had previously sent a list of editors and media experts who would be proposed for a meeting to reach an agreement. Shortly thereafter, the bill was again removed from the agenda, as some members of parliament emphasized during the discussion that they were unwilling to support the bill until it had been agreed upon with the media community.

title: 27-Year-Old Missouri Man Admits Role in Failed Bitcoin Kidnapping Plot
body: Bitcoin Magazine 27-Year-Old Missouri Man Admits Role in Failed Bitcoin Kidnapping Plot A St. Louis man has admitted his part in a violent scheme to steal bitcoin from a Connecticut family. Martel Williams, 27, pleaded guilty Monday in federal court in Hartford to conspiracy to interfere with commerce by robbery, commonly called Hobbs Act robbery. The charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. U.S. Attorney David X. Sullivan announced the plea. The plot began in August 2024. Prosecutors say the people coordinating the attack wanted bitcoin belonging to a man who had taken part in a theft worth hundreds of millions of dollars. To get it, they recruited Williams and two associates from St. Louis. The crew was supposed to force its way into the target’s home, threaten him, and demand that he move the cryptocurrency into accounts the conspirators controlled. Williams and others traveled to Connecticut between August 21 and August 24, 2024. They rented vehicles and gathered supplies, including air rifles, walkie-talkies, and a laptop computer. For two days, they stalked the target and his parents, waiting for an opening to get inside the house. Cameras, frustration, and a failed bitcoin break-in The opening never came. Williams and his associates feared they had been captured on home security cameras. They also grew frustrated with the plan and with a lack of communication from their coordinators. They left Connecticut without carrying out the job. Shortly afterward, a second crew of six men from Florida arrived to carry out the scheme again. On August 25, 2024, Danbury police arrested those six men after a violent carjacking. The men beat and kidnapped two people inside the vehicle. Those two victims were the parents of the target. Local outlets have tied the target to a bitcoin theft in the range of $230 million to $245 million, though the exact figure varies from report to report. The federal case itself centers on the attempted robbery, not the original theft. Federal agents arrested Williams on July 17, 2026. He remains free pending sentencing, and no sentencing date has been set. The FBI New Haven Violent Crimes Task Force, FBI Los Angeles, FBI St. Louis, and the Danbury Police Department investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Karen L. Peck and Stephanie T. Levick prosecuted it. Other defendants in the Danbury case have also pleaded guilty, according to local reporting. Poetic bitcoin justice Earlier this month, a scammer who had stolen about 60 bitcoin (roughly $4.8 million) through a fake-review task scam lost it all when thieves emptied three Ledger addresses where the scammer had moved the proceeds on October 9. Blockchain analysts at Chainalysis said the transfers went into one wallet reported as stolen, while the wider Ledger incident, in which a criminal group allegedly implanted seed-phrase-reading devices sold through Malaysian reseller CryptoBilis, may have drained about $86 million. Ledger said it was working with law enforcement and has confirmed no other vendors were targeted, following a July attack on Coldcard that cost users close to $120 million through a firmware bug. This post 27-Year-Old Missouri Man Admits Role in Failed Bitcoin Kidnapping Plot first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman .

title: Ex-Deputy Economy Minister Perelyhin joins businessman Butkevych's BGV Group as Chief Mining Officer
body:
Yehor Perelyhin, who served as deputy minister of economy and environment from July 2025 until October 20, has joined the team of investment group BGV Group Management as deputy CEO and a member of its board of directors, the investment group said in a statement on Tuesday. The group is active in the mining sector and was founded by Hennadiy Butkevych, co-owner of ATB, Ukraine's largest retail chain.
"Essentially, this is a Chief Mining Officer position, using the Western equivalent and terminology. There are many plans and objectives. They include establishing and developing production and businesses in the critical minerals and other strategic materials sector, developing a commercially viable business model, structuring new investment and commercial agreements, attracting capital for strategic projects, establishing and overseeing the relevant operational processes, and implementing a very ambitious strategy," Perelyhin wrote on Facebook on Tuesday.
He said he was pleased to join the team led by Oleksandr Naumik, which was among the first in Ukraine to recognize the strategic importance of mining and processing critical minerals and had consistently invested financial resources and expertise in geological exploration, laboratory work, processing technology development, project preparation and reserve assessments in accordance with Western standards.
As reported, at the Ministry of Economy, Perelyhin was responsible for coordinating and overseeing the work of the Investment Attraction and International Organizations Cooperation Department, the Financial Policy and War Risk Insurance Department, and the Subsoil Use Directorate.
Perelyhin received his higher education in France (ISEG, ISG) and the United States (St. John's University) and holds an MBA. Before his appointment to the government, he held senior positions in the banking sector and headed Petro-Consulting (now European Lithium Ukraine LLC). He also served twice as head of United Mining and Chemical Company JSC (UMCC) in 2021–2025, bringing it to the privatization stage. In April 2025, he was appointed deputy minister of environmental protection and natural resources. Following the reorganization and merger of the ministries, he was the only deputy to move to the position of deputy minister of economy, environment and agriculture.
Perelyhin was also delegated as an authorized representative to the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF). After he left his position as deputy minister, former Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko replaced him in that role.
In early October, URIF approved the creation of a joint investment platform with BGV Group Management to develop a portfolio of critical minerals projects in Ukraine. The arrangement provides for the possibility of investing up to $30 million in individual projects, as well as attracting Ukrainian and international co-investors, financial institutions, technology companies, industrial companies and strategic partners to specific projects.
According to the company, BGV Group Management's investments in mining already exceed $125 million. After 10 years of operating in the sector, the company has the largest portfolio of specialized projects in Ukraine across six critical minerals segments involving graphite, beryllium, zirconium, titanium, molybdenum and rare earth elements.
BGV Group Management was founded in 2015. It develops five main business areas: mining, energy, real estate development, retail, and education and sports.

title: SCOTUS won't restore policy that lets immigration judges close deportation cases
body:
The regulation give judges discretion to temporarily pause removal proceedings.
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to unfreeze a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration judges to use their discretion to temporarily close deportation cases for immigrants.
In an unsigned order, the court rejected a request from three cities with large migrant populations -- Baltimore as well as Columbus, Ohio and New Haven, Connecticut -- to pause an agreement between Texas and the Trump administration that threw out the policy.
The regulation, known as "administrative closure," gives immigration judges discretion to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for migrants while the migrants seek humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the country.
The Trump administration has pushed to curtail judicial processes for unlawful migrants, and the high court's conservative majority has been largely deferential to executive authority in the area of immigration policy.
Deportation hearings in immigration court are legal proceedings initiated by the Department of Homeland Security in which an immigration judge determines whether a migrant should be removed from the United States. Often, an immigration judge will pause or dismiss a case to allow the individual to pursue legal relief.
While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown , began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.
Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts -- in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.
In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted "efficiency" and protected "due process rights." They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.
In June, the state of Texas sued the federal government, arguing that the policy granted "indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."
