title: How companies disbursed Kogi LG funds through ‘in-and-out’ paper transactions – EFCC investigator
body:
An Economic and Financial Crimes Commission ( EFCC ) investigator narrated on Tuesday how three companies received some Kogi State local government funds and tried to hide the disbursements of the money through what he described as “in-and-out” transactions.
The transactions allegedly took place during the tenure of former Governor Yahaya Bello, who along with two others is facing charges of diverting billions of naira in Kogi State funds at the FCT High Court in Abuja
EFCC detective John Justice, who testified as the 20th prosecution witness in the corruption trial of Mr Bello and co-defendants, said some records showed that the companies withdrew the local government funds as cash without trace of the beneficiaries.
The witness said further investigations showed that funds were transferred straight to different accounts through paper transactions, rather than being completely disbursed in cash as indicated in certain records.
The in-and-out transactions, according to Mr Justice, refer to a practice where a customer goes into a bank and simultaneously fills out a withdrawal slip for one account and a deposit slip for another, moving the exact same amount of money between accounts on paper. In such transactions, the customer does not physically handle or leave with any actual cash.
The witness said a review of CCTV recordings of the banks revealed that the transactions were just paper transactions and not just cash withdrawals.
“We invited the banks (Access and Zenith) because of the voluminous nature of the withdrawals. We requested CCTV footage of the banks, and it revealed that the customers were not taking the cash out of the banks.
“The banks explained that those transactions were treated as in and out. When we asked the banks what they meant, they explained that the customer walked into the bank, filled a cheque withdrawal and filled a deposit slip to a different account,” Mr Justice said.
Mr Justice listed the companies at the centre of the transactions as Hazyman Investment Limited, Bimas Ventures Limited and Fazad.
The EFCC suspects the LG funds transferred to the companies are part of N110.4 billion that Mr Bello, alongside his co-defendants – Umar Shuaibu Oricha and Abdulsalami Hudu – allegedly diverted from Kogi State’s coffers while he served as governor between January 2016 and January 2024.
The trio are facing 16 counts of criminal breach of trust involving N110.4 billion allegedly diverted from the Kogi State treasury.
EFCC alleged that part of the funds was used to buy properties in highbrow areas of Abuja.
The anti-graft agency also accused Mr Bello, who is vying for the Kogi Central Senatorial District seat in 2027 on the platform of the All Progressives Congress, of using part of the diverted funds to make upfront payments for his children’s school fees.
However, Mr Bello and his co-defendants, whom EFCC said conspired with him to commit the crimes, have denied the allegations.
Mr Justice, who described himself as an experienced Asset Tracing and Procurement Fraud and Anti-Money Laundering expert, gave an overview of EFCC investigations into the former governor.
He said the EFCC received intelligence regarding the activity of the Kogi State LGs, and three companies (mentioned earlier) were recurrent in the investigation process.
Mr Justice and his procurement and fraud section team headed by Emeka Okonjo carried out a BVN search on the companies, and found that Yakubu Siyaka was among the alter egos of the companies.
He said the team also wrote to Access and Zenith banks asking for tickets of the companies’ transactions.
According to him, the banks’ responses revealed that Keyless Nature benefitted from the transactions.
Mr Justice said the team received the companies’ statements of account, “they were analysed, and most of the inflow coming into these accounts was from LGs of Kogi State on a monthly basis.”
He said a BVN search conducted on Keyless Nature revealed a connection with Abba Adaudu.
“Analysis of the accounts revealed that these companies were receiving inflow from Kogi State. Most of the transactions were treated as cash withdrawals,” the witness said.
Trial judge Maryann Anenih adjourned the case till 24 November.
In February, the EFCC presented the account statements of 13 companies, including the companies the witness mentioned on Tuesday.
The investigator’s testimony aligns with that of a compliance officer who detailed slews of transfers from some local governments in Kogi State to companies’ accounts.
Mr Adaudu’s name has featured in some witnesses’ testimony. For instance, a bureau de change operator, Jamiu Abdullahi, said he received N1.4 billion through his accounts from Mr Adaudu between 15 December 2021 and 21 February 2022, during Mr Bello’s time in office, to purchase US dollars.
A bureau de change (BDC) operator testified in previous proceedings this month explaining his roles in the payments of the dollar-denominated school fees of the children of Mr Bello at the American International School Abuja (AISA). The prosecution believes the funds were illegally sourced from Kogi State Government’s treasury, an allegation Mr Bello and his co-defendants have denied.

title: Russia sought diplomatic solutions to Iranian conflict since its onset — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russia has been advocating for an end to hostilities and the search for a diplomatic solution since the very beginning of the Iranian conflict, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday.
"As you may well know, Your Highness, Russia has been advocating for a cessation of hostilities and the search for a political and diplomatic solution to the conflict surrounding Iran from the very beginning," Putin said at his meeting with Tamim bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, the Emir of Qatar.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on February 28. In June, Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding providing for an immediate cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including in Lebanon.
However, in the early morning hours of July 8, the US resumed large-scale strikes against Iran, accusing it of violating the terms of the agreements reached on the Strait of Hormuz.
Nearly 25% of global oil trade and about 20% of the liquefied natural gas trade are transported through the strait. The US administration then effectively indicated that it would stop using large-scale military force against Iran and instead seek to economically strangle the country through sanctions.

title: Ukrainian side has yet to confirm trilateral talks will take place on Nov 4
body:
The Ukrainian side has not yet confirmed that trilateral talks between Ukraine, the United States, and Russia will take place in Abu Dhabi on November 4, as announced by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

As Head of the Servant of the People parliamentary faction David Arakhamia stated in comments to TSN, Ukraine cannot yet confirm that the meeting will take place on that specific date.

"The parties are still finalizing the date and awaiting confirmation from the U.S. delegation, which is acting as a mediator in these talks," Arakhamia said.

The president's communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn was also unable to confirm the date.

"Let's wait at least until the end of October. It's too early to make an announcement," Lytvyn old reporters on Tuesday, October 27.

As previously reported, Tusk stated that talks in Abu Dhabi (UAE) between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States at the team level are tentatively scheduled for November 4 of this year.

title: Zelenskyy: Russia fires over 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv, Kyiv region in two weeks
body:
Since October 14, Russia has launched more than 100 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Kyiv region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Just this October, since October 14, there have already been several Russian ballistic missile attacks. In fact, in two weeks, more than 100 ballistic missiles have been fired at Kyiv and Kyiv region," he said in an evening video address on Tuesday.
According to Zelenskyy, the delivery of air defense packages is being delayed, and there is a particular shortage of missiles for the Patriot systems.
"Unfortunately, there are very significant constraints on deliveries, and these air defense packages have been delayed. I want to thank all our partners who provide their support in a timely manner. But, unfortunately, there are also delays. And everyone hears and sees that it is currently difficult for us to defend ourselves against Russian ballistic missiles," he said.
The president also said that Russian strikes have damaged buildings, a subway station, and subway lines in Kyiv. Russian missiles also struck the South Bridge, which is one of the capital's key logistical arteries.
"We are doing everything possible to preserve our energy sector, our infrastructure, and our logistics. And the task is very difficult. Unfortunately, there have been casualties," Zelenskyy said.

title: Intel, Oracle, IBM Join Objections to OKX-ICE Tokenized Stock Venue, Bringing Total to 26
body:
The tech sector’s resistance to tokenized stocks keeps building.
Intel, Oracle, IBM, and quantum computing firm IonQ are the latest companies to object to having their shares traded on OKXICE TSV, according to an updated public notice from the venue dated Monday.
The planned platform, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, now lists 26 objecting issuers.
That’s up from 22 in its Oct. 23 notice, which added Wells Fargo , Cisco, and Marvell. The tally stood at 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15, when the first batch included Verizon, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group . In less than two weeks, the list has nearly tripled.
Technology companies dominate the roster. Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom , Qualcomm, Arm, Cisco, and now Intel and Oracle have all objected, along with banks Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo.
IBM and IonQ add two quantum computing players. As before, the notices don’t explain the companies’ reasons or what an objection means for whether a stock can trade on the platform.
OKXICE TSV plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.
Users must pass identity and sanctions checks and hold a nontransferable “soulbound” token to trade. The venue is set to operate under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.
The latest notice highlights a key risk for investors. Each token represents a claim on a real share held by a third-party “tokenizer” through a registered broker-dealer. If that broker-dealer failed, the notice says, it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in a self-custodied wallet would count as customer property or be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which protects brokerage customers when firms fail.
The notice also says trades must be fully funded, with no margin or borrowing. Liquidity providers don’t have to be registered market makers and can pull their liquidity at any time.
OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before unveiling plans for the venue this month.

title: ICC to elect prosecutor in December 2027
body:
THE HAGUE, October 27. /TASS/. The International Criminal Court (ICC) will elect a new prosecutor to replace recently resigned Karim Khan in December 2027, the Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties said.
It noted that in February, after the end of the application process, information about all candidates will be posted on the assembly's website. Their portfolio will be evaluated by the Advisory Committee on Nominations of Judges, as well as the Independent Oversight Mechanism, a subsidiary body of the court that verifies compliance with its standards. At the same time, the Assembly admits that the terms of the prosecutor's election may be changed if "the process requires."
On July 24, President of the Assembly of States Parties, Ms. Paivi Kaukoranta said that the supervisory authority had removed Khan from office in connection with allegations of sexual harassment with 82 out of 125 ICC countries voting for his dismissal.

title: Full statement: Wontumi’s reflections from prison
body: RE: CHAIRMAN WONTUMI’S REFLECTIONS FROM PRISON – CALLS FOR DEDICATED PRISON HOSPITAL, CONJUGAL VISITATION, AND TOTAL REFORM Following my consistent visits to Chairman Bernard Antwi Boasiako (Chairman Wontumi) since his remand on July 20th, 2026, I wish to share his full reflections on the state of Ghana’s prisons and his humble appeal for urgent reforms. Chairman Wontumi notes that his incarceration has been a period of deep reflection. He has had first-hand interaction with prison officers, inmates, and the conditions under which the Ghana Prison Service operates – a system he says has seen little structural improvement since 1962. He emphasizes that “Not all prisoners are prisoners” and that our correctional system must move from punishment to true reform, welfare and productivity. His detailed observations and appeals: Prison Officers’ Welfare and Pay Calls on government to urgently review pay, accommodation and conditions of service for prison officers. Dedicated Prison Hospital No dedicated, well-equipped prison hospital, no ambulance, no standby generator in many prisons. Seriously sick inmates with terminal illnesses including tuberculosis are managed under difficult conditions. He calls for construction of a dedicated, ultra-modern Prison Hospital for all facilities, and in the interim, emergency linkage with 37 Military Hospital and Police Hospital. Classification of Inmates Minor offenders sleep with armed robbery convicts. Persons on trial for treason and terrorism are mixed with ordinary inmates – a security risk. Youth, Defilement and Behavioural Concern Majority are young men 18-35 years for defilement cases. He observes that due to prolonged incarceration and lack of counselling, these cases often end up engaging in same-sex activities and becoming gays and lesbians within prison. Calls for proper classification and counselling. Family and Conjugal Visitation Calls for a dedicated private area for spouses and children to visit. It is the prisoner who is in prison, not the children or spouse. Regulated visitation for love and intimacy will reduce tension, preserve marriages and aid reformation. Overcrowding and Infectious Diseases Inmates with tuberculosis sleep with healthy inmates. LGBTQI+ Management Calls for clear policy direction on LGBTQI+ classification. Prison Agriculture Service has vast lands and skilled labour but only one tractor for food and garbage. Pleads with Ministry of Food and Agriculture to support prison farms. Justice Sector Collaboration Regional Prison Commanders should be included in jury and justice deliberations because “the real job begins after judgement.” Infrastructure Since 1962 little investment apart from pure water production. Calls on government and private sector to build ultra-modern facilities and factories. Parliamentary Involvement – Key to Reform: Chairman Wontumi makes a special appeal to Parliament of Ghana for these changes to happen. He calls on: 1. The Speaker of Parliament to lead the conversation on prison reform as a matter of human rights and national development. 2. The Majority Caucus and Minority Caucus to work together in a bipartisan manner to pass a new Prison Reform Act, approve budgetary allocation for a dedicated Prison Hospital, ambulance service, generators, and agricultural equipment. 3. The Parliamentary Select Committees on Defence and Interior, Health, and Food and Agriculture to pay working visits to prisons across the country to see conditions firsthand. He believes that without Parliament – Majority and Minority working together with the Speaker – the needed legal and budgetary reforms cannot happen. Continental Lesson African prisons must change – even the name must change. Ghana can lead Africa. “At this experience since July 20th till date, prison doesn’t reform as it should be. I pray that the entire Africa will learn from Ghana.” Appeal: Chairman Wontumi respectfully appeals to the Speaker, Majority Leader, Minority Leader, Attorney General, Chief Justice and Government to prioritize prison welfare. He remains in high spirits. Signed: Dr. Palgrave Boakye-Danquah Spokesperson to Chairman Wontumi

title: Ukraine intercepting more Russian Geran-4 jet-powered drones, General Staff says
body:
Ukraine's air defenses have intercepted nearly 60% of Russian Geran-4 jet-powered attack drones over the past three months, with interception rates reaching 80% during some attacks, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces said.
Fighter jets, including F-16s , Mirage aircraft, and MiG-29s , play a significant role in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, according to the General Staff .
It did not mention interceptions rates of the more advanced Geran-5 drone.
Ukraine is also working to strengthen its short-range air defenses amid a shortage of surface-to-air missiles.
These defenses include Gepard and Shilka anti-aircraft systems, newer platforms such as Skynex, Skyranger, and Terrahawk Paladin, interceptor drones, and mobile fire groups operating across Ukraine's Defense Forces.
Mobile fire groups are equipped with machine guns and man-portable air defense systems (MANPADS), which Ukrainian troops have successfully used to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones.
The General Staff said Ukraine is also seeking cheaper ways to counter the threat , including testing new interceptor drones. Some of the systems being tested have already shot down dozens of Russian jet-powered Geran drones, according to the military.
Russia has increasingly used jet-powered drones to attack Kyiv and the surrounding region since late summer, adding to the threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles.
The newer Geran-5 drones fly higher and faster than other drones, making them significantly harder to intercept. Their growing numbers have also challenged Ukraine's existing interceptor drones, which have proved effective against slower Russian drones.
Ukraine is racing to develop faster interceptors to counter the evolving threat, while Russia is expanding production of jet-powered drones.
Ukraine previously achieved interception rates of around 95% against conventional Shahed-type drones.

title: Alexander Solzhenitsyn warned against a war between Russians and Ukrainians. He also wanted to redraw Ukraine’s borders.
body: On October 20, a monument to Alexander Solzhenitsyn was dismantled in central Vladivostok, where it had stood since 2015. It was supposed to be moved to a park commemorating victims of political repression, but the very next day it was unexpectedly put back . The official explanation was that it was too large for the new site. Vladivostok’s role in this story is no coincidence. It was there that Solzhenitsyn began his journey across Russia in 1994, after 20 years in exile. The writer traveled across the country to Moscow by train. After returning, he became active in politics, criticizing Gorbachev and Yeltsin but speaking favorably of Putin. The feeling is mutual: Putin honors Solzhenitsyn’s memory despite the writer’s views on the USSR and its suppression of dissent. At Meduza’s request, historian Alexey Uvarov explains how Solzhenitsyn’s contradictory views took shape — and how they foreshadowed the Russian-Ukrainian war. From Kislovodsk to Vermont: How Solzhenitsyn survived war and the camps and ended up in exile Alexander Solzhenitsyn was born in Kislovodsk in 1918. His father died before he was born, and his mother raised him alone in Rostov-on-Don. The family was poor, but Solzhenitsyn developed a love of literature as a child. While still in school, he dreamed of writing a novel about the 1917 revolution. Like many of his peers, he sincerely believed in communism and saw the revolution as the first step toward building a just society. In 1936, Solzhenitsyn enrolled in the physics and mathematics department at Rostov University. He continued to dream of a writing career. Solzhenitsyn was drafted into the army in 1941. After artillery school, he was sent to the front, where he commanded a sound-ranging battery, rose to the rank of captain, and received two military decorations. During the war, however, he began to question Joseph Stalin’s policies. Solzhenitsyn had not yet rejected communism itself. He believed Stalin had distorted Lenin’s ideas and that the Soviet system needed to return to its original principles. He discussed these thoughts in letters to his school friend Nikolai Vitkevich. Military censors read the letters, and in February 1945 Solzhenitsyn was arrested at the front. In July, the Special Council of the NKVD, the Soviet internal affairs agency, sentenced him to eight years in labor camps on charges of anti-Soviet agitation and attempting to establish an anti-Soviet organization. Solzhenitsyn’s views gradually changed in prison. In conversations with other prisoners, he encountered criticism of Marxism itself as well as of Stalin. In time, the writer concluded that repression was inherent in the Soviet system, rather than simply a consequence of Stalin’s mistakes. He abandoned communism and returned to the Christian faith in which he had been raised. Solzhenitsyn spent part of his sentence in a “sharashka,” a secret research institute staffed by prisoners, and the final three years in a camp for political prisoners in Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan. After his release in 1953, he was sent into indefinite internal exile in Kazakhstan. Only in 1956 was Solzhenitsyn able to return to the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic; a year later, his conviction was overturned and his name cleared. He settled in Ryazan, took a job as a schoolteacher, and continued writing. The Soviet “Thaw” gave him an opportunity to publish his work. In 1962, Alexander Tvardovsky, editor in chief of the journal Novy Mir, secured Nikita Khrushchev’s personal permission to publish Solzhenitsyn’s novella “Odin den Ivana Denisovicha” (“One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich”) . The work attracted enormous interest and immediately made its author famous. But while the Soviet leadership was prepared to condemn Stalin’s crimes, it would not condemn the system of party dictatorship itself. After Khrushchev’s removal in 1964, Solzhenitsyn’s works were gradually barred from publication. The writer had no intention of renouncing his work. In 1967, he openly challenged censorship, while his novel “V kruge pervom” (“In the First Circle”) and novella “Rakovy korpus” (“Cancer Ward”) circulated in samizdat — clandestinely copied editions — and were published abroad. In 1969, Solzhenitsyn was expelled from the Writers’ Union. A year later, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. His conflict with the authorities culminated in the publication of “Arkhipelag GULAG” (“The Gulag Archipelago”), which Solzhenitsyn had worked on in secret for many years. Drawing on his own experiences and the testimony of hundreds of former prisoners, he showed that mass repression had begun under Lenin and was rooted in the very nature of the Soviet state. The first volume was published in Paris in December 1973. By then, Solzhenitsyn was offering his own vision of the country’s future as well as criticizing its rulers. That same year, he sent the Soviet leadership his “Pismo vozhdyam Sovetskogo Soyuza” (“Letter to the Soviet Leaders”), calling on them to abandon communist ideology and concentrate on domestic problems. The writer did not, however, advocate a transition to Western liberal democracy and was open to retaining authoritarian rule. In February 1974, Solzhenitsyn was arrested, stripped of his Soviet citizenship, and expelled to West Germany. He later moved to Switzerland, then to the United States in 1976. The Vermont recluse: How Solzhenitsyn became a critic of both the USSR and the West In 1976, Solzhenitsyn settled with his wife and children in the small town of Cavendish, Vermont. He bought a house surrounded by woods, where he could work away from journalists and public attention. His main project was the historical epic “Krasnoye Koleso” (“The Red Wheel”), which he had conceived in his youth. In it, the writer sought to understand the causes of the 1917 revolution and the Bolsheviks’ rise to power. He studied archival documents and eyewitness accounts, then spent months working on the manuscript. Solzhenitsyn also maintained his ties to the USSR. After the publication of “The Gulag Archipelago,” he had established a fund to help Soviet political prisoners and their families, donating royalties from the book’s sales. Human rights activists secretly distributed the money inside the country. In 1977, Alexander Ginzburg, one of the fund’s leaders, was arrested, but the organization continued its work. Solzhenitsyn also collected Russian émigrés’ recollections to preserve accounts of the revolution, wars, and Soviet repression. Although the writer rarely appeared in public, he continued to make political statements. His views differed markedly from those of many other critics of the USSR. Solzhenitsyn considered communism a destructive ideology, but he did not see Western society as a model for Russia’s future. This became particularly clear in June 1978, when he addressed Harvard University’s graduating class. Instead of praising American democracy, the writer criticized Western materialism, the excessive emphasis on individual rights, the influence of the press, and politicians’ unwillingness to confront communist regimes. The speech prompted debate in the press: Many critics accused Solzhenitsyn of ingratitude toward the country that had given him refuge and of rejecting liberal democracy. Solzhenitsyn speaking at Harvard University. June 8, 1978 Solzhenitsyn also clashed with other émigrés from the USSR. His dispute with the writer Andrei Sinyavsky was particularly bitter. In “Nashi plyuralisty” (“Our Pluralists”), an article published in 1983, Solzhenitsyn accused some émigré intellectuals of having collaborated with the Soviet authorities and now claiming the right to determine Russia’s future. His opponents, in turn, criticized his Russian nationalism and authoritarian views. Christianity was central to Solzhenitsyn’s worldview. In May 1983, he received the Templeton Prize for his contribution to religious thought. Speaking in London to mark the award, the writer said that society’s abandonment of faith in God was the main cause of Russia’s 20th-century tragedies. He saw this loss of faith as the source of both Soviet totalitarianism and the moral crisis in Western society. In 1985, Solzhenitsyn remained one of the world’s best-known Russian writers, but his works were still not being published in his homeland. The possibility of returning to Russia seemed remote. Perestroika and the return to Russia: How Solzhenitsyn planned the country’s future from exile Mikhail Gorbachev’s rise to power in 1985 changed conditions in the USSR. His policies of perestroika and glasnost allowed previously forbidden subjects, including Stalinist repression, to be discussed openly. The authorities were in no hurry to allow Solzhenitsyn’s works back into print, however. In 1987, Novy Mir editor in chief Sergei Zalygin said the journal planned to publish “Cancer Ward,” and the following year he approached the writer himself. But Solzhenitsyn set a condition: “The Gulag Archipelago” had to be published in the USSR first. He believed readers needed access to this book about the Soviet system’s crimes before any of his other works. In 1989, Novy Mir finally began publishing chapters of “The Gulag Archipelago.” Other works by the writer soon began appearing in the USSR, and he again became a subject of public debate. In August 1990, Gorbachev restored Solzhenitsyn’s citizenship and that of his wife. The writer was not yet planning to return, however. He wanted to finish “The Red Wheel” and secure the formal dismissal of the treason charge brought against him before his expulsion in 1974. Solzhenitsyn was already taking an active part in discussions about the country’s future. In September 1990, Komsomolskaya Pravda and Literaturnaya Gazeta published his article “Kak nam obustroit Rossiyu?” (“Rebuilding Russia: Reflections and Tentative Proposals”), with a print run of nearly 27 million copies. The writer took it as a given that the communist system was doomed and proposed his own plan for transforming the state. He called for abandoning imperial ambitions and not using force to hold on to republics seeking independence. At the same time, Solzhenitsyn advocated preserving a union of Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. He also proposed redrawing some republics’ borders because he considered parts of their territory historically Russian. The writer envisioned Russia as a state with strong local self-government, grounded in national and Christian traditions rather than Western political models. The article provoked fierce debate. Many welcomed the call to abandon communism and focus on domestic problems. But the proposals concerning Ukraine’s and Kazakhstan’s borders drew sharp criticism. Gorbachev also rejected the plan, considering Solzhenitsyn’s views too conservative. Events moved faster than the writer had anticipated. In December 1991, the USSR collapsed, and his proposed union never materialized. By then, the legal barriers to Solzhenitsyn’s return had also been removed. In September 1991, the Soviet Prosecutor General’s Office dismissed the case against him, finding that his actions did not constitute a crime. But the writer remained in Vermont for almost another three years. He continued working on his books and following Russian politics. Solzhenitsyn welcomed the fall of the communist regime, but Boris Yeltsin’s economic reforms and the population’s impoverishment left him increasingly disillusioned . On May 27, 1994, 20 years after his expulsion, Solzhenitsyn finally returned to Russia with his wife and son. He deliberately chose a route through the Far East so that he could cross the country by train and see how it had changed. His plane landed first in Magadan, then in Vladivostok. From there, the writer traveled west by rail, arriving in Moscow on July 21. Solzhenitsyn talking with Siberian Cossacks at a meeting in Irkutsk. June 17, 1994 From support to disillusionment: How Solzhenitsyn became an unyielding opponent of Yeltsin After returning to Russia, Solzhenitsyn had no intention of confining himself to literature. Over his 20 years in exile, he had developed his own vision of how the country should be organized after communism, and now he wanted to join the debate over its future. But what he saw on his journey across Russia disappointed him. The writer spoke of poverty, corruption, and a privatization process that had put state property into the hands of a small group of people. He called the political system a “sham democracy” and “an ingenious fusion of bureaucrats, Soviet party officials, and hardened wheeler-dealers.” The Kremlin initially counted on his support. Solzhenitsyn’s biographer Lyudmila Saraskina writes that Yeltsin was certain the writer would be “on our side.” Reformers saw him as an ally against communism, but his criticism of the economic changes increasingly echoed the rhetoric of the communist opposition. The liberal press began calling Solzhenitsyn “the choirmaster of the doomsayers.” Solzhenitsyn laid out his views most fully in a speech to the State Duma on October 28, 1994. Lawmakers had spent several months debating whether to invite the writer, with the pro-presidential Russia’s Choice faction voting against it. Solzhenitsyn spoke for about an hour. He said Russia had “no democracy, only oligarchy” — rule by “a small, closed circle of people.” He proposed developing local self-government along the lines of the prerevolutionary zemstvos, elected bodies responsible for schools, hospitals, and roads. The writer did not oppose a strong presidency and believed it should be preserved, but he thought its powers should be increasingly limited at lower levels of government, with residents making their own decisions at the local level. Solzhenitsyn also expressed mixed views on the idea of having the president appoint regional leaders. He warned lawmakers that parliament risked sharing the fate of the prerevolutionary Dumas if it could not stand up to the executive branch. Lawmakers gave the speech a cool reception: No one asked questions, and the applause was tepid. The writer’s supporters saw this as evidence of politicians’ indifference to the country’s troubles. Reformers, meanwhile, considered Solzhenitsyn’s proposals outdated. Yegor Gaidar said with regret that the speech had pleased the communists. His relationship with Yeltsin was also difficult. In August 1991, Solzhenitsyn welcomed Yeltsin’s resistance to the State Committee for the State of Emergency, which had attempted a coup, but soon began criticizing his economic policies. In June 1992, they spoke by phone for 40 minutes, and the writer said he had “failed to convince him of anything.” The president also publicly challenged his prominent critic. In “Zapiski prezidenta” (“The Struggle for Russia”), he responded to Solzhenitsyn’s question about whether he would treat his own mother with shock therapy: “I would use shock therapy on myself, and not just one time.” On November 16, 1994, they met in person, with their wives and without journalists. Yeltsin’s press secretary, Vyacheslav Kostikov, recalled that the president was nervous and that his advisers had tried to talk him out of the meeting. The conversation lasted about four hours and, in Kostikov’s words, proceeded “without glossing over political differences.” Solzhenitsyn recounted his journey across the country and outlined his proposals. But no noticeable changes in government policy followed. Another source of disagreement soon emerged. In December 1994, Russian troops entered Chechnya, which had effectively been outside Moscow’s control since 1991. Solzhenitsyn considered the decision to go to war a “grave political mistake.” In 1992, he had advised Yeltsin to let Chechnya go if it wanted to secede. Later, the writer proposed recognizing the republic’s independence, but separating it from Russia with a line of military posts along the border and retaining the territory on the left bank of the Terek River as part of Russia. In 2000, after Chechen militants invaded Dagestan, he acknowledged that his earlier advice to Yeltsin had been a mistake. Solzhenitsyn also tried to reach television audiences. Beginning in April 1995, his 15-minute addresses aired on ORT every two weeks. He spoke about schools, the army, elections, the situation of Russians outside Russia, and the war in Chechnya. But the program was canceled after 12 episodes. The 13th episode, devoted to people’s disillusionment with politics and criticism of the authorities, never aired . “They’ve shut me up, just as I expected,” Solzhenitsyn said. ORT’s management said it had made the decision because of the approaching parliamentary elections and the need to maintain political balance. But because other critical programs were taken off the air at the same time, the decision prompted suspicions of political censorship. Solzhenitsyn no longer had a regular television audience, though he continued to travel around the country and express his views in the press. Solzhenitsyn at his country home in Troitse-Lykovo during the filming of Alexander Sokurov’s film about him By the late 1990s, his criticism of Yeltsin had grown even harsher. In May 1998, he published “Rossiya v obvale” (“Russia in Collapse”). In it, Solzhenitsyn accused the authorities of carrying out unfair privatization, destroying industry and science, impoverishing the population, and giving in to the West. He did not call for a return to the Soviet system, but he considered the existing political order unacceptable. The book appeared three months before the August debt default, which gave his criticism added weight. His differences with Yeltsin came to a head in December 1998. To mark the writer’s 80th birthday, the president awarded him the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle, Russia’s highest state honor. Solzhenitsyn had sent the presidential administration a written refusal in advance, but Yeltsin signed the decree anyway. On December 11, his birthday, at the premiere of Yury Lyubimov’s play “Sharashka” (“The Prison Research Institute”) at the Taganka Theater, he said from the stage: “I cannot accept an award from the country’s highest authority, which has brought Russia to its present disastrous state.” The writer did, however, accept Yeltsin’s personal birthday greetings. Putin and Solzhenitsyn: How a dissident and a KGB officer grew close Solzhenitsyn entered 2000 as an unyielding critic of Yeltsin. He reacted sharply to Yeltsin’s resignation and acting President Putin’s decree granting the former head of state immunity. Speaking at the Russian State Library in May 2000, he said: “I consider it disgraceful to absolve Yeltsin of responsibility. And probably not just Yeltsin — another hundred or two should stand trial along with him!” Solzhenitsyn was initially wary of the country’s new leadership as well. In interviews with NTV and Novaya Gazeta, he criticized Putin’s intention to continue Yeltsin’s reforms: “So far, we have seen no encouraging steps from the new authorities to put things right.” Within a few months, however, his attitude toward the new president had become noticeably more favorable. On September 20, 2000, Putin and his wife visited Solzhenitsyn at his country home in Troitse-Lykovo. The following day, the writer said the president had made a good impression on him. He praised Putin’s quick mind and described his decisions as “prudent and sound,” saying Putin had “no thirst for personal power.” Solzhenitsyn said the two did not always agree, but listened carefully to each other’s arguments. The meeting provoked debate. To many former Soviet dissidents, the growing closeness between the author of “The Gulag Archipelago” and a former KGB officer seemed paradoxical . Andrei Sakharov’s widow, Yelena Bonner, wondered how “the regime’s most fearless opponent became friends with a KGB colonel.” Still, Solzhenitsyn’s approval of the president did not mean he stopped criticizing the authorities. In December 2000, while accepting an award from the French Academy of Moral and Political Sciences, he sharply criticized the political elite, which he believed was dominated by “unrepentant members of the old nomenclatura” and “rapacious former heads of the Komsomol.” Answering journalists’ questions after the ceremony, the writer recounted what he had told Putin at their private meeting: “Strengthening the state is necessary for Russia’s unity, but strengthening the state will not make Russia flourish. Russia can flourish only when millions are free to speak, when they are free in word and deed to shape their own destiny.” Solzhenitsyn and Putin agreed above all on the need to strengthen the state. The writer believed that the collapse of the USSR and the economic upheavals of the 1990s had left Russia in a deep crisis, and that the new president was trying to rebuild the state. In a July 2007 interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel, Solzhenitsyn said Putin had inherited a country that had been “ransacked and knocked off its feet” and had begun gradually rebuilding it. The writer also said he was “dismayed” by the slow development of local self-government and regretted the absence of a sizable, constructive political opposition in Russia. In the same interview, he called Putin’s decision to abolish elections to the State Duma in single-member districts a mistake. In private conversations, Solzhenitsyn could be even more explicit in criticizing Putin’s decisions. In April 2008, a few months before his death, he met with U.S. Ambassador William Burns. According to a diplomatic cable published later, the writer called the abolition of gubernatorial elections a “mistake.” He said citizens should be able to choose their own representatives in government and hold them accountable. As an example, Solzhenitsyn recalled town meetings in Vermont, which he called the very essence of democracy. Putin and Solzhenitsyn also had similar views on relations with the West. Solzhenitsyn had long criticized Western policy, but his judgments became even harsher after NATO’s bombing of Yugoslavia in 1999. In a 2006 interview with Moskovskiye Novosti, he said NATO’s expansion was intended to encircle Russia and strip it of its sovereignty. A year later, the writer called Putin’s foreign policy “quite reasonable and more foresighted,” while criticizing NATO’s efforts to bring former Soviet republics, particularly Ukraine, into its orbit. The Russian State Prize, awarded to Solzhenitsyn in 2007 “for outstanding achievements in humanitarian work,” symbolized the closeness between the writer and the president. Solzhenitsyn had refused the Order of St. Andrew from Yeltsin in 1998, but accepted Putin’s award. He explained his decision by noting that the prize had been awarded by a panel of experts rather than by the president personally. In his Der Spiegel interview, Solzhenitsyn also answered a question about Putin’s past: “Vladimir Putin — yes, he was an officer of the intelligence services, but he was not a KGB investigator, nor was he the head of a camp in the gulag.” Putin and Solzhenitsyn meeting. June 2007 On June 12, 2007, the writer’s wife, Natalia, accepted the award at the Kremlin. Solzhenitsyn himself was unable to attend because of his health. After the ceremony, Putin visited him at home for another conversation . The president told journalists that many of the authorities’ actions were in keeping with Solzhenitsyn’s ideas. Life after death: How the authorities put Solzhenitsyn’s legacy to work for them Solzhenitsyn died on August 3, 2008, at 89. By then, Putin had become prime minister, and Dmitry Medvedev was president. Both paid their respects to the writer: Putin attended the public memorial service, and Medvedev the funeral at the Donskoy Monastery. On the day of the funeral, Medvedev signed a decree commemorating Solzhenitsyn. Scholarships were established in his honor, and Moscow’s Bolshaya Kommunisticheskaya Street was soon renamed Alexander Solzhenitsyn Street, despite protests from the Communist Party of the Russian Federation. Later, an abridged version of “The Gulag Archipelago,” prepared with the involvement of the writer’s widow, Natalia, was produced for schoolchildren. The Russian authorities continued to honor Solzhenitsyn’s memory in the years that followed. In December 2018, to mark the centenary of the writer’s birth, Putin personally unveiled a monument to him in Moscow. In his speech, the president called Solzhenitsyn a “true patriot” who, even in exile, “opposed any manifestations of Russophobia.” In this way, Solzhenitsyn’s devotion to Russia and defense of its national interests — not just his fight against Soviet repression — took on special prominence in the official portrayal of the writer. Vladimir Putin and Alexander Solzhenitsyn’s widow, Natalia, at the unveiling of a monument to the writer in Moscow. December 11, 2018 The writer’s widow, Natalia Solzhenitsyna, plays an important role in preserving and interpreting his legacy. In a 2018 interview with the French newspaper Le Figaro, she supported the annexation of Crimea, calling it a restoration of historical justice. Solzhenitsyna also acknowledged that the peninsula’s annexation was contentious under international law and opposed Russian intervention in the Donbas. She said the intervention was an enormous mistake that the country would come to regret. In 2022, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the publisher AST released “S Ukrainoy budet chrezvychayno bolno” (“Ukraine Will Be an Extremely Painful Problem”), a collection compiled by Solzhenitsyna. The book continued a project begun in 2018 with the collection “Rossiya. Zapad. Ukraina” (“Russia. The West. Ukraine”). It brought together Solzhenitsyn’s statements on Russian-Ukrainian relations, disputed territories, and Western policy. In the foreword, the writer’s widow repeated her husband’s arguments about the injustice of Ukraine’s Soviet-era borders and Western countries’ responsibility for the deterioration in relations between Russia and Ukraine. Yet in May 2022, Natalia Solzhenitsyna also signed a written pledge vouching for opposition politician Vladimir Kara-Murza, who had been arrested on charges of spreading “fake news” about the Russian army. Solzhenitsyn, Ukraine, and Kazakhstan: How the writer’s views grew more radical Solzhenitsyn’s views provoked particularly fierce debate in Ukraine and Kazakhstan. The writer recognized peoples’ right to self-determination and opposed forcibly keeping republics within a common state. Yet he considered large parts of Ukrainian and Kazakhstani territory historically Russian. This contradiction persisted in his statements for decades. Solzhenitsyn’s early reflections on Ukraine seemed fairly conciliatory. In “The Gulag Archipelago,” the bulk of which he finished writing in 1968, the writer recalled his conversations with Ukrainian nationalists in Soviet camps. He criticized the authorities’ habit of labeling them bandits and considered Ukrainians’ desire for independence understandable. Despite their shared history, Russians and Ukrainians had failed over several centuries to learn to live in harmony, Solzhenitsyn acknowledged. “Ukraine will be an extremely painful problem,” he warned. But he considered it unacceptable to hold on to Ukraine by force. Ukrainians themselves, he believed, should decide their country’s future. The writer nevertheless hoped that a peaceful separation would eventually allow the two peoples to reunite. In May 1975, Solzhenitsyn recorded an Easter radio address to Ukrainians in Canada. In it, he recalled his own Ukrainian roots: His mother was almost entirely of Ukrainian descent, and his maternal grandfather spoke Ukrainian. The writer said he did not speak Ukrainian fluently but understood it well. He recalled Ukrainians’ suffering, including the famine of the 1930s, and his friendships with Ukrainian prisoners in Soviet camps. Polish historian Grzegorz Przebinda of Jagiellonian University said the address was included in neither the 2018 collection “Russia. The West. Ukraine” nor the 2022 volume “Ukraine Will Be an Extremely Painful Problem,” both prepared by the writer’s widow. Hi, I’m Katya. I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe. Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza. The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work. Even during this period, however, Solzhenitsyn’s attitude toward Ukraine was becoming more contradictory. Przebinda found that, when preparing a new edition of “The Gulag Archipelago” in 1980, the writer added a remark to his earlier reflections saying that Khrushchev had arbitrarily transferred Crimea to Ukraine. At the same time, some sympathetic statements about the Ukrainian national movement disappeared from the book. Solzhenitsyn nevertheless continued to oppose violence between the two peoples. In 1981, he sent a letter to the organizers of a conference on Russian-Ukrainian relations in Toronto. In it, the writer urged that no one be held by force and promised that “never, under any circumstances, shall I take part in a Russian-Ukrainian clash or allow my sons to do so.” By the early 1990s, territorial claims were becoming increasingly prominent in his thinking. In “Rebuilding Russia,” Solzhenitsyn proposed letting most Soviet republics go while preserving a union of Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and Kazakhstan. He denied that a distinct Ukrainian people had existed since the early Middle Ages, calling such ideas “a recently invented falsehood.” The writer also maintained that the Kherson region, the area around the Sea of Azov, Crimea, and the Donbas had never been part of historical Ukraine. He considered Kazakhstan’s territory an artificial creation of the Soviet authorities and proposed keeping its northern regions within Russia. Solzhenitsyn still recognized Ukrainians’ and Kazakhs’ right to independence in principle, but he believed that each region should decide separately which state it would belong to. Solzhenitsyn in the United States in 1989 These proposals provoked a sharp reaction. In September 1990, participants in a rally in Alma-Ata against Solzhenitsyn’s territorial claims publicly burned a newspaper containing his article. The Lviv Regional Council also condemned the writer’s statements. His critics included former Ukrainian political prisoners who, like Solzhenitsyn himself, had endured the Soviet camps. In August 1991, before the Soviet Union collapsed, Solzhenitsyn called on Yeltsin to reconsider the Soviet republics’ borders. He asked the president to ensure that votes in Ukraine’s forthcoming independence referendum would be counted separately in each region. In the writer’s view, residents should decide for themselves which state their territories belonged to. In a 1994 interview with Forbes, he again said he wished Ukraine success, but only within borders that he himself considered ethnically justified. In his final years, Solzhenitsyn’s views on Ukrainian politics hardened further. In 2006, he called the alleged suppression of the Russian language in Ukraine “an act of atrocity” and again questioned Ukraine’s right to Crimea and its eastern regions. In April 2008, four months before his death, he published an article in Izvestia titled “Possorit rodnye narody?” (“ Swallowing Shameless Lies ”). The writer opposed recognizing the famine of 1932–1933 as a genocide of Ukrainians and compared the Ukrainian authorities’ arguments to Bolshevik propaganda. The article outraged former Ukrainian political prisoners. Levko Lukyanenko and other human rights advocates called on Russian intellectuals not to support this interpretation of the Holodomor. They also expressed hope that Solzhenitsyn himself would find the courage to “live not by lies” — a reference to his own 1974 essay, “Zhit ne po lzhi” (“Live Not by Lies”). How to view Solzhenitsyn in 2026 It would be wrong to reduce Solzhenitsyn either to his “great-power” views or to his condemnation of Soviet camps and repression. He was a complex person whose political convictions changed throughout his life. Though he did not support Western liberal democracy, the writer defended freedom of speech, human dignity, and local self-government. But in today’s Russia, the “great-power” side of his legacy has come to the fore. Putin found ideas that matched his own views in the writer’s reflections on a strong state and national interests. As a result, Solzhenitsyn, who remains unacceptable to many admirers of the Soviet past, has gained a prominent place in the state’s efforts to shape historical memory. Other parts of his legacy, meanwhile, increasingly conflict with the Russian authorities’ actions. Even as the state honors the author of “The Gulag Archipelago,” a Moscow museum devoted to Soviet repression has been closed and replaced by a museum of victims of Nazi crimes. Still more striking is the contradiction with the principle of “protecting the people,” which Solzhenitsyn considered one of the state’s main responsibilities and which Putin himself quoted in 2006. The war against Ukraine, with its enormous loss of life, is difficult to reconcile with that principle. In closing, all that remains is to quote Solzhenitsyn once more, from his essay “‘Russky vopros’ k kontsu XX veka” (“The ‘Russian Question’ at the End of the Twentieth Century”): We do not need to be a world arbiter, to compete for international leadership (stronger volunteers will surface); all our efforts must be directed inwards, towards assiduous inner development. title: President honours flydubai crew for courage during September 30 mid-air attack
body: President Sheikh Mohamed conferred the First Class Order of Zayed II on the crew of flydubai flight 1073 and commended their bravery during the mid-air emergency on September 30, which ensured the safety of passengers. Sheikh Mohamed received the crew at a council attended by senior members of the UAE's leadership, including Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid, Vice President and Ruler of Dubai. The honours were presented by Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed, Crown Prince of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Defence, who commended the crew’s actions and sense of responsibility. During the meeting, the leaders paid tribute to the crew for the high level of responsibility they showed in maintaining passenger safety and security. They stressed that preserving human safety and security is the UAE's highest priority and ultimate value. Prestigious civilian honour The First Class Order of Zayed II is one of the UAE's state civil honours, conferred directly by the UAE President. Named in honour of the UAE’s founding father, Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the award recognises individuals who demonstrate distinguished national service, heroic actions, exemplary dedication to public safety, or significant contributions to strengthening international relations and strategic partnerships with the UAE. The award is conferred on both UAE citizens and foreign nationals, including diplomats, civil servants, and everyday individuals who perform exceptional acts of bravery or service. 'First Class' denotes the highest tier within the Order of Zayed II merit system. What happened on flydubai flight Flydubai Flight 1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv plunged 17,000 feet in less than a minute when the first officer attacked pilot Capt Smit Machchhar and seized control of the plane. In an exclusive interview with The National , Capt Machchhar spoke of the moment his co-pilot repeatedly struck him with an axe before sending their Boeing 737 plunging towards the Arabian Desert. According to the UAE prosecutors, a flydubai co-pilot tried to seize control of a passenger jet and crash it into Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion International Airport. An investigation into the incident found that the aircraft's Omani co-pilot carried out a terrorist plot to cause mass casualties at the Israeli airport. The suspect, aged 29, was inspired by the attacks on September 11, 2001, and had pursued a career in aviation specifically to carry out such an operation, according to his confession. After Capt Machchhar managed to get the cabin door open, crew members and passengers restrained the suspect and rescued the injured captain. During the event in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, Sheikh Mohamed praised the crew for their swift and decisive actions that saved lives on board. The crew members thanked the President and expressed their pride in receiving the honour. The gathering was attended by other senior officials, including: Sheikh Maktoum bin Mohammed, First Deputy Ruler of Dubai, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance; Sheikh Saif bin Zayed, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Interior; and Sheikh Hamdan bin Zayed, Ruler's Representative in Al Dhafra Region. Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, chairman of the Dubai Civil Aviation Authority and chairman and chief executive of the Emirates Group, also attended, as did Sheikh Nahyan bin Mubarak, Minister of Tolerance and Coexistence, and a number of sheikhs, officials and guests.

title: Nearly 50 recon and intel Marines headed to undersea cable guard duty in Europe
body: A team of close to 50 reconnaissance and intelligence-focused Marines are being sent to join a NATO mission that oversees the network of undersea internet cables and pipelines in the Baltic Sea. The Marines are being sent to join the NATO-led operation due, at least in part, to their expertise with unmanned reconnaissance drones and other tactical intelligence-gathering skills. In a Marine Corps press release, the senior officer in the Finnish Navy said the Marines would work alongside Finns and other NATO forces to monitor waters in the Baltic, which are crisscrossed with data cables and natural gas pipelines. “The experience, skills and systems of the U.S. Marine Corps are perfectly suited for supplementing our situation picture and supporting our monitoring of the Baltic Sea,” said Chief of Operations of the Finnish Navy Capt. Johan Tillander. The roughly four dozen Marines are from the 2nd Reconnaissance Battalion, 2nd Marine Division, and the II Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group, both of which are based at Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, North Carolina. News Space Force wants to embed more guardians into the joint force By Nicholas Slayton News US expands alcohol restrictions for troops in Japan By Nicholas Slayton News Air Force special ops trainees are graduating months faster in revised pipeline By Patty Nieberg Reconnaissance Marines are widely known as the service’s elite light infantry, but their primary capabilities are the passive skills of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance, or ISR. The Information Group is an intelligence analysis unit trained to keep commanders apprised of ISR sources like those collected by recon units. Both units were in Europe on training rotations, the Marine release said, when they were reassigned to the Baltic operation, dubbed Enhanced Vigilance Activity Baltic Sentry , to “operate alongside the Finnish Coastal Brigade to provide advanced expeditionary surveillance and tactical reconnaissance capabilities. The rotation will leverage the unique capabilities of Reconnaissance Marines, including small Unmanned Aerial Systems and littoral sensors, to feed vital data directly into the shared NATO common operational picture.” The waters of the Baltic Sea — and the seafloor beneath them — have been an increasingly active front in the simmering conflict between Russia and NATO after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. In September 2022, an undersea explosion broke the Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines between Germany and Russia. A Ukrainian intelligence officer went on trial this month in Germany on charges related to the destruction. Since the Nord Stream attacks, more than half a dozen other attempts have been made to disable or cut pipelines or data networks on the floor of the Baltic. The post Nearly 50 recon and intel Marines headed to undersea cable guard duty in Europe appeared first on Task & Purpose .

title: Enugu governor appoints two Nollywood stars as special assistants
body:
Governor Peter Mbah of Enugu State has appointed popular Nollywood actress and filmmaker, Eucharia Anunobi, as his senior special assistant on women mobilisation for the Enugu North District.
PREMIUM TIMES reports that Ms Anunobi’s appointment was announced in a statement issued in September by the Secretary to the Enugu State Government, Chidiebere Onyia.
The Nollywood actress, who is also a gospel minister, was among 101 new aides appointed to various positions, including special adviser, senior special assistant, and special assistant roles in the state.
Apart from Ms Anunobi, the governor also appointed another Nollywood actress, Rachael Okonkwo, as his senior special assistant on Film and Creative Industry Development.
But Ms Anunobi only announced the appointment in a post on his Facebook page on Tuesday.
“Behold the latest Honourable. Great people of my great nation, Nigeria and the world at large, it is official !!!,” she wrote.
“I am the Senior Special Assistant on women mobilisation, Enugu North Zone to the Governor of Enugu State, Peter Ndubuisi Mbah.”
Born in Owerri, Imo State, Ms Anunobi rose to prominence in Nollywood during the 1990s, starring in over 90 films before becoming a gospel minister.
The 61-year-old joins the list of Nollywood stars who have been given political appointments in Nigeria.
Nkiru Sylvanus, another Nollywood actress, was appointed special assistant on Lagos State Affairs to the then-Imo State Governor Rochas Okorocha in July 2011.
In April 2022, Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State appointed Nollywood actor Bob-Manuel Udokwu as his special adviser on Entertainment, Leisure and Tourism.

title: Zelenskyy announces new contacts with European partners in coming weeks
body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced new engagements with major European countries in the coming weeks.

"We will be engaging in new communications with powerful European countries in the coming weeks," Zelenskyy said in a video address on Tuesday evening.

He said Ukraine is coordinating efforts with its European partners to secure new support packages and organize diplomatic meetings.

According to the president, Ukraine is looking forward to a trilateral meeting between representatives of Ukraine, the United States, and Russia in November and insists on Europe's participation in all diplomatic processes and decision-making.

"So that no one is left out of the process. I want to thank everyone who is actively involved and helping us," he added.

title: Russian electronics billionaire Dmitry Alekseyev publicly defends jailed election expert Alexander Kynev, denouncing his detention conditions
body: Dmitry Alekseyev, president and co-owner of the retail chain DNS, wrote a Facebook post defending political scientist Alexander Kynev, who was arrested on charges of attempting to sell drugs. ”[…] I get it — the elephant in the room, the times we’re living in. But you know what? They’ve just released a series based on ‘ Hard to Be a God .’ There’s not much left of the Strugatsky brothers’ work in it, but even there, persecuting scholars is portrayed as an outrageous example of medieval barbarism. Kynev is one of those scholars. A scholar who’s now sitting in an overcrowded cell with a hole in the floor for a toilet. Surely this isn’t what our traditional values are about? Or is humanism a forbidden word now, too?” Alekseyev asked. The news outlet Agentstvo, which drew attention to Alekseyev’s post, said it was a rare instance of a prominent Russian businessman speaking out in defense of a victim of political repression. Alexander Kynev is a well-known expert on Russian regional politics. He was arrested in a drug case on September 25. He was beaten when he was detained, and his shinbone was broken in two places. On October 26, it emerged that he had gone on a hunger strike in pretrial detention. His lawyer said Kynev shares a cell with 34 other people and that the toilet is a hole in the floor, which Kynev cannot use because his leg is in a cast. Dmitry Alekseyev’s DNS is one of Russia’s largest retailers of electronics and home appliances. Forbes estimates Alekseyev’s net worth at $1.6 billion. Alekseyev has criticized the authorities before, including after Alexey Navalny’s death in pretrial detention. Read more Russian elections expert Alexander Kynev stayed in the country to keep studying its politics. After criticizing the latest vote, he was arrested on drug charges. The Strugatsky brothers’ Soviet sci-fi classic ‘Hard to Be a God’ took aim at dictatorship. Russia’s new state-backed TV adaptation strips away the politics. title: Senior Russian diplomats discuss West’s steps to contain Russia, its militarization push
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. A Russian Foreign Ministry board meeting chaired by Russia’s top diplomat Sergey Lavrov on Tuesday condemned the West’s militarization push, restrictions on navigation and the course toward containing Russia, Russia’s MFA said.
"Issues regarding the military and political situation in the region, including the West’s unfriendly steps in militarization, restrictions on navigation and `broader containment of Russia’ were discussed in detail," the ministry revealed.
In addition, threats and challenges to Russia’s national interests, ways to overcome those and prospects for unlocking the potential of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor in logistics as well as issues of ensuring security of the Kaliningrad Region were analyzed.

title: Flavio Bolsonaro headed to the US after losing Brazil election, sources say - report
body: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday's presidential election and refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports, two sources said.The US Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's lawyer also did not respond.It was not immediately clear where Bolsonaro was heading, what time he would arrive or whether he would seek asylum. US President Donald Trump's administration has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.Flavio's departure for the United States threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a US State Department campaign to restore them to office.Lula's office did not respond to a request for comment.Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to leftist Lula.On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, leading to his documents being canceled.Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee."I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me." Bolsonaro follows father's pathJair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former US President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.His son has yet to officially concede defeat - saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities - but his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point.Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move."If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

title: Unclaimed $40M Lotto Max ticket expires Wednesday, OLG says
body:
An unclaimed Lotto Max ticket worth $40 million will expire Wednesday, the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG) says.
The winning ticket from the Oct. 28, 2025, Lotto Max draw was bought at an authorized retailer somewhere in Grey County, the OLG said in a news release Tuesday.
It will expire Wednesday – one year since the draw was held.
With only hours remaining, the OLG is urging anyone who purchased a Lotto Max ticket in Grey County, or anyone who visited the area around the time of the draw, to check their tickets immediately.
Grey County is made up of communities like Owen Sound, Meaford, The Blue Mountains, Flesherton, Markdale, Durham and Hanover.
“Because Grey County is a popular destination for tourists, cottagers and day-trippers, there is possibility that the winning ticket may not belong to a local resident,” the OLG said.
“Someone visiting the area could have purchased the ticket, tucked it away and never realized they were holding a $40 million jackpot winner.”
The winning numbers for the Oct. 28, 2025, Lotto Max draw are 6, 14, 17, 19, 26, 43, 45, with 27 being the bonus number.

title: Benue police arrest 60-year-old man over defilement of minor
body: records other breakthroughs By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Benue State Police Command has arrested a 60-year-old man over the alleged defilement of a 10-year-old girl in Igumale, Ado Local Government Area, LGA, of the state. The Commissioner of Police, CP, Cletus Nwadiogbu, disclosed this on Tuesday while briefing journalists on the security situation and operational achievements recorded by the command in October 2026. According to him, the incident was reported to the police on October 13, prompting the arrest of the suspect, while the victim was taken for medical examination and necessary treatment. Nwadiogbu said, “the Command recorded an arrest in an alleged defilement case reported on 13th October 2026 in Igumale, Ado Local Government Area, involving a 10-year-old girl. “A 60-year-old suspect was arrested, while the victim was taken for medical examination and necessary treatment. Investigation is ongoing, and the Command will ensure that the matter is handled in accordance with the law, with the privacy and welfare of the victim protected.” The Police Commissioner added that the case was among several serious offences being investigated by the command as part of efforts to protect vulnerable persons and bring suspected offenders to justice. He also disclosed that “the Command rescued 29 kidnapped victims during the period under review through intelligence-led operations and collaboration with other security agencies and community-based security groups.” According to him, “four passengers abducted after a commercial vehicle was attacked along Uzer Village axis of Ayilamo-Tse-Abi Road in Logo LGA on October 5 were rescued following a joint operation involving the police, Operation Whirl Stroke, Benue State Civil Protection Guards and local hunters.” The Commissioner said “17 farmers were also rescued from Tse-Acha and Tse-Wuam communities in Bamun Village, Tombo District, Logo LGA, on October 7, while eight kidnapped victims, including a Reverend Father, were rescued in Ohimini LGA following their abduction along the Ugbokolo-Ajegbe-Awume Road on October 13.” He disclosed that “the Command also arrested 34 foreign nationals during separate operations, comprising 16 Cameroonians apprehended in Otukpo LGA on October 9 and 18 Nigeriens intercepted at Orokam on October 22.” He said investigations were ongoing to establish their immigration status and circumstances of movement. Nwadiogbu further reported the arrest of suspects in separate operations against cultism, unlawful possession of firearms and violent crimes, with seven locally fabricated firearms and 16 rounds of ammunition and cartridges recovered during the period under review. The Commissioner also disclosed that one suspected bandit was neutralised during an encounter involving personnel of Operation Zenda Joint Task Force along Amaafu-Abaji Road in Katsina-Ala LGA on October 2, while a locally fabricated firearm was recovered. He urged residents to remain vigilant and provide credible information to security agencies, stressing that public cooperation was essential to preventing crime and protecting lives and property across the state. CP Nwadiogbu expressed gratitude to the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, for his continued support and commitment to strengthening policing operations and ensuring the safety of lives and property across the country. He also appreciated the Benue State Governor, Rev. Fr. Hyacinth Alia, for his constant support to the command and commitment to peace, security and stability in the state, while acknowledging the contributions of other security agencies, community leaders, local vigilantes and members of the public whose cooperation continues to support efforts to maintain law and order. The post Benue police arrest 60-year-old man over defilement of minor appeared first on Vanguard News .
