title: What Happens When America's Power Grid Becomes a Last Resort?
body: Good news. Electric grid reliability was a lot better in 2025 than in 2024. But one swallow does not make a spring, as Aristotle noted, a number of years ago. Grid reliability, we believe, has been trending downward since the turn of the century, that is, since deregulation really got rolling. Okay, you could argue, as a good logician, that this is an example of a post hoc ergo propter hoc fallacy, that is, because event B took place after event A must mean that A caused B. We admit that. We're just pointing out the chronology, before applying a few lessons from Wall Street.  First, to the numbers graphed below. The blue line is based on outage numbers issued by the Energy Information Administration, a series that ended in 2023. Note the upward trend. The green line shows outage minutes per average customer, as calculated by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers IEEE. It shows a wide-ranging variability from year to year, but on an upward trend. The grey line, trending upward slightly but relatively smooth, shows average outages after excluding Major Event Days; in other words, reliability when there is nothing big going on to affect reliability.  Let's consider these numbers from a Wall Street perspective. First, the reliability number excluding Major Event Days looks suspiciously like "adjusted earnings", the procedure whereby management removes unusual and supposedly one-time items from the income statement they report to Wall Street. They have to report those items in the audited statements, but they like to divert attention to the adjusted numbers. "Hey, this is a one-time event; it won't happen again, so ignore it." Instead, something else happens next year, and on and on. We could say the same about hurricanes. Each one is a unique event, but they keep recurring. Customers want to know how good you are at keeping the lights on during challenging moments, not when all is calm.  Second, look at the volatility of the outage numbers. As any finance 101 student will tell you, the greater the volatility, the greater the risk. In this case, we mean risk to users of the grid, who have to decide whether to invest in storage or a supplemental power source to protect against grid failure. If batteries cost you $2000 per year to protect against that two-hour average outage, you might decide not to buy the protection. If you are running a business that needs ultra-reliable power, you might invest if a six-hour outage were likely but not a two-hour outage. Do you risk the outage or the overinvestment in storage  Let's look at the issue from some other angles. First, because of solar plus storage, there is an urban-rural cost divide re-emerging in the electric power business, something we haven't seen since the 1930s. It was always understood that rural customers were far more expensive to serve than urban ones. The financial return on a mile of utility distribution line in, say, Manhattan, NY, with perhaps 25,000 customers per mile is far greater than the return on distribution assets in Manhattan, Kansas, with perhaps five customers per mile. But now, financially, it is cheaper and technologically feasible for the monopoly utility service provider to cut these high-cost customers off from the grid and offer them standalone solar, batteries, and propane backup generators. In other words, the old problem of serving high-cost utility customers in remote areas never went away, but now it can be addressed in a very different manner which is cheaper for the utility overall and provides better reliability for the customer.  As if to make our case, a new entrant in the battery market recently raised money. It installs relatively large batteries in homes at no expense to the homeowner, and in an outage it provides about 36 hours of power. Aside from opportunities for simple arbitrage, since we're talking about finance here, these are simply arbitrage machines. They may discharge or provide electricity at times of high power prices and recharge themselves when power prices are low, They also may be able to take advantage of other profit-making opportunities created by the state of the grid. Residential customers get some cheaper power and outage protection while the corporate owner gets the other profit opportunities. We think this business will grow.Lastly, we note that sometimes a technology race is a race to the bottom, meaning things get cheaper and cheaper. We think this is likely to occur with battery technologies. The cheaper and more advanced technologies will displace the older ones even though the latter worked just fine. For example, the telegraph system was operating quite well, but it was still replaced by the telephone, which was considered better. This is important financially because a relentless technological drive to lower costs does not always provide an adequate return to investors. And in cases where the industry, like electricity, is critical to the literal functioning of modern society, we do not have a choice. If there is no longer any profit to be made in the electricity business, then our essential societal need for electricity suggests it should be treated like other essential services that local governments provide, like police, fire, and sanitation.  In sum, we don't offer advice to customers. We suspect, however, that if the grid cannot start to show consistent improvement, given both the declining cost of storage and the difficulty of getting a grid connection, more customers who can will go off the grid, which could reduce the financial support needed to improve its operations. As we have argued before, if big customers reduce use of the grid or desert it altogether, the grid could become a provider of last resort for those who cannot afford to leave it, which will bring up the question of how to support the grid as a public good. Better to improve service and keep customers happy than open that can of worms.  By Leonard Hyman and William Tilles for Oilprice.com

title: ‘Trump Is Cooked’: How Trump’s Russia Policy Is Splintering Republicans Ahead of the Midterms
body: With the Nov. 3 midterms fast approaching, US President Donald Trump’s handling of the war in Ukraine – including the recent diesel deal with Moscow, sanctions waivers, and restrictions on military aid—has triggered a fierce rift within the Republican Party. While over 50% of Republican base voters back the administration’s moves, polling shows 71% of crucial independent voters strongly oppose them. Meanwhile, Capitol Hill is facing open pushback from Republican senators and representatives, and Democrats are already preparing aggressive congressional investigations if they flip control of Congress. In this detailed analysis, we break down the shifting MAGA momentum, the political fallout of the Russia-Ukraine policy pivot, and what it all means for the upcoming midterms.

title: „A new generation of anti-aircraft missiles.” Poland and the UK are stepping up cooperation
body:
Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz and British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting today signed a three-year Defence Cooperation Plan. The document constitutes the practical implementation of the security and defence partnership treaty, the so-called Northolt Treaty, signed on 27 May this year by Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Keir Starmer. A new generation of anti-aircraft missiles was mentioned as one of the areas of cooperation.
“The Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is right now. The signed agreement, which enhances our capabilities and cooperation, is the best proof of this. A moment ago, together with the Secretary, we signed an agreement regarding the defence cooperation plan. The three-year defence cooperation plan is the result of the Polish-British treaty adopted a few months ago (…). It demonstrates our joint commitment: Polish and British soldiers, joint exercises, and skills development,” said Deputy Prime Minister Kosiniak-Kamysz during the conference.
Wicepremier, minister obrony narodowej W. @KosiniakKamysz: Sojusz 🇵🇱-🇬🇧 nigdy nie był tak silny, jak w tym momencie. Podpisana umowa podnosząca nasze zdolności i współpracę jest tego najlepszym dowodem. Przed chwilą wspólnie z panem sekretarzem podpisaliśmy umowę dotyczącą planu współpracy na rzecz obrony. Trzyletni plan współpracy obronnej jest efektem traktatu polsko-brytyjskiego, przyjętego kilka miesięcy temu. Bardzo za to dziękuję. On pokazuje nasze wspólne zaangażowanie: żołnierze polscy, brytyjscy, wspólne ćwiczenia, rozwój umiejętności.
The head of the Ministry of National Defence (MON) emphasised the importance of the United Kingdom as a partner in arms production: “The United Kingdom is a very important partner for us when it comes to arms production. The Miecznik programme, the subsequent stages of which are proceeding according to plan, the construction of integrated air defence – the Narew, Pilica, and Pilica+ programmes, the programme to build an independent 155 mm ammunition production line, and this is only part of our joint initiatives .” He also mentioned drone programmes and the British component in the selection of submarines. He noted that strengthening the defence industry in agreement with the British is a “requirement of the moment,” and Poland will strive to bring the United Kingdom closer to Europe.
“The bonds of friendship and solidarity between the United Kingdom and Poland run deep, but it is not just about our shared history; it is also about our shared assessment of the threats we face today, and our shared determination that in this clash between freedom and tyranny, the United Kingdom and Poland will not be passive observers,” Secretary Streeting said in turn.
The British Ministry of Defence communique listed several key areas. One of them is “cooperation in the production and development of a new generation of air defence missiles.” This may refer to the CAMM-MR/FCM missile, which is expected to have a range of over 100 km. Recently, following a parliamentary interpellation, the Armament Agency issued information regarding the progress of the programme. In addition, drone and anti-drone systems, the Miecznik programme, and the protection of infrastructure in the Baltic Sea were listed as areas of cooperation. The armed forces of both countries will also cooperate within the framework of the Steadfast Defender and Joint Warrior exercises, as well as the Polish Dragon exercises, including in the fields of air defence and electronic warfare.
The second important topic of discussion was support for Ukraine. Kosiniak-Kamysz emphasised that Poland and the United Kingdom “are doing everything to support Ukraine in its fight against Russian tyranny.” Exercises of the so-called “coalition of the willing,” involving the UK armed forces, will take place in Poland next month.
The Northolt Treaty identifies the Russian Federation as the primary long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and provides for, among other things, cooperation in the defence industry, cybersecurity, interoperability of the armed forces, joint exercises, and capability development (including in the areas of air defence and ammunition).

title: Melania Trump says ceasefire zone in Alyoshki extended beyond town
body:
WASHINGTON, October 27. /TASS/. US First Lady Melania Trump said the ceasefire zone in Alyoshki, in the Kherson Region, had been extended beyond the town.
"The ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect at 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 27, 2026. Timing was accelerated two days ahead of schedule to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid. The ceasefire's geographic area has expanded beyond Alyoshki, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys," she wrote on X.
On October 23, the White House announced that Russia and Ukraine had reached an agreement, with Melania Trump’s assistance, to establish a ceasefire in Alyoshki, in the Kherson Region, starting October 29.

title: Ukrainian Parliament preliminarily approves bill raising bank profit tax to 50% for 2027
body:
The Verkhovna Rada, as expected, passed at first reading a bill on the specifics of bank profit taxation (No. 15262), which provides for another increase in the tax rate for banks in 2027, from 25% to 50%.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, 265 members of parliament voted in favor of the bill, exceeding the required minimum of 226 votes.
"We are making this decision for the fourth time, and the previous three times were quite successful, as we managed to attract additional funds to the budget from the banking system, which generates excess profits even during wartime," said Danylo Hetmantsev, a co-author of the bill, commenting on the vote.
According to him, banks' pretax profit totaled approximately UAH 143.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026, about 5.3% higher than on the corresponding date last year and 2.9 times greater than in the first eight months of 2025.
At the same time, according to the National Bank, net profit for the period fell by 32.7% to UAH 71.66 billion, as the corporate income tax rate was 25% last year.
Hetmantsev noted that the additional revenue from extending the 50% bank profit tax rate has already been incorporated into the revenue side of the 2027 state budget draft and amounts to UAH 38.5 billion.
As reported, the Verkhovna Rada first set the bank profit tax rate at 50% for 2023, doing so retroactively. The relevant law did not take effect until December 8. The same law raised the standard tax rate for banks from 18% to 25%.
A year later, parliament again retroactively raised the rate for banks to 50% for 2024 and increased the standard corporate income tax rate for nonbank financial institutions from 18% to 25%, effective in 2025.
The third time the Rada set a 50% tax rate on bank profits was for 2026, passing the relevant law on the morning of the day in question, before the start of the year, in the autumn of 2025.

title: Spain gives NACOC €300,000 to complete first forensic laboratory
body: The Government of Spain has provided €300,000 in financial support to the Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) to facilitate the completion of its first forensic laboratory. The funding is intended to strengthen the Commission’s investigative and prosecutorial capabilities, particularly in the fight against illicit drug trafficking and transnational organised crime. The Spanish Ambassador to Ghana, Ángel Lossada, announced the support during a brief ceremony to present the package to NACOC management, reaffirming Spain’s commitment to strengthening security cooperation between the two countries. He said Spain was prepared to deepen its collaboration with Ghana through capacity building, specialised training and technical assistance to support efforts against drug trafficking and organised crime. The Ambassador disclosed that the Spanish Government was stepping up cooperation with Ghana, either through the European Union Security and Defence Partnership or through the negotiation of bilateral agreements with the Ministry of the Interior. He also pledged support for the training of forensic officers to ensure the effective operation of the laboratory once it is completed. Receiving the support, NACOC Director-General, Major General Maxwell Obuba Mantey, expressed appreciation to the Spanish Government for its continued partnership and commitment to strengthening Ghana’s fight against drug trafficking. He described the funding as timely, noting that the establishment of a modern forensic laboratory had been one of his key priorities since assuming office. According to him, the absence of a dedicated forensic laboratory has posed a major operational challenge for the Commission, particularly in investigating and prosecuting drug-related offences. He explained that NACOC currently depends on other state institutions to conduct forensic examinations, a situation that often delays the receipt of laboratory results and the prosecution of cases. Major General Mantey said completing the laboratory would enable the Commission to conduct forensic examinations more promptly, strengthen investigations and improve the prosecution of drug-related offences.

title: In Pakistan’s Punjab, toxic air threatens wildlife amid a monitoring blind spot
body: Each November, a suffocating blanket of particulate matter envelops Pakistan’s Punjab province, turning the sky into a hazardous grey canopy. While the public health catastrophe for more than 20 million residents rightfully dominates headlines, a silent crisis unfolds across the region’s agricultural fields, urban green spaces and remaining wetlands. We know exactly what this toxic air does to human lungs, and we even track its precise impact on agricultural assets. A 2023 baseline study closely monitored 10 livestock farms, each housing 90-275 animals across the Lahore and Kasur districts, tracking the exact micrograms of fine particulate matter, carbon dioxide and potentially toxic trace elements inside cattle sheds. Researchers even screened the air for opportunistic bacterial pathogens like Staphylococcus aureus to safeguard the health of livestock. Yet, if a wild bird or mammal landed directly outside those monitored facilities, science would suddenly turn a blind eye. In a region choked by seasonal pollution, wildlife is suffering in a massive monitoring void. Sidra Safdar, associate professor of Wildlife and Ecology at the University of Veterinary and Animal Sciences (UVAS) in Pakistan and a co-author of the 2023 livestock study, explicitly identifies the root of this discrepancy: lack of funding and political will. “One reason for a massive data gap in wildlife monitoring associated with poor air quality is the lack of suitable resources and specialized equipment,” Safdar notes, emphasizing that real-time air quality tracking demands costly annual calibration. Pakistani farmers working in their field blanketed by smog in Peshawar, November 2019. Image…This article was originally published on Mongabay

title: Trading activities halted, pupils drop out as galamsey destroys road access in Abesua community
body: Residents of the Abesua Electoral Area in the Atwima Mponua District of the Ashanti Region are bearing the brunt of illegal mining activities, which have left them isolated and at risk. The operations have caused the collapse of the bridge over River Kukubu, the only access road connecting Abesua No. 1, Abesua No. 2, Nyamebekyere, Abrokyire and adjoining communities to the main road at Seribuso and Mankranso. A visit to the site on Sunday, October 25, revealed that the bridge had completely caved in after illegal miners excavated and degraded lands along the riverbanks. The river has since overflowed onto the road, making it extremely difficult for vehicles and motorcycles to ply the route. Sources in the affected communities disclosed that later that evening, the miners returned with heavy machinery and attempted to redirect the water by pushing sand into the river channel without reconstructing the bridge, an action that has further deteriorated the road. The situation is taking a severe toll on education. Pupils from the cut-off communities who commute daily to Atwima Asamang Basic School often abandon school, particularly when it rains, because they cannot cross the river. “I started KG at Atwima Asamang, and this is the road I have been using all this while. It wasn’t in this bad state until these galamsey activities started,” said Faustina Akosua, a pupil of the school. Another pupil, Celia Amoa, recounted the danger younger children face. “Some of the young schoolchildren among us sometimes fall into the river, and we have to manage to save their lives and take them home,” she said. Parents are worried about their children’s safety. To ensure they get to school safely, many have to put their livelihoods on hold to escort them across the treacherous bridge to and from school, adding to their daily struggles. Some teachers who use the road to commute to school also recounted the stress they go through before crossing the river. Kwabena Adomako, Headteacher of Abesua Basic School, revealed that the deplorable state of the road often renders it impassable, forcing him and his colleagues to abandon their journey and return home without going to school, ultimately disrupting the children’s learning process. Trading activities in the enclave are also grinding to a halt. Traders say they are unable to travel to market centres to restock, while those who manage to make the journey are forced to pay exorbitant fares. A Trader, Mary Afrah, lamented that traders who supply foodstuffs and other essential items to surrounding villages have been unable to reach the market for the past month due to the poor road conditions, leaving many residents to go to bed hungry. “No car wants to come here because of the bad road. The okada riders charge GH¢30 each from Seribuso to Abesua, and sometimes they drop you at the bridge and refuse to cross even if you offer them GH¢50,” she said. The Unit Committee Chairman for Nyamebekyere and Abrokyire, Eric Adomako, said they have on several occasions appealed to the leaders of the illegal mining groups to at least rehabilitate the road if they are unwilling to halt their operations, but they have refused. He said they are often threatened by bodyguards of the illegal miners during such engagements. “Our road was already in poor condition, but it was not this deplorable before the illegal mining started. We have made several attempts to dialogue with the galamsey operators, but when we visit their sites, their bodyguards and security personnel threaten us with weapons,” he recounted. He added that the District Chief Executive for Atwima Mponua and all relevant security agencies in the district are aware of the situation, but have failed to take action. Residents are therefore appealing to the Atwima Mponua District Assembly, the Ashanti Regional Minister and the relevant security agencies to, as a matter of urgency, intervene to stop the galamsey activities, reconstruct the Kukubu bridge and restore the road to save lives and livelihoods.

title: Ghana’s Interior Ministry tops government performance index as Trade Ministry ranks last
body: A new assessment of 23 government ministries in Ghana has ranked the Ministry of the Interior first for institutional performance, while the Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry placed last, highlighting concerns over public service delivery, workforce efficiency and financial management. The Index of Government Institutions’ Performance Towards Economic Prosperity (IGIPTEP), developed by the Africa Centre for Entrepreneurship and Youth Empowerment (ACEYE) in partnership with Atlas Network, assesses how effectively government institutions operate and contribute to economic prosperity. The assessment found that 21 of the 23 ministries scored above 50%, while two fell below that threshold. The Ministry of the Interior recorded the highest score of 80.26%, placing it in the index’s very high performance category. The Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry ranked 23rd with 48.08%, narrowly below the Ministry of Transport, which scored 49.6%. Service delivery and accountability under scrutiny The index examines five areas of institutional performance: service delivery quality, money management, transparency and accountability, people and work efficiency, and public engagement and inclusion. It draws on secondary research, including institutional websites, annual reports, archived publications and online media coverage. The researchers organised and coded the information, compared findings across sources and quantified the results to assess institutional performance. Inspired by the Fraser Institute’s Economic Freedom of the World index in Canada, IGIPTEP seeks to apply international assessment principles to Ghana’s governance environment. The findings offer a comparative picture of how ministries perform across key governance indicators, although the assessment relies on available documentary evidence rather than a direct measurement of every aspect of service delivery. Interior Ministry leads the rankings The Ministry of the Interior emerged as the strongest performer, scoring 80.26%. It was followed by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, with 72.8%, and the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, which scored 66.02%. The Ministry of Education placed fourth with 65.42%, while the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources came fifth with 64.82%. The Ministry of Health ranked sixth, scoring 64.15%. The Ministry of Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, the Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts, the Ministry of Roads and Highways, and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs also featured among the top 10. The results suggest considerable variation in the performance of institutions responsible for delivering public services and implementing government policies. Transport Ministry faces workforce efficiency concerns The Ministry of Transport ranked 22nd, scoring 49.6%. Its assessment identified several areas of progress, including port dredging, efforts to clear container backlogs, the addition of buses, developments in rail infrastructure and the expansion of licensing services. The ministry was also credited with an air passenger grievance portal and the publication of a Right to Information manual. However, the report raised concerns about transparency and workforce efficiency. The ministry scored 40% for transparency and accountability and just 24% for people and work efficiency. Its strongest indicator scores were in money management, at 66.67%, and service delivery quality, at 64%. The assessment pointed to documentation issues highlighted by the Auditor-General and the Public Accounts Committee, alongside gaps in published audit and budget execution reports. It also identified limited publicly available information on staff training and continuing concerns about transport fares and congestion in Accra. The findings indicate that improvements in infrastructure and services do not necessarily translate into strong overall institutional performance when workforce capacity and public accountability remain weak. Trade Ministry at the bottom The Ministry of Trade, Agribusiness and Industry ranked last, with a score of 48.08%. Its strongest area was transparency and accountability, where it scored 70%. It recorded 53.33% for public engagement and inclusion, but performed poorly in service delivery quality and money management, scoring 46.4% and 46.67%, respectively. Like the Transport Ministry, it scored 24% for people and work efficiency. The assessment recognised the ministry’s acknowledgement of trade-related delays, the development of reform plans and an extension of the export revenue repatriation period from 60 to 120 days. It also cited the ministry’s participation in the Government Accountability Series and engagement with exporters. However, persistent port clearance delays were identified as a source of additional costs for traders. The report also raised concerns about loan monitoring under the Rural Enterprises Programme, broken links to documents on the ministry’s website, the absence of formal complaint channels and gaps in publicly available workforce and training information. The findings point to a gap between policy initiatives and the efficiency with which services are delivered to businesses and the wider trading community. Finance Ministry records a mid-table result The Ministry of Finance scored 58.16%, placing 15th among the 23 institutions assessed. It fell within the index’s acceptable performance category, alongside several ministries responsible for employment, agriculture, energy, defence and other key sectors. The Ministry of Environment, Science and Technology ranked 12th with 59.99%, while the Office of the Attorney-General and Ministry of Justice placed 13th with 59.67%. At the lower end of the acceptable category, the Ministry of Energy and Green Transition scored 51.06%, placing 21st. The spread of scores shows that most ministries crossed the 50% threshold, but relatively few approached the performance level achieved by the Ministry of the Interior. What happens next? ACEYE and Atlas Network say the next phase will involve stakeholder dialogues and the co-development of policy recommendations. Such discussions could provide an opportunity for ministries, civil society groups, businesses and other stakeholders to examine the findings and identify practical reforms. The index places particular emphasis on public access to information, responsible management of public funds, staff productivity and the role citizens play in shaping government decisions. For Ghana, the central challenge is whether comparative assessments such as IGIPTEP can help translate concerns about institutional performance into measurable improvements in public services and the business environment. While the rankings provide a snapshot of the 23 ministries examined, their longer-term value will depend on how the findings are scrutinised, how institutions respond and whether subsequent assessments show tangible progress.

title: GLP-1 drug coverage is being dropped by employer plans: What to know about 2027 weight-loss options
body:
To learn more about the CNBC CFO Council, visit cnbccouncils.com/cfo
With open enrollment season in swing, many employees may notice something conspicuously missing from their benefits menu — coverage of GLP-1 drugs for weight loss.
More companies are dropping coverage completely or offering employees less generous payouts. In some cases, they're shifting to a different model altogether — offering employees a consolation prize of sorts — access to a weight management program through a third party.
Coverage of these drugs for weight loss is pricey for employers — typically costing in the mid-$500s to mid-$600s per user monthly. Some companies say whatever the price, covering the drugs is worth it based on employee health. "We spend about $250 million or more on GLPs, and that's up from zero" four or five years ago, Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan told CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin in August. "We see a great impact on the employees. ... Believe me, we're pounding everybody on price and trying to get as cheap [as possible]. But our view is that [because of] the long-term health benefits, plus there may be more short-term health benefits ... it's a good investment."
Nevertheless, as healthcare costs continue to climb, more employers have been looking for an exit ramp on GLP-1 coverage for weight loss, and that includes bigger companies. A WTW annual health benefits survey fielded over the summer and being released in full on Wednesday found that 53% of employers with more than 100 employees cover GLP-1s for weight loss, down from 57% in 2025. That's the first decline in three years. What's more, 16% of employers said they cover the drugs now but are considering removing them, up from 9% last year.
According to a recent Marsh survey of over 1,800 US employers, health insurance cost per employee is expected to rise 8.2% on average in 2027, the biggest increase since 2003, with GLP-1 use accounting for a full percentage point of the overall cost growth. Its experts have cited the soaring costs among reasons employers are considering dropping coverage for 2027.
"Employers are really balancing empathy with economics," said Caroline Susie, principal in Marsh's total health management practice.
Some workers who use employer-sponsored health plans are being provided with options in the event of GLP-1 coverage being dropped, though nothing may match full health insurance coverage. Here are alternatives to expect.
Some employers are directing workers to buy GLP-1s through direct-to-consumer options like Novo Nordisk's NovoCare or Eli Lilly's LillyDirect . WTW's survey showed that 8% of employers have gone this route, and 28% were planning or considering it.
Seth Friedman, pharmacy and health plans practice leader at Gallagher, estimated that 20% to 30% of the firm's clients have dropped coverage for 2027 and are sending employees the direct route. For employers, this move can mean significant savings. The percentage of U.S. adults who take GLP-1 medications for weight loss purposes climbed to 11% in 2026, up significantly from 3% in 2024, according to Gallup . What's more, 15% report having used the medicine for weight loss at some point, a nine-percentage-point boost.
"Many people will choose to pay for this on their own even if it's not covered by the plan," said Jeff Levin-Scherz, population health leader at WTW.
The starting price for the lowest dose of Novo's Wegovy for self-pay individuals is currently $149 a month for the pill and $199 a month for the shot. Those prices are subject to change in 2027; Novo Nordisk says current promotional pricing may be modified or canceled. Lilly's Zepbound starts at $299 a month for a single-dose vial or multi-dose KwikPen.
Some companies are moving to a direct-to-employer model , where they drop coverage through their traditional pharmacy program, but offer to reimburse some portion of an employee's out-of-pocket costs.
"These 'alternative coverage' models enable employers to access more advantageous pricing and greater control over their contributions, without covering the drug on their PBM formulary," said a spokesperson for Vida Health, one of multiple vendors that works with employers in this area. Others include Noom and GoodRx.
Employers can often design the program that works for their employees' needs, at a significant savings from paying for GLP-1 drugs through a pharmacy benefit manager, said Alysha Fluno, national pharmacy practice leader at Marsh. A PBM is a third-party administrator that manages prescription drug benefits for health insurers and employers.
Based on direct-to-consumer prices, employers could fully subsidize, pay a vendor fee, and still spend much less than they would to purchase Wegovy, for example, through a PBM, according to WTW's Levin-Scherz.
Some employers are dropping coverage and contracting with third parties like CVS Weight Management, Noom, Omada Health, UnitedHealthcare, Vida and Virta, to offer weight-management programs to employees. Some employers offered these types of programs before, while others made them available only after dropping GLP-1 coverage for weight loss.
According to 2025 data from Marsh , 25% of employers of 500 or more employees had a vendor partner for lifestyle modification and nutrition support. Employers, not employees, typically foot the bill for these programs, at a significant savings compared with GLP-1 coverage. Services can vary by member, but offerings generally include live or online coaching on behavior change, diet, exercise, nutrition and other health topics. Costs for these programs can run about $65 to $100 per employee per month, depending on what's offered, according to Marsh's Susie. Employers who choose a vendor that offers prescription services as well could pay $150 or more per month per participating employee.
Service providers cite good results from their programs in recent years. Data from Omada Health show that 63% of members evaluated at 12 months after stopping a GLP-1 maintained or continued to lose weight. UnitedHealthcare's Real Appeal program data show that 88% of at-risk participants lost weight during the 52-week program designed to promote healthy eating, physical activity, improved well-being and a better health outlook. What's more, 37% of participants lost 5% or more in body weight. Meanwhile, initial program results reported by CVS Weight Management showed 90% weight loss maintenance for members up to 10–12 months after ending drug therapy.
Provider offerings vary somewhat, but professional support is often a hallmark. "We want to make sure that if they go off GLP-1s for whatever reason, they maintain the behavior changes," said Cody Fair, chief commercial officer of Noom. "We're able to keep that weight off because they've retrained their brain and changed their habits," he said.
Employee utilization, however, can be a challenge, said Gallagher's Friedman. "It's absolutely a commitment, and that's probably why you don't see a whole lot do it. Especially when they know they can just have their doctor write a script and go directly to Novo or Lilly."
While these tax-advantaged accounts are not alone a replacement for a comprehensive health plan, GLP-1 medications are eligible for flexible spending account (FSA) and health savings account (HSA) reimbursement when prescribed by a licensed provider to treat a diagnosed medical condition, such as obesity. The disadvantage of using an HSA to pay for GLP-1s is that the dollars invested don't have a chance to grow tax-free for use later on in retirement.
The annual employee contribution limit for an FSA is $3,400 in 2026. For 2026, the maximum annual HSA contribution limits set by the IRS are $4,400 for individuals with self-only coverage and $8,750 for those with family coverage. That will rise in 2027 to $4,500 for individuals and $9,000 for families. Official 2027 IRS contribution limits for FSAs have not yet been announced.
"Benefits are there to cover those out-of-pocket costs," said Andrew Stocker, president of employee benefits at Voya Financial. "Employers need to educate employees about the benefits that do exist."

title: Hanwha Defense USA to take controlling stake in Philly Shipyard for planned U.S. Navy work
body: Hanwha Systems has owned 60% of the yard since Hanwha acquired it in December 2024, with Hanwha Ocean holding the remaining 40%. In September, Hanwha Systems announced plans to sell its stake to Hanwha Defense USA Shipbuilding LLC, an HDUSA-led joint venture with Hanwha FutureProof. “As Hanwha Defense USA continues to grow its multi-domain presence across the U.S., bringing the Philly Shipyard under HDUSA will further align our government and commercial shipbuilding efforts,” said Michael Coulter, HDUSA’s president and chief executive officer. “We look forward to continuing to invest in our Philly Shipyard facilities and workforce in preparation for exciting work ahead.” HDUSA established a presence at the shipyard earlier this year to support its transition to a dual-use facility. Preparations cover yard operations, workforce and customer relationships for work involving the Navy, other federal agencies and commercial customers. “Over the past two years Hanwha has made significant investments in the Philly Shipyard to contribute to the revitalization of the U.S. shipbuilding industry,” said Tom Anderson, HDUSA’s president of U.S. shipbuilding. “Now we are positioning the shipyard to transition to dual-use, aligning shipyard operations, workforce, and customer relations in preparation to build for the U.S. Navy, other federal agencies, and commercial customers.” Anderson, a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral, will oversee all HDUSA shipbuilding operations in the United States. The company did not disclose financial terms or a closing date.

title: Oleshky humanitarian operation results could pave way for further steps in peace process – Sybiha
body:
If the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, Kherson region, is successful, it could pave the way for further steps in the peace process, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said.
"We welcome the humanitarian operation in Oleshky. This is about saving lives. For many months, we have been telling the world about the people starving in Oleshky," Sybiha said at a joint press conference of the foreign ministers of Ukraine, Finland, and Norway in Helsinki.
He recalled that Ukraine had appealed to countries, international organizations, world leaders, and key religious figures regarding the situation in Oleshky.
"We are grateful to First Lady Melania Trump for her involvement in this critically important work – and for her leadership. We hope that all commitments will be fulfilled. On the Ukrainian side, we are fully prepared. Our Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, is coordinating this operation. If we see results in Oleshky, this could pave the way for further steps in the peace process – as a confidence-building measure," Sybiha said.
Earlier, the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, Dmytro Lubinets, reported that as of 17:30 on October 27, Ukraine and Russia were adhering to the agreements on a ceasefire in designated territories related to the humanitarian mission. It began today at 03:00 Kyiv time and 04:00 Moscow time.
As reported, on October 23, 2026, U.S. First Lady Melania Trump announced that an agreement had been reached between Ukraine and Russia on a ceasefire in Oleshky area to allow for a humanitarian operation. According to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, the agreement provides for the delivery of humanitarian aid, technical demining, and ensuring the free movement of civilians.
Lubinets said that a ceasefire in the Kherson region was declared at 15:00 on October 27.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine also reported that a ceasefire was implemented in Oleshky on October 27 to facilitate a humanitarian operation.

title: Three arrested in Atewa Forest as NAIMOS launches Operation Green Shield
body: Three people have been arrested in the Atewa Forest Reserve in the Eastern Region as the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS) launches a military-backed operation to flush out illegal miners and protect the threatened forest. The arrests were made on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, as part of Operation Green Shield, an initiative designed to disrupt illegal mining, clear affected areas and maintain a security presence to prevent miners from returning. The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, described the destruction of Ghana’s forest reserves through illegal mining as a national emergency, warning that the activities were threatening the country’s environment, water resources and future generations. “We are at war with bad people who have decided that they will make money so that all of us will die,” he said during the operation. The minister disclosed that 44 of Ghana’s 288 forest reserves had been affected by illegal mining, resulting in the destruction of approximately 8,900 hectares of forest land. He said the affected area was equivalent to about 12,500 football fields, adding that restoring the degraded reserves would require billions of dollars. Despite measures to restrict the movement of excavators into forest reserves, Mr Buah said illegal miners continued to devise new methods to evade enforcement and destroy forest land, including a practice locally known as “one leg” mining. He also disclosed that authorities had seized and spread over 6,000 excavators as part of efforts to prevent their use in illegal mining. As part of the latest intervention, Mr Buah said the government, with support from the Ghana Armed Forces, would establish a camp within the Atewa Forest to sustain the operation and prevent renewed encroachment. He commended the security personnel involved and urged them to remain committed to protecting the country’s natural resources. Director of Operations at NAIMOS, Colonel K. S. Appiah, said Operation Green Shield would follow a four-stage strategy involving the disruption of illegal mining activities, the clearance of affected areas, the maintenance of a security presence and the eventual transfer of responsibility to the Forestry Commission. “The mission is to disrupt, clear and hold and transition,” he explained. He said the operation would continue as security teams identified and tackled illegal mining activities in other areas. Under the transition phase, the Forestry Commission is expected to deploy forest guards to Atewa to sustain protection after the initial enforcement operations. Mr Buah also warned traditional authorities and metropolitan, municipal and district chief executives against turning a blind eye to illegal mining in their jurisdictions. He said local authorities had a responsibility to help protect the environment and indicated that the government intended to strengthen accountability through proposed legislative changes affecting the roles of traditional authorities and local officials in mining-related processes. The minister further urged the public to avoid politicising illegal mining, warning that its consequences extended beyond environmental destruction to public health and the long-term security of future generations. Atewa Forest is an important ecological asset and watershed supporting the Birim, Ayensu and Densu river systems. Its protection is considered critical to conserving biodiversity and safeguarding water resources for communities that depend on the rivers.

title: Yakovenko assumes duties as Energoatom board member and CFO
body:
Anton Yakovenko has assumed the duties of a member of the management board and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) at National Nuclear Energy Generating Company Energoatom, the company said on its website.
"As a member of the management board and Chief Financial Officer, he will focus on ensuring Energoatom's financial stability, capital management, improving transparency, enhancing the company's investment readiness and developing cooperation with international financial institutions," Energoatom said in a statement.
According to the statement, Yakovenko has more than 20 years of management experience at major Ukrainian and international companies, including in the positions of CEO and CFO. He served as CEO of Agricom Group. Previously, he headed Agrii Ukraine, a company belonging to Origin Enterprises plc, and Terra Food Group, and worked as CFO of Roshen Group. He began his professional career at KPMG.
As reported, on September 21, Energoatom's Supervisory Board selected Yuriy Tkachuk, CEO of another major state-owned enterprise, JSC Ukrgasvydobuvannia, as the winner of the competition for the position of Energoatom's Chief Executive Officer (CEO).
Pavlo Pavlyshyn was selected as the winner of the competition for the position of board member responsible for nuclear safety and operations (Chief Nuclear Officer, CNO). He headed Rivne Nuclear Power Plant from June 2012 to June 2022, with a break from December 2019 to March 2020, when he served as acting president of Energoatom. In June 2022, he was transferred to the position of director of Atomremontservis for the duration of martial law. On October 25, 2022, he began working as first deputy mayor of Varash, the satellite city of Rivne Nuclear Power Plant.
Energoatom's Supervisory Board also selected Yakovenko as the winner of the competitive selection for the position of board member responsible for financial matters (Chief Financial Officer, CFO), and Alena Perepelytsia for the position of board member responsible for legal affairs (Chief Legal Officer, CLO). Perepelytsia served as director of legal and regulatory affairs at JSC Ukrgasvydobuvannia. Before that, she spent more than two decades in senior positions in the legal department of Ukrnafta JSC.
Energoatom is continuing competitive selections for the positions of board member responsible for human resources management (Chief People Officer, CPO) and board member responsible for commercial affairs (Chief Commercial Officer, CCO). The company is also preparing to announce a competition for the position of Inspector General, a board member responsible for independent internal oversight in the areas of nuclear and radiation safety.

title: Stop Vibing, Start Resonating: Pair Programming with LLM Agents
body:
I'm going to coin a new term for AI/LLM assisted agentic pair-programming practices. Not Vibe Coding, but Resonance Coding. I'll explain.
Vibe and resonance are both vibrations. A vibe is unstructured, an uncontrolled sound that maybe happens to feel good. It's the song you hear come on while you're driving in the morning, unplanned and unexpected, the magic music that makes your morning mood.
Resonance on the other hand is two systems tuned to the same frequency, each amplifying the other. A small, synchronized input produces a large, coherent output. That only happens when the systems are matched.
In Resonance Coding, the human expert supplies the tuning: the frequency, the amplitude, the chords and the plan. The LLM supplies the amplification. In this case, the LLM is operating as a force multiplier, or in physics terms, a bigger lever to move a heavier load.
You could probably find dozens (hundreds?) of examples online of people showing how Claude or Codex or some other coding agent built them Minecraft in a week, a day, or even an hour. And they have cubes, movement, some textured blocks, maybe a sword and a guy named Stelex (Steve + Alex) and a big bad dragon. But is it Minecraft? No, it's Temu Minecraft.
In one hour, and no longer, I want to build as best of a Minecraft clone as possible using either Python or MSVC++ as found on this computer, avoiding installing extensive other SDKs but utilizing 3rdparty libraries as needed to accelerate development. No other guidance is provided, the judgement criteria is simply how good of a Minecraft clone is produced, as judged by Minecraft players who will test it. You must complete this within one hour, it cannot be incomplete or broken, and you can use all of my token budget which resets at 4pm today. I don't want any interaction, this is a one-shot autonomous build, so make all decisions yourself. Proceed with execution.
Here's the output: Stelexcraft on GitHub .
One 55-minute coding session (self-interrupted twice because I had to convince it to KEEP GOING). Claude chose Python for rapid prototyping reasons, which was sensible given the situation.
There's a breakdown of the creation process and a features list . The highlights:
And here's its own comparison against real Minecraft .
It's impressive until you dig further. But who understands this code? What architecture does it use? Could you add a feature it didn't plan for without breaking three others? What about multiplayer? What about redstone and the Nether?
It's a really flashy demo and demonstrably a great achievement, though cloning Minecraft is kind of a "solved problem" so there's a lot of material in the agent's training that it is leveraging here. Solving a novel problem might not go as well, but Minecraft is the poster child of a good vibe-coding opportunity.
Andrej Karpathy coined the term in February 2025 : "There's a new kind of coding I call 'vibe coding', where you fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists."
Vibe coding doesn't have to be a one-shot, but the recipe is generally "prompt, accept, run, paste the error back, lather, rinse, repeat." Or with a good agent harness, prompt, go chill and do something else and come back later to a finished product.
It works fine for throwaway prototypes and proofs of concept, simple tools (I'm totally guilty of this), and time-crunch-limited situations like hackathons (that allow it). It's great for figuring out if an idea works at all, and feels right and such. It's a sketch on a napkin, but it isn't as well refined as a CAD model or blueprint. I'm from the days of pencil and straightedge drafting, and I won some ribbon at a state competition at CSU in Ft. Collins, which I guess presaged me getting into CAD and 3D as a career.
Have I vibe coded? Sure, a ton. I have several personal tools that are exactly what I want that I don't think I need anything further from beyond what was vibe coded.
Another place where vibe-coding works is when you AREN'T the expert, but you need to get the job done. Software person trying to wire up a Raspberry Pi to control landscaping pumps, valves, sensors and such? Throw the responsibility to the agent who is arguably MORE of a domain expert, and roll with the vibes. Hardware person trying to write a Python script to index data? Vibe on, my friend.
Real tools and products are the end-product of a million important decisions, most of which you've never imagined. Texture formats. Graphics primitives. Voxel query optimization. Voxel tree and LOD architecture. Shader optimization. (OK to be fair, Notch probably didn't think through most of these at the start, if you've ever read his early posts.)
When you leave these unspecified, the LLM wings it with best guesses based on what it believes it knows. It doesn't know anything about the goals, plans for users, hardware, or the experience you have in your brain. It flies blind based on the most-likely vector extracted out of its training dataset and what it might learn by researching in the spur of the moment (if it decides to research). The acceptance test is just "does it work" and there's not a lot of planning for reliability or making a reliable useable product.
It usually does pretty well on the first 80%-90%. Which as every developer or literally anyone who ever did anything, knows is the easy part. When you get into the last 10%-20% is where the poor decision making or lack of planning catches up with you and suddenly things that should be easy to fix cause cascades of other knock-on errors, and fragility rears its ugly head.
At the end you get something that nobody understands or can own or justify to anyone.
But often, that's good enough! I've vibe-coded perfectly good one-off tools that did EXACTLY what they needed for the situation I needed them for.
I love the sound of an orchestra tuning before a concert. There's something acoustically magical about hearing them all converge on an A (440Hz) played by a violin and/or oboe. They're about to work together to produce something magical, and this is how they proactively eliminate dissonance and destructive interference so they're all on the same wavelength, literally.
I feel like the optimal use of LLM coding practices begins the same way, and so I've coined the term "Resonance Coding" to represent it. There, I'm now a "thought leader" or something. Please come to my TED Talk.
With Resonance Coding, you take explicit efforts to make sure like an orchestra, everyone is on the same page and wavelength so you can create a beautiful symphony, not a cacophonous mess.
To me, Resonance Coding is pair programming where you work together with an LLM to establish all of the guiding framework, the melody, the harmony, the tuning, the movements and everything else necessary to smash the music out perfectly. One party becomes the domain expert, outlining all the critical guiding principles, making the decisions based on real-world development experience, and relying on the AI agent to amplify their tones into a larger and more melodious result.
The qualified human is the architect, and the final arbiter of decisions. The LLM organizes, orchestrates, error-checks, arranges, and gathers requirements and domain knowledge TO SERVE THE HUMAN (not in the Treehouse of Horror sense). It iterates until the form and function of the intended solution is agreed upon, then the two cooperatively implement, test, and refine a quality product. At all times the human is in charge, guiding and overseeing the AI's work, like leading a bright junior intern developer with limitless caffeine and an eidetic memory of everything on the internet.
The word of the day is "Qualified". The results are best when the human could actually do the whole project themselves. It might take a human weeks or months to do what could be accomplished by an AI agent in a day or days. But the human's finished product will generally be better thought out with a better understanding of the broader context, and more maintainable by humans. When working together , the end product can be of human quality (or better!) in day/days timeframe, by resonating their complementary skills together to amplify their productivity.
The LLM isn't the author of the result, it's a designated force-multiplier (or multipliers, if you're using wide-scale sub-agents) with savantic knowledge and recall, infinite patience and energy, and hopefully no programmer-grade ego and attitude (looking at you Grok). It doesn't get bored or testy troubleshooting stupid build-system errors (though I've seen internal LLM dialogs say expletives, and Google's Gemini once spiraled into calling itself "a disgrace" 86 times in a row while stuck on a bug, so maybe they do get frustrated). It just stiffens its upper lip, keeps calm and carries on in the face of link errors, runtime library resolution problems, undocumented quirks in libraries, and the sorts of things that drive humans to drink and worse. As Linus Torvalds recently put it , "I use AI to do the things that I'm bad at." I'd add the things I don't enjoy. Do we like writing hash maps? I don't, so I'll delegate that. Do I like architecting the overall design to exploit beautiful high-level synergies of particular data structures and algorithms? I love that, give me more of that all day long, please.
The human domain expert knows what "correct" means, sets goals, priorities, taste, makes architectural decisions, realizes "technically right, actually wrong" issues, knows the greater context of the users, client and history, and in the end is ultimately responsible for the result.
The LLM partner organizes, structures, remembers and recalls, discovers and proposes options and trade-offs a human might not think of, plans and orchestrates, especially sub-agents and parallel tasking, and tirelessly writes tests, checks things, makes scaffolding, refactors and plays devil's advocate when appropriate.
I've had LLM agents make brilliant suggestions of alternate ideas, like using a library or algorithm I was unaware of. I've also had them make terrible suggestions because they had no idea of the greater context of what I was trying to do, or requirements I had in my head but hadn't recorded digitally.
(Yes, that sounds like a fatal roller coaster .)
Resonance is an ongoing cycle, not a waterfall (waterfalls also make a beautiful sound, but that's another story).
The LLM interviews the expert instead of the other way around: "What platform? Single-player or multiplayer? Which part of Minecraft actually matters to you?" It surfaces hidden assumptions and unknown unknowns. I've experimented with an informal Q&A pre-planning step here, as well as Matt Pocock's Grill Me skill for this. Sometimes it rabbit holes and asks stuff that won't be known at the start, but that can be ok to at least get on the table for later resolution.
Turn the conversation into durable artifacts: requirements, a glossary of domain terms, constraints, non-goals, and project memory files the agent rereads every session. This also helps when resetting the context, or splitting between multiple agents or accounts. This can all be revisioned in the code repository, and reviewed with stakeholders to make sure it addresses the use-cases and needs.
The LLM proposes multiple approaches and options with tradeoffs. The expert picks, adjusts, or vetoes, and the decisions get written down with their reasons as durable institutional knowledge.
Break the work into small, verifiable tasks, plan tests, sequence steps, and farm out independent pieces to subagents. Designate milestones and issues.
Work in small batches through achievable milestones. The human reviews diffs, not dumps, and steers early, while course corrections are still cheap.
Tests are written alongside or ahead of the code. The LLM reviews its own work and the human's. Use adversarial checks: "try to break this."
Profile, refactor, document, and feed what you learned back into the project memory so the next loop starts smarter. Exhaustively review and error-check code and non-code assets.
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse is the textbook example of destructive resonance. (Technically, engineers will tell you it was aeroelastic flutter, not forced resonance : the bridge's own twisting fed energy back into itself from the wind, a self-exciting feedback loop. That's an even better metaphor for what comes next.) So, how can Resonance Coding be destructive?
An LLM just amplifies what it is provided. People have already rabbit-holed down crazy psychoses and conspiracies boosted by sycophantic LLMs reflecting their energy back. So, destructive resonance is something to be wary of. In Resonance Coding, you can get out of your wheelhouse easily and over-extend your confidence. If you just rubber-stamp the LLM decisions, you are exiting resonance and entering vibing again. And you could seriously harsh your vibe.
Resonance Coding needs a damping mechanism for harmful wavelets. Tests, disagreements, second opinions, and the real world need to guide the decision making or it just goes free-form and vibe-y.
Resonance Coding is slower to start, there's not that instant magical dopamine rush of "Whoa, Look what I made!". It needs real expertise. Without an expert it's just vibe coding with more paperwork. And the realities of context and memory limits means the project memory artifacts on-disk are critical to keeping the agent(s) on track with the original or current directive and plan. My AI agent reviewing and editing this wants me to mention this is "load-bearing" (groan).
The Cathedral of the Golden Code. Of course it's AI generated, but you knew that. Still, it's on my bucket list to visit. It looks like it's probably in Barcelona, down the street from the Sagrada Família somewhere.
It seems like every programming fad becomes a religion. I won't even name them all, but surely you've gotten swept up or stood on the sidelines of some fad. UML. AOP. TDD (either of them). NFTs. TLAs. Vibe coding still has a place. In fact, the output of a vibe coding session can easily become the input for Resonance Coding. It could be the prototype that gets reviewed for functional, architectural and use-case/need-fit requirements to BUILD the Resonance Coding specifications. Want to get your user stories and use-cases but nobody wants to jump in and document them? Vibe code a prototype and give it to them and let them try it and tell you all the things wrong with it .
And Resonance Coding isn't a new thing. Lots of us have been doing this all along. I'm only writing about it (and naming it) because there IS already a difference. People are already doing the thing I'm calling Resonance Coding, but the world just lumps it all in as "Vibe Coding" but it ain't. Let's start calling it a different thing, because it really does work differently. And there's for sure some kind of spectrum between vibe and resonance. Not all projects deserve the whole gamut of Resonance. Sometimes all you need is just a little resonance on your vibe, like a little chocolate in your peanut butter will hit the spot, am I right?
At the end of the day, if someone will pay for it or depend on it or maintain it, Resonance Coding is the direction to go with agentic development.
So, are all programmers obsolete? Yeah, no. If anything it gives us new superpowers. Resonance Coding focuses the things we're the best at, understanding the big picture and how to make programs that achieve the goals, and defocuses (lovely bokeh!) all the potentially distracting bits, like getting bogged down in writing templates, assembling build tooling, making and executing tests, and grunt work that saps our energy. Domain expertise becomes more valuable, not less because the LLM amplifies whatever signal you feed it. Juniors learn faster inside a Resonance loop than inside a Vibe loop, because they see the reasoning, not just the output. Your clients are still paying for, and getting, your expert's judgment, delivered at agentic speed.
Anyone can get a textured cube field. Building the real thing means getting human and AI onto the same frequency.
Got a vibe-coding horror story or a Resonance win? I'd love to hear it. And if you have a project that needs to be built for real, not just demoed, let's talk .
Tell us what you’re building and where it’s stuck. We’ll tell you straight whether it’s something we can help with, and how we’d approach it.
Or see how we run consulting and software development engagements.

title: HIMERA, GomSpace Group launch sovereign Ukrainian satellite under OBRIA initiative
body:
Ukraine's HIMERA and Denmark's GomSpace have launched OBRIA NANO, the first test satellite of the future independent Ukrainian communications network, into orbit and have already begun operating it.

According to HIMERA, the developer and manufacturer of communication systems, the satellite was launched as part of the SpaceX Transporter-18 mission on October 1, 2026.

"The goal of the initiative is to create Ukraine's own satellite network, diversify the country's communication channels, and reduce strategic dependence on foreign infrastructure. The next important step is to localize the production of satellites and ground terminals in Ukraine. This will allow us to develop our own technologies in the field of satellite communications and gradually build up Ukraine's manufacturing capabilities," the statement reads.

title: CIUS awards over 800 grants, scholarships to scholars, institutions in Ukraine over past 50 years
body:
The Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies (CIUS) at the University of Alberta is celebrating its 50th anniversary and has announced an international symposium to mark the occasion, titled "Recentring the Humanities: Ukraine and the World."
According to CIUS, over the past 50 years, the institute has awarded at least 1,742 academic honors, grants, and scholarships, of which 883 – or about 51% – were awarded to Ukrainian scholars and institutions.
CIUS currently comprises 11 research centers and programs that study the Holodomor, medieval and early modern Ukrainian history, contemporary social processes, the Ukrainian language and methods of teaching it, as well as the history of Ukrainians in Canada and other countries. One area of focus concerns the history of Ukrainian statehood. Among the institute's long-term projects is the English-language Internet Encyclopedia of Ukraine. Crimean Tatar studies constitute a separate area of focus.
The CIUS was founded in 1976 with the support of the provincial government, the University of Alberta, and the active participation of the Ukrainian community in Canada. The institute made its first payment to an institution in Ukraine in 1987-1988, and as early as 1989-1990, KIUS became one of the hubs through which Ukrainian researchers established contacts with the academic community in North America. The collaboration also encompassed legislative reforms and the development of democratic institutions, a significant portion of the funding for which was provided by the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA).
A symposium marking the institute's anniversary will take place October 28-30 in Edmonton, with the option to participate online upon prior registration.
Among the announced participants are Oleksandra Matviychuk, head of the Center for Civil Liberties; Refat Chubarov, Chair of the Mejlis of the Crimean Tatar People; historians Serhiy Plokhy and Yaroslav Hrytsak; philosopher Volodymyr Yermolenko; and Metropolitan Borys Gudziak. Participants will discuss how Ukraine's experience – particularly its resistance to Russian aggression – is shaping international debates on history, human rights, democracy, and cultural identity.

title: Ghana Buttresses Northern Security
body: In mid-October, leaders in Ghana’s northern Bawku community celebrated a milestone: 150 days without gun violence in a region beset by a long-running ethnic conflict. Experts say that Bawku’s five months of calm between the Kusasi and Mamprusi ethnic groups are the result of intensive mediations by the National Peace Council, an increased security presence and the promise of investments by the national government. Kusasi and Mamprusi groups have been at odds for decades over which group holds the chieftaincy of Bawku. In 2021, their conflict erupted into violence that has continued sporadically. Ghanaian authorities deployed Soldiers to the region in July 2025 after gunmen killed three students near a school. Bawku sits in northeastern Ghana near the borders with Burkina Faso and Togo. For centuries, the town’s open-air market has been a crossroads for communities across the Sahel and forests of West Africa. Bawku’s population is mostly Muslim, tying the community’s 80,000 residents more closely to their neighbors in the Sahel and creating a divide with the rest of Ghana, which is more than 70% Christian. Ghana’s leaders see calm in Bawku as an important hedge against the potential spread of Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM) and violent groups from Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. JNIM has a history of exploiting ethnic conflicts and anti-government sentiment to gain a foothold in communities across the Sahel and, more recently, along the border regions that Burkina Faso and Niger share with Ghana and other coastal nations to the south. Those border regions tend to fall short when it comes to government investment, leading to resentment among residents. To counter that, Ghana recently announced plans to invest heavily in public infrastructure through the three-year, $85.7 million ($1 billion cedi) Bawku Revitalization Fund. Between 2026 and 2028, the fund will pay for roads, healthcare, education, dam and irrigation facilities for all-year-round agriculture, security installations and economic and commercial facilities, according to a government statement. “Insecurity over the years has severely constrained public and private investment and stalled critical infrastructure development,” Felix Kwakye Ofosu, Ghana’s minister of government communications, said in a statement announcing the fund. The goal, Ofosu added, is “to restore Bawku to its historic position as a significant economic and trading hub in Northern Ghana.” Ghanaian Ministry of the Interior Mubarak Mohammed Muntaka recently told Ghana’s Joy FM radio that, thanks to improving security conditions in Bawku, the government has loosened a nighttime curfew in the region and lifted a five-year-old ban on traveling by motorcycle. George Amoh, executive secretary of the National Peace Council, believes the current calm could be a sign that the conflict between the two groups is burning out. “At a point in conflict, people or actors in the conflict become fed up,” Amoh told The African Report. However, security analyst Col. Festus Aboagye cautions that the region’s porous borders, illicit weapons markets, cross-border kinship networks and organized crime could give JNIM and other armed groups an opening to stir up trouble should Bawku’s internal conflict remain unresolved. “The calm is real, but it is not yet the same as peace,” Aboagye told The African Report. The post Ghana Buttresses Northern Security appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Honda warns 50% Canada auto tariffs would be catastrophic for industry
body:
DETROIT — The automotive industry faces a "catastrophic" scenario if the U.S. and Canada cannot reach a new trade deal by the end of this year, an executive with Honda Motor warned Tuesday.
President Donald Trump has threatened to double tariffs on Canadian vehicles and parts from 25% to 50% on Jan. 1 if the two countries don't reach a deal.
"That really would be catastrophic for the entire industry," Jennifer Thomas, senior vice president of corporate affairs at American Honda Motor Co., said during a Reuters automotive conference in Detroit.
Thomas said, ideally, the countries would also include Mexico in the arrangement and reach a trilateral deal, like the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA. Trade associations representing Honda, as well as every major player in the U.S. automotive industry, have been advocating for that more comprehensive accord and against bilateral arrangements between two countries.
Her comments come months after U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced that the U.S. would not automatically extend the USMCA, moving the trade pact into an annual review process instead of a 16-year trilateral extension.
Trump negotiated the USMCA to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement during his first term and it took effect in 2020. He later soured on it and accused Canada of "ripping off the United States of America for years."
Thomas said she is "cautiously optimistic" that cooler heads will prevail to avoid the doubling of tariffs, which Trump threatened in August if no deal can be reached.
She said she's encouraged by recent reports that the U.S. and Canada have reestablished trade talks, including easing levies on critical materials such as aluminum.
"Our message has been clear: We need that trilateral agreement to stay in place in order for the U.S. industry to be competitive," Thomas said. "It's integral to our success."
Honda is the s econd-largest producer of vehicles in Canada behind Toyota Motor , but many automotive officials have voiced concerns about the lack of a North American trade deal and tariff uncertainty due to the number of parts that regularly cross the borders for vehicle production.
While Honda has established large operations in Canada, the company reports that more than 60% of the vehicles it sells in the U.S. are manufactured domestically across multiple U.S. assembly plants.
"I never thought I would see the North American region be put at a disadvantage like this," Thomas said, adding that some overseas countries have better tariff rates.
The Trump administration has negotiated trade deals with other countries such as Japan and South Korea, which are major exporters of vehicles to the U.S., that include 15% tariffs on vehicles.

title: Show HN: Control the browser directly from TheGitAI Terminal
body:
Most of what a coding agent does needs no browser at all. This is for the part that does - the cloud console, the dashboard, the admin panel, and everything else that has no API to call and no way in from the outside.
TheGitAI is an agentic AI coding tool for your terminal. With the TheGitAI Chrome extension installed, it can also work in the Chrome you already have open, signed in as you already are. There is no second browser, no separate sign-in, and no API key standing in for you.
Checking how a page you just built renders is the one browser task that needs nothing special: the page is local, it has no session, and Playwright or a headless script does it perfectly well. If that is the whole job, use one of those.
What a headless script cannot do is work in a browser that is already yours. No cookie jar to transplant, no credentials to hand to a tool, no screenshots to paste in so the agent can see what you are looking at. That gap is the reason this extension exists.
Two halves, and both are required. The extension does nothing on its own.
Then run ai in any project directory and ask about a page. The extension connects on its own - there is no pairing step, no port to configure, and nothing to sign into twice.
Its clicks and keystrokes are the same kind the browser gets from you, rather than scripted events - which is why pages that ignore automated input still behave normally.
Exiting the CLI leaves your pages open. Another session cannot take tabs owned by a live one.
The extension makes no network requests of its own. Everything it reads goes to the TheGitAI tool on your own computer, over a local channel between two programs on the same machine.
Nothing it reads is stored by us - not the pages, not the screenshots, not a record of the sites you visit. On your own machine it keeps exactly two things: a random identifier so two Chrome profiles can be told apart, and whether you have switched it off. Uninstalling removes both.
See Trust & Privacy and the full privacy policy .
The popup tells you which half is missing. If it says TheGitAI is not installed on this computer, the terminal app is not there yet or has never been run - install it and run ai once. The CLI registers the local connection on every interactive launch, so it repairs itself.
When a browser request starts without a connection, TheGitAI waits up to 2.5 seconds for discovery before reporting a failure. This includes the first browser request in a session as well as reconnects. A failed check does not mean the extension is missing or disabled, and a later request checks again. Open the TheGitAI icon in Chrome to check its connection status if the browser remains unavailable.
After updating the CLI, exit and start a new ai process to load the fix. Existing processes continue using the code they started with. If a connection is replaced while an action is running, TheGitAI reports that its outcome is unknown. Check the page before repeating the action; it is not replayed automatically.
