title: Will Nabeela Syed’s data centre concerns propel her to the Illinois Senate?
body: Voter concerns about the proliferation of US data centres remain high ahead of next week's crucial midterm elections that could alter the trajectory of President Donald Trump's final two years in office. For Democrat Nabeela Syed, 27, a Muslim American who is in the Illinois House of Representatives, voter worries about data centres have long been a focal point. "Data centres consume enormous amounts of power, and the companies driving that demand should be the ones covering the cost of it," a statement on her campaign website reads. It says Ms Syed believes that ultimately, the cost of data centres "should not be showing up in our electricity bills" – an issue that recent polling shows is increasingly important to US voters. She stood behind Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, a fellow Democrat, when he signed a bill that he described as "the strongest AI safety accountability bill in the nation". She also endorsed his decision to pause tax incentives for new data centres amid mounting concern from residents in her district about the environmental impact, noise and other issues related to the projects. Now she is campaigning to take a Republican-held state Senate seat, focusing much of her campaign on promises to act on voter worries about data centres and increasingly powerful technology companies. Polling in recent months has shown that Democrats are more likely than Republicans to have concerns about AI and data centres. But surveys also show that some lifelong Republicans are dissatisfied with the proliferation of data centres throughout the country. Even in conservative states such as Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott announced a slowdown in data centre construction in response to apparently bipartisan worries. In general, Republican politicians have been less likely to be critical of data centres, causing them to lose ground with independent voters as the November 3 midterms approach. According to Axios , an internal Republican memo showed party leaders encouraging candidates in close races to try to shift their views on AI and data centres. The proposed message focuses on ensuring voters are aware that data centres will only be built with the approval of local people and that the company pays for its own utility use, with an emphasis on the importance of the US winning the AI race over China. #OhioSenate In the memo, obtained by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee says Democrats have made data centers a "centerpiece" of their campaign to defeat Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) — and that it's working. "If he loses and data centers get the blame,… https://t.co/Ncx8vi9qAZ pic.twitter.com/qNI25uGDEA — Politics & Poll Tracker 📡 (@PollTracker2024) August 19, 2026 Back in the 26th district of Illinois, Republican incumbent Darby Hills seems to have also felt the quickly expanding anti-data centre mood of the electorate. "I hear you," she posted on her campaign's social media pages, pointing out that she introduced legislation that she says will do a better job of holding data centre developers accountable. "I filed Senate Bill 1050 to strengthen local control and make sure our communities have a meaningful voice before these massive developments move forward." According to Journal & Topics , a news organisation that focuses on Chicago's northwest suburbs, during a candidate forum both Hills and Syed said that an important distinction needed to be drawn between between traditional data centres and AI-hyperscale data centres, with the latter being more intrusive, noisy and environmentally disruptive. In Michigan, a similar scenario unfolded with Republican Mike Rogers, who is running against Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a US Senate seat. Mr Rogers surprised many in recent months by announcing that he supported a data centre moratorium in the state, a stance that his opponent Mr El-Sayed has long maintained. The sudden about-face by Mr Rogers led the El-Sayed campaign to express scepticism about the Republican's change in tune. What's causing data centre resentment? In recent weeks, President Donald Trump has said that he felt concerns about unregulated AI and fears about data centres were hoaxes. Yet earlier in the year, his administration seemed keenly aware of the displeasure throughout the US as data centre construction was booming and electricity bills were rising. In February, he promoted a largely non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which Big Tech companies and data centre developers promise to provide electricity for their sites instead of taking from the existing grid. Despite the widely publicised move, opposition to data centres has continued to grow, but there are benefits that they are providing to some communities. Javier Palomarez, president and chief executive of the US Hispanic Business Council, says those economic benefits are real. "Construction can generate hundreds of well-paying, if temporary, jobs for electricians and other building trade workers, and the tax benefits can be substantial," he said, adding that in Loudon County, Virginia, data centres accounted for 38 per cent of the government's general fund revenue. "That revenue helps fund schools, roads and emergency services while reducing pressure on residential taxpayers ... it's the case leaders need to bring to Americans." Mr Palomarez said that government revenue aside, the overall economic benefits from data centres have been blunted by the electricity they use. "Those [data centre] benefits won’t mean much to someone worried about paying next month’s electric bill," he said. After the coming elections, Mr Palomarez said there will be plenty of time for technology companies and data centre developers to win hearts and minds. "There is room to earn public support, but people need more than a promise that the benefits will eventually reach them," he said. "They need to know they won’t be left with the bill."

In Michigan, a similar scenario unfolded with Republican Mike Rogers, who is running against Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for a US Senate seat. Mr Rogers surprised many in recent months by announcing that he supported a data centre moratorium in the state, a stance that his opponent Mr El-Sayed has long maintained. The sudden about-face by Mr Rogers led the El-Sayed campaign to express scepticism about the Republican's change in tune. What's causing data centre resentment? In recent weeks, President Donald Trump has said that he felt concerns about unregulated AI and fears about data centres were hoaxes. Yet earlier in the year, his administration seemed keenly aware of the displeasure throughout the US as data centre construction was booming and electricity bills were rising. In February, he promoted a largely non-binding ratepayer protection pledge in which Big Tech companies and data centre developers promise to provide electricity for their sites instead of taking from the existing grid. Despite the widely publicised move, opposition to data centres has continued to grow, but there are benefits that they are providing to some communities. Javier Palomarez, president and chief executive of the US Hispanic Business Council, says those economic benefits are real. "Construction can generate hundreds of well-paying, if temporary, jobs for electricians and other building trade workers, and the tax benefits can be substantial," he said, adding that in Loudon County, Virginia, data centres accounted for 38 per cent of the government's general fund revenue. "That revenue helps fund schools, roads and emergency services while reducing pressure on residential taxpayers ... it's the case leaders need to bring to Americans." Mr Palomarez said that government revenue aside, the overall economic benefits from data centres have been blunted by the electricity they use. "Those [data centre] benefits won’t mean much to someone worried about paying next month’s electric bill," he said. After the coming elections, Mr Palomarez said there will be plenty of time for technology companies and data centre developers to win hearts and minds. "There is room to earn public support, but people need more than a promise that the benefits will eventually reach them," he said. "They need to know they won’t be left with the bill."

title: El Fasher massacre one year on: Sudanese human rights groups demand truth about crimes, attrocities at fall of seige
body: Four Sudanese human rights organisations have called for the protection of civilians, independent investigations into alleged crimes, and accountability for those responsible in a joint statement marking the first anniversary of the fall of El Fasher , the capital of North Darfur. The Sudanese Human Rights Monitor, the African Centre for Justice and Peace Studies, the Darfur Bar Association, and the Al Khatim Adlan Centre for Enlightenment and Human Development said ending impunity required independent and transparent investigations, accountability based on evidence, guaranteed humanitarian access, and redress for victims without discrimination or selectivity. The organisations said the anniversary was an opportunity to call on all parties to fulfil their legal and moral responsibilities and renew their commitment to protecting civilians, establishing the truth, and securing justice without discrimination. The four signatories reaffirmed their commitment to independently and professionally monitoring and documenting violations, defending victims’ rights and dignity, strengthening the rule of law, and pursuing justice and guarantees against the recurrence of abuses. The statement stressed that protecting civilians required an end to violations, independent investigations, and accountability for those responsible for crimes. Victims’ rights must be upheld on the basis of evidence and individual responsibility, with guarantees of a fair trial. Siege of El Fasher and incitement to violence El Fasher came under a large-scale assault in late October 2025 following a prolonged siege and a severe deterioration in humanitarian conditions. Numerous credible reports have documented serious violations against civilians , including killings, detention, torture, widespread sexual violence, looting, the destruction of infrastructure essential to civilian life, and attacks on people fleeing the city. The organisations expressed concern over the growing use of ethnic rhetoric, hate speech, and incitement to violence and revenge. They warned that such language, including statements by individuals or entities linked to the warring parties and material circulated through the media and digital platforms, posed a direct threat to social cohesion and risked fuelling further violence. They urged the warring parties, political and military leaders, community representatives, and media organisations to reject incitement to violence, discrimination, and collective revenge. They also called for investigations into incitement to crimes and accountability for those responsible, in accordance with the law and available evidence, while respecting legitimate freedom of expression. The four organisations stressed that criminal responsibility was individual and must not be attributed to entire population groups or used to justify collective punishment on ethnic or political grounds. Protection of detainees and transparent investigations The organisations called on those controlling detention facilities to disclose where detainees were being held and the grounds for their detention, notify their families, guarantee access to lawyers, allow detainees to challenge the legality of their detention, and provide the necessary care. They also demanded independent investigations into deaths in custody and allegations of torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance, and arbitrary detention, as well as access to detention facilities for independent bodies. The signatories expressed concern that the findings of several announced investigative committees examining serious violations and incidents during the war had not been published. They urged the relevant authorities to disclose investigation findings, recommendations, and the outcomes of referrals for judicial proceedings. Establishing investigative committees, they stressed, did not replace independent criminal investigations or prosecutions where there were legal grounds to pursue them. Humanitarian crisis and aid access The humanitarian crisis in Darfur and Kordofan is worsening as a result of fighting and displacement, amid the near-total collapse of essential infrastructure, declining agricultural production and income sources, funding shortages, insecurity, and restrictions on humanitarian access. The four organisations called for unjustified obstacles to aid deliveries to be removed. These include security and logistical restrictions, administrative and bureaucratic delays involving registration, permits and approvals, and restrictions on the movement of aid workers and supplies. They condemned attacks on relief trucks carrying assistance to people facing starvation. They also highlighted restrictions on volunteers working in emergency response rooms and community initiatives, who face limitations on their movement and ability to serve their communities, including arrest, enforced disappearance, and killing. The signatories called on the authorities in Port Sudan and Nyala, each within the areas under their effective control, to review procedures obstructing humanitarian operations and ensure that they were transparent, proportionate, and processed promptly. All parties to the conflict and other actors exercising effective control were urged to protect humanitarian workers, facilitate the safe passage of supplies, and prevent aid from being looted or unlawfully diverted. Accountability and reparations The organisations stressed the need to investigate crimes and violations and hold accountable anyone found responsible for committing them, ordering them, or contributing to them, in accordance with international human rights law, international humanitarian law, and the rules applicable to each case. Military rank, official status, or political and organisational affiliations must not shield individuals from criminal accountability under Article 25 of the Rome Statute, the statement said. The signatories called on relevant national, regional, and international mechanisms to continue documenting violations, conducting investigations, preserving evidence, and supporting independent and effective judicial processes, including the work of the International Criminal Court on Darfur. They also stressed that victims had the right to know the truth and the fate of missing people, and to access effective remedies and reparations. These should include compensation, rehabilitation, and guarantees against the recurrence of violations. Survivors and victims’ families must also be protected from reprisals and stigmatisation. Recommendations The organisations urged the parties to the conflict and armed groups to respect the rules protecting civilians, halt unlawful attacks, prevent incitement to violence and collective revenge, release detainees, and stop violence against humanitarian workers. Those controlling detention facilities were called on to disclose the whereabouts of detainees and the grounds for their detention, safeguard their legal rights and basic needs, allow independent bodies access to them, and investigate deaths and allegations of torture, ill-treatment, and enforced disappearance. The Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces, both of which have established investigative committees, were urged, alongside the judicial authorities, to publish investigation findings and the measures taken in response, clarify the outcomes of judicial referrals, ensure the independence of investigations, and protect victims and witnesses. The organisations also called on the authorities, parties to the conflict, and those controlling supply routes to remove unjustified obstacles to humanitarian assistance, guarantee the safe passage of aid workers and supplies, and refrain from using administrative procedures or security restrictions to obstruct relief operations without legitimate grounds. Finally, they urged donors, humanitarian organisations, and international mechanisms to take concrete steps to protect civilians. These should include supporting international investigative mechanisms, ensuring humanitarian access, applying pressure to end violations, providing the funding needed to address food insecurity and malnutrition, expanding essential services in affected areas, and supporting independent documentation, evidence preservation, and relevant judicial processes. Share article The post El Fasher massacre one year on: Sudanese human rights groups demand truth about crimes, attrocities at fall of seige appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .

title: Lavrov describes diesel deal as business agreement with no additional conditions
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov described the Russian-American diesel deal as a "purely business agreement" with no additional conditions.
"Regarding the agreements announced following the phone call between President [of Russia Vladimir] Putin and President [of the United States Donald] Trump concerning supplies of diesel fuel, the deficit of which the United States considers inadequate to the current requirements of the global market, this is a purely business agreement," Lavrov said at a meeting with editors-in-chief of African media outlets.
"No conditions such as we’ll buy diesel fuel from you, provided you take certain actions on the political front or regarding security issues, whether in the Strait of Hormuz or anywhere else, there were no such linkages whatsoever," he stressed. "This is a purely pragmatic approach taken by sensible leaders who are concerned about both their own national economies and the global economy, considering the interests of their citizens above all else, rather than focusing on resolving various geopolitical issues," the minister added.

title: Red Sea Insecurity Highlights Eritrea’s Strategic Value
body: Eritrea is seeing its strategic value to regional security and the global economy rise as conflict affects traffic on the Red Sea. Houthi rebel attacks on commercial vessels have disrupted commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, shifting attention to Eritrea’s 2,234-kilometer coastline. The Red Sea is one of the world’s most important routes for global shipping. Each year, up to 15% of global maritime trade worth more than $1 trillion transits the waterway, which extends from the Suez Canal in the north to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the south. Analysts say sustained disruptions in the Red Sea would fuel serious supply-chain delays, ratchet up energy prices and further destabilize global trade. Eritrea and Yemen are separated by about 37 kilometers at the Bab el-Mandeb Strait chokepoint. This makes Eritrea’s location “particularly interesting, as Yemen is in a state of crisis and maritime security in the region is at risk,” Abdurahman Sayed, director of the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration in London, told German broadcaster Deutsche Welle (DW). “The only safe route in this area runs through Eritrea, where there are currently no security concerns.” In July, diplomatic discussions in Cairo involving Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and the U.S. underscored Eritrea’s growing role in coordinating approaches to facilitate trade and address security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. After meeting with Eritrean Foreign Minister Osman Saleh, U.S. Senior Adviser for Africa Massad Boulos said they explored ways to enhance cooperation on regional economic development, trade and security, particularly the need to “work together constructively to address regional conflicts and advance lasting peace, stability, and prosperity in the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa,” Boulos said in an Al Jazeera report. Amid the Red Sea concerns, Eritrea remains embroiled in tensions with Ethiopia, which has for years demanded access to the Red Sea through Eritrea’s port of Assab. Ethiopia lost access to the sea in 1993 when Eritrea gained independence. According to Michael Woldemariam, a researcher at the School of Public Policy at the University of Maryland and the Atlantic Council, escalating tensions with Ethiopia are key to understanding Eritrea’s strategic moves in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea. “Asmara is seeking to forge partnerships that can serve as a counterweight to Addis Ababa,” Woldemariam told DW. “Its recent diplomatic outreach to Egypt, Somalia, the United Arab Emirates’ armed forces, Saudi Arabia, Ethiopian opposition groups, and even the U.S. should be viewed against this backdrop.” Matters are complicated by ongoing violence in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, situated along Eritrea’s southern border. Eritrean troops in the first week of October reportedly crossed into the Ethiopia town of Zalambessa, residents said. The town was once controlled by Tigrayan rebels who seek overthrow the Ethiopian government. Addis Ababa has accused Asmara of supporting the rebels. About one week later, Ethiopian troops entered the town, but it was unclear if Eritrean troops remained. Asmara has argued that Addis Ababa’s accusations of an invasion by Eritrean forces ⁠was a “declaration of war.” “With Addis Ababa and Asmara ​now on opposing sides again, conflicts raging elsewhere in the region and tensions high across the Red Sea, there are fears of broader contagion of violence this time around,” Martin Plaut, a journalist specializing in the Horn of Africa and Southern Africa, wrote on his website. Fighting between the countries on their shared border in Tigray would mark a drastic turn of events. Hundreds of thousands of people died in the Tigray War that ended with a peace deal in 2022. Eritrea then supported Ethiopia against the TPLF. “When Ethiopian forces reach the border of Eritrea, this will bring the two forces head-to-head,” Mehari Taddele Maru, an expert on the Horn of Africa and a former senior official inthe African Union, told The New York Times. “There is a high probability of a war between the two countries that may end in Ethiopian control of Assab and potentially regime change” in Eritrea, he added. Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki has ruled the country as a strict one-party authoritarian regime since 1993. “The country is ruled by a single man, and there are no constitutional institutions,” Sayed told DW. “That makes the state very vulnerable should this strongman be removed from power.” The post Red Sea Insecurity Highlights Eritrea’s Strategic Value appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: Family announces burial arrangements for Nigerian actor Steve Echendu
body:
The family of late actor Steve Echendu has announced his burial arrangements.
His death was announced hours after veteran actor Francis Duru’s passing sent shockwaves through the entertainment industry.
In a statement posted on actress Clarion Chukwura’s Instagram page on Tuesday and signed by his son, Kamsiyochukwu Echendu, the family announced a three-day funeral programme for the 52-year-old actor.
The family said a wake-keep ceremony will take place on 27 November, ahead of his burial on 28 November in his hometown of Umuokwara Umuohiri, Isiala Mbano, Imo State.
A thanksgiving and outing service will follow on 29 November, bringing the funeral activities to an end.
“Your life was a blessing, your memory a treasure; you will always be loved and deeply missed”, said the family.
According to the family, the actor leaves behind his wife, children and brothers.
Mourning his death, Chukwura recalled his contributions to Nollywood during its formative years, when the industry was still finding its feet.
She described his death as a painful loss, saying his exit was hard to bear.
“This is hard. Indeed, a painful exit. A major pillar in the early days of Nollywood, the most professional, hardworking and respectful production manager I ever worked with in the foundational years of Nollywood. Rest in Peace, Steve”, she noted.
Echendu wore several hats in the industry, working as an actor, producer and director. His film credits include “Knockout Blessing”, “Fury”, “Infant at Heart”, among others.
As of press time, his family had not disclosed the cause of his death.
Meanwhile, colleagues paid tributes to his contributions to Nollywood during the industry’s formative years, as the home-video sector expanded.

title: Next Week’s Midterms Could Stall the CLARITY Act and Test Crypto’s Political Clout: TD Cowen
body: Bitcoin Magazine Next Week’s Midterms Could Stall the CLARITY Act and Test Crypto’s Political Clout: TD Cowen Washington’s crypto agenda hinges on next week’s midterm elections, according to a new policy note from TD Cowen, shared with Bitcoin Magazine. Analyst Jaret Seiberg warned in the note that the probable results could make it difficult for Congress to pass the CLARITY Act over the next two years. The bill would set the rules for bitcoin and other digital assets, and the industry has spent $176 million on more than 100 races to shape the outcome. Here are a couple of the results: A Democratic sweep is the most probable outcome Prediction markets cited in the report give Democrats a 90% chance of winning the House and a 62% chance of winning the Senate. TD Cowen considers this the most negative scenario for bitcoin and the broader crypto sector. Under it, Sen. Elizabeth Warren would become Senate Banking Committee chair. Seiberg describes her as a crypto skeptic who has led opposition to the CLARITY Act, and he expects her to conduct tough oversight of federal regulators. Warren cannot stop regulators from adopting policies that favor the industry. Seiberg expects President Trump to remain favorable toward crypto, so he would veto any bill that limits his regulators’ authority. Democrats would lack the votes to override him. As a result, policy changes are expected to focus on tokenization , perpetual futures, and stablecoins . A split Congress with Republicans holding the Senate The second scenario keeps Democrats in control of the House while key Senate races stay close enough to break for Republicans. Sen. Tim Scott would keep his Banking Committee gavel. TD Cowen views this outcome as a better result for bitcoin, because Rep. Maxine Waters could trade support for parts of the market structure bill in exchange for investor protections and action on her other priorities. Adverse legislation would be blocked from reaching the president’s desk. A Republican sweep is the least likely but best outcome for crypto Kalshi gives Republicans a 10% chance to keep the House and a 35% chance to keep the Senate. TD Cowen calls this the best path for crypto policy , though the margins matter. A wider Senate majority would improve the odds that leaders advance the CLARITY Act in 2027 or 2028, and they could attempt a revival during the lame-duck session . A narrow majority, by contrast, would leave the bill stalled, as Democrats keep pushing ethics provisions that the president opposes. When the Senate blocked the bill , Bitcoin-related stocks tumbled. For background, the CLARITY Act would create federal rules for digital assets. The House passed its version in July 2025 by a 294-134 vote. The Senate Banking Committee approved its own version in May 2026 by a 15-9 vote, with two Democrats joining Republicans. On the Senate floor, a cloture vote failed 49-50 on September 15. Democrats want ethics language that would bar senior officials, including the president, from profiting from crypto ventures. Republicans and industry groups resist those limits. Stablecoin yield is another dispute. Each side says the other is blocking progress, and the bill is stuck. This post Next Week’s Midterms Could Stall the CLARITY Act and Test Crypto’s Political Clout: TD Cowen first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Micah Zimmerman .

title: Radio-tagged Monarch butterflies
body:
New technology allows butterflies to tagged with devices that report time and location
Who knew a Monarch butterfly could borrow a cell phone to check in with friendly people he met on his journey?
That is essentially what happens now that new technology has reduced the weight of a radio-pulse tag to less than half a gram. Those tags use Bluetooth technology to send information back to the researchers in the U.S. and Canada, including Jennifer Weber, Ph.D. '25, and Shawn Kurtzman from the Conservation Management Institute , to collect far more data than has ever been available about the paths and speed of Monarch butterflies as they migrate from a vast range in continent’s temperate areas to nature preserves in Mexico and Central America.
International calls are welcome, as some of the butterflies tagged in Virginia are now in Mexico.
Weber gave some of the Monarchs names and keeps up with their perilous migratory journeys. Sneezy, tagged here in the New River Valley in September, was detected in Mexico on Oct. 17. Addison and Sleepy, also part of the mountain cohort, checked in from Texas but now seem to be travelling outside of range of cell service. Two other recent visitors to Virginia Tech, Hahn and Sandman, are now in Alabama and South Carolina, respectively. Orion and Walker were in Georgia, dealing with tropical storm Isaias, before heading west again.
Thomas is the real traveller. Tagged in Fort A.P. Hill near Fredricksburg, he was last detected in Mississippi, then pinged again a thousand miles away in southern Mexico.
"We figured he would follow the Gulf Coast and make his way to the wintering grounds," Weber said. "Imagine our shock when he pinged yesterday at lunchtime all the way across the gulf. His latest ping put him a little bit east of a city named Coatzacoalcos, well south of the wintering grounds."
Weber said Thomas and a few other radio tagged monarchs were picked up by a swirling storm system and deposited on the Mexican coast.
To say Monarchs are checking in with cellphones is not hyperbole. The new tags emit a pulse detectable by Bluetooth-enabled smartphones, vehicles, and cellular towers which send a signal through a background function to the researchers to create a continuous, real-time map.
"It’s citizen science, but crowd-powered," Weber said.
No information about the device itself is sent — just the tag number and location. It also means a Monarch flying over wilderness could go days without being located, leaving Weber to wonder if the tag stopped working, fell off, or the butterfly perished.
Kurtzman said the estimated survival rate is 25 to 28 percent.
Following a flight path at hundreds of data points reveals micro-level behaviors, such as whether monarchs utilize highway corridors, how they react to major weather disruptions, and where they pause to feed on available nectar along their route.
Weber and Kurtzman outfitted 35 Monarchs with pulse tags and follow their path to winter quarters. The cost of the radio-pulse tags is still high enough that most butterflies are tagged with a small sticker on a wing that includes contact information for anyone who found it. This message-in-a-bottle strategy returns data from a tiny percentage of Monarchs.
With new technology, scientists are able to see the flight path of the Monarchs with dozens of data points. The blue and purple lines were Monarchs tagged in the New River Valley in mid-September, the red and orange lines represent Monarchs tagged at Fort A.P. Hill, and the coastal group have green lines indicating their route. Photo courtesy of Jennifer Weber.
The CMI researchers tagged Monarchs on federal land around military installations in three Virginia locations — the Radford Arsenal for a mountain population; Fort A.P. Hill for a Piedmont population; and Oceana Naval Air Station and Joint Base Langley-Eustis to identify a coastal population. Monarchs tagged on the Tech campus were included in the mountain cohort. By deploying tags across mountain, Piedmont, and coastal locations, researchers want to determine whether monarchs from different geographic regions in Virginia follow the same migration corridors to Mexico or take distinct paths, such as heading south into Florida.
A butterfly that flits around doesn’t seem to be moving rapidly in any specific direction, but just two hours after being tagged in September on the Virginia Tech campus, one Monarch was flying near the New River in Giles County, having crossed two ridgelines on its way west.
The research will be used by Project Monarch , a collaborative initiative, along with Monarch Joint Venture and the Xerces Society for Invertebrate Conservation , two nonprofits working to understand and preserve Monarchs, a threatened species. Researchers from dozens of universities and research groups are partnering with these agencies to reveal how these insects navigate around or through challenging areas throughout eastern North America.
“We're all kind of throwing our data in the same pot,” Weber said. “Hopefully, that data will be available for anyone who needs it so we can help these little guys.”
Learning more about the migratory routes will guide land management choices in the future. Whether it’s a large expanse of federal land or a yard owned by a butterfly aficionado, encouraging plants than benefit Monarchs is ecologically important. Milkweed, goldenrod, thistle, and wingstem are a few of the species Monarchs need.
“You can't just provision the caterpillars and do nothing for the adults, because milkweed doesn't last into the fall,” Weber said “Then we start relying on the wingstem, we rely on the thistle, we rely on the goldenrod. So having a wide variety of plants and plants that provision them at every portion of the year is super important.”

title: CEC denies Likud's request to extend Israeli election voting time past 10 p.m.
body: The Central Election Committee (CEC) denied a Likud formal request on Tuesday to extend voting hours due to congested polling stations nationwide.The CEC ruled that there was no justification for extending voting hours, citing, among other factors, high voter turnout across all sectors of the population.The committee clarified that anyone who arrives at a polling station before it closes will be allowed to vote.However, voting in Hebron was extended until 10 p.m. due to a power outage.Likud, Shas, People of Israel, and Otzma Yehudit push to extend voting timesOfer Winter's People of Israel, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit, and the haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Shas party joined Likud in calling for an hour-long extension. “Our representatives on the ground are reporting unusual crowding at polling stations,” Winter explained in a statement regarding the request. “This situation risks denying party supporters their right to vote. We must ensure that as many People of Israel voters as possible are able to cast their ballots.”"I am very concerned about the apathy in the Haredi and right-wing strongholds," said Shas Chairman Arye Deri in a Tuesday statement. "The high voter turnout in the strongholds of the Left and in the Arab sector is deeply worrying.""According to the data we have, numbers like these have not been seen since 1973.""There are massive lines at polling stations in Bedouin communities in the Negev and in Tel Aviv, yet, regrettably, in our own camp, among the Haredi and right-wing strongholds, there is a sense of complacency," Deri said.Decision to extend voting hours can only be made by SohlbergEarlier on Tuesday, Israeli media reported that the weather could also factor into the debate over whether to extend voting hours.The decision can only be made by CEC Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg.The Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, opposed Likud's request to extend voting hours in a statement of its own."No unusual incident has occurred to justify granting this request," the party stated, "which is intended to lay the groundwork for claims challenging the integrity of the election, in line with the lies Netanyahu has been spreading since this morning."

title: Europe can't keep head above water in information war against Russia — Lavrov
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Europe is trying to keep the public on its side via its information war against Russia, while finding that harder to do these days, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at a meeting with the editors-in-chief of the African media.
"The West is depending on disinformation to keep public opinion on its side, trying to hold on for dear life. It's with this information war that they are trying to keep their heads above water. But it's getting harder and harder for them to do that."

title: Ukrainian forces have successfully adapted Russian tactics, Zelensky on Operation Veles
body:
Zelensky announced this in a Facebook post, Ukrinform reports.
“An important operation is underway on the Kupiansk axis. Mykhailo Drapatyi, Ihor Obolenskyi, and Pavlo Palisa briefed me on the initial results and progress of Operation Veles, which is being conducted by the National Guard of Ukraine’s 2nd Khartiia Corps. More than 100 Russian occupiers have already been eliminated, and more than 30 have been taken prisoner. Ukrainian forces have advanced more than 15 kilometers underground,” the statement said.
Russian forces had previously attempted to use underground gas pipelines to move through Ukrainian positions and launch assaults, Zelensky said.

title: Lockheed Martin invests C$10 million in Canadian AI to improve Hercules fleet maintenance
body: Lockheed Martin Canada is developing the platform with the RCAF and Canadian AI company Contextere. The investment contributes to Lockheed Martin’s economic impact commitments under the CC-130J In-Service Support program. iMAPLE stands for Intelligent Maintenance, Asset, Personnel and Learning Environment. It draws on Contextere’s work turning institutional knowledge into practical guidance for people maintaining and operating complex equipment. “Lockheed Martin’s investment in iMAPLE reflects a shared belief that the future of sustainment depends on connecting people, knowledge, and technology,” said Gabriel Batstone, Contextere’s chief executive officer and co-founder. “Together, we are building on Canadian intellectual property that supports our armed forces, strengthens our industrial base, creates opportunities for skilled trades, and showcases how Canadian AI can deliver value on the global stage.” Beyond the funding, Lockheed Martin will advise on the design, testing and optimization of AI components throughout the project. It will also provide validated machine-learning methodologies, quality reviews and knowledge transfer. “Today’s announcement demonstrates meaningful results for Canadians through Canada’s Industrial and Technological Benefits Policy. This partnership invests in a Canadian-developed artificial intelligence solution that supports the Royal Canadian Air Force’s CC-130J Hercules fleet,” said Stephen Fuhr, Canada’s secretary of state for defense procurement. The partners see potential for broader applications and exports alongside the work supporting the Hercules fleet. Lockheed Martin said the project aligns with Canada’s Defence Industrial Strategy and national AI strategy, AI for All. “This collaboration with the Royal Canadian Air Force and Contextere offers something truly special,” said Kristen Leroux, Lockheed Martin’s vice president and regional executive for Canada and Latin America. “We’re proud to be a part of the development of iMAPLE and to work alongside Contextere in support of our air force and the CC-130J fleet, demonstrating how Canadian innovation can build a sovereign defence and dual-use ecosystem right here at home.” Lockheed Martin said Canada’s purchase and associated support of 17 CC-130J Super Hercules aircraft have delivered more than C$4.7 billion in economic benefits under the Industrial and Technological Benefits Policy. The company also reported contributing C$3.6 billion to Canadian gross domestic product over the past five years and supporting an average of 4,561 jobs annually.

title: ‘It’s campaign slush fund’, Atiku asks N’Assembly to reject Tinubu’s loan request
body: Former Vice-President and African Democratic Congress (ADC) Presidential Candidate, Atiku Abubakar, has said President Bola Tinubu’s request for approval to borrow $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion vindicates his October 12 warning about a loan plan of up to $20 billion. Atiku said the President’s failure to identify the specific projects the loans would fund raises serious concerns that borrowed public money could be channelled through the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, now rerouted inland, to political campaigners and favoured contractors. In a statement issued by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said: “On October 12, I warned Nigerians that President Tinubu was reportedly preparing to borrow up to $20 billion in connection with the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway. I asked him to confirm or deny the plan and publish the accounts. He did neither. Today, he has asked the Senate to approve $20.52 billion and €1.045 billion in external loans. My warning has been vindicated. “The President has listed broad sectors but has not provided a project by project account of what this enormous borrowing will fund. Nigerians have not been given clear project details, costs, locations or contractors to scrutinise. “That silence is especially troubling given the highway’s inland rerouting. Nigerians have every right to ask whether it is becoming a pipeline for borrowed money to reach Tinubu’s campaigners and favoured contractors. Barely 12 weeks before an election, how can the President ask lawmakers to saddle Nigerians with more than $20 billion and €1 billion in debt without identifying the projects and their costs? Is this a development plan for Nigerians or a campaign financing scheme dressed up as infrastructure? “You cannot continue taking frivolous loans on the eve of your departure from office. Let it be on record that one of the first responsibilities I will undertake as President is to scrutinise and investigate every kobo borrowed, especially loans taken in the final year of your tenure. Nigerians will ask questions, and we will find the answers by every lawful means. “I put local and international lenders on notice: any loan granted to this winding down administration must meet all constitutional, statutory and due process requirements. Upon assumption of office, I will scrutinise every such loan. Any borrowing found to have been obtained without proper authorisation or process will be challenged and will not be allowed to stand. “The National Assembly must not approve a single dollar until the President publishes every project, contract, cost, contractor, loan term and repayment obligation. No public money should be borrowed in the dark, and no lawmaker should sign a blank cheque against Nigeria’s future.” Atiku said the burden was on Tinubu to prove that the borrowing would serve the country, not his political interests. He urged lawmakers to publish the proposal and supporting documents and subject them to rigorous scrutiny before any decision.

title: Circle Pushes Deeper Into Latin America With USDC Settlement in Colombia
body:
Circle is extending its reach across Latin America, teaming up with payments-technology firm ACI Worldwide to fold USDC settlement into the region’s existing banking rails, starting with a pilot in Colombia.
Announced Tuesday, the collaboration pairs Circle’s USDC infrastructure with ACI Connetic, ACI’s cloud-based payments orchestration platform, to show financial institutions how stablecoin settlement can run alongside traditional payment systems rather than replace them.
The initial focus is Colombia, where ACI built the central infrastructure behind Bre-B, the country’s interoperable instant-payments network. The idea is to test how a digital dollar like USDC can slot into that real-time, account-to-account system to create what the companies call a multi-rail ecosystem.
The framing reflects a shift in how banks are approaching stablecoins. Rather than debating the technology itself, institutions increasingly want to know how digital dollars fit into the treasury operations, governance and settlement processes they already run.
“The conversation around stablecoins is moving from possibility to practicality,” said Craig Ramsey, ACI’s global head of account-to-account payments, describing the effort as a way to integrate regulated stablecoins into workflows banks already trust.
Kash Razzaghi, Circle’s chief commercial officer, said financial institutions across Latin America are increasingly looking at how stablecoins can support the evolution of payments “within the infrastructure they already use,” framing USDC as a bridge between traditional finance and the digital economy.
The move builds on Circle’s steady regional expansion. The company has pushed into dozens of emerging markets as stablecoins go mainstream, and earlier gained a Latin American foothold when Argentina’s Mercado Pago added USDC .
Colombia is a logical next target, given high cross-border remittance volumes and a population well-acquainted with dollar-denominated savings as a hedge against inflation.
Circle positioned the pilot as technology-agnostic: while it runs on USDC, ACI’s platform is built to support other payment networks and digital-asset providers over time. For Circle, the deal is another step in weaving its stablecoin into the plumbing of mainstream finance, this time in a fast-growing payments market where instant-payment adoption is already accelerating.

title: Kano Assembly approves state police
body: By Hadiza Yusuf The Kano State House of Assembly has approved the proposed constitutional amendment to allow state governments to establish and operate their own police forces. The approval was confirmed by the Majority Leader of the Assembly, Lawan Hussaini Dala, shortly after plenary on Tuesday. Dala said the lawmakers had considered and approved the proposed constitutional review to provide for the establishment of state police. “We have approved the constitutional review for the establishment of state police at plenary today,” he said. The approval followed deliberations on the proposed amendments to the 1999 Constitution, as amended, which seek to give state governments the legal authority to establish and operate their own police forces. During plenary, the lawmakers considered the constitutional alteration bill in the Committee of the Whole, deliberating on clauses one to 26 of the proposed amendment. The lawmakers had earlier adopted a motion to consider the constitutional amendment bill in the Committee of the Whole before proceeding with deliberations on its provisions. The post Kano Assembly approves state police appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: ANALYSIS: Nigeria’s first methane disclosure raises questions over repeated figures, missing data
body:
Nigeria has taken an important step towards improving transparency in its oil and gas sector by publishing company-level greenhouse gas emissions data for the first time.
The disclosure, released by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (NEITI) in its 2023 oil and gas audit report , is expected to help citizens, regulators and investors understand how much pollution companies emit and whether the country is making progress towards its climate commitments.
However, an independent review of the data has identified several issues that may undermine confidence in the disclosures if left unresolved.
Using the Emissions Monitoring and Accountability Tool (EMAT), an interactive platform that organises and compares emissions data published by NEITI, this analysis found repeated emissions figures across different companies, missing methane information, and inconsistencies in the number of companies reported as having submitted emissions data.
The findings do not suggest wrongdoing by any company. Rather, they highlight areas where Nigeria’s emissions reporting framework could be strengthened to improve transparency, data quality and public confidence.
One of the most striking observations is that Chevron Nigeria Limited and the Shell Petroleum Development Company (SPDC) reported exactly the same methane emissions figures for 2022.
Both companies reported 173,578,759.2 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) and 6,943,150.368 kilograms of methane.
The values are identical across virtually all reported fields except for halons.
The figures appear in Appendix 12 of NEITI’s 2022 and 2023 Oil and Gas Industry Reports, which contain Nigeria’s first publicly available company-level greenhouse gas disclosures.
This became immediately visible because EMAT allows users to compare company data side by side, identical figures that may be difficult to notice in static tables.
The Chevron-SPDC entries are not isolated cases.
Another example is Aradel Holdings Plc, which reported exactly the same methane values in both 2022 and 2023: 133,522,033 kilograms CO₂e and 5,340,877 kilograms of methane.
Similarly, Network E&P reported 112 kilograms CO2e and 3.64 kilograms methane in both reporting years.
Repeated figures do not automatically mean the data are inaccurate. Companies with similar operations, shared production facilities, or common reporting boundaries could legitimately report similar emissions. However, exactly identical values reported to several decimal places warrant further verification against the original submissions.
Another case concerns Pillar Oil, where the same numerical value appears repeatedly across different greenhouse gases.
For example, in 2022, the value 1,610,170.7872 appears across several gases, including carbon monoxide, nitrous oxide, nitric oxide and sulphur dioxide. The same pattern appears in 2023 with 2,389,859.8050.
The published report does not explain why these different gases share identical values.
The analysis also found that methane reporting is far from complete.
Of the 30 company-year records reviewed in Appendix 12, only 12 contain information across all three methane reporting fields.
The remaining 18 records contain missing information, and some of the omissions are difficult to interpret.
For instance, NAE reported 963,970 kilograms of methane in 2022 but recorded zero for the corresponding carbon dioxide equivalent.
In 2023, the company again reported methane emissions but left the carbon dioxide equivalent field blank.
Similarly, Chevron and Heirs Energies reported methane only as carbon dioxide equivalent in 2023 without providing the underlying methane mass.
Heirs Energies reported 217.4 million kilograms CO₂e, one of the highest methane-related figures in the dataset, yet the absence of the methane mass makes it impossible to independently verify the conversion.
In another case, Platform Petroleum appears on the reporting sheet, yet all of its methane fields are blank for both years.
The report provides no explanation of whether blank cells indicate that no emissions occurred, that no data were submitted, or that emissions were not calculated.
This distinction matters because a blank field is not the same as reporting zero emissions.
The analysis also raises questions about how many companies actually submitted emissions data.
NEITI states that 15 out of 62 audited companies submitted greenhouse gas information, while 47 companies did not.
However, the appendix presents 15 companies on the reporting sheets, and 58 entries on the non-reporting sheet.
Taken together, the lists contain 73 entries, rather than the 62 companies referenced by NEITI.
Further review shows that Platform Petroleum appears on both the reporting and non-reporting lists.
In addition, some entries refer to joint venture interests or individual oil fields rather than clearly identifiable legal entities, making it difficult to determine exactly which companies reported emissions.
For example, the non-reporting list includes the NEPL (55 per cent) and Shoreline (45 per cent) interests in OML 30, while the reporting sheets separately list Esso’s Erha and Usan fields.
A reconciled list that clearly distinguishes legal entities, operators, and production assets would significantly improve transparency.
Nigeria has committed to ending routine gas flaring by 2030 and reducing fugitive methane emissions from the oil and gas sector by 60 per cent by 2031.
Measuring progress towards these goals depends on reliable baseline data.
Because Appendix 12 represents Nigeria’s first public company-level greenhouse gas disclosure, it effectively serves as the benchmark against which future emissions reductions will be measured. If the baseline contains gaps or inconsistencies, assessing future progress becomes more difficult.
Several practical improvements could strengthen future disclosures, including publishing the original reporting templates submitted by companies, clearly distinguishing between reported zeros and missing information, identifying the legal entity responsible for each reported asset, providing explanatory notes for unusual entries and maintaining a public log of corrections where errors are identified.
NEITI was asked, through a Freedom of Information request, to respond to the issues identified in the analysis, including questions concerning the methodology used by companies, duplicate figures, missing or zero values, emissions intensity, the number of reporting companies, verification procedures, and the accessibility of the published data.
NEITI explained that under EITI Requirement 3.4, greenhouse gas reporting is encouraged rather than mandatory.
According to the agency, its reporting template requested companies to provide greenhouse gas emissions data and information on the methodology used, including emission factors, direct ground based sensors, satellite estimates, and other recognised approaches.
However, the template did not require companies to provide the Global Warming Potential values used, the specific IPCC or other scientific assessment from which those values were derived, or the time horizon used to convert emissions into CO₂ equivalents.
The agency said it did not convert, normalise, recalculate or adjust the data submitted by companies. The published figures, therefore, reflect the information provided by the companies.
NEITI also said there is currently no established national verification framework for these disclosures and that its role is focused on transparency, collection, and publication rather than on independent technical validation or methodological harmonisation.
Regarding repeated entries and identical figures identified in the analysis, NEITI acknowledged the observations and said it would conduct an internal review.
The agency said necessary adjustments had been reflected in the published data. It added that the original company templates and internal validation records were not intended for public disclosure.
NEITI said that any corrections or clarifications resulting from its internal review would be reflected in the published dataset. It acknowledged the observations and said it would take the feedback into account as it updates the published information.
NEITI’s first company-level greenhouse gas disclosure represents an important starting point for public scrutiny of emissions in Nigeria’s oil and gas sector.
The data provide journalists, researchers, civil society organisations and policymakers with information that was previously difficult to access at the company level.
At the same time, the analysis shows that the value of the disclosure will depend on improvements in the way emissions information is collected, standardised, verified and published.
The immediate priority should be to establish a clearer and more consistent reporting framework that enables users to distinguish between zero emissions, missing information and non-applicable data; understand the methodology behind reported figures; identify the companies and assets covered; and reproduce emissions-intensity calculations.
As Nigeria works towards its methane-reduction commitments, the quality of the underlying data will be as important as the targets themselves.
The first disclosure has opened the window of transparency. The next challenge is ensuring that the information available through that window is complete, consistent and reliable to support meaningful public accountability.
This report was supported by the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development(CJID) as part of the Deepening Methane Emissions Transparency Initiative-Stream II

title: Sports, art, energy ties should unite, not divide peoples, says Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Sports should unite peoples rather than dividing them, while some international sports organizations are "undermining cooperation" in this humanitarian sphere, Russian President Vladimir Putin said on Tuesday.
"Thank you very much for the offer regarding the sports aspect," the president thanked Minister of Energy and Petroleum of Senegal El Hadji Abdourahmane Diouf after he invite him to attend the Youth Olympic Games in his country.
"All of this is indeed important for cooperation and for creating the right conditions," Putin said addressing participants at the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow, the Russian capital.
"We unfortunately are witnessing some actions in the sports environment and in international sports organizations that undermine cooperation in this crucial humanitarian sphere," Putin continued.
"We [Russia] adhere to the principle that sports, just like art and cooperation in the energy sphere, is undoubtedly something that should unite, rather than divide, peoples," the Russian president added.
The International Olympic Committee (IOC) announced a decision on July 7 to provisionally lift an earlier-imposed suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) and also recommended lifting restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes in all international tournaments.
On February 28, 2022, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) issued recommendations to international sports federations to prohibit athletes from Russia and Belarus from participating in international tournaments, citing Moscow’s special military operation in Ukraine as the reason.
Following the IOC’s recommendations in late February 2022, the majority of global sports federations decided to bar athletes from Russia and Belarus from all international sports tournaments.
In late March, 2023, the IOC recommended allowing individual athletes from Russia and Belarus to participate in international sports tournaments, but only under specific conditions. Specifically, athletes from the two countries should not be "actively supporting" Russia’s special military operation in Ukraine and must compete under a neutral status. Russia and Belarus were also banned from participating in international team events.
On October 12, 2023, the IOC suspended the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) until further notice after the Russian organization included the Olympic councils of the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics (DPR and LPR), the Zaporozhye and Kherson Regions as its members.

title: Military drone outfit Anduril partners with Qualcomm to build laptops on US soil with new BlueChip venture
body: Defense contractor Anduril, which is known for its military drones, just announced that it’s building laptops in the U.S., with the company saying that it will begin taking orders in 2027. According to its press release , it will call its laptop product line BlueChip and will use a Snapdragon X Series SoC for its core computing capabilities. It also said that it already has functional prototypes, with 90% of the procurement cost of the components used to build it coming from suppliers in the U.S. and other allied countries. However, it’s also aiming for a fully domestic supply chain in the long term. This means that Anduril is not only sourcing domestically produced semiconductors but also uses other made-in-the-U.S. parts, like batteries, the external casing, and even the glass for its screen. “Other companies might design their computers in the U.S., Anduril makes them here,” the Anduril founder Palmer Luckey said in the Anduril YouTube video. “We’re making parts out of metals that the U.S. knows how to extract, knows how to refine, knows how to process, and knows how to mill at scale at a reasonable price; and that goes for the entire laptop. The same thing goes for the battery technology.” Luckey has been planning to launch a fully U.S.-made laptop since last year but said that it’s going to cost 20% more than a comparable device. Still, it seems that the company is targeting critical industries — government, defense, first responders, and public safety — which might be willing to spend more to ensure the security of their computer systems. Anduril is also better placed to start building a domestically designed, built, and sourced laptop today as the White House’s efforts to bring back semiconductor manufacturing have resulted in massive fabs like TSMC Arizona and Samsung’s Taylor, Texas site . Taiwan’s plan to support smaller companies key to TSMC’s supply chain by funding industrial parks in the U.S. will also likely benefit BlueChip, as it would make it easier for the company to source needed parts it would otherwise have to order from abroad. Anduril has acknowledged the progress in the U.S.’s efforts to bring back computer manufacturing to its shores but also acknowledged the challenges that it faces when it comes to building a 100% domestic supply chain. “…manufacturing complete computers also requires circuit boards, displays, batteries, and other components still largely produced overseas. Restoring domestic computer manufacturing requires rebuilding that broader industrial base,” it said in its press release. “BlueChip will take a phased approach, beginning with expanding domestic sourcing and manufacturing, progressing toward eliminating reliance on foreign suppliers, and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.”

title: Melania Trump: Ceasefire area expanded beyond Oleshky
body:
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump announced that the area covered by the local ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which took effect early Tuesday morning, has been expanded beyond the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region.

"Timing was accelerated two days ahead of schedule to protect the safety of civilians and to facilitate the delivery of critical humanitarian aid. The ceasefire's geographic area has expanded beyond Oleshky, within the Kherson Region, to provide safe passage for the humanitarian convoys," Mrs. Trump said on X social media platform.

She also said she had received this information from General Valery Gerasimov, Joint Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.

As previously reported, a ceasefire in the area around the city of Oleshky in Kherson region was declared at 03:00 on October 27. It will last until 22:59 on November 1 as part of U.S. First Lady Melania Trump's initiative to reopen the city.

title: ‘We're stranded’: Flash floods block Israeli voters from reaching polling stations
body: Polling stations in small communities in the Arava region of southern Israel are set to close at 8 p.m. Tuesday, but stormy weather and flash floods have left residents stranded on roads, unable to reach their polling stations.  Residents of the Tamar Regional Council area, particularly Neot HaKikar south of the Dead Sea, have been stuck in their vehicles because of police roadblocks. Those who have yet to vote fear they will not make it home before polling stations close.     Earlier, police closed Route 90 and roads connecting Eilat with Dimona and Ein Gedi in both directions because of the severe weather. Yoni Stern, a resident of Neot HaKikar, said: "Many Arava residents, myself included, are stuck on the road and cannot exercise our right to vote. We're getting no response from the Central Elections Committee, and no response from the police. I'm stuck at Arava Junction and need to get to my polling station. They need to extend voting hours or reopen the road," he demanded. Earlier, Likud appealed to Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, demanding an extension of voting hours. The request was subsequently backed by Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit party, Aryeh Deri's Shas and Ofer Winter's Amcha Yisrael. Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! party opposed the request, joined by Naftali Bennett's Yachad and Yair Golan's Democrats. The Central Elections Committee announced that it would discuss the request.       Heavy rain across southern Israel on Tuesday caused flash floods in streams from the Eilat area through the Negev to the northern Arava and Dead Sea region. All roads leading into and out of Eilat have been closed to traffic, although residents are still permitted to leave the city to reach Ramon Airport. Police urged drivers to avoid closed roads, remain patient and follow instructions from officers at the scene. Rain also began falling in central Israel and the lowlands. Several highways in southern Israel were closed to traffic. Route 90 was blocked from Lido Junction to Eilat, with additional closures in the Dead Sea area at the hotel roundabout, Masada Junction, Nahal Arugot and David Roundabout. Route 57 was closed in both directions between Adam Junction and Bekaot Junction. Route 25 was blocked between Tzafit Junction and Arava Junction, as well as from Oron Junction toward Route 206 at Ma'ale Akrabim. Route 40 was closed between Mitzpe Ramon and Tzihor Junction, Route 13 between Menuha Junction and Tzihor Junction, and Route 12 between Eilat and Neot Smadar. At Mount Shagov near Eilat, 17 millimeters of rain were recorded in just three hours. Neot Smadar in the Arava also received an unusually large amount of rain for the area, 8.4 millimeters, roughly a quarter of its annual rainfall. In Ma'ale Adumim, 8 millimeters of rain fell from midday, while a similar amount was recorded Monday evening in Masada, south of the Sea of Galilee.

title: Lockheed Martin Showcases 1000 km PrSM Inc 4 Prototype
body: Lockheed Martin’s Precision Strike Missile (PrSM) Increment 4 prototype will use ramjet technology and an advanced sensor suite to strike moving ships over 1,000 kilometers away. “As threats evolve throughout the global theater, the Army needs a modernized precision missile that can perform at ranges far beyond current capabilities. When fired from a HIMARS launcher, PrSM Increment 4 is expected to hit both moving maritime and relocatable land targets at least 1,000 km away,” reads the Lockheed Martin release. According to a Monday release, Lockheed Martin’s PrSM Inc 4 prototype submission will use a propulsion system from L3Harris and existing guidance systems. Work from company’s Strigo Product Center, a department specializing in the development of data links, frequency sensors and missile seekers, will inform the munition’s guidance suite. The statement highlighted the “battle-proven” guidance and control systems from PrSM Inc 1. This is in reference to the missile’s engagements during Operation Epic Fury against Iranian targets. Lockheed Martin’s current PrSM Inc 1 and 2 missile production line at Camden, Arkansas, can support the production of the firm’s Inc 4 offering. According to the release, the use of existing lines will achieve “economies of scale for all versions of the missile.” The American defense firm is one of five companies down selected by the U.S. Army for the extended-range maritime strike program. Lockheed Martin’s prototype will go against submissions from Anduril, Castelion, Mach Industries and RTX. Tests in 2027 and 2028 will inform the Army’s final award. Derived from the ground branch’s operational needs , PrSM Inc 4 will form a key component of Washington’s ground-based anti-shipping capabilities against China. From launchers such as the M142 High Mobility Rocket Artillery System, U.S. forces plan to hold Chinese forces under threat from archipelagos in the First Island Chain. Canada and Australia also plan to field maritime strike PrSM variants on their HIMARS launchers. The post Lockheed Martin Showcases 1000 km PrSM Inc 4 Prototype appeared first on Naval News .

title: Algeria to Use Desert Prison in Fight Against Drug Trafficking
body: In remote southern Algeria, the Sahara Desert is known for its inhospitable conditions. In the summer, temperatures regularly exceed 51 degrees Celsius. Annual rainfall is under 20 millimeters. Vast fields of sand and extreme heat mean that there is very little life present, but soon that will change, as the government announced plans to build a prison there to hold convicted drug lords and traffickers. Algeria’s Supreme Security Council, chaired by President Abdelmadjid Tebboune, ordered the “conversion of a barracks belonging to the People’s National Army in the Grand Sahara at Tanezrouft, in the Bordj Badji Mokhtar area in Algeria’s far south, into a high-security prison for drug barons and traffickers.” The council also decided to create a special security agency to combat the country’s worsening illicit drug trade, it said in a September 2 statement. “This significant decision means that the Algerian state has decided to move from legislative deterrence to punitive deterrence in its war on drug barons and the illicit trade in psychotropic pills, because the issue of drugs has become very serious and threatens civil peace,” security expert Mabrouk Kahi told The New Arab website. Algeria has suffered from a sharp rise in drug trafficking in recent years. In a population of about 46 million there were 3 million drug addicts in 2024, according to figures released by the National Office for the Fight Against Drugs and Drug Addiction. Drug seizures have been on the rise in scale and frequency. On August 21 in Oran, police intercepted more than 10 million capsules of pregabalin, a psychotropic substance, along with 33 kilograms of cocaine in what was described as one of Algeria’s largest-ever drug seizures. Authorities recently arrested two Algerian drug kingpins who were leading major criminal networks in France. The men were thought to be hiding in Algeria to take advantage of the country’s poor diplomatic relations with France. Abdelatif Mehdi Laribi, regarded as the founder of the DZ Mafia, was arrested on July 20 under an international warrant issued by two investigating magistrates in Marseille. His cartel has established itself as one of the most powerful criminal organizations and is involved in large-scale drug trafficking and money laundering. “We are compelled to protect citizens from these scourges,” Tebboune said in an October 4 interview with several Algerian news outlets. He reiterated that the government will apply the death penalty for major drug offences. “It has become a war, a war against Algeria.” Kahi said Algeria’s plan for the Tanezrouft desert could include more than one prison. “There was a need to build prisons in the far southwest, in the areas of Bordj Badji Mokhtar, Tinzaouatine and Ain Guezzam, in the far south of the country, as a deterrent option, especially as these areas are relatively isolated, and establishing prisons there would spread fear among consumers and even traffickers,” he said. The post Algeria to Use Desert Prison in Fight Against Drug Trafficking appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: “Missiles from Israel, Firings from Greece”: Turkish Media Reacts to Joint Exercise North of Crete
body: Turkish media outlets have sharply criticized a joint naval exercise conducted by Greece and Israel in the northern Cretan Sea, describing the activity as a “dirty alliance” and warning of rising tensions in the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean. The exercise, held around 21 October 2026, focused on acceptance firings of Israeli SPIKE NLOS and ER guided missiles by the Hellenic Navy. Greek vessels, including a Machitis-class gunboat and a Mark V special operations craft, launched the missiles. The drill culminated in the sinking of the decommissioned Greek frigate Bouboulina (F-463), which was struck by SPIKE missiles and then finished off by a heavy SUT torpedo fired from a Greek submarine. Senior officers attended the event, including Hellenic National Defence General Staff Chief General Dimitrios Houpis, Hellenic Navy Chief Vice Admiral Dimitrios-Eleftherios Kataras, and Israeli Navy Chief Vice Admiral Eyal Harel. Frigates, submarines, missile boats, helicopters, special operations units, and air assets from both countries participated. The exercise also served to improve interoperability between the two navies. Coverage in Turkish media was notably critical. CNN Türk ran the headline “Missiles from Israel, firings from Greece! Dirty alliance north of Crete,” framing the drill as heightened military activity in the Eastern Mediterranean and highlighting Greece’s use of Israeli weapons systems. The newspaper Akşam used similar language, calling the cooperation a “dirty alliance in the Eastern Mediterranean” and repeating the phrase “Missiles from Israel, firings from Greece.” The pro-government newspaper Star was even more pointed, headlining: “A move that will increase tension in the Aegean! Greece fired the missiles it bought from Israel.” It focused on the operational use of the SPIKE NLOS systems and linked the exercise to closer Athens-Tel Aviv military ties. By contrast, Habertürk and the Anadolu Agency adopted a more restrained tone, simply reporting that Greece and Israel had conducted a joint training exercise and concentrating on its military aspects without using the “dirty alliance” label. The drill took place a day after the parliament in eastern Libya ratified a 2019 maritime memorandum with Turkey—an agreement rejected by Greece and condemned by Israel. It also fits into a broader pattern of deepening Greek-Israeli defense cooperation, which includes recent deals such as the multi-billion-euro “Achilles Shield” air and missile defense package. Turkish outlets presented the exercise as a signal of increased military coordination between Athens and Jerusalem in a region already marked by competing maritime claims and energy projects.
