title: US Asphyxiating, Illegal and Genocidal Blockade Policy Has Been the Main Factor Preventing Cuban Devt and That of Its People — Cuban Ambassador to Nigeria
body: Miriam Morales is the Cuban Ambassador to Nigeria. She believes her country has been held back by several sanctions imposed by Washington and calls on Nigeria and other well-meaning countries to put an end to the sanctions that have brought sorrow, tears and blood to the people of Cuba. Michael Olugbode brings you an excerpt. You have been in this country for some time now. What is your impression of Nigeria, its numerous cultures and its people? It is a breathtaking and unforgettable positive impression. Multiculturalism enriches culture and, in general, the lives of people and countries. Nigerian culture is diverse and beautiful, and so are Nigerians. Getting along with Nigerians and learning every day about the country’s history, traditions and spiritual richness have been an enormous privilege. Can you tell us about the highs and lows of your tour of duty so far in the country? For every Cuban ambassador, the central objective is to develop friendly, mutually respectful and advantageous cooperation and relations, both with the peoples and the governments of the respective host countries. For a Cuban, being posted as an ambassador to an African country, in my case Nigeria, constitutes a great challenge, taking into consideration our great African heritage. Our histories and cultures are so deeply intertwined that only good things can come from relations between our peoples and governments. That alone makes any highs and lows totally irrelevant. Anyway, life itself is full of highs and lows, and it is only our inner strength and resilience that enable us to move forward, find solutions and grow. What is the bilateral relationship like between Nigeria and Cuba, and what are the trade figures? Bilateral relations between Cuba and Nigeria were established in July 1974, and their 52nd anniversary was celebrated in July 2026. These relations are founded on deep historical, cultural and ancestral ties, as well as mutual respect. We maintain a close partnership, traditionally focused on sectors such as health, education, human resource development, science and sports, including the exchange of scholarship recipients and the presence of Cuban medical personnel. There is a shared commitment to strengthening economic, political and cultural links for the benefit of both peoples. Which areas do you think need improvement? The current world situation, in which sanctions, blackmail, impositions and wars are being used instead of cooperation and diplomacy, is imposing heavy burdens on countries worldwide. That constitutes an undeniable fact, and I am not speaking specifically about Nigeria. But let me tell you that your question could strongly stimulate the mind of any ambassador and lead to a situation in which there would not be enough space in your very important newspaper to publish the answers. But, going straight back to your question, the global situation I was talking about is particularly demanding for a small country like Cuba. Cuba is the only country in the world subjected to the longest and most inhumane blockade in modern history, now coupled with new sanctions introduced weekly, a fuel blockade and the permanent threat of military aggression. All these measures are intended to turn my country back into a subjugated colonial state under US rule, as it was until January 1959. However, Cuba has made resistance and creativity the core of its current endeavours. A new economic and social policy and programme is deeply transforming economic, trade, financial and investment relations, backed by powerful and enduring legislative activity. All these efforts are bringing Cuba into line with international standards for investment, cooperation and business in general, without abandoning the powerful social justice components that have always characterised our definition of socialism and will continue to do so. I am confident that this entire process is already offering new possibilities for further developing a bilateral relationship such as that between Cuba and Nigeria, which has traditionally been guided by positive mutual interests. An ambassador would rarely favour mentioning specific, isolated issues or areas where more could be done. Both countries will continue working together in areas where positive results have been achieved and will surely find new and diverse avenues to strengthen their bilateral relationship. Nigerians used to go to Cuba for training in medicine, but that seems to have changed. What changed? Bilateral relations between Cuba and Nigeria have always rested on mutual respect. The doors of the Latin American School of Medicine and those of every other higher education institution in Cuba will always be open to Nigerian students. Cuba was a country that was on an upward trajectory, but this seems to have changed over time. What could have been responsible for this? Almost immediately after the triumph of the Cuban Revolution, the US broke off relations and adopted a very hostile policy towards my country. From the very beginning, the main goal was to destroy the beacon of independence and sovereignty that the Revolution represented to all the subjugated countries in the Latin American region, which had suffered for decades under the oppression of successive dictatorships with direct political, financial and military support from Washington. The current blockade policy is merely the codification and highest expression of all the aggressive actions set in motion by the US since the early years of the Revolution, including the military invasion internationally known as the Bay of Pigs invasion, which represented, for the US, its first military defeat in Latin America. Cuba was then compelled to restructure all its economic, trade and financial relations and find new partners around the world. The former socialist countries of Eastern Europe, led by the Soviet Union at the time, became new partners for Cuba, based, in general terms, on shared political and ideological positions. Some other countries outside that bloc, in Africa, the Middle East and even Europe, also entered into this new relationship to varying degrees. When the so-called socialist bloc in Eastern Europe collapsed and the former Soviet Union disintegrated, Cuba was once again left with almost no markets, trade, financial cooperation or investment. That dramatic situation led to the establishment of what became known as the Special Period in my country, severely affecting the upward trajectory you have referred to. My country was once again compelled to rebuild all its external economic relations. Important socioeconomic changes were also introduced to adjust to the new and challenging situation. These included opening the country to mass international tourism and beginning to transform the Cuban legal system in relation to foreign investment. Despite navigating a very difficult economic path, the country was eventually able to begin a new period of upward growth. The situation in Latin America had started to change with the successive defeat of dictatorships and the establishment of progressive governments with different political characteristics. Strong South-South cooperation, in line with contemporary concepts, emerged but was attacked by Washington through various means. All this raised hopes across the region by opening the way for a new, qualitative form of cooperation. In the case of Cuba and Venezuela, contrary to US propaganda, a highly mutually beneficial relationship developed, which also had a positive impact on the Latin American region. So, once again, to return to your question, this ushered in a new period of upward growth. It is necessary to take into consideration that US hostility and its blockade policy against Cuba have persisted for more than six decades. Only changes in our region temporarily opened the way for Cuba, to use your words, to move upwards again. Throughout this period, we never lost sight of the fact that the US’s aggressive policy against my country was being permanently reinforced. It escalated immensely during Donald Trump’s first presidency and acquired a genocidal character with his return to the White House. There have been weekly announcements of new sanctions, the introduction of a fuel blockade and constant threats of possible military aggression. I am sure you know the rest of that history, including the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and everything that followed. These developments have created a new and complicated environment, not only for Cuba but for the entire Latin American region. Could the death of your great leader, Fidel Castro, have accounted for this, or perhaps the American blockade? Or is it that communism is no longer in vogue and your allies have dried up? Without any country having truly experienced life under communism—which, in our view, cannot simply emerge from a proclamation—we consider it the highest level of socioeconomic development, social justice and well-being for all, without simplistic egalitarianism. It is an alternative for humanity to what several left-wing politicians, economists and philosophers have described as savage capitalism. But that is only a rough definition. The overwhelming majority of Cubans still mourn, and will continue to mourn, the death of Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro. His deeds and legacy remain, and will continue to remain, a political and human inspiration for the Cuban people as we continue building an alternative to brutal capitalism. We call it socialism. The achievements and example of the Cuban Revolution are historically linked to Fidel Castro and the heroism of the Cuban people. Their influence extends far beyond our country, as you have surely seen in the celebrations of Fidel Castro’s centenary this year in Cuba and around the world. The example and influence of the Cuban Revolution must, without any doubt, be immensely strong if we consider the genocidal and irrational hostility of the world’s foremost economic and military superpower in its attempts to destroy it. The US’s asphyxiating, illegal and genocidal blockade policy has always been the main factor preventing the development of Cuba and its people, and it continues to be so today. As the week drew to a close, Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel Bermúdez and Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla strongly rejected aggressive statements and threats made against Cuba by President Trump. During a campaign rally in Fort Myers, Florida, Trump claimed that US warships would “pass by” Cuba upon returning from a war in Iran and stated that he would send Marco Rubio to “close the deal”—or, in other words, to negotiate the situation in the country. Subsequently, Marco Rubio, writing on his X account, publicly urged Cuban citizens to collaborate discreetly with the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to push for political change on the island. If not, what could explain US Secretary of State Marco Rubio leading a campaign of defamation, lies and hatred against the island and its people, while threatening, blackmailing and intimidating independent, sovereign states with the spectre of illegal sanctions in an effort to change their longstanding position of support for the UN resolution calling for the elimination of the economic, trade and financial embargo against Cuba on October 28? What is the relationship between your country and America like? What about other countries, especially China and Russia, which have deep roots in socialism? The Cuban government and people have no negative or hostile feelings towards the American people. In fact, there has been a growing sentiment among the American people in favour of a change in policy towards Cuba, with calls for the elimination of the blockade and descriptions of it as useless and obsolete. That sentiment is stronger today than ever before. As for those in the White House, the Cuban government, even under the current circumstances, has reiterated its readiness to discuss any issue relating to bilateral relations on an equal footing. It also believes there are concrete areas for mutually beneficial cooperation. In Cuba’s position, there is no room for impositions of any kind, dictating the type of political system Cuba should have or imposing changes in the Cuban leadership. Cuba will never surrender its independence and sovereignty. Some communication channels remain open, although it has not been possible to establish an agenda for dialogue. Nevertheless, high-ranking representatives of the US government, including President Donald Trump, continue to claim from time to time that talks are taking place, as part of what we consider a disinformation campaign and an irresponsible appetite for fake news. These claims have been accompanied by persistent hostile actions, such as last week’s decision by Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier to charge Army General Raúl Castro with conspiracy to commit first-degree murder. The charge was based largely on a federal indictment announced last May that included allegations concerning the downing of an aircraft belonging to the organisation “Brothers to the Rescue”, which Cuba considers a terrorist organisation. There was also the US mission to the United Nations orchestrating an anti-Cuba event at UN headquarters, in what we consider a direct violation of the UN Charter, as part of the campaign surrounding the October 28 UN resolution on the blockade. Our relations with Russia and China are based on deep-rooted historical ties, cooperation and exchanges in almost all areas of mutual bilateral interest, including international affairs. They also involve diverse organisations striving to place international collaboration in a different perspective, emphasising mutually beneficial projects and programmes within the framework of South-South cooperation. Have you thought of meeting America halfway for the blockade to be lifted? The Cuban government has reiterated several times that it is open to dialogue and negotiations on the basis I have already explained. The blockade is really affecting Cuba. Do you think the international community has done enough to assist Cuba in getting it lifted? On October 27 and 28, the UN General Assembly will consider, for the 34th time, the resolution entitled “Need to put an end to the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed by the United States of America against Cuba”. The overwhelming majority of UN member states have historically rejected the US blockade against Cuba, regardless of the potential risks. Threats, impositions, manoeuvres and blackmail have always existed, although never before as part of such an open international campaign, now prioritised by what remains of US foreign policy, which openly and shamelessly exhibits its brutal imperial characteristics. For the first time, following the considerations made last July, the UN General Assembly will take a position through a resolution against the energy blockade, the fuel blockade and the collective punishment that such a policy represents for the entire Cuban people. For decades, the international community has maintained a clear, longstanding and almost unanimous position in support of the immediate and unconditional elimination of the blockade against Cuba. What is new, as I have already said, is the existence of such a brutal campaign, exemplified by an official US State Department document sent to its embassies, instructing them to exert pressure on host governments not to vote in favour of what it describes as “Cuban propaganda”. This is as though the blockade and its humanitarian consequences were not part of a reality that nobody can deny. Even under these unbelievable circumstances, Cuba remains confident that the resolution will receive majority international support. I would like to take this opportunity to express the profound gratitude of the Cuban government and people for Nigeria’s support in the international arena, most notably regarding its vote in the United Nations General Assembly against the economic, commercial and financial blockade imposed on Cuba. I reiterate that the vote will take place on October 28. I am grateful to the newspaper THISDAY for providing the opportunity to present the situation in my country within the current context experienced by the Cuban people.

title: US Visa Bond: Full list of countries, including Nigeria, required to pay up to $20,000
body: The United States has listed 50 countries whose citizens must pay a visa bond of up to $20,000 when applying for certain visitor visas, including Nigeria, according to the US Department of State. The measure applies to eligible applicants for B-1 business and B-2 tourist visas travelling on passports issued by the listed countries. The bond amounts are $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, with the specific amount determined by a consular officer during the visa interview. In a notice published on October 2, 2026, the Department of State outlined the countries subject to the visa bond programme and their respective implementation dates. The programme operates under Section 221(g)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, with the department stating that the requirement applies regardless of where an applicant submits their visa application. Full list of countries subject to US visa bonds The 50 countries listed by the US Department of State, alongside their implementation dates, are: Algeria — January 21, 2026 Angola — January 21, 2026 Antigua and Barbuda — January 21, 2026 Bangladesh — January 21, 2026 Benin — January 21, 2026 Bhutan — January 1, 2026 Botswana — January 1, 2026 Burundi — January 21, 2026 Cabo Verde — January 21, 2026 Cambodia — April 2, 2026 Central African Republic — January 1, 2026 Côte d’Ivoire — January 21, 2026 Cuba — January 21, 2026 Djibouti — January 21, 2026 Dominica — January 21, 2026 Ethiopia — April 2, 2026 Fiji — January 21, 2026 Gabon — January 21, 2026 The Gambia — October 11, 2025 Georgia — April 2, 2026 Grenada — April 2, 2026 Guinea — January 1, 2026 Guinea-Bissau — January 1, 2026 Kyrgyz Republic — January 21, 2026 Lesotho — April 2, 2026 Malawi — August 20, 2025 Mauritania — October 23, 2025 Mauritius — April 2, 2026 Mongolia — April 2, 2026 Mozambique — April 2, 2026 Namibia — January 1, 2026 Nepal — January 21, 2026 Nicaragua — April 2, 2026 Nigeria — January 21, 2026 Papua New Guinea — April 2, 2026 São Tomé and Príncipe — October 23, 2025 Senegal — January 21, 2026 Seychelles — April 2, 2026 Tajikistan — January 21, 2026 Tanzania — October 23, 2025 Togo — January 21, 2026 Tonga — January 21, 2026 Tunisia — April 2, 2026 Turkmenistan — January 1, 2026 Tuvalu — January 21, 2026 Uganda — January 21, 2026 Vanuatu — January 21, 2026 Venezuela — January 21, 2026 Zambia — August 20, 2025 Zimbabwe — January 21, 2026 How much must Nigerians pay for a US visa bond? Nigerian citizens applying for B-1 business or B-2 tourist visas may be required to post a bond of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 if they are otherwise eligible for the visa. The amount is determined during the visa interview. The bond is an additional financial requirement and does not guarantee that the applicant will receive a visa. Applicants must submit Department of Homeland Security Form I-352 and agree to the bond’s terms through the US Department of the Treasury’s Pay.gov platform. The department warns applicants not to pay a bond before being instructed to do so by a consular officer. Applicants are expected to use the specific payment link supplied through official instructions. The bond may be paid by the applicant or a third party, such as a relative, friend or business associate. However, the name of the person identified as the bond obligor on Form I-352 must match the name of the person making the payment. If the bond conditions are satisfied, the money is refundable under the programme’s terms. US visa bond holders restricted to commercial air entry The programme also imposes travel conditions on people who post visa bonds. According to the State Department, bond holders must enter and leave the United States through designated commercial air ports of entry, including US Customs and Border Protection preclearance locations. They are not permitted to use charter aircraft, general aviation, land borders or sea ports of entry under the stated bond conditions. Failure to comply with the designated entry and exit requirements could result in problems with entry or the recording of a traveller’s departure. When will the US refund visa bonds? The department outlined several circumstances under which a bond may be cancelled and the deposit returned automatically. These include cases where the visa expires and the holder has not travelled to the United States, or where the holder has complied with the visa conditions and departed within the authorise Vanguard News The post US Visa Bond: Full list of countries, including Nigeria, required to pay up to $20,000 appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Senate Passes bill to jail oil polluters, impose heavier fine
body: By Henry Umoru ABUJA- THE Senate has passed a bill that would strengthen the National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA) with powers to impose heavier fines and criminal penalties for oil spill violations. The bill is titled National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (Establishment) Act (Amendment) Bill, 2026, was passed after the Senate adopted the report of its Committee on Environment. The bill seeks to amend the NOSDRA Establishment Act 2006 to provide statutory backing for adequate fines and criminal sanctions to enforce environmental laws in the petroleum sector. In his presentation of the report, Chairman Senator Olubiyi Fadeyi, Senate Chief Whip Senator Tahir Monguno (Borno North) said the amendment addresses persistent pollution in the Niger Delta. He said oil spills have continued to devastate the environment and destroy livelihoods, particularly fishing and farming, in oil-producing communities. According to Monguno, existing penalties have failed to deter offenders, necessitating tougher sanctions. “The fines are not deterrent enough to deter offenders,” he told the Senate, adding that the bill introduces criminal liability for spills that damage the environment and deprive residents of their means of livelihood. The Senate dissolved into Committee of the Whole to consider the bill clause by clause and approved Clauses 1 to 12, including the short title, explanatory memorandum and long title. Upon reverting to plenary, the Senate read the bill a third time and passed it. The law is expected to boost NOSDRA’s enforcement capacity and provide a stronger framework for tackling oil spill violations. The President Godswill Akpabio hailed the Environment Committee for its work and congratulated NOSDRA on the additional powers granted by the legislation. ENDS The post Senate Passes bill to jail oil polluters, impose heavier fine appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Boeing commercial aircraft losses more than double despite production recovery
body:
Boeing's commercial aircraft business more than doubled its operating loss in the third quarter of 2026 despite continued progress in the production of the 737 and 787.
Boeing Commercial Airplanes lost US$697 million between July and September, compared with US$322 million in the previous quarter. Revenue reached US$10.72 billion, down from US$11.13 billion in the second quarter.
The manufacturer attributed the weaker result to a less favorable mix of aircraft delivered, higher expected costs associated with future production-rate changes and increased estimates for supply-chain expenses.
Compared with a year earlier, the division's loss fell sharply from US$5.35 billion. That comparison is distorted, however, by a US$4.9 billion charge related to the 777X that Boeing recorded in the third quarter of 2025.
Follow Air Data News: WhatsApp | Instagram | LinkedIn | Twitter | Facebook
For the first nine months of 2026, Commercial Airplanes generated US$31.67 billion in revenue, 5% more than a year earlier, while its operating loss fell from US$6.45 billion to US$1.58 billion.
The continued losses contrast with a manufacturing operation that has been gradually recovering from years of disruptions and restrictions.
Boeing said 737 production is progressing toward a stable rate of 47 aircraft per month. The company had been producing 38 per month a year ago before receiving approval from the Federal Aviation Administration to increase output.
The 787 is currently stable at eight aircraft per month, another increase from the seven-per-month rate reported a year earlier.
Boeing delivered 161 commercial aircraft during the third quarter, virtually unchanged from the 160 handed over during the same period in 2025. The total comprised 124 737s, 22 787s, ten 767s and five 777s.
Deliveries reached 475 aircraft during the first nine months of 2026, compared with 440 a year earlier. The 737 accounted for 367 of the total, followed by 62 787s, 26 767s and 20 777s.
While Boeing continues working to increase production, the number of aircraft it has already sold but still needs to build has grown further.
Commercial Airplanes ended September with more than 6,300 aircraft in its backlog, valued at a record US$612 billion. A year earlier, the backlog comprised more than 5,900 aircraft worth US$535 billion.
The manufacturer recorded 300 net commercial aircraft orders during the third quarter, including business from Turkish Airlines, Ethiopian Airlines and Lufthansa.
The combination of a growing backlog and higher production rates makes the cost of increasing output particularly important. Boeing specifically cited expenses associated with future rate changes and higher supply-chain cost estimates among the factors affecting the third-quarter result.
Boeing also cleared two major certification milestones during the period.
The 737-7 received its amended type certificate from the FAA during the third quarter, clearing the smallest member of the current MAX family for service after years of delays.
The 737-10 followed in October . The largest MAX variant received FAA certification on October 20, completing approval of all four passenger versions of the family: the 737-7, 737-8, 737-9 and 737-10.
The 777X remains Boeing's major commercial aircraft program still undergoing certification. Flight testing of the 777-9 continues, with the manufacturer maintaining its expectation of delivering the first aircraft in 2027.

title: Finnish and Norwegian leaders discuss Ukraine peace with Putin as a source close to the Kremlin warns of escalating hybrid warfare with Europe
body: Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre. October 20, 2026 Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin. Western leaders initiated the call to discuss Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts to end it. The Finnish president’s office said the call was meant “to convey messages directly regarding future negotiations to help to end the war to President Putin” ahead of meetings to be held in Abu Dhabi. It was Putin’s first contact with European leaders supporting Ukraine since July 2025, when he spoke with French President Emmanuel Macron. The Kremlin confirmed the call, saying Putin “assessed the current situation” in Ukraine and reminded participants of the “root causes of the conflict.” Putin also pointed to the “confrontational policy of EU and NATO countries, which is prolonging the fighting,” the Kremlin’s press service said. Volodymyr Zelensky said Stubb and Støre briefed him on their call with Putin. “Alex and Jonas made it clear to the Russian leader that real de-escalatory steps are needed regarding our energy and infrastructure,” Zelensky said. He added that the Finnish and Norwegian leaders had discussed preparations for a trilateral meeting between negotiating teams from Ukraine, the United States, and Russia. Stubb’s office said the call “was a follow-up of the meeting in Oslo on October 20 and held in consultation with Ukraine.” The Norwegian capital hosted talks that day between Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and Zelensky, with Støre and Stubb also taking part. Witkoff then traveled to St. Petersburg to meet with Putin before returning to Oslo and flying home to the United States. Those trips produced an agreement on a trilateral meeting between the United States, Ukraine, and Russia, to be held in Abu Dhabi. The meeting will take place after November 4, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said. The day before, on November 3, the United States will hold midterm elections in which Republicans could lose their congressional majority. Announcing the timing, Ushakov said the peace talks would also have to involve “all of Europe.” Europe has long sought a negotiator to represent the European Union’s interests in talks on ending the war between Russia and Ukraine. Stubb has repeatedly been named as a candidate for the role, having built a good relationship with Trump, including on the golf course, and emerged as one of Trump’s main points of contact with European leaders. The Telegraph has also named Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and Czech President Petr Pavel among the candidates. After Stubb and Støre’s call with Putin, Frederiksen criticized the initiative, saying she was “skeptical” and that the talks had not been coordinated with other European leaders. She added that she sees no sign that Russia wants peace with Europe, either in the hybrid war that continues every day or in Ukraine. The independent Russian political newsletter Faridaily says contacts between European leaders and the Kremlin amount to “a significant shift in position.” European leaders had “mostly preferred not to talk to Putin at all” since the war began. However, a source close to the Kremlin said that “events are moving toward escalation, including an intensification of hybrid warfare with Europe.” According to the source, Putin is convinced NATO is waging a hybrid war against Russia and blames Ukraine’s European allies for “comprehensive assistance” in attacks on Russia, including helping identify targets and guide strikes. A source close to the Kremlin told Reuters that Putin told Stubb and Støre that Russia would not abandon its goal of capturing all of the Donbas. The European leaders responded that a “just” peace was necessary, the source added. The war in photographs. title: Oil tanker on fire after hitting mines in Hormuz: Iran Army
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – The Iranian army on Tuesday said an oil tanker hit mines and caught fire while attempting to cross the Strait of Hormuz via a route not authorized by Tehran.
"A few hours ago, an oil tanker in breach of regulations, having switched off its tracking systems and attempted to cross a prohibited and dangerous area east of the Strait of Hormuz, struck naval mines, causing damage and a fire," the army said in a statement carried by local Iranian media.
The Iranian military has reported on multiple occasions that tankers struck naval mines while attempting to transit areas Tehran considers off-limits.

title: Anthropic's IPO could be 'speculative fiction' or a 'generational moment' — investors are split
body:
Anthropic's IPO prospectus is chock-full of details for investors to celebrate — and worry about.
The company's bulls are cheering its 1,300% annual sales growth, 900% net revenue retention and 85% implied gross margin. But its bears are pointing to roughly $80 billion in half-year net losses, hundreds of billions of dollars' worth of compute commitments and more than 90 pages of risk factors .
From either camp, the numbers are staggering, and they put Anthropic in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history . The IPO is also pushing investors firmly into uncharted territory as they work to value the first pure-play artificial intelligence company to go public at a time of rising interest rates and growing concerns about the size of the AI buildout.
Anthropic was valued in May at $965 billion, and is reportedly looking for an IPO valuation in the range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, which would instantly make it one of the 10 most valuable U.S. tech companies.
"This is a generational moment, and we'll look back in a decade, and this was the biggest paradigm shift in technology that will shape our lives like nothing else has," Denny Fish , a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told CNBC's "The Exchange" on Monday. "The devil comes down to the details, and we still don't have all the details yet."
Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a group of researchers who defected from OpenAI , is best known for its Claude AI models and services sold through enterprise contracts and subscriptions.
In its long-awaited prospectus on Monday , Anthropic said its enterprise customer base included more than 11,900 customers with at least $100,000 spend over the prior year, more than 1,900 clients spending $1 million or more and roughly 250 customers spending $10 million or more. In the first nine months of 2026, five customers accounted for about a quarter of its revenue.
"I think it's really easy to lose sight of how early it is, and to see a business like Anthropic doing this well this early on in the journey is incredibly impressive," Erica Brescia , a managing director at Redpoint Ventures, told CNBC's "The Exchange" on Monday.
"There's still an astronomical opportunity ahead for Anthropic," said Brescia, whose firm is an investor in the company. "And I think this is a really exciting opportunity for retail investors to get a piece and to get to participate in this transformation outside of buying chip stocks."
For many investors focused on business fundamentals, Anthropic is a tough sell.
The company lost $80.7 billion in the first six months of this year, after reporting a loss of $12.9 billion over the same stretch in 2025, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Meanwhile, its compute commitments are soaring while competition is picking up from lower-cost open-weight models.
David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, describes Anthropic's upcoming offering as "a huge Wall Street grift."
Trainer has built a reputation on Wall Street as a notorious bear on IPOs. His firm published a report last month arguing that Anthropic is the " most ridiculous IPO of 2026 " and that it will be an "unprecedented test of investor gullibility."
Having reviewed the prospectus, Trainer told CNBC in an interview on Tuesday that his position hasn't changed. He said AI will be an "amazing tool for society," but not so much for businesses, and he's worried about Anthropic's competitive position, its "opaque" insider selling schedule, and the fact that its commitments and liabilities dwarf its cash.
"All these people have stakes in Anthropic. They want to be able to cash out," Trainer said. "Having lived through the tech bubble, having lived through the great financial crisis, having been on Wall Street during those times, having seen how the sausage is made, it's like a slow-moving train wreck for me."
Roger McNamee, an early investor in both Google and Facebook, told CNBC on Tuesday that the Anthropic IPO is a "very dangerous thing for investors," adding that the industry still has a lot to prove.
"We should view this S-1 as speculative fiction because it's a great story, it's a really great story, but it's hundreds of pages, and those hundreds of pages are not there to clarify the story," McNamee, co-founder of Elevation Partners, told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "And based on the feedback I get on [X], a lot of people who disagree with me are sitting there going, 'I love this story,' and I go, 'Look, God bless, it's your money.'"
Anthropic's public filing brings it one step closer to its IPO, but there are still hurdles to clear to reach the starting line.
On its roadshow, the company will have to woo prospective investors, gauge demand, set the IPO offer price and allocate shares. Once all of that is complete, it will finally list on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol "ANT."
Investors will be watching each development and detail closely.
Gil Luria , managing director at D.A. Davidson, said he wants to know a lot more before the company's debut. That includes the path to long-term profitability and, importantly, the valuation. He said in an interview on Tuesday that if the IPO is priced correctly, it will likely do "very well."
"We can talk about the risks, but as we sit here right now, and based on what we know right now, Anthropic is still the main AI company, and it's a pure play," Luria said. "So the IPO should go well because investors will want exposure to the pure play."

title: Ukraine Moves Closer to Its Own Satellite Network as Test Craft Reaches Orbit
body:
Ukrainian communications company Himera and Danish satellite manufacturer GomSpace have sent Obria nano, a test satellite, into orbit as the first step toward an independent Ukrainian communications network.
Himera told Ukrainska Pravda on Tuesday, Oct. 27, that the satellite reached orbit aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission on Oct. 1, and is reportedly already operating.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
“The technical trials should provide the practical experience needed for the project’s further development into Ukrainian national infrastructure,” Himera said.
While the launch relied on a SpaceX rocket, the satellite itself will be controlled by a Ukrainian operator and will serve Ukraine’s strategic security needs. The project comes as Kyiv seeks to reduce its dependence on SpaceX’s Starshield service amid recent disruptions and diplomatic tensions with Washington.
Ukraine’s dependence on foreign-made technology creates strategic risks, especially during wartime, Himera argued. Building capabilities domestically, the company said, would widen the country’s communication options and strengthen its security.
In the long term, the company plans to deploy a satellite constellation covering all of Ukraine’s territory.
The network would also complement existing European satellite systems and form the basis of a sovereign Ukrainian communications system.
Moving production of satellites and ground terminals to Ukraine is Himera’s next priority, as this could help Kyiv build its own expertise in satellite communications, while gradually expanding domestic manufacturing.
Ukraine also signed seven agreements with Finland on Oct. 22, including deals to expand Kyiv’s use of Finnish satellite capabilities through Nokia and ICEYE.
“We agreed that we will make greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities,” President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier. “This is important for our defense and for Ukraine’s resilience.”
A unit of the Main Directorate of Intelligence ( HUR ) had tested Himera’s tactical radios – HIMERA G1 PRO radios and HIMERA B1 repeater – in real combat conditions, the company said in a statement on Oct. 15.
HUR testers reportedly praised the devices’ durable casing, simple setup, compact repeater and a long battery life.
According to Himera, the radios ran for up to four days on a single charge, even in low temperatures and high humidity.
However, the main improvement users requested was much better sound quality for the G1 PRO. At the time, Himera said it had already sent some users a beta version and reported collecting their feedback for the next update.
Meanwhile, Russia is working on its own, domestic alternative to Starlink.
Built by the Russian company Bureau 1440, Rassvet is a low-orbit satellite broadband service that users can connect to through dedicated terminals that relay data to satellites overhead.
Major General Ilya Pavlenko, who served as deputy chief of the Defense Ministry’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) from 2015 to 2020 told Interfax-Ukraine that Russia’s growing Rassvet satellite network could eventually allow its forces to control long-range drones over Ukraine in real time.
He cautioned against writing off the project because of problems with its first satellites , arguing that the network could later be used as another tool for hybrid warfare against Europe.
Bureau 1440 says the finished system will operate at an altitude of about 800 kilometers (497 miles), deliver speeds of up to 1 Gbps with delays of up to 70 milliseconds, and use 5G non-terrestrial network standards and laser links between satellites.
According to Pavlenko, Russia is also moving its jet drone factories underground, which could further limit Ukraine’s ability to break manufacturing cycles or destroy the drones.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

title: Google Deepmind's Genie 4 puts a modern spin on agent designs that predate LLMs
body:
Genie 4 is supposed to simulate interactive worlds in real time, including sound and talking characters. Gemini models plan in the background what happens next in the simulation. Only select testers can try the world model for now.
Google Deepmind has introduced Genie 4 , the successor to Genie 3 , which the company showed in August 2025. The world model doesn't produce finished videos but calculates a scene frame by frame, reacting to input as it goes. Users move through the scene with the keyboard and steer events with text prompts.
According to Deepmind, Genie 4 is the company's first real-time world model that generates sound directly. The company says each world has its own background audio, such as wind in the trees. Genie 4 also handles dialogue, with characters that are supposed to talk to each other and react in real time to user input or events. Ad
Deepmind sees the biggest gain in realism in how the model renders people. Characters are supposed to move naturally and react to their surroundings, and users should be able to control them directly. Ad
According to Deepmind, Genie 4 builds on capabilities of the video model Gemini Omni so the world looks and behaves realistically. Other Gemini models help plan the simulation to keep it consistent.
If a user changes the weather with a text prompt, Gemini is supposed to adapt the instruction to the running scene. Deepmind says Gemini also steers events between inputs so the world keeps developing in a way that makes sense. Ad
Deepmind explains the process with multistep tasks. Gemini 3.8 Flash watches the scene continuously, breaks a goal into steps, and uses new frames to check whether each step worked. If the world changes or the user steps in, the model adjusts its plan.
Deepmind is also testing Gemini 4 Argon to tie its Genie work to its robotics research, Gemini Robotics. In one demo, Argon breaks the task of playing checkers into steps. Genie 4 gets these as text instructions and uses them to simulate Apptronik's humanoid robot Apollo playing the game, with no real robot involved. Ad
Deepmind calls Genie 4 an early, experimental model. According to the company, the world stays consistent over short sessions, but visual details can shift and objects don't always persist in longer simulations or after several complex prompt changes. Ad
Deepmind says it's still researching complex physical interactions, accurate real-time sound, and readable text.
For now, Genie 4 is only available to select testers as a research preview. It's set to reach Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Project Genie web app soon, along with partners who have early access to the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.
Google says all videos and audio tracks will carry its SynthID watermark, which invisibly marks AI-generated content.
Once they mature, world models could serve as training environments where robots and AI agents learn from simulated experience rather than just from data. Deepmind sees pairing Gemini with Genie as an early step toward hybrid world models that combine the reasoning of language and code models with pixel-level simulation.

title: Sultan Of Sokoto To Turban Peter Igho As Kakakin Daular Usmaniyya
body: The Sultan of Sokoto, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar III, will formally turban veteran broadcaster and television producer, Chief Peter Igho, as Kakakin Daular Usmaniyya on Sunday, November 1, 2026. A statement from the Sultan’s Palace in Sokoto said the ceremony would take place at the palace, following the conferment of the traditional title on Igho on September 10, 2025. The title was bestowed on Igho in recognition of his contributions to the development of the Sultanate Council, Sokoto State and Nigeria. The ceremony is expected to attract prominent Nigerians from different walks of life and across the country, with the aim of strengthening cordial relations and promoting national unity among Nigeria’s diverse communities. Igho is a veteran Nigerian broadcaster, television producer and media personality who served as an Executive Director at the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA). He is best known for producing and directing Cock Crow at Dawn, one of Nigeria’s pioneering television dramas, as well as other programmes that helped shape the country’s broadcasting industry. He has received several national and international awards for his contributions to broadcasting and has mentored generations of media professionals. A native of the Niger Delta, Igho is also recognised for his cultural advocacy, community leadership and philanthropy. The Sultan of Sokoto, who will preside over the ceremony, is the 20th occupant of the throne and President-General of the Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs (NSCIA). He ascended the throne on November 2, 2006. A retired Brigadier-General of the Nigerian Army, Sultan Abubakar is widely respected for his advocacy for peace, interfaith dialogue, education and national unity. The Sultanate traces its heritage to the Sokoto Caliphate, also known as Daular Usmaniyya, founded in 1804 by Islamic scholar and reformer, Shehu Usman Dan Fodio. At its peak, the Caliphate was the largest state in West Africa and became known for its scholarship, administration, justice and promotion of Islamic values. Today, the Sultanate Council remains a major custodian of that heritage and an important institution for Islamic leadership, peacebuilding and national cohesion in Nigeria. The post Sultan Of Sokoto To Turban Peter Igho As Kakakin Daular Usmaniyya appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Lawmakers move to make formal identification compulsory for renting apartments in Abuja
body:
The Senate on Tuesday resolved to initiate legislation requiring tenants in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja, to present valid means of identification before renting apartments as part of efforts to curb criminal activities.
The Senate President, Godswill Akpabio , directed the Senate Leader, Opeyemi Bamidele, to draft the bill for consideration by the National Assembly.
Mr Akpabio gave the directive during the plenary while lawmakers were debating a report by the Senate committees on Diaspora and Non-Governmental Organisations; Judiciary, Human Rights and Legal Matters; Foreign Affairs; and Special Duties on the need to protect Nigerians from being trafficked to Libya for slavery.
The report was presented by Aniekan Bassey, chair of the Senate Committee on Diaspora and Non-Governmental Organisations.
Mr Akpabio expressed concern that many property owners rent out their properties to strangers without obtaining adequate information about their identities, occupations and other relevant details.
He argued that the lack of proper documentation makes it difficult for security agencies to trace suspects when crimes are committed, allowing perpetrators to escape without leaving a clear trail.
“A lot of people just give their properties to strangers. They don’t even have any papers to know where they come from. In some instances, the phone number that is used in renting the property does not even belong to the occupant of the house. So when something happens, the person will escape and then leave no trace,” he said.
The Senate President urged Mr Bamidele to consider legislation that would strengthen tenancy regulations and make landlords more accountable for verifying prospective tenants’ identities.
“People enter people’s properties with very nefarious intentions and, at the end of the day, they will just commit some crimes, traffic people’s children and make money while living in the house itself. It is something that we must tighten the laws on tenancy,” he said.
Mr Akpabio proposed adopting an approach similar to the banking sector’s Know Your Customer (KYC) policy, which requires financial institutions to verify customers’ identities.
“As you know in the bank, they say, know your customer; this one we can say, know your tenants. Let’s make the necessary law for the FCT, for instance. We can enact an Act for the FCT that says know your tenants so that nobody will come and live in the house and perpetrate crime,” he said.
He said the proposed legislation could also cover the rental of shops and other commercial spaces, arguing that inadequate identity verification could expose occupants and business owners to criminal attacks.
Mr Akpabio said people renting shops should provide verifiable identification, including a driver’s licence or international passport, to help security agencies trace them if they are implicated in criminal activities.
He said the lack of reliable tenant information could leave property owners unable to identify or help locate people who used their premises to commit crimes.
“And then even those that are going to do shoplets, we can use that opportunity to regulate shoplets because people go into secluded environments and then do shoplets, and then they move in and they rob them in the night and escape.
“So people who want to do shoplifting should have clear identities; you should be able to show either a driver’s licence or an international passport and other means of identification so that if you stay in somebody’s property and then you go and commit a crime, when they trace and come there and find out that this was where you live, the owner of the property may not even have an idea of who you were.”
To support his argument, Mr Akpabio recalled measures his administration introduced to tackle kidnapping when he was governor of Akwa Ibom State.
He said his government prescribed the death penalty for kidnapping and introduced measures involving the destruction of property used as hideouts by criminals.
The Senate President noted that the measures encouraged landlords to monitor activities on their premises and report suspicious behaviour for fear of losing them.
He said similar measures could help deter criminals from using rented apartments and commercial premises as bases for criminal activities.
If enacted as envisaged by the Senate President, the proposed legislation would require landlords in the FCT to verify prospective tenants’ identities before letting out their property.
The proposal is intended to help security agencies trace people suspected of committing crimes from their residential addresses and discourage criminals from using rented apartments and commercial premises as hideouts.
However, its effectiveness would depend on the legislation’s details, including how identities would be verified, what records landlords would be required to keep, and how compliance would be monitored.
If enacted, the law could make it easier for investigators to establish the identities of tenants linked to rented property. It could also impose additional responsibilities on landlords and property agents, potentially requiring them to retain identification records and provide relevant information to authorised authorities when legally required.
The proposal could, however, raise concerns about privacy, the security of tenants’ personal information and the possibility of landlords using the requirement to discriminate against prospective tenants or deny accommodation to people who cannot readily provide the prescribed documents.
The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 provides a framework for lawful, secure handling of personal information. Any system requiring landlords to collect and retain tenants’ identification details would need to comply with applicable data protection obligations.
The proposal remains in the drafting stage, based on the proceedings described by the Senate President. It would need to go through the legislative process before becoming law.

title: Third Russia-Africa Summit Follows Unmet Expectations
body: As Vladimir Putin prepares to host his third Russia-Africa Summit at the end of October, observers are looking at previous summits for clues about how to evaluate the promises and deals expected to be inked in Moscow. The first summit held in Sochi in 2019 was met with “enthusiasm” by the 43 African heads of state who attended, according to Dr. Joseph Siegle, director of research at the Africa Center for Strategic Studies. “There was a sense that Russia may represent a new source of investment and trade that would open up more economic opportunities,” Siegle told ADF. So far, those opportunities have failed to materialize. At the first summit, Russia pledged to double trade with Africa in five years from about $20 billion to $40 billion. What happened, instead, was a contraction of trade to $14 billion over five years. It has since rebounded to about $27 billion, but that total is lopsided in favor of Moscow, which exports about seven times more than it imports from Africa. Russia accounts for less than 1% of foreign direct investment on the continent. “There was a recognition that Russia didn’t really have a lot to offer economically to the continent,” Siegle said, adding that, “by 2023 there was a lot more skepticism toward Moscow.” The 2023 summit in St. Petersburg occurred a year after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with only 17 heads of state in attendance. The meeting took place as Russia was attacking commercial vessels on the Black Sea and blockading vital shipments of grain and fertilizer to the continent. One of the highlights of the summit was a pledge by Putin to donate 25,000 to 50,000 tons of grain to six African countries. But observers noted that this pledge to preferred countries accounted for only a small fraction of the hundreds of thousands of tons being held up by Russia’s blockade of shipments on the Black Sea. “The donations were a drop in the bucket to the constrictions on grain, fertilizer, and fuel that have been caused,” Siegle said. As of 2026, attacks on commercial vessels continue. In July alone, Russia launched at least 23 strikes against the port infrastructure of Greater Odesa, where most of Ukraine’s wheat and agricultural products are stored and shipped. Goods destined for Africa and elsewhere continue to be stuck in storage facilities in Ukraine and Russia due to the war. Prices of food and fertilizer remain elevated. Egypt, the top global buyer of wheat from the region, will receive about one-tenth of the amount it did last year, Reuters reported. “When Russia attacks vessels in Odesa Bay, it is not merely disrupting Ukraine’s exports — it is increasing the risk of a genuine global food crisis,” Illia Kabachynskyi wrote for United24 Media. “This global price effect falls hardest on countries that already spend a disproportionately large share of their budgets on food imports.” The 2023 summit was marked by a pledge to forgive $23 billion in Soviet-era debt owed by African countries. But observers noted that this debt was so old that it was unserviceable by modern Russia. Siegle called the pledge “symbolic.” “Those debts were incurred so far back that they weren’t actually adding to the interest and debt burdens that African countries were paying and therefore did not change the economic picture that they are facing,” he said. “So, officially, it wipes the slate clean and allows relationships to move forward, but from a practical standpoint it didn’t mean that much.” Another feature of the summits has been the signing of military cooperation agreements. More than 40 African countries have reportedly signed such agreements with Russia. However, experts have pointed out that military-to-military cooperation remains very small in scope. The primary tool of engagement continues to be mercenaries with the state-backed Africa Corps present in the Central African Republic, Libya, Mali and elsewhere. Writing for Nigeria’s This Day news site, researcher Oumarou Sanou said the pitch to African nations at the summit is principally one of “regime protection” made to the increasing numbers of leaders who take power through coups or other non-democratic means. “Moscow’s pitch to Africa rests on a narrower premise than its rhetoric suggests, not development, not shared prosperity, but protection, delivered through private military contractors and now the state-run Africa Corps,” Sanou wrote. As the third summit approaches, observers are tallying a lack of tangible results from earlier events, including the proposal that summits would soon take place in Africa. “Between the promise of a rotating host country which never materialized, unmet trade goals, and economic commitments that remain limited, several announcements made at previous summits are struggling to produce the results that were hoped for,” analyst Mustapha Bature Sallama wrote for the Modern Ghana website. Approximately 17 heads of state have confirmed attendance for the 2026 event with some delegations reportedly questioning why they are being asked to fly to an active war zone. Sallama said the location alone highlights what he describes as an unequal partnership. “The fact that a third consecutive summit is being held in Russia illustrates the disconnect between the rhetoric of a ‘partnership of equals,’ and a relationship whose agenda, priorities and organization continue to be defined, largely, from Moscow,” Sallama said. Tale of the tape: Promises meet reality as third Russia-Africa summit approaches Pledge In 2019, Russia promised to double trade with Africa to $40 billion annually. Reality Trade dropped to $14 billion and has only rebounded to $27 billion, with the trade balance heavily in favor of Russian exports. Pledge Russia said it would donate wheat and fertilizer to address disruptions caused by its war against Ukraine. Reality Blockades continue to disrupt shipping in the Black Sea and attacks on commercial infrastructure have sent shockwaves through grain and fertilizer markets. Russia delivered 25,000 to 50,000 tons of grain to six countries, but that represents a small fraction of pre-war exports. Pledge Russia announced a debt forgiveness program for African countries Reality The $23 billion in forgiven debt was from the Soviet era and, experts say, was unserviceable and does not affect the debt burden of modern African countries. Pledge Russia announced military cooperation agreements with 40 African countries. Reality Moscow’s security engagement on the continent remains largely conducted by Africa Corps mercenaries which operate in a handful of countries. Billed as counterterror forces, they have failed to halt the spread of terror in the Sahel and now mainly offer “regime protection” for autocratic leaders. Pledge Statements at the 2023 summit indicated a future summit would take place on the African continent. Reality The 2026 summit is set to take place in Moscow, forcing attendees to travel to an active war zone. The post Third Russia-Africa Summit Follows Unmet Expectations appeared first on Africa Defense Forum .

title: US Army looks to high-flying balloons to help see, strike along front lines with China
body: To burst China’s anti-access/area-denial bubble, the U.S. Army is looking at using high-flying balloons with payloads that can monitor the battlefield, relay communications and strike adversaries. The Army has tinkered with high-altitude balloons for some time, but interest and experimentation have grown in recent years. Against China’s growing arsenal in the vastness of the Pacific , those balloons could provide a cheaper, lower-signature platform that can be employed from dispersed positions, Maj. Gen. Bernard Harrington, commander of the Army’s 7th Infantry Division/Multi-Domain Command-Pacific, or MDC-P, said at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington, D.C., earlier this month. Harrington’s command was recently established to merge the ground-maneuver elements of the 7th Infantry Division and long-range capabilities of the 1st Multi-Domain Task Force. Part of the unit’s mission is to operate in space, cyberspace and the electromagnetic spectrum and use long-range fires to help the rest of the Joint Force maneuver, including by opening gaps in China’s anti-access/area-denial network — the air, sea and land-based sensors and weapons designed to keep U.S. forces at bay. “For us in the Pacific, we really are looking at a specific pacing threat and an anti-access/area-denial network,” against which MDC-P aims to create “windows of opportunity for that Joint Force, whether it be a carrier strike group that’s going to pulse into the weapons engagement zone , whether it be a bomber task force, whether it be a ground unit doing a joint forcible-entry operation,” Harrington said. High-altitude balloons, or HABs, could facilitate that by carrying “launched effects” — the Army’s term for an aerial system deployed from crewed and uncrewed vehicles for reconnaissance, communications, strikes and other missions. HABs would give MDC-P soldiers more ways to employ attack drones and munitions that are cheaper than “exquisite” missiles, available in greater numbers and harder for adversaries to spot. Interest in HABs has grown in part due to technological improvements that allow them to stay aloft for weeks or months at a time and give operators more control over where they go. That enhances balloons’ value as platforms for radars and other sensors which, at operating altitudes above 60,000 feet, can see far into rival territory while remaining in international airspace. They also offer a cost-effective complement to satellites, which are more expensive and whose orbits limit their time over any one area. Harrington described high-altitude balloons as part of “an ecosystem” of data-collecting assets in space, in the air, on land and at sea. HABs in particular could compensate if space-based assets are taken out , Harrington said. “So our ability to employ HABs [and] have HABs be persistent enables both our collection and targeting as well as us [to] provide that information to the Joint Force for their collection and targeting.” Harrington also described a role for balloon- or unmanned surface vessel-launched effects in kinetic strikes. With the right timing and enough precision, those strikes may not even need to eliminate their target to create an opening. “Maybe I don’t necessarily need to sink a ship, but if I take out certain systems on that vessel, well, then it creates this temporal window of opportunity,” Harrington said. “We saw great value [in] that maybe I don’t have to use specifically or unmask an exquisite system to achieve that effect. If I can achieve effect of mass utilizing lower-cost systems, maybe that will get me there,” Harrington added. “So we modeled that, and what we saw was — particularly with our unmanned surface vessels, long-range one-way attack, long-range launched effects — the ability to synchronize and mass that could potentially get us to achieve that effect.” Harrington’s command experimented with some of those systems during Bayonet Quest 26, an exercise held in Michigan and on Lake Huron from late September to early October. An official video showed soldiers working with air and maritime drones, including a quadcopter launched from a surface vessel and a fixed-wing drone hooked up to a balloon. Harrington said Bayonet Quest tested MDC-P’s ability to “orchestrate those systems” by launching them, gathering data from their sensors, and using AI and LLMs to process that data and produce tasking orders. “If you see [a potential target], then task a UAS to be able to come over and actually validate if that meets the target folder,” Harrington said, describing the approach. “Then I can task long-range one-way attack [or] an attack USV to be able to achieve that effect or I could send that as a potential fire mission to a more exquisite munition to be able to close that kill chain.” That reduces the need for a large, easily targetable ground presence, Harrington added: “This is all about integration: Integrate multiple systems into one data layer, be able to lay something like a large language model on top of it, and allow orchestration so we don’t have a lot of soldiers in fixed sites on ground control stations.” Harrington’s comments come amid a flurry of HAB-related experiments by the Army in North Africa , the Middle East , Europe and the Pacific. At exercise Valiant Shield in Guam this summer, soldiers experimented with HABs and launched effects “within an island-chain operational construct.” One test sent a HAB aloft towing a long-endurance drone “to evaluate stratospheric payload deployment capabilities.” Soldiers tested the same balloon-drone combo in Japan during Orient Shield in September. The Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Europe has done dozens of HAB launches over the past year to examine the logistics of employing balloons and to test sensing and communications capabilities using “ experimental payloads .” Speaking alongside Harrington this month, MDC-E commander Brig. Gen. Steven Carpenter said HABs have a role, alongside other sensors and weapons, in opening “windows of opportunity” against anti-access/area-denial networks, in particular by providing resilient communications and additional strike platforms. “We like to proliferate the stratosphere with high-altitude balloons, but I mean 200, 300 at a time. We like to use them as drones, [communications retransmission], electromagnetic sensing, electronic attack, and then to drop them down and have air-launched effects,” Carpenter said. “During different seasons, the flight paths are different. We study that. We understand during what seasons, where the best places are to launch those high-altitude systems and then, again, to hold enemy cities and capabilities at risk at any time.”

HABs would give MDC-P soldiers more ways to employ attack drones and munitions that are cheaper than “exquisite” missiles, available in greater numbers and harder for adversaries to spot. Interest in HABs has grown in part due to technological improvements that allow them to stay aloft for weeks or months at a time and give operators more control over where they go. That enhances balloons’ value as platforms for radars and other sensors which, at operating altitudes above 60,000 feet, can see far into rival territory while remaining in international airspace. They also offer a cost-effective complement to satellites, which are more expensive and whose orbits limit their time over any one area. Harrington described high-altitude balloons as part of “an ecosystem” of data-collecting assets in space, in the air, on land and at sea. HABs in particular could compensate if space-based assets are taken out , Harrington said. “So our ability to employ HABs [and] have HABs be persistent enables both our collection and targeting as well as us [to] provide that information to the Joint Force for their collection and targeting.” Harrington also described a role for balloon- or unmanned surface vessel-launched effects in kinetic strikes. With the right timing and enough precision, those strikes may not even need to eliminate their target to create an opening. “Maybe I don’t necessarily need to sink a ship, but if I take out certain systems on that vessel, well, then it creates this temporal window of opportunity,” Harrington said. “We saw great value [in] that maybe I don’t have to use specifically or unmask an exquisite system to achieve that effect. If I can achieve effect of mass utilizing lower-cost systems, maybe that will get me there,” Harrington added. “So we modeled that, and what we saw was — particularly with our unmanned surface vessels, long-range one-way attack, long-range launched effects — the ability to synchronize and mass that could potentially get us to achieve that effect.” Harrington’s command experimented with some of those systems during Bayonet Quest 26, an exercise held in Michigan and on Lake Huron from late September to early October. An official video showed soldiers working with air and maritime drones, including a quadcopter launched from a surface vessel and a fixed-wing drone hooked up to a balloon. Harrington said Bayonet Quest tested MDC-P’s ability to “orchestrate those systems” by launching them, gathering data from their sensors, and using AI and LLMs to process that data and produce tasking orders. “If you see [a potential target], then task a UAS to be able to come over and actually validate if that meets the target folder,” Harrington said, describing the approach. “Then I can task long-range one-way attack [or] an attack USV to be able to achieve that effect or I could send that as a potential fire mission to a more exquisite munition to be able to close that kill chain.” That reduces the need for a large, easily targetable ground presence, Harrington added: “This is all about integration: Integrate multiple systems into one data layer, be able to lay something like a large language model on top of it, and allow orchestration so we don’t have a lot of soldiers in fixed sites on ground control stations.” Harrington’s comments come amid a flurry of HAB-related experiments by the Army in North Africa , the Middle East , Europe and the Pacific. At exercise Valiant Shield in Guam this summer, soldiers experimented with HABs and launched effects “within an island-chain operational construct.” One test sent a HAB aloft towing a long-endurance drone “to evaluate stratospheric payload deployment capabilities.” Soldiers tested the same balloon-drone combo in Japan during Orient Shield in September. The Army’s Multi-Domain Command-Europe has done dozens of HAB launches over the past year to examine the logistics of employing balloons and to test sensing and communications capabilities using “ experimental payloads .” Speaking alongside Harrington this month, MDC-E commander Brig. Gen. Steven Carpenter said HABs have a role, alongside other sensors and weapons, in opening “windows of opportunity” against anti-access/area-denial networks, in particular by providing resilient communications and additional strike platforms. “We like to proliferate the stratosphere with high-altitude balloons, but I mean 200, 300 at a time. We like to use them as drones, [communications retransmission], electromagnetic sensing, electronic attack, and then to drop them down and have air-launched effects,” Carpenter said. “During different seasons, the flight paths are different. We study that. We understand during what seasons, where the best places are to launch those high-altitude systems and then, again, to hold enemy cities and capabilities at risk at any time.”

title: Greek–Indian Chamber chief: Quality exports and legal labour from India are the priorities
body: Strengthening economic and trade ties between Greece and India, promoting Greek products, and attracting more Indian visitors represent significant opportunities for the Greek economy. At the same time, meeting the labour needs of Greek businesses has become a critical issue, particularly in tourism, construction, and other productive sectors. Angelos Tsavdaris, President of the Greek–Indian Chamber of Commerce & Economy, spoke to Dimokratiki about the potential for cooperation between the two countries, the strategy for approaching the vast Indian market, and the upgrade of the “Eustopia” programme for the legal recruitment of workers. He also explained why skills certification, safety training, and more effective oversight of procedures are essential both for protecting workers and for the smooth operation of Greek businesses. What are the main priorities of the Greek–Indian Chamber of Commerce & Economy today for developing relations between Greece and India? The relations that have developed between the two countries create significant prospects that we are trying to exploit. Our core objective is to strengthen trade and increase Greek exports to India — a huge market with great potential. Greece does not need to compete on volume of production; it needs to highlight the quality of its products. We have excellent products that can find their place in the Indian market, provided we promote them with the right strategy. At the same time, we aim to further develop cooperation in tourism and establish Greece as an attractive destination for Indian travellers. How can Greece attract more Indian tourists? We want to attract more tourists from India’s middle class, who travel to Europe and are looking for new destinations. The goal is for Greece to become one of their main choices. To achieve this, we must promote not only the well-known tourist destinations but also the opportunities offered by the rest of the Greek regions. Every place has its own identity, its own products, its gastronomy, and its hospitality. We want the Indian visitor to get to know Greece in greater depth — to taste local products, discover different areas, and realise that our country offers much more than its beaches and sights. In this way, tourism can be meaningfully linked to local production and create additional benefits for regional economies. The shortage of workers is a major concern for Greek businesses. What is the Chamber’s role in this area? We have developed the “Eustopia” programme, which concerns the legal process of recruiting workers from India to meet the needs of Greek businesses. Recently we upgraded it after examining the needs and problems that appear in the Greek market. We found that a company may request workers of a specific specialisation and end up receiving staff with different skills from those required. This creates difficulties in planning and operations. That is why we moved to an upgraded framework with emphasis on training and certification. We want the Indian worker who comes to Greece to genuinely possess the knowledge for the position he or she is going to take up. How will it be ensured that workers have the required skills? A basic prerequisite is that training and certification of their specialisation has already taken place through a recognised European certification body. They must also know the safety rules that apply in the European Union and be able to meet the requirements of their profession. With the upgraded platform, the Greek employer will be able to select candidates according to the specialisation they are looking for, conduct online interviews, and examine their certificates. For example, they will be able to check whether a candidate electrician holds the required certification and has passed the relevant safety-rule checks. This process allows the employer to evaluate the candidate before proceeding with the selection. Our aim is to correctly match the specialisation with the actual need of the business. There are, however, cases (and complaints) of workers entering Greece for a purpose other than work. How is this phenomenon being addressed? It is a serious issue that must be tackled in an organised way by the competent authorities. The Chamber does not monitor every Indian national who enters Greece. Our role concerns the procedures and the workers who are included in our own programme.
