title: Norway, Ukraine sign new energy cooperation agreement
body:
Norway and Ukraine have signed an agreement on cooperation in the energy sector, with a key focus on facilitating private investment in the industry, the Norwegian Ministry of Energy announced.
"Norway and Ukraine are strengthening their cooperation in the energy sector. Today, a cooperation agreement on energy was signed during Norwegian Minister of Energy Terje Aasland's visit to Ukraine," the ministry stated on its website on Tuesday.
Closer collaboration, mutual learning, and facilitating private investments in the energy sector are central points in the agreement
The Ministry of Energy explained that an energy cooperation agreement between the two nations had already been established in 2024; it has now been updated to align with a joint declaration on a strategic partnership (the so-called Ellisiv Declaration) signed in August 2026 by Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
"The cooperation agreement we have signed today underscores that Norway has much to contribute, but also much to learn from Ukraine's experiences with energy preparedness and securing critical infrastructure. We are committed to facilitating a cooperation that can strengthen expertise in both countries," said Minister of Energy Terje Aasland, as quoted in the statement.
The Minister said that Norway has supported Ukraine since the onset of Russia's full-scale war and will continue to contribute to sustaining energy production.
As reported, in May 2026, Norway announced a EUR 40 million grant to support Ukraine's energy resilience.

title: In Memory of Roza Aitmatova
body: Roza Aitmatova died on October 26, 2026, at the age of 89. She was the younger sister of Chingiz Aitmatov, one of the most important writers of the 20th century. With her death, Kyrgyzstan has lost an invaluable witness to its history. She succeeded in turning the tragedies endured by her family into part of her nation’s collective memory. Roza was born in Moscow on March 8, 1937. She was just six months old when her father, Torekul Aitmatov, a prominent political figure who had played a role in establishing the state institutions of the young Kyrgyz Republic, was arrested during Stalin’s purges. He was executed in November 1938, but his family remained unaware of his fate for decades. His wife, Nagima Abduvalieva, left alone with four children, continued to hope that her husband was still alive, somewhere in a distant Soviet labor camp. Roza grew up alongside her brothers and sister, Chingiz, Ilgiz and Lyutsiya, in an atmosphere of hardship and uncertainty. As the children of an “enemy of the people,” they faced discrimination and financial difficulties. During the war, the family lived in modest homes in the Talas region, relying on the support of relatives and fellow villagers. Chingiz, the eldest child, had to take on adult responsibilities at an early age: while still a teenager, he worked as secretary of the village council. For Roza, her elder brother had been a source of support and a role model since childhood. It was Chingiz, then a young agronomist, who told the family in 1953 that they might be able to move to the capital, Frunze, now Bishkek. Before leaving, Nagima wanted to have a photograph taken with all four of her children. As Roza later recalled, this seemingly simple gesture symbolized the end of their most difficult years and the beginning of a new life. In the years that followed, Chingiz gained international recognition with works such as Jamila , The First Teacher and Mother Earth . Roza had by then devoted herself to the natural sciences, having studied physics and mathematics. She followed her brother’s literary achievements closely. Yet their relationship remained, above all, a deeply personal family bond, built on intimate conversations, shared memories and boundless love for their mother. One episode recounted by Roza reveals just how closely the writer’s work was connected to his family history. In 1962, following a severe deterioration in Nagima’s health, Roza went into her brother’s study to tidy his desk. Among the pages of a new manuscript, she discovered a dedication to their parents: to their father, whose burial place was still unknown, and to their mother, who had raised four children on her own. It was the first draft of Mother Earth , a novella in which Roza recognized many aspects of Nagima’s life, her courage and her resilience. When their mother died in 1971, Roza saw her brother, by then a celebrated writer, weeping inconsolably in a hospital corridor. Behind the image of a man known throughout the world was still the boy who had lost his father and feared losing the last remaining link to his childhood. A turning point came in 1991, when a mass grave containing victims of Stalin’s purges was discovered at Chon-Tash, near Bishkek. Among those buried there was Torekul Aitmatov. After more than half a century, the family finally learned the truth. Chingiz took part in the ceremony to rebury the remains and proposed naming the site Ata-Beyit, meaning “Grave of the Fathers.” For Roza, who had never had the chance to truly know her father, the discovery marked a new mission. She sought to reconstruct his life and restore the names and personal histories that the years of terror had sought to erase. The result of this work was the book White Pages of History , first published in 2009. Other books and memoirs followed, devoted to her parents and to her brother, who had died in 2008. Alongside this work, Roza made a significant contribution to education and women’s rights, heading Kyrgyzstan’s Women’s Assistance Center. In the final years of her life, she continued to collect memories and personal accounts, including in collaboration with her nephew, Asan Akhmatov. In a work published in 2024, by which time she was the last surviving child of Torekul and Nagima Aitmatov, Roza recalled her brother Chingiz’s words: “You can always come to an understanding with another person, whoever they may be. But there is one thing you cannot negotiate with. That is time.” While Chingiz used literature to tell the stories of his people’s suffering and hopes, Roza devoted much of her life to reconstructing her family’s history and preserving the memory of those who had been consigned to oblivion. She gathered documents, photographs and testimonies so that future generations, too, could know their past. Now that she, too, is gone, the responsibility of keeping her memory alive falls to others.

title: Canada-EU summit will kick off formal talks on closer ties: Carney
body:
The Canada-EU Summit being held this week in Montreal will serve to launch more formal negotiations on a deeper partnership over the next year, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday,
Carney will meet with European Union President Ursula von der Leyen and other EU officials on Thursday and Friday in Montreal, where they are expected to announce the next stage of an enhanced alliance.
“This is the launch of further formal discussions, negotiations, over the course of the next year,” Carney said on his way into the weekly cabinet meeting.
The exact nature of the pact between Canada and the EU has been unclear — even to the leaders themselves.
In September, von der Leyen said the new arrangement could make Canada an “associate” member of the 27-member bloc. But “associate membership” does not actually exist in the EU and Canadian officials have downplayed the use of that term.
“It doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature. What matters is the difference that it will make to lives of Canadians, young Canadians, in terms of opportunities to study work and travel, our Canadian businesses in terms of new opportunities,” Carney said Tuesday, adding it could open up new research opportunities as well.
Carney used the term “alliance of the future” to describe the deal, which was first made public when he spoke to the EU Parliament in Strasbourg, France, last month.
Jonathan Wilkinson, who took on the Canadian ambassadorship in Brussels earlier this year after spending more than five years in the Liberal cabinet, told The Canadian Press the labour policy discussions with Europe are focused on “specialized areas” where employers on both sides of the Atlantic could benefit from access to a shared labour pool.
He said any measures that would make it easier for workers and students to move between the two jurisdictions must be approached in a “thoughtful way.”
“We’re not talking about free movement of labour between Europe and Canada. But what we are talking about is, in some specialized areas, it may be actually interesting and useful for both countries to have the ability to tap into labour pools,” Wilkinson said.
The ambassador did not cite specific sectors where labour mobility between Canada and the EU could be eased. The EU and Canada have been discussing increased collaboration on critical minerals, technology, defence and clean energy.
Wilkinson pointed to work already done by Canada and Europe on mutual accreditation for architects and said any future decisions about labour mobility would be focused on areas of “mutual benefit.”
Canada has also discussed joining Erasmus+, the European Union’s student exchange program, which offers study and training opportunities in member nations.
Michelle Rempel Garner, the Conservative immigration critic, has called on the government to explain what these negotiations mean for people coming to Canada.
“Canadians are already struggling with the cost of living due to immigration levels which are too high and have contributed to jobs becoming more scarce and workers getting paid less. Canadians deserve transparency on any EU immigration deal and how it would impact our jobs, homes, and health care,” she said in a statement.
The summit appears to be a source of friction between Carney and the new Parti Québécois government in Quebec.
A spokesperson for Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon St-Pierre Plamondon said in a written statement that Ottawa denied the premier the chance to speak at the summit and refused to allow Quebec to host a reception on the sidelines, following a request submitted by the former government in mid-September.
Following the cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Carney said in French that St-Pierre Plamondon declined an invitation to join him and the other premiers for a dinner with European officials during the summit. Carney said the federal government has had three consultation sessions with Quebec about the talks with the EU.
Joel Lightbound, Carney’s Quebec lieutenant, said Tuesday that St-Pierre Plamondon is welcome to attend the summit and the dinner but this is still a meeting between Canada and the EU.
This week’s summit will take place on the 10th anniversary of the signing of the Canada-Europe Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, or CETA.
Nine EU members — France, Italy, Belgium, Ireland, Poland, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Greece and Hungary — have not yet ratified that trade deal.
Wilkinson said he’s spoken with all 27 of his EU member nation counterparts and there is momentum in Europe to get more countries behind CETA. He did not name specific nations.
One of the EU’s leading nations may have a new government soon. Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right National Rally, is the current polling favourite to succeed Emmanuel Macron as president this spring.
Le Pen delivered a nearly hour-long speech to supporters Sunday that focused on her party’s nationalist, anti-immigrant positions.
Wilkinson said politics is always dynamic and Europeans and Canadians will go on sharing values regardless of which party is in power in a particular nation.
“I think in France, it’s a very important debate that they are having. And I think that if in fact the government were to change, people will have to take stock of that,” he said.
“But I do think that the European Union is a much bigger project than any one government in any one country. And I have a lot of confidence that Europeans will find their way through this and be just fine.”
Wilkinson said energy and critical minerals — including natural gas, hydrogen and nuclear power — will play a crucial role in the enhanced partnership between Canada and the EU.
“We’re looking at … how can we, for example, encourage significant additional European investment in Canadian minerals projects. We’re talking about how can we think about things like stockpiling together so that we actually can help to stabilize the market,” Wilkinson said.
The European Investment Bank applied for an exemption from Canadian foreign banking rules earlier this month that would allow the state investor to operate in Canada as part of a critical minerals agreement.
Wilkinson said Canada and the European Union are both looking for ways to build up the infrastructure to refine and ship critical minerals and reduce China’s market dominance.
“That’s not a dependency that’s good for Canada. That’s not a dependency good for the European Union. So we are looking at that,” he said.

title: Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence
body:
Today, we’re excited to announce LFM3 , our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.
Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.
The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face , our Playground , and the Liquid AI API . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.
LFM3 instances are ideal candidates for specialized intelligence. Fine-tune them on your own data, and deploy them where your application runs. Enjoy the article.
LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention could run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. Its design came from our automated hardware-in-the-loop architecture search . For LFM3, we used this search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts.
We also expanded the hardware in the loop, from CPUs in one phone and one laptop for LFM2 to 14 device and backend combinations for LFM3: phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15), a Raspberry Pi 5, laptops (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen AI), and Arm and x86 cloud CPUs, plus GPUs and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.
Gated short convolutions still make up over half the layers. To add capability without slowing down long contexts, we tried swapping some of them for other sequence blocks, and sliding-window attention (SWA) gave the best quality–speed tradeoff. We kept the other changes described below only where they improved quality without a meaningful speed cost. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster.
Tri-hybrid layer mix. LFM3 combines three operators: gated short convolutions, sliding-window attention (SWA), and global attention. Of its 24 layers, 13 are convolutions, 5 are SWA with a 256-token window, and 6 are global attention. The convolutions also use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.
Head-wise gated attention. A sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization and improve training stability .
Partial RoPE. Global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head and leave the low-frequency half unrotated, so those dimensions match on content regardless of distance . SWA layers keep full RoPE.
Sandwich norm. Each block normalizes both its input and its output, which helps keep activations well-scaled.
LFM3 uses the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B , built to tokenize non-Latin scripts more efficiently.
Training. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens. Compared with LFM2, the mix adds more scientific papers, repository-level code, a wider range of knowledge sources, and considerably more math. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated, higher-quality data, with a larger share of agentic traces and diverse tool calls to prepare the model for agentic post-training. This stage also extends the context window to 256K tokens.
The first LFM3 release includes six models, all branched from the same LFM3-1.7B-Base backbone and all around 2B parameters. Four of them cover different input modalities (text, vision, audio, and omni), and the last two are decision models specialized from the vision and omni models. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you can pick the one that fits your use case, customize it, and run it on-device.
For a deeper dive into the performance and inference results behind these models, refer to the respective model cards.
LFM3-1.7B is a text model for local agents and specialized applications with a 256K-token context window.
It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It can triage your inbox, manage your calendar, research topics on the web, send you morning briefings on WhatsApp, and use tool search to find the right tool among thousands of options. Since tokens are free, dozens of agents can run continuously in the background. You can adapt it to your domains, harnesses, and tools with a short fine-tuning run on a single GPU.
AA-Omniscience non-hallucination (public)
On agentic tasks, LFM3-1.7B competes with models several times its size. It leads on instruction following and function calling on BFCL and ToolSandbox, and beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps (WebArena-Verified, AutomationBench). Larger models still win on agentic coding and knowledge, where size matters most, but search helps close the knowledge gap, nearly doubling its score on Humanity's Last Exam.
To achieve these results, the model went through four stages of post-training:
On-device, we measure metrics with llama.cpp at Q4_0 and a 32K-token context. LFM3-1.7B is the fastest model on all three devices, decoding 1.8 to 2.8 times faster than the next one, and it uses the least memory. Long contexts stay cheap: a full 128K-token context needs 1.6 GB of KV cache, against 4.3 GB for Qwen3.5-4B and 5.6 GB for MiniCPM5-2B.
On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-1.7B can produce 3.6 billion tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests, more than any other model in this comparison.
To show what this throughput makes possible, we ran more than 300,000 LFM3-1.7B agents in parallel to investigate the Enron email archive.
LFM3-1.7B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like online fraud detection when run on Liquid RIPL . P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.
LFM3-VL-2B can watch, reason, and understand the physical world:
LFM3-VL-2B is a leap in performance over the LFM2.5-VL series. Across 62 vision benchmarks, LFM3-VL-2B scores significantly ahead of all models of similar size by at least 7.4 points, and despite its size, it matches the performance of Gemma 4 12B, a model more than 6 times larger, surpasses Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and is within 2 points of GPT-5.6 Luna. For more details, see the model card.
Notes: Each category score is the unweighted mean of its benchmark scores. The Average row is the unweighted mean across all 62 evaluations.
All of this can be run efficiently on-device, which enables everyday use of intelligence without the data leaving your device or the need for a cloud connection. On-device, LFM3-VL-2B has the highest prefill throughput and lowest memory footprint across all measured devices, compared to other models of its size class.
On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-VL-2B can produce over 12,000 tokens per second, higher than any other model of the same size class.
LFM3-VL-2B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like image asset tagging when run on Liquid RIPL . P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.
In addition to improvements to the LFM3 backbone, LFM3-VL comes with our new in-house vision encoder which uses 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.
The Liquid vision encoder combines convolution and attention to make it significantly more efficient than its ViT counterpart at the same quality. The performance-efficiency graph below illustrates this. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B’s vision encoder at 55.9% average accuracy across 13 vision-language model benchmarks, while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs.
For video, the encoder jointly embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice of visual features, halving the temporal sequence length before further encoding. Together, these choices make the encoder a foundation for both richer image understanding and efficient video processing.
LFM3-Audio-2B is a compact, fully featured audio model that runs locally on laptops and edge devices. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both.
LFM3-Audio-2B uses a new architecture with an audio encoder and codec developed in-house. It outperforms LFM2.5-Audio in speech quality and now supports 18 languages. New capabilities include audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling.
Multilingual (avg. across en, es, pt, de, fr, it, zh, ja, ko)
English TTS (UTMOSv2, 1-5, higher is better) (WER, %, lower is better)
VoiceBench, Tool calling, Audio understanding (audio in, text out, %, higher is better)
Our new LFM-based audio encoder is built from a mixture of sliding-window attention and short-convolution layers, keeping memory utilization bounded. The new encoder is fully causal, allowing the model to process live microphone input and perform prefill while you speak. This reduces the wait after you finish, with time to the first token as low as 50 ms.
LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, powers multilingual speech generation in both LFM3-Audio and LFM3-Omni. Built on the LFM3 architecture, LiquidCodec turns generated tokens into speech at about 87× real time on a single CPU thread (Apple M4 Max), supporting streaming decoding.
Quantization compresses each 80 ms of speech into 12 discrete tokens and, in contrast to previous LFM Audio models, allows multiple tokens to be predicted iteratively in parallel rather than requiring sequential prediction. As the backbone generates new tokens, the detokenizer progressively converts them into speech, all faster than real-time so that conversations are smooth and responsive.
LFM3-Omni-2B is our first omni model, bringing vision, audio, and language together in a single model that can see, listen, and talk back:
LFM3-Omni supports cross-modal interactions that require understanding visual and auditory information together. Users can ask spoken questions about images, or provide videos with synchronized audio and ask questions that depend on both what is seen and what is heard.
In addition to cross-modal understanding, LFM3-Omni retains the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and language instruction following.
LFM3-Omni-2B is designed for efficient deployment in resource-constrained environments. Its capabilities enable conversational assistants that can provide context-aware guidance, support hands-free interactions, and help users complete tasks through natural voice commands. By combining visual understanding, spoken dialogue, and tool calling, it can support applications ranging from personalized education and everyday assistance to navigation of digital interfaces and robotic systems.
At 2.2B parameters, it brings this kind of multimodal assistant on-device. Examples include a tutor that looks at your handwritten math and answers your spoken question, a tablet you can walk around with and ask about what it sees, and in-car assistants that combine what the camera sees with what the driver says.
This release also brings two new decision models: d1-2B , built on LFM3-VL-2B, reads text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B , built on LFM3-Omni-2B, also listens. Instead of writing an answer, they decide in milliseconds. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability.
Beyond the new LFM3 backbone, the big change since d1-3B is typed answers . On top of yes/no, choices, and scores, both models can now:
Ask as many questions as you like: they’re read in one pass over the same input.
Smaller and stronger. d1-2B replaces our previous d1-3B, with a third fewer parameters:
Decision Bench (real enterprise records)
ImajevBench (decisions from photos and rules)
Our Meta index (117 private and public benchmarks)
Decisions you can speak. d1-Omni-2B takes the same questions over audio, so a voice request can be routed, checked, or answered just like a typed one. Asked by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy:
DecisionBench (business routing and triage)
Typed Decisions (customer service cases)
It also recognizes everyday sounds (84.5% on ESC-50) and tells which of 43 languages is being spoken (92.5% on FLEURS).
Pick d1-2B for text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B when your inputs include audio. Both run on-device, and turn a stream of tickets, documents, calls, or camera frames into structured decisions without a round trip to the cloud.
In the following demo, d1-2B runs on a MacBook. You describe what to find in plain language, and it draws a bounding box around every match in a single forward pass, using the new Point answer type.
LFM3 is built to be specialized. The 2B-class models are small enough to fine-tune on your own data and run where your application lives. The following two examples show this with LFM3-VL-2B. The first is a short fine-tune that turns it into an inspection model for one narrow industrial task. The second is a research extension that turns it into a robot controller.
While frontier models are powerful generalists, they are not necessarily experts in your particular use case. In this demo, we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to find and classify defects in drone photos of wind turbine blades. Training used about 3,000 public photos ( WTBs2025 ) with SFT and GRPO for a few hours on one A100. We then compared it with the base model and GPT-6 Luna on about 1,400 held-out photos.
Out of the box, LFM3-VL-2B and GPT-6 Luna correctly identify these defect types in fewer than 10% of images. A short fine-tune raises LFM3-VL-2B’s classification accuracy to 67% and improves detection F1 from 0.003 to 0.11, compared with 0.01 for GPT-6 Luna. Lightning-strike images illustrate the difference, where GPT-6 Luna often locates the defect correctly but labels it incorrectly, while the fine-tuned model correctly identifies a lightning strike. Beyond classification and detection, the model can answer natural-language questions about the same image. For example, it can locate visible damage or write a brief inspection finding including the defect type, supporting evidence, and location.
We investigate how LFM3-VL-2B can serve as a basis for robotics applications. We consider three complementary directions: (1) high-level tool orchestration, (2) vision-language navigation, and (3) low-level manipulation.
Orchestration. Building on LLM-based robot planning and control (SayCan, Code as Policies) and recent physical orchestrators (VoLo, Gemini Robotics ER 2), we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to operate a robot arm through tools. Given a request and the current camera image, it reasons step by step, grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, and manipulates them via motion planners. It then checks each outcome in the next image and reports back, including when a request is out of reach or ambiguous. The tasks feature relational selection, sorting by measured properties, and environment perturbations, all simulated in Isaac Sim. No architectural change was needed. A rank-32 LoRA adapter was trained on about 40,000 samples, combining manipulation trajectories with general tool-use and pointing data, and took about six GPU-hours on a single AMD Instinct MI325X. Paired with a fine-tuned d1-2B skill monitor, we can further double recovery success under disturbances such as slips, jams and drags.
Navigation. For vision-and-language navigation, LFM3-VL-2B reads a route description and a short history of RGB frames to predict navigation targets and residual-quantized trajectory primitives, inspired by the action interface of LightNav-0. Each decision consists of five tokens: two spatial/control tokens and three hierarchically quantized codes encoding a ten-waypoint path that a velocity controller can track. We only repurpose 2,068 vocabulary tokens; the architecture is otherwise unchanged. We train on 2.8 million samples for 72 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs. In unseen validation scenes, the resulting model achieves success rates of 53% on R2R and 43% on RxR under a strict continuous-control evaluation protocol with wall sliding disabled and explicit stopping required. We further observe robustness across varying camera angles and instruction languages. On a Jetson AGX Orin, our navigation model updates waypoint trajectories at over 2.5 Hz using TensorRT FP16 without visual prompt caching.
Manipulation. To turn LFM3-VL-2B into a vision-language-action (VLA) model, we adopt parallel action prediction inspired by OpenVLA-OFT and StarVLA-α: a small residual MLP maps the hidden states of eight action-query tokens to an eight-step chunk of continuous robot actions in a single forward pass. Proprioception is provided both as discretized text and through an embodiment-specific learned projection, and the whole network is fine-tuned end to end. We trained a single generalist checkpoint for 170 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs, on simulated and real-robot data from 15 embodiments, ranging from single arms and mobile manipulators to bimanual platforms and a humanoid. The resulting VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks. On a Jetson AGX Orin, it can generate action chunks in under 50 ms using TensorRT at FP16 precision.
Start building today with LFM3, available on Hugging Face and the Liquid AI API .
With LFM3, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:
We are grateful to our day-0 launch partners for their support. LFM3 is ready to use today across these platforms: Ambarella, AMD, Arm, Intel via OpenVINO, NVIDIA, OpenRouter, Qualcomm via Qualcomm AI Hub and GenieX, and Vercel. Thanks to Mercedes-Benz and Shopify for partnering on pre-release testing and evaluation.
Thank you to our builder ecosystem for its support: Atomic, Cactus, Hugging Face, llama.cpp, LM Studio, MLX, Ollama, RadixArk on SGLang, .txt, Unsloth, vLLM, and ZML.
For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:
Liquid AI, "Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence", Liquid AI Blog, October 2026.
For press inquiries, email us at press@liquid.ai

title: Finnish president says he discussed limiting military operations in Ukraine, food security with Putin
body:
The issues of limiting military operations in Ukraine-in particular, strikes on energy facilities-as well as food security were discussed during a phone call between Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gar Støre, which took place on Tuesday morning and lasted about an hour and a half, according to a report on the website of Finland's national broadcaster Yle.
Stubb said the call was coordinated with Ukraine and the U.S., and during it, he conveyed direct messages from Ukraine to Putin. "Finland never discusses Ukraine-related issues without general approval, bypassing Ukraine," he noted.
According to the Finnish president, the impetus for the call was a meeting in Oslo that took place a week ago. Commenting on the meeting in Oslo, Stubb said they had a strong sense that the peace talks were reaching an impasse. He added they managed to get them back on track and improve relations between the United States and Ukraine.
He said Finland and Norway are trying to facilitate progress in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, and that during the conversation with Putin, they discussed an energy truce and, more broadly, a mutual cessation of attacks on infrastructure facilities between Ukraine and Russia, as well as food security and the exchange of prisoners.
The president said that at the end of the conversation, a willingness to continue negotiations was expressed, but there was no agreement of any kind regarding at what stage or how this would take place.
For his part, Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov stated following the conversation that Stubb and Støre had informed Putin "of Zelenskyy's active interest in negotiating directly with our leader," but, according to him, Putin replied that he would hold them only on Russian territory. "Our leader reiterated that if Zelenskyy wants to hold direct negotiations, he should come to Moscow, where all conditions will be provided for him, particularly in terms of security," Ushakov said.
Furthermore, according to the aide to the leader of the aggressor state, contact at the level of the leaders of Ukraine and Russia is allegedly possible only after the negotiation process concludes with the drafting of a document regarding a long-term settlement. "The negotiators would be ready to brief them on the documents, and the leaders, in turn, would be ready to sign them," Ushakov said.
As reported, Zelenskyy discussed with Stubb and Støre their conversation with Putin and thanked them for "this active support for our diplomacy and our joint peace efforts with all partners." According to the Ukrainian president, the Finnish president and the Norwegian prime minister told the Russian leader that concrete de-escalation measures are needed regarding Ukraine's energy sector and infrastructure. They also discussed preparations for the trilateral Ukraine-United States-Russia meeting, scheduled for November in Abu Dhabi (UAE) at the working-level.

title: Obuasi SHTS sexual misconduct: Families of victims consider relocation over stigma and victimization
body: Families of girls allegedly sexually abused at Obuasi SHTS are considering fleeing their communities as stigma and victimization deepen. Gender Minister, Dr. Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, says some families are being pushed into hiding, adding to the trauma of the alleged abuse, as she says some victims are now harbouring suicidal thoughts. Addressing the gathering, the minister recounted the psychosocial distress some of the victims are enduring. “There is an incident where one of the girls doesn’t want to return to school or engage in any activity in life anymore. She has regretted telling her story and blaming herself. Most of them are harbouring suicidal thoughts,” she said. A delegation from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, led by the sector minister, met with opinion leaders in the Obuasi municipality over the allegation of sexual abuse against 19 girls of Obuasi Senior High and Technical School. Including religious leaders, civil society organisations, assembly members, old students of Obuasi SHTS and other stakeholders, the community dialogue focused on empowering victims of the alleged sexual misconduct. The deliberation also centered on devising robust structures and mechanisms to protect children and the youth in the town against any sexual misconduct. Dr. Momo Lartey further disclosed that some families are now relocating to avoid stigma. “Some families are considering relocation because people are pointing fingers at them. People are rather victimizing them instead of supporting them,” she added. As calls for justice intensify, the minister is rallying community support for the victims. Seven families of the girls allegedly sexually abused by the headmaster are preparing to press charges against him, amidst the reported threats, intimidation and attempts to blackmail those seeking justice. The opinion leaders want a meticulous and independent probe into the allegation.

title: Greek Orthodox Patriarch tells 'Post' 'minority group of radicals' conducted Jordan attack
body: The terror attack on the Church of Saint George in Hammoud, in Jordan's Al-Karak province, last week “was a heinous and cowardly act of violence perpetrated by a minority group of radicals who seek to intimidate and divide the community,” Theophilos III, the Greek Orthodox Patriarch of Jerusalem, told The Jerusalem Post in a statement on Tuesday, when asked about anti-Christian radicalization in the region.Theophilos III, whose Greek Orthodox Patriarchate has a longstanding presence in Jordan, told the Post that the attack, which sought to divide Jordan's Christian community, had instead “strengthened the bonds of all Jordanians,” who came together to mourn the nine churchgoers killed on Friday.“We gathered two days after the attack to remember the martyrs who lost their lives, weep with all who are mourning, visit the injured, and pray for a more peaceful future,” he said. “This violence has only drawn our community closer together, deepened our roots in this land.”Around 40 people were wounded on Friday when gunmen opened fire on a funeral procession at the church.Theophilos III shared that he met with Jordanian King Abdulla and other members of the royal family who “all offered their heartfelt condolences and commitments of support.”Jordanian society united against radicalism, Theophilos III says“I return to Jerusalem certain of two things, by the grace of the Divine: we as Christians stand firm and remain steadfast in our faith - Christians in this land will never falter, and that the Jordanian society as a whole is united against radicalism of all forms,” he continued, adding that the “heinous” attack “runs entirely contrary to the moderate Islam practiced in Jordan.”“We hold an absolute conviction that Jordanian society will remain united, vigilant and strong against any extremist ideologies that target the peaceful,” he continued. “For many within my community, Jordan is home, and I applaud His Majesty King Abdullah II, Custodian of the Muslim and Christian Holy Sites in the Holy Land, and the entire Royal Family, for the leadership they have shown in response to this evil attack. This response and their commitments of protection to the Christian community - not only in word but also in deed - are a model to be replicated across the region, where too many Christians live in intimidation and fear.”Theophilos III's remarks come as Jordan navigates its dual role as a close US ally and a Muslim-majority country with a significant Christian minority.Viral video highlights tension between religions in JordanAn interaction between a Christian woman and Jordan's minister of religious endowments has gone viral online after the woman said some Jordanians had told her that mourning Christians was haram, or forbidden under Islamic law. In response, the minister described anyone unwilling to mourn alongside the Christian community as an extremist and said Christians were an integral part of Jordanian society.Though Jordan is considered to offer a high level of religious freedom, the non-denominational Christian charity organization Open Doors US reported that Christians often experience discrimination in employment, government monitoring, and restrictions on public preaching.The American charity reported that the war in Gaza has fueled Islamic conservatism and that Muslims were pressured to create distance from the Christian community.

title: A judge halted D.C. golf course renovations. Trump says they'll still start next month
body:
President Trump, seen touring the East Potomac Golf Links in late June, says his administration will appeal the judge's ruling and close the course for renovations next month. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
After weeks of tense hearings and late-night court filings, a federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from making any further alterations to East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to redevelop into a championship-level venue.
The long-simmering legal battle kicked into high gear in recent weeks, after the government cut down 430 trees on the golf course with less than a day's notice. That prompted a pair of lengthy court hearings that at times turned heated, with government officials repeatedly insisting that the tree-clearing was unrelated to the renovations President Trump had touted on social media. They contradicted the president's own social media posts from that very morning by saying there was no final plan for those renovations at all.
"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting president," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes wrote in her 70-page opinion . "And yet, here we are."
Reyes extended what was initially a two-week halt to tree removal, ordering the government not to cut down "or substantially prune or otherwise damage or impair" any trees at East Potomac Park without a court order. She also ordered it to provide "no less than ten business days' written advance notice" before closing or making any "irreversible modification" to any parts of the park while the legal battle plays out.
"By issuing this preliminary injunction, the Court does not end the round: it simply marks the ball until the parties can fully and fairly litigate this case," Reyes wrote.
Monday's ruling is a win for the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers who sued to prevent renovations earlier this year — and for the growing grassroots movement to protect the municipal course and the surrounding recreational area, which is beloved by runners, cyclists, birders and others.
"We are grateful the court intervened to stop the Trump-Vance administration's greed and lawlessness while the case continues, and we are eager to argue the case in court," said Skye Perryman, the president of the nonprofit Democracy Forward, which is representing the plaintiffs.
In a Truth Social post late Monday, Trump said the Department of the Interior will appeal the ruling. NPR has reached out to the Department of Interior but did not hear back in time for publication.
Trump also doubled down on his earlier announcement that construction will begin on Nov. 15 and keep the park closed for 15 months, adding that the "judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project."
"To have to give advanced notices to a judge who has no expertise in Golf, Architecture, Landscaping, Construction, or anything else having to do with building such a World Class Project, is not fair, appropriate, or Constitutional," Trump wrote.
Reyes herself has said she is not interested in policing the federal government's landscaping efforts.
That's why, as she explained in Monday's opinion, she repeatedly declined to intervene in the case — instead issuing repeated warnings against any unannounced major alterations — until "the Government did what it assured all it would not do."
"The Court earlier stated, 'I am not the Lorax. I do not speak for the trees,'" Reyes concluded. "The Court still does not speak for the trees. It speaks only for the rule of law."
On Tuesday afternoon, Reyes made a record of Trump's post and gave the government about 24 hours to clarify whether a plan exists to close East Potomac in mid-November and, if so, "how that can be reconciled" with what its lawyers previously told the court. She said she will schedule a status hearing for either Friday or Monday.
A golfer plays near some of the 430 trees that were cut down at East Potomac earlier this month. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Reyes' strongly-worded 70-page opinion came exactly a week after a seven-hour hearing in which she clashed repeatedly with the government's lawyers. She had already rejected the administration's request to recuse herself from the case because of alleged bias.
Last week's hearing featured sworn testimony from several officials from the Department of the Interior and National Park Service, to provide a fuller account of the origins and purpose of the controversial tree-clearing. But it teed up bigger questions about whether the administration had misled the court and the public over its intentions for the golf course.
"This started as a case about golf. That good walk spoiled. But it has become much more," Reyes wrote on Monday. "It now forces the Court to reconcile assertions by President Donald J. Trump with the sworn testimony of multiple government employees and the argument of senior Department of Justice attorneys."
Much of Reyes' opinion examines the gap between what Trump has said publicly and what his administration has told the court.
The most notable: Trump posted online the morning of last week's hearing that work would begin on the golf course "immediately." But hours later, in the courtroom, administration officials said in sworn testimony that they were not aware of any final plan.
Weaving together timelines and testimonies, Reyes ultimately agreed with plaintiffs that there does seem to be a golf course renovation plan (they refer to it as the "Washington National Plan") despite the administration's repeated denials.
"To be sure, the Court cannot pinpoint the exact date at which the Plan became final," Reyes wrote. "But it determines without hesitation that it occurred at some point well before October 15, 2026."
She doesn't accept the government's explanation that it cleared hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on such short notice to enact vegetation recommendations from a 2019 National Park Service Report (whose other recommendations, including for the city's other two municipal golf courses, went largely unaddressed in the last seven years). She called that justification "pretextual."
She took particular aim at the credibility of one witness, Gregory Wischer — a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department — who was photographed carrying rolled-up concept plans while accompanying Trump and golf course architect Tom Fazio on a tour of East Potomac in June.
"Yet Wischer maintains that he — as Deputy Chief of Staff to the Secretary of the Interior — just spontaneously became interested in tree and vegetation management. In mid September. At the East Potomac Golf Course," Reyes wrote.
Reyes said the government "has made no compelling factual rebuttal." At one point, the administration accused the plaintiffs of conjecture "based on a handful of tweets." Reyes shut that down in Monday's opinion.
"The 'handful of tweets' are not complaints about the Red Sox's latest blown lead in the ninth. They are statements from the President of the United States, and from the Secretary of the Interior, about actions within their purview," she wrote. "And the posts say, in no uncertain terms, that a plan exists and that construction will start imminently — one even contains a final schematic of the Course's redesign."
East Potomac Park, seen from the observation deck of the Washington Monument in July. The manmade peninsula is home to a municipal golf course and recreational areas, including a 3-mile road around the perimeter. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Trump said as recently as Monday night that he believes the renovations do not require approval. But, as Reyes pointed out in her opinion, administration officials acknowledged in a July hearing that major renovations would require federal environmental and historic preservation reviews.
Last week, however, administration lawyers presented an "alternative argument" that the renovations actually cannot be reviewed under the Administrative Procedure Act.
"It says, Emily Litella-style: 'Never mind,'" Reyes wrote, referring to the perpetually about-facing Saturday Night Live character . "But parties cannot change course whenever and however the evidence suits them … And so the Court does not credit this new argument."
Plaintiffs in the lawsuit argue that the government is purposefully approaching the golf course renovations as smaller projects — like dumping debris from the White House East Wing demolition last year or cutting down hundreds of trees this month — to avoid federally required environmental reviews.
That argument seems to hold water with Reyes, who said, the Interior Department likely violated the National Environmental Protection Act "by impermissibly segmenting its review of the Plan's environmental effects."
Monday's ruling — and the administration's promised appeal — could slow that process even more. Trump said on social media that work "must begin, immediately, if it is to be completed in a timely and seasonal manner."
But there are still many questions about the final product.
The rendering Trump shared earlier this month shows the park's three courses of varying ability levels combined into one that overtakes the entire peninsula, seemingly removing the perimeter road that runners and bikers use every day and raising questions about whether the historically affordable golf course could soon be less accessible.
Trump said Monday the redeveloped course will be able to host events like the PGA Championship and Ryder Cup, but will also be "open to the Public, at a reduced rate for those living in Washington, D.C."
The project is one of many ways he's looking to make his mark on the nation's capital, from building the White House ballroom to adding his name to the Kennedy Center to pushing through plans for a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
body: Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs , which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job. With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure. SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks. This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs. The challenge SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk. For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime. How SOCI indexing works Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it. A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid. SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly: Scenario What happens The image includes a SOCI index SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes The image has no SOCI index Standard download, no change in behavior The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed The job falls back to a standard download and continues running Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow. What we measured We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed. Setup Eight images , 1.8–35.4 GB compressed. GPU and CPU instances ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.g6, ml.g6e, ml.g7, ml.g7e, ml.p4d, ml.p5, and ml.m7i, from xlarge to 48xlarge, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1). Download time measured from the start of the image pull until the container is ready to run. All figures are medians of repeated runs. Result 1: Download time drops from minutes to seconds at every image size Image size (compressed) Standard download Lazy loading Improvement 1.8 GB 48 s 3-11 s ~8x 13.2 GB 3 min 42 s ~6 s ~34x 35.4 GB 7 min 17 s 3-11 s ~38x The following chart compares container image download time for a standard Docker pull against SOCI lazy loading across eight image sizes, from 1.8 GB to 35.4 GB. Each image size shows two bars. The Docker download time bar (blue) grows steadily with image size, from 48 seconds at 1.8 GB to 7 minutes 17 seconds at 35.4 GB. A speedup label above each pair shows the ratio of Docker time to SOCI time. Speedups range from approximately 10x for the smallest image to over 35x for the largest. Figure 1: Container image download time, standard Docker pull compared to SOCI lazy loading, across eight image sizes Standard download time grows with image size because every file is decompressed and written. Lazy loading stayed at 3–11 seconds regardless of size, an 8x–46x improvement. The bigger the image, the more minutes you save. Result 2: The saving holds on every instance type and size Running the 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type/size combinations, standard download ranged from 3 min 16 s to 4 min 20 s, while lazy loading held at 6-8 s. That is about 34x faster on every configuration. You don’t need to change instance type or size to benefit. Figure 2: Download time for a 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type and size combinations Result 3: Training performance is unaffected beyond a first-epoch penalty We ran two kinds of full training jobs from the Docker-pulled and from the SOCI-indexed image and compared every epoch: Image classification on ResNet-50 on Imagenette (9,469 images) Container images: PyTorch (13.2 GB DLC) and TensorFlow (9.9 GB DLC) Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g7e.48xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, ml.g6e.12xlarge, ml.g6e.24xlarge, and ml.g6e.48xlarge. Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Qwen2.5-0.5B on alpaca-cleaned (51,760 examples) with the Hugging Face Trainer. Container image: 9.4 GB Hugging Face PyTorch DLC. Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g6.48xlarge. The following chart breaks job startup into image download time and first training epoch time, comparing a standard Docker pull with a SOCI-indexed image across GPU and CPU configurations for both workloads. Figure 3: Job startup split into image download time and first training epoch time, standard Docker pull compared to a SOCI-indexed image From the second epoch on, time per epoch is the same (within run-to-run variation) on every instance, for both workloads. The first epoch takes 3–16 s longer from the lazy-loaded image, while files the framework touches for the first time are fetched. This first-epoch cost is the same on every instance size. Net: each job finished 1-6 min sooner. That is the download saving minus the one-time first-epoch cost, a fixed saving per job. Test this on your own workload These numbers are from the two workloads described earlier. The first-epoch cost depends on your image and what your code touches at startup: Lazy loading wins when the first training step needs only a fraction of the image, the rest streams in while you train. If your entry point reads most of the image before training starts (for example, scanning, checksumming, or preloading its contents), the first epoch waits for roughly the same bytes a full pull would have fetched. The net improvement would be small. Front-loaded starts still came out ahead in our tests: torch.compile and a just-in-time (JIT) built CUDA extension added 7-15 s to the first epoch (net saving still 3 min 25 s–3 min 56 s) A 6 GB model baked into the image streamed its weights at load time, adding 2-3.5 min, but the overall job still finished 2-2.5 mins sooner on the indexed image. Getting started You can adopt SOCI indexing two ways: use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container or create an index for your own custom image. Option 1: Use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container AWS publishes SOCI-indexed variants of several popular Deep Learning Containers, identified by the -soci suffix on the image tag: 763104351884.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/pytorch-training:2.9-gpu-py312-cu130-ubuntu22.04-sagemaker-v1-soci Pre-indexed variants are available for PyTorch Training, TensorFlow Training, vLLM, and SGLang, including arm64 variants for some frameworks. To adopt lazy loading, update the image tag in your job definition to the -soci variant. Browse the full list in the AWS Deep Learning Containers Gallery . Note: If you build your own image FROM a DLC base image, you must create a SOCI index for your final image. The index from the base image does not carry forward to derived images. Option 2: Create a SOCI index for your own image To index a custom image, you need a Linux host (such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance running Amazon Linux 2023) with containerd , the SOCI snapshotter , and either Finch or nerdctl installed. Set your environment variables . ACCOUNT_ID="111122223333" REGION="us-east-1" REPOSITORY_NAME="my-training-image" ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0" SOCI_IMAGE_TAG="v1.0-soci" REGISTRY="$ACCOUNT_ID.dkr.ecr.$REGION.amazonaws.com" Install the required tools . sudo dnf install -y containerd fuse soci-snapshotter runfinch-finch sudo systemctl start soci-snapshotter sudo systemctl restart containerd Authenticate to Amazon ECR . aws ecr get-login-password --region "$REGION" \ | sudo nerdctl login -u AWS --password-stdin "$REGISTRY" Pull your original image . sudo nerdctl pull "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG" Create the SOCI-indexed image . sudo nerdctl image convert --soci \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$ORIGINAL_IMAGE_TAG" \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" Push the indexed image . sudo nerdctl push --platform linux/amd64 \ "$REGISTRY/$REPOSITORY_NAME:$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" This creates two artifacts in your repository: the SOCI index and an OCI-compliant image index manifest linking your image to the index. Your original image and its digest remain unchanged. Automate index creation in CI/CD To generate indexes automatically on every push, deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder . It uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect Amazon ECR image push events and build the index. No changes to your build pipeline are required. Use the indexed image in your SageMaker AI job Reference your SOCI-indexed image exactly as you would any other image. No API changes are needed. Only the tag differs. Training example (SageMaker Python SDK) from sagemaker.train import ModelTrainer from sagemaker.train.configs import Compute trainer = ModelTrainer( training_image="111122223333.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-training-image:v1.0-soci", role="arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/SageMakerExecutionRole", compute=Compute( instance_type="ml.g5.12xlarge", instance_count=2, ), ) trainer.train() Verify that your image includes a SOCI index Before launching, confirm your tag resolves to an indexed image: aws ecr batch-get-image \ --repository-name "$REPOSITORY_NAME" \ --image-ids imageTag="$SOCI_IMAGE_TAG" \ --accepted-media-types \ "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json" \ --query 'images[0].imageManifest' --output text \ | jq '.manifests[] | {mediaType, artifactType}' Look for a child manifest whose artifactType begins with application/vnd.amazon.soci.index. alongside your platform manifest. If it isn’t there, the tag does not point to an indexed image. Things to keep in mind Amazon ECR private repositories only. Images in other registries, or pulled through a private Docker registry (TrainingRepositoryAccessMode set to Vpc), are not eligible for lazy loading. Improvement scales with image size. Images smaller than roughly 4 GB see relatively small improvements. Check for Docker-specific assumptions. SOCI-indexed images run on a containerd-based runtime. Review entry points and setup scripts for code that calls the Docker CLI, reads /var/run/docker.sock, or derives identifiers from cgroup paths. SageMaker AI mounts a /.dockerenv marker for backward compatibility, but avoid adding new dependencies on it. SOCI indexing for SageMaker AI jobs is available across all AWS Regions. Conclusion With SOCI indexing, you can minimize container image download time from your SageMaker AI training and processing jobs. Add a SOCI index to your images, or switch to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container. Either way, you cut startup time from minutes to seconds, reduce total job cost, and accelerate your machine learning (ML) iteration cycle. And your existing job definitions, API calls, and data pipelines stay exactly the same. To learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI and start using SOCI indexing, explore the following resources: Pick a SOCI-indexed Deep Learning Container. Browse the Deep Learning Containers Gallery and append -soci to your image tag. For framework-specific guidance, see SOCI index for AWS Deep Learning Containers . Index your own custom image. Follow the step-by-step walkthrough in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide , or refer to the SOCI snapshotter getting-started guide for advanced options. Automate indexing in your CI/CD pipeline. Deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder to generate indexes automatically on every image push. No pipeline changes are required. Test locally with Finch. Use the Finch lazy-loading walkthrough to validate your image on a containerd-based runtime before you submit a job. Dive deeper into the technology. Read Reducing container cold start times using SOCI index on DLAMI and DLC on the AWS Machine Learning Blog for benchmarks, or explore Under the hood: Lazy loading container images with Seekable OCI and AWS Fargate on the AWS Containers Blog to understand the lazy-loading mechanism in detail. Faster container startup is only one image tag away. Try it on your next SageMaker AI job and see the difference. About the authors Kanwaljit Khurmi Kanwaljit is a Senior Manager of Solutions Architecture and Data Scientists at Amazon Web Services, specializing in AI and ML. He collaborates with AWS product teams, engineering, and customers to provide guidance and technical assistance for maximizing the value of their hybrid GenAI solutions on AWS. Kanwaljit specializes in helping customers with containerized, data science, and machine learning applications. Mona Mona Mona currently works as Sr AI/ML specialist Solutions Architect at Amazon. She is a published author of three books and her latest book is AI Agents on AWS. She has authored 20+ blogs on AI/ML and cloud technology and a co-author on a research paper on CORD19 Neural Search which won an award for Best Research Paper at the prestigious AAAI (Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence) conference. Michael Oguike Michael is a Product Manager for Amazon SageMaker AI. He is driven by the application of technology and AI to solve real-world problems. At AWS, he helps customers across industries build, train, and deploy AI/ML models at scale. Before AWS, Michael designed and operated offshore oil and gas wells and facilities. Outside of work he enjoys exploring behavioral science and psychology through books and podcast. Deep Shah Deep is a Software Development Engineer on the Amazon SageMaker team, where he works on the infrastructure that powers model training on AWS. When he’s not scaling training systems, he enjoys sim racing, reading, and traveling.

title: 45,000 Nvidia Blackwell GPUs Cleared for Kazakhstan Data Center
body:
Goldman Sachs Raises December Brent Oil Price Forecast to $105
Eurasianet is an independent news organization that covers news from and about the South Caucasus and Central Asia, providing on-the-ground reporting and critical perspectives on…
Kazakhstan marked perhaps the high point of its presidentially proclaimed “year of artificial intelligence” with a visit by technology titan, Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, who said the Central Asian state has the potential to become “a global hub for Physical AI.”
Huang and Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev met on October 23 for talks aimed at bolstering collaboration between the chipmaking giant and Kazakh companies. Huang praised the Kazakh tech ecosystem as possessing all the prerequisites to become an AI power.
“This new industry requires energy at its foundation, it also requires a population dedicated to science, math and technology. You have richness in both,” Huang was quoted as telling Tokayev during their meeting.
Speaking later at a public forum with Kazakh Minister of AI Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang painted a picture in which Kazakhstan retools its energy sector to power data centers and AI development. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said.
Huang went on to predict that AI would transform every sector of the Kazakh economy from mining to agriculture. “AI will lift your people,” he said. Madiyev indicated that emphasis is being placed on the development of Kazakh-language models.
Huang’s visit coincided with the expansion of an Armenian-American AI infrastructure firm, Firebird.ai , into Kazakhstan. According to an Nvidia blog post , Firebird has obtained an export license for 45,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs for use in a data center built in conjunction with Kazakhtelecom. The first phase of the project is under construction, with a launch date set for the third quarter of 2027.
Firebird’s infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan could reach 500 megawatts once a planned second phase is completed. Firebird also intends to establish a lab to foster the development of human capital and AI startups.
Firebird CEO Razmig Hovaghimian said the collaboration with Kazakhstan came together quickly. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together,” Hovaghimian said after meeting the Kazakh leader. “We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.”
The Firebird- Nvidia project, officially known as Firebird AI KZ Ltd. , can help cement Kazakhstan’s position in a US initiative known as Pax Silica, which is designed to ensure AI and supply-chain reliability for Washington, while opening access to advanced technology and chips for participating states. Kazakhstan joined Pax Silica this past June.
But questions about Kazakhstan’s continuing membership in the group were raised after Astana also joined a competing Chinese initiative, dubbed WAICO . Over the summer, a draft State Department note reportedly stated that any nation that joined WAICO would be ineligible for participation in Pax Silica.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, during his recent visit to Central Asia, walked back the notion that Kazakhstan would have to make a choice between the two programs for AI development, saying Central Asian states were free to cooperate with any nation in building out their AI infrastructure.
