title: The Super Mouse puts a touchscreen macro pad under your hand
body:
A company called Arctic Fox Technologies has announced a new multifunction mouse that forgoes a myriad of customizable shortcut buttons peppered across its surface for a compact touchscreen sitting beneath your hand. The Super Mouse may not prioritize ergonomics with its boxy design, but it can replace other peripherals on your desk, like a trackpad, macro pad, or streaming controller. If you’re faster at typing on your phone, the Super Mouse could potentially even replace a full-size keyboard with a smartphone-sized alternative that even includes swipe typing.
The Super Mouse is now available for preorder through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign in which it’s discounted to $199 for backers, while full retail pricing will be $249. Delivery is expected to start in February 2027, but take that estimate with a grain of salt, as many Kickstarter campaigns have faced unforeseen delays.
That price makes the Super Mouse more expensive than other companies’ attempts to merge mice and touchscreens. But while alternatives like Turtle Beach’s Command Series MC7 has just a 2.25-inch narrow display on the side, the Super Mouse features a 3.1-inch, 720 x 720 touchscreen positioned front and center beneath a pair of standard mouse buttons, a scroll wheel, and two customizable “hyper keys.”
[Image: The Super Mouse doesn’t include a rechargeable battery and draws all the power it needs from a USB-C port, so using it wirelessly isn’t an option. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/supermouse2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all]
That touchscreen will be most useful as a way to quickly launch apps through what its creators call a “Control Panel” that can include up to 16 shortcuts, macros, or launchers. The display’s functionality will change contextually and will present relevant shortcuts based on what app you’re using. If you’re working with video in Adobe Premiere, for example, the touchscreen will include editing and playback shortcuts. But if you have a specific workflow need, or the app you’re using isn’t recognized, the Super Mouse’s functionality can be customized using the company’s Flow desktop app.
[Image: The Super Mouse will present app-specific controls such as playback and editing shortcuts for Adobe Premiere. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/10/supermouse.gif?quality=90&strip=all]
Other touchscreen features include event and meeting reminders when synced with Google Calendar, voice-to-text capabilities processed locally on the mouse itself, multiple user profiles, focus timers, and productivity tracking. The mouse also includes a gyroscope so you can control slideshows or scrub video by just moving it around. The only feature seemingly missing is the ability to go wireless. Instead of a rechargeable battery, the Super Mouse draws all the power it needs from a USB-C port, so you’ll always need to keep it tethered to your PC.

title: FireFly finds copper-gold system near idle mill
body: FireFly Metals (TSX, ASX: FFM) has found a new copper-gold system near its idle Nugget Pond mill in Newfoundland, adding a potential satellite deposit to its Green Bay development plans. Hole FFR26-071 at Mount Joy cut 22.5 metres grading 1.87% copper and 0.64 gram gold per tonne from 109 metres downhole. The prospect is 35 km east of the Ming mine, the main Green Bay deposit, which is about 360 km northwest of St. John’s. “We view the discovery as an encouraging early indication of the regional exploration potential at Green Bay, with several additional targets yet to be tested,” BMO Capital Markets analyst Rene Cartier wrote in a note Tuesday. The discovery, just 2.6 km from Nugget Pond, gives FireFly another target to test alongside its proposed Ming restart and expansion. A larger regional resource base could support more production over a longer mine life, although Mount Joy’s size and economics have yet to be established and the company has yet to establish how it might fit into its development plans. Shares gained 9.2% to $1.42 by midday in Toronto, valuing FireFly at about $1.32 billion (US$941 million). The stock closed 9.3% higher in Sydney at A$1.41. Shallow discovery The Mount Joy intercept included nine metres grading 2.95% copper and 0.95 gram gold from 112 metres. The initial hole, FFR26-064, returned 6.45 metres grading 0.81% copper and 1.19 grams gold from 15.55 metres downhole. A survey inside the first hole identified a conductive target about 80 metres to the south, leading FireFly to drill FFR26-071. Such surveys measure electrical conductivity to help locate sulphide bodies beyond a drill hole. Follow-up hole FFR26-076 cut about 40 metres of semi-massive sulphides between 240 and 280 metres downhole. Assays are pending and expected within about four weeks. Visual sulphides alone don’t establish metal grades or economic value. The company interprets a fault between the mineralization in the latter two holes. More conductive targets remain to be tested and FireFly plans a winter access road from Nugget Pond to support drilling early next year. FireFly described Mount Joy as a volcanogenic massive sulphide, or VMS, system with characteristics similar to Ming and Tilt Cove. It lies along the same geological contact as the former Tilt Cove mine. Restart plans FireFly has budgeted $16.7 million for regional exploration in fiscal 2027, with three surface rigs working across its targets. An initial resource for the separate Main Mine prospect, less than 3 km from Ming, is due in the first quarter. Six underground rigs are converting and expanding Ming’s resources ahead of an updated estimate and feasibility study due in the first quarter of 2027. FireFly expects to consider a final investment decision around mid-year and targets copper production in 2029. The Green Bay inferred resource published in August totals 60.2 million measured and indicated tonnes grading 1.9% copper and 0.5 gram gold, containing about 1.16 million tonnes of copper and 908,000 oz. gold. The total includes Ming and Little Deer. An August preliminary economic assessment outlined a base case processing 1.8 million tonnes annually over more than 32 years. Newfoundland and Labrador has approved selected early works, including clearing and a construction camp. Electrical and wastewater-treatment upgrades are underway. “In our view, continued exploration success, and growth in resources, will further support FireFly’s investment case for an upscaled centralized processing facility with higher production rates over a longer mine life,” Cartier wrote.

title: A fast and secure tar parser for the Rust ecosystem
body:
Starting with 0.13 1 , uv uses tar-codec to parse source distributions.
tar-codec is roughly twice as fast as our previous tar implementation ( astral-tokio-tar ) while also reducing uv's exposure to parser differentials and other security risks.
This blog post is about tar-codec itself: what it is, and what compelled us to build and optimize it. Read on if you, too, would like to know too much about tar archives.
What follows is an extended digression on the tar format. If all you care about is tar-codec , skip to it .
As a Python packaging tool, uv is in the business of resolving and installing Python packages. uv requests installable distributions from various sources (principally package indices like PyPI ) and installs them on the user's behalf. This is how you go from uv add urllib3 to something you can actually import and use in your own Python codebase.
Installable distributions come in two primary forms:
"Built" 2 distributions, also known as bdists or (most commonly) wheels , are essentially ZIP archives containing structured metadata and a fixed layout. Installers handle these by (more or less) plopping their contents into the right destination directory.
Many people think that bdist is short for "binary distribution," since wheels often contain compiled native code. This one common way to use wheels, but wheels can also contain pure Python. They're just another (and frequently better) way to package and install a distribution.
"Source" distributions, also known as sdists , are essentially tar archives. Unlike built distributions, a source distribution is essentially 3 just a rollup of a source tree's state at release time.
By definition, source distributions execute arbitrary code at installation time. This makes them very powerful, but brittle (missing build tools or dependencies) and also a security risk (an attacker who controls the sdist can run code without the user needing to import anything).
Wheels are generally produced by running a build backend on a source distribution. Examples of that include uv's own uv_build , maturin , and flit .
Consequently, at a bare minimum, a Python package installer needs to understand at least two different archive formats: ZIP for wheels, and tar for sdists.
We've already talked a bit before about ZIPs on the Astral blog, and we'll certainly be talking about them again soon enough. But today we'll be focusing on tar.
It's fair to ask: why does uv want a new tar parser?
In short: security and performance, but mostly security.
Up until 0.13, uv used astral-tokio-tar for its tar operations, including both parsing and creation (in uv build ). astral-tokio-tar is itself a fork of edera-dev/tokio-tar , which is a fork of vorot93/tokio-tar , which is a fork of dignifiedquire/async-tar , which is an async adaptation of composefs/tar-rs .
Around a year ago, we began to receive a number of security reports in astral-tokio-tar . This spurred us into looking more into our compression and archive handling stack, where we found additional problems.
Many of these boiled down to differentials that could cause a full parser desynchronization 4 : given an identical tarball, uv , pip , and other package tooling could be made to see different contents for the same package distribution. We found this particularly concerning in the context of archives that would appear "safe" to an index (like PyPI) but could extract dangerously when parsed by an installer like uv or pip .
This could the take the form of an "append" differential (where the attacker can append new files or new contents to existing files for a specific victim parser), or even a "full" differential (where the attacker can fully separate the extraction contents for each parser):
In the context of uv , the attacker model for these kinds of vulnerabilities is somewhat subtle: tar is only used for source distributions which, per above and unlike wheels, are assumed to execute arbitrary code at build time. Consequently, Python packaging mostly considers tar differentials to be a minor concern, since any attacker who would use them has a much more direct and official route towards writing arbitrary contents to disk (or executing arbitrary code).
Still, these findings unnerved us, and we embarked on a project to eliminate every differential we could find in astral-tokio-tar .
tar-codec grew directly out of that effort: we ultimately came to the conclusion that the tokio-tar family was too lenient by design , and that retrofitting constraints to it would be more troublesome and error-prone (including for existing non-Astral users of its APIs) than developing our own, ground-up implementation of tar. This would also give us the opportunity to systematically understand the tar format, and ensure that our assumptions around which aspects are (or aren't) differential risks hold true.
Similarly, we determined that our performance goals around tar parsing would be impossible to meet in the existing code base, at least not without refactors that would be tantamount to a rewrite.
It's important to understand that one does not simply build a tar parser from scratch. One must first understand how the tar format evolved into its current state 5 .
tar is an interesting format. Or more precisely, it's an interesting family of formats.
To summarize, there are three (and a half) variants that matter in practice:
There's UNIX V7 tar, which is the "original" tar. Very few tar implementations write this format by default anymore, but virtually all still read it. For example, Python's tarfile module will happily parse V7 tar files.
The UNIX V7 format is not widely used anymore because it comes with significant limitations on per-member file sizes (approximately 8 GiB) and path lengths (100 bytes).
Then there's the UStar/pax tar family 6 . This family is widely supported by tar implementations for both reading and writing. As far as tar goes, UStar and pax are what passes for a "gold standard" in terms of clarity of specification and documentation.
At this juncture, the main thing to know about the UStar/pax family is that it's derived from the UNIX V7 format, but with certain restrictions lifted:
GNU tar is documented in the GNU tar manual , but is not standardized per se . The source code of GNU tar (the CLI) is the de facto standard for GNU tar.
Like UStar/pax, GNU tar is derived from UNIX V7 tar. It's also derived from an early draft of UStar .
Also like pax, GNU tar makes file sizes and path/link lengths (effectively) unlimited. It does so in a completely different and much funnier way than pax does.
If you've ever written a parser for a binary format before, then you probably have a preconception for what a binary format should look like. To first, second, and third approximations, binary formats tend to look something like this:
Within this, too, certain idioms appear: binary formats typically use some form of TLV encoding , use different magics to signal different endiannesses, &c.
The tar format does not look like this, regardless of the variant. tar is fundamentally a block format , owing to its origins as a tape archival format 8 .
As a block format, a tar archive is comprised of one or more fixed-length blocks. There is no file-level header; instead, many of its blocks are headers, while other blocks contain actual member 9 data:
In all flavors of tar, all blocks (including the header blocks) are always 512 bytes. Each header block declares metadata for the member that follows it. This includes important things like the size of the member and its filepath.
Member contents don't always fit cleanly into multiples of 512 bytes, so a tar that wants to encode a file member of N bytes will allocate ceil(N / 512) blocks and pad out the remainder of the last block. This doesn't affect extraction, since the reader knows (via the header block) exactly how many bytes out of the allocated space are actual file content.
Conventionally, the padding or "holes" in a tar archive are filled with NUL bytes. However, nothing stops a tar producer from filling them with uninitialized memory, or lines from the Bee Movie, or anything else. A recurring theme with tar (of all flavors) is that it has no opinions about what goes in the holes of the format. This malleability makes it very prone to parser differentials, since it gives the attacker ample space to place surprising data.
tar's block design also makes it relatively space-inefficient 10 by modern standards. For example, a 513-byte file occupies an absolute minimum of 1,536 bytes when encoded as a tar member: one 512-byte block for the header, and two blocks for the content (one of which has only 1 "real" byte, followed by 511 bytes of padding). Similarly, a tar archive containing 1000 one-byte files requires a minimum of 1025 KiB of encoding (1 MiB for the headers and contents, and then 1 KiB for the trailing zero blocks).
So far, this all sounds pretty sane. It's not a "normal" file format by modern standards, but there's a simple state machine one could write to formalize a parse for the tar example above:
Unfortunately, it's not that simple. The state machine above is accurate for a V7 tar, but not for anything else in the tar format family.
To understand why, we have to remember V7 tar's limitations. All of those limitations come down to the C structure that represents a V7 member header, which we've annotated here:
Three big limitations stand out, and each member of the tar family tries to solve them in various different ways:
Let's see how each family works around these.
UStar's half-solution is to preserve the existing physical header block, while impressing some of its fields and padding into new roles.
This partially lifts the member name restriction (by raising it to 255 bytes), but retains the file size and linkname limitations.
pax fixes these remaining limitations by doing away with the single-block metadata design. Instead, pax has extensions that rely on two new UStar typeflags:
In both cases, an extended header block indicates its member's "size." But that size isn't for a file: instead, it's for the extension data itself.
So, what's in the extension data? pax calls it an extended header , and it's an entirely different encoding format. An extended header contains one or more pax "records," and each record is a string that looks like this:
This can be hard to visualize, so here's a concrete example:
Despite being a new encoding, the way that pax records work is relatively simple: if there is an effective pax record that corresponds to a tar member header's state, the pax record's value takes precedence. In the example above, this means that the subsequent member's size is 8000 bytes, even if the member's own header records a different size.
This is where the difference between global and local extensions comes in as well: global extended headers take precedence over all subsequent members in the archive, while local extended headers only affect the next file in the archive. Local extended headers also take precedence over any global headers, so we have the following precedence ordering:
(This, too, is simplified. More on that later.)
For this example, a pax-conforming tar implementation should extract two members:
hasdrubal.txt , with a payload of 10737418240 bytes and an mtime of 100 .
Observe that this is both greater than the UStar size limit of 8 GiB and does not use the UStar header's own name (of hannibal.txt ) or size (of 0 ), since the member's header is preceded by an x extended header that overrides those values 13 .
Moreover, the archive also contains a g extended header that overrides mtime for all subsequent members and x does not contain its own mtime , so the global extended header's mtime=100 also takes effect.
hamilcar.txt , with a payload of 1234 bytes and an mtime of 100 .
Observe that, unlike hasdrubal.txt , there is no x extended header for this member. As a result, the UStar member states are used, with the exception of those overridden by the effective g extended header. Thus hamilcar.txt ends up with mtime=100 , even if its UStar header sets a different value.
GNU tar takes a very different approach. First, here's the GNU tar header:
Observe that, unlike the UStar format, there is no char prefix[155] field. Furthermore, instead of pax extended headers with a fully general keyword/value format, GNU tar does two things:
It goes way harder than UStar on trying to re-use the existing 512-byte V7 member header. In particular, GNU tar adds its own base-256 encoding: if the first byte in a numeric field has its high bit set, then the remaining octets in that field are binary, rather than tar's normal octal form.
This effectively expands the per-byte entropy in numeric fields from 3 bits to 8 bits. For a char size[12] , that makes the effective size limit 2**80 14 or one yobibyte.
Instead of general x and g extended headers, GNU tar introduces a bunch of specialized typeflags for its own extensions.
Many of these are not relevant to the post, or even to modern tar archives at all. But two are:
These two typeflags effectively fill the role of the pax path and linkpath records, respectively.
For this example, a GNU tar implementation should extract two members:
hasdrubal.txt with a payload of 10737418240 bytes.
Observe that this size, which exceeds 8 GiB, was encoded directly in the header. However, the effective filename of hasdrubal.txt comes from overriding the header's original filename of hannibal.txt via the preceding GNU L extension.
publius.txt , which links to another file named africanus.txt .
Observe that publius.txt originally declared publius.txt -> scipio.txt as its link, but this gets overridden to africanus.txt by the preceding GNU K extension.
Finally, while GNU tar does not have pax's notion of global vs. local precedence, GNU tar extensions can stack . For example, to override a member's name and linkname at the same time, you'd have a tar header sequence like this 15 :
Now that we understand very roughly how the various tar family formats look and work, let's see what tar-codec has to do to parse them safely and efficiently.
First we'll revisit the state machine. Our nice and simple V7 state machine now understands the different pax and GNU states, and has become this monstrosity:
(Note that the error transitions in this state machine are dramatically simplified: in practice, any I/O or validation failure at any point also results in a Failed state.)
What in the world happened? A few different things:
Our state machine begins with a "classification" stage, which effectively locks the remainder of the parse to a single family (either UStar/pax or GNU 16 ) based on the identity (magic and version) of the first block.
This is done for differential reduction reasons: while researching tar-codec 's design, we realized that many other widely used tar parsers attempt to merge states across various tar families, with inconsistent results.
For example, with some tar parsers, it's possible to stack headers like so:
This has unclear semantics: GNU tar expects an L or K to apply to the next "file" member, but the next physical member in the stream is a pax local extension that also wants to modify the next "file" member. In practice we've seen other parsers do all kinds of things in this state, including attempting to merge the extensions, honoring one over the other(s), attempting to apply the L state to x instead of the file member, and so forth. Each of these is a potentially exploitable differential!
Instead, tar-codec will reject a tar archive if its individual headers don't agree about what family of tar it is. Real-world tar encoders don't mix tar families (there's no good reason to), so this doesn't pose a significant breakage risk.
The GNU part of the state machine is slightly more strict than the GNU documentation implies: the GNU documentation allows stacking of L / K extensions, including multiple of the same kind , in any order.
tar-codec tightens that to allowing L and K in any order, but only one of each per underlying member.
The UStar/pax part of the state machine models local and global extended headers rigidly.
There's a significant amount of complexity beneath this: pax allows x and g anywhere in the tar stream. For example, this is a perfectly valid extension sequence in pax:
This brings us to one of the most painful parts of pax that we glossed over before: extended headers don't shadow each other fully, they compose depending on what state the "stack" of effective pax records is in. The state of any given pax record can be:
Undeclared : no effective pax record exists anywhere in the current stack of local and global extensions, which means that the member's own UStar header's state takes precedence.
Active : there's an effective pax record in the stack, and it has a value.
Tombstoned : there's an effective pax record in the stack, but it has no value (for example, 8 path=\n instead of 12 path=abc\n ).
You would think that this would be the same as the Undeclared state, but it's not! pax considers this record explicitly deleted, and prescribes :
If the <value> field is zero length, it shall delete any header block field, previously entered extended header value, or global extended header value of the same name.
This has fascinating consequences for the state machine, because it means that an effective-but-deleted path record means...a file with no path? How are you supposed to extract that 17 ?
Needless to say, tar-codec tries to follow this faithfully. In particular, it attempts to be diligent about rejecting logically-consistent-but-nonsense states that fall out of pax's strange record state machine, including empty paths and global extended headers that try to declare size and other key states for all members.
One of the early design choices we made with tar-codec was to isolate the implementation into a few layers. From lowest to highest:
The tar-framing crate is responsible for taking a stream of blocks and turning it into a stream of frames. This happens in two refinement stages:
The stream or "physical" API honors the big state machine above and yields each block in a given state, one block at a time.
The "logical" API consumes the blocks produced by the "physical" API, and yields them as a stream of assembled members. Each assembled member is essentially its "header" (which is the physical header, merged with any effective extension state that affected the physical framing), a separate extension state for non-framing extensions (such as GNU L and K ), and a readable payload for the member's actual contents.
The tar-codec crate takes the "logical" API from tar-framing and turns it into something that can be extracted in memory or onto disk.
Extracting an archive (of any format) onto disk is its own can of worms, with its own differential risks 18 . Another one of our early observations is that every archive implementation tends to have its own extract-to-disk implementation, with its own edge cases.
We built archive-trait to address that. archive-trait exposes Archive and ArchiveBuilder traits (along with associated types and machinery) that allow any format to expose uniform APIs for reading and creating archives. We then built archive-trait 's own filesystem extraction on top of cap-std , giving us the ability to "anchor" extraction into a single directory and avoid a large class of link and path traversal footguns.
Writing a differential-resistant tar parser is surprisingly hard, given how ubiquitous tar files of all flavors are, and how simple the original (V7) format is.
This post has only scratched the surface in terms of complexity. To recap:
Each tar family has its own state machine, which is not always clearly laid out in that family's documentation or reference implementation. It is imperative that these state machines do not mix, but real-world tar parsers regularly allow them to.
Each tar family has its own, non-trivial rules for determining the precedence of state (pathname, linkname, and size) attached to archive members.
Some of this state affects the framing of the parser itself, meaning that faithfully handling e.g. pax archives means handling size and similar records up-front, rather than trying to abstract the parse across individual 512-byte header blocks.
Separately, there were numerous places where we had to compromise on strict pax conformance because of observed behavior from other implementations:
The pax spec is explicit that pax record values must be UTF-8. However, both GNU tar and star historically emitted some vendor-specific records 19 as raw binary. See this bug-tar thread for more context .
UStar and pax are explicit that uname and gname should be NUL-terminated in the UStar header, meaning that each can be at most 31 bytes long. However, CPython's tarfile (and probably others) will happily fill either to 32 bytes, only overflowing to the pax record at 33 bytes or more. See CPython#159322 for more context.
More generally, tar implementations will frequently leave mode , uid , gid , and mtime as all NUL, rather than zeroed or similar. This doesn't pose a framing/parser synchronization risk, so tar-codec tracks them as "missing" rather than assigning an arbitrary default value.
Finally, in the process of designing and implementing tar-codec, we found many parser differential primitives that cause various tar implementations to behave very differently on identical inputs. Some of these are currently being disclosed as security vulnerabilities. However, some of the general classes we saw:
pax/GNU state machine confusion, as mentioned above. In particular, some tar implementations can be fooled into applying a pax extension's states to a GNU extension (or vice versa) instead of to the subsequent member, often resulting in full desynchronization and different extraction results.
Mis-handling of pax extension precedence, in particular both global ( g ) extended headers and record "tombstoning." For example, some implementations will accept a g header with size=1234 but ignore it, despite pax saying clearly that such a size record overrides any UStar size fields. This also typically results in a full desynchronization primitive.
Mis-handling of pax record parsing. For example, some implementations will ignore the <length> prefix and instead assume that pax records can be safely split on \n . This is not true, since the <value> of a pax record can contain a verbatim \n . As you may have guessed, this also typically results in a full desynchronization primitive.
More generally, we found a great deal of variety in how lax various tar implementations are when it comes to parsing integer fields: many use their language's native "integer from string" API, which can behave surprisingly in the presence of different (non-Western Arabic) numeral forms, leading and trailing whitespace, and so forth. These small variations can percolate into two different implementations parsing the same size field as different integers, once again resulting in desynchronization.
Decode and encode performance was not the hard part: we found a lot of low-hanging fruit while optimizing both, including optimizing tar's checksum generation and calculating pax record length prefixes.
We also picked up significant performance gains by ensuring that tar-codec reuses allocations and batches/buffers its work wherever possible (and where doing so does not weaken the API's internal consistency or cancellation correctness in an async setting).
Conversely, performant secure extraction is somewhat hard: directory capability tracking (of the kind that cap-std does) adds measurable overhead to many of our filesystem operations, particularly when extracting on hosts that lack openat2(2) or an equivalent system call 20 . This negatively impacts extraction on macOS in particular.
All in all, tar-codec 's design rests on well-worn principles for secure parser design: we are conservative rather than liberal in what we accept, and we enforce correctness by construction through increasingly constrictive layers (from member framing to streaming to extraction). These design choices have made us confident that tar-codec is more resistant to differentials (by correctly rejecting them) than other tar implementations.
The fractured and under-specified nature of tar makes it impossible for us to say that we are entirely devoid of differentials, or that new differentials won't be discovered in the future. However, we believe that tar-codec 's primitives are the correct ones if and when those contingencies occur.
This is not the end of our work, on several levels:
While tar-codec is essentially feature-complete for our own purposes (within uv ), we're interested in making sure that it also solves problems that the larger Open Source community has around secure and performant tar parsing.
To that end, we'll be looking at supporting other, more niche aspects of the various tar families (like sparse files, and more control over vendor-specific pax records) as the need arises.
Separately, we'll be working with others in the community on improving the correctness of other tar implementations. In particular, we see Harmen Stoppels's nascent tar-minefield project as a promising way to test and re-align other implementations with stricter, more differential-resistant interpretations of the tar family formats.
Separately, as you may have guessed from our decision to build a generic archive-trait library: tar is not the only format we're thinking about here!
We're also actively looking into replacing uv's ZIP parsing, for similar reasons. We hope to share our lessons from that work soon, along with material benefits to uv itself.
tar-codec has been available since 0.12, but was disabled by default behind the --preview-features tar-codec flag. As of 0.13, it is the default and can be disabled by setting UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1 . ↩
The term "built" is the source of a great deal of confusion for newcomers when they first encounter Python packaging. In the context of Python packaging, "built" refers to the fact that the distribution is produced by a "build backend", i.e. contains structured metadata that a source distribution is not guaranteed to have.
It does not imply that the wheel contains shared libraries or other native code, although it can. Pure Python packages are also regularly distributed as built distributions, because installing them is faster and more reliable. ↩
Historically, a source distribution was literally just a source archive, with the convention of having a pyproject.toml or setup.py at the archive's root. More recent Python packaging standards state that source distributions must contain a PKG-INFO file containing standard metadata. See PEP 643 for more on that.
As a result, many source distributions contain no metadata other than the build system itself, which must be executed to access the distribution's metadata. ↩
We recommend Edera's " TARmageddon " blog post for a detailed treatment of one such differential. ↩
Martin Dørum has a great blog post on the original tar format and how it evolved over time into the constellation of variants that currently exist. We highly recommend reading his post. ↩
Whether or not UStar and pax should be clumped together in the same family is doubtless extremely controversial to the dozen-or-so other people on Earth who have thought about the tar format this much. I consider them to be in the same family, since pax is effectively a strict superset of UStar and comes from the same standards body (POSIX) that produced UStar. ↩
There are actually two different GNU tar formats: there's oldgnu i.e. "old GNU" and gnu i.e. "new GNU". The difference between these two is minor (relative to everything else) and GNU tar itself emits "new GNU" as of tar 1.12, which was released in 1997. So that's enough about "old GNU." ↩
"tar" of course being short for "Tape ARchive." Magnetic tapes (like all mass storage) store their contents in sequences of fixed-sized blocks, and tar seals 1979's glorious 512-byte blocks in amber.
tar is also far from the only block-style file format. cpio is another well-known one. ↩
Archive members are things like files and directories, but also things like sockets and device files. I'm not really clear on what it means to archive a socket, but both UStar/pax and GNU tar will happily let you express that you've done so! ↩
Before compression, of course. tar knows nothing about compression. It's just the format that encodes one or more files into a single file. ↩
V7 tar handles directories in two ways: it creates directories that are implied to exist (for example, a member whose name is foo/makeme/bar will create foo and foo/makeme if needed), and it will explicitly create a directory if a regular file member ends with a slash, e.g. foo/makeme/ . ↩
In other words, it's a self-describing length. This is somewhat unusual when compared to a "normal" TLV/LTV encoding, where the length component is typically either a fixed length or something with only limited length variation, like LEB128 . ↩
You might be thinking: why bother putting states in the member's UStar header at all, if they're just going to be overridden by the pax extended header? Why not just fill those parts of the block with NULs?
The answer has to do with backwards compatibility: both GNU and pax do a disgusting hack interesting trick where the extension/extended header's own name field is also a valid path, conventionally a specially formatted one like %d/PaxHeaders.%p/%f , where %d is the dirname of the pax path record, %p is the current PID, and %f is the basename of the same path record.
The theory behind this is (probably) that a subsequent tool can repair the extraction, by looking at the pax headers which have been extracted as a regular file instead. In practice I suspect this doesn't work well in the greater-than-8 GiB case, which is one of the cases where it matters the most. ↩
This is 2**80 instead of 2**96 because we lose size[0] to the base-256 sign bit and size[11] to the NUL byte. Implementations that don't require a NUL terminator for fields like size could in principle allow up to 2**88 instead. ↩
The order of GNU extensions before the member they affect does not appear to matter in any implementation. In other words, you can have L -> K -> 1 or K -> L -> 1 . ↩
That's correct: we don't support parsing V7-style tar files. An early review revealed that they're nonexistent in the Python packaging ecosystem, probably because Python's own tarfile never supported creating them. The gap between V7 and UStar is small, however, so adding it would not be difficult if needed. ↩
Many tar implementations do random things here, like trying to extract to an empty path (which of course fails), or picking some previous filename or extended header state. ↩
Extraction differentials themselves are out of this post's scope, but to summarize: extraction depends heavily on the target filesystem and its state, including any pre-existing symbolic and hard links.
Nuances abound, including how to handle files that differ in casing inside the archive but not on the filesystem itself (macOS and Windows), how to handle symlinking on systems where symbolic links are privileged (Windows), and how to handle "funky but valid" filenames (non-UTF-8, UTF-8 with NULs, control characters, &c.). ↩
A pax "vendor record" is a normal pax record, but with a name like VENDOR.keyword instead of keyword . pax itself does not specify their semantics and various implementations do wildly different things with them, so tar-codec rejects them by default (with an option to skip/ignore them instead). SCHILY.xattr.* is one common example of a vendor record namespace. GNU also has their own vendor namespace, e.g. GNU.sparse.* for sparse members. ↩
Without openat2(2) or a similar source of RESOLVE_BENEATH semantics, cap-std needs to open each directory component in a path, which means that its system calls scale linearly with the depth of the paths it needs to track. This is on top of the system call overhead for the extraction I/O itself. ↩

title: Outcome of Oleshky humanitarian operation could pave the way for further steps in peace process, Sybiha says
body:
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this at a joint press conference with Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen and Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide in Helsinki, Ukrinform’s correspondent reports.
“If we see results in Oleshky, this could open the way for further steps in the peace process as a confidence-building measure,” Sybiha said.
For months Ukraine had been drawing the international community’s attention to the situation in Oleshky, where people are going hungry, appealing to countries, international organizations, world leaders, and prominent religious figures, Ukraine’s FM said.
Sybiha also thanked U.S. First Lady Melania Trump for her involvement in these efforts and her leadership.
“We hope that all commitments will be fulfilled. The Ukrainian side is fully prepared for this,” the minister said.
As previously reported, the ceasefire in the Oleshky area is scheduled to remain in effect from October 27 until 10:59 p.m. on Sunday, November 1.

title: France and 10 European countries plan to deploy nuclear-capable French jets to deter Russia, WSJ reports
body: A French Rafale fighter jet with ASMP-A missiles France is working with 10 other European countries to establish a new nuclear deterrence framework aimed at Russia, The Wall Street Journal reported. The initiative, which President Emmanuel Macron called “forward deterrence,” was unveiled in March 2026. It calls for deploying nuclear-capable French Rafale fighter jets to other European countries. Participants also intend to create a joint system for early warning and intelligence sharing. The United Kingdom, Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Poland, Greece, Finland, Norway, Sweden, and Denmark have joined France in the initiative. The three Baltic states, which are most vulnerable to Russian aggression, are not part of the project, while Italy declined to participate. Finland said it would like to take part but does not plan to host nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime. French officials believe the new deterrent could be more credible because the security of France’s European neighbors matters far more to Paris than to Washington. European officials also emphasize that the new system should supplement, rather than replace, the American “nuclear umbrella” over the continent and create further strategic uncertainty for Russia. Experts say the French ASMP-A cruise missiles carried by Rafale fighters are more effective in modern warfare than American B-61 nuclear bombs. The American bombs were developed in the 1960s, and advances in Russian air defenses limit their use. Macron also said France plans to resume producing nuclear weapons for the first time in decades. The country currently has about 290 nuclear warheads but will no longer disclose information about its arsenal. In practice, however, France will retain full control over its nuclear forces. “The French will let us participate in their nuclear deterrence as much as the Americans,” said a minister from one of the countries involved in the project. France is holding bilateral talks with its partners and has set up 10 separate groups for those discussions. Defense officials across Europe have had to hold frequent calls to keep one another informed about the negotiations, military officials said. title: How is the Western world reporting on Israel's 26th Knesset elections?
body: Israel's elections are taking center stage in international media coverage on Tuesday, with headlines framing the vote as a test of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political future and a decision on the country's direction after three years of war.Alongside discussion of a possible change of government, the outlets surveyed also emphasize the uncertainty surrounding the outcome: the election could end without a clear result that would allow either camp to form a government.“Netanyahu's political survival on the line as Israel votes,” reads the Reuters headline.The Associated Press opted for more direct wording: “Israeli voters decide whether to oust Netanyahu after three years of war.” Both headlines place the prime minister at the center of the first election since the October 7 attack and the wars that followed.Britain's Financial Times chose the headline “Israelis head to polls in historic election.”Germany's Tagesschau described the vote as a “fateful election,” while Spain's El País framed its significance in terms that extended beyond Israel's borders: “Netanyahu puts his future on the line in an election decisive for the entire Middle East.”'Yes or no to Bibi'Alongside straight news reporting, some outlets published sharply worded opinion headlines.In the American magazine The Atlantic, the headline “Netanyahu Enters Full Panic Mode” appeared above an article by commentator Graeme Wood. Germany's Der Spiegel used similar language: “Netanyahu shifts into panic mode.” In both cases, the headlines reflect analysis of Netanyahu's conduct and campaign messaging, rather than reporting on the election results.The Italian edition of Euronews summed up the election's personalized framing with the headline “'Yes or no to Bibi': Israel's election has become a referendum on Netanyahu.”By contrast, Brazil's Folha de S.Paulo focused on the figures surrounding the two main contenders: “Israel's election pits Netanyahu against a former general, but other leaders may determine who governs the country.”British coverage also highlights the gap between winning at the ballot box and actually forming a government.The Times published a guide to the electoral system, the candidates, and possible scenarios. The Wall Street Journal emphasized in its subheadline that Israel's parliamentary system could leave the outcome unclear for weeks.In France, Le Monde took a more personal approach to the election, publishing a field report on Israelis living abroad who are returning to the country to vote. The headline opens with the words “'What is at stake is existential!',” quoting one of the people interviewed. The report describes voters traveling from various countries to take part in the election.Elections on 'a knife's edge'On election day, Der Spiegel also published a news report with a different focus: “Families remember Hamas victims, and demand answers.” Thus, alongside its sharp commentary on Netanyahu, the magazine also gave space to families demanding an investigation into the failures surrounding the attack.The drama surrounding the election is also reflected in Australian headlines. SBS described the vote as being “on a knife's edge,” while ABC focused on Netanyahu's increasingly hard-line security rhetoric in the run-up to the election.Across the coverage examined, one distinction repeatedly emerges: the question of which party or candidate will receive the most votes is not the same as the question of who will ultimately be able to govern. That second question may remain unresolved even after the polls close.

title: Zamfara moves against Ebola virus threat, steps up surveillance, screens travellers at Gusau airport
body:
Zamfara Government has stepped up surveillance against Ebola threat by conducting mass screening at the Gusau International Airport and across motor parks. This was done to prevent possible spread of the virus in the state.
The State Commissioner for Health, Dr Nafisa Maradun, disclosed this while flagging-off the response team at the Gusau International Airport on Friday.
She said the state government initiated the response measure following the arrival of a passenger, an indigene of Zamfara, from Saudi Arabia via EgyptAir, who presented with high temperature.
Maradun said the measures were aimed at preventing an outbreak of the virus in the state.
She said the government had also intensified screening of passengers and commuters arriving at Gusau motor parks and other entry points, noting that raising public awareness remained key to curbing possible spread of the virus.
The move, according to the commissioner, follows the reported index case in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention had disclosed that the index patient diagnosed with the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus in Nigeria is a Ugandan-born woman who arrived in the FCT with her husband on 3 October.
Flagging off the response at the airport, Maradun said: “It becomes necessary as the surveillance team identified a passenger arriving from Saudi Arabia via EgyptAir with high temperature.”
She said officials had been deployed to the airport to screen passengers arriving in Zamfara by air to ensure no one imports the Ebola virus into the state.
Also, the Nigerian Medical Association (NMA), Zamfara Chapter, said it was collaborating with major stakeholders to intensify surveillance and preventive measures against Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) in the state.
The State NMA Chairman, Dr Muhammad Murtala, stated this at a press briefing in Gusau on Friday, marking the 2026 Physicians’ Week.
The theme for this year’s Physicians’ Week is “Securing the Future of Medicine in Nigeria.”
Dr Murtala, who is the Incident Manager, Polio Emergency Operations Centre in the state, said the NMA, in collaboration with the state Ministry of Health and partners, had developed an incident action plan to create public awareness on Ebola.
According to Dr Murtala said the Ministry of Health had already met with critical medical stakeholders and public health experts to ensure active surveillance against the disease.
“Therefore, we are fully engaged and prepared to manage the situation in case of any Ebola case, to ensure it is carefully managed and to prevent further spread,” he said.

title: 2027: APM in coalition talks, says Daura
body: By Juliet Umeh Vice-presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, Lawal Daura, says the party is involved in coalition discussions ahead of the 2027 general elections. Daura disclosed this on Channels Television’s Sunrise Daily, where he also called for an inclusive approach to governance, saying Nigeria needed a “reset” to address what he described as recurring political and social problems. “We are involved right now in the discussion for the coalition,” he said. Explaining the APM’s “reset agenda,” Daura said Nigeria had been “moving in cycles without really making much or any progress.” He said the agenda would bring Nigerians together to discuss the country’s direction and agree on how it should be governed. “The reset agenda should be an all-inclusive thing. Let us get together as Nigerians.” According to him, a government formed under the agenda would involve stakeholders beyond those who helped it win an election. “Where you make an election or win your election to be the winner-takes-all is not going to help Nigeria,” he said. Daura, a former Director-General of the Department of State Services, said his decision to enter politics was motivated by his desire to contribute to the country’s development. “I felt maybe there is a need for me to come out and contribute,” he said, adding that joining the political process would allow him to contribute “more and better than when it is just maybe by the sidelines.” He said his years in public service had given him insights into the country’s challenges, but added: “I play politics, but within the definition given by politicians in Nigeria, I would say I am not a politician.” Daura said he initially sought the governorship of Katsina State after senior citizens approached him over insecurity in the state, which he described as an “epicentre” of banditry and kidnapping. “I have made myself very clear right from the onset that whatever my people requested me to do, I would do. At my level, I can even become a local government chairman. I wouldn’t mind.” He said his governorship bid through the African Democratic Congress did not proceed as he had hoped, citing the absence of primaries and concerns about compliance with electoral law. He said he declined suggestions that he seek a Senate seat instead. Daura said he chose the APM after considering other parties, which he alleged faced internal leadership disputes or court cases. He called the APM “the only healthy party” at the time he joined and said it was expanding its reach. “Right now, as I speak, APM is a party to beat,” he said. Asked why he did not seek a Senate seat, Daura said the security situation required urgent action. “The Senate is not really a fire brigade station. The insecurity situation in Nigeria now or today demands a kind of a fire brigade approach.” On the 2018 incident in which security operatives blocked access to the National Assembly while he headed the DSS, Daura said carrying out his duties did not make him undemocratic. He declined to disclose what he said was behind the action, saying the relevant material remained classified. “If the same scenario appeared today, I would do the same,” he said. The post 2027: APM in coalition talks, says Daura appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Airbus receives order for two more Galileo satellites with stronger anti-jamming protection
body: The European Space Agency awarded the contract on behalf of the EU Agency for the Space Programme, under a delegation from the European Commission. Airbus said the additional pair would use manufacturing capabilities established for the six satellites already on order. “With these contracts, ESA and European industry are safeguarding the continuity of Europe’s satellite navigation services, responding to the evolving needs of users, and strengthening Europe’s strategic autonomy,” said Laurent Jaffart, ESA’s director of resilience, navigation and connectivity. “These contracts represent an investment in Europe’s ability to navigate its own future, independently and with confidence.” The new antennas are intended to improve navigation accuracy, while the digital payloads can be reconfigured in orbit. This will allow new signals and services to be introduced as user requirements change. Each satellite will have an enhanced atomic clock configuration and links to other satellites for communication and data cross-checking. The spacecraft will weigh more than two tonnes each and are designed to operate for 15 years. “We are committed to delivering these next-generation satellites which are vital to augment navigation capabilities for European security and defence and wider societal benefits,” said Alain Fauré, head of Space Systems at Airbus. Manufacturing, integration and testing will draw on facilities in Backnang, Friedrichshafen, Getafe, Ottobrunn and Toulouse. Galileo is funded by the European Union and managed by the European Commission. ESA leads the design, development and qualification of its space and ground systems, while EUSPA provides services and oversees operations and deployment.

title: Russia-Iran trade turnover growing — Putin
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Trade turnover between Moscow and Tehran is growing: it increased by more than 10% in the first eight months of this year, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a meeting with President of the Islamic Republic of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian.
"Russian-Iranian trade turnover grew by 10.4% in the first eight months of this year," he said.

title: Fubara Reaffirms Support For Tinubu, Wike-Led Rainbow Coalition
body: Rivers State Governor, Siminalayi Fubara, has reaffirmed his support for President Bola Tinubu and the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, pledging to work for the victory of the Rainbow Coalition in the 2027 general elections. Fubara spoke on Tuesday at the unveiling of the coalition’s candidates in Rivers State, where he urged members to put past leadership disputes behind them and work together. The governor described the coalition as family, expressing happiness at being reunited with political allies after a crisis that divided the group. “I’m really happy to be here, not just being here, but standing in the midst of my family,” he said. Fubara acknowledged Wike and other political leaders for their roles in his emergence as governor, expressing gratitude that they had come together again for what he described as the collective good of Rivers State. He pledged to support the coalition’s candidates, saying he would do everything within his power to secure their victory. The governor also thanked Tinubu for standing by him during his most difficult period and reaffirmed his commitment to the political bloc led by Wike. “I’m here with all my heart, my soul, and my body, and I will do everything within my power to ensure that we have victory, not just for Mr President, who has stood for me in my most difficult time, but also to ensure that this power still remains in our own bloc,” Fubara said. He described the unveiling as an honour and expressed optimism about the candidates’ performance in the January 2027 elections. The Rainbow Coalition comprises seven political parties that have aligned to field consensus candidates for the elections in Rivers State. They are the All Progressives Congress (APC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Action Alliance (AA), All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA), Labour Party (LP), Allied Peoples Movement (APM) and Boot Party. However, candidates from only the APC and PDP emerged as the coalition’s consensus candidates for the 2027 elections. The coalition, led by Wike, who is also the national leader of the PDP, unveiled its candidates at a ceremony in Port Harcourt on Tuesday. Former Minority Leader of the House of Representatives, Kingsley Chinda, emerged as the coalition’s governorship candidate on the APC platform, with the current Majority Leader of the Rivers State House of Assembly, Major Jack, as his running mate. For the three senatorial districts, the APC has two candidates, while the PDP has one. Felix Amaechi Obua is the APC candidate for Rivers West, while Senator Allwell Onyesoh is the party’s candidate for Rivers East. Senator Olaka Nwogu of the PDP is the candidate for Rivers South-East. The coalition’s House of Representatives list has 13 candidates, comprising 10 APC members and three PDP members. Among the APC candidates is the Speaker of the Rivers State House of Assembly, Martin Amaewhule, who is contesting for Obio/Akpor Federal Constituency. The PDP candidates include Kelechi Nwogu for Etche/Omuma, Arthur Uchendu for Ikwerre/Emohua and Achinike Wonodi for Port Harcourt I. For the Rivers State House of Assembly, the coalition has 32 candidates, with 21 contesting on the APC platform and 11 on the PDP platform. The post Fubara Reaffirms Support For Tinubu, Wike-Led Rainbow Coalition appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Boundary Dispute: Ifo chairman, Ogun urges Lagos to call Ojodu counterpart to order over signpost
body:
The Chairman of Ifo Local Government in Ogun State, Kusimo Idris Olalekan, has urged the Lagos State Government to call the Chairman of Ojodu Local Government to order over the erection of a signpost bearing the inscription, “Welcome to Lagos State,” at a disputed location along the Yakoyo–Ojodu Road.
Olalekan said the placement of the signpost had raised concerns about the boundary between Ogun and Lagos states, particularly around Yakoyo in Isheri-Ojodu Ward, where Ifo Local Government maintains that the location falls within Ogun State’s territorial jurisdiction.
The council expressed concern that the signpost, which indicates the beginning of Lagos State, could create confusion among residents and road users over the actual boundary between the two neighbouring states.
The development comes amid concerns over the territorial limits of the two states in the affected area, following the construction of a road by the Ogun State Government under Governor Dapo Abiodun.
Ifo Local Government maintained that the disputed location falls within its jurisdiction and called on the Lagos State Government to intervene by directing the Ojodu Local Government chairman to desist from actions that could aggravate the boundary disagreement.
According to the council, the issue of territorial jurisdiction around the Yakoyo–Ojodu axis has generated concerns over the years, with what it described as repeated attempts by Lagos State to assert control over areas claimed by Ogun State.
The council warned that such developments could create unnecessary tension and uncertainty for residents, stressing the need for both state governments and their respective local government authorities to handle the matter with caution and responsibility.
It called for an objective determination of the boundary through official records, approved survey coordinates and other relevant government documents to establish the precise territorial limits of both states.
The council noted that a resolution based on authoritative records would help prevent further misunderstandings, protect the interests of residents and promote peaceful relations between Ogun and Lagos states.
Olalekan further urged the Lagos State Government to ensure that the actions of local government officials did not undermine efforts to maintain cordial relations between the two states, particularly in communities located around their shared boundary.
Reaffirming Ifo Local Government’s commitment to protecting its territorial interests, the chairman said the council would continue to defend the rights of its residents while pursuing a resolution of the matter through appropriate channels.
The council also called on all parties to exercise restraint and respect established territorial boundaries pending an authoritative clarification of the disputed area

title: A $3M Hedge, a Midterm Test and Retail's Rise: Prediction Markets at NEXTPredict
body:
Prediction markets spent two days in the spotlight at NEXTPredict, which brought the industry's biggest exchanges, trading firms and policymakers to Convene Hudson Yards in New York on October 22 and 23.
With the U.S. midterms less than two weeks away, elections dominated the conversation, but executives were just as keen to talk about what comes next.
The conference opened with a trade that didn't pay out. NEXTPredict had paid a $12,000 premium on Kalshi for contracts that would have returned around $3 million if more than half of scheduled arrivals at New York's JFK airport were cancelled the day before the event.
"We ended up losing that trade yesterday, right?" NEXTPredict co-founder Pierre Lindh said on Thursday's "Hedging the Unhedgeable" panel. "And I can only say I'm very happy that we lost that trade, because that means we're all here today."
Traditional event insurance covers cancellation, Lindh explained, but "most of these type of force majeure situations won't cancel the event. It will severely damage the event."
Joe Grubb, head of business development at Susquehanna, which took the other side of the trade, said the firm modeled the risk in-house in about a day or two. "It's sort of in our DNA at Susquehanna to price strange things," he said.
Kalshi's director of business development, Nicolas Hull, said small businesses were now hedging on the exchange, starting with a New York bar that covered a Knicks playoff promotion. As long as a contract is certified with the CFTC and has a verifiable data source, "we can list almost anything on our exchange," he said.
This is the team behind NEXTPredict Summit New York.
Months of planning. More late nights than we'll admit. And then, last week, it all came together at Convene, 30 Hudson Yards.
2,000+ of you in the room. 180 speakers. 47 countries. Two weeks before the midterms, the… pic.twitter.com/KCA9TpDCV4
— NEXTpredict (@nextpredictio) October 26, 2026
Todd, the former NBC News political director, had told Lindh before the event that he was "open minded" about whether markets or pollsters would call the midterms better. By Friday's "Who Calls the Midterms" panel, he sounded closer to a convert.
"This is my argument of why I'm bullish on prediction markets for the future of journalism and that it should be this, in its own way, a fact checker," Todd said. "With money being involved, there's more incentive to get it right."
He argued that prediction markets have effectively replaced exit polls on election night, but pushed back on the idea that polling is broken. "You can still do a good poll. It just costs a lot," he said.
His panelists were more cautious. "Speed is not necessarily the same as accuracy," said Columbia University professor Rajiv Sethi, while PredictIt CEO John Phillips reminded the audience that "it's called wisdom of crowds, not wisdom of whales."
That caution looked well placed days later. Before Brazil's presidential runoff on Sunday, Polymarket gave Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva only about a 20% chance of beating Flávio Bolsonaro, but he went on to win a fourth term, Decrypt reported . Experts blamed Brazil's ban on prediction markets, which left the odds largely to traders outside the country.
For Robinhood, elections were only the starting point. "When I started doing this two years ago, it was about elections," JB Mackenzie, the brokerage's vice president and general manager for futures and prediction markets, told CNBC 's Contessa Brewer, one of several working journalists the organizers booked for the program. "Then it transformed into politics and sports, and now it's moving into economics and financials."
Sports remain the biggest category, Mackenzie said, but contracts on Bitcoin , crude oil and gold are now the fastest-growing. "The simplicity of a probability is much more consumable for customers," he said.
Polymarket's Bailey Springer, who works on regulatory strategy outside the U.S., said regulators in global financial hubs increasingly recognize that "prediction markets aren't going away" and have real uses for investment and hedging. "At Polymarket, our position is that these are derivatives and should be regulated as such," she said.
Speed was another theme. On Thursday's "Race to Zero Latency" panel, Farokh Sarmad , president and co-founder of Decrypt Media, said ordinary traders are usually a step behind professional firms when news breaks. "By the time you open Polymarket or Kalshi or Myriad or all the other prediction markets, you're usually a little too late," he said.
His answer is to cut out the gap between reading and trading, which Decrypt is doing with its Solana -based Information Exchange . "The best way to reduce that latency is to be able to consume it and trade it directly on the same platform," Sarmad said, adding that for any of this to work, "everything has to move on chain."
Institutional money also featured heavily, with Morgan Stanley leading sessions on the second day.
Lindh, for his part, sees the industry's next debate already taking shape. "I think the next step will be the comparison between prediction markets and insurance," he said.
Disclosure: Myriad is a prediction market developed by Decrypt's parent company, Dastan.

title: New Brunswick signs deal for Canadian firm to explore old antimony mine
body:
The New Brunswick government announced progress on a pair of mining projects officials see as proof the sector is back on the rise in a province where it used to be an economic cornerstone.
Natural Resources Minister John Herron twice took to the stage at a mining conference in Fredericton this week to tout what he called an “audacious” vision to reignite the industry in his province.
“Our vision is to build a modern mineral sector that drives sustained economic growth, supports high quality jobs (and) strengthens regional economies — whether it’s through exploration, development or supply chain activity,” Herron said.
The province’s Liberal government has pushed a new minerals strategy this year to position New Brunswick as a jurisdiction ready for investment.
That’s as the federal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has made critical mineral development a top economic and national security priority amid global demand.
“We have what the world wants,” Herron said Monday, speaking at the annual Exploration, Mining and Petroleum Conference hosted by the provincial government.
Neil Jacobson, one of the conference organizers from the province’s Department of Natural Resources, said nearly 500 executives, investors and other industry professionals attended the three-day forum, which he said was more than double the attendance from recent years.
On Monday, the government said it signed an exploration deal with a U.S.-based firm that plans to extract minerals from a long-closed mining site in northern New Brunswick.
Regeneration Enterprises wants to pull metals from rock and chemical waste left at the Nigadoo mine site, and then fund environmental clean up of the mine using revenue generated from selling the metals.
Production at the Nigadoo mine, located near Bathurst, N.B., first started in 1956, according to a University of New Brunswick research paper. The mine was permanently shuttered in 1977 after repeated closures.
“This project will convert something that has been a liability for decades and turn it into new investment, good jobs and a cleaner site,” Herron said in a statement.
Then on Tuesday, he announced an agreement with a Canadian firm that hopes to reopen a major antimony mine.
The deal gives Toronto-based Avenir Minerals the exclusive rights to explore the former Lake George mining site, located southwest of Fredericton.
The abandoned mine used to be one of North America’s largest producers of the critical mineral antimony, and operated intermittently from 1876 to 1996.
The shiny grey metal is mainly used as a flame retardant, but it is also used in solar panels, lead-acid batteries and more recently in infrared missiles, nuclear weapons and night vision goggles.
The agreement comes after the province announced it had started negotiations with Avenir Minerals in July.
Alden Greenhouse, chief executive of Avenir Minerals, said his company has 30 months to study the mine’s potential for antimony and other critical minerals.
He said the exploration process will likely include drilling. As well, he said his company will consult with First Nations and nearby communities.
Both projects are funded only by private capital, without an ask for provincial taxpayer dollars.
“There’s a buzz, we’re just here to unlock that potential,” said Jacobson, an acting deputy minister for the lands and mines division of the Department of Natural Resources.
We call ourselves air traffic controllers. We want the runway to be cleared for companies and New Brunswick to prosper off what potential economic opportunities that are coming.”
Others are uncertain about reviving the sector.
“It’s not a good legacy,” Beverly Gingras, executive director of the Conservation Council of New Brunswick, said Tuesday.
“People come in, they make money, and then they leave. And New Brunswickers are left taking responsibility, paying the environmental, social, and economic costs of other people making money.”
Terry Richardson, chief of Pabineau First Nation, said there needs to be a balance between taking care of the environment and boosting the provincial economy.
Either way, he said, Indigenous buy-in will be required.
“We hold the keys,” he said in an interview. His Mi’kmaq community signed an agreement with Regeneration Enterprises for the Nigadoo mine exploration project that could lead to financial benefits.

title: OpenAI Proves ETH Is False, and Crypto Twitter Has Questions
body:
OpenAI says ETH is false, and Crypto Twitter reacted exactly the way you would expect. “Damn algo traders just slaughtered $ETH,” a user called Takumi posted on X, while Andrew Jiang quipped: “Vitalik has been real quiet since this came out.”
But chill out, degens, the ETH in question is the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a computer-science conjecture from 1999 that has nothing to do with Ethereum, its price, or co-founder Vitalik Buterin. So, crypto bros, you can breathe.
OpenAI published a 67-page paper claiming its AI found a way around the hypothesis, and the people who proposed it are now checking the work.
Computer scientists Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi proposed ETH with Francis Zane, and it says a classic logic puzzle called 3-SAT (finding true-or-false settings that satisfy a pile of rules, three options at a time) cannot be solved much faster than by trying every combination. Hundreds of papers assume it to show that problems in graph theory, computational biology, databases and geometry cannot be solved quickly, per OpenAI .
In other words, ETH is a map of what computers will probably never do fast, and OpenAI says its model just redrew it. “The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become,” the company wrote on its blog , “and may help guide the search for better algorithms.”
The paper, dated October 17 and revised October 25, describes a deterministic algorithm (one with no randomness) that counts every satisfying assignment of such puzzles in subexponential time, meaning the work grows more slowly than any exponential in the number of variables. Counting solutions is harder than deciding if one exists, so the harder job brings the easier one along for free.
OpenAI says its AI found the disproof on October 16 and that it was formalized in Lean, software that verifies every logical step mechanically, on October 17. Both sit on GitHub, the same route as its 722 math manuscripts earlier this month, of which only 162 came with a computer-checked main result.
Impagliazzo, Paturi, and MIT’s Ryan Williams lead the independent examination, and they are careful about their role. “Our involvement should not be taken as certification of the claim,” the three wrote in an open letter , adding that “a result of this significance requires careful, independent scrutiny and an understanding that others can reconstruct, question, and build upon.”
OpenAI says participants signed no non-disclosure agreements and work unpaid, and the company agreed to publish all raw data and fund a conference on the result.
Practical payoffs are far off: “Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research,” OpenAI wrote. The paper itself says the result does not show that every NP problem can be solved in subexponential time, so P versus NP, the question of if every problem with an easy-to-check answer is also easy to solve, stays open.
In simple terms, P is the class of problems that computers can solve efficiently, while NP is the class of problems whose proposed solutions can be checked efficiently. So P versus NP — the question of whether every problem whose answer is easy to check is also easy to solve — stays open.
Anthropic, not wanting to lose the math wars, then posted a paper credited to Claude titled “A 2^o(n) Time Algorithm for 3-SAT” and dated October 26. The repository, which also tackles the ETH problem, says an internal research Claude model discovered the algorithm, and “the result is purely asymptotic and says nothing about solving formulas in practice.”
Claude formalized Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean in September, and Terence Tao saw this kind of overlap coming. “We have now seen that even the rumor of someone working on a problem can trigger a massive amount of AI-powered effort to flatten it before the original research project has time to reach its full potential,” the mathematician wrote in September.
OpenAI’s recent $5 million contribution to the Simons Foundation will fund workshops, conferences and special programs to help researchers examine and build on AI-produced results.
