title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
body: This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder. The engineering team at Property Finder , a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock . Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live. Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage. The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker. In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads. The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock. Figure 1: Prompt optimization loop architecture The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization. Your evaluation might be lying Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough. But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness. Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed. Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types. In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace. Building ground truth you can trust To break the cycle, you need human experts with real domain knowledge doing fresh annotations independently. No reference to previous model outputs. No access to what the incumbent predicted. Dataset scope Property Finder’s team hand-annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images. The team selected these from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments. This post reports results on the UAE images. The Egypt images served as a cross-regional check on 230 images and are not reported here. The first 256 UAE images to be annotated formed the development set for tuning. The evaluation set for the final model comparison uses all 356, adding 100 images annotated after the development runs. A set of 356 images is roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models. Rare classes within individual attributes have fewer examples, so smaller differences on those attributes might not be detectable. Expert annotation A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images. They brought specialized knowledge of real estate listing quality standards. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team conducted systematic quality reviews through dedicated clarification sessions. Those reviews settled ambiguous cases and kept the labeling consistent across the dataset. Multi-label transition Real estate images frequently show multiple rooms through doorways or display overlapping quality characteristics. The switch from single-label to multi-label classification alleviated a major source of artificial ambiguity. A hallway photo showing a bedroom through a doorway is genuinely both. After you allow multiple labels, you measure what the model gets right rather than penalizing it for reasonable secondary predictions. A hybrid approach could complement this methodology: models from different families surface candidate labels and disagreements, and human experts adjudicate every case, so no model output is used directly as a label. This would reduce the annotation burden for future dataset expansion. Metrics selection Micro F1 served as the primary metric because it weights each prediction equally, which matches the business goal of overall label correctness. Macro F1 was reported alongside it because Micro F1 is dominated by frequent classes and can hide weak performance on rare attributes. Per-label precision and recall helped identify specific failure modes. Per-sample intersection over union (IoU) measured how closely each image’s predicted labels overlapped the expert’s labels. The nine single-label attributes, such as rotation or watermark detection, have one right answer per image. The AWS team also scored them with exact-match accuracy, the share of images where the answer matches the expert label. Prompt optimization as reinforcement learning With unbiased evaluation in place, you can start improving. You cannot improve what you cannot measure correctly. The optimization follows a loop analogous to reinforcement learning. Think of each prompt version as an agent, the Micro F1 score as the reward signal, and error analysis as the gradient for improvement. The idea resembles GEPA (Genetic-Pareto reflective prompt evolution) , where you mutate prompt components, evaluate fitness, select survivors, and iterate. In this engagement, the AWS team refined most versions from error analysis, with AI assistants reviewing failed images and proposing changes. MIPROv2 , an automated prompt optimization framework from the DSPy library, complemented this manual process for the photo classification task in v27. Where it started The first prompt (v0) used generic classification instructions, simplified here for illustration: “Classify this image into one of the following categories: Living Room, Kitchen, Bedroom, Bathroom…” Proprietary model A, Property Finder’s production baseline, scored a Micro F1 of 0.55 on the 256-image development set. It used v22, a prompt tuned for its model family. Scores before v21 used the earlier single-label setup and aren’t directly comparable. Iteration by iteration The AWS team tested early versions on several candidate models and added structured output formatting and attribute-specific definitions. The most instructive fix came from image-level error analysis. In the early single-label versions, the model consistently classified rooms visible through doorways as the secondary room type. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team added explicit instructions to classify based on the room occupying the majority of the frame. The later switch to multi-label output kept the main room as a label and allowed rooms visible through doorways as additional labels. Regional customization produced the next gain. In some regions, listing photos carry decorative Arabic text overlays that are not watermarks. Rules for that text removed a whole category of false positives. The v21 prompt switched photo classification and room category to multi-label output and became the shared starting prompt for every model. With it, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct from Meta scored a Micro F1 of 0.75 on the development set. From there, the AWS team tuned each model’s prompt separately. For this model, v24 targeted room size overestimation, multi-label handling, and output format. Then v25, an automatically optimized version, moved the critical tasks first. In v27, MIPROv2 restructured the photo classification task, and the model’s Micro F1 on that task reached 0.76. Where it ended The final prompt, v27_PF, is v27 plus rules that Property Finder added for renders, images with borders or frames, and corridors. Like v27, it keeps the Arabic text rules and output format instructions. A normalization step after each model call handles remaining format differences. With v27_PF, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct scored a Micro F1 of 0.80 on the 356-image evaluation set, where proprietary model A scored 0.56 with v22. The evaluation set includes the 256 development images, and both models’ prompts were tuned on those images. These scores are therefore optimistic. The switch from proprietary model A to Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, each on its own tuned prompt, lifted Micro F1 from 0.55 to 0.81 on the development set. That is a 47 percent relative gain. Prompt tuning alone, on Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, raised it from 0.75 with the shared v21 prompt to 0.81 with v27. Lessons from failed approaches Not everything succeeded. The 2-bucket approach put the watermark attributes and the other attributes in two separate API calls. It brought no meaningful accuracy gain. Boxed-image detection also dropped sharply. Without the watermark attributes in the same prompt, the models mistook watermark overlays for image borders. Generic prompts also failed regardless of which model you ran them on. Real estate imagery has too much domain specificity for a one-size-fits-all instruction. Results: Cost, accuracy, and speed The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team evaluated multiple models on Amazon Bedrock with the unbiased evaluation framework. All models started from the shared v21 prompt and were then tuned for their model family on the development set. Proprietary model A got one tuning round, v22. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct got several, v24 to v27, plus Property Finder’s edge-case rules, so it had more tuning effort behind it. The final comparison against proprietary model A used the 356-image evaluation set. Property Finder selected Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct for their production workload based on accuracy across all 11 attributes and cost efficiency. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The following table shows the exact-match accuracy that Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct (v27_PF) reached on each single-label attribute, scored on the 356-image evaluation set. It scored 90 percent or higher on six of the nine, and matched or exceeded proprietary model A on all 11 attributes. On photo classification, which can have several labels per image, the two scored the same. Attribute Exact-match accuracy Rotation detection 100% People detection 97% Boxed-image detection 97% Watermark detection 94% Render detection 93% Furnished status 91% Room under construction 81% Room size 65% Watermark text extraction 55% Cost per 1,000 images Property Finder scores tens of thousands of images a day, so per-image cost matters. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct is a cost-effective open-weight model, and the pipeline gets all attributes for an image in a single call. Result Value Estimated cost per 1,000 images $2.35 Cost reduction compared with Property Finder’s previous setup 86% These figures are estimates as of December 2025 in the US East (Ohio) Region. The Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct figure assumes 9,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens per image, from the original two-call cost analysis. A single call with the production prompt carries about 7,500–8,000 input tokens, so this is an upper estimate. The 86 percent compares it with the cost analysis estimate for Property Finder’s previous setup, which used the v21 prompt. The accuracy comparison used v22, which was tuned from v21, so its cost might differ. For current pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing . Inference speed Property Finder runs this optimized pipeline in production, processing tens of thousands of images daily with Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct on Amazon Bedrock. In their own monitoring, Property Finder observed a 40–60 percent reduction in inference latency compared with their previous setup. Apply this to your workloads Start by auditing your evaluation labels. If they came from model predictions rather than human experts, you have the same bias problem Property Finder found. Build domain-expert ground truth for a few hundred representative samples, and keep a separate test split that you never use for tuning. Adopt multi-label metrics where your classification task involves overlapping attributes. Then iterate on prompts using image error analysis, treating each iteration as a generation in an evolutionary optimization loop. When you deploy a pipeline like this, add responsible AI controls. For example, you can use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content policies and filter inappropriate model outputs. The attribute predictions in this pipeline don’t come with a calibrated confidence score, so use a practical signal to choose images for human review. Model disagreement is one such signal. When two models give different answers for an attribute, the image is often ambiguous. A second model on every image adds cost, so you can start with a sample. Check how often the signal catches real errors on your development set before you rely on it. Conclusion In this post, we walked through how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to achieve better accuracy at lower cost through model selection on Amazon Bedrock. Three elements needed to come together for this result: unbiased evaluation to measure honestly, the flexibility to evaluate and switch between model families without re-platforming, and carefully evolved prompts tailored to the domain. Amazon Bedrock provided the foundation. It gave Property Finder access to multiple model families through a single API, inherited AWS governance and security controls, and the ability to adopt new models as they become available without changing their infrastructure. To get started with model evaluation and selection on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock documentation . If you process vision workloads at scale and want help building an unbiased evaluation framework, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center . Share your experiences with model evaluation and prompt optimization in the comments. Acknowledgments Additional contributors from AWS include Yousuf Albannai, Amine Sehili, Thomas Ounnas, Aris Tsakpinis, Rafik Soliman, Nikhil Ulhas Pandit, and Sneh Sharma. About the authors Khaled Thabit Khaled Thabit is the Director of Data Engineering at Property Finder, where he leads the company’s data and AI strategy. He is passionate about using AI and data to shape the future of the property marketplace in MENA. Meriem Boughrara Meriem Boughrara is a Senior Data Engineer at Property Finder, where she leads AI and data engineering initiatives across the platform. She oversees project delivery for AI-driven solutions and works closely with cross-functional teams to bring them to production. Mohamed Desouky Mohamed Desouky is a Data Engineer at Property Finder, where he builds and maintains data pipelines powering AI-driven listing quality systems across MENA markets. He enjoys building scalable data solutions that drive measurable business impact. Mina Metias Mina Metias manages the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team in the MENA region, overseeing customer engagements from discovery through production deployment and supporting delivery of measurable business outcomes. Vadim Selyutin Vadim Selyutin is a Senior Data Scientist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center. He provides technical leadership on customer engagements, partnering with organizations to design, build, and deliver generative AI solutions from ideation through production deployment. Mohamed Noordeen Alaudeen Mohamed Noordeen Alaudeen is a Data Scientist at the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center, where he builds and deploys generative AI solutions that solve real-world business problems for enterprise customers across industries. He enjoys tackling complex technical challenges and turning them into production-ready solutions.

title: ADC-PCC to N’Assembly: Reject Tinubu’s $21bn loan over lack of transparency
body: By Luminous Jannamike The African Democratic Congress Presidential Campaign Council (ADC-PCC) has urged the National Assembly to reject President Bola Tinubu’s proposed $20 billion and £1 billion foreign borrowing unless the Federal Government provides full details of the facilities and demonstrates their benefits to Nigerians. The council said the fresh borrowing would add to the burden on Nigerians already battling rising living costs and increased taxation, questioning why the government was seeking more loans without accounting for previous borrowings and savings from fuel subsidy removal. In a statement by its Director of Media and Publicity, Kola Ologbondiyan, the ADC-PCC faulted the administration’s borrowing plans, demanding evidence that the funds would translate into tangible improvements in citizens’ lives. “What exactly is President Tinubu borrowing all this money for? Where are the roads, the electricity, the hospitals, the jobs and the critical infrastructure that should justify this relentless accumulation of debt? Nigerians deserve answers,” Ologbondiyan said. He questioned why the government was returning to international creditors while millions of Nigerians struggled to survive the effects of its economic policies. The council warned that continued borrowing without transparent spending and measurable returns could deepen Nigeria’s debt burden, restrict future governments’ policy options and threaten the country’s economic sovereignty. “This is not a sustainable path to national development. It is a dangerous attempt to mortgage the future of Nigeria and generations yet unborn,” Ologbondiyan said. The ADC-PCC demanded that Tinubu publish a comprehensive account of all domestic and foreign borrowing since May 29, 2023, including a breakdown of revenue realised from subsidy removal and how the funds had been spent. It also called for full disclosure of the proposed loans’ purposes, interest rates, repayment periods, fees, conditions and any collateral or guarantees attached to the facilities. “Nigeria cannot borrow its way out of poor economic management. Borrowing must be tied to clearly defined national priorities, transparent expenditure and measurable outcomes. Anything less is an injustice to the Nigerian people,” the council said. It urged lawmakers to insist on accountability and refuse to approve the facilities until the Federal Government establishes their necessity, sustainability and tangible benefits to Nigerians. The post ADC-PCC to N’Assembly: Reject Tinubu’s $21bn loan over lack of transparency appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Ghostty 1.4
body:
Release notes for Ghostty 1.4.0, released on October 27, 2026.
Ghostty 1.4.0 is a major release that includes large performance and memory improvements, a 100% complete Kitty graphics implementation including animation and relative placements (the first non-Kitty terminal to do so), SSH integration improvements, and hundreds more improvements and fixes across all platforms.
This release features 7 months of work with changes from 172 contributors over 2,889 commits . Thank you to all the contributors, maintainers, community moderators, translators, packagers, and users who each helped make this release possible.
These release notes are painstakingly and lovingly hand-crafted by human Ghostty maintainers, including the full changelog. They take a combined 16+ hours to write, so please enjoy. 🥰
Note: I requested CVEs for the above advisories weeks ago, but GitHub hasn't assigned them yet. If/when they're assigned, I will update the above with proper CVE numbers.
Ghostty 1.4 supports macOS 27 (Golden Gate). Most of the work was compatibility fixes:
Ghostty 1.4 remains fully compatible with prior macOS versions back to and including macOS 13 (Ventura). See the system requirements for more details.
Ghostty 1.3.1 works on macOS 27, but it has some of the visual issues listed above, such as the gray tab bar.
PRs: #13943 #13939 #13935 #13934 #13893 #13933 #13389 #13270 #13281
Ghostty now supports Kitty graphics animation and relative placements . These were the last major features of the Kitty graphics protocol that Ghostty didn't support.
Programs that display animated images with the Kitty protocol, such as an animated GIF shown with kitten icat , now animate in Ghostty instead of showing a single still frame. Frame transmission, composition, and playback control are all supported, and animations pause while the terminal isn't visible. Relative placements let a program position one image relative to another image's placement, so the child image moves along with its parent.
We also did a full conformance pass against the specification and Kitty itself, fixing dozens of behavioral differences. For example, images now scroll with text inside scroll regions ( #4323 ), retransmitting an image ID replaces the old image ( #6711 ), and invalid image data now gets an error response instead of silence, which could leave clients hanging. The full list is in the terminal capabilities section.
Kitty graphics are faster, too. Image payloads are now parsed in bulk with SIMD instead of one byte at a time, making large image transfers about 16x faster to parse in our benchmarks (64 MiB of image data, x86_64 Linux), and drawing images costs much less per frame.
Our Kitty graphics implementation now covers 100% of the published specification, making Ghostty (and libghostty) the first terminal to do this outside of Kitty itself.
PRs: #13264 #13473 #13240 #13245 #14130 #14137 #14138 #14017
Ghostty now transparently compresses scrollback that isn't visible, reducing the physical memory those pages use by 70% to 90% for typical text-heavy history. Compression only runs while the terminal is idle and pages are decompressed on demand when you scroll back or search, so it has no measurable impact on I/O throughput.
Thanks to compression, the default scrollback limit has been raised from 10 MB to 50 MB per terminal. On platforms that support compression, a full scrollback still generally uses less physical memory than the old 10 MB limit did.
Compression lowers resident (physical) memory, not virtual memory, so look at resident memory when measuring it. It is currently available on macOS and 64-bit Linux.
Beyond scrollback, memory usage is lower in many places:
PRs: #13209 #13220 #13226 #13227 #13537 #13827 #13587 #14011 #13722 #14035 #12760
There are performance improvements across the board in Ghostty 1.4 that yield significant gains compared to prior Ghostty versions.
The biggest win came from a surprising discovery: on macOS, the kernel caps every read from a pty at about 1 KiB no matter how large the read buffer is. Previously, Ghostty processed each read as it arrived, so per-read overhead was paid every kilobyte, and the program writing output sat blocked while we parsed. Ghostty now drains the pty on one thread while parsing on another, raising end-to-end I/O throughput by 25% to 55% on macOS (M4 Max, plain and Unicode text) over Ghostty 1.3.x.
VT processing itself is also much faster. In parser benchmarks, plain ASCII text went from 128 MB/s to 725 MB/s (5.7x), CJK text got 3.4x faster, and a 2.6 GB dataset of real-world terminal recordings from asciinema is processed about 25% faster. Together, these changes took cat -ing a 150 MB text file on macOS from 1.5 seconds to 566 milliseconds.
The GTK app has a new rendering pipeline. It no longer uses GtkGLArea . Instead, the renderer draws with EGL on its own thread, exports each frame as a DMABUF, and hands it to GTK to display. Rendering is now triple-buffered, which should greatly reduce tearing, and no OpenGL calls run on the main thread anymore, which let us remove a number of workarounds.
The most visible result is crisp text under fractional scaling. Text and box-drawing characters are no longer blurry with fractional display scaling such as 125% or 150% ( #1938 ). We fixed this once before, but it came back after upstream GTK changes. Ghostty now renders at the window's true fractional scale, so every rendered pixel maps to exactly one pixel on screen.
The new render surface needs a system EGL library (see Changes for Package Maintainers ). On GPU drivers that can't export DMABUFs, Ghostty falls back to copying frames through the CPU, which is slower but works.
PRs: #13962 #13993 #13995 #13998 #14002 #14061
Ghostty now implements the Kitty clipboard protocol (OSC 5522) on both macOS and GTK. Ghostty 1.3 could parse the protocol but didn't implement it.
OSC 52 can only read and write plain text. The Kitty clipboard protocol lets programs running in the terminal read and write any kind of clipboard data, such as images or HTML, and lets them pick among the formats on the clipboard. Programs can also enable paste events (mode 5522), which tell the program what formats a paste contains so it can read the one it wants. This is how a terminal program can accept a pasted image, for example.
Clipboard access follows the existing clipboard-read and clipboard-write configurations. By default, reads prompt for permission and writes are allowed. The permission prompt shows a preview of the clipboard contents, including images. Programs that send a password can have your answer remembered for the rest of that terminal session. A new clipboard-write-limit-bytes configuration limits the size of a single write (default 64 MiB). A write over the limit fails and leaves the clipboard untouched.
You can now rearrange splits on GTK by dragging them, matching the macOS feature introduced in Ghostty 1.3. When a tab has two or more splits, each split shows a drag handle at the top. Grab the handle and drop the split onto any other split, including splits in other tabs and windows. An overlay shows which side of the target split it will land on. The terminal contents, working directory, and running processes all move with it.
A new drag-handle configuration controls when drag handles are shown on both macOS and GTK: auto (default), always , or never . With never , splits can't be rearranged with the mouse. Hiding the handles was a common request from users who found them in the way.
On GTK, splits can only be dropped onto other splits. Dragging a split out to create a new tab or window is macOS-only.
PRs: #14454 #13494 #14483 #14538 #14673 #14375 #14144
Ghostty 1.4 includes dozens of improvements to core terminal emulation. We now run esctest , Thomas Dickey's terminal conformance suite, against Ghostty's terminal core in CI. Alongside that, we fixed many differences from xterm in cursor movement within margins, tab stops, character sets, mode reports, and more. You can find the full list of related changes in the terminal capabilities section.
Ghostty also supports several new sequences, including soft terminal reset (DECSTR), extended cursor position reports (DECXCPR), backarrow key mode (DECBKM), and screen size reports in characters ( CSI 19 t ). Programs can also now ask whether the terminal is visible using visibility reports (mode 2033), so they can stop rendering while hidden.
Keyboard encoding also matches xterm more closely, with fixes for modifyOtherKeys mode 2 and legacy Alt-as-Escape encoding of non-ASCII keys.
Two new sequences are disabled by default because they can be abused by untrusted programs, including ones running on a remote machine:
PRs: #12582 #12814 #13533 #13844 #14472 #14854
Ghostty 1.2 introduced SSH shell integration features as a work in progress. In Ghostty 1.4, they're backed by a new ghostty +ssh CLI action: a drop-in ssh wrapper that prepares the remote session for Ghostty and then runs the real ssh with your arguments forwarded unchanged.
Before connecting, +ssh installs Ghostty's terminfo on the remote host so the proper xterm-ghostty TERM value can be used, and forwards COLORTERM , TERM_PROGRAM , and TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION . If the terminfo install fails (for example, tic isn't available on the remote), it falls back to TERM=xterm-256color . Flags such as --terminfo=false , --forward-env=false , and --verbose control each step.
The ssh-env and ssh-terminfo shell integration features (still opt-in) now call +ssh too. Previously, each shell integration carried its own copy of this logic, which made up roughly a third of our shell integration scripts. Now bash, zsh, fish, elvish, and Nushell all behave identically, and you can get the same behavior from scripts or anywhere else by calling ghostty +ssh directly.
The terminfo install itself is also more reliable. Ghostty now always installs its own bundled terminfo rather than accepting whatever xterm-ghostty entry the remote already has, and it reinstalls automatically when a Ghostty update changes the terminfo. It also no longer needs infocmp or Ghostty's terminfo on the local machine. Installs are cached per host and port, so two machines behind one address no longer share a cache entry. And ssh-env no longer silently overrides SetEnv entries in your ~/.ssh/config ( #11518 ).
The +ssh-cache command that manages this cache now takes positional destinations ( ghostty +ssh-cache user@example.com ) and has a new --prune=30d flag. See the breaking changes if you script against +ssh-cache .
macOS: The minimum required macOS version for Ghostty 1.4 remains unchanged (macOS 13 Ventura). Ghostty is now compatible with macOS 27.
GTK: Ghostty 1.4 requires GTK 4.18 and libadwaita 1.7 , up from GTK 4.14 and libadwaita 1.5 in Ghostty 1.3. This aligns with our GTK/Adwaita version policy . Notably, Ubuntu 24.04 LTS doesn't meet this requirement. Systems with older GTK or Adwaita versions can work around this requirement by using an older version of Ghostty or the Flatpak package. #14330
OpenGL (GTK): The minimum required OpenGL version remains 4.3, but Ghostty now renders through EGL instead of GTK's OpenGL widget. This should be invisible for nearly everyone, but if Ghostty fails to start with an EGL error, please make sure your GPU driver provides a working EGL implementation.
We previously announced that Ghostty 1.4 would require macOS 14. Nothing forced our hand to do this in this release, so we kept macOS 13 support. We still plan to drop macOS 13 in a future release. Apple dropped security support for macOS 13 in the fall of 2025, so we recommend upgrading regardless.
The following behaviors have changed in 1.4.0:
The list below contains deprecations that remain compatible today through a compatibility layer, but may break in a future release if they are ignored:
There is no set timeline to remove these deprecations, but we recommend adapting to the new configurations sooner rather than later to avoid any possible disruptions in the future.
Ghostty 1.4 introduces full localization for the command palette and adds support for 4 new languages :
Localization is maintained by volunteer contributors. If you want to help localize Ghostty in your language, please open a discussion on the GitHub repo. Thank you to all the volunteers who contributed to Ghostty's localization!
As with 1.3, libghostty isn't directly part of the Ghostty 1.4 release. But a large part of the 1.4 development cycle went into libghostty, so here's an update.
Over the past 6 months, the C API for libghostty-vt has grown from a parser and a few encoders into a complete terminal emulator API, adopted by dozens of free and commercial terminal emulators used by millions of people. It's hard to quantify exactly, but the number of people using a libghostty-based terminal is confidently several times the number of people using the Ghostty GUI.
libghostty-vt now builds for macOS, Linux, Windows (MSVC and GNU), FreeBSD, Android, iOS, and WebAssembly, and CI continuously verifies every one of these targets. The goal is for libghostty-vt to be generally usable everywhere, within reason, so if you want more target support, let us know!
It's also easier to integrate libghostty-vt into existing build systems. There's CMake support, Nix packaging, an xcframework, and a source tarball, in addition to the existing pkg-config file. libghostty-vt no longer needs libc++, and it can build freestanding.
The API is still marked as a work in progress and broke compatibility several times during this cycle, so expect more breaking changes before a tagged release. The API documentation and the Zig, C, C++, Swift, and WebAssembly examples (now over 30) are kept up to date with main .
We're going to do a final pass over the C API, break ABI one more time, and then likely tag a libghostty 1.0 release very soon.
Ghostty is a non-profit project , fiscally sponsored by Hack Club . All of our finances are public on HCB , so you can see exactly where every dollar goes.
During the 1.4 cycle, we paid $41,820 to contributors under contract and spent about $1,260 on infrastructure such as website hosting.
I'm happy to share that we've now signed our first two 12-month contracts , which give contributors stable, long-term paid work on Ghostty and help ensure the ongoing stability and sustainability of the project:
If you'd like to support Ghostty, please visit our sponsorship page .
The primary focus of the roadmap continues to be libghostty functionality, stability, and portability. During the last release cycle, I said I aimed to tag a libghostty release. We haven't done that yet, but I'm confident we will do so before Ghostty 1.5.
libghostty is a project that continues to be the tide that lifts all boats. libghostty improvements tie directly to Ghostty GUI improvements as well as dozens of other large projects in the ecosystem. As more large projects adopt libghostty, libghostty tends to get more testing and attention, and this creates a cycle that yields the most gain for terminal emulators everywhere.
macOS and GTK builds of Ghostty have talented, capable maintainer teams that are continuing to improve them, so they're not neglected by any means! As a project, we've decided to drop any roadmap for Windows support in the Ghostty GUI. libghostty fully supports Windows (and we test it in CI), and the official stance now is that downstream projects should use that.
Our release cycle remains 6 months. This release was delayed by one month, but Ghostty 1.5 is planned for March 2027. libghostty will have a separate release cycle.
