title: Anthropic’s elaborate plan to keep Wall Street at bay
body:
Anthropic wants to have it both ways. With its impending IPO, it wants to tap the vast riches of the public markets and insists it doesn’t want to compromise its core mission of developing AI safely and for the benefit of humanity. But greater model capabilities bring greater risks, and shareholders eager for returns may have little patience for costly safety measures that slow products on their way to market.
Sam Altman, the CEO of Anthropic’s archrival, OpenAI, has cited investor pressures as one reason the company is not pursuing an IPO this year. Anthropic hopes it can resist investor pressures with a mind-boggling governance structure.
University of Pennsylvania law professor Elizabeth Pollman told The Verge that Anthropic has proposed going public with a “unique and complicated governance structure that has not been used before” and that has been “creatively designed for this founder-led and mission-driven company.” Experts say it should give Anthropic freedom to pursue profits without letting shareholders force it to cut corners on safety or rush systems out before they’re adequately tested. But even the strongest legal protections can only go so far, and no corporate structure, no matter how well designed, can completely insulate a public company from the demands of the market.
Foremost, Anthropic is a public benefit corporation. Simply put, it is legally required to focus on more than just maximizing shareholder returns, balancing these with its stated social mission and the interests of stakeholders, such as employees and specific communities. Patagonia and Kickstarter are among the better-known examples, with missions centered on environmental conservation and supporting creative communities, respectively.
Another key safeguard aims to protect Anthropic’s mission by limiting shareholder influence over one of the biggest levers of corporate power: the company’s board of directors. Directors oversee the company and appoint its leadership, including the CEO. Directors can also hold executive roles, as is the case with Anthropic, with CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei both sitting on the board.
Shareholders typically have considerable sway over who sits on the board, giving them a means to replace directors or push for changes if they are unhappy with how the company is being run. For example, if shareholders are unhappy at what they perceive as unnecessary delays to market for optional safety testing, they may remove directors and replace them with ones more aligned with their interests, such as making money and being less cautious.
Under Anthropic’s proposed governance structure, ordinary shareholders won’t have much of a say over who is on the board at all. Instead, four of the board’s seven directors will be chosen by a special body called the long-term benefit trust, explains Jens Dammann, a professor in business and commercial law at the University of Texas School of Law. It is a highly unusual setup for a major technology company.
The trust is made up of “five financially disinterested voting trustees” with expertise in “AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” Through a special class of share called Class T stock, the trustees can appoint or remove directors in pursuit of their stated purpose: ensuring “that Anthropic responsibly balances the financial interests of stockholders with the interests of those affected by Anthropic’s conduct and our public benefit purpose.” The trust is designed to operate independently of the company’s commercial pressures, allowing it, in theory, to put Anthropic’s mission first.
Ordinary shareholders technically have a say in the board’s three remaining seats. However, Anthropic has created another safeguard that keeps power firmly in the hands of its founders, called “Founder LLC,” which will control 50.1 percent of the voting power on shareholder matters. Given that many shareholder votes are decided by a simple majority, Founder LLC basically gives Anthropic’s founders the ability to block or force through decisions, regardless of how other shareholders vote. This means that they will effectively choose the remaining three directors, Columbia Law School professor Dorothy Lund told The Verge.
The prospectus says Founder LLC will “initially” be seven of Anthropic’s founders: Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah. “Our seven co-founders will initially be the sole members.” Notably absent is another cofounder, Ben Mann, who co-leads the company’s experimental Anthropic Labs arm, as reported by The San Francisco Standard.
All in all, the arrangements would give Anthropic’s founders and the trust “tremendous power” over the company’s direction, shielding it from many of “the pressures associated with being a public company,” Dammann told The Verge. “Given the unusual governance structure Anthropic has chosen, I don’t see how going public, by itself, would undermine its ability to prioritize safety over commercial interests.”
Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Law School, agreed, telling The Verge that, legally speaking, “Anthropic is entirely insulated from profit seeking pressures, in the sense that ordinary shareholders have no ability to select the board or make business decisions.” But Lipton cautioned that the founders themselves have financial stakes in the company, which could influence their decisions.
And there’s a big difference between legal protections and immunity from market pressures. Anthropic, like all AI companies, “desperately needs capital,” Lipton said. “It’s not clear to me that any governance structure will protect against the market reality that unless Anthropic takes advantage of profit making opportunities at a faster pace than its competitors, it will not be able to fund its operations.” Lund expressed similar concerns. Anthropic will still “need to stay in the good graces of their investors,” she said, adding that “competitive pressure and capital needs can erode safety commitments over time.” Anthropic did not respond to The Verge’s request for comment on whether it felt the company could actually resist shareholder pressure to massively accelerate AI at the cost of safety.
Another potential vulnerability emerges if Anthropic’s founders start leaving. In its prospectus, the company says its success is “highly dependent on the continued service” of its senior team, particularly its founders. Dario and Daniela are singled out as being especially “critical” to advancing the company’s research and mission. But beyond the loss of leadership, their departure could trigger significant changes in how the company is structured, potentially stripping away some of the safeguards preventing Anthropic from pursuing profit over safety.
Under the proposed structure, Founder LLC would “sunset” if a majority of its members leave or the group chooses to dissolve it. Once that happens, ordinary shareholders could gain the power to weaken the trust’s protections, even against the wishes of the trustees, and without the support of the founders or employees, who hold different classes of stock, Dammann told The Verge. Other means of subverting the trust also exist, he explained, including coordinated action by the public shareholders, employee stockholders, and founders.
For now, it seems, Anthropic can probably have it both ways. But the protections designed to preserve its commitment to AI safety are far from ironclad, and much depends on market pressures, whether its founders stick around, and directions of the trust. Dammann said he sees a “fundamental dilemma that cannot be resolved in a fully satisfactory way” between Anthropic’s mission and investor demands. As long as things are going well, this tension may be manageable. “Investors may not mind their lack of voice as long as things go well,” Dammann said. “But if things go sour, they may become quite frustrated.”

title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
body: Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it. In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost. The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies. The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably. A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons: The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it. It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops. Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously. This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely. They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge. Solution overview Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targets: the edge and the cloud. Exowatt implemented this approach on the Qwen3-1.7B model for the first use case, edge alarm triage, then applied the same approach to the Qwen3-14B model for the second use case, cloud energy-market analysis. The company plans to reuse this solution to build smaller, task-specific models across the fleet. Figure 1: Exowatt fine-tuning and deployment pipeline, spanning the build, cloud-serving, and edge-serving stages The following seven AWS services power the AI pipeline, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints to manage: AWS Service Purpose Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) Data, manifests, model artifacts, and test sets Amazon SageMaker AI serverless fine-tuning Every fine-tune run, launched from Public Hub recipes Amazon SageMaker AI serverless evaluation 2,000 answers per candidate scored as a managed job SageMaker Model Registry Every completed fine-tune with its evidence and metrics Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import Hosts the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B for Cloud EMS, invoked privately from the Cloud EMS service. No idle cost Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Qwen3) Paraphrase (three rewrites per answer in the training data) and frontier model benchmarking Alarm-triage paraphrases use Qwen3-VL-235B on Amazon Bedrock. Energy-market paraphrases use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. AWS Lambda + Amazon EventBridge Serverless-evaluation scorer and a scheduled keep-warm invocation of the custom model The workflow is organized into three stages: Model customization (cloud): Exowatt fine-tunes open-weight base models using serverless model customization, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SageMaker AI. Because serverless training allocates capacity on demand, the team runs multiple experiments per day rather than waiting for self-selected GPU. After evaluation, the best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry. Edge deployment: For latency-sensitive, connectivity-constrained work such as alarm triage, the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B model is frozen, quantized to the GGUF format, and run with llama.cpp inside Kubernetes pods at the edge using on-site controllers. This path requires no GPU and operates without internet connectivity. Cloud deployment (elastic): For internet-connected, fleet-level analysis, the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B energy-market model is served through Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, which runs with no idle cost and bills only while the model is active. Why Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization service provides a wide selection of open-weight models with ready-made fine-tuning recipes from the SageMaker Public Hub, so the team avoided building and optimizing a custom training container, work that can otherwise take weeks. For Exowatt, this turned fine-tuning from a scarce, scheduled event into a routine, on-demand one. This makes a rapid experimentation-and-test loop practical while keeping experimentation cost low. Fine-tuning on provisioned GPUs requires choosing a specific instance type, requesting that capacity, waiting for it to become available, running the job, and paying for the instance for as long as it is held. The held time typically includes the idle time between experiments when a dedicated instance is kept running. For a small team running many experiments, this slows down innovation and increases cost. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization automatically manages and orchestrates the infrastructure required to run the fine-tuning job, removing the pain of capacity management, and charges only for the time the fine-tuning job runs. Use case 1: Edge alarm triage with Qwen3-1.7B Exowatt sites raise alarms around the clock. A compact on-site model reads each alarm together with the site’s own status and telemetry and returns one of a small fixed set of classifications with cited evidence (such as an offline system, derated component, or sensor mismatch) or an explicit abstention when the evidence is insufficient. Model selection and training data The team first tried Qwen3-8B with prompting and guardrails, which plateaued below the target (0.735 macro-F1). A fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B changed that: it outperformed the Qwen3-8B plus prompting setup on this narrow, single-turn task at roughly one-fifth the parameters, while staying small enough for GPU-free edge inference. Thirteen fine-tuned Qwen3-8B candidates across 12 dataset versions never beat the prompted 8B baseline. The smaller model with more varied data did. The training set was small and curated: 2,522 examples built from 684 verified decisions on generated site scenarios plus 1,838 certified paraphrases that kept each decision fixed while rewriting the prose. The paraphrases were generated by Qwen3-235B on Amazon Bedrock for about $3.72. Each paraphrase was kept only if deterministic checks confirmed that the decision, labels, evidence citations, and every number were unchanged (1,838 of 2,218 candidates passed). One fault family was held out of training entirely, and 320 cases were reserved for testing. Training and deployment Training completed in about 32 minutes on SageMaker serverless fine-tuning for roughly $20–$25. Quantized to 8 bits (about 1.71 GiB), the model runs offline in a 6 GiB llama.cpp pod on the site’s existing CPU server. It also runs on a t3.2xlarge instance type. Use case 2: Cloud energy-market analysis with Qwen3-14B Dispatchable storage turns timing into an operational decision: each site must continually decide how much stored energy to hold for its load and when to release it, and for grid-connected sites market conditions feed into that choice. The fine-tuned model reads a six-hour packet of live market data (about 90 rows of real-time prices, day-ahead forecasts, and grid notices) and returns one of five market events (such as a price spike or scarcity adder) in about four seconds. Every claim is tied to a specific data row to inform the dispatch strategy. Why Qwen3-14B Qwen3-14B was chosen because it is supported by Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, it ships as a SageMaker Public Hub model with a ready LoRA recipe (no custom container or instance type to manage), and at about 28 GiB it is small enough to serve cost-effectively. Training data and process Exowatt fine-tuned the model on public Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market data drawn from five years of history (about 163 million rows across 12 tables). The team rule-labeled this data into 25,000 examples (22,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,000 held out for testing). They then expanded the training set to 86,281 rows by having Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock rewrite the prose of each example while its labels and numeric fields stayed fixed. Training was a single LoRA epoch (rank 16, alpha 32), completed in about 8.5 hours of managed serverless fine-tuning with up to four jobs running at once. The team ran 23 jobs and about 155 hours of managed training in the six days from initial plan to a champion model serving in Cloud EMS. The decisive improvement came from paraphrase diversity: adding three rewrites per answer lifted macro-F1 from 0.950 to 0.975. The base model scored only 0.415 macro-F1. It produced valid JSON but did not yet know the market. Fine-tuning fixed that. Deployment The merged checkpoint was imported to Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import in about 14 minutes. The model runs with no idle cost and bills at $6.86 per hour only while active. Benchmark results On the edge alarm-triage task the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B went from a model that couldn’t produce a valid answer to 0.911 macro-F1 with 320 test cases, ahead of every frontier baseline. Applying the identical fine-tune-and-evaluate loop to the energy-market task with 2,000 test cases, the Qwen3-14B reached 0.975 macro-F1, again ahead of the frontier baseline and at a fraction of the cost. In both cases a small, fine-tuned model beat far larger general-purpose models on the specific task. Both models return strict JSON in which every claim cites a specific input data row. Any unsupported claim is dropped before it reaches an operator, which is what lets the team trust small models in autonomous, physical settings. Model Macro-F1 $ / 1,000 decisions Offline? Claude Haiku 4.5 0.519 ~$4.70 No Claude Opus 4.7 0.680 ~$22 No Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.698 ~$15 No Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B 0.911 $0 * Yes Base Qwen3-1.7B No score (failed the validity gate) Table 1: Edge alarm triage results, fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B compared to frontier models $0 per 1,000 decisions means no metered API or GPU inference cost. The quantized model runs on the site’s existing CPU. Model Macro-F1 Event Acc. Valid JSON $ / 1,000 answers Base Qwen3-14B 0.415 0.54 0.834 $0.64 Claude Sonnet 4.6 0.538 0.584 0.991 $17.79 Claude Opus 4.7 0.625 0.718 0.9995 $29.26 Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B 0.975 0.983 1.000 $0.60 Table 2: Cloud energy-market analysis results, fine-tuned Qwen3-14B compared to frontier models Costs are Amazon Bedrock list prices times measured tokens per answer. Fine-tuning lifted an open model from last place to first: +0.35 macro-F1 over Claude Opus 4.7 (95 percent confidence interval 0.324 to 0.371) at about 49× lower cost per 1,000 answers ($0.60 compared to $29.26). The model held 0.968 macro-F1 on a second, later test set. Business benefits Faster iteration and faster time to market: Exowatt moved its customized model from experimentation to production in only nine days. This process could have taken months if the team had to build and optimize custom containers and training recipes, provision GPUs, and manage infrastructure. With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, the team trained Qwen3-1.7B in about 32 minutes and Qwen3-14B in about 8.5 hours, with no capacity requests and up to four training jobs running concurrently. For the energy-market use case, Exowatt ran 23 jobs totaling about 155 hours of managed training and moved from the base model to a fine-tuned model serving in Cloud EMS in six days. The merged checkpoint was imported into Amazon Bedrock in about 14 minutes. The end-to-end pipeline used seven AWS serverless services, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints for Exowatt to manage. Higher accuracy compared to frontier models: Both fine-tuned models beat the larger frontier models on their own task: Qwen3-1.7B at 0.911 macro-F1 (compared to 0.698 for Claude Sonnet 4.6) and Qwen3-14B at 0.975 (compared to 0.625 for Claude Opus 4.7). Lower cost across both deployments: In the cloud, the Qwen3-14B serves at $0.60 per 1,000 answers versus $29.26 for Claude Opus 4.7 (about 49× lower), with no idle cost and $6.86 per hour only while active on Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. At the edge, the quantized Qwen3-1.7B runs on the site’s existing CPU with no per-inference cost and no dependency on connectivity. Grounded, low-risk outputs: Across both models, the evidence fence removed every uncited claim (any evidence citation whose source, field, or value does not literally match the input), and the edge model abstains rather than guesses when unsure. This is what let the team run it autonomously in shadow mode on a cloud-hosted replica of a site. Lessons learned For specific tasks, smaller fine-tuned large language models can outperform large frontier models: Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B models each outperformed frontier models on the target task, delivering higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost with significantly smaller models. Data quality and variety outweigh raw volume and extra epochs: For tightly scoped tasks, data quality mattered more than model size or data volume. On the alarm-triage model, more verified training variety moved macro-F1 from 0.584 (trained on the 684 verified decisions alone) to 0.911 (with the paraphrase-expanded 2,522-row set). Simply running more epochs over the same rows did worse: a control run that trained on the 684 original rows for 11 epochs (the same number of steps) reached only 0.879. Curated data mattered more than dataset size throughout. Removing the provisioning step changes how a team works: When a training run no longer requires waiting for GPU capacity, fine-tuning shifts from a rare event to a routine, iterative one. One training pipeline serves two deployment targets: Separating model training from deployment lets Exowatt use the same pipeline for both offline edge deployment and connected fleet-level analysis, simplifying operations and accelerating model deployment in the cloud. Conclusion Exowatt now has one reusable AI pipeline that took a task from model specific data preparation to model deployment. Rather than tuning one model for different tasks, Exowatt plans to apply the same fine-tuning principles to different tasks, each with its own data, specific models, and evaluations, across the fleet as new device types and market tasks come online. The pattern generalizes beyond energy industry segments. AI engineers, data scientists, and customers across industry segments can adopt the same principles. Use Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization as a low-overhead AI pipeline to fine-tune small, task-specific models, then deploy them where the work happens: at the edge when connectivity or latency requires it, and through a managed cloud endpoint such as Amazon SageMaker AI for elastic workloads. To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization and Amazon Bedrock . About the authors Purna Sanyal Purna is a GenAI Specialist Architect at AWS, helping customers to building Agentic AI applications with custom model and inferencing at scale with successful adoption of cloud native architecture. He has specialization in data strategy, GenAI Infra and Applied AI. He is passionate about architecting scalable AI systems that drive innovation and user impact. Tim Child Tim is Chief Engineer of Software and AI at Exowatt, where he leads the software, AI and digital systems behind the company’s clean, dispatchable energy for AI datacenters. He leads Exowatt’s energy management system that runs Exowatt’s sites, the company’s AI strategy, and the AI tools and agents the whole company depends on. Before Exowatt, he earned a PhD in Physics (quantum computing) at the University of British Columbia. Felipe Arce Felipe is a Lead Software Engineer at Exowatt, working where AI meets energy infrastructure. He built the fine-tuned model factory and helps build the energy management system that runs Exowatt’s sites and the digital twins that bring them to life in simulation. Before Exowatt, he spent four years on Microsoft Azure’s incident platform. He loves infrastructure, especially the platforms other engineers build on. Jingchao Yang Jingchao is a Senior Solutions Architect for Startups at AWS, where he specializes in building lakehouse architectures for agentic systems. Jingchao brings 8+ years of data engineering experience with a PhD in Geoinformation Science.

title: Stubb, Støre's phone call with Putin coordinated with Ukraine – Sybiha
body:
The meeting between the leaders of Finland and Norway – Alexander Stubb and Jonas G. Støre – with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin was coordinated with Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said, calling it "the right move."
"We discussed the morning phone calls between the leaders of Norway and Finland and Putin, and later with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and the peace process. This call was coordinated with us, and this is the right approach," Sybiha said at a joint press conference of the foreign ministers of Ukraine, Finland, and Norway in Helsinki.
Earlier, the Office of the President of Finland and the Norwegian government reported on a phone call between Stubb and Støre and Russian President Putin, which took place on Tuesday, October 27.
"The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighboring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Later, Dmytro Lytvyn, an adviser to the Ukrainian president, reported that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was speaking by phone with Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gar Støre following their phone conversation with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin.

title: Putin holds talks with Iranian president in Kremlin
body:
MOSCOW, October 26. /TASS/. Russian Leader Vladimir Putin is holding talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in the Kremlin for the second time in a month, a TASS correspondent reports.
The meeting takes place within the framework of the eighth summit of the Forum of Gas Exporting Countries.
Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, head of the Federal Customs Service Dmitry Shugayev, Transport Minister Dmitry Yadrov, Deputy Prime Minister, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, Energy Minister Sergey Tsivilyov, Deputy head of the Presidential Administration Maxim Oreshkin, Deputy head of the Presidential Administration, Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov, Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov, Gazprom CEO Alexey Miller participate.
Putin and Pezeshkian met quite recently, in early October in Turkmenistan at the CIS summit to discuss the cooperation development, the growth of trade turnover (increased by 21% in 2025) and the situation in the Middle East. Putin declared Russia's readiness to help resolve the crisis around Iran.

title: Iran, Russia presidents hold meeting in Moscow
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin held a meeting in Moscow on Tuesday.
Putin received Iran’s President Pezeshkian at the Kremlin following the 8th Gas Exporting Countries Forum Summit in Moscow on Tuesday evening.
Putin announced in remarks published on Tuesday, after meeting with Masoud Pezeshkian in the Kremlin: Russia is fulfilling all its commitments regarding projects in Iran. The construction of the Bushehr nuclear power plant in Iran is underway.
The Russian President continued: In a bilateral meeting with Pezeshkian, I discussed the situation in the Middle East (West Asia); an issue that is causing concern. We hope that developments in the Middle East will move in a positive direction.
Vladimir Putin then added: I am always pleased to meet with you. Trade exchanges between Russia and Iran have increased by 10.4 percent in the first 8 months of this year. The summit of the leaders of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum was very productive.

title: Oil Tanker Tycoon’s WhatsApp Messages Drive Big Market Moves
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
By Alex Longley, Archie Hunter and Weilun Soon (Bloomberg) — The messages from the world’s biggest supertanker owner often begin with pleasantries: “Dear Ladies and Gentlemen.”
Within minutes, the WhatsApps are the talk of the oil-tanker industry, a multibillion-dollar corner of the energy market that’s been plunged into chaos by the Iran war this year, and where word of mouth is the main way information spreads. The details vary, but the messages to shipbrokers from Sinokor Group, the South Korean company controlled by tycoon Ga-Hyun Chung, mostly boil down to the same thing — one of its vessels has just been hired at a new sky-high rate to ferry oil out of the Persian Gulf.
Some messages detail a new contract, listing the ship, counterparty and eyewatering price. Others just refer loosely to negotiations underway. The format fluctuates from terse strings of numbers and names to full sentences and florid signoffs: “Very respectfully. Thank you very much and best regards,” concludes one message sent to brokers in August, and seen by Bloomberg. Usually, in the days that follow, the global benchmark price set by London’s Baltic Exchange takes another leap higher.
What would simply be fodder for gossip in most industries, brokers say that Sinokor’s WhatsApp messages have for months played an outsized role in setting the cost of transporting oil around the world. Rates for very-large crude carriers — the biggest kind of oil tanker — have soared more than 1,600% this year amid disruptions caused by the war, creating an unprecedented boom for the industry, but throwing a spotlight on the arcane system used to price the world’s shipping contracts, and the centuries-old institution that manages it.
The world of oil tanker rates is coming under fresh scrutiny this week, as hearings begin in a London lawsuit brought against the Baltic Exchange by trader Mercuria Energy Group, which argues that the benchmark rate is no longer fit for purpose because of the disruptions caused by the Iran war. Mercuria has complained to the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority about the benchmark, according to its legal filings, and at least one other market participant has also contacted the regulator, according to a person with knowledge of the complaint, who asked not to be identified because it is not public.
The Mercuria case doesn’t refer to Sinokor or its role in the market. Mercuria argues that a near-cessation of normal commercial shipments through the Strait of Hormuz since the war began meant that there was no basis on which to calculate the oil tanker market’s most important reference price, known as TD3C, which measures the cost of shipping oil from inside the Persian Gulf to China.
But the war is also shining a light on wider questions about how the benchmark is determined, especially as Sinokor’s dominance of the market has expanded. Every day, a select number of shipbrokers submit assessments of the market to the Baltic Exchange, which uses them to publish a price for the TD3C index.
While Middle Eastern state producers are having growing success in moving their oil out of the gulf, the trade is still largely covert by nature, reducing the flow of verifiable data.
The result, shipowners, traders and brokers say, is that Sinokor’s swaggering Whatsapps are often a key source of information available for assessing the Persian Gulf tanker market, and therefore for setting the global cost of shipping oil.
Sinokor has “a huge influence on the market dynamics and the fundamentals of what’s happening on the VLCC market,” said Joel Grau, chief executive officer at shipping insurer Zostera Marine and a professor at the National Maritime College of Ireland.
To be sure, the tanker market is being supported by a genuine supply squeeze, with more vessels tied up on longer and unusual routes or waiting to collect oil outside the gulf, and as Iran escalates missile and drone strikes on ships.
But nearly two decades after uproar over the Libor rate of borrowing, the scrutiny of the Baltic Exchange’s main tanker rate is once again raising questions over the reliability of a financial benchmark that prices billions of dollars in derivatives and is set not by trades but by the assessments of market participants.
“I will of course still carry out my duties, but have we (the Baltic) taken any legal advice on the questionable market situation,” Christopher Loveday, an assessor for TD3C at the Baltic Exchange, asked a colleague in mid-March, according to a Mercuria legal filing. He expressed concern that the Baltic could face “issues” with market participants “like the Libor situation a decade or so ago,” according to the filing. (There’s no suggestion in Mercuria’s legal filings that the wrongdoing that led to the Libor scandal is at play at the Baltic Exchange, nor has any regulator or other party suggested as such.)
The importance of TD3C itself is already being eroded. Open interest on the underlying derivatives contracts has declined, and industry insiders say they’re increasingly focused on a new Baltic index called TD34 that prices the cost of shipping oil from just outside of the Strait of Hormuz to Asia.
This story is based on interviews with over a dozen people involved in oil tanker markets, most of whom asked not to be identified discussing private interactions and business dealings.
Sinokor didn’t respond to requests for comment. The Baltic Exchange and Mercuria declined to comment. The FCA said it can’t comment on engagement with individual firms and that it has been monitoring the impact of the Iran war since the conflict began.
In its defense, the Baltic Exchange, which is owned by Singapore Exchange Ltd., has said that its decision to keep publishing TD3C wasn’t taken lightly. Mercuria is asking the court to retroactively suspend the index. However, the Baltic’s lawyers said that doing so would mean dissolving more than eight months of pricing and that “such a claim is without precedent in this jurisdiction or, to the Baltic’s knowledge, in any other.”
It was barely two weeks into the Iran war, on March 12, when brokers received a notification from Sinokor that it had hired out a ship to sail from the United Arab Emirates port of Zirku to Asia at a rate of at least 700 Worldscale points — far above the Baltic’s assessment for that day of 348.89. The Worldscale system is a standardized way of comparing tanker freight rates across different routes.
At the time, prices had already been soaring for months after Sinokor, until then a relatively smaller player, suddenly embarked on a massive supertanker buying spree with backing from container shipping giant MSC Mediterreanean Shipping Co.
The aggressive move gave Chung — the deeply private scion of a Korean shipping family — a level of influence in the tanker market that insiders say is unprecedented, and meant that Sinokor was positioned to reap huge profits when the war started.
By the time of Sinokor’s March WhatsApp, the Baltic Exchange was facing turmoil of its own, as shipbrokers grappled with how to calculate the cost of shipping from a Saudi Arabian port that was effectively inaccessible due to the war. Some began using a still-functioning Saudi port on the Red Sea for their TD3C assessments, but the exchange intervened and insisted that the benchmark price must continue to reflect loadings from inside the Persian Gulf.
By March 16, the Baltic’s rate jumped to almost 600 Worldscale points, equivalent to $602,000 a day, as traders struggled to assess a trade that appeared to have stalled, and with barely any visibility of deals being done other than Sinokor’s notice.
Prices continued to swing wildly in the coming weeks, and in late April Mercuria filed a lawsuit alleging that it had suffered losses in the hundreds of millions of dollars as a result of distortions in the benchmark, though its lawyers said in May that it was not looking to “extract money from an exchange.” The company since removed the figure from its claim.
Mercuria argues that the index should be suspended immediately, and that since the Iran war began the route no longer serves its intended function. For its part, the Baltic’s argues that would be an unprecedented move and that if that request were granted there would be “chaotic market-wide consequences,” including for the multibillion-dollar derivatives market linked to TD3C.
For decades, the Baltic Exchange’s Middle East to Asia benchmark has stood at the heart of the oil tanker market, used as a reference point in long-term contracts for supertanker deals — including for vessels sailing elsewhere in the world — and underpinning a large derivatives market. The original TD3 route measured the cost of traveling to Japan, but was replaced about a decade ago with TD3C, to reflect China’s growing dominance as an oil importer.
The rate is published just after 4 p.m. London time every day, based on the average of assessments provided by nine brokers. The individual brokers submit their estimates shortly before the price is issued, although the Baltic Exchange can occasionally ask for justification for the figures, one of the people said.
Mercuria’s lawsuit alleged that TD3C was being distorted, and its lawyers argued that the handful of ships transiting Hormuz in the early months of the war should not qualify as fixtures for setting the benchmark rate.
By the summer, however, the flow of oil out of the Persian Gulf was becoming a steady stream, as producers and traders settled into a new “dark shuttle” system — using dedicated tankers making return journeys under cover of night before offloading oil onto ships waiting empty just outside the gulf.
Bloomberg reported in early July that Sinokor had emerged as a major owner of supertankers moving crude through the strait of Hormuz. But the level of information about ships and cargoes operating in the region for the most part remained extremely limited.
It was around that time that the Sinokor messages — referred to among industry insiders as “blasts” — began to accelerate. Sinokor owner Chung already had a reputation in shipping circles for creating sprawling WhatsApp groups with representatives from individual brokerage firms or counterparties, usually including large numbers of Sinokor employees as well.
In late July, when TD3C had begun to retreat following the interim peace deal between the US and Iran that notionally lowered the risk of attack in Hormuz, Sinokor “blasted” out that it had hired out a ship at 465 Worldscale points, about 60 points higher than where the market was assessed that day. The difference is the equivalent to just over $60,000 a day in earnings.
Sinokor sent out at least five missives in August, each announcing progressively higher rates. By Aug. 21, the company told the market that it hired a ship out at 1,350 Worldscale points, almost three times the level of just under a month earlier.
In the months to come, the market went parabolic, surging from around 400 points in late July, to almost 1,320 points in October. Supertankers in the Persian Gulf — and any deals still tied to TD3C— were now earning more than $1.4 million a day.
The potential payoff for Sinokor and its partner MSC is huge. Sinokor is listed as the manager of 83 supertankers on the Equasis maritime database, many of which are operating in or around the Middle East. Most industry figures see the company controlling more vessels than that in reality when charter deals are added in too.
Using a gauge of average supertanker earnings across the world, a fleet of 83 ships would have pulled in on average of about $143 million a month last year. That jumped to $509 million by July this year, $1.4 billion in September, and $2.1 billion in October, based on the average for the month so far. In reality, it depends where the vessels are sailing, and those figures don’t account for costs and days where ships aren’t hired. (Some of the company’s ships have been hit in Hormuz recently, potentially reducing the number of days its tankers can earn money while they undergo repairs.) By comparison, Sinokor’s revenue for the whole of 2025, which also includes a container shipping arm, was $5.5 billion, according to accounts published in South Korea.
While the financial rewards for companies like Sinokor willing to take the risk of crossing Hormuz are significant, the journeys also ultimately provided a vital lifeline to global energy markets. Worst case-scenario forecasts of $200 a barrel crude oil prices never materialized, partly as a result of the ships that continued to cross Hormuz. Sinokor itself carried an estimated 37% of the oil that passed through the Strait of Hormuz last month, Bloomberg reported last week.
For many in the industry, the crucial question is how literally to take the Sinokor messages, which have become less frequent since the summer.
Several people involved in tanker markets said Sinokor’s WhatsApps can leave room for interpretation around parts of the rate being publicized, like who pays for insurance, or the ship’s destination.
And the already opaque shipping market has become even harder to track as a result of the Iran war, as most ships in the Middle East have stopped broadcasting satellite signals that make their movements easy to follow.
Tracking and satellite images show that while some of the bookings the company broadcast went exactly as advertised, others are less clear. At least one ship that Sinokor said would sail from the Middle East to Asia in early August hasn’t left the Indian Ocean and Persian Gulf since then.
To be sure, charterers and shipowners will sometimes privately agree to change the route they’re due to sail, while bookings can also fall through.
The Baltic Exchange’s policies say that panelists should use discretion over the relative value they attribute to data they gather and — in cases where there is little or no activity on a route for a period of time — must apply their “expert judgement of the wider market” to provide an assessment.
Of 130 published days between early March and early September, the Baltic Exchange said in its defense that there were 12 instances where one broker didn’t provide the Baltic with an assessment for the route, citing difficulties in assessing the market. Last month, a different broker said that it would no longer input data for the route on an indefinite, but temporary basis, the exchange added in its defense for the court case.
“There is an element of trust when you are determining the price of shipping oil,” said Halvor Ellefsen, a London-based director at Fearnleys Shipbrokers UK Ltd. “With such a dominant player making bullish uncorroborated proclamations, although lacking underlying contractual details, it has never been more difficult to figure out where in reality TD3C sits. TD34 has by and large taken over from TD3C as a reliable benchmark.”

title: Nasarawa NDC Publicity Secretary quits party, declares support for SDP candidate
body: By Edwin Philip, Lafia The Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in Nasarawa State, Mr Joseph Danjuma, has resigned from the party and declared support for the Social Democratic Party (SDP) governorship candidate, former Inspector-General of Police, Abubakar Adamu. Danjuma announced his resignation in a letter titled “Letter of Resignation” addressed to the state chairman of the NDC, citing a lack of opportunity to perform his duties as the party’s spokesperson. “I wish to humbly resign my membership and position as the Publicity Secretary of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Nasarawa State Chapter, with immediate effect,” he stated. Explaining his decision, he added: “My decision follows the lack of opportunity to perform my role as the spokesperson of the party in the state.” Following his resignation, Danjuma declared his intention to join Adamu’s campaign ahead of the 2027 governorship election. “With this development, I hereby fully join the campaign train of Ex-IGP Adamu. Thank you,” he said. Danjuma, a journalist who has worked with print and broadcast media organisations, previously served as Chief Press Secretary to former Nasarawa State Deputy Governor, Hon. Dameshi Luka. He had earlier expressed support for Adamu at a rally organised under the auspices of the Alago Support Group. Speaking at the event, Danjuma said the group was formed out of a desire for the Alago people to participate actively in decisions concerning the political future of Nasarawa State. He said the group considered Adamu a suitable candidate based on his record of public service and experience as a former police chief. Danjuma also highlighted Adamu’s connections with the Alago community, noting that he had attended school with some prominent sons and daughters of the area in Obi and had maternal ties to the people. “We have resolved that we will no longer be onlookers or fence-sitters while the political destiny of our dear state is being decided. The time to participate, to take a stand and to take our destiny in our own hands is now,” he said. He maintained that members of the Alago community should be free to support candidates of their choice, citing Section 40 of the 1999 Constitution, which guarantees freedom of peaceful assembly and association. Efforts to obtain a reaction from the NDC chairman in Nasarawa State, Hon. Dogo Shammah, regarding Danjuma’s resignation and his stated reason for leaving the party were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report. The post Nasarawa NDC Publicity Secretary quits party, declares support for SDP candidate appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: Serbian public broadcaster apologizes for years of one-sided news coverage during Aleksandar Vučić’s rule
body: Radio Television of Vojvodina (RTV) apologized to viewers live on air for having “turned a blind eye to many things,” Serbian outlets reported . ❗️Dnevnik RT Vojvodine u 17h. V.d glavnog i odg. urednik RTV je podneo ostavku. Ali ovo izvinjenje i jedan otkaz nisu dovoljni! Potrebna je odgovornost, otkaz, i njegova i SVIH onih koji su dosad ćutali na javnom servisu svih građana. 🧹 pic.twitter.com/8dBKmjfsEl — MoreofSea 🌅📷 (@MoreofSea) October 26, 2026 A news broadcast showed footage of people in Serbia celebrating after the election. Anchor Goran Eror then said the footage showed only some of what RTV had failed to show viewers the previous night. “For many years, the public broadcaster failed to fulfill its role. Things went unsaid, a blind eye was turned, information was one-sided, reporting was uncritical, and the right questions were not asked — or no questions were asked at all. And for that, we owe our viewers an apology,” the anchor said, reading a statement on air. He said some employees had fought to allow journalists and editors to work freely but that “we did not win the battle in time.” “But we believe it is important to carry on that fight,” he said. Following the apology, Nenad Čačić, acting editor-in-chief of RTV’s main channel, RTV 1, resigned. Serbia held an early parliamentary election on October 25. Former President Aleksandar Vučić, who had resigned a month earlier, ran in the election, hoping to become prime minister if he won. His party lost to the “Student List” movement, which grew out of protests that began in 2024. A similar episode unfolded in Hungary, where Viktor Orbán stepped down after 16 years in power when the government changed in spring 2026. The new government later announced a reorganization of the public broadcaster MTVA, while the television channel M1 apologized to viewers for lying and for “doing it all these years.” Serbia’s election Serbia’s student-backed opposition has defeated Vučić at the ballot box. He says the winners will impose sanctions on Russia — but they say otherwise. Can Serbia’s student protesters stop Aleksandar Vučić from becoming prime minister? title: Kaduna: ADC guber candidate blames El-Rufai for insecurity
body: The Kaduna State gubernatorial candidate of the African Democratic Congress(ADC), Hon Isa Ashiru, has blamed the Malam Nasir El-Rufai’s administration for the escalation of insecurity in Kaduna State. Speaking in an interview with Trust TV on Tuesday, Hon Ashiru attributed the insecurity in Kaduna State to retrenchment of many Traditional rulers by the previous administration, which has created a lot of ungoverned spaces. ‘’For instance, when the APC government came, they retrenched so many village heads and district heads. They left these places ungoverned. The report that is usually transmitted from the village head to district head head, to the Emir, for onward transmission to the Governor and Security Council meeting is no more,’’ he said. It will be recalled that El-Rufai’s government had reverted to 77 districts and 1,429 village units that existed prior to 2001, effectively sacking the 313 district heads and 4,453 village heads appointed after the year 2001 by administration of former Governor Ahmed Mohammed Makarfi. The then Governor had enacted the Traditional Institutions Law N0 21 of 2021 in June, which replaced the Chiefs (Appointment and Deposition) Law Cap 25 of 1991, to undertake sweeping controversial reforms to the traditional and emirate council system in Kaduna State. In the interview with Trust TV, Hon Ashiru promised that his administration will bring the traditional rulers on board, so as to close the ungoverned spaces, pledging to provide operational vehicles for security agencies and give them incentives for putting their lives on the line. The ADC candidate also said that his government will deploy the use of Artificial Intelligence ‘’because of the sophistication in the industry now,’’ adding that insecurity has become an industry because of the millions involved in the payment of ransom. Decrying the security situation in the state, he expressed optimism that the matter will be reduced to the barest minimum, if not brought to an end, when his administration brings back the retrenched traditional rulers, deploys AI and gives incentives to security agencies, and provide them with operational vehicles.

title: Houthis claim to have hit Saudi Ras Tanura oil refinery, defense ministry with ballistic missiles
body: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday they had hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery, the ⁠biggest in the kingdom, with a ballistic missile.The Houthis also said they had attacked Saudi military aircraft and repelled an advance by Saudi-backed forces near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, an important Red Sea shipping route.Intensifying hostilities between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia have further disrupted oil supplies and heightened the risk of a wider regional conflict, eight months since the Iran war began.The Houthis' military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said the strike on the Ras Tanura refinery had caused a fire at the complex, which also includes a shipping terminal and is located on the Gulf, west of the Strait of Hormuz.Saree also claimed that the Houthis had hit the Saudi Ministry of Defense with a ballistic missile and Abha International Airport with a drone.Saudi authorities did not confirm any of the strikes.Ras Tanura, which has a capacity of 550,000 barrels per day, was shut for a period in the early months of the Iran war as a precautionary measure.Nearly all Saudi Arabia's oil exports flow through two main ports: Ras Tanura in the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea, both of which the Houthis have attacked in the past.Bloomberg News cited a person familiar with the matter as saying Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near Ras Tanura's terminal.Houthis claim to have hit two military transport jetsThe ​Houthis said they had attacked two military transport jets at Najran Airport and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation of the attacks.On Tuesday afternoon, civil defense authorities briefly issued an air raid alert in the Saudi capital Riyadh.The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in support of Yemen's internationally recognized government said it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Riyadh.The Houthis said they had repelled an advance by forces they described as Saudi-backed from the southern approaches to the Bab al-Mandab Strait.Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces earlier this month pushed the Houthis out of coastal areas they had seized in September, loosening the group's grip on a vital Red Sea oil route.Houthi media claims Saudi struck MochaHouthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV reported Saudi strikes on the Yemeni city of Mocha. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.The fighting has shattered a 2022 UN-brokered truce between the coalition and the Houthis, who control the Yemeni capital Sanaa.On Monday, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran to try to reduce regional tensions.Parliament in Egypt, which has said it is considering joining the three countries in a mutual defence pact, authorised Egypt's military on Monday to help defend Saudi Arabia if asked.

title: Iran, Tajikistan to expand cultural cooperation
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 27 (MNA) – ran’s Deputy Culture Minister Mohsen Javadi and the Minister of Culture of Tajikistan Matlubakhon Sattoriyon emphasized the formation of a specialized working group to follow up and implement the two countries’ agreements.
The two sides met and held talks on October 24 on the sidelines of the 14th Dushanbe International Book Fair in Tajikistan, ISNA reported.
In the meeting, which was held with the aim of deepening the longstanding cultural and literary ties between the two countries, the two sides exchanged views on practical solutions for expanding the level of cooperation in various areas of the printing industry, book publishing, and book reading.
Among the most important axes of the talks in the meeting were coordination, synergy, and planning in the field of collating, printing, and publishing the works of the literary and historical luminaries and figures shared by the two countries.
The cultural officials of Iran and Tajikistan described the ancient heritage of Persian speakers as a valuable asset and emphasized that its preservation and proper publication require the continuous cooperation of specialized organizations and institutions in both countries. Cooperation in the field of introducing and translating the works of contemporary writers of both countries and designing an ecosystem for the Persian language in cyberspace were among other topics raised in the meeting.
In order to follow up on the approved measures and operationalize the agreements reached, it was decided that a specialized joint working group be formed between cultural representatives of Iran and Tajikistan. This working group will be responsible for continuous follow-up and facilitating the process of implementing bilateral cooperation programs.
The 14th Dushanbe International Book Fair was held from October 22 to 24 at the National Museum of Tajikistan.
Iran Book and Literature House presented more than 300 titles at the fair, promoting Iranian literature and opportunities for cultural cooperation.
The Iranian pavilion featured classical and contemporary literature, Iranian studies, and children’s and young adult books.
Iran Book and Literature House also held meetings with Tajik cultural officials and participated in specialist sessions to explore cooperation in publishing, translation, and literary exchange.
Iran has regularly attended the Dushanbe fair, and Tajikistan has participated in the Tehran International Book Fair (TIBF). Tajikistan was the special guest of the TIBF in 2023.

title: Finding panics with Call Graph Analyzer
body:
We often get asked "How can I eliminate panics in my Rust code?" There have been several attempts to tackle this issue. Under the Open Device Partnership and working together with Microsoft, we have developed and released the Call Graph Analyzer (CGA) , a tool to extract the callgraph from monomorphized MIR . This callgraph can be used to track down what functions in the compiled binary can panic.
We often get asked "How can I eliminate panics in my Rust code?" There have been several attempts to tackle this issue. Under the Open Device Partnership and working together with Microsoft, we have developed and released the Call Graph Analyzer (CGA) , a tool to extract the callgraph from monomorphized MIR . This callgraph can be used to track down what functions in the compiled binary can panic.
For example, when you run cargo cga check on your code, you get:
In this blogpost we discuss why this new approach is both better and worse than pre-existing approaches at finding panics.
Before discussing the Call Graph Analyzer, we should first consider why panics are useful, and in what cases it might be beneficial to minimize or perhaps even completely eliminate any possible panic. This topic has been explored extensively by others [ 1 ][ 2 ][ 3 ][ 4 ], but it is useful to summarize here. Lets start with a brief description:
Rust provides a mechanism to prevent a function from returning normally, and instead âpanic,â which is a response to an error condition that is typically not expected to be recoverable ...
These unrecoverable error conditions may either be caused by a bug in the implementation of a function, or constitute violated entry conditions for a function (so a bug in the function itself or a mistake by the caller of that function).
An example is calling 1.strict_add(u32::MAX) , which would result in a panic in response to the caller passing invalid arguments to the operation. Similarly a normal addition 1 + u32::MAX in Rust will panic if overflow-checks are enabled.
Instead of panicking, error conditions can be dealt with by:
However striving for zero panics is very hard and quite foolish: code is rarely void of assumptions. Returning Result<T, AssumptionViolated> everywhere just pushes the burden up the call stack, until you will abort anyway at the root. This essentially yields the same behaviour as if you were to panic.
It is useful to make panics explicit though. It is better to know about your panic paths and to reason about them, than to just accidentally include panics and ignore that they exist. Having regression analysis on your panic paths is also very useful, notifying you of any new panic paths introduced in your code.
Having said that, in the following cases it might be justified to eliminate some of your panics:
Striving for no unrecoverable error conditions is extremely hard in practice. Generally it is better to implement top-level recovery mechanisms. In embedded this would entail using a Watchdog timer which resets the device if it is stuck, and a recovery image to restore the device to a working state. On a host machine this could mean catching unwinding panics using catch_unwind . Note that the latter is not fool-proof and comes with a few caveats. Externally accessible services should be redundant and fast to recover.
In conclusion, it is useful to find unintentional panics.
Currently, ways to extract callgraphs or detect panics include:
You can download any of these projects, and with the exception of Charon (which is not explicitly meant for this usecase) it is very easy to get started.
Linker-based panic detection methods work by triggering an error in the linker when it tries to link in a special panic handler. This detection approach only works if not a single panic is included in your binary. It also only works on binaries and not on libraries.
ELF debug info analysis looks at the DWARF debug info that is included in ELF artifacts like binaries and Rust libraries compiled to object files. It is limited in what callgraph information it can provide: the panic machinery can be completely inlined or disappear during the linker phase.
And finally we have HIR, MIR and rust-analyzer based approaches, which use the various Intermediate Representations (IRs) of your code generated by the compiler (and rust-analyzer) to extract the callgraph from. In a sense all these approaches take your original Rust code, have the compiler process it, and spit out what it thinks is happening. Theoretically these approaches work on any Rust crate.
The HIR-based analysis can only analyze the code in your specific crate. This analysis can check if you explicitly write panic! in your own crate. However, it is unaware of any code in your dependencies, such as the standard library. Hence it can not trigger on panics that occur within dependencies. The compiler can also insert assertions like bound checks, which are not even a call to panic until very late in the code generation pass depending on your compiler flags.
The MIR-based analysis is ideal, as it can theoretically see all code from dependencies, before they are optimized away, including panics originating in the standard library. Hence Call Graph Analyzer uses this approach. The only downside is that this analysis is done before LLVM is able to remove unreachable code, and hence we get some false positives.
All these previous approaches take what the compiler is already doing when compiling your crate, and interrupt the compilation process to look at a snapshot of the compilation state to find out whether you are calling a panic.
The rust-analyzer approach is slightly different, as it does not depend on the compiler at all. Rust-analyzer has duplicated the Rust-HIR-MIR pipeline from the compiler, which they adapted for their process. This separate pipeline for rust-analyzer is pretty fast, can be stored in memory and supports updating the state while you are actively writing and changing your Rust code. However, it can not always analyze code that rustc is happy to compile. Most notably it often struggles with complex proc_macros like we use a ton of in Rust Embedded. As an end-user you notice this when your code editor stops giving any helpful suggestions. (The team behind rust-analyzer is working hard to prevent this!) The upside of rust-analyzer is that it does not depend on the Rust compiler.
For our usecase we needed a method that:
We decided on a MIR-based callgraph exporter, which became the Call Graph Analyzer (CGA). Next up, we will discuss the design and functionality of CGA.
CGA extracts the callgraph directly from MIR as a rustc-driver . Clippy similarly is a rustc-driver. Like Clippy, CGA therefore depends on a specific version of the rust compiler, which gets us to the first real downside of CGA:
A note of caution: CGA compiles your crate with a specific (probably different) version of the rustc compiler, standard library, and potentially different compiler flags. Hence you will not get the exact callgraph as included in your binary.
Having a specific (nightly) version of rustc as a dependency using rustc-private also means that CGA can not be installed as a crate from crates.io . Instead the repository needs to be checked out locally, after which cargo install --path . needs to be run (which uses a specific version of the Rust toolchain automatically).
This user experience might be improved when rustc_public contains everything that CGA needs. Though, that scenario isn't really likely. Instead, if CGA becomes popular enough, it might be maintained alongside rustc, just like Clippy currently has this special status. Any breaking change in rustc is also applied to Clippy, and you can install Clippy for your specific toolchain using Rustup. For more information on this, you can watch the excellent talk on "Out of tree access to the compiler state" by Alona Enraght-Moony .
As a rustc-driver, the CGA binary has the same API as rustc itself. You can use cargo to run CGA using cargo cga check . Internally rustc will run as if you were to run cargo check . However CGA does some additional work to gather the call graph, which for a typical crate means that compilation with CGA is roughly 2x-3x as slow as running cargo check .
When CGA is done running all the compiler passes that are normally part of cargo check , it forces the compiler to yield all so-called roots or entrypoints of your crate. Intuitively, this is any part of your crate that is accessible from the outside when compiled. These include:
For this analysis we are explicitly not interested in all the functions that are compiled as part of const blocks, including static value initialization, as only the outcomes of these computations are included in the final binary.
From these roots outward we perform a reachability analysis by walking through the MIR tree. Every time a function is called, that function is also explored. Thus all unused functions are not visited. In Rust, like in C++, a function with Generic arguments is monomorphized when it is called using the concrete types used to call it.
Thus we do not only gather the called functions, but the concrete instantiation of each function, as the implementations can differ wildly depending on the type arguments passed.
This process gets a little bit tedious when considering:
After walking through the MIR tree of your crate and its dependencies, we get a collection of callgraphs. We can now choose to either extract them to JSON or GraphViz dot files, or to check them for any panics or blacklisted functions.
When extracting, all the callgraphs are put in your /target folder as <crate>.callgraph.json . We finally merge them together and export the global callgraph with separate roots using:
To quickly illustrate what this looks like, please consider the following example using dyn objects:
This results in a graph with an arrow for every entry in the vtable:
Image 1: Graphviz Callgraph example (you can zoom in for better readability)
As you can imagine, this quickly becomes quite large and unreadable. If you have a suggestion for a GUI application that can meaningfully display callgraphs, please reach out as that would be very helpful!
Secondly, like Clippy, we can ask CGA to check our code for any panic paths by running:
This will take the callgraph, find panic paths, and will try to give a helpful insight in how this panic path relates to your crate. One of the lints emitted for the above code looks like this:
Note that it shows the backtrace, along with the possible vtable resolution, and the last call from our current crate context. These diagnostics are generated heuristically , meaning that out of all the panic paths, we choose a single one for each callsite in our local crate. We try to choose the best of all these paths using a scoring mechanism.
For any serious crate that was not developed with minimizing panics in mind, the amount of lints generated by CGA is not really manageable. To help with this, CGA comes with a few configurable parameters.
As an example, if you trust a function to not panic (even though panic paths are being emitted for it), you can add the function to the whitelist. Any panic path that includes that function will be ignored. These rules can match on both simplified function names as well as full canonical Rust paths with all generic parameters included.
Alternatively, functions can be put on a blacklist. Besides panics, if you want a crate and its dependencies to never use some function, it is possible to exlude it. For example, you might want to exclude interaction with the filesystem, the network or processes.
An example of a cga.toml configuration file
Then if we feed the following program to CGA:
Note that this feature does not actually preclude a process from being spawned in any of your crates or dependencies: within Rust it will forever remain possible to link to some external object file or use assembly directly, which CGA can not analyze. Blacklisting with CGA is, however, an interesting capability.
Having detailed what CGA can and can not do, it is useful to know there are some caveats and downsides to the approach CGA uses.
Traversing monomorphized MIR is not trivial. Resolving vtables is quite finnicky; the compiler inserts shims sometimes and actual calls are inserted later; coroutines need to be unpacked to find the async paths; and there are implicit assertions which eventually also end up being a panic. All of which is to say: the analysis is hard and it is inevitable that some parts of it are not completely correct. When the toolchain is updated, the resulting MIR can vary dramatically, which also has an impact on the call graph. It might be that down the line some part of the analysis breaks if rustc works differently.
This is to be expected: Rust MIR is unstable and will remain to be so for the foreseable future. Consequently CGA will be a bit fragile.
Depending on your compiler flags but in particular your opt-level , the MIR CGA gathers contains panics that are unreachable.
For example, the expression 1 + 1 has an implicit overflow bounds check included. If you were to const evaluate the expression, it is exceedingly obvious that the expression can never panic. With opt-level=2 (optimize for speed) this expression is optimized to 2 by an earlier compiler pass before CGA gets the MIR. However with opt-level="z" (optimize for size) this panic path is included in the MIR. Instead, the optimization is left to LLVM to perform (which it does).
Your compiler and cargo options really matter with regards to the callgraph being emitted, similarly to how they matter to the final binary generated by rustc and the linker.
I advise people to use opt-level=2 for CGA, even if the shipped binary uses something different, as generally no reachable panic will be missing with opt-level=2 (thus fewer false positives and no false negatives).
CGA has been tested on a few real-world binaries, and typically it works out of the gate. Sometimes however it does not. This is either because the project does not compile with build-std yet (which CGA requires), or because the build.rs expects the application to be built with stock rustc and not with a rustc-driver like CGA ( example ).
If CGA does not work for your project, or if the callgraph does not seem to be correct, please open an issue ! The tooling can only evolve by testing it against real software.
With Call Graph Analyzer (CGA) you can extract callgraphs and detect panics. If you were wondering how many panics your application secretly contains, even though you are not using unwrap , give it a spin and let us know what you find!
A special shoutout to Jyn for this blogpost and the work by Ferrocene , which heavily inspired our work on the Call Graph Analyzer.
