title: Tinubu Seeks Law to Bring Nigerians Convicted Abroad Home to Serve Jail Terms
body: * President transmits amendment bill to Senate, seeks framework for prisoner transfers under bilateral agreements * Senate orders probe of travel agencies over suspected human trafficking networks in Libya Sunday Aborisade in Abuja President Bola Tinubu has asked the Senate to amend the law governing the transfer of convicted offenders, seeking to empower Nigeria to enter into agreements with foreign governments to enable eligible Nigerians convicted abroad to serve their prison sentences at home. The proposed legislation, known as the Transfer of Convicted Offenders Enactment and Enforcement Amendment Bill 2026, seeks to amend the Transfer of Convicted Offenders Enactment and Enforcement Act, Cap 216, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria, 2004. Tinubu transmitted the bill to the Senate in a letter read by Senate President Godswill Akpabio during plenary on Tuesday. The president explained that the proposed amendment would provide a legal framework for Nigeria to enter into agreements with other countries for the transfer of convicted offenders, while also enabling the country to honour similar requests from foreign governments under mutually agreed conditions. In the letter, Tinubu said the bill sought to give effect to agreements between Nigeria and other countries on the transfer of convicted persons. He stated: “The Transfer of Convicted Offenders Enactment and Enforcement Amendment Bill 2026 seeks to amend the Transfer of Convicted Offenders Enactment and Enforcement Act, Act Cap 216, Laws of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 2004, to give effect to the provisions of any scheme or agreement for the transfer of convicted offenders between the Federal Government of Nigeria and the government of any other country.” The president further explained that the proposed amendment would empower him to extend the application of the law to countries with which Nigeria had entered into relevant agreements through an order published in the Federal Gazette. According to him, the provision would facilitate the implementation of prisoner-transfer arrangements, particularly with countries outside the Commonwealth. After reading the president’s letter, Akpabio referred the bill to the Senate Committee on Rules and Business for further legislative consideration. The proposed amendment comes amid several high-profile cases involving Nigerians convicted by foreign courts, including former public officials and political figures. Among them is former Delta State Governor James Ibori, who was sentenced to 13 years’ imprisonment in the United Kingdom in 2012 after pleading guilty to money-laundering offences. He was released in 2016. Former Deputy Senate President Ike Ekweremadu was sentenced to nine years and eight months’ imprisonment in the UK in 2023 over his role in an organ-trafficking conspiracy involving a young man. Similarly, Abidemi Rufai, a former aide to Ogun State Governor Dapo Abiodun, was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment in the United States in 2022 for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft. Nigeria and the United Kingdom already have a prisoner-transfer arrangement that allows eligible prisoners to serve their sentences in their home countries, subject to applicable legal requirements and the agreement of both governments. The proposed amendment seeks to strengthen the domestic legal framework for implementing similar arrangements with countries outside the Commonwealth. However, the proposed legislation would not automatically entitle every Nigerian convicted abroad to return home to serve a sentence. Any transfer would depend on the terms of the relevant agreement, the eligibility of the prisoner and the applicable legal conditions. Meanwhile, the Senate has directed a comprehensive investigation into suspected human-trafficking networks and travel agencies allegedly connected to the trafficking, exploitation and abuse of Nigerians in Libya. The resolution followed the adoption of a report on the urgent need to protect Nigerians from trafficking, slavery and other human rights abuses in the North African country. Presenting the report on behalf of the joint committees on Diaspora, Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Special Duties, Senator Anthony Yaro, representing Gombe South, said the committees had consulted relevant stakeholders, received memoranda and examined the circumstances surrounding the abuses before making their recommendations. He said the recommendations were designed to strengthen Nigeria’s institutional response to human trafficking, improve the protection of victims and disrupt criminal networks responsible for exploiting vulnerable Nigerians. The motion for the consideration and adoption of the report received the support of Senator Victor Umeh, representing Anambra Central. In its resolutions, the Senate called for stronger enforcement of existing anti-trafficking laws, increased funding for the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) and other relevant agencies, and a comprehensive investigation into suspected trafficking networks and their associated travel agencies. The lawmakers also called for the establishment of a national reintegration and protection programme for returning victims of trafficking. They recommended that the National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons coordinate the programme in collaboration with NAPTIP and other relevant institutions to ensure that returning victims received appropriate protection and support. The Senate further urged the Federal Government to intensify diplomatic engagement with Libya through bilateral and multilateral channels to combat trafficking and promote safe and legal migration. Contributing to the debate, Senator Neda Imasuen, representing Edo South, said the country’s major challenge was not the absence of laws against human trafficking but the failure to enforce existing legislation effectively and hold offenders accountable. Imasuen’s position underscored concerns about the gap between Nigeria’s legal framework and the effective prosecution of individuals and networks involved in trafficking and exploitation. In his remarks, Akpabio called for stronger deterrent measures against perpetrators of serious crimes, arguing that laws must carry sufficient consequences to discourage criminal conduct. Recalling his tenure as governor of Akwa Ibom State, the Senate president said he had signed an anti-kidnapping law prescribing the death penalty and the forfeiture of property where a kidnapped victim was found. He also advocated a strict Know-Your-Tenant policy, arguing that landlords should be able to provide information about their tenants when crimes were committed. Akpabio warned that landlords who failed to provide relevant information could face questions over their possible complicity in criminal activities. As part of its resolutions, the Senate directed NAPTIP to work with the Nigeria Police Force, the Nigeria Immigration Service, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to investigate identified travel agencies. The agencies are expected to interrogate their directors, officers and agents to establish the extent of their involvement, if any, in recruitment networks, financial transactions and travel arrangements connected to the trafficking and exploitation of Nigerians abroad. The investigation is expected to help identify the individuals and organisations facilitating the movement of victims, expose the financial channels sustaining trafficking operations and strengthen measures to prevent further exploitation. The Senate’s resolutions also placed renewed emphasis on victim protection, the reintegration of returning Nigerians and diplomatic cooperation with Libya, alongside stronger law enforcement against suspected traffickers.

title: Meta’s $25 billion legal loss just put blood in the water
body:
When attorneys general from across the US announced a $17 billion settlement with Meta this summer, the sum was unprecedented. But a ruling last week by a New Mexico judge blew that number out of the water. The judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion to resolve claims that Meta misled users around the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal and related incidents. Similar claims were resolved by the settlement with most other states. The outcome raised an obvious question: Should these states have asked for more?
The answer depends on a mix of factors, including whether the $25 billion order stands up to Meta’s legal challenges. Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement that the company is “confident we will prevail on appeal” and called New Mexico’s lawsuit an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” If the fine sticks, however, it could create a new appetite for Big Tech’s opponents to stick it out in court — or ask for bigger payouts to settle.
“For the settling AGs, they’re going to look at this and maybe experience some regret for all the claims that they waived, and start looking around and trying to figure out what’s left that they didn’t waive, if they can try to get some money like this too,” says Daphne Keller, director of platform regulation at the Stanford Program in Law, Science & Technology. For the many individuals, school districts, and tribes with outstanding claims, “this is very encouraging and will make them hopeful that continuing to litigate aggressively will lead to a big payout,” Keller says.
The $25 billion court order covered millions of violations of New Mexico’s unfair practices law, after a jury found Meta had misled users about how it protected their data and policed misinformation and hate speech – claims stemming from the 2018 Cambridge Analytica scandal. In most states, such claims were covered by a section of the kids online safety settlement, resolved with a $459 million payment.
While that number looks comparatively puny, there were upsides to taking it. A settlement provided more certainty and an expedited payout for states even though Meta will be making the payments over 10 years. It also secured product commitments from Meta, like restrictions on teen usage, that might have been more difficult to get from a court ruling. And it allowed those to be implemented soon after the settlement was approved, which advocates say is important to prevent further harm to kids. Other state attorneys general also may have been working with different laws or evidence that could result in outcomes different from those obtained in New Mexico.
But New Mexico’s win, combined with other recent legal victories for AGs and private plaintiffs — including a separate judgment of nearly $1 billion against Meta in New Mexico — may embolden anyone still litigating privacy and kids online safety cases. “Assuming that even a fraction of this award gets upheld, then they clearly took pennies on the dollar compared to New Mexico,” Keller says of the settling states. Imagining she’s an AG with similar claims — like public false statements about privacy or content moderation — “I become less willing to settle in those cases,” Keller adds. “Or if I do settle, I ask for more.”
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier, whose state avoided joining the Meta settlement, seemed to take the latest New Mexico ruling as a validation. “As I said at the time, the multi-state settlement with Meta was a slap on the wrist,” Utheimer wrote on X. “Florida isn’t going to sell out to Meta. We’re going to hold them accountable.” The District of Columbia could be the next place to test whether New Mexico’s win can be replicated since it did not settle its Cambridge Analytica claims and has continued pursuing its lawsuit in court.
While the AGs who joined the settlement can’t pursue covered claims against Meta anymore, they could still push for more in cases against other social media defendants, including TikTok, YouTube, and Snap. And those who weren’t part of the Meta settlement, including school districts and individuals, may be encouraged to continue pushing ahead. “Realistically, there’s so many cases, it’s not feasible that every single case can have an outcome like this,” says Keller. “Meta actually would go broke because the multipliers are so large. But any one, or 10, or 50 of them could hit the jackpot.”
States have stepped in to pursue tech policy and competition cases where the federal government has declined to, but the wide range of potential outcomes for each state presents its own challenges. As Congress has stalled on major tech policy bills and the Trump administration has often favored lighter regulation on tech, Colorado Law associate professor Blake Reid sees recent cases as a “move toward state-level tech policy.”
“The trick of that is, now you have 50 states that all have different sets of resources, and different sets of politics, and different sets of incentives, and frankly just different skill levels in terms of the sophistication that it takes to do litigation at this scale,” Reid says. “And it’s the same Meta, but now it’s up to 50 small opponents that are going to break in different ways.”
As for whether the $25 billion ruling makes other states rethink their strategy, Reid says there could be a range of approaches, depending partly on whether the figure is upheld on appeal and whether Meta loses yet more cases. “Is that a game that every state attorney general wants to play?” he asks. “And I think the settlement in the other case suggests maybe not.” Still, the new figure may change what AGs think they can achieve in court. And the more losses Meta and other tech companies rack up, the more ambitious they might get.

title: Ebonyi Assembly passes State Police Bill
body: By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The Ebonyi State House of Assembly has passed into law the State Police Bill transmitted to it by the National Assembly for concurrence. The bill seeks to alter the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria (as amended) to provide a legal framework for the establishment of State Police Services across the federation, while retaining the Nigeria Police Force at the federal level. The State Assembly, during plenary at the Assembly Complex, Nkaliki Road, Abakaliki, saw all 24 members vote unanimously in favour of the bill after extensive deliberations and consultations with their constituents. The Speaker of the House, Rt. Hon. Moses Ije Odunwa, who presided over the session, said the unanimous vote underscored the Assembly’s commitment to constitutional reforms aimed at strengthening security architecture, enhancing access to criminal intelligence and protection of lives and property. Odunwa noted that the demand for a sub-national policing system has been a long-standing clamour among Ebonyi people, adding that the state had formally presented its position in support of State Police during the public hearing organised by the National Assembly on the constitution review. “The passage of this bill reflects the wishes of Ebonyians who desire a policing system that is closer to the people and more responsive to local security challenges,” the Speaker stated. The Leader of the House and member representing Afikpo North-West Constituency Hon. Kingsley Ikoro, in his contribution said the establishment of State Police would significantly increase manpower and improve effectiveness in tackling crime and criminality at the grassroots. Also speaking, Hon. Victor Chidi Nwoke, representing Abakaliki North Constituency, Hon. Oluchukwu Ukie Ezeali, representing Afikpo North East Constituency, and the Chief Whip of the House, Hon. Nkemka Okoro Onumah, in their separate contributions, emphasised the need to bring policing closer to the people as a panacea to the nation’s security challenges. Following the passage, the Speaker directed the Clerk of the House, Mrs. Uche Edene, to transmit a formal memo communicating the resolution of the House to the National Assembly. The post Ebonyi Assembly passes State Police Bill appeared first on Vanguard News .

title: US taps Poland to host European PAC-3 missile maintenance facility
body: WARSAW, Poland — The United States government has selected Poland to host a new European maintenance facility for Patriot Advanced Capability-3 (PAC-3) interceptors, produced by Lockheed Martin , according to U.S. and Polish officials. “Today’s announcement puts partnership into action. By investing national resources to establish this critical sustainment capability on NATO’s Eastern Front, Allies are sending a clear message: the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action,” Pentagon acquisition chief Michael Duffey was quoted as saying in a statement. This new regional hub will rely on transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration to be led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, according to the statement. The investment is expected to shorten turnaround times and reinforce deterrence along the alliance’s eastern flank. Related Germany, US to expand shared production of Patriot interceptors, strike missiles German and U.S. defense leaders have signed an agreement positioning Germany as an additional production hub for scarce American defense equipment. “Poland has sought very hard to have these competencies and infrastructure in Poland. We were contending against several ambitious competitors,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Tuesday. The latest development comes as European allies are advancing talks with the U.S. on the possibility of enabling local production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors, seeking to address supply chain shortfalls. Alongside Germany , the governments of Poland and Ukraine, among others, have also lobbied Washington to allow the newest generation of Lockheed Martin missiles to be manufactured at domestic facilities. In March 2018, Poland signed a contract worth around $4.75 billion to acquire two Configuration 3+ batteries for the country’s mid-range air-defense system. The country launched the program’s second phase in May 2022, requesting the U.S. to deliver a further six Patriot batteries with related gear. In December 2025, the Polish government announced that the first two batteries reached full operational readiness.

title: Ten Decrees: Old Masters, New Money
body: Bitcoin Magazine Ten Decrees: Old Masters, New Money On August 15, 1971, Richard Nixon announced that he had directed Treasury Secretary John Connally “to suspend temporarily the convertibility of the dollar into gold.” The suspension was never lifted. Fifty-five years later to the day, Lucho Poletti unveiled the first of ten drawings responding to that decree. Europe had experienced its own monetary upheavals. Hieronymus Bosch and Pieter Bruegel the Elder worked during an era of expanding banking, credit, and speculation. Antwerp, where Bruegel worked, became one of Europe’s great commercial centers. Both painters populated their compositions with hundreds of figures, constructing elaborate worlds in which human behavior, social order, and moral judgment could be examined simultaneously. Master Cuts Out The Stone (after Hemessen), Pepenardo (2025) Bitcoin artists have increasingly returned to this visual tradition. Pepenardo’s Master Cuts Out the Stone , exhibited by BMAG earlier this year, reimagined Jan Sanders van Hemessen’s The Surgeon as a study of who extracts and who is extracted from. Carlijn Kingma’s The Waterworks of Money , shown at Bitcoin Amsterdam last year, depicted the modern monetary system as an interconnected landscape. Complex systems seem to invite pictures that hold everything in a single frame. Lucho Poletti has made bitcoin-related art since 2017, describing his practice as visual propaganda for the monetary revolution. A contributor to the Bitcoin Conference art gallery since 2021, he returns to Bitcoin Amsterdam this November with Ten Decrees . The series reimagines ten paintings, four by Bosch and six by Bruegel, around money. Fiat , Latin for “let it be done,” becomes the organizing principle. Nine titles issue commands: let there be fury, profit, chaff, a game, folly, hunger, refuge, collapse, and ash. The tenth, Ultima Fiat , reverses that authority: let it be the last. Furia Fiat: Let there be fury , Lucho Poletti (2026) Unveiled on August 15, 2026, the anniversary of Nixon’s announcement, the series follows a biweekly release schedule beginning August 29 and concluding January 3, 2027, the anniversary of Bitcoin’s Genesis Block. Each drawing contains hundreds of figures and objects, with inscriptions often visible only at close range. The 30-by-20-inch prints, produced in editions of ten, form a composition spanning approximately four meters when arranged in two rows of five. Five drawings have been released, most recently Fiat Moria , after Bruegel’s Netherlandish Proverbs , on October 24. The sixth, Fiat Fames , follows November 7. Ahead of Bitcoin Amsterdam , November 5–6, I spoke with Poletti about the recurring influence of Bosch and Bruegel on bitcoin art, the relationship between allegory and propaganda, and translating his densely detailed drawings to the conference’s main-stage LED installation. The Garden of Earthly Delights , Hieronymus Bosch (c. 1490–1510) BMAG: Bosch and Bruegel seem to be having a synchronistic moment among artists interested in Bitcoin. Both worked in what is now Belgium and the Netherlands, during a period when Antwerp was emerging as a major financial center and the Habsburgs were debasing coinage. What is it about transitional periods (like the current one) that draws artists back to Bosch and Bruegel and their densely populated landscapes? Lucho Poletti: Because they had already solved the problem I was stuck with: how do you draw a whole society going wrong at once? Bosch and Bruegel put hundreds of people in a single frame, each busy with their own concerns. The system shows up in the sum of it. You don’t look at a Bruegel, you search it. It’s a great way to depict the effects of money, which nobody really sees and everybody feels. They also lived through a money problem a lot like ours. Silver from the Americas poured into Europe through Seville and on to the bankers in Antwerp. Prices across Western Europe rose sixfold over 150 years. Philip II defaulted in 1557 and the crash spread across all of Europe. Two years later Bruegel painted Netherlandish Proverbs, a village where everyone is absorbed in something foolish and nobody can see the whole. The four Bosch pieces are about appetite: the temptation, and the bill that shows up after. The six Bruegels are about the crowd, and how society behaves once the rules stop making sense. Fiat Lucrum : Let there be profit , Lucho Poletti (2026) BMAG: The series draws on the original meaning of the F-word every bitcoiner knows. Nine of your titles use fiat as a command, while the tenth, Ultima Fiat , seems to reverse that authority. How did you arrive at Latin as the language of the series, and why does the final decree change speaker? Lucho Poletti: Fiat was never a noun. In Latin it’s a verb, “let it be done.” It’s the word God speaks in the Latin Genesis before the light comes on: fiat lux. Someone with authority says so and it happens. That’s a literal description of how fiat money comes into existence, so I wanted the verb in every title. Latin wasn’t a stretch for me. I’ve titled work in it for years: Moneta Divina, Cypher Deos, and Novus Moneta Seclorum dating back to 2020. The dollar already speaks it, too. Turn over a one-dollar bill and there are three Latin mottos on the back. Ultima Fiat, Fiat Lucrum and Furia Fiat had their names before the series did. Once there were three decrees in concept, I kept going until I had ten, and the name for the whole series became obvious. Ten Decrees has the Ten Commandments sitting under it, which suits work rebuilt out of painted sermons. In Fiat Lucrum there’s a lighthouse at the top left with FIAT LUX GENESIS 1:3 engraved into it. The title is the phrase rewritten for the money printers: let there be light turned into let there be profit. Fiat Lucrum (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) Nine of the decrees are issued to you, in the flat voice an institution uses. Let there be profit, let there be hunger, let there be a game. The tenth is the only one we get to say back. Ultima fiat means “let it be the last,” which is closer to a plea than an order. Every one of us has been living under the first nine since 1971, whether we noticed or not, and Bitcoin is how we issue the tenth. It closes the series on January 3, the anniversary of the Genesis Block, which also happens to be my birthday. BMAG: Bosch and Bruegel constructed extraordinarily complex visual worlds where allegory, satire, religious symbolism, and everyday life coexist. Their paintings invite close inspection but rarely offer a single, definitive interpretation. In Ten Decrees , you’re borrowing their compositions while introducing a more explicit critique of the monetary system. How do you approach the relationship between ambiguity and message in your work? Lucho Poletti: The words carry the message so the people don’t have to. Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights doesn’t have a single word in it. Fiat Lucrum has more than fifty lettered objects, and some are as blunt as a protest sign: four money presses lettered QE-1, QE-2, QE-3 and QE-∞, and a little hand-lettered card on a broker’s desk that reads genius, we print, you pay, have a nice day. Nobody has to wonder what I think of the money system. Fiat Palea (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) I keep the ambiguity in the people. In Fiat Lucrum there’s a crowd cheering a woman who holds up a $ on a golden staff under a sign that says ETF, and that crowd is wearing my mask. So is the man signing the leverage contract, and so is the woman taking the mortgage. In Fiat Palea a man in the mask is knee-deep in a pile of printed bills. Bosch drew his own neighbors into the middle of the garden, and I drew mine. If the ₿ on a forehead were a badge of honor, I wouldn’t hand it out like that. It’s more a badge of the aware, the initiated. Knowing the money is broken doesn’t make one a saint. I’m careful with endings too. These pieces show the exit while not promising a way out. Near the middle of Fiat Moria there’s a lit doorway with MONEY ₿ BETTER WORLD over the arch, and a plain-faced man on the step looking back at the square. He hasn’t gone in yet, and nobody’s stopping him. Where you’d be standing in that picture is your call. Fiat Palea: Let there be chaff , Lucho Poletti (2026) BMAG: In Fiat Lucrum , your reinterpretation of Bosch’s Garden of Earthly Delights , you introduce a system of waterworks: pipes, reservoirs, and flowing liquidity. Bosch often allowed viewers to recognize things that the figures within his paintings could not. What possibilities does that kind of visual allegory offer you when depicting something as abstract as the monetary system? Lucho Poletti: What Bosch never had in his garden was plumbing, so I gave it some. Water organizes the whole of Fiat Lucrum. It starts clean high in the mountains on the left, pours out of a machine in Eden and settles in a reflecting basin. Cut into the basin’s wall there’s an inspection window with fish swimming behind the glass. Somebody built a viewing port into the reservoir so you could check it, and every full node on the Bitcoin network is that window. Downstream the water widens into a lake. In the middle sits a glass tank lettered FRESH LIQUIDITY, with BOTTOMLESS engraved on the bowl, and eight people are having the party of their lives inside it. The valve wheel that controls the flow is on top of the dome, outside the glass, where none of them can reach it. Monetary policy gets set by someone who isn’t at the party. And the tank leaks. From there the water runs orange, down a stream and over a waterfall into a pool where a tick with a $ on its cheek drinks it through a hose. Fiat Lucrum (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) That’s the Bosch trick you’re describing. The bathers can’t see the leak or the valve, and you can see both from across the room. Richard Cantillon worked out around 1730 that new money helps whoever gets it first and costs whoever gets it last. I drew it as a watercourse because everybody already understands water: whoever’s upstream drinks first, and everyone downstream gets what’s left. BMAG: Looking across the series, are there particular details, references, or artistic decisions that you feel are especially important but might be overlooked by viewers? What would you want someone encountering these drawings for the first time to spend more time looking at? Lucho Poletti: Up close is where these work, and most of what matters in them is small. Start with the plain faces. Everybody spots the Satoshi masks and the $ skulls first because they’re the loud ones, but the plain faces belong to the people the system is happening to. In Furia Fiat a line of bald men crawl on their hands and knees with red tubes plugged into the backs of their skulls, and the red is the same color as the fluid in a bowl a few meters away that says TIME. That’s what’s being drained out of them. In Fiat Palea, Adam and Eve stand under a serpent with a $ for an eye. They’re wearing the mask, but neither of them has a ₿ on the brow yet. Furia Fiat (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) Then look at how characters connect across a distance. In Fiat Ludus a sack lettered STIMULUS sits on a bench next to an older figure, and a little way off a kid walks away with the same sack on his back, lettered THE BILL. A blindfolded boy feels around with his arms out while the man lunging in beside him holds up a bunch of $ balloons the boy can’t see. Even the enrollment forms are signed by Seymore Debt and Max D. Out. Fiat Ludus (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) Fiat Ludus (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) In Fiat Palea a broken crate stenciled EXECUTIVE ORDER 6102 sits in the straw, and further back, bolted across a vault, a plate reads WINDOW, NO REDEMPTION. Roosevelt took the gold in 1933 and Nixon closed the window in 1971, and I put the two close enough that you read one and then find the other. Up higher in the same piece, a guy in the mask with WHOOPS across his vest is pouring gasoline on a burning bank. In Furia Fiat, the $ skulls stand on GNOSIS and clutch books of knowledge, keeping them for themselves. The bubbles are dated. Fiat Ludus has a sphere with tulips growing out of the top, marked 1637 and 1720, and another with a hen sitting on a WALL STREET egg, marked 1929 and 2008. Variety’s front page the day after the 1929 crash read WALL ST. LAYS AN EGG. Some of the skies have thin straight lines of cloud behind the smoke, the kind a plane leaves. Fiat Ludus (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) Watch the prices, too. A price in dollars only goes up: at CANTILLON’S hot dog stand in Fiat Ludus the 5¢ is crossed out and the sign says $9. A price in sats only goes down: a fish stall in Fiat Moria has 4000 crossed out, then 2000, and now it’s 1000 SATS. In Fiat Ludus, the carrots changing hands have dropped from 7,500 to 3,000 SATS on the chalkboard next to the dollar hopscotch. Fiat Ludus (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) The Latin is there to be read. MORITURI TE SALUTANT, those who are about to die salute you, is carved around the rim of the arena in Fiat Ludus. EX NIHILO, out of nothing, is cut over an empty vault in Fiat Palea. In Fiat Moria the $ skull leaning out of the window has a plaque on either side of him: MUNDUS VULT DECIPI, the world wants to be deceived, and $TULTORUM INFINITUS EST NUMERUS, the number of fools is infinite, with a $ for the S. Fiat Lucrum has a little panel that runs a whole life in four stops: school, debt, work, death. And in Fiat Moria there’s a small round time machine with NO RETURN on its side and 1944-2026 on the dial. A man is climbing out of it, staring at the village. 1944 is Bretton Woods, when the world tied its money to the dollar and the dollar to gold. He left then and he’s only just arrived, and he can’t quite believe what he’s looking at. Fiat Moria (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) None of that comes with a caption. You find it by standing close for a long time, the way you would with a Bruegel, and the finding is the whole point. Fiat Ludus: Let there be a game , Lucho Poletti (2026) BMAG: Each drawing is 18,000 pixels wide, populated by hundreds of figures, with every Satoshi mask drawn by hand and details that only reveal themselves up close. You’ve described the work as “crafted, not generated.” At a time when AI can convincingly imitate the Old Masters, what significance does that labor have for you, and how does it shape the way you want these works to be experienced? Lucho Poletti: “Crafted, not generated” is a phrase I came up with to sum up where the work in these pieces actually is. There are machines in my process, but they’re only one part of it. A model I trained on years of my own work does the rough first pass on a composition. I think of it as an apprentice. Bosch came out of a family workshop, and the masters of his day leaned on assistants for the groundwork so their own hours could go into the meaning. Mine roughs out the scene and gives me a base to build toward the standard they set. Then I spend weeks on each piece in a grueling manual process in Photoshop, making the decisions and drawing in hundreds of figures, objects, symbols and phrases until the art says what I mean. Fiat Moria (detail), Lucho Poletti (2026) AI can imitate the look of a Bosch or a Bruegel pretty convincingly now. What it can’t do is mean anything. It won’t decide that the valve on the liquidity tank in Fiat Lucrum belongs outside the glass, where the bathers can’t reach it. It won’t decide that the slop on the ground should be piggy banks wired into the money presses, each with its own name: SAVINGS, PENSION, NEST EGG. It doesn’t make jokes either. It’s never going to sit a fool in a jester’s cap on a platform lettered TAKE IT AT FACE VALUE while a $ skull does his makeup. My personal philosophy is that if I don’t do the majority of the work, it’s not my art. I hold myself to that, and anyone who looks at these up close can see a person made the decisions that matter. That’s how I’d like people to take these in: up close, and for a long time. I don’t ask anyone to trust me on how they were made. The work answers that better than I can. Fiat Moria: Let there be folly , Lucho Poletti (2026) BMAG: You’ve been part of the Bitcoin Conference since 2021, and this November Ten Decrees comes to the main stage at Bitcoin Amsterdam, not far from the historical centers where Bosch and Bruegel worked. These drawings are extraordinarily detailed, designed to reward close inspection. How are you approaching their translation to monumental LED screens, and does exhibiting them in the Netherlands carry any particular significance for you? Lucho Poletti: The prints were meant for one person standing close to search the work and find details that speak to them. An LED wall gets a thousand people at fifty meters, which is an amazing opportunity to create a visual experience for the still pieces, so I’ve done my best to create a compelling one for each piece. Each one gets fifteen seconds, in the order they were released. The big center wall carries the center of each piece in one slow pass from left to right, so the room gets the shape of it. The screen on the right opens on the Bosch or Bruegel it came from, with its name and date, and halfway through it wipes across to mine. The screen on the left side pulls out lateral details you’d never catch from the floor, like the ship of fools riding the mast in Fiat Moria, or the pigs feeding at the DEBASED trough. All five released so far play back to back as one loop, old master and new money side by side the whole way through. Ten Decrees , Bitcoin Amsterdam main-stage visualization rendering, Lucho Poletti (2026) The Netherlands matters to me. Bosch spent his whole life in ’s-Hertogenbosch, about an hour south of Amsterdam by train. Some of Bruegel’s proverbs are still in use in Dutch: people still say someone hangs his cloak to the wind when he turns with the crowd, and in Fiat Moria, a man wearing a Satoshi mask jumps off a mountain, holding his cloak in his hand—a reference to the Dutch proverb about changing one’s position to suit the prevailing winds. Amsterdam has its own chapter in this story. The Bank of Amsterdam opened in 1609 to give merchants a money nobody could debase, and for over a century its bank guilder traded at a premium over ordinary coin because people trusted the silver was in the vault. David Hume held it up as the model of a fully backed bank. It had been lending to the Dutch East India Company quietly, and when that became public in 1790 the premium vanished and the bank declared itself insolvent. I can’t think of a better city to show a series about monetary decrees and trust, two months before the last one lands on the Genesis Block anniversary. The Tower of Babel, Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563) Exhibition & Further Reading Lucho Poletti’s Ten Decrees will be on view on the main stage at Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 5–6, 2026, as part of the Bitcoin Museum & Art Gallery (BMAG) programming. Explore Poletti’s detailed write-ups on each Decree for a deeper look at the artwork, symbolism, and historical references throughout the series, and follow him on X . Read more from BMAG’s Bitcoin Amsterdam series: The Undercurrent: Three European Artists on Making Money Visible and The Architecture of Money: Mapping Financial Power in the Age of Bitcoin . The Bitcoin Museum & Art Gallery (BMAG) organizes international exhibitions, auctions, and artist collaborations exploring bitcoin and its cultural implications. Join us at Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 5–6, 2026, and use code BA26-BMAG20 for discounted admission. Get your tickets here . This post Ten Decrees: Old Masters, New Money first appeared on Bitcoin Magazine and is written by Dennis Koch .

title: Filian, Fil-C binaries on Debian
body:
I'm impressed with the level of compatibility of the new memory-safe C/C++ compiler Fil-C (filcc, fil++). Many libraries and applications that I've tried work under Fil-C without changes, and the exceptions haven't been hard to get working.
I've accumulated miscellaneous notes on this page regarding usage of Fil-C. My selfish objective here is to protect various machines that I manage by switching them over to code compiled with Fil-C, but maybe you'll find something useful here too.
Is it affordable? As some data points, I've posted a graph showing nearly 9000 microbenchmarks of Fil-C vs. clang on cryptographic software (each run pinned to 1 core on a Zen 4). Typically code compiled with Fil-C takes between 1x and 4x as many cycles as the same code compiled with clang.
Can I use Fil-C to compile replacement packages for my Debian machine? I'm working on Filian , which adapts Debian packages to use Fil-C. On a Debian 13 system, Filian downloads Fil-C, compiles Fil-C, installs Fil-C, downloads selected Debian source packages, compiles those packages with Fil-C, and installs those packages.
Are there other package managers that support compiling with Fil-C? Yes: Filnix from Mikael Brockman adapts Nix packages to use Fil-C. For example, an unprivileged user under Debian 12 with about 10GB of free disk space can download, compile, and install Fil-C, and run a Fil-C-compiled Nethack, as follows:
Are binary packages available precompiled with Fil-C? I'm not distributing Filian binaries for now, but if you run multiple Debian systems with synchronized package versions then you can compile once and share the binary packages. For Filnix, some binary packages are already cached via Cachix . You can also use various packages from the /opt/fil binary distribution from the Fil-C author.
Is the supply chain safe? As a starting point in answering this question, I've posted a script to help auditors see how Fil-C differs from upstream sources (clang, glibc, ...).
I think everything later on this page is superseded by Filian, except for some package notes that I haven't integrated into the Filian database yet. Filian definitely supersedes filian-install-packages version 20251030 posted here, filian-install-compiler versions 20251029 , 20251030 , 20251104 posted here, the build-parallel script posted here, and the libgc replacement posted here.
Timings below are from a mini-PC named phoenix except where otherwise mentioned. This mini-PC has a 6-core (12-thread) AMD Ryzen 5 7640HS (Zen 4) CPU, 12GB RAM, and 36GB swap. The OS is Debian 13. (I normally run LTS software, periodically upgrading from software that's 4â5 years old such as Debian 11 today to software that's 2â3 years old such as Debian 12 today; but some of the packages included in Fil-C expect newer utilities to be available.)
Current recommendations for things to do at the beginning as root :
I created an unprivileged filc user. Everything else is as that user.
This isn't just the compiler; there's also glibc and quite a few higher-level libraries and applications. There are also binary Fil-C packages, but I've worked primarily with the source package at this point.
There are also options to use musl instead of glibc, but musl is incompatible with some of the packages shipped with Fil-C: attr needs basename , elfutils needs argp_parse , sed 's test suite needs the glibc variant of calloc , and vim 's build needs iconv to be able to convert from CP932 to UTF-8.
I had originally configured the server phoenix with only 12GB swap. I then had to restart ./build_all_fast_glibc.sh a few times because compiling the Fil-C compiler ran out of memory (from automatically parallelizing the compilation across 12 threads; presumably compiling clang on the same machine would have the same issue). Switching to 36GB swap made everything work with no restarts; monitoring showed that almost 19GB swap (plus 12GB RAM) was used at one point. A larger server, 128 cores with 512GB RAM, took 8 minutes for Fil-C plus 6 minutes for musl, with no restarts needed.
Fil-C includes a ./build_all_slow.sh that builds many more libraries and applications (sometimes with patches from the Fil-C author). I wrote a replacement script https://cr.yp.to/2025/build-parallel-20251023.py with the following differences:
On phoenix , running time PATH="$HOME/bin:$HOME/fil-c/build/bin:$HOME/fil-c/pizfix/bin:$PATH" ./build-parallel.py went through 61 targets in 101 minutes real time (467 minutes user time, 55 minutes system time), successfully compiling 60 of them.
libcap. This is the one that didn't compile: /home/filc/fil-c/pizfix/bin/ld: /usr/libexec/gcc/x86_64-linux-gnu/14/liblto_plugin.so: error loading plugin: libc.so.6: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
util-linux. I skipped this one. It does compile, but the compiled taskset utility needs to be patched to use sched_getaffinity and sched_setaffinity as library functions rather than via syscall , or Fil-C needs to be patched for those syscalls. This is an issue for build-parallel since build-parallel relies on taskset ; maybe build-parallel should instead use Python's affinity functions.
attr, bash, benchmarks, binutils, bison, brotli, bzip2, bzip3, check, cmake, coreutils, cpython, curl, dash, diffutils, elfutils, emacs, expat, ffi, gettext, git, gmp, grep, icu, jpeg-6b, libarchive, libcap, libedit, libevent, libpipeline, libuev, libuv, lua, lz4, m4, make, mg, ncurses, nghttp2, openssh, openssl, pcre2, pcre, perl, pkgconf, procps, quickjs, sed, shadow, simdutf, sqlite, tcl, tmux, toybox, vim, wg14_signals, xml_parser, xz, zlib, zsh, zstd. No problems encountered so far (given whatever patches were already applied from the Fil-C author!). The benchmarks package is supplied with Fil-C and does a few miscellaneous measurements.
I did export PATH="$HOME/bin:$HOME/fil-c/build/bin:$HOME/fil-c/pizfix/bin:$PATH" before these.
boost 1.89.0 : Seems to mostly work. Most of the package is header-only; a few simple tests worked fine.
I also looked a bit at the compiled parts. Running ./bootstrap.sh --with-toolset=clang --prefix=$HOME ran into vfork , which Fil-C doesn't support, but editing tools/build/src/engine/execunix.cpp to use defined(__APPLE__) || defined(__FILC__) for the no-fork test got past this.
Running ./b2 install --prefix=$HOME toolset=clang address-model=64 architecture=x86_64 binary-format=elf produced an error message since I should have said x86 instead of x86_64 ; Fil-C said it caught a safety issue in the b2 program after the error message: filc safety error: argument size mismatch (actual = 8, expected = 16) . I didn't compile with debugging so Fil-C didn't say where this is in b2 .
cdb-20251021 : Seems to work. One regression test, an artificial out-of-memory regression test, currently produces a different error message with Fil-C: filc panic: src/libpas/pas_compact_heap_reservation.c:65: pas_aligned_allocation_result pas_compact_heap_reservation_try_allocate(size_t, size_t): assertion page_result.result failed.
libcpucycles-20250925 : Seems to work. I commented out the first three lines of cpucycles/options .
libgc : I replaced this with a small gcshim package ( https://cr.yp.to/2025/gcshim-20251022.tar.gz ) that simply calls malloc etc. So far this seems to be an adequate replacement. (Fil-C includes a garbage collector.)
libntruprime-20241021 : Seems to work after a few tweaks but I didn't collect full notes yet. chmod +t crypto_hashblocks/sha512/avx2 disables assembly and makes things compile; configured with --no-valgrind since Fil-C doesn't support valgrind; did a bit more tweaking to make cpuid work.
lpeg-1.1.0: Compiles, maybe works (depends on lua, dependency of neovim): cd PREFIX=$(dirname $(dirname $(which lua))) wget https://www.inf.puc-rio.br/~roberto/lpeg/lpeg-1.1.0.tar.gz tar -xf lpeg-1.1.0.tar.gz cd lpeg-1.1.0 make CC=`which filcc` DLLFLAGS='-shared -fPIC' test cp lpeg.so $PREFIX/lib
luv-1.51.0: Compiles, maybe works (depends on lua, dependency of neovim): cd PREFIX=$(dirname $(dirname $(which lua))) wget https://github.com/luvit/luv/releases/download/1.51.0-1/luv-1.51.0-1.tar.gz tar -xf luv-1.51.0-1.tar.gz cd luv-1.51.0-1 mkdir build cd build LUA_DIR=$HOME/fil-c/projects/lua-5.4.7 # lua install should probably do this: cp $LUA_DIR/lua.h $PREFIX/include/ cp $LUA_DIR/lauxlib.h $PREFIX/include/ cp $LUA_DIR/luaconf.h $PREFIX/include/ cp $LUA_DIR/lualib.h $PREFIX/include/ # and then: cmake -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=`which filcc` -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$PREFIX -DWITH_LUA_ENGINE=Lua -DLUA_DIR=$HOME/fil-c/projects/lua-5.4.7/ .. make test make install
mutt-2-2-15-rel (depends on ncurses): wget https://github.com/muttmua/mutt/archive/refs/tags/mutt-2-2-15-rel.tar.gz tar -xf mutt-2-2-15-rel.tar.gz cd mutt-mutt-2-2-15-rel CC=`which clang` ./prepare --prefix=$HOME/fil-c/pizfix --with-homespool make -j12 install Seems to work, at least for reading email.
tig (depends on ncurses and maybe more): wget https://github.com/jonas/tig/releases/download/tig-2.6.0/tig-2.6.0.tar.gz tar -xf tig-2.6.0.tar.gz cd tig-2.6.0 CC=`which filcc` ./configure --prefix=$(dirname $(dirname $(which git))) make -j12 make test make -j12 install Seems to work, at least for viewing the Fil-C repo.
w3m (depends on gcshim and ncurses): Seems to work. I tried the Debian version: git clone https://salsa.debian.org/debian/w3m.git . I used CFLAGS=-Wno-incompatible-function-pointer-types (which is probably needed for clang anyway even without Fil-C).
I've built and installed some replacement Debian packages using Fil-C as the compiler on a Debian 13 machine, as explained below. Hopefully this can rapidly scale to many packages, taking advantage of the basic compile-install-test knowledge already built into Debian source packages, although some packages will take more work because they need extra patches to work with Fil-C.
Structure. Debian already understands how to have packages for multiple architectures (ABIs; Debian "ports") installed at once. For example, dpkg --add-architecture i386; apt update; apt install bash:i386 installs a 32-bit version of bash, replacing the usual 64-bit version; you can do apt install bash:amd64 to revert to the 64-bit version. Meanwhile the 32-bit libraries and 64-bit libraries are installed in separate locations, basically /lib/i386-linux-gnu or /usr/lib/i386-linux-gnu vs. /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu or /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu . (On Debian 11 and newer, and on Ubuntu 22.04 and newer, /lib is symlinked to /usr/lib .)
I'm following this model for plugging Fil-C into Debian: the goal is for apt install bash:amd64fil0 to install a Fil-C-compiled ( amd64fil0 ) version of bash, replacing the usual ( amd64 ) version of bash, while the amd64 and amd64fil0 libraries are installed in separate locations.
[Filian uses amd64filc0 , with libraries in /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnufilc0 .]
The include-file complication. Debian expects library packages compiled for multiple ABIs to all provide the same include files: for example, /usr/include/ncurses.h is provided by libncurses-dev:i386 , libncurses-dev:amd64 , etc. This is safe because Debian forces libncurses-dev:i386 and libncurses-dev:amd64 and so on to all have the same version. An occasional package with ABI-dependent include files can still use /usr/include/x86_64-linux-gnu etc.
Fil-C instead omits /usr/include in favor of a Fil-C-specific directory (which will typically be different from /usr/include : even if Fil-C is compiled with glibc, probably the glibc version won't be the same as in /usr/include ). This difference is the top source of messiness below. I'm planning to tweak the Fil-C driver to use /usr/include on Debian. [This is done in Filian.]
Something else I'm planning to tweak is Fil-C's glibc compilation, so that it uses the final system prefix. [This is also done in Filian.] The approach described below instead requires /home/filian/fil-c to stay in place for compiling and running programs. Building Debian packages. How does Debian package building work? First, more packages to install as root: apt install dpkg-dev devscripts docbook2x \ dh-exec dh-python python3-setuptools fakeroot \ sbuild mmdebstrap uidmap piuparts Debian has multiple options for building a package. The option that has the best isolation, and that Debian uses to continually build new packages for distribution, is sbuild, but for fast development I'll focus on directly using the lower-level dpkg-buildpackage. [Filian also uses dpkg-buildpackage for the moment.] Baseline 1: using sbuild without Fil-C. In case you do want to try sbuild, here's the basic setup, and then an example of building a small package (tinycdb): mkdir -p ~/shared/sbuild time mmdebstrap --include=ca-certificates --skip=output/dev --variant=buildd unstable ~/shared/sbuild/unstable-amd64.tar.zst https://deb.debian.org/debian mkdir -p ~/.config/sbuild cat << "EOF" > ~/.config/sbuild/config.pl $chroot_mode = 'unshare'; $external_commands = { "build-failed-commands" => [ [ '%SBUILD_SHELL' ] ] }; $build_arch_all = 1; $build_source = 0; $source_only_changes = 1; $run_lintian = 1; $lintian_opts = ['--display-info', '--verbose', '--fail-on', 'error,warning', '--info']; $run_autopkgtest = 1; $run_piuparts = 1; $piuparts_opts = ['--no-eatmydata', '--distribution=%r', '--fake-essential-packages=systemd-sysv']; EOF mkdir -p ~/shared/packages cd ~/shared/packages apt source tinycdb cd tinycdb-*/ time sbuild Baseline 2: using dpkg-buildpackage without Fil-C. Here's what it looks like compiling the same small package with dpkg-buildpackage: mkdir -p ~/shared/packages cd ~/shared/packages apt source tinycdb cd tinycdb-*/ time dpkg-buildpackage -us -uc -b The goal: Using dpkg-buildpackage with Fil-C. [Filian handles the following differently; see filian-onetime :] As root, teach dpkg basic features of the new architecture, imitating the current line amd64 x86_64 (amd64|x86_64) 64 little in the same file: echo amd64fil0 x86_64+fil0 amd64fil0 64 little >> /usr/share/dpkg/cputable

For me this worked and produced three ../*.deb packages. Installing them as root also worked:
Compiling a deliberately wrong test program with the newly installed library also works, and triggers Fil-C's run-time protection:
libc-dev. [Handled automatically in Filian:] Some packages depend on libc-dev, so let's build a fake libc-dev package (probably there's an easier way to do this):
libmd. Seems to work. At first this didn't install since the compiled version (for amd64fil0) was 1.1.0-2 while the installed version (for amd64) was 1.1.0-2+b1. Debian requires the same version number across architectures (see above regarding include-file compatibility), so apt said that 1.1.0-2+b1 breaks 1.1.0-2. I resolved this by compiling and installing 1.1.0-2 for both amd64 and amd64fil0. This is a downgrade since "+b" refers to a "binNMU", a "binary-only non-maintainer upload", a patch beyond the official source; I don't know what the patch is. [Filian automatically synchronizes +b versions.]
readline. Needs ln -s /usr/include/readline /usr/include/x86_64+fil0-linux-gnu/readline after installation. Could have tweaks in debian/rules (which seems to predate *.install ), but this is in any case an example of the messiness that I'm planning to get rid of. [Filian cleans this up.]
lua5.4. Seems to work. Depends on readline.

title: Nordic countries have provided Ukraine with nearly $50B in aid since full-scale invasion began, Sybiha says
body:
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this at a press conference alongside his counterparts Elina Valtonen of Finland and Espen Barth Eide of Norway in Helsinki, Ukrinform reports.
“Putin is still showing no genuine willingness to end the war. That is why it is critically important to strengthen Ukraine. Finland and Norway, along with Denmark, Iceland, and Sweden, are demonstrating true leadership in this regard. Since February 2022, the five Nordic countries have provided about $50 billion in assistance,” Sybiha said.
At the same time, he emphasized that Ukraine is not merely a recipient of aid but also a partner contributing to the common security of Europe and the entire transatlantic community.
He recalled that Ukraine had signed agreements with Finland and Norway on cooperation in the field of unmanned systems.
“Now we must turn these agreements into joint production. Ukrainian experience and Nordic technologies can strengthen our entire continent,” the foreign minister emphasized.
Sybiha also highlighted Ukraine’s urgent need to strengthen its air defenses, particularly by securing additional interceptors for PAC air defense systems, and called on partners to continue contributing to the PURL initiative.
Ukraine’s FM said the country had fulfilled its part of the joint FREYJA project, which aims to develop European capabilities to counter ballistic missiles.
“Now it is our allies’ turn. Today, we discussed how to accelerate this process,” the minister said.
Sybiha also said the parties had agreed on further steps to increase pressure on Russia, including imposing new sanctions targeting its war machine. In this context, he noted that “more can be done to counter the shadow fleet.”
“Our Nordic partners play a particularly important role here. Your geographical location makes you key participants in these efforts,” Sybiha said.
As reported, on Tuesday, October 27, the Norwegian government announced that it would provide 500 million Norwegian kroner (nearly $54 million) in energy support for Ukraine ahead of winter.

title: 2027: Atiku Not A Man You Can Take His Word To The Bank – Wike
body: The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike, has questioned the credibility of former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, accusing him of frequently changing his position on political matters. Wike spoke on Tuesday at the unveiling of candidates of the Rivers State Rainbow Coalition, where he criticised the consistency of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) presidential candidate. Drawing on his past political dealings with Atiku, Wike recalled supporting the former vice-president’s presidential ambition in 2019 and running against him in the Peoples Democratic Party’s (PDP) presidential primary in 2022. “I pray you never know him, [Atiku Abubakar]. I ran with him in the 2022 presidential primaries. In 2019, I was one of the biggest sponsors for that presidential election,” he said. Wike questioned Atiku’s reliability, declaring, “He’s not a man that you can go to the bank with his words.” ﻿ The minister alleged that Atiku frequently changed his position, making it difficult to rely on his statements. “He tells you one thing in the morning, he tells you another thing in the afternoon. He tells you something in the evening, the next morning he tells you a different thing,” Wike said. He then challenged his audience to consider whether Atiku was a leader worth following, asking, “Is he the man you follow?” The post 2027: Atiku Not A Man You Can Take His Word To The Bank – Wike appeared first on Channels Television .

title: Russia Ships Less Crude Even as Key Baltic Port’s Flows Rebound
body:
Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe.
Fuga Bluemarine crude oil tanker lies at anchor near the terminal Kozmino in Nakhodka Bay near the port city of Nakhodka, Russia, December 4, 2022. REUTERS/Tatiana Meel
(Bloomberg) — Russia shipped the least crude in more than a month, even as operations at its key Baltic port recovered strongly from an earlier halt.
In the four weeks through Oct. 25, overseas crude flows edged lower to 3.55 million barrels a day, tanker data compiled by Bloomberg showed. That was down by 30,000 barrels a day from the period to Oct. 18, to the lowest in five weeks. The drop came despite a rebound in weekly flows.
A total of 12 tankers left the Primorsk terminal near St. Petersburg last week. That compared with just four the previous week, which saw a three-day gap in arrivals and departures. Similar interruptions in the past were linked to maintenance.
Russia’s war on Ukraine is hitting global supplies of fuel and food, compounding the impact of the conflict in the Persian Gulf and sending crude prices to the highest since the early days of the full-scale invasion, when the Brent benchmark briefly topped $120 a barrel.
A recent lull in Kyiv’s attacks on Russian refineries has allowed Moscow to boost processing rates, likely diverting crude that would otherwise have been exported. There were no reported strikes on Russian oil processing plants in the seven days to Oct. 25, amid moves to initiate trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US.
If the halt to attacks on refineries continues, the amount of Russian crude available for export could fall in the coming weeks, as previously damaged plants are repaired and brought back into operation.
At the same time, buyers in India may be turning away from Russian barrels amid sky-high shipping costs and cheaper alternatives from the Persian Gulf. The shift comes as crude flows from the Middle East return to near pre-war levels. Whether those flows can be maintained if the Iran conflict flares up after the US mid-terms and the Israeli election remains to be seen.
In the week to Oct. 25, some 37 tankers loaded 26.93 million barrels of Russian crude, vessel-tracking data and industry reports show. The volume compared with a slightly revised 21.87 million barrels on 31 ships the previous week.
Shipments jumped by 730,000 barrels a day last week to average 3.85 million barrels a day, the highest in a month.
Flows from Primorsk rebounded after a gap in ship movements of several days during the previous week that suggested that loading operations may have been suspended for maintenance at the port or the pipeline that supplies it.
Weekly shipments can be volatile, affected by weather, maintenance work, sanctions, military activity and the timing of departures.
There was one shipment of Kazakhstan’s Kebco grade from Novorossiysk during the week. Since the start of September, Moscow has diverted all shipments of Kazakh crude through the Black Sea port, freeing up more capacity for its own barrels at Ust-Luga on the Baltic, which is seen as safer.
The amount of Russian crude on the water rebounded last week, driven by the jump in shipments from the country’s Baltic ports.
On a four-week average basis, the gross value of Moscow’s oil shipments was little changed at $2.61 billion a week in the 28 days to Oct. 25, close to the previous week’s three-week low. The small drop in total flows and lower prices for Russia’s key Urals crude were offset by higher prices for the Pacific ESPO grade.
On a weekly basis, the value of exports jumped by about $430 million to a wartime high of $2.76 billion, with lower Urals prices more than offset by the jump in shipments and an eighth straight weekly increase in ESPO values.
China and India remain the biggest buyers of Russian crude by a considerable margin. But it’s not always possible to assign a final destination to individual cargoes until well into their voyage, leaving many of the more recent shipments on tankers showing interim destinations, such as Suez, Port Sudan, or Singapore. These are recorded as “Unknown Asia” until a credible final destination is available. Ships still showing their destinations as their Russian loading ports, or places such as Gibraltar, are recorded as “Other Unknown.”
Observed shipments to Russia’s Asian customers, including those showing no final destination, edged lower to to 3.42 million barrels a day in the 28 days to Oct. 25, down from a revised 3.45 million in the period to Oct. 18.
Shipments to Moscow’s remaining customers in the Mediterranean region were unchanged from the revised figure for the period to Oct. 18. That figure was revised down to about 130,000 barrels a day after one tanker heading toward Turkey changed its destination to the Suez Canal.
That took flows to Turkey to about 80,000 barrels a day in the four weeks to Oct. 25, unchanged from the earlier period.
An earlier flurry of shipments to Egypt, which took flows to as much as 160,000 barrels a day in mid-June, has fallen back to about 50,000 barrels a day in the most recent period.
Flows to Syria have fallen to zero since August after the Mediterranean nation agreed to “drastically” reduce Russian oil imports in negotiations with the US on lifting remaining sanctions.
Shipments to the region may be revised higher once destinations for almost 1.8 million barrels a day of crude become clear. Historically, most cargoes on ships showing intermediate destinations have been delivered to India or China.

title: As holiday shopping approaches, seasonal hiring gives 'mixed signals,' experts say
body:
On Oct. 20, Amazon said it plans to employ more than 300,000 full-time, part-time and seasonal workers ahead of the peak shopping period, according to a press release . In 2025, Amazon pledged 250,000 holiday jobs, marking a 20% increase in jobs.
UPS, one of the largest U.S. shipping companies, announced on Oct. 7 it would hire 100,000 seasonal employees in 2026, down nearly 10% from the company's 2025 holiday hiring target.
These announcements, together with fewer retailers providing recruitment headcounts ahead of the holidays are part of why experts say seasonal hiring is giving them "mixed signals," says Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer of outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
"I don't expect this to be an explosive seasonal hiring year like we saw in '21 and '22," Challenger tells CNBC Make It. Following Amazon's announcement, Challenger says "there's reason to be a little bit more positive than we originally thought."
Seasonal job postings as of Sept. 30, 2026 surpassed 2025 levels during the same period, according to an Oct. 15 report from Indeed Hiring Lab , the job board's economic research wing. Experts say non-retail jobs are driving the growth.
Indeed's report found that seasonal hiring in 2026, as measured by the number of job postings, is up 10% from 2025. Researchers scrubbed Indeed and other job boards for seasonal jobs, which they define as roles with at least one holiday-related descriptor in the title. Indeed director of economic research Laura Ullrich tells CNBC Make It that the data reflects "a large percentage of jobs" — even those whose companies did not pay Indeed to upload their openings on the site.
While many retailers have been silent about their seasonal hiring plans, "We've seen some positive additions," Challenger said of Amazon's hiring plans. "We did see UPS is down a little bit. Exporting goods is down a little bit."
Retail has long dominated seasonal hiring, but its stronghold has faltered. In 2019, jobs in retail accounted for around 66% of all seasonal roles, according to Indeed. Today, retail adds 61% of all seasonal work opportunities.
Loading and stocking roles, which accounted for 3.5% of seasonal hiring posts in 2019, now represent 9% of all holiday job listings as of Sept. 30, 2026. The warehouse category is the fastest-growing among retail, sales, customer service, transportation and food preparation, according to Indeed.
As for individual roles, the five most in-demand, non-retail titles include customer service representative, unloader, delivery driver, photographer and stocker, the Indeed report found.
Experts at Indeed say the shift in seasonal hiring reflects how e-commerce has reshaped holiday shopping. The share of Americans who shop online is up to 87%, according to data from the Statista Research Department , and experts forecast e-commerce retail sales growth of 6% every year until 2030.
Bain & Company projects a $1 trillion breakthrough in holiday retail sales across the U.S. in 2026, a historic first boosted by inflation . Challenger says the figure "doesn't necessarily mean more sales or more revenue or profit."
Instead, the forecast shows that while the high cost of necessities like food and gas are changing consumer habits, inflation "hasn't totally dampened consumers' expectations of participating in shopping this holiday season," Challenger explains.
To prepare for the holiday season, retailers are posting more permanent part-time jobs in place of seasonal roles, says Ullrich.
Non-seasonal, part-time roles accounted for 38% of retail jobs in September 2025, and today make up 49% of the holiday retail job market. Seasonal roles accounted for just 20% of retailers' overall holiday job posts in September 2026, a decline from the same period in 2025.
In response to sales forecasts, retailers have taken different approaches to seasonal hiring. Spirit Halloween said it would hire 52,000 employees on June 11 and Michaels plans to onboard over 10,000 workers for the holidays. Per Target's website , the company said it would lean on its existing workforce before looking for seasonal hires. The big-box store did not announce headcounts.
Ullrich sees the trend to hire more permanent employees across retail "as a positive" and says retailers "realize they need more employees on a permanent basis."
Seasonal work is also in high demand for job seekers. Desktop searches for seasonal and holiday terms are up 28% in 2026 against 2025 search data on Indeed, a sign that workers hope to earn extra cash before the year concludes.
An Indeed report from June 9 found that 16% of active job seekers already hold multiple jobs. On average, workers with multiple jobs tripled their application volume in the month leading up to landing their second role.
Workers with service jobs, characterized by high turnover rates and inconsistent scheduling, are the most likely to hold another job. Among active job seekers, Food preparation workers make up the largest share, 17%, looking for additional employment.
