title: Europeans looking to squeeze themselves into Ukraine talks, nothing new here — Lavrov
body:
MOSCOW, October 27. /TASS/. Europe is only looking to squeeze itself into the negotiating process on Ukraine, and there is nothing new to its approach, Russia’s top diplomat Sergey Lavrov said, commenting on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s phone call today with the Norwegian and Finnish leaders.
"Today, President Putin held a phone call with the Norwegian prime minister and the Finnish president at their request. I have not seen the transcript yet but, apparently, no new ideas were voiced," Russia’s top diplomat said at a meeting with editors-in-chief of African media outlets. "This only shows the Europeans’ ambitions to squeeze themselves into the negotiating process," he added. According to Lavrov, "for the time being, we do not see a change in Europe’s approach.".

title: Galaxy Books $323 Million Q3 Profit as Its Own Investments Rebound
body: Galaxy Digital (Nasdaq: GLXY) reported a $323 million net profit for the third quarter on Oct. 27, with most of the improvement coming from the segment that holds the firm’s own digital asset and investment positions. The company lost $85 million in the second quarter. In the three months ended Sept. 30, its Treasury & Corporate segment generated $419 million of Galaxy’s $569 million in adjusted gross profit , after posting a $42 million loss on that measure in Q2. Adjusted EBITDA came to $455 million , compared with negative $77 million a quarter earlier. Both adjusted figures are non-GAAP measures. Founder and CEO Mike Novogratz said in the release that Galaxy “delivered a strong third quarter, reflecting the strength of our established Digital Assets franchise, significant appreciation across our investments portfolio, and the growing contribution from our Data Centers business.” Diluted EPS was $0.66, and adjusted EPS was $0.83. A year earlier, in the third quarter of 2025, Galaxy reported net income of $505 million. Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter . Digital Assets Segment Posts Small Adjusted EBITDA Loss The Digital Assets segment, which includes Galaxy’s trading, lending and asset management businesses, recorded adjusted gross profit of $71 million, up 9% from Q2. Its adjusted EBITDA was negative $9 million, compared with negative $11 million in the second quarter. Galaxy said its trading volumes rose 12% from the prior quarter and its average loan book grew 27% to $1.8 billion. Combined assets under management and assets under stake reached $10.4 billion , up 46%. Data Centers Add Revenue The Data Centers unit earned $79 million in adjusted gross profit, up from $20 million, in its first full quarter of revenue under the Helios I, Phase I lease. All 133 MW of that phase had been delivered to CoreWeave by the end of Q2. Galaxy completed a $3.5 billion senior secured notes offering to fund Helios I, Phase II, where it expects data hall deliveries to start in the second quarter of 2027. The company said it is in talks with prospective tenants for 830 MW of approved Helios II capacity that is not yet leased, and that its gross power pipeline now exceeds 5.7 GW. On Oct. 26, the board authorized a new share buyback of up to $200 million . The Department of Defense is preparing for a potential "doomsday" scenario in which America's power grid collapses, supply chains grind to a halt, and military installations are forced to operate for three months without outside support, according to Fox News .
The unprecedented plan, branded FORTRESS by Pentagon planners, aims to make major military bases across the continental United States capable of functioning independently for at least 90 days, according to documents obtained by the news outlet.
U.S. Air Force airmen and civilian contractors prepare a containerized nuclear power reactor for airlift aboard a C-17 Globemaster III at March Air Reserve Base, California, Feb. 13, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo by Staff Sgt. Monique Bright)
"We don't want to rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense. We just simply can't. It's an intolerable risk," DoD spokesperson Sean Parnell said .
The Pentagon is exploring portable nuclear reactors, massive battery installations, and independent microgrids that would allow bases to disconnect from civilian power systems during prolonged blackouts. Officials have long feared that the lose of electricity could cripple communications, logistics, weapons production, and military command structures.
FORTRESS also reportedly calls for stockpiling ammunition, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts, and medical supplies, while preparing civilian factories to rapidly transition into wartime production.
The Pentagon also plans recurring industrial stress tests and mobilization exercises, alongside measures to protect military communications and navigation systems from satellite disruptions and GPS jamming.
"I realized that a lot of the way we think about homeland defense was built around the antiquated assumption that two oceans would protect us," Parnell said . "President Trump understands that world is gone, and he's already paved the way for new thinking: Golden Dome, a renewed focus on the Western Hemisphere, Greenland, Panama."
"The next conflict will likely be fought on multiple fronts. Look at the geopolitics behind any major war. When that happens, global supply chains will break," the official added . "You don't want to be making these decisions in the middle of a global multi-front conflict. We have to have a plan."
The ongoing threats to America's power grid come from both foreign adversaries and domestic saboteurs.
In February 2024, the NSA and other federal agencies warned that Chinese state-sponsored hackers linked to Volt Typhoon had compromised critical U.S. infrastructure networks, including energy, water, transportation, and communications systems.
In December 2022, gunmen attacked two electrical substations in North Carolina, plunging roughly 45,000 customers into darkness and leaving some without power for five days.

Matic, the company behind my favorite robot vacuum , is launching its first new model since its 2023 debut : the Matic Serene . The new robotic floor cleaner has one key upgrade: noise reduction. With a promised output of just 52 decibels at its highest suction level, the Serene claims to be about as quiet as a running refrigerator. It costs $1,695, $200 more than the original Matic’s current price, and is available now . The good news is the company is offering an upgrade path for existing Matic owners.
The Serene targets people “who are extremely noise sensitive,” cofounder and president Mehul Nariyawala tells The Verge. But beyond noise levels, it’s “exactly the same Matic.” The upgrade comes via a new hardware stack, and existing Matic owners can request a Serene hardware upgrade for their current model in early 2027.
Loud robot vacuums often get shut off by annoyed owners, meaning they don’t finish their job and frustrate owners even more. (This happens a lot in my household.) That is why many bots have the option of a quiet mode, but these modes generally mean lower suction and less effective cleaning. The Matic Serene will clean on max power at just 52 decibels. “It’s very quiet on carpets, on hard surfaces; you mostly hear brush roll now,” says Nariyawala. The original Matic, which costs $1,495 and will continue to be sold, operates at 55 decibels.
Matic takes a new approach to robot vacuums, with a form factor and navigation system different from most lidar-based disc robots sold by brands like iRobot, Roborock, Dreame, and others. Nariyawala told me that when the company developed Matic, they designed it to address the “seven deadly sins of robot vacuums,” with noise high on that list , along with getting stuck and dying under the couch.
Many of today’s robot vacuums have a quiet mode that runs around 55 to 60 decibels, but they achieve this reduction by lowering suction power. In high-power mode, most are closer to 70 decibels. Matic launched with a claim of 55 decibels on its highest level and is now dropping by 3 more decibels, which could be a big deal for people who like to run their vacuums while at home. I’ve found I can use the Matic while working from home, but I sometimes need to shut it off if I am on a phone call. At 3 decibels quieter, I might not need to interrupt its work.
Existing owners can upgrade their Matic for the difference between their original purchase price and Serene’s price of $1,695. Matic has seen several price increases since it launched. The current model costs $1,495. However, someone may have purchased it for $1,095 when it first launched, meaning the upgrade could cost $600. That’s probably a tough sell. But if you gave up on robot vacuums because of noise, the Serene could be the solution you’ve been waiting for. I’ll be testing it soon and will have a full review.

Google announced today its Genie 4 world model for generating interactive experiences using AI. The company says the model has four main updates: It allows for more realistic worlds, lets users update an experience in real time with a natural language prompt, can generate audio, and uses Gemini 3.8 Flash under the hood to help with its simulations. It also can create experiences that are about two minutes long, up from one minute for the previous Genie 3 model.
Google is pitching Genie 4 as a tool that could be helpful for things like pre-visualization for filmmakers, prototyping game ideas, and making training scenarios for robots. But the company warns that, as simulations run longer, details and object permanence can shift over time.
I haven’t been able to try Genie 4 for myself — it’s launching first as a “research preview” to “trusted testers” — so I can’t tell you how it compares to the Genie 3-powered Project Genie, which I used to generate bad Nintendo knockoffs . But here are some examples from Google demonstrating what’s possible with the new model.
Genie 4 will be “coming soon” to Google AI Ultra subscribers, Google says, and the company has opened a waitlist where you can apply to be able to try it in Project Genie.

title: 'This is America!' Waltz says as he and Cubans get into shouting match at UN
body:
Things got testy as the Cubans approached the podium as Waltz was speaking.
Tension between the U.S. and Cuba was on full display at the United Nations on Tuesday as the Trump administration's envoy to the body, Ambassador Mike Waltz, and Cuba's foreign minister engaged in a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly.
During the U.N.'s annual debate on the U.S. blockade against Cuba, Waltz took the podium and began delivering a speech that was hotly critical of the Cuban regime.
Shortly after Waltz began his remarks, Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla and the rest of the Cuban delegation began challenging him from the audience -- shouting and gesturing as the president of the assembly banged his gavel and fruitlessly asked them to quiet down.
"I hope everyone, Mr. President, is listening to the delegation right now," Waltz said with a smile. "Imagine what happens when someone ask these questions in Havana, not in a room of ambassadors and cameras! Imagine what happens to those people if this is the intimidation and disruption that we see!"
Rodríguez Parrilla and Waltz traded more remarks, with Waltz declaring "This is America, this is the United Nations, this isn't your communist dictatorship. You can't silence me or you cannot silence my colleagues!
Rodríguez Parrilla, whose comments could not be clearly heard on a U.N. livestream of the meeting, approached the front of the hall.
Waltz yelled, "Mr. President, this individual needs to back away from this podium. He's not going to intimidate me in the United States of America! I'm the representative of the United States of America! Back up!"
At that point, the assembly president suspended the meeting. After recounting the U.N.'s rules for the event, the president then gave Rodríguez Parrilla a chance to issue a point of order on the condition he limit his grievances to procedure rather the substance of Waltz's remarks.
Rodríguez Parrilla returned to his seat and used the opportunity to speak to protest Waltz's claims, accusing him of "grossly lying."
Waltz finished his speech without major incident, ending by urging the chamber to vote against the resolution under consideration on Wednesday. Waltz finished his remarks without major incident -- urging the chamber to vote against the resolution under consideration on Wednesday.
Following the incident, Rodríguez Parrilla doubled down on X, writing that Waltz "with his arrogance and hubris, forgets that he is at the United Nations, not at the US National Security Council, nor in a Green Berets unit, nor in a Signal group, where he has repeatedly shown his incompetence and incapacity."
Waltz, a former Green Beret, came under scrutiny last year while serving as national security adviser for inadvertently inviting a journalist to a Signal chat with Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, Vice President JD Vance and other top national security officials discussing details of the strike on the Houthis in Yemen.
President Donald Trump nominated Waltz to the U.N. post at the same time he announced Secretary of State Marco Rubio would also serve as national security adviser.

title: Photos show record-breaking tides flooding homes, roads in California
body: Photos show extensive flooding in some parts of Southern California amid record-breaking high tides that have swamped homes and highways. The so-called king tide — the highest tides of the year caused by the full moon — reached 8 feet, 2 inches Tuesday in the Los Angeles Harbor, breaking a record set just the day before. The Pacific Coast Highway was inundated, and people in the area said water was coming up through the storm drains.Linda Holle, who works at a marine fueling station in Newport Beach, told CBS News her office was flooded, and that she had never seen flooding like this before.  Experts say king tides during full moons in November and December could be even worse. If the king tide next month coincides with a winter storm and pounding surf, it could cause significant problems.Photos show flooding in Southern California

title: Finland and Japan sign new defence agreement
body:
"The agreement will open up significant growth opportunities for our defence industry and technology companies," Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) said.
Finland and Japan have signed an agreement on transferring defence equipment and technology, according to the Finnish defence ministry.
Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) signed on Finland's behalf during his visit to Japan this week, the ministry said in a press release. Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi signed on behalf of Japan.
"I would like to thank the Japanese Minister of Defence for the good negotiation process. The agreement will open up significant growth opportunities for our defence industry and technology companies," Häkkänen said in the release.
"The international security environment requires democratic countries to cooperate more closely in the development of the defence industry and technology. Japan is an important partner for Finland," he continued.
According to the ministry, the agreement outlines the terms and conditions for transferring defence equipment and technology. Cooperation may include research, development or production projects, coordinated by a joint committee from both countries.
Häkkänen has been in Japan for the past few days, accompanied by a business delegation of 20 Finnish defence and dual-use tech companies.
According to a separate release issued by the Finnish embassy in Tokyo, Häkkänen was scheduled to meet with Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi.
Finnish companies joining the trip will present their latest technologies at business seminars and meetings in search of commercial opportunities.

title: President declares to implement Leader’s directives
body:
TEHRAN, Oct. 28 (MNA) – Iranian president pledged that his administration will implement Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei’s directives aimed at fulfilling Iran’s conditions for ending the current state.
Addressing a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, President Masoud Pezeshkian referred to the Leader’s recent directive to Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei to pursue the fulfillment of conditions set by Iranian officials to move beyond the “no war, no peace” situation.
Describing the directive as conveying “a great and important message” and outlining the country’s future prospects, the president stressed that the entire government would work with full capacity to realize the specified objectives and measures.
Pezeshkian also underscored the need for executive bodies to remain prepared to deal with changing circumstances in the country. He said all ministers, heads of executive bodies and their deputies are required to maintain full readiness while prioritizing management and cost reduction in line with existing conditions.
He emphasized that Iran would stand firm with strength and unity against any threats, sanctions and external pressure.
“Enemies must not imagine that by increasing pressure and threats, they can weaken the will of the Iranian nation and force the country to surrender,” Pezeshkian stated.
The Leader recently met with Rezaei, describing the Supreme National Security Council and its Secretariat as the “crossroads of policymaking” in the country’s affairs.
During the meeting, Ayatollah Hosseini Khamenei also emphasized national unity, mutual trust between the people and officials, the use of constitutional capacities to help the president and executive bodies resolve problems, and the protection of national and regional security
The Leader also called for fulfilling the conditions set by Iranian officials for ending the war and bringing the current “neither war nor peace” situation to an end.

title: Iran claims 4 tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz
body:
Updated on: October 30, 2026 / 3:18 AM EDT / CBS News
Follow updates on the war in the Middle East for Friday, Oct. 30, here . See earlier developments below.
The U.S. Department of Defense has added two more service member deaths to its official account of casualties since the war with Iran started more than eight months ago, bringing the overall death toll to 23.
Both of the newly noted deaths on the Defense Casualty Analysis System portal were noncombat related. In total the DCAS portal says 11 service members have been killed by enemy fire during the war, and 12 others have died under circumstances deemed nonhostile, which includes accidents and sickness.
Both of the service members recently added as nonhostile deaths were airmen, including one who died of an illness and the another from unspecified causes that remain under investigation, The Washington Post quoted the Air Force as saying.
The two deaths added to the DCAS system are listed under Overseas Operations , which includes deaths recorded by the Pentagon after it stopped using the name Operation Epic Fury for the offensive against Iran in May, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared the operation over.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Friday it intercepted and destroyed a drone in the Mecca region that had been fired by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels.
"A drone launched by the terrorist Houthi militia has been intercepted and destroyed in the Mecca region," the coalition wrote in a post on X.
The Houthis denied any attempt to strike Saudi Arabia on Friday, the Reuters news agency reports.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on social media that the group hadn't conducted any operations aimed at Saudi territory, adding that the Houthis only target Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
Explosions rocked the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh on Thursday hours after the Iran-backed Houthis reported deadly strikes earlier in the day on residential areas of western Yemen that the Houthis said killed at least 12 people.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said on Thursday it had downed two ballistic missiles launched by the group towards Riyadh, soon after Agence France-Presse correspondents heard fresh explosions in the capital.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said on X.
Earlier, AFP correspondents in Riyadh had heard at least eight explosions as authorities warned the city was "under a hostile aerial threat" in a phone alert.
Saudi civil defense had issued warnings for "potential danger" in Riyadh, Kharj and the southern city of Najran that were lifted shortly afterward.
The Houthis have ramped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, including by launching deadly strikes on the Riyadh airport that forced its shuttering for two weeks as flagship events were canceled, threatening the kingdom's economic diversification plans.
The Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government have exchanged daily attacks since a yearslong truce fell apart over the summer.
A tanker was struck by a projectile in the Strait of Hormuz around 7:30 p.m. local time (noon Eastern time), according to the U.K. Marine Trade Operations Centre .
The ship was exiting the strait along the southern route, promoted by the U.S., when it came under fire.
"There are no reported injuries to the crew or environmental impact … at this time," the UKMTO said.
While it wasn't clear who fired the projectile, Iran has taken credit for several ships hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday and has been targeting ships along the southern route at an increased rate.
Iran has not yet responded to a letter sent by Vice President JD Vance to the secretary of the Iranian Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, according to the semi-official Tasnim News agency, which is closely affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Tasnim said in a Thursday post on its official Telegram social media account that Tehran was not prepared to drop any of its core conditions for a ceasefire, which include lifting the American blockade of Iran's ports, easing sanctions and giving Iran access to its frozen financial assets held abroad, among other things.
Multiple news outlets have reported that Vance's letter to Rezaei was an attempt to restart peace negotiations, but President Trump said Wednesday that it was a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Iran's navy said a tanker it described as violating maritime restrictions was damaged and caught fire after striking sea mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving the vessel unable to continue sailing.
In a statement, the navy said the incident occurred before noon on Thursday as the tanker was sailing through an area designated as prohibited and unsafe by Iran
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a shipping route in the south of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has insisted vessels can only use northern routes it has authorized.
The navy's statement warned that the Strait of Hormuz was closed "to violating vessels that, without coordination and relying on the lies of the U.S. president, intend to pass through prohibited and unsafe areas."
"These uncoordinated transits through high-risk areas have exposed and will continue to expose vessels and their crews to serious dangers," it added.
Qatar has categorically denied allegations of interfering in Israel's elections or funding efforts to influence their outcome, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of launching a disinformation campaign to drag the small Persian Gulf state into domestic Israeli political disputes.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majid al-Ansari said in a statement that Qatar would not be used as a scapegoat for Israeli politicians' failures, insisting that Doha had no involvement in Israel's political competition and would continue its mediation efforts between Iran and the U.S., as well as wider diplomatic engagement and support for the Palestinian people.
His comments come after Israeli President Benjamin Netanyahu alleged that Tuesday's national elections were "stolen by Arab parties" and claimed foreign interference in the vote.
Israel's Shin Bet internal security service is investigating possible Qatari and Turkish funding used in an effort to influence the election outcome, according to reports by the Jerusalem Post and Israel's Channel 13.
"These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure," al-Ansari said. "The repeated invocation of Qatar in Israeli electoral rhetoric reveals an excessive obsession with our country among certain Israeli political and media figures."
Iran's navy has carried out more than 20 operations against U.S. warships and approximately 300 operations targeting American interests in various locations during the war, Iranian Army Navy Coordinating Deputy Rear Admiral Jalil Moghadam said in an interview published Thursday by the official state-run news agency IRNA .
Moghadam claimed the operations involved missiles and drones and said Iran's navy remains operational despite repeated claims by President Trump and other U.S. officials saying it has been destroyed.
"If the Iranian Navy has been destroyed, why have these forces not come closer than 500 or 600 kilometers to the Strait of Hormuz, or closer than 300 kilometers to our maritime borders? There is a force standing in their way, and that force must be the Navy," he said.
Moghadam did not offer any evidence to substantiate his claims.
IRGC spokesperson Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Mohebi challenged U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) to provide independent evidence for its claims of mine-clearing operations in the Strait of Hormuz.
"Prove your claim of mine-clearing in the Strait of Hormuz with independent evidence, not a statement!" demanded Mohebi in a post on X , adding that "the reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the skies, on land and at sea — not on social media or in America's media-warfare rooms."
Earlier Thursday the IRGC said three oil tankers had been disabled after striking mines in the strait, and the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center confirmed one vessel in the area was seen on fire.
In late August, President Trump and CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper insisted the primary shipping lanes of the Strait of Hormuz had been demined and were safe for commercial vessels.
In a statement posted online, Cooper said the U.S. military had "meticulously and quietly" cleared mines previously laid by the IRGC.
"Internationally recognized transit routes in the strait are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military," he said. "Today, international shipping lanes are open, and momentum is building."
Iran's Houthi allies said Thursday that a Saudi strike on a residential area in Yemen's western Taiz province killed 12 people, as the two sides continued to exchange fire in the reignited Yemeni civil war.
"As an initial toll, 12 citizens were killed and three others were critically injured when the Saudi enemy targeted the homes of the families of Ibrahim Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz and Al-Raabi Saeed Mohammed Ahmed Al-Qouz in Al-Barah, Maqbana district," the Houthi health ministry said in a statement shared by the group's Saba news agency.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis. The Saudis, who back Yemen's government, have engaged in fighting with the Houthi rebels along the Red Sea coast and in deadly back-and-forth strikes.
Iran has used some 5,000 agencies to help it slip past the U.S. naval blockade to import hardware, explosives and trucks needed for its drone and missile programs over land, sea and air, according to a report by the Reuters news agency .
The secret network of military agencies has helped Iran usher at least $2 billion in components into the country since 2025, evading Western sanctions and, since earlier this year, the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.
Some of the agencies are linked to Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), others to business conglomerates run by the country's elite, Reuters said.
Between January 2025 and June 2026, before the U.S. blockade was imposed but with myriad U.S. and international sanctions in place, a single company, MOD 346428, imported large quantities of rocket propellants, explosives and weapons parts crucial for drones and missile production, as well as trucks that can be used as missile launchers. The hardware was brought in from China, Russia and Germany, Reuters reported.
The agencies all use the address of Iran's Ministry of Defense and Armed Forces Logistics in Tehran. Most were established in 2013, when Iran was struggling under international sanctions, the investigation found.
Iran's Intelligence Ministry said Thursday that it had dismantled four alleged terrorist cells and arrested 16 suspects in the central and southern parts of Sistan and Baluchestan Province, while detaining three more individuals accused of gathering and transmitting information about security and defense sites in the country's southeast.
In a statement, the provincial intelligence directorate said the operations were carried out in recent days following public tips and ongoing intelligence and operational surveillance, in cooperation with other provincial security forces. It alleged that the cells were affiliated with terrorist groups linked to the United States and Israel.
The ministry said some of the 16 detainees had arrived from abroad. It also alleged that several were involved in the killing of law enforcement personnel in Iranshahr. The suspects have been handed over to judicial authorities, according to the statement, carried by Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Security forces reportedly seized a cache of weapons and ammunition, including nine Kalashnikov rifles, two American-made M4 rifles and seven handguns.
In a separate operation, authorities arrested three people accused of collecting and transmitting information on the locations of military headquarters and defense and security facilities in southern Sistan and Baluchestan to networks the ministry described as linked to U.S. and Israeli intelligence and media operations.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said Thursday that its electronic warfare unit had intercepted and safely landed a U.S. reconnaissance drone west of the Strait of Hormuz, claiming the craft had been conducting surveillance of Iranian air defense systems along the Persian Gulf coastline and the strait.
"Through an offensive electronic warfare operation, the fighters of the IRGC Navy's electronic warfare unit, with the help of Almighty God, successfully managed to safely land an American terrorist army reconnaissance and deception drone of the MQM-170 type in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, after detecting and identifying it and taking control of its guidance and control systems," a statement from the IRGC navy read.
The bulletin added that the IRGC had "determined that the aircraft had taken off from the coast of one of the countries on the southern shores of the Persian Gulf."
Vice President JD Vance has sent a letter to Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei seeking to restart peace negotiations, according to multiple reports, but President Trump insists it is a focused outreach intended only to help get medical supplies into Iran.
Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he is still mulling whether to resume major military operations against Iran or make a peace deal after next week's midterm elections, according to various outlets.
The Wall Street Journal first reported that Vance was engaging directly with Mohsen Rezaei, one of Iran's most powerful hard-liners, in an effort to revive negotiations, citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter.
Vance sent the letter to Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' longest-serving former commander, at President Trump's direction, according to The Journal. The initiative seeks to establish whether Washington and Tehran can find common ground to avert a renewed conflict, the paper reported.
According to The New York Times , the letter, sent last week via Qatari mediators and delivered to Rezaei on Sunday, proposed an early meeting between American and Iranian officials, with Vance offering to lead the U.S. negotiating team.
The Times said Rezaei was expected to issue a formal response by Thursday. The letter did not specify a date or location for negotiations, but U.S. and Iranian officials were quoted by the newspaper as saying direct talks could begin as soon as next week in Qatar or Turkey.
According to Axios , Vance's letter explicitly stated that any negotiations aimed at preventing new U.S. military strikes would require discussions on Iran's nuclear program.
Asked Wednesday about Vance's contact with Iranian officials, Mr. Trump told reporters he had not sought to renew peace talks, but "what that is, they [Iran] need help with medical supplies and various things. He [Vance] asked me what I thought and I said, 'If you want to do that that's okay.' Basically it's getting supplies in to help people who are not well."
An official briefed on the diplomacy confirmed to CBS News Wednesday that Qatari mediators had presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war.
A response is expected from Tehran by the end of the week, most likely Saturday, the official added.
On Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' said Thursday that three oil tankers exploded and caught fire after striking naval mines while attempting to transit what it described as "the unauthorized southern route" through the Strait of Hormuz.
In a statement, the IRGC Navy's public relations office said the incidents occurred over the past 24 hours, adding that the vessels were subsequently stranded along the southern shores of the strait.
The U.S. has encouraged shippers to use a southern shipping lane through the vital waterway, which President Trump himself declared mine-free at the end of August. Iran insists vessels can only transit the strait through routes it administers closer to its coast in the north of the strait, in coordination with Iranian authorities.
"These oil tankers had switched off all their radar and navigation systems," the IRGC added, referring to a common practice for vessels trying to avoid either U.S. or Iranian-imposed blockades in the strait and surrounding waters.
The vessels, "disregarding warnings from the IRGC Navy, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized southern route of the Strait of Hormuz when they struck naval mines and exploded," the IRGC said.
The IRGC said it held the vessels' owners and crews responsible for using the route that Tehran has warned against for months.
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth has fired the Pentagon's top military planner, Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, a Pentagon official has told CBS News, after he was accused of leaking classified information related to the Iran war.
Sylvia was removed on Wednesday as head of strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff, becoming the latest in a series of generals to be ousted by Hegseth.
U.S. officials have told several Middle Eastern countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military action against Iran after next week's midterm elections – as well as the possibility that Iran will attempt to retaliate against them, two diplomats briefed on the matter told the Associated Press.
President Trump has not made a final decision on whether to carry out new strikes against Iran, the diplomats, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, stressed. He has, however, repeatedly said that he is weighing ordering new military action once the critical Nov. 3 elections are over.
Those threats and the fresh U.S. urgings for allies to prepare for potential retaliation have put the region on alert for a possible return to major operations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday in a post on X that Tehran "continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed" and is working with mediators to review ideas that Tehran included in a proposal floated last month, which was summarily rejected by Mr. Trump, but which Iran still wants to see used as the basis for a new ceasefire agreement.
The U.S. has told regional allies that a new round of military action could last for just several days, but regional officials are bracing for Iran and its proxy groups to retaliate, which could bring longer-term fighting, the diplomats told the AP.
The allies have also been urged by U.S. officials to take precautionary measures in anticipation that Iran's response would include retaliatory strikes on energy facilities and other crucial infrastructure.
The master of a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz reported seeing another vessel on fire nine nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, on Thursday, a monitoring agency run by the British military said.
The crew's status wasn't known and there was no damage assessment or report on the incident's environmental impact, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre added.
The strait is a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies. Since the start of the Middle East war in February, Iran has sought to control the waterway and has attacked ships it accuses of passing through the waterway without authorization.
The United States has responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the group at the kingdom's eastern region.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward the Eastern Province," coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia has this month come under sustained attack from the Iran-backed Houthis, including a strike on Riyadh's international airport that was the kingdom's deadliest in years.
The Houthis said this week they had targeted the Ras Tanura refinery in the oil-rich Eastern Province with a ballistic missile.
Tehran has denied having anything to do with attacks by the Houthis after Saudi Arabia accused Iran of having encouraged the group's escalation against the kingdom.
Following an uneasy four-year truce, fighting reignited in Yemen in July, months into the U.S.-Iran conflict that has plunged the wider region into crisis.
Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said Wednesday the Iran-backed Lebanese movement was not concerned with the results of Israel's election , vowing to continue its "resistance" against the neighbouring country no matter who wins.
With 85% of ballots counted, the right-wing bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had a slight lead over the main opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, but was still short of a majority after Tuesday's election.
"We do not concern ourselves with who governs Israel, but let it be perfectly clear that it cannot continue its occupation and must leave our land," Qassem said in a written statement.
"The resistance will continue ... and will stand up to the aggression directed against it and against Lebanon, and there is no room to discuss the disarmament" of Hezbollah "as long as the occupation persists and its aggression continues," he added.
The group, which once dominated political life in Lebanon, has been weakened by the two wars it has waged against Israel since 2023.
U.K. Treasury chief John Healey used his first budget Wednesday to offer households and businesses some support with energy bills this winter in the face of what he termed "global economic storms."
He said that his "choice in the budget today is to give families and businesses some breathing space now," as the consequences of the Middle East conflict play out.
"For families, that means higher prices at the pump, higher energy bills and higher mortgages," he said in his statement, one of the main dates of the parliamentary calendar. "For businesses, higher running costs and more expensive loans. And the impact is felt in the public finances, too."
Among the measures announced was a 100-pound ($133) one-off payment this winter for 20 million lower- and middle-income households, proportionately more of whom live in the electoral battlegrounds in northern England.
Other measures include the extension of a cut in the sales tax on electricity bills and the abolition of a charge paid on gas bills.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through widespread fraud and called on Shin Bet, Israel's security agency, to investigate.
"We demand from the police and the Shin Bet a thorough investigation into the election theft by the Arab parties and the full prosecution of the criminals," Netanyahu's Likud party shared on his X account , translated from Hebrew. "This is a serious blow to Israeli democracy and the voting rights of Israeli citizens. The law enforcement agencies must act with an iron fist and in an immediate manner."
Netanyahu's party leads in the latest vote counts , but all of the parties will fall short of the majority needed to control the Knesset, Israel's parliament. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%, according to official election data.
Local media projected 53 seats for the Likud party, 48 seats for the Yahar and other opposition parties and 19 seats for the Arab-led parties. In order to reach a majority (61 of 120 seats) and pick a prime minister, deals will have to be made.
Amid reports Iran had rejected the latest proposal for peace from Qatari intermediaries, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that his country continues to review ideas for a diplomatic solution to the eight-month war.
"While our Brave Armed Forces are fully prepared to defend the Homeland, Iran continues to give diplomacy a chance to succeed," Araghchi wrote. "We remain in close and ongoing contact with intermediaries to review ideas that can ensure implementation of our 7-Day Plan in even less than a week."
The seven-day plan was presented to the U.S. shortly after the U.N. General Assembly in September. However, President Trump rejected the idea presented by Iran for a seven-day ceasefire and then phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
Earlier Wednesday, a senior Iranian official denied Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal on Sunday, saying instead Qatar had only come with "unacceptable" ideas , Reuters reported.
A source had earlier reported there were concerns Israel could begin a new bombing campaign after its election, according to Reuters.
Kuwait summoned Iran's envoy in protest on Wednesday, after Tehran denied one of its citizens, sentenced to death in Kuwait, was involved in an assassination plot targeting a top government figure.
Earlier this week, two Kuwaiti judicial sources told the AFP news agency that the Gulf state had condemned three Shia men to death for plotting the assassination of Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Fahad al-Yousef, collaborating with Iran; and for membership in Hezbollah.
Iran's embassy in Kuwait said earlier Wednesday it "rejects the Kuwaiti government's claim regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate figures or in any other act that could harm Kuwaiti national security."
It added that the person in question had been outside Kuwait for 10 years.
It said it regretted a "negative approach towards Iran, manifested, among other things, in the repetition of flimsy and worn-out scenarios concerning Iranian interference in Kuwaiti affairs."
In response, Kuwait summoned Iranian ambassador Mohammad Toutounji over the statement, which it said "constituted blatant interference in the internal affairs of the State of Kuwait and an infringement upon its sovereignty and the independence of its judiciary."
Abdulredha Haydar Dahqani was among those who had been sentenced to death, the judicial sources told AFP.
Dahqani, an Iranian national, had already been handed the death penalty in 2016 after he was tried in absentia along with 25 Kuwaitis. He was convicted of spying for Iran and plotting attacks.
Another was Hussein Abdallah al-Maatouq, a religious dignitary and secretary-general of the National Islamic Alliance, Kuwait's most influential Shia movement, the sources said.
Israel's defense minister on Wednesday denounced opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot for urging the military to resist post-election pressure from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who has threatened new strikes on Iran.
"His call to senior military officials not to obey the directives of the prime minister or me or of other relevant security authorities, on the grounds that 'they have his support,' is an anti-democratic statement detached from reality," Israel Katz wrote on X .
Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a speech to supporters after Tuesday's election that Netanyahu was a caretaker prime minister lacking a mandate and the military should serve the state rather than the premier.
"Stand firm in the face of any attempt to challenge you. You have my unequivocal backing. Netanyahu, do not dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened in recent days to renew strikes on Iran.
Media reports, denied by Netanyahu, said military chief Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir pushed back immediately before the election on the prime minister's new plans on Iran.
Eisenkot's comments were the latest in "a campaign of lies" about tension between Netanyahu and the military over Iran, Katz said.
Yemen's Ministry of Transport has warned of risks to civil aviation safety after Aden International Airport was targeted in a missile attack attributed to the Houthi group for the sixth time, Saudi Arabia's Asharq News reported.
The missile strike shook parts of the southern city, raising fresh concerns over the safety of airport operations and the potential threat to civilian air traffic.
Airport authorities had evacuated all employees and workers from the facility following Houthi threats to target the airport.
Iran is finalizing a protocol with Russia to accelerate joint development of small modular nuclear reactors, Behrouz Kamalvandi, spokesman and deputy for international, legal and parliamentary affairs at the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran, has announced.
Speaking to Iran's Shabakeh Khabar television network , Kamalvandi said the agreement would facilitate closer cooperation on the construction of small modular reactors, a technology attracting growing international interest as countries seek reliable, low-carbon electricity sources. SMRs are far smaller than traditional large-scale reactors.
Kamalvandi also highlighted rising global electricity demand, driven in part by artificial intelligence, digital technologies and the electrification of transport. He said nuclear power could provide stable baseload electricity while helping reduce emissions.
He claimed Iran's nuclear industry had reached a mature stage and said the country had developed substantial domestic capabilities in nuclear plant construction, fuel-cycle technology and nuclear safety. He also stated political pressure had delayed some Iranian projects but had not halted the country's nuclear activities.
Kamalvandi made the remarks while discussing Iran's participation in an international ministerial conference on nuclear energy in South Korea. He said the Iranian delegation was using the event to promote international cooperation and argue that countries party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty should have their rights respected alongside their obligations.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Wednesday that any Israeli-instigated attack in the Gulf region would have a "devastating impact" on global markets.
"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Araghchi said in a post on X .
The United States and Israel have in recent days raised the prospect of renewed attacks on Iran in the war, which began in late February with strikes on the Islamic republic.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking to form a new government after close elections, said on Wednesday he could work with President Trump to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.
Iran's Embassy in Kuwait has categorically rejected the Kuwaiti government's allegation that an Iranian citizen was involved in a plot to assassinate public figures or in any other activity that could undermine Kuwait's national security.
The embassy said in a statement that it "categorically rejects the allegation made by the Kuwaiti government regarding the involvement of an Iranian citizen in a plot to assassinate public figures or in any other act that could undermine Kuwait's national security, and recalls that the aforementioned individual has not been present in Kuwait at any time during the past ten years."
A Kuwaiti State Security and Terrorism Criminal Court sentenced three men to death on Monday over an alleged plot to assassinate First Deputy Prime Minister and Interior Minister Sheikh Fahad Al-Yousef, with prosecutors accusing the defendants of spying for Iran, communicating with Iranian-linked entities and joining Hezbollah, two judicial sources told the AFP news agency Tuesday.
The court also sentenced eight other defendants to varying prison terms.
According to Kuwaiti newspaper Al-Rai , the defendants were accused of communicating with Iran and entities allegedly operating in its interests, including Lebanese group Hezbollah, to carry out hostile acts against Kuwait following the killing of Iran's Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei on Feb. 28, at the beginning of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Wednesday Saudi Arabia killed dozens of people with strikes in Yemen. The group also said it had targeted the perimeter of an airport in government-held Aden
Houthi broadcaster Almasirah reported 14 dead "and 10 wounded, including women and children in a preliminary toll," in attacks blamed on Saudi Arabia that hit a market and a petrol station in the northwestern Jawf province.
In Aden, a Houthi missile fell inside the perimeter of the airport shortly before the Iran-backed group issued a call to evacuate the area, a local police source told the AFP news agency.
The source added that the strike hit while a Saudi military aircraft was at the airport, but the plane "was not hit and took off shortly afterward."
He spoke on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said in a post on Telegram that the cargo plan was "transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people."
The Houthis have targeted Aden several times in recent weeks. They have also intensified attacks on their Saudi foe, while they battle the government it backs in Aden.
The United States has told its Gulf allies to prepare for a brief but intense campaign against Iran after the midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing people briefed on the matter.
The U.S. military is shipping a Patriot antimissile system from Texas to Israel and has transferred troops off bases where they may have been vulnerable, officials familiar with the decisions told the outlet.
American forces across the Middle East have been restocking munitions and aircraft have been preparing for strikes, the paper reported, while an additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine unit are set to join the 20 or so warships in the region, though some other vessels could be withdrawn.
The Houthis have called on people in Aden International Airport in southern Yemen to evacuate immediately, claiming that a Saudi military cargo aircraft is transporting weapons there intended to kill Yemenis.
Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said in a post on X : "Our armed forces call on those present at Aden Airport to evacuate the airport immediately, due to the presence of an enemy Saudi military cargo aircraft transporting weapons to kill the sons of the Yemeni people."
Aden is the seat of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, and has been since the Iran-backed Houthis took the country's capital, Sanaa, in 2014.
A senior Iranian official denied Wednesday that Qatar had presented Tehran with a new peace proposal, saying instead that Qatar had come with "unacceptable" ideas, the Reuters news agency reported.
Reuters reported earlier Wednesday that Qatari mediators handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war on Sunday, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Dismissing the idea that they had been given a new peace proposal, the Iranian official speaking to the news agency said Tehran would show no flexibility on the nuclear issue.
Qatari mediators on Sunday handed Iran a new draft deal to end the war, the Reuters news agency reported, citing an official briefed on the negotiations.
Tehran is considering the proposal and set to respond by the end of the week, the agency reported Wednesday.
The source added that there were concerns in Tehran before the meeting on Sunday that Israel could resume its bombardment of Iran this week.
The cost of the Iran war has risen to an estimated $47 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. military's Central Command obtained by CBS News Tuesday.
Like previous estimates, it does not include damage to U.S. military bases in the Middle East. The bulk of the cost, $29 billion, is for replacing expended munitions.
According to a report released by the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office in September, the Iran war could cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month for as long as it continues.
Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition in Tuesday's election, but his Likud party still emerged as the largest party among all the contenders. Neither bloc, Netanyahu or the opposition, has a clear majority.
While Netanyahu appears to have won fewer votes than his main challenger, according to the early exit polls, both candidates will likely struggle to cobble together a coalition.
One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.
Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.
Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

title: Stubb's call with Putin draws praise, criticism at home and abroad
body:
Critics are asking how much the government knew ahead of the 90-minute call.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb 's phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin this week has sparked reactions in Finland and Russia, among other places.
Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre jointly spoke with the Russian leader on Tuesday . Stubb and Støre met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo last week .
According to Stubb's office, the aim was to give Putin a direct message about upcoming negotiations in Abu Dhabi to help end Russia's war in Ukraine.
Some of the reactions in Finland came from Tuomas Forsberg , a geopolitics expert from the University of Tampere and Timo Soini , a co-founder of the Finns Party and former foreign minister.
They spoke about the significance of the leaders' call on Yle TV's discussion show A-studio on Tuesday evening — starting with the question of whether it was the right time for the conversation.
According to Forsberg, there had been discussions over the past year about the need for a call to the Kremlin, but the expectation was that Russia would offer a positive gesture that would provide a motive and opportunity for such a call.
This didn't happen. Instead, he said a round of US negotiations forced Europeans to jump in to relay their own — and Ukraine's — messages to Moscow.
The call has received a mixed reception outside of Finland. According to Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen , the call wasn't coordinated with other European countries. She told Danish public broadcaster DR that it's important for Europeans to remain united. Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson has also said he wasn't informed in advance about the call with Putin.
According to Støre, all of Finland's and Norway's allied countries received advance notice about the call with Putin. Stubb also claimed all the Nordic countries were informed beforehand.
According to Forsberg, once the process of arranging the call began, things advanced quickly.
"This naturally came together quickly once the process got moving. In that sense, it's difficult to agree with all European states on how to proceed. That might take too much time if you think a fire needs putting out," he said.
However, former foreign minister Timo Soini criticised what he characterised as the independent nature of the leaders' phone call. According to him, the matter should have been discussed in advance in Finland.
"Under the constitution, foreign policy is led by the president in cooperation with the government, without interruption. At what point did this cooperation happen, and who exactly was aware of it?" Soini said.
According to Soini, the call's talking points should have been formed together in advance, rather than Stubb speaking to Putin first and only afterwards explaining what was discussed.
"That's not any kind of policy-setting, to say 'I'll make the call, and once I've made it, I'll tell you what I talked about.'"
According to Stubb, the roughly ninety-minute call included topics such as limiting military operations particularly in regard to energy infrastructure, as well as matters related to food security.
The call laid the groundwork for a November meeting in Abu Dhabi involving Ukraine, the United States and Russia. Stubb said on Tuesday at a Nordic Council meeting that the meeting will also include European representation.
According to Stubb, the call with Putin was prepared in cooperation with Ukraine and the United States.
Zelensky thanked Stubb and Støre for the call on X that afternoon.
"Alex and Jonas made clear to the Russian leader that real action is needed to reduce attacks on our energy system and infrastructure," Zelensky said of the call.
According to a Kremlin statement, Stubb, Støre and Putin agreed to maintain phone contact in future as well.
Russian media has extensively covered the phone call between Stubb, Støre and Putin, largely drawing on official statements.
Newspaper Kommersant reported that Putin agreed with Stubb and Støre to continue direct contacts, with all parties welcoming the resumption of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US in Abu Dhabi.
State broadcaster Vesti noted that Finland's president and Norway's PM participated as leaders of their own countries, not on Europe's behalf. Other outlets highlighted discussions on Baltic Sea stability and adherence to international maritime law.
Russian politicians largely welcomed the phone conversation.
Grigory Karasin , who chairs the Federation Council's international affairs committee, suggested that "common sense" was returning to European political thinking, though he emphasised that gestures need to be followed by concrete agreements.
Duma member Andrei Klimov said the call signalled that Europeans had realised nothing could be resolved without Russia, calling it a global power whose opinion must be considered. He suggested Finland and Norway were chosen as negotiators partly because they are Russia's neighbours.
Political researcher Nikolai Toropin tempered expectations, saying no major breakthrough had occurred, "but this is better than nothing."
Business paper Vedomosti reported that Putin accused EU and Nato countries of pursuing policies prolonging the war, as he emphasised that Russia's interests need to be considered in the conflict's resolution.
Russian outlets also revisited speculation that Stubb could become the EU's mediator in peace negotiations, citing reports from Germany's Berliner Zeitung and Politico. However, Russian media group RBK noted Putin previously said he'd prefer former German chancellor Gerhard Schröder as mediator.

title: Yle names Krista Taubert as new head of news and sports
body:
Taubert will begin working in the role from 1 November.
The Finnish Broadcasting Company Yle has appointed Krista Taubert as Director and Editor-in-Chief of the News and Sports unit.
"We promise to offer our audience a truthful and balanced picture of Finland and the world every day. We create the nation's greatest shared experiences and most lasting memories," Taubert said.
In the role, Taubert will be responsible for Yle's news, current affairs, sports, event and local content across all distribution channels, in all languages except Swedish or Sámi. The News and Sports division also includes Yle's news in English, Russian, Ukrainian, Somali, Arabic, and sign language.
She will take up the position on 1 November.
Her appointment was announced to staff on Wednesday morning by Yle CEO Marit af Björkesten .
"In the current state of the world, the importance of reliable information is greater than ever," af Björkesten remarked. "I am very pleased that we have such an experienced journalist and ambitious leader to take our news journalism into the future."
Taubert has served as acting Director and Editor-in-Chief since June, when her predecessor Panu Pokkinen became seriously ill while on holiday in Portugal. He died on 8 July after suffering a second cardiac arrest at home.

title: At least 64 killed in train collision on high-speed line in Spain
body:
The collision occurred near the towns of Mora, Orgaz and Urda.
LONDON -- At least 69 people were killed after two trains collided on Spain's Madrid-Seville high-speed line on Wednesday, officials said.
The collision occurred at around 8:30 a.m. local time at kilometer marker 118 near Urda. The crash involved a Renfe train and an Iryo train, both traveling from Madrid to Seville, Spain's Transport Ministry told ABC News.
The collision was also the second major train crash in Spain this year on the same high-speed train line, involving the same trains from the same rail operators. In January, two high-speed Iryo and Renfe trains collided near Adamuz in the province of Cordoba, killing 46 people. Authorities said one of the trains derailed and another train collided with the derailed cars.
The Spanish Interior Ministry said in a statement Thursday that six more victims were added to the death toll overnight, bringing the total number of people who perished in the crash to 74. The office of the president and the Transportation Ministry later revised that number downward to 69 dead.
During a news conference Wednesday, Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente called the crash "truly unbelievable." He said the preliminary investigation indicates the crash was caused by an "inexplicable" order by the rail controllers to allow one train to proceed despite a safety failure that halted a train on the tracks further ahead.
According to Puente, a computer failure led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.
"In the event of a system failure, the control center takes over," Puente said, adding it was the control center which decided to allow the trains to move again without any speed restrictions. That decision, Puente said, resulted in the Renfe train crashing into the Iryo train, which was stationary on the tracks further ahead.
In addition to those killed, at least 15 people were seriously injured and were taken to area hospitals, and more than 50 were hospitalized with lesser injuries, Emiliano Garcia-Page, president of the Castilla-La Mancha Region, said during a separate news conference on Wednesday.
Garcia-Page said 24 victims who were killed were found on the Renfe train and the remainder were on the Iryo train. He said search-and-rescue crews are using canines to comb through the wreckage looking for victims.
"All of Spain is mourning. We express our solidarity and deepest sympathy to the relatives of the victims," Garcia-Page said.
Garcia-Page continued, "The ministry is trying to determine the causes of this terrible tragedy and understand how and why it happened. We are going to get to the bottom of this. And if there was any negligence, it will come to light. If there were failures in the safety system, we will address them decisively."
The incident marked the deadliest high-speed train crash in Spain since 2013, when 80 people were killed and more than 170 were injured when a train traveling from Madrid to Ferrol derailed in Galicia in northwest Spain.
"We have suffered two terrible high-speed rail tragedies in a single year. Everything appears to indicate that the causes of both accidents are unrelated, but it is not for me to say," Garcia-Page said at Wednesday's news conference. "That is the role of the independent railway accident investigation commission."
He added, "If we need to further strengthen safety in order to restore confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have."
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who traveled on Wednesday to the site of the crash, said in a social media statement that he is "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo."
"We extend all our solidarity to the families of the victims and to the injured, to whom we wish a speedy recovery. Our main priority is the victims," Sánchez said.
The government of Spain announced on Wednesday that it has declared three days of official morning, from Thursday to Saturday, to honor those killed and injured in the crash.
"We'd like to convey to the families our condolences, our sorrow, our support and our affection at such a hard, difficult time," Spain's King Felipe VI said in a statement.
As part of the preliminary investigation of Wednesday's crash, authorities said the Renfe train probably struck the Iryo train from behind, causing two coaches to derail and plummet down an embankment.
The Iryo train was carrying 146 passengers, including one baby, while the Renfe train had 397 passengers, according to the transport ministry.
"It was a terrible crash. The carriage partially overturned. We saw carriages next to it completely wrecked," crash survivor Miguel Ángel Pérez told RTVE, the Spanish national radio and television public broadcasting network.
Ángel Pérez said he was riding with work colleagues in the last car of the Renfe train when the crash occurred. He said that prior to the crash train operators warned that the train was stopping due to "an overload on the track."
"Then it started moving again, and that's when we felt immense impact. We felt the train move, derail and we were tilted. It was a terrible few seconds," Ángel Pérez said.
An American tourist named Dire and his wife said they were headed to Andalusia and were also on the train that had stopped on the tracks before they felt "a huge crash."
"The train moved, things flew everywhere," Dire of Florida told the Spanish news station, Canal 24 Horas. "I looked out the window and saw that the train was completely destroyed. People were screaming, crying, covered in blood... I told my wife, 'We have to leave now,' because we were afraid the train would overturn."
Another passenger, Ana, told reporters that she was traveling on one of the trains with her sister and her dog when the crash occurred, according to Reuters.
"Suddenly, I only heard screams," Ana, who suffered injuries to her face and leg, told Reuters.
In the aftermath of the crash, Ana said passengers broke windows and that firefighters pulled her from the wreckage. "I was covered in blood," she said.
She described the horrific scene of seeing people dying in front of her.
"Some people were fine, and others were really bad. You could see them dying, and you could do nothing," said Ana, who added that she and her sister, who was also injured, were taken to a hospital by ambulance.
In a statement, Iryo said its service 6076, traveling from Madrid to Seville, was involved in the accident near Urda. The company said it had activated all emergency protocols and was working closely with authorities to manage the situation.
As a result of the crash, all Iryo services departing from Madrid-Puerta de Atocha and traveling along the Southern Corridor have been canceled. The company said it had no estimate for when service would resume.
Spain's Health Minister Monica Garcia said the government was mobilizing resources and coordinating with relevant institutions to respond to the crash.
“We are mobilizing all the resources at our disposal and coordinating with all the relevant institutions,” Garcia said. “I’m working with the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha to provide any resources it may need. My full support and gratitude go to the emergency personnel dispatched to the area."
The U.S. State Department confirms that several U.S. citizens were injured.
"The Department of State and the U.S. Embassy in Madrid are working closely with local authorities to assist Americans,” a department spokesperson said. "We extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of all those affected.”
The department is asking Americans in need of assistance and those concerned about the safety of loved ones in Spain to get in contact. So far, it has not indicated that any U.S. citizens are among the dead.

title: Why California's election results take longer than other states
body:
Alaska and Pennsylvania could also see election results later than other states.
While Election Day is on Nov. 3, at least some of California's midterm election results may not be projected until days or even weeks later.
Not only is there a plethora of ballots to count because California is the most populous state, with 23 million registered voters, but it also relies on a large number of mail-in ballots, with some not arriving until a week after voting ends.
According to the California secretary of state , "vote-by-mail ballots postmarked on or before Election Day and received within seven days after the election, as well as any provisional ballots cast, must still be counted."
Earlier this year, the Supreme Court upheld a Mississippi law allowing tabulation of late-arriving mail-in ballots so long as they were postmarked by Election Day. The decision was a loss for the Republican Party, which brought the case, and the Trump administration, which has pushed to override state election rules nationwide by imposing strict federal limits on voting by mail.
The Supreme Court last month also rejected the Trump administration's attempt to limit mail-in voting for now, keeping in place a lower court decision blocking the U.S. Postal Service from implementing new restrictions.
In addition to late-arriving mail ballots, the California secretary of state told ABC News that there is an arduous process of counting mail ballots and validating voters' signatures, as each envelope signature must match the signatures on file. County election officials have up to 30 days after the election to count ballots.
More than 89% of Californians that voted in the June 2 primary election did so by mail, according to California Secretary of State Shirley Weber. On July 10, Weber announced that the primary results were certified.
ABC News projected the two candidates advancing to the state's gubernatorial general election about one week after the primary election: Democrat Xavier Becerra was projected to advance on June 5, and Republican Steve Hilton was projected to advance on June 9.
California's long ballot-counting process often opens floodgates for criticism, with President Donald Trump frequently claiming without evidence that elections in the state are "rigged."
"In the end, they're not going to let you win it. They just won't let you win it because it's a rigged state," Trump said during a Newsmax interview earlier in October.
In his claims of election fraud, Trump has repeatedly referenced Republican Spencer Pratt's loss in the Los Angeles mayoral primary. While Pratt was initially in second place on primary night, he was eventually edged out by Democrat Nithya Raman once ballots were fully counted -- which can happen given the state's vote-counting process.
"Spencer Pratt was doing great. And at the end of the election, Election Day, his opponent was crying. Oh, she's lost so badly. She was crying. Then all of a sudden, like a week and a half later, you hear that she's surging. Nobody ever heard of her. You know, people that nobody ever heard of don't surge. The only time they surge is when they cheat," Trump claimed in early October.
The University of Florida's Election Lab has found that so far, 50% of mail ballots that have been accepted by the state of California are from registered Democrats and 29% are from registered Republicans, as of Oct. 25. The remaining 21% of ballots are from those with no party affiliation or registered with a minor party.
An October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll found that among likely California voters who said they would probably or certainly vote -- or who already had -- 65% said they would vote by mail. Just 11% of California voters said they would vote in person at a polling place on Election Day.
The president has also railed against mail-in ballots for years, despite himself voting by mail twice during Florida elections this year. A White House spokesperson said that Trump has supported "commonsense exceptions" to allow Americans to use mail-in ballots, including for "illness, disability, military, or travel," but that he opposes universal voting by mail due to it being "highly susceptible to fraud."
An analysis from the Brookings Institution from November 2025 found that voter fraud is rare in voting by mail.
As the president blitzes the country ahead of the midterms, he has continued to sow doubt in mail-in voting while simultaneously encouraging Republicans to vote any way they can . Speaking to Newsmax earlier this month, Trump claimed without evidence that Democrats are sent multiple ballots and that Republicans sometimes do not receive a ballot at all.
"They send out millions and millions of ballots. Democrats get, in some cases seven, in some cases one, but in some cases they get much more than one. Republicans oftentimes don't get any, they have to call in for their ballot," Trump claimed.
Ahead of the general election, officials and state leaders have emphasized the security of California elections and mail ballots.
"Voting in California is secure, reliable, and part of California's tradition of encouraging participation in our democracy," Weber, the secretary of state, said earlier this month.
"Voting is safe, vote-by-mail is accessible to any and all who need it. And I encourage every Californian to make their voice heard this November," California Gov. Gavin Newsom also said in October.
California is not the only state where election results take an extended amount of time. Alaska, for instance, accepts some ballots up to 15 days after the election and certification cannot be done before then.
The Alaska Division of Elections says that the "process is intentionally slow and methodical so that accuracy is obtained."
Pennsylvania also prevents counties from opening ballots until 7 a.m. on Election Day, meaning early votes cannot be counted upon receipt.
