title: Winter speed limits take effect on Finnish roads this week
body:
Speed limits on main roads will generally be lowered to 80 km/h, though some limits will drop to 70.
Winter and darkness-related speed limits will take effect on Finland's main roads this week, according to the Finnish Transport Infrastructure Agency.
The agency said the main changeover day is Wednesday, though limits will be switched by Friday at the latest.
Speed limits on main roads will generally be lowered to 80 km/h, though on some road sections limits will drop to 70 km/h. On motorways, speed limits will go down to 100 km/h.
Decisions on winter restrictions are made by regional Centres for Economic Development, Transport and the Environment.
However, as in recent years, Fintraffic can raise variable speed limits on motorways to 120 km/h until the end of November. This measure requires that weather and road conditions, as well as the road-specific speed limit, allow it.
The switch to winter season speed limits comes at the end of October, as a large proportion of road traffic now occurs in darkness, following the end of daylight saving time last Sunday .

title: Video: Hero dog Martta saves neighbour from chilly fate
body:
"We're certainly proud of our dog for doing something like this. A great dog, a really great dog," her owner said.
Lapp Reindeer dog Martta lives in Kittilä, Finnish Lapland with her owners Pekka and Anu Nevalainen .
One day she caught their attention with an unusual bark.
For some reason, Martta really wanted to go outside, and took her owners with her.
Pekka and Anu followed Martta onto their neighbour's property and found him stuck in the cold water of a wastewater pit.
By then the man had completely run out of strength, and without help the icy water would likely have claimed his life.
The Nevalainens couldn't manage to lift the man out of the pit, but managed to keep him afloat until rescue services arrived. They struggled to hold onto their neighbour for around half an hour before help came.
Pekka said the worst part of the ordeal was knowing the man's likely fate if they lost their grip.
In recognition of her heroic instincts, Martta will receive the Hero Dog title from the Finnish Kennel Club, alongside seven other brave pups, at the Helsinki Dog Fair in December.
But Martta has already received rewards of ice cream and plenty of praise.
"We're certainly proud of our dog for doing something like this. A great dog, a really great dog," Pekka said.
Besides Martta, seven other dogs will also receive heroic awards in December. What unites the special canines is that at least one person likely owes their life to each of them.
The awards ceremony will take place on 13 December at the Dog Fair in Helsinki, where 14 other dogs will receive honourable mentions.

title: Lockheed Martin Welcomes Dedicated PAC-3® Missile Maintenance Facility in Poland
body:
BRUSSELS, Oct. 27, 2026, In coordination with the United States Government, Lockheed Martin is pleased to announce plans to establish a dedicated PAC-3 ® Missile Maintenance Facility (MMF) in Poland. This historic step strengthens NATO's integrated air and missile defense across Europe.



The PAC-3 MMF in Poland will support the growing community of NATO Allies operating PAC-3 interceptors by performing onsite repair, refurbishment, lifecycle support and re-certification, enabling rapid turnaround for resupply and integrated testing. The facility will build on a deeply integrated transatlantic industrial partnership, with Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden— original signatories to the agreement alongside the US and Poland—playing important roles in the supply chain.

"For more than 75 years, Lockheed Martin has been a trusted partner to Europe— strengthening regional sustainment, expanding production capacity and accelerating the delivery of critical missile defense capabilities. The PAC-3 MMF represents the next evolution of that partnership, bringing essential sustainment support to our European allies and ensuring these advanced defense systems remain available when and where they are needed most," said Tim Cahill, president, Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control.

The new facility will be fully integrated with Poland's existing defense industrial ecosystem, creating high‑skill jobs, expanding opportunities for local suppliers, and investing in local communities to enhance the resilience of the allied industrial base.

"Lockheed Martin is a permanent part of Europe's security landscape. Lockheed Martin's growing footprint here underpins European collective strength and prosperity," said Jay Pitman, President, Lockheed Martin International. "This announcement establishes deeper industrial partnerships in Poland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden, and we are expanding opportunities for American and European suppliers, strengthening supply chain resilience on both sides of the Atlantic and investing in capabilities that reinforce our shared defense industrial base. Together, these efforts are building lasting transatlantic industrial strength and reinforcing security and readiness for decades to come."

Lockheed Martin will continue to be an enduring partner to Europe, advancing its security, industrial strength and prosperity. Together with European industry, the company is building the capacity and resilience needed for deterrence today while building a diverse range of partnerships across Europe to create a stronger, more autonomous and interoperable European defense ecosystem well into the future.

Demand for PAC-3 MSE, the world's most advanced air and missile defense interceptor, continues to grow worldwide, driven by its combat-proven performance. This year, the US government awarded Lockheed Martin $58.62 billion to continue accelerating PAC-3 MSE production, ensuring US allies have the advanced air and missile defense capabilities they need to defend what matters most.

title: Bolsonaro lands in US days after election defeat: Sources
body:
Incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva defeated Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by authorities in Brazil, fled his country and landed in the U.S. Wednesday morning.
Bolsonaro landed at Miami-Opa Locka Executive airport in Florida shortly after 9 a.m. ET, accompanied by his family.
Images captured the plane touching down in South Florida and Bolsonaro, who was defeated by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday's runoff election, coming off the jet.
The family was being shielded from photographers by umbrellas as they left the airport.
President Donald Trump's administration is issuing Bolsonaro and his family visas, a State Department official told ABC News.
On Tuesday, Brazilian authorities said they were unaware were investigating whether he fled to the U.S., according to authorities familiar with the investigation.
The former presidential candidate is under investigation over a sports betting case and for a probe into the production of a movie about his father, Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil's president from 2019 to 2023, according to Brazilian authorities.
Bolsonaro released a statement Wednesday afternoon thanking Argentina's government and Trump for helping him leave Brazil.
He claimed, without any evidence, that there was fraud in Sunday's elections.
"Given the political weaponization of justice in Brazil, I brought my family to the United States, where we are safe," Bolsonaro said in a statement.
"I did not flee Brazil. I left Brazil -- left a state of exception -- so I could be the leader my people deserve," he added.
Trump was asked about the situation by reporters Wednesday and refused to say who he believed won Brazil's presidential election.
"But I know that we gave him a pass to come into the country, so we'll see," Trump told reporters on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews Wednesday.
"But I won't get involved. It was a very strange election, that's for sure," he added.
When asked by reporters why he granted a visa to Bolsonaro and his family to come to the U.S., Trump said that he thought they had been "treated very unfairly" in Brazil. The president said Wednesday he had not spoken to the presidential candidate.

title: Judge to appoint special master in California voting case in setback to Trump admin
body:
The judge appeared skeptical of the DOJ's request for a restraining order.
The federal district judge overseeing the Justice Department's lawsuit asking California to segregate roughly 20,000 ballot belonging to individuals it claims are "likely" noncitizens appeared skeptical of the DOJ's efforts to seek emergency action just a week from the state's election.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said in court Tuesday he intends to appoint a special master to probe DOJ's process that led it to compile the list of alleged 20,000 likely non-citizens, dealing a setback to the Trump administration's attempt to quickly intervene in the election.
Judge Carter did not rule by the conclusion of the hearing on the DOJ request for a temporary restraining order against the state, though he appeared skeptical of the department's late-stage attempt to force what he described as a "monumental change" in California's ongoing administration of its election.
Carter told the parties he intends to issue some kind of ruling governing proceedings on the case moving forward by tomorrow.
Bill Essayli, a controversial Trump-installed leader of the U.S. Attorney's Office in the Central District of California, argued in the hearing that the administration was simply pushing for the state to be in compliance with federal law barring non-citizens from casting votes.
But state officials and other legal advocates opposing the DOJ lawsuit countered that the litigation violated longstanding Constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections -- and could have chaotic consequences for the state in tabulating final vote counts in the weeks ahead.
Notably in closing out the hearing, Judge Carter appeared to admonish the administration over its recent letters to state officials around California suggesting it could prosecute them if they are involved in tabulating ballots that could be from the list of alleged likely noncitizens.
"This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately," Carter said. "Good night."
On Monday, a federal appeals court rejected a request from the DOJ to issue an order requiring California to set aside the 20,000 ballots from its list, kicking the back to the district court.
Earlier this month, the DOJ filed suit against California , accusing the state of failing to review the list of alleged noncitizens that the Trump administration claimed were sent mail-in ballots for next week's midterm election.
In court papers filed earlier last week, Los Angeles officials said a preliminary analysis of 200 of the names on the 20,000-person list, included a "high percentage" of individuals who say they were born in the U.S. and many more who have no voting history at all.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Alex Pretti's parents seek answers from DOJ months after son's killing
body:
No one has been charged in connection with the killing of the VA nurse.
It's been more than nine months since Veterans Affairs nurse Alex Pretti was shot by federal immigration agents in Minnesota, and his parents said that they have received no updates, no information and no support from the federal government.
On Tuesday, Susan and Michael Pretti made a public emotional plea to the Justice Department, which has not issued any charges in connection with the Jan. 24 shooting, to release all the evidence it has into its investigation and provide more accountability.
"Michael and I are not asking for any special treatment. We do not want to be on TV we are not political activists, nor do we want to become political activists. All we want is justice for Alex," Susan Pretti told reporters.
The couple held back tears as they spoke to the press, surrounded by pictures of the incident that sparked protests and backlash against the Trump administration, Immigration Customs and Enforcement and other federal agencies.
"The federal government went on TV and lied about Alex, they tried to slander his memory to cover up their crime," Susan Pretti said.
Then Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem alleged their son "committed an act of domestic terrorism," during a news conference hours after the shooting.
A Justice Department spokesperson responded to the Prettis' claims in a statement to ABC News on Tuesday.
"The timing is consistent with how these types of investigations proceed. As is standard practice, communications with family members, if any, come at a later stage of a case, such as indictment, initial appearance, plea, trial, or sentencing," the official said. "Those communications do not typically occur during an investigation."
A spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney's Office in Minnesota declined comment to ABC affiliate KSTB in St. Paul.
Eyewitness videos reviewed by ABC News show that the 37-year-old nurse appeared to be recording on Jan. 24 when a federal officer shoved a woman into him.
Alex Pretti appeared to try to help her, and then both of his hands are visible -- one holding a phone and the other held up, seemingly to protect himself from pepper spray -- when he's wrestled to the ground.
His firearm, which he had a legal permit to carry, was removed by an officer while he was on the ground and before approximately 10 shots were fired, the videos show.
Noem later said that she did not have all of the information about the incident before she alleged Pretti was a terrorist.
However, she repeatedly refused to retract her statement or apologize when asked by the press and congressional leaders on multiple occasions.
"We are working in those situations where there's a tragic loss of life and that there is something that our agents are involved in, that we continue to deliver information," she said during a Senate hearing in March when asked about the shooting.
Noem was removed from her position days after that hearing. Since her ouster as DHS secretary, Noem was named by Trump to be the special envoy to the "Shield of Americas," a coalition between the U.S. and governments in Latin America.
Michael Pretti said no one from the federal government reached out to his family despite repeated requests. The family says Attorney General Todd Blanche and Dan Rosen, the U.S. attorney for the District of Minnesota, have not provided any more details about the investigation.
The Justice Department said the investigation into the incident is ongoing.
"What we have been treated to is cruelty," Michael Pretti said.
"At every turn they have ignored us, misled us and shielded Alex's killers," he added.
Steve Schleicher, an attorney representing the couple, told reporters the Hennepin County Attorney's Office was reviewing the case and needed access to all available evidence to determine what happened and whether criminal charges were warranted.
In a statement provided to ABC News, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said: "The federal government continues to obstruct our investigation into Alex Pretti's killing. That's why we continue to pursue our lawsuit in federal court to access the evidence that is being wrongly withheld."
The statement added: "We have repeatedly asked for the cooperation to resume. Those requests have fallen on deaf ears. Alex Pretti died at the hands of federal agents and their bosses continue to hide evidence. It's disgusting behavior that reflects how little they care for the American people, who deserve transparency about a fatal shooting by a federal agent."
Michael Pretti directly addressed Blanche and Rosen during the news conference asking them to cooperate with local investigators.
"Look in your heart and do what is right. Share the evidence now so prosecutors can follow the facts and hold these men accountable," Michael Pretti said.
The father added the family would consider any available legal options as they continue seeking justice for their son.
"We're heartbroken to be here today. We wish we didn't have to be here. We wish Alex was alive," Michael Pretti said.
-ABC News' Luke Barr contributed to this report.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Man accused of fatally choking ex on same day they appeared on court TV show: Warrant
body:
Michelle Parker has been missing since 2011.
Authorities allege a Florida man choked his former fiancée to death shortly after they appeared in an "embarrassing" episode of the reality show "The People's Court" that aired following days of heated messages and threats from the mother to restrict access to their twins, according to a newly unsealed affidavit.
Michelle Parker, a 33-year-old mother of three, vanished in 2011 hours shortly after the pre-taped episode of "The People's Court" aired featuring a dispute about her engagement ring, according to police. Her body has never been found and she is presumed dead, according to police.
Her former fiancé, 55-year-old Dale Smith Jr., was arrested earlier this month and charged with second-degree murder in connection with her presumed death, Orlando police said. He has pleaded not guilty and maintains his innocence, his lawyer said.
According to the 46-page arrest warrant affidavit for his arrest, which was released Tuesday after an Orange County judge ordered it unsealed, authorities believe Smith choked Parker to death when she came to his house on Nov. 17, 2011, to drop off their 3-year-old twins.
Her sister reported her missing that night, after Parker never showed up for her shift at the bar where she worked or returned to the home she shared with her mother, according to the affidavit.
While being interviewed by detectives the following day, Smith was photographed with "recent scratches and abrasions that detectives now believe are defensive wounds from the victim," the affidavit stated.
He had scratches near his mouth and on his lower lip and on his left wrist, as well as abrasions on the back of both of his elbows, according to the affidavit.
"There are no records of detectives asking what the above injuries were from," the affidavit stated.
Smith was named the only suspect in Parker's disappearance during a news conference on Nov. 28, 2011, according to the affidavit. Police allege in the affidavit that Smith has "a violent history" and "cannot handle stressful situations."
During the preliminary investigation, detectives "learned of a history of domestic violence between the victim and suspect, none of which was ever documented by law enforcement," with Parker's family and friends describing their relationship "as tumultuous, with the suspect oftentimes being violent and controlling toward the victim," the affidavit stated. Police also learned Smith was found guilty in 2001 of domestic violence against his wife at the time, according to the affidavit.
Smith was arrested on Oct. 14, nearly 15 years after Parker disappeared, with Orlando Police Chief Eric Smith saying investigators "reexamined testimony and conflicting statements made by the suspect and used advanced digital forensics to uncover and analyze additional evidence."
According to the affidavit, this year, an Orlando Police Department homicide analyst reviewed the original cellular data records obtained in 2011 and "recognized there was additional data in the records that had not been analyzed."
"It is likely this data was not readable to detectives in 2011. The data revealed more precise location and user data, to include messages, for the suspect's and victims' phones," the affidavit stated.
In the weeks leading up to her disappearance, Parker sent what police described as "several offensive messages to the suspect." According to the affidavit, she texted that she hated him and threatened that his visitation rights would be taken away.
"My kids are better off with out u n their life," she texted him in one instance on Nov. 3, 2011, according to the affidavit.
Later, in text messages, Parker accused Smith of trying to bribe her for sex, according to the affidavit. "Thought about your offer.... & will have to decline. I'd rather have a personal legal loan, than feel like a whore," she allegedly texted him on Nov. 10, 2011, according to the affidavit.
Smith denied offering to have sex in exchange for money, saying he simply wanted to spend time with her, the texts included in the affidavit show.
Two days before she disappeared, the two discussed custody of their twins during the upcoming weekends and holidays, during which Parker texted, "Ur so------- impossible! Everything is about YOU your still so ------- selfish!" according to the affidavit.
During his initial interview with police, Smith said he didn't know what happened to Parker but "thought she was 'laying low' after the People's Court show aired" and that he believed she was embarrassed by it, and that he wanted her to come home safe for the sake of their kids.
"[H]owever, according to his phone records, he never called or messaged her ever again after November 17, 2011," the affidavit stated, noting that in the nearly seven weeks prior to Parker's disappearance, the two exchanged 1,013 text messages and 21 voice calls, according to the affidavit.
"It is believed the suspect killed the victim in his house after days of offensive messages, declining sex for cash, the embarrassing People's Court episode airing, and threatening to restrict his access to his children," the affidavit stated.
Citing cellular data, investigators allege that Smith lied to police about how long Parker was at his home to drop off the twins. According to the affidavit, he testified that she arrived at his house around 4 p.m. and was gone 10 minutes later. Her phone usage "proves the victim arrived at the suspect's house at 15:18 hours, stayed there for over an hour, and the victim does not respond to anyone ever again," the affidavit stated.
According to the affidavit, investigators reviewed surveillance video against the new cellular data and, based on that evidence, they allege that Smith deleted messages off Parker's phone from until 4:27 p.m. on Nov. 17, 2011, then threw it into Lake Conway, where the phone was later recovered.
They also allege that cellular records and video evidence show that Smith lied to police about when he said he left his home and the route he took to his parents' house after getting the twins on Nov. 17, 2011.
Smith remains held without bond following his initial court appearance on Oct. 15.
His attorney, Rajan Joshi, told ABC News that Smith has maintained his innocence since Parker's disappearance.
"When he was originally questioned, when this initially happened, he was very cooperative with law enforcement. He let them search his house. He talked to them. He came in voluntarily without a lawyer, gave an interview," Joshi said following Smith's arrest. "It was clear that law enforcement was only looking at him as the sole suspect."
The judge this week granted a motion limiting what the state and defense can say about the case.
According to the affidavit, Smith and Parker taped the episode of "The People's Court" in June 2011, and it aired on Nov. 17, 2011, at 2 p.m., just prior to Parker arriving at Smith's house.
"Both the raw footage and the aired footage were not flattering to either the suspect or the victim," the affidavit stated.
Smith was seeking $5,000 over a lost engagement ring, saying in the episode that Parker had thrown the ring at him during an argument at an Atlanta hotel and it went over a balcony.
During the episode, the exes discussed their on-again, off-again relationship and contentious co-parenting situation for their twins. Parker, who had an older child from a prior relationship, described Smith as "pretty malicious and vindictive."
The show's judge, Marilyn Milian, found both were at fault and that Parker owed Smith $2,500 for her half of the ring.
According to the affidavit, this was not the first time Smith had issues regarding an engagement ring.
A woman who was previously engaged to Smith told police that after their engagement failed in 2006, she "refused to return the engagement ring and the suspect sued her through a courtroom television show," according to the affidavit.
After that, the woman "advised the suspect told her he would make her disappear," according to the affidavit.

title: DOJ fails to get indictment against ex-Trump aide Cassidy Hutchinson: Sources
body:
The Justice Department had sought charges of lying to Congress.
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., has refused to indict former Trump White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson on charges of lying to Congress over her testimony before the House Select Committee that investigated the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol, sources familiar with the matter confirmed to ABC News.
The failed indictment is the latest setback for the Justice Department in its support of what critics call a campaign of retribution by President Donald Trump, who has long accused Hutchinson of lying to the committee regarding his actions surrounding the Capitol assault.
Republicans have long sought to undercut Hutchinson's testimony regarding a story she said had been relayed to her secondhand about President Trump lunging for the steering wheel of his presidential limo following his speech on the Ellipse on Jan. 6.
Trump has vehemently denied the account and other White House employees did not corroborate the specific detail about Trump lunging.
The Washington Post first reported that a grand jury refused to indict Hutchinson.
Former special counsel Jack Smith, who indicted President Trump for his efforts to overturn his 2020 election loss, has said he opted not to treat Hutchinson as a material witness after determining much of her testimony was based on hearsay. Trump pleaded not guilty to all charges related to Jan. 6 and Smith's case against him was ultimately dismissed .
Hutchinson has maintained that she stands by her testimony. She could not immediately be reached for comment on Tuesday.
A Justice Department spokesperson also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

title: Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years in federal sex trafficking case
body:
The jury found Alon, Oren and Tal Alexander guilty on all counts.
The Alexander brothers were each sentenced to 30 years in prison on Tuesday, after being found guilty on all counts in their federal sex trafficking trial in New York City.
The former real estate titans, Oren and Alon Alexander, 39-year-old twins, along with their brother, Tal Alexander, 40, were accused by prosecutors of a "decade-long sex trafficking and sexual abuse scheme."
The three brothers will have to participate in sex offender treatment programs in prison, the judge said. In addition to their prison terms, the brothers were each sentenced to 10 years of supervised release.
Oren and Alon Alexander were also ordered to pay $300,000 each in fines, and Tal Alexander was ordered to pay $350,000 in fines, as well as restitution, which will be determined by attorneys from both sides. Oren Alexander, who was also convicted of sexually exploiting a minor by distributing homemade child sex abuse material of a 17-year-old girl in 2009, was ordered to pay an additional $50,000 immediately.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa asked the judge for the maximum sentence -- life in prison -- for all three brothers, arguing that the government does not believe one is more culpable than the others in what prosecutors called an "immense" sex trafficking scheme.
"They spent years designing, executing, and perfecting their playbook of luring victims with promises of luxury, drugging victims so they could not resist, and then forcibly raping them," prosecutors wrote in a sentencing memorandum filed ahead of Tuesday's hearing. "The defendants carried out their playbook time and time again, drugging, raping, and assaulting dozens of victims. Over 70 women came forward with harrowing accounts of assault that stripped them of their dignity and autonomy."
Defense attorneys argued that the brothers should serve lighter sentences -- 15 years, the minimum for sex trafficking -- while maintaining their innocence.
"At no time did Alon, Oren or Tal rape or sexually assault another person. At no time did Alon, Oren or Tal entice, harbor, or maintain a woman to have commercial sex. At no time did Alon, Oren or Tal administer a drug or other substance to a woman against her will or without her knowledge. At no time did Oren intentionally make or distribute child pornography," defense attorneys wrote in their sentencing memorandum on behalf of the three brothers. "They are innocent of these charges, and they show honor and respect to our system of justice by vowing to fight for their innocence with all of their power for as long as is required, confident in the notion that one day they will be free to live out their lives with their children and families."
The brothers' friends and family members also submitted letters to Judge Valerie Caproni asking for leniency, describing their character and dedication to family.
The brothers addressed the court prior to learning their sentences during Tuesday's hearing in Manhattan, continuing to claim that they never sexually assaulted or drugged anybody.
Judge Caproni admonished the brothers for continuing to maintain their innocence.
"You did not have to stand up and say you’ve never raped anyone," Caproni said while handing down their sentences. "That's a lie and you know it."
A dozen women delivered victim impact statements during Tuesday's hearing, including six who testified during the federal trial.
Prosecutors thanked those who came forward in the case "to ensure that the defendants can no longer harm others."
"The defendants preyed on women and young girls, using drugs and violence to incapacitate them so they could rape them. The defendants did this for years --inflicting unspeakable harm on so many young women. And, for years, the defendants used their careers and social status to conceal the danger they posed," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement. "Today's sentence makes clear that this craven, sinister conduct is extraordinarily serious and will be met with serious punishment."
Throughout the five-week trial , 11 women testified that they were sexually assaulted by one or more of the brothers. At least eight of the women claimed they were drugged by one of the Alexanders.
The brothers denied sexually assaulting anyone or running a sex trafficking conspiracy, as prosecutors have charged. They pleaded not guilty. A spokesperson for the Alexander family called the verdict "deeply disappointing."
"We believe there are substantial problems with the evidence and the way this case was presented," the spokesperson, Juda S. Engelmayer, said in a statement following the jury's verdict in March. "The legal process does not end here. We will continue fighting every day until justice is done and the three brothers regain their freedom."
Oren and Tal Alexander gained notoriety in New York's luxury real estate market through their company, Alexander Group, and have been under federal investigation alongside Alon since late 2024.
They have been accused of luring women to nightclubs and parties, then drugging and sexually assaulting them.
In his closing statement during the spring trial, federal prosecutor Andrew Jones said there is "crushing evidence" that the brothers "masqueraded as party boys when really they were predators" who committed an "array of federal sex offenses."
Jones recounted the graphic accounts of the alleged victims and said the wealthy brothers had a "playbook" of luring women with exclusive parties, yachts and luxury travel so they could assault them.
During closing arguments, defense attorney Howard Srebnick conceded the brothers could be "obnoxious" and their conduct "inappropriate," but he told the jury, "Nobody was being assaulted, nobody had been trafficked."

title: Judge admonishes Trump administration over plans for Washington, DC, golf course
body:
Trump said he plans to close the course Nov. 15.
A federal judge has ordered a top Department of Justice official back into court after President Donald Trump posted on his social media account affirming that East Potomac Golf Course will close Nov. 15 for renovations — directly contradicting repeated assertions from administration officials in a hearing last week.
District Judge Ana Reyes has ordered Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward to clarify whether his prior statements to her that there were no plans to close the course remain accurate.
She further ordered Woodward's attendance at a hearing either Friday or Monday where she is expected to press the government for more updates on its compliance with her injunction barring further construction at East Potomac.
In a sharply worded 70-page ruling, Reyes criticized the Trump administration over its plans for the historic golf course in Washington, D.C., and concluded the administration likely violated environmental laws in the process.
"Rarely, if ever, has the United States Department of Justice urged a federal court not to believe the sitting President," Reyes wrote. "Not to believe him that a cabinet secretary has 'developed' a federal land project. Not to believe him that the secretary's agency will destroy a historic golf course already on the land. Not to believe him that 'Restoration work' will begin 'IMMEDIATELY!' Not to believe him that the course 'will be closed' for over a year. Not to believe what the President has repeatedly told the American public. And yet, here we are."
The case began over golf and long walks, Reyes said, but has now morphed into an effort to reconcile sworn statements made by members of the administration with statements made by Trump.
The administration must give "ten business days' written advance notice before making any irreparable modification to any forms or features of East Potomac Park, pending the outcome of this litigation," Reyes said.
Hours before the hearing was set to start, the president had posted on social media that construction on East Potomac Golf Course would begin immediately, despite the administration suggesting to the court that it would not.
"If, as DOJ insists, President Trump is wrong, Secretary Burgum can just say so," Reyes wrote. "He has not. That said, at this juncture Plaintiffs carry the burden of showing a final plan likely exists. They have done so. This is confirmed not just by the President's and Secretary's many posts, but also by the Government's actions, not the least of which is the removal of hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees on no real notice."
The tree removal had been scheduled a week earlier, but Reyes concluded that those involved in the lawsuit had little notice to stop the cutting.
The administration also likely violated environmental laws — specifically the National Environmental Policy Act -- by "segmenting" the environmental impacts of the construction, she said.
Trump said his administration will appeal the ruling, insisting he will move forward with his plans to shut down the course on Nov. 15 to start the project.
"We are closing the East Potomac Golf Course Site as scheduled on November 15th in order to renovate and rebuild for Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons," Trump wrote on his social media platform overnight.
He said the judge's request for updates is "unconstitutional."
"We believe this Project is totally 'as of right,' and that the judge does not have the Constitutional Right to 'ask for or receive notices,' which are time-consuming, unnecessary, expensive, and unconstitutional. We will immediately appeal this decision," Trump wrote.
During a gaggle with reporters on Monday night after his Mississippi rally, Trump also said he has a "go-ahead" to work on the renovations and blasted the judge for being an "architectural critic of golf courses."
"It's not my golf course, it's a public course being built in Washington D.C. and it has a go-ahead," Trump said.
He added that the current public course is "extremely dangerous to play" because it is too close together and that he was asking the D.C. Circuit Court for "immediate remedy."

title: How often should you update your financial plan?
body: A financial plan can give you a framework for everything from managing monthly expenses to saving for retirement, but the assumptions behind that plan won't necessarily stay the same for long. Your income can change, unexpected expenses can emerge and financial goals that made sense a few years ago may no longer reflect what you're working toward today.Changes outside of your control can matter, too. The interest rate climate can affect what you earn on savings and what it costs to borrow, while inflation can change how far your budget stretches. Tax rules, investment returns and insurance costs can also shift over time, potentially leaving parts of an otherwise solid financial strategy out of sync with your current circumstances.That doesn't mean you need to overhaul your finances every time the economy changes or your monthly spending fluctuates, though. But leaving a financial plan untouched for too long can create its own problems. According to New York Life's 2026 Wealth Watch Midyear Outlook survey, 56% of Americans have updated their retirement strategy, and 37% plan to make changes to their investment portfolio or strategy this year. So, how frequently should you revisit your plan, and what circumstances should prompt you to take another look?Find out more about your New York Life coverage options here.How often should you update your financial plan?There's no single schedule that works for everyone, but reviewing your financial plan at least once a year can help ensure that it still reflects your income, expenses, goals and overall financial situation. An annual review also provides a natural opportunity to catch smaller issues before they have years to compound.During that review, look at the major components of your financial life rather than focusing only on your investment portfolio. For example, check whether your emergency fund is still large enough to cover several months of current expenses, particularly if your housing, insurance or other essential costs have increased.You should also revisit your debt. If you've paid off a loan or credit card balance, you may be able to redirect that monthly payment toward another financial goal. Conversely, if your balances have increased or high-rate debt is taking up a growing portion of your budget, your repayment strategy may need to change.Retirement savings deserve attention as well. Consider whether you're contributing enough to remain on track for your goals and whether changes to your income create room to increase those contributions. It can also make sense to review your investment allocation periodically to determine whether market movements have pushed it significantly away from the level of risk you intended to take.And don't overlook the administrative pieces of your plan, either. Beneficiary designations, insurance coverage, estate-planning documents and tax strategies can become outdated even when the rest of your finances appear relatively stable.That said, an annual review should generally be viewed as a baseline rather than a rule that requires you to wait 12 months between updates. Certain changes can make it worthwhile to revisit your plan much sooner.Learn how a New York Life insurance policy could benefit you today.When should you review your financial plan sooner?Major financial or personal changes can alter your priorities quickly. Waiting until your next scheduled review could leave you working from outdated assumptions. In these situations, it can make sense to reassess the affected parts of your plan as they occur:Your income or employment changedA substantial raise, job loss, career change or move from salaried work to self-employment can affect your budget, taxes, retirement contributions and emergency savings needs. Updating your plan can help you determine how much of a higher income to save or where to cut back if your earnings decline.You experienced a major life eventGetting married or divorced, having a child, buying a home or losing a spouse can fundamentally change your financial obligations. These events may require more than a budget adjustment. You may also need to update insurance coverage, beneficiaries, estate plans, savings goals or the amount of cash you keep available for emergencies.Your debt situation changedTaking on a mortgage, accumulating a significant credit card balance or paying off a major debt can change how you allocate your money. If high-rate debt has become difficult to manage, for example, the original plan of making extra payments may no longer be enough. At that point, it may be worth exploring other approaches.Your goals changedFinancial plans are ultimately built around what you want your money to accomplish. If you decide to retire earlier, purchase a home, start a business or prioritize another goal, the amount you need to save — and where you put that money — may also change substantially. Updating the plan allows your day-to-day financial decisions to reflect those new priorities.The numbers no longer workYou don't necessarily need a major life event to justify an update to your financial plan. If you're consistently overspending, drawing from savings to cover routine bills or falling behind on a goal despite following your original plan, that's useful information. Rather than continuing with a strategy that no longer fits, reassess the assumptions behind it and adjust accordingly.The bottom lineFor many people, reviewing a financial plan once a year provides a reasonable starting point, but the calendar shouldn't be the only factor that determines when you revisit it. Significant changes to your income, debt, family situation or financial goals can all warrant an earlier review.And updating your plan doesn't necessarily mean rebuilding it from scratch. In many cases, a few targeted adjustments are enough to keep your savings, spending and longer-term goals aligned. What matters most is treating your financial plan as something that evolves along with your finances rather than a document you create once and leave untouched.New York Life paid for the creation of this article. CBS News independently wrote and produced the article in accordance with its editorial standards.

title: Trump continues red-state campaign push with days until midterms
body:
Trump is set to attend campaign rallies in Texas on Tuesday.
President Donald Trump is barnstorming deep-red states across the country to defend GOP majorities in Congress as Democrats make inroads in some unlikely places.
As of Tuesday afternoon, the president has made 20 stops to states he handily won and six to battlegrounds since Sept. 9, according to ABC News tracking. Those include four in Texas, two in Ohio, two in Tennessee, and visits to states that for some observers may be surprising: Oklahoma, Kentucky and Alabama.
The president made his fourth campaign season trip to Texas -- a state he won in three presidential elections -- on Tuesday, where he is attending two rallies; Vice President JD Vance will be in Texas for a rally later this week. Trump's Tuesday trip and Vance's upcoming one means the president and vice president will have visited Texas -- typically reliably red -- eight times since Labor Day weekend.
An early October ReconMR poll found that among likely Texas voters, Texas Democratic state Rep. James Talarico had 48% support while Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton had 44% support, within the poll's margin of error.
Trump's red-state travels come with just days until the high-stakes midterm elections where control of Congress is at stake.
As Democratic candidates largely center their campaigns around affordability and ending the Iran war, they are fending off attacks from Republicans, largely on taxes, culture war and transgender issues. At the same time, Republicans are calling on the president and his Cabinet officials to heed voter economic concerns.
As Republicans look to shore up support among the MAGA faithful, Trump's approval ratings have suffered. His approval rating recently reached a record low of 33% in the ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll . About 7 in 10 Americans say that gas is unaffordable and that the country is headed in the wrong direction, according to the same poll.
On Monday, Trump hit the campaign trail in Mississippi, where no Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate since 1982. Trump carried the state by a 23-point margin in the 2024 presidential election. GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is defending her seat against Democrat and district attorney Scott Colom.
"A lot of folks ain't gonna be able to make this rally because they can't afford the gas to get up here," Colom said at a press conference in Corinth ahead of Trump's rally in the city.
Trump said on Monday that he was supporting Hyde-Smith in the state because he "can't take a chance."
"I can't take a chance. She's got no problem. The only problem is sometimes, and this happens, and sometimes when you think somebody's doing so well, nobody wants – they all stay home," Trump said -- later adding "so that's why I'm here."
Last week, Trump campaigned in Kansas for Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall, who is fighting in what ABC News is rating a toss-up race for reelection against Democrat Rev. Adam Hamilton. Vance stumped for the one-term incumbent in September and again on Monday.
Hamilton could break a 94-year losing streak for Democrats -- he is split even with Marshall among likely Kansas voters, according to a September New York Times/Siena University poll .
Trump is headed back to Kansas on Saturday in Salina, where he will need to run up the score in a county he carried by more than 30 points in 2024.
Several Republicans -- including Trump, Vance, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Speaker Mike Johnson -- have visited Wisconsin's closely watched 3rd Congressional District, where Democrat Rebecca Cooke is facing off against GOP incumbent Rep. Derrick Van Orden. ABC News recently shifted its rating from "toss-up" to "lean Democrat."
Trump surrogates are also flocking to Iowa, a state Trump won in the last three presidential elections. The president has already paid a visit to Sioux City and will headline a rally in Dubuque just two days before the midterms.
Iowa Democratic Senate candidate Josh Turek, a state lawmaker, is running against Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to succeed outgoing GOP Sen. Joni Ernst.
Hinson has praised the president but also sought to distance herself at times and recently called for an end to the Iran war.
But Turek told ABC News it is "good" for Trump to see how healthcare funding cuts and tariffs have affected Iowans.
"I think that the war in Iran has hurt Iowa more than any other state," Turek said.
Kennedy is stumping for Iowa Republican gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn on Wednesday. Johnson is headlining a rally for GOP incumbent Rep. Zach Nunn in the state's 3rd Congressional District that same day.
At least nine cabinet members visited Iowa in August, underscoring just how competitive the House races, open Senate and governor races have become.

title: FBI agents charged with lying about Hunter Biden probes accuse DOJ of 'serious abuse'
body:
Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides have been charged with lying to Congress.
A magistrate judge blasted Justice Department attorneys during a hearing Tuesday after the department, in an overnight court filing, added a charge of obstruction to two charges of lying to Congress that were brought Friday against two former FBI agents who investigated Hunter Biden .
The Justice Department on Friday charged Nikki Floris, the former deputy assistant director for FBI's Counterintelligence Division, and Bradley Benavides, another former senior counterintelligence official, with allegedly making false statements to Congress stemming from a probe into whether investigators in the lead-up to the 2020 election sought to suppress or discredit the veracity of material on the laptop of former President Joe Biden's son that included embarrassing photos and videos.
The DOJ early Tuesday added an obstruction of a congressional proceeding charge -- but in a contentious hearing, magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui slammed the Justice Department for the overnight filing, which prosecutors posted to the case docket without receiving signoff from the judge.
The FBI agent who swore out the complaint also did not include his signature.
"I think they should have filed nothing," Judge Faruqui said. "They never had complaints filed on their record that are unsigned, waiting for a judge to make a probable cause finding. I think that it is inappropriate and harms the defendant. I'm frustrated that I got it in the middle of the night, but I'm much more concerned that it's filed on the public record."
The assistant U.S. attorney in the hearing, John Borchert, struggled repeatedly as Faruqui asked him to explain the government's conduct, which the judge said was unlike any case he had ever seen in the history of D.C.'s district court.
Faruqui ultimately granted the request from Flores' and Benavides' attorneys to strike the amended complaint from the docket and said he would continue Tuesday's hearing to determine whether prosecutors established probable cause in their initial complaint filed last week.
"Why today on this one case have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?" Faruqui asked of Borchert. "What is it? It appears that -- it makes it look like the United States is afraid of me trying to find probable cause."
"Let me address that squarely. We are not afraid of a probable cause finding," Borchert said.
The Justice Department alleges that Floris and Benavides knowingly lied to Congress on two separate occasions -- on July 19, 2023, for Floris, and on Sept. 28, 2023, for Benavides.
"The evidence further establishes that probable cause exists to believe that Floris and Benavides made these statements for the purpose of minimizing or concealing [the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force's] engagement with, and communications about, the Hunter Biden investigations and to impede the Congressional investigation," according to the documents filed overnight.
The affidavit alleges that both congressional and FBI witnesses, along with FBI documents, prove that the pair were aware of the Hunter Biden investigation.
"The government's last-ditch filing before the pre-scheduled preliminary hearing in this case is not merely procedurally improper and substantively deficient," Floris' attorneys said. "It represents a serious abuse of the criminal charging process, a troubling disregard for the judicial safeguards governing the initiation of criminal proceedings, and a calculated effort to evade judicial scrutiny and shield the government's allegations from adversarial testing at the scheduled preliminary hearing."
"In our combined decades of DOJ service, we have never seen or even heard of something like this being filed. That's because the public lodging of criminal charges must be authorized by the grand jury, a judge, or the defendant herself," the attorneys said. "We have asked to address this outrageous government conduct against a decorated public servant at today's court hearing."
Judge Faruqui appeared on Friday to be skeptical of the charges -- saying the "facts appear to be old" and there are "questions that need to be answered" -- before setting a hearing for Tuesday to consider whether the government established probable cause in its complaint.
Faruqui said the judge who signed off on the complaint needed extra time to determine if there was probable cause or not. "Rare charges" that are "this old" are never charged by complaint, according to the judge.
It was not immediately clear why prosecutors chose to charge the pair through a criminal complaint and not an indictment, which would have required approval by a grand jury instead of a magistrate judge.

title: SCOTUS won't restore policy that lets immigration judges close deportation cases
body:
The regulation give judges discretion to temporarily pause removal proceedings.
The Supreme Court on Tuesday declined to unfreeze a Biden-era policy that allowed immigration judges to use their discretion to temporarily close deportation cases for immigrants.
In an unsigned order, the court rejected a request from three cities with large migrant populations -- Baltimore as well as Columbus, Ohio and New Haven, Connecticut -- to pause an agreement between Texas and the Trump administration that threw out the policy.
The regulation, known as "administrative closure," gives immigration judges discretion to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for migrants while the migrants seek humanitarian protections or other forms of legal status in the country.
The Trump administration has pushed to curtail judicial processes for unlawful migrants, and the high court's conservative majority has been largely deferential to executive authority in the area of immigration policy.
Deportation hearings in immigration court are legal proceedings initiated by the Department of Homeland Security in which an immigration judge determines whether a migrant should be removed from the United States. Often, an immigration judge will pause or dismiss a case to allow the individual to pursue legal relief.
While dismissals were viewed as a positive outcome for migrants, immigration attorneys have said the Trump administration, as part of its immigration crackdown , began to use dismissals to detain people at immigration courts and place them into expedited removal without allowing them to fight their case.
Last year, federal agents arrested hundreds of migrants at immigration courts -- in some cases after their deportation cases were dismissed.
In court filings, the cities argued that administrative closure promoted "efficiency" and protected "due process rights." They also argued that the practice has existed in various forms for decades.
In June, the state of Texas sued the federal government, arguing that the policy granted "indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."

title: CDC's deputy director resigns after being hired in April
body:
Dr. Jennifer Shuford's last day will be Nov. 12.
Dr. Jennifer Shuford, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's deputy director, has resigned, the agency said in a statement on Tuesday.
Shuford, who also served as chief medical officer, was hired for the role in April. Her last day will be Nov. 12, the CDC said.
"I am leaving to spend more time with my family," Shuford said in a statement. "I am so thankful to President Trump and Secretary Kennedy for giving me the opportunity to help lead CDC. It has been an amazing experience and I will be forever grateful for it."
In a separate statement, Dr. Erica Schwartz, the CDC's director, thanked Shuford for her time at the federal health agency.
"I am deeply grateful for Dr. Shuford's outstanding leadership and commitment to CDC and public health, especially as she has navigated an exceptionally demanding, high-profile and constantly evolving environment over the past several months," Schwartz said.
In the interim, Satish Pillai will serve as acting CDC chief medical officer and deputy director.
Shuford is board-certified in internal medicine and infectious diseases and received her medical degree from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical School, according to her bio on the CDC website .
Before joining the CDC, Shuford served as Texas' chief state epidemiologist, later becoming commissioner of the Texas Department of State Health Services.
"In this role, Dr. Shuford oversaw statewide public health programs, including infectious disease response, health promotion, epidemiology and emergency preparedness," her bio reads.
Shuford was appointed in April with two others at the same time Schwartz was nominated by President Donald Trump to serve as the next CDC director.
"These Highly Respected Doctors of Medicine have the knowledge, experience, and TOP degrees to restore the GOLD STANDARD OF SCIENCE at the CDC," Trump wrote in a social media post at the time.
Shuford has been a vocal supporter of vaccination, saying areas with declining measles vaccination rates are at an increased risk of outbreaks.
In February 2025, when a measles outbreak was spreading in western Texas, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said measles outbreaks were "not unusual," adding that they happen every year.
But in an appearance on CNN the same month, Shuford described Texas' measles outbreak as "unusual" for the state.
"We haven't had this sort of an outbreak since the early 1990s and it's seriously impacting the population in that region," she said. "This community has had some falling vaccine coverage rates in recent years and so we're trying to correct that, trying to get vaccines out there to protect our population and to try to get rid of this measles outbreak that's affecting them right now."
Additionally, during the COVID-19 pandemic, while still in her role as chief state epidemiologist, Shuford appeared in a video posted on Facebook explaining how COVID-19 vaccines work, including efficacy and side effects.

title: Likud rep. accuses CEC of ignoring instances of voter fraud in favor of high voter turnout
body: The Likud party's election integrity representative, Sagi Keisler, accused the Central Elections Committee (CEC) of ignoring alleged instances of voter fraud in favor of maintaining a high voter turnout on Election Day.Likud claimed to have submitted 775 complaints to the CEC alleging documented incidents of improper conduct and attempted fraud at polling stations in Arab-majority localities. Earlier on Tuesday, Likud said that it had received 620 reports of unusual incidents and suspected irregularities at polling stations in the Arab sector, collected through a network of over 1,500 representatives across the country. About one-third of the reports concern the recording of voters' personal information and the transmission of information outside polling stations. Some 66 reports concern irregularities involving ballot papers and envelopes, 26 involve difficulties verifying voters' identities and exercising polling station committee members' authority, and 17  concern violence and threats. The remaining reports involve staffing deficiencies, election campaigning, and documentation issues. Envelopes reported missingIn one incident, 10 sealed envelopes were reported missing from a polling station in Fassuta and in another, a discrepancy of 11 envelopes between the number of envelopes and the recorded number of voters was found in Jadeidi-Makr, the headquarters said.Likud's election integrity headquarters also criticized an instruction from the director-general of the Central Elections Committee to prevent overcrowding, saying it could undermine adherence to voter identification requirements and voting procedures. "The Elections Committee is cutting corners precisely where stricter oversight is needed. We are receiving hundreds of reports of suspected irregularities, including missing envelopes and the unauthorized transmission of information."Instead of strengthening oversight, pressure is being applied to prevent overcrowding at polling stations. We demand an immediate investigation into these suspicions, the deployment of independent observers, and guarantees of a proper and transparent voting process," said Sagi Kaisler, head of Likud's election integrity headquarters for the Arab sector.

title: Trump admin demands Washington set aside 400 ballots it says are from noncitizens
body:
Washington's secretary of state expressed skepticism about the request's timing.
The Justice Department is asking election officials in Washington state to set aside hundreds of ballots it says may belong to noncitizen voters, the latest move by the Trump administration to intervene in a state-run election just days before the midterms.
The move sparked backlash from state officials who said the Justice Department’s intention in publicizing these allegations so close to an election was to create "unfounded suspicion."
Federal prosecutors in Washington state claimed in a statement Monday that the more than 400 individuals on the list represented “only the tip of the iceberg.” The statement accompanied a letter sent by the state’s two U.S. attorneys demanding that election officials set aside any ballots belonging to individuals on the list. ABC News has not seen the letter.
The Justice Department’s messaging in Washington on Monday echoes steps it took ahead of a lawsuit it filed last week against California, where it has sued to prevent the state from counting more than 20,000 ballots it claims may belong to noncitizen voters.
The Trump administration has promoted a number isolated cases of alleged noncitizen voting in recent weeks as evidence of rampant election fraud. But all available evidence suggests voter fraud and noncitizen voting remains exceedingly rare , and certainly not widespread enough to alter the outcome of any election.
A federal appeals court declined to intervene in that matter and said that the "emergency" the DOJ claimed was in part "self-constructed."
Local officials in Los Angeles said a sampling of the 20,000 ballots surveyed showed a "high percentage" of people who say they were born in the U.S.
"We saw what happened in California and don't want Washingtonians to be harassed," Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a statement on Monday responding to the Justice Department's letter.
Hobbs wrote in his response that at least one of the individuals on the Justice Department’s list dates back to 1994. Since then, 113.5 million primary and general election ballots have been cast in Washington, according to the secretary of state’s office.
"The timing of this request -- one week before the General Election -- is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results," Hobbs added. "We are carefully reviewing the request and assessing the information sought to ensure that our response complies with applicable state and federal laws."
